sub_talks.title: [NSS-20-01] Development and validation of the Forward Feature Extractor Prototype for high-speed data processing in the ATLAS L0Calo trigger systems (#2816)
sub_talks.speaker: A.C. ATLAS Collaboration
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] ATLAS Collaboration, CERN, Geneva, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present the development and validation of the Forward Feature Extractor (fFEX) prototype module, a key component of the ATLAS Experiment's Phase-II Level-0 Calorimeter (L0Calo) trigger system for real-time event filtering and feature extraction. The prototype module has been produced and validated through an extensive test campaign. Hardware validation demonstrates stable power delivery, full main-board core functionality, reliable FPGA operation including high-speed transceivers and bit-error-rate tests at 25.8 Gbps per link, robust clock distribution including jitter cleaners and fanout stages, and complete control and monitoring functionality. In addition, integration tests with other ATLAS Phase-II subsystems have been carried out and the results are reported, confirming interoperability and being suitable for operation within the experiment's complex trigger and data-acquisition architecture. The system achieves a total throughput of 2.5 Tbps per main FPGA, including real-time processing and data-handling operations. On the firmware side, a modular design has been implemented, comprising the infrastructure layer, including an implementation of the Interlaken protocol (Core1990) and a simple-packet based protocol called IPBus, the readout firmware, and the algorithmic firmware. In this article, particular emphasis is placed on the readout path and the handling of multiple data types and trigger objects, including the formatting, error-correction and flow-control aspects. The algorithmic firmware supports the identification of jets, electromagnetic clusters, and hadronic tau candidates, and the calculation of global quantities such as missing transverse energy (MET). These results demonstrate the technical readiness of the fFEX prototype for further system-level integration, timing and performance studies.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-20-02] Lessons Learned from the sPHENIX Experiment (#1595)
sub_talks.speaker: M. L. Purschke
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Brookhaven National Laboratory, Physics, Upton, New York, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The sPHENIX experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC), and RHIC itself, concluded their beam operations on Feb. 6, 2026. RHIC and the experiments are now being decommissioned to begin construction of the Electron-Ion Collider. This marks the end of 25 years of Heavy-Ion and polarized proton-proton Physics at the facility. sPHENIX was designed as a high-rate detector optimized for precision measurements of jets, heavy flavor, and quarkonia in Relativistic Heavy-Ion collisions. Following a successful commissioning phase, the experiment collected high-quality data in p-p , Au-Au, and O-O collision systems. To summarize our key performance numbers: The sPHENIX DAQ system has exceeded the design event rate of 15 kHz We were able to sustain a DAQ data rate of more than 70 GB/s We accumulated just under 300 PB of data on tape with beam, and crossed the 300 PB threshold with the post-shutdown calibration data. We present key lessons learned from the design, commissioning, and operation of the sPHENIX data acquisition system. We also briefly discuss ongoing analysis efforts and the anticipated physics legacy of the sPHENIX program.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-20-03] Architecture and Performance of a Versatile Trigger, Tracking and Readout System for Particle Detector Beam Tests (#1917)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Congedo (Autores: L. Congedo , R. Pillera , D. Cerasole , G. De Robertis , L. Di Venere , F. Gargano , M. Giliberti , F. Licciulli , A. Liguori , R. Liotino , P. Loizzo , F. Loparco , L. Lorusso , M.N. Mazziotta , N. Nicassio , G. Panzarini)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Bari, Bari, Italy [2] Dipartimento di Fisica "M. Merlin", Università e Politecnico di Bari, Bari, Italy [3] Dipartimento di Fisica, Università di Trento, Trento, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents the development and validation of a Trigger, Tracking, and Readout System for the beam test characterization of novel particle detectors, designed to address the challenges of providing precise reference tracking for event reconstruction while integrating heterogeneous front-end electronics. The system combines a scalable tracking apparatus based on scintillating fibers coupled to Silicon Photomultipliers, a Centralized Control Unit for trigger generation and system synchronization and a modular readout architecture based on Field Programmable Gate Arrays. A dedicated software platform provides unified control of data acquisition, configuration and monitoring, ensuring efficient system operation. The overall design approach relies on hardware modularity and the use of commercial components, complemented by adaptable firmware and software to interface multiple detector technologies with minimal customization effort. The system has been validated during beam test campaigns of a Ring Imaging Cherenkov detector prototype for the future ALICE3 experiment, foreseen at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider. The results demonstrate accurate event reconstruction capability, with a data matching efficiency among independent readout boards exceeding 99%, ensuring reliable synchronization across different subsystems. In addition, a time resolution at the level of a few tens of picoseconds have been measured, highlighting the remarkable timing performance of the system and its suitability for the characterization of high-precision timing detectors. The results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed system as a cost-effective, flexible, scalable, and portable solution that can be readily employed for the development and beam test validation of future particle detectors based on a wide range of technologies.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-20-04] TD-Link: A Daisy-Chain Optical Architecture for Integrated Data Readout and Deterministic Timing Distribution in Large-Scale Detector Systems (#1971)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Abba (Autores: A. Abba , V. Arosio , G. Becuzzi , M. Bianchini , F. Caponio , S. Carsi , A. Cusimano , C. Maggio , A. Mati , D. Ninci , A. Picchi , C. Tintori , Y. Venturini)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Nuclear Instruments SRL, Lambrugo, Italy [2] CAEN SPA, Viareggio, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract TD-Link is a versatile optical communication architecture combining high-throughput data readout and sub-nanosecond timing synchronization over a single optical fiber for large-scale detector systems. The protocol adopts a multidrop daisy-chain ring topology connecting one Data Concentrator to up to sixteen FERS front-end boards per link, with multiple independent links per concentrator, enabling scalable instrumentation with reduced optical infrastructure. Operating at 3.25 Gb/s, TD-Link transports data, synchronization, and control traffic within the same serial stream through a token-based protocol minimizing per-hop latency and supporting packet fragmentation. The synchronization system distributes a global time reference (T0) with deterministic latency. On the concentrator, transmitter lane alignment exploits the half-full condition of the transceiver elastic buffer as a 1-bit phase detector. A firmware state machine iteratively adjusts the TX phase interpolator until the write-to-read pointer difference reaches half the buffer depth, locking the lane to a deterministic phase condition. A Digital Dual Mixer Time Difference (DDMTD) circuit is used only for inter-concentrator synchronization, compensating the phase offset between the recovered transceiver clock and the FPGA fabric reference clock. On FERS boards, recovered clocks are cleaned through an external zero-delay PLL and retransmitted downstream, preserving phase coherence along the daisy chain. Deterministic T0 latency is ensured by disabling elastic buffers and routing timing signals through calibrated delay paths. Experimental validation with CERN PicoTDC-equipped FERS boards demonstrates a synchronization sigma of 6 ps for boards sharing the same coaxial clock reference and below 25 ps for boards connected to different concentrators. The performance remains stable across repeated power cycles, confirming the robustness of the phase alignment strategy.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-20-05] Design and test of a readout board for the ePIC dRICH detector (#2620)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Falchieri (Autores: D. Falchieri , P. Antonioli , L. Barion , M. Contalbrigo , F. Cossio , G. Della Casa , S. Geminiani , R. Malaguti , M. Panza , R. Preghenella , L. P. Rignanese , G. Torromeo)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] INFN Sezione di Bologna, Section of Bologna, BOLOGNA, Italy [2] INFN Sezione di Ferrara, Section of Ferrara, Ferrara, Italy [3] INFN Sezione di Torino, Section of Torino, Torino, Italy [4] INFN Bologna and UNIBO, Section of Bologna and UNIBO, Bologna, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This paper presents the design of a board named RDO (ReaDOut module) which is the main building block of the readout system for the dual-radiator RICH (dRICH) of the ePIC experiment at the future Electron-Ion Collider (EIC). The main purpose of the board is to provide an interface towards the front-end ASICs (the ALCOR chips) and towards the main data acquisition system (the FELIX boards) through a high-speed optical link based on the CERN VTRx+ optical transceiver. Among the many requirements, the board needs to fit a very limited size and must withstand a moderately hostile radiation environment. The board has already been used in a test-beam at CERN and it has also undergone irradiation tests of its main components: the most significant results will be presented and discussed.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-20-06] Performance evaluation of SPIDER and ICECAL65 for the upgrade II of the LHCb calorimeter detector (#2654)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. Picatoste (Autores: A. López , J. Altet , L. Alvado , X. Aragonés , N. Arveuf , E. Barajas , E. Bechetoille , D. Breton , G. Blanchard , S. Gómez , B. Joly , L. Leterrier , J. Maalmi , S. Manen , D.D. Marín , D. Mateo , H. Mathez , J. Mauricio , J. Mazorra , E. Picatoste , J. Serrano , C. Sylvia , P. Vallerand , R. Vandaele)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universitat de Barcelona, ICCUB, Barcelona, Spain [2] Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya, Departament d'Enginyeria Electrònica, Barcelona, Spain [3] Universitat de Valencia, IFIC, Valencia, Spain [4] Université de Paris-Saclay, CNRS / IN2P3 / IJCLab, Orsay, France [5] Université Clermont-Auvergne, CNRS / IN2P3 / LPCA, Clermont-Ferrand, France [6] Université de Caen Normandie, CNRS / IN2P3 / LPC, Caen, France [7] Université de Lyon, CNRS / IN2P3 / IP2I, Lyon, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The LHCb Phase-II electromagnetic calorimeter upgrade, known as PicoCal, requires new radiation-tolerant front-end electronics capable of providing precise energy and timing measurements under the demanding conditions expected after the High-Luminosity LHC upgrade. Two dedicated ASICs are being developed for this purpose in TSMC65 technology: ICECAL65 for energy measurement, and SPIDER for picosecond timing reconstruction. ICECAL65 follows the scheme in the ASIC currently used in the LHCb calorimeter. Nonetheless, it adopts a dual-gain architecture with time-interleaved subchannels to achieve 12-bit precision over a wide dynamic range while eliminating dead time between input samples. The analog chain integrates configurable shaping, tunable integration, and high-speed track-and-hold stages synchronized through an integrated PLL. Post-layout simulations indicate a power consumption of 40 mW per channel, output noise compatible with 12-bit precision, linearity errors below 1%, and spillover below 2.5%. SPIDER is a waveform digitizer ASIC dedicated to ultra-fast timing measurements. Based on the Waveform Time-to-Digital Converter concept, it samples detector signals inside programmable windows synchronized with the 40 MHz LHC clock. The architecture combines analog memory banks, embedded discriminators, DLL-based timing control, and massively parallel Wilkinson ADC conversion. Configurable sampling frequencies from 1.6 to 20 GS/s enable timing resolutions well below 10 ps rms. While post-layout simulations of ICECAL65 are still pending verification, first measurements of SPIDER_V0 demonstrate a Time Difference Resolution of 7.13 ps rms between two asynchronous pulses, corresponding to a single-channel precision close to 5 ps. Together, ICECAL65 and SPIDER provide a complete front-end solution for the PicoCal upgrade and represent a promising platform for future fast-timing detectors in high-energy physics.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-20-07] Design and Performance of the Fermilab Constant-Fraction Discriminator (FCFD) Readout ASIC for ePIC Barrel Time-of-Flight Detector (#2797)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Gong (Autores: A. Apresyan , C. V. Gingu , D. Gong , N. S. Kharwadkar , S. Los , C. Pena , C. Syal , S. Wu , S. Xie , T. Zenger , T. Zimmerman)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, Batavia, Illinois, United States of America [2] California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present the design and performance of the FCFD1.1 constant-fraction discriminator ASIC for precision timing detectors based on AC-LGAD sensors. The chip, implemented in 65 nm CMOS, achieves ~ 40 ps time resolution and 15-20 μm spatial resolution in beam tests, with full detection efficiency over the sensor surface. The design integrates on-chip time-walk correction, reducing reliance on offline calibration. Building on this result, we introduce FCFD1.2, a six-channel full-chain prototype for AC-LGAD readout. Each channel includes a constant-fraction discriminator, an ADC block, and a self-calibrated TDC, while the six channels share a common readout block that packs the data into frames and outputs them through a serializer. The chip was submitted in April 2026, and preliminary test results are expected to be presented at the conference. Its architecture targets ~ 45 ps overall timing resolution, with less than 10 ps contribution from the internal electronics, enabling scalable, low-power timing readout for future detector systems.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-20-08] LDMX Timing Distribution and Data AcquisitionSystem (#2940)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. A. Reese (Autores: B. A. Reese , C. Bakalis , R. Herbst , T. K. Nelson , L. Tompkins , E. Berzin , M. Weaver)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, Menlo Park, California, United States of America [2] Stanford University, Stanford, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Light Dark Matter eXperiment (LDMX) will search for sub-GeV dark matter with a fixed-target missing-momentum technique requiring time-aligned detector data from several independent subsystems, including the Trigger Scintillator, Silicon Tracker, Electromagnetic Calorimeter, and Hadronic Calorimeter. This work presents the LDMX trigger and data acquisition (TDAQ) system for timing distribution, fast control, and event tagging. The central timing node is implemented on an APx ATCA board originally developed for CMS. It receives the LCLS-II accelerator timing stream and recovers the 185.714 MHz timing clock and timing frames. Firmware combines accelerator pulse identifiers, run state, and Global Trigger decisions into fixed-latency 3.714 Gbps PGP Fast Control (PGPFC) messages for endpoints. Timing Messages carry a 56-bit pulse ID, 4-bit run state, and state-changed flag. Readout Request (RoR) messages, analogous to Level-1 Accept triggers, carry pulse ID and a 6-bit bunch count. Endpoints recover the fast-control clock, derive a 37.14 MHz bunch clock, align RoRs to bunch boundaries, and write the common timestamp into DAQ event headers. Common firmware blocks provide fast-control reception and event formatting for subsystem designs, enabling offline alignment and future real-time event building. Run states support trigger-data alignment and RoR-latency calibration before physics. In a 2025 beamline test at End Station A at SLAC, this architecture acquired coherent data at 10 Hz for up to 12 hours with aligned contributions from participating reduced-scale detector-subsystem slices.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-09-01] 4π Visualization of Extended, Low-Level GammaEmission Sources Using a Rotating 3-D PositionSensitive CdZnTe Imager (#1204)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. O. Lamm (Autores: A. O. Lamm , P. Hotvedt , Z. He)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Michigan, Nuclear Engineering and Radiological Sciences, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Direct image reconstruction methods for Compton imaging such as Simple Back Projection (SBP) are widely used for their simplicity and robustness. Difficulties arise when imaging low-activity, non-point sources that span a significant portion of the detector's field of view (FOV). The detector's directional photopeak efficiency will heavily skew the collected data, and may result in a biased image that does not accurately visualize the extent and intensity of the whole object. This work proposes a SBP imaging algorithm with rotational corrections that smooth out the directional efficiency of the CdZnTe detector and generate a 4π FOV Compton image that accurately visualizes the distribution of an extended radioactive source. Experimental results demonstrate the ability to differentiate between naturally occurring radioactive material (NORM) such as Ra-226 and Th-232 found in the concrete masonry unit (CMU) walls and the lack of NORMs from the windows. This was achieved by placing the detector 6" away from a CMU wall and a floor-to-wall window of roughly the same size and rotating it continuously as it collected data. The resulting Compton image clearly showed regions of high and low intensity corresponding to the locations of the CMU wall and window, successfully mitigating the effects of directional efficiency. Further work will investigate source-to-detector distance dependence and field applications, with the goal of applying similar methods to environmental monitoring and surveying scenarios to visualize areas of elevated radiation levels and contamination.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-09-02] High-Energy Gamma Transmission Imaging with a 3D-CZT Detector Using Ring Localization (#1362)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. G. Hotvedt (Autores: P. G. Hotvedt , Y. Zhu , M. Granados , Z. He)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Michigan, Nuclear Engineering and Radiological Sciences, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Transmission imaging requires a backing photon-sensing detector to accurately measure the interaction site and energy of each incident photon in future systems for material identification. 3D-CdZnTe detectors currently approximate the centroid of each electron cloud as the gamma interaction site with subpixel position sensing, but at high photon energies this measure may be biased by several millimeters from the true gamma interaction position, creating a noisy image. The ring localization technique constructs a ring of potential locations of the interaction site. The ring has its center at the measured centroid and has a radius equal to the average displacement between the interaction site and the centroid. Overlapping multiple rings on a per-event basis recovers this positional error. To demonstrate this recovery, a Th-228 source was placed behind a tungsten collimator with a 0.5-mm gap, which was aligned across a row of pixel electrodes to create centroid and ring images. Images were made using suspected Compton scattering events with a total event energy > 2 MeV. Two specific pixels were investigated in both images: one in the exposed region and one in the shielded region. The ring localization image shows an improved signal-to-noise ratio in both the exposed and shielded pixels compared to the centroid image. The pixels in the ring image also demonstrate a statistically significant difference between the average signal in the exposed and shielded regions. Subdividing the pixels reveals a count gradient on the investigated pixel, with the higher average signal in line with the collimator region. Future work will add more event types to get a better measure of the image resolution.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-09-03] A 128-Channel Mixed-Signal Readout ASIC for 3D Position-Sensitive CZT Detectors with Integrated ADC and TDC (#2014)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Yang (Autores: Z. Yang , H. Chang , Y. Huang , X. Zheng , J. Zhu , Y. Tian , Y. Li , F. Liu , H. Feng , W. Shen , M. Zeng)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [2] MicroParity Tech Inc., Hangzhou, China [3] Chinese Academy of Sciences, Institute of High Energy Physics, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Three-dimensional position-sensitive Cadmium-Zinc-Telluride (3D-CZT) detectors are promising in astrophysics. However, the specific space environment and scientific observation requirements impose numerous challenges on the readout electronics, including achieving low noise, high timing precision, and high count rates, while balancing high integration with low power consumption. Thus, we propose MPT3128, a 128-channel mixed-signal application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) for 3D-CZT detectors. Each channel integrates a low-noise charge-sensitive amplifier (CSA), fast and slow shapers, a 12-bit ADC (shared between two channels), and a time-to-digital converter (TDC) with a resolution of 312.5 ps. Specifically, for cathode timing, it features an adjustable fast-shaper peaking time and a triple-threshold timing scheme. Experimental results demonstrate that the analog front-end achieves low timing jitter (~2 ns even at 4.5 fC charge input), low electronic noise (202 e - rms), and high energy resolution (5.7 keV FWHM at 511 keV), while featuring fully digital output and control interfaces, facilitating system integration. Furthermore, with all channels active, the triggering rate reaches 55 kHz per channel. The unit has a relatively low power consumption (6.34 mW/channel), making it a promising solution for advanced radiation applications.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-09-04] X-ray direct detectors from solution-processed CdZnTe quantum dots (#2395)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Ruggieri (Autores: M. Ruggieri , M. Waqas , M. Scagliotti , M. Rapisarda , A. Valletta , P. Branchini , L. Tortora , A. Fabbri)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] INFN, Roma Tre Section, Rome, Italy [2] CNR, IMM, Rome, Italy [3] Roma Tre University, Dep. of Sciences, Rome, Italy [4] Padova University, Padova, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The growing role of solution-processable materials in novel, sensible radiation detectors has established materials like organic semiconductors and perovskites as promising alternatives to traditional ones. Solution-processable materials posses the unique characteristic to be semiconductors that can be processed in liquid form, and thus are extremely useful to develop thin, large-area and inexpensive devices. Quantum Dots have only recently started to draw attention as candidates for innovative, tunable detectors. These nanoparticles possess wide tunability possibilities, facile synthesis, ambient stability and are constituted often of High-Z elements such as Pb, Cd, Se etc. QDs' optoelectronic properties are strongly dependent on their size, which is tunable during synthesis. Within a size range for every QD material, it is then possible to select the best ones for each application. Recent results suggest that QD-based detectors have high X-ray sensitivity even with low-power operation, are radiation hard and retain their stability under ambient condition. However, a still unexplored and exciting question is if the best materials for direct radiation detection could still perform efficiently in QD form. A positive answer would mean a new, unprecedented way to fabricate such detectors, exploiting the advantages of solution-processable materials such as low-cost, large-area deposition, casting on flexible substrates etc. With this question in mind, and inspired by the excellent detection characteristics of CdZnTe detectors, in this work we synthesized CZT QD and employed them in drop-cast photodetectors. We assessed their X-ray detection capabilities in the 5-50 keV range with low-power biasing, observing a ready, repeatable response to the radiation. This result, albeit still early, seems to suggest a positive answer to our question, paving the way for the use of already established materials (CZT) in QD form for the development of new, advanced direct detectors.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-09-05] High-Flux Performance of a Photon-Counting Detector for Spectral CT Based on the ColorCT ASIC (#1491)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Brambilla (Autores: A. Brambilla , A. Peizerat , K. Abdoul-Carime , A. Poizat , J. Jonsson , D. Tran , L. Verger)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Univ. Grenoble Alpes, CEA-Leti, DOPT, Grenoble, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract ColorCT is a novel readout ASIC for energy-resolved photon-counting detectors (ER-PCDs) dedicated to spectral X-ray computed tomography (CT). It is designed to sustain very high photon fluxes while preserving spectral performance under strict power consumption constraints. The ColorCT test chip features an 11 × 11 pixel matrix (330 µm pitch) and 8 energy bins. A fast analog front-end delivers short pulses (13 ns peaking time, 24 ns FWHM), enabling high count rate capability. A Digital Reset circuit mitigates pile-up and prevents detector paralysis, ensuring a monotonic increasing behavior of the count rate with the X-ray flux with a saturation value of 30 Mcps. A digital charge sharing correction (CSC) improves the spectral accuracy. The ASIC was coupled to a CdTe crystal to perform X-ray characterizations. Experimental results demonstrate improved count rate and spectral response obtained with the Digital Reset and the CSC, with a power consumption of 3 mW/mm² at 3 10 7 cps/px (3 10 8 cps/mm²).

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-09-06] A CZT Readout ASIC for Double-Layer Compton Imaging Applications (#2191)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 W. B. Wright (Autores: W. B. Wright , T. Prakash , C. Grace , M. Turqueti , J. Caravaca)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Engineering Division, Berkeley, California, United States of America [2] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Nuclear Science Division, Berkeley, California, United States of America [3] University of California San Francisco, Department of Radiology & Biomedical Imaging, San Francisco, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract CZT Compton cameras have demonstrated great promise for nuclear medicine. We are designing a dual layer CZT Compton camera to enhance angular resolution with respect to current single-layer cameras. An application specific integrated circuit (ASIC) that provide excellent 3D position, energy resolution and high data throughout is required for this. A multi-channel ASIC is presented in this work to overcome these challenges. It is composed of 16 anode readout channels, plus a cathode channel, that each contain a charge sensitive amplifier (CSA), pulse shaper, programmable gain amplifier (PGA), peak detector, and configurable peak detector reset dissipating 12 mW per channel to support low-noise and high dynamic range. The channels are designed for a target energy of 218keV & 440keV used in 225 Ac Compton imaging, with a worst-case 0.81% non-linearity over the dynamic range of 30 keV to 2.2 MeV. Each channel can handle up to 2 nA of leakage current without performance degradation and yields 1.33% FWHM at 662 keV with a single-pixel capacitance of 29.1 pF for each (1.225 mm)x(1.225 mm) pixel. The rise time of each CSA is 150 ns while the shaper peaking time is 320 ns to enable fast readout with a configurable gain of 7, 13, 45, 81, and 132 mV/fC from the PGA. This work demonstrates a compact, scalable readout platform for CZT-based Compton imagers and other room-temperature semiconductor detector systems requiring high energy resolution.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-09-07] Performance evaluation of CZTS grown with higher purity CdSe starting material (#2698)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 U. N. Roy (Autores: U. N. Roy , J. Kleppinger , R. James)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Savannah River National Laboratory, ELM, Aiken, South Carolina, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract CdZnTe (CZT) has been the most commercially successful semiconductor material for room-temperature X-ray and gamma-ray radiation detector applications. It is considered as the gold standard for detector applications that require spectral and often spatial information in a compact instrument. However, CZT still contains a high density of performance-limiting defects such as high concentrations of sub-grain boundary networks, Te inclusions and compositional inhomogeneity in as-grown ingots. Adding a small amount of selenium (Se) in the CZT matrix was found to successfully mitigate the performance-limiting defects and provide for better compositional homogeneity. Thus, the new quaternary Cd x Zn 1−x Te y Se 1−y (CZTS) is emerging as a next-generation compound semiconductor, potentially surpassing the material quality of CZT. However, the purity of CZTS material is not on par with commercial CZT, principally due to the lack of availability of commercial high-purity CdSe. The presence of the impurities in CZTS caused by the lower-purity CdSe starting material was found to impose a detrimental effect on the charge transport properties of CZTS, resulting in adverse effects on the charge collection and detector performance. Here, we report for the first time on the growth and characterization of Cd 0.9 Zn 0.1 Te 0.98 Se 0.02 grown by vertical Bridgman and by the traveling heater method (THM) using higher-purity CdSe starting material.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-09-08] Merit-Function-Guided Porosity Control in Directional Solidification of CZT (#2985)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. E. Gheribi (Autores: A. E. Gheribi , K. Younsi , N. Chorbadzhiev , E. Hammoutene , F. Belanger)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] 5Nplus, R&D, Montreal, Québec, Canada
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Directional solidification (DSM) enables rapid growth of cadmium zinc telluride (CZT) ingots with superior scalability and geometric flexibility compared to the travelling heater method (THM). However, the strongly non-equilibrium conditions inherent to DSM promote gas bubble nucleation, growth, transport, and coalescence, leading to porosity that degrades detector performance. Bubble-induced defects distort internal electric fields, enhance charge trapping, reduce the carrier mobility-lifetime product ($\mu\tau$), and increase leakage current and electronic noise through impurity segregation and secondary phase formation. In contrast, THM operates closer to thermodynamic equilibrium and therefore minimizes such defects, albeit at reduced growth rate and scalability. DSM-grown CZT typically exhibits axial heterogeneity, with increasing bubble density and size toward the last-to-solidify region. This results from coupled interactions between volatile-species thermodynamics, buoyancy-driven transport, capillarity, coalescence, and solidification kinetics. Bubble coalescence and accumulation in the upper melt region significantly amplify porosity near the end of solidification, producing larger pores that are more easily entrapped and more detrimental to detector uniformity. To describe these mechanisms, a physics-based dimensionless framework is introduced using transport, thermodynamic, and interfacial scaling parameters, including an escape number comparing bubble migration and interface growth velocities, as well as Bond and Capillary numbers governing deformation and stability. Within an atomistic-informed thermophysical model at 5N Plus, temperature- and composition-dependent properties are used to evaluate these parameters and define a predictive merit function for DSM optimization. This framework identifies conditions that promote bubble escape, suppress coalescence and entrapment, and reduce porosity while preserving the advantages of rapid CZT crystal growth.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-21-01] Development of a Cost-Effective PCCT Detector Based on Sub-Millimeter EQR SiPM and LYSO Array with High Count Rate and Adequate Energy Resolution (#6)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Yan (Autores: Y. Yan , M. Huang , X. Zhang , K. Liang , R. Yang , D. Han)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Normal University, school of Physics and Astronomy, Beijing, China [2] Beijing Normal University, Applied Optics Beijing Area Major Laboratory, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Among the detector candidates for clinical photon-counting CT (PCCT), SiPM-based fast-scintillation photon-counting detectors (PCD) represent a cost-effective solution. However, their practical implementation is constrained by the incompatible trade-off between count-rate capability and energy resolution. To address this limitation, we developed a scintillation PCD designed to achieve both high counting rate and improved energy resolution. The detector consists of a 26-channel pixelated LYSO scintillator array coupled to an epitaxial-quenching-resistor (EQR) SiPM array with a 0.5-mm pixel pitch and 15-μm microcells. Benefiting from the EQR architecture, the SiPM pixels exhibit a fast recovery time of 3.2 ns, a 64% fill factor, and a photon detection efficiency exceeding 40% at 420 nm. A multi-channel FPGA-based photon-counting readout circuit with per-channel pole-zero cancellation was developed to suppress signal tailing and mitigate pulse pile-up. This PCD achieved a maximum count rate of 46.3 Mcps/mm² while maintaining an energy resolution of 33.7% at 59.5 keV. The spatial resolution of 1.86 lp/mm (537 μm) was achieved under 120-keV X-rays, which agreed closely with the 0.5-mm physical pixel pitch of the detector. A more sophisticated PCD based on a 64-channel EQR SiPM array with 0.25-mm pixel pitch and 10-μm microcells, coupled to a corresponding pixelated LYSO scintillator array, will also be presented. Those results indicate that the proposed scintillation PCD is a promising cost-effective candidate for clinical PCCT applications.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-21-02] First Characterisation Results on Backside-Illuminated SiPM Prototypes from the IBIS Project (#2930)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Preghenella (Autores: R. Preghenella , F. Acerbi , P. Antonioli , E. Bertolin , F. Carnesecchi , F. Caso , D. Elgewaily , G. Fadini , A. Ficorella , C. Forza , A. Gola , P. Kachru , E. Montagna , A. Montanari , R. Nania , L. Parellada-Monreal , G. Paternoster , R. Ricci , L. Rignanese , E. Rovati , B. Sabiu , G. Sirri , N. Tosi , C. Trippl , O. Villarreal)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Bologna, Bologna, Italy [2] Fondazione Bruno Kessler, Trento, Italy [3] Università di Bologna, Bologna, Italy [4] Università di Milano Bicocca e INFN Sezione Milano Bicocca, Milano, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We report on the development and characterisation of innovative Backside-Illuminated Silicon Photomultipliers (BSI-SiPMs) within the INFN IBIS and IBIS_NEXT projects. The BSI architecture relocates the photon entrance window to the back side of the device, enabling high fill factor and improved photon detection efficiency while preserving compatibility with advanced front-end electronics integration, and offering the potential for enhanced sensitivity in the VUV region. A preliminary experimental campaign has been performed on partially processed BSI prototype devices, including electrical characterisation over a wide temperature range, dark count rate measurements, irradiation studies, annealing tests, and timing performance evaluation using both pulsed laser excitation and minimum ionising particles (MIPs) at CERN. Irradiation up to 10 9 n eq /cm 2 results in an increase in dark count rate. Preliminary annealing studies show recovery of dark current by nearly one order of magnitude. Timing measurements yield resolutions of order ~100 ps, demonstrating the potential of BSI-SiPMs for fast timing applications in high-energy physics.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-21-03] Photon-to-Digital Converters Enabling Event Classification Through Pulse Shape Discrimination (#1301)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. A. Charlebois (Autores: G. Lessard , C. M. Pepin , T. Rossignol , N. Roy , F. Vachon , R. Espagnet , G. Lemaire , A. L. Steinhebel , P. Hausladen , L. Fabris , R. Lecomte , R. Fontaine , J.-F. Pratte , S. A. Charlebois)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Université de Sherbrooke, Interdisciplinary Institute for Technological Innovation and Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Sherbrooke, Québec, Canada [2] Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, Tennessee, United States of America [3] Université de Sherbrooke, Sherbrooke Molecular Imaging Center and Department of Medical Imaging and Radiation Sciences, Sherbrooke, Québec, Canada
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Digital silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) are being developed to circumvent many of the shortfalls inherent to analog SiPMs and their associated readout electronics. We design 3D-integrated digital SiPMs, called Photon-to-Digital Converters (PDCs), to simultaneously optimize the photosensitive area, remove analog noise contributions, and embed signal processing. With a low-power-optimized readout architecture providing high timing resolution, we demonstrate fully digital measurement approaches and their benefits across multiple fields, including time-of-flight medical imaging and neutron imaging. Leveraging the high-timing precision of the PDC through pulse shape discrimination, the components of an LGSO (Fast/Slow) phoswich scintillator assembly are precisely classified, while maintaining the expected energy resolution for the scintillators irradiated with calibration isotopes such as a 68Ge source. Coincidence timing resolution is also assessed for this configuration. These results position PDCs as great candidates for depth-of-interaction reconstruction in PET imaging, ToF measurement in CT imaging, and particle identification in neutron imaging.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-21-04] Progress on Single-cell-access TSVs for 3D-integrated microSiPM readout in fast-timing SiPM detectors (#2683)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Gola (Autores: A. Gola , S. Bisi , C. Bruschini , E. Charbon , S. Gundacker , K. Herweg , P. Kachru , L. Parellada Monreal , G. Paternoster , M. Penna , M. Ruzzarin , D. Schug , V. Schulz , N. Zorzi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK), Trento, Italy [2] Ecole Polythechnique federale de Lausanne (EPFL), AQUA Lab, Neuchatel, Switzerland [3] University Hospital RWTH Aachen, Aachen, Germany [4] Austrian Academy of Sciences, Institute of High Energy Physics, Vienna, Austria [5] RWTH Aachen University, Institute of Imaging and Computer Vision, Aachen, Germany [6] Hyperion Hybrid Imaging Systems GmbH, Aachen, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Segmentation of the SiPM active area into smaller, independently read out elements is one of the most promising routes to improve the single-photon time resolution (SPTR) required by next-generation time-of-flight PET systems. We report on Single-Cell Access through-silicon vias (SCA-TSVs), a custom TSV technology under development at Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK), Trento, and applied to the NUV-HD-MT SiPM platform. SCA-TSVs exploit the deep-trench isolation (DTI) already present in this technology to physically separate and independently access each SiPM microcell from the backside, with essentially no loss of fill factor. A backside redistribution layer (RDL) can then regroup microcells with an arbitrary segmentation level, according to application requirements. The first implementation targets the DIGILOG project, where a 3 × 3 mm² SiPM with 50 µm cells is segmented into 3 × 3- or 6 × 6-cell clusters, referred to as microSiPMs. These units are designed to be read out independently by a matched ASIC developed at EPFL and connected through chip-to-chip 3D integration. This approach preserves the SPTR of a single SPAD, approximately 25 ps FWHM, while avoiding the complexity of full single-cell readout. The first SCA-TSV learning cycle (LC1) required modifications to the original NUV-HD-MT technology, mainly an increase of the DTI depth beyond 20 µm. Front-side characterization showed that the timing performance was preserved. The first backside integration runs also revealed a reduced TSV yield. The analysis identified both layout-related and backside-process-related limitations, which are being addressed through optimized LC1 backend process splits and in the second technology learning cycle (LC2). The presentation will discuss the SCA-TSV concept, LC1 fabrication and characterization results, and the latest LC2 developments toward 3D-integrated microSiPM/ASIC chips for fast-timing applications.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-21-05] PlatonSPAD: A Scalable Sensor for Elementary Particle Detection (#1496)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Kaneyasu (Autores: K. Kaneyasu , T. Dieminger , J. Soerensen , D. Sgalaberna , C. Bruschini , E. Charbon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Ecole polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Advanced Quantum Architecture lab, Neuchatel, Neuchâtel, Switzerland [2] ETH Zurich, Institute for Particle Physics and Astrophysics, Zurich, Zürich, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Precise detection of elementary particles such as neutrinos, gammas, or electrons in an unsegmented scintillating volume requires three-dimensional tracking with sub-nanosecond timing resolution [1], [2]. However, conventional detectors based on analog silicon photomultipliers are inherently constrained by trade-offs between spatial resolution and scalability, making them less suitable for large-scale implementations [3]. To overcome these limitations, CMOS single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD)-based detectors have emerged as a promising alternative for high-resolution particle detection [4], [5]. Here, we propose a dedicated large-format SPAD array sensor fabricated in 110 nm CMOS image sensor (CIS) technology, targeting both high timing precision and scalability. The sensor incorporates a high photon-detection-efficiency SPAD pixel architecture that triggers time-to-digital converters (TDCs) in an event-driven manner with a resolution of 200 ps to detect sparse photons generated by probabilistic events such as particle interactions. All TDCs are synchronized with a global reference clock distributed through an on-chip phase-locked loop, ensuring precise timing alignment across the entire sensor array. Furthermore, a tunable clock shifting feature is implemented to compensate for clock skew in multiple-chip operation. As a result, this chip serves as a fundamental building block for a scalable, multi-chip tiled detector system in which all timing information is globally synchronized, enabling future large-scale, high-resolution particle tracking applications.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-21-06] Study of neutron irradiated CMOS SPADs for RICH detector applications (#2502)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Dolenec (Autores: R. Dolenec , H.K. Yildirim , G.V. Tran , A.G.P. Domenech , B.C. Efe , W.Y. Ha , U. Karaca , P. Singh , G.G. Taylor , S. Korpar , P. Križan , R. Pestotnik , A. Seljak , E. Charbon , C. Bruschini)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Jožef Stefan Institute, Ljubljana, Slovenia [2] University of Ljubljana, Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, Ljubljana, Slovenia [3] École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne, AQUA Laboratory, Neuchâtel, Switzerland [4] University of Maribor, Faculty of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Maribor, Slovenia
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Single-photon avalanche diodes (SPAD) produced in CMOS technologies are increasingly being considered as photodetector candidates for future Ring imaging Cherenkov (RICH) detectors. CMOS SPAD based sensors with integrated electronics can be designed and optimized specifically for RICH detector applications, making it easier to achieve the high photon detection efficiency, excellent single photon timing resolution and hardness to neutron radiation as required in the planned high energy physics experiments. To help guide the design of first digital SiPM targeting RICH detector applications being developed in the spadRICH project, existing single SPADs as well as a 144x32 SPAD array were studied in terms of their operation after neutron irradiation. Dark count rates were measured for neutron irradiation as high as 10 12 1-MeV neutron equivalent/cm 2 . Thermal annealing and operation at temperatures down to liquid nitrogen were explored. In terms of cryogenic operation, afterpulsing probability and behavior of the photon detection efficiency were also studied. Simulations were used to assess the possible performance of microlenses specifically for the highly collimated Cherenkov photon light as expected in the upgraded LHCb RICH detector.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-21-07] Comparative Study of NIEL Effects on Dark Count Rate in 110 nm CMOS SPADs Under Neutron, Proton and Electron Irradiation (#1251)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) fabricated in a 110 nm CMOS technology were irradiated with neutrons, protons, and electrons over a range of fluences up to 10 11 1 MeV neutron-equivalent cm -2 . The dark count rate (DCR) evolution was systematically characterized as a function of displacement damage dose; online monitoring during neutron and proton irradiation allowed individual scattering events and short-term annealing dynamics to be resolved at the single-pixel level, providing direct insight into defect formation and recovery. Statistical characterization of the DCR distributions reveals that the average DCR alone is insufficient to describe radiation-induced degradation in SPAD arrays: the particle type critically determines both the magnitude and spatial uniformity of damage. These differences reflect distinct defect morphologies - clustered damage for hadrons, isolated point defects for electrons - a key aspect not captured by NIEL scaling alone.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-21-08] First developments of NUV-DJ SiPM arrays forcryogenic operation for the LHCb SciFi tracker Upgrade II (#2830)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C.A. Trippl (Autores: C.A. Trippl , F. Acerbi , E. Curras Rivera , G. Haefeli , O. Marti Villareal , S. Sheng , A. Gola)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Fondazione Bruno Kessler, CRS, Trento, Italy [2] École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, LPHE, Lausanne, Vaud, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents the first cryogenic performance evaluation of the novel Near-Ultraviolet Deep-Junction (NUV-DJ) SiPM technology developed by Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK). By relocating the high-electric field region deeper within the substrate, the NUV-DJ architecture achieves a state-of-the-art photo-detection efficiency of approximately 70% at 420 nm and a timing resolution of 60 ps FWHM at room temperature with a 4 x 4 mm 2 SiPM. We report on a comprehensive dark characterisation of these sensors from 300 K down to 77 K, extracting the activation energy (Ea​) to identify dominant carrier generation mechanisms, and evaluating the stability of correlated noise and gain. These studies serve as a foundation for a new dedicated production run for the LHCb Scintillating Fibre (SciFi) Tracker Upgrade II, in collaboration with EPFL, featuring custom 0.4 mm2 geometries and advanced afterpulsing suppression. The main goal is to assess whether the enhanced blue-green sensitivity of NUV-DJ, which is advantageous for the readout of irradiated blue-emitting scintillating fibres, can be combined with radiation tolerance and stable cryogenic operation at liquid-nitrogen temperature.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-22-01] Learning Real-World Spectral Templates from a City-Scale Radiological Sensor Network (#1381)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Parrilla (Autores: H. Parrilla , N. Abgrall , M. Bandstra , R. Cooper , Y. Kim , M. Salathe , R. Sankaran , S. Shahkarami)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, California, United States of America [2] Argonne National Laboratory, Lemont, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Spectral templates used for radiological anomaly detection and isotope identification are most commonly derived from simulation, yet real-world source encounters are subject to a diversity of shielding configurations, scattering geometries, and encounter dynamics that simulation does not fully capture. The PANDAWN sensor network - fourteen statically deployed, multi-modal radiological detection nodes distributed across Chicago, IL - provides a unique opportunity to learn spectral templates directly from real-world data. In this talk, we present the application of regularized Non-Negative Matrix Factorization clustering to anomalous gamma-ray spectra, which recovers multiple spectrally distinct templates for nuisance isotope encounters observed across the network, each corresponding to physically interpretable differences in source attenuation and encounter geometry. Examining how these cluster components trigger isotope identification during known source encounters reveals distinct temporal patterns, further demonstrating that the learned templates capture meaningful structure in the real-world encounter environment. We will discuss what these results reveal about source encounters across the network, present an assessment of template transferability across nodes, and examine how developing a taxonomy of data-driven source templates of this kind can improve detection and isotope identification performance.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-22-02] Spatially-derived Enhancement of Time-domain PSD and Spectroscopy Measurements (#1991)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. M. Collins-Price (Autores: P. M. Collins-Price , I. Tsitsimpelis , M. D. Aspinall , M. J. Joyce)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lancaster University, Engineering, Lancaster, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Geometrical event removal (GER) via a position-sensitive multianode photomultiplier tube (MAPMT) is used to enhance mixed-field pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) in an organic EJ-276 scintillator and gamma spectroscopy peak-to-continuum ratio in a CeBr3 crystal scintillator. Significant (~21.3%) improvements in PSD figure-of-merit (FoM) are shown without the need for an energy cut-off, allowing for real-time spectrum-agnostic enhancement of time-domeain PSD methods. This allows greater separation of the neutron and gamma plumes at low energies without the need for a low-energy cutoff, thereby preserving the ability to measure across the full range of neutron spectra. The position sensitivity of the detector has also been exploited to create 2D flux map images of gamma fields attenuated through various lightweight 3D-printed collimators, and to identify the isotope and relative direction of individual point gamma sources in a multi-isotope combined field.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-22-03] Impact of Air Activation on Tritium Monitoring in Fusion Energy Systems (#2627)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. D. Clarke (Autores: S. D. Clarke , D. Breitenmoser , M. Y. Hua , S. A. Pozzi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Michigan, Department of Nuclear Engineering & Radiological Sciences, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America [2] Helion Energy, Inc., Everett, Washington, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Robust tritium monitoring is essential for fusion energy systems, where rapid detection of low-level airborne releases is needed to support safe operation and accident response. However, intense neutron fields in fusion environments activate surrounding air and produce radioactive products that can contribute beta, gamma-ray, and X-ray backgrounds, complicating tritium detection. In this work, we investigate the impact of air-activation products on a proposed tritium detection concept that combines a thin plastic scintillator beta cell with a surrounding NaI(Tl) anti-coincidence shield. The plastic scintillator provides sensitivity to the low-energy beta particles from tritium decay, while the NaI(Tl) detector enables rejection of coincident photon backgrounds. Monte Carlo simulations were performed using MCNP6 to estimate the detector response to tritium and relevant air-activation radionuclides, including beta emitters such as 13N, 14C, 39Ar, 39Cl, and 41Ar, as well as associated gamma-ray, X-ray, and bremsstrahlung contributions. A 1.3-mm-thick plastic scintillator cell was modeled to match commercially available thin-walled beta cells used in radioxenon detection. Preliminary results show that several air-activation products produce signals in the same low-energy region as tritium and may represent important background contributions, particularly when gamma rays are not detected in coincidence. Subsequent simulations will be performed using the MCNPX-PoliMi code to accurately treat the correlated detection of electrons and photons in the plastic and NaI(Tl) cells.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-22-04] Attention-Biased Additive Point Source Localization (#2925)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. Rofors (Autores: E. Rofors , B. J. Quiter , V. Negut)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present Attention-Biased Additive Point Source Localization (ABAPSL), a fast reconstruction method for localizing multiple radioactive point sources from mobile gamma-ray measurements. The method extends our prior gridded multi-source localization work, which found sources one at a time and added confirmed sources into a growing background model. ABAPSL instead re-fits all active sources at each reconstruction while using an attention metric to place fine test points only where the data support high sensitivity or high source likelihood. This provides local 10cm-scale refinement without requiring a uniformly fine grid over the full survey area. We also introduce multi-resolution spatial measurement binning, replacing fixed time bins with trajectory-aligned spatial bins that remain fine near candidate sources yet are coarser in background-dominated regions. The resulting system matrix is small enough for online reconstruction on mobile computers such as the onboard compute used in a Localization and Mapping Platform (LAMP) system. We demonstrate the approach with simulations around multiple radioactive point sources, with LAMP measurement validation to follow.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-22-05] VETTR: A Robotic Landmine Detection System via Associated Particle Imaging (#2957)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Pavlovsky (Autores: R. Pavlovsky , P. Freeman , V. Goicoecheaca , S. DuBridge , J. Ellin , J. Oshiro , B. Bilyeu , E. Suzuki , A. Haefner , K. Vetter)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Gamma Reality Inc, Berkeley, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Gamma Reality Inc has developed and demonstrated, to our knowledge, the first robotic deployment of Associated Particle Imaging (API) for the application of rapid-assessment, detection and 3D imaging of buried landmines. We utilize a deuterium-tritium (DT) reaction to generate momentum-tagged neutrons, at rates up to 5E8 n/s, that stimulate characteristic gamma-ray emissions. The result is 3D voxel-spectral information that we combine with contextual sensed scenes, via 3D LiDAR, providing a centimeter resolution map of isotopic compositions within a specific scene. There are many non-destructive assay applications for such a system, however we identify landmine detection as our first application space. Modern landmine detectors are sensitive to secondary characteristics of mines, such as low mass-metal content within the mines, and struggle with false-positive probabilities. Our method targets the primary characteristics of mines, which has the potential for a very large reduction in false positive rate compared to current methods, which can be 30 to 1 or often worse. In this paper we present results of our field demonstrations and domestic tests, where we identify surrogate mine materials constructed of ammonium nitrate and carbon against common background and nuisance objects (organic materials, metal objects, & etc). We present results for 20 min, 5min and 1min detections over mine surrogates in soil. We will also present the results of field-testing over TNT and other explosive fills in replica casings.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-22-06] Development of a Real-time Dose Rate Monitoring System Reading with Optical Fiber under the High-Dose Rate Condition (#3167)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Kurosawa (Autores: S. Kurosawa , A. Yamaji , C. Fujiwara, C. Fujiwara , Y. Urano, Y. Urano)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Nagoya University, Graduate School of Engineering, Nagoya, Japan [2] Kyoto University, Institute for Integrated Radiation and Nuclear Science, Kumatori, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dosimetry under the high dose-rate conditions is required such as internal survey of the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant for the decommissioning. We have developed a dose-rate monitor consisting of optical fiber and scintillators. Since the optical fiber has lower collection efficiency of the scintillation photons compared to that of direct contacting between a scintillator and photomultiplier tube, higher light output was required. Moreover, long emission wavelength of over 650 nm is required to obtain sufficient sensitivity. Cr-doped oxides are expected to have emission wavelength in the red or infra-red region, and garnet crystals can be optimized the emission wavelength by changing crystal fields. Thus, we focused on Cr-doped (Y, Gd) 3 (Al, Ga) 5 O 12 materials as red oxide scintillators, and Gd 3 (Ga 0.995 Cr 0.005 ) 5 O 12 (Cr:GGG) single crystals grown by the micro-pulling-down method had an emission wavelength of Cr:GGG was 731 nm, which achieved the emission goal. Using this Cr:GGG sample we have developed the real-time dose monitor, and such system was found to operate the survey even under the high dose rate of around 1 kSv/h. Moreover, we evaluated the absorption dose with different gamma-ray energies with geant4 (gamma-ray energy response), and the result was consistent with gamma-ray irradiation test with 137 Cs and 60 Co sources.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-06-01] Minkhole Collimators for SPECT: Minkowski-Sum Aperture Geometry and Closed-Form Ray Tracing (#1605)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Li (Autores: Y. Li , H. Li)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] United Imaging Healthcare North America, MI, Houston, Texas, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) pinhole collimators trade isotropic resolution against detector coverage: circular apertures cover only 78.5% of a square detector. Rectangular pinholes (rectholes) fill the detector but introduce anisotropic resolution. Lofthole collimators linearly interpolate between a circular aperture and a rectangular exit; their non-developable lateral surfaces complicate fabrication and geometric calibration. We present the minkhole collimator, a knife-edge geometry whose half-frustum equals the Minkowski sum of a circular waist and a rectangular exit. The half-frustum boundary decomposes exactly into ten analytic patches: two caps, four ruled side planes, and four corner quadrics. Convexity of each half-frustum bounds a ray to at most two boundary intersections, giving a closed-form ray tracer of six linear and four quadratic solves with no iteration. We implement the 10-patch intersection and compare the minkhole to pinhole, recthole, and lofthole collimators on a common geometry. At matched sensitivity and field of view, minkhole projections are more symmetric than the recthole's and show less diagonal elongation than the lofthole's, while fully covering the detector. Its piecewise-developable surface (planar and sheared-conical patches) admits a compact analytic form that simplifies calibration, making the minkhole a practical building block for multi-aperture SPECT.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-06-02] Monte Carlo simulation model of the ring CZT based VERITON SPECT-CT system (#2273)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Sarrut (Autores: A. Etxebeste , M.H.H. Bui , M. Erojo , T. Baudier , J.N. Badel , M. Hakulinen , D. Sarrut)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CREATIS, INSA-Lyon, CNRS UMR 5220, Lyon, France [2] Centre de lutte contre le cancer Léon Bérard, Lyon, France [3] Diagnostic Imaging Center, Kuopio University Hospital, Kuopio, Finland [4] University of Eastern Finland, Department of Technical Physics, Kuopio, Finland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The aim of this study was to develop and evaluate a GATE Monte Carlo model of the ring CZT based VERITON SPECT-CT system against experimental data. System spatial resolution was evaluated using planar images with 99m Tc point-like sources. Good agreement was obtained between both experimental and simulated data with consistent values within one sigma, except for the studied distances closest to the collimator surface (5 and 7 cm) where relative discrepancies of 25% and 7% were observed along X-axis. A tomographic acquisition, corresponding to 4 gantry rotations and 60 swivel positions per detector head, using the NEMA IEC body phantom was simulated within GATE 10. A qualitative comparison of profiles showed good agreement between both reconstructions. We plan to further evaluate this model regarding quantitative imaging and extend it to additional radionuclides. Such a model could have a significant impact on the optimisation of acquisition protocols, image reconstruction and system design.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-06-03] Intraoperative Position-Sensitive Positron Emission Counter (PEC): A Simulation Study (#2337)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Ohashi (Autores: R. Ohashi , S. Ito , M. Takahashi , T. Yamaya)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology, Chiba, Japan [2] Chiba University, Graduate School of Science and Engineering, Chiba, Japan [3] Mirai-Imaging Corporation, Fukushima, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract For metastatic lymph-node localization in esophageal cancer surgery with 18 F-FDG injection, we have been developing an intraoperative positron emission counter (PEC). This device employs two BGO scintillators (∼10×5×15 mm 3 ) on the tip of a forceps and it provides coincidence detection. The current design of the PEC is not position sensitive; however, quantitative radioactivity measurement requires recovery of the source distribution within the compact field of view (FOV) of the PEC, because position-dependent detection efficiency renders the integral count rate ambiguous. In this paper, we investigate the feasibility of source distribution visualization on a position-sensitive PEC variant featuring 2×2 segmentation of each scintillator (yielding 16 lines of response, LORs) together with a machine-learning (ML) decoder mapping these 16 LORs to a source distribution. Specifically, we designed a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with a spatial-softmax head defined over the FOV. The MLP was trained with Kullback-Leibler (KL)-divergence supervision on random-walk phantoms (each yielding a 16-LOR expected count vector via Geant4 simulation, Poisson-sampled at a 100-count budget), with mixed single- and synthetic 2-source training samples. The pitch of the FOV reconstruction grid was 0.5 mm. On held-out single-source test phantoms, the predicted distribution provides the source center-of-gravity (CoG) with a median 3D Euclidean mean-absolute-error (MAE) of 0.73 mm and the per-axis source extent within ≤16% (sigma MAE 0.13-0.24 mm vs. ground-truth 1.2-1.5 mm). On disjoint 2-source pairs, 90.1% of the detected peaks lie within 2.5 mm of a true source (per-detected-peak median 1.40 mm; per-true-source median 1.58 mm). These results indicate that a position-sensitive PEC with an MLP-based decoder achieves not only the source localization but also the source distribution visualization from only 16 LOR counts.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-06-04] A metascintillator-based, ultra-ToF enabled, brain PET scanner simulation (#2563)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Konstantinou (Autores: G. Konstantinou , P. Lecoq)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] EPFL, PV lab, Neuchatel, Neuchâtel, Switzerland [2] Metacrystal SA, Geneve, Switzerland [3] CERN, Geneve, Genève, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Metascintillator systems composed of LYSO:Ce and 2D organic lead halide perovskites were recently measured in the laboratory with high end electronics. The timing behavior of this metascintillator rendered two dominant subsets: 44% of fast, perovskite-led and shared events at 46 ps and 56% of slow, LYSO:Ce events at 110 ps. As this design reaches ultrafast ToF regimes, an opportunity to better understand the effect of such CTR on final image quality arises. The possibility of adapting this configuration to a photonic-driven semi-monolithic metascintillator also offers very good depth-of-interaction discrimination, at 4 mm. To benchmark this detector architecture, a brain PET scanner was designed in GATE, with a Hoffman brain and Derenzo phantoms for benchmarking. A series of reconstruction approaches, for instance using the fast subset as priors or weighing in on the different subsets been performed, but the drive for this exercise is to invite the reconstruction community to experiment with and demonstrate the potential of new generation high end ToF detectors for medical imaging.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-06-05] Towards the Ultimate Sub-0.4 mm Resolution: GATE Simulation of a Mouse Brain PET System (#1832)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H.G. Kang (Autores: H.G. Kang , H. Tashima , T. Yamaya)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology (QST), Advanced Nuclear Medicine Sciences, Chiba, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Last year, we developed a sub-0.5 mm resolution positron emission tomography (PET) system using staggered 3-layer depth-of-interaction (DOI) detectors for mouse brain imaging. However, the crystal pitch of 0.8 mm limited the spatial resolution to 0.45 mm, which sparked our pursuit of the ultimate resolution. In this study, we investigate the spatial resolution of a newly proposed mouse brain PET system that uses a reduced crystal pitch as we move towards sub-0.4 mm resolution. The proposed system provides 48 mm inner diameter and 22.6 mm axial coverage. It consists of 32 DOI detectors with 2-ring geometry. Each DOI detector has staggered 3-layer LYSO crystals (crystal pitch=0.6 mm) with a crystal layer thickness of 3+3+5 mm, thereby providing a 11 mm total thickness. We used GATE simulation to investigate the performance of the proposed PET design. For spatial resolution evaluation, an NEMA 22 Na source (D=0.25 mm) was scanned from the field-of-view center to the 15 mm radial offset position and it was reconstructed by using an FBP algorithm. For imaging performance evaluation, a resolution phantom having six different rod diameters was used. The PET images were reconstructed by using the OSEM algorithm. Compared to results of our previous work, the spatial resolution was improved from 0.75±0.02 mm to 0.55±0.07 mm. Unlike the previous work, the 0.4 mm rods of the resolution phantom were resolved with a valley-to-peak ratio of 0.763. In conclusion, the simulation showed that our proposed mouse brain PET system provided 0.4 mm resolution in resolution phantom imaging. As a next step, we plan to develop a prototype mouse brain PET scanner to achieve 0.4 mm resolution experimentally.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-07-01] Experimental Feasibility of Dual-Mode C-arm CT/SPECT Imaging Using a Commercial X-ray Detector for Online Brachytherapy Delivery Verification (#1805)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Sung (Autores: S. Sung , H.-J. Choi , S.W. Jeong , S.H. You , C.H. Min)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yonsei University, Department of Radiation Convergence Engineering, Wonju, Republic of Korea [2] Yonsei University Wonju College of Medicine, Wonju Severance Christian Hospital, Department of Radiation Oncology, Wonju, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Online brachytherapy delivery verification requires two complementary capabilities: anatomical verification of the applicator prior to irradiation and dynamic tracking of the radioactive source during dose delivery. This study experimentally evaluated the feasibility of a dual-mode C-arm CT/SPECT imaging concept using a single commercially available X-ray flat-panel detector. The core paradigm repurposes a standard X-ray detector into a shared hardware platform: an uncollimated mode for structural visualization, and a collimator-attached mode for radioactive source tracking. The experimental setup utilized a DRTECH EXT1616R digital detector. In the uncollimated X-ray mode, projection images of a PMMA-agar phantom containing a two-ovoid applicator were acquired at 90 kV and 10 mAs during rotational acquisition. The acquired projections successfully distinguished the applicator, air cavities, and phantom tissue surrogate layers. For the SPECT mode, a parallel-hole tungsten collimator was attached to the identical detector. Projection frames of a 58.12 GBq Co-60 source were acquired continuously at 1 frame/s during rotation. Following image intensity enhancement, the Co-60 source profile yielded full width at half maximum values of 3.80 mm and 2.91 mm in the x and y directions, respectively. Furthermore, to demonstrate the ultimate clinical utility of this dual-mode concept, a high-quality reference CT image of a patient-specific 3D-printed pelvic phantom was overlaid with the reconstructed SPECT source distribution, successfully illustrating CT/SPECT fusion feasibility. These findings robustly support the experimental viability of utilizing a commercial X-ray detector for both anatomical assessment and frame-based source delivery verification.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-07-02] Development of Biological Microenvironment Imaging Technique Using 111 In Cascade Gamma-Ray Correlation (#3120)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Feng (Autores: B. Feng , M. Hamdan , T. Tatsumi , S. Miyao , A. Sugiyama , M. Uenomachi , H. L. Mizuno , Y. Anraku , N. Akimitsu , K. Shimazoe)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The University of Tokyo, Graduate School of Engineering, Tokyo, Japan [2] Fukushima Institute for Research, Education and Innovation (F-REI), Fukushima, Japan [3] The University of Tokyo, Isotope Science Center, Tokyo, Japan [4] Institute of Science Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan [5] Hoshi University, Tokyo, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study explores nuclear medicine imaging toward visualization of both radiotracer distribution and microscopic chemical environment using 111 In cascade gamma-ray correlation. PAC coefficients of 111 In-labeled agents were quantitatively evaluated under different pH conditions to assess local chemical-environment sensitivity. Cell experiments using 111 In-labeled molecular probes were performed to examine applicability to biological samples. In vivo DPECI visualized 111 In-labeled agent biodistribution in mice, showing liver and tumor signals consistent with ex vivo organ biodistribution. These results provide a basis for future multimodal imaging that integrates PAC-derived microscopic chemical information with DPECI-based spatial visualization.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-07-03] SmartBrain-EEG: First-in-Human Wearable PET/EEG Imaging in Epilepsy (#2207)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Liu (Autores: H. Liu , W. Qu , Y. Lin , K. Hu , X. Yu , D. Liang , Y. Lin , X. Zhang , J. Tao , D. Shi , W. Li , H. Zhao , Y. Zhang , Q. Peng)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China [2] Harbin Institute of Technology, College of Artificial Intelligence, harbin, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In presurgical epilepsy evaluation, noninvasive localization remains challenging in patients with negative or suspicious magnetic resonance imaging findings or inconsistent multimodal results. Positron emission tomography provides metabolic information, while electroencephalography records abnormal electrical activity. However, conventional fixed PET systems usually require supine and constrained positioning, limiting simultaneous monitoring during seizure-related states, task conditions, or near-natural behaviors. To address this limitation, we integrated scalp electroencephalography with an ultra-light wearable motion-following brain PET system to evaluate the feasibility of simultaneous metabolic-electrophysiological imaging in epilepsy subjects. Compatibility was first assessed using an electroencephalography-equipped brain phantom. Phantom images acquired with and without electroencephalography electrodes showed comparable structures, and electroencephalography waveforms remained interpretable with and without PET operation. Initial human evaluation was then performed in an epilepsy patient. Wearable brain PET imaging and simultaneous wearable PET/EEG acquisition were successfully completed. During prolonged acquisition, the subject fell asleep, causing detector displacement and motion artifacts in reconstructed PET images. These results demonstrate the technical feasibility of simultaneous wearable metabolic-electrophysiological brain imaging and highlight the need for improved fixation, motion tracking, and motion correction in future natural-state neuroimaging studies.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-07-04] Human Subject and Phantom Imaging Performance of PETcoil Gen II Brain-Dedicated PET System (#2894)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. H.-S. Park (Autores: G. H.-S. Park , M. N. Ullah , G. Chinn , C. S. Levin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Stanford University, Radiology, Stanford, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract PETcoil Gen II is a second-generation RF-penetrable time-of-flight (TOF) positron emission tomography (PET) brain insert designed for simultaneous PET/MRI. We evaluated initial imaging performance using a 3D Hoffman brain phantom and present the first clinical ¹⁸F-FDG brain PET images acquired with the system. Randoms correction was performed using delayed-window (DW) estimates. A computed tomography (CT)-based attenuation (μ) map was generated and extrapolated to 511 keV using piecewise linear interpolation, while scatter fractions were estimated via OpenSSS. In the Hoffman phantom and research subject scan, full corrections improved signal-to-background ratio from 3.48 to 4.50 and from 2.69 to 3.20, respectively, with improved visualization of cortical and subcortical structures. These results indicate that the correction methods are functioning and demonstrate the ability of the PETcoil Gen II to produce high-quality images.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-07-05] Development of SIAT 9.4T MRI compatible animal PET scanner (#1791)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Li (Autores: H. Li , H. Huang , S. Yang , Z. Kuang , N. Ren , Z. Hu , Y. Yang , Z. Liu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Chinese Academy of Sciences,, Paul C. Lauterbur Research Center for Biomedical Imaging, Shenzhen Institute of Advanced Technology, Shenzhen, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study aims to develop a 9.4 T MRI-compatible small-animal PET insert with sub-millimeter spatial resolution and system-level magnetic compatibility. The PET insert consists of 84 dual-ended readout detector arrays arranged in 7 axial rings, with 12 detector modules per ring. Each detector array contains a 28 × 28 LYSO crystal matrix with a crystal size of 0.75 × 0.75 × 20 mm³. Compact front-end amplification electronics, row-column multiplexed readout, non-magnetic mechanical support, and inner/outer carbon-fiber tubes were integrated to meet the spatial and electromagnetic compatibility requirements of a 9.4 T MRI scanner. Point-source imaging was performed to evaluate spatial resolution. A prototype PET insert was developed and integrated. 22 Na point-source images reconstructed using OSEM with 5 iterations demonstrated sub-millimeter spatial resolution, indicating high-resolution imaging capability for 9.4 T small-animal PET/MRI applications.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-23-02] CMOS-Based QUBO Solver ASIC for Charged Particle Tracking (#1611)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Kim (Autores: H. Kim , J. Bae , C. Park , C. Shim , B. Kim , L. Rota , A. Pena-Perez , B. Markovic , L. Fanals-i-Batllori , A. Gupta , H. Hernandez , P.-C. Huang , G. Liu , V. Turbiner , A. G. Schwartzman , R. Bartoldus , R. Herbst , A. Dragone)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, Menlo Park, California, United States of America [2] Kwangwoon University, Seoul, Republic of Korea [3] Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia, United States of America [4] Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [5] University of California - Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, California, United States of America [6] Stanford University, Menlo Park, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present a CMOS-based QUBO solver ASIC architecture and its application to charged particle track reconstruction for high-energy physics. The solver implements a fully parallel spin-update engine operating on the Ising Hamiltonian Y = −(SUMij si Jij sj − Hi si) with 8-bit fixed-point coupling interaction coefficients, which gets mapped to Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization(QUBO) problems via the standard spin-to-binary substitution xi = (si + 1)/2. The QUBO encodes track-finding physics through diagonal terms (geometric edge quality) and off-diagonal terms (triplet collinearity rewards and bifurcation penalties) derived from the Denby-Peterson formulation. The solver is evaluated as a front-end edge discriminator in a two-stage track reconstruction pipeline on TrackML simulated data. Unlike prior quantum annealing-inspired approaches that rely on a Gaussian KDE trained on ground-truth edge features, our method requires no supervised training or labeled-edge fitting - edge quality is determined entirely by the solver's combinatorial optimization over local neighborhoods. The pipeline achieves F1 = 84.1% (precision 89.3%, recall 79.6%), within 4% of the KDE-dependent baseline while exceeding it in precision.
