sub_talks.title: [NSS-23-01] A Timing ASIC for Large-area SiPM Readout with Channel Delay Compensation (#2660)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Fu (Autores: Y. Fu , W. Wu , M. Wang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Institute of Nuclear and Particle Physics, School of Physics and Astronomy, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The detector of TRopIcal DEep-sea Neutrino Telescope (TRIDENT) will use large-area silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) arrays combined with photomultiplier tubes to boost photon detection efficiency and pointing capability. An application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) is being developed to aim at high-resolution time measurement of large-area SiPM arrays. 16 front-end channels are embedded in the ASIC, with output logical-ORed on LVDS output to interface external TDC. Each channel includes a front-end buffer and a discriminator, both in current mode for higher bandwidth while reducing power. To compensate for inconsistency of propagation delay due to detector array layout and process variation, a programmable delay line is introduced for each channel. The delay line consists of coarse and fine delay cells with 165 ps and 33 ps resolution respectively and a dynamic range of 3000 ps. When connected to 16 2s2p SiPM (Hamamatsu S13360-3050PE) arrays with a total area of 5.76 cm², the system achieved a timing jitter of <500 ps FWHM.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-23-03] Scalable FPGA-Based Dual-Threshold Time-Over-Threshold Readout Circuit for Fast-Component Discrimination in BaF₂ (#3182)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M.H. Son (Autores: M.H. Son , J. Jung , J.H. Jung , Y. Choi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Sogang University, Department of Electronic Engineering, Intelligent Signal Processing System (ISPS) Laboratory, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract BaF₂ emits a prompt fast component with a sub-nanosecond decay time (~0.6 ns), ideal for ultrafast timing applications. Previous studies proved discriminated fast-component-dominant events based on pulse amplitude and slew rate characteristics could improve coincidence time resolution (CTR) in BaF₂. In this work, the fast-component discrimination method was implemented using FPGA-based dual-threshold time-over-threshold (DTOT) readout circuit, providing scalable architecture for multi-channel systems. To reproduce the pulse amplitude and slew-rate characteristics used in previous full-waveform analysis using oscilloscope, the proposed DTOT method extracted amplitude-related, slew-rate-related parameters using two voltage thresholds applied to the pulse. Low-threshold TOT width provided amplitude-correlated parameter, while the timing difference between low- and high-threshold crossings provided pulse slew rate. Because fast-component-dominant events exhibited steeper rising edges, these parameters enabled fast-component discrimination without full waveform sampling. The FPGA-based DTOT readout circuit consisted of BaF₂ coupled to VUV-MPPC SiPM, two-stage high frequency amplifier designed to provide sufficient gain with preserving rising-edge profile of fast component, low-latency comparators for accurate slew-rate extraction, and FPGA-based TDC for timestamping threshold crossings. In previous full-waveform analysis, CTR improved from 115 ps to 98 ps (14.8%) using the fast-component-dominant events. With the FPGA-based DTOT readout circuit, CTR improved from 126 ps to 109 ps (13.2%) using the fast-component-dominant events. These results demonstrated that FPGA-based DTOT readout circuit could identify the fast-component events and achieved considerable CTR improvement without full waveform sampling, providing a scalable and practically implementable method for ultrafast timing applications.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-23-04] A Flexible Multi-Mode Digital Readout Architecture for High-Precision Low-Rate Time-of-Flight Detectors (#2425)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Viqueira Rodríguez (Autores: M. Viqueira Rodríguez , J. Mauricio Ferré , A. Espinya Rojas , J.M. Fernández-Tenllado Arribas , M. Ribalda Galvez , R. Manera Escalero , J.J. Silva García , S. Portero Castillo , G. Bergamin , R. Ballabriga Sune , D. Gascón Fora)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CERN, EP-ESE-ME, Meyrin, Genève, Switzerland [2] Universitat de Barcelona, Institut de Ciències del Cosmos de la Universitat de Barcelona (ICCUB), Barcelona, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract As chip design costs and complexity rises, the industry is increasingly shifting toward application versatility. The digital readout of the PoETIC chip, designed for custom Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) detectors within the PetVision project, embodies this philosophy, supporting Positron Emission Tomography (PET), mass spectrometry, and other high- precision low-rate (≤1 MHz) Time-of-Flight (ToF) applications. The architecture has 16 channels, with three thresholds each: (1) ≤1 photon Low Threshold (ThL), (2) a few-photons High Threshold (ThH), and (3) above ten photons Trigger Threshold (ThT). ThL and ThH are connected to dedicated Time-to-Digital Converters (TDCs), while the ThT signals are ORed into two groups of eight channels, connected to a separate TDC channel. Each TDC channel provides a ToF of 24.4ps time-bin and a Time-over-Threshold (ToT) of 390ps. Each channel integrates a track-and-hold circuit connected to an ADC for linear energy measurements. To optimize data transmission across diverse applications, the readout supports multiple operational modes and configurations. In low-bandwidth setups, several PoETIC chips can be daisy-chained to share a single communication link, reducing the required system resources. For data compression, a trigger operation mode reduces the data volume by transmitting a full bit-width reference ToF timestamp grouped with delta- encoded timestamps of other hits. For systems requiring external validation, the TDC digitizes the trigger validation signal generated by an external coincidence system so that only validated trigger events are transmitted. A data-driven operation mode allows the transmission of all hits in independent packets. The chip also offers control over ToF, non-linear energy measurement (ToT), and linear energy measurement data, allowing users to configure which information is sent, bit widths, and filtering to balance precision and bandwidth according to the specific requirements of the target application.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-23-05] Analog Neural Network ASIC for In-Detector Processing: Experimental Validation of an Advanced Prototype (#2723)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Ronchi (Autores: M. Ronchi , M. Amadori , M. Carminati , G. Borghi , C. Fiorini)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Politecnico di Milano, Department of Electronics, Information and Bioengineering (DEIB), Milano, Italy [2] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare (INFN), Sezione Milano, Milano, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Analog neural networks (ANN) are promising solutions for achieving fast and efficient data processing, usually trading-off accuracy for ultra-low power operation. For instance, in scintillator-based PET and SPECT gamma cameras, analog processing embedded in the analog acquisition chain can simplify the system design, reducing throughput, power consumption and scanner cost. After a first proof-of-concept, last year we proposed the design of a more advanced version of an Analog Neural Network ASIC (ANNA). We now present the preliminary experimental results of this ANNAv2 chip, fabricated in 110 nm CMOS technology. It features a fully analog charge-domain processing architecture enabling the implementation of configurable feedforward fully connected ANN. Each neuron consists of an efficient inverter-based charge integrator. Thanks to this programmability, its employment is not limited to emission tomography, but can be tailored to other scenarios in processing signals of "intelligent" detectors. The maximum supported complexity is 70 analog inputs with 5 weighted layers, up to 32 neurons per layer, and 32 analog outputs. Weights are quantized over 63 analog levels, with programmable non-linear activation functions. Preliminary measurements performed on the ASIC validate the correct operation of the proposed architecture and demonstrate the feasibility of fully analog end-to-end inference (with an energy cost of 2nJ/inference) for sensor front-end applications.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-23-06] ASIC Development of Rad-hard Embedded FPGA in 28nm for Machine Learning in Particle Detector (#2082)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Gupta (Autores: A. Gupta , L. Ruckman , Q. Liu , L. Wu , J. Gonski , L. Rota)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] SLAC National Laboratory, Technology Innovation Directorate, Menlo Park, California, United States of America [2] Stanford University, Physics, Palo Alto, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Embedded FPGAs (eFPGAs) combine the performance and efficiency of custom silicon with the flexibility of programmable logic as reconfigurable digital logic can directly be integrated into ASICs. When designed with radiation tolerance techniques such as Triple Modular Redundancy (TMR), eFPGAs can support fault-tolerant and intelligent front-end processing. This enables systems to adapt to evolving data handling needs and environmental conditions, while also supporting local data reduction to lower cabling, power and backend processing demands. Building on previous prototype developments in 130nm and 28nm at SLAC, this paper details the ASIC development of a radiation-hardened eFPGA in 28nm CMOS using radiation-mitigation techniques to realize a reconfigurable logic fabric capable of reliable operation under fault-inducing conditions.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-24-01] GEM detectors for the CMS muon system (#1040)
sub_talks.speaker: C. Aimè
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Pavia, Pavia, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The High-Luminosity upgrade of the Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) will subject the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) experiment to unprecedented particle rates and radiation levels. To maintain high-efficiency muon triggering and reconstruction in this challenging environment, CMS is upgrading its forward muon system, including Gas Electron Multiplier (GEM) technology. This program introduces two key stations: GE1/1 and ME0. The GE1/1 station, composed of triple-GEM detectors, was installed during Long Shutdown 2 to complement the existing Cathode Strip Chamber stations in the 1.6 < |η| < 2.15 region. Operational since the start of Run 3, GE1/1 has significantly enhanced redundancy and Level-1 trigger performance. This presentation reviews the operational experience gained during Run 3, focusing on detector performance, electronics optimizations, and the continuous improvements implemented to ensure seamless system integration. Looking further ahead, the ME0 station is designed for installation during Long Shutdown 3 to extend the muon system's coverage up to |η| = 2.8. To withstand the high-rate environment of the HL-LHC, ME0 incorporates advanced design optimizations and robust background rejection capabilities. We present the current status of the ME0 project, including results from the latest prototype studies, time resolution performance, and the progress of the ongoing mass production. Together, these GEM upgrades are pivotal for extending the physics reach of CMS, ensuring high-quality muon identification and tracking in the most demanding regions of the detector.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-24-02] A new detector technology for the LHCb Muon system in the high luminosity era (#2159)
sub_talks.speaker: F. Debernardis
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] INFN-Bari, Fisica, Bari, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A novel Micro-Pattern Gaseous Detector (MPGD) technology based on μ-RWELL is under development as a potential replacement for the most irradiated regions of the LHCb muon system at CERN, in view of the Upgrade II program. The μ RWELL is a resistive MPGD featuring a compact single-stage amplification structure with typical gains up to 10 4 , making it well suited for operation in harsh radiation environments. An improved detector layout, the G-RWELL, is currently under study. This configuration enhances the standard μ-RWELL design by introducing a single GEM pre-amplification stage, allowing gains up to 10 5 under stable operating conditions. These features make the technology suitable for the extreme rate capability required at the future LHC high-luminosity conditions, where peak luminosity of L = 1.5×10 34 cm −2 sec −1 is planned. The presentation will focus on the ongoing research activities on these detector technologies in the context of the LHCb muon Upgrade II. Particular emphasis will be given to recent testbeam campaigns at the CERN PS beam line, involving the use of the FATIC front-end electronics, currently under development, and a dedicated data analysis framework optimized for this readout.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-24-03] A Straw Tube Chamber Prototype for the Inner Detector of a Future e + e - Collider Experiment (#2774)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Okfen (Autores: O. Kortner , S. Kortner , H. Kroha , N. Meier , J. Okfen , R. Richter , J. Zimmermann)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Max Planck Institute for Physics, ATLAS Research Group, Munich, Bavaria, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Future Circular electron-positron Collider, proposed as future flagship at CERN, offers a unique opportunity for precision measurements of the Higgs boson and electroweak properties. To meet the stringent requirements of a future Inner Tracker in terms of momentum resolution, particle identification, and minimal material budget, a scalable, ultra-light gaseous detector concept based on straw tubes is under development. This contribution presents the design and construction of a 1.5 m-long straw tube chamber prototype. As part of the mechanical feasibility study, the importance of the tube wall pre-tensioning during assembly was identified to prevent a drift radius asymmetry. Via a CERN test beam validation a comprehensive study of the prototype has been performed. The applied grounding scheme was successful, since the noise rates are below 100 Hz. Through a muon detection efficiency of 100% except for a narrow region close to the tube wall and a spatial resolution of 118 μm, the suitability of the straw tube tracker for an inner detector of a future e + e - collider experiment is demonstrated. Combining the test beam data with Garfield++ simulations allows for a prediction of the expected the particle identification capabilities, yielding a π/K separation mostly better than 3σ up to momenta of 10 GeV. Owing to their reduced material budget, straw tubes exhibit a low gamma conversion probability, although the resulting Compton electrons are not stopped within the thin tube wall. Subsequently, crucial input for the optimization of future prototypes is provided, which is directly addressed in the next generation 4 m-long straw tube chamber prototype. This contribution will additionally present the latest performance results from the up-scaled 4m prototype, obtained during the upcoming CERN test beam campaign in July.

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents performance measurements of the first neutron detector module developed for the Cold Neutron Spectrometer (CSPEC) hosted at the European Spallation Source (ESS). Designed and built at the Laue-Langevin Institute (ILL), the detector employs a two-dimensional Multitube architecture to meet the CSPEC requirements in terms of spatial resolution count rate capability and amplification gain stability and uniformity. Experimental tests completed at the CT2 detector test beamline of ILL, confirm compliance to these detection features while validating the production process for the next modules.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-24-05] Characterization of a High-efficiency Multi Element Thick Gas Electron Multiplier Based Neutron Dosemeter (#1312)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Wang (Autores: H. Wang , S.H. Byun)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] McMaster University, Department of Physics and Astronomy, Hamilton, Ontario, Canada [2] McMaster University, Radiation Sciences Graduate Program, Hamilton, Ontario, Canada
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We report characterization of a high-efficiency multi-element neutron dosemeter built by the Thick Gas Electron Multiplier (THGEM) technology. The multi-element configuration is an excellent way to increase neutron detection efficiency and is well suited for the development of tissue-equivalent proportional counters (TEPCs) for microdosimetric measurements in low-intensity neutron fields. Compared to conventional TEPCs, the THGEM-based design eliminates the need for anode wire structures, thereby simplifying fabrication and assembly processes. Moreover, the capability of cascading multiple THGEM layers to achieve higher gain, combined with its low cost, mechanical robustness, and large-area scalability, are advantageous features of the THGEM for building multi-element detectors. Following the successful development of an initial prototype consisting of twenty-one gaseous sensitive volumes, an upgraded detector with ninety-five sensitive volumes has been developed to increase neutron efficiency even higher. Experimental characterization of the new detector is currently underway using 238 PuBe and 7 Li(p,n) neutron sources at the McMaster Accelerator Laboratory. The signal performance and dosimetric response of the detector will be presented and compared with Monte Carlo simulation results.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-24-06] Xe-SF 6 mixtures for negative-ion detectors (#3195)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. P. Marques (Autores: A. P. Marques , J. F. Sousa , A. M.F. Trindade , D. S. Rodrigues , F. I.G.M. Borges , F. P. Santos)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Coimbra, Department of Physics, Coimbra, Portugal [2] Laboratory of Instrumentation and Experimental Particle Physics, Coimbra, Portugal
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Conventional gaseous detectors rely on electron drift, but this transport is intrinsically limited by diffusion, particularly in noble-gas mixtures and over long drift distances. Electronegative additives offer an attractive alternative because they rapidly capture electrons and form negative ions, which drift with much smaller diffusion, enabling improved spatial resolution. In this work, Xe-SF 6 mixtures were investigated using a dedicated experimental setup to study electron attachment, ion mobility, electron detachment, charge multiplication, and electroluminescence. Near-total electron attachment was observed in all cases, confirming the efficient formation of negative ions in Xe-SF 6 mixtures. In the low-field regime, two negative-ion species, SF 6 - and clustered SF 6 - (SF 6 ), were identified, with reduced mobilities remaining independent of the electric field. High electric fields inside GEM holes enabled electron detachment and subsequent amplification, with EL and multiplication thresholds shifting to lower fields and gas gains increasing as the SF 6 concentration decreased. Xenon electroluminescence was also observed in these mixtures, both inside the GEM and after, although strongly quenched by the electronegative additive. The increase in the thresholds for both scintillation and charge multiplication with increasing SF 6 fraction, highlight the central role of the detachment processes in the amplification mechanisms. These results demonstrate that even a very small addition of SF 6 can substantially modify xenon transport properties. However, the usual amplification stages are not immune to these changes.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. L. Hutcheson (Autores: A. L. Hutcheson , B. F. Phlips , W. N. Johnson , M. V. Johnson-Rambert , A. M. Thompson)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] U.S. Naval Research Laboratory, Washington, DC, United States of America [2] Technology Service Corporation, Arlington, Virginia, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The objective of the Neutron Radiation Detection Instrument (NeRDI) series of experiments is to space qualify and characterize the long-term performance of these new detector technologies in on-orbit radiation environments. The second of this series of experiments, NeRDI-1B, launched on 21 April 2025 to the International Space Station as part of the Department of Defense Space Test Program-Houston 10 (STP-H10) mission. The NeRDI-1B instrument comprises two arrays of Domino microstructured semiconductor neutron detectors (MSNDs), a single separate MSND sensor, and an EJ-270 plastic scintillator read out by a custom array of silicon photomultipliers. Here we describe the NeRDI-1B instrument and present an analysis of its first year of on-orbit operations, with particular focus on the characterization of the MSNDs.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-25-02] High-speed single-photoelectron detection for Cherenkov astronomy (#1412)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Giangrande (Autores: L. Giangrande , M. Heller , T. Montaruli)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Geneva, Particle and nuclear physics, Geneva, Genève, Switzerland [2] University of Geneva, Département de physique nucléaire et corpusculaire - DPNC, Geneva, Genève, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Silicon photomultipliers are increasingly replacing photomultiplier tubes in Cherenkov telescope cameras, but achieving single-photoelectron resolution with nanosecond timing in a low-noise, scalable detector system emains challenging. We present a co-designed SiPM sensor and front-end application specific integrated circuit (ASIC) that meets these requirements. The custom hexagonal sensor, developed with Hamamatsu Photonics, incorporates an integrated optical filter and fourfold pixel segmentation. The readout is performed by a second prototype of the FANSIC ASIC, optimized for this application and fabricated in 65 nm standard CMOS technology, provides eight channels with on-chip analog summing of sub-channels on a 3.5×3.5 mm2 die, while consuming only 24 mW per channel. We demonstrate clear single-photoelectron peak separation with a gain of 2.7 × 10−12 V · s , and an impulse response below 4 ns full width at half maximum with a 1.7 ns rise time, preserving the nanosecond-scale structure of Cherenkov pulses. The system esponds linearly from 1 to 130 photoelectrons, and 55 distinct photoelectron peaks are resolved by varying the source intensity.These results demonstrate that the integrated sensorelectronics architecture delivers the speed, resolution, and dynamic range required for imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes, and provides a scalable path toward large-area camera modules.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-25-03] Experimental demonstration of thermal neutron effects and their suppression in a sampling-type veto detector (#1440)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Matsumura (Autores: T. Matsumura , G. Y. Lim , K. Kotera , K. Shiomi , H. Nanjo , H. Watanabe , T. Nomura , M. Ukai , T. O. Yamamoto)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Defense Academy of Japan, Department of Applied Physics, Yokosuka, Japan [2] High Energy Accelerator Research Organization (KEK), Institute of Particle and Nuclear Studies, Tsukuba, Japan [3] Osaka University, Department of Physics, Toyonaka, Japan [4] Japan Atomic Energy Agency, Advanced Science Research Center, Tokai, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This paper reports on the effects of thermal neutrons in a plastic-scintillator-based sampling calorimeter for a rare kaon decay experiment and the results of experimental studies demonstrating their suppression. We prepared a prototype detector consisting of a lead/scintillator sampling calorimeter with a transverse size of 25 × 25 cm² and 25 alternate layers of 1-mm-lead and 5-mm-scintillator. The prototype can accommodate 50 boron carbide sheets (0.1 mm thick), detachably mounted between the lead and scintillator layers to absorb thermal neutrons. We irradiated the prototype detector with a 0.9 GeV/c π - beam at J-PARC and demonstrated the existence of late signals which are thought to be γ-rays from capture of thermal neutrons induced by the interaction of charged pions. Furthermore, we separately confirmed, by utilizing a radioactive neutron source, that the insertion of boron carbide sheets reduces the detection of thermal neutrons. These results demonstrate that boron loading is effective in suppressing accidental signals originating from pion-induced thermal neutrons.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-25-04] A High-Performance Mid-Format SiC based Detection System for Radioactive Ion Beam Tagging and Diagnostics (#2221)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Guazzoni (Autores: L. Acosta , C. Altana , A. Barbon , G. Cardella , A. Castoldi , G. D'Agata , E. De Filippo , S. de Luca , F. De Pretto , E. Geraci , C. Guazzoni , C. Maiolino , A. Mason , E. V. Pagano , S. Pirrone , G. Politi , L. Quattrocchi , M. Pozzi , F. Risitano , F. Rizzo , P. Russotto , M. Trimarchi , S. Tudisco , C. Zagami , R. Zambolo)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CSIC, Madrid, Spain [2] INFN, LNS, Catania, Italy [3] Universita' degli Studi di Catania, Dipartimento di Fisica e Astronomia, Catania, Italy [4] INFN, Sezione di Catania, Catania, Italy [5] Politecnico di Milano and INFN, Dipartimento di Elettronica, Informazione e Bioingegneria, Milano, Italy [6] INFN, Sezione di Milano, Milano, Italy [7] Universita' di Messina, Dip. di Scienze MIFT, Messina, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Radioactive Ion Beams (RIBs) are the frontier in Nuclear Physics, allowing investigations of low cross-section reactions and of nuclei far from the stability valley. Silicon carbide (SiC) material can overperform Silicon as a charged-particle detector, offering nearly zero leakage current and visible-light blindness thanks to the high bandgap. The high displacement energy of SiC is synonymous of radiation hardness and the saturation velocity higher than Si makes SiC an excellent material for fast, high-rate radiation detectors in nuclear and medical physics. In order to provide effectively RIBs tagging, even in the case of high intensity beams, like the ones foreseen at the Laboratori Nazionali del Sud of INFN in Catania (Italy), produced by the novel high intensity Radioactive Ion Beams (RIBs) facility named FRAISE, novel detection systems for the diagnostics and the tagging of RIBs along the transport line and in the measurement chamber are requested. To this aim and for the need of other particle accelerators around the world, we are developing a novel high performance, mid-format detection system, based on an array of Silicon Carbide (SiC) diodes, readout by an optimized fast frontend electronics. This contribution deals with the design, the study and the experimental qualification of the performance of the proposed mid-format detection system with particular care in the characterization of the timing properties and in the analysis of the limiting factors affecting the time resolution. For deposited energies above 2 MeV the time resolution keeps below 100 ps rms at zero added input capacitance. At 22pF added capacitance, the measured time resolution is below 100 ps rms above 5 MeV injected energy.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-25-05] The General Antiparticle Spectrometer (GAPS) Instrument: Design, Performance, and First Antarctic Flight (#2247)
sub_talks.speaker: K. Yee
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The General Antiparticle Spectrometer (GAPS) is an Antarctic balloon experiment designed to search for low-energy cosmic antiparticles as signatures of dark matter. The GAPS instrument flew on an Antarctic long-duration balloon platform for 25 days in the 2025 austral summer, proving several novel technologies for the first time in flight. The detection method employed by GAPS involves a low-energy antiparticle slowing to a stop within the tracker, forming an exotic atom; the subsequent decay releases characteristic X-rays and nuclear annihilation products that are detectable by the instrument. GAPS utilizes a plastic scintillator time-of-flight (TOF) system that measures energy depositions and velocities and provides a system trigger, together with a tracker consisting of over 1000 lithium-drifted silicon (Si(Li)) strip detectors that provides energy and position measurements, as well as X-ray detections. The tracker operating temperature of < -35 o C is achieved with a novel multi-loop capillary heat pipe (MCHP) thermal system that passively transfers heat generated in the tracker to a large-area radiator. This contribution details the instrument design, performance from ground commissioning, and first Antarctic flight of the GAPS instrument.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-25-06] The Future of In-Beam Gamma-ray Spectroscopy at RIBF: CeBr 3 Development for the HYPATIA Array (#2810)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Tetley (Autores: L. Tetley , T. Gao , J. Sharpe , W. Marshall , S. Chen , T. Ayers , J. Flatt , D. Hesp , B. Hide , P. Joshi , M. Labiche , D. O'Donnell , D. Seddon , R. Shearman , F. Thomson , C. Unsworth , P. Doornenbal , S. Paschalis , M. Petri)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of York, School of Physics, Engineering and Technology, York, United Kingdom [2] STFC, Daresbury Laboratory, Warrington, United Kingdom [3] University of the West of Scotland, School of Computing, Engineering & Physical Sciences, Paisley, United Kingdom [4] University of Liverpool, School of Physical Sciences, Liverpool, United Kingdom [5] National Physical Laboratory, Nuclear Metrology Group, Teddington, United Kingdom [6] RIKEN, Radioactive Isotope Physics Group, Wako, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract HYPATIA is a next-generation scintillator detector array under development for in-beam gamma-ray spectroscopy of exotic nuclei at the Rare Isotope Beam Factory (RIBF), at the RIKEN Nishina Center for Accelerator-Based Science. When completed, the array will consist of 1008 advanced scintillator detector crystals (384 HR-GAGG and 624 CeBr 3 ), in a hybrid configuration to deliver improved energy resolution, fast timing, enhanced background suppression and peak-to-total. This work presents the development and characterisation of CeBr 3 detector modules produced at the University of York for integration into the HYPATIA array. Each module consists of four CeBr 3 crystals coupled to silicon photomultiplier arrays within a compact, hermetically sealed housing, designed to ensure the long-term performance stability of the hygroscopic scintillators, whilst optimising the detection efficiency. Experimental characterisation demonstrates an energy resolution of 4.1% - 4.3% at 662 keV and a timing resolution of approximately 0.6 ns (FWHM) for the coincident 60 Co gamma rays. These results validate the module design and confirm its suitability for the high-precision spectroscopic measurements required to explore the limits of nuclear stability.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-10-01] Energy-Resolved Effective Focal-Spot Characterization of a CdTe-Timepix3 Nanofocus XCT System Using Orthogonal Slanted-Edge Measurements (#1354)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. A. Roque (Autores: G. A. Roque , M. K. Schütz , J. S. Useche , S. Procz , M. Fiederle)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Albert-Ludwigs-Universität Freiburg, FMF, Freiburg, Baden-Württemberg, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Spatial resolution in high-magnification X-ray imaging is limited by the detector's pixel aperture and the X-ray source focal spot size. The latter caps the achievable geometric magnification, and depends on photon energy, observation direction, and sample X-ray attenuation. This work presents an energy-resolved characterization of the effective focal spot size of the Freiburg Materials Research Center nanofocus X-ray imaging system, that combines the Hamamatsu L10711-03 Tungsten-anode nanofocus X-ray tube with a 12 × 1 Timepix3 spectroscopic photon-counting detector (PCD) array equipped with 1 mm thick Cadmium Telluride (CdTe) sensors. A single high-absorbing Steel slanted edge is used to implement the double-distance edge-response method, applied in horizontal and vertical orientations to measure the focal spot size in both principal directions. For energy bins from 15 keV to 50 keV, an in-contact edge image captures detector-generated blur, while a magnified edge image embeds both detector blur and source penumbra. After energy calibration, flat-field correction, and event declustering, edge-spread functions are oversampled, differentiated to obtain line-spread functions (LSF), and Fourier-transformed to obtain energy-resolved Optical Transfer Functions, OTF(E). The per-bin ratio of the mixed and contact OTF removes the detector contribution to image blur and yields a source-plane OTF and LSF, from which the effective focal spot size is extracted. Preliminary analysis suggests measurable variation in the recovered source-plane profiles across energy windows and between horizontal and vertical orientations, indicating that the effective focal spot cannot be treated as energy-independent. The study relies on a practical method for source characterization in spectroscopic photon-counting X-ray systems, to achieve a thorough resolution characterization of the nanofocus imaging system.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-10-02] Digital Signal Processing of Large-Volume, Pixelated CsPbBr 3 for Gamma-ray Spectroscopy (#1601)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Streicher (Autores: M. Streicher , M. Petryk , J. Palmer , I. Pandey , S. Abraham , R. Parsons)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] H3D, Inc., Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America [2] Actinia, Inc., Evanston, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Over the course of the past decade, CsPbBr 3 has emerged as perhaps the most promising alterative room temperature semiconductor material for gamma-ray spectroscopy. CsPbBr 3 has been shown to be grown quickly, and relatively inexpensively, while being surprisingly defect tolerant. Fifteen 1-cm-thick CsPbBr 3 samples, attached to printed circuit boards with a low-temperature melting alloy, were evaluated over the course of this project. A custom evaluation system containing COTS preamplifiers and oscilloscopes was used to correct these samples for depth-of-interaction effects. While yields were initially fairly poor, the best sample achieved better than 1.5% FWHM energy resolution at 662 keV for the entire 0.25 cm 3 volume. Eight of the nine pixels in the device achieved energy resolution better and 1.5% FWHM at 662 keV. The device exhibited predicable conditioning effects. The device has been operating for several months, albeit not at continuous bias. The failing samples tended to have attachment issues; either the attachment failed and the CsPbBr 3 disconnected from the carrier board or all pixels exhibited poor performance and instability which could also be due to issues with the device attachment to the substrate. At the time of the conference, the authors expect to have preliminary results of a CsPbBr 3 gamma-ray spectrometer with volume greater than 1 cm 3 read out with pulse-waveform sampling preamplifiers integrated into an Application Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC).

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-10-03] A spectroscopic CdZnTe/CMOS hybrid linear array detection system based on wedge-bondable HDI interposer (#2346)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Mele (Autores: F. Mele , J. Quercia , Y. Zhu , L. Abbene , M. Bettelli , T. Brookes , A. Buttacavoli , N. Ghorbanian , F. Principato , M. C. Veale , A. Zappettini , G. Bertuccio)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Politecnico di Milano, Department of Electronics, Infomration and Bioengineering, Milano, Italy [2] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare (INFN), Sezione di Milano, Milano, Italy [3] University of Palermo, Department of Physics and Chemistry (DiFC), Palermo, Italy [4] Istituto Materiali per l'Elettronica e il Magnetismo (IMEM), Parma, Italy [5] UKRI STFC Rutherford Appleton Laboratory, Didcot, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In this work, we present a CdZnTe/CMOS spectroscopic linear-array detection system enabled by a wedge-bondable High Density Interconnect (HDI) interposer that allows bump-bonding on the detector side and wedge-bonding toward the readout electronics, significantly simplifying the interconnection constraints between the two elements [1],[2],[3]. The interposer layout is optimized to suppress inter-channel parasitics, yielding measured pixel-to-pixel and pixel-to-guard capacitances of 10.2 fF and 25.7 fF, respectively. Two custom 8-pixel CdZnTe detectors (500 μm pitch, 25 μm gap with 1 mm and 2 mm thickness respectively) were integrated with an 8-channel ultra-low-noise SIRIO charge-sensitive amplifier [4],[5] and characterized at room temperature. After integration, spectroscopic characterization was performed with 55Fe, 241Am, and 57Co radioactive calibration sources, demonstrating the capability of the system to cover a wide energy range (5-150 keV). Using a 50 ns peaking time on an external digital pulse processor, an average FWHM of 744 eV (Detector 1) and 850 eV (Detector 2) was measured on the pulser line, recording an optimum energy resolution of 1.4% at 122 keV, and paving the way for additional studies on larger detector arrays in high-flux spectroscopy applications.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-10-04] Stabilizing the Detector Response of CsPbBr 3 Gamma-Ray Detectors (#2010)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Petryk (Autores: M. Petryk , M. Streicher , R. Parsons , S. Abraham , J. Palmer , I. Pandey)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] H3D, Inc., Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America [2] Actinia Detectors, Inc., Evanston, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract With greater photopeak efficiency and lower temperature growth processes, CsPbBr 3 is a promising alternative to CdZnTe (CZT) for room temperature semiconductor-based gamma-ray detectors. H3D, Inc. has characterized the stability of both single-pixel and pixelated 10mm thick CsPbBr 3 gamma-ray detectors. The best pixelated devices show a pattern of conditioning, whereby the device response stabilizes after 60 hours of bias. The best resolution obtained is 1% at 662 keV on a by-pixel basis, and 1.5% overall. The most stable detectors show clear photopeaks from 137 Cs during over 1200 hours of continuous operation. Though the stability is improved by contact engineering, surface polishing, and encapsulation, there is still significant drift in the peak over time. This drift causes the resolution to deteriorate over time and invalidates earlier calibrations. H3D has developed an algorithm to stabilize the response of these CsPbBr 3 detectors further by utilizing the known relationships between photopeaks and escape peaks. The algorithm operates on a per-measurement basis, requiring no knowledge of what isotope is being measured nor the past history of the device. This enables it to be applied in the field to arbitrary measurements, without requiring a convenient check source for pre-measurement calibration. sub_talks.title: [RTSD-10-05] Neutron Irradiation Effects in β-Ga₂O₃ Radiation Detector Materials Investigated by Raman and Positron Annihilation Spectroscopy (#2161)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Noor (Autores: S. Noor , M. Liu , A. Wells , G. Yang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] NCSU, Nuclear Engineering, Raleigh, North Carolina, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Gallium oxide (Ga₂O₃) is an emerging material for next-generation nuclear sensors due to its ultra-wide bandgap, high thermal stability, and large critical breakdown field. However, its radiation tolerance and defect evolution mechanisms in reactor environments remain insufficiently understood, limiting predictive assessment of long-term device reliability and performance. In this work, we systematically investigate the effects of neutron irradiation with simultaneous thermal annealing on β-Ga₂O₃ using positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS), Raman spectroscopy, and polarized optical microscopy to probe irradiation-induced changes across atomic, defect, and microstructural length scales, providing complementary insight into defect formation, evolution, and recovery mechanisms under neutron exposure. Monoclinic β-Ga₂O₃ samples were irradiated in the North Carolina State University PULSTAR reactor at room temperature (RT) and 700 °C. Microstructural characterization and PALS confirmed vacancy-type defects in the RT irradiated samples, while their absence at high temperature suggests thermally activated point defect suppression through increased atomic mobility. Raman spectroscopy revealed irradiation-induced microtilting in both cases, whereas the absence of Raman modes associated with gallium-clusters and oxygen-vacancy indicates overall defect concentrations remained low though detectable by the highly sensitive PALS technique. Together, these results show β-Ga₂O₃ is a promising material for nuclear sensing while unveiling key insights into its behavior under irradiation.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-04-01] Development of a PET/MRI Compatible Fluorescence Microscope for Simultaneous Cell Tracking in a Small Animal PET/MRI Scanner (#2535)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. Renn (Autores: P. Renn , J. Schäfers , N. Jurisa , C. Pilger , T. Huser , K. Schäfers)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Münster, European Institute for Molecular Imaging, 48149, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [2] Bielefeld University, Biomolecular Photonics Research Group, Department of Physics, 33615, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Cell tracking in vivo is a key challenge in translational medicine. Positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offer complementary strengths for this task, yet the validation of tracking algorithms against a reliable ground truth remains unresolved. Fluorescence microscopy can fulfill this role, but its integration into the highly constrained PET/MRI environment poses significant technical challenges. Here, we present a fluorescence microscope (FM) designed for simultaneous operation inside a small-animal PET/MRI scanner, with all custom structural and housing components 3D printed in polylactic acid (PLA). The assembled instrument has a total length of 95 cm and fits within the 35 mm PET insert bore, accommodating sample diameters of up to 21 mm. The imaging probe is rotated via a non-ferromagnetic, friction-driven mechanism, enabling multi-angle acquisition without repositioning the sample, and reliable rotation over the full 360° range was demonstrated under manual control. The system follows an epi-fluorescence configuration with 10× magnification, an excitation wavelength of 488 nm, and a 500 nm longpass filter in the detection path. Characterization with a calibration slide and a Convallaria majalis test specimen yielded a pixel pitch of 0.144 μm/pixel (6.96 pixels/μm), a spatial resolution of 2.32 μm (FWHM), a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 7.21, and a field of view (FoV) of 0.55 × 0.31 mm2 (3816 × 2160 pixels), sufficient to resolve individual cells. These results establish the feasibility of integrating fluorescence microscopy into a PET/MRI scanner and provide the basis for future multimodal cell tracking studies with a reliable optical ground truth.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-04-02] Hybrid PGI-PET Imaging for Ion-Range Monitoring in Hadron Therapy (#2044)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Balibrea Correa (Autores: J. Balibrea Correa , V. Babiano-Suárez , J. Lerendegui-Marco , P. Torres-Sánchez , I. Ladarescu , C. Domingo-Pardo , A. Tarifeño-Saldivia , M. Pallás , B. Brusasco , J. Wulff , C. Baümer , S. Rossomme , A. Warnier)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto de Física Corpuscular (CSIC-University of Valencia), Física Nuclear Experimental, Valencia, Spain [2] Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya, Física Nuclear, Barcelona, Spain [3] West German Proton Therapy Centre, Essen, Germany [4] Ion Beam Applications, Louvain, Belgium
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Hadron therapy is a highly conformal cancer treatment technique that enables superior dose delivery to the tumor while sparing surrounding healthy tissues. However, its full clinical benefit is still limited by uncertainties in proton range within tissue, mainly due to the indirect estimation of ion stopping power from X-ray CT images. These uncertainties lead to safety margins that reduce treatment precision. Real-time, high-accuracy ion-range verification is essential to improve dose delivery and further enhance the therapeutic potential of proton therapy. Among the available approaches, PGI and PET are regarded as the most promising, as they provide complementary information. PGI offers direct correlation with the Bragg peak during irradiation, whereas PET yields high-resolution activity distributions from beta+ emitters produced along the proton path. In this work, we report recent developments and experimental results obtained with a hybrid PGI-PET system for in situ proton range verification. The system is based on four high-efficiency two-plane Compton imagers arranged in a cross configuration, specifically optimized to enhance PGI sensitivity at the expense of a reduced PET field of view. Experimental campaigns were carried out at commercial IBA Proteus Plus and Proteus One proton therapy facilities using 100 and 125 MeV pencil beams delivered at minimum clinical currents. Polyethylene phantoms were irradiated at controlled positions and data were acquired during both in-spill and off-spill periods. The first reconstructed 2D images demonstrate that PGI can directly identify the Bragg peak position through the maximum of the PGI distribution over a broad field of view, while PET provides a narrower and higher-resolution distribution associated with the induced beta+ activity. These results confirm the feasibility and complementarity of the hybrid PGI-PET approach and support its potential for accurate, clinically relevant proton range verification.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-04-03] Intercrystal Compton Scattering Detection in Pixelated LYSO Detectors via Quantum Localization (#2993)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Hashemi (Autores: A. Hashemi , X. Zhang , H. Sabet)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Harvard Medical School/Massachusetts General Hospital, Radiology Department, Boston, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We introduce a novel quantum-inspired method for identifying intercrystal Compton scattering in pixelated scintillation detectors. The approach treats each SiPM readout as a spatial signal and converts it into a discrete eigenfunction representation using a Hamiltonian built from the measured intensity distribution. Event structure is then assessed through quantum localization, quantified by the participation ratio. Single-site events produce highly localized dominant modes, whereas Compton-scattered events produce multiple localized modes associated with distinct interaction sites. A dual criterion based on quantum localization and eigenvalue proximity is used to classify multi-site events without calibration-intensive response modeling or supervised training. The method was evaluated with Geant4 optical photon simulations and measurements from LYSO:Ce detector arrays with thicknesses from 2 to 25 mm. Experimental classification agreed closely with simulation, with differences below 1% for most thicknesses and below 5% in all cases. These results indicate that the proposed representation captures the topology of gamma-ray interactions directly from detector signals.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-04-04] PETRARCA: a Positron Emission Tomography Real-Time Analog Re-Configurable ANN Detector (#2827)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Pandocchi (Autores: M. Pandocchi , M. Amadori , M. Ronchi , G. Borghi , M. Carminati , C. Fiorini)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Politecnico di Milano, Dipartimento di Elettronica Informazione e Bioingegneria, Milano, Italy [2] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Milano, Milano, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positron emission tomography systems are becoming increasingly complex due to the growing number of detector channels and the large amount of data generated, especially in total-body imaging configurations. In this work, we present PETRARCA, a positron emission tomography detector system integrating an analog neural network ASIC (ANNA) for real-time edge computing of gamma-ray interaction coordinates within a monolithic scintillation crystal. The system consists of a 32 mm × 32 mm × 10 mm monolithic LYSO crystal coupled to an 8 × 8 SiPM matrix read out by dedicated front-end electronics. The detector architecture includes both a conventional digital acquisition path and a parallel analog inference path based on the ANNA ASIC, enabling simultaneous acquisition of sensor data and hardware neural-network predictions. A first evaluation of the system has been carried out using simulated data and the real ASIC response to emulate a reduced-scale configuration using a 4 × 4 SiPM array coupled to a 26 mm × 26 mm × 10 mm monolithic crystal. The performances of the ASIC in predicting the interaction coordinates were tested, and proved to have a mean absolute error (MAE) of around 1 mm on both the x and y axes. The preliminary results demonstrate the feasibility of analog neural-network edge computing for spatial localization in PET detectors and support further developments toward fully integrated real-time detector systems.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-04-05] MIMOSA: Medical IMaging MOnte Carlo Simulation Algorithms for fast proton therapy range monitoring (#2751)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. D. Garvey (Autores: D. D. Garvey , G. Llosá , F. Hueso González)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] IFIC, CSIC-UV, Valencia, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Monte Carlo simulations play a vital role in many aspects of proton therapy treatment, including proton depth of penetration monitoring. A key limiting factor of full simulation engines is computation time: simulations can take several days, far longer than the time between treatment fractions. This project aims to develop a Monte Carlo simulation software, MIMOSA, for prompt gamma-ray based proton range verification, that is fast enough to be deployed before the next treatment fraction. Clinically acceptable gamma pass rates above 99% for 2%/2 mm and 97% for 1%/1 mm with respect to TOPAS were achieved on both homogenous and heterogenous phantoms. To benchmark computational speed, state-of-the-art GPU codes MOQUI and FRED were tested on the same computer. Comparatively, MIMOSA achieved a notable speed increase, able to simulate 1e9 primary protons with a 200 MeV energy in approximately 3 minutes. Along with maintaining accuracy and increasing computational speed, the project uses the hardware agnostic SYCL standard, and will be available with an open-source license and extensive documentation. Ongoing work is devoted to simulating realistic radiotherapy treatment plans, and including prompt gamma-ray transport and detector response.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-04-06] Analytical modeling and inclusion of object scatter in non-TOF 3D PET for low-count data (#1275)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Roser (Autores: J. Roser , H. P. Vo , M. Rafecas)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universität zu Lübeck, Institute of Medical Engineering, Lübeck, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Compton scattering in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is commonly seen as an important degrading factor for the image quality. In particular, object scattering is known to reduce image contrast and distort quantification. Conventional scatter correction techniques do not model scatter directly in the system matrix, despite its potential to better handle low-count data scenarios. In this work, we propose an analytical model for single Compton scattering events and subsequently derive expressions of the system matrix and sensitivity. We validate the obtained expressions with Monte Carlo simulations. Ongoing work includes studying the impact of such approach by using low-count simulated data, and a comparison of the proposed method with conventional scatter correction techniques.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-04-08] Validated Optical Simulation for High-Energy Gamma Response in a 3-Layer LYSO DOI Detector (#1668)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Jiang (Autores: S. Jiang , G. Lovatti , F. Evangelista , P. Thirolf , K. Parodi , M. Nitta)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, München, Bavaria, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We have developed a 3-layer staggered LYSO de tector with DOI capability within the project SIRMIO (Small animal proton irradiator for research in molecular image-guided radiation-oncology) for proton range verification via PET imag ing. To evaluate the feasibility of detecting prompt gamma rays for quasi-instantaneous monitoring of proton beams, we propose a workflow that includes the validation of optical simulation settings and the implementation of the saturation effect of the SiPM photonsensor in the Geant4 simulation. Measurement data with 152 Eu, 22 Na and 137 Cs radioactive sources are utilized for modeling the saturation effect of SiPM, and also for validating optical boundary settings in Geant4. The measured spectra of 22 Na and 137 Cs point sources are well reproduced with the proposed simulation workflow. The responses to prompt gamma rays are then simu lated. According to the floodmaps and profiles, LYSO pixel can be identified at 2.2, 4.4 and 6.2 MeV, but the contrast decreases strongly when energy reaches 6.2 MeV. The peak-to-valley ratios drop by up to 53% at 4.4 MeV and 62% at 6.2 MeV (relative to 2.2 MeV), primarily due to the energy deposition occurring more frequently in multiple LYSO pixels. These predictions suggest the detector's potential for detecting prompt gamma rays, while accurately recovering or rejecting inter-crystal scatter events is essential to maintain detector performance at higher gamma energy.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-04-09] Identification of ICS Pixels in a high-resolution 3-Layer DOI-PET Detector Using a CNN (#2619)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Jiang (Autores: S. Jiang , G. Lovatti , F. Evangelist , P. Thirolf , K. Parodi , M. Nitta)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, München, Bavaria, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We have developed a 3-layer staggered LYSO DOI detector for the SIRMIO (Small animal proton irradiator for research in molecular image-guided radiation-oncology) project, with a crystal pitch of 1.0 mm. Due to the small crystal size, inter-crystal scatter (ICS) events degrade spatial resolution, while discarding them causes significant sensitivity loss. In our detector, ICS events account for approximately 50% of all interactions at 511 keV and result in a median lateral positioning error of approximately 2 mm. To solve this problem, we propose a dual-head convolutional neural network (CNN) for separating the 8×8 MPPC total response of two-pixel ICS events into two individual response matrices, from which the pixel positions and energy fractions can be obtained-a precondition for recovering the ICS events. The CNN correctly identifies both scattering pixels in 69.3% of test events, and in 26.4% of cases one pixel is correctly identified. Among the events with one pixel mismatched, the lateral error of the misidentified pixel falls within 1.0 mm in 91.0% of cases. Meanwhile, the median energy fractions prediction error is 0.016 per pixel. The results demonstrate that CNN-based MPPC response decomposition can serve as the enabling foundation for complete ICS recovery in 3-layer staggered DOI detectors, addressing a limitation explicitly acknowledged in recent physics-based ICS studies.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-04-10] Study on the axial extension of the small-fish PET scanner MERMAID (#2065)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Kolodziej (Autores: M. Kolodziej , J. Roser , S. Seeger , H. P. Vo , R. Kantorek , M. Rafecas)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Luebeck, Institute of Medical Engineering, Luebeck, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany [2] University of Luebeck, Isotope Laboratory of the Natural Science Section, Luebeck, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract MERMAID is the first PET scanner prototype dedicated to study small aquatic animals. Particularly, it aims to support the use of adult zebrafish as a model of human diseases. The current prototype, which consists of four detection modules composed of LYSO:Ce crystals, has demonstrated the capability of providing images with submillimeter resolution. An extension of MERMAID by another four modules is planned, aimed to increase the system sensitivity and allow for shorter scan times, making it more suitable for in-vivo imaging. In the presented work, various configurations for the extended MERMAID system are characterized by means of simulations and tailored reconstruction framework; modifications of imaging protocol for the system are investigated.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-03-01] MRI-Informed SPECT-only Spatial Normalization for Reliable Brain Perfusion Quantification (#1410)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. You (Autores: E. You , Y.J. Seol , H.G. Ryoo , S.K. Kang , J.S. Lee)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Seoul National University, Interdisciplinary Program in Bioengineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] Seoul National University, Integrated Major in Innovative Medical Science, Seoul, Republic of Korea [3] Seoul National University, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea [4] Samsung Ventures, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Spatial normalization enables standardized volume-of-interest quantification in brain perfusion single-photon emission computed tomography, but accurate alignment is difficult because of low resolution, noise, partial volume effects, and uptake-dependent variation. We propose a MRI-informed, SPECT-only framework that distills anatomical deformation fields and feature guidance from a magnetic resonance imaging registration teacher. The student disentangles anatomical and uptake-related representations to suppress functional-uptake interference while requiring only single-photon emission computed tomography at inference. In 173 paired imaging datasets, the method improved standardized uptake value ratio consistency between subject and template spaces, especially for fine-grained volumes of interest, supporting MRI-free, single-pass template-based quantification.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-03-02] Developments in fabrication and design flexibility of amorphous silicon microchannel plates (#2584)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Konstantinou (Autores: G. Konstantinou , L. Barraud , C. Baillif , N. Wyrsch)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] EPFL, Neuchatel, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The technology of amorphous silicon-based micro-channel plates (AMCPs) uses a versatile approach to stack hydrogenated amorphous silicon in thicknesses up to 100 μm, using plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) and etch microchannels of diameter below 2 μm every 5 μm, on a hexagonal pattern, by deep reactive ion etching. With gains up to 1000 for reverse bias less than 300 V, the design is possible to build on arrays of sensitive transimpedance amplifiers, integrated in read-out circuits with high channel density, such as for instance 15 by 15 μm. This ensures single photon detection with quantum efficiency up to 30% and noise rates below 50 Hz/cm², if combined with state of the art photocathodes such as the hi-QE from Photonis. Current fabrication runs focus on direct integration of the stack on ASICs, to be integrated with the photocathode over the next months. Measurements show timing response with jitter below 10 ps, making this high-precision photodetector ideal for radiation detectors combining ultra-fast photon emission and low light yield, such as Cherenkov.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-03-03] Fabrication of diamond detectors with graphitic contacts for tissue equivalent dosimetry (#2040)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 I. Lopez Paz (Autores: I. Lopez Paz , C. Guardiola , G. Rius)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institut de Microelectronica de Barcelona (IMB-CNM, CSIC), Bellaterra, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Diamond-based dosimeters are popular for medical dosimetry in view of their fast response, radiation hardness and tissue equivalence. However, some design improvements to achieve better accuracy in signal readout and approach tissue equivalence are possible by the removal of the metallic contacts, sometimes covering the active area of said devices. In this contribution, we explore the use of a simple processing and scalable solution to obtain non-metal, low Z electrical contact. Thus, the fabrication of diamond detectors with graphitic contacts at the Microelectronics Institute of Barcelona are shown. Several approaches are explored, some of which never utilised before for radiation detector fabrication, namely pyrolytic photoresist film, nickel catalysis and ion surface graphitisation. A prototype of such device using the pyrolytic photoresist film process for the first time has been produced and was tested under a 60 kV X-ray tube. We report the fabrication and preliminary performance results of such device. Although the substrate material quality is not ideal for radiation detection, it was possible to observe radiation response using the PPF as an interface material. The prototype features a linearity better than 3% as tested in a laboratory X-ray chamber, proving it a promising technology for detector operation. Finally, the technology challenges are finally discussed to assess the feasibility of PPF-diamond technology for dosimeter batch production.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-03-04] Scintillation Properties of (Lu,Y)₂O₃:La Ceramic Pixels for PET (#2881)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Glodo (Autores: J. Glodo , S. Kim , A. Kim , M. Muller , C. Sosa , J. Xie , S. R. Cherry , J. Du)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Radiation Monitoring Devices, Inc., Watertown, Massachusetts, United States of America [2] University of California, Davis, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Lutetium oxide-based scintillators are of growing interest for positron emission tomography (PET) because of their high density and high effective atomic number, which provide efficient stopping of 511 keV annihilation photons. Lanthanum-doped (Lu,Y) 2 O 3 (LYO:La) is a transparent ceramic variant that retains the favorable stopping power of Lu 2 O 3 while being easier to fabricate, making it an attractive candidate for next-generation PET detector arrays. In this work we report a scintillation characterization of LYO:La pixels in two geometries relevant to PET, 1×1×10 mm 3 for high-resolution preclinical and dedicated-organ imaging, and 3×3×10 mm 3 for whole-body clinical systems. Pixels were cut from LYO:La ceramic disks, polished on all faces, and evaluated with a range of side reflectors (Teflon, Tyvek, ESR film, and Spectralon) in both flat and upright coupling orientations. We measured X-ray-excited radioluminescence emission spectra, 22 Na (511 keV) pulse height spectra, relative light yield, energy resolution, scintillation decay time profiles, and timing resolution. The results illustrate the influence of pixel geometry, coupling face, and reflector choice on light collection and energy resolution, and show that LYO:La pixels offer a promising combination of stopping power, light yield, and timing performance for PET detector modules.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-03-05] Ultrahigh Spatial Resolution Perovskite-based Direct X-ray Imagers for Low-lag Medical Applications (#3045)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Datta (Autores: B. Dunham , S. Motakef , A. Datta)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CapeSym, Inc., Research and Developement, Natick, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dynamic medical X-ray imaging requires detectors that combine high quantum efficiency, low residual lag, and high spatial resolution without the optical spread and afterglow of scintillator-based flat panels. We report a fully inorganic perovskite-based direct-conversion perovskite X-ray imager fabricated from phase-pure orthorhombic Cesium Lead Bromide (CPB) sensor material and integrated with active-pixel readout arrays. Phase-pure CPB was obtained by controlled crystal growth and converted into dense blade-coated films; non-phase-pure starting materials containing secondary phases produced nonuniform films and degraded images, confirming the importance of phase control for reproducible detector performance. The optimized CPB detector demonstrated high linear X-ray response, sensitivity of 55,400 μC Gyair⁻¹ cm⁻² at 30 keV and 0.5 V/μm, a limit of detection of 417 pGyair s⁻¹, a mobility-lifetime product of 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ cm² V⁻¹, and a calculated detective quantum efficiency near 85% at practical dose levels. In flat-panel imaging, CPB imagers reached 6.9 lp/mm at 20% modulation transfer function on a 100 μm-pitch amorphous-silicon array and resolved 20 lp/mm after integration with a CMOS readout. Most importantly for low-lag medical applications, improvements in phase purity and charge-transport stability reduced residual detector lag from 8.9% to 1.1%. These results show that all-inorganic perovskite direct conversion can provide a path to low-dose, low-lag, high-resolution imaging for fluoroscopy, tomosynthesis, dental cone-beam computed tomography, and other image-guided procedures.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-03-06] PhysiCal-PET: Physics-based neural networks for the rapid position Calibration of PET Scanners (#2036)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Abushawish (Autores: M. Abushawish , P. Galve , I. Colmenarejo Allavena , S. Gaitan Dominguez , C. Galindo Morata , V. M. Nouvilas , J.M. Udias)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Grupo de Física Nuclear, EMFTEL & IPARCOS, Madrid, Spain [2] Health Research Institute of the Hospital Cínico San Carlos (IdISSC), Madrid, Spain [3] Spanish National Research Council (CSIC), Institute for Physical and Information Technologies "Leonardo Torres Quevedo", ITEFI, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Total-body positron emission tomography (PET) increases system sensitivity and enables whole-body dynamic imaging, but its extended axial field of view makes accurate depth-of-interaction (DOI) calibration essential for maintaining uniform spatial resolution and reducing parallax error. Conventional DOI calibration requires mechanically scanned collimated sources or detector-specific reference measurements, which become impractical as the number of detector modules increases. PhysiCal-PET introduces a physics-based neural-network framework for autonomous in-system DOI calibration of PET scanners. The method trains a network to map raw detector signals to DOI using coincidence data acquired with an uncollimated positron source at known positions. For each event, the loss function enforces annihilation geometry by requiring the predicted line of response to be consistent with the source position, thereby providing supervision without measured DOI labels. The framework was tested on realistic PET simulations and applied to data from a real preclinical PET scanner. Using this procedure, the DOI response of all 144 detector modules was calibrated in less than 2 hours of point-source measurement time. These results demonstrate that the annihilation physics can replace labor-intensive DOI calibration hardware and enable rapid, routine calibration of high-resolution PET systems. PhysiCal-PET therefore provides a scalable path toward autonomous calibration for total-body PET and other systems that rely on accurate DOI positioning.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-03-07] Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Denoising for Low-Dose Fluoroscopy via Motion-Gradient Weighting (#2582)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. León (Autores: N. León , X. Ye , J. L. Longas , J.M. Arco , J.M. Ortega , M. Pérez-Liva , J. L. Herraiz , A. Sisniega)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Sedecal Molecular Imaging, Madrid, Spain [2] Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Nuclear Physics Group and IPARCOS, Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A spatio-temporal denoising training strategy for low-dose fluoroscopy is proposed, based on a spatially-adaptive temporal consistency metric. This approach acts on a small set of consecutive frames coupling a conventional denoising operator with an adaptive motion-gradient attention gate to selectively modulate the temporal consistency terms within the loss function, ensuring effective noise suppression and flickering reduction while maintaining high anatomical fidelity in dynamic regions. The proposed method was used to train a denoising operator in which a three-frame temporal window is used as input. The model was trained across multiple dose reduction factors (qF), and demonstrated superior structural recovery and enhanced temporal stability in the processed image sequences, compared to single-frame models. Quantitative and qualitative evaluation of image quality, along with stability maps-defined as the Normalized Cross-Correlation (NCC) of temporal Coefficient of Variation (CV) maps-confirms high fidelity relative to high-dose reference acquisitions, effectively mitigating stochastic fluctuations without introducing motion artifacts.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-03-08] An Ensemble of Deep-Learning Classifiers for 3D Anatomical Change Reconstruction in Carbon-Ion Radiotherapy (CIRT) (#2644)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Martisikova (Autores: P. Schlegel , R. Kirchgässner , P. Ochoa-Parra , E. Bartelme , R. Mikut , O. Jäkel , M. Martisikova)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] DKFZ, Division of Medical Physics in Radiation Oncology, E040, Heidelberg, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [2] Heidelberg Institute for Radiation Oncology (HIRO), National Center for Research in Radiation Oncology (NCRO), Heidelberg, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [3] University, Heidelberg, Medical Faculty, Heidelberg, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [4] Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT), Institute for Automation and Applied Informatics (IAI), Karlsruhe, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Carbon-ion radiotherapy (CIRT) combines high biological effectiveness with outstanding treatment precision. Since treatment plans are based on the most recent Computed Tomography (CT), anatomical changes during multi-week treatments may compromise dose delivery accuracy. To address the increasing uncertainty about the patient's anatomical state with time elapsed since the planning CT, our group developed an in vivo monitoring method using secondary charged particles emitted during therapy. This non-invasive approach requires no additional dose and reduces uncertainty about patient anatomy and thus, loss of treatment accuracy. It uses a custom detection system to detect nuclear fragments emmited from the patient and allows approximating their origin. To reconstruct these changes in 3D, we utilize our recently published method for detecting the depth (z) of changes along the beam axis and apply it to a sliding window (x,y) along the transverse plane. However, splitting reconstructed nuclear fragment origins into smaller subsets reduces the statistical stability of each subset distribution. In this study, we present an approach to robustly distinguish whether a windowed subset belongs to a region with or without an anatomical change based on correlation matrices generated by our depth detection method. These images contain location-wise correlations of joined frequency band variations between projections of nuclear fragment measurements from different treatment days. To classify regions of change and approximate change depth, we train an ensemble of deep learning-based image classifiers with different architectures (i.e. ResNet, RegNet and ConvNeXt) and combine their outputs into an ensemble decision. The approach was validated using dedicated irradiation measurements with coin-sized cavities inserted into PMMA head phantoms. Despite limited training data, we achieved robust improvements in change localization using an ensemble of different deep learning architectures.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-03-09] Zero-Shot PET Image Super-Resolution via Cross-Modal Mutual Information Guidance (#2526)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. He (Autores: Y. He , Y. Lv)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shanghai United Imaging Medical Technology Co., Ltd, Molecular Imaging Business Unit, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Diffusion models have shown strong potential for improving PET image quality. However, existing methods based on unconditional pretrained diffusion priors often struggle to balance realism and fidelity, particularly in preserving high-resolution details. To address this issue, we propose MI-ResShift, a zero-shot mutual information-guided diffusion model with residual shifting for PET image super-resolution. MI-ResShift introduces a differentiable local-wise mutual information layer to guide the denoising process using structural information from CT or MRI, enabling robust cross-modal feature alignment in the statistical domain. By combining mutual information guidance with residual shifting, the proposed method enhances PET detail fidelity and robustness while reducing diffusion-based inference to only four steps. Experiments on PET/MR brain datasets demonstrate that MI-ResShift improves image quality over classical interpolation methods and provides an efficient solution for cross-modal PET super-resolution.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-03-10] 3D Photon Position Estimation Using Neural Networks in Monolithic-Based PET Systems (#2663)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Freire (Autores: P. Piera-Sapiña , M. Freire , F. Lopez-Berenguer , A. Gonzalez-Montoro , A. J. Gonzalez)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto de Instrumentación para Imagen Molecular (I3M), Centro Mixto CSIC-Universitat Politècnica de València,, Valencia, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Neural Network (NN) models have emerged as a promising tool for determining 3D photon impact positions in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) detectors based on monolithic scintillators. Nevertheless, NNs typically require long acquisitions of reference data training, becoming a time-consuming process that requires extensive experimental data for each individual detector module. To reduce calibration time, we propose a new methodology based on NNs trained entirely using simulated data to predict the 3D impact position of gamma rays. The feasibility of the proposed approach was verified using a real preclinical PET system composed of two rings of 8 LYSO:Ce monolithic scintillators each. The simulation of a single detector was implemented in GATE and reference data moving a pencil beam in 1 mm steps was simulated to train two Multilayer Perceptrons (MLPs), MLP X and MLP Y , to predict the x - and y - impact positions, respectively. To validate the introduced methodology at reconstructed image level, experimental data was acquired using a 22 Na point source at the center of the preclinical system and processed using both the presented framework and the system's standard calibration methodology. Results have demonstrated that similar spatial resolution was obtained with both approaches, thus demonstrating that NNs trained exclusively with Monte Carlo simulations can generate coherent reconstructed images and thus eliminate the need for calibration measurements for each individual detector module.

sub_talks.abstract: For more than 20 years, the GATE toolkit has been a reference open-source platform for Monte Carlo simulations in medical physics, supporting applications in PET, SPECT, CT, radiation therapy, and dosimetry. The recent release of GATE 10 marks a major step forward for the platform. This new generation of GATE, featuring a Python-based user interface, enables the design, execution, and analysis of complex simulations within a modern scientific computing environment. By bridging Monte Carlo simulations with data analysis, image processing, artificial intelligence, and high-performance computing tools, GATE 10 empowers the development of current and next-generation methodologies for medical imaging and therapy. Continuing a long-standing tradition of bringing together the GATE community at this conference, we invite users and developers to join the GATE Users Workshop to discover the latest developments and contribute to the program by sharing their scientific projects. Whether you are an experienced user or new to GATE 10, this meeting is an opportunity to connect with the community and explore GATE potential for your research. Registration for the GATE User Meeting is now full, but you are still very welcome to attend the meeting and join the discussions. Please note, however, that lunch boxes can only be provided to registered participants, as they had to be ordered in advance.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-08-01] Sensitivity-Informed Network for Image Restoration in Sparse-Detector PET (#1881)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Hou (Autores: Y. Hou , Y. Chen , F. Zhan , J. Jiang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Normal University, School of Physics and Astronomy, beijing, China [2] The First Affiliated Hospital of USTC, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Hefei, China [3] Jiangnan University, Wuxi School of Medicine, Wuxi, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positron emission tomography (PET) requires dense detector crystals and associated electronics, resulting in high manufacturing costs. Sparse detector configurations can reduce hardware complexity but may degrade image quality due to reduced coincidence events, incomplete line-of-response coverage, and geometry-dependent artifacts. In this study, different sparse detector configurations were investigated for clinical PET imaging, and a sensitivity-informed network, termed SIU-Net, was proposed to recover image quality from sparse ring reconstructions. The residual sensitivity image was used as structural guidance to improve the restoration of degradation caused by detector sparsity. Experiments on 303 clinical brain datasets showed that the 1/2-TS-AR configuration achieved the best image quality among the evaluated sparse designs. SIU-Net consistently outperformed the baseline models across seven degraded image settings. These results demonstrate the potential of combining optimized sparse detector geometry with sensitivity-guided deep learning restoration for cost-effective PET imaging.
