sub_talks.title: [MIC-08-02] Anatomy-Guided Null-Space Learning for Self-Supervised Blind PET Deblurring (#2189)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Zhou (Autores: Z. Zhou , Z. Liu , T.-A. Song , F. Yang , J. Dutta)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Massachusetts Amherst, Biomedical Engineering, Amherst, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The intrinsically limited spatial resolution of positron emission tomography (PET) confounds image quantitation. Post-reconstruction deblurring is an ill-posed inverse problem in which the blur kernel is often unknown, and noise renders direct inversion infeasible. We present a principled framework for self-supervised blind PET image deblurring that incorporates high-resolution MRI anatomical guidance in a data-consistent way. The central contribution is an observation-dependent spectral decomposition of the PET image into a practical range space, i.e., the set of spatial frequencies recoverable from the blurry PET observation at a specified signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) threshold, and a complementary practical null space whose content cannot be estimated from the PET data alone, regardless of the estimator. A self-supervised deep learning framework, Anatomy-Guided Null-Space Learning (AGNS), instantiates this decomposition with three jointly optimized components: a blind 3D kernel estimation network, a range-space Wiener deconvolution, and an MRI-guided null-space imputation network. Joint optimization proceeds via the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). Methodological evaluation is performed through clinical paired-resolution validation using images from the HRRT and NeuroEXPLORER (NX) scanners, where the NX images are only used as the validation ground-truth. AGNS produces strong qualitative and quantitative benchmarks relative to competing unsupervised and non-AI approaches.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-08-03] Brownian Bridge Diffusion Model for Ultra-Low-Dose Total-Body PET Denoising (#1889)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Aghakhanolia (Autores: N. Aghakhanolia , A. Rafiei Sardouei , J. Fowler , A. L´opez Montes , K. Shi , P. L. Esquinas , A. Rahmim)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of British Columbia, School of Biomedical Engineering, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada [2] University of British Columbia, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada [3] University of British Columbia, Department of Physics & Astronomy, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada [4] Bern University Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Bern, Bern, Switzerland [5] University of British Columbia, Department of Radiology, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada [6] BC Cancer Research Institute, Department of Basic and Translational Research, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract PET imaging enables quantitative assessment of disease burden and treatment response, but performance is constrained by a trade-off between radiation dose and image quality. Reducing injected adiotracer activity decreases patient exposure, yet increases image noise, degrading lesion detectability and quantitative accuracy. Total-body PET systems, with substantially increased sensitivity, enable significant dose reduction. However, ultra-low-dose acquisitions remain highly noisy, limiting their clinical utility. In this work, we investigate Brownian Bridge Diffusion Models (BBDM) as a novel framework for ultra-low-dose PET denoising. BBDM formulates dose-level image translation as a stochastic bridge between paired standard- and low-dose PET images, with the diffusion process constrained at both endpoints. This formulation is well-suited for dose translation. The proposed method was evaluated on a multi-center, multi-scanner total-body 18F-FDG PET/CT dataset of 80 patients. Paired full-dose and simulated 1/10-dose datasets were generated through statistical count reduction in the list-mode data. The model was trained with T = 1000 diffusion steps, and inference was accelerated using S = 200 sampling steps. On the held-out test cohort, BBDM achieved substantial gains across both global image-quality and lesion-level quantitative metrics. Compared with low-dose inputs, BBDM increased PSNR by approximately 26.6% and SSIM by 8.9%, while reducing RMSE by 60.0%. Across evaluated lesions, SUVmean and SUVmax biases decreased by 54.5% and 70.9%, respectively. Lesion noise was also reduced by 45.8%. The approach effectively preserves both image quality and lesion quantification at substantially reduced dose levels, highlighting its potential for ultra-low-dose total-body PET imaging.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-08-04] Self-Supervised Low-Dose SPECT Denoising from a Single Standard-Dose Scan via Poisson Thinning (#2519)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Zheng (Autores: H. Zheng , L. Cheng , L. Gao , S. Wang , Z. Wu , H. Liu , Y. Liu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Beijing, China [2] Chengdu NOVEL MEDICAL Equipment Co., Ltd., Chengdu, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Low-dose or fast-scan single-photon emission computed tomography/computed tomography (SPECT/CT) suffers from Poisson noise, but clinical archives usually provide only one noisy standard-dose projection per patient and no noise-free target. A common single-scan workaround synthesizes a low-dose input from the standard-dose scan and uses the original projection as the supervised target. This creates a nested pair because the target contains the input photons, so the objective can learn a noisy full-dose image with input-noise leakage. We propose a self-supervised projection-domain framework based on mutually exclusive Poisson thinning. Each standard-dose projection is partitioned online into K∈{2,3,4,5} disjoint equal-dose subsets by multinomial assignment, and two subsets are randomly paired for Noise2Noise training. These paired subsets contain disjoint photons and are conditionally independent given the underlying count rate while preserving the same dose; mean-square or Poisson-likelihood training therefore targets the clean same-dose conditional mean rather than a noisy full-dose target. A three-dimensional residual U-Net is trained only from thinned noisy pairs and applied before OSEM reconstruction. Training used 225 clinical bone SPECT/CT cases. On 31 held-out cases evaluated by patient-specific controlled Poisson resampling over 1×--5× fast-scan factors, the method achieved 45.72 dB PSNR and 0.9862 SSIM in the projection domain, outperforming an architecture-matched low-to-standard-dose supervised baseline by 2.68 dB; the paired gain increased from 1.82 dB at 1× to 3.34 dB at 5×. The framework enables low-dose bone SPECT/CT denoising from routinely stored projections without clean ground truth or repeated acquisitions.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-08-05] VLM-Guided Conditional Flow Matching for CT-Free total-body PET Correction (#2298)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Rong (Autores: J. Rong , S. Li , C. Yang , L. Li , J. Liu , R. Chen , Z. Huang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Research Center for Medical AI, Shenzhen, China [2] Ren Ji Hospital, School of Medicine, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate attenuation and scatter correction is important for positron emission tomography (PET) to improve diagnosis. Conventional PET correction pipelines rely heavily on CT-derived attenuation information, which inevitably increases radiation exposure during clinical examinations, especially in total-body PET/CT imaging. In this study, we introduce a vision-language-model-guided conditional flow framework for CT-free PET attenuation and scatter correction. Specifically, non-corrected PET slices are analyzed to generate organ-aware textual prompts, which are subsequently encoded as semantic representations and integrated into a latent-space flow generation process. Then, a cross-modal attention mechanism is further designed to establish interactions between semantic prompts and PET image features under multiple scales during conditional flow matching. Experiments were performed on 264 clinical subjects under total-body PET/CT scans. Comparison methods consist of several representative deep learning approaches, including UNet, Uformer, CycleGAN, latent diffusion models, and VM-UNet. Quantitative evaluation demonstrated that the proposed framework achieved the highest metric index, reaching 38.66 dB PSNR and 0.9754 SSIM on the testing dataset. Visual assessment and Correlation Analysis additionally confirmed improved anatomical continuity and more accurate tracer uptake recovery. The study suggests that semantic-aware flow modeling offers an effective strategy for CT-free PET correction.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-08-06] Implicit Neural Representations for Joint Motion-Resolved PET Reconstruction and Respiratory Gating (#3089)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. De Bie (Autores: N. De Bie , M. Colarieti Tosti)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Department of Biomedical Engineering and Health Systems, Stockholm, Sweden
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Respiratory motion during acquisition degrades image quality in positron emission tomography (PET). Data-driven gating (DDG) extracts a respiratory signal directly from the measurement data, but classical methods such as axial center-of-mass and principal component analysis (PCA) degrade under irregular breathing and at low count rates. We propose a self-supervised framework based on implicit neural representations (INRs) that jointly estimates a respiratory gating signal and a motion-corrected reconstruction. Two coordinate-based networks parametrize a motion-free canonical activity image and a deformation field conditioned on learnable per-frame latent codes that encode the respiratory state. We evaluate the framework on XCAT thoracic phantom simulations of an 18F-FDG acquisition at clinically realistic count levels under regular and irregular breathing. The recovered gating signal achieves Spearman correlations of 0.87 (regular) and 0.85 (irregular) with the ground-truth respiratory signal, exceeding center-of-mass (0.62; 0.30) and PCA-based (0.74; 0.34) DDG baselines, and the framework simultaneously produces a motion-resolved reconstruction with PSNR comparable to maximum likelihood expectation maximization (MLEM) reconstruction.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-08-07] Towards CT-Free Multi-Time-Point [ 18 F]PSMA-1007 LAFOV PET Protocols: Evaluation of Synthetic Attenuation Maps Versus Elastic Co-Registration for Longitudinal Imaging (#1865)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. Olyaei (Autores: E. Olyaei , J. Schaefferkoetter , E. Calderón Ochoa , C. P. Reinert , L. S. Kiefer , C. la Fougère , F. P. Schmidt)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University Hospital Tuebingen, Department of Nuclear Medicine and Clinical Molecular Imaging, Tuebingen, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [2] Eberhard-Karls University Tuebingen, Werner Siemens Imaging Center, Department of Preclinical Imaging and Radiopharmacy, Tuebingen, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [3] Siemens Medical Solutions USA, Inc, Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America [4] University Hospital Tuebingen, Cluster of Excellence iFIT (EXC 2180) "Image Guided and Functionally Instructed Tumor Therapies",, Tuebingen, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [5] University Hospital Tuebingen, Diagnostic and Interventional Radiology, Tuebingen, Baden-Württemberg, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Long axial field-of-view (LAFOV) PET enables imaging at very late timepoints but requires repeated CT acquisitions for attenuation correction (AC) in multi-time-point protocols, increasing radiation exposure. This study evaluates two CT-free AC strategies for [¹⁸F]PSMA-1007 LAFOV PET at delayed imaging timepoints: synthetic μ-maps derived from non-attenuation-corrected PET imaging using a ResNet-based model (Synth-AC) and elastic co-registration of CT-based μ-maps from the initial scan (CoReg-AC). Ten patients were scanned on a Siemens Biograph Vision Quadra LAFOV system at 90 min, 3 h, and 5 h p.i. Quantitative evaluation was performed based on relative differences in SUV mean across seven major organs. Lesion quantification was assessed for SUV mean (28 lesions at 3 h p.i., 20 lesions at 5 h p.i.) using Bland-Altman analysis and linear regression. Visually, synthetic μ-maps appeared smoother, while co-registration preserved more anatomical detail but showed localized inconsistencies. In PET images, Synth-AC exhibited smaller and more homogeneous deviations (±5%), whereas CoReg-AC showed more pronounced peripheral differences. At organ level, reduced variability was observed at 5 h for both methods. CoReg-AC showed a positive bias in high-uptake organs (liver +1.7% to +4.3%, spleen +2.7% to +4.3%), while Synth-AC shifted from near agreement at 3 h to moderate negative bias at 5 h (liver −2.1%, heart −13.5%). Both methods demonstrated a pronounced positive bias in lung regions. Linear regression demonstrated strong agreement with CT-based AC (R² = 0.993-0.998), and Bland-Altman analysis at 3 h p.i. showed a mean bias of −0.97% with limits of agreement [−12.11%; +10.17%] for Synth-AC and +1.40% [−8.71%; +11.52%] for CoReg-AC. Both CT-free approaches enable robust quantitative imaging in delayed LAFOV PET. Observed differences are primarily driven by organ-level bias patterns, while lesion quantification remains stable.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-08-08] 3D Latent Implicit Diffusion for Scalable Volume Generation (#2875)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. De Paepe (Autores: Y. Mellak , A. Bousse , A. De Paepe , D. Visvikis)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Université de Bretagne Occidentale, LaTIM, INSERM, UMR 1101, Brest, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Full-volume 3-D medical image generation at clinical resolutions remains a significant challenge due to GPU memory constraints. Direct voxel-space generative modeling becomes increasingly difficult once spatial resolution exceeds 256³, especially on single-GPU hardware. Latent diffusion approaches reduce this burden by performing generation in a compact representation [1], but decoding onto a dense fixed grid remains costly at high resolution. Implicit neural representations offer an attractive alternative, as they reconstruct images by querying continuous spatial coordinates rather than materializing a full voxel grid [2], making them naturally suited to memory-efficient volumetric generation. We propose a memory-efficient 3-D latent implicit diffusion framework that combines a lightweight 3-D encoder with a coordinate-conditioned local implicit decoder, inspired by [3]. The encoder compresses the input volume into a compact latent grid, while the implicit decoder reconstructs the volume by querying continuous spatial coordinates from learned latent features, avoiding the need to materialize the full voxel grid during training. A full-volume 3-D diffusion model is then trained directly in this compact latent space. At inference, new volumes are generated by sampling from the diffusion model and rendering the full grid through the implicit decoder. We validate our framework on CT and MRI volumes at resolutions up to 512³ on a single consumer-grade GPU, demonstrating coherent full-volume generation across axial, coronal, and sagittal planes without materializing the full voxel grid at any stage of training.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-09-01] Deep learning-based estimation of individual scintillation photon arrival times for enhanced TOF resolution (#1210)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Onishi (Autores: Y. Onishi , R. Ota , F. Hashimoto , K. Ote , G. Akamatsu , H. Tashima , T. Yamaya)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Hamamatsu Photonics K.K., Central Research Laboratory, Hamamatsu, Japan [2] Chiba University, Graduate School of Science and Engineering, Chiba, Japan [3] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology, Department of Advanced Nuclear Medicine Sciences, Chiba, Japan [4] University of Florida, J. Crayton Pruitt Family Department of Biomedical Engineering, Gainesville, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The coincidence time resolution of scintillation detectors plays a critical role in time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET) and it is fundamentally limited by the emission, transport, and detection processes of scintillation photons. Although previous analytical and Monte Carlo simulation studies have suggested that exploiting multiple timing information of scintillation photons could approach the theoretical timing limits, direct experimental access to all detected photon timestamps remains unavailable with standard PET detectors using analog silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs). To address this challenge, we previously proposed a deep learning-based approach to recover photon timestamps on an event-by-event basis by removing the SiPM degradation factor from detector waveforms within an unsupervised learning framework. Our experimental evaluations demonstrated that the recovered photon behavior is consistent with previous findings, although the absence of ground-truth timestamps inevitably limited a rigorous and quantitative assessment of its validity and reliability. In this study, we evaluate the proposed method using Monte Carlo simulation data with fully known photon-level information. The recovered photon timestamps were quantitatively compared with the true timestamps in terms of timing bias, timing uncertainty, and total photon count fidelity. The results showed that the proposed method achieves timing biases within approximately 10 ps and maintains acceptable timing precision across photons while accurately preserving the number of detected photons per event. With the optimized parameter settings, we will further improve temporal precision in timestamp recovery using experimental data.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-09-02] Inter-Crystal Scattering Recovery in Semi-Monolithic Crystals: an Experimental and Simulation Study (#1581)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Pagano (Autores: F. Pagano , F. Loignon-Houle , D. Sanchez , E. Elmoujarkach , N. Karakatsanis , J. Cateret , S. Nehmeh , A. Gonzalez)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CSIC-Universitat Politècnica de València, Institute for Instrumentation in Molecular Imaging (I3M), Valencia, Spain [2] Oncovision, Valencia, Spain [3] Weill Cornell Medical College, Department of Radiology, New York, New York, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In positron emission tomography (PET), inter-crystal scattering (ICS) is a major source of uncertainty contributing to spatial resolution. While rejecting ICS events can improve the resolution, it comes at the cost of sensitivity. Accurately recovering the first interaction position is therefore crucial for maintaining both high sensitivity and spatial resolution. In this work, we apply ICS recovery to experimental data from semi-monolithic detectors, with a 2:1 slab-to-SiPM ratio using both analytical and deep-learning (DL) approaches. We developed a GATE Monte Carlo simulation framework tuned to reproduce experimental signals for data augmentation. A multilayer perceptron (MLP) achieved ~78% exact layer prediction, with an additional ~15% misassigned by only one slab, leaving just ~7% exceeding 1.5 mm (one slab thickness). This outperforms analytical methods, particularly for ICS-only events, where the MLP is 16 percentage points more accurate, and the analytical method fails entirely at edge slabs. We show simulated signals closely match experimental data; additional tuning will enable their use in training networks for experimental application. This study takes a first step toward combining simulated and experimental data for DL-based ICS recovery, which could bypass individual detector array calibration.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-09-03] A High Resolution Semi-Monolithic GAGG Detector Aiming for SPECT Imaging (#2693)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Zhao (Autores: Y. Zhao , K. Wang , J. Dang , W. Huang , Z. Yan , Z. Gu , Q. Wei)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Science and Technology Beijing, School of Automation and Electrical Engineering, Beijing, China [2] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract High-resolution SPECT imaging requires detectors with high intrinsic spatial resolution, good energy resolution, and high detection efficiency. Pixelated scintillator arrays are commonly used to improve the intrinsic spatial resolution, but sub-millimeter pixels increase fabrication complexity and cost, and inter-crystal gaps may reduce detection efficiency. In this work, we developed and evaluated a semi-monolithic GAGG SPECT detector composed of 29 stacked continuous crystal slabs. Each slab measured 25.8 × 0.8 × 6 mm³, and adjacent slabs were separated by 0.08 mm-thick BaSO 4 reflectors. The detector was coupled to a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) array (Hamamatsu MPPC S14161-3050HS) and read out using a PETsys TOFPET2 ASIC. A tungsten parallel-slit collimator with 13 slits, a 2 mm pitch, and a 0.8 mm slit width was placed directly in front of the detector entrance surface for flood image, energy resolution (ER), and intrinsic spatial resolution (ISR) measurements. Most pseudo-pixels (defined as discrete areas on the flood image based on the crystal look-up table) were clearly resolved in the flood image, except for several edge crystal pixels, with average peak-to-valley ratios of 5.4 ± 2.1 and 7.4 ± 3.9 in the X and Y directions, respectively. Within a 110-170 keV energy window, DOI-based energy correction improved the average ER from 15.37% ± 1.75% to 11.07% ± 0.77% at 140 keV. The average ISR were 1.02 ± 0.36 mm and 0.42 ± 0.29 mm in the X and Y directions, respectively. In conclusion, these results demonstrate that the proposed semi-monolithic GAGG detector can achieve good energy resolution and sub-millimeter-level intrinsic spatial resolution, showing potential for high-resolution SPECT imaging.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-09-04] Feasibility of Cherenkov-only Radiation Emitters Coupled to SiPMs for PET (#1180)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. X. Pinto (Autores: A. X. Pinto , N. Kratochwil , L. Rebolo , A. H. LeBeau , R. Hernandez , J. Veloso , B. Mehadiji , P. Correia , A. L. Silva , G. Ariño-Estrada)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Aveiro, I3N Physics Department, Aveiro, Portugal [2] University of California Davis, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America [3] Institut de Física d'Altes Energies - Barcelona Institute of Science and Technology (IFAE-BIST), Barcelona, Spain [4] University of California, Department of Radiation Oncology, School of Medicine,, Davis, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Recent applications of Positron Emission Tomography (PET) in dosimetry such as Pair Production Tomography (P2T) or Proton Range Verification (PRV) require a detector count rate capacity far beyond the conventional range for diagnostic-oriented PET. Most commonly used PET detectors use scintillation crystal coupled to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs). For high count rate situations the scintillation decay time in the range of tens of nanoseconds can lead to undesired pile-up effects. In this work, we explore the feasibility of using Cherenkov-only emitter based on PbF₂ coupled to SiPMs to overcome the limitation posed by the long scintillation tails. While Cherenkov-only emitters have been proposed and tested for ultra-fast timing in time-of-flight PET (TOF-PET), the goal of this work is to evaluate the feasibility of using them in readily scalable setup. We used 3×3×3-20 mm³ PbF₂ crystals coupled to Broadcom NUV-MT SiPMs (4×4 mm²) and custom low-noise high-frequency (LN-HF) readout electronics. SiPM over-voltages from +2 to +8 V and different trigger levels were evaluated to determine the optimal performance for this type of application, focusing on the true coincidence fraction (TCF), coincidence ratio and coincidence timing resolution (CTR), in order to assess if the Cherenkov signals are discernible from background noise. Additionally, we tested the same setup read out by an ASIC (FastIC evaluation board) to understand the impact of an integrated system-applicable readout. Using LN-HF-readout electronics and an excess bias voltage of +4 V we measure a TCF of 81% and a CTR of 240±2 ps. Using the FastIC ASIC, the best results were a TCF of 81% and a CTR of 506±6 ps. Our results demonstrate the potential of Cherenkov-only radiators for high count rate PET applications.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-09-05] Scan Time and Effective Dose Reduction using an Ultra-Fast Molecular Breast Imaging System (#2691)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Cherlin (Autores: A. Cherlin , M. Exley , N. Atkins , K. Erlandsson , I. Baistow , B.F. Hutton , M. O'Connor , C. Hruska , K. Thielemans)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Kromek Ltd., Sedgefield, United Kingdom [2] University College London, Institute of Nuclear Medicine, London, United Kingdom [3] Mayo Clinic, Department of Radiology, Rochester, Minnesota, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A prototype stationary tomographic ultra-fast Molecular Breast Imaging system (UFMBI) has been developed and characterised using phantom studies. The system combines ultra-high resolution CZT detectors with depth‑of‑interaction (DOI) sensitivity and wide‑angle sampling from densely packed multi‑pinhole (MPH) collimators, together with novel de‑multiplexing reconstruction to mitigate multiplexing artefacts. This approach enables substantial reductions in scan time (∼40 min) and radiation dose (∼2.4 mSv) compared with conventional MBI, supporting wider adoption as a supplemental screening tool for women with dense breast tissue. A dual-head prototype with a field-of-view of 132mm x 88mm has been designed and built. Each head consists of a 6x4 array of 5 mm thick CZT detectors with 11x11 grid of 2 mm pixels. Raw detector data are processed using a machine learning model providing 10x10 sub-pixelisation and DOI sensitivity. Image reconstruction uses OSEM algorithm incorporating attenuation, collimator blurring, septal penetration and multiplexing effects. Performance was evaluated using uniform and spherical lesion phantoms (5-9 mm) at tumour‑to‑background ratios of 10-20:1, with comparison to a clinical planar MBI system by imaging 99m Tc-infused gel phantoms. Dose/time reduction factors (DRF) were evaluated by resampling measured data relative to the reference equivalent to current clinical practice. Lesion detectability was assessed using contrast‑to‑noise ratio (CNR) and the Rose criterion (CNR>3). Sphere studies demonstrated detectability of 5-7 mm lesions at DRF = 8. Gel phantom experiments showed that UFMBI achieved ~2.9× higher CNR than the clinical system at reference conditions and ~2× higher at DRF = 6. These results demonstrate the feasibility of UFMBI as a high‑throughput tomographic extension of conventional MBI, with potential application as a supplemental screening tool for women with dense breasts.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-09-06] Scalable Cherenkov-Enhanced Timing in BGO with FastIC+ (#1562)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Loignon-Houle (Autores: F. Loignon-Houle , F. Pagano , D. Mazzanti , A. Olmos-Risen , N. Cucarella , D. Guberman , O. de la Torre , S. Gomez , D. Gascon , A. J. Gonzalez , A. Gonzalez-Montoro)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institute for Instrumentation in Molecular Imaging (i3M), CSIC-UPV, Valencia, Spain [2] Institute of Cosmos Science, University of Barcelona, Barcelona, Spain [3] Universitat Politècnica de Cataluña, Barcelona, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The ultrafast nature of Cherenkov photon emission offers an avenue to improve the coincidence time resolution (CTR) of time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET) detectors. Bismuth germanate (BGO) provides a higher Cherenkov photon yield than conventional lutetium-based crystals, but its slow scintillation component induces large variations in signal shape. Measuring the rise time of the signals, obtained from the time difference between two threshold crossings, enables classification of events by Cherenkov yield and time-offset correction to improve the CTR. While this principle has been demonstrated with dedicated fast electronics, scalable implementation remains a challenge. Here, we exploit the dual-threshold capability of the new FastIC+ ASIC to extract rise-time information in BGO-based detectors and study the influence of bias voltage, settings of thresholds, and rise-time correction methods on CTR performance. We obtained a 32% CTR improvement, from 577 to 395 ps FWHM, with 3×3×15 mm 3 polished BGO coupled to 3×3 mm 2 FBK NUV-MT SiPMs biased at 49 V, and we show trade-offs between noise rejection and rise-time correction efficiency as a function of the two selected thresholds. This work marks a concrete step toward a scalable approach to exploiting BGO's mixed Cherenkov-scintillation emission in TOF-PET imaging.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-09-07] An Optimized Two-Layer PET&SPECT Shared Detector based on a Scintillator-as-Collimator Design (#1674)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Zhao (Autores: Y. Zhao , C. Huang , X. Zeng , H. Yang , W. Huang , X. Jiang , X. Zhang , M. Niu , Y. Liang , Q. Wei , Z. Gu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China [2] University of Science and Technology Beijing, University of Science and Technology Beijing, Beijing, China [3] Cancer Hospital Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Shenzhen, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Simultaneous PET and SPECT imaging enables concurrent characterization of multiple biological processes, but conventional multi-modality systems typically require separate detector subsystems. We previously proposed a scintillator-as-collimator design for a PET&SPECT shared detector, and demonstrated PET, SPECT, and simultaneous PET&SPECT imaging capabilities. Nevertheless, the scintillator-as-collimator volume (SCV) lacked depth-of-interaction (DOI) discrimination in PET mode, and the thickness of the SPECT Detector volume (SD) was not optimized, compromising its time-of-flight (TOF) PET performance. To address these limitations, we developed an optimized two-layer PET&SPECT detector with a top 16×16 LYSO array (1.53×1.53×10 mm³) and a bottom 8×8 LYSO array (3×3×10 mm³), separated by two 2-mm light guides. The block was coupled to an MPPC array and read out by a PETsys TOFPET2 ASIC. To evaluate the effect of hole drilling on performance, two prototype detectors were fabricated: a drilled detector with holes in the top LYSO array and light guides, and a non-drilled reference. Both detectors used unpolished crystal sides with BaSO 4 reflectors. Flood images, energy resolution (ER), DOI resolution, and coincidence time resolution (CTR) were evaluated. ​​​​​​​The drilled detector achieved effective DOI discrimination in both SCV and SD. After excluding ICS events, DOI resolutions of 3.60 ± 0.43 mm and 2.18 ± 0.15 mm were obtained in the top and bottom layers, with a bottom-to-bottom CTR of 259 ps. The DOI and CTR are comparable to those of the non-drilled reference detector. In conclusion, these results validate the optimized two-layer scintillator-as-collimator design and demonstrate its potential for a PET&SPECT shared detector with high DOI and TOF performance. Future work will evaluate the capability of the SD region in detecting 140 keV gamma photons and develop a prototype system for imaging validation.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-09-08] Unlocking Next-Generation Time-of-Flight Imaging with the PoETIC ASIC (#1270)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Gascon (Autores: J. M. Fernandez-Tenllado , M. Ribalda , J. Mauricio , A. Espinya , M. Viqueria , J. J. Silva , S. Portero , G. Bergamin , D. Mazzanti , L. J. Imas , D. Guberman , A. Sanuy , J. A. Alozy , O. de la Torre , M. Penna , R. Dolenec , C. Trippl , J. M. Benlloch , D. Sanchez , S. Majewski , A. Gola , G. El Fakhri , R. Pestotnik , R. Ballabriga , D. Gascon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universitat de Barcelona (UB), Institut de Ciències del Cosmos (ICCUB), Barcelona, Spain [2] Conseil Européen pour la recherche nucléaire (CERN), Microelectronics Section, Meyrin, Genève, Switzerland [3] Jožef Stefan Institute (JSI), Experimental Particle Physics, Ljubljana, Slovenia [4] Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK), Custom Radiation Sensors, Trento, Italy [5] Consejo Superior de Investigaciones Cientificas (CSIC), Institute for Instrumentation in Molecular Imaging (I3M), Valencia, Spain [6] Oncovision, Valencia, Spain [7] Yale University, PET Center at Yale School of Medicine, New Haven, Connecticut, United States of America [8] Univeristy of California, Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Time-of-Flight Positron Emission Tomography requires readout electronics capable of extracting precise timing information. The Positron Emission Tomography Integrated Circuit (PoETIC) has been developed to bridge the performance gap between the intrinsic timing resolution of the detector and that achievable with integrated readout solutions, while remaining scalable in channel count and power consumption. PoETIC introduces a novel channel architecture based on two fully independent analog front-ends per channel, separately optimized for timing and energy measurements, and thereby relaxing conflicting design requirements at the input stage. Fabricated in 65 nm CMOS technology, the PoETIC die integrates fast low-noise front ends, dual-threshold discriminators and a TDC with 24.4 ps time binning. Four 16-channel dies are combined into a 64-channel 2.5D Integrated Circuit. A custom high-speed serial interface supports daisy-chained data and trigger distribution, significantly reducing interconnect complexity. The power consumption is 10 mW per channel. Measurements of a first prototype show a single-photon time resolution of 57 ± 1 ps FWHM and 85 ± 1 ps FWHM using FBK NUV-HD-MT SiPMs of 1×1 mm² and 3×3 mm², respectively. Preliminary measurements yield a coincidence time resolution of 74 ± 1 ps FWHM with the 3×3 mm² SiPMs and LGSO crystals of 2×2×3 mm³. To the best of our knowledge, these results represent state-of-the-art timing performance for an ASIC and suggest that PoETIC approaches the intrinsic timing performance of scintillator crystals while offering a flexible and scalable readout solution for next-generation PET systems and other fast-timing applications.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-26-01] Emergent Physical Interpretability in Transformer Encoders for Radiation Anomaly Detection (#1513)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. M. Mowen (Autores: D. M. Mowen , M. Alamaniotis)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Texas at San Antonio, Electrical Engineering, San Antonio, Texas, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Constraining a Transformer decoder to a known physical generative structure induces emergent interpretability in the encoder's self-attention without labels or supervision. We demonstrate this in gamma-ray spectroscopy, where measurements are Poisson-sparse at one-second mobile survey dwell times, environments are nonstationary, and labeled decompositions are unavailable. Observed spectra arise as nonnegative additive superpositions of source contributions, which we encode using a Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (NMF)-constrained decoder paired with a Transformer encoder. The learned representations organize into physically meaningful components, separating environmental substructures and recovering known photopeak features at correct energies. In contrast, an identical Transformer with an unconstrained decoder produces unstructured latent representations, with 48.6% of weights taking negative values that are inconsistent with photon-counting physics, isolating the decoder constraint as the causal mechanism. The proposed architecture achieves state-of-the-art anomaly detection on 6,221 field-collected spectra, outperforming linear baselines and unconstrained autoencoders while exhibiting reduced run-to-run variance, demonstrating that embedding known generative structure into decoder design can induce interpretable representations across domains governed by additive physical processes.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-26-02] Ground-Truth-Free Validation of Surface Radiation Mapping via Forward-Simulation Round-Trip (#1723)
sub_talks.speaker: B.-J. Kim
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Changwon National University, Nuclear Engineering, Changwon, Republic of Korea [2] Reversible Inc., Changwon, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Reconstruction of surface radiation contamination from sparse airborne measurements has matured rapidly with deep learning, but a validation gap persists: the surface activity is rarely measurable in operational deployments, leaving no oracle for evaluating predictions. We address this by reframing airborne mapping as an inverse deconvolution problem in which a known forward operator maps surface activity to aerial fluence via altitude blur and detector response. The framing yields a ground-truth-free validation protocol: each candidate surface reconstruction is forward-simulated through the operator and compared to held-out aerial measurements. We characterize the protocol on a synthetic benchmark with a 64-by-64 ground-truth surface of Gaussian hotspots, a fixed Gaussian forward kernel, 150 sparse aerial samples per scene, and 200 held-out validation points. Four reconstructions are compared: inverse distance weighting (IDW), ordinary kriging, IDW followed by Wiener deconvolution, and a small encoder-decoder convolutional network. Across 40 scenes per method, the round-trip aerial-space root-mean-square error correlated with the oracle surface-space root-mean-square error, with a pooled Pearson correlation of 0.871 across methods and within-method correlations from 0.71 to 0.82. The protocol identified the encoder-decoder network as the most accurate reconstruction in agreement with the oracle ranking, without access to ground truth. These findings suggest that round-trip forward-simulation residuals can serve as a practical proxy for surface reconstruction quality, supporting evaluation and benchmarking of radiation mapping methods when direct surface ground truth is limited or unavailable.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-26-03] Backscattered Spectral Network Imaging Method Based on a Combined Long-ShortCrystal Detector (#2600)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Li, J. Li (Autores: J. Li , J. Li , Y. Xiao, Y. Xiao)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [2] Key Laboratory of Particle & Radiation Imaging (Tsinghua University), Ministry of Education, Beijing, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Compton backscatter imaging (CBST) is a promising non-contact technique for nondestructive testing of complex structures, but its performance is limited by the trade-off between detection efficiency and spatial resolution. In this work, we propose a backscattered spectral network imaging framework based on a combined long-short crystal (CLSC) detector and a spectral fusion neural network. The CLSC detector integrates alternating long and short scintillation crystals to improve photon detection efficiency while retaining geometric selectivity, and segmented metal collimation is introduced to provide depth-dependent scattering information. The acquired multi-crystal spectra are processed by a dual-branch fusion network that jointly exploits spectral and spatial features for defect reconstruction. Geant4 simulations with varying defect sizes and depths under realistic noise conditions demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms conventional count-based and collimator-free approaches under low-count conditions, enabling more reliable detection of deep and small defects.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-26-04] A Machine Learning Approach to Inter-Crystal Scattering Kinematics for Multiple Emission Tomography (#2796)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Presotto (Autores: L. Arnone , M. N. Colombo , G. Terragni , F. Pennazio , M. Paganoni , L. Presotto , E. Auffray , M. Pizzichemi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Milano-Bicocca, Milan, Italy [2] CERN, Geneva, Switzerland [3] INFN Torino, Turin, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract High spatial resolution and sensitivity in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) are essential for early diagnosis and treatment monitoring. However, in modern pixelated detectors, a large fraction of coincidence events involves Inter-Crystal Scatter (ICS), where a gamma ray deposits its energy across multiple scintillators through a Compton interaction followed by photoelectric absorption.These events are difficult to exploit because the sequence of interactions cannot be directly determined, degrading the reconstruction of the Line of Response and, consequently, the spatial resolution. For this reason, ICS events are often discarded, leading to a significant loss in sensitivity. The Multiple Emission Tomography (MET) project aims to recover these events and use them to enable a hybrid imaging approach combining PET and Compton camera capabilities. In conventional approaches, ICS reconstruction relies on analytical methods based on chi-squared minimization and manually tuned selection cuts. Although effective, these methods are computationally intensive and strongly dependent on user-defined criteria, limiting both efficiency and scalability. In this work, we introduce a Machine Learning (ML) pipeline integrated into the MET prototype to automatically identify ICS events and determine their interaction sequence. By replacing the analytical reconstruction with XGBoost classifiers and a Convolutional Neural Network, the proposed approach provides a more flexible and efficient solution, improving the identification of the first interaction point and enabling a more effective use of multi-crystal events.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-26-05] Real-Time Data Compression Using Machine Learning for the ARGO Dark Matter Detector (#1376)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Esmaeilzadeh (Autores: S. Esmaeilzadeh , C.-E. Granger , H.E. Rahali , K. Gracequist , S. Viel , A.C. Therrien)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Sherbrooke universuity, Interdisciplinary Institute for Technological Innovation(3IT), Sherbrooke, Québec, Canada [2] Carleton University, Department of Physics, Ottawa, Ontario, Canada
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Abstract-The search for dark matter requires increasingly advanced detectors and data processing systems. The ARGO detector, under development, uses liquid argon as the detection medium and will deploy Single Photon Avalanche Diodes (SPAD) over approximately 200 m2. These SPAD matrices, arranged in mm2 units, will generate millions of data channels, with potential drawbacks such as high power consumption, complex cabling, and costly high-speed data storage. To address these challenges, we investigate a unified real-time machine learning (ML) approach capable of simultaneously performing particle identification and event position reconstruction. The proposed Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture classifies events as nuclear recoils (NR), electron recoils (ER), or alpha decays, while concurrently reconstructing the interaction position inside the detector. This multi-task approach reduces computational resources, making it well suited for resource- constrained edge environments near the detector. Future work will focus on optimizing the models and implementing them on edge hardware.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-26-06] Machine-Learning Based Rapid Characterization of HPGe Detectors Based on Full-Energy Peak Efficiency Responses (#1052)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Zhang (Autores: K. Zhang , P. Su , Z. Wu , A. Hu , H. Zhang , J. Li , R. Qiu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [2] Key Laboratory of Particle & Radiation Imaging, Tsinghua University, Ministry of Education, Beijing, China [3] Nuctech Company Limited, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Full-energy peak efficiency (FEPE) is a critical quantity for quantitative gamma-ray spectrometry using HPGe detectors. However, the FEPE response may vary during long-term operation because of operational history and environmental conditions. Conventional detector characterization usually requires repeated Monte Carlo simulations, in which selected geometrical parameters are manually adjusted until the simulated FEPE curve agrees with experimental measurements. This iterative procedure is computationally expensive and strongly dependent on operator expertise. To address this limitation, this work proposes a machine-learning-based rapid characterization framework using a sparsely connected multilayer perceptron (MLP) with multiple attention heads. By taking experimentally determined FEPE values and fixed detector parameters as inputs, the network directly determines key characterization parameters, including the crystal radius, crystal length, and dead layer thickness. On a test set comprising 13 detector instances with different specifications, the proposed framework performed detector characterization, and the simulated FEPEs of the characterized detectors agreed closely with the corresponding experimental FEPEs, demonstrating the broad applicability of the approach. Owing to the feed-forward nature of the MLP architecture, the characterization procedure can be completed rapidly through a single forward pass, providing an efficient alternative to the conventional manual Monte Carlo adjustment workflow.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-26-07] Comprehensive Strategy for Track Signal Extraction in the COMET Phase-I Experiment using Deep Learning Algorithms (#2397)
sub_talks.speaker: J. Sato
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yokohama National University, Deapartment of Physics, Yokohama, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The COMET Phase-I experiment searches for the neutrinoless muon-to-electron conversion with a target sensitivity of $7 \times 10^{-15}$. A critical challenge is identifying signal hits amid a high background occupancy of approximately 40\% in the Cylindrical Drift Chamber (CDC). Traditional methods struggle under such dense environments. We present a deep-learning-based hit filtering strategy using a U-Net architecture with an EfficientNet backbone. By optimizing image formats and multi-hit handling, we achieved a purity of 98\% and a retention of 90\%, significantly surpassing design goals. This framework establishes a robust foundation for track reconstruction in high-occupancy environments.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-26-08] Signal Electron Extraction and Energy Resolution the COMET Experiment (#1795)
sub_talks.speaker: Y. Kojima
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yokohama National University, Graduate School of Engineering Science, yokohama, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Charged lepton flavor violation (CLFV) is a promising probe of physics beyond the Standard Model. The COMET Phase-I experiment searches for coherent muon-to-electron conversion (μ⁻-e⁻ conversion), which produces a mono-energetic electron with an energy close to 105 MeV. However, Decay-In-Orbit (DIO) electrons form a major background near the signal region, requiring precise track reconstruction and energy estimation. In this study, a U-Net-based deep-learning method was applied to Cylindrical Drift Chamber (CDC) hit information represented as two-dimensional images. Hit wires with deep-learning scores above a threshold were treated as signal hits and passed to GenFit for track reconstruction. Quality cuts based on the p-value, the number of degrees of freedom (NDF), and reduced χ² were also applied to improve the reconstruction quality. The ROC curve evaluation demonstrated effective discrimination between signal-electron hits and background hits. Furthermore, applying the selected hits to GenFit improved the momentum residual distributions compared with the conventional reconstruction method. In particular, the combination of hit selection and quality cuts suppressed events with large momentum residuals contributing to the DIO background and reduced the overlap between the DIO background and the signal region. Smearing evaluations using the obtained momentum residual distributions and the theoretical DIO spectrum indicated improved energy reconstruction performance under the condition corresponding to a conversion rate of CR = 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁵. These results suggest that deep-learning-based hit selection can improve track reconstruction and energy estimation performance in the COMET experiment.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-27-01] Measurement of the Cross Section of 14 N(n, p) 14 C Reaction Using Sample-Added Scintillator (#2201)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Li (Autores: G. Li , T. Katabuchi , Z. Zhu , M. C. Maloney , R. Kunitomo , Z. Shao , A. Kimura , S. Endo , R. L. Gerard)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institute of Science Tokyo, Department of Transdisciplinary Science and Engineering, Tokyo, Japan [2] Japan Atomic Energy Agency, Ibaraki, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Conventional measurements of neutron-induced charged-particle emission cross sections with semiconductor detectors are limited by particle energy loss in samples and stringent experimental constraints.The ¹⁴N(n, p) reaction is critical for dose evaluation in boron neutron capture therapy, as it dominates radiation dose to healthy tissue under thermal and epi-thermal neutron irradiation. High-precision cross-section data with uncertainties below 5% are indispensable for safe treatment planning, while existing datasets are currently under re-evaluation. This work aims to accurately measure the ¹⁴N(n, p) reaction cross section from 2.6×10⁻³ to 1.8 eV using a homemade sample-added scintillator detector. The scintillator consists of a base matrix, ¹⁴N-containing luminescent agent, wavelength shifter and photoinitiator. Pure scintillators and sample-added scintillator with lithium fluoride and gold powder are fabricated as active targets, attached directly on the surface of a photomultiplier tube, and aligned on the neutron beam. Experiments are carried out at the ANNRI beamline of the MLF of the JPARC with a flight length of 28.41 m. Waveform signals were recorded by a digitizer, with long-gate pulse height area, short-gate pulse shape discrimination area and time-of-flight data acquired for each event. The ¹⁴N(n, p) cross section was determined relative to the ⁶Li(n, α) reaction. Results indicates that the cross sections obtained in the present work show an overall energy dependence consistent with the expected low-energy 1/v behavior, and the measured values are consistent within uncertainty with the past experimental values and evaluated cross section data. This study demonstrates the feasibility of using self-made sample-added scintillators for measurements.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-27-02] Development of thermal neutron detector using co-doped Ce:LaBr₃/⁶LiBr Eutectic Scintillators for High Gamma-Ray Backgrounds (#2226)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Kamada (Autores: K. Kamada , K.J. Kim , M. Yoshino , M. Kaburagi , J. Ishii , T. Matsumoto , S. Manabe , A. Masuda , H. Harano , M. Kato , K. Shimazoe , A. Yoshikawa)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tohoku Univ., Sendai, Japan [2] C＆A corp., Sendai, Japan [3] National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology, Tsukuba, Japan [4] The University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Thermal-neutron detection in intense gamma-ray fields is required for fuel-debris monitoring and criticality safety during nuclear decommissioning. We developed co-doped Ce:LaBr₃/⁶LiBr eutectic scintillators in which the ⁶LiBr phase converts thermal neutrons through the ⁶Li(n,α)³H reaction and the Ce:LaBr₃ phase produces fast scintillation light. Building on eutectic-scintillator design concepts that enable higher Li content than stoichiometric single crystals, Sr²⁺ and Ba²⁺ co-doping were investigated to improve pulse-shape discrimination (PSD). Sr co-doping produced only limited improvement in the eutectic because Sr-rich secondary regions were formed, whereas Ba co-doping gave clearer α/γ PSD mapping. A Ce:LaBr₃/⁶LiBr detector was then evaluated in the same ²⁵²Cf-neutron/¹³⁷Cs-gamma mixed-field configuration and digital processing scheme as the optimized LiCAF:Ce detector benchmark. Neutron-source detection was demonstrated up to 5.4 Gy/h with an effective thermal-neutron sensitivity of approximately 0.3 cps/nv, indicating the potential of Ba,Ce:LaBr₃/⁶LiBr eutectics for compact neutron monitoring in decommissioning environments.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-27-03] Scintillators based on 2D perovskite single-crystals for the detection of rapid neutrons and gamma/neutron discrimination. (#1344)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Thorimbert (Autores: F. Thorimbert , E. Gros-Daillon , D. Tisseur , O. Llido , V. Buridon , D. Tromson , J.-M. Verilhac)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Université Grenoble Alpes, CEA/LITEN, Grenoble, France [2] Université Grenoble Alpes, CEA/LETI, Grenoble, France [3] CEA, IRESNE, Saint-Paul les Durance, France [4] Université Paris-Saclay, CEA/LIST, Palaiseau, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Fast neutron detectors are essential for quantifying neutron flux in nuclear reactors, imaging the internal structure of large equipment, and detecting contraband or radioactive nuclear materials. However, no ideal technology currently enables efficient, accurate, and real-time detection of fast neutrons, which are high-energy, highly penetrating particles. There is a growing interest in hybrid organic-inorganic halide perovskites, which exhibit scintillation under X-rays, gamma rays, and fast neutrons within a single material platform. In particular, two-dimensional (2D) perovskites contain both light elements, such as hydrogen in long organic cations, which are suitable for neutron detection, and heavy elements, such as lead, which enhance X- and gamma-ray absorption [1,2]. In this presentation, I will present our approach to grow from solution by solvent evaporation, centimeter-sized single crystals of 2D perovskites, namely PEA 2 PbBr 4 . The optical characterizations of this single-phase, perfectly ordered crystal present two photoluminescence (PL) peaks, at 411 and 426 nm, attributed respectively to the emission from the surface and the bulk, a PLQY (Photoluminescence Quantum Yield) of 26 %, and a time decay of ≈ 3 ns. The radioluminescent measurements show a result of 20000 to 30000 Ph/MeV vs LYSO, which is better than organic scintillators, like EJ200~10000 Ph/MeV. In a second step, we will dope the reference material with cations such as Zn²⁺ or Mn²⁺ to enhance the light yield and increase the Stokes shift in order to reduce the self-absorption. We will also investigate the effects of dimensionality and halide composition to achieve a PL redshift. All synthesized materials will be evaluated under realistic neutron flux conditions, with particular attention to their stability. In parallel, their ability to discriminate between neutron and gamma radiation will also be investigated on a laboratory bench, using a 252 Cf source.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-27-04] Optimization of Cs₂LiLa(Br,Cl)₆:Ce Scintillation Crystals for Neutron Detection and n/γ Discrimination (#1789)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Cai (Autores: Z. Cai , X. Zhang , Z. Yin , J. Liu , Z. Kang , Q. Zhao , T. Wang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Northwestern Polytechnical University, State Key Laboratory of Solidification, Xi'an, China [2] Crystalab Corporation Ltd, Xi'an, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Cs 2 LiLa(Br,Cl) 6 :Ce (CLLBC) is a promising Elpasolite scintillator for compact gamma-ray spectroscopy and thermal-neutron detection, but the effect of Ce concentration on neutron-gamma pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) remains insufficiently quantified. In this work, CLLBC crystals with 20% Cl substitution and nominal Ce concentrations of 2%, 3%, and 4% were grown by the vertical Bridgman method. When Ce concentration increasing from 2.05% to 5.46%, the 662 keV energy resolution improved from about 3.5% to 3.2%, the relative light output increased by 9.4%, and the neutron-gamma figure of merit (FOM) increased from 1.6 to 2.0. Scintillation-decay measurements and coupled rate-transport calculations indicate that higher Ce concentration enhances energy transfer and excitation-density-dependent quenching, making neutron-like pulses more distinct from gamma-ray pulses. Continued growth optimization further enabled a 1 inch SiPM-coupled CLLBC detector that achieved 3.19% energy resolution at 662 keV and FOM = 2.37. These results demonstrate a practical route for improving CLLBC scintillators for compact mixed-field radiation detectors.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-27-05] Development of Tl and 6 Li Co-Doped Cs 3 Cu 2 I 5 for Remote Thermal Neutron Detection (#1524)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Fujiwara (Autores: C. Fujiwara , Y. Urano , A. Yamaji , N. Matsubayashi , T. Takata , H. Tanaka , M. Hunyadi , L. Csige , S. Kurosawa)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tohoku University, Department of Materials Science, Graduate School of Engineering, Sendai, Japan [2] Nagoya University, Graduate School of Engineering, Nagoya, Japan [3] Kyoto University, Institute for Integrated Radiation and Nuclear Science, Osaka, Japan [4] HUN-REN Institute for Nuclear Research,, Debrecen, Hungary [5] Osaka University, Institute of Laser Engineering, Osaka, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Tl- and ⁶Li-co-doped Cs 3 Cu 2 I 5 crystals were grown by the Bridgman method and evaluated as thermal neutron scintillators for application in fiber-optic-coupled neutron flux monitoring systems. The grown crystals (5 × 5 × 3 mm) exhibited a light yield of approximately 140,000 ph./n th excited thermal neutron, which is approximately 24 times higher than that of the conventional and widely used GS20 neutron scintillator. A detector was constructed by optically coupling a small crystal piece (1 × 1 × 0.2 mm) to the tip of a 20 m optical fiber. Neutron irradiation experiments were conducted at the Kyoto University Research Reactor. The neutron excited radioluminescence spectra of Tl, 6 Li doped Cs 3 Cu 2 I 5 were confirmed. In addition, the scintillation intensity varied linearly with neutron flux, with a coefficient of determination of R ² = 0.996. These results indicate that ⁶Li- and Tl-co-doped Cs 3 Cu 2 I 5 is a highly promising scintillator material for real-time neutron dosimetry in high-flux environments such as boron neutron capture therapy.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-27-06] Gamma-Neutron Detection with Intrinsic and Doped Ternary Halide Scintillators (#2873)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. Ariesanti (Autores: E. Ariesanti , R. Hawrami , R. Hermann , M. Loyd)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Fisk University, Life and Physical Sciences (Physics), Nashville, Tennessee, United States of America [2] Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, Tennessee, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Traditionally dual-mode radiation detection requires a combination of two or more radiation detectors that work synchronously. In recent years more novel and advanced scintillation detector materials for dual-mode detection have been discovered and developed. Recent elpasolite scintillators, such as cerium doped CLYC, CLLB, and TLYC, which contain neutron sensitive materials, have been investigated as dual mode detectors. Because of the complexity of their phase diagrams, crystal growth yield, including bulk uniformity and detection performance, is lower than ideal, which eventually leads to a high final product cost. As a result, there is not a widespread interest in using these scintillators due to their high costs and scarcity although they have good detection and gamma-neutron performance. Simpler compounds like binary and ternary halides have less complicated phase diagrams due to fewer reacting compounds in the growth systems. This paper describes the efforts to grow scintillators that are capable of simultaneous neutron and gamma ray detection with lithium-doped or containing ternary halide compounds. The presence of lithium, whether it be natural or enriched 6 Li, improves the neutron sensitivity of the compounds and allows for simultaneous detection of gamma-ray and thermal neutrons. Fast or scattered neutron detection is also possible with ternary chloride compounds. This paper presents the growth and characterization of lithium based ternary halide scintillation crystals for dual-mode neutron-gamma detection and imaging. Early results show an energy resolution about 4% (FWHM) for 662 keV gamma-rays and a primary decay constant about 800 ns. Other properties, such as melting points, transmittance and absorbance spectra, x-ray excitation optical emission spectra, as well as preliminary neutron gamma discrimination and crystal structure measurements will be presented.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-27-07] Neutron and Gamma Ray Pulse Shape Discrimination in Small, Fiber-Coupled Organic Glass Scintillators (#1730)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Tyler (Autores: S. Tyler , O. Stennes , S. Clarke , S. Pozzi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The University of Michigan, Department of Nuclear Engineering and Radiological Sciences, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Miniature fiber-coupled organic scintillators are promising candidates for distributed neutron measurements in confined or high-radiation environments where remote placement of photodetectors and electronics is desirable. In this work, organic glass scintillator (OGS) droplets coupled to polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) optical fibers were characterized to investigate how optical transport distance affects pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) behavior and neutron-sensitive response. Measurements were performed using direct coupling and fiber lengths up to 12 m with 252 Cf and 137 Cs sources. Tail-to-total PSD was used to compare neutron and gamma-ray event populations under fixed photomultiplier operating conditions. Increasing fiber length produced substantial attenuation and broadening of both pulse populations, with the gamma-ray band degrading more rapidly than the neutron band. Low-light transport effects, coupling conditions, and threshold migration also significantly altered the PSD morphology as fiber length increased. Although low-energy calibration features were difficult to interpret due to the small scintillator geometry and probable electron escape effects, measurable neutron-sensitive PSD structure remained observable across all tested fiber lengths. These results suggest that long PMMA optical transport may preferentially suppress gamma-ray response while preserving neutron-sensitive discrimination capability relevant to neutron-signature analysis and remote neutron monitoring applications.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-27-08] Pulse Shape Discrimination in a 3D-Printable Perovskite-Polysiloxane Nanocomposite Scintillator (#2064)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Polo (Autores: M. Polo , S. M. Carturan , M. Cinausero , S. Moretto , G.-F. Dalla Betta , A.P. Caricato , A. Quaranta)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Trento, Department of Industrial Engineering, Trento, Italy [2] INFN-TIFPA, Trento, Italy [3] University of Padova, Department of Physics and Astronomy, Padova, Italy [4] INFN-LNL, Legnaro, Italy [5] INFN-Padova, Padova, Italy [6] University of Salento, Department of Physics and Mathematics, Lecce, Italy [7] INFN-Lecce, Lecce, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Scintillators, which convert ionizing radiation into visible photons, are essential in applications ranging from high-energy physics to medical imaging. Plastic scintillators are especially attractive due to their low cost, fast response, and simple fabrication. However, their limited radiation hardness and poor geometrical adaptability restrict their use in demanding environments such as hadron therapy and real-time dosimetry. In this work, a novel nanocomposite scintillator designed for 3D printing is investigated. The material consists of a photocurable polysiloxane matrix embedding metal-halide perovskite (CsPbBr3) nanocrystals, enabling the fabrication of complex detector geometries. Beyond its manufacturability, the composite exhibits an unusual scintillation response: under alpha-particle excitation, the emitted signal shows a significantly longer decay time compared with the fast emission typical of pure perovskites. These temporal features allow effective pulse shape discrimination between gamma photons and alpha particles, representing, to the best of the authors' knowledge, the first demonstration of this capability in hybrid perovskite-based scintillators. Preliminary optical characterization was carried out through spectrofluorimetric analysis to study the interaction between the polymer matrix and the perovskite phase, while UV--visible transmittance measurements confirmed adequate transparency for efficient light transport. Scintillation performance was then evaluated using an alpha source. Comparison with a commercial plastic scintillator benchmark highlights the potential of the proposed nanocomposite for advanced and customizable dosimetry applications, especially where flexible detector geometries and particle discrimination are required.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-28-01] Methylpiperazinium Perovskitoid for High‑Performance X‑Ray Detection (#2343)
sub_talks.speaker: H. Li
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] wuhan university of technology, HuBei, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Abstract - Metal halide perovskites are promising for direct X‑ray detection, but phase impurity in conventional quasi‑2D systems limit device performance. Here we report a methylpiperazinium (MPZ) based quasi‑2D perovskitoid, (mpz) 5 Pb 8 Br 26 ·2H 2 O. The crystal features a unique segmented architecture: four corner‑sharing PbBr 6 octahedra form 3D‑like conduction blocks, separated by 2D spacer regions where MPZ 2+ . This design simultaneously achieves a high mobility‑lifetime (μτ) product of 6.1×10 -3 cm 2 V -1 . A direct X‑ray detector fabricated in the out‑of‑plane configuration exhibits a sensitivity of 33.18 μC Gy -1 cm -2 and a detection limit of 6.2 nGy s -1 , representing a record among lead‑based quasi‑2D perovskites. The successful construction of quasi-2D single crystals provides a versatile platform for high-performance optoelectronics, proving its efficacy for applications spanning photodetection, solar energy conversion, and light-emitting devices even under the most rigorous material requirements

sub_talks.title: [NSS-28-02] Design and Evaluation of Graphene Strip Arrays for Radiation Detection (#2400)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Turqueti (Autores: M. Turqueti , A. Lindman , A. Poon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Engineering Division, Berkeley, California, United States of America [2] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Nuclear Science, Berkeley, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Graphene has emerged as a promising material for next-generation sensing systems due to its exceptional carrier mobility, low electronic noise, mechanical flexibility, and high electrical conductivity. In this work, we present the design and evaluation of graphene strip arrays for radiation detection applications. The detector architecture employs segmented graphene sensing strips integrated connected to low-noise front-end electronics to investigate radiation-induced signal generation, spatial sensitivity, and charge transport characteristics. Conventional semiconductor radiation detectors often face challenges associated with fabrication complexity, radiation damage, and limitations in scaling toward lightweight and flexible detection systems. Graphene-based detectors provide an alternative approach with potential advantages in fast signal response, compact integration, and scalable fabrication. The proposed detector consists of patterned graphene strip arrays fabricated on an silicon substrate with optimized strip geometry and differential signal readout. Radiation-induced charge variations are detected through low-noise charge amplification and signal conditioning electronics. Preliminary experimental characterization demonstrates measurable detector response under controlled irradiation conditions and stable electrical operation across multiple bias configurations. The segmented strip geometry enables position-sensitive radiation detection and supports scalability toward larger-area detector systems. The presented work demonstrates the feasibility of graphene strip arrays as compact, low-noise radiation detectors for advanced nuclear science and charged-particle instrumentation.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-28-03] Geometry-Defined Impact Ionization in Two-Stage Mesa-Type Silicon Electron Multipliers (#1064)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Sonobe (Autores: H. Sonobe , N. Kamiya , T. Kobayashi , R. Shiozaki , Y. Matsunaga)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Hamamatsu Photonics K.K., Solid State Division, Hamamatsu, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A silicon electron multiplier (SiEM) that achieves internal multiplication without a dedicated doped gain layer is demonstrated. The device employs a two-stage mesa-type architecture in which impact ionization occurs in a localized high-field region formed by geometric field crowding within a cylindrical mesa. A buried gate electrode independently controls carrier injection into the multiplication region. Devices were fabricated in a sub-micron CMOS process line. The structure consists of an injection stage and a multiplication stage. The injection stage uses a buried polysilicon gate to electrostatically steer carriers toward the center of the pixel, while the multiplication stage confines the high electric field within a constricted cylindrical mesa. Three-terminal operation enables independent control of multiplication through the gate bias. Electro-optical measurements were performed using 905 nm illumination with an absorption depth of approximately 30-35 µm in silicon. The devices exhibit a multiplication factor exceeding 100 for |Vgate| < 50 V. Scaling of the cylindrical mesa geometry shows that smaller diameters and reduced mesa height lower the bias required for multiplication. For example, reducing the mesa diameter from 3.0 µm to 1.6 µm increases the multiplication factor from approximately 1.5 to greater than 3 at |Vgate| = 40 V, and gains exceeding 400 are obtained at |Vgate| ≈ 50 V. Temperature measurements from −40 °C to 40 °C show a multiplication sensitivity of dVgate/dT = 24-30 mV/°C at constant gain (M = 10). This value is significantly smaller than those typically reported for gain-layer detectors. These results demonstrate geometry-defined impact ionization with electrostatically controlled carrier injection. The proposed SiEM provides a design framework for radiation-tolerant silicon detectors with internal multiplication.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-28-04] Electrical and UHDR characterization of trench-isolated thin segmented silicon detectors (#2529)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Montalvan Olivares (Autores: D. Montalvan Olivares , U. Deut , M.G. Bisogni , M. Boscardin , M. Centis Vignali , S. De Astis , M. Ferrero , S. Giordanengo , F. Mostardi , R. Sacchi , A. Vignati)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Università degli Studi di Torino, Deparment of Physics, Turin, Italy [2] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Turin, Italy [3] Università di Pisa, Pisa, Italy [4] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Pisa, Italy [5] Fondazione Bruno Kessler, Trento, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Thin segmented silicon sensors have attracted increasing interest for beam monitoring and microdosimetry in emerging radiotherapy modalities such as FLASH and spatially fractionated radiotherapy, owing to their excellent temporal response, high spatial precision, and robustness. In this study, thin planar silicon sensor manufactured by Fondazione Bruno Kessler and implementing different electrode-isolation strategies were investigated through electrical characterization and irradiation tests under ultra-high dose rate electron beams. The investigated devices included sensors with two different trench technologies, which were compared with segmented silicon detectors based on p-stop and Junction Termination Extension isolation techniques. Electric characterization was performed through current-voltage and capacitance-voltage measurements to extract relevant operational parameters. In addition, the detectors were exposed to electron beams delivered by a LINAC at dose-per-pulse values of 2.2 Gy in a 4µs pulse. Preliminary results showed comparable electrical performance for all detector technologies, with leakage currents in the nanoampere range and stable operation up to 200 V bias voltage. Nevertheless, segmented sensor without trench isolation exhibited deviations between collected charge and pad areas ratios, suggesting geometry-dependent contributions to charge collection, likely related to perimeter effects. Ongoing studies aim to evaluate whether trench isolation mitigates these effects and improves sensitive volume definition, as well as to assess the radiation hardness of the proposed detector technologies.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-28-05] Development and Electrical Performance Characterization of 3D Column-Trench Detector (#2488)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Ji (Autores: H. Ji , M. Liu , Z. Li , X. Li , J. Luo)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] the Key Laboratory of Fabrication Technologies for Integrated Circuits, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China [2] the Institute of Microelectronics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China [3] Institute of High Energy Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In this work, a novel 3D column-trench detector based on a 30 $\mu $m thick high-resistivity P-type epitaxial silicon is proposed and experimentally validated. The detector is fabricated on the standard CMOS process platform of the Institute of Microelectronics, Chinese Academy of Sciences (IMECAS), featuring a hybrid 3D configuration that combines N-type column electrodes and P-type strip trench electrodes. Electrical characterizations performed on single-pixel device with central N-type electrode demonstrate that the proposed detector achieves a low leakage current of 0.3 nA and a small capacitance of 0.3 pF under a reverse bias voltage of 30 V. According to the analysis of current-voltage (IV) and capacitance-voltage (CV) characteristics, the device exhibits a full depletion voltage of approximately 3 V and a high breakdown voltage up to 130 V. In addition, the device design, layout, and electrical performance of the 3DCTS are systematically elaborated in this paper. The electrical test results indicate that the proposed device possesses promising application prospects in high-energy physics experiments, medical imaging, and space radiation detection.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-28-06] Large-Area Silicon Pixel Sensor Processing on 8-Inch High-Resistivity Wafers (#2906)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Kalliopuska (Autores: J. Kalliopuska , J. Marles , S. Andoh , M. Ilosalo , N. Giri , O. Shtepura , M. Järvenpää , S. Vähänen)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] ADVAFAB, Helsinki, Finland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The transition from 6-inch to 8-inch high-resistivity silicon wafer processing has been implemented for the fabrication of large-area pixel sensors for photon-counting applications. The upgraded production line enables a doubling of usable wafer area compared to conventional 6-inch wafers, allowing either larger sensor formats or increased number of sensors per wafer. Prototype 8- inch wafers were processed using stepper lithography with stitching to realize multiple sensor layouts compatible with Medipix3, Timepix3 and Timepix4 readout ASICs. Electrical characterization was performed prior to under-bump metallization (UBM) and flip-chip assembly. Leakage currents at a reverse bias of -300 V were compared with reference data from 6-inch production batches of 500 μm thick sensors. An approximately 60% increase in leakage current for sensors fabricated on 8-inch wafers is attributed to a non-uniform radial resistivity distribution observed in the prototype 8-inch material. 8-inch wafer processing has been successfully demonstrated for silicon pixel sensor fabrication. The process is compatible with existing 6-inch technology and supports large-area sensor production. Although an increased leakage current was observed due to resistivity non-uniformity, the results confirm the feasibility of the approach. Future 8-inch production wafers are expected to have an improved resistivity profile, which is anticipated to reduce the leakage current and improve sensor uniformity.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-28-07] Results from irradiated nLGAD sensors (#1742)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Ferrero (Autores: M. Ferrero , V. Sola , G. Paternoster , A. Morozzi , A.R. Altamura , R. Arcidiacono , A. Bisht , M. Boscardin , N. Cartiglia , M. Centis Vignali , M. Costa , T. Croci , A. Fondacci , S. Galletto , O. Hammad Ali , L. Lanteri , L. Massaccesi , F. Moscatelli , M.M. Obertino , D. Passeri , N. Pastrone , F. Siviero , M. Tornago , R. White)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare (INFN), INFN Torino, Torino, Italy [2] Università degli Studi di Torino, Department of Physics, Torino, Italy [3] Fondazione Bruno Kessler, Trento, Italy [4] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare (INFN), INFN Perugia, Perugia, Italy [5] Università degli Studi del Piemonte Orientale, Novara, Italy [6] 6CNR-IOM, Sede secondaria di Perugia, Perugia, Italy [7] Università degli Studi di Perugia, Perugia, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This contribution will present the first results on the radiation resistance of p-in-n Low-Gain Avalanche Diodes (nLGAD) produced at Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK), where signal multiplication is achieved through a high-concentration n-type dopant implant. The sensors are fabricated on thin epitaxial n-type substrates with an active thickness of 55 µm and incorporate a redesigned p ++ ohmic contact and n + gain layer, optimized to account for dopant activation and diffusion effects. Fourteen wafers were produced, exploring different implant depths, diffusion profiles, and employing two n-type dopants, Phosphorus and Arsenic. These devices provide a unique platform to study the donor removal mechanism at concentrations of ~10¹⁶ atoms/cm³, offering key input for the development of radiation-hard p + -n + compensated LGADs for operation at extreme fluences. We will present the first results on nLGAD sensors irradiated with neutrons in the fluence range 10¹⁴-10¹⁵ n eq /cm². The characterization pre- and post-irradiation focuses on the evolution of gain and charge collection, providing a first direct assessment of the radiation hardness of nLGAD in this fluence regime. The study of the radiation resistance of the gain layer will be further supported by the characterization of the n + implant, through the characterization of irradiated Van der Pauw structures.
