sub_talks.title: [NSS-28-08] Insights into DC-coupled Resistive Silicon Detector (DC-RSD) results (#2041)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Ferrero (Autores: M. Ferrero , R. Arcidiacono , N. Cartiglia , G. Bardelli , M. Boscardin , M. Centis Vignali , A. Cassese , T. Croci , A. Fondacci , O. Hammad Ali , M. Durando , A. Morozzi , L. Menzio , F. Moscatelli , D. Passeri , G. Sguazzoni , F. Siviero , V. Sola , L. Viliani , G. Paternoster)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Istituto nazionale di Fisica Nucleare (INFN), INFN Torino, Torino, Italy [2] Università del Piemonte Orientale, Novara, Italy [3] Istituto nazionale di Fisica Nucleare (INFN), INFN Firenze, Firenze, Italy [4] Fondazione Bruno Kessler, Povo, Italy [5] TIFPA-INFN, Trento, Italy [6] Istituto nazionale di Fisica Nucleare (INFN), INFN Perugia, Perugia, Italy [7] CERN, Meyrin, Genève, Switzerland [8] CNR-IOM, CNR Perugia, Perugia, Italy [9] Università degli Studi di Perugia, Perugia, Italy [10] Università degli Studi di Torino, Torino, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Recent progress in sensor technology has paved the way for high-resolution 4D-tracking silicon detectors capable of simultaneously measuring position and time of passage of charged particles. This is achieved through the innovative concepts of Low Gain Avalanche Diodes (LGAD) and Resistive Silicon Detectors (RSD). While standard LGADs aim at excellent temporal resolution, the RSD design also achieves high spatial resolution through signal sharing. This contribution presents the latest advancements in the DC-coupled RSD (DC-RSD) design, which utilizes trenches for cell isolation and signal sharing control. A major milestone of the 2026 campaign is the integration of the FAST3 ASIC, a custom-designed chip specifically optimized for high-precision timing measurements with LGAD-based sensors. For the first time, this readout electronics is employed to characterize the performance of DC-RSD sensors in a test beam environment before and after radiation exposure. We will present the results of an experimental campaign conducted on DC-RSD sensors irradiated at fluences 2×10¹⁴ and 4×10¹⁴ neq/cm². These measurements will represent the first test beam characterization performed on irradiated DC-RSD sensors. The analysis focuses on the evolution of timing and spatial resolution as a function of fluence, comparing the performance of the FAST3 chip with previous readout solutions. The results, obtained at the DESY and CERN test beam facilities, offer insights into the radiation hardness and robustness of the DC-RSD principle.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 2Poster Number:MIC-10-002] Detection efficiency of a lead-loaded plastic scintillator for positron emission tomography detectors : A Monte Carlo study (#1086)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Yamazaki (Autores: M. Yamazaki , M. Sato)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Gunma Prefectural College of Health Sciences, Department of Radiological Technology, School of Radiological Technology, Gunma, Japan [2] Shinshu University, Graduate School of Medicine, Science and Technology, Nagano, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Lead-loaded plastic scintillators are promising candidates for next-generation positron emission tomography (PET) detectors, combining the fast timing response and low cost of organic scintillators with enhanced gamma-ray stopping power due to heavy-element doping. This study evaluates the 511-keV photon detection performance of EJ-256, a commercially available plastic scintillator containing 5 wt% lead, relative to a conventional polyvinyltoluene (PVT) scintillator using Monte Carlo simulations. All simulations were performed in Geant4 (v11.1.1). Monoenergetic 511-keV gamma rays were incident on scintillator blocks with a fixed cross-section of 4 × 4 mm² and thicknesses ranging from 20 to 200 mm in 5-mm increments. For each configuration, 100,000 primary events were simulated, and the resulting energy-deposition spectra were analyzed in ROOT. Detection efficiency was defined as the fraction of incident photons depositing 505-515 keV within the scintillator volume. EJ-256 exhibited a distinct fullenergy peak at 511 keV, whereas the reference PVT scintillator showed only a broad Compton continuum. Detection efficiency for EJ-256 increased from 0.9% at 20-mm thickness to 2.9% at 200 mm, consistent with enhanced photon absorption at greater thicknesses. However, efficiency gains became marginal beyond approximately 135 mm, indicating practical saturation. The energy resolution remained approximately constant at ~10% full width at half maximum across the investigated thickness range. These results indicate that moderate lead loading enhances 511-keV photon detection in plastic scintillators without compromising spectral stability, supporting the potential of EJ-256 as a cost-effective candidate for PET detector modules.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 5Poster Number:MIC-10-005] Exploring CTR improvement through structural refinement of orthogonally stacked PET detector (#1253)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Ota (Autores: A. Sanzen , Y. Onishi , R. Ota)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Hamamatsu Photonics K.K., Central Research Laboratory, Hamamatsu, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Time of flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET) plays an important role in the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease and cancer because it enables localized estimation of lesion positions. Improving coincidence time resolution (CTR) is essential for enhancing the precision of lesion position estimation. Currently, commercially available PET systems achieve a CTR of approximately 200 ps full width at half maximum(FWHM), while the next goal is to reach 100 ps FWHM at the system level. However, commercial PET systems employ thick scintillators for high detection efficiency, resulting in a trade-off between CTR and detection efficiency due to photon transport time spread. To overcome this trade-off, we proposed xDetector, a readout scheme in which detector groups are orthogonally stacked. xDetector employs shorter scintillators than conventional detectors to improve CTR, while maintaining detection efficiency through multiple layers stacked. In addition, by orthogonally stacking detector groups via air coupling, it is possible to estimate the interaction position within the scintillator, which contributes to further CTR improvement. In previous study scintillator crystals and multi pixel photon counters (MPPC)s with 4.2 mm pitch were optimized for CTR measurements together with a high-frequency readout circuit. However, it was demonstrated that the CTR of xDetector with 3.2 mm pitch was 10% faster than that with 4.2 mm pitch, which can be attributed to faster time response of 3 mm MPPC than 4 mm. Thus, in this study, we aimed to further improve CTR by leveraging geometric flexibility and adopting small crystals with the same cross-sectional pitch of MPPCs compared to previous configurations. Through this investigation, we explore the potential of xDetector towards realizing 100 ps CTR.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 8Poster Number:MIC-10-008] A Cost-Effective Neural Network Approach for DOI Estimation in a State-of-the-Art PET Detector (#1688)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Q. Liu (Autores: Q. Liu , D. Arutinov , K.G. Ciantar , G. Wagenknecht , N.J. Shah , C. Lerche)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Forschungszentrum Jülich GmbH, Institute of Neuroscience and Medicine 4, Jülich, Germany [2] Chengdu University of Technology, College of Nuclear Technology and Automation Engineering, Chengdu, China [3] Forschungszentrum Jülich GmbH, Peter Grünberg Institute 4, Jülich, Germany [4] RWTH Aachen University, Department of Physics, Aachen, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Depth-of-interaction (DOI) estimation can reduce parallax error in PET imaging, but conventional pixelated detectors usually require additional DOI-encoding hardware or modified detector geometries. This study investigates a cost-effective neural network approach to recover DOI information from a state-of-the-art air-coupled pixelated PET detector using only compact engineered features, which could be extracted directly by front-end ASICs without digitizing all silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) channels. A Geant4 optical simulation was performed, and neural networks were trained for both 3D position regression and DOI-bin classification. The feature-only model achieved DOI performance comparable to models using the full raw SiPM counts, with an MAE z of 1.107±0.001 mm, and an F1 score of 0.790 for DOI-bin classification, with most classification errors occurring between neighboring bins. These results demonstrate a practical and cost-effective pathway to enable DOI capability without changing the detector geometry, while reducing readout complexity, system cost and power consumption.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 11Poster Number:MIC-10-011] X-ray Imaging Performance of Mg Co-doped Y 3 (Al,Ga) 5 O 12 :Ce for Photon-counting CT (#1759)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Suezumi (Autores: H. Suezumi , K. Kamada , M. Yoshino , L. Gushchina , K. Nakanishi , R. Murakami , S. Ishizawa , Y. Yokota , A. Yoshikawa)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tohoku University, Graduate School of Engineering, Sendai, Japan [2] Tohoku University, Institute for Materials Research, Sendai, Japan [3] C&A corporation, Sendai, Japan [4] Tohoku University, New Industry Creation Hatchery Center, Sendai, Japan [5] Nagoya University, Department of Integrated Health Science, Graduate School of Medicine, Nagoya, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Photon-counting computed tomography (PCCT) has attracted attention because of its potential for high spatial resolution, low-dose imaging. Although semiconductor detectors are widely studied for PCCT, indirect-conversion detectors with fast and bright scintillators combined with silicon-photomultipliers arrays (SiPMs) have recently emerged as promising alternatives owing to their potential for the scalability and cost effectiveness. Though Gd 3 (Al,Ga) 5 O 12 or (Lu,Y) 2 SiO 5 shows an excellent scintillation properties, Kα escape peak of Gd (43 keV), and Lu (55 keV) degrade the accurate photon counting. Instead, Mg co-doped Y 3 (Al,Ga) 5 O 12 :Ce (YAGG) garnet scintillators with lower Kα escape peak (<15 keV) is developed for X-ray imaging applications. The effect of Mg co-doping on scintillation properties results in representing 5-7 folds increase in the light yield of 35,000 photons/MeV@662 keV and the decay time of <50 ns. In addition, synchrotron X-ray imaging performance demonstrates that the spatial resolution of Mg co-doped Y 3 Al 3 Ga 2 O 12 :Ce is comparable to that of LuAG:Ce with the 1 mm sample thickness. Although the density of YAGG:Ce,Mg (5.08-5.33 g/cm) is lower than that of LuAG:Ce (6.67 g/cm), there is a concern regarding X-ray stopping power and deterioration of spatial resolution, the linear attenuation coefficients at 12.4 keV are sufficiently high (273-350 cm −1 for YAGG:Ce,Mg and 943 cm −1 for LuAG:Ce), resulting in X-ray absorption efficiencies exceeding 99.99% for 1 mm thickness samples, indicating negligible influence on imaging performance in the lower energy range. Moreover, we also demonstrate the feasibility of YAGG:Ce,Mg to medical field from the success in clear imaging of small, dried fish. These results show that YAGG:Ce,Mg scintillators are promising candidates for next-generation X-ray imaging detectors and can be applied for indirect-conversion PCCT applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 14Poster Number:MIC-10-014] Optimal Radiator Refractive Index for Cherenkov-Radiator-Integrated PET Detectors: A Simulation Study (#1942)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Ishikawa (Autores: T. Ishikawa , R. Ota , H. Haneishi , T. Yamaya)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Chiba University, Graduate School of Science and Engineering, Chiba, Japan [2] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology, Institute for Quantum Medical Science, Chiba, Japan [3] Hamamatsu Photonics K.K., Central Research Laboratory, Hamamatsu, Japan [4] University of California, Davis, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America [5] Chiba University, Center for Frontier Medical Engineering, Chiba, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In positron emission tomography, time-of-flight information can localize source positions along lines of response. Cherenkov-radiator-integrated microchannel-plate photomultiplier tubes (CRI-MCP-PMTs) with a 3.2-mm-thick lead glass window (n~1.5) have achieved 30-ps coincidence time resolution (CTR). However, improving coincidence detection efficiency remains a challenge, as increasing the radiator thickness degrades the CTR. In this study, we focused on the radiator refractive index. Based on the Frank-Tamm formula, we hypothesized that ultraviolet-transparent materials with a high refractive index would increase Cherenkov photon production, reducing event loss. Furthermore, increased Cherenkov photon detection would improve effective single-photon time resolution, thus enhancing CTR. We tested this hypothesis using Geant4 simulations of point-source measurements with paired CRI-MCP-PMTs incorporating optical and detector characteristics. Assuming wavelength-independent refractive indices from 1.7 to 3.0, we found coincidence detection efficiency increased from 1.1% to 3.0% whereas CTR deteriorated from 41.5 to 49.6 ps. Contrary to our expectations, the reduced speed of light in the medium increased timing jitter, overriding the CTR benefits from detecting more Cherenkov photons. A similar simulation for lead fluoride radiators (n~1.7-2.1)-expected to improve efficiency while maintaining the CTR-showed a worse CTR (46.4 ps) was obtained than for the wavelength-independent cases (~42.0 ps). Wavelength-resolved analysis showed a CTR of 53.3 ps for 240-340 nm photons, which was unexpectedly worse than that of 39.9 ps for 540-640 nm photons, despite the higher theoretical photon production in the shorter band. One possible cause is the steep refractive index dispersion in the shorter band. In summary, while higher refractive indices improve coincidence detection efficiency, they can degrade CTR. Minimizing refractive index dispersion is critical for fast timing.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 17Poster Number:MIC-10-017] Fabrication of diamond detectors with graphitic contacts for tissue equivalent dosimetry (#2040)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 I. Lopez Paz (Autores: I. Lopez Paz , C. Guardiola , G. Rius)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institut de Microelectronica de Barcelona (IMB-CNM, CSIC), Bellaterra, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Diamond-based dosimeters are popular for medical dosimetry in view of their fast response, radiation hardness and tissue equivalence. However, some design improvements to achieve better accuracy in signal readout and approach tissue equivalence are possible by the removal of the metallic contacts, sometimes covering the active area of said devices. In this contribution, we explore the use of a simple processing and scalable solution to obtain non-metal, low Z electrical contact. Thus, the fabrication of diamond detectors with graphitic contacts at the Microelectronics Institute of Barcelona are shown. Several approaches are explored, some of which never utilised before for radiation detector fabrication, namely pyrolytic photoresist film, nickel catalysis and ion surface graphitisation. A prototype of such device using the pyrolytic photoresist film process for the first time has been produced and was tested under a 60 kV X-ray tube. We report the fabrication and preliminary performance results of such device. Although the substrate material quality is not ideal for radiation detection, it was possible to observe radiation response using the PPF as an interface material. The prototype features a linearity better than 3% as tested in a laboratory X-ray chamber, proving it a promising technology for detector operation. Finally, the technology challenges are finally discussed to assess the feasibility of PPF-diamond technology for dosimeter batch production.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 20Poster Number:MIC-10-020] Experimental Evaluation of Classification MLP for Position Estimation in Semi-Monolithic LYSO Cassettes for Ultra-High-Performance Brain PET (#2111)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. A. Karakatsanis (Autores: E. Elmoujarkach , F. Pagano , F. Loignon-Houle , A. J. Gonzalez , D. Sanchez , J. V. Catret , M. Sabuncu , N. A. Karakatsanis , S. A. Nehmeh)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Weill Cornell Medical College, Department of Radiology, New York, New York, United States of America [2] CSIC-Universitat Politècnica de València, Institute for Instrumentation in Molecular Imaging (I3M), Valencia, Spain [3] Oncovision, Valencia, Spain [4] Cornell University, School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Ithaca, New York, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate localization of annihilation γ-ray interaction positions within detector block is essential for achieving high spatial resolution in positron emission tomography (PET). Conventional high-resolution PET detectors often use finely pixelated scintillator arrays resulting in increased system cost due to the larger number of crystal elements and number of readout-channels. Semi-monolithic scintillator detectors offer an alternative solution by enabling signal-based position estimation with reduced readout. In this work, we experimentally evaluated a classification-based multilayer perceptron (class-MLP) for estimating the γ-photons interaction position direction within each semi-monolithic LYSO detector slab across a cassette of 40 mini-modules (mM), each comprised of 16 LYSO slabs coupled to 8x8 SiPMs and read by 16 readout channels, developed for the Ultra-High-Performance Brain PET (UHB-PET) system. Calibration data were acquired from each of the 40 mM, and operated on a benchtop setup using a 0.5mm slit-collimated source translated in 0.5mm steps. The class-MLP used 24 multiplexed readout and classified events into 49 position bins spanning 0-24mm along the monolithic. Independent MLPs were trained for the individual mM. After correction for the finite collimator resolution, the mean positioning-error FWHM was 1.29±0.13mm (range: 0.85 to 1.41mm). The corresponding FWTM was 3.91±0.29mm (range: 3.29 to 4.73mm). Our results demonstrate that class-MLP can achieve near-millimeter detector mean spatial resolution along the monolithic dimension in 20mm-thick semi-monolithic LYSO detectors with minimal variability across all mM of a UHB-PET cassette. Future work will focus on acquiring calibration data from all cassettes in the fully assembled UHB-PET scanner to characterize its system-wide detector spatial resolution using the current calibration strategy per mM.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 23Poster Number:MIC-10-023] AI-based DOI determination for hexagonal monolithic LYSO scintillators with hexagonal cells engraved with laser: A simulation/experiment study (#2234)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Udias (Autores: M. Abushawish , J. Udias , C. Golhen , C. Galindo-Morata , P. Galve , V. Sánchez-Tembleque , L. J. Algarra , D. Pérez Benito , L. Batres , J.J. Vaquero)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Grupo de Física Nuclear, EMFTEL & IPARCOS, Madrid, Spain [2] Hospital Clínico San Carlos, Health Research Institute of the Hospital Cínico San Carlos (IdISSC), Madrid, Spain, Madrid, Spain [3] Spanish National Research Council (CSIC), Institute for Physical and Information Technologies "Leonardo Torres Quevedo", ITEFI,, Madrid, Spain [4] Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, Departamento de Bioingeniería, Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Laser engraving of monolithic scintillators to create pixel boundaries has been around already for some time, with the promise of good pixel identification as in conventional pixelated detectors, but at a much lower cost. However, their use is hindered by the fact that the pixel boundaries are semi-transparent, making it difficult to identify the pixel of interaction with the algorithms applied to fully pixelated detectors. The RETIMAGER project proposes laser-engraved (LE) pixelated LYSO blocks, with optimized transparency of pixel boundaries that might be exploited to obtain depth-of-interaction (DOI) based on the light spread in the SiPM array, while keeping crystal pixel identification. Hexagonal SiPM arrays, scintillators and pixel cells are introduced, improving packing fraction and reducing gaps in between detectors, but adding difficulty when applying ordinary vertex identification strategies. We present the experimental DOI performance for several RETIMAGER detectors, engraved with different optical densities (and thus trasparencies) por hexagons of 1.25 mm side. Data is acquired in a testbench with a collimated source, and employed to train an NN algorithm, to predict DOI. For a 13 mm thick crystal, DOI assignation uncertainty ranges from 2.4 to 3.2 mm FWHM, depending on the trasparency of the boundaries, with the highest trasparency detectors exhibiting the best results. Experimental results follow the trend of the simulations, which can be used to further optimize the DOI performance and to reduce bias.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 26Poster Number:MIC-10-026] Exploring the Performance of Light-Sharing Based Single-ended BGO DOI-PET Detectors (#2339)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y.H. Sul (Autores: Y.H. Sul , M. Yi , G.B. Ko , J.S. Lee)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Seoul National University, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] Seoul National University, Interdisciplinary Program in Bioengineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea [3] Seoul National University, Integrated Major in Innovative Medical Science, Seoul, Republic of Korea [4] Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Department of Nuclear and Quantum Engineering, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [5] Brightonix Imaging Inc., Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Bismuth germanate (BGO) is a high-density and cost-effective scintillator for PET detectors, but depth-of-interaction (DOI) encoding with single-ended readout remains challenging due to its relatively low light yield. This study investigated a light-sharing based BGO detector using paired crystals for DOI encoding. The effects of reflector geometry and lateral surface treatment were evaluated to optimize detector performance. Among the unpolished configurations, the trapezoidal reflector provided the best DOI encoding capability, achieving an average DOI resolution of 5.29 mm FWHM and an energy resolution of 20.4%. Partial surface polishing improved energy and timing performance but degraded DOI encoding capability. After applying timing correction based on DOI and rise-time correction, the timing resolution of the unpolished trapezoidal configuration improved from 427 ps to 353 ps FWHM. These results suggest the feasibility of a single-ended DOI approach for BGO PET detectors with potential time-of-flight (TOF) applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 29Poster Number:MIC-10-029] Experimental Evaluation of Coincidence Time Resolution in LYSO Scintillators with Photonic Crystal Pattern (#2465)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Hyeon (Autores: S. Hyeon , S. Choi , G.B. Ko , M.S. Lee)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Daegu Gyeongbuk Institute of Science and Technology (DGIST), Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Daegu, Republic of Korea [2] Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), Nuclear and Quantum Engineering, Daejeon, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Time-of-flight (TOF) positron emission tomography (PET) performance is governed by the coincidence time resolution (CTR), which is fundamentally constrained by the number and arrival-time distribution of scintillation photons reaching the photosensor. To enhance both quantities, we fabricated nano-scale line- and hole-type photonic crystal (PhC) patterns with a 1.2 μm period on the polished 3×3×20 mm³ surfaces of lutetium-yttrium oxyorthosilicate (LYSO) scintillators via flex-mold soft lithography using a UV-curable optical resin (n = 1.5). Six SiPM coupling conditions were evaluated: bare LYSO with and without grease, and line- and hole-type PhC patterns each with and without grease. The intrinsic scintillation photon arrival-time distribution was reconstructed by deconvolving each measured waveform with the single-photoelectron (SPE) response of a photomultiplier tube (PMT), and the absolute light gain of each PhC geometry was independently assessed in an airgap PMT configuration by comparing the photopeak before and after patterning. PhC-patterned crystals achieved a 42.8% reduction in deconvolved rise time and light gains of 1.20 (line) and 1.18 (hole). To quantify the redistribution of photon arrivals, fractional yields were computed within three time windows - early (0-1 ns), mid (1-10 ns), and late (10-50 ns) - normalized to the total yield over 0-50 ns. The early-window yield increased from 0.7% to 0.9% (a 33.5% relative gain), the mid-window yield rose from 19.8% to 21.2%, and the late-window yield decreased from 79.5% to 77.9%, confirming a redistribution of photon arrivals toward the earlier windows. In SiPM CTR measurements, the line-type PhC combined with grease achieved the best CTR of 180.6 ps, a 29.5% improvement over the bare crystal. These findings demonstrate that nano-scale PhC patterning improves CTR in LYSO-based TOF-PET by enhancing both the absolute light yield and the prompt photon density.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 32Poster Number:MIC-10-032] X-ray fluorescence imaging for breast cancer characterization within the IMMPRINT project (#2531)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Brzeziński (Autores: K. Brzeziński , S. Parashari , O. Elesgaray , K. Kumar , C. Hoeschen , C. Lacasta , M. Mikuz , A. Studen , J. Treis , J. Ninković , G. Llosá)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto de Física Corpuscular (IFIC), CSIC-UV, Valencia, Spain [2] Otto von Guericke University, Magdeburg, Germany [3] Jozef Stefan Institut, Ljubljana, Slovenia [4] MPG Halbleiterlabor, Garching, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract X-ray fluorescence imaging (XFI) is an emerging molecular imaging technique that combines high sensitivity with high spatial resolution, offering significant penetration depth in tissues while minimizing ionizing radiation exposure compared to other existing methods. This makes XFI a promising tool for tumor characterization and personalized treatment. The IMMPRINT project aims to develop a proof-of-principle demonstrator that leverages X-ray fluorescence computed tomography as a novel hybrid modality for tumor profiling, with a focus on breast cancer. The pnCCD silicon sensors produced by MPG HLL, Munich, have been chosen for the proof-of-principle studies. Fluorescence photons are generated when gold nanoparticles are excited by incident X-rays and are detected by the pnCCD. A specific system has been designed to operate up to four pnCCDs, including a cooling system to stabilize sensors' temperature between 0ºC and 20ºC, and it is under construction. Simulations are also performed which support the system design.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 35Poster Number:MIC-10-035] Characterization of DOI-enabled Three-Layer Trapezoidal Pixelated LYSO Detector (#2616)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Parashari (Autores: S. Parashari , K. M. Popov , F. Hueso-Gonzalez , M. Nitta , P. G. Thirolf , K. Parodi , G. Llosa)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto de Fisica Corpuscular (IFIC), CSIC-UV, Valencia, Spain [2] Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität, Department of Physics, Munich, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In the context of the "Small Animal Proton Irradiator for Research in Molecular Image-guided Radiation Oncology" (SIRMIO) project, a high-resolution depth-of-interaction (DOI) LYSO-based detector has been developed for a small-animal in-beam PET scanner. In addition to PET applications, the DOI detector may also be suitable for the detection of high-energy prompt gamma rays originating from excited nuclei such as 12C and 16O, enabling potential applications in Compton camera imaging for ion-beam therapy monitoring. However, the interaction mechanisms of high-energy gamma rays differ from those of 511 keV annihilation gamma rays, particularly in terms of the relative contributions of photoabsorption and Compton scattering processes. In this study, we experimentally investigated the performance of the DOI detector for high-energy gamma-ray detection to gain a better understanding of its applicability to prompt gamma imaging. The detector consists of a three-layer pixelated scintillation block coupled to a 64-channel silicon photomultiplier array. The use of the PETsys TOFPET2 ASIC, employed in the Compton camera MACACOp developed by the IRIS group, is a potential alternative to the current electronics employed in the SIRMIO project, which enables individual channel readout. The study demonstrates the feasibility of operating the detector with PETsys electronics, and characterizes its response with 60Co and 22Na sources.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 38Poster Number:MIC-10-038] PETRARCA: a Positron Emission Tomography Real-Time Analog Re-Configurable ANN Detector (#2827)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Pandocchi (Autores: M. Pandocchi , M. Amadori , M. Ronchi , G. Borghi , M. Carminati , C. Fiorini)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Politecnico di Milano, Dipartimento di Elettronica Informazione e Bioingegneria, Milano, Italy [2] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Milano, Milano, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positron emission tomography systems are becoming increasingly complex due to the growing number of detector channels and the large amount of data generated, especially in total-body imaging configurations. In this work, we present PETRARCA, a positron emission tomography detector system integrating an analog neural network ASIC (ANNA) for real-time edge computing of gamma-ray interaction coordinates within a monolithic scintillation crystal. The system consists of a 32 mm × 32 mm × 10 mm monolithic LYSO crystal coupled to an 8 × 8 SiPM matrix read out by dedicated front-end electronics. The detector architecture includes both a conventional digital acquisition path and a parallel analog inference path based on the ANNA ASIC, enabling simultaneous acquisition of sensor data and hardware neural-network predictions. A first evaluation of the system has been carried out using simulated data and the real ASIC response to emulate a reduced-scale configuration using a 4 × 4 SiPM array coupled to a 26 mm × 26 mm × 10 mm monolithic crystal. The performances of the ASIC in predicting the interaction coordinates were tested, and proved to have a mean absolute error (MAE) of around 1 mm on both the x and y axes. The preliminary results demonstrate the feasibility of analog neural-network edge computing for spatial localization in PET detectors and support further developments toward fully integrated real-time detector systems.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 41Poster Number:MIC-10-041] Scintillation Properties of (Lu,Y)₂O₃:La Ceramic Pixels for PET (#2881)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Glodo (Autores: J. Glodo , S. Kim , A. Kim , M. Muller , C. Sosa , J. Xie , S. R. Cherry , J. Du)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Radiation Monitoring Devices, Inc., Watertown, Massachusetts, United States of America [2] University of California, Davis, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Lutetium oxide-based scintillators are of growing interest for positron emission tomography (PET) because of their high density and high effective atomic number, which provide efficient stopping of 511 keV annihilation photons. Lanthanum-doped (Lu,Y) 2 O 3 (LYO:La) is a transparent ceramic variant that retains the favorable stopping power of Lu 2 O 3 while being easier to fabricate, making it an attractive candidate for next-generation PET detector arrays. In this work we report a scintillation characterization of LYO:La pixels in two geometries relevant to PET, 1×1×10 mm 3 for high-resolution preclinical and dedicated-organ imaging, and 3×3×10 mm 3 for whole-body clinical systems. Pixels were cut from LYO:La ceramic disks, polished on all faces, and evaluated with a range of side reflectors (Teflon, Tyvek, ESR film, and Spectralon) in both flat and upright coupling orientations. We measured X-ray-excited radioluminescence emission spectra, 22 Na (511 keV) pulse height spectra, relative light yield, energy resolution, scintillation decay time profiles, and timing resolution. The results illustrate the influence of pixel geometry, coupling face, and reflector choice on light collection and energy resolution, and show that LYO:La pixels offer a promising combination of stopping power, light yield, and timing performance for PET detector modules.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 44Poster Number:MIC-10-044] Ultrahigh Spatial Resolution Perovskite-based Direct X-ray Imagers for Low-lag Medical Applications (#3045)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Datta (Autores: B. Dunham , S. Motakef , A. Datta)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CapeSym, Inc., Research and Developement, Natick, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dynamic medical X-ray imaging requires detectors that combine high quantum efficiency, low residual lag, and high spatial resolution without the optical spread and afterglow of scintillator-based flat panels. We report a fully inorganic perovskite-based direct-conversion perovskite X-ray imager fabricated from phase-pure orthorhombic Cesium Lead Bromide (CPB) sensor material and integrated with active-pixel readout arrays. Phase-pure CPB was obtained by controlled crystal growth and converted into dense blade-coated films; non-phase-pure starting materials containing secondary phases produced nonuniform films and degraded images, confirming the importance of phase control for reproducible detector performance. The optimized CPB detector demonstrated high linear X-ray response, sensitivity of 55,400 μC Gyair⁻¹ cm⁻² at 30 keV and 0.5 V/μm, a limit of detection of 417 pGyair s⁻¹, a mobility-lifetime product of 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ cm² V⁻¹, and a calculated detective quantum efficiency near 85% at practical dose levels. In flat-panel imaging, CPB imagers reached 6.9 lp/mm at 20% modulation transfer function on a 100 μm-pitch amorphous-silicon array and resolved 20 lp/mm after integration with a CMOS readout. Most importantly for low-lag medical applications, improvements in phase purity and charge-transport stability reduced residual detector lag from 8.9% to 1.1%. These results show that all-inorganic perovskite direct conversion can provide a path to low-dose, low-lag, high-resolution imaging for fluoroscopy, tomosynthesis, dental cone-beam computed tomography, and other image-guided procedures.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 47Poster Number:MIC-10-047] Timing and Spatial Properties of HRPPD coupled to LGSO/LYSO for TOF-PET Applications (#3103)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C.-M. Kao (Autores: Y. Wang , M. Popecki , H. Kim , A. Lyashenko , M. Nemallapudi , M. Minot , C.-M. Kao , C.-T. Chen)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Chicago, Radiology, Chicago, Illinois, United States of America [2] Incom Inc., Research and Development, Charlton, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Large-area microchannel plate photomultipliers (MCP-PMT) such as the Large-Area Picosecond Photon Detector (LAPPD) and High-Rate Picosecond Photon Detector (HRPPD), are attractive for time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET) due to their superior single-photon time resolution (SPTR) and low-cost potential. However, when coupling them with popular TOF-PET scintillators, it was previously reported worse-than 250 ps coincidence time resolutions (CTR) for annihilation photons. In this work, by applying a custom high-frequency (HF) amplifier to the outputs of an HRPPD (10×10cm 2 window) coupled to a 3×3×3 mm³ LGSO crystal and an SiPM-based reference detector, we measured a 144 ps CTR. In addition, we showed that individual crystals of a 4×4 array of 3×3×10 mm³ LYSOs can be resolved using this HRPPD whose output was 4×4 pads having a 25 mm pitch. We also constructed a detector model for investigating key factors affecting CTR. These factors include scintillation yield, light transport in the crystal and HRPPD window, photon detection efficiency and charge collection of the HRPPD, and electronics contributions, with parameters derived from analytical calculations, Geant4 simulations, or experimental measurements. This model predicted a CTR that was consistent with the measured value. Based on this model, a development roadmap with quantitative performance targets and near-term milestones is presented.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 50Poster Number:MIC-10-050] Analytical modeling and inclusion of object scatter in non-TOF 3D PET for low-count data (#1275)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Roser (Autores: J. Roser , H. P. Vo , M. Rafecas)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universität zu Lübeck, Institute of Medical Engineering, Lübeck, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Compton scattering in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is commonly seen as an important degrading factor for the image quality. In particular, object scattering is known to reduce image contrast and distort quantification. Conventional scatter correction techniques do not model scatter directly in the system matrix, despite its potential to better handle low-count data scenarios. In this work, we propose an analytical model for single Compton scattering events and subsequently derive expressions of the system matrix and sensitivity. We validate the obtained expressions with Monte Carlo simulations. Ongoing work includes studying the impact of such approach by using low-count simulated data, and a comparison of the proposed method with conventional scatter correction techniques.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 53Poster Number:MIC-10-053] Noise Modeling of Three Material Dual Energy Computed Tomography with a Pathlength Constraint (#1443)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. E. Ferretti (Autores: A. E. Ferretti , E. Sidky , J.P. Phillips , X. Pan)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Chicago, Department of Radiology, Chicago, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dual energy computed tomography (DECT) utilizes transmission measurements through a sample with two distinct X-ray spectra to produce a two material decomposition. By introducing a path-length constraint to DECT measurements, it is possible to obtain a three material decomposition. In both cases, the stability of the resulting decompositions and noise properties of the virtual monochromatic images (VMIs) are sensitive to acquisition choices like beam energy. We aim to extend a theoretical noise-propagation framework for choosing optimal beam energies and VMI energy for two material decompositions to the three material case. We then demonstrate the utility of this framework for a proposed use-case of contrast enhanced breast tomography. In particular, by assuming linear propagation of noise through material sinogram estimation and filtered backprojection, a compound Poisson noise process in X-ray measurements, and Gaussian-distributed distance constraints, we obtain analytic expressions for the Jacobian of the material sinogram-to-data transformation, the variance of VMI pixels, and the VMI contrast to noise ratio (CNR). We then use the VICTRE software to generate a realistic computational breast phantom, modeled as consisting of glandular tissue, adipose, and iodine contrast agent. For this phantom, we find that tube potential pairings of 30-40 kVp and 55-80 kVp give a high value of the material sinogram-to-data transformation Jacobian determinant, indicating good stability and minimal noise propagation. For this phantom and spectra, we compare analytically predicted and empirically realized VMI CNR versus monoenergy, and find good agreement between them with a maximum CNR of 9.6 for a VMI monoenergy of 65.5 keV in both cases.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 56Poster Number:MIC-10-056] Optimization of Pinhole Diameter in Fully Stationary Multi-Pinhole Brain SPECT: Prioritizing Spatial Resolution via CNN-Based Correction (#1530)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Akatsuka (Autores: T. Akatsuka , K. Ogawa)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Hosei University, Applied Informatics, Graduate School of Science and Engineering, Koganei, Japan [2] Hosei University, Applied Informatics, Faculty of Science and Engineering, Koganei, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Multi-pinhole SPECT enables static data acquisition without rotating the detectors, reducing patient burden. In brain SPECT, particularly for diagnosing neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's, high spatial resolution is critical for visualizing minute regional functions. However, increasing the number of pinholes to secure sufficient sensitivity causes projection overlaps on the detector. Furthermore, physical factors such as gamma-ray attenuation and scattering within the object degrade the quantitative accuracy of reconstructed images. In addition to these issues, a significant trade-off exists regarding the pinhole aperture size. While a larger diameter (e.g., 5 mm) increases photon counts and reduces statistical noise, it exacerbates projection blur and degrades spatial resolution. Conversely, a smaller diameter (e.g., 2 mm) preserves resolution but suffers from increased noise. Previously, we proposed a convolutional neural network (CNN) approach using U-Net++ for a three-detector multi-pinhole SPECT that simultaneously performs overlap separation and various physical corrections. In this study, we applied this framework to brain SPECT to determine the optimal aperture size by comparing 2-mm and 5-mm pinhole diameters. Our results demonstrated that the 2-mm aperture, which maintains spatial resolution, outperformed the 5-mm aperture across quantitative image quality metrics, including NMSE, PSNR, and SSIM, confirming its superiority for detailed brain imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 59Poster Number:MIC-10-059] Validated Optical Simulation for High-Energy Gamma Response in a 3-Layer LYSO DOI Detector (#1668)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Jiang (Autores: S. Jiang , G. Lovatti , F. Evangelista , P. Thirolf , K. Parodi , M. Nitta)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, München, Bavaria, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We have developed a 3-layer staggered LYSO de tector with DOI capability within the project SIRMIO (Small animal proton irradiator for research in molecular image-guided radiation-oncology) for proton range verification via PET imag ing. To evaluate the feasibility of detecting prompt gamma rays for quasi-instantaneous monitoring of proton beams, we propose a workflow that includes the validation of optical simulation settings and the implementation of the saturation effect of the SiPM photonsensor in the Geant4 simulation. Measurement data with 152 Eu, 22 Na and 137 Cs radioactive sources are utilized for modeling the saturation effect of SiPM, and also for validating optical boundary settings in Geant4. The measured spectra of 22 Na and 137 Cs point sources are well reproduced with the proposed simulation workflow. The responses to prompt gamma rays are then simu lated. According to the floodmaps and profiles, LYSO pixel can be identified at 2.2, 4.4 and 6.2 MeV, but the contrast decreases strongly when energy reaches 6.2 MeV. The peak-to-valley ratios drop by up to 53% at 4.4 MeV and 62% at 6.2 MeV (relative to 2.2 MeV), primarily due to the energy deposition occurring more frequently in multiple LYSO pixels. These predictions suggest the detector's potential for detecting prompt gamma rays, while accurately recovering or rejecting inter-crystal scatter events is essential to maintain detector performance at higher gamma energy.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 62Poster Number:MIC-10-062] A Mesh-Type Reference Computational Phantom Platform for Multi-Modality Monte Carlo Simulation in OpenGATE (#1743)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Jegal (Autores: J. Jegal , K.B. Kim , Y.S. Yeom , J. Yang , C.H. Choi , J.-I. Kim , Y. Seo , Y. Huh)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Institute of Radiological and Medical Sciences, Department of Radiation Ocology, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] Seoul National University Hospital, Department of Radiation Ocology, Seoul, Republic of Korea [3] Yonsei University, Departement of Radiation Convergence Engineering, Wonju, Republic of Korea [4] UT Southwestern medical Center, Department of Radiology, Texas, United States of America [5] University of California, Department of Biomedical Imaging and Radiology, San Francisco, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Mesh-type Reference Computational (MRCP) Phantoms provide anatomically realistic tetrahedral organ structures, but their practical use in OpenGATE-based imaging and dosimetry simulations remains limited. In our previous work, a simplified tetrahedral phantom was imported using a tessellated-solid-based workflow and evaluated with heart and body geometries. In this study, we extended the approach to a whole-body tetrahedral phantom framework using parameterised tetrahedral geometry construction and region-aware dose scoring. The updated workflow reads mesh, material, organ-region, and visualization information, constructs the complete phantom in OpenGATE, and enables selected-organ three-dimensional dose scoring while preserving full-phantom particle transport. A copy-number-based filtering method was introduced to associate tetrahedral elements with anatomical regions, avoiding material-name-based selection. The complete phantom, including all anatomical organs, was successfully loaded with a memory usage of 23.84 GB. Three-dimensional deposited energy and dose distributions were generated for selected organs. Multi-threaded performance was evaluated using 8 million x-ray beam particles, reducing computation time from 2453.13 s with 1 CPU thread to 429.43 s with 8 CPU threads, corresponding to a 5.7-fold speed improvement. In the 8-thread simulation, dose scoring for four selected organs, including blood, heart wall, and both lungs, was completed in approximately 5 minutes. These results demonstrate the feasibility of multi-threaded, organ-specific MRCP dosimetry and provide a basis for extending mesh-type phantom simulation to CT, PET, SPECT, and linac workflows in OpenGATE.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 65Poster Number:MIC-10-065] Inter-Crystal Scattering in LYSO-SiPM PET: Integrated Analysis via Geant4/GATE Simulation, CNN, and Multi-Pitch Experiments (#1859)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Deng (Autores: T. Deng , Q. Zhang , H. Zhang , X. Cai , C. Zhang , Y. Yin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lanzhou University, School of Nuclear Science and Technology, Lanzhou, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study integrates GEANT4/GATE Monte Carlo simulations with hardware experiments to investigate and correct inter-crystal scattering (ICS) in Lutetium Yttrium Oxyorthosilicate (LYSO) Positron Emission Tomography (PET) detectors. In the simulation phase, 10 7 valid events from a 511 keV gamma-ray point source were tracked across a 16 x 16 LYSO array (2.1 mm pitch) to analyze 3D energy spread and depth of interaction (DOI) characteristics. To correct ICS-induced parallax errors, we designed a physics-guided Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) with an energy masking constraint to recover the initial interaction coordinates. Furthermore, we established a physical experimental platform using arrays of various pitches (2.1 mm, 3.2 mm, and 4.1 mm). Deploying the pretrained CNN on physical hardware and conducting preliminary iterative training with empirical data demonstrated the predictive potential of machine learning for measured signals. During system image reconstruction, perfect CNN prediction of ICS events could theoretically improve spatial resolution from 1.45 mm to 1.21 mm. By synergistically applying algorithmic ICS correction and DOI information, the full width at half maximum (FWHM) can be further compressed to 0.99 mm. This study provides a conceptual solution and initial attempt for mitigating inter-crystal scattering in future high-resolution PET detectors.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 68Poster Number:MIC-10-068] Design of a brain SPECT scanner based on high intrinsic resolution CZT detectors and multi-pinhole collimators (#1985)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Thielemans (Autores: K. Erlandsson , F. Fraioli , A. Cherlin , B. F. Hutton , K. Thielemans)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University College London, Institute of Nuclear Medicine, London, United Kingdom [2] Kromek Ltd, Department of imaging, Sedgefield, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract SPECT is useful for investigating a range of neurological and psychiatric conditions, such as Parkinson's disease, epilepsy and schizophrenia. Most clinical brain SPECT studies are performed with rotating gamma-cameras with parallel-hole collimators, which results in sub-optimal image quality. Multi-pinhole (MPH) collimators can provide an improved sensitivity vs. resolution trade-off, while Cadmium-Zinc-Telluride (CZT) detectors offer better intrinsic spatial resolution as well as superior energy resolution compared to scintillation detectors. In collaboration with Kromek Ltd, we have developed a molecular breast imaging system based on CZT detectors and MPH collimators. Here we report initial results on designing a dedicated brain SPECT scanner using similar technology. The system will consist of a polygon of planar detectors and will be completely stationary, allowing for dynamic imaging. We performed computer simulations for various design configurations, based on a 20-cm diameter spherical field-of-view (FOV), assuming an intrinsic detector resolution of 0.4x0.4 mm and a depth-of-interaction (DOI) resolution of 1 mm. The simulations were based on an analytical system model, and images were reconstructed using an ML-EM algorithm. Our initial evaluations involved two different digital phantoms: A grid of 7x7 point-sources with a non-zero background; and the Hoffman brain phantom. With the target resolution set to 9 mm at the center and a degree of multiplexing of ~30%, the sensitivity was ~6×10 -4 . An average reconstructed resolution of ~5 mm FWHM was obtained, going from 9 mm at the center down to 2-3 mm towards the edge of the FOV. In conclusion, our initial results show that high image quality can be obtained with this type of SPECT system.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 71Poster Number:MIC-10-071] Modeling analog SiPMs with temporal crosstalk integration for fast timing in medical imaging (#2021)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Kratochwil (Autores: N. Kratochwil , E. Roncali , G. Ariño-Estrada)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California, Davis, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America [2] Barcelona Institute of Science and Technology in Barcelona, Institut de Fisica d'Altes Energies, Barcelona, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) coupled to scintillators are widely used in medical imaging, particularly in fast-timing applications such as time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET) . While significant progress has been made in modeling detector response and correlated noise, recent advances in SiPM technology and fast readout electronics require a reassessment of the full analog signal formation process. In particular, the transition from idealized digital timestamps to realistic analog signals introduces information loss due to bandwidth limitations, electronic noise, and correlated effects such as optical crosstalk. We present a comprehensive simulation framework that bridges this gap by modeling both analog waveform formation and generation-dependent optical crosstalk with explicit temporal structure. The framework enables systematic separation of different degradation mechanisms affecting timing performance. We investigate the impact of bandwidth limitation, electronic noise, and correlated noise on coincidence time resolution, as well as the information loss transitioning form digital to analog signals. Our results show a clear degradation of timing resolution when moving from ideal timestamps to realistic analog readout conditions, in agreement with experimental measurements. Furthermore, we observe that optical crosstalk can, in certain scintillator configurations, improve timing performance by effectively enhancing early signal amplitude, while simultaneously degrading higher-level temporal information relevant for event characterization. The presented framework provides a flexible tool for disentangling these effects and guiding SiPM and readout optimization for future fast-timing detector systems.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 74Poster Number:MIC-10-074] Study on the axial extension of the small-fish PET scanner MERMAID (#2065)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Kolodziej (Autores: M. Kolodziej , J. Roser , S. Seeger , H. P. Vo , R. Kantorek , M. Rafecas)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Luebeck, Institute of Medical Engineering, Luebeck, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany [2] University of Luebeck, Isotope Laboratory of the Natural Science Section, Luebeck, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract MERMAID is the first PET scanner prototype dedicated to study small aquatic animals. Particularly, it aims to support the use of adult zebrafish as a model of human diseases. The current prototype, which consists of four detection modules composed of LYSO:Ce crystals, has demonstrated the capability of providing images with submillimeter resolution. An extension of MERMAID by another four modules is planned, aimed to increase the system sensitivity and allow for shorter scan times, making it more suitable for in-vivo imaging. In the presented work, various configurations for the extended MERMAID system are characterized by means of simulations and tailored reconstruction framework; modifications of imaging protocol for the system are investigated.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 77Poster Number:MIC-10-077] Design and Modeling of BetaBox 2.0: a System for Quantitative Measurement of Beta Emitters in Single Cells (#2271)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Klein (Autores: K. Klein , J.A. Leal Doblado , D. Prout , P. Clark , M. van Dam , A. Chatziioannou)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California Los Angeles (UCLA), Pharmacology, Los Angeles, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Single cell radiation measurements are an integral part of interrogating the biological heterogeneity of cancerous tumors. Identifying cell types present in bulk tumors via FDG uptake can elucidate cell types resistant to treatments, that would potentially be obscured via macroscopic FDG PET imaging. The BetaBox 1.0 was previously constructed to perform these single cell radiation measurements, but suffers from a lack of scale and inability to isolate cells after radiation measurement for further study. To address these challenges, we are constructing the BetaBox 2.0, which will be a high-sensitivity, low-noise device capable of performing many simultaneous single cell radiation measurements via the detection of beta particles in a pixelated array of organic scintillators coupled to SiPMs. The design of BetaBox 2.0 is considered and modeled in GATE simulations, which are used to determine an optimal organic scintillator thickness for the device. These simulations are then expanded on via experimental measurements taken with a SiPM pixel read out by PETsys readout electronics. These datasets jointly suggest the BetaBox 2.0 will be capable of isolating the signal from single cells, and quantitatively assessing their radiation uptake.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 80Poster Number:MIC-10-080] Hardware Ray-Tracing-Accelerated Optical Photon Transport in TOPAS on Apple Silicon (#2319)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Goh (Autores: Y. Goh , K. M. Back , U.-S. Lee , S.-W. Kim , S. Y. Song)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Asan Medical Center, Department of Radiation Oncology, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Optical photon transport in scintillator-based imaging detectors dominates TOPAS Monte Carlo wall time because each primary spawns tens of thousands of secondary photons, and TOPAS itself has no released GPU backend. We present MetalOpticalPhoton, a TOPAS extension that ports the optical physics chain to Apple Metal hardware ray tracing while reusing existing TOPAS material/surface/geometry tables. On an Apple M3 Ultra (80 GPU cores), execution wall time on a 100K-event scintillator-plus-lens benchmark is 25-28× shorter than a 30-thread M3 CPU baseline and about 10× shorter than a 90-thread AMD 7995WX baseline, sustaining roughly 33×10 6 photons/s GPU throughput. Two corrections to vanilla OpenTOPAS-a parallel-world envelope coincident-boundary loop suppressing 75-80% of the sensor-integrated CPU optical fluence, and a primary polarization initialization typo-were required for a self-consistent CPU reference and are relevant to TOPAS optical Monte Carlo independently of GPU acceleration. After patching, CPU-GPU agreement reaches the sub-1% level reported for production GPU optical Monte Carlo (sensor-integrated fluence sum ratio 0.993 ± 0.002 over five seeds).

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 83Poster Number:MIC-10-083] Identification of ICS Pixels in a high-resolution 3-Layer DOI-PET Detector Using a CNN (#2619)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Jiang (Autores: S. Jiang , G. Lovatti , F. Evangelist , P. Thirolf , K. Parodi , M. Nitta)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, München, Bavaria, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We have developed a 3-layer staggered LYSO DOI detector for the SIRMIO (Small animal proton irradiator for research in molecular image-guided radiation-oncology) project, with a crystal pitch of 1.0 mm. Due to the small crystal size, inter-crystal scatter (ICS) events degrade spatial resolution, while discarding them causes significant sensitivity loss. In our detector, ICS events account for approximately 50% of all interactions at 511 keV and result in a median lateral positioning error of approximately 2 mm. To solve this problem, we propose a dual-head convolutional neural network (CNN) for separating the 8×8 MPPC total response of two-pixel ICS events into two individual response matrices, from which the pixel positions and energy fractions can be obtained-a precondition for recovering the ICS events. The CNN correctly identifies both scattering pixels in 69.3% of test events, and in 26.4% of cases one pixel is correctly identified. Among the events with one pixel mismatched, the lateral error of the misidentified pixel falls within 1.0 mm in 91.0% of cases. Meanwhile, the median energy fractions prediction error is 0.016 per pixel. The results demonstrate that CNN-based MPPC response decomposition can serve as the enabling foundation for complete ICS recovery in 3-layer staggered DOI detectors, addressing a limitation explicitly acknowledged in recent physics-based ICS studies.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 86Poster Number:MIC-10-086] Impact of PET energy window extent on trues normalization and reconstructions (#2712)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Noë (Autores: S. Noë , S.A. Zaman Pour , A. Reeves , A. Rezaei , J. Nuyts , G. Schramm , K. Thielemans)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] KU Leuven, Department of Imaging and Pathology, Nuclear Medicine & Molecular imaging, Leuven, Belgium [2] University College London, Institute of Nuclear Medicine and the Hawkes Institute, London, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract PET systems require (among others) normalization corrections for the geometric sensitivity of the scanner, the result of the spatial arrangement of the detector crystals and energy readout area. It is estimated for a given extent of the photon energy acceptance window, and must be re-estimated if the lower energy threshold (LET) is changed, e.g. when optimizing the number of noise-equivalent counts for a given object, or to improve joint estimation of activity and attenuation. To investigate the effect of changing the LET on the geometric sensitivity, we performed a simulation study in SimSET and compared sensitivity sinograms, reconstructions and properties of accepted photons. We found that the effects are dependent on detector location and photon incidence angle, and likely due to the finite extent of the energy readout area.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 89Poster Number:MIC-10-089] MIMOSA: Medical IMaging MOnte Carlo Simulation Algorithms for fast proton therapy range monitoring (#2751)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. D. Garvey (Autores: D. D. Garvey , G. Llosá , F. Hueso González)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] IFIC, CSIC-UV, Valencia, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Monte Carlo simulations play a vital role in many aspects of proton therapy treatment, including proton depth of penetration monitoring. A key limiting factor of full simulation engines is computation time: simulations can take several days, far longer than the time between treatment fractions. This project aims to develop a Monte Carlo simulation software, MIMOSA, for prompt gamma-ray based proton range verification, that is fast enough to be deployed before the next treatment fraction. Clinically acceptable gamma pass rates above 99% for 2%/2 mm and 97% for 1%/1 mm with respect to TOPAS were achieved on both homogenous and heterogenous phantoms. To benchmark computational speed, state-of-the-art GPU codes MOQUI and FRED were tested on the same computer. Comparatively, MIMOSA achieved a notable speed increase, able to simulate 1e9 primary protons with a 200 MeV energy in approximately 3 minutes. Along with maintaining accuracy and increasing computational speed, the project uses the hardware agnostic SYCL standard, and will be available with an open-source license and extensive documentation. Ongoing work is devoted to simulating realistic radiotherapy treatment plans, and including prompt gamma-ray transport and detector response.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 95Poster Number:MIC-10-095] Effects of Beam Filtration on Time-of-Flight-Based Scatter Rejection in Computed Tomography (#3162)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Lee (Autores: J. Lee , S. Kim , G. Ko , W. Sung)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The Catholic University of Korea, Department of Biomedical Engineering, College of Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] The Graduate School of The Catholic University of Korea, Department of Medical Sciences, Seoul, Republic of Korea [3] The Catholic Medical Center of The Catholic University of Korea, CMC Institute for Basic Medical Science, Seoul, Republic of Korea [4] The Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), Department of Nuclear and Quantum Engineering, Daejeon, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Computed tomography image quality is degraded by scattered photons, which reduce image contrast and quantitative accuracy. Time-of-flight-based scatter rejection has been proposed as a method to distinguish primary and scattered photons using their arrival-time differences, but the influence of beam filtration under polychromatic x-ray spectrum has not been fully evaluated. This study investigated the effects of tube voltage and beam filtration on time-of-flight-based scatter rejection using Monte Carlo simulation. X-ray spectrum were generated at 40 and 120 kVp, and four filtration conditions were compared: no filter, 1.06mm aluminum, 0.15mm copper, and 0.6mm tin. Polymethyl methacrylate phantoms with thicknesses of 50 and 200 mm were simulated. Scatter rejection performance was evaluated using the scatter rejection rate as a function of timing jitter from 0 to 1000 ps, and the area under the curve was used as a summary metric. At 120 kVp, tin filtration increased the area under the curve by 11.1% in the 200mm phantom and by 30.6% in the 50mm phantom compared with the no-filter condition. In contrast, at 40 kVp, the filtration effect was small, with a maximum area under the curve difference of 0.010 in the 50mm phantom. These results indicate that tin filtration improves timeof-flight scatter rejection at 120 kVp, whereas filter optimization has a limited effect at 40 kVp.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 98Poster Number:MIC-10-098] Hybrid PGI-PET Imaging for Ion-Range Monitoring in Hadron Therapy (#2044)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Balibrea Correa (Autores: J. Balibrea Correa , V. Babiano-Suárez , J. Lerendegui-Marco , P. Torres-Sánchez , I. Ladarescu , C. Domingo-Pardo , A. Tarifeño-Saldivia , M. Pallás , B. Brusasco , J. Wulff , C. Baümer , S. Rossomme , A. Warnier)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto de Física Corpuscular (CSIC-University of Valencia), Física Nuclear Experimental, Valencia, Spain [2] Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya, Física Nuclear, Barcelona, Spain [3] West German Proton Therapy Centre, Essen, Germany [4] Ion Beam Applications, Louvain, Belgium
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Hadron therapy is a highly conformal cancer treatment technique that enables superior dose delivery to the tumor while sparing surrounding healthy tissues. However, its full clinical benefit is still limited by uncertainties in proton range within tissue, mainly due to the indirect estimation of ion stopping power from X-ray CT images. These uncertainties lead to safety margins that reduce treatment precision. Real-time, high-accuracy ion-range verification is essential to improve dose delivery and further enhance the therapeutic potential of proton therapy. Among the available approaches, PGI and PET are regarded as the most promising, as they provide complementary information. PGI offers direct correlation with the Bragg peak during irradiation, whereas PET yields high-resolution activity distributions from beta+ emitters produced along the proton path. In this work, we report recent developments and experimental results obtained with a hybrid PGI-PET system for in situ proton range verification. The system is based on four high-efficiency two-plane Compton imagers arranged in a cross configuration, specifically optimized to enhance PGI sensitivity at the expense of a reduced PET field of view. Experimental campaigns were carried out at commercial IBA Proteus Plus and Proteus One proton therapy facilities using 100 and 125 MeV pencil beams delivered at minimum clinical currents. Polyethylene phantoms were irradiated at controlled positions and data were acquired during both in-spill and off-spill periods. The first reconstructed 2D images demonstrate that PGI can directly identify the Bragg peak position through the maximum of the PGI distribution over a broad field of view, while PET provides a narrower and higher-resolution distribution associated with the induced beta+ activity. These results confirm the feasibility and complementarity of the hybrid PGI-PET approach and support its potential for accurate, clinically relevant proton range verification.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 101Poster Number:MIC-10-101] Development of a PET/MRI Compatible Fluorescence Microscope for Simultaneous Cell Tracking in a Small Animal PET/MRI Scanner (#2535)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. Renn (Autores: P. Renn , J. Schäfers , N. Jurisa , C. Pilger , T. Huser , K. Schäfers)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Münster, European Institute for Molecular Imaging, 48149, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [2] Bielefeld University, Biomolecular Photonics Research Group, Department of Physics, 33615, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Cell tracking in vivo is a key challenge in translational medicine. Positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offer complementary strengths for this task, yet the validation of tracking algorithms against a reliable ground truth remains unresolved. Fluorescence microscopy can fulfill this role, but its integration into the highly constrained PET/MRI environment poses significant technical challenges. Here, we present a fluorescence microscope (FM) designed for simultaneous operation inside a small-animal PET/MRI scanner, with all custom structural and housing components 3D printed in polylactic acid (PLA). The assembled instrument has a total length of 95 cm and fits within the 35 mm PET insert bore, accommodating sample diameters of up to 21 mm. The imaging probe is rotated via a non-ferromagnetic, friction-driven mechanism, enabling multi-angle acquisition without repositioning the sample, and reliable rotation over the full 360° range was demonstrated under manual control. The system follows an epi-fluorescence configuration with 10× magnification, an excitation wavelength of 488 nm, and a 500 nm longpass filter in the detection path. Characterization with a calibration slide and a Convallaria majalis test specimen yielded a pixel pitch of 0.144 μm/pixel (6.96 pixels/μm), a spatial resolution of 2.32 μm (FWHM), a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 7.21, and a field of view (FoV) of 0.55 × 0.31 mm2 (3816 × 2160 pixels), sufficient to resolve individual cells. These results establish the feasibility of integrating fluorescence microscopy into a PET/MRI scanner and provide the basis for future multimodal cell tracking studies with a reliable optical ground truth.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 104Poster Number:MIC-10-104] Toward Simultaneous PET/SPECT/MR System for Theranostic Imaging (#2904)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Jin (Autores: Y. Jin , J. Du , S. R. Cherry , L.-J. Meng)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Illinois at Urbana and Champaign, Department of Nuclear, Plasma, and Radiological Engineering, Urbana, Illinois, United States of America [2] University of California at Davis, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America [3] University of Illinois at Urbana and Champaign, Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology, Urbana, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We report a design study for a combined preclinical scanner that integrates PET, SPECT, and MRI for simultaneous acquisition of PET, SPECT, and MR images for broad-band multi-isotope imaging capability critical for theranostics applications. The PET subsystem provides a very high-sensitivity and benefits from a wide variety of existing tracers. The SPECT subsystem allows for broad-band multi-isotope imaging capability critical for imaging therapeutic radioisotopes and their daughters. MRI offers unmatched soft-tissue contrast and high-resolution anatomical reference. The PET/SPECT insert consists of 12 detector rings. The central four PET rings are integrated with four rings of micro camera elements (MCEs) that are "looking at" the object through the small gaps between the PET detector blocks. This compact design provides approximately 16% PET sensitivity at the center and 1-mm PET imaging resolution across the 8-cm transverse by 28-cm axial FOV. The 64 CZT SPECT cameras provide approximately 1-mm spatial resolution over a 6-cm transverse and 9-cm axial FOV. To support simultaneous PET/SPECT operation, the design incorporates our previously developed anti-coincidence rejection strategy to suppress PET-induced contamination in SPECT data. Prior F-18/Tc-99m PET/SPECT simulations demonstrated up to 83.7% rejection of scatter contamination in projection-domain analysis, supporting the feasibility of acquisition-level cross-modality rejection. These design elements resulted in a compact and high performance tri-modality imaging platform for simultaneous PET/SPECT/MR imaging for preclinical theragnostic applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 107Poster Number:MIC-10-107] Development of a Preclinical Simultaneous Ultrasensitive SPECT and PET Imager (#3109)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Zhu (Autores: R. Zhu , C. Ling , F. Ahmed , A. Jha , J. O'Sullivan , Y.-C. Tai)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Washington University in St. Louis, Imaging Science, saint louis, Missouri, United States of America [2] Washington University in St. Louis, Mallinckrodt Institute of Radiology, saint louis, Missouri, United States of America [3] Washington University in St. Louis, Biomedical Engineering, saint louis, Missouri, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We previously proposed a Broadband Ultrasensitive Gamma Imager (BUGI) that uses a sensing collimator imager to encode and detect gamma rays without a metal collimator. When combined with fast scintillators, this approach enables simultaneous high-sensitivity SPECT and time-of-flight-capable PET imaging, with potential applications in monitoring alpha-particle radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT). Unlike conventional simultaneous PET/SPECT systems, which use high-energy collimators that reduce PET sensitivity to SPECT levels, BUGI raises SPECT sensitivity toward that of PET.In this study, we evaluated two preclinical BUGI detector designs using GATE Monte Carlo simulations: a pinhole-inspired geometry and a parallel-hole-inspired geometry. The scanner consists of an octagonal arrangement of 8 detector blocks, each containing 1 × 4 arrays of self-collimating mini-modules built from 3×3×3 mm³ GAGG crystals. A dual-isotope cylindrical phantom was simulated with a ⁹⁹ᵐTc background, a ⁹⁹ᵐTc spherical tumor, and an ¹⁸F spherical tumor, with a tumor-to-background ratio of 4:1. SPECT events and PET coincidence events were reconstructed independently using a GPU-based MLEM framework.Both detector geometries produced usable simultaneous SPECT and PET images with comparable tumor contrast . The parallel-hole design showed better background uniformity, improved preservation of the cylindrical phantom shape, and sharper tumor edges.The pinhole design showed an octagonal artifact pattern that may be reduced with increased angular sampling. PET images were sharp and visually similar between the two designs. Future work will focus on developing and validating multi-energy-window SPECT and PET reconstruction methods for the BUGI system.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 110Poster Number:MIC-10-110] A Dual-Ring Super-Resolution PET System (#1259)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C.-M. Kao (Autores: Y. Lang , Q. Xie , C.-M. Kao)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Biomedical Engineering Department, Wuhan, China [2] Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Institute of Artificial Intelligence, Wuhan, China [3] University of Science and Technology of China, Department of Electronic Engineering and Information Science, Hefei, China [4] University of Chicago, Department of Radiology, Chicago, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Building upon previous works that explored the feasibility of super-resolution (SR) positron emission tomography (PET) by applying the principle of structured illumination microscopy (SIM), in this work we propose the concept of a dual-ring SR PET system design. Such a PET system contains a rotatable inner detector ring that serves the dual purpose of creating the needed measurement modulation for performing SIM-based SR as well as increasing event detection to eliminate a major drawback of the previous approach in which the modulator could considerably diminish the imaging sensitivity. We simulated a 2d PET system comprising 576 4.2 mm (transaxial) x 4.2 mm (axial) x 20 mm (radial) LYSO crystals on a 770 mm diameter ring. On the other hand, the inner ring consisted of repeating 2.8 mm-width attenuating material or detector and 5.6 mm-width air. The attenuating material was either 5 mm thick tungsten (W) or 10 mm thick LYSO. The outer detector was 20 mm thick LYSO. Axially, the inner ring was uniform and had the same 4.2 mm length as the outer detector ring. An SR dataset was made of three measurements acquired at three rotational positions of the inner ring. We also considered point-spread function (PSF) reconstruction when not using the inner ring, and also the situation when detector wobble motion was introduced to increase sampling. Our simulation results show that the dual-ring image can resolve 1.2 mm sources in the case of noise-free data and the image quality is visually superior to the PSF and Wobble+PSF images. For a noisy data set, it yields an overall better image quality than the other two SIM-based SR images using W or LYSO modulators for it has higher coincidence detection sensitivity. Quantitative performance evaluation based on the contrast-recovery-coefficient versus the background noise also shows superior results with the dual-ring system.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 113Poster Number:MIC-10-113] Performance Evaluation of a DOI-Enabled Dedicated Brain PETCT System (#1479)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Q. Peng (Autores: D. Liang , Y. Lin , H. Liu , X. Yu , H. Zou , Y. Xu , H. Zhao , J. Tao , W. Zhu , Y. Lin , W. Ma , W. Li , Y. Zhang , D. Shi , J. Zeng , Q. Ren , Z. Xie , W. Liu , Q. Peng)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dedicated brain positron emission tomography (PET) systems can achieve higher sensitivity and spatial resolution than whole-body PET scanners due to their compact detector geometry. However, the reduced detector aperture introduces parallax error, making depth-of-interaction (DOI) capability important for maintaining spatial resolution uniformity across the field of view. In this work, we present a comprehensive performance evaluation of a DOI-enabled dedicated brain PET system based on light-sharing window (LSW) detector technology. The system consists of ten detector panels with an axial field of view of 280.6 mm and employs 2.0 × 2.0 × 20.0 mm³ LYSO crystal arrays with DOI encoding capability. Performance measurements were conducted following the NEMA NU 2-2018 standard, including spatial resolution, sensitivity, count rate performance, scatter fraction, and time-of-flight (TOF) resolution. The measured sensitivity reached 14.31 cps/kBq at the center of the field of view and 15.08 cps/kBq at a radial offset of 10 cm. The peak noise-equivalent count rate (NECR) was 39.54 kcps at 5.11 kBq/mL. The TOF resolution was 298 ps at peak NECR and improved to 281 ps at low activity concentrations. Spatial resolution measurements demonstrated that DOI encoding significantly mitigated parallax error at large radial offsets. Preliminary clinical imaging studies further demonstrated the capability of the proposed system for high-resolution brain PET imaging
