sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 116Poster Number:MIC-10-116] Design and Preliminary Validation of a Heart-Dedicated TOF-PET Scanner with Sub-250ps Timing Resolution (#1614)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Q. Peng (Autores: Y. Lin , H. Zou , D. Liang , Z. Zhao , H. Liu , X. Yu , J. Tao , H. Zhao , X. Zhang , W. Zhu , W. Li , D. Shi , Y. Zhang , Q. Peng)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract General-purpose positron emission tomography scanners often face challenges with the high-frequency motion and small target volumes inherent in cardiac imaging. This study introduces a heart-dedicated positron emission tomography prototype featuring twenty detector panels in a cylindrical geometry with a 493.28 millimeter aperture and a 236.4 millimeter axial field of view. The detectors utilize lutetium-yttrium oxyorthosilicate crystals coupled to multi-pixel photon counters with depth-of-interaction capability. Performance was validated through Geant4 Application for Tomographic Emission simulations, detector bench tests, and in vivo experiments. Results demonstrate a coincidence resolving time of 234 picoseconds full width at half maximum and a spatial resolution of 1.0 millimeter under idealized conditions. Furthermore, electrocardiogram-gated imaging in rat and rabbit models successfully captured eight cardiac phases from end-systole to end-diastole, providing distinct myocardial structures without significant motion blur. These results validate the system's high sensitivity and timing precision, establishing a foundation for extracting functional parameters such as ejection fraction. Future work will implement depth-of-interaction correction across the full field of view to maintain high peripheral resolution for precise cardiovascular research and clinical diagnostics.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 119Poster Number:MIC-10-119] Design and Quantitative Characterization of a High-Performance Brain-Dedicated PET System via Virtual Pinhole PET Technique (#1919)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Chen (Autores: Y. Chen , Z. Yuan , Y. Chen , C. Li , K. Wang , Y. Hou , Y.-C. Tai , J. Jiang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Normal University, School of Physics and Astronomy, Beijing, China [2] Washington University in St. Louis, Mallinckrodt Institute of Radiology, St. Louis, Missouri, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positron emission tomography (PET) is an indispensable tool in neuroscience, yet its efficacy in early lesion detection and advanced brain research is often constrained by the fundamental trade-offs between spatial resolution and sensitivity. To surpass these limitations, this study introduces the NeuroEXPLORER with Insert (NXI), a high-performance dedicated brain PET system that integrates Virtual Pinhole (VP-PET) technology into the NeuroEXPLORER (NX) platform. We developed a comprehensive quantitative reconstruction framework incorporating a full suite of physical correction techniques tailored for the NXI's asymmetric geometry. The system's performance was rigorously validated through Monte Carlo simulations using GATE. Point-source evaluations demonstrated a enhancement in overall sensitivity, driven by an increased proportion of high-resolution insert-scanner (IS) coincidence events in the vicinity of the insert. An ablation study performed on uniform cylinder data, demonstrated the effectiveness of the integrated correction suite, including normalization, attenuation, random, and scatter corrections. In Derenzo phantom experiments, the NXI system successfully resolved 0.6 mm hot rods, a benchmark that remained unresolvable by the standard NX configuration. Furthermore, high-resolution digital brain phantom studies confirmed the system's clinical potential, showing a 5.74% increase in data acquisition volume and a 19.31% improvement in the contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) of gray and white matter compared to the NX system. By synergizing optimized hardware design with specialized reconstruction algorithms, this work verifies that the NXI architecture substantially elevates both sensitivity and spatial resolution, providing a robust technical pathway for the development of next-generation dedicated brain PET instrumentation.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Hohnholz (Autores: J. Hohnholz , L. U. Rauscher , M. Judenhofer , E. Olyaei , H. P. Vo , M. Rafecas , B. Pichler , F. Schmidt)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Werner Siemens Imaging Center, Department of Preclinical Imaging and Radiopharmacy, University of Tuebingen, Tuebingen, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [2] Siemens Medical Solutions USA, Inc., Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America [3] University Hospital Tuebingen, Nuclear Medicine and Clinical Molecular Imaging, Tuebingen, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [4] Institute of Medical Engineering, University of Luebeck, Luebeck, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany [5] Cluster of Excellence iFIT (EXC2180) "Image Guided and Functionally Instructed Tumor Therapies", Tuebingen, Baden-Württemberg, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract To improve diagnostic accuracy in hybrid breast imaging, we develop a dedicated PET/MR breast insert for integration into a clinical whole-body PET/MR system. The final insert consists of two cylindrical detector rings (⌀ = 178 mm, height = 95 mm), each comprising five rings with 32 detector blocks per ring. A sparsely populated (18/32 blocks) single-ring prototype was realized, using dual-layer, depth-of-interaction capable 10×10/9×9 LSO scintillator arrays (1.6×1.6×9.8 / 5.2 mm³) and SiPM readout connected via 30 cm flexible cables to MRI-compatible front-end electronics. Detector calibration and bias voltage optimization demonstrated changes in CRT of up to 100 ps between 42-47V. A bias voltage of 45 V was selected as a stable operating point, maintaining consistent energy resolution and coincidence count rates. Reliable crystal identification was achieved for both layers, with a peak-to-valley ratio of 3.7. At this operation point, the prototype achieved energy resolutions of 13.1 ± 1.8% FWHM (top layer) and 11.8 ± 2.4% (bottom layer). CRT depended on the applied energy window, yielding 383 ± 34 ps FWHM for 430-610 keV and improving to 349 ± 32 ps for a 511±50 keV window, while degrading to 483 ± 175 ps for 250-760 keV. Compared to previous system configurations (>500 ps), the updated readout enabled a substantial improvement in timing performance. These results demonstrate robust energy and timing performance of a sparsely populated, DOI-capable PET/MR insert under realistic integration constraints, including extended signal routing and MRI-compatible system design. The findings support the scalability towards a fully populated double-ring system currently under construction, enabling systematic evaluation of PET/MR performance under stress-test sequences and realistic breast imaging conditions within a clinical PET/MR scanner.

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents a low‑cost small‑animal PET system based on BGO crystals with depth‑of‑interaction (DOI) capability. A 10×8 BGO array (1.5×1.5×20 mm³) is coupled to an MPPC array in a 2×2 configuration, and a 6‑mm light‑sharing window (LSW) encodes DOI‑dependent light sharing. Using a rapid calibration method (vertical line source + histogram matching), the detector achieves an average DOI resolution of 4.9 mm FWHM and an energy resolution of 17.4% at 511 keV. System‑level evaluation shows a spatial resolution of 1.43 mm FWHM at the center and resolves 1.5‑mm hot rods. The design eliminates labor‑intensive mechanical collimation, offering an affordable, maintainable solution for high‑sensitivity preclinical imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 128Poster Number:MIC-10-128] Nested plastic scintillator PET detector geometries have distinct spatial resolution advantages (#2558)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Rädler (Autores: M. Rädler , P. Moskal)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Jagiellonian University, Centre for Theranostics, Kraków, Poland [2] Jagiellonian University, Faculty of Physics, Astronomy and Applied Computer Science, Kraków, Poland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The J-PET (Jagiellonian Positron Emission Tomography) collaboration is developing a large Field-Of-View (FOV) Total-Body J-PET (TB-J-PET) scanner [1,2,3,4] enabling, among others, low dose imaging, short scan times, and dynamic imaging. The key distinctive feature, i.e., the utilization of cost-effective plastic scintillators, could facilitate a wider adoption of large FOV scanners. In this work, we study the benefit of combining the TB-J-PET with a Brain PET Insert (BI) via Monte Carlo simulations. We show that the proposed detector configuration has unique advantages enhancing the spatial resolution. For this purpose, we first developed a rigorous and accurate scheme to estimate spatial resolution from Maximum Likelihood Expectation Maximization (MLEM) reconstructions. We thereby address known challenges of MLEM-based spatial resolution assessment [5], which is discouraged by NEMA standards that continue to rely on the suboptimal Filtered Back-Projection (FBP). We then investigate the impact of the detector geometry on the resolution. The BI uses narrower scintillators than the TB-J-PET (4 vs. 6 mm). We show that this is a resource‑efficient approach to achieve high resolution inside the BI, since the coincidences between TB-J-PET and BI (~50% of sensitivity) have particularly low uncertainty. We also show that this detector configuration is geometrically optimal and suppresses the non-collinearity effect. We back up our findings with theoretical analyses. We also investigate other factors influencing spatial resolution, including event selection, detector scattering, phantom scattering, and positron range. We provide intuitive insights, offering compelling arguments for the experimental realization of the detector geometry under investigation.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 131Poster Number:MIC-10-131] Adapt-PET: A Hardware-Algorithm Co-evolution Framework for Versatile, Ultra-High-Resolution Targeted Imaging (#2661)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Liao (Autores: R. Liao , Z. Yuan , K. Wang , Y. Chen , Y. Chen , Y. Tai , J. Jiang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Normal University, School of Physics and Astronomy, Beijing, China [2] Washington University in St. Louis, Mallinckrodt Institute of Radiology, St. Louis, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract PET remains a cornerstone of molecular imaging,yet the trade-off between spatial resolution,sensitivity,and system versatility persists.While integrating high-resolution inserts into existing systems can enhance performance within a targeted field-of-view,conventional designs lack geometric symmetry in insert-scanner(IS)and insert-insert(II)LORs.This asymmetry necessitates exhaustive,configuration-specific normalization data,severely limiting the mobility and clinical adaptability of the insert.To overcome these limitations,we propose the Adapt-PET(Adaptive-geometry PET)design strategy,which utilizes a "Hardware-Algorithm Co-evolution" approach featuring a movable,DOI-capable insert.The insert geometry is derived by proportionally downscaling the base scanner's transaxial dimensions while maintaining axial consistency,followed by systematic crystal subdivision.This configuration enables a unified geometric mapping strategy that projects IS and II LORs onto a standard scanner-scanner(SS)space.By exploiting intrinsic symmetries,our approach achieves geometric compression ratios comparable to baseline systems,effectively decoupling system normalization from hardware geometry and eliminating the need for re-normalization upon insert relocation.The proposed strategy was validated through GATE simulations of two prototypes integrated with a Siemens Biograph Vision scanner.Positioned at an inner radius of 200-mm,each insert comprised 24 modules of 30×40 subdivided crystal arrays(1.047×0.749×15 mm³)with a sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 137Poster Number:MIC-10-137] Performance evaluation of the third generation of TOF-DOI Prism-PET detector modules (#3032)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Shabani Sichani (Autores: S. Shabani Sichani , Z. Wang , W. Tan , D. A. Muller , J. Qi , G. C.-Y. Chiang , A. H. Goldan)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Weill Cornell Medicine, Radiology, New York, New York, United States of America [2] Cornell University, Physics, Ithaca, New York, United States of America [3] Cornell University, Applied Physics, Ithaca, New York, United States of America [4] University of California, Davis, Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Poor spatial resolution and partial volume effect (PVE) limit PET's ability to accurately quantify radiotracer uptake in small brainstem nuclei such as the locus coeruleus, one of the earliest sites to undergo neuropathological changes in the early stages of tau accumulation associated with Alzheimer's disease. Prism-PET is designed to improve spatial resolution and mitigate the PVE by combining ultrahigh-resolution detector modules with high scanner sensitivity in a practical and cost-effective system. Latest generation of Prism-PET detector module was evaluated using both qualitative and quantitative performance assessments. The module's flood map was examined to assess crystal separation, pattern stability, and the reliability of crystal identification across the detector module. The tested module produced a clear and stable flood map with well-separated crystal patterns, indicating robust event localization. Quantitatively, we measured the detector's energy resolution, depth-of-interaction (DOI) resolution, and coincidence timing resolution. The tested module achieved 10.34% energy resolution, 3.23 mm FWHM DOI resolution, and 337 ps coincidence timing resolution. In the future work, we will report on the performance of the third generation Prism-PET scanner.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 140Poster Number:MIC-10-140] Clinical Validation of MoDeCo: A Motion Detection and Correction Method for a Dedicated Brain PET Scanner (#3187)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. Muñoz (Autores: E. Muñoz , D. Sánchez , P. Bascuñana , M.N. Cabrera-Martín , J.V. Catret)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Oncovision, Image Department, Valencia, Spain [2] Oncovision, CTO, Valencia, Spain [3] Hospital Clínico San Carlos, Nuclear Medicine, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Patient motion during PET acquisition is a well-known source of image degradation. In dedicated brain PET systems such as CareMiBrain (Oncovision), patients occasionally slide downward during acquisition despite head immobilization, compromising diagnostic quality in a clinically relevant subset of studies. We present MoDeCo (Motion Detection and Correction), a modified iterative reconstruction algorithm that detects and compensates for intra-acquisition rigid head motion without requiring external tracking hardware. The listmode data are split into temporal fragments; fast preliminary reconstructions are co-registered to the first fragment to estimate rigid transformations, and a modified MLEM/OSEM algorithm applies them within each subiteration to combine the partial back-projections. Head motion was quantified on 256 [18F]FDG patient studies acquired at Hospital Clínico San Carlos (Madrid), and a qualitative clinical comparison was performed on 15 selected studies. Maximum head displacement during acquisition exceeded 5 mm in 14% of patients. In the high-motion subset (n = 10), MoDeCo was rated significantly superior to standard OSEM in 60% of cases and moderately superior in 20%; mild-motion studies (n = 5) were rated as equivalent. No case showed standard reconstruction outperforming MoDeCo. MoDeCo improves image quality in patients with significant motion while preserving equivalence in those without appreciable motion.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 143Poster Number:MIC-10-143] Impact of beam hardening and detector response function corrections when using photon-counting imaging detectors (#1206)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Hayashi (Autores: H. Hayashi , R. Nishigami , D. Kobayashi , T. Kasue , N. Kimoto , T. Asahara)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Kanazawa University, College of Transdisciplinary Sciences for Innovation, Kanazawa, Japan [2] Kanazawa University, Graduate School of Medical Sciences, Kanazawa, Japan [3] Junshin Gakuen University, Department of Radiological Science, Faculty of Health Sciences, Fukuoka, Japan [4] Okayama University, Faculty of Health Sciences, Okayama, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Photon-counting detectors (PCDs) can perform quantitative imaging by utilizing the differences in the individual energies of X-ray photons, but this analysis requires various corrections, such as charge sharing, to determine the correct attenuation amount. The purpose of this study is to quantitatively clarify the importance of beam hardening and detector response corrections, which can be applied by software processing, when performing imaging with polychromatic X-rays using a line-sensor-type PCD having an anti-coincidence mode. Our PCD was a CdTe detector manufactured by Varex Imaging (pixel size 0.1 mm, thickness 0.75 mm). The response characteristics were calculated using the Monte Carlo simulation code EGS5, and the charge summing effect related to the "anti-coincidence mode" in the four clustered pixels was reproduced in a simple way. The evaluation method involved examining the reproducibility of quantitative values in the effective atomic number (Z eff ) images. Simulations using various virtual phantoms and experiments using a non-destructive testing system with the PCD-type line sensor were conducted. As a result, we demonstrated that by including our proposed correction procedure with the anti-coincidence mode, it is possible to generate highly quantitative Z eff images. In conclusion, this study verified that when using PCDs, it is important to implement software-based beam hardening and detector response function corrections in addition to using the anti-coincidence modes.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 146Poster Number:MIC-10-146] Evaluation of Lead-Free Composite for X-ray Shielding using LD-V1 Film (#1319)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Park (Autores: D. T. Tran , M. Kim , S. Park)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Institute of Radiological and Medical Sciences, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] University of Science and Technology, Radiological and Medico-Oncological Sciences, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study evaluated a lead-free BaSO 4 -silicone composite for diagnostic X-ray shielding (60-100 kVp) using LD-V1 film, combining MCNP6 simulation with experimental validation. Evaluation of a 2 mm thick composite demonstrated shielding efficiencies ranging from 68.79% to 83.50%. Simulated results showed good agreement with experimental measurements, with a maximum deviation of 10.28%. Furthermore, the two-dimensional dose distribution map revealed an average radiation reduction of approximately 60.34% across the material. This result confirms effective attenuation of X-ray radiation across the irradiated field. The dose reduction was also spatially uniform over the entire protected area. In addition, the consistent dose reduction pattern indicates a homogeneous dispersion of BaSO 4 particles within the silicone matrix. These findings establish the BaSO 4 -Si composite as an effective lead-free alternative and demonstrate the utility of LD-V1 film for both quantitative dosimetry and spatial validation in clinical X-ray systems.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 149Poster Number:MIC-10-149] Evaluation of image resolution for Novel Dual-energy X-ray Absorptiometry System (#1441)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Leem (Autores: H. Leem , Y. Ahn , S. Min , M. Oh , C. Kwon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Osteosys Corp., RnD center, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract DXA has evolved beyond standard BMD measurement to include sarcopenia diagnosis and bone quality assessment via the TBS. As TBS is now a recognized modifier in the WHO FRAX Tool , image resolution has become the paramount technical factor determining the performance of DXA systems. This study evaluates the image resolution of iNSiGHT C510 (Osteosys, Korea), the novel DXA model designed for high-resolution whole-body imaging within 3 minutes. The image resolution of iNSiGHT C510 was quantitatively assessed using a line phantom. The system achieved a vertical resolution of 0.63 lp/mm and a horizontal resolution of 0.9 lp/mm, demonstrating superior resolution capabilities compared to the industry-leading GE Prodigy. Anatomical discriminability was further verified using the spine phantom with increasing BMD levels. Analysis of peak-to-valley ratios, which represent the contrast clarity between bone and intervertebral discs, confirmed that iNSiGHT C510 maintains excellent discriminability despite its longitudinal scan architecture. These quantitative results suggest that the system minimizes ROI setting errors, ensuring high clinical reproducibility for TBS calculations that are highly sensitive to subtle signal variations. This study confirms that iNSiGHT C510 provides image resolution equivalent to global standards. Hardware architecture establishes a technical foundation for reducing identification errors in spinal measurements and improving ROI precision. Consequently, iNSiGHT C510 satisfies the performance requirements demanded by the high-precision sarcopenia diagnostic market. Future work will involve integrating ToF technology to suppress scatter noise inherent in wide fan-beam architectures.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 152Poster Number:MIC-10-152] Physics-Guided Retinexformer for Beam Hardening Artifact Correction in Rock CBCT (#1537)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Ma (Autores: Y. Ma , L. Li)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Beam hardening in cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) of high-density rock causes cupping artifacts and nonlinear CT value deviations, hindering quantitative mineral analysis. Conventional deep learning methods often over-smooth microstructures due to a lack of physical constraints. We propose a physics-informed Retinexformer framework that reformulates the polychromatic X-ray degradation as a multiplicative Retinex model. Under this paradigm, the non-uniform hardening field is treated as a degraded illumination map, while the pristine rock structure represents the ideal reflectance. A pre-trained Denoising Diffusion Implicit Model (DDIM), combined with mask-guided moment matching, is utilized to explicitly generate a statistically aligned physical hardening field prior. Furthermore, a multi-scale feature encoder extracts high-frequency structural details from the residuals between the input and the prior to guide the denoising process. Experiments on a 10-cm diameter underground rock dataset show that our method significantly corrects CT value deviations while preserving the fine structure. Quantitatively, it achieves a PSNR of 37.13 dB and an SSIM of 0.940, reducing RMSE to 0.0149-significantly outperforming SOTA baselines (NAFNet, Retinexformer, MambaIRv2). Notably, our model achieves this with only 2.00M parameters and 19.42G FLOPs, offering a highly efficient and interpretable solution for CT artifacts correction in dense media.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 158Poster Number:MIC-10-158] Mitigating Scatter-Induced BMD Errors in Wide Fan-Beam DXA Using Anti-Scatter Grids (#2260)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Oh (Autores: M. Oh , Y. Ahn , S. Min , H. Leem , C. Kwon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Osteosys Corp., R&D Center, seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) is the clinical standard for bone mineral density (BMD) assessment. Modern wide fan-beam DXA architectures (fan angle ≥ 20°) shorten whole-body acquisition to under three minutes but enlarge the irradiated volume, raising the scatter-to-primary ratio with field size. Conventional DXA omits anti-scatter grids, relying on the long object-to-image-detector distance (OID > 580 mm) for scatter rejection via the air-gap effect. Whether this assumption holds for wide fan-beam DXA has not been directly tested. We investigated residual scatter in an experimental wide fan-beam DXA system using three complementary experiments on step-wedge and anthropomorphic phantoms. First, we implemented an outer-channel scatter probe and detected measurable scatter at outer channels even at OID > 580 mm. Second, with an 8:1 anti-scatter grid we quantified the dual-energy mass attenuation difference Δ(μ/ρ); at the maximum phantom configuration (25 cm polycarbonate + 4.9 cm aluminum), scatter caused an inversion of Δ(μ/ρ) in the no-grid configuration (−0.018 cm²/g); the 8:1 grid restored Δ(μ/ρ) to 0.076 cm²/g - a partial recovery only. Third, a 14:1 grid successfully suppressed the spurious BMD elevation. Compared to the no-grid baseline which showed a severe thickness-dependent BMD bias (coefficient of variation of approximately 19%), the 14:1 grid reduced the variability to 3% across 0-140 mm of added polycarbonate layers. These findings establish that explicit scatter compensation - whether through anti-scatter grids or software-based correction - is essential for thick-patient measurements at wide fan-beam DXA.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 161Poster Number:MIC-10-161] Empirical Decomposition for Quantification of Multi-Contrast-Agent (#2472)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Wang (Autores: P. Chen , Z. Wang , C. Wang , T. Jia , S. Xie , C. Wei)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institute of High Energy Physics, Beijing Engineering Research Center of Radiographic Techniques and Equipment, Beijing, China [2] University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, School of Nuclear Science and Technology, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Contrast agents play an important role in spectral CT because they enhance the visibility of vessels, organs, tumors, and lesions, thereby improving image interpretation and lesion identification. However, accurately quantitative contrast-agent decomposition remains challenging. Conventional material decomposition algorithms still suffer from limited quantitative accuracy even in contrast-agent imaging. This problem becomes more severe when multiple contrast agents coexist. To address this limitation, we propose an empirical multi-agent decomposition method. The proposed method first applies conventional empirical decomposition to obtain initial decomposition results and estimate the corresponding decomposition errors. Then, bivariate error surfaces are constructed to model the relationship between iodine and gadolinium concentrations and their decomposition errors. These fitted error surfaces are subsequently used to compensate for the errors produced by conventional empirical decomposition. Simulated experiments demonstrate that the proposed method can simultaneously decompose iodine and gadolinium with improved quantitative accuracy, and the global MAPE and NRMSE are effectively reduced compared with the image-domain decomposition method for the test phantoms.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 164Poster Number:MIC-10-164] Empirical Correction of Detector Response for Quantitative X-Ray Transmission Modelling and its Application to Computed Tomography (#2574)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Q. Chen (Autores: Q. Chen , B. James , Y. Liu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation, Mineral Resources, Lucas Heights, Australia
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract X-ray computed tomography (CT) relies fundamentally on accurate transmission measurements to reconstruct meaningful attenuation maps. However, detector response non-linearity systematically biases transmission measurements away from the values predicted by the polychromatic forward model, propagating these errors into reconstructed data. To address this, a combined spectral modelling and empirical calibration framework was developed for a high-resolution flat-panel detector, enabling prediction of measured transmission values across a broad range of sample thicknesses and compositions. A polychromatic spectral model was constructed by combining tube-spectrum estimates with Beer-Lambert attenuation using NIST/XCOM coefficients, convolved with an effective CsI scintillator response function. Predicted transmission values were compared against experimental measurements obtained using high purity elemental foils spanning a wide range of thicknesses. Consistent and reproducible discrepancies between modelled and measured values revealed a structured detector response non-linearity not captured by the forward model. A first-order empirical correction was derived from the model-experiment residuals, yielding a fitted detector-response exponent of α = 1.47 applied to model predictions to reproduce experimental detector behaviour. The calibrated model can therefore generate realistic transmission values consistent with measured detector output across a range of sample configurations. These findings highlight the broader potential of this framework, particularly for dual-energy CT, where material decomposition relies critically on the relative contrast between acquisitions at different tube voltages. A calibrated forward model of this kind offers a pathway toward improved relative CT threshold accuracy, supporting more reliable separation of materials with overlapping attenuation properties and more robust quantitative interpretation of reconstructed data.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 167Poster Number:MIC-10-167] Synthetic generation of the dental anatomy for cone-beam CT simulation from patient data (#2593)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 I. Tatachak (Autores: I. Tatachak , L. Kabongo , N. Papadakis , X. Ripoche , S. Rit)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Creatis, INSA-Lyon, Universite Claude Bernard Lyon 1, CNRS, Inserm, CREATIS UMR 5220, U1294, F-69373, Lyon, France [2] Univ. Bordeaux, CNRS, Inria, Bordeaux INP, IMB, UMR 5251, Bordeaux, France [3] ACTEON Group, Mérignac, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This paper develops a pipeline for generating synthetic cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) projections from real dental CBCT acquisitions, providing a reference for supervised learning. To this end, we segment and synthesize fine structures from real CBCT acquisitions to obtain a material map of the head volume. Using the characteristics of the CBCT scanner, notably the effective spectrum, we simulate the acquisitions by modeling a polychromatic X-ray source and adding compound Poisson noise. The results demonstrate the realism of the generated synthetic CBCT acquisitions, as well as the plausibility of the simulated artifacts.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 170Poster Number:MIC-10-170] Image Quality Evaluation of Cone Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) in an O-arm Fluoroscopy Machine Using the SedentexCT IQ Phantom (#2974)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J.P.R. S. De Guzman (Autores: J.P.R. S. De Guzman , A. Peralta)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Philippine General Hospital, Department of Radiology, Manila, Philippines [2] University of Santo Tomas, The Graduate School, Manila, Philippines
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The O-arm fluoroscopy machine, an application of cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) for interventional procedures, lacks a dedicated image quality (IQ) phantom for system image performance evaluation. This study aimed to investigate the viability and limitations of using the SedentexCT IQ phantom, a phantom originally designed for dental CBCT, to assess the image quality of resultant CBCT images of an interventional O-arm unit. Six CBCT image quality tests were performed (i.e. Uniformity, Image Noise, Geometric Accuracy, Voxel Intensity Values, Contrast Resolution, and Spatial Resolution), and corresponding parameters were assessed as baseline data in the low dose, standard dose, high dose, and enhanced cranial modes of the O-arm machine. The procedures were structured to the EFOMP-ESTRO-IAEA CBCT quality control protocol. An observed limitation of the phantom was the evaluation of the spatial resolution (lp/mm), since the lowest resolution of the SedentexCT IQ phantom is 1.0 lp/mm. Overall, since the phantom was applicable for the required CBCT image quality tests, the SedentexCT IQ phantom can be considered as a viable tool for image quality testing of the O-arm machine.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 173Poster Number:MIC-10-173] Validation of conventional mammography material decomposition using VICTRE simulated breast data (#3018)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 X. Pan (Autores: J. Phillips , E. Sidky , I. Reiser , Z. Zhang , K. Kulkarni , X. Pan)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The University of Chicago, Department of Radiology, Chicago, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The purpose of this work is to validate basis material decomposition in breast cancer screening mammography using a conventional single-kV scan. We employ mammography system physics modeling and a pathlength constraint to enable estimation of the basis material images. Using 3D breast phantoms and low noise Monte Carlo projection data generated with the FDA VICTRE software, we decompose transmission data into pathlength basis images of adipose and glandular tissue. The decomposition recovered adipose and glandular maps with mean absolute errors of 3.47 mm and 1.83 mm respectively. Accuracy along the skinline and nipple is degraded due to material mismatch. The results indicate material decomposition in mammography using a single energy acquisition is feasible to enable the quantitative recovery of adipose and glandular material maps.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 179Poster Number:MIC-10-179] Development of a 64-Channel Energy and Timing Acquisition System for TOF-DXA (#3146)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S.-H. Chun (Autores: S.-H. Chun , J. Jung , J. Nam , S. Kwon , J.H. Jung , Y. Choi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Sogang University, Department of Electronic Engineering, Intelligent Signal Processing System (ISPS) Laboratory, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Time-of-flight dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (TOF-DXA) is proposed as a method for enhancing material decomposition by incorporating timing information into conventional dual-energy attenuation measurements. In this study, a 64-channel energy and timing acquisition system was developed for TOF-DXA. The detector consisted of a 64-channel LYSO array with a pixel size of 3 × 3 × 3 mm³, coupled to four 16-channel Broadcom NUV-MT SiPM arrays. Detector signals were split into independent energy and timing paths. For the energy path, signals were processed through differential amplifiers and digitized using 10-bit multichannel analog-to-digital converters. Timing signals were processed using front-end comparators and a Kintex-7 FPGA-based tapped delay line (TDL) time-to-digital converter. The TDL was implemented using a single-chain architecture based on CARRY4 primitives. This dual-path configuration enabled synchronized acquisition of energy and timing information on an event-by-event basis. The FPGA logic measured energy values through peak detection and synchronized them with timing data stored in a timing FIFO to ensure event-by-event alignment. The energy resolution was evaluated using a Co-57 source at 122 keV, while the timing resolution was evaluated in coincidence with a reference detector using a Na-22 source. X-ray spectra were acquired using an X-ray generator operated at 83 kVp and 0.2 mA with a Ce filter (K-edge: 40.4 keV) to evaluate system performance in the DEXA energy range. The energy resolution was 16.3% at 122 keV, and the coincidence timing resolution was 104 ps at 511 keV. The low- and high-energy peaks were clearly resolved in the acquired X-ray spectrum. These results demonstrated that the developed 64-channel acquisition system could simultaneously measure energy and timing information for TOF-DXA. Optimization of the acquisition board is currently in progress, and comprehensive system performance results will be presented at the conference.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 182Poster Number:MIC-10-182] GARM: Geometry-Aware Reconstruction Method for Static CT Generalizable across Diverse Scanning Strategies (#1076)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. Song (Autores: P. Song , C. Chen , Z. Chen , Y. Xing)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [2] Tsinghua University, Key Laboratory of Particle & Radiation Imaging, Ministry of Education, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Static computed tomography (SCT) enables fast, task-specific imaging through ultrafast and flexible firing among distributed focal spots. However, it introduces irregular and incomplete data acquisition, which poses great challenges to reconstruction. In this work, we propose Geometry-Aware Reconstruction Method (GARM) for SCT across diverse scanning strategies. The Geometry-Guided Dimension Reduction (G2DR) Network first transforms irregular 3D projections into slice-wise 2D fan-beam projections using geometric information derived from ray positions. A 2D dual-domain network then suppresses sparse-view artifacts guided by geometric and Radon-space information. Simulated experiments demonstrate that GARM achieves high-quality reconstruction from irregular and incomplete projections with strong generalization capability across diverse scan strategies.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 185Poster Number:MIC-10-185] Impact of Small-Angle Event Selection in Compton Cone Imaging (#1168)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. Medina (Autores: E. Medina , M. Kolstein , J. Caravaca , M. Chmeissani , B. Mehadji , G. Ariño-Estrada)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institut de Física d'Altes Energies - Barcelona Institute of Science and Technology (IFAE-BIST), Medical Physics Group, Bellaterra, Barcelona, Spain [2] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, CA, United States of America [3] University of California Davis, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Davis, CA, United States of America [4] University of California Davis, Department of Radiology in the School of Medicine, Davis, CA, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Compton cameras are imaging systems that detect Compton-scattered gamma rays using two position-sensitive detectors, typically called the scatterer and the absorber. Each interaction pair defines a Compton cone enabling three-dimensional image reconstruction. In this work, we investigate how the selection of low scattering angle events influences image quality. A GATE-based simulation of a Si/CdTe Compton camera system was developed to generate Compton cone data. A 511 keV rod phantom with source cylinders of radii from 1.5 mm to 0.75 mm was implemented, and 100 M primary photons were simulated. Images were reconstructed from subsets obtained by applying a maximum threshold on Compton electron energy in the scatterer. Energy selections of 5, 10, and 15 keV (corresponding to scattering angles of 8°, 11.4°, and 14°) were used, along with a reference dataset without any energy cut for standard CC reconstruction comparison. We show that for two rods of 1.5 mm and 1.25 mm radius, the peak-to-valley ratio (PVR) without any energy selection is approximately 3.5. By selecting energy deposits below 15 keV (14°) the PVR nearly triples, with further improvements observed for lower energy thresholds, reaching a value of 13.8 for a 5 keV energy cut For smaller rod radii, the PVR remains below 3, although low-energy event selection still yields enhancements of approximately 60%, 30%, and 17% for radii of 1 mm, 0.75 mm, and 0.51 mm, respectively. These findings support event-selection strategies for CC systems capable of triggering at low energies in the scatterer. Restricting to the most informative events can reduce computational load and improve reconstruction performance, with the strongest benefits observed for rods with radii above 1 mm.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 188Poster Number:MIC-10-188] Deep Learning-based 3D SPECT Reconstruction from Biplanar Projections and CT Scout Views (#1262)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Huang (Autores: J. Huang , Q. Yao , H. Han , H. Xie , G. Cao , Y. Lv)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] ShanghaiTech University, School of Biomedical Engineering,, Shanghai, China [2] Shanghai United Imaging Healthcare, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dual-view SPECT planar imaging is a widely used method in clinical bone scan screening due to its efficiency and low radiation dose compared to whole-body SPECT/CT imaging. However, its diagnostic efficacy is often limited by anatomical overlap and the absence of depth information. Achieving high-quality 3D image from only two projections remains a challenge for traditional methods. Furthermore, existing deep learning-based approaches for ultra-sparse-view SPECT reconstruction are mainly designed for cardiac imaging and cannot be directly adapted to bone scintigraphy. To address these limitations, we propose a deep learning framework for 3D SPECT reconstruction from orthogonal biplanar projections and CT Scout views. The framework comprises a 3D condition map generation module and a structure-guided 2D conditional diffusion module, facilitating a two-stage reconstruction process including an initial coarse reconstruction followed by iterative refinement via a diffusion model. Quantitative results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves better recovery coefficients for bone tissues and metastatic lesions, as well as improved LPIPS scores for perceptual quality. Qualitative assessments further reveal that the reconstructed images exhibit highly realistic textures and shows strong agreement with standard full-view scans. This method provides a fast, low-radiation 3D reconstruction strategy with considerable potential to optimize clinical bone scan workflows, enhance diagnostic accuracy and improve patient comfort.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 191Poster Number:MIC-10-191] The Inverse Problem of Spatiotemporal Emission Reconstruction from Prompt Gamma Timing Data (#1478)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Werner (Autores: J. Werner , M. Schmidt , J. Roser , J. Kasprzak , Y. Feng , V. Ferrero , F. Pennazio , M. Rafecas)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Luebeck, Institute of Medical Engineering, Lübeck, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany [2] Universitá degli Studi di Torino, Department of Physics, Torino, Italy [3] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Torino, Torino, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Reconstructing the emission distribution of prompt gamma radiation in time and space offers a unique advantage: it reveals the primary particle motion inside the irradiation target during particle therapy. Similar to typical tomographic emission reconstruction scenarios, the measurement process based on Prompt Gamma Timing can be described by a linear system model and Poisson-distributed measurement data. However, the structure of the emission domain (emission time and position of the prompt gammas) and the detection domain (detector index and event time difference relative to a primary particle signal) are unique. In this work, we inspect some features of this inverse problem and analyze related fundamental limitations based on reconstructions with ideal data and the singular value decomposition of the system matrix. The results show a need for regularization and help identify possible improvements to the approach. Additionally, understanding this inverse problem in-depth also supports the development of other Prompt-Gamma-Timing-based techniques.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 194Poster Number:MIC-10-194] Recent updates to STIR, a community effort of a quarter century (#1658)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Efthimiou (Autores: N. Efthimiou , D. Deidda , V. Dao , Z. Li , C. Tsoumpas , K. Thielemans)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] UMCG, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Groningen, Netherlands [2] National Physical Laboratory, Teddighton, United Kingdom [3] UCL, Institute of Nuclear Medicine, London, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Software for Tomographic Image Reconstruction (STIR) is a long-standing open-source platform for PET and SPECT reconstruction that has supported tomographic imaging research for more than two decades. Public STIR documentation dates to the early 2000s, and the project remains actively developed, with a current public release in November 2025 and a GitHub repository reporting 9,409 commits, 146 stars, and 108 forks. Recently there have been major contributions, that have expanded substantially the framework in scanner support, motion correction, and raw-data interoperability. Advances include support for the Siemens Biograph Vision Quadra long axial field-of-view PET/CT system, a data-driven rigid head motion-correction workflow for brain PET, and PETSIRD as a vendor-independent raw-data interface. Here, we demonstrate the impact of motion on clinically relevant quantitative measures. Together, these developments reinforce STIR's position as a mature, community-driven platform for modern PET reconstruction research.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 197Poster Number:MIC-10-197] Developments in fabrication and design flexibility of amorphous silicon microchannel plates (#2584)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Konstantinou (Autores: G. Konstantinou , L. Barraud , C. Baillif , N. Wyrsch)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] EPFL, Neuchatel, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The technology of amorphous silicon-based micro-channel plates (AMCPs) uses a versatile approach to stack hydrogenated amorphous silicon in thicknesses up to 100 μm, using plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) and etch microchannels of diameter below 2 μm every 5 μm, on a hexagonal pattern, by deep reactive ion etching. With gains up to 1000 for reverse bias less than 300 V, the design is possible to build on arrays of sensitive transimpedance amplifiers, integrated in read-out circuits with high channel density, such as for instance 15 by 15 μm. This ensures single photon detection with quantum efficiency up to 30% and noise rates below 50 Hz/cm², if combined with state of the art photocathodes such as the hi-QE from Photonis. Current fabrication runs focus on direct integration of the stack on ASICs, to be integrated with the photocathode over the next months. Measurements show timing response with jitter below 10 ps, making this high-precision photodetector ideal for radiation detectors combining ultra-fast photon emission and low light yield, such as Cherenkov.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 200Poster Number:MIC-10-200] A Universal Geometric Calibration Method for CBCT Systems with Arbitrary Trajectories (#1877)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Jia (Autores: T. Jia , C. Wang , B. Liu , Y. Wang , L. Wei , Z. Wang , C. Wei)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institute of High Energy Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing Engineering Research Center of Radiographic Techniques and Equipment, Beijing, China [2] University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Nuclear Science and Technology, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a universal calibration method based on spatial vector decomposition to address the challenge of dynamically changing and difficult-to-calibrate geometric parameters in cone-beam computed tomography (CT) systems with complex scanning trajectories. The proposed method enables high-precision and robust calibration for a broad range of CT imaging systems. First, the projection matrix at each scanning angle is computed using a calibration phantom. This matrix is then decomposed into spatial vectors representing the system's geometric state, including the position of the X-ray source, the detector reference point, and orientation vectors. These vectors can be directly used for image reconstruction or converted into device-specific parameters. A vector-based detector mapping algorithm is also introduced to facilitate efficient projection data correction. Experiments on Micro-CT, CL and robotic-arm CT systems confirm that the method significantly improves image clarity, suppresses artifacts and distortions, and accurately reconstructs the actual motion trajectories of the X-ray source and detector. The method demonstrates high accuracy and versatility, providing a reliable calibration solution for high-degree-of-freedom CT systems.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 203Poster Number:MIC-10-203] CT-less Attenuation Maps as Priors for Robust Joint Activity-Attenuation Estimation in TOF and Non-TOF PET (#2048)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. Emond (Autores: E. Emond , Z. Chalampalakis , A. Mehranian , K.-H. Su , S. Ahn , F. Kotasidis)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] GE HealthCare GmbH, Düsseldorf, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [2] GE HealthCare, Buc, France [3] GE HealthCare, Oxford, United Kingdom [4] GE HealthCare, Zurich, Switzerland [5] GE HealthCare, Waukesha, United States of America [6] GE HealthCare Technology and Innovation Center, Niskayuna, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract CT‑less attenuation correction in PET has gained increasing interest as a means to reduce patient radiation exposure, with recent AI‑based methods providing anatomically plausible attenuation estimates from emission data and complementary inputs. However, residual inaccuracies in such attenuation maps can still impact PET quantification. Joint estimation of activity and attenuation provides a physics‑based framework to mitigate these effects, but remains less well constrained in the absence of time‑of‑flight (TOF) information. This work evaluates the use of AI‑generated CT‑less attenuation maps as spatial priors for joint estimation of activity and attenuation in TOF and non‑TOF PET. Using a maximum‑a‑posteriori formulation, the CT‑less attenuation map is employed both as an initial estimate and as a regularising prior. Experiments on paediatric PET datasets show that this approach stabilises joint reconstruction and recovers anatomically plausible attenuation maps, including in the non‑TOF case. These results support the use of CT‑less attenuation maps as effective priors for robust PET reconstruction.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 206Poster Number:MIC-10-206] Convergence-Informed AI-Assisted Reconstruction for Dual-Panel PET Imaging (#2078)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Saberi Manesh (Autores: A. Saberi Manesh , M. Amini , Y. Salimi , G. Hajianfar , K. Doroud , H. Arabi , H. Zaidi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Geneva, Department of Medical Imaging, Geneva University Hospital, Geneva, Genève, Switzerland [2] Picotech, St Genis Pouilly, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dual-panel positron emission tomography (PET) scanners offer compact, cost-effective, and organ-dedicated imaging geometries, but their limited angular coverage introduces anisotropic resolution loss and elongation artifacts. This work presents a convergence-informed artificial intelligence (AI)-guided iterative reconstruction framework for the ProVision dual-panel PET system. The proposed approach exploits voxel-wise convergence information (VCI) extracted from the first 15 iterations of list-mode multi-ray maximum likelihood expectation maximization (MLEM) reconstruction. VCI was incorporated into five reconstruction strategies: analytic VCI-guided MLEM, multilayer perceptron-based VCI-guided MLEM, standalone 3D Swin-UNet reconstruction, AI-guided maximum a posteriori reconstruction (AI-MAP), and AI-initialized MLEM (AI-MLEM). Training and evaluation were performed using Monte Carlo simulations, a scaled NEMA image quality phantom, an external simulated patient test set, and an experimental anthropomorphic pelvis phantom. Compared with conventional MLEM, the proposed hybrid methods substantially improved contrast recovery, background uniformity, and geometric fidelity. AI-MLEM increased the contrast recovery coefficient from 53.16% to 82.35%, reduced background variability from 12.38% to 8.25%, and reduced the elongation ratio from 1.48 to 1.15. On the external simulated patient test set, AI-MLEM improved structural similarity from 0.446 to 0.816 and reduced normalized mean absolute error from 0.405 to 0.215. Experimental phantom results further confirmed improved lesion conspicuity and reduced vertical spreading. These results demonstrate that early-iteration convergence behavior provides useful voxel-wise guidance for mitigating limited-angle artifacts while preserving data consistency in dual-panel PET reconstruction.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 209Poster Number:MIC-10-209] Anatomically Guided Adaptive Gaussian Representation for PET Image Reconstruction (#2133)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Li (Autores: Z. Li , Z. Wang , X. Zhao , Y. Yuluo , Y. Huang , Z. Xie)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Peking University, The Institute of Medical Technology, Beijing, China [2] Peking University, National Biomedical Imaging Center, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We propose a continuous Gaussian representation for PET reconstruction, modeling the activity distribution with normalized Gaussian basis functions. This reformulates PET reconstruction as a compact differentiable optimization problem by coupling an analytical Gaussian forward model with Poisson likelihood. The key component is an anatomically guided adaptive density control strategy, which dynamically prunes, splits, and clones Gaussian primitives according to contribution, gradient, and MRI-derived mask constraints, thereby allocating representation capacity to informative regions while suppressing redundant components. Image-domain Huber-TV regularization is incorporated to stabilize reconstruction. Experiments on 2D simulations demonstrate competitive performance across count levels and clear advantages under low-count conditions, suggesting the potential of adaptive continuous representations for PET reconstruction.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 212Poster Number:MIC-10-212] MRI guided PET reconstruction in meningioma [ 68 Ga]DOTATOC patients, pituitary adenoma [ 18 F]FET, and neurodegenerative [ 18 F]FDG patients (#2361)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. L. Andersen (Autores: E. S. Christensen , A. Clemmensen , P. Lehmann , J. Cabello , O. M. Henriksen , I. Law , A. Kjaer , T. L. Andersen)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Copenhagen University Hospital, Department of Clinical Physiology and Nuclear Medicine, Copenhagen, Denmark [2] University of Copenhagen, Department of Biomedical Sciences, Cluster for Molecular Imaging, Copenhagen, Denmark [3] Siemens Healthcare A/S, Ballerup, Denmark [4] Siemens Medical Solutions USA, Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America [5] University of Copenhagen, Department of Clinical Medicine, Copenhagen, Denmark
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The latest generation of simultaneous positron emission tomography and magnetic resonance imaging (PET/MRI) scanners is now at the forefront of hybrid imaging. As of now, the reconstruction of both modalities is independent, but research is ongoing in MRI-guided (MRIg) PET reconstruction, where information from the MRI is used as prior information in the iterative PET reconstruction. We present three different clinical cohorts: meningioma patients (n=8) scanned with [ 68 Ga]DOTATOC, a single pituitary adenoma scanned dynamically with [ 18 F]FET and a neurodegenerative cohort (n=10) scanned with [ 18 F]FDG. The cohorts have been analyzed with standard OSEM reconstruction (b=0) versus MRIg reconstruction. The meningioma cohort showed an increased volume with standardized uptake values (SUV) above 2.5 when using MRIg reconstruction, and an increased SUV max in the tumor. The pituitary adenoma showed increase time-activity curve both for β=1 and β=2. The neurodegenerative cohort showed stable SUV ratios of the cerebral-to-cerebellar cortex down to 3 minutes. This preliminary work shows the clinical value in utilizing the information from the MRI in PET reconstruction with applications both to increase image quality and resolution, but also to facilitate faster imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 215Poster Number:MIC-10-215] A Hybrid Neural Network Model for DaTscan Diagnosis of Neurodegenerative Disorders (#2498)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. Roupas (Autores: E. Roupas , A. Koukopoulou , E. Mitsou , E. Stiliaris)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, Medical School, Athens, Greece [2] National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, Department of Physics, Athens, Greece
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study presents the development of a hybrid Neural Network designed to simultaneously reconstruct medical images from their sinograms and to predict diagnostic parameters for neurodegenerative disorders, specifically Parkinson's disease. The training pipeline utilizes simulated Dopamine Transporter Scan (DaTscan) brain images and their corresponding sinograms, generated via a custom Monte Carlo based framework that employs analytically driven functions to model realistic hotspot and background noise characteristics. The architecture integrates image reconstruction and disease-specific parameter estimation into a unified framework. Key diagnostic features include the bilateral asymmetry of radiotracer uptake within the caudate nuclei; deviations in spatial distribution or intensity within predefined Regions of Interest (RoIs) serve as primary indicators of neuropathology. This dual-function approach advances automated, AI-assisted functional neuroimaging, offering a robust pathway for early, non-invasive diagnosis of neurodegenerative conditions.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 218Poster Number:MIC-10-218] A Global-Local Latent Diffusion Model for Limited-Angle CT Reconstruction (#2642)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Q. Xu (Autores: Y. Wang , C. Wei , Q. Xu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institute of High Energy Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China [2] University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, School of Nuclear Science and Technology, Beijing, China [3] Jinan Laboratory of Applied Nuclear Science, Jinan, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Limited-angle computed tomography (LACT) reconstruction is highly ill-posed because missing projection views lead to severe artifacts and incomplete boundaries. This work proposes a global-local latent diffusion framework for limited-angle CT reconstruction. The proposed method performs diffusion reconstruction in the latent space of a variational autoencoder and jointly incorporates U-Net-based local modeling and transformer-based global modeling into the denoising process. The U-Net component captures multiscale spatial details and boundary continuity, whereas the transformer component models long-range dependencies and global structural relationships associated with missing-angle information. These complementary priors are adaptively integrated to guide latent-space denoising. During sampling, a physics-guided data-consistency constraint is further introduced. Specifically, the intermediate latent prediction produced by the model is decoded back to the image domain, processed with a projection-consistency operation, and then re-encoded into the latent diffusion trajectory. Preliminary experiments on a simulated data set show favorable reconstruction quality, indicating that the proposed global-local diffusion framework can improve structural fidelity and projection consistency for limited-angle CT reconstruction.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 221Poster Number:MIC-10-221] Iterative proton CT reconstruction from list-mode data of a sandwich time-of-flight scanner (#2821)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Coussat (Autores: A. Coussat , J.M. Létang , S. Rit)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] INSA-Lyon, Université Claude Bernard Lyon 1, CNRS, Inserm, CREATIS, UMR 5220, U1294, F-69373, Lyon, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Proton CT is a promising alternative to X-ray CT for proton therapy treatment planning, allowing direct estimation of the relative stopping power map within the patient body without relying on conversion from Hounsfield units. Conventional list-mode proton CT scanners measure the energy loss of each individual proton to estimate the integral of the relative stopping power along its path, the water-equivalent path length, but do not meet the requirements for clinical use due to their low acquisition rates. An alternative proton CT scanner design was recently proposed where the time-of-flight of each proton is measured between two detectors located before and after the patient along the proton beam. The main advantages of this sandwich time-of-flight design are its compactness and high acquisition rates. However, conversion from sandwich time-of-flight data to water-equivalent path length is not possible. In this work, we propose an iterative reconstruction of the sought relative stopping power map based on the non-linear forward problem. The method is assessed using Monte Carlo simulations of the acquisition of four simple phantoms. Although computationally expensive, this method accurately recovers the relative stopping power map.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 224Poster Number:MIC-10-224] Direct normalization correction for a brain PET system with multi-resolution detector design (#2848)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Yang (Autores: C. Yang , H. Ye , C. Huang , Z. Wu , H. Liu , Q. Wei , Z. Gu , J. Wu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Normal University, Center for Advanced Quantum Studies, School of Physics and Astronomy, Beijing, China [2] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China [3] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [4] University of Science and Technology Beijing, School of Automation and Electrical Engineering, Beijing, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A high-sensitivity, high-resolution brain PET system with a multi-resolution detector design has been developed. However, image reconstruction without normalization correction produces pronounced image artifacts. In this study, we implemented list-mode reconstruction with direct normalization correction using normalization factors derived from simulation data for this multi-resolution PET system. The effect of normalization correction on reconstructed image quality was evaluated using Monte Carlo simulations and real scan data from a modified image-quality phantom. The results showed that normalization-corrected reconstruction substantially reduced image artifacts and improved image uniformity in simulated data, while residual nonuniformity remained in real scan data due to the lack of experimentally measured crystal efficiencies. Overall, this work demonstrates the feasibility of normalization correction for the dual-layer brain PET system and provides a basis for further experimental normalization using measured crystal efficiencies

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 227Poster Number:MIC-10-227] Effect of Cardiac Reorientation on Deep Learning-Based Denoising for Low-Dose Cardiac SPECT (#2932)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. G. Brankov (Autores: M. Toumi , Y. Yang , M. King , J. G. Brankov)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Illinois Institute of Technology, Electrical and Computer Engineering, Chicago, Illinois, United States of America [2] University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School, Department of Radiology, Worcester, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In low-dose (LD) myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI) with single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), radiation exposure is reduced at the expense of image quality, potentially impairing perfusion defect detection. Deep learning methods have shown promise in reducing noise in LD MPI images. However, clinical data exhibit varying cardiac orientations, increasing the complexity of the learning task for denoising models. We hypothesize that standardizing cardiac orientation with respect to a common reference prior to training can reduce this complexity and improve denoising performance. We evaluated this approach with a previously proposed edge-aware convolutional autoencoder (EdgeCAE) across four levels of trade-off between edge preservation and mean-squared error (MSE) fidelity. The model was trained on 738 clinical subjects and tested on 300 noise realizations derived from two independent patient anatomies, with and without pre-reorientation. Our results demonstrated that cardiac reorientation consistently reduced the MSE compared to the full-dose reference images. This was also supported by visual assessment on an independent patient cohort.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 230Poster Number:MIC-10-230] Ghost Artifact Suppression in Multiplexed Self-Collimating SPECT via Total Variation Regularization (#2996)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Yao (Autores: S. Mehta , H. Tripathi , T. Methuku , T. Skirsky , L. Ying , T. Ma , R. Yao)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The State University of New York at Buffalo, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Buffalo, New York, United States of America [2] The State University of New York at Buffalo, Department of Radiology, Buffalo, New York, United States of America [3] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [4] The State University of New York at Buffalo, Biomedical Department, Buffalo, New York, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Multiplexing in SPECT renders the measurement operator underdetermined. In symmetric multi-source configurations, iterative ambiguity reinforcement sustains persistent ghost artifacts. Established mitigation strategies require supplemental single-beam nonmultiplexed projections, constraining collimator design and sacrificing sensitivity. Sparsity in gradients for common tracer distributions motivate total-variation (TV) regularization as a natural demultiplexing strategy: ghost artifacts produce extra gradient support that TV prior penalizes, breaking the ambiguity cycle. We demonstrate that MAP-TV (maximum a posteriori total variation) acts as an active reconstruction-stage demultiplexer, a supplemental approach to modifying the projection set in the data acquisition stage.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 233Poster Number:MIC-10-233] Integrating In-Patient Scattered Events in PET Reconstruction via a Monte Carlo Projector (#3119)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Moulin (Autores: M. Moulin , G. Montémont , H. De Las Heras Gala , J.M. Létang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CEA-LETI, Université Grenoble-Alpes, Grenoble, France [2] INSA-Lyon, Université Claude Bernard Lyon 1, UJM- Saint Etienne, CNRS, Inserm, Lyon, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In this paper, we propose a new projection method for PET, called Monte Carlo Point Projectors (MCPP), which back-projects measured gamma interactions in the detector by sampling potential positions of the event source within the field of view (FoV). We apply this method to scattered events using a projector for scattered lines of response (ScLoR), as well as a combination of scattered lines of response and Compton cones of response (CoR). The simulated system is a cylinder with a radius of 15~cm and a length of 16~cm, composed of 12 Cadmium Zinc Telluride panels, with a 7~cm radius water sphere at the center to simulate in-patient scatter. We show that for this system, the point spread function (PSF) resolutions were 8.3~cm for CoR and 5.3--4.7~cm for the proposed ScLoR projector and the combination with the CoR, demonstrating the advantage of using scattered events with the MCPP method. We also studied how the missing energy of scattered events influences the PSFs obtained with MCPP, noting that lower missing energy yields better resolution. Its combination with a scatter classification method on experimental data is being evaluated. In conclusion, the MCPP approach facilitates the integration of different projectors to process a maximum of detected events.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 236Poster Number:MIC-10-236] List-Mode Subspace-Based Dynamic PET: 1-Second Temporal Resolution on the NeuroEXPLORER (#3210)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Marin (Autores: Y. Djebra , Y. Najmaoui , D. Szezurek , Y. Chemli , K. Fontaine , J.-D. Gallezot , T. Toyonaga , M. Normandin , G. El Fakhri , C. Ma , T. Marin)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dynamic PET imaging is becoming increasingly valuable in neuroimaging and cardiac imaging, thanks to its ability to track functional changes over time. Conventional approaches to dynamic PET imaging need to find a balance between frame duration and noise: shorter temporal frames can provide important information on rapid physiological processes, but at the expense of increased noise. Traditional filtering strategies aim at reducing noise, but inherently cause loss of spatial and/or temporal resolution. In this work, we represent dynamic PET images using a subspace model during image reconstruction to substantially reduce noise while preserving spatial and temporal information, thereby exploiting the spatiotemporal correlations in dynamic images. We demonstrate the power of the proposed approach on an in-vivo scan of a nonhuman primate performed on the high-sensitivity, high-resolution NeuroEXPLORER scanner. Dynamic images reconstructed at 1-second frames exhibit high resolution and dramatically reduced noise compared to conventional reconstructions, enabling the visualization of early tracer perfusion, respiratory motion and contrast changes in the whole body, without any gating. The proposed method shows promise for short-frame imaging of the brain and body.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 239Poster Number:MIC-10-239] Hierarchical ROI-free Learning for GFR Category Stratification in Dynamic 99m Tc-DTPA Renography (#1527)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Xu (Autores: Z. Xu , J. Li , C. Li , J. Zhong , W. Sun , J. Chen , J. Dong , Z. Sun , Y. Zeng , H. Xiao , J. Sun)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Hainan University, Department of Data Science and Big Data, Haikou, China [2] The First Affiliated Hospital of Hainan Medical University, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Haikou, China [3] Hainan General Hospital, Haikou, China [4] The Second Affiliated Hospital of Hainan Medical University, Department of Radiation Oncology, Cancer Treatment Center, Haikou, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dynamic 99m Tc-diethylenetriaminepentaacetic acid (DTPA) planar renography is widely used for quantitative renal function assessment, but Gates-based glomerular filtration rate (GFR) estimation depends on manually defined kidney and background regions of interest (ROIs), which is time-consuming and operator-dependent. We developed RFVGG, an ROI-free hierarchical deep learning framework that learns directly from dynamic renography image sequences using routinely available Gates-derived labels. This retrospective study included 728 consecutive patients who underwent dynamic 99m Tc-DTPA planar renography. RFVGG was built on a shared 3D VGG-style backbone with hierarchical task-specific heads for three-, five-, and six-category GFR stratification. Model development followed five-fold cross-validation, and RFVGG was compared with CNN, ResNet-18, and DenseNet under identical evaluation settings. Classification performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and specificity. RFVGG achieved accuracies of 0.842±0.020, 0.705±0.043, and 0.606±0.042 for the three-, five-, and six-category tasks, respectively. The corresponding precisions were 0.846±0.017, 0.668±0.037, and 0.614±0.034; recalls were 0.843±0.024, 0.689±0.045, and 0.642±0.039; and specificities were 0.915±0.012, 0.920±0.012, and 0.920±0.008, respectively. These results indicate that RFVGG can perform automated ROI-free GFR category stratification from dynamic 99m Tc-DTPA planar renography without contour-based kidney or background ROI tracing

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 242Poster Number:MIC-10-242] Design and Construction of Physical and Digital Phantoms for Image-Derived Input Function Validation Studies in Brain PET Imaging (#1866)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 U. Khalid (Autores: U. Khalid , C. Memis , L. Tellmann , M. Lennartz , T. Meurer , P. Lohmann , H. Iida , M. Wiesmann , H. Herzog , J. Scheins , N. J. Shah , C. W. Lerche , C. R. Brambilla)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Forschungszentrum Jülich GmbH, Institute of Neuroscience and Medicine, INM-4, Jülich, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [2] RWTH Aachen University, Faculty of Medicine, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [3] Forschungszentrum Jülich GmbH, Institute of Energy Technologies (IET), Jülich, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [4] RWTH Aachen, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [5] University of Turku, Turku PET center, Institute of Biomedicine, Faculty of Medicine, Turku, Finland [6] Uniklinik Aachen, Clinic for Diagnostic and Interventional Neuroradiology, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [7] RWTH Aachen, Department of Neurology, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Quantitative brain PET studies often require arterial input functions (AIF), which can be derived from radiotracer concentrations through the internal carotid arteries (ICAs) in dynamic PET images. Image-derived input function (IDIF) methods avoid invasiveness; however, challenges in precise quantification of dynamic flow conditions and correction of partial volume effects (PVE) persist. Recently developed dedicated PET systems for brain imaging, such as the RETIMAGER System, offer excellent spatial and temporal resolution, which is of high relevance for IDIF determination. In addition, hybrid systems offer complementary information for improved IDIF validation. This study shows the design and development of digital and physical phantoms for future validation of IDIF methods in Brain PET systems. A two-phase approach employs the design and construction of a cylindrical phantom with an ICA insert matching real structural geometries. Phase 1 uses a digitalized phantom with Monte Carlo (MC) simulations to validate and optimize acquisition and reconstruction parameters. Phase 2 is in progress for experimental versus simulation validations using a physical phantom with an ICA insert to simulate flow dynamics using an injector. Additionally, a 3D head phantom incorporating gray matter (GM), white matter (WM), scalp, and ICA structures has been designed and is in fabrication for future comprehensive validation.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 245Poster Number:MIC-10-245] TRACE: A New Phantom for Simultaneous Multi-Method Assessment of PET Spatial Resolution (#2135)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Choudhary (Autores: D. Choudhary , B. Mehadji , R. D. Badawi , N. Omidvari , B. A. Spencer)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] UC Davis Health, Radiology, Sacramento, California, United States of America [2] UC Davis, Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Spatial resolution assessment in positron emission tomography (PET) typically relies on the full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) of point-like line sources reconstructed with filtered back-projection (FBP), yet modern clinical imaging predominantly uses iterative reconstruction methods, motivating the need for phantoms that evaluate resolution under clinically relevant protocols. To address this, we present TRACE (Tapered Rod Array for Continuous-resolution Evaluation), a 3D-printed phantom enabling simultaneous spatial resolution assessment via four complementary methods - FBP FWHM, modulation transfer function (MTF), Rayleigh criterion, and visual assessment - in a single acquisition. TRACE consists of a tapered cone with continuously decreasing fillable conical rod diameters (4.8-1.2 mm over 10 cm) and three integrated capillary slots for NEMA-compatible line source measurements. The phantom was scanned on the uEXPLORER total-body PET scanner in transverse (XY) and axial (XZ) orientations. FBP FWHM yielded mean transverse resolutions of 3.0 ± 0.2 mm (radial) and 3.4 ± 0.2 mm (tangential), and 2.9 ± 0.5 mm axially. Under OSEM reconstruction, the Rayleigh criterion and visual assessment resolved rods down to 1.8 mm (XY) and 2.0 mm (XZ), while the 50% and 10% MTF were achieved at 2.8 mm and 1.6 mm (XY), and 2.6 mm and 1.7 mm (XZ), respectively. TRACE bridges standardized and clinically relevant resolution assessment, delivering all four metrics in a single acquisition and offering a comprehensive framework for PET spatial resolution characterization

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 248Poster Number:MIC-10-248] A Reconstruction-Agnostic Paper Made Fan Phantom for Task-Relevant PET Spatial Resolution Assessment (#2307)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Mehadji (Autores: B. Mehadji , R. Badawi , L. Nardo , B. A. Spencer)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] UC Davis, Radiology, Sacramento, California, United States of America [2] UC Davis, Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Conventional methods for assessing PET spatial resolution, such as the NEMA NU-2 protocol and ACR guidelines, provide limited insight into the effective resolution achieved with modern clinical reconstruction techniques. In this work, we propose a simple and low-cost fan-pattern paper phantom enabling modulation transfer function (MTF)-based analysis for continuous spatial resolution characterization. The phantom consists of laser-cut paper in a fan geometry with gap sizes decreasing from 5 mm to 1 mm which is briefly immersed in an F-18 solution. Reproducibility and repeatability were evaluated on a uEXPLORER PET/CT system. Images were reconstructed using filtered back projection (FBP) and multiple clinical reconstruction algorithms, including OSEM and artificial intelligence (AI)-based methods. Spatial resolution full width at half maximum (FWHM) was derived from the MTF using the 50% frequency criterion. Results demonstrate an average radial resolution of 3.23 ± 0.034 mm for reproducibility and 3.22 ± 0.054 mm for repeatability, consistent with NEMA NU-2 measurements but with lower uncertainties, which can be attributed to the robustness of the MTF evaluation method. The proposed approach enables rapid (<5 min), robust, and continuous assessment of spatial resolution, including under clinical and AI-based reconstruction conditions. The proposed phantom provides a practical tool for PET system characterization and reconstruction optimization and will be made available to facilitate wider adoption.
