sub_talks.title:
[Poster panel: 251Poster Number:MIC-10-251] Quantitative Image Quality Evaluation of 177 Lu
SPECT Using a NEMA NU 4-based SPECT IQ
Phantom (#2365)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Zhang (Autores: Y. Zhang , D. Boreel , M. Boswinkel , R. M. Ramakers , K. Chatzipapas , M. C. Goorden)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] TUDelft, Radiation Science & Technology Department, Delft, Netherlands [2] Radboud University Medical Center, Department of medical Imaging, Nijmegen, Netherlands [3] MILabs B.V, Utrecht, Netherlands
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Lutetium-177, a combined gamma and beta emitter, is gaining significant attention as a theranostic isotope with clinical applications in metastatic prostate cancer and neuroendocrine tumors. Quantitative imaging of 177 Lu in a preclinical setting is important for therapy optimization. This study evaluates the image quality performance of a small-animal SPECT scanner equipped with an ultra-high-sensitivity collimator for 177 Lu using a SPECT IQ phantom adapted from the NEMA NU 4 PET phantom. Whole-body acquisitions were performed using a multi-bed protocol, and projection data were reconstructed with an iterative algorithm under different post-filtering conditions. Image quality was assessed using recovery coefficients (RCs) for rods of varying diameters, and image noise was quantified as the percentage standard deviation (%STDunif ) within a uniform region. The results show that RC varies with rod size, iteration number, and post-reconstruction filtering. Effective recovery was observed for 1.35 mm rods (RC ∼0.77), while RC values decreased to approximately 0.38 and 0.23 for 1.15 mm and 0.95 mm rods, respectively, indicating that reliable recovery is achieved for rod sizes of about 1.5 mm. Image noise increases with iteration number and decreases with stronger smoothing, reflecting the expected resolution-noise trade-off. These initialfindings demonstrate the capability of the SPECT IQ phantom for quantitative performance evaluation and protocol optimization in high-resolution SPECT imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 254Poster Number:MIC-10-254] Investigation of the stability of energy-based scatter estimation in PET (#2546)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. ZamanPour (Autores: S. ZamanPour , A. Rezaei , J. Nuyts , G. Schramm)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] KU Leuven, Department of Imaging and Pathology, Leuven, Belgium
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Energy-based scatter estimation in PET estimates scatter from the energy information of detected photon pairs, without relying on an attenuation map. Recent work demonstrated promising results using a model that decomposes the 2D energy histogram into true and scattered coincidences via three basis functions. This model rests on two fundamental assumptions. First, that the shape of the scattered energy spectrum is sufficiently stable across varying activity distributions and time-of-flight (TOF) bins to be represented by fixed weights on two basis functions (c 1 p 1 + c 2 p 2 ). Second, that the scattered and true energy distributions remain statistically distinguishable given the finite energy resolution of the scanner: when low-angle Compton scatter dominates (as in LORs through high-contrast hot regions at central TOF bins) the scatter spectrum shifts towards 511 keV and the two distributions may become so spectrally similar that reliable decomposition is mathematically infeasible, regardless of counting statistics. In this work, we investigate the validity of both assumptions using long MCGPU-PET Monte Carlo simulations of an elliptical phantom with hot-sphere inserts of radii 1, 3, and 5 cm and contrast ratios of 1:10 and 1:100. Scattered energy spectra are extracted and inspected across TOF bins, hot-region sizes, and contrast ratios; challenging cases are identified for each assumption; and the feasibility of the nine-component 2D energy histogram decomposition from S.A. Zaman Pour et al. is evaluated.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 257Poster Number:MIC-10-257] A Quantitative Comparison of PET Image Reconstruction Methods for Amyloid-Beta Plaque Identification in Alzheimer's Disease (#2744)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Azeez (Autores: A. Azeez , M. Khalighi , A. Sokolowski , E. Mormino , C. Young , F. Boada)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Stanford School of Medicine, Radiological Sciences Laboratory, Palo Alto, California, United States of America [2] Stanford School of Medicine, Department of Neurology and Neurological Sciences, Palo Alto, California, United States of America [3] University of California Davis, Department of Radiology, Davis, Davis, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The accurate quantification of amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques with Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is critical for the early diagnosis and management of Alzheimer's Disease (AD). However, the diagnostic accuracy of PET imaging is heavily dependent on the image reconstruction algorithm employed. This study provides a quantitative comparison of three distinct PET image reconstruction methods to determine their efficacy for Aβ plaque identification. Using a clinical AD dataset, each of the three algorithms was applied to generate enhanced PET images. The resulting Aβ burden was quantified using the standardized Centiloid scale(CL), and a rigorous statistical analysis was performed to evaluate the performance differences between the methods. Identifying the optimal reconstruction technique is paramount, as its implementation can lead to more sensitive early detection of AD, improved monitoring of disease progression, and ultimately, the enhancement of therapeutic outcomes.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 260Poster Number:MIC-10-260] Dose-Dependent Electron Density CT Images for PET Attenuation Correction (#2877)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Niekämper (Autores: D. Niekämper , S. Mostafapour , L. Tellmann , S. Faby , H. Alrakh , J. Scheins , J. Braaksma , D. Overbeek , M. J.W. Greuter , N.J. Shah , C. Tsoumpas , C. Lerche)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Forschungszentrum Jülich GmbH, Institute of Neuroscience and Medicine 4, Jülich, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [2] University of Groningen, University Medical Center Groningen, Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging, Groningen, Netherlands [3] University of Groningen, University Medical Center Groningen, Department of Radiology, Groningen, Netherlands [4] Siemens Healthineers AG, Department of Computed Tomography, Forchheim, Germany [5] RWTH Aachen University, Department of Neurology, Aachen, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Generating accurate attenuation maps from CT images is essential for quantitative PET/CT imaging, while minimising radiation exposure is also important. In conventional CT, the attenuation contributions from Compton effect and photoelectric absorption are combined into a single attenuation value and transformed together from the CT energy spectrum to the PET imaging energy, despite their different energy dependencies. In contrast, spectral CT enables separate electron density and effective atomic number images to be reconstructed. This allows to transform the relevant Compton attenuation contribution independently by applying a scaling factor to the electron density image. In this study, we compare attenuation maps obtained using this approach with those obtained via a bilinear transformation. Measurements of phantoms containing various tissue-equivalent inserts are performed using a PET/CT with twin-beam dual-energy capability and a photon-counting CT. In additional measurements, selected inserts are replaced by compartments containing activity in order to evaluate the effect of the different attenuation maps on reconstructed PET images. The measurements are performed across a wide dose range to investigate how far the radiation dose can be reduced while still obtaining accurate attenuation maps. Preliminary results show good agreement between attenuation values obtained at different dose levels, with the highest discrepancies between both transformation methods observed for bone-equivalent inserts. Using electron density and effective atomic number reconstructions from spectral scanners to generate attenuation correction values may improve quantitative PET imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 263Poster Number:MIC-10-263] TOF-Aware Single Scatter Simulation in STIR: Implementation and Validation Against Monte Carlo (#2967)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Sabeur (Autores: M. Sabeur , S. ZamanPour , S. Stute , Y. Moussaoui , S. Moussaoui , K. Thielemans)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Nantes Université, Ecole Centrale de Nantes, LS2N, Department of Medical Imaging, Nantes, France [2] CHU Nantes, Section of Nuclear Medicine, Nantes, France [3] University College London, Institute of Nuclear Medicine, London, United Kingdom [4] KU Leuven, Department of Imaging and Pathology, Leuven, Belgium
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Single scatter simulation (SSS) combined with tail-fitting is the standard analytical method for scatter correction in PET. Extending SSS to time-of-flight (TOF) data requires non-trivial adaptations to the scatter kernel. The open-source Software for Tomographic Image Reconstruction (STIR) library has a widely used implementation of SSS for non-TOF data. Here, we present a fully TOF-aware SSS implementation in STIR with two contributions: (i) the TOF kernel ε t in the scatter-arm emission integral is computed via erf (error function) as opposed to central point approximation in Watson, avoiding the need for an extra normalisation step. (ii) re-use of cached integrals from the non-TOF implementation. The implementation is validated against MCGPU Monte Carlo on a 9-ring compact PET scanner (27 TOF bins, 169 ps, uniform phantom), confirming strong agreement with MC single scatter (r=0.985 full 4-D sinogram; r=0.994 TOF-summed spatial). This contribution opens the door to fully quantitative PET reconstructions for TOF-PET in STIR.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 266Poster Number:MIC-10-266] Event-by-Event Energy-Based Scatter Correction via Bayesian Likelihood Estimation (#3026)
sub_talks.speaker: M. Teimoorisichani
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Siemens Medical Solutions USA Inc., Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Energy-based scatter (EBS) correction is increasingly utilized in PET image reconstruction. This work introduces a novel EBS framework that assigns scatter probabilities to individual listmode events via analytical Bayesian calculations. The method utilizes pre-defined energy distributions of scatter kernels as basis functions. By analyzing the global energy spectrum, the algorithm estimates the fractional probability for each event type and subsequently calculates the likelihood of Compton scattering for individual coincidences. The approach was validated using two phantom datasets acquired on a Biograph Vision PET/CT scanner (Siemens Healthineers). Reconstructed images were compared against standard vendor-implemented single-scatter simulation (SSS) with tail-fitting. Results demonstrate high consistency, with scatter fraction estimates differing by less than 3% from SSS. Furthermore, uniform and NEMA image quality phantom analyses showed less than 1% divergence in contrast recovery and background variability. These findings suggest that the proposed EBS method provides a robust, computationally efficient alternative for scatter estimation in clinical PET reconstruction.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 269Poster Number:MIC-10-269] Synthetic CT Generation for Attenuation Correction in Respiratory-Gated Rb-82 Cardiac PET Using 3D Diffusion Models (#3061)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Yu (Autores: B. Yu , W. Qi , J. Kolthammer , K. Gong)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Florida, J. Crayton Pruitt Family Department of Biomedical Engineering, Gainesville, Florida, United States of America [2] Canon Medical Research USA, Inc., Vernon Hills, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate attenuation correction (AC) using computed tomography (CT) is critical for quantitative PET imaging. However, in respiratory-gated cardiac PET, respiratory phase mismatch between gated PET and CT can compromise the accuracy of CT-based AC, while acquiring additional phase-matched CT scans is impractical due to radiation dose concerns. To address these limitations, we employed a 3D Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) to generate synthetic CT images directly from non-attenuation corrected (NAC) PET data for gated PET AC. The model was trained using paired non-gated Rb-82 myocardial perfusion PET scans and CT-derived attenuation maps, and directly applied to respiratory-gated PET without retraining. Visual evaluation showed that 3D DDPM generated synthetic CT images with superior anatomical fidelity and improved respiratory phase alignment with gated PET compared with 3D GAN, 3D UNet, and 2D DDPM. Regional quantitative analysis near the diaphragm further demonstrated that 3D DDPM achieved improved attenuation correction in regions most affected by respiratory mismatch.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 272Poster Number:MIC-10-272] Beyond the Single-Tissue Voxel:A Spin-Echo-Based Multi-Tissue Decomposition Framework with Implications for Synthetic MRI and Machine Learning Diagnosis (#1194)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Zeng (Autores: H. Li , Q. Luo , M. J. Pomeroy , H. Li , Y. Kee , X. J. Zhou , Z. J. Liang , L. Zeng)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Stony Brook University, Electrical and Computer Engineering, Stony Brook, New York, United States of America [2] University of Illinois College of Medicine at Chicago, Radiology, Chicago, Illinois, United States of America [3] Stony Brook University, Biomedical Engineering, Stony Brook, New York, United States of America [4] Stony Brook University, Radiology, Stony Brook, New York, United States of America [5] Utah Valley University, Computer Sience, Orem, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Conventional synthetic MRI generates contrast images from a single effective set of voxel-wise quantitative parameters: proton density (PD), T1, and T2, which may be insufficient when any two or all three of gray matter (GM), white matter (WM), and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) coexist within the same image voxel. This work presents an exploratory framework using the standard spin-echo signal generation model with a purity-weighted Expectation-Maximization algorithm for tissue prototype estimation that systematically quantifies the prevalence of such multi-tissue voxels. From three co-registered spin-echo MR brain images at distinct Time to Echo (TE), Time to Repetition (TR) settings, per-voxel PD, T1, and T2 relaxation maps are recovered via a robust nonlinear inversion pipeline and validated by re-synthesizing the original images. Each voxel is then decomposed into fractional contributions of GM, WM, and CSF using three methodologically independent models: a Signal-Domain Mixture Model, Parameter-Domain Mixture Model and Mean Parameter-Domain Mixture Model. All three consistently show that 52% - 62% of brain image voxels contain contributions from multiple tissue types, demonstrating model-independently that the single-effective-parameter representation is insufficient in most brain voxels and that conventional synMRI parameter maps can be systematically biased. A tissue-aware synthesis framework is proposed that generates physically grounded MRI contrasts across the full spin-echo (TE, TR) measurement space, providing a quantitative basis for more reliable synthetic MRI. Future work will extend this framework to multi-subject validation and evaluate the synthesized contrast library for machine learning-based lesion diagnosis.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 275Poster Number:MIC-10-275] Assessment of Cortical Defect Discriminability in Reduced-Dose Pediatric Tc-99m DMSA Renal SPECT (#1422)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. A. King (Autores: W. Fu , Y. Yang , N. Kwatra , S.T. Treves , F. Fahey , M. A. King)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Illinois Institute of Technology, Electrical and Computer Engineering, Chicago, Illinois, United States of America [2] Harvard Medical School, Radiology, Boston, Massachusetts, United States of America [3] Boston Children's Hospital, Radiology, Boston, Massachusetts, United States of America [4] University of Massachusetts Medical Center, Radiology, Worcester, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In prior work, deep-learning (DL) based denoising was demonstrated to be capable of yielding images comparable to standard-dose studies when the imaging dose is reduced several-fold in pediatric Tc-99m DMSA renal SPECT, based on both quantitative image quality metrics and visual assessment by clinical experts. In this study, we further evaluate the diagnostic utility of DL-denoised images by employing a DL-based classifier to perform a task-based assessment of cortical defects, where a 3D convolutional neural network (CNN) was used to differentiate kidneys with cortical defects from those with normal uptake. We demonstrated this approach with a set of clinical data acquired from 956 subjects, with performance quantified using receiver-operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. The results showed that, without DL denoising, the quarter-dose data achieved a lower classification performance than the full-dose in terms of the area under the ROC curve ( p -value < 0.001); however, with DL denoising, the quarter-dose data achieved a statistically comparable performance to that of the full-dose data ( p -value = 0.452).

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 278Poster Number:MIC-10-278] Automated Coronary Artery Extraction up to Distal Vessels Based on Hessian Matrix and 3D Skeletonization to Compensate for Incomplete Labels (#1528)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Ide (Autores: R. Ide , K. Ogawa)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Hosei University, Applied Informatics, Graduate School of Science and Engineering, Tokyo, Japan [2] Hosei University, Applied Informatics, Faculty of Science and Engineering, Tokyo, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract While deep learning has become the mainstream approach for coronary artery extraction from coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) images, its reliance on training data makes it difficult to accurately extract fine distal vessels using existing datasets with insufficient annotations. Therefore, this study proposes a hybrid extraction method utilizing image feature analysis. This method consists of three stages. First, an initial extraction is performed based on anatomical features and CT values. Second, a chained connection algorithm combining tubular structure enhancement via the Hessian matrix and three-dimensional (3D) skeletonization is employed to connect vessel fragments through local search, thereby recovering continuity. Third, volume expansion is performed using an adaptive threshold corresponding to local intensity to restore the accurate vessel diameter. Application of this method to an open dataset demonstrated extreme robustness against CT value degradation caused by insufficient contrast agent perfusion. We successfully extracted and reconstructed fine distal vessels that were missing in the existing labels while maintaining their continuity. Future work involves collaborating with clinical specialists to reconstruct high-quality ground truth labels and conduct rigorous quantitative evaluations.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. J. Martinez-Murcia (Autores: M. Rodriguez-Rubio , F. J. Martinez-Murcia , J. E. Arco , I. A. Illán , F. Segovia , C. Jimenez-Mesa , C. Vazquez-Garcia , J.M. Gorriz , J. Levin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Granada, Department of Signal Theory, Networking and Communications, Granada, Spain [2] Andalusian Research Institute in Data Science and Computational Intelligence, Granada, Spain [3] Mind, Brain and Behavior Research Center (CIMCYC), Granada, Spain [4] Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Department of Neurology, LMU University Hospital, Munich, Bavaria, Germany [5] German Center for Neurodegenerative Diseases (DZNE), Munich, Bavaria, Germany [6] Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Institute of Clinical Neuroimmunology, Biomedical Center and University Hospital, Munich, Bavaria, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Optical coherence tomography (OCT) provides non-invasive retinal biomarkers that may reflect the distinct neurodegenerative patterns of underlying proteinopathies. This study evaluates a machine learning framework to classify synucleinopathies (Parkinson's disease [PD] and multiple system atrophy [MSA]) and tauopathies (progressive supranuclear palsy [PSP]) using retinal layer morphometry. Several classification tasks were assessed, ranging from healthy control (HC) discrimination to the differential classification of proteinopathic groups. XGBoost was employed as the primary classifier and evaluated using nested cross-validation. To minimize intra-subject variability, only the most recent visit per patient was included, with features aggregated as the average of both eyes to represent bilateral neurodegenerative involvement. The model demonstrated notable efficacy in distinguishing synucleinopathies (PD+MSA) from tauopathies (PSP), achieving an accuracy of 0.704 ± 0.057. This performance was comparable to the binary classification of HCs vs. all pathological cases (0.724 ± 0.079). In contrast, multi-class settings proved more challenging. These findings suggest that while fine-grained clinical subtype differentiation remains a challenge, OCT-derived biomarkers are highly effective at capturing the broad divergent impacts of alpha-synuclein and tau pathology on the retina.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 284Poster Number:MIC-10-284] Multi-step Nonlinear Iteration Method for ECT Energy Spectrum Decomposition (#1885)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Mu (Autores: J. Mu , Z. Lu , J. Peng , Z. Yu , D. Bi , S. An)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] United Imaging Healthcare Co., Ltd, MI BU Detector R&D Center, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Theranostic radionuclide molecular imaging represents a core technology in precision nuclear medicine. However, its clinical application is hindered by scatter interference and complex background signals in spectral analysis. To address this bottleneck, this paper proposes a multi-step nonlinear iterative method for energy spectrum background subtraction and full-energy peak analysis, suitable for emission computed tomography detectors. The method realizes high-precision background subtraction and peak stripping via a systematic workflow consisting of peak localization, Log-Log-Square root transformation, interval iterative calculation, and Gaussian fitting. Experimental validation is conducted under both single-nuclide and multi-nuclide conditions. The results demonstrate that the proposed method can effectively separate full-energy peaks submerged by scatter in single-nuclide spectra. For the CsI detector, the energy resolution is improved from 12.9% to10.97%. For multi-nuclide and multi-peak spectra, it successfully separates overlapping peaks, suppresses Compton continuum interference, and optimizes energy resolution to around 10.6%. This method improves detector energy resolution, provides solid technical support for the clinical translation of theranostic radionuclide molecular imaging, and exhibits favorable adaptability and correction accuracy. Future work will focus on optimizing iterative efficiency and extending the method's applicability to more complex clinical scenarios.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 287Poster Number:MIC-10-287] Residual Scatter Correction Using Grid-Wall Shadow Sampling in Cone-Beam CT with a Two-Dimensional Anti-Scatter Grid (#2293)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Cho (Autores: J. Park , S. Cho , H. Yang , D. Jeon , D.Y. Han , H. Cho)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yonsei University, Department of Radiation Convergence Engineering, Wonju, Republic of Korea [2] Yale School of Medicine, Department of Therapeutic Radiolog, New Haven, Connecticut, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Residual X-ray scatter degrades image contrast, uniformity, and quantitative accuracy in cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT). A two-dimensional (2D) anti-scatter grid physically suppresses scattered photons, but conventional gain correction using a matched flood projection only compensates the multiplicative grid-wall footprint and does not remove additive residual scatter, which persists as low-frequency nonuniformity in reconstructed images. This work proposes a projection-domain residual scatter correction method that exploits grid-wall shadows as internal sampling positions for scatter estimation. After gain correction, primary signals equalize between wall-shadow and neighboring hole pixels by design; any remaining signal mismatch is therefore attributed to additive residual scatter. Sparse scatter estimates at wall-shadow locations are expanded into a full-field scatter map via Gaussian-weighted interpolation and subtracted from the raw projection before logarithmic conversion and filtered backprojection reconstruction. This approach requires no additional hardware or dedicated scatter measurements, as it utilizes the intrinsic grid-wall structure already present in every grid projection. We evaluate the method using an ACR 464 phantom scanned at 80 kVp and 50 mA with 720 views on a 1516 × 1516 flat-panel detector (0.28 mm pixel pitch). Compared with no-grid and grid-only reconstruction, the proposed correction reduces residual shading artifacts and improves image uniformity. The contrast-to-noise ratio increases from 1.63 (no grid) and 3.27 (grid only) to 3.69 with the proposed method, with improved contrast visibility. These results demonstrate that grid-wall shadows provide practical sampling positions for estimating and correcting additive residual scatter in grid-based CBCT systems.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 290Poster Number:MIC-10-290] Low-Dimensional Embeddings of Structural MRI for Multi-Disease Brain Morphometry (#2362)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Jimenez Mesa (Autores: C. Jimenez Mesa , M. Mamalakis , C. Vazquez-Garcia , F.J. Martinez Murcia , J. E. Arco , F. Segovia , J. Ramirez , A. Ortiz , J. Suckling , J.M. Gorriz)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Malaga, Department of Communications Engineering, Malaga, Spain [2] University of Granada, DaSCI Andalusian Institute of Data Science and Computational Intelligence, Granada, Spain [3] University of Cambridge, Department of Psychiatry, Cambridge, United Kingdom [4] University of Cambridge, Cancer Research United Kingdom Cambridge Institute, Cambridge, United Kingdom [5] University of Granada, Department of Signal Theory, Telematics and Communications, Granada, Spain [6] University of Granada, Mind, Brain, and Behavior Research Center, Granada, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The differential diagnosis of neurological disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and multiple sclerosis (MS) remains a clinical challenge due to overlapping neuroanatomical atrophy patterns in structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). This work investigates whether low-dimensional embeddings derived from T1-weighted MRI can reveal a consistent neuroanatomical organisation across these conditions. Using a dataset of 528 subjects, we compared two feature extraction strategies: (i) high-dimensional voxel-wise representations and (ii) regional embeddings based on the Automated Anatomical Labeling (AAL) atlas (116 regions). Dimensionality reduction was performed using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) followed by Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) to project subjects into a two-dimensional manifold embedding. Our results demonstrate that the neuroanatomical manifold is remarkably scale-invariant as both voxel-wise and regional embeddings yielded consistent topological distributions. Centroid distance analysis in the embedding space revealed a progressive deviation from the HC baseline across disorders. Interestingly, while the model was built on the HC-AD axis, MS and FTD cohorts exhibited the largest structural displacements (d MS =7.24, d FTD =5.59) compared to AD (dAD=3.57) and PD (d PD =4.27). These findings suggest that low-dimensional manifold representations derived from structural MRI are robust to spatial aggregation and may provide an interpretable framework for studying shared and disease-specific brain alterations across heterogeneous neurological disorders.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 293Poster Number:MIC-10-293] Detector design in the AIDER Compton Camera Using Neural Networks: A Hybrid CNN-DNN Approach (#2484)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Rodriguez Almora (Autores: D. Rodriguez Almora , J. Altube , L. Barrientos , A. Brunamonti , K. Brzezinski , C. Fiorini , F. Ghisio , A. Hanna , A. Iltis , S. Parashari , J. Pérez Curbelo , G. Llosá)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This paper presents the development of a high-performance Compton camera for targeted radionuclide therapy within the framework of the European project AIDER. The camera is composed of two detector planes, each made of four LaBr 3 or CeBr 3 monolithic crystals of 50 mm x 50 mm size coupled to Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) arrays. In order to determine the optimum pixel size, a hybrid analysis approach based on convolutional neural networks (CNN) and dense networks (DNN) has been developed to estimate the interaction position of the photons. Starting from Monte Carlo simulation data (GATE v7.0) and using a reference based on an analytical model, the proposed alternative incorporates the systematic error of this model as an additional input for the NNs. This achieves active correction of the edge effect and improves the overall spatial resolution (FWHM) from a range of 1.80-2.25 mm down to 0.63-0.70 mm. Results show the benefits of the combined NN approach and indicate the possibility of employing SiPM arrays with large pixel sizes, effectively restricting the amount of readout channels. Experimental tests are ongoing.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 296Poster Number:MIC-10-296] Impact of Spatial Normalization on the Performance of Deep Learning-Based Systems for Neurodegenerative Disease Classification (#2537)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Segovia (Autores: F. Segovia , R. López , C. Vázquez-García , A. Hernández , Á. Zorrilla , C. Jiménez-Mesa , F. J. Martínez-Murcia , I. Á. Illán , J. Ramírez , T. Martín-Noguerol , J. M. Górriz)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Univiersity of Granada, Department of Signal Theory, Networking and Communications,, Granada, Spain [2] University of Malaga, Department of Communications Engineering, Málaga, Spain [3] Andalusian Institute of Data Science and Computational Intelligence (DaSCI ), Granada, Spain [4] HT Medica, Radiology department, Granada, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study evaluates the suitability of spatial registration in deep learning for neuroimaging, focusing on the balance between reducing inter-subject anatomical variability and preserving data fidelity. We hypothesize that processing images in their native anatomical space avoids morphological distortions introduced by registration, enabling neural networks to detect subtle structural biomarkers that may be altered in normalized spaces. To test this, a standard densely connected neural network was used to classify two balanced cohorts: one focused on the diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) and the other on the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease (AD). The experimental design compared four input modalities: whole-brain volumes and gray matter maps, each in native space and registered to a standard reference space. For PD classification, native and registered spaces achieved similar accuracy, although registration produced a marked imbalance between sensitivity and specificity. For AD, the best performance was obtained using gray matter in native space, confirming that preserving topological integrity is critical in pathologies with pronounced atrophy. These findings suggest that spatial registration should not be considered an indispensable preprocessing step in deep learning-based neuroimaging, but rather a methodological choice that must be evaluated based on the task and dataset. Processing in native space is an effective alternative that simplifies preprocessing while preserving diagnostically relevant information, opening future research directions on model robustness to anatomical variability without prior transformation.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 299Poster Number:MIC-10-299] Edge-Guided Deformation Field Fusion for Robust PET Motion Correction (#2650)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 W. Qi (Autores: Q. Liu , W. Qi , J. Kolthammer)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Canon Medical Research USA, Vernon Hills, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Non-rigid motion correction for gated PET is challenging due to low contrast and high noise in homogeneous regions, where deformation estimates may drift, while strong smoothness regularization can oversmooth boundaries and suppress localized motion near lesions. We propose an edge-guided flow fusion method that combines two deformation fields predicted by identical registration architectures trained with different smoothness weights. For each moving--fixed PET pair, we compute an edge probability map from the gradient magnitude of the Gaussian-smoothed absolute intensity difference, followed by percentile normalization and logistic mapping. After thresholding and morphological dilation, the resulting mask defines an edge-dominant region. We fuse the two predicted flows by selecting the low-regularization flow near edges and the high-regularization flow in homogeneous background regions, then warp the moving PET volume using a spatial transformer. This approach preserves deformation flexibility at boundaries while maintaining smooth motion in low-contrast regions, without changing network architecture.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 302Poster Number:MIC-10-302] Simulation Trained Convolutional Neural Network For Clinical Inter-Crystal Scattering Filtering (#2835)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 O. Bubon (Autores: H. Maa-Hacquoil , E. De Benetti , A. Reznik , O. Bubon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lakehead University, Department of Physics, Thunder Bay, Ontario, Canada [2] Radialis Inc., Thunder Bay, Ontario, Canada
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract PET detectors often use a Center of Gravity (CoG) algorithm applied to the output signal of sensor modules to perform coordinate reconstruction. CoG assumes that the spread of optical photons emitted by a pixelated scintillator crystal is symmetric about the point of interaction. A photoelectric (PE) event, where energy is deposited within a single scintillator pixel, produces such a distribution. Inter-crystal scatter (ICS) events, however, occur when a gamma photon deposits energy into multiple scintillator pixels, producing multiple photon distributions that degrade CoG accuracy and spatial resolution. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have proven effective for identifying and recovering ICS events in simulated data and in real systems when trained on experimentally acquired datasets, typically obtained using collimated measurements to isolate scintillator pixels. However, acquiring collimated datasets is time-consuming and requires high precision, motivating the use of simulated data as a primary training source. In this work, PET data was generated using GATE and used to train a small CNN to identify and remove ICS events based on softmax confidence values for a detector consisting of a 24×24 LYSO array coupled to an 8×8 SiPM array. A NU-4 image quality phantom and Na-22 point source acquired on a clinical system demonstrated improvements in recovery coefficient (RC) and peak-to-valley ratio for all RC five rod sizes, along with modest improvements in spatial resolution and spill-over ratio. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using imulated data as a primary training source for ICS filtering and recovery. Thus, a hybrid approach incorporating limited real data may further improve performance without requiring a large number of collimated acquisitions.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 305Poster Number:MIC-10-305] Temporally and Spatially-Variant Penalty for Dynamic PET Reconstruction (#2858)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Taheri (Autores: N. Taheri , T. Carlier , S. Stute)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CRCI2NA, INSERM UMR 1307, Nantes University, Nantes, France [2] Nuclear Medicine Department, Nantes University Hospital, Nantes, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dynamic PET reconstruction is challenging due to strong temporal variations in count statistics, leading to non-uniform noise and spatial resolution across frames. In this work, we simply extend previous works to propose a temporally and spatially-variant regularization strategy for dynamic penalized maximum-likelihood (PML) reconstruction based on a time-and-space-dependent modulation factor derived from the Fisher information matrix. A modified estimation of the modulation factor is used to improve robustness in low-count conditions by removing dependence on noisy measurements. The method was evaluated using dynamic FDG simulations based on the 2D Zubal brain phantom and compared with OSEM and PML reconstruction without modulation. Results showed improved preservation of anatomical structures and lower RMSE values in the cortex, putamen, and caudate regions while avoiding the excessive smoothing observed with conventional PML reconstruction. These results suggest that automatic temporally and spatially adaptive regularization can improve image quality and quantitative accuracy in dynamic PET imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 308Poster Number:MIC-10-308] SAR-Based Brain Aging Validation Using Functional Connectivity Correlation Matrices from UK Biobank (#3186)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Hernández (Autores: A. Hernández , I. A. Illán , J. Ramírez , F. Segovia , D. Salas-González , C. Jiménez-Mesa , C. Vázquez-García , F. J. Martínez-Murcia , J. Levin , J. M. Górriz)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Granada, Department of Signal Theory, Networking and Communications, Granada, Spain [2] University of Malaga, Department of Communications Engineering, Málaga, Spain [3] Andalusian Institute of Data Science and Computational Intelligence (DaSCI ), Granada, Spain [4] Ludwig-Maximilians-University, Department of Neurology, Munich, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study applies the Statistical Agnostic Regression (SAR) methodology to validate predictive model for brain aging using gray matter functional connectivity derived from fMRI data from the UK Biobank database. The method evaluates significant linear relationships between age and functional connectivity correlation matrices, by resampling and estimating an upper bound on the expected risk through a Bayesian threshold under the worst-case scenario. The SAR power quantifies the probability of detecting a true linear relationship using the expected risk statistic, via Monte Carlo simulations under the null distribution. Predictive performance is assessed through Principal Component Analysis (PCA) applied to the global correlation matrices, which are constructed from subjects whose ages fall within the extreme percentiles (below the 15th and above the 85th percentile). This framework enables the identification of connectivity signatures associated with aging within a unified representation of functional brain connectivity dynamics. Functional connectivity matrices of gray matter were computed from preprocessed fMRI data by extracting region-wise time series and estimating pairwise statistical dependencies using Pearson correlation coefficients. The results support the development of a statistically significant model for predicting age from functional connectivity correlation matrices and demonstrate that combining rigorously validated predictive models with SAR and PCA methodologies can characterize age-related variability in functional connectivity and improve understanding of brain aging using large-scale population neuroimaging data.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 311Poster Number:MIC-10-311] Interpreting Prognostic [ 18 F]FDG PET Radiomic Signatures Using Parametric Tumour Simulation (#1849)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. M. Bonney (Autores: L. M. Bonney , K. M. Bradley , A. B. Hassan , D. R. McGowan)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Oxford, Sir William Dunn School of Pathology, Oxford, United Kingdom [2] Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Department of Medical Physics and Clinical Engineering, Oxford, United Kingdom [3] Cardiff University, Wales Research and Diagnostic Positron Emission Tomography Imaging Centre (PETIC), Cardiff, United Kingdom [4] University of Oxford, Department of Oncology, Oxford, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Radiomic features derived from [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT imaging can quantify intratumoural spatial heterogeneity and have demonstrated prognostic utility across multiple oncological indications, including sarcoma. However, the biological interpretation of radiomic risk scores remains poorly understood, partly due to confounding in clinical datasets and the absence of ground-truth tumour parameters. A simulation-based approach offers a controlled framework for mapping image-derived features to biologically and physically meaningful tumour properties. In this study, a parametric tumour model incorporating eight biologically motivated parameters-including uptake intensity, radial signal gradients, compartmental structure, multifocal uptake, and morphological deformation-was used to generate 1,024 synthetic tumour volumes across physiologically plausible parameter ranges. In parallel, a prognostic radiomic risk score was derived from [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT images of 115 sarcoma patients enrolled in the Oxford Precision Oncology for Sarcoma (OxPOS) study. This trained model was subsequently applied to each simulated volume to infer a radiomic risk score, and correlation analysis identified simulation parameters most strongly associated with predicted risk. Three parameters; baseline uptake intensity, radial signal gradient, and fractional high-uptake volume, exhibited moderate but statistically significant correlations with the model-derived risk score (|r|= 0.41, 0.38, and 0.52, respectively). These findings provide mechanistic insight consistent with known tumour biology; for example, elevated radial signal gradients are characteristic of tumours with necrotic cores. This work demonstrates the utility of simulation for enhancing biological interpretability and communicability of radiomic prognostic models. Ongoing work aims to expand the simulation framework and integrate genomic data to further elucidate the biological underpinnings of radiomic signatures in sarcoma.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 314Poster Number:MIC-10-314] Parameter Estimation of Arterial Input Function Using Nonlinear Mixed-Effects Modeling With Reduced Sampling (#2685)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Du (Autores: J. Jiang , Z. Jiang , J. Chen , Y. Du)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Department of Radiology, Baltimore, Maryland, United States of America [2] Johns Hopkins University Whiting School of Engineering, Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics, Baltimore, Maryland, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dynamic positron emission tomography (PET) requires dense arterial blood sampling to estimate arterial input functions (AIFs), creating substantial clinical burden and limiting practical implementation. To reduce number of samples, we developed a data-driven method for AIF estimation under sparse sampling conditions using nonlinear mixed-effects modeling. The study dataset included 90-min dynamic brain PET AIF data from 26 healthy subjects acquired with the 11C-DPA-713. A three-exponential nonlinear mixed-effects model was used to characterize the AIF, with fixed effects representing population-level kinetics and random effects capturing inter-individual variability. The AIF was modeled using a deterministic five-point subsampling strategy that selected representative early, intermediate, and late decay-phase observations. Model parameters were estimated using the stochastic approximation expectation maximization algorithm, and reduced-sampling predictions were compared with reference ground truth generated from the full dataset. The reduced five-point strategy produced AIF estimates that closely matched the full-data reference, yielding a root mean squared error of 0.37 and a mean relative error of ranging from 19% to 27.8%. Visual comparisons further demonstrated strong agreement between predicted and reference AIFs across subjects, indicating that plasma activity characteristics were preserved despite reduction in sampling density. These findings suggest that sparse sampling combined with nonlinear mixed-effects modeling can provide reliable AIF estimation while reducing the burden of arterial blood collection in dynamic PET studies.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 317Poster Number:MIC-10-317] Orbital MRI radiomics in thyroid eye disease: A multi-structure stability analysis using perturbation-based methods (#3226)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Semnani (Autores: F. Semnani , S.S. Aarabi , A. Jafarizadeh , M. Abbasi , A. Doostparast , M. Abdollahi , R. Alizadehsani , J. M. Gorriz)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] School of Medicine, Tehran University of Medical Sciences (TUMS), Tehran, Iran (Islamic Republic of) [2] Nikookari Eye Center, Tabriz University of Medical School, Tabriz, Iran (Islamic Republic of) [3] School of Medicine, Hormozgan University of Medical Sciences (HUMS), Bandar Abbas, Iran (Islamic Republic of) [4] Eye Research Center, Mashhad University of Medical Sciences, Mashhad, Iran (Islamic Republic of) [5] School of medicine, Queensland University of Technology, Brisbane, Australia [6] Data Science and Computational Intelligence Institute, Universidad de Granada,, Granada, Spain [7] Department of Psychiatry, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Thyroid eye disease (TED), the most common autoimmune orbital disorder and a major cause of orbital morbidity, is still assessed largely through subjective clinical measures. Although orbital MRI radiomics offers potential quantitative biomarkers for disease activity and treatment response, the reproducibility of these features under real-world imaging variability has not been systematically evaluated, limiting clinical translation. We performed a perturbation-based stability analysis using 150 patients from the public TOM500 dataset, extracting 293 radiomic features from seven Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI)-compliant families across nine bilateral orbital structures using original and Laplacian-of-Gaussian filtered MRI images. We used ten perturbations per patient with combined rigid transformations, Gaussian noise, and 1-voxel mask modifications, and assessed stability using ICC(A,1). Across 2,637 structure-feature combinations, mean ICC was 0.72, and 53% of features achieved Good or Excellent stability (ICC ≥ 0.75). The medial rectus (ICC 0.84), followed by superior rectus and optic nerve (both 0.81) were the most robust structures, whereas the eyeball (0.55) and lateral rectus (0.61) were least stable. Laplacian-of-Gaussian filtering improved texture feature reproducibility, increasing median texture ICC from 0.73 to 0.80 and enhancing stability in medial rectus, lacrimal gland, and orbital fat features. Stability rankings were nearly identical between active and inactive disease groups (Pearson r = 0.92), indicating that disease severity did not influence feature reliability. These findings provide the first large-scale reproducibility assessment of orbital MRI radiomics in TED and establish a foundation for future biomarker and predictive modeling studies.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Bäumer (Autores: J. N. Esser , C. M. Bäcker , A. Hammi , B. Timmermann , J. Weingarten , J. Wulff , C. Bäumer)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The aim of the study was to investigate whether proton therapy fields can be verified in vivo during treatment using film-based transit portal dosimetry. Potential clinical treatment plans were checked for downstream dose contributions. The complete proton portal imaging workflow was verified in experiments with an anthropomorphic phantom. Head-and-neck, mediastinal, thoracic, abdominal and cranio-spinal axis irradiations (CSIs) yielded downstream dose areas, which enable portal imaging. The cranial fields of CSI plans were deemed as most suitable and tested with the phantom in a simplified setup. Radiochromic films, mounted on top of the patient couch, served as portal imaging detectors. Phantom tests indicate that the patient setup can be verified within an accuracy of ≈1 mm per direction. In conclusion, a novel, straight-forward procedure has been developed for in-vivo dosimetry in proton therapy for some patients with specific indications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 323Poster Number:MIC-10-323] A Feasibility Study of Patient-Specific Integral Dose Verification Using a 3D-Printed Tumor Model Scintillator for Radiosurgery (#1239)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H.J. Yang (Autores: H.J. Yang , T.H. Kim , Y.K. Kim , H. Kim , H.-T. Chung)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Cancer Center Korea, Proton Therapy Center, Goyang, Republic of Korea [2] Radexel Inc., Research and Development Team, Seoul, Republic of Korea [3] Hanyang University, Department of Nuclear Engineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea [4] Seoul National University College of Medicine, Department of Neurosurgery, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We developed a patient-specific volumetric dosimetry system using a tumor-shaped plastic scintillator derived from patient MR images for integral dose verification in Gamma Knife radiosurgery. Three tumor model scintillators (TMSs) representing a vestibular schwannoma (0.39 cm³) were irradiated using a nine-shot plan prescribing 8 Gy to the 60% isodose line. The integral dose, defined as the energy absorbed over the entire tumor volume, was measured and compared with the value calculated by the Leksell GammaPlan® treatment planning system. Two independent calibration methods were employed: calibration at a secondary standard dosimetry laboratory and Monte Carlo simulation-based calibration using Geant4. The integral dose measured by the simulation-based calibration was (2.00 0.76)% higher than the planned value of 5.01 mJ, falling within the acceptable 3% tolerance for Gamma Knife absolute dosimetry. The laboratory-based calibration yielded an integral dose (5.84 3.56)% lower than the reference value of 4.30 mJ; the larger deviation is attributed to probe reassembly uncertainty and the angular dependence of the calibration coefficient. These results demonstrate that the TMS system can serve as a practical tool for verifying the three-dimensional integral dose calculated by a treatment planning system.

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Compton cameras are being explored as a promising technique for treatment monitoring of targeted alpha therapy, by imaging the gamma emissions produced during the decay of the alpha-emitting radionuclides. To improve image accuracy, attenuation correction is essential. Here we analyze the effects achieved by incorporating attenuation correction into the list-mode MLEM reconstruction of MACACO III+ synthetic data using ideal simulation. The results demonstrate that, without attenuation correction, contrast recovery coefficients of 97.2%, 84.7%, 73.5%, 47.8% are achieved for rods with diameters of 6, 5, 4 and 3 mm, respectively, using a total activity of 0.135 MBq of 440 keV gammas, a major gamma peak in the decay of 225 Ac and a hot to background ratio 10:1, simulated over 2 hours. Combined energy reconstruction at 218 and 440 keV yields improved image contrast when attenuation correction is applied. This work was carried out within the frame of the Advanced Imaging DEtector for targeted Radionuclide therapy (AIDER) project.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Q. Xie (Autores: R. Liu , D. Mu , J. Zhu , A. Qiu , T. Hu , W. Li , Y. Nitta , J. Liu , L. Wan , P. Xiao , J. Zhu , Q. Xie)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Wuhan, China [2] Huazhong University of Science and Technology, School of Software Engineering, Wuhan, China [3] University of Science and Technology of China, Department of Electronic Engineering and Information Science, Hefei, China [4] Zhejiang Cancer Hospital, Hangzhou Institute of Medicine (HIM), Chinese Academy of Sciences, Department of Radiation Oncology, Hangzhou, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positron emission tomography (PET) is an effective non-invasive modality for in vivo range verification in carbon-ion therapy. This study evaluates an all-digital PET system for in-beam monitoring of carbon-ion treatment plans. Clinical DICOM RT plans were converted into a GATE/Geant4 model of single-field pencil beam scanning (PBS) carbon-ion irradiation in a polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) phantom. Simulated dose and positron-emitter distributions were compared with treatment planning system (TPS) dose and measured PET data. TPS and GATE showed good dosimetric agreement, with nearly identical planning target volume (PTV) D50% and a 3D gamma passing rate of 97.66% (2%/2 mm). PET validation yielded R50,sim = 124.33 mm and R50,exp = 125.00 mm, corresponding to ΔR50 = 0.67 mm. These results support millimeter-level PET-based range verification for carbon-ion therapy.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 332Poster Number:MIC-10-332] Performance of a state-of-the-art ToF-PET detector in a proton therapy in-beam radiation environment (#1485)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Fogg (Autores: T. Fogg , P. Dendooven)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University Medical Center Groningen, Particle Therapy Research Center & Department of Radiation Oncology, Groningen, Netherlands
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In-vivo positron emission tomography (PET) imaging of positron emitters produced by the therapeutic proton beam in the patient is a well-studied irradiation verification tool. Adaptive treatment planning benefits from fast feedback, down to the sub-second time scale, requiring an in-beam PET scanner operating during beam delivery for N-12 imaging. Use in clinical routine requires that the performance of such detectors is not significantly affected by radiation exposure over time. We have studied the performance of four state-of-the-art time-of-flight Hamamatsu C13500-4075YC-12 (ToF)-PET detectors in a proton therapy radiation environment. A 150 MeV proton beam (pulsed with intensities of 0.3, 1 and 3 nA at 10% and 1.5% duty cycles) was stopped in PMMA phantoms whilst PET data was acquired. The coincidence energy spectra obtained in-beam (both with the beam on and between beam pulses) show the N-12 511 keV peak. As the experiment progressed, the data output shows cumulative faults from an increasing percentage of corrupt events. Whilst the accumulation of these faults was partially mitigated by system resets during the experiment, comparison of data acquisitions with a combined Na-22 & Ga-68 source before and after the experiment show that the performance degradation is long-lasting, although the detectors show signs of recovery 5 months later.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 335Poster Number:MIC-10-335] In-Beam All-Digital PET for Dose-Guided Particle Therapy: Vision, Roadmap, and Progress (#1518)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Qiu (Autores: A. Qiu , Q. Xie)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Wuhan, China [2] University of Science and Technology of China, Department of Electronic Engineering and Information Science, Hefei, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Proton and heavy-ion therapy exploits the Bragg peak to concentrate dose within the tumor while sparing surrounding normal tissues; however, range uncertainties necessitate conservative safety margins and restrict clinical indications. To address this, we are developing an in-beam All-Digital positron emission tomography (PET) platform for dose-guided particle therapy. Two prototype systems have been designed, built, and tested at multiple proton and heavy-ion therapy centers: a 12-module pre-clinical partial-ring system for phantom and small-animal studies, and a 16-module research-clinical open-ring system for human-subject trials. Both employ lutetium-yttrium oxyorthosilicate scintillators read out via the multi-voltage threshold digitization architecture. In-beam PET imaging of proton-induced positron activity has been demonstrated in polymethyl methacrylate phantoms with approximately 1 mm range agreement, and in live rats where biological washout effects on image contrast were observed. A three-phase development roadmap is presented, progressing from online range monitoring to adaptive therapy and ultimately real-time feedforward therapy, aiming to narrow safety margins, broaden treatment indications, and provide the verification infrastructure for FLASH therapy.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 338Poster Number:MIC-10-338] Feasibility Study of In-Beam Range Verification Using Pixelated CZT Detectors in Carbon Ion Therapy (#1646)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Guo (Autores: D. Guo , J. Shao , X. Cai , C. Zhang , Y. Yin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lanzhou University, LanZhou, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract To overcome the limitations of existing beam range verification methods in terms of detection efficiency, system complexity, and real-time capability, this study proposes a carbon ion beam range verification method based on a pixelated cadmium zinc telluride (CZT) detector and machine learning. The pixelated CZT detector was used to measure the secondary particle response generated during carbon ion irradiation of a polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) target, and a machine learning regression model was then applied to predict the beam range. The experimental results demonstrate that the pixelated CZT detector can accurately measure secondary particle responses. In addition, the effects of different detection regions, defined by pixel ranges, were investigated at a monitor unit (MU) setting of 6 × 10⁶. Using data from a 16 × 16 pixel region, the proposed method achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.79 mm. These results indicate that the proposed approach provides a feasible technical strategy for online range verification in carbon ion beam therapy

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 341Poster Number:MIC-10-341] Experimental setup for radiobiological studies with laser-accelerated protons at high dose rates (#1921)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Velasco Peñarrubia (Autores: L. Velasco Peñarrubia , L. Martín Fernández , J. Juan Morales , D. de Luis Blanco , J.L. Henares González , J.I. Apiñaniz Aginako , M. Seimetz)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto de Instrumentación para Imagen Molecular (i3M), CSIC-Universitat Politècnica de València, Valencia, Spain [2] Centro de Láseres Pulsados (CLPU, Salamanca, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Laser-driven sources of ionizing radiation provide unique possibilities for studying ground-breaking phenomena and for exploring novel applications of compact accelerators. An outstanding example is the controlled irradiation of biological samples with laser-accelerated, high-energy particles. After a pilot experiment at the Spanish Pulsed Laser Center (CLPU), the aim of the present study is an increase of the single-shot dose and the mean dose rate on monolayer cell cultures. Two possible scenarios at the same laboratory have been considered. On the one hand, the previous setup at the VEGA-3 laser line may be upgraded through a set of permanent quadrupole magnets to focalize the proton beam closely behind the laser target. On the other hand, a similar, more compact arrangement inside the VEGA-2 target vessel benefits from shorter flight paths and a 10-fold higher repetition rate. Particle tracking simulations with realistic beam control elements point towards a 5-15 times increase in proton fluence and single-shot dose.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 344Poster Number:MIC-10-344] Design and Development of a BGO-based PET Scanner for Dose Verification after Proton Therapy (#1975)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Freire (Autores: Ó. Pietrzyk , M. Freire , M. Gil , L. F. Vidal , M. Balcerzyk , A. J. Gonzalez)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto de Instrumentación para Imagen Molecular (I3M), Centro Mixto CSIC-Universitat Politècnica de València, 46022 Valencia, Spain, Valencia, Spain [2] Bioaraba Health Research Institute, Vitoria, Spain [3] IKERBASQUE, Basque Foundation of Science, Bilbao, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Proton therapy is an advanced radiotherapy modality whose clinical advantage arises from the highly localized dose deposition produced at the Bragg peak. However, this feature makes the technique highly sensitive to uncertainties in patient positioning, anatomical changes, and beam delivery. Verifying the dose delivered to patients after treatment session is therefore essential to ensure treatment safety and reducing planning margins. During proton irradiation, nuclear interactions generate positron‑emitting isotopes that can be detected with Positron Emission Tomography (PET). In this work, we focus on the detection of 18 F, whose long half‑life enables offline PET acquisitions 60-150 min after treatment, when short‑lived isotopes have decayed. Because the expected in‑vivo 18 F activity is very low (0.1-1 Bq/mL), we propose a PET system optimized for low‑count imaging, based on BGO scintillation crystals to avoid the intrinsic background of lutetium‑based detectors typically used in commercial scanners. The proposed PET prototype ( INSPIRE ) consists of 16 detector modules arranged in a single ring, each comprising a two‑layer pixelated BGO block (19×19 and 20×20 arrays) coupled to a 12×12 SiPM array, thus enabling Depth of Interaction (DOI) information. The system, which has an inner diameter of 26 cm and an axial length of 5 cm, is intended for brain studies. In this work we present the design of the INSPIRE system and the experimental characterization of the detector modules, including pixel resolvability, layer separation, and energy performance, together with preliminary proton‑irradiation simulations that illustrate the suitability of the 18 F signal for offline PET imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 347Poster Number:MIC-10-347] A Software Framework for Real-Time Prompt Gamma Range Verification (#2107)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Urban (Autores: L. Santini , K. Urban , E. S. Bellotti , B. Foglia , A. Forgione , M. Piroddi , C. Riboldi , A. Contangelo , G. Borghi , M. Carminati , S. Agosteo , D. Mazzucconi , D. Bortot , K. Parodi , A. Mereghetti , C. Fiorini)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Politecnico di Milano, Department of Electronics, Information and Bioengineerin, Milano, Italy [2] Politecnico di Milano, Department of Energy, Milano, Italy [3] National Institute for Nuclear Physics, Section of Milan, Milano, Italy [4] Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität Munich, Department for Medical Physics, Garching, Germany [5] Centro Nazionale di Adroterapia Oncologica, Pavia, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Real-time monitoring in hadron therapy is essential to account for anatomical shifts and setup uncertainties that may compromise dose delivery. This work evaluates a software framework designed for online range verification via monitoring of the Prompt Gamma (PG) profile, which is know to be correlated to the Bragg peak position. The architecture employs a decoupled simulation pipeline: PG emission is modeled using MC codes, while the detector response is characterized through a dedicated Python-based tool, PGIPY. This simulated new profile, computed spot by spot, is then compared with measurement inside the software. To ensure spot-by-spot clinical correspondence, the software utilizes machine log files to synchronize simulated data with actual delivery sequences. Experimental validation with an homogenoeus phantom was performed at the CNAO facility (Pavia, Italy). A high degree of correlation was observed between simulated and experimental profiles, confirming that the framework is free from significant systematic modeling errors. These results demonstrate that the proposed pipeline provides a robust, validated baseline for clinical integration, ensuring that any detected profile deviations during treatment are attributable to physical range shifts.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 350Poster Number:MIC-10-350] Construction and positioning accuracy of a prototype Portable Organ Dosimetry Device (PODD) for RPT (#2213)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 W. C. Hunter (Autores: W. C. Hunter , R. S. Miyaoka)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Washington, Radiology, Seattle, Washington, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Purpose: To enable personalization dosage of 177 Lu-based Theranostic radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT), we are developing a Portable Organ Dosimetry Device (PODD) for at-home use to monitor activity in regions of interest (ROI) such as tumors and organ at risk (OAR). To accurately estimate OAR activity, knowledge of the relative positions of probes and ROIs is required. This can be achieved either by consistency of initially measured locations, or by verifying locations for each measurement. Methods: We have constructed a prototype PODD, and we examine the variation of ROI-location estimates of an NEMA IQ phantom in the PODD reference frame by measuring PODD and ROI features from repeat x-ray CT scan with the phantom removed and replaced in the PODD between measurements. Results: The standard deviations of ROI translational location with the phantom in a supine orientation was 1.0mm axially, 0.2mm horizontally, and 0.1mm vertically. Standard deviations of rotational position were 0.7 degree in tilt and less than 0.1 degrees in roll about the PODD and CT scanner axis. Conclusion: Locating uncertainty of a rigid body phantom within our prototype PODD will not significantly affect the accuracy of time-integrated activity estimates using longitudinal measurements with the phantom removed and replaced in the PODD between measurements. We must repeat these measurements for a realistic deformable phantom or with real subjects.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 353Poster Number:MIC-10-353] 224 Ra Experimental and simulation studies with the MACACO III+ Compton camera prototype (#2389)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Barrientos (Autores: L. Barrientos , K. Brzeziński , D. Rodríguez Almora , S. Parashari , M. Strugari , I. Torres-Espallardo , G. Llosá)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto de Física Corpuscular (IFIC-CSIC/UVEG), Valencia, Spain [2] La Fe Hospital (HUiP), Nuclear Medicine department, Valencia, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Compton cameras are showing promise for targeted radionuclide therapy (TRT). The IRIS group of IFIC (Valencia, Spain) has developed a scintillator-based Compton camera prototype for medical imaging applications which is being assessed in TRT. The prototype MACACO III+ consists of two detector planes, with the second having an active area four times larger than the first. Previous tests performed on phantoms and small animals using 131 I demonstrated the suitability of the system for radiotracer imaging. The system is being employed to obtain initial experimental data with different radionuclides to validate the simulations carried out within the European project AIDER, which will develop a high performance Compton camera. In this work, experimental measurements with MACACO III+ were carried out at La Fe Hospital (Valencia, Spain) to image a vial filled with 224 Ra. GATE simulations were also performed to compare with experimental data. In addition, the prototype MACACO IV, composed of two planes with four detectors each, is under development. Simulation studies also include the configuration of the new prototype to assess influence of detector geometry on the overall system performance.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 356Poster Number:MIC-10-356] AIDER Compton Camera for Targeted Radionuclide Therapy (#2559)
sub_talks.speaker: G. Llosá
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto de Física Corpuscular (IFIC), CSIC-UV., Valencia, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Targeted radionulclide therapy (TRT) is a cancer treatment modality that employs radiopharmaceuticals to selectively deliver radiation to cancerous cells at specific target organs. Its use has increased drastically in the last years, and it has been extended to novel radiopharmaceuticals. The secondary photons emitted by the therapeutic radionuclides can be employed for imaging the compound distribution in the patient's body for treatment assessment and dosimetry. A precise quantification of the radiation dose delivered to lesions and organs at risk is crucial for improving patient treatment safety and reducing related side effects. Conventional imaging modalities are not optimized for such secondary emission, in particular in the case of alpha-emitting radionuclides, which are gaining prominence due to their exceptional cytotoxicity. For targeted alpha therapy (TAT), image-based dosimetry is an unmet need as currently used gamma cameras are not effective in the case of these high energy and low activity emitters. The European project AIDER aims at developing a high-performance scintillator-based Compton camera to improve imaging in TRT and to enable image-based dosimetry in TAT. The project, coordinated by the IRIS group of IFIC, includes four academic partners, two hospitals, an SME and a patient association. Within the project, the system will be developed and tested with phantoms and patients. Initial work on system design optimization and image reconstruction, as well as detector and electronics development has been carried out.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 359Poster Number:MIC-10-359] Gamma Detection for Source Localisation in Targeted Alpha Therapy (#2678)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Williams (Autores: C. De Sio , L. AbuSabah , J. Duan , Y. Shi , S. Williams , J. Velthuis)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Bristol, School of Physics, Bristol, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Targeted alpha therapy delivers highly localised dose, so treatment planning and delivery verification depend on whether the radionuclide source remains at the intended deposition site or is redistributed by diffusion or biological transport. This simulation study tests whether decay-chain gamma emissions can provide a detectable source-localisation signal in an AlphaGlue-like geometry. Photon transport was modelled for a thin loaded glue layer on a water phantom surrounded by six detector panels, with each photon entry into a panel counted as one hit. Seven source configurations were analysed: a retained-source baseline, broad redistribution of 10%, 50%, or 90% of the source in water, and localised displacement of 20%, 40%, or 60% of the source to a compact water region. Each configuration used ten repetitions of 10,000 primary decays and was normalised to a 3 μCi reference source. Total detector-hit yield changed only modestly, but baseline-subtracted spatial hit profiles showed strong source-dependent structure. The central glue-facing signal fell to 0.94, 0.72, and 0.47 of baseline for the broad-redistribution cases, and to 0.84, 0.67, and 0.50 for the localised-displacement cases. Profile-shape features recovered the broad diffusion fraction with an R2 value of 0.998, while a secondary-source metric identified all localised displaced-source cases. The reconstructed displaced-source position was centred at approximately 525-531 mm, compared with the simulated 500 mm source region. Time-window analysis showed that large redistributions reached three-standard-deviation thresholds within 30 minutes to 2 hours; the weakest broad redistribution required about 6 hours, and the 20% localised displacement produced detectable displaced-region excess within about 1 hour. These results indicate that gamma-hit patterns provide source-location information beyond total count rate and could support activity verification and treatment-delivery monitoring.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Belcari (Autores: N. Belcari , L. Pesce , G. Sportelli , C. Catarinicchia , L. Menichetti , D. Panetta , L. Colagiorgio , A. Leso , D. Serafini , A. Arzenton , L. Cansolino , C. Alberghina , F. P. Cammarata , C. Bonanno , M. Ippolito , F. Scopelliti , G. Grosso , A. Gandini , A. Donzella , E. Mariotti , G. S. Valli , A. Andrighetto)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Pisa, Department of Physics, Pisa, Italy [2] INFN, Sezione di Pisa, Pisa, Italy [3] University of Pisa, CISUP, Pisa, Italy [4] CNR, IFC, Pisa, Italy [5] Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna, Pisa, Italy [6] INFN, Laboratori Nazionali di Legnaro, Legnaro, Italy [7] University of Padova, Department of Physics and Astronomy, Padova, Italy [8] University of Pavia, Department of Clinical Surgical Sciences, Pavia, Italy [9] INFN, Sezione di Pavia, Pavia, Italy [10] CNR, IBSBC, Cefalù, Italy [11] INFN, Laboratori Nazionali del Sud, Catania, Italy [12] University of Catania, Department of Chemical Sciences, Catania, Italy [13] Cannizzaro Hospital, Catania, Italy [14] LENA, Pavia, Italy [15] University of Brescia, Department of Mechanical and Industrial Engineering, Brescia, Italy [16] University of Siena, Department of Physical Sciences, Earth and Environment, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present a low-cost lensless radiomicroscopy system for cellular-scale imaging of theranostic radiopharmaceutical uptake using a commercial CMOS image sensor. The device enables simultaneous brightfield and β-emission imaging with sub-10 μm spatial resolution, allowing direct correlation between morphology and radionuclide distribution. The system was validated using β⁻-emitting 111Ag and β⁺-emitting 18F-FDG sources, demonstrating quantitative linearity and accurate radioactive decay measurements. Live-cell experiments on MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells showed detectable intracellular uptake of 111Ag, while imaging of U87 glioblastoma spheroids revealed spatially localized 18F-FDG accumulation in a warm background environment. These results demonstrate the potential of lensless radiomicroscopy as a compact and affordable platform for quantitative in vitro evaluation of theranostic agents at single-cell and multicellular levels.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 365Poster Number:MIC-10-365] Intercrystal Compton Scattering Detection in Pixelated LYSO Detectors via Quantum Localization (#2993)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Hashemi (Autores: A. Hashemi , X. Zhang , H. Sabet)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Harvard Medical School/Massachusetts General Hospital, Radiology Department, Boston, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We introduce a novel quantum-inspired method for identifying intercrystal Compton scattering in pixelated scintillation detectors. The approach treats each SiPM readout as a spatial signal and converts it into a discrete eigenfunction representation using a Hamiltonian built from the measured intensity distribution. Event structure is then assessed through quantum localization, quantified by the participation ratio. Single-site events produce highly localized dominant modes, whereas Compton-scattered events produce multiple localized modes associated with distinct interaction sites. A dual criterion based on quantum localization and eigenvalue proximity is used to classify multi-site events without calibration-intensive response modeling or supervised training. The method was evaluated with Geant4 optical photon simulations and measurements from LYSO:Ce detector arrays with thicknesses from 2 to 25 mm. Experimental classification agreed closely with simulation, with differences below 1% for most thicknesses and below 5% in all cases. These results indicate that the proposed representation captures the topology of gamma-ray interactions directly from detector signals.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 368Poster Number:MIC-10-368] A Learned Unfolded Deconvolution Framework for Partial Volume Correction in Total-Body PET Imaging (#3021)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. S. Azimi (Autores: M. S. Azimi , V. Felfelian , M. Cheraghi , A. Alavi , H. Arabi , H. Zaidi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Obuda University, Doctoral School of Applied Informatics and Applied Mathematics, Budapest, Hungary [2] Obuda University, University Research and Innovation Center, Budapest, Hungary [3] Shahid Beheshti University, Department of Medical Radiation Engineering, Tehran, Iran (Islamic Republic of) [4] Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Tehran, Iran (Islamic Republic of) [5] University of Pennsylvania, Department of Radiology, Philadelphia, United States of America [6] Geneva University Hospital, Division of Nuclear Medicine & Molecular Imaging, Geneva, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Total-body PET imaging provides unprecedented sensitivity and extended axial coverage but remains affected by partial volume effects (PVE), particularly in small lesions and regions with spatially varying resolution. Conventional deconvolution approaches, such as Richardson-Lucy (RL), can improve spatial resolution but often suffer from noise amplification and inaccuracies in point spread function (PSF) modeling. In this work, we propose a learned unfolded deconvolution framework for robust PVE correction in total-body PET imaging. The method reformulates RL deconvolution as a fixed-depth network in which each iteration explicitly incorporates the system PSF while learnable parameters enable adaptive regularization and noise suppression. Standard-dose [¹⁸F]FDG PET images were used as network inputs to isolate the PVE correction problem from low-count noise effects. The model was trained in a self-supervised manner using RL-generated surrogate references, eliminating the need for voxel-wise ground-truth images. Evaluation was performed on multicenter total-body PET datasets acquired from uEXPLORER and Biograph Vision Quadra systems. Quantitative assessment on an independent test set demonstrated high structural fidelity (PSNR = 47.38 ± 5.71, SSIM = 0.98 ± 0.01) and low reconstruction error (RMSE = 0.005 ± 0.003), while maintaining acceptable SUV bias (12.2% ± 23.1%). Qualitative analysis showed improved lesion delineation and enhanced uptake contrast without visible noise amplification. Bootstrap-based analysis further demonstrated stable performance with narrow confidence intervals across metrics. The proposed framework provides an interpretable and robust solution for PVE correction, improving image quality and quantitative consistency in total-body PET imaging.
