sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 371Poster Number:MIC-10-371] Direct Theranostic Dose Estimation using a Multi-Pinhole Model of the Sparse Portable Organ Dosimetry Device (#3220)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. M. Alessio (Autores: G. Maliakal , R. S. Miyaoka , W. C. Hunter , A. M. Alessio)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Michigan State University, Institute for Quantitative Health, Biomedical Engineering, CMSE, and Radiology, East Lansing, Michigan, United States of America [2] University of Washington, Radiology, Seattle, Washington, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Many studies have proposed methods to estimate internal dosimetry, enabling patient-specific adjustment of radiopharmaceutical therapy. We are developing a practical, low-cost multi-pinhole collimated system (PODD) with on the order of 10 sensors at fixed locations around a subject. Estimation of internal dosimetry to organs at risk is extremely ill-posed with this sparse sensor placement. In this work, we hypothesize that use of objective functions with an accurate forward model and multiple regularization terms can directly estimate total accumulated activity using simulated PODD acquisitions of realistic distributions of Lu-177 DOTATATE. Methods: We developed a custom GPU-based forward projector enabling rapid multi-pinhole detection simulation. We propose an objective function for direct estimation of wash-in, wash-out, and total integrated activity (TIA) kinetic parameters from multi-time point, sparse sensor measurements. This objective function includes regularization based on a) matching sensor measurements to initial time-point SPECT acquisitions and b) promoting kinetic parameters similar to population kinetics. Evaluation was performed by simulating sensor acquisitions from public 4-time point SPECT/CT images (Dewaraja et al, 2021, Lu-177 DOTATATE Anonymized Patient Datasets). Conclusion: Direct estimation of clinically relevant TIA can be performed with on the order of 10 to 20 pinhole-collimated sensors acquiring data at four times post treatment.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 374Poster Number:MIC-10-374] FastPET for low-count reconstruction scenarios (#1498)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 V. Nadig (Autores: V. Nadig , D. Bharkhada , M. Millardet , V. Panin , J. Schaefferkoetter , Y. Zheng , M. Zhang , N. Murthy , S. Liu , P. Schleyer)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Siemens Healthcare Limited, London, United Kingdom [2] Siemens Medical Solutions, Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America [3] University of Pennsylvania, Radiology Department, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Highly sensitive long-axial-field-of-view (LAFOV) positron emission tomography (PET) scanners require fast and reliable reconstruction methods, where accurate quantification in short temporal frames is key to kinetic modeling applications. We extended FastPET - a direct neural network reconstruction method based on image loss - with an additional forwardprojection step and data loss penalty, modified the training database to specifically account for short temporal frames and evaluated its PET quantification accuracy in high- and lowcount regimes on the Biograph Vision Quadra. Compared to ordered subset expectation maximation (OSEM, 4i5s, all pass) reconstructions, FastPET based only on image loss resulted in smoothed images and an overshoot in the contrast recovery coefficient (CRC) by up to 20%. A combination of data loss and image loss counteracted this effect but still showed a degraded CRC for frame lengths ≤5s. Including low-count training data in the training stablized the image quality and slightly improved the CRC of small structures in short frames ≤5s.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 377Poster Number:MIC-10-377] Quantitative Reconstruction and Correction for Long-Axial FOV PET: Optimizing Component-Based Normalization and Scatter Estimation (#1897)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Jiang (Autores: Y. Chen , R. Liao , Y. Hou , J. Jiang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Normal University, school of physics and astronomy, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The extension of the axial field-of-view (AFOV) advances in positron emission tomography (PET), offering unprecedented sensitivity and enabling ultra-low-dose 4D total-body imaging. However, long-axial field-of-view (LAFOV) systems introduce significant challenges, including prohibitive computational loads and complex quantitative corrections necessitated by expanded axial acceptance angles. A primary obstacle is the extreme sparsity of acquired data relative to the vast lines-of-response (LOR) space. We present a robust quantitative correction strategy integrated into QuanTOF, a GPU-accelerated, list-mode reconstruction framework. Our primary contribution is the implementation of a modified component-based normalization (CBN) strategy tailored for axial-dependent variations, effectively mitigating noise amplification in sparse data environments. Furthermore, we introduce a simplified calibration protocol utilizing 0.5 m thin-ring and FOV-length line sources to derive geometric and plane efficiencies-an efficient alternative to conventional through-axial rotating rods. To ensure correction accuracy despite data sparsity, a moderate rebinning strategy was employed for scatter and random estimation. The framework was validated via GATE simulations of the 1.5 m uMI Panorama GS system. Reconstruction of a 1.5 m uniform cylinder phantom (8cm radius) demonstrated superior axial uniformity, with intensity fluctuations constrained to less than 2% within 70% of the FOV. Additionally, Derenzo phantom simulations confirmed the framework's high-resolution capabilities, successfully resolving 2.4 mm hot rods. These results show this framework successfully overcomes the inherent challenges of LAFOV data sparsity, securing the quantitative fidelity essential for total-body molecular imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 380Poster Number:MIC-10-380] Optimized Partial Field-of-View Reconstruction by Limited TOF Axial Rebinning in Long-Axial PET (#2235)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 I. Hong (Autores: I. Hong , Z. Burbar)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Siemens Healthineers, R&D, Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work addresses efficient partial axial field-of-view (aFoV) reconstruction for long-axial PET systems, where reconstructing the full long-axial dataset and subsequently cropping to a target aFoV is computationally expensive. This need may arise when CT coverage is intentionally limited (e.g., organ-focused protocols or pediatric imaging). However, simply limiting the PET aFoV reduces the effective sensitivity of a long-aFoV scanner to that of a shorter-aFoV system. We propose a limited axial rebinning strategy that retains a subset of oblique lines of response that would otherwise be discarded when truncating data to a partial aFoV, thereby leveraging the sensitivity of the long-aFoV system. The approach selects a starting rebin segment and a bounded set of additional oblique segments (up to a maximum rebin segment), and rebins eligible events into target segments while preserving time-of-flight (TOF) geometry. In an FDG human study on a long-aFoV system, the proposed limited rebinning substantially increases retained true counts for a Vision-equivalent aFoV versus truncation without rebinning, while maintaining comparable axial resolution and avoiding the cost of reconstructing the full long-aFoV image.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 383Poster Number:MIC-10-383] Generalizable CT-Free Low-Dose PET Restoration: Few-Shot Adaptation Across Multi-Scanners (#2478)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 X. Qiao (Autores: X. Qiao , H. Wang , B. Yao , J. Yu , Z. Zhuang , Q. Huang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Ruijin Hospital, Shanghai, China [2] Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Department of Cardiology, Ruijin Hospital, Shanghai, China [3] Wageningen University and Research, Wageningen, Netherlands [4] Macao Polytechnic University, Faculty of Applied Sciences, Macao, China, Macao Special Administrative Region
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract PET/CT radiation exposure arises from both the injected PET radiotracer and the accompanying CT scan used for attenuation and scatter correction. Reducing PET dose while eliminating CT-based correction is therefore an attractive strategy for lower-radiation PET/CT imaging, but this setting substantially degrades image quality. In this study, we propose a deep learning framework for CT-free low-dose [18F]FDG PET restoration based on a Noise-Level-Estimation network and systematically evaluate its generalizability across different PET scanners. The model restores attenuation- and scatter-corrected PET images from reduced-dose non-corrected inputs using a mixed-dose training strategy. It was trained on a main cohort from Ruijin Hospital, acquired with [18F]FDG on a uEXPLORER scanner, comprising 5,731 reconstructed PET volumes derived from 1,163 examinations. Scanner-domain validation was performed on 640 reconstructed PET volumes derived from 320 examinations acquired on three different scanners, including Discovery MI, Vision 450, and uMI 780. Direct pretrained inference, few-shot scanner-domain finetuning, and from-scratch training were compared. Direct application of the uEXPLORER-trained model showed performance degradation under scanner shifts, whereas few-shot finetuning consistently improved restoration fidelity. In the most challenging uMI 780 cohort, median PSNR increased from 35.24 dB to 47.58 dB after finetuning. These results demonstrate the feasibility of scanner-generalizable CT-free low-dose FDG PET restoration.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 386Poster Number:MIC-10-386] 3D Photon Position Estimation Using Neural Networks in Monolithic-Based PET Systems (#2663)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Freire (Autores: P. Piera-Sapiña , M. Freire , F. Lopez-Berenguer , A. Gonzalez-Montoro , A. J. Gonzalez)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto de Instrumentación para Imagen Molecular (I3M), Centro Mixto CSIC-Universitat Politècnica de València,, Valencia, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Neural Network (NN) models have emerged as a promising tool for determining 3D photon impact positions in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) detectors based on monolithic scintillators. Nevertheless, NNs typically require long acquisitions of reference data training, becoming a time-consuming process that requires extensive experimental data for each individual detector module. To reduce calibration time, we propose a new methodology based on NNs trained entirely using simulated data to predict the 3D impact position of gamma rays. The feasibility of the proposed approach was verified using a real preclinical PET system composed of two rings of 8 LYSO:Ce monolithic scintillators each. The simulation of a single detector was implemented in GATE and reference data moving a pencil beam in 1 mm steps was simulated to train two Multilayer Perceptrons (MLPs), MLP X and MLP Y , to predict the x - and y - impact positions, respectively. To validate the introduced methodology at reconstructed image level, experimental data was acquired using a 22 Na point source at the center of the preclinical system and processed using both the presented framework and the system's standard calibration methodology. Results have demonstrated that similar spatial resolution was obtained with both approaches, thus demonstrating that NNs trained exclusively with Monte Carlo simulations can generate coherent reconstructed images and thus eliminate the need for calibration measurements for each individual detector module.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 389Poster Number:MIC-10-389] Depth Attention and Volume Attention Module for 3D Medical Image Segmentation (#1088)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 X. Kan (Autores: X. Kan , K. Ogawa)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Hosei University, Graduate School of Science and Engineering, Tokyo, Japan [2] Hosei University, Faculty of Science and Engineering, Tokyo, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract 3D medical image segmentation of CT and MRI volumes is essential for clinical diagnosis and treatment planning. While deep learning methods such as 3D U-Net, Attention U-Net, and nnU-Net achieve strong performance, conventional 3D CNNs treat all slices equally along the axial direction, causing insufficient learning of lesion-containing slices. Existing attention mechanisms such as Attention U-Net focus on height×width (H×W) planar spatial attention without explicitly modeling slice-wise importance along the depth (D) axis. This paper proposes two attention modules to address these limitations. First, a Depth Attention Module (DAM) automatically learns the importance of each slice and integrates it into each decoder layer via residual connection. Second, a volume Attention Module (VAM) extends DAM to independently learn importance along H, W, and D axes, combining three independent axis-wise attention maps to achieve disease-adaptive spatial importance learning. DAM achieves Dice improvements of 7.61%, 4.71%, and 3.72% over 3D U-Net on brain hemorrhage CT (HemSeg-200), kidney CT, and ischemic stroke MRI, respectively, and 8.52% over nnU-Net on lung cancer CT (MSD Task06). On brain hemorrhage CT, DAM further improves over Attention U-Net by 4.54% and over nnU-Net by 1.03%. VAM achieves improvements of 7.76% over 3D U-Net on brain hemorrhage CT and 2.83% over nnU-Net on lung cancer CT. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed modules across multiple diseases and imaging modalities.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 392Poster Number:MIC-10-392] Comparing the anatomical accuracy of a PET(O15) reconstructed algorithm (AGR) on Moyamoya Patients (#1252)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Azeez (Autores: A. Azeez , A. Zhang , M. Zhao , G. Zaharchuk , F. Boada)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Stanford School of Medicine, Radiological Sciences Laboratory, Palo Alto, California, United States of America [2] Stanford School of Medicine, Department of Neurosurgery, Palo Alto, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract PET(O15) is the gold standard for assessing cerebral perfusion in vivo. Assessment of perfusion deficits before surgical interventions in Moyamoya patients with PET(O15) is hampered by poor spatial resolution and low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). We investigate the use of anatomically-guided reconstruction (AGR) for improving the assessment of baseline perfusion metrics in Moyamoya patients. To evaluate PET(O15) perfusion metrics in Moyamoya patients with and without the use of anatomically guided reconstructions. We assess perfusion metrics across different anatomical brain parcellations to evaluate the differences between the conventional and AGR-enhanced PET(O15) images. Regions that overlap with clinically relevant regions are significantly different in signal intensity when comparing the use of the reconstruction method. Many of which overlap with those reported in the Moyamoya literature. Implementation of the anatomy-guided PET reconstruction(AGR) algorithm can provide clinicians with a better understanding of the disease progression, especially if data integrity is limited, and of low resolution. Particularly in cases of radioisotopes with short decay half-life, such as O15, or when studying diseases of tissue perfusion and oxygen metabolism.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 395Poster Number:MIC-10-395] MRI-Informed SPECT-only Spatial Normalization for Reliable Brain Perfusion Quantification (#1410)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. You (Autores: E. You , Y.J. Seol , H.G. Ryoo , S.K. Kang , J.S. Lee)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Seoul National University, Interdisciplinary Program in Bioengineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] Seoul National University, Integrated Major in Innovative Medical Science, Seoul, Republic of Korea [3] Seoul National University, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea [4] Samsung Ventures, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Spatial normalization enables standardized volume-of-interest quantification in brain perfusion single-photon emission computed tomography, but accurate alignment is difficult because of low resolution, noise, partial volume effects, and uptake-dependent variation. We propose a MRI-informed, SPECT-only framework that distills anatomical deformation fields and feature guidance from a magnetic resonance imaging registration teacher. The student disentangles anatomical and uptake-related representations to suppress functional-uptake interference while requiring only single-photon emission computed tomography at inference. In 173 paired imaging datasets, the method improved standardized uptake value ratio consistency between subject and template spaces, especially for fine-grained volumes of interest, supporting MRI-free, single-pass template-based quantification.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 398Poster Number:MIC-10-398] When Do TAC and ROI Features Help? Residual Multimodal Learning for GFR Estimation in Dynamic 99m Tc-DTPA Renography (#1697)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Zhu (Autores: Y. Zhu , J. Li , C. Li , J. Zhong , W. Sun , Z. Xu , J. Chen , Y. Zeng , J. Sun , H. Xiao)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Hainan University, Department of Data Science and Big Data, Haikou, China [2] The First Affiliated Hospital of Hainan Medical University, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Haikou, China [3] Hainan General Hospital, Pediatric Intensive Care Unit, Haikou, China [4] The Second Affiliated Hospital of Hainan Medical University, Department of Radiation Oncology, Cancer Treatment Center, Haikou, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dynamic 99m Tc-DTPA renography provides both spatiotemporal image information and clinically interpretable time-activity curve (TAC) and region-of-interest (ROI) descriptors for renal functional assessment. However, how these heterogeneous information sources should be integrated for automated Gates-derived total glomerular filtration rate (GFR) estimation remains unclear. This study developed a residual multimodal learning framework in which a 3D CNN image branch first estimated Gates-derived total GFR from multi-frame renography sequences, and selected TAC/ROI descriptors were then used to predict a residual correction term rather than being directly concatenated with image features. A total of 471 complete paired examinations were retrospectively included, with 376 cases for training and 95 cases for held-out testing. Representative image-only, TAC-only, direct-fusion, ROI/TAC tabular, and residual-correction models were compared under the same test split. The dynamic image-only model outperformed perfusion TAC-only, function TAC-only, and pure ROI/TAC tabular models, indicating that the multi-frame renography sequence was the dominant information source. Direct fusion of image and TAC inputs did not improve image-only prediction. In contrast, the proposed residual-correction model achieved the best overall performance, with the lowest mean absolute error of 8.21 and root mean square error of 10.93. These findings suggest that TAC/ROI descriptors are more useful as clinically interpretable residual correction cues than as standalone predictors or directly fused inputs. The proposed framework provides a practical strategy for approximating total GFR from routine dynamic 99m Tc-DTPA renography while clarifying the complementary role of TAC/ROI descriptors.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 401Poster Number:MIC-10-401] Uncertainty-Guided Localized Diffusion Refinement for Lumbar Spine MRI Segmentation (#1924)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Q.V. Pham (Autores: Q.V. Pham , S. Sung , H.J. Choi , S. Jeong , S.W. Nam , H. Kim , C.H. Min)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yonsei University, Department of Radiation Convergence Engineering, Wonju, Republic of Korea [2] Hanoi University of Science and Technology, Faculty of Engineering Physics, Hanoi, Viet Nam [3] Yonsei University Wonju College of Medicine, Department of Radiation Oncology, Wonju, Republic of Korea [4] Wonju Severance Christian Hospital, Wonju College of Medicine, Yonsei University, Department of Rheumatology, Wonju, Republic of Korea [5] Wonju Severance Christian Hospital, Wonju College of Medicine, Yonsei University, Department of Radiology, Wonju, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Lumbar spine MRI segmentation is an important prerequisite for quantitative spine image analysis; however, it remains challenging due to complex anatomy, low contrast, and high inter-patient variability. Recent diffusion-based approaches have shown potential for medical image segmentation; nevertheless, preserving anatomically consistent boundaries remains challenging, particularly in low-contrast regions. We propose a conditional diffusion-based framework for lumbar spine MRI segmentation with uncertainty-guided localized refinement. The model integrates a UNet-based denoising backbone with multi-scale feature encoding to preserve anatomical structures during the diffusion process. Furthermore, an entropy-driven uncertainty mechanism is introduced to identify ambiguous regions, enabling localized refinement and selective diffusion re-sampling in low-confidence regions to support boundary delineation. The framework is evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation on multi-contrast (T1- and T2-weighted) MRI data, achieving Dice scores of 0.87-0.89 with low surface errors (ASSD ≈ 1-2 mm, HD95 < 10 mm). The current results demonstrate consistent segmentation performance across spinal canal, vertebral bodies, and intervertebral discs, indicating the feasibility of automated multi-structure lumbar MRI segmentation. These results suggest that the proposed framework can serve as a technical foundation for automated quantitative spine MRI analysis. In future work, this framework will be extended to vertebral body and corner-region analysis for edema detection, assessment of corner changes, and quantitative MRI evaluation of axial spondyloarthritis.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 404Poster Number:MIC-10-404] PhysiCal-PET: Physics-based neural networks for the rapid position Calibration of PET Scanners (#2036)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Abushawish (Autores: M. Abushawish , P. Galve , I. Colmenarejo Allavena , S. Gaitan Dominguez , C. Galindo Morata , V. M. Nouvilas , J.M. Udias)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Grupo de Física Nuclear, EMFTEL & IPARCOS, Madrid, Spain [2] Health Research Institute of the Hospital Cínico San Carlos (IdISSC), Madrid, Spain [3] Spanish National Research Council (CSIC), Institute for Physical and Information Technologies "Leonardo Torres Quevedo", ITEFI, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Total-body positron emission tomography (PET) increases system sensitivity and enables whole-body dynamic imaging, but its extended axial field of view makes accurate depth-of-interaction (DOI) calibration essential for maintaining uniform spatial resolution and reducing parallax error. Conventional DOI calibration requires mechanically scanned collimated sources or detector-specific reference measurements, which become impractical as the number of detector modules increases. PhysiCal-PET introduces a physics-based neural-network framework for autonomous in-system DOI calibration of PET scanners. The method trains a network to map raw detector signals to DOI using coincidence data acquired with an uncollimated positron source at known positions. For each event, the loss function enforces annihilation geometry by requiring the predicted line of response to be consistent with the source position, thereby providing supervision without measured DOI labels. The framework was tested on realistic PET simulations and applied to data from a real preclinical PET scanner. Using this procedure, the DOI response of all 144 detector modules was calibrated in less than 2 hours of point-source measurement time. These results demonstrate that the annihilation physics can replace labor-intensive DOI calibration hardware and enable rapid, routine calibration of high-resolution PET systems. PhysiCal-PET therefore provides a scalable path toward autonomous calibration for total-body PET and other systems that rely on accurate DOI positioning.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 407Poster Number:MIC-10-407] Nonsubsampled Contourlet Transform-based Generative Adversarial Networks for Anatomical Structure-Preserving Low Dose CT Denoising (#2204)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Cho (Autores: H. Cho , S. Cho)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yonsei University, Department of Radiation Convergence Engineering, Wonju, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a Nonsubsampled Contourlet Transform-Based Generative Adversarial Network (NSCT-GAN) for low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) denoising. LDCT reduces radiation exposure but introduces quantum Poisson and electronic Gaussian noise, which blurs anatomical structures. Conventional deep learning methods using mean-squared error loss produce over-smoothed images, while existing image-domain generative adversarial networks (GANs) struggle with high-frequency CT noise. To address this, the proposed NSCT-GAN extracts multi-scale, multi-directional, and shift-invariant high-frequency features using the NSCT. The network trains a discriminator on these high-frequency images to distinguish noise from anatomical edges. The generator utilizes a U-Net architecture to maintain spatial consistency. The objective function combines a Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty adversarial loss for high-frequency reconstruction, an L1 loss for accurate CT number recovery, and a multi-scale structural similarity (MS-SSIM) loss for global and local structural consistency. The method was evaluated using the 2016 NIH-AAPM-Mayo Clinic Low-Dose CT Grand Challenge dataset and compared against five deep learning-based denoising methods: WavResNet, SMGAN, CPCE, DU-GAN, and WDLP. Quantitative results demonstrate that NSCT-GAN achieves a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 27.1850 dB, a structural similarity index (SSIM) of 0.8215, and a feature similarity index (FSIM) of 0.9698, yielding the highest SSIM and FSIM values among the tested models. Qualitative evaluations show the method restores continuous vascular boundaries in the lungs and maintains heterogeneous parenchymal patterns in the liver without introducing over-smoothing or artifacts.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 410Poster Number:MIC-10-410] Preliminary Results of Generative Model-Based Positron Range Correction in PET Imaging (#2359)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Hou (Autores: Y. Hou , J. Ni , Y. Chen , F. Zhan , J. Jiang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Normal University, School of Physics and Astronomy, Beijing, China [2] The First Affiliated Hospital of USTC, Department of Nuclear Medicine,, Hefei, China [3] Jiangnan University, Wuxi School of Medicine, Wuxi, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positron range is an inherent physical factor that degrades the spatial resolution of positron emission tomography (PET), particularly for radionuclides with high positron energies. This study investigated the feasibility of deep learning-based positron range correction for PET brain imaging. A total of 304 brain datasets acquired using a Siemens Biograph Vision PET/CT scanner at the First Affiliated Hospital of the University of Science and Technology of China were voxelized to generate brain phantoms. These phantoms were used as activity maps for GATE simulations with three emission settings: 18 F, 68 Ga, and back-to-back sources. The 18 F and 68 Ga simulations represented mild and severe positron range effects, respectively, whereas the back-to-back simulation served as the range-free reference. Two deep learning-based correction methods were evaluated, including a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model (C-DDPM) and a residual U-Net (Res-UNet). Visual results showed that C-DDPM better restored fine sulcal and gyral structures and achieved closer agreement with the back-to-back reference, especially for the more severe 68 Ga correction task. Although Res-UNet achieved superior PSNR, SSIM, and NRMSE values, its restored images exhibited noticeable oversmoothing and partial loss of subtle anatomical details. These findings suggest that diffusion-based generative restoration is a promising strategy for positron range correction, with the potential to reduce positron range induced blurring while preserving fine anatomical structures.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 413Poster Number:MIC-10-413] Wavelet-Conditioned Rectified Flow for Efficient Whole-Body Low-Dose PET Denoising (#2431)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Xie (Autores: L. Xie , W. Duan , J. Yan , H. Zhang , S. Wang , Z. Wu , H. Liu , Y. Liu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Low-dose positron emission tomography (PET) reduces injected activity and acquisition time, but low-count statistics introduce strong noise, impaired lesion conspicuity, and unstable standardized uptake value (SUV) quantification in whole-body imaging. Recent 3D diffusion models improve PET denoising, and wavelet-conditioned diffusion further shows that the Haar low-frequency LLL subband can serve as a robust structural prior. However, diffusion sampling is computationally expensive for large 3D PET volumes. We propose Wavelet-Conditioned Rectified Flow (WCRF), a deterministic whole-body PET restoration framework that integrates wavelet-domain structural guidance with rectified-flow matching. To establish robust structural guidance, WCRF isolates the lowest-frequency (LLL) subband via a single-level 3D Haar decomposition. This frequency-derived information is then combined with the original noisy input to form a resilient conditioning signal. A lightweight ControlNet-style branch injects this condition into a time-conditioned rectified-flow network, which learns the velocity field from low-dose to full-dose PET along a straight transport path. During inference, WCRF restores full 3D volumes using sliding-window Euler integration with only a small number of function evaluations. Experiments against low-dose input, 3D U-Net, 3D GAN, and 3D DDPM baselines at the 1/20-dose setting show that WCRF achieves competitive overall restoration performance among the evaluated methods, while substantially reducing inference cost relative to DDPM.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 416Poster Number:MIC-10-416] Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Denoising for Low-Dose Fluoroscopy via Motion-Gradient Weighting (#2582)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. León (Autores: N. León , X. Ye , J. L. Longas , J.M. Arco , J.M. Ortega , M. Pérez-Liva , J. L. Herraiz , A. Sisniega)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Sedecal Molecular Imaging, Madrid, Spain [2] Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Nuclear Physics Group and IPARCOS, Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A spatio-temporal denoising training strategy for low-dose fluoroscopy is proposed, based on a spatially-adaptive temporal consistency metric. This approach acts on a small set of consecutive frames coupling a conventional denoising operator with an adaptive motion-gradient attention gate to selectively modulate the temporal consistency terms within the loss function, ensuring effective noise suppression and flickering reduction while maintaining high anatomical fidelity in dynamic regions. The proposed method was used to train a denoising operator in which a three-frame temporal window is used as input. The model was trained across multiple dose reduction factors (qF), and demonstrated superior structural recovery and enhanced temporal stability in the processed image sequences, compared to single-frame models. Quantitative and qualitative evaluation of image quality, along with stability maps-defined as the Normalized Cross-Correlation (NCC) of temporal Coefficient of Variation (CV) maps-confirms high fidelity relative to high-dose reference acquisitions, effectively mitigating stochastic fluctuations without introducing motion artifacts.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 419Poster Number:MIC-10-419] An Ensemble of Deep-Learning Classifiers for 3D Anatomical Change Reconstruction in Carbon-Ion Radiotherapy (CIRT) (#2644)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Martisikova (Autores: P. Schlegel , R. Kirchgässner , P. Ochoa-Parra , E. Bartelme , R. Mikut , O. Jäkel , M. Martisikova)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] DKFZ, Division of Medical Physics in Radiation Oncology, E040, Heidelberg, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [2] Heidelberg Institute for Radiation Oncology (HIRO), National Center for Research in Radiation Oncology (NCRO), Heidelberg, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [3] University, Heidelberg, Medical Faculty, Heidelberg, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [4] Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT), Institute for Automation and Applied Informatics (IAI), Karlsruhe, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Carbon-ion radiotherapy (CIRT) combines high biological effectiveness with outstanding treatment precision. Since treatment plans are based on the most recent Computed Tomography (CT), anatomical changes during multi-week treatments may compromise dose delivery accuracy. To address the increasing uncertainty about the patient's anatomical state with time elapsed since the planning CT, our group developed an in vivo monitoring method using secondary charged particles emitted during therapy. This non-invasive approach requires no additional dose and reduces uncertainty about patient anatomy and thus, loss of treatment accuracy. It uses a custom detection system to detect nuclear fragments emmited from the patient and allows approximating their origin. To reconstruct these changes in 3D, we utilize our recently published method for detecting the depth (z) of changes along the beam axis and apply it to a sliding window (x,y) along the transverse plane. However, splitting reconstructed nuclear fragment origins into smaller subsets reduces the statistical stability of each subset distribution. In this study, we present an approach to robustly distinguish whether a windowed subset belongs to a region with or without an anatomical change based on correlation matrices generated by our depth detection method. These images contain location-wise correlations of joined frequency band variations between projections of nuclear fragment measurements from different treatment days. To classify regions of change and approximate change depth, we train an ensemble of deep learning-based image classifiers with different architectures (i.e. ResNet, RegNet and ConvNeXt) and combine their outputs into an ensemble decision. The approach was validated using dedicated irradiation measurements with coin-sized cavities inserted into PMMA head phantoms. Despite limited training data, we achieved robust improvements in change localization using an ensemble of different deep learning architectures.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 422Poster Number:MIC-10-422] Reduction of Breathing and Metallic Implant Artifacts in PET with Synthetic CT Attenuation (#2684)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Wilson (Autores: J. Edwards , Z. Wilson , S. Wollenweber , R. Johnsen , H. Ratner , A. Mehranian , K. M. Bradley , D. R. McGowan)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Oxford, Oncology Department, Oxford, United Kingdom [2] Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Department of Medical Physics and Clinical Engineering, Oxford, United Kingdom [3] GE HealthCare, Chicago, Illinois, United States of America [4] University Hospital of Wales, Wales Research and Diagnostic Positron Emission Tomography Imaging Centre, Cardiff, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Despite its widespread use for compensating attenuation in positron emission tomography (PET), computed tomography (CT)-based attenuation correction has limitations which can create imaging artifacts associated with breathing motion and metallic implants. Using deep learning networks to create synthetic attenuation correction maps represents a data-driven, non-ionizing alternative with the potential to reduce the frequency and/or intensity of such errors. In this study, the authors aimed to demonstrate that using synthetic maps would reduce breathing motion and metallic implant artifacts. To achieve this, ten anonymized whole-body F 18 -Fluorodeoxyglucose exams were assessed. Scans were divided into two Cohorts; Cohort 1 comprised exams with breathing motion artifacts, whilst Cohort 2 contained scans of patients with hip replacements. Each scan was corrected separately with CT-based attenuation correction and synthetic maps prior to identical reconstruction. Quantitative assessments of standardized uptake value (SUV) parameters were performed, and differences were tested for statistical significance. Additionally, each image's lesion detectability, diagnostic confidence and overall image quality were scored on a Likert scale by an experienced radiologist. After assessment, no statistically significant differences in SUV quantification were detected (p > 0.05). Images corrected with synthetic maps were preferred by the radiologist in Cohort 1, but no preference was expressed in Cohort 2. Moreover, a single Cohort 1 case was identified in which breathing motion artifacts impacted clinical diagnosis only for the image treated with CT-based attenuation correction. Thus, it was concluded that synthetic maps reduce breathing motion artifacts to an extent which may support clinical diagnoses, although their effects on metallic implant artifacts require further investigation.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 425Poster Number:MIC-10-425] Frozen Stable Diffusion VAE as a Slice-Wise Encoder for Scalable 3-D Medical Image Generation (#2828)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. De Paepe (Autores: Y. Mellak , A. De Paepe , A. Bousse , D. Visvikis)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Université de Bretagne Occidentale, LaTIM, INSERM, UMR 1101, Brest, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Full-volume 3-D medical image generation at clinical resolutions remains a significant challenge due to GPU memory constraints. Existing voxel-space generative methods are difficult to scale to large clinical volumes, as memory and compute costs grow rapidly with spatial resolution. Latent diffusion approaches offer a more scalable alternative [1], but they typically require training a dedicated medical autoencoder for each modality or dataset before generative modeling can begin, making the compression stage itself a major bottleneck [2], [3], [4]. A lighter alternative is to encode axial slices independently with a 2-D autoencoder and stack the resulting latent maps into a 3-D tensor [5]; however, this still requires training a modality-specific encoder from scratch, limiting generality across modalities and resolutions. We propose a scalable latent flow framework that eliminates this bottleneck by using a frozen pretrained Stable Diffusion VAE as a ready-to-use slice-wise encoder for medical volumes, requiring no modality-specific retraining or adaptation. Each axial slice is resampled to a common resolution, intensity-normalized, and encoded independently by the frozen encoder, yielding a high in-plane compression factor compared to dedicated medical autoencoders. The resulting latent maps are stacked into a compact 3-D tensor, on which a full-volume 3-D U-Net flow model is trained directly. The objective predicts clean latents and supervises in velocity space [6], ensuring stable optimization and sharp generations in high-dimensional latent spaces, avoiding the blurriness and instability observed with standard diffusion objectives. We validate our framework on CT, PET, and MRI volumes at clinical resolutions, demonstrating strong encoding fidelity and coherent full-volume generation across axial, coronal, and sagittal planes on a single consumer-grade GPU, without any modality-specific autoencoder training.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 427Poster Number:MIC-10-427] Deep learning-based 3D SPECT generation model for 225Ac-DOTATATE quantification using CT and 2D Planar images (#2434)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Yang (Autores: J. Yang , M. Almaslamani , I. Lee , I. Lim , S.-K. Woo)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Institute of Radiological and Medical Sciences, Division of Applied RI, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] University of Science & Technology, Radiological & Medico-Oncological Sciences, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [3] Korea Institute of Radiological and Medical Sciences, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Targeted alpha therapy using 225 Ac-DOTATATE has shown promise for patients with metastatic or inoperable neuroendocrine tumors. Image-based dosimetry is important for treatment optimization and toxicity assessment; however, quantitative 225 Ac SPECT imaging is challenging due to low injected activity and limited gamma-ray count statistics. This study aimed to investigate the feasibility of generating 225 Ac-DOTATATE SPECT images from planar and CT images using a deep learning-based image generation framework. Five patients were administrated administered with 205 µCi of 225 Ac-DOTATATE were included. Planar, SPECT and CT imaging was performed 24 h after administration using a dual-head Symbia T2 scanner with energy windows centered at 78, 218, and 440 keV. Fusion images were generated from planar and CT images using the conjugate view method described in MIRD Pamphlet No. 16. Planar images, fusion images, and CT images were used as multimodal inputs to a 3D U-Net encoder-decoder network to generate quantitative SPECT images. All images were resized to 128 × 128 × 128 voxels and normalized. The model was optimized using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 2 × 10⁻⁵, batch size of 1, and 500 epochs, using L1 loss. The generated SPECT images showed uptake patterns comparable to acquired SPECT images. Quantitative organ-level analysis showed similar uptake distributions across major organs and tumor regions, with relative uptake error below 15% in most organs. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of planar-to-SPECT image generation using deep learning and suggest its potential to support 225 Ac-DOTATATE image-based dosimetry by providing three-dimensional radiopharmaceutical distribution from clinically practical planar and CT images.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 428Poster Number:MIC-10-428] No CT, No Problem: Synthetic PET Enables Attenuation Correction in Dedicated Brain Scanners (#2919)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Merino-Balaguer (Autores: A. Merino-Balaguer , D. Perez-Benito , C. J. Brooks , J. J. Vaquero , J. E. Iglesias , D. Izquierdo-Garcia)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, Dpt. Bioengineering, Madrid, Spain [2] Instituto de Investigación Sanitaria Gregorio Marañón, Madrid, Spain [3] Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Dpt. Radiology, Boston, Massachusetts, United States of America [4] Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dedicated standalone brain positron emission tomography (PET) scanners have emerged in recent years as a promising technology for neuroimaging, offering high spatial resolution, increased sensitivity, reduced injected dose and shorter acquisition times. However, unlike hybrid PET/computed tomography (PET/CT) or PET/magnetic resonance imaging (PET/MRI) systems, these scanners do not provide an anatomical image from which attenuation information can be derived. We present a SynthSR-based framework to predict CT-derived attenuation maps from non-attenuation-corrected (NAC) PET images, aiming to enable attenuation correction in standalone brain PET. Building on SynthSR, a large and widely variable set of synthetic PET volumes is generated to sample a space larger than the potential clinically viable PET images, and thus increasing the robustness and clinical applicability of the model. The synthetic PET volumes are generated on-the-fly from anatomical labels using label-conditioned Gaussian-mixture intensity sampling, spatial/intensity augmentation and PET-specific priors estimated from real normalized PET data. A PET appearance model introduces count-based noise, correlated texture, smoothing, and controlled intensity variability. Finally, spatial transformations are used to increase sample diversity while preserving voxel-wise alignment. A three-dimensional U-Net was trained to predict normalized attenuation maps from synthetic PET, while validation and testing were performed on never-seen real PET/CT data. The model was optimized with 24,000 on-the-fly synthetic samples and evaluated on held-out real PET/CT data. The best validation checkpoint achieved MAE=0.03 (3%), PSNR=25.74 dB, and Pearson correlation r=0.859. On the independent test subject, the model achieved MAE=0.027 (2.7%), PSNR=26.35 dB, and r=0.854. These results support the feasibility of CT/MRI naive pseudo-CT generation for PET attenuation correction in novel standalone dedicated brain PET scanners.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 431Poster Number:MIC-10-431] Alpha-CenterNet: A Heatmap-Based Detector for Alpha-Particle Localization in Scintillator-Camera Imagery (#3015)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Kang (Autores: D. Kang , S. Kim , W. Sung)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Agency for Defense Development, Chem-Bio Technology Directorate, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [2] The Catholic University of Korea, Department of Biomedical Engineering, College of Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea [3] The Catholic University of Korea, Department of Medical Sciences, Graduate School, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Targeted Alpha Therapy with actinium-225 induces double-strand DNA breaks through individual alpha decays, motivating quantitative imaging of single-event distributions for dose assessment. We address point detection in a cerium-doped gadolinium aluminum gallium garnet scintillator coupled to an electron-multiplying camera, in which each alpha produces a point-spread function of approximately 2-micrometer diameter at 10 to 150 events per 100-millisecond frame. We compare three method groups on Monte Carlo simulated images: 20 classical preprocessing-and-clustering pipelines, two deep learning detectors based on the U-Net and YOLOv8-nano architectures, and Alpha-CenterNet, a heatmap-based detector that adapts CenterNet with a feature pyramid network and a modified focal loss. The highest-F1 classical pipeline attains 0.641 with 447-nanometer mean localization error. U-Net reaches F1 = 0.978 with 302-nanometer error; YOLOv8-nano reaches 185-nanometer error with F1 = 0.938; the two metrics produce divergent rankings. Alpha-CenterNet (3.78 million parameters) achieves F1 = 0.965 and 244-nanometer error, reducing localization error by 19 percent relative to U-Net at 26 percent of its parameter count, and reaching the validation F1 plateau of 0.98 in 29 versus 86 epochs-a 2.97-fold convergence speedup within the same ablation. The modified focal loss decouples F1 from localization error: F1 changes by 0.0004 while the mean error decreases by 76 nanometers, and this effect persists across all tested densities. The method generalizes to clustered and edge source distributions at unseen densities, supporting point detection for Targeted Alpha Therapy monitoring.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 434Poster Number:MIC-10-434] AI-Assisted Circuitry Design for a Timing-Sensitive SiPM Front-End Readout (#3235)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Wang (Autores: Z. Lv , Z. Hao , X. Lai , P. Xie , B. Wang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] ShanghaiTech University, School of Biomedical Engineering, Shanghai, China [2] Shanghai United Imaging Healthcare Advanced Technology Research Institute Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Artificial-intelligence-assisted PCB layout is an emerging capability that promises to reduce design iteration time and enable rapid exploration of placement and routing alternatives, which is particularly valuable for complex, multi-channel analog front-end boards where manual layout is labor-intensive and experience-dependent. In this work, we explore the application of an AI-assisted layout workflow to a timing-sensitive silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) front-end readout board for time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET) detectors. A four-channel RF front-end readout board, extending a validated single-channel timing topology, underwent automated placement and routing via AI layout tools. To establish a performance baseline, a single-channel prototype of the same RF topology was fabricated and characterized using a coincidence measurement setup with LYSO scintillators, achieving a coincidence time resolution of 100.78 ps and confirming the near-100-ps timing capability of the front-end design. Preliminary evaluation of the AI-generated four-channel layout shows that the tool achieved high routing completion and produced a viable candidate layout. Based on these encouraging results, we plan to fabricate the AI-generated board and systematically compare its timing performance, energy response, and channel consistency against our manually designed baseline, providing a direct, measurement-level assessment of AI-assisted layout quality for timing-sensitive detector electronics.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 437Poster Number:MIC-10-437] Simultaneous Dual Tracer PET Separation in reconstruction: Validation on LAFOV Data (#1161)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Li (Autores: Z. Li , N. Efthimiou , S. L.M. Viol , G. Luurtsema , T. van Meerten , K. Thielemans , A. H. Brouwers , A. A. Lammertsma , C. Tsoumpas)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University Medical Center Groningen, Department of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging, Groningen, Netherlands [2] VU University Medical Center, Department of Radiology and Nuclear Medicine, Amsterdam UMC, Amsterdam, Netherlands [3] University Medical Center Groningen, Department of Hematology, Groningen, Netherlands [4] University College London, Institute of Nuclear Medicine, London, United Kingdom [5] University College London, UCL Hawkes Institute, London, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Simultaneous dual tracer PET provides complementary physiological information compared with single tracer imaging. For example, combining [⁸⁹Zr]labeled monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) with [¹⁸F]fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) enables the assessment of both targeted uptake and glucose metabolism, potentially improving patient selection [1]. Existing dual tracer separation methods exploiting differences in tracer kinetics are typically applied post-reconstruction in the image domain. However, these approaches may be sensitive to noise propagation. In this work, we evaluate a sinogram-domain iterative separation method that is incorporated directly into the reconstruction process, enabling direct generation of single tracer images.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 440Poster Number:MIC-10-440] High-Energy Proton Scattering Radiography of a Geant4 Hand Phantom under Constant-Energy Loss (#1435)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. S. Ughade (Autores: R. S. Ughade , S. Chatzidakis)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Proton radiography and tomography often use residual energy or water equivalent path length (WEPL) to estimate relative stopping power (RSP). Since the maximum likelihood path (MLP) formalism of Schulte et al. (2008), proton trajectories in tissue have been modeled as curved paths constrained by entry and exit tracking. In full proton CT, this path estimation is coupled to energy dependent multiple Coulomb scattering and longitudinal energy loss, which becomes computationally and physically complex at low residual energies. Most MLP based reconstructions use the estimated path mainly to assign WEPL or RSP contributions to voxels. Here, we examine a thin object regime in which scattering itself provides imaging contrast. For high energy protons traversing a human hand, the integrated energy loss is small, allowing the scattering relevant βcp factor to be approximated as constant along the path. Under this constant energy approximation, we reconstruct a volumetric scattering density map using an M-value calculated from each proton scattering angle and kinetic energy, together with the μTRec Bayesian voxel attribution algorithm developed for muon scattering tomography. The method is demonstrated in Geant4 using an anthropomorphic hand phantom containing bones, muscles, tendons, and skin. A single orientation 200 MeV parallel proton beam with 10^7 protons is simulated and reconstructed on a 0.3 mm voxel grid. The resulting proton radiograph resolves carpals, metacarpals, and phalanges, and detects a submillimetre osteochondral gap at the thumb interphalangeal joint. These results suggest that constant energy, MLP inspired scattering radiography can provide a computationally lightweight alternative or complement to energy loss based proton imaging for thin anatomical sites.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 443Poster Number:MIC-10-443] Multiple Emission Tomography: A High-Sensitivity Single-Layer Simultaneous PET Compton-Camera (#1838)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Pizzichemi (Autores: M. Pizzichemi , G. Terragni , F. Pennazio , F. Sgarbi , L. Cassano , L. Arnone , M. N. Colombo , E. Fiorina , F. Cossio , M. Fadavi Mazinani , M. Paganoni , E. Auffray , L. Presotto)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Milano-Bicocca, Milano, Italy [2] CERN, Geneva, Genève, Switzerland [3] INFN Torino, Torino, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The growing importance of theranostics and research with long‑lived isotopes demands imaging systems far more sensitive than standard PET or SPECT. Many emerging isotopes lie outside current detector capabilities, resulting in low sensitivity, high background, and poor quantification, as seen with 90 Y verification and 124 I or 89 Sr imaging. The Multiple Emission Tomography (MET) project introduces a novel imaging device based on inorganic scintillators, capable of operating in dual modes: PET-style coincidence detection of 511 keV photon pairs and single-photon Compton-scattering detection in a single-layer configuration. The technical configuration of the MET prototype utilizes a DOI-capable light-sharing scheme. Each module consists of a 16x16 matrix of 1.53x1.53x20 mm 3 depolished LYSO crystals coupled to an 8x8 array of 3x3 mm 2 Hamamatsu Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs). The detector's readout electronics are based on the ALCOR ASIC, a low-power, mixed-signal device featuring single-photon sensitivity, a high bandwidth of up to 2 Mevents/s per channel, and a fine 25 ps time binning. Supported by a combination of analytic algorithms and a machine learning pipeline, the MET detector can successfully solve the temporal sequence of inter-crystal scatters, and determine the points of interaction and the energies deposited. To fully leverage these recovered events, a dedicated Compton image reconstruction algorithm has been developed, employing an event-by-event statistical model with ad-hoc projector functions. This technology is expected to significantly impact theranostics, collimator-less SPECT, and in-vivo range verification for CPT.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 446Poster Number:MIC-10-446] A Scalable NaI(Tl)-SiPM Photon-Counting Scintillator Detector for Gold and Gadolinium XRF Imaging (#2151)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. L.M. Silva (Autores: A. L.M. Silva , B. Casanelli , D. Batista , T. Ferreira , P. Correia , R. Figueroa , J. Veloso)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] I3N -University of Aveiro, Physics Dpt., Aveiro, Portugal [2] Center of Excellence in Physics and Engineering in Health (CFIS), University of La Frontera (UFRO),, Temuco, Chile
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Gold and gadolinium-based nanoparticles have been investigated as theranostic agents whose characteristic X-ray fluorescence (XRF) emissions enable non-invasive, element-specific biodistribution imaging. This work presents the design, assembly, and characterization of a scalable NaI(Tl)-SiPM scintillation detector module developed as a building block for a 16-element detector array for the Confocal Orthovoltage X-Ray--Induced Radiation System (COXIRIS) Project. Each module comprises a 25.4x25.4x4 mm 3 monolithic NaI(Tl) crystal optically coupled to a custom SiPM array and read out by the TOFPET2 ASIC. The architecture targets the K-shell fluorescence lines of gold ( K α = 68 keV) and gadolinium ( K α = 43 keV), while providing a large active area at low cost. Four modules were characterized with a 2.0 μ Ci 241 Am source, whose 59.5 keV emission lies within the 40--80 keV target interval. The peak was clearly identified in all modules, with energy resolutions ranging from 47% to 65%. Per-pixel gain calibration produced an additional relative improvement of approximately 2% for each module. These results support the feasibility of the proposed assembly approach as a detector building block for XRF imaging applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 449Poster Number:MIC-10-449] A Preclinical PET System for Simultaneous Acquisition and Separation of Multiple Tracers (#2209)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. W. Foster (Autores: J. W. Foster , W. He , M. N. Ullah , Y. B. Shah , G. Chinn , C. S. Levin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Stanford University, Electrical Engineering, Stanford, California, United States of America [2] Stanford University, Radiology, Stanford, California, United States of America [3] Stanford University, By courtesy Electrical Engineering, Bioengineering, Physics, Stanford, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positron emission tomography (PET) is traditionally limited to scanning one tracer per session. Positron and prompt gamma emitters may be used to form triple coincidences that allow for signal separation based on energy. We present a proof-of-concept, preclinical PET system designed for detecting and distinguishing prompt gamma and annihilation photons in the same detector. We describe the data processing pipeline with advances for estimating randoms, scatter, and sensitivity of the prompt gamma photon. System performance is characterized with NEMA and Derenzo phantom studies. Next, we present multi-isotope studies using 52 Mn and 18 F in a custom image quality phantom. We compare two reconstruction methods and find alternating updates yield faster convergence and higher image quality. After correcting for injected activity and decay, the mean voxel intensity ratio between 18 F and 52 Mn across background ROIs is 0.95 ± 0.06, where 1 represents perfect quantitative agreement. The uncertainty reflects variability across ROIs and dose calibrator uncertainty (±2%), suggesting unmixing accuracy is within dose calibrator tolerance. Further, we scan the phantom after 18 F decay to determine the relative image quality between single ( 52 Mn only) and dual ( 52 Mn with 18 F) acquisition. We find the 52 Mn image has similar contrast recovery (0.65/0.62) and crosstalk ratio (0.24/0.24) between the single and dual acquisition. Due to low triples sensitivity, simultaneous acquisition of both radionuclides reduces the contrast to noise from 10.2 to 4.7. Despite limitations on axial field of view, data rate, and the high background from 52 Mn's 3 gamma cascade, we achieve high quantitative accuracy. Future studies will scale up the system, use more favorable tracers, add regularization to mitigate noise propagation and include preclinical animal scans.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 452Poster Number:MIC-10-452] On the Pseudo Dark-Field Signal in X-Ray Scattering Tensor Tomography (#2316)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Liu (Autores: R. Deng , R. Liu , P. Song , J. Lu , L. Zhang , Z. Wang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract X-ray scattering tensor tomography retrieves directional dark-field projections from the focused, structured illumination produced by 2D diffractive optics, and is increasingly attractive as a route to anisotropic micro-structural imaging on laboratory sources. Quantitative tensor reconstruction requires the focused reference field to cancel out exactly in the Fourier-domain retrieval, a condition met only under monochromatic illumination. We show that beam hardening through an absorbing sample reshapes this focused reference field non-uniformly across its bright core and the surrounding plateau, so the retrieval assigns a non-zero scattering tensor to a purely absorbing object-a pseudo dark-field signal. We derive a closed-form expression for the pseudo dark-field signal, prove its exact isotropy arising from the circular symmetry of the focal spot, and identify the retrieved observables that are biased by beam hardening versus those that are not. The standard angular-consistency metric is blind to this bias, so a dedicated calibration is required. We describe a step-wedge calibration protocol that compresses the family of pseudo dark-field signals into a single thickness-dependent function suitable for per-pixel correction. Removing this artefact is a prerequisite for quantitative X-ray scattering tensor tomography on laboratory sources.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 455Poster Number:MIC-10-455] A Proof-of-Concept Tri-Mode PET and SPECT Imager with a Shared Scintillator-as-Collimator Detector (#2390)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 X. Zeng (Autores: X. Zeng , H. Yang , M. Niu , W. Huang , X. Jiang , C. Huang , Y. Zhao , J. Tian , X. Zhang , Q. Wei , J. Wu , Y. Liang , Z. Gu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] shenzhen bay laboratory, Shenzhen, China [2] University of Science and Technology Beijing, School of Automation and Electrical Engineering, Beijing, China [3] Beijing Normal University, School of Physics and Astronomy, Beijing, China [4] Cancer Hospital Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, Shenzhen, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Simultaneous dual-radionuclide imaging offers complementary information for diagnosis, stratification, treatment planning, and therapy evaluation. However, the fundamental differences between PET and SPECT present significant challenges for integrated imaging. We propose a scintillator-as-collimator detector enabling both PET and SPECT. It consists of three scintillator layers separated by two light guides. Parallel holes in the upper portion function as a SPECT collimator, referred to as the scintillator-as-collimator volume (SCV). The lower portion serves as the SPECT detector (SD). In PET mode, the entire detector acts as a multi-resolution TOF-DOI PET detector. Thus, it serves as a self-collimated SPECT or TOF-DOI PET detector. A dual-panel prototype was developed with rotational acquisitions for PET, SPECT, and simultaneous imaging. SPECT events are selected using flood image mask, maximum SiPM channel energy (Pmax), and DOI-integrated charge (QDC). SPECT resolution reaches ~5 mm. PET performance is preserved, with best SD-SD CTR of 352 ps and two-layer DOI. The introduction of holes has minimal impact on PET detection, enabling high-quality PET images. In simultaneous imaging, a unified timing framework rejects 511 keV down-scatter, and residual artefacts were further mitigated using a 200-240 keV energy window for scatter correction. Phantom experiments validate tri-mode imaging. This detector eliminates external collimators, supports multi-tracer imaging, and offers a cost-effective single-detector-set PET&SPECT system.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 458Poster Number:MIC-10-458] Zero-Shot PET Image Super-Resolution via Cross-Modal Mutual Information Guidance (#2526)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. He (Autores: Y. He , Y. Lv)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shanghai United Imaging Medical Technology Co., Ltd, Molecular Imaging Business Unit, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Diffusion models have shown strong potential for improving PET image quality. However, existing methods based on unconditional pretrained diffusion priors often struggle to balance realism and fidelity, particularly in preserving high-resolution details. To address this issue, we propose MI-ResShift, a zero-shot mutual information-guided diffusion model with residual shifting for PET image super-resolution. MI-ResShift introduces a differentiable local-wise mutual information layer to guide the denoising process using structural information from CT or MRI, enabling robust cross-modal feature alignment in the statistical domain. By combining mutual information guidance with residual shifting, the proposed method enhances PET detail fidelity and robustness while reducing diffusion-based inference to only four steps. Experiments on PET/MR brain datasets demonstrate that MI-ResShift improves image quality over classical interpolation methods and provides an efficient solution for cross-modal PET super-resolution.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 461Poster Number:MIC-10-461] Extracting total and Compton attenuation coefficients via ghost imaging-like photon counting (#2895)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. R. Romanchek (Autores: G. R. Romanchek , P. G. Bharathi , S. Abbaszadeh)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Department of Nuclear, Plasma, and Radiological Engineering, Urbana, Illinois, United States of America [2] University of California Santa Cruz, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Santa Cruz, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Coincidence-based imaging with the back-to-back 511 keV photon pairs emitted during positron annihilation enables transmission imaging with reduced quantum noise. Conventional transmission imaging recovers only a single attenuation-related quantity per voxel or pixel. In this work, we extend coincidence-based imaging to simultaneously recover both the total and the Compton-scatter linear attenuation coefficients from a single acquisition, providing a second axis for material identification. Forward-scattered photons collected in coincidence within an analytically defined polar window, obtained by integrating the Klein-Nishina differential cross section over a 20-to-30-degree band, enable direct estimation of the Compton macroscopic cross section, while the idler channel provides the incident count for the total coefficient. We evaluate the approach using Monte Carlo simulations of opposing cadmium zinc telluride panels viewing a water phantom of thickness 2 to 10 millimeters. Idler-normalized transmission was recovered to within 0.1 percent across all thicknesses, while the extracted total and Compton coefficients exhibited 1 to 4 percent absolute error, with the Compton coefficient transitioning from over- to underestimation near 6 millimeters. These deviations arise from logarithmic amplification of small counting errors and from competing air-scatter contamination at thin phantoms and self-attenuation of scattered photons at thicker ones. The results establish that scatter data from coincidence-based annihilation imaging can recover a second material descriptor, motivating further development toward dose-efficient material identification.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 464Poster Number:MIC-10-464] Enhancement of Charged-Particle Shielding via Lightweight Nanocomposites (#2978)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Grey (Autores: G. Grey , N. Speck , D. Vecchio , K. Cotterill , A. Taub , M. Hammig)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Michigan, Materials Science & Engineering Department, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America [2] University of Michigan, Nuclear Engineering & Radiological Sciences, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America [3] Amphionic, LLC., Plymouth, Michigan, United States of America [4] University of Michigan, Department of Math, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America [5] University of Michigan, Department of Physics, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The development of lightweight radiation shielding materials is of high interest for a broad range of defense, space, and medical applications. In particular, mass-savings are desired in vehicles (ground, naval, and/or aerospace) and as wearable fabrics in high dosage environments such as those encountered in the medical setting. Here we investigate the potential of enhanced shielding via radiation attenuation of nanostructured materials which take advantage of interfacial and nanocrystalline loss processes increase the multiplicity of energy loss mechanisms within the shielding solid. In this work, colloidal metallic nanoparticles grown in an aqueous environment (such as palladium (Pd) and silver (Ag)) with sizes in the 5 - 50 nm range are imbedded in a polymeric matrix material (epoxy or aramid nanofiber (ANF)) to demonstrate photon and electron shielding while maintaining mechanical properties such as strength, durability, and form-factor flexibility. The mechanisms of energy loss at the interfaces of the nanomaterials and overall in the solid are quantified through transport modeling as well as the unorthodox usage of the Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM), in which a focused electron beam and state-of-the-art detector system are utilized to measure the effects of particle interactions within our material system to a near single particle resolution. Therefore, this work encompasses both an investigation of the potential enhancement of radiation attenuation by nanostructured materials while also introducing an innovative nanocomposite material system with manufacturing versatility enabling lightweight, flexible shielding.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 467Poster Number:MIC-10-467] Detector Geometry Optimization of a Sensing Collimation Imager (SCI) (#3067)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Cai (Autores: L. Cai , H. Xia , S. Aggarwal , F. Ahmed , J. A. O'Sullivan , A. K. Jha , Y.-C. Tai)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Washington University in St. Louis, Imaging Science, St. Louis, Missouri, United States of America [2] Washington University in St. Louis, Department of Biomedical Engineering, St. Louis, Missouri, United States of America [3] Washington University in St. Louis, Department of Electrical and Systems Engineering, St. Louis, Missouri, United States of America [4] Washington University in St. Louis, Mallinckrodt Institute of Radiology, St. Louis, Missouri, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Sensing Collimation Imager (SCI) is an ultrasensitive gamma detector that integrates multi-pinhole, coded aperture, and self-collimation imaging into a single compact device, achieving substantially higher sensitivity than conventional gamma cameras. Maximizing the spatial encoding capability of the SCI module requires optimizing the crystal arrangement over a high-dimensional combinatorial design space, which is too large for exhaustive search. We propose an information-theoretic detector geometry optimization framework that uses the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) spatial correlation map as a computationally efficient performance metric. The metric requires only computing the FWHM of the FIM column vector (O(n)), avoiding the O(n³) cost of inverting the FIM for the Cramér-Rao bound, enabling broad geometry searches. A genetic algorithm (GA) guided by this metric searches over fixed-cardinality crystal arrangements to identify high-performing designs. Applied to the SCI module, the GA converged within 50 generations and identified an optimized arrangement producing narrower FIM correlation peaks throughout the field of view than a heuristic design. GATE Monte Carlo simulations of a Derenzo phantom confirmed improved recovery of the 8 mm sphere group with clearer feature separation, validating the optimization framework.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 470Poster Number:MIC-10-470] Toward Whole-Body Whole Gamma Imaging: Monte Carlo Simulation of 89 Zr PET-Compton Hybrid Imaging (#3156)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Miyahara (Autores: M. Miyahara , H. Tashima , M. Suga , S. Takyu , F. Nishikido , G. Akamatsu , T. Yamaya)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Chiba University, Graduate School of Science and Engineering, Chiba, Japan [2] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology, Institute for Quantum Medical Science, Chiba, Japan [3] Chiba University, Center for Frontier Medical Engineering, Chiba, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Whole gamma imaging (WGI) is a novel imaging technique that combines PET and Compton imaging by inserting a scatterer detector ring inside a PET detector ring. One of the suitable nuclides for WGI is 89 Zr. 89 Zr emits a 909 keV single gamma ray after undergoing positron emission or electron capture to form 89m Y. Because these 909 keV gamma rays are emitted approximately four times more frequently than positrons, hybrid imaging of WGI combining both modalities is expected to improve image quality compared to conventional 89 Zr-PET which uses only annihilation gamma rays. In this study, we aimed at finalizing the design of a clinical whole-body WGI system. The hybrid imaging method was applied to Geant4-simulated data of a whole-body WGI system. We modeled a system employing HR-GAGG crystals as the scatterer and LGSO crystals as the absorber. Measurement of an 89 Zr-filled NEMA IEC body phantom placed at the center of the field of view was simulated. Images were reconstructed using the hybrid reconstruction method combining PET and Compton events and compared with PET images reconstructed by the list-mode OSEM algorithm using only PET events. We calculated the percent contrast (Q H,j ) and percent background variability (N j ) for each sphere size j (10-37 mm). The results showed that, for large spheres with diameters of 22 mm or more, hybrid imaging reduced N j , but the maximum achievable Q H,j was lower than that of PET. In contrast, for small spheres with diameters of 17 mm or less, hybrid imaging demonstrated a specific advantage by suppressing noise amplification while accelerating contrast recovery in the early iterations. In conclusion, although the overall image quality improvement was limited in certain aspects, the potential to enable novel applications such as multi-isotope imaging and positronium lifetime imaging using appropriate position emitters was suggested.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-11-01] Toward Clinical Deployment of Complex PET Designs via Fast In-System Calibration (#1486)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Thull (Autores: J. Thull , Y. Kuhl , B. Weissler , D. Schug , V. Schulz)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] RWTH Aachen University, Chair of Imaging and Computer Vision, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [2] Hyperion Hybrid Imaging Systems GmbH, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate positron emission tomography (PET) depends on calibration of detector alignment, gamma interaction positioning, and coincidence timing, which jointly define line-of-response (LOR) and time-of-flight (TOF) information. Conventional workflows calibrate these quantities in separate stages using dedicated acquisitions, hardware, or phantoms. This is particularly burdensome for light-sharing detectors, where these quantities are coupled through the detector response but are typically treated as separate calibration tasks. We introduce a differentiable in-system calibration framework that enables rapid scanner-level calibration by replacing staged workflows with a single coincidence-level optimization. A shared neural network predicts local interaction positions and timing corrections from single-event readouts, while learnable detector poses map predictions into scanner coordinates. Singles are processed independently, and coincidence information enters only via physical LOR and TOF construction. This prevents source-label access at the network input while enforcing scanner-level consistency. The framework was trained on 28M coincidences from 450 randomized 22Na point-source positions acquired on a semi-monolithic preclinical PET system. In hot-rod reconstructions, the proposed calibration achieved image quality on par with a conventional blueprint and fan-beam workflow, as assessed by peak signal-to-noise ratio, structural similarity, coefficient of variation, recovery coefficients, and peak-to-valley ratios. Differentiable in-system calibration therefore compresses labor-intensive staged workflows into a unified physics-constrained optimization completed in hours, reducing effort and mechanical constraints without sacrificing reconstruction performance.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-11-02] A Compact Preclinical PET Scanner Achieving NEMA-Standard Sub-0.5 mm Spatial Resolution via Analytic FBP Reconstruction (#1867)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Li (Autores: C. Li , H. Wen , Y. Jiang , Y. Hou , K. Wang , J. Jiang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Normal University, Key Laboratory of Beam Technology of Ministry of Education, School of Physics and Astronomy, Beijing, China [2] Beijing Normal University, Key Laboratory of Radiopharmaceuticals of the Ministry of Education, NMPA Key Laboratory for Research and Evaluation of Radiopharmaceuticals (National Medical Product Administration), College of Chemistry, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract PET is a cornerstone of preclinical imaging, where achieving ultra-high spatial resolution is paramount for the precise quantification of sub-regional metabolism. While commercial scanners typically yield 1.0-1.5 mm resolution, advanced research prototypes target sub-millimeter precision. This study introduces a compact preclinical PET scanner achieving NEMA-standard sub-0.5 mm spatial resolution via the analytic filtered back-projection (FBP) algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first reported system demonstrating such resolution through FBP. The dual-ring scanner features a 64 mm transaxial and 53.2 mm axial field of view, integrating 16 modules of 44 × 44 LYSO crystal arrays (0.497 × 0.497 × 5 mm 3 elements). These arrays are coupled to Hamamatsu Multi-Pixel Photon Counters (MPPCs, S14161-3050HS-08) and managed by a PETsys TOFPET2 ASIC system. System performance was characterized following NEMA NU 4-2008 protocols. The scanner demonstrated an overall energy resolution of 13.43% and an absolute sensitivity of 0.87% (350-650 keV). Peak true and noise equivalent count rates (NECR) were 7.61 kcps and 6.02 kcps, respectively, with a scatter fraction of 8.92%. FBP reconstruction of a point source demonstrated the system achieved average FWHM resolutions of 0.90 mm, 0.86 mm, and 0.69 mm in the radial, tangential, and axial directions, respectively, reaching a peak resolution of 0.48 mm. Imaging of a Micro-Derenzo phantom resolved 0.4 mm rods via iterative reconstruction. In vivo studies using 18 F-FDG and 18 F-Florbetazine delineated precise tracer distributions within sub-regional structures. While the 5-mm scintillator thickness involves a trade-off in sensitivity, the system establishes a benchmark for spatial fidelity in preclinical instrumentation. Future work will integrate thicker crystals with depth-of-interaction capabilities to enhance sensitivity without compromising spatial precision.
