sub_talks.title: [MIC-11-03] Development of a ring-type Quantum Entanglement PET Imaging System and Application of a Novel Image Reconstruction Algorithm to In-Vivo Imaging (#1680)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Nakamura (Autores: K. Nakamura , M. Fujimoto , P. Caradonna , M. Uenomachi , L. Stephenson , D. Watts , K. Shimazoe)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The University of Tokyo, Department of Nuclear Engineering and Management, Graduate School of Engineering, Tokyo, Japan [2] The University of Tokyo, Department of Bioengineering, Graduate School of Engineering, Tokyo, Japan [3] Institute of Science Tokyo, Institute of Integrated Research, Tokyo, Japan [4] University of York, York, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Current positron emission tomography (PET) imaging is fundamentally limited by physical background noise, such as scatter and random coincidences, which significantly degrade image quality and quantitative accuracy. Quantum-entangled PET (QEPET) is a promising solution that utilizes the inherent orthogonal polarization correlation of annihilation photon pairs to physically reject noise. However, its practical application to in-vivo imaging has been a major challenge due to the severe reduction in usable event statistics caused by strict event selection. In this study, we developed a triple-ring PET scanner consisting of 24 Ce:GAGG modules (8×8 arrays of 2.5×2.5×9.0 mm³ pixels at 3.2 mm pitch; 1536 pixels in total) arranged in three axial rings with an inner radius of 36.7 mm, read out by SiPMs via dynamic time-over-threshold circuits, achieving an energy resolution of 9.5% at 511 keV and a coincidence timing resolution of 16.8 ns. By selecting events within a scattering-angle range of 70°-121° and an azimuthal-angle difference of 80°-100°, we obtained a modulation contrast ratio of 1.91, which clearly exceeds the classical limit of 1.63, confirming the entanglement of annihilation photon pairs. Furthermore, to overcome the limited counting statistics of conventional QEPET, we developed a novel reconstruction algorithm that seamlessly integrates the high-statistics structural information of standard PET into the iterative MLEM process. In phantom experiments, this approach improved the SBR to ~1.25× that of raw QEPET while preserving an SNR ~1.27× that of standard PET, achieving the highest CNR among the compared methods. Finally, we performed in-vivo QEPET imaging of a tumor-bearing mouse. The developed method effectively suppressed the granular noise characteristic of conventional QEPET while demonstrating highly localized tracer accumulation, thereby verifying its superiority over both standard PET and conventional QEPET.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-11-04] SIMPLE-DIP: Positronium Lifetime Image Reconstruction Using Deep Image Prior (#2252)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Huang (Autores: B. Huang , J. Qi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California, Davis, Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positronium lifetime tomography (PLT) is an emerging imaging modality for imaging positronium lifetime in vivo. Previously, we developed SIMPLE (Statistical IMage reconstruction of Positron Lifetime via time-wEighting), a reconstruction framework for estimating average positron lifetime images, and demonstrated high-resolution imaging on a phantom at clinical activity levels. However, the reconstruction problem remains highly ill-posed, particularly under low-count and high-random conditions. In this work, we propose SIMPLE-DIP, a deep image prior (DIP)-based reconstruction method that regularizes SIMPLE without requiring external training data. The proposed approach employs a single patient-specific U-Net that takes a prior anatomical image as input and jointly constrains both the activity and lifetime-weighted images during reconstruction. Computer simulations using a brain phantom show that SIMPLE-DIP effectively suppresses image noise while preserving lifetime contrast and improving lesion recovery, outperforming the compared SIMPLE formulations regularized by the quadratic penalty or independent DIPs. These results suggest that the proposed SIMPLE-DIP is a promising method for high-resolution positronium lifetime imaging.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-11-05] AI-Based Predictive Dosimetry from PET for 177Lu-PSMA Radiopharmaceutical Therapy for Prostate Cancer (#2210)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Lei (Autores: B. Lei , T.-A. Song , F. Yang , V. Balaji , J. Dutta)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Massachusetts Amherst, Biomedical Engineering, Amherst, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Personalized 177Lu-PSMA-617 radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) for prostate cancer requires patient-specific dosimetry, but post-therapy SPECT imaging for dose computation is not universally performed. In contrast, pre-therapy PSMA PET is widely available and often mandatory for patient selection. PET-based predictive dosimetry therefore has the potential to enable personalized treatment planning before RPT administration. We developed a machine learning framework for organ-level predictive dosimetry from pre-therapy PET, where PET-derived organ features are used to predict kinetic parameters of post-therapy SPECT time-activity curves (TACs). Organ masks for the liver, spleen, and bilateral kidneys were used to extract PET features. Serial 177Lu-PSMA SPECT images at multiple post-injection time points provided reference organ activity values, from which mono-exponential fitting yielded organ TACs and time-integrated activities (TIAs). Absorbed dose was computed from TIAs using the MIRD formalism with organ-specific S values. Our deep learning model predicting kinetic parameters outperformed a comparable deep learning model predicting TIA directly, as well as three classical machine learning models predicting kinetic parameters. This workflow demonstrates the feasibility of forecasting organ absorbed dose from pre-therapy PET, supporting individualized therapeutic regimen planning.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-11-06] Event-Resolved Parent-Progeny Discrimination Using CMOS Lensless Radiomicroscopy for 225 Ac Targeted Alpha Therapy (#2026)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Chu (Autores: H. Chu , J.S. Lee)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Seoul National University, Interdisciplinary Program in Bioengineering, College of Engineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] Seoul National University, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea [3] Seoul National Graduate School, Integrated Major in Innovative Medical Science, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Although targeted alpha therapy (TAT) using 225 Ac has demonstrated high therapeutic efficacy, clinical translation remains limited due to redistribution of daughter isotopes, leading to off-target dose. Therefore, discriminating localized emissions from redistributed emitting progeny is significant for small-scale dosimetry and radiopharmaceutical evaluation. Here, we propose a low-cost CMOS-based lensless radiomicroscopy system for direct / discrimination using cluster morphology. Event level features extracted from 210 Po and 90 Sr measurements were used for classification applying both a physics-driven probability density function (PDF) approach and a data-driven multilayer perceptron (MLP). Both methods achieved > 98% accuracy with AUC > 0.99. Mixed-source experiments mimicking 225 Ac decay conditions demonstrated robust event-level discrimination. These results indicate that cluster morphology encodes sufficient physical information to monitor daughter isotope migration, enabling pathway toward quantifying parent and progeny distributions in radiopharmaceutical imaging.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-11-07] Physics-Guided Implicit Neural Representation for 3D Ac-225 Compton Imaging (#1786)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Song (Autores: G. Song , B. Das , J. Kim , Y. Seo , J. Kim , G. Cho , J. Caravaca)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Department of Nuclear and Quantum Engineering, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [2] University of California, San Francisco, Department of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging, San Francisco, California, United States of America [3] Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [4] University of California, Berkeley, Department of Nuclear Engineering, Berkeley, California, United States of America [5] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Nuclear Science Division, Berkeley, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Actinium-225 (Ac-225) is a promising alpha-emitting radionuclide for targeted alpha therapy, and Compton cameras have emerged as a potential imaging solution for this radionuclide. We developed a physics-guided implicit neural representation (PG-INR) framework for Ac-225 Compton image reconstruction that does not require any ground truth data. Unlike conventional deep learning approaches, the proposed method incorporates physical laws directly into the training process by embedding physics-based loss terms, including maximum-likelihood estimation and Klein-Nishina differential cross section. This enables unsupervised learning solely guided by the measurement results. Furthermore, by representing the reconstructed image as a continuous implicit neural function, the framework achieves resolution enhancement beyond the native voxel grid. The proposed method was evaluated against a conventional ordered subsets expectation maximization (OSEM) algorithm using measured Compton imaging data from a mouse phantom and a Monte Carlo-simulated resolution phantom (from 1.0 to 2.5 mm). For the mouse phantom experiments, PG-INR achieved up to 18-fold faster reconstruction compared to OSEM at comparable resolution. For the resolution phantom simulation, PG-INR successfully resolved 1.0 mm diameter rods with up to 4.8 dB peak signal-to-noise ratio improvement and 0.25 structural similarity index measure enhancement over OSEM. These results suggest that the PG-INR performs significantly better than standard OSEM for Ac-225 Compton imaging.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-11-08] Attenuation Map Estimation from NAC Brain PET Images Using a 3D Patch-Based U-Net: A Multi-Tracer Study on the NeuroEXPLORER (#1934)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Keppens (Autores: M. Keppens , G. Schramm , H. Goesseye , K. Van Laere)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] KU Leuven, Department of Imaging and Pathology, Leuven, Belgium
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Attenuation correction in PET/CT imaging typically uses a CT-derived attenuation map (μ-map), prone to misalignment artifacts, CT-induced artifacts, and additional radiation dose. CT-free alternatives are therefore clinically attractive, and deep learning methods are a promising solution. As clinical PET centres increasingly adopt diverse tracer protocols beyond FDG, a single attenuation correction model that generalizes across tracers without retraining would further reduce deployment complexity. In this work, we investigate the feasibility of supervised μ-map estimation from non-attenuation-corrected (NAC) brain PET images using a 3D patch-based U-Net, trained and evaluated on patient data from the NeuroEXPLORER, a brain- dedicated PET/CT scanner. A dataset of 353 scans across 12 different tracers was used to study the effect of tracer composition on model generalizability. To our knowledge, this is the first study to systematically assess how training tracer composition affects cross-tracer generalization in deep learning-based CT- free attenuation correction, using a large multi-tracer cohort. The tuned U-Net outperformed Attention U-Net, HighResNet, and Swin UNETR under matched conditions. FDG-only training showed poor generalization to non-FDG tracers, with Normalized Root Mean Squared Error (NRMSE) on average 5× higher in the brain for non-FDG tracers than multi-tracer models across different dataset sizes. Notably, a model trained without any FDG data produced FDG μ-maps as well as a FDG-only model, suggesting the network learns anatomy-based priors that generalize across tracer distributions. Tracer diversity during training did not degrade FDG performance and improved generalization. Weighted resampling to correct FDG/non-FDG imbalance worsened performance when the non-FDG patient pool was small. These results indicate that training set diversity, rather than size or tracer-specific data, is an important driver of generalization.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-12-01] Direct clinical imaging of alpha therapy in a PET/CT scanner via cascade gamma-rays imaging (#1380)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Caravaca (Autores: J. Caravaca , Y. Seo , J. Cabello , S. Siegel , R. R. Flavell , T. A. Hope)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Applied Nuclear Physics, Berkeley, California, United States of America [2] University of California San Francisco, Radiology, San Francisco, California, United States of America [3] Siemens Medical Solutions USA, Inc., Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Targeted alpha therapy is a very promising treatment modality for numerous types of cancer. Although PET presents an excellent resolution and signal-to-noise ratio, this modality is limited to radionuclides that emit positrons and cannot be used to image alpha radionuclides such as Ac-225 and Pb-212. Therefore, SPECT is the imaging modality of choice for these radionuclides, despite its poor signal-to-noise ratio and low quantitative accuracy due to the extremely limited sensitivity of this modality. We propose a new approach that enables imaging of alpha-emitting radionuclides in PET/CT scanners: time-of-flight cascade gamma-ray imaging. Our methodology exploits the coincidence detection of gamma-ray cascades emitted by 225 Ac or 212 Pb to perform tomography of non-positron emitters in PET/CT scanners. Our technique is evaluated with Ac-225 and Pb-212 phantoms at low concentrations of ~44kBq/mL and short scan sessions under 5-minutes in a commercial clinical PET/CT. We also present the first clinical image of a prostate cancer patient injected with 225Ac-PSMA-617 in a clinical PET/CT system. Lastly, we predict via simulations that next-generation long-axial field-of-view PET/CT scanners will achieve a sensitivity several orders of magnitude higher than SPECT with similar or better spatial resolution.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-12-02] From MeV Gamma to PET Signal: Experimental Demonstration of Pair Production Tomography for Theranostic Imaging (#2289)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Das (Autores: B. Das , R. Peter , J. Caravaca , Y. Seo)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California, San Francisco, Department of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging, San Francisco, California, United States of America [2] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Applied Nuclear Science Division, Berkeley, California, United States of America [3] University of California, San Francisco, Department of Radiation Oncology, San Francisco, California, United States of America [4] University of California, Berkeley, Department of Nuclear Engineering, Berkeley, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Imaging of theranostic radionuclides that emit high-energy (MeV range) γ rays remains extremely challenging with conventional imaging systems. SPECT performance degrades at MeV energies due to scatter and collimator penetration, while PET is inherently restricted to positron-emitting radionuclides. Pair production tomography (PPT) offers a new approach enabled by the high-energy γ interactions with matter to detectable coincidence signals. When a photon with energy ≥ 2m e c 2 (=1.022 MeV) undergoes pair production, the positron generated from this pair production leads to annihilation with the medium electron and emission of two 511 keV photons, enabling PET imaging. In this study, we experimentally demonstrate PPT using the 212 Pb decay chain, exploiting 2.617 MeV γ rays from 208 Tl. Monte Carlo simulations indicate that, despite long photon transport distances, the spatial distributions of pair production and annihilation events remain localized at the millimeter scale. Phantom experiments were performed on both clinical time-of-flight (TOF) PET and preclinical non-TOF PET systems without hardware modification using clinically and preclinically relevant 212 Pb activity levels. Reconstructed PPT images successfully recovered the spatial distribution of activity, with improved contrast observed when TOF information was available. Corresponding SPECT measurements under identical conditions showed reduced visibility for smaller structures. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of PPT for imaging high-energy γ-emitting radionuclides and suggest a route to extend PET beyond conventional principles requiring positron emissions directly from radionuclides.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-12-03] Quantitative evaluation of pair-produced positrons using a clinical linear accelerator for pair-production tomography (#2445)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Ota (Autores: R. Ota , Q. Lyu , B. Das , B. Faddegon , Y. Seo , K. Sheng , S.I. Kwon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California, Davis, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America [2] Hamamatsu Photonics K.K., Central Research Laboratory, Hamamatsu, Japan [3] University of California, San Francisco, Department of Radiation Oncology, San Francisco, California, United States of America [4] University of California, San Francisco, Department of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging, San Francisco, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract X-ray based radiotherapy is indispensable in modern cancer treatment yet has challenges because it is an open-loop treatment, with limited ability to verify during treatment whether the delivered dose matches the treatment plan. To address this problem, we investigated the use of positrons which are generated in a patient body during X-ray radiotherapy through pair production interactions between matter and MV X-rays, and proposed a novel imaging modality termed pair-production tomography (P2T). This is possible because the X-ray energy used for radiotherapy is a few MeV, and pair production can occur when the photon energy is higher than 1.022 MeV, producing an electron-positron pair. Their simulation results showed opportunities to utilize pair-produced positrons to not only monitor the treatment but also differentiate materials with similar density but different effective atomic numbers, which remains challenging in conventional computed tomography. However, to our best knowledge, there has been no experimental evidence of pair-produced positron detection using a clinical linear accelerator (LINAC). Therefore, in this study, we performed experimental detection of pair-produced positrons using a LINAC. Experiments were conducted using a LINAC and a pair of radiation detectors composed of photomultiplier tubes and LYSO scintillator crystals. We successfully observed positrons generated in various phantoms via pair production. Furthermore, we quantitatively investigated sensitivity of P2T by adjusting the effective atomic number of phantoms, showing consistent results with the previous simulation results. These results provide an important step toward experimental validation of P2T.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-12-04] Terbium-149: a Laboratory for Three-Photon Events (#2764)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Mercolli (Autores: L. Mercolli , P. V. Grundler , A. N. Moiseeva , L. Eggimann , S. Braccini , U. Köster , N. P. van der Meulen , W. M. Steinberger)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Inselspital, Bern University Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Bern, Bern, Switzerland [2] University of Bern, Albert Einstein Center for Fundamental Physics (AEC), Laboratory for High Energy Physics (LHEP), Bern, Bern, Switzerland [3] PSI Center for Life Sciences, Center for Radiopharmaceutical Sciences, Villigen, Aargau, Switzerland [4] Institut Laue-Langevin, Grenoble, France [5] PSI Center for Nuclear Engineering and Science, aboratory of Radiochemistry, Villigen, Aargau, Switzerland [6] Siemens Medical Solutions USA, Inc, Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Terbium-149 ( 149 Tb) is a promising radionuclide for targeted α therapy that also emits positrons and prompt photons γ across a wide energy range, which makes it a candidate for ortho-positronium (oPs) lifetime imaging (oPsLI). We present the first demonstration of oPsLI with a therapeutic radionuclide and with γ energies below 511 keV on a commercial long-axial field-of-view PET/CT system. Using a three-lifetime-component Bayesian fitting model, we determined the oPs lifetime for the following three γ energy windows: 310 to 420 keV, 590 to 710 keV and above 720 keV. The medium- and high-energy windows yielded oPs lifetime values consistent with each other and with literature values, while the low-energy window produced systematically lower values. Voxel-wise oPsLI with small voxel size was successfully demonstrated using a single γ energy window. These results establish 149 Tb as a versatile probe for exploring γ energy window effects in oPsLI, with future potential for in vivo microdosimetry and chelator stability studies.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-12-05] The first in vivo quantum entanglement imaging of a human subject (#3065)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. Moskal (Autores: P. Moskal , D. Kumar , S. Sharma , E. Ł. Stępień)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Jagiellonian University, Institute of Physics, KRAKOW, Poland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present the first in-vivo imaging of the degree of quantum entanglement in a human subject. The reported investigations were conducted at the Cracow University Hospital in Poland using a 50 cm long, multi-photon J-PET scanner capable of registering and imaging the degree of quantum entanglement of photons originating from electron-positron annihilations in the patient's body. A 48-year-old male patient, administered 145 MBq of [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-TATE, was scanned for 20 minutes starting 90 minutes post-injection, following the completion of his routine diagnosis. Data were collected in a triggerless mode, enabling the simultaneous registration of annihilation photons and Compton scattered photons. Event selection was based on the position, time, and energy deposition of the annihilation and scattered photons. The angular distributions between the scattering planes of annihilation photons in the patient's liver and spleen were determined. These distributions were used to extract the degree of quantum entanglement for these organs. The obtained degree of quantum entanglement is larger than expected for separable photons and lower than expected for maximally entangled photons. These results demonstrate, for the first time, the feasibility of measuring the degree of quantum entanglement in annihilation photons originating from patients during positron emission tomography. This finding motivates the further development of detectors for the construction of PET systems capable of simultaneously capturing annihilation and Compton-scattered photons, and supports future studies aimed at uncovering medically useful information gained by imaging the degree of quantum entanglement.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-12-06] Constraining CP Invariance in Ortho-Positronium Decays at 7 T with NeuroSphere MR-Compatible PET Modules (#3078)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. S. Allen (Autores: M. S. Allen , M. Scipioni , C. Silva , N. Efthymiou , M. Hiradfar , O. Hen , C. Catana)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] MGH and Harvard University, A. A. Martinos Center and Harvard Medical School, Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States of America [2] MIT, Physics, Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In addition to medical imaging applications, Positron Emission Tomography (PET) systems can be used to study fundamental physics. One pathway for positron-electron annihilation is the formation of ortho-positronium (oPs), an intermediate bound state that decays to photons after a short lifetime. The lifetime and decay kinematics of oPs can be used to probe material properties and test the Standard Model. Additional sources of charge conjugation-parity (CP) symmetry violation are required to explain the observed matter-antimatter imbalance in the Universe, and CP violation can be constrained by measuring decays under the reversal of an applied magnetic field. A dedicated physics measurement platform was constructed from the architecture of the NeuroSphere brain PET insert for 7-T MRI, including a PET detector array, positronium target with lifetime trigger, and motorized gantry for control of the system orientation inside the 7-T environment. GATE simulations were used to inform the development of a custom data analysis pipeline for oPs event selection and multi-coincidence processing. Systematics were mitigated by combining runs with various target and detector positions (to average out artificial asymmetries caused by assembly or detector efficiency) and by applying a baseline correction from events in a kinematic region with vanishing analyzing power (to account for drift and more field- and material- related effects). decays in polyvinyltoluene (PVT) were measured at 7 T, finding a lifetime of 98.7 ± 1.0 ns and constraining CP violation to be zero at a level of 2 × 10 −2 . This work demonstrates the unique opportunity provided by PET/MR instrumentation to perform high-field physics measurements, a pathway toward a leading measurement of CP violation in positronium, and proof-of-concept for measuring positronium decays with the full NeuroSphere system.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-12-07] Novel Spatial Encoding Using Larmor Precession in Nuclear Medicine: A Study on Imaging Robustness (#1753)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Suzuki (Autores: H. Suzuki , B. Feng , M. Fushimi , K. Shimazoe , H. Takahashi , M. Sekino)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The University of Tokyo, Department of Electrical Engineering and Information Systems Graduate School of Engineering, Bunkyo, Japan [2] The University of Tokyo, Department of Nuclear Engineering and Management, Department of Bioengineering, and Institute of Engineeing Innovation, Bunkyo, Japan [3] Keio University, Department of Applied Physics and Physico-Informatics, Faculty of Science and Technology, Bunkyo, Japan [4] The University of Tokyo, Department of Bioengineering, School of Engineering, Yokohama, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In nuclear medicine, positron emission tomography (PET) and single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) exhibit high detection sensitivity by detecting γ-rays emitted from radiopharmaceuticals, but they are limited by poor spatial resolution. Conversely, Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) achieves high spatial resolution by encoding positional information through Larmor precession induced by magnetic field gradients. To improve the spatial resolution in nuclear medicine, we propose a novel image reconstruction framework that integrates magnetic field-based spatial encoding, as utilized in MRI, with γ-ray detection as employed in PET and SPECT. By incorporating the effect of Larmor precession in perturbed angular correlation (PAC), we formulated a forward model that enables image reconstruction as an inverse problem. Numerical simulations demonstrated that our method can stabilize 7 by 7pixels imaging on a small-animal scale. Furthermore, condition number analysis revealed that the imaging process becomes increasingly stable as the neodymium magnets are scanned. However, since each magnetic field distribution requires several hours of measurement, future work will focus on designing more detailed field distributions to reduce measurement time while further enhancing spatial resolution.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-12-08] Real-Time Task-Based Adaptive SPECT Imaging via Optimized System Sampling Strategies Using a Robotic Clinical SPECT Platform (#2916)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Jin (Autores: Y. Jin , L.-J. Meng)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Illinois at Urbana and Champaign, Department of Nuclear, Plasma, and Radiological Engineering, Urbana, Illinois, United States of America [2] University of Illinois at Urbana and Champaign, Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology, Urbana, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Task-based adaptive SPECT imaging has long been limited by the computational complexity associated with optimizing acquisition strategies over high-dimensional system configuration spaces. In this work, we present a computational framework for adaptive SPECT imaging based on direct optimization of imaging time distribution (ITD) over discretized detector poses. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of this scheme on a simulated robotic SPECT platform. The framework finds the best imaging strategy by finding an optimized imaging noise property based on the modified uniform Cramér-Rao bound (MUCRB). We further improve the computation efficiency using a non-uniform object-space pixelation (NUOP), which makes it possible to compute the optimum imaging geometry in real time. A StarGuide-inspired multi-head robotic SPECT was simulated and evaluated using a Hoffman brain phantom and hot- and cold-rod resolution-phantoms. Compared with conventional whole-view and uniform ITDs under identical total acquisition time, the optimized ITDs achieved substantially improved region-of-interest (ROI) image quality in all three phantoms and ROIs. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework enables efficient task-specific optimization of acquisition strategies for highly reconfigurable SPECT systems.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-13-01] Cramér-Rao-Efficient Timing with Photon Counting: Theory and Proof-of-Concept Demonstration for Cherenkov TOF-PET (#1437)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Kratochwil (Autores: N. Kratochwil , S. Lee , J. W. Cates , G. Ariño-Estrada)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California, Davis, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America [2] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Nuclear Science Division, Berkeley, California, United States of America [3] Barcelona Institute of Science and Technology, Institut de Fisica d'Altes Energies, Barcelona, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Fast timing with Cherenkov luminescence has attracted significant interest in the medical imaging community over the last decade. While detector time resolutions of 100-200ps FWHM have been reported, we recently demonstrated that current timing estimators fail to fully exploit the prompt nature of Cherenkov emission. In particular, simulations of a small BGO crystal coupled to a state-of-the-art silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) yield a detector time resolution (standard deviation) of σ t = 158ps when using only the first detected photon, whereas the Cramér-Rao lower bound (CRLB) predicts a ≈ 4.5-fold improvement to σ t = 35ps for the same configuration. To approach this limit, we apply a maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE) framework incorporating the full photon arrival time distribution. Using all detected photons, we obtain a harmonic average detector time resolution of σ t = 35 ± 2ps, demonstrating statistically efficient timing estimation consistent with the CRLB. The MLE framework also enables event classification, identifying variations in Cherenkov photon yield and time biases from light transport and photon production. Simulations suggest a 2-fold timing improvement compared to state-of-the-art classifiers such as the signal rise time. To validate this approach experimentally, we apply the method to a semi-monolithic BGO photon-counting detector (42 × 2 × 20 mm 3 ) measured in coincidence with a reference detector and read out by 16 SiPMs. Events with different Cherenkov photon yield can be identified, improving time resolution from 199ps (all events) to 165ps and 140ps FWHM for tighter log-likelihood selections. We observe a stronger improvement over the first timestamp for Cherenkov-rich events and shallow interaction depths. These results demonstrate that photon-counting-based MLE can fully exploit the information content of Cherenkov emission, enabling a pathway toward CRLB-limited timing performance for improved TOF-PET imaging.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-13-02] Sparse-to-Dense SiPM Readout Upsampling for Position Estimation in PET Detectors (#1583)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Loignon-Houle (Autores: F. Pagano , P. Muñoz Izquierdo , A. Gonzalez , F. Loignon-Houle)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CSIC-Universitat Politècnica de València, Institute for Instrumentation in Molecular Imaging (I3M), Valencia, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Signal readout strategies of positron emission tomography detectors have an inherent compromise between resolution and complexity, where finer photosensor sampling improves interaction localization but increases the number of readout channels and associated hardware demands. Channel-reduction methods are therefore central to detector design, though they typically can incur some loss in performance. Recent advances in deep learning offer a pathway to mitigate this compromise by recovering information lost through reduced readout. In this work, we propose a neural network-based sparse-to-dense mapping that reconstructs high-resolution (8×8) silicon photomultiplier signals from low-resolution (4×4) inputs. Data was acquired using a semi-monolithic scintillator array with pinhole collimation across both the monolithic and depth-of-interaction directions. An initial upsampling network is trained to transform 4×4 signals into 8×8 representations, which are then used as input to a second network for interaction position estimation. Performance is evaluated by comparing positioning accuracy across four configurations: native 8×8 readout, reduced 4×4 readout, upsampled 4×4-to-8×8 signals, and a conventional row-column summation (8+8) scheme. Results demonstrate that the proposed upsampling approach effectively reconstructs higher-resolution signal structure, helping to improve the monolithic and DOI resolution compared to both 4×4 and 8+8 readouts. This approach could therefore remove the need for additional hardware coming with conventional multiplexing techniques, while recovering the benefits of denser photosensor sampling.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-13-03] Crosshair Light-Sharing Detectors with Diode-based Multiplexing for High-Resolution TOF-DOI PET (#2227)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H.G. Kang (Autores: H.G. Kang , E. Yoshida , G. Akamatsu , T. Yamaya)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology (QST), Advanced Nuclear Medicine Sciences, Chiba, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Last year, we developed diode-based row-column multiplexing boards that can reduce the number of silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) channels by a factor of four without compromising the coincidence timing resolution (CTR). This technology is key to reducing the production costs of next-generation clinical whole-body time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET) systems. However, we used one-to-one coupling detectors with a crystal pitch of 3.2 mm, which cannot provide depth-of-interaction (DOI) information. For brain PET applications, for example, DOI measurement capability with a finer crystal pitch is required. On the other hand, our group has developed crosshair light-sharing (CLS) detectors that can offer both TOF and DOI information with a crystal pitch half that of the SiPM pitch. In this work, therefore, we explored the performance of the CLS detectors with the multiplexing board in combination with a TOFPET2 ASIC module for high-resolution TOF-DOI brain PET imaging. The CLS detectors had a 14×14 array of fast-LGSO crystals (crystal pitch=1.6 mm, crystal thickness=15 mm) and an 8×8 SiPM array (Hamamatsu, S14161-3050HS). The multiplexed SiPM signals were digitized by the TOFPET2 ASIC module. We evaluated CTR at eight different detector positions of the multiplexing boards by shifting the CLS detector pairs and a 22 Na source. The diode multiplexing did not degrade the CTR and energy resolution compared to the case without multiplexing. The average CTR of 366±6 ps was obtained across the eight detector positions. In the future, we plan to further improve the CTR by using DOI information.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-13-04] High-performance 4×4-channel microchannel plate photomultiplier tubes with bismuth germanate window faceplate (#2331)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Ota (Autores: R. Ota , Y. Ichikawa , T. Sasaki , K. Kuramoto , K. Shimano , T. Moriya , S. R. Cherry , S.I. Kwon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California, Davis, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America [2] Hamamatsu Photonics K.K., Central Research Laboratory, Hamamatsu, Japan [3] Hamamatsu Photonics K.K., Electron Tube Division, Iwata, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positron emission tomography can benefit from time-of-flight information between a coincident pair of PET detectors to enhance image quality. Improved coincidence time resolution (CTR) can not only improve image quality but also obviate the need for image reconstruction when the spatial uncertainty derived from CTR becomes sufficiently small to directly localize positron annihilation events within the patient body, potentially making PET systems more compact and flexible. The first reconstruction-free positron emission imaging termed direct positron emission imaging (dPEI), was demonstrated using detectors with 32 ps CTR; however, limitations such as low detection efficiency, lack of energy information due to the use of a pure Cherenkov radiator, and a small active area resulting from the single-channel detector system remain. To address these limitations and make dPEI more practical, we developed the first prototypes of a multi-anode bismuth germanate-integrated microchannel plate photomultiplier tube (MA-BGO-IMP). The MA-BGO-IMP is position-sensitive and has a two-dimensional 4 × 4 anode array with a 5.75 mm readout pitch. At the detector level, the transit time spread and quantum efficiency were measured to be ~40 ps full width at half maximum (FWHM) without circuit optimization and 31.4% at 380 nm without Fresnel reflection correction, respectively. A coincidence experiment was conducted using a 22 Na point source paired with a barium fluoride-integrated microchannel plate photomultiplier tube. The preliminary energy resolution and CTR were 26% FWHM at 511 keV and 56.2 ps FWHM, respectively. These results were obtained using signals from only one anode. At the conference, we will present more detailed characterization of these newly developed MA-BGO-IMPs with 511 keV-based coincidence results, including energy resolution, CTR, and spatial resolution using a pair of MA-BGO-IMPs.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-13-05] Achieving Sub-100 ps CTR and Sub-2 mm DOI Resolution in TOF-PET Modules (#2370)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Terragni (Autores: G. Terragni , E. Ucari , M. N. Colombo , J. W. Cates , M. Pizzichemi , E. Auffray)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CERN, Meyrin, Genève, Switzerland [2] Boston University, Boston, Massachusetts, United States of America [3] University of Milano-Bicocca, Milan, Italy [4] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Low-dose imaging and small-animal positron emission tomography (PET) require detectors with both high sensitivity and high spatial resolution. In this study, we investigate the performance of high-density scintillator matrices, such as BGO and LYSO:Ce, combined with multi-channel, low-noise, low-power, high-frequency (HF) readout electronics to enhance the Time-of-Flight (TOF) and Depth-of-Interaction (DOI) performance of pixelated detectors. High-frequency SiPM readout has demonstrated significant improvements in coincidence time resolution (CTR) by enabling the detection of ultrafast optical-photon production processes, such as Cherenkov emission in BGO and fast scintillation in LYSO:Ce. Two DOI-encoding detector designs are compared in this work: a double-sided readout and a single-sided readout employing a light guide to achieve DOI encoding through light sharing in laterally depolished crystal matrices. Experimental results demonstrate that they can achieve a timing resolution comparable to that of a standard pixelated matrix while also providing accurate DOI information. In particular, using 20 mm-long LYSO:Ce crystals, the light-sharing approach achieves a CTR of 133 ± 2 ps FWHM together with a DOI resolution of 2.2 ± 0.1 mm FWHM. Using a double-sided readout further improves the performance, reaching a CTR of 90 ± 2 ps FWHM and a DOI resolution of 1.9 ± 0.1 mm. Both DOI encoding methods provide similar DOI performance with LYSO:Ce matrices, while the advantage of collecting light from both ends of the scintillator becomes more evident with BGO crystals. In this case, the double-sided readout achieves a DOI resolution of 4.4 ± 0.1 mm, compared with 7.2 ± 0.2 mm obtained using the light-sharing approach. Future work will investigate the scalability of these detector concepts by extending the study from 16 to 64-channel prototypes and by comparing different readout electronics.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-14-01] Deep Learning Limited Angle Artefact Correction for dual panel PET in Shearlet Domain (#2587)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Maebe (Autores: J. Maebe , M. Abi Akl , B. Vervenne , S. Vandenberghe)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Ghent University, Gent, Belgium
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dual-flat-panel positron emission tomography (PET) systems offer strong advantages such as improved sensitivity but suffer from reconstruction artefacts due to missing projection data. We propose a deep learning model to correct these artefacts in the shearlet domain. The shearlet transform provides a multiscale, multidirectional analysis of the image, decomposing it into its shearlet coefficients, each corresponding to a subset of projections. A U-Net is used to correct for artefacts in these coefficients, but by only modifying coefficients corresponding to missing projection data, we can obtain an overall more robust algorithm. The model is trained and evaluated on data from a dual-panel PET system simulated in GATE, using real patient PET scans as the ground truth activity maps. The resulting artefact-corrected images showed good visual agreement with reference images from a system with full angular sampling. The standardized uptake value (SUV) mean of a hotspot also showed improvement (being closer to the reference value), but further investigation is required with regards to the consistency of quantitative accuracy of the model. Future work will also include an extension to 3D, to better leverage projection data along the axial dimension.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-14-02] Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization of Self-Collimating SPECT System Design Using Quantitative Imaging Metrics (#3200)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. O. Shah (Autores: S. O. Shah , H. Tripathi , T. Methuku , K. M. Parmer , T. Skirsky , L. Ying , T. Ma , R. Yao)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] State University of New York at Buffalo, Engineering Science (Artificial Intelligence), Buffalo, New York, United States of America [2] State University of New York at Buffalo, Radiology, Buffalo, New York, United States of America [3] State University of New York at Buffalo, Computer Science and Engineering, Buffalo, New York, United States of America [4] State University of New York at Buffalo, Biomedical Engineering, Buffalo, New York, United States of America [5] Tsinghua University, Engineering Physics, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Self-collimating (SC) SPECT employs a multi-layered, interspaced mosaic array detector structure to enable simultaneous gains in sensitivity and resolution. The complex configuration, however, demands a new set of imaging metrics and strategy to guide system design and optimization. In this work, we propose a Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization (MOBO) framework based on four voxel-wise imaging metrics calculated from the projection probability density functions (PPDF) of the system: Angular Sampling Completeness Index (ASCI), average PPDF FWHM (full-width at half-maximum), Multiplex Index (MPXI), and sensitivity, to predict a design's performance and efficiently navigate the design space. Through analytical simulations, we study a SC small animal SPECT that consists of a cylindrical tungsten high-resolution collimator ring surrounded by four concentric detector rings. In an initial test, we seek optimal design parameters for the aperture diameter, the number of apertures on the collimator ring, and crystal counts in two independent detector rings. The MOBO agent uses independent Gaussian process surrogates with log noisy expected hypervolume improvement to propose Pareto-improving configurations sequentially. Results of MOBO search confirm that the four objectives genuinely conflict, which is desired, and provide recommended parameters balancing resolution, sensitivity, angular coverage, and multiplexing. Validation studies of the MOBO recommendations are underway.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-14-03] Sensitivity-Aware Gated Deep Reconstruction for Cascade γ Coincidence Imaging (#2567)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Jia (Autores: H. Jia , H. Liu , T. Gong , Y. Liu , Z. He)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, School of Biomedical Engineering, Beijing, China [2] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [3] Tsinghua University Changgeng Hospital, Changgeng Hospital, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Cascade γ coincidence imaging can provide stronger geometric constraints than conventional single-photon imaging by exploiting the coincident detection of two cascade photons, but its reconstruction is challenging due to the complex system response and spatially non-uniform sensitivity. This work proposes a physics-prior-driven deep reconstruction framework for small-animal cascade γ coincidence imaging. A direct back-projection(DBP) reconstruction image was used as a physics-informed initialization, and a cascade sensitivity map was incorporated into a gated 3D ResUNet as a system-level spatial prior. Patch-based training was further adopted for sparse point-source reconstruction to reduce foreground-background imbalance. Monte Carlo simulations showed that, for a single-point source, the proposed method reduced the mean FWHM from 1.50 mm to 0.87 mm, increased the PSNR from 43.85 dB to 54.48 dB, and reduced the peak localization error from 0.25 mm to nearly 0 mm compared with DBP reconstruction. For the hotrod phantom, the foreground MAE decreased from 0.886 to 0.142, indicating improved recovery of extended active structures. The sensitivity map comparison further showed that different incorporation strategies lead to different trade-offs between foreground recovery and background suppression. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides a feasible route toward fast, sensitivity-aware, and physically informed reconstruction for cascade γ coincidence imaging.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-14-04] Two-Stage Retrieval-Augmented 3D Detection of Bone Metastatic Lesions via SPECT/CT (#2324)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Lin (Autores: Y. Lin , D. Li , N. Dang , F. Weng , W. Chen , G. Chen , Y. Liang , Q. Huang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Macao Polytechnic University, Applied Sciences, Macao, China [2] Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and Peking Union Medical College, National Cancer Center/National Clinical Research Center for Cancer/ Cancer Hospital & Shenzhen Hospital, Shenzhen, China [3] Guangxi University of Foreign Languages, School of Digital Technology, Nanning, China [4] Vplus Technology Ltd., Research and Development Department, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Bone metastases are common in advanced malignancies, and SPECT/CT provides complementary 3D radiotracer uptake and anatomy for screening and follow-up. Automatic whole-body lesion localization can reduce reading burden and improve consistency in patient-level assessment. However, it remains challenging because a detector needs to balance high-recall whole-body search, false-positive suppression, and fine-resolution local detail under memory and runtime constraints. To address this challenge, we propose a two-stage retrieval-augmented lesion detection framework: a 3D Swin Transformer-FPN-FCOS detector retrieves candidates from coarse-voxel-spacing whole-body SPECT/CT, and a candidate query retrieves fine-voxel-spacing local/context SPECT/CT evidence tokens for classification, box refinement, and rescoring. In validation, the base model achieves free-response receiver operating characteristic (FROC) scores of 0.511/0.471 for Mean-FROC/Low-FROC and reduces inference time from 14.9 to 3.6 s/patient; a final reranker raises Mean-FROC to 0.530 at 5.5 s/patient.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-14-05] Data Augmentation Strategy Analysis for Noninvasive Lung Cancer Subtype Classification (#2187)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 X. Hu (Autores: X. Hu , X. Lin , R. Yang , D. Huang , Q. Yao , R. Yan , K. Li , L. Geng)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beihang University, Beijing, China [2] Department of Radiation Oncology, Cancer Center, Peking University Third Hospital, Beijing, China [3] Department of Technology, CAS Ion Medical Technology Co., Ltd., Beijing, China [4] Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Lung cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related death, and distinguishing between the two major non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) subtypes, adenocarcinoma (ADC) and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), is essential for treatment planning. To evaluate whether data augmentation strategies can improve subtype classification on computed tomography (CT) images with reduced annotation burden, we compared pseudo-color mapping, adaptive histogram equalization, pixel inversion, and rotation-based augmentation in combination with tumor-centric and lung-centric region extraction. Using the public NSCLC-Radiomics dataset, features were extracted with a pretrained ResNet-50 network and classified with support vector machine (SVM) and k-nearest neighbors (KNN) models, with all augmentation and feature selection performed within each cross-validation fold. Rotation consistently improved classification, with the best single model reaching 89.36% patient-level classification accuracy. Tumor-centric and lung-centric strategies showed complementary error patterns, and an ensemble of five complementary models achieved 100% patient-level classification accuracy on this cohort. The findings suggest that complementary augmentation pathways can diversify feature representations and improve classification stability in small-sample studies.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-06-01] Development of a Dual-Modality Imaging Capsule for Laparoscopic Radio-Guided Surgery (#2174)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Patel (Autores: K. Patel , L. Confalonieri , S. Huh , M. Wilson , D. Caprotti , N. Ikoma , E. M. Zannoni)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The University of Texas at Austin, Walker Department of Mechanical Engineering, Austin, Texas, United States of America [2] The University of Texas at Austin, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Austin, Texas, United States of America [3] Rutherford Appleton Laboratory, Science and Technology Facilities Council, Didcot, United Kingdom [4] MD Anderson Cancer Center, Department of Surgical Oncology, Houston, Texas, United States of America [5] The University of Texas at Austin, Department of Diagnostic Medicine, Austin, Texas, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Minimally-invasive radio-guided surgery requires simultaneous functional nuclear guidance and anatomical visualization to enable precise intraoperative localization of radiolabeled targets [1]. We propose a dual-modality imaging drop-in capsule designed for deployment through a standard 15-mm laparoscopic trocar. It consists of a 2-mm thick semiconductor detector with a sub-millimeter pixel pitch [2,3], a custom lofthole collimator embedded within a 3D-printed tungsten capsule, and two miniaturized stereoscopic micro-cameras. Preliminary results show: real-time 3D depth maps validated against an ultrasonic distance sensor; a seamless 360° panoramic view stitched from sequential frames using cylindrical warping and multi-band Laplacian blending [4,5]; spectral localization of multiple isotopes 57 Co and 241 Am within a scattering biological medium; and a preliminary 2D co-registration overlaying the functional dataset onto the anatomical scene. We will present the system design and components, and discuss the steps towards a fully integrated prototype for laparoscopic radio-guided surgery.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-06-02] Development of a High Sensitivity Cascade Gamma Photon Coincidence Imaging System (#2224)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Q. Wei (Autores: Q. Wei , Y. Zhao , K. Wang , Z. Yan , S. Xu , X. Zhou , J. Dang , H. Jia , H. Ye , Z. Hang , W. Huang , Z. Gu , H. Liu , J. Wu , Y. Liu , Z.-X. He)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Science and Technology Beijing, Beijing Engineering Research Center of Industrial Spectrum Imaging, School of Automation and Electrical Engineering, Beijing, China [2] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China [3] Tsinghua University, School of Biomedical Engineering, Beijing, China [4] Beijing Normal University, Center for Advanced Quantum Studies, School of Physics and Astronomy, Beijing, China [5] Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Beijing, China [6] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Lutetium-177 ( 177 Lu) is one of the most representative radionuclides in integrated nuclear medicine theranostics. To image 177 Lu, we have developed a full-ring, high-sensitivity cascade gamma photon coincidence imaging system. This work presents the system construction and preliminary performance evaluation. The detector ring consists of 40 continuous LaBr₃ crystal modules arranged in 10 radial × 4 axial configuration (each 50 × 50 × 6 mm³). The inner diameter of the ring is 110 mm, with axial module spacing of 60 mm. Each crystal is coupled to four MPPC arrays and read out via PETsys FEM256 electronics, with three FEB/D boards and one DAQ for data acquisition. Both the ASICs and MPPCs are cooled by a water-cooling system, maintaining water at 8 °C and ASIC temperature below 20 °C. The collimator assembly comprises 10 tungsten plates (26 × 128 × 8 mm³), each covering four axial detector modules. Plates are arranged alternately with pinholes and slits (1 mm), placed at a vertical distance of 36.5 mm from the ring center, creating an imaging field of Φ30 × 30 mm. The prototype hardware has been fully assembled and is capable of normal data acquisition. Simulation results indicate a coincidence sensitivity of 2.97 × 10⁻⁵ at the central field of view, spatial resolution of ~1.7 mm, and hot cylindrical object resolution up to 1.2 mm. Preliminary experimental tests have validated the feasibility of the system. Ongoing optimization includes crystal position calibration, energy resolution improvement, and collimator geometry alignment. The full system performance evaluation is expected to be completed before the upcoming conference.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-06-03] Quantum entanglement of annihilation photons as a function of the annihilation mechanism (#2454)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Kumar (Autores: D. Kumar , S. Sharma , P. Moskal)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Jagiellonian University, Faculty of Physics, Astronomy and Applied Computer Science, Krakow, Poland [2] Jagiellonian University, Center of Theranostics, Krakow, Poland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In matter, a positron annihilates with an electron into two photons through several mechanisms, including direct annihilation and the formation of positronium, a metastable bound state that exists as either para-positronium or ortho-positronium. Each channel has a characteristic lifetime, allowing their contributions to be distinguished in time. The two photons are predicted to be entangled in their polarizations [1], and recent measurements indicate that the degree of entanglement depends on the annihilation channel [2]. In particular, the ortho-positronium decay is sensitive to the local concentration of molecular oxygen, and can serve as a probe of tissue hypoxia in PET imaging [3]. The Jagiellonian Positron Emission Tomograph is a scanner built from plastic scintillators, in which 511 keV photons interact predominantly through Compton scattering [4]. The Compton scattering plane of each photon is correlated with its polarization. We measure annihilations of positrons emitted by a sodium-22 source embedded in porous polymer. Sodium-22 emits a positron accompanied by a 1274 keV prompt photon, which provides a time reference for the positron lifetime. The polarization correlation distribution of the annihilation photon pairs is consistent with quantum entanglement, between the limits for maximally entangled and classically separable states [2]. Selecting events by positron lifetime reveals distinct polarization correlation distributions for different annihilation channels. A detailed comparison will be presented at the conference. These results motivate quantum-informed PET imaging, with tissue hypoxia as a clinical biomarker.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-06-04] First In-Vivo Positronium Ratio Imaging (PRI) using F-18 FDG: A Preliminary Study with Phantom and a Mouse Model (#2615)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Fujimoto (Autores: M. Fujimoto , K. Nakamura , R. Sato , P. Caradonna , A. Ostuka , S. Ohta , M. Uenomachi , L. Stephenson , A. Montgomery , D. P. Watts , K. Shimazoe)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The University of Tokyo, Department of Bioengineering, Bunkyo, Japan [2] The University of Tokyo, Department of Nuclear Engineering and Management, Bunkyo, Japan [3] Institute of Science Tokyo, Laboratory for Zero-Carbon Energy, Meguro, Japan [4] University of York, School of Physics, Engineering and Technology, York, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This research presents the development and first in-vivo demonstration of Positronium Ratio Imaging, a novel functional imaging technique that uses the three-photon to two-photon decay ratio of positronium. While conventional Positron Emission Tomography primarily maps radiopharmaceutical distribution, Positronium Ratio Imaging provides insights into the tissue microenvironment by exploiting the sensitivity of ortho-positronium to local oxygen levels and morphology. We characterized the system's geometric stability using a four-rod phantom with varying dimensions and evaluated the results against Monte Carlo simulations using the Geant4 toolkit. The phantom study identified a size-dependent uncertainty baseline of approximately twenty percent, primarily arising from detector sensitivity and geometric factors. Furthermore, we achieved the first in-vivo ratio imaging using a tumor-bearing mouse model administered with fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose. Quantitative analysis revealed that the three-photon to two-photon ratio in brown adipose tissue was approximately two and a half times higher than in the heart and bladder. This significant contrast is consistent with theoretical trends derived from tissue-specific positronium lifetimes and far exceeds the established hardware-induced uncertainty. These findings validate the feasibility of using standard positron emitters for functional three-photon imaging without the need for specialized prompt-gamma emitters. Future work will focus on refining quantitative calculation methods, evaluating signal-to-noise ratios, and implementing hardware-specific calibrations to enhance absolute quantification. This technology lays a foundation for clinical applications such as the non-invasive visualization of tumor hypoxia and metabolic characterization of the tissue microenvironment, offering a breakthrough in functional molecular imaging.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-06-05] Quantitative 4D PET Imaging of Photosynthate Transport and Rhizosphere Carbon Partitioning in Intact Plant-Soil Systems (#3049)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M.N. Ullah (Autores: M.N. Ullah , D. Hastings , D. Anders , W. Cheng , S. Abbaszadeh , C. S. Levin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Stanford University, Department of Radiology and Molecular Imaging Program at Stanford ( (MIPS)), stanford, California, United States of America [2] University of California Santa Cruz, Department of Environmental Studies, Santa Cruz, California, United States of America [3] University of California Santa Cruz, Electrical and Computer Engineering, Santa Cruz, California, United States of America [4] Stanford University, Departments Physics, Electrical Engineering, and Bioengineering, Stanford, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present quantitative 4D PET imaging of photosynthate carbon transport and rhizosphere exudation in intact Phaseolus vulgaris plant-soil systems using the R-PET (Rhizo-PET) scanner with the ¹¹C radiotracer (t₁/₂ = 20.3 min). Across N = 6 plants, time-activity curves (TACs) extracted from 225 cross-pattern ROIs per dataset-spanning 3 roots × 3 axial depths × ±3 mm radial extent-reveal a reproducible source-to-sink carbon allocation hierarchy: upper root zones receive ≈50% of total plant carbon, while root 2 (primary taproot) dominates at 20.8 ± 6.3%. Time-to-peak (TTP) increases from 31.5±4.4 min (upper) to 48.0±13.1 min (lower root 2), corresponding to a phloem transport velocity of ≈2.4 mm min⁻¹. Rhizosphere carbon exudation follows an exponential decay AUC(r) = A e⁻ᵏʳ with k = 0.10-0.20 mm⁻¹, placing the active deposition zone within 4-14 mm of the root surface-the first spatially resolved 3D+t measurement of this process in intact soil.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-06-06] Comparative Evaluation of Respiratory Motion Correction Methods for Upright Walk-Through PET Using XCAT Simulations (#1444)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Aziz (Autores: R. Aziz , T. D'Hulster , J. Maebe , C. Vanhove , S. Tao , S. Vandenberghe)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Ghent, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Ghent, Belgium [2] Shenzhen Institute of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shenzhen, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Walk-through positron emission tomography (WT-PET) is an emerging upright imaging geometry based on two vertically opposing flat detector panels. Although this design may improve patient comfort and acquisition efficiency, respiratory motion remains a major source of image degradation. This study evaluates respiratory motion correction strategies for WT-PET using XCAT anthropomorphic simulations. A 30s acquisition was simulated in a WT-PET geometry and reconstructed using an in-house MLEM-based algorithm. Data-driven amplitude- and phase-based respiratory gating were followed by non-rigid motion correction using Advanced Normalization Tools (ANTs) and Fast Algorithms for Motion Correction (FALCON). Overlapping-frame reconstruction using 0.9375s windows shifted every 0.3125s was also evaluated to assess the effect of temporal smoothing. Performance was quantified against a motion-free reference using normalized root mean square error (NRMSE), diaphragm edge width, and line profile analysis. ANTs phase-based 4-gate correction achieved the best performance, reducing NRMSE from 64% to 6% and restoring the diaphragm edge width to the motion-free reference level (25.10 mm vs. 25.79 mm). FALCON phase-based 4-gate correction reduced NRMSE to 12% but showed limited recovery of diaphragm sharpness, with an edge width of 28.40 mm compared with 28.62 mm for no motion correction. Overlapping-frame ANTs correction reduced NRMSE to 15% and yielded an intermediate edge width of 27.13 mm, although line profiles indicated residual local displacement and smoothing. These findings show that data-driven respiratory gating combined with deformable registration can substantially improve image quality in upright WT-PET.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-06-07] Dementia Risk Estimation From a Positron Emission Tomography-Derived Latent Biomarker (#2058)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Vázquez García (Autores: C. Vázquez García , F. J. Martínez Murcia , J. Ramírez Pérez de Inestrosa , F. Segovia Román , A. Forte Deltell , I. Álvarez Illán , A. Hernández Segura , C. Jiménez Mesa , J.M. Górriz Sáez)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Granada, Department of Signal Processing and Biomedical Applications, Granada, Spain [2] University of Valencia, Department of Statistics and Operations Research, Valencia, Spain [3] University of Málaga, Department of Communication Engineering, Málaga, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We investigated whether a positron emission tomography-derived latent biomarker can serve as a compact prognostic signal after longitudinal modeling. The study used 3,458 scans from 1,624 participants in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. A Bayesian mixed-effects model was fitted to the biomarker trajectory and evaluated in two practical settings: forecasting future visits for previously observed subjects and estimating short-term dementia risk from predicted biomarker values. For subjects already observed during training, future visits were predicted with a mean root mean squared error of 0.298 and a mean absolute error of 0.250. For entirely new subjects, a change-from-baseline formulation reduced prediction error to a mean root mean squared error of 0.217 and a mean absolute error of 0.171 after an initial scan. A training-only logistic calibration applied to held-out predictions reached an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.826 for future dementia risk estimation. These results suggest that the latent biomarker can move beyond representation learning and support short-term longitudinal forecasting and clinically interpretable risk stratification.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-06-08] Data-Driven Selection of Representative Motion Models for Simulation in Dynamic Cardiac PET (#2952)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Nemati (Autores: N. Nemati , O. Rainio , S. Palonen , E. Lehtonen , T. Maaniitty , J. Teuho , J. Tuisku , M. Irfan , N. Miller , L. Nummenmaa , J. Knuuti , R. Klén)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Turku and Turku University Hospital, Turku PET Centre, Turku, Finland [2] Turku University Hospital, Department of Clinical Physiology, Nuclear Medicine and PET, Turku, Finland [3] Turku University of Applied Science, ICT and Industrial Engineering, Data Engineering and AI technologies, Turku, Finland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Patient motion remains a common challenge in dynamic cardiac positron emission tomography (PET), as it degrades image quality and complicates reliable evaluation of motion correction methods. Realistic motion simulation requires motion models that capture the variability observed in clinical data, but this remains difficult when simulations rely on only a limited set of motion patterns. In this work, we propose a data driven framework for motion model selection and simulation in dynamic cardiac PET. We characterize motion trajectories using physically interpretable features and analyze them using clustering and trajectory similarity based on dynamic time warping to identify a compact set of representative motion models. These models are integrated with patient-specific motion scaling for frame-wise simulation of motion-corrupted PET data. The proposed framework produces stable normalized error levels across 1308 patient-model evaluations while using only a small number of representative motion models. The results suggest that the selected models effectively capture dominant motion behaviors observed in the dataset and enable realistic PET motion simulation.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-06-09] A Quality Control Framework for Deep Learning-based Attenuation Map Synthesis in PET (#2579)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Lu (Autores: Z. Ji , Y. Li , C. Jiang , C. Sun , X. Wang , Y. Lu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] ShanghaiTech University, School of Information Science and Technology, Shanghai, China [2] Shanghai United Imaging Healthcare Co., LTD, Molecular Imaging Business Unit, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Deep learning-based attenuation correction (DL-AC) offers potential advantages over conventional CT-based attenuation correction (CT-AC) in PET imaging, including avoidance of additional radiation exposure and reduced susceptibility to PET-CT misalignment. However, in DL-AC application scenarios, when CT-derived attenuation maps (CT-μ) are unavailable as reference images, quality control (QC) of deep learning-derived attenuation maps (DL-μ) often relies on manual inspection. To address this limitation, we propose a patch-level 3D convolutional neural network (3D CNN) framework for automated anomaly detection and localization in DL-μ without requiring CT during inference. During training, CT-μ was used to assist patch-level annotation of DL-μ, and artifact-free CT-μ patches without observer-identified abnormalities were incorporated as normal samples to help the model learn normal attenuation patterns. During inference, only DL-μ was used, and sliding-window prediction was used to aggregate patch-level anomaly probabilities into a voxel-wise anomaly probability map. On the validation set (51 cases), the framework yielded patch-level performance with an AUC of 0.9984, an F1-score of 0.9802, a sensitivity of 97.06%, and a specificity of 98.86%. These results suggest that the proposed framework can provide spatial cues for DL-μ, potentially supporting efficient evaluation and reducing reliance on manual QC inspection.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-06-10] Characterizing Noise in Clinical Nuclear Medicine Modalities via Quantum-Inspired Framework (#2977)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Hashemi (Autores: A. Hashemi , S. Abdar Esfahani , P. Silva , A. Sinagra , P. Heidari , H. Sabet)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Harvard Medical School/Massachusetts General Hospital, Department of Radiology, Boston, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Quantum-inspired denoising is employed for clinical PET/CT, PET/MR, and SPECT imaging by treating images analogous to disordered materials and analyzing the eigenfunctions of an associated Hamiltonian. Quantum localization is quantified by the participation ratio, enabling filtering of non‑localized, high‑participation modes that dominate the mid‑frequency range and are associated with diffusive noise. By suppressing these modes and reconstructing from the remaining localized modes, noise is reduced without training data or manual regularization. The framework is applied to 46 multi‑vendor, multi‑tracer patient datasets from Massachusetts General Brigham to characterize scanner‑dependent noise structure and its impact on image appearance. Across the cohort, quantum‑inspired filtering yields consistent decreases in blind image quality scores (PIQE and BRISQUE) together with increases in entropy and Laplacian variance, indicating lower perceived noise and enhanced structural detail in the denoised clinical images.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-05-01] Pixelated Cherenkov Crystals for Prompt-Gamma Imaging in Proton Range Verification (#1181)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Rebolo (Autores: L. Rebolo , S. Moreno Gomez , M. Kolstein , M. Backfish , M. Novotny , R. Sahebzada , S. St. James , B. Mehadji , E. Prebys , P. M. Correia , A.L. Silva , G. Ariño-Estrada)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidade de Aveiro, Física, Aveiro, Portugal [2] University of California Davis, Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America [3] University of California Davis, Physics, Davis, California, United States of America [4] University of Utah, Huntsman Cancer Institute, Salt Lake City, Utah, United States of America [5] Crocker Nuclear Laboratory, Davis, California, United States of America [6] Institut de Fisica d'Altes Energies - Barcelona Institute of Science and Technology (IFAE-BIST), Bellaterra, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Proton range verification (PRV) in proton therapy is an outstanding clinical need. Prompt-gammas (PG) emitted along the proton track constitute a strong signal to determine the Bragg Peak position. However, the high energy of PGs (1-7 MeV), the high particle flux and the presence of significant background radiation make prompt-gamma imaging (PGI) challenging. We report on the development of pure Cherenkov pixelated detectors for PRV. The detector consisted of an 8×8 pixelated PbF2 crystal array coupled to an 8×8 S14161-3050HS-08 SiPM array from Hamamatsu, read out by a row-column signal processing board. Two analytical event reconstruction algorithms were evaluated: rise-to-the-power with k=2 (RTP2) and k=3 (RTP3). The detector was exposed to both a sealed 228Th source and a 67.5 MeV proton beam at a current of 100 pA. Floodmaps were obtained using both RTP2 and RTP3 methods to resolve the 8×8 matrix of the crystal under laboratory source irradiation. Similar results were obtained under proton beam irradiation, showing the robustness of this detector concept. In this contribution we demonstrate for the first time the ability of a pixelated pure Cherenkov detector to provide spatial resolution information in clinically relevant proton beam conditions. The prompt emission of Cherenkov light and exclusive sensitivity to highly energetic PGs offer a very high count rate capability, effective background rejection, and capacity to multiplex signals, enabling to use less channels and low power readout electronics. Future work will focus on quantitative floodmap quality metrics, detector modeling to optimize the detector geometry, and acquisition of additional data in the proton beam line at higher proton energies and beam currents.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-05-02] Coded-Mask PGI for Proton Range Verification With Pure Cherenkov Crystal Detectors (#1159)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. M. Gómez (Autores: S. M. Gómez , M. Kolstein , C. Gomà , S. Marcatili , A. Wrońska , M. Rafecas , G. Ariño-Estrada)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institut de Física d'Altes Energies - Barcelona Institute of Science and Technology (IFAE-BIST), Medical Detector Instrumentation and Imaging Physics group, Cerdanyola del Vallès, Spain [2] Institut d'Investigacions Biomèdiques August Pi i Sunyer (IDIBAPS), Translational genomics and targeted therapies in solid tumours, Barcelona, Spain [3] Laboratoire de Physique Subatomique et de Cosmologie (LPSC), Physics at the service of energy and health - Medical Applications, Grenoble, France [4] Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique (CNRS), Grenoble, France [5] Marian Smoluchowski Institute of Physics, Jagiellonian University, Department of Hadron Physics (ZFH), Kraków, Poland [6] Universität zu Lübeck, Biomedical Engineering - Medical Imaging, Lübeck, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany [7] University of California Davis, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate proton range verification (PRV) in proton therapy (PT) is an unmet clinical need and is essential to exploit the full potential of PT to maximize treatment effectiveness and minimize toxicity. We present a Monte Carlo (GATE 10) study of a Cherenkov-based prompt gamma imaging system combining an array of PbF2 crystal detectors with a MURA coded-aperture collimator for real-time PRV. The detector response was studied through detected Cherenkov photon distributions generated by prompt-gammas with energies ranging from 0.5 MeV to 7.0 MeV in steps of 0.5 MeV. A threshold of 15 detected Cherenkov photons was applied to reject low-energy background, which effectively suppressed 511 keV annihilation gammas and sub-MeV contributions while retaining the prompt gammas of interest. Image reconstruction was performed using the Maximum Likelihood Expectation Maximization algorithm, with the system matrix computed with 4.4 MeV point-like sources. The imaging performance was validated on isotropic gamma point sources in both 1D and 2D coded-mask configurations across a field of view of ∼130 mm. A direct comparison between discrimination based on energy deposition (E > 1 MeV) and discrimination based on the number of detected Cherenkov photons (nckv ≥ 15) showed comparable performance, with position residuals consistent with zero within statistical uncertainties in both cases. For the proton beam measurements, background rejection was performed exclusively via the Cherenkov photon count threshold. Under realistic proton beam conditions, the distal fall-off position was reconstructed with a systematic residual below 1.5 mm and a statistical precision of less than 2 mm for beam intensities above 10^8 protons, corresponding to approximately 10 ms of irradiation at a standard proton current of 2 nA (1.25 × 10^10 protons/s). This work presents the concept and shows the feasibility of using Cherenkov-based coded-aperture imaging for PRV by means of a simulation framework.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-05-03] Deep Learning-based CT-Free Deformable Registration for PET-CT Misalignment Correction (#1875)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Mehranian (Autores: A. Mehranian , S. Wollenweber , F. Kotasidis , Z. Chalampalakis , A. Lulinsky , H. Ratner , R. Johnsen , G. Kovalski)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] GE HealthCare, Oxford, United Kingdom [2] GE HealthCare, Waukesha, United States of America [3] GE HealthCare, Zurich, United Kingdom [4] GE HealthCare, Buc, France [5] GE HealthCare, Haifa, Israel
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Respiratory phase mismatches between PET and CT commonly cause artifacts in PET/CT, especially at lung-liver and lung-spleen interfaces. Since CT captures a single respiratory phase while PET reflects an average over breathing, this misalignment leads to attenuation correction errors and inaccurate lesion quantification, particularly near the liver dome. We propose a deep learning framework that uses PET-based pseudo-CT to guide deformable CT-to-PET alignment. A retrospective dataset of 10 18F-FDG exams with respiratory phase mismatch (banana) artifacts, scanned on a Total-Body BGO-based PET/CT scanner, was used for evaluation. A previously trained 3D residual neural network was used to generate pseudo-CT images from non-attenuation corrected (NAC) PET images. The pseudo-CT images, inherently aligned with the PET data, were then used as a reference for deformable registration of the CT images. The original and registered CT images were used for attenuation correction and reconstruction of the PET data using a BSREM algorithm. Regions of interested were placed in dome of the liver to quantitatively measure the SUV changes in those regions affected by the artifacts. Compared to baseline PET/CT without correction, the proposed method effectively reduced or eliminated respiratory-induced PET/CT misalignment artifacts were significantly reduced or eliminated. Quantitatively, the method achieved improvements in liver SUVmean towards the expected values. By leveraging the native alignment between PET and the generated pseudo-CT, the method avoids direct multimodal registration and instead enables accurate deformable alignment of CT to PET space. This approach improves attenuation correction and quantitative accuracy, with potential to enhance diagnostic confidence in routine clinical PET/CT imaging
