sub_talks.title: [M-LT-05-04] Evaluation of TOF-DOI Crystal Topologies for the HD-MetaPET MRI Insert (#2140)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Meyer (Autores: T. Meyer , G. Terragni , D. Schug , Y. Kuhl , B. Weissler , E. Gegenmantel , O. Muelhens , H. Radermacher , M. Pizzichemi , E. Auffray , V. Schulz)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] RWTH Aachen University, Chair of Imaging and Computer Vision, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [2] CERN, Geneva, Switzerland [3] Hyperion Hybrid Imaging Systems GmbH, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [4] University of Milano-Bicocca, Milan, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The HD-MetaPET project is developing a high-resolution positron emission tomography insert for simultaneous magnetic resonance imaging. The insert will consist of 120 Hyperion Visor Max detector tiles with an area of 56.5 x 56.5 mm 2 , arranged in two semi-circles and coupled to LYSO:Ce crystal scintillators. A crucial optimisation parameter for the upcoming system performance is the crystal topology. This study evaluates Time-of-Flight and Depth-of-Interaction positioning performance across several crystal topologies: continuous slabs, pseudoslabs, and pixelated arrays with a light guide coupled to the face opposite the photosensitive detector. The study utilizes the Hyperion Visor Max and a custom development board, both featuring the TOFPET2 ASIC. Experimental measurements are performed using a 22 Na point source. The preliminary results with crystals of different materials show that pixelated arrays with light guides outperform continuous slabs. Specifically, pixelated designs achieved a Coincidence Time Resolution of ≈235 ps, compared to >400 ps for the slabs. The results indicate that the pixelated designs utilizing the light guide also demonstrated superior accuracy in the evaluation of the Depth-of-Interaction. The pixelated light-guide topology shows promising performance, circumventing the traditional compromise between spatial depth accuracy and timing resolution. Consequently, this configuration emerges as a good candidate for integration into the upcoming HD-MetaPET scanner. While these preliminary results are promising, the comprehensive evaluations utilizing final-scale crystals of the same material and the final scanner electronics will be presented at the conference.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-05-05] Noise-Robust Bayesian Parameter Estimation of Two-Tissue Compartment Kinetic Model for dynamic SPECT imaging (#1051)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Zhang (Autores: D. Zhang , H. Liu , J. Qin , Y. Gu , W. Fang , L. Wang , J. Wu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Normal University, School of Physics and Astronomy, Beijing, China [2] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [3] Fuwai Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences & Peking Union Medical College/National Center for Cardiovascular Diseases, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Tracer kinetic modeling using the two-tissue (2T) compartment model remains challenging in dynamic SPECT imaging, particularly under realistic noise conditions. In this study, we propose a noise-robust Bayesian parameter estimation method that incorporates physiological prior information for the 2T model in dynamic SPECT imaging. To validate the proposed method, we conducted both simulation study and dynamic 99m Tc-4BOH clinical study. The proposed method was compared with the conventional nonlinear least-squares (NLS) method. In the simulation study, the proposed method yielded lower relative bias in the estimated kinetic parameters ( K 1 , k 2 , k 3 , and k 4 ) than the NLS method under both low and high noise conditions. In the clinical 99m Tc-4BOH study, K 1 estimated using the proposed method demonstrated significantly stronger agreement and lower relative bias with respect to head-to-head 13 N-NH 3 PET myocardial blood flow (MBF), which was used as the reference standard, than the NLS method. In conclusion, the proposed method substantially improved the accuracy and precision of parameter estimation for the 2T model compared with the NLS method.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y.J. Seol (Autores: Y.J. Seol , S.K. Kang , E.T. Kim , J.S. Lee)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Seoul national university, Interdisciplinary Program in Bioengineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] Seoul national university, Integrated Major in Innovative Medical Science, Seoul, Republic of Korea [3] Samsung Ventures, Seoul, Republic of Korea [4] Seoul National University Bundang Hospital, Department of Psychiatry, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We propose a kinetic-consistent conditional flow matching framework for dynamic [11C raclopride PET SRTM parametric imaging. Conventional indirect SRTM fitting is vulnerable to frame-wise count noise, causing unstable voxel-wise R1 , k2 , and BPND maps. Using 105 scans from 35 subjects, count-reduced datasets were generated at 50%, 25%, and 10% of the original counts. The model refines reduced-count indirect SRTM estimates toward full-count SRTM pseudo-reference maps using kinetic consistency, count/noise conditioning, and physiological constraints, reducing BPND deviation, high-percentile errors, and kinetic-parameter disagreement compared with indirect SRTM and denoising and regularization-based baselines

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-05-07] Attenuation Images from Time‑of‑Flight PET for Metal Artifact Reduction: A Phantom Study (#1406)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A.-K. Lüvelsmeyer (Autores: F. L. Peltzer , A.-K. Lüvelsmeyer , C. M. Bäcker , J. Wulff , M. Teimoorisichani , W. Jentzen , B. Timmermann , C. Bäumer)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University Medicine of Essen, West German Proton Therapy Centre Essen, Essen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [2] University Medicine of Essen, West German Cancer Centre Essen, Essen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [3] TU Dortmund University, Physics, Dortmund, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [4] Siemens Medical Solutions USA Inc., Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America [5] University Medicine of Essen, Clinic for Nuclear Medicine, Essen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [6] University Medicine of Essen, Department of Particle Therapy, Essen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Metal implants can degrade CT image quality and introduce artifacts that affect dose calculation in particle therapy. This study investigates attenuation images (µ‑MLAA) reconstructed from time‑of‑flight PET data using maximum‑likelihood reconstruction of attenuation and activity for metal artifact reduction. The linearity of a calibration curve relating CT number to relative electron density was first evaluated using a PMMA phantom with metal and tissue‑equivalent inserts. Metal artifacts were then studied in a water phantom containing a Ti6Al4V total endoprosthesis (TEP) implant. µ‑MLAA attenuation images reconstructed from PET list mode data and CT images reconstructed using iterative metal artifact reduction (iMAR) were evaluated using gamma index analysis (10%, 1 mm) relative to an artifact‑free reference slice. The calibration curve remained linear in the presence of metal inserts ( R 2 > 0.999 ). For the TEP phantom, µ‑MLAA images achieved a higher gamma pass rate (96.3%) than iMAR CT (70.8%). Using the calibration curve, the relative electron density of the TEP shaft was estimated as n e, rel = 3.58±0.12 corresponding to a 3.5% deviation from reported reference values. These results indicate the potential of µ‑MLAA images for reducing metal artifacts and supporting implant characterization in radiotherapy imaging.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-05-08] An FPGA-based data acquisition system for remote wireless radiation monitoring (#1302)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Miyaoka (Autores: P. S. Guntha , E. Ingalls , T. M. Whalen , M. Kim , W. C. Hunter , G. Jones , S. Hauck , R. Miyaoka)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Washington, Radiology, Seattle, Washington, United States of America [2] University of Washington, Electrical Engineering, Seattle, Washington, United States of America [3] Microsoft, Azure, Redmond, Washington, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Purpose: We are developing a Personalized Remote Radiation Tracking Portable Organ Dosimetry Device (PRRT PODD) for at-home monitoring of patients receiving radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT). We report on an FPGA-based data acquisition system capable of wireless communication in support of this goal. Methods: Our acquisition system supports16-radiation detectors and outputs an energy histogram for each using a time-over-threshold (ToT) energy measurement. The electronics consists of a custom analog board that converts each detector's analog signal into a digital ToT signal; an FPGA board for signal processing; and a microcontroller board that serves as the system controller. The microcontroller communicates with the FPGA via UART to retrieve energy histogram data, manages system configuration parameters, and provides Bluetooth Low Energy connectivity to a mobile Android app. The electronics fits within the PODD's base assembly and can operate on cell phone battery power. Each detector has a small thermistor for individual probe temperature monitoring and to characterize MPPC gain versus temperature. An Android app was developed to control data acquisition and wireless transfer of data to a remote workstation. The detector and electronics acqusition system was tested using Tc-99m, Na-22 and Lu-177 radioactive sources at clinically relevant counting rates. Results: Sixteen channel operation of our FPGA-based data acquisition system has been validated using a variety of radionuclides. The output properties of the probes have been characterized versus temperature to enable post acquisition normalization of signals. Conclusion and future work : A compact, wireless 16-channel gamma spectroscopy system for remote monitoring of Lu-177 RTP was designed and tested. Future work includes implementing real-time temperature compensation based on continuous temperature readings, ensuring stable operation without post-processing.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-05-09] Energy-Shifting: an efficient approach for Monte Carlo Particle Therapy Dose Calculation (#3092)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Bert (Autores: C.-H. Pham , D. Benoit , V. Bourbonne , U. Schick , D. Visvikis , J. Bert)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Brest, LaTIM, INSERM-UMR1101, Brest, France [2] Brest Hospital University, Radiotherapy Department, Brest, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract While recent deep learning techniques for accelerating Monte Carlo (MC) radiotherapy dose calculation have shown promising results, most state-of-the-art methods rely on a denoising paradigm. This approach aims to predict a high-sampling (HS) reference dose map from a fast low-sampling (LS) input. However, information loss and stochastic noise in LS inputs often limit the accurate recovery of fine structural details and dose gradients, and may lead to hallucinations. To address these limitations, we propose a novel learning framework, Energy-Shifting, which reconstructs a time-intensive polyenergetic HS dose distribution from a GPU-accelerated monoenergetic dose map. Our results demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms conventional denoising approaches in accuracy.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-05-10] Treatment Monitoring System for Proton Therapy Based on Beam Range Measurement (#1067)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Jang (Autores: S. Jang , J. Cho , G. Lee , T. Eom , J. Lee , J.H. Jeong , S.H. Kim , S. Cho , K. Jo , C.H. Kim)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Hanyang University, Nuclear Engineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] National Cancer Center, Proton Therapy Center, Goyang, Republic of Korea [3] Samsung Medical Center, Department of Radiation Oncology, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In proton therapy, range uncertainties can result in insufficient dose delivery to the tumor or unintended dose delivery to organs at risk (OARs). To address this, several range verification methods have been investigated, and prompt gamma imaging is considered a promising method due to the strong correlation between the dose profile and prompt gamma distribution at the distal dose fall-off location. Based on prompt gamma imaging, a treatment monitoring system was developed to measure the in vivo beam range and detect range shifts during the treatment. The developed system consists of a 72-slit parallel collimator, 144 CsI(Tl) scintillation detectors, a dedicated field-programmable gate array (FPGA)-based data acquisition (DAQ) system, and a dedicated program with a graphical user interface (GUI). The DAQ system calculates pulse height and timing of each signal from 144 detectors. The dedicated program reconstructs 1D prompt gamma distribution using pulse data and determines the beam range of each spot using a dedicated range estimation algorithm [1]. The system's performance was evaluated using a clinical proton beam prescribed to deliver 0.5 Gy to a spherical clinical target volume (CTV) with 50 mm diameter in a homogeneous PMMA phantom. To evaluate range shift detection performance, range shifts were induced at both the global range shift (1-10 mm) and local range shift (5 and 10 mm) conditions. At the same time, the computation time for range deviation analysis was evaluated. The system detected global range shifts with an accuracy of 1 mm and identified the presence and location of local range shifts exceeding 5 mm. Furthermore, the time required for range deviation analysis per layer was found much shorter than energy layer switching time. These results demonstrate the system can verify the in vivo beam range during treatment in clinical practice.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 3Poster Number:MIC-15-003] Dual-ended Redout PET Detectors based on 0.25 mm pitch LYSO/GAGG arrays (#1104)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Xie (Autores: J. Xie , H. Wang , J. Qi , R. D. Badawi , S. R. Cherry , J. Du)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California at Davis, Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Spatial resolution and sensitivity are the two most critical characteristics of a positron emission tomography (PET) scanner, as they determine the accuracy and precision of reconstructed images. Achieving uniform ultra-high spatial resolution across the field of view (FOV) while maintaining sufficient sensitivity requires PET detectors capable of resolving ultra-fine, high-aspect-ratio crystals and extracting precise depth-of-interaction (DOI) information to mitigate parallax errors. In this study, we developed and evaluated two dual-ended readout detectors for small-animal brain PET applications. Each detector comprised a 36 × 36 array of lutetium yttrium oxyorthosilicate (LYSO) or gadolinium aluminum gallium garnet (GAGG) coupled to two linearly-graded silicon photomultipliers (LG-SiPMs). The crystal element size of the two crystal arrays was 0.20 × 0.20 × 9 mm³, while the pitch of the two crystal arrays was 0.25 mm. Despite the crystal element aspect ratio reaching 45:1, most crystal elements in both detectors were resolved, yielding average energy resolutions of 37.3 ± 5.6% and 31.7 ± 5.7%, respectively, for the LYSO and GAGG arrays, resepectively. The mean coincidence timing resolutions (CTRs) of the central 32 × 32 crystal elements, measured using a 200-1000 keV energy window to select events, were 1025 ± 40 ps (LYSO array) and 1205 ± 62 ps (GAGG array). Additionally, the average DOI resolutions across crystal elements were 1.48 ± 0.10 mm and 1.47 ± 0.10 mm, respectively, for the LYSO and GAGG arrays, respectively.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 6Poster Number:MIC-15-006] Study of the response of comercial CMOS sensors to soft X-rays (#1477)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Velasco (Autores: L. Velasco , J. Juan-Morales , T. Cebriano , N. Lara , J.L. Henares , J. Hernandez-Toro , P. Vicente , D. De Luis , E. Flores , M. Seimetz , J.I. Apiñaniz Aginako)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Center of Pulsed Lasers (CLPU), Villamayor, Spain [2] Instituto de Instrumentación para Imagen Molecular (I3M), CSIC-Universitat Politècnica de València, Valencia, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract High-repetition-rate (HRR) operation is a key limitation in laser-driven particle and photon sources, requiring diagnostics compatible with repetition rates of order 1 Hz or higher. We investigate standard industrial CMOS imaging sensors as soft X-ray detectors, analysing their single-photon response in the 5.5--12.6 keV range. The response is linear, and the sensors are calibrated in terms of generated electron--hole carriers versus incident photon energy. X-ray interactions in pixel sensors produce single-pixel (SPE) and multi-pixel events (MPE), which are analysed independently; removing MPEs significantly improves spectral resolution. This work is a first step toward the systematic study of commercial CMOS sensors under exposure to high-energy particles and photons, including response, radiation tolerance and dynamic range. Their compact size, low cost, and intrinsic compatibility with high-repetition-rate operation make them suitable for laser-plasma, nuclear and particle physics, and biomedical applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 9Poster Number:MIC-15-009] Asymmetric dual-ended readout using diode-based multiplexing circuits for TOF-DOI PET detectors (#1717)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Dai (Autores: R. Dai , X. Jiang , X. Zeng , X. Zhang , W. Huang , Y. Zhao , J. Hua , H. Yang , M. Niu , Z. Gu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China [2] University of Science and Technology Beijing, School of Automation and Electrical Engineering, Beijing, China [3] Harbin Institute of Technology, School of Electronics and Information Engineering, Harbin, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract To address spatial resolution and sensitivity limitations in whole-body PET for small-organ imaging, such as heart, breast and prostate, this study developed an asymmetric dual-ended readout for TOF-DOI PET detectors. The asymmetric readout design utilizes a 4×4 SiPM array (6×6 mm² pixels) with individual channel readout at the front end, for good timing performance . At the back end, an 8×8 SiPM array (3×3 mm² pixels) is read out using a diode-based row-column summing multiplexing circuit to facilitate event position decoding while reducing the number of readout channels. Specifically, the multiplexing scheme reduces the back end channels from 64 to 16, lowering the total channels per detector from 80 to 32. LYSO arrays with three crystal dimensions were evaluated: an 8×8 array (3.10×3.10×20 mm³ crystals), a 13×13 array (1.88×1.88×20 mm³ crystals), and a 16×16 array (1.50×1.50×20 mm³ crystals). Detector performance was evaluated in an array-to-array coincidence setup, with two identical detector modules placed face-to-face. Flood images show all crystals in the three evaluated arrays can be clearly resolved under both non-multiplexed and multiplexed readout conditions. The average energy resolutions for the 8×8, 13×13, and 16×16 arrays are 12.49%, 11.71%, and 10.92%, respectively, which are comparable to those obtained with non-multiplexed readout . A preliminary evaluation of CTR for the 8×8 array yields 327 ps (non-multiplexed) and 365 ps (multiplexed), indicating limited timing degradation due to multiplexing. The proposed asymmetric multiplexed readout design maintains acceptable spatial, energy, and timing resolution while substantially reducing electronic complexity . This configuration is suitable for developing cost-effective, high-performance organ-specific PET scanners . Future work will focus on optimizing the MPPC operating overvoltage and PETsys threshold settings, as well as implementing an interleaved multiplexing circuit to improve CTR performance.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 12Poster Number:MIC-15-012] Development of a TOF-DOI PET Detector Using Dual-ended Interleaved Multiplexing Readout (#1813)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 X. Jiang (Autores: X. Jiang , R. Dai , X. Zhang , H. Yang , Y. Zhao , X. Zeng , W. Huang , M. Niu , Z. Gu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China [2] Harbin Institute of Technology, School of Electronics and Information Engineering, Harbin, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Time-of-flight (TOF) and depth-of-interaction (DOI) information improve the spatial resolution and signal-to-noise ratio of PET imaging, but typically requires numerous readout channels, increasing system complexity and cost. In this work, we developed a TOF-DOI PET detector using a novel dual-ended interleaved multiplexing (DiMux) readout. The detector consists of an 8×8 LYSO crystal array with polished surfaces, where each crystal measures 3.1 × 3.1 × 20 mm 3 with a 3.2 mm crystal pixel pitch, and is optically isolated using BaSO 4 reflectors. Both ends are one-to-one coupled to 8×8 SiPM arrays and read out by two complementary interleaved multiplexing circuits, which use Schottky barrier diode-based charge division. In this approach, each crystal is encoded as a row signal on one end and a column signal on the opposite end, with multiplexed signals digitized by PETsys TOFPET2 ASICs. This dual-ended, complementary design enables accurate position decoding using a conventional center-of-gravity (CoG) method, eliminating the need for deep learning-based decoding. Flood images with clearly resolved crystals are generated from the summed signals of both ends. The detector achieves a average DOI resolution of 2.97 mm and a coincidence time resolution (CTR) of 257 ps, which further improves to 234 ps after excluding inter-crystal scattering (ICS) events. Compared with a non-multiplexed dual-ended reference detector, the DiMux scheme reduces the number of readout channels by a factor of four while maintaining comparable TOF and DOI performance. These results demonstrate that the DiMux readout provides a high performance, low complexity, and scalable solution for clinical PET imaging systems.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 15Poster Number:MIC-15-015] Design of a Single-Ended Readout DOI PET Detector with BGO and Deep Learning (#1952)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Hong (Autores: S. Hong , J.H. Jung , J. Jung , Y. Choi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Sogang University, Department of Electronic Engineering, Intelligent Signal Processing System (ISPS) Laboratory, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The purpose of this study was to design a single-ended readout PET detector with BGO providing DOI, to investigate the effects of lateral surface treatments and inter-crystal coupling conditions on detector performance, and to improve the performance using deep learning. A detector consisting of an 8 × 8 array of 3 mm × 3 mm × 20 mm BGO, each one-to-one coupled with a SiPM, was modeled using DETECT2000. Photon distributions were estimated for four detector configurations: polished + air (PA), polished + glue (PG), unpolished + air (UA), and unpolished + glue (UG). The x-, y-, and z-positions were analytically estimated using photon distribution information. To improve positioning accuracy, a deep learning model combining CNN and MLP was implemented. The CNN extracted features from photon distributions, and the MLP estimated the fine position using CNN-derived features concatenated with analytically calculated positions. The difference between the ground-truth and the estimated positions was evaluated using the mean absolute error (MAE). The accuracy of DOI estimation was assessed by evaluating the DOI identification accuracy in 20 mm long BGO divided into three equal segments. For x- and y-position estimations, the MAE values showed minimal variations (< 0.1 mm) across the four detector configurations, regardless of the estimation methods. For DOI estimation, the UA and UG achieved lower MAE (3.8 and 3.6 mm) and higher DOI identification accuracies (63% and 66%) than the other detector configurations. By applying deep learning, the MAE values for UA and UG were reduced to approximately 1 mm, and the DOI accuracies increased to 92% and 91%, respectively. These results indicate that three-level DOI identification can be achieved using photon distribution information obtained from a simple single-ended readout detector. In particular, the UA provided superior DOI estimation performance, and the incorporation of deep learning further enhanced DOI positioning accuracy.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 18Poster Number:MIC-15-018] A pulse-train model for X-ray photon-counting scintillation detectors with pile-up (#2023)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Schröder (Autores: L. Schröder , D. R. Schaart)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Delft Univeristy of Technology, Radiation Science & Technology, Delft, Netherlands
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract To investigate potential applications of indirect photon-counting detectors, we developed a model to simulate pulse trains with pile-up for a combination of scintillator and silicon photomultiplier (SiPM). We generated pulse trains for various input rates, and the output count rate (OCR) and the spectral degradation factor (SDF) were analyzed. This was performed for two scintillators and counting algorithms, various cut-off frequencies of the applied low-pass filter, event energy thresholds, and a mono- and a polychromatic source. The results were compared to experiments. For the OCR, the model and measurements produced very similar results for all investigated parameter combinations. While the SDF values of the simulations tended to show some differences compared to the measurements, the general trend was similar.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 21Poster Number:MIC-15-021] Monte Carlo Simulations of a Penumbra-Based Collimator-less SPECT Detector for Targeted Radionuclide Therapy Monitoring (#2115)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 I. Neves (Autores: I. Neves , B. Casanelli , A. L.M. Silva , P. M.M. Correia)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Porto, Faculty of Sciences, Porto, Portugal [2] University of Aveiro, Institute for Nanostructures, Nanomodelling and Nanofabrication (i3N), Department of Physics (DFis), Aveiro, Portugal
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work investigates a collimator-less scintillator-based detector that uses penumbra maps to reconstruct the spatial origin of radioisotopes without photon losses from collimation, motivated by the need for in-vivo dosimetry monitoring during targeted radionuclide therapy (TRT) and the limitations for its broader clinical adoption. Monte Carlo simulations were performed in GATE to evaluate the method's viability, using a 218 keV mono-energetic point-like source to replicate the first gamma emission on Ac-225's decay scheme. Given its favorable photoelectric fraction for this energy, BGO was chosen as the detector's material on the simulations. Geometrical parameters such as crystal dimensions, inter-crystal spacing, and array layout were systematically varied. Results show that inter-crystal spacing significantly shapes the photon distribution pattern, the larger 0.4mm value produced a distinct visual artifact. Depth profiles vary with source position in a predictable manner and provide information regarding the radiation's penetration depth. The implemented dual-layer checkerboard geometry demonstrated complementary detection behavior between layers, improving spatial discrimination over single-layer designs. These findings support the feasibility of collimator-less gamma imaging and show that geometric optimization shapes the detector's spatial response.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 24Poster Number:MIC-15-024] A covariance-based framework for quantifying circuit and intrinsic CTR limits in TOF-PET detectors (#2237)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Shim (Autores: H. Shim , G.B. Ko)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Department of Nuclear and Quantum Engineering, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [2] Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Mechanical Engineering Research Institute, Daejeon, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract CTR in PET detectors is a quadrature combination of scintillator photon statistics, intrinsic detector physics, and front-end circuit electronics, but conventional measurement reports only the combined FWHM, leaving the relative contributions indeterminate. This hinders rational optimization between circuit-side and detector-side improvements. We introduce a covariance-based framework that decomposes the CTR noise budget from a single coincidence measurement by simultaneously extracting timestamps from two independent readouts-the timing chain and the energy chain. The covariance Cov(ΔT T , ΔT E ) isolates the common-mode intrinsic contribution, while variance differences identify chain-specific circuit noise in closed form, requiring no calibration beyond standard CTR acquisition. Applied to a 4 condition of LSO and GAGG:Ce (3×3×20 mm³) with Broadcom NUV-MT and NUV-DJ SiPMs, the framework extracts a circuit noise floor σ nT = 11.2-18.5 ps per detector across all conditions, supporting its interpretation as a detector-independent electronics floor. Intrinsic contributions cluster sharply by crystal type (LSO 28-31 ps, GAGG 49-56 ps), exceeding the analytical CRLB by 1.42-1.62× due to DOI and transport effects. A walk asymmetry ρ(ΔT E , dE)/ρ(ΔT T , dE) = 1.42-1.82× reflects front-end pulse-shape physics. The decomposition quantifies circuit-improvement leverage: LSO configurations retain 11-15% potential CTR reduction, while GAGG configurations operate within 2-6% of their photon-statistics bound. The framework provides a single-measurement diagnostic for prioritizing circuit-side versus detector-side investments in PET front-end development, and also provides the first quantitative noise-budget characterization of NUV-DJ SiPMs.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 27Poster Number:MIC-15-027] Identification and Mitigation of Inter-Crystal Scatter in Dual-Layer DOI Configurations Under Highly Multiplexed Readout (#2354)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. U. Rauscher (Autores: L. U. Rauscher , M. Judenhofer , J. Hohnholz , E. Haas , E. Olyaei , H.P. Vo , M. Rafecas , B. Pichler , F. P. Schmidt)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University Hospital Tuebingen, Department of Preclinical Imaging and Radiopharmacy, Tuebingen, Germany [2] Siemens Medical Solutions, Inc, Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America [3] University of Luebeck, Institute of Medical Engineering, Luebeck, Germany [4] University Hospital Tuebingen, Department of Nuclear Medicine and Clinical Molecular Imaging, Tuebingen, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Stacked scintillator configurations to obtain depth-of-interaction (DOI) information, combined with small crystal pitch, are commonly used to improve spatial resolution and maintain uniform performance across the field of view. Such configurations are prone to inter-crystal scatter (ICS), where energy deposition is shared across multiple crystals, leading to event mis-assignment and degradation of detector performance, including incorrect DOI estimation. Correction of these effects typically benefits from individual channel readout, which is often limited in highly multiplexed systems. In this work, we investigate ICS in a dual-layer LSO detector with 1.6 mm pitch, employing a 10×10/9×9 stacked crystal configuration coupled to a 4×4 SiPM array. The detector uses a highly multiplexed readout scheme with only three output channels (x, y, and total energy), imposing additional constraints on event discrimination. To analyze ICS effects, a hybrid simulation framework was developed, pairing Geant4-based modeling of gamma interactions with custom light transport and readout model. The simulations reproduce characteristic structures observed in experimental data, including patterns in floodmaps and energy-dependent light spread distributions. Based on these results, a light-pattern-based metric was introduced to identify ICS events using an energy-dependent threshold derived from single-interaction event distributions. This approach indicates that 32.9 ± 5.5% of events per crystal are affected by ICS and assigned to a non-optimal crystal, including mis-assignment between layers. Reassignment of these events to the most likely interaction crystal increased effective sensitivity by 4.1% and improved energy resolution from 10.6 ± 1.8% to 10.2 ± 1.8% FWHM. These results demonstrate that ICS as major effect in finely pixelated, DOI-capable detectors and that its identification and partial correction is feasible under highly multiplexed readout conditions.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 30Poster Number:MIC-15-030] Characterization of a multiplexed SiPM readout with free-running ADC for BGO PET detectors (#2466)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Belcari (Autores: N. Belcari , M. Morrocchi , G. Sportelli)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Pisa, Department of Physics "E. Fermi", Pisa, Italy [2] INFN - Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Pisa, Pisa, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present a modular FPGA-based data acquisition and real-time processing architecture for SiPM-based PET detectors, developed in the context of compact, low-cost PET imaging. The system combines a multiplexed readout of a SiPM array with free-running high-speed ADCs and on-chip FPGA processing to extract event energy, timestamp, and interaction position in real time. The approach emphasizes compactness, scalability, and low-latency operation, while reducing channel count and system complexity. First measurements demonstrate correct operation and clear crystal identification in flood maps, highlighting both the potential and current limitations of SiPM multiplexing, such as the limited CTR. This work aims to enable cost-efficient, flexible, and scalable PET imaging systems.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 36Poster Number:MIC-15-036] Evaluating a novel type of silicon photomultiplier for X-ray photon-counting CT applications (#2659)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Schröder (Autores: L. Schröder , M. Snoeyink , D. R. Schaart)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Delft University of Technology, Radiation Science & Technology, Delft, Netherlands
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Photon-counting computed tomography (PCCT) is a rapidly emerging (medical) imaging technology. PCCT commonly relies on finely pixelated room-temperature semiconductor detectors (RTSD). Scintillation detectors have long been considered too slow to handle the high X-ray fluence rates encountered in clinical PCCT. However, the fast signals provided by modern scintillators and silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) allow us to reconsider this paradigm. SiPM-based scintillation detectors offer excellent image quality and are known to operate reliably in clinical time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET) scanners. Recent research indicates that the combination of ultrafast SiPMs and scintillators could potentially provide a robust, scalable, and affordable X-ray photon-counting detector (PCD) technology. Here, we evaluate a novel type of silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) for this application. The SiPM is based on small (< 15 m) single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs), which have an innovative design that enables a fast recharge time (< 7 ns) as well as a high geometric efficiency (fill factor), resulting in high photodetection efficiency (PDE) (~ 50%) over a broad wavelength range. These benefits can be exploited to mitigate the classical trade-off between dynamic range and PDE, which is of high interest for X-ray photon-counting applications. We perform experiments with different design variations of the new SiPM, coupled to small pixels of commercially available scintillators (e.g. LYSO:Ce, LaBr3:Ce). We report on the pulse shape, count-rate capability, and spectral performance achieved with different combinations of SPAD design and scintillator.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 39Poster Number:MIC-15-039] Ultra-High-Definition, 8 µm pitch, Low-Dose X-ray Detector for Microfocus Clinical Applications: From Dental to Medical Imaging (#2814)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Sannino, M. Sannino (Autores: M. Sannino , M. Sannino , R. A.D. Turchetta , D. Uzbelger Feldman , A. Bofill-Petit , E. Simons , R. Raible)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] IMASENIC SL, Barcelona, Spain [2] Real Time Imaging Technologies, LLC, Charlotte, North Carolina, United States of America [3] Blur Product Development, Cary, North Carolina, United States of America [4] University of Virginia Health Science Center, Charlottesville, Virginia, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present the design and characterization of a 11.6 million pixel, 8 µm pitch, low noise (1.5 e rms), high dynamic range (93.5 dB), backside-illuminated (BSI) CMOS image sensor with microlenses (M) coupled to a scintillator for X-ray detection. Characterisation with a microfocus X-ray source shows high MTF, in excess of 30-line pairs per mm (lp/mm), while operating at an air kerma of 20.9 mGy per image.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 42Poster Number:MIC-15-042] Dual-Ended Readout PET Detector Based on Semi-Monolithic Laser-Engraved Scintillators (#2831)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 V. Sánchez-Tembleque (Autores: V. Sánchez-Tembleque , L. J. Algarra , L. Batres , D. Perez-Benito , D. Izquierdo-Garcia , J. J. Vaquero)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidad Carlos III, Biomedial science and engineering lab, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents the development of a semi-monolithic laser-engraved PET detector with dual-ended readout for continuous Depth of Interaction (DOI) estimation. The detector is based on a monolithic LYSO scintillator structured using Subsurface Laser Engraving (SSLE) techniques, enabling controlled light sharing between neighboring pixels while pre-serving the simpler readout and calibration typically associated with pixelated detectors, together with the accurate interaction vertex determination characteristic of monolithic designs. The main objective of this work is to determine the optimal placement of a reduced number of photodetectors in order to maximize DOI performance while minimizing the system's complexity. The study is based on the direct experimental measurement of light sharing inside the scintillator crystal. For this purpose, two 61- channel SiPM matrices are coupled to both faces of a LYSO scintillator matrix featuring a honeycomb laser-engraved pattern of 181 crystals. Taking advantage of the fact that the existing electronics can process up to 64 channels, the light distribution measured on one side of the detector is combined with the signal collected by only three selected photodetectors on the opposite side to estimate the DOI and evaluate different configurations for these additional channels. Using fully instrumented matrices on both faces allows the evaluation of different three-SiPM configurations and provides a detailed understanding of scin-tillation light-sharing behavior. The proposed approach aims to identify compact dual-ended configurations capable of achieving continuous DOI estimation with reduced readout complexity for future high-resolution PET detectors.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 45Poster Number:MIC-15-045] PETVision: An Ultra-High TOF Resolution PET System with 2.5D Modular Flat-Panel Detectors (#3008)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Zhuo (Autores: Y. Zhuo , T. Marin , D. Gascon , A. Gola , J.M. Benlloch Baviera , D. Sanchez Gonzalo , R. Ballabriga Sune , W. Weber , J. Barberá Ballester , G. Bergamin , J.V. Catret Mascarell , R. Dolenec , J.M. Fernández-Tenllado , L. Garrido , K. Grogg , I. Hany , P. Kachru , S. Korpar , P. Križan , M. Leban , S. Majewski , J. Mauricio , D. Mazzanti , S. Merzi , L. Moliner Martinez , T. Mulnix , Y. Najmaoui , S. Nekolla , M. Orehar , G. Palu , L. Parellada Monreal , G. Paternoster , N. Pavon Hernandez , M. Penna , S. Portero , I. Rauscher , G. Razdevšek , M. Ribalda , A. Sanuy , A. Seljak , A. Studen , O. de la Torre Perez , C. A. Trippl , M. Viqueira Rodriguez , D. Žontar , R. Pestotnik , G. El Fakhri)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yale University, Yale Biomedical Imaging Institute (YBII) at Yale School of Medicine, New Haven, Connecticut, United States of America [2] University of Barcelona (IEEC-UB), Dept. Física Quàntica i Astrofísica, Institut de Ciències Del Cosmos (ICCUB), Barcelona, Spain [3] Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK), Povo TN, Italy [4] Instituto de Instrumentación Para Imagen Molecular (CSIC-UPV), Valencia, Spain [5] Oncovision, Valencia, Spain [6] CERN, Geneva, Switzerland [7] Technical University of Munich (TUM-MED), Munich, Germany [8] Jožef Stefan Institute, Ljubljana, Slovenia [9] University of Ljubljana, Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, Ljubljana, Slovenia [10] University of Maribor, Faculty of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Maribor, Slovenia [11] University of California Davis, Davis, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We report updates on the development and current progress of PETVision, a modular flat-panel positron emission tomography (PET) system designed to achieve ultra-high Time-of-Flight (TOF) resolution. Traditional cylindrical PET scanners often face limitations due to high crystal volume costs and geometries that restrict simultaneous medical intervention. By leveraging unprecedented Coincidence Time Resolution (CTR), the PETVision architecture enables limited-angle, flat-panel geometries that reduce material costs while maintaining high image resolution. The Photo-Detection Module (PDM) of the PET system is utilizing a 2.5D integration configuration, where Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) arrays and readout ASICs are coupled to opposite sides of a passive interposer. The sensing layer employs state-of-the-art NUV-HD-MT technology, featuring custom "glass-less" Through Silicon Vias (TSVs) to achieve a Photon Detection Efficiency (PDE) of up to 65% and a Single Photon Time Resolution (SPTR) with Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) as low as 20 ps. Readout electronics development is proceeding in two stages: an initial 32-channel FastIC+ BGA chiplet demonstrating a CTR of (85±1) ps FWHM with 2×2×3 mm3 LYSO:Ce:0.2%Ca scintillator crystals. This is followed by the 64-channel Positron Emission Tomography Integrated Circuit (PoETIC) ASIC, which targets an electronics jitter contribution below 12 ps r.m.s. to support the 10-picosecond challenge. This modular approach aims to provide a high-performance, cost-effective PET imaging system suitable for diverse clinical and research applications, including simultaneous PET/intervention procedures.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 48Poster Number:MIC-15-048] Comparative Evaluation of NUV-MT and NUV-DJ SiPM Timing Performance for TOF-PET Detector Application (#3213)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Choi (Autores: S. Choi , H.S. Shim , G.B. Ko)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Department of Nuclear and Quantum Engineering, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [2] Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Mechanical Engineering Research Institute, Daejeon, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Recently developed Broadcom NUV-DJ SiPMs have improved photon detection efficiency (PDE) by placing the high-field region deeper than that of NUV-MT SiPMs. PDE is one of the major factors affecting coincidence timing resolution (CTR), and its performance varies depending on the scintillation light wavelength. Therefore, this study comparatively evaluated the CTR performance of LYSO:Ce, GAGG:Ce, and BGO scintillators, which have different peak emission wavelengths, coupled with NUV-MT and NUV-DJ SiPMs. The detectors consisted of 6 × 6 mm² NUV-MT and NUV-DJ SiPMs coupled with 3 × 3 × 20 mm³ LYSO:Ce and GAGG:Ce crystals and 3 × 3 × 3 mm³ BGO crystals using optical grease. Timing and energy signals were processed using a high-frequency (HF) readout board and acquired using an oscilloscope. CTR measurements were performed as a function of overvoltage for each detector. In addition, quartile-based rise-time analysis was conducted for the BGO detectors to investigate the effect of prompt Cherenkov photon detection on timing performance as indirect indicators. The detectors coupled with NUV-MT SiPMs achieved CTRs of 109.0 ps (LYSO:Ce), 182.8 ps (GAGG:Ce), and 210.8 ps (BGO) at an overvoltage of 12 V, whereas those coupled with NUV-DJ SiPMs achieved CTRs of 103.0 ps (LYSO:Ce), 172.4 ps (GAGG:Ce), and 187.2 ps (BGO), respectively. Compared with the NUV-MT SiPMs, the NUV-DJ SiPMs improved CTR by 5.2%, 4.5%, and 11.2% for LYSO:Ce, GAGG:Ce, and BGO, respectively. The quartile analysis further showed improved timing performance for fast rise-time events when using the NUV-DJ SiPMs. These results indicate that the improved PDE of the NUV-DJ SiPM enhances prompt photon detection and contributes to improved CTR performance for BGO scintillators. Therefore, the proposed detector configuration may be beneficial for future TOF-PET and BGO-based timing detector applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 51Poster Number:MIC-15-051] Decomposing Optical Photon Transport in PET Detectors: Geometric Priors and Generative Models of Residual Stochasticity (#1379)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Naunheim (Autores: S. Naunheim , N. Kratochwil , E. Melton , B. Pardi , E. Roncali)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California, Davis, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America [2] University of California, Davis, Department of Computer Science, Davis, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Monte Carlo simulations of optical photon transport are the gold standard for modeling PET detectors, but their step-by-step nature makes large-scale optical systems computationally prohibitive. Generative models are an attractive alternative, and we previously demonstrated conditional generative adversarial networks for single crystals and crystal arrays, in which physics knowledge enters the model through architectural extensions and a physics-informed loss. In this work, we propose a fundamentally different way of incorporating physics. Instead of acting on the loss, prior physical information is injected directly into the conditioning pathway of the generative model. A lightweight, geometry-agnostic light transport estimator (GALTE) propagates photons through the segmented crystal geometry under a simplified physical model and produces a compact descriptor of the expected sensor-level light response. This descriptor replaces the bare emission coordinates as conditioning input, leaving the generative model to capture only the residual stochastic structure that the analytical prior cannot resolve. We instantiate the framework with a conditional GAN whose architecture and trainable parameter count matches the published OptiGAN baseline, so that observed differences can be attributed to the conditioning rather than to model capacity. On a 3×3 BGO array, the GALTE-conditioned model preserves the distributional fidelity of the OptiGAN baseline across the full crystal array while reproducing physically interpretable structures of the joint position-momentum distribution more closely, particularly in regimes of high reflection multiplicity. Most notably, the GALTE-conditioned model reaches its best performance after roughly one third of the training epochs required by the OptiGAN baseline. Physics-informed conditioning thus opens a path toward generative models that combine physical priors with machine learning.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 54Poster Number:MIC-15-054] Scaling TOF-PET Timing Calibration via Structured Detector-Wise Learning (#1493)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Thull (Autores: J. Thull , Y. Kuhl , T. Meyer , M. Henning , B. Weissler , D. Schug , V. Schulz)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] RWTH Aachen University, Institute of Imaging and Computer Vision, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [2] Hyperion Hybrid Imaging Systems GmbH, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Time-of-flight positron emission tomography (PET) timing calibration is especially challenging for light-sharing detectors, where biases arise from interaction-dependent light transport, silicon photomultiplier response, and effects of readout electronics. Conventional skew and walk corrections are robust but leave high-dimensional event signatures underused. We introduce an in-system approach that learns detector-wise corrections from coincidence data without requiring pair-specific models. A shared network conditioned by detector embeddings estimates single-interaction offsets from singles observables, yielding a structured model with linearly scaling detector-specific parameters. We evaluate the method on two prototype PET systems: a 24-module semi-monolithic detector scanner and a 28-module multi-layer segmented-crystal detector scanner. For both, data were acquired at 450 randomized 22Na point-source positions and split by source position for fivefold cross-validation. We studied a residual multilayer perceptron, a geometry-aware transformer, and a lightweight edge multilayer perceptron. Across scanners and energy windows, learned models improved coincidence timing resolution over time-skew and time-walk correction. The residual multilayer perceptron achieved the best timing resolutions, reaching 431ps and 382ps for scanners 1 and 2. Transformer and edge variants performed similarly with smaller models and generalized to detector pairs excluded during training. Feature ablation identified light spread as the dominant auxiliary cue, with local position and energy adding further improvements. These results establish detector-wise learning as a practical route to scalable timing calibration for PET systems with complex light-sharing detector topologies.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 57Poster Number:MIC-15-057] GPU-Accelerated Monte Carlo Simulation for SPECT Imaging (#1616)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Zhou (Autores: F. Zhou , Z. Liu , Y. Li , B. Gao , S. Tang , C. Sun , L. He)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] United Imaging Healthcare, Shang hai, China [2] United Imaging Healthcare North America, Houston, Texas, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Monte Carlo simulation (MCS) is essential for PET and SPECT system modeling and optimization. However, existing CPU-based toolkits such as GATE and Geant4 remain too slow for iterative system design. We present a GPU-accelerated SPECT simulation module within the United-Imaging Healthcare (UIH) Molecular-imaging Innovation Platform (uMIP), extending its validated PET capability to single-photon imaging with native support for both multi-pinhole and parallel-hole collimator geometries. The key innovation is a closed-form analytic ray-aperture intersection algorithm for multi-pinhole collimators, which eliminates iterative geometric traversal and enables massively parallel GPU execution. Its speed is approximately 2~3 orders of magnitude faster than a CPU-based simulation toolkits. Quantitative validation against Geant4 demonstrates excellent agreement for both multi-pinhole and parallel-hole configurations: point-source projection profiles across six field-of-view positions yield NRMSE <0.80% and Pearson correlation >90%, while transmitted-photon spatial distributions and energy spectra show consistent results at both 140 keV and 440 keV. The proposed framework provides a practical, high-fidelity simulation platform for rapid SPECT collimator design and imaging protocol optimization.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 60Poster Number:MIC-15-060] Monte Carlo Validation of a Positron Emission Mammography Scanner Using GATE 9.4: Sensitivity Analysis with an Aluminum Sleeve Phantom (#1652)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. H. El-Sallabi (Autores: S. H. El-Sallabi , O. Bouhali , H. Fayad , A. Ghujeh , J. Ji)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Texas A&M University at Qatar, Electrical & Computer Engineering, Doha, Qatar [2] Hamad Medical Corportation, Occupational Health and Safety, Doha, Qatar [3] Hamad Bin Khalifa University, Electrical Engineering, Doha, Qatar [4] Texas A&M University, Electrical & Computer Engineering, College Station, Texas, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate Monte Carlo simulation of Positron Emission Mammography (PEM) scanners is essential for optimizing detector design, reconstruction algorithms, and dosimetry in dedicated breast imaging. This work presents a GATE 9.4 simulation of the Naviscan PEM scanner validated against clinical sensitivity measurements at Hamad Medical Corporation, Doha, Qatar. Scanner geometry was implemented from published specifications, with detector efficiency derived from LYSO crystal attenuation via the Beer-Lambert law (approximately 70% for 13 mm crystals, mu = 0.86 cm-1 at 511 keV). A cylindrical aluminum sleeve phantom in five configurations (zero to four 2.5 mm sleeves) was simulated using a 0.58 ns coincidence timing window and a 350-650 keV energy window, matching the hospital protocol. True coincidences were counted following clinical convention, including scattered events within the energy window. The base-case configuration achieved 96.8% agreement with hospital measurements. Mean agreement across all five configurations was 70.3%, with the correct exponential attenuation trend reproduced across increasing sleeve thicknesses. Systematic underestimation at higher attenuation is consistent with known GATE aluminum cross-section limitations and the absence of scatter recovery corrections. All parameters were derived from first principles without empirical tuning. Preliminary results demonstrate a rigorous, reproducible simulation framework for PEM, with complete validation to be presented at the conference.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 63Poster Number:MIC-15-063] Heuristic seeding for GA-based optimization of halbach magnets for PET-compatible low-field MRI (#1747)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M.S.H. Akram (Autores: M.S.H. Akram , F. Nishikido , M. Suga , T. Obata , T. Yamaya)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology (QST), Imaging Physics Group, Advance nuclear medicine science, Chiba, Japan [2] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology (QST), Applied MRI Research, Chiba, Japan [3] Chiba University, Center for Frontier Medical Engineering, Chiba, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This paper presents an optimization framework for Halbach magnet arrays targeting PET-compatible portable low-field MRI. Positioning an MRI system within existing PET rooms offers a practical alternative to PET-in-MRI inserts, as it simplifies compliance with radioisotope regulations. However, achieving high field uniformity in a 200-magnet Halbach array requires optimizing discrete rotation angles within an exponentially large search space. To address this, we developed a genetic algorithm (GA) utilizing adaptive mutation and dynamic elitism. To prevent premature convergence caused by rapid diversity loss in high-dimensional spaces, we investigated five population seeding strategies, including a novel Segmented Stochastic Progression (SSP) method using stratified complexity sampling. Performance was evaluated via fitness convergence and Hamming distance using progressive mutation step-size ranges (sigma = 6 to 1 and 10 to 1). Our results demonstrated that heuristic seeding maintained population diversity 1.3 to 2.6 times more effectively than random initialization. Specifically, the SSP method provided superior global search stability, yielding highly ordered magnetic flux streamlines across a 10 cm target region within a 20 cm diameter ring. Furthermore, mean time to solution (MTTS) remained consistent (0.94-1.00 relative to baseline), indicating the search quality was improved without increasing the computational overhead. This approach offers a robust, transferable methodology for complex electromagnetic design optimizations.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Atieh (Autores: M. Atieh , E. Durand , O. Kochebina)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Assistance publique - Hôpitaux de Paris (AP-HP), Department of Biophysics and Nuclear Medicine, Le Kremlin-Bicêtre, France [2] Université Paris-Saclay, BioMaps Laboratory, Service Service Hospitalier Frédéric Joliot, CEA, Orsay, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a GATE Monte Carlo model and its preliminary validation of the uMI Panorama 35™ PET system, which combines a 35 cm axial field-of-view with sub-200 ps time-of-flight performance. The model was validated for coincidence time resolution (CTR) and against NEMA NU 2-2018 measurements of sensitivity and noise equivalent count rate. The coincidence time resolution of 197 ps obtained with the model is comparable to 194 ps measured experimentally, and a system sensitivity of 21.0 versus 23.5 kcps/MBq. It also reproduced count-rate performance, with a peak noise equivalent count rate of 615 kcps at 43.7 kBq/mL, compared with 687 kcps at 43.2 kBq/mL experimentally. These results show the preliminary work on its validation and focuses mainly on the main counting performance characteristics of the scanner. Future work will extend validation to additional image tests, including spatial resolution and image quality.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 69Poster Number:MIC-15-069] Experimental and simulation-guided light-sharing characterization of hexagonal laser-engraved PET detectors. (#2003)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. N. Golhen Mateo (Autores: C. N. Golhen Mateo , M. Abushawish , P. Galve Lahoz , V. Sanchez-Tembleque , D. Pérez-Benito , L. Batres , L. J. Algarra , J. Udias , J.J. Vaquero)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Departamento de Estructura de la Materia, Física Térmica y Electrónica, Madrid, Spain [2] UC3M, Madrid, Spain [3] Spanish National Research Council (CSIC), Institute for Physical and Information Technologies "Leonardo Torres Quevedo", ITEFI, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract PET image quality depends on accurate identification of the gamma-ray interaction point. RETIMAGER proposes laser-engraved (LE) pixelated LYSO blocks, where inter-crystal transparency can be tuned through engraving density. This controlled light sharing can preserve crystal identification while providing XY position information. Previous GOSS optical simulations combined with artificial intelligence (AI) predicted the transparency range expected to optimize XY resolution for 1.25 mm pitch hexagonal crystals. Here, we extend this simulation-guided strategy to experimental data by analysing four LE matrices with different engraving densities and effective transparencies. For each event, the seven largest SiPM signals were used to characterize the light-sharing pattern. A χ² classifier was developed from reference patterns associated with the two main configurations imposed by the hexagonal geometry: crystals above one SiPM and crystals close to a vertex shared by three SiPMs. GOSS simulations with different transparency values were processed with the same procedure and used to select a representative configuration and define the ROI criterion for extracting the χ² reference distributions. This criterion was transferred to the experimental matrix, separating the expected 1-SiPM-like and 3-SiPM-like populations. These results show that simulation-guided light-sharing analysis supports classification of the experimental response and future application of AI-based XY identification to LE matrices, aiming to determine the transparency that maximizes detector performance and enables intracrystal positioning.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 72Poster Number:MIC-15-072] Microstructure-Informed Single-Grid Dark-Field X-ray Imaging for Breast Microcalcification Typing (#2061)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Choi (Autores: S. Choi , S. Park , J.-T. Kang , J. Yeon , J.-W. Jeong)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute, Materials and Components Research Division, Daejeon, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dark-field X-ray imaging (DFXI) measures ultra-small-angle scattering from sub-resolution density fluctuations and provides contrast complementary to attenuation mammography. We present a wave-optics simulation of a compact single-grid spatial-harmonic imaging (SHI) DFXI system for breast microcalcification typing, focusing on type-II hydroxyapatite (HAp) and type-I calcium oxalate dihydrate (COD). Instead of a generic monodisperse-sphere model, the simulation uses a calibrated γ ( ξ )-based microstructure interface: HAp is represented as a Gaussian-random-field medium, whereas COD is represented as a compact-crystal scatterer with weak surface-dominated dark-field response. For a 17.5 keV source, 20 μ m focal spot, 47 μ m grid period, and 2.0 m source-to-detector distance, the operating autocorrelation length is ξ G =249 nm. Simulations with simplified Bakic-style Voronoi backgrounds over BI-RADS A--D show that large HAp clusters remain detectable under anatomy-limited conditions and that the dark-field-to-absorption ratio, r =Δ I df /Δ(1- T ), separates HAp-like and COD-like clusters more robustly than either channel alone. These results support compact tabletop SHI-DFXI for specimen-level microcalcification characterization and surgical-margin assessment.

sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Hospital Clínic de Barcelona - IDIBAPS, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Barcelona, Spain [2] University of Santiago de Compostela, Center for Research in Molecular Medicine and Chronic Diseases (CiMUS), Santiago de Compostela, Spain [3] University Medical Center Groningen, Department of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging, Groningen, Netherlands [4] University of Washington Medical Center, Department of Radiology, Seattle, Washington, United States of America [5] University College London, Institute of Nuclear Medicine, London, United Kingdom [6] University Hospital Tuebingen, Department of Nuclear Medicine and Clinical Molecular Imaging, Tuebingen, Germany [7] Eberhard Karls University Tuebingen, Werner Siemens Imaging Center, Department of Preclinical Imaging and Radiopharmacy, Tuebingen, Germany [8] Eberhard Karls University Tuebingen, Institute for Astronomy and Astrophysics, Tuebingen, Germany [9] Instituto de Salud Carlos III, Biomedical Research Networking Center of Bioengineering, Biomaterials and Nanomedicine (CIBER-BBN), Barcelona, Spain [10] University of Barcelona, Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences, Biophysics and Bioengineering Unit, Barcelona, Spain [11] Instituto de Salud Carlos III, Reina Sofía Alzheimer Centre, CIEN Foundation, Madrid, Spain [12] Instituto de Salud Carlos III, Biomedical Research Networking Center on Neurodegenerative Diseases (CIBERNED), Santiago de Compostela, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Total Body Positron Emission Tomography (TBPET) scanners offer a substantial sensitivity increase compared to traditional scanners, leading to lower doses or acquisition times. In parallel, interest in modelling such tomographs through Monte Carlo simulations has raised. In this work, a faster framework to simulate TBPET scans is presented by modelling the Siemens Biograph Vision Quadra scanner. SimPET platform is used for simulation, which combines the use of SimSET and STIR. To assess its performance, spatial resolution, sensitivity and image quality NEMA tests were run. Spatial resolution shows reasonable agreement, with an average deviation of 0.6 mm. Although our model overestimates the experimental sensitivity, as expected for a simple cylinder model, a calibration factor is proposed. Concerning image quality, recovery coefficients align with experimental data, while background variability is higher due to reduced maximum ring difference. To sum up, our approach represents a faster alternative (projected x40 speed-up), which could make feasible the large-scale databases simulation when fully adjusted and optimized.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 78Poster Number:MIC-15-078] Performance Comparison of Low-Multiplexing and High-Multiplexing Multi-Pinhole Collimators for a Large-Animal Cardiac SPECT System (#2308)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Yan (Autores: J. Yan , D. Zhang , W. Duan , S. Wang , Z. Wu , H. Liu , Y. Liu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Large-animal preclinical studies are essential for translating cardiovascular imaging technologies toward clinical applications; however, dedicated SPECT systems optimized for large-animal cardiac imaging remain limited. In this study, we propose a full-ring large-animal cardiac SPECT system composed of six detector heads and investigate the impact of multi-pinhole multiplexing on system performance. Two collimator configurations are compared: a low-multiplexing reference design with 6 pinholes per plate and a high-multiplexing system with 36 pinholes per plate. The 36-pinhole configuration is generated using a Halton sequence, serving as a specific high-multiplexing representative rather than an optimized arrangement. System performance is evaluated using sensitivity maps and multiple digital phantoms, including a Defrise disk phantom for axial sampling assessment, a Derenzo phantom for spatial resolution evaluation, and a hot-sphere phantom for contrast analysis. All studies employ analytic projection and the Maximum Likelihood Expectation Maximization reconstruction. Results demonstrate that the high-multiplexing system achieves a higher peak sensitivity (2.04 × 10⁻³ vs. 3.87 × 10⁻⁴), improved hot‑rod resolution (3.5 mm clearly resolved vs. 4.5 mm marginally resolved), and a smaller detectable hot‑sphere diameter (4 mm vs. 5 mm). In conclusion, high-multiplexing multi-pinhole design may benefit spatial resolution and detectability in stationary SPECT systems, although projection-overlap-induced artifacts must be carefully managed.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 81Poster Number:MIC-15-081] Is 20 mm Still Optimal? Revisiting Scintillator Length in Modern TOF-PET Systems (#2332)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Furuta (Autores: M. Furuta , H.G. Kang , H. Tashima , G. Akamatsu , T. Yamaya)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology (QST), Institutes for Quantum Medical Sciences, Chiba, Japan [2] Chiba University, Faculty of Engineering, Chiba, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Scintillator length of 20 mm has been considered a standard in positron emission tomography (PET); however, recent advances in time-of-flight (TOF) performance necessitate a re-evaluation of this assumption. While shorter scintillators improve coincidence timing resolution (CTR) at the expense of detection efficiency, enhanced TOF information may compensate for this loss in terms of image quality. In this work, we experimentally investigated the effects of crystal thickness on CTR and performed simulations of a clinical PET scanner to evaluate image quality. We used fast-LGSO crystals with a cross section of 4 × 4 mm2 and varying lengths, each coupled to a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM; Hamamatsu Photonics) that had an effective area of 4.0 × 4.0 mm². The timing and energy signals of the SiPM were extracted using a custom-made high frequency readout circuit and digitized with a CAMAC digitizer. The measured CTRs of 10 mm, 15 mm, and 20 mm fast-LGSO crystals were 121 ps, 129 ps and 134 ps, respectively. Based on the experimental results, we investigated the effects of crystal thickness on the image quality of a clinical PET scanner (ring diameter= 675 mm, axial coverage= 158 mm) by Geant4 simulation. Image quality was evaluated using an IQ phantom based on the NEMA NU 2 standard, and metrics including contrast recovery and background variability. Among the three crystal thicknesses, the 20 mm thickness provided the highest contrast while keeping the background variability. At this stage, we have concluded that longer scintillators appear to provide better image quality. We are still investigating the performance of even longer lengths such as 25 mm and 30 mm, and their performance will be discussed at the conference.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 84Poster Number:MIC-15-084] Comparison Between GATE and SimSET Monte Carlo Simulations on GE Omni Legend PET scanner geometry (#2495)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. ZamanPour (Autores: S. ZamanPour , A. Reeves , S. Noe , A. Rezaei , J. Nuyts , K. Thielemans , G. Schramm)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] KU Leuven, Department of Imaging and Pathology, Leuven, Belgium [2] University College London, Department of Medical Physics and Biomedical Engineering, London, United Kingdom [3] University College London, Institute of Nuclear Medicine and the Hawkes Institute, London, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Monte Carlo (MC) methods are powerful tools for simulating physical processing such as estimating in positron emission tomography (PET) scattered and true coincidences in PET, with GATE considered the gold standard. However, the high computational costs can limit its clinical applicability. SimSET offers a substantially faster alternative while retaining the key photon-interaction physics required for accurate PET simulation. In this work, we present a systematic concordance study between SimSET and GATE for the GE Omni Legend PET scanner geometry. The two simulators are compared across four metrics: sensitivity sinograms for the true coincidences, 2D energy spectra, trues-only reconstructed images, and scatter fraction, using a uniform cylinder and a realistic [18F]PE2I brain phantom as test cases. Strong agreement was observed across all metrics, with scatter fractions differing by less than 0.03 percentage points (25.65% vs. 25.63%). SimSET was found to be approximately ~59x times faster than GATE for almost equivalent simulation conditions. These results demonstrate that SimSET reproduces GATE outputs with high fidelity on this state-of-the-art scanner geometry, establishing it as an efficient and accurate platform for MC-based scatter estimation in clinical PET imaging workflows.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 87Poster Number:MIC-15-087] Hybrid Least-Square and k-Nearest-Neighbour Event Positioning for a Compact Gamma Camera with Monolithic NaI(Tl) Scintillator (#2718)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Wu (Autores: X. Zhang , Y. Qi , A. Fabbri , V. O. Cencelli , H. Zou , J. Zheng , Q. Du , Z. Wu , B. M.W. Tsui)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Suzhou Institute of Biomedical Engineering and Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Department of Medical Imaging, Suzhou, China [2] University of Wollongong, Centre for Medical Radiation Physics, Wollongong, Australia [3] I.N.F.N, Roma, Italy [4] Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing University, Medical School, Suzhou, China [5] Johns Hopkins University, Department of Radiology, Baltimore, Maryland, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The purpose of this study is to develop an accurate event positioning algorithm for a compact scintillation camera to enhance its intrinsic resolution and useful field-of-view (FOV). The compact camera consists of a 50×50×7mm 3 continuous NaI(Tl) crystal directly coupled to a Hamamatsu H12700 position-sensitive photomultiplier tube (PSPMT) with an 8×8 multi-anode readout array. Two kinds of reference libraries of detector responses for event positioning were built by analytical model of scintillation light distribution in a monolithic crystal and GENT4-based GATE Monte Carlo (MC) simulation, respectively. Each entry of the discrete grids-based library contains a detector response distribution corresponding to a known interaction position in crystal volume. Then a hybrid event positioning framework combining least-square estimation (LSE) and k-nearest-neighbour (k-NN) was developed and experimentally validated using Tc-99m flood sources. Preliminary test results show that the proposed hybrid event positioning method with MC simulation-based reference library exhibits good positioning linearity and edge-event positioning accuracy to enhance detector's spatial resolution and useful FOV as compared to the conventional centroid positioning method. Experimental results also demonstrate that the hybrid algorithm provides robust and computationally efficient event positioning. In conclusion, the approach combing hybrid algorithm with MC simulation-based reference library offers a practical and accurate solution for next-generation monolithic gamma-camera systems requiring high throughput and high intrinsic resolution. Further experimental evaluations are continued under investigations.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 90Poster Number:MIC-15-090] Ultra-fast Positron Range Simulator for Patient-Specific PET Imaging (#2851)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R.J. Paneque-Yunta (Autores: R.J. Paneque-Yunta , N. Encina-Baranda , J.L. Herraiz , K.M. Abushab , J.M. Udias , P. Ibañez)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Complutense University of Madrid (UCM), Nuclear Physics Group and IPARCOS, Madrid, Spain [2] Instituto de Investigación Sanitaria Hospital Clínico San Carlos (IdISSC), Nuclear Techniques and Instrumentation in Biomedicine, Madrid, Spain [3] Al-Azhar University-Gaza, Medical Physics, Gaza, State of Palestine
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positron range (PR) degrades spatial resolution in positron emission tomography (PET), with its efect being radionuclide- and medium-dependent. Current accurate PR simulators are computationally intensive and cannot be used in clinical applications. This work presents the Hybrid Monte Carlo (HMC) PR simulator, a GPU-accelerated condensed-history code in CUDA Fortran for 3D annihilation imaging in heterogeneous voxelized geometries derived from CT images and μ-maps. Pre-computed interaction tables covering 24 reference-tissue materials and support for arbitrary β + emitters up to 3.55 MeV end-point energies ( 68 Ga, 82 Rb, etc.) allow both GPU and CPU implementations. Maximum speeds reach 4.77·10 5 (Intel Core i9-14900KF) and 3.32·10 8 (NVIDIA GeForece RTX 5080) histories/s, surpassing prior CPU-only PR simulators by up to 4 orders of magnitude. Close agreement with PenEasy 2024 is demonstrated: point-source simulations reach FWHM residuals are below 0.1 mm at 10 7 histories, and voxelwise R 2 =0.982 and PSNR≈30.8 dB are achieved in a realistic myocardium phantom while decreasing the simulation time from 6 hours to 1 second (using HMC GPU). The resulting annihilation maps enable PET resolution modeling and patient-specific PR correction within clinically practical time frames.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 93Poster Number:MIC-15-093] Analytic Determination of Minkhole Collimator Sensitivity With Penetration (#3082)
sub_talks.speaker: Y. Li
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] United Imaging Healthcare North America, MI, Houston, Texas, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Multi-pinhole collimation in single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) trades aperture penetration against sensitivity and spatial resolution. Closed-form analytic sensitivities with penetration are known for the circular pinhole and the rectangular pinhole (recthole), but not for the recently introduced minkhole: a Minkowski-sum aperture lofting a circular waist into a rectangular exit. We close that gap with three knife-edge closed forms—an Anger three-term penetration expansion, an exact on-axis Stieltjes form in elementary moment integrals, and a Stieltjes-corrected hybrid—anchored to a two-dimensional level-set integral as the point-source-exact reference. The three-term expansion shares the universal penetration-order scaling of the circular-pinhole and recthole results; the minkhole’s first-order coefficient carries a disk-rectangle Steiner cross-term that vanishes at the recthole limit and is structurally absent from the cylindrical circular pinhole. The on-axis Stieltjes route recovers the Metzler–Moore recthole closed form term-by-term as the waist radius vanishes. Validation against a three-dimensional ray-tracing reference on a 12-panel benchmark grid gives worst relative errors of 1.01% (Anger), 0.69% (hybrid), and 0.39% (level-set exact). The hybrid enables sub-millisecond sensitivity evaluation for minkhole-based SPECT system-matrix construction.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 99Poster Number:MIC-15-099] Performance evaluation of Compton-PET with MACACO-PET system (#2666)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Parashari (Autores: S. Parashari , K. Brzezinski , L. Barrientos , N. Castellanos , F. Hueso-González , A. Ros , J. Roser , M. Rafecas , G. Llosa)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto de Fisica Corpuscular (IFIC) CSIC-UV, Valencia, Spain [2] University of Luebeck, Institute of Medical Engineering, Luebeck, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Integration of Compton cameras (CC) with PET can be advantageous for multitracer imaging and to improve the resolution for simultaneous β + -γ emitters. This technology is showing potential to become a viable option. The combination of PET and SPECT faces challenges due to collimation in SPECT and poor performance at high photon energies. CCs overcome this limitation and are more suitable for high-energy and multiple gamma emitting radiotracers. The IRIS group of IFIC (Valencia) has shown via simulations that combined CC and PET imaging of a Derenzo-like phantom with 89 Zr, 124 I, and both 18 F and 95 Tc is feasible, demonstrating the ability of Compton-PET to image multiple radionuclides. In continuation of this work, a performance evaluation of an experimental Compton-PET prototype is ongoing. An identical geometry is also studied through GATE simulations. The geometry consists of four identical detectors, of which two are combined as a CC and the other two are placed as PET detectors facing each other at either side of the geometrical center of the system. Image reconstruction is performed using a custom algorithm developed by the IRIS group. We present reconstructed images of a 22 Na source array obtained with the simulated Compton-PET system. Successful imaging results pave the way for subsequent laboratory testing of the Compton-PET system, enabling simultaneous β + -γ and multitracer radionuclide imaging.
