sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 102Poster Number:MIC-15-102] Dosimetry Assessment and Noise Scaling Laws in Proton Computed Tomography (#2724)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Bruzzi (Autores: C. Civinini , A. Falivene , L. Noferini , F. Rossi , M. Scaringella , A. Taddeucci , F. Tommasino , E. Verroi , M. Bruzzi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] INFN - Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Firenze, Sesto Fiorentino (FI), Italy [2] A.O.U. Careggi, U.O. Fisica Sanitaria, Firenze, Italy [3] USL Toscana Centro, SOC Fisica Sanitaria Firenze ed Empoli, Firenze, Italy [4] University of Trento, Department of Physics, Trento, Italy [5] INFN - Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, TIFPA, Povo (TN), Italy [6] University of Florence, Department of Physics and Astronomy, Sesto Fiorentino (FI), Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Proton Computed Tomography (pCT) is an emerging imaging modality designed to reduce uncertainties in proton therapy planning by directly mapping the Relative Stopping Power (RSP) of tissues. This study provides a comprehensive performance evaluation of the INFN pCT prototype, focusing on experimental dosimetric characterization and the determination of noise scaling laws. Utilizing a silicon tracker and a YAG:Ce calorimeter, measurements were conducted at the APSS Trento center with a 211.2 MeV proton beam. Dosimetry performed with TLD-100 thermoluminescent dosimeters revealed an absorbed dose of 1.4-1.5 mGy per10 8 trigger events, resulting in a total dose of 11.6 mGy for a high-quality 9-rotation scan. The investigation into image noise demonstrated that the system operates in a purely statistical regime, with the standard deviation of RSP following the inverse square root of the product of dose and voxel volume. No significant additive noise floor was detected. Analysis identified a 1 mm³ voxel volume as an optimal benchmark, constrained by Multiple Coulomb Scattering physical limits. At this resolution, measured noise levels ranged from 0.3% to 0.7%, significantly outperforming the 1% clinical requirement. These results validate the system's ability to provide high-accuracy RSP maps at low patient doses.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 105Poster Number:MIC-15-105] Feasibility of 511 keV photon detection in the presence of scattered x-rays for simultaneous PET and CT imaging (#2946)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. E. Kinahan (Autores: C. Hayward , C. Rabin , W. Hunter , R. Miyaoka , I. Sechopoulos , P. E. Kinahan)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Washington, Department of Radiology, Seattle, Washington, United States of America [2] Instituto de Física, Universidad de la República, Montevideo, Uruguay [3] Department of Medical Imaging, Radboud University Medical Center, Nijmegen, Netherlands
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In PET/CT scanners the x-ray source is turned off during the PET acquisition for several reasons, including preventing saturation of the PET detectors due to pulse pile-up from lower-energy scattered x-rays. We conducted simulation and experimental studies to evaluate if there are operating conditions where simultaneous PET and CT imaging is feasible. Simulation studies were used to estimate the flux and energy distribution of scattered x-rays for a dedicated breast PET/CT scanner using a tungsten x-ray tube operated at 65 kVp. The x-ray tube spectrum was used for tracking of x-rays scattered at roughly 90 deg into a PET detector. We also evaluated using metal filters in front of the PET detector to preferentially absorb the lower energy scattered x-rays. We then conducted experimental studies of 511 keV photon detection by a LYSO scintillator in the presence of scattered x-rays. The x rays were generated from a mammography scanner operated at 49 kVp. The scattering object was a water phantom in the mammography field of view. The PET detector was located at 90 deg to the x-ray beam direction. The outputs were evaluated in terms of timing and energy spectra. The simulation studies indicated that for the CT and PET scanner geometry, the scattered x-ray flux was overall reduced by 90 %. The addition of 1 mm of Ag or Cu in front of the PET detector reduced the flux of scattered x-rays incident on the PET detector by 99.5% or 96.5%, while reducing the flux of 511 keV photons by only 9% or 16%. The experimental studies demonstrated the expected dominance of the scattered x-rays on the PET detector output. The use of 1 mm of Cu filtration restored the photopeak signal, except for the predicted 16% loss. Both simulations and experimental studies indicate that simultaneous PET and x-ray imaging may be possible under certain conditions of x-ray tube technique, scanner geometry, and pre-detector PET filtration.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 108Poster Number:MIC-15-108] Integrating X-ray Dark-Field and Fluorescence Modalities for Molecular Imaging in Personalized Medicine: Initial Specifications of Setup Design and Integration Parameters (#3110)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 X. Yan (Autores: K. Kumar , X. Yan , X. Yan , M. Abboush , M. Abboush , C. Riani , C. Riani , C. Hoeschen , C. Hoeschen)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg, Institute for medical technology, Chair of Medical Systems Technology, Magdeburg, Saxony-Anhalt, Germany [2] University of Pavia, Department of Physics "A. Volta",, Pavia, Italy, Italy [3] University of Pavia, Department of Physics "A. Volta",, Pavia, Italy, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract As innovative imaging tools, both X-ray dark-field and X-ray fluorescence imaging show significant potential for medical applications. However, each modality has technical trade-offs that can limit its effectiveness when used in isolation. While molecular imaging plays a crucial role in modern diagnostics by enabling early detection and personalized therapy, existing in vivo methods often suffer from low sensitivity, limited resolution, or high ionizing radiation exposure. To address these challenges, this proof-of-principle study proposes a hybrid approach leveraging the synergistic advantages of X-ray dark-field imaging (DFI) and X-ray fluorescence (XRF) imaging. DFI-characterized by high sensitivity to micro-level structural abnormalities at a low radiation dose-is utilized to identify targeted regions of interest (ROIs), thereby overcoming the inherent resolution and dose constraints of XRF. By confining XRF scans exclusively to DFI-guided ROIs, the distribution of molecular nanoprobes (nanoparticles) can be mapped with high precision. This approach ensures that the high radiation doses typical of body-wide nuclear imaging are restricted to localized areas, significantly enhancing patient safety. In this work, specifications for both modalities were investigated via simulations and experiments to establish optimal integration parameters. Subsequently, a CAD model was developed and implemented to assemble the final integrated setup.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 111Poster Number:MIC-15-111] A Dual-Head Positron Imaging System (#1322)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Streun (Autores: M. Streun , A. Chlubek , R. Koller , R. Metzner , D. Pflugfelder , B. Scherer , N. Schramm , P. Wüstner , E. Zimmermann , G. Natour)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Forschungszentrum Jülich GmbH, Institute of Technology and Engineering (ITE), Jülich, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [2] Forschungszentrum Jülich GmbH, Institute of Bio- and Geosciences (IBG-2), Jülich, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In this paper we will introduce a system for two-dimensional imaging of positron emission. It has been developed for the investigation of plant roots grown in rhizotrones. A rhizotron is a narrow, transparent flower pot that forces the roots to grow in a virtually two-dimensional manner. For this reason, a 3D reconstruction, as done in a PET scanner, is not necessary, and for a 2D projection two opposing planar detector heads are sufficient. The heads cover an area of 134x134 mm 2 and each contains 4096 LYSO scintillation crystals of 1.85x1.85x10 mm 3 each. Digital Silicon Photomultipliers (Philips DPC) detect the scintillation events which are stored as list mode data on disk and are already used to instantly visualize an online image of the activity distribution. We will present first images and characterize the system based on evaluation measurements.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 114Poster Number:MIC-15-114] Development of the CT extension of the MERMAID PET prototype (#1586)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Kantorek (Autores: R. Kantorek , S. Seeger , M. Rafecas)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Luebeck, Institute of Medical Engineering, Lübeck, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany [2] University of Luebeck, Isotope Laboratory of the Natural Science Section, Lübeck, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Zebrafish play an important role in biomedical research as a key vertebrate model for disease studies and drug screening; however, PET imaging has not yet been translated to this animal model. To fill this gap, the PET prototype MERMAID has been specifically conceived for imaging adult zebrafish and other small aquatic animals. Initial studies have proven the feasibility of the concept, as well as the need for anatomical reference information. For the latter, we are developing a cone beam CT system to be integrated into MERMAID. Challenges are the low soft tissue contrast in zebrafish and its small thickness, the attenuation of the water-filled imaging chamber, and potentially high radiation doses for the target animal. Although synchrotron radiation and contrast agents have both proved successful in providing high resolution and contrast zebrafish CT images, neither is suitable for our case, nor phase-contrast CT imaging techniques. The current CT setup consists of a cesium iodide flat panel detector and a handheld x-ray tube with a tungsten filament. For image reconstruction simultaneous algebraic reconstruction technique (SART) adapted from the reconstruction toolkit (RTK) is used. This setup allows a resolution smaller than 0.4 mm. We have successfully imaged several characterization phantoms as well as adult zebrafish ex-vivo, allowing visualization of the skeleton and small soft tissue changes in both air and water. Further work will include image registration, soft-tissue contrast enhancement, and integration with the PET component.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 117Poster Number:MIC-15-117] Initial performance evaluation of a dual-panel, high-resolution TOF-DOI PET prototype (#1796)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Niu (Autores: M. Niu , H. Yang , X. Jiang , X. Zeng , W. Huang , R. Dai , X. Zhang , J. Hua , Y. Zhao , Q. Wei , Y. Liang , Z. Gu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China [2] University of Science and Technology Beijing, School of Automation and Electrical Engineering, Beijing, China [3] National Cancer Center, Cancer Hospital & Shenzhen Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Shenzhen, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study presents an initial evaluation of a dual-panel PET prototype with TOF-DOI capabilities for high-resolution local human organs imaging. The system consists of two flat panel detectors, offering an open geometry suitable for small anatomical regions. Each panel has a 212 × 212 mm² active area and consists of dual-layer, multi-resolution LYSO detectors. An interleaved multiplexing circuit was implemented to reduce the readout channels by a factor of four, with signals processed by TOFPET2 ASIC electronics. At the detector level, clear flood images were obtained with well identified crystals. The average energy resolutions were 14.60% and 14.09% for the top and bottom layers. The bottom layer achieved an average DOI resolution of 3.37 mm. The best coincidence timing resolution was 280 ps for bottom-bottom events after excluding inter-crystal scatter events. With a panel distance of 30 cm, the spatial resolutions at the center of the FOV were 1.15, 1.53, and 3.63 mm FWHM in the three orthogonal directions. The peak sensitivity was 4.29% at the FOV center and 2.14% at a 5 cm axial offset. For phantom imaging, 1.6-mm rods were clearly resolved at the FOV center and remained discernible at a 5 cm off-center when four DOI bins were used in reconstruction. These initial results indicate that the dual-panel TOF-DOI PET prototype is promising for high-resolution imaging of localized human anatomy and small lesions detection. Its open and flexible geometry may also support dose monitoring in proton therapy. Further work will focus on correction methods, a more comprehensive performance evaluation, and practical imaging demonstrations.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 120Poster Number:MIC-15-120] Development of a Four-Layer DOI Detector Based Preclinical PET System (#1863)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Yang (Autores: H. Yang , X. Zhang , X. Jiang , W. Huang , Y. Zhao , X. Zeng , M. Niu , Y. Liang , Z. Gu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China [2] Harbin Institute of Technology, School of Astronautics, Harbin, China [3] National Cancer Center/National Clinical Research Center for Cancer/Cancer Hospital & Shenzhen Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and Peking Union Medical College, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Shenzhen, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents a Monte Carlo-based performance evaluation of a preclinical PET system based on a four-layer depth-of-interaction (DOI) detector. The detector with optimized layer thickness design comprises two LYSO arrays and two BGO arrays. The first and third layers adopt 60×30 LYSO arrays with pixel dimensions of 0.78×0.78×4 mm3 and 0.78×0.78×6 mm3, respectively, the second and fourth layers employ 40×20 BGO arrays with pixel dimensions of 1.21×1.21×4 mm3 and 1.21×1.21×10 mm3, respectively. System spatial resolution and sensitivity were characterized via Monte Carlo simulations following the NEMA NU 4 protocol. The single-ring system achieves the peak sensitivity of 16.6% and an average spatial resolution of 0.69 mm across the field of view (FOV). The complete dual-ring complete system could further improve the sensitivity to >25%. Compared with the two-layer detector system, the proposed four-layer DOI design exhibits significantly improved sensitivity while maintaining high and uniform spatial resolution. Experimental validation using the four-layer detector with total size of 51.6×25.8×25.5 mm3 demonstrated CNN classification accuracies of 84% for the LYSO layers and 76% for the BGO layers. Flood images using 45° oblique collimated incidence showed distinct event clustering patterns between upper- and lower-layers Future work will focus on developing the single-ring validation prototype and further improving the DOI layer discrimination accuracy.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 123Poster Number:MIC-15-123] Experimental Evaluation of 3D Imaging Point Spread Function for the Ultra-High Performance Brain PET (UHB-PET) Scanner (#2170)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. A. Karakatsanis (Autores: N. A. Karakatsanis , F. Pagano , F. Loignon-Houle , D. Sanchez , E. Munoz , E. Elmoujarkach , J. V. Catret , A. J. Gonzalez , S. A. Nehmeh)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Weill Cornell Medical College, Department of Radiology, New York, New York, United States of America [2] Instituto de Instrumentacion para Imagen Molecular (i3M), Valencia, Spain [3] Oncovision SA, Valencia, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We report preliminary experimental results on the 3D imaging point spread function response performance of the Ultra-High Performance Brain PET (UHB-PET) system employing semi-monolithic LYSO slabs, machine-learning-based event positioning, and list-mode 3D point spread function (PSF) reconstruction. Detector calibration was previously performed using a slit-collimated 22-Na point source translated across monolithic and depth dimensions. A previous multilayer perceptron (MLP) estimated monolithic and depth positions of interaction, while axial positioning was derived via a previous center-of-gravity algorithm. List-mode coincidence events were registered encoding time, energy, time-of-flight, module pair and within-module 3D coordinates, discretized into virtual detector pixels (50 transaxial × 50 axial × 20 depth) and mapped to global cylindrical coordinates after depth-of-interaction correction. A list-mode MLEM algorithm with an optimized Gaussian PSF model kernel width was employed. The system 3D imaging PSF was evaluated from 3-min acquisitions by placing a 0.25 mm 22-Na point source across 25 axial positions spanning the full axial FOV along the transaxial FOV center. 3D PET images free of visual artifacts were obtained. A uniform 3D PSF with mean relative absolute deviation from FOV center of 5.83%, 5.87% and 7.32% for both FWHM and FWTM was observed in radial, tangential and axial PSF components, respectively, across all axial locations demonstrating an axially homogeneous 3D imaging PSF for UHB-PET. Ongoing work includes implementation of classification-based MLP positioning with improved detector resolution, incorporation of experimentally derived spatially variant PSF kernels, and validation with an extended set of phantoms to further optimize 3D imaging PSF response and its uniformity in all directions across the entire FOV.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 126Poster Number:MIC-15-126] System integration of a Breast PET/MR Insert in a Whole-Body PET/MRI System: Data Driven Temperature Drift Correction and Synchronization (#2428)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Hohnholz (Autores: J. Hohnholz , L. U. Rauscher , M. Judenhofer , E. Olyaei , H. P. Vo , M. Rafecas , B. Pichler , F. P. Schmidt)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Werner Siemens Imaging Center, Department of Preclinical Imaging and Radiopharmacy, University of Tuebingen, Tuebingen, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [2] Siemens Medical Solutions USA, Inc., Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America [3] University Hospital Tuebingen, Nuclear Medicine and Clinical Molecular Imaging, Tuebingen, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [4] Insitute of Medical Engineering, University of Luebeck, Luebeck, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany [5] Cluster of Excellence iFIT (EXC2180), "Image Guided and Functionally Instructed Tumor Therapies", Tuebingen, Baden-Württemberg, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Our PET/MR breast insert currently under development is designed to be compatible with a whole-body 3T PET/MRI system. The proposed insert comprises a ring geometry based on dual layer LSO detector blocks coupled via FFC cables to SiPM arrays. Such integration in the confined and RF-shielded PET/MR environment introduces challenges related to thermal stability, which are addressed using data-driven temperature monitoring and correction. In an isothermal setup, the photopeak remains stable (898.7 ± 0.5). Under a temperature gradient, a drift from 901.1 to 914.1 (~ 1.1 to 8.5 keV) within 30 min is observed, resulting in a shifted and broadened energy spectrum (photopeak 907.8, FWHM 76.9). After scaling energy values via the derived ratio of the peak shift to the reference, the photopeak is restored to 899.1 with reduced FWHM (75.7). In parallel, combined operation of insert and whole-body PET systems requires alignment of independent timestamp domains to enable mixed-coincidence reconstruction. Two detector blocks were operated with independent local clocks, a synchronized reference was established and desynchronized by introducing a delay. A data-driven algorithm estimates this offset via a sliding-window coincidence search (±100 ns), where the offset is determined by the maximum coincidence counts within the timing window. After correcting for the delay, time difference spectra within a narrow ±3 ns time window could be restored while preserving a 430 ps coincidence resolution time. These results demonstrate that data-driven correction and synchronization enable stable PET/MR operation and potentially enable mixed-coincidence imaging across independent systems. Future work will focus on scaling to multi-ring systems, enhancing in-situ temperature sensing during MR operation, and evaluating mixed-coincidence imaging between independent PET systems enabled by the proposed synchronization approach.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. E. Enriquez-Mier-y-Teran (Autores: F. E. Enriquez-Mier-y-Teran , J. Bec , M. Judenhofer , S. Siegel , S. I. Kwon , S. Cherry , A. Kyme , S. Meikle)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The University of Sydney, Faculty of Medicine and Health, Sydney, Australia [2] The University of Sydney, Brain and Mind Centre, Sydney, Australia [3] University of California Davis, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America [4] Siemens Healthineers, Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America [5] The University of Sydney, School of Biomedical Engineering, Sydney, Australia
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Conventional brain PET imaging of small rodents necessitates anesthesia to prevent motion artefacts. However, anesthesia may alter brain function and preclude the simultaneous assessment of brain function and animal behavior. The Motion-Adaptive Molecular and Behavioral Observation (MAMBO)-PET system aims to overcome these limitations by enabling brain imaging in awake, freely moving mice. The system consists of four detector panels. Two panels have been assembled, while the remaining two are in the final stages of assembly. Here, we report the initial performance of the two-panel MAMBO-PET system. The mean detector panel energy resolution ranged from 14.9% to 15.0%. The FWHM of the radial and tangential PSF profiles at the center of the FOV were 0.9 mm and 5.7 mm, respectively. Future work includes the NEMA characterization of the full 4-panel system.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 132Poster Number:MIC-15-132] First experimental and phantom results of the DC-SPECT scanner: a cardiac-dedicated SPECT with Laser-Processed CsI:Tl Detector Modules (#2799)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 X. Zhang (Autores: X. Zhang , A. Sitek , M.P. Ottensmeyer , F. Han , H. Sabet)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Harvard Medical School, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Our group is developing Dynamic Cardiac SPECT (DC-SPECT) featuring laser-processed CsI: Tl scintillators with converging pixels to avoid depth-of-interaction blurring. This work reports, for the first time, the initial imaging performance of the DC-SPECT scanner featuring laser-processed CsI: Tl detector modules with converging pixels. A 50×50×8.05 mm³ CsI: Tl crystal was laserprocessed into a 25×25 converging-pixel array. The crystal was coupled to an 8×8 multi-pixel photon counter array , read out by a custom 64-channel analog front-end board and a 12-bit waveform digitizer. Three decoding algorithms were evaluated: MLE-Bicubic, MLE-Nearest, and a deep neural network (NN) decoder. A ⁵⁷Co point source and a ⁹⁹ᵐTc three-line source phantom were imaged using list-mode MLEM reconstruction. For the point source, FWHM values of 6.24, 6.58, and 5.67 mm were obtained for MLE-Bicubic, MLE-Nearest, and NN at 20 iterations, with NN yielding the sharpest response. At 50 iterations, FWHM values improved to 4.63, 4.98, and 5.02 mm, with MLE-Bicubic achieving the sharpest response. For the three-line source phantom, sources located near the center of the field of view yielded mean FWHM values as low as 3.55 mm (NN) and 4.04 mm (MLE-Bicubic). Sources near the field-of-view edge exhibited broader responses, consistent with the known degradation of detector sensitivity toward the detector periphery. The converging-pixel architecture effectively eliminates depth-of-interaction ambiguity without additional hardware, further supporting the practical viability of this detector design. Future work will focus on optimization of reconstruction parameters, and further phantom and cardiac imaging studies toward clinical deployment of the DC-SPECT system.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 135Poster Number:MIC-15-135] Validation of an Image Based Method of Estimating Mechanical Offsets in a Rotating Flat-Panel PET Scanner with Phantom and Clinical Data (#2997)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Shahi (Autores: A. Shahi , B. Baldassi , B. Komarov , U. Metser , A. Reznik , O. Bubon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lakehead University, Physics, Thunder Bay, Ontario, Canada [2] Radialis Inc., Thunder Bay, Ontario, Canada [3] Princess Margaret Cancer Center, Medical Imaging, Toronto, Ontario, Canada [4] Thunder Bay Regional Health Research Institute, Thunder Bay, Ontario, Canada
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate geometric calibration is essential for high-resolution 3D PET image reconstruction because detector element mispositioning can introduce spatial misalignment of lines-of-response (LORs) and image blur. This challenge is particularly important in rotating flat-panel PET scanners, where opposing detector panels rotate during acquisition to improve angular coverage and enable fully 3D reconstruction. In this work, we developed and evaluated an image-based calibration method for estimating linear offsets between detector centers and the axis of rotation in the Radialis PET Imager, an organ-targeted rotating flat-panel PET scanner. The calibration was performed using a 22 Na point source acquired with twelve step-and-shoot detector rotations from -90° to +75°. Four point source experiments were performed at different source locations. An iterative algorithm was implemented to estimate linear offsets by minimizing distances between reconstructed point sources from different detector angles and the target image acquired at 0°. The estimated offsets were fed into transformation matrices used for composite image reconstruction of list mode data from all detector angles. Performance was evaluated using spatial resolution measurements from composite images, Hoffman brain phantom scans, and a clinical 18 F-Florbetaben brain scan. Offset calibration improved the average spatial resolution (FWHM) from 3.3 mm to 2.9 mm, with axial FWHM improving from 5.2 mm to 3.0 mm. Hoffman phantom images reconstructed with offset calibration demonstrated improved contrast and visualization of internal structures. The calibration of 18 F-Florbetaben clinical brain images demonstrated improved visualization of anatomical features, including the septum pellucidum, as well as improved contrast and reduced apparent cortical tracer uptake relative to image reconstructed without offset calibration.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 138Poster Number:MIC-15-138] Detector Stability and Effects on Time and Energy Resolution in Novel Clinical Brain PET Scanners (#3125)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Batres (Autores: L. Batres , L. J. Algarra , M. Vidal , D. Perez , J.J. Vaquero)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, Departamento de Bioingeniería, Leganés, Spain [2] Instituto de Investigación Sanitaria Gregorio Marañón, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Compact PET scanners based on highly integrated front-end ASICs require stable thermal conditions to preserve detector gain, timing response, energy resolution, and inter-module uniformity. This is especially relevant in low-footprint PET systems, where high channel density and closed mechanical integration limit conventional forced-air cooling. This work presents a thermal stabilization strategy designed for a new family of clinical and preclinical PET scanners: BuckyPET, BrainPET and UltraPET. The solution combines adaptive SiPM bias compensation with active liquid cooling of the ASIC electronics using a cascade proportional--integral (PI) controller. The outer loop regulates an exponentially filtered high-percentile aggregate of ASIC temperature deviations from a learned baseline, while the inner loop controls the coolant temperature through the chiller command. Saturation, setpoint slew-rate limiting and anti-windup mechanisms are included to improve robustness under variable conditions. The proposed strategy maintained the ASIC thermal deviation within the tolerance band for different ambient conditions and high data throughput acquisitions. Preliminary measurements show improvements of up to 15% in energy resolution and up to 8% in coincidence time resolution compared with worst-case thermal drift conditions. The architecture enables compact, silent, and patient-friendly scanner designs, while preserving reproducible PET performance.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 141Poster Number:MIC-15-141] Counting loss correction of photon counting detector: the need to consider the effective atomic number of the target object in clinical applications (#1049)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Kimoto (Autores: N. Kimoto , R. Nishigami , T. Asahara , Y. Kanazawa , A. Katsumata , S. Yamamoto , H. Hayashi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Junshin Gakuen University, Department of Radiological Science, Faculty of Health Sciences, Fukuoka, Japan [2] Kanazawa University, Graduate School of Medical Sciences, Kanazawa, Japan [3] Okayama University, Department of Radiological Technology, Faculty of Health Sciences, Okayama, Japan [4] Kumamoto University, Faculty of Life Science, Kumamoto, Japan [5] Asahi University, Oral Radiology and Artificial Intelligence, Mizuho, Japan [6] JOB CORPORATION, Yokohama, Japan [7] Kanazawa University, College of Transdisciplinary Sciences for Innovation, Kanazawa, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Correcting counting loss phenomena caused by pulse pile-up and dead time is essential for the medical application of an energy-resolving photon counting detector (ERPCD). At the IEEE 2025 MIC conference, we proposed a counting loss correction algorithm applicable to objects, but it was limited to an effective atomic number (Z eff ) of 7-13. In this study, we propose a novel counting loss correction algorithm that extends the target object to Z eff = 3-20 to cover biological samples, and evaluate the quantitative performance of the Z eff images related to the algorithm. The novelty is to estimate the effect of counting loss on objects with Z eff = 3-20 using experimentally derived counting loss correction functions for polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA, Z eff = 6.5) and aluminum (Al, Z eff = 13). Using the correction function for each Z eff , the measured counting rate can be converted to the expected counting rate under ideal conditions without counting loss. Since the Z eff of the object is unknown at the beginning of the analysis, corrections for Z eff = 3-20 are tentatively performed. The corrected counting rate is then applied to the material identification algorithm, which was proposed in a previous study, and Z eff is derived. Finally, the Z eff of an object is determined when the entire algorithm works properly. To demonstrate our method, reference samples with known Z eff (PMMA, Al, bilayer structures of PMMA and Al, and Si powder) and tooth samples were measured using a prototype ERPCD system equipped with a cadmium zinc telluride (CZT) semiconductor detector. When applying the correction to the measurement of reference samples, the accuracy of the Z eff image was +/-1 under general radiography conditions. For a dental sample, tooth structure and resin can be observed with proper Z eff . This result demonstrates that counting loss correction is important for the clinical application of ERPCD.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 144Poster Number:MIC-15-144] An algorithm to generate effective atomic number and mass density images from photon-counting CT: application for lung disease assessment (#1211)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Asahara (Autores: T. Asahara , R. Nishigami , N. Kimoto , M. Mitani , N. Akagi , M. Honda , T. Iguchi , T. Hiraki , H. Hayashi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Okayama University, Department of Radiological Technology, Faculty of Health Sciences, Okayama, Japan [2] Kanazawa University, Graduate School of Medical Sciences, Kanazawa, Japan [3] Junshin Gakuen University, Department of Radiological Science, Faculty of Health Sciences, Fukuoka, Japan [4] Okayama University Hospital, Division of Radiological Technology, Medical Support Department, Okayama, Japan [5] Okayama University, Department of Radiology, Faculty of Medicine, Dentistry and Pharmaceutical Sciences, Okayama, Japan [6] Kanazawa University, College of Transdisciplinary Sciences for Innovation, Kanazawa, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Photon-counting CT (PC-CT) enables acquisition of energy-resolved images. Analyzing these images provides potential for quantitative diagnosis based on material composition. This study aims to develop an algorithm that simultaneously generates effective atomic number (Z eff ) and effective mass density (ρ eff ) images from virtual monoenergetic images (VMIs) acquired by clinical PC-CT. To demonstrate the feasibility of our algorithm, phantom experiment and clinical lung datasets were analyzed as representative applications. In our algorithm, Z eff and ρ eff values are estimated voxel-wise from two VMIs. The CT values are converted to μ values, and their ratio is converted to the Z eff value using a reference curve created from a known database of mass attenuation coefficient (μ/ρ). In addition, the tentative mass densities as a function of atomic number are estimated by fitting μ/ρ data of each atomic number to the measured μ values, and the ρ eff is uniquely determined using the Z eff information. The algorithm was validated using an in-house low-density phantom and clinical chest CT images from 10 patients. We analyzed Z eff and ρ eff values in diseased and normal lung tissue regions. From the phantom study, the measured ρ eff values were consistent with the reference density of the samples. In clinical analysis, lung diseases exhibited characteristic changes in ρ eff . A metastatic lung nodule showed a similar Z eff value compared to normal lung tissue, but its ρ eff value was clearly higher. During pneumonia follow-up, ρ eff values decreased by approximately 56% after one month of disease regression, while Z eff values remained nealy unchanged. Our algorithm generates Z eff and ρ eff images from PC-CT data, allowing quantitative interpretation of conventional CT values. These results suggest that ρ eff provides a useful quantitative indicator for lung lesion assessment.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 147Poster Number:MIC-15-147] Dual-Energy CT Metal Artifact Reduction Using VMI-Guided Iterative Reconstruction Refinement (#1325)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Park (Autores: S. Park , Y. Lim , S. Lee , H. Cho)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yonsei University, Department of Radiation Convergence Engineering, Yonsei University, Wonju, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Metal artifacts in computed tomography (CT) degrade image quality and reduce quantitative reliability, particularly in the presence of metallic objects. Conventional metal artifact reduction (MAR) methods, such as sinogram interpolation and normalized correction, rely heavily on accurate metal segmentation and often fail to preserve fine anatomical structures. Although dual-energy CT (DECT) provides additional spectral information for material characterization, its potential has not been fully utilized in prior-guided iterative MAR frameworks. In this study, we propose a prior-guided iterative MAR method for DECT that incorporates virtual monoenergetic image (VMI) priors for improved artifact suppression and structural preservation. Metal regions are first identified in the image domain using residual-based metal segmentation from initial dual-energy reconstructed images, and the resulting metal mask is forward-projected to generate the metal trace in the projection domain. Dual-energy projection data are then corrected in the projection domain using prior-guided interpolation to reduce metal-induced inconsistencies. Material decomposition is then performed to generate VMIs, which provide structurally consistent priors for subsequent image-domain reconstruction refinement. The final images are obtained by iterative prior-guided reconstruction that enforces data consistency while incorporating VMI-based edge guidance and artifact-suppression regularization to suppress residual artifacts and preserve anatomical boundaries. Quantitative evaluations on simulated datasets demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces root mean square error and improves structural similarity compared with normalized MAR. These results indicate that the proposed framework effectively suppresses metal artifacts while maintaining structural fidelity and quantitative accuracy.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 150Poster Number:MIC-15-150] Magnification Effect Evaluation for Novel Dual-Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry System (#1442)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Kwon (Autores: C. Kwon , Y. Ahn , S. Min , H. Leem , M. Oh)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Osteosys Co., Ltd., R&D Center, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate BMD measurement is essential for osteoporosis diagnosis and fracture risk assessment. Wide fan-beam DXA systems provide faster scan acquisition than pencil-beam systems; however, their geometric characteristics can introduce magnification errors when the distance between the X-ray source and the subject changes. These distortions affect bone mineral content (BMC), projected bone area, and ultimately BMD accuracy. The iNSiGHT C510 (OsteoSys Co., Korea) employs a 25° fan beam with a SID distance of 812 mm, substantially wider than the 4.5° narrow fan beam geometry of the PRIMUS, which operates at a 634 mm SID. To compensate for magnification-induced distortion, the iNSiGHT C510 incorporates the geometric correction within the LUCIDA software platform. The correction algorithm was evaluated using a custom lumbar spine phantom elevated from 0 to 200 mm above the tabletop in 10 mm increments, with 10 repeated measurements obtained at each height. Without correction, the iNSiGHT C510 showed BMD deviations ranging from approximately +40% to −40%. After applying the correction algorithm, residual BMD variability was reduced to within ±5%, comparable to the ±4-5% variation observed with the PRIMUS under identical conditions. Correlation analysis between corrected iNSiGHT C510 measurements and corresponding PRIMUS values demonstrated strong agreement, with a coefficient of determination (R²) of 0.934 and a standard error below 2%. These results indicate that the proprietary correction algorithm effectively compensates for magnification errors inherent to the wide fan-beam geometry, enabling the iNSiGHT C510 to achieve clinically equivalent BMD accuracy suitable for routine bone density assessment.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 153Poster Number:MIC-15-153] Transient radiative transport equation solution for ToF-CT ballistic X-ray photons (#2208)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Fromont (Autores: M. Fromont , R. Fontaine , Y. Bérubé-Lauzière)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Université de Sherbrooke, Département de génie électrique et de génie, Sherbrooke, Québec, Canada [2] Université de Sherbrooke, Institut interdisciplinaire d'innovation technologique - 3IT, Sherbrooke, Québec, Canada
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Computed tomography (CT) has made significant advances in reducing X-ray exposure while preserving image quality. A novel project to improve CT imaging involves subsituting anti-scatter grids with filtering out scattered photons using time-of-flight (ToF) measurements. A first approach resorting to ToF filtering was developed to eliminate the noise due to scattered photons, thereby improving the contrast-to-noise ratio. Additionally, ToF-CT has the potential to exploit both detected ballistic and scattered photons for reconstructing both 3D images of absorption and scattering using model-based image reconstruction. In this approach, an X-ray radiation propagation model must be resorted to. For this purpose, a transient radiative transport equation is presented herein. It is divided into ballistic and scattering propagation components. The present study focuses on the ballistic component, with the aim of evaluating various numerical methods to achieve better numerical temporal accuracy.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 156Poster Number:MIC-15-156] Characterization of a Photon-Counting CT Modality for Preclinical PET/CT (#2155)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. F.C.A. Veloso (Autores: R. G. Oliveira , A.L. M. Silva , P. M.M. Correia , J. F.C.A. Veloso)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Aveiro, Physics, Aveiro, Portugal
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The easyPET/CT is a multimodal imaging system that integrates positron emission tomography and computed tomography (CT), using LYSO:Ce scintillator crystals coupled to silicon photomultipliers. CT acquisition is done in photon-counting (PC) mode, enabling energy discrimination and improving contrast-to-noise ratio. The radiation source used is a 241 Am radioactive source (2.89 MBq), which simplifies system integration. This work presents the first characterization of the integrated CT modality of the easyPET/CT of through simulation, evaluating CT number calibration, noise, and uniformity. A non-linear system response between pixel intensity and Hounsfield units was observed and successfully corrected using a second-order polynomial fit (R 2 =0.99). Noise and uniformity assessment revealed peripheral non-uniformity attributed to reconstruction artifacts. Spatial resolution characterization is ongoing. These results establish a foundation for a compact, portable PCCT system with strong potential for multimodal preclinical imaging applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 159Poster Number:MIC-15-159] Characterization of a LYSO:Ce/SiPM detector array for photon-counting CT (#2348)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J.F. C.D.A. Veloso (Autores: R. G. Oliveira , A.X. Pinto , A.L. M. Silva , P.M. M. Correia , J.F. C.D.A. Veloso)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Aveiro, Physics, Aveiro, Portugal
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work characterizes the LYSO:Ce/SiPM detector array of the easyPET/CT, a compact multimodal preclinical imaging platform. The characterization of the 16×2 array of LYSO:Ce crystals, coupled one-to-one to SiPMs was assessed per crystal in terms of energy resolution (ER), count rate, and sensitivity using a 241 Am radioactive source (59.5 keV). The mean ER was 33.8 ± 1.8% FWHM at 59.5 keV, competitive with current LYSO:Ce-based photon-counting detector systems reported in the literature. The mean count rate and sensitivity were 62.4 ± 5.3 photons/s and 0.7 ± 0.1 counts-photon -1 , respectively, both displaying a uniform spatial distribution across the array. The overall uniformity of the detector response validates the shared PET/CT hardware architecture as a viable approach for photon-counting CT, confirming that using the PET detector for CT operation preserves detector integrity. Future work will address pile-up characterization at higher count rates to further define the dynamic range of the system.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 162Poster Number:MIC-15-162] Linearizing the Transformation from CT Hounsfield Units to Linear Attenuation Coefficient for PET Attenuation Map Generation using Virtual Non-Contrast Images (#2486)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Alrakh (Autores: H. Alrakh , L. Tellmann , O. Nikoubashman , S. Faby , D. Niekämper , A. Abu arra , M. Wiesmann , N.J. Shah , C. Lerche)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Forschungszentrum Jülich GmbH, INM-4, Jülich, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [2] RWTH Aachen University, Department of Neurology, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [3] RWTH Aachen University, Department of Diagnostic and Interventional Neuroradiology, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [4] Siemens Healthineers AG, Department of Computed Tomography, Forchheim, Bavaria, Germany [5] An-Najah National University, Department of Biophysics and Medical Imaging, Nablus, State of Palestine
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Attenuation correction (AC) is crucial for artefact-free PET/MR images. Currently, CT-derived PET attenuation maps (AMs) are based on transformation schemes from conventional CT scanners with data from polyenergetic X-ray spectra. It is known that converting from polyenergetic CT image data to monoenergetic 511 keV linear attenuation coefficients (LACs) introduces systematic errors in the LACs employed for AC in PET imaging. To address this issue, we investigated spectral CT to obtain more accurate AMs. Spectral CT offers advantages over conventional CT scanners by providing the possibility of material decomposition. It also allows to reconstruct virtual monochromatic images (VMI) from the inherently multiple polyenergetic data sets of CT. The spectral information can also be used to obtain virtual non-contrast (VNC). In our approach, we use angiographic spectral CT scans with an administration of iodinated contrast agents and computed VNC images from the obtained dataset. The linear transformation scheme from monochromatic CT images to LACs at 511 keV was obtained from VNC images for different tissue types using an electron density phantom and a photon counting (PC) CT scanner. The use of VNC images effectively simplifies the transformation from HUs to LACs requiring only a single linear function. It further minimizes residual deviations of the LACs for soft-tissues mimicking materials. Deriving the LACs from VNC images instead of standard CT images may lower the systematic errors of CT-based attenuation correction for PET scanners equipped with dual energy CT systems.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 165Poster Number:MIC-15-165] Effects of Deep Learning Model Optimization for Metal Artefact Reduction in Spectral Photon-Counting Computed Tomography (#2581)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Y. Raja (Autores: O. S. Khan , B. Tariq , A. Behouch , N. Maalej , M.S. Jouini , A. Y. Raja)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Khalifa University, Physics, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates [2] Khalifa University, Mathematics, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Metal-induced artifacts in spectral photon-counting computed tomography (SPCCT) degrade image quality and, critically, corrupt material decomposition (MD) accuracy by introducing spectral distortions across energy bins. This paper presents a generalized optimization pipeline applied to a residual dense U-Net, developed through a two-stage process combining manual grid search and Optuna-based automated machine learning (AutoML) to tune the optimizer, learning rate, loss configuration, and dense block depth. The pipeline is evaluated using a dual-phase framework that covers energy analysis and MD performance on hydroxyapatite and iodine density images. RDU-Net+ achieves a mean signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 35.34, root mean squared error (RMSE) of 0.0045, and structural similarity index (SSIM) of 0.954, while improving hydroxyapatite classification accuracy to 92.37\% and iodine accuracy to 91.86\%. All improvements over the baseline are statistically significant ($p < 0.001$). The proposed pipeline provides a structured, reproducible optimization framework for deep learning-based metal artifact reduction in SPCCT.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 168Poster Number:MIC-15-168] Image Improvement in X-ray Fluorescence Computed Tomography Using Deep Image Prior with X-ray Transmission Images (#2730)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Zeniya (Autores: T. Ono , S. Kusakari , F. Hashimoto , R. Abe , M. Kobayashi , T. Sasaya , N. Sunaguchi , S. Takeda , H. Kawashima , T. Yuasa , T. Zeniya)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Hirosaki University, Graduate School of Science and Technology, Hirosaki, Japan [2] University of Florida, J.Crayton Pruitt Family Department of Biomedical Engineering, Gainesville, Florida, United States of America [3] Yamagata University, Graduate School of Science and Engineering, Yonezawa, Japan [4] High Energy Accelerator Research Organization, Institute of Materials Structure Science, Tsukuba, Japan [5] Fukushima Institute for Research, Education and Innovation, Namiemachi, Japan [6] Kyoto Pharmaceutical University, Radioisotope Research Center,, Kyoto, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract X-ray fluorescence computed tomography (XFCT) enables nanoparticle imaging and biological function imaging without radioisotopes. We successfully improved image quality by applying Deep Image Prior (DIP), a self-supervised deep learning technique that does not require training datasets, to XFCT images. However, conventional DIP, which uses randomly generated input images, has problems such as reduced spatial resolution and deviation from the true image distribution. To address these problems, we propose CT-DIP, a modified DIP framework in which the network input is replaced with projection images acquired from simultaneous X-ray transmission computed tomography (XTCT). Monte Carlo simulations using Geant4 were performed to generate both XFCT and XTCT projection images of a mouse brain phantom, with iodine used as a contrast agent to mimic cerebral blood flow. Image reconstruction was carried out using the ordered subsets expectation maximization (OS-EM) algorithm after DIP denoising. Visual evaluation and quantitative evaluation using Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) demonstrated that CT-DIP outperformed conventional DIP, Gaussian filtering, and only OS-EM reconstruction. Furthermore, CT-DIP reduced training time from 75.3 minutes to 4.2 minutes, representing an approximately 18 times speedup. These results suggest that CT-DIP has strong practical potential for XFCT imaging in low-count environments, and future work will focus on validation with real measurement data.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 171Poster Number:MIC-15-171] Experimental Characterization and Materials-Driven Optimization of Fine-Pitch CZT Detectors for Photon-Counting CT (#2994)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Ikhlef (Autores: A. Ikhlef , S. Arnab , R. Luhta , S. Utrup , C. Vrettos)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Analogic Corporation, Salem, New Hampshire, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The performance of fine-pitch cadmium zinc telluride (CZT) photon-counting detectors is strongly governed by experimentally measurable charge transport and leakage current characteristics. We present the fabrication and experimental characterization of a pixelated CZT detector array with a nominal pixel pitch of 441 × 441 μm², targeting high-channel-count architectures for computed tomography (CT). CZT material properties were characterized using a custom-built time-of-flight (TOF) measurement system to extract electron mobility and lifetime under controlled electric field conditions. Dark current behavior was systematically measured as a function of bias voltage and pixel geometry to assess operational limits imposed by material quality. Experimentally derived transport and leakage parameters were used to perform a detector-level trade-off analysis linking CZT material properties, pixel pitch, and bias field. The results establish experimentally grounded constraints and design guidelines for scaling CZT detector arrays toward advanced photon-counting CT systems.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 174Poster Number:MIC-15-174] Longitudinal Cone-Beam CT and MRI Integration for High-Fidelity Synthetic CT Generation (#3003)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 V. Jaouen (Autores: V. Jaouen , V. Bourbonne , J. Bert , U. Schick , P.-H. Conze , D. Visvikis)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] IMT Atlantique, Brest, France [2] U1101 LaTIM, Inserm, Université de Bretagne Occidentale, Brest, France [3] Brest University Hospital, Brest, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Cross-modality synthesis from cone-beam CT (CBCT) to CT is central to online adaptive radiotherapy and accurate dose recalculation. Although planning MRI provides valuable soft-tissue information, daily CBCT captures the patient's updated anatomy on the treatment couch. Its direct use remains limited by scatter artifacts and imperfect Hounsfield Unit (HU) calibration. This study investigates whether aggregating sequential on-treatment CBCTs improves deep learning-based synthetic CT (sCT) generation compared with single-fraction CBCT or static MRI priors alone. We developed a conditional GAN with Residual-in-Residual Dense Blocks to generate high-fidelity sCTs. The model was evaluated on 190 patients with brain metastases, split into 152 training cases and 38 independent test cases. Each patient had a planning CT used as ground truth, a planning T1-weighted MRI, and up to three daily CBCT scans. Four input settings were compared: 1 CBCT, 1 CBCT+MRI, 3 CBCTs, and 3 CBCTs+MRI. Adding temporal and multimodal information improved sCT accuracy. The single-CBCT baseline achieved 67.79 HU MAE and 29.12 dB PSNR, while the full 3 CBCTs+MRI configuration reached the best performance, with 59.81 HU MAE and 30.82 dB PSNR. Importantly, temporal accumulation alone using 3 CBCTs achieved 60.01 HU MAE, outperforming the static multimodal 1 CBCT+MRI setting at 65.98 HU. This suggests that longitudinal CBCT redundancy provides stronger density and attenuation constraints than a single CBCT complemented by a rigid planning MRI prior. Sequential CBCT aggregation, especially when fused with MRI, improves HU calibration and reduces daily setup artifacts, supporting robust automated sCT generation for online adaptive radiotherapy.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 177Poster Number:MIC-15-177] Dynamic hepatocyte-specific liver imaging using a two-dimensional SiPM-based photon counting CT: Comparison between healthy and liver tumor mouse models (#3095)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Lucyana (Autores: F. Lucyana , M. Arimoto , M. Oshima , Y. Futura , S. Midorikawa , H. Kawashima , S. Kobayashi , K. Okumura , A. Mizutani , N. Ohno , J. Kataoka , T. Ro , R. Minagawa , K. Murakami , S. Terazawa , Y. Maeno)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Kanazawa University, Kanazawa, Japan [2] Waseda University, Tokyo, Japan [3] Ishikawa Prefectural University, Nonoichi, Japan [4] Proterial Ltd., Osaka, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Photon counting computed tomography (PC-CT) enables energy-resolved imaging and material-specific analysis through individual X-ray photon detection. In this study, dynamic hepatocyte-specific imaging was performed in healthy and liver tumor mouse using a developed two-dimensional (2D) PC-CT system consisting of a 16 × 64-channel YGAG scintillator array coupled with MPPC array, with a voxel size of 1×1×1 mm 3 . Gd-EoB was intravenously administered, and time-resolved imaging was conducted before and after contrast injection. Reconstructed CT images in the 50-60 keV energy range and estimated Gd concentration maps were evaluated around the liver and bladder regions. Dynamic enhancement was observed after Gd administration in both healthy and liver tumor mice, with differences in temporal enhancement behavior and estimated Gd concentration tendency between the two models. Although the tumor region was not clearly distinguishable because of its small size and current image quality limitations, temporal changes in CT value and estimated Gd concentration were still observable. MRI comparison demonstrated a positive relationship between MRI signal intensity and PC-CT-derived Gd concentration, although quantitative tendencies differed because of differences in imaging mechanisms and contrast sensitivity between MRI and PC-CT. These results demonstrate the feasibility of scintillator-based PC-CT for dynamic hepatocyte-specific imaging in vivo.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 180Poster Number:MIC-15-180] Improved Material Decomposition Method in DXA Using Scatter-Induced Arrival Time Difference (#3163)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Kwon (Autores: S. Kwon , J. Jung , S.-H. Chun , J. Nam , J.H. Jung , Y. Choi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Sogang University, Department of Electronic Engineering, Intelligent Signal Processing System (ISPS) Laboratory, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Material decomposition is commonly based on the R-value, defined as the ratio of attenuated intensities measured at low-high X-ray energies. However, materials with similar compositions, such as fat and muscle, can exhibit overlapping R-values, limiting the accuracy of material decomposition. This study investigates the feasibility of improving material decomposition using scatter-induced arrival time difference. Scattered photons travel longer paths than primary photons, resulting in delayed arrival times. Photons with arrival time delay exceeding a threshold were distinguished as scattered photons. The scatter ratio (SR), defined as the ratio of scatter counts in low to high energy regions, was used for an additional identifier for material decomposition. DXA system was simulated using GATE with a detector consisting of 240 × 24 LYSO pixels with dimensions of 3 × 3 × 5 mm³, an X-ray source operated at 83 kVp and 0.2 mA with a 0.025 mm Ce filter, and the source-to-detector distance set to 1000 mm. Fat, muscle, and bone phantoms were placed at the center between the source and detector. The arrival time delay threshold was set to 20 ps since the maximum time difference of direct photons within the 5 mm pixel depth is 16 ps under ideal timing resolution of 0 ps. Each material was represented in feature space using the R-value and SR. Material separability was evaluated using a separability index based on the difference between feature means and standard deviations. In the feature space, fat, muscle, and bone formed distinct clusters. SR derived from photon arrival time difference improved the separability index for all material pairs. For fat-muscle, the separability index increased from 13 to 17, achieving a 25% increase. For fat-bone and muscle-bone pairs, separability improved by 84% and 62%, compared with the R-value. These results demonstrate the feasibility of improving the material decomposition in DXA using scatter-induced arrival time difference.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 183Poster Number:MIC-15-183] Limited-Angle and Few-View Image Reconstruction Using Point Spread Functions (#1111)
sub_talks.speaker: G. Zeng
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Utah Valley University, Department of Computer Science, Orem, Utah, United States of America [2] University of Utah, Radiology, Salt Lake City, Utah, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Limited-angle tomography and few-view tomography are extremely ill-conditioned problems. A usual way to reconstruct an image in limited-angle tomography or in few-view tomography is via an iterative algorithm that minimizes a two-term objective function. The objective function consists of a data fidelity term and a Bayesian term. A common Bayesian term is the total variation (TV) norm of the image. This paper proposes a different way to reconstruct the image in limited-angle tomography and few-view tomography by iteratively deconvolving the point spread function (PSF). Two PSFs are considered: the PSF of the filtered backprojection (FBP) and the PSF of pure backprojection. The method of using the PSF of pure backprojection gives better results.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 186Poster Number:MIC-15-186] Accelerating CGCIS Iterative Reconstruction Based on Location Priors from the DBP Algorithm (#1203)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Wang (Autores: K. Wang , Y. Zhao , S. Xu , Z. Hang , H. Liu , J. Wu , Y. Liu , Z. He , Q. Wei)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Science and Technology Beijing, Beijing Engineering Research Center of Industrial Spectrum Imaging and School of Automation and Electrical Engineering, Beijing, China [2] Tsinghua University, Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital, Beijing, China [3] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [4] Beijing Normal University, Center for Advanced Quantum Studies, School of Physics and Astronomy, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract To address the high computational complexity and low efficiency caused by traversing all field-of-view (FOV) voxels during image reconstruction in full-ring cascade gamma coincidence imaging systems (CGCIS), we propose a location priors algorithm to significantly accelerate image reconstruction. By restricting system matrix calculations, forward projection and back-projection operations to the ROI. This reduces the computational complexity from O( N x × N y × N z ) to O( m × n × l ), thereby significantly improving reconstruction efficiency. Experimental results demonstrated that, compared to conventional iterative algorithm, the proposed location priors algorithm achieved an approximate 37.05-fold acceleration in reconstruction speed while preserving high imaging quality. Ultimately, this advancement provides robust technical support for real-time, dynamic imaging monitoring utilizing theranostic nuclides.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 189Poster Number:MIC-15-189] DeepDreaming SPECT: Gradient-Based Reconstruction via Differentiable Physics Simulation (#1364)
sub_talks.speaker: F. Massanes
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Siemens Medical Solutions USA Inc, MI SPECT Research, Hoffman Estates, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present a gradient-based SPECT reconstruction framework that treats the physics-based forward model as a frozen differentiable operator and optimizes the 3D activity volume through backpropagation, an approach directly analogous to Google's DeepDream algorithm. The forward model is implemented as a PyTorch module comprising gantry rotation via trilinear interpolation, photon attenuation correction, and depth-dependent detector blur via per-slice convolution with measured point response function (PRF) kernels. Reconstruction minimizes the Mighell modified chi-square, a Poisson-appropriate cost function, using adaptive gradient descent. We evaluate four first-order optimizers (Adam, AdamW, RMSprop, SGD) on a hot/cold sphere phantom acquired on a Siemens Symbia Intevo with LEHR collimation and demonstrate that RMSprop achieves the fastest cost reduction. Preliminary reconstructions at 20 iterations recover the phantom geometry with visible hot sphere contrast, validating both the forward model accuracy and the gradient-based reconstruction pipeline.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 192Poster Number:MIC-15-192] Plug-and-Play Learned Regularization in PET Reconstruction: Integration of DeepInverse and STIR through SIRF (#1578)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Chandrasekaran (Autores: K. Chandrasekaran , G. Webber , A. Denker , M. J. Ehrhardt)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Bern, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Inselspital (Bern University Hospital), Bern, Bern, Switzerland [2] King's College London, School of Biomedical Engineering and Imaging Sciences, London, United Kingdom [3] Deutsches Elektronen-Synchrotron DESY, Helmholtz Imaging, Hamburg, Hamburg, Germany [4] University College London, Department of Computer Science, London, United Kingdom [5] University of Bath, Department of Mathematical Sciences, London, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents a modular software integration framework that bridges physics-based PET reconstruction with modern deep learning regularization. While deep learning has shown significant promise in medical imaging, integrating learned priors into established reconstruction pipelines remains a challenge. We address this by developing a direct interface between the DeepInverse library and the Synergistic Image Reconstruction Framework (SIRF), which wraps the Software for Tomographic Image Reconstruction (STIR) engine. This integration enables the direct deployment of learned priors, such as the Deep Residual UNet (DRUNet) and Weakly Convex Ridge Regularizers (WCRR), within accurate physics-based forward models. To demonstrate the framework's flexibility, we integrate and evaluate three reconstruction strategies using learned regularization: PnP-PD3O (WCRR), PnP-SVRG (DRUNet), and PnP-HQS (DRUNet). Performance is validated using a simulated 2D thorax phantom, comparing the proposed framework against Ordered Subsets Maximum A Posteriori One Step Late (OSMAPOSL), corresponding to standard Ordered Subsets Expectation Maximization (OSEM) reconstruction when no prior is applied, and OSMAPOSL with Relative Difference Prior (RDP) baselines. Quantitative results demonstrate improved image fidelity using learned regularization. As a representative example, the PnP-SVRG approach achieved a Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) of 45.90 dB, compared to 39.52 dB for baseline OSEM, showing improved reconstruction quality using this unified interface. The framework suppresses noise while preserving structural details. By providing an open-source Python-based bridge, this work lowers the barrier for evaluating state-of-the-art inverse-problem techniques in realistic clinical PET imaging scenarios.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 195Poster Number:MIC-15-195] Optimization of CT Reconstruction for Improved Image Quality in Lithium-Ion Battery Modules for Electric Wheelchairs (#1761)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Kim (Autores: D. Kim , H.-J. Choi , C.H. Min)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yonsei Unuversity, ﻿Department of Radiation Convergence Engineering, Wonju, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) are widely used in electric wheelchairs, and their safety is a critical concern due to the risk of thermal runaway caused by internal defects. In practical applications, batteries are operated as multi-cell modules, and periodic inspection is required as their condition degrades over time. X-ray computed tomography (CT) is widely used for non-destructive testing. However, CT inspection of compact multi-cell modules is challenging since overlapping attenuation from neighboring cells can lead to reconstruction artifacts and reduce defect contrast. In this study, CT reconstruction strategies for multi-cell LIB modules were evaluated using a Geant4-based simulation framework. Projection data were generated under the simulated conditions, and various combinations of projection processing and reconstruction methods were compared. Reconstructed image quality and defect detectability were quantitatively evaluated using the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and detectability index (d′). The results show that the combination of unfiltered projection data, OS-SART reconstruction, and Gaussian smoothing achieved the highest mean d′ across the nine cells. Compared with the baseline reconstruction, SNR, CNR and d′ improved by 233%, 119% and 117%, suggesting improved defect-to-background separation. These results indicate that reconstruction strategy significantly affects defect detectability, and optimization of reconstruction methods is necessary. In future work, experimental validation will be conducted on a prototype radiography system.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 198Poster Number:MIC-15-198] Frequency Guided Network for Quantitative PET Reconstruction with Improved Scatter Correction (#1823)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Hou (Autores: Y. Hou , Y. Chen , H. Wen , F. Zhan , J. Jiang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Normal University, School of Physics and Astronomy, beijing, China [2] The First Affiliated Hospital of USTC, Division of Life Sciences and Medicine, Hefei, China [3] Jiangnan University, Wuxi School of Medicine, Wuxi, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract PET reconstruction aims to recover the activity distribution from coincidence measurements, while accurate quantitative imaging relies on comprehensive modeling of the physical processes spanning positron annihilation, photon propagation, and detector response. Existing deep learning approaches commonly rely on end-to-end supervision using iterative reconstructions as reference labels, which limits quantitative accuracy and does not explicitly account for the physical degradation mechanisms governing PET measurements. In this work, we propose Wiener Wavelet Net (WieNet), a degradation aware reconstruction framework that models the geometric time of flight probabilistic (GTP) image as a blurred and bias contaminated observation of the underlying activity distribution. A two-stage learnable Wiener filtering strategy is introduced to address TOF induced spatial blurring through frequency domain deconvolution, while a wavelet attention fusion module performs multi energy guided scatter correction by selectively incorporating reliable low frequency information. A 3D denoiser suppresses residual stochastic noise, and an absolute activity calibration module restores the quantitative intensity scale using patient and acquisition parameters. Experiments on clinical and simulated datasets demonstrate that WieNet provides improved scatter compensation and quantitative accuracy compared with fully corrected OSEM and other baseline methods. These findings suggest that degradation aligned reconstruction integrating blur restoration, scatter correction, and quantitative calibration offers a principled alternative to purely supervised deep learning PET reconstruction.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 201Poster Number:MIC-15-201] Image-guided depth-of-interaction recovery for parallax-mitigated PET image reconstruction (#2033)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Galindo-Morata (Autores: C. Galindo-Morata , P. Galve , I. Colmenarejo , M. Abushawish , J. Udias)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Grupo de Física Nuclear, EMFTEL & IPARCOS, Madrid, Spain [2] Health Research Institute of the Hospital Cínico San Carlos (IdISSC), Madrid, Spain, Madrid, Spain [3] Spanish National Research Council (CSIC), Institute for Physical and Information Technologies "Leonardo Torres Quevedo", ITEFI, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Depth-of-interaction (DOI) information is essential to reduce parallax-related spatial blurring in PET systems using thick scintillation crystals, especially in compact preclinical scanners. We present an image-guided DOI estimation method for a preclinical PET scanner with dual-ended readout, aimed at DOI calibration from both signals. The method follows a superiterative reconstruction strategy. An initial image is reconstructed with a fixed DOI assignment and then used as a spatial prior. Then, from the list-mode file, for each event LOR indicated by a crystal-pair, several DOI candidates are compared for the said crystal pair, generating several possible DOI-LORs. Each candidate LOR is forward-projected onto the previous image, and the value of such projection is used as a compatibility metric. The DOI combination with the highest compatibility is selected to update the DOI-LOR for the given event. To assess consistency, the dual-ended energy ratio was represented as a function of the estimated DOI. The ratio-DOI distributions show a clear depth-dependent trend, indicating that the proposed method provides a DOI response correlated with detector light sharing.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 204Poster Number:MIC-15-204] Patient-Adaptable Smoothing with Deep Learning Denoising for Cardiac-gated SPECT Studies (#2052)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 X. Zhang (Autores: X. Zhang , Y. Yang , J. G. Brankov , M. A. King)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Illinois Institute of Technology, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Chicago, Illinois, United States of America [2] University of Massachusetts Medical School, Department of Radiology, Worcester, Massachusetts, United States of America [3] Hunan University of Technology and Business, School of Frontier Crossover Studies, Changsha, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In cardiac-gated SPECT studies, the acquired data counts can exhibit significant inter-subject variability. Consequently, the reconstructed images are often processed with post-reconstruction filtering in which the smoothing level needs to be adjusted individually among subjects for optimal noise suppression. In this study, we investigate an operator-interpolation approach to achieve an adaptable level of smoothing with a deep learning (DL) denoising network for processing cardiac-gated images, enabling real-time, patient-specific adjustments without retraining the DL network. We assessed the performance of this approach on a set of 20 clinical gated acquisitions using a DL network pre-trained at two nominal smoothing levels on image data from 862 studies. The results indicate that the proposed approach could achieve nearly identical denoised output images compared to retraining the DL network for a specific target smoothing level, with an average relative mean-squared-error (rMSE) below 0.15% and the structural similarity index measure (SSIM) above 0.982.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 207Poster Number:MIC-15-207] LAFOV scanner SAFOV imaging: Sensitivity Restoration by Local Tomography Approach (#2099)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 V. Panin (Autores: V. Panin , D. Bharkhada , M. Millardet)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Siemens Medical Solutions USA, Molecular Imaging, Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America [2] University of Pennsylvania, Department of Radiology, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The application of organ-specific imaging on axially long field-of-view (LAFOV) scanners is currently emerging, where an axially shorter CT acquisition defines the target region of imaging. Nevertheless, the PET system naturally acquires additional measurements, where high-polar-angle data contain contributions from both the CT-defined region and the region extending beyond it. Estimation of correction factors, including attenuation and scatter, requires knowledge of the object in the extended region using traditional approaches. The modern scanner has TOF resolution of a few centimeters, and the TOF local tomography property can be exploited for this task. High-polar-angle PET data, truncated in the TOF domain, can be used, as they contribute to the targeted region. This paper investigates this approach with the goal of faster reconstruction of the target region of interest. Scatter correction is performed using quantitative knowledge of the object obtained from reconstruction of the subset of data for which correction factors are fully known (residual scatter approach). Attenuation can be obtained by a similar approach or by the ML-ACF method using full or TOF-truncated emission data. Alternatively, the attenuation map can be estimated from the full-extent emission data compressed into a single backprojection image using a fast DL method. Preliminary investigations on the Siemens Vision Quadra show that the sensitivity of the targeted region can be restored with accurate quantification.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 210Poster Number:MIC-15-210] Clinically Feasible Deep-Learning-Enabled Dual-Gating Reconstruction for Cardiac PET (#2156)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K.-H. Su (Autores: K.-H. Su , R. Keshet , A. Langholz , B. Yuzefovich , S. Novofastovski , E. Stern , S. Peleg-Cohen , A. Lulinsky , Y. Grobshtein , G. Kovalski)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] GE HealthCare, Chicago, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Cardiac PET imaging is significantly affected by respiratory and cardiac motion, leading to image blurring and reduced quantification accuracy, particularly in motion-sensitive myocardial regions. Although dual-gating techniques can mitigate motion artifacts, their clinical adoption remains limited due to substantial noise amplification and degraded image quality. In this work, we propose a clinically feasible dual-gating reconstruction framework that integrates deep-learning-based denoising with motion-compensated reconstruction to address this fundamental limitation. The proposed method was evaluated using both XCAT simulations with known ground truth and clinical datasets from 18 patients undergoing Flyrcado and Rubidium (Rb) cardiac PET imaging. A deep-learning denoising model is applied to enhance gated images and improve the robustness of motion estimation. Motion fields are estimated using a symmetric normalization approach and incorporated into a novel multi-pose reconstruction framework, where motion information is directly embedded into forward and backward projections for efficient motion-aware reconstruction. Simulation results demonstrate accurate recovery of myocardial defects that are blurred or indistinguishable in standard reconstructions without motion correction. Clinical results show improved image sharpness, enhanced myocardial delineation, and preserved count statistics across both tracers, indicating consistent performance under realistic imaging conditions. By effectively addressing the noise-motion trade-off while maintaining computational efficiency, the proposed framework enables practical clinical implementation of dual-gated cardiac PET imaging. This approach has the potential to improve diagnostic confidence and quantitative accuracy in routine cardiac PET applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 213Poster Number:MIC-15-213] Regularized Tomographic Reconstruction for Fast Ultrasound-Modulated Optical Tomography (#2444)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Duclos (Autores: L. Duclos , A. Louchet-Chauvet , F. Ramaz , M. Bocoum , J.-L. Gennisson , C. Comtat)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Université Paris Saclay, Inserm, CNRS, CEA, Laboratoire d'Imagerie Biomédicale Multimodale, Orsay, France [2] ESPCI Paris, Université PSL, CNRS, Institut Langevin, Paris, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Ultrasound-modulated optical tomography (UOT) is a hybrid biomedical imaging modality that uses a laser beam and ultrasound (US) to reveal optical properties deep within scattering living tissues. It exploits the acousto-optic effect and is based on the detection of photons whose frequency is shifted by the US frequency. Traditionally, focused US waves are used to directly sample the optical image pixel by pixel. To improve the signal-to-noise ratio of the optical image and reduce the acquisition time, US plane waves can be used, resulting in a tomographic problem. However, the finite numerical aperture of the US probe introduces a limited-angle problem, resulting in a loss of lateral resolution. To mitigate this issue, structuration of the plane waves (SW) has been successfully tested for long acquisition times. The objective of the study is to evaluate the performances of Least Squares with Total Variation (LS-TV) tomographic reconstruction in SW UOT for shorter acquisition times, using simulated data with realistic noise levels. We show first that reducing the number of configurations of the US plane wave structuration from 1353 initially to 41 maintains reconstruction quality for a fixed total acquisition time. Then, we increase gradually the acquisition frame rate from 0.002 Hz initially to 3 Hz. Analysis with adapted regularization parameter reveals a trade-off between frame rate, noise in the reconstructed image, and contrast recovery coefficient (CRC) for an optical absorber mimicking a 1.35 mm radius tumor. Noise increases with frame rate while CRC remains stable below 0.19 Hz and drops significantly above 1.5 Hz. This study shows for the simulated setup that LS-TV reconstruction enables SW UOT imaging up to a frame rate of 1.5 Hz. It also shows that noise is the primary limiting factor for high-speed UOT rather than sparsity in undersampled SW data.
