sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 216Poster Number:MIC-15-216] Multiresolution Proximal Stochastic Denoising Regularization for Accelerated Sparse-View CT Reconstruction (#2515)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. De Paepe (Autores: A. De Paepe , D. Visvikis , A. Bousse)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] LaTIM, Inserm, UMR 1101, Brest, France [2] Université de Bretagne Occidentale, Brest, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Sparse-view CT reconstruction can reduce radiation dose and acquisition time, but it leads to a severely ill-posed inverse problem. Recent denoiser-based methods such as SNORE provide effective image priors for this setting, yet remain computationally expensive at full resolution. In this work, we propose a multiresolution extension of Prox-SNORE for sparse-view CT. The method solves a sequence of reconstruction problems from coarse to fine resolution levels, using each intermediate solution to initialize the reconstruction at the next finer level. This strategy improves the conditioning of the optimization in the early stages and accelerates convergence at high resolution. Experiments on 30-view CT show that the proposed approach achieves a better time-quality trade-off than standard and annealed Prox-SNORE, while reaching comparable final reconstruction quality. These results suggest that multiresolution optimization is a simple and effective way to make stochastic denoiser-based reconstruction more practical for accelerated CT reconstruction.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 219Poster Number:MIC-15-219] MLEM Positron Range Corrector for PET/CT (#2681)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J.L. Herraiz (Autores: J.L. Herraiz , R.J. Paneque-Yunta , N. Encina-Baranda , J.M. Udias)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Complutense University of Madrid, Grupo de Fisica Nuclear, EMFTEL & IPARCOS, Madrid, Spain [2] Health Research Institute of the Hospital Clínico San Carlos (IdISSC), Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positron range introduces a spatially variant, density-dependent blur in positron emission tomography (PET) images of high-energy emitters such as 68 Ga and 82 Rb, degrading quantification at tissue interfaces. We present a graphics-processing-unit (GPU) implementation of a heterogeneous maximum-likelihood expectation-maximization (MLEM) positron range correction with a joint expectation-maximization/total-variation (EM-TV) update, built on an exact density-weighted forward/adjoint pair derived from a recently published multi-branch range parametrization supporting eight isotopes. The forward operator combines near-field volume integration with far-field Fibonacci-sphere ray traversal of a CT-derived density volume; the adjoint is the matched transpose, and the iterative update conserves total counts exactly. The code corrects a clinical-scale 192x192x335 68 Ga-PSMA volume in 2 minutes (1 iteration, 8 subsets, RTX 3090) and produces visibly sharper structures on a 68 Ga mouse acquisition with a preclinical scanner in 45 seconds. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/jlherraiz/PRC_OSEM.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 222Poster Number:MIC-15-222] Lutetium-176-Aided Joint Activity and Attenuation Reconstruction in TOF-PET Using Trust-Region Cubic Surrogate Optimization (#2772)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 X. Zhao (Autores: X. Zhao , Z. Zhao , Z. Wang , Z. Xie)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Peking University, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Joint Maximum Likelihood Activity and Attenuation (MLAA) provides a promising CT-less attenuation correction framework but suffers from global scaling ambiguity. Intrinsic Lu-176 background radiation provides patient-specific transmission information to reduce this issue, while introducing a highly nonlinear and ill-conditioned joint likelihood. We propose the Separable Cubic Surrogate with Trust Region (SCS-TR) algorithm, utilizing an analytical Lipschitz constant and a vectorized solver to ensure strictly monotonic convergence and avoid local optima. The reconstruction is initialized with Maximum Likelihood Transmission Reconstruction (MLTR) results. GATE simulations studies demonstrate that SCS-TR effectively recovers clear bone structures and smooth uniform regions without explicit regularization. The proposed method recovered clear bony structures and uniform soft-tissue regions without explicit regularization, and maintained structural fidelity under 20% count statistics.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 225Poster Number:MIC-15-225] Organ-based Motion Correction for PET Image Reconstruction using Artificial Intelligence to Segment Organs (#2922)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Bharkhada (Autores: E. Lieffrig , V. Panin , J. Schaefferkoetter , D. Bharkhada)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Siemens Medical Solutions USA, Inc., Molecular Imaging, Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America [2] Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Respiratory, cardiac and patient motion during positron emission tomography imaging create artifacts in reconstructed images and can bias their interpretation. In this study, we propose a data-driven, organ-based method to correct motion. Our framework utilizes deep learning-based organ segmentation on no motion corrected images, followed by motion gating derived from centroid of tracer distribution computed within the segmented regions of interest on histo-images. Motion vector fields between the gated images are estimated using the Lucas-Kanade algorithm. Motion is subsequently corrected for in the corresponding gated sinograms and the motion-corrected image is reconstructed from the motion-free sinograms. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to the liver, enabling accurate estimation and correction of respiratory motion. Qualitative and quantitative results show that our method significantly improves the quality of the reconstructed images compared to no motion correction, and that the organ-specific approach also outperforms motion correction based on motion estimation on the whole abdominal tracer uptake. The average mean and maximum lesion intensities increased by 23.4% and 26.9%, respectively. Combined with better contrast observed on the reconstructed image, these findings suggest that the organ-based approach can recover some true signal that would otherwise be lost due to motion. The proposed framework paves the way for more precise, organ-focused motion correction strategies, enabling the reconstruction of high-quality images tailored to specific anatomical regions.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 228Poster Number:MIC-15-228] Multi-information Joint Iterative Reconstruction Algorithm for Cascaded Gamma Photon Coincidence (#2956)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Xu (Autores: S. Xu , X. Liu , K. Wang , Z. Yan , G. Liu , Q. Wei , H. Liu , J. Wu , Y. Liu , Z. He)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Science and Technology Beijing, School of Automation and Electrical Engineering, Beijing, China [2] China Nuclear Power Engineering Co., Ltd, Beijing, China [3] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [4] Beijing Normal University, School of Physics and Astronomy, Beijing, China [5] Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In cascaded gamma photon coincidence imaging, coincidence events offer superior spatial localization accuracy. However, their low cascade branching ratio limits detection efficiency compared to single-photon events, resulting in elevated statistical noise and prolonged acquisition times. Since simultaneously acquired single-photon events also encode the spatial distribution of the radionuclide, we propose a multi-information joint iterative reconstruction algorithm. This method fuses coincidence and single-photon events to construct a joint cost function. Given the incomplete spatial sampling of single-photon events, linearly integrating these modalities via the MLEM algorithm causes high-count single-photon data to overwhelm the high-resolution coincidence features. This leads to image distortion and edge blurring. To overcome this, we introduce a Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimation framework. Discarding the conventional image-domain spatial smoothing prior, the algorithm utilizes single-photon information simultaneously for direct image reconstruction and projection-domain regularization. Within this framework, a data weighting factor, α, governs the integration of single-photon data in the likelihood term, while a prior penalty factor, β, modulates the anti-distortion penalty. For ultra-low dose or rapid scanning protocols, increasing α leverages the high detection efficiency of single photons to bolster effective statistical counts, suppress Poisson noise in count-starved coincidence events, and enhance sensitivity. Concurrently, synergizing with β to counteract image distortion yields substantial improvements in image quality and the contrast-to-noise ratio.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 231Poster Number:MIC-15-231] Detector-Block-Level Geometric Calibration for Full-Ring Multi-Aperture SPECT Using Analytical Ray-Tracing Simulation (#3028)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Q. Wang (Autores: Q. Wang , H. Li , Y. Li)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] United Imaging Healthcare North America, Houston, Texas, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Full-ring multi-aperture single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) can provide excellent spatial resolution, but geometric misalignments of collimator apertures and detector blocks can substantially degrade image quality. We developed and evaluated a detector-block-level geometric calibration method for full-ring SPECT systems using analytical ray-tracing simulation. The simulated system used the geometry of Alpha-SPECT, consisting of 34 detector modules arranged on a ring with a 40.4-cm radius. Each module contained a 2 (transaxial) × 8 (axial) detector-block array, and each block comprised 40 × 40 CZT crystals with dimensions of 0.5 × 0.5 × 6 mm³. Each module was paired with an 18-mm-thick tungsten collimator containing sixteen 2-mm-diameter pinholes, each focused onto one detector block and separated from the detector surface by 3.1 cm. The proposed calibration estimated source-position offsets and local pinhole and detector-block misplacements by fitting three source-shift parameters and four pose-perturbation parameters for each pinhole-block pair. Simulated projection were generated by ray tracing from a 3 × 3 × 3 grid of 140-keV point sources with 2.5-cm spacing, after applying realistic random perturbations to source positions and system geometry. For each pinhole-block pair, nonlinear least-squares fitting minimized the discrepancy between measured and estimated block projections using independent multistart global optimization followed by two-stage local refinement. Across all detector blocks, the estimated geometric perturbations closely matched the known applied perturbations. Reconstruction of a small Jaszczak phantom using the calibrated geometry showed significantly improved image quality compared with reconstruction using the perturbed geometry. These results demonstrate that detector-block-level calibration can accurately recover local geometric misplacements and support robust high-resolution full-ring multi-aperture SPECT imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 234Poster Number:MIC-15-234] A flexible convex optimization framework for list-mode PET reconstruction with explicit regularization using Primal-Dual Hybrid Gradient (#3122)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Lopez Montes (Autores: A. Lopez Montes , Z. Ren , J. Steiner , R. Foygel Barber , A. Rominger , C.-M. Kao , K. Shi , E. Sidky)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Bern, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Bern, Bern, Switzerland [2] University of Bern, Department of Digital Medicine, Bern, Bern, Switzerland [3] University of Pennsilvania, Department of Statistics and Data Science, The Wharton School, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States of America [4] University of Chicago, Department of Radiology, Chicago, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Image reconstruction in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is conventionally performed using Maximum Likelihood Expectation Maximization (MLEM) or Ordered Subsets Expectation Maximization (OSEM). While highly successful clinically, these approaches are limited in their ability to incorporate general regularization functions, particularly non-smooth penalties such as Total Variation (TV). In practice, most clinical reconstruction workflows combine OSEM with post-processing Gaussian filtering, which may lead to oversmoothing or residual noise in low-count acquisitions. In this work, we propose a Chambolle-Pock Primal-Dual Hybrid Gradient (CP-PDHG) framework for PET reconstruction compatible with both sinogram and list-mode representations. The proposed formulation introduces a stacked operator representation enabling simultaneous treatment of complete sinogram and list-mode likelihood terms while naturally incorporating convex regularization functions. We derive closed-form dual updates for the Poisson likelihood and implement Huber-regularized reconstruction as a differentiable approximation to TV. The method was evaluated on simulated IQ phantom data with count levels ranging from 10 6 to 10 8 detected coincidences and on clinical long axial field-of-view (LAFOV) PET acquisitions acquired on a Siemens Biograph Vision Quadra system. In noiseless simulations, CP-PDHG achieved convergence rates comparable to MLEM, while in low-count scenarios it demonstrated substantially improved noise behavior. Regularized CP-PDHG consistently outperformed MLEM with Gaussian post-filtering in both simulated and clinical low-count reconstructions, showing improved lesion conspicuity and reduced noise propagation.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 237Poster Number:MIC-15-237] Investigation of hybrid CT-free attenuation correction framework with TOF-MLAA and deep learning (#1209)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Onishi (Autores: Y. Onishi , K. Ote , T. Isobe)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Hamamatsu Photonics K.K., Central Research Laboratory, Hamamatsu, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positron emission tomography (PET) attenuation correction (AC) is essential for achieving quantitative accuracy and is conventionally performed using computed tomography (CT). However, CT-based AC introduces challenges such as image misregistration and additional radiation exposure. Although deep learning-based CT-free AC methods have shown promising performance, concerns remain regarding the reliability and physical consistency of purely data-driven attenuation estimates. In this study, we investigate a hybrid CT-free AC framework that combines deep learning-based attenuation estimation with maximum likelihood reconstruction of attenuation and activity using time-of-flight information (TOF-MLAA). As an initial step toward this integration, we focus on evaluating the TOF-MLAA performance for attenuation-map reconstruction using emission data alone. Monte Carlo simulation was conducted using a realistic digital brain phantom and a brain-dedicated PET scanner geometry. The results demonstrate that TOF-MLAA can reconstruct attenuation maps with anatomically plausible structures and physically meaningful spatial distributions, despite residual noise and quantitative inaccuracies. As a next step, tracer-agnostic deep learning-derived attenuation estimates will be incorporated into the TOF-MLAA framework. This integration is expected to improve the stability and quantitative performance of attenuation reconstruction while enhancing the reliability and physical consistency of deep learning-generated attenuation maps.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 240Poster Number:MIC-15-240] Crystal-Wise Dead-Time Correction: Application to VRAIN (#1619)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Tashima (Autores: H. Tashima , G. Akamatsu , Y. Iwao , T. Yamaya)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology, Institute for Quantum Medical Science, Chiba, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dead-time correction is important for quantitative PET imaging; however, typical methods are approximate, as global dead-time correction is applied using system-level count-rate information. Even with more refined methods, such as block-wise correction, limitations remain. On the other hand, one-to-one coupled detectors, which provide independent signal readout for each crystal, may exhibit crystal-dependent variations in count rate and dead-time behavior. In this study, therefore, we developed a crystal-wise dead-time correction method for the brain-dedicated PET system VRAIN, in which each scintillator crystal is coupled to an individual SiPM. Singles count rates for each crystal were calculated from singles event data acquired during measurement of an 18 F-filled phantom over a wide range of radioactivity levels and the rates were used to estimate dead time. Dead-time factors representing sensitivity reduction due to count loss were modeled using both non-paralyzable and paralyzable models. The factors were estimated for arbitrary acquisition time frames and incorporated into the forward projection model of a list-mode OSEM reconstruction algorithm. To evaluate the proposed method, pool phantom measurements were performed and compared with a detector-wise correction method. The proposed method showed improved linearity with radioactivity compared with the detector-wise approach. Comparable performance was observed between the two dead-time models, while the non-paralyzable model showed slightly better linearity. These results demonstrate the feasibility of crystal-wise dead-time correction for improving quantitative accuracy in brain PET systems with one-to-one coupled detectors.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 243Poster Number:MIC-15-243] Beyond NEMA Standards: Spatial Resolution Assessment of a Dual-Rotation Preclinical PET System (#2011)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. M. Ribeiro (Autores: F. M. Ribeiro , L. Moutinho , A. C. Carvalho , A. C. Santos , P. M.M. Correia , A. L.M. Silva , J. F.C.A. Veloso)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Aveiro, Department of Physics, i3N, Aveiro, Portugal [2] University of Coimbra, iCBR, CIMAGO, CIBB, CEMMPRE, Coimbra, Portugal
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The easyPET.3D system is a preclinical positron emission tomography (PET) scanner featuring a non-conventional acquisition geometry based on the dual-rotation of two opposing detector modules, combining a fan rotation for angular sampling and an axial rotation for volumetric coverage. Its performance was previously evaluated following the NEMA NU 4-2008 standard, demonstrating consistent spatial resolution across the field-of-view. However, such assessment relies on filtered back projection, an analytical reconstruction method that may not accurately represent the performance of systems with unconventional geometries, where its application can be challenging, thereby limiting the direct applicability of the standard protocol. In this work, the easyPET.3D spatial resolution was further investigated using a micro-Derenzo phantom and iterative reconstruction (LM-MRP), enabling a more realistic and application-oriented evaluation. A quantitative metric based on the smallest resolvable rod diameter was introduced to formalize the commonly adopted smallest resolvable rod criterion and provide a simple and reproducible indicator under practical imaging conditions. The analysis was performed for the three predefined acquisition modes of the system (fast, medium, slow), previously established based on optimized operating parameters. These modes differ in axial rotation step angle and acquisition time, reflecting distinct sampling conditions while preserving the same hardware configuration. This work explores a more application-oriented approach for assessing spatial resolution in preclinical PET systems with non-conventional geometries.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 246Poster Number:MIC-15-246] PET Spatial Resolution Repeatability and Reproducibility Following the NEMA NU 2 Standard (#2134)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. A. Spencer (Autores: B. A. Spencer , Y. Wu , Y. Dong , L. Nardo , B. Mehadji)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] UC Davis Health, Radiology, Sacramento, California, United States of America [2] United Imaging Healthcare, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The NEMA NU 2 protocol provides the standard for positron emission tomography (PET) spatial resolution evaluation and benchmarking, yet its reproducibility and repeatability have not been rigorously evaluated for modern PET systems. In this study, we investigated the variability of NEMA spatial resolution measurements using the uEXPLORER total-body PET scanner under controlled experimental conditions. A total of 195 point source measurements were acquired to determine an estimate of NEMA spatial resolution uncertainty along with the effects of capillary size, activity concentration, and acquired counts. Spatial resolution was computed following the NEMA standard using in-house code and a vendor provided tool for filtered back projection reconstruction. Despite controlled experimental conditions, statistically significant differences were observed in 16 of 86 comparisons indicating limited reproducibility across experiments. From our measurements we determined that a single NEMA spatial resolution measurement exhibits an uncertainty of approximately 0.2 mm (≈5%), improving to 0.1 mm (≈3%) with repeated acquisitions. There was no observed impact to spatial resolution from capillary size (0.3-1.0 mm) or total counts acquired, while a potential dependence on activity concentration was identified but requires further validation. These findings highlight a discrepancy between reported precision in the literature and practical measurement variability. We recommend incorporating repeated measurements and reporting uncertainty to ensure meaningful benchmarking. Revisions to the NEMA protocol may be necessary to better reflect the performance of modern PET systems

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 249Poster Number:MIC-15-249] Characterization and Correction of Dynamic Changes in Sensitivity Patterns for the Jülich BrainPET-7T (#2315)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. J. Scheins (Autores: J. J. Scheins , L. Tellmann , D. Niekämper , N. J. Shah , C. W. Lerche)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Forschungszentrum Jülich GmbH, Institute of Neuroscience and Medicine (INM-4), Jülich, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [2] RWTH Aachen University, Department of Neurology, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In PET, the large dynamic range of activity in the scanner field-of-view (FOV) represents a significant challenge in accurately detecting and quantifying all incoming photons and coincidences. Block pileup and deadtime, well-known effects that increase non-linearly with the activity exposure, are unavoidable for all types of detector hardware. Thus, the observed global sensitivity at the block-level, as well as the detection efficiency at the crystal-pixel level, can be strongly impacted. The adequate characterization and correction of these sources of bias is imperative to obtain artifact-free quantitative images from the reconstruction process. In this work, we characterize such activity dependencies for our Jülich BrainPET-7T insert, which is designed as hybrid PET/MR system for advanced neuroscience applications. The new BrainPET-7T insert comprises 120 detector blocks with a three-staggered-layer design using a 12x12 matrix of digital silicon photomultipliers (dSiPM) from Philips DPC to detect light. A 11 C-decay experiment using a homogeneously filled cylinder was performed to quantify changes in terms of individual block deadtime and crystal efficiency maps as a function of the FOV activity. Assuming the low activity regime is (approx.) unbiased allows quantification of deviations with respect to higher activities by extrapolation of ground truth values. A block deadtime of 11-13% was found for a total FOV activity of 195 MBq. Furthermore, the crystal efficiency patterns showed a continuous evolution over the covered activity range, necessitating compensation in terms of dynamic adjustment of the scanner normalization to prevent streak artifacts in reconstructed images in the high activity regime.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 252Poster Number:MIC-15-252] Evaluation of the Impact of Motion Correction on PET Quantification of Early Diagnosis of Alzheimer's Disease (#2407)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 V. A. Dao (Autores: V. A. Dao , E. Mikhaylova , D. Lesnic , C. Tsoumpas)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Leeds, School of Mathematics, Leeds, United Kingdom [2] Positrigo AG, Zurich, Zürich, Switzerland [3] University Medical Center Groningen, University of Groningen, Department of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging, Groningen, Netherlands
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In this work we apply the fully automated motion correction algorithm using open source Software for Tomographic Image Reconstruction (STIR) with automated motion detection for [ 18 F]-Flutemetamol ([ 18 F]-FMM) tracer for β-amyloid accumulation in the brain cortex region. The visual results show significant improvement in contrast in the Pons and Cerebellum region with decrease blurring at the edges around the cortex region of the brain. The quantitative results shows statistically significant agreement of centiloid, a metric for early diagnosis Alzheimers' disease, between the motion corrected [ 18 F]FMM tracer and the noisy longest frame without detectable motion using the single sided Wilcoxon test at 5% compared to no motion correction.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 255Poster Number:MIC-15-255] Investigation of PET-only Data-driven Motion Detection and Correction Methods (#2633)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Beriashvili (Autores: N. Beriashvili , L. Tellmann , C. R. Brambilla , K. G. Ciantar , J. J. Scheins , E. Pfaehler , M. Chikhradze , N. J. Shah , C. W. Lerche)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Forschungszentrum Jülich, Institute of Neuroscience and Medicine 4, Jülich, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [2] Georgian Technical University, Faculty of Engineering Physics, Tbilisi, Georgia [3] RWTH Aachen University, Faculty of Medicine, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [4] RWTH Aachen University, Department of Neurology, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Spontaneous patient motion degrades image quality and compromises quantitative accuracy in brain PET imaging. In this work, we present and evaluate three data-driven approaches for rotational motion detection using list-mode PET data: a point-cloud-based principal component analysis (PCA) method operating on LOR midpoint coordinates, a PCA method applied to backprojected images, and a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based approach. Controlled measurements were performed using an anthropomorphic head phantom on a custom holder allowing isolated single-plane rotations, with ground truth determined via MRI at each position. The PCA-based methods achieved an angular precision of 1-3 degrees, with the backprojection-based implementation additionally reducing signal cross-talk between projection planes. A full comparison of all three methods will be presented at the conference.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 258Poster Number:MIC-15-258] Rigorous and accurate estimation of spatial resolution of MLEM reconstructions in PET (#2749)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Rädler (Autores: M. Rädler , P. Moskal)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Jagiellonian University, Centre for Theranostics, Kraków, Poland [2] Jagiellonian University, Faculty of Physics, Astronomy and Applied Computer Science, Kraków, Poland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positron Emission Tomography (PET) detector systems are continuously being developed and optimized to enhance sensitivity and spatial resolution. Standards, such as those defined by the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA), are essential for reliable performance assessment. However, little has changed between the first (NU 2-1994) and the latest (NU 2-2024) NEMA standard on spatial resolution assessment of PET scanners. Also, the small animal PET scanner standard (NU 4) has not been updated since 2008. Reconstructing point sources with outdated filtered back-projection remains mandatory. Although Maximum Likelihood Expectation Maximization (MLEM) algorithms are favored for achieving higher resolution and lower noise, their use for spatial resolution assessment is discouraged, since reconstructed point sources can become arbitrarily small with many iterations [1]. In this work, we propose a protocol for rigorous and accurate estimation of the spatial resolution of MLEM-reconstructed images. Our method relies on the Derenzo phantom [2], yet, any hot-rod phantom may be used. Spatial resolution is assessed in two steps. First, Modulation Transfer Function (MTF) values are extracted at spatial frequencies defined by the rod sizes. Then, a parametric MTF model is fitted to derive the resolution from the associated Point Spread Function (PSF). We show that this method converges, removing the dependence on the number of iterations. We further demonstrate that it yields spatial resolution values consistent with theoretical expectations. Therefore, we recommend updating the upcoming NEMA NU 2 and NU 4 standards to reflect established iterative reconstruction practices and enable a robust assessment of spatial resolution across PET systems.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 261Poster Number:MIC-15-261] Randomand Scatter Correction for a Brain PET System Based on List-Mode Data (#2899)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Wu (Autores: Z. Wu , H. Yang , H. Li , C. Huang , X. Jiang , W. Huang , X. Zeng , M. Niu , Z. Gu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shen zhen, China [2] Southern University of Science and Technology, Shen zhen, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In this work, random and scatter corrections were developed for N-PET, a dedicated brain PET system, using the correction framework supported by CASToR. Each detector module contains dual-layer LYSO scintillator arrays with four DOI encoding bins. Random coincidences were estimated using the delayed window method, while scatter coincidences were estimated using a GATE Monte Carlo simulation model. Both random and scatter estimates were incorporated as additive terms in the iterative reconstruction model. To improve the statistical stability of sparse LOR-level estimates, each 2×2 neighboring crystal array was grouped as one block. For each block-pair, the random and scatter counts from all corresponding crystal-level LORs were summed and evenly redistributed to the LORs within the same block-pair. Random correction was evaluated experimentally with an image quality phantom containing three hot spheres with diameters of 13 mm, 22 mm, and 37 mm. The results showed that random correction reduced background noise outside the phantom, and normalization and attenuation correction further improved image uniformity and hot sphere visibility. Scatter correction was preliminarily evaluated using GATE simulation. The proposed method increased the CRC of the 13 mm hot sphere from 0.49 to 0.60, which was comparable to the scatter-free reconstruction result of 0.59. These results show that the proposed list-mode-based random and scatter correction method improves the reconstructed image quality of the N-PET system. Future work will validate the scatter correction with experimental data and further optimize the accuracy of both corrections.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 264Poster Number:MIC-15-264] Attenuation Correction Strategies for Bain Scans in State-of-the-art TOF PET/MRI (#2990)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Teimoorisichani (Autores: M. Teimoorisichani , J. Schaefferkoetter , J. Cabello , P. Lehmann , F. L. Andersen , T. L. Andersen , P. Schleyer)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Siemens Medical Solutions USA Inc., Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America [2] Siemens Healthcare A/S, Ballerup, Denmark [3] Siemens Healthineers AG, Research & Clinical Translation, Magnetic Resonance, Erlangen, Germany [4] Copenhagen University Hospital Rigshospitalet, Department of Clinical Physiology and Nuclear Medicine, Copenhagen, Denmark [5] University of Copenhagen, Department of Clinical Medicine, Copenhagen, Denmark
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate patient attenuation maps ( μ -maps) are essential for precise PET quantification. In this study, we compared four methods for generating brain µ -maps in TOF PET/MRI scans and evaluated their impact on reconstructed PET images. We analyzed MRI segmentation, MLAA-based attenuation correction, and two deep learning (DL) approaches: convolutional neural networks (CNN) and denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DM). Two clinical studies utilizing [ 18 F]-FDG and [ 18 F]FE-PE2I tracers on a Siemens BIOGRAPH One PET/MRI (Siemens Healthineers) were examined. The MR-based technique occasionally misclassified skull bone and paranasal sinuses as soft tissue. Both DL networks produced reasonable µ -maps for [ 18 F]-FDG but struggled with the [ 18 F]FE-PE2I data, which was absent from the training set. While MLAA-based µ -maps assisted in recovering missed bone and sinuses, they were more susceptible to noise. For [ 18 F]-FDG, µ -map variations did not cause major PET quantification differences, though MLAA showed a slight overcorrection. Conversely, for [ 18 F]FE-PE2I, CNN-based attenuation led to an activity underestimation of up to 10% in the striatum. This study highlights the importance of µ -map selection, and future work will utilize PET/CT for a systematic "ground truth" comparison.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 267Poster Number:MIC-15-267] Performance Evaluation of DSAC in LYSO and Plastic Scintillators: A Comparative Simulation Study for CT-less PET (#3027)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Tiwari (Autores: S. Tiwari , S. Sharma , P. Moskal)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Jagiellonian University, Faculty of Physics, Astronomy and Applied Computer Science, Kraków, Poland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Quantitative PET requires attenuation correction (AC) to compensate for the loss of annihilation photons due to absorption and scattering within the patient's body [1]. The current clinical gold standard is CT, but it increases radiation dose, hardware costs, and registration complexity [2]. These limitations motivate the exploration of CT-less AC approaches in PET imaging [3]. One such method is Detector Scattered Attenuation Correction (DSAC), which uses detector-scattered photons to estimate the attenuation map from the PET data itself [4]. In DSAC, detector-scattered (DS) coincidences are used. These coincidences define lines of response (LORs) in which a gamma ray undergoes Compton scattering in one detector module and then deposits its remaining energy in another detector module after passing through the patient. As these photons pass through the phantom, attenuation information is encoded through photoelectric absorption and scattering. In this comparative study, we use GATE simulations [5] with two different materials, plastic and LYSO, to estimate attenuation maps via DSAC. The results show that plastic scintillator based JPET Scanner [6,7] yield a significantly higher DS-coincidence fraction (47%) than LYSO (1.2%), representing a 6.3-fold increase in useful statistics despite the lower raw registration efficiency of plastic. Single Slice Rebinning (SSRB) reconstructions show lower absolute error, better uniformity, and reduced cupping for plastic, while the phantom remains visible for LYSO despite its lower DS statistics. Our study concludes that DSAC is feasible for PET imaging with both scintillator types, with plastic offering stronger DS statistics and improved preliminary quantitative metrics

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M.N. Ullah (Autores: M.N. Ullah , G. Chinn , G. H.-S. Park , D. Anders , S. Abbaszadeh , C. S. Levin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Stanford University, Department of Radiology and Molecular Imaging Program at Stanford ( (MIPS)), stanford, California, United States of America [2] University of California Santa Cruz, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Santa Cruz, California, United States of America [3] Stanford University, Departments Physics, Electrical Engineering, and Bioengineering, stanford, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate randoms correction in PET is typically achieved via delayed-window (DW) or singles-product (SP) methods, both requiring dedicated hardware unavailable on many research PET systems. We present Non-imaging Pairs Random Estimation (NPR), a calibration-free estimator that uses detector pairs whose lines of response (LORs) lie outside the reconstruction field of view (FOV) as a random-coincidence baseline. Per-pair randoms are estimated in three closed-form steps from prompt list mode data alone. Validated against GATE Monte Carlo ground truth on data acquired across 38 simulations spanning random fractions 9-99%, NPR achieves per-pair MAE = 0.45%, matching DW (0.50%) and SP (0.35%) for spatially distributed sources. Under a 5×-singles-asymmetry hot-sphere stress test, NPR retains 1.96% MAE (matching DW, which is also robust) while SP fails by +230%/-33%. A 20-pair FPGA configuration supporting NPR45 (neighbor pairs only, MAE = 0.50%) is demonstrated on R-PET with an ¹⁸F capillary phantom.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 273Poster Number:MIC-15-273] An Exponential Total Variation Functional to Replace the Total Variation Norm (#1061)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. L. Zeng (Autores: G. L. Zeng , Y. Li)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Utah Valley University, Computer Science, Orem, Utah, United States of America [2] Utah Valley University, Mathematics, Orem, Utah, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In iterative image restoration, the total variation (TV) norm is the most common regulator to control noise and enforce sharp edges in the images. This paper proposes an exponential version of the TV norm. This exponential version of the TV norm behaves similar to the L p norm for 0 < p < 1 and it promotes sharp image edges better than the TV norm. This exponential TV is easy to implement. We use computer simulations to compare the effectiveness of preserving sharp edges by the TV regulator and by the exponential version. The image restoration task is image denoising. The exponential regulator is demonstrated as more effective in obtaining piecewise-constant images than the popular TV regulator.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 276Poster Number:MIC-15-276] Comparative Evaluation of Respiratory Motion Correction Methods for Upright Walk-Through PET Using XCAT Simulations (#1444)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Aziz (Autores: R. Aziz , T. D'Hulster , J. Maebe , C. Vanhove , S. Tao , S. Vandenberghe)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Ghent, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Ghent, Belgium [2] Shenzhen Institute of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shenzhen, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Walk-through positron emission tomography (WT-PET) is an emerging upright imaging geometry based on two vertically opposing flat detector panels. Although this design may improve patient comfort and acquisition efficiency, respiratory motion remains a major source of image degradation. This study evaluates respiratory motion correction strategies for WT-PET using XCAT anthropomorphic simulations. A 30s acquisition was simulated in a WT-PET geometry and reconstructed using an in-house MLEM-based algorithm. Data-driven amplitude- and phase-based respiratory gating were followed by non-rigid motion correction using Advanced Normalization Tools (ANTs) and Fast Algorithms for Motion Correction (FALCON). Overlapping-frame reconstruction using 0.9375s windows shifted every 0.3125s was also evaluated to assess the effect of temporal smoothing. Performance was quantified against a motion-free reference using normalized root mean square error (NRMSE), diaphragm edge width, and line profile analysis. ANTs phase-based 4-gate correction achieved the best performance, reducing NRMSE from 64% to 6% and restoring the diaphragm edge width to the motion-free reference level (25.10 mm vs. 25.79 mm). FALCON phase-based 4-gate correction reduced NRMSE to 12% but showed limited recovery of diaphragm sharpness, with an edge width of 28.40 mm compared with 28.62 mm for no motion correction. Overlapping-frame ANTs correction reduced NRMSE to 15% and yielded an intermediate edge width of 27.13 mm, although line profiles indicated residual local displacement and smoothing. These findings show that data-driven respiratory gating combined with deformable registration can substantially improve image quality in upright WT-PET.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 279Poster Number:MIC-15-279] Multi-parametric calibration and correction procedures for clinical and preclinical PET scanners: improving timing and energy resolution (#1593)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 I. Colmenarejo Allavena (Autores: I. Colmenarejo Allavena , M. Abushawish , C. Galindo Morata , P. Galve , J. Udias)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Grupo de Física Nuclear and IPARCOS, Madrid, Spain [2] Spanish National Research Council (CSIC), Institute for Physical and Information Technologies "Leonardo Torres Quevedo", ITEFI, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Modern Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scanners are increasingly complex, incorporating a large number of modular detectors that require meticulous synchronization. Precise calibration of detector parameters, such as energy response, depth-of-interaction (DOI), and time-alignment, is essential to maintain image quality. This work presents a robust multi-parametric correction pipeline applied to two LYSO based, DOI capable PET scanners: a preclinical (12 cm transaxial FOV) device and a extended Field of View clinical geometry (23 cm transaxial FOV) scanner, targeting four primary sources of systematic degradation: crystal-by-crystal energy centroid offsets, individual crystal gain non-uniformities, time alignment, and DOI-dependent energy and time variations. Calibration data were acquired from reference point sources and specialized phantoms to ensure statistical reliability. The timing alignment pipeline, which iterates recursively over crystal- and detector-level centroids, improved the Coincidence Time Resolution (CTR) by 50% through the effective mitigation of electronic offsets and time-walk effects. Furthermore, DOI-dependent energy corrections linearized the crystal response, improving energy resolution from 25.0% to 12.6% FWHM. These results demonstrate that a modular multi-parametric calibration framework significantly optimizes timing and energy performance across heterogeneous PET architectures, providing a scalable solution for high-sensitivity molecular imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 282Poster Number:MIC-15-282] Dementia Risk Estimation From a Positron Emission Tomography-Derived Latent Biomarker (#2058)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Vázquez García (Autores: C. Vázquez García , F. J. Martínez Murcia , J. Ramírez Pérez de Inestrosa , F. Segovia Román , A. Forte Deltell , I. Álvarez Illán , A. Hernández Segura , C. Jiménez Mesa , J.M. Górriz Sáez)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We investigated whether a positron emission tomography-derived latent biomarker can serve as a compact prognostic signal after longitudinal modeling. The study used 3,458 scans from 1,624 participants in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. A Bayesian mixed-effects model was fitted to the biomarker trajectory and evaluated in two practical settings: forecasting future visits for previously observed subjects and estimating short-term dementia risk from predicted biomarker values. For subjects already observed during training, future visits were predicted with a mean root mean squared error of 0.298 and a mean absolute error of 0.250. For entirely new subjects, a change-from-baseline formulation reduced prediction error to a mean root mean squared error of 0.217 and a mean absolute error of 0.171 after an initial scan. A training-only logistic calibration applied to held-out predictions reached an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.826 for future dementia risk estimation. These results suggest that the latent biomarker can move beyond representation learning and support short-term longitudinal forecasting and clinically interpretable risk stratification.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 285Poster Number:MIC-15-285] Affine rotation and scaling transformations directly over the sinogram domain images for data augmentation (#2059)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Sanz-Sánchez (Autores: A. Sanz-Sánchez , F. B. García-Aparisi , J. Prats-Climent , J. R. Vergara Quezada , M. J. Rodríguez-Álvarez)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universitat Politècnica de València, Instituto de Instrumentación para Imagen Molecular (I3M), Consejo Superior de Investigaciones Científicas, Valencia, Spain [2] Universidad Tecnológica Metropolitana, Informática y Computación, Santiago, Chile
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Data augmentation techniques applied in state-of-the-art image reconstruction with deep learning in the positron emission tomography (PET) modality are performed in the reconstructed image domain and subsequently forward-projected to the sinogram domain. In this work, we present a method for applying affine rotation and scaling transformations to sinogram images obtained from a series of simulations in GATE. The proposed algorithms were validated on 100 2D sinogram slices from Nema-like and Jaczack-like phantoms. The preliminary results from this study indicate that the proposed methods are visually indistinguishable from those obtained by applying the transformation in the image domain and then forward projecting to the sinogram domain. The quantitative evaluation was performed using the metrics Zero Mean Normalized Cross-Correlation (ZNCC), which yielded mean values over 0.95, and the Gradient Normalized Cross-Correlation (GNCC), which yielded mean values over 0.66, for both the rotation and scaling transformations. These preliminary results show that the implemented algorithms could be considered the first of their kind, designed to tackle data augmentation directly in the sinogram domain.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 288Poster Number:MIC-15-288] Multi-Hit Event Recovery in Multiplexed PET (#2294)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Narita (Autores: K. Narita , J. W. Foster , T. Yamaya , C. S. Levin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology (QST), Institute for Quantum Medical Sciences, Chiba, Japan [2] Chiba University, Graduate School of Science and Engineering, Chiba, Japan [3] Stanford University, Molecular Imaging Program, Stanford, California, United States of America [4] Stanford University, Department of Electrical Engineering, Stanford, California, United States of America [5] Stanford University, Department of Radiology by courtesy the Department of Bioengineering, Electrical Engineering, and Physics, Stanford, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Multiplexed positron emission tomography (mPET) is an emerging method that enables two or more tracer distributions to be separated from data acquired in one PET scan. The technique requires high detection efficiency for triple coincidences resulting from a prompt-gamma and two annihilation photons emitted from a positron+prompt gamma emitter. In this study, we focus on multi-hit events occurring within the same coincidence timing window inside the same detector, which are typically discarded as multi-photon hits or inter-crystal scatter (ICS). We propose a recovery method for both annihilation and prompt-gamma events from these multi-hit events, thereby improving the detection sensitivity for triple coincidences. We first generated a new charge‑to‑digital converter (QDC)-based energy window derived from single‑hit 511 keV events for each crystal. This crystal‑specific window was then applied to each hit in multi‑hit events, and then each hit was classified as either an ICS, annihilation photon, or prompt‑gamma event. Evaluation with a 22 Na point source placed at the center of the scanner showed increases of 3.5% in annihilation photon singles, 10.8% in prompt‑gamma singles, 1.1% in double coincidences, and 9.1% in triple coincidences. These results indicate that the proposed method recovers useful events and enhances triple‑coincidence sensitivity for mPET.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 291Poster Number:MIC-15-291] Hyperion DAQ: A Versatile Data Acquisition and Processing Platform (#2422)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Schug (Autores: D. Schug , O. Muelhens , E. Gegenmantel , B. Weissler , Y. Kuhl , T. Meyer , J. Thull , H. Radermacher , M. Breuer , V. Schulz)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] RWTH Aachen University, Chair of Imaging and Computer Vision, Aachen, Germany [2] Hyperion Hybrid Imaging Systems GmbH, Aachen, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present the Hyperion DAQ (data acquisition platform), a versatile MRI-compatible infrastructure for PET detector data acquisition. It combines firmware on a sensor-tile FPGA and a mainboard FPGA with a software stack that splits between a Data Acquisition and Processing System (DAPS) host - receiving and processing the ASIC data over a 10 Gig Ethernet downstream link - and a separate control computer that coordinates the platform components. The firmware handles ASIC configuration, capture and per-packet annotation; the higher-level calibration routines run in software. We have integrated the PETsys TOFPET2 ASIC as the first front-end digitization chip and built an end-to-end calibration suite on top of the platform: breakdown determination via bias sweeps, signal-level and threshold calibration via discriminator sweeps, a charge-to-digital converter (QDC) linearization sampled by on-tile test pulses and stored as a per-bin lookup table, and a time-to-digital converter (TDC) calibration driven by the natural random trigger stream from a 511 keV source. All four routines run in-system on the assembled scanner. We further report on the ASIC's test-pulse insensitivity window, showing that its position depends on the end phase of the test pulse rather than its start phase - a finding relevant to anyone calibrating the TDC with a test-pulse-based code-density method. On a Visor Max detector pair (8×8 6 mm Broadcom SiPMs read out by a single TOFPET2 ASIC, 64 LYSO crystals per tile), three ²²Na sources, 5 V over-voltage and 17°C cooling, we measure an energy resolution of 10.7 % FWHM at 511 keV and a coincidence time resolution of 248 ps FWHM. An end-to-end evaluation of the data-rate handling of the firmware and software acquisition chain will be presented at the conference. The platform is being prepared for the next generation of Hyperion-based PET/MRI scanners.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 294Poster Number:MIC-15-294] Quantifying the Effect of Partial Volume Correction on Lesion Dosimetry in ¹⁶¹Tb-FAPI-2286 and ¹⁷⁷Lu-FAPI SPECT/CT imaging (#2883)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. S. Azimi (Autores: M. S. Azimi , M. Peer-Firozjaei , M. Cheraghi , G. Divband , S. Dash , V. Malasani , K. Yadav , R. Vatsa , P. Thakral , P. Ashok , N. Sanchety , V. Hari , H. Dadgar , M. Assadi , H. Arabi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Obuda University, Doctoral School of Applied Informatics and Applied Mathematics, Budapest, Hungary [2] Obuda University, University Research and Innovation Center, Budapest, Hungary [3] Babol University of Medical Science, Student Research Committee, Babol, Iran (Islamic Republic of) [4] Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences, PET-CT Unit, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Tehran, Iran (Islamic Republic of) [5] Jam Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Tehran, Iran (Islamic Republic of) [6] Sarvodaya Hospital, Dept. of Nuclear Medicine & Molecular Theranostics, Faridabad, India [7] ABX-CRO Advanced Pharmaceutical Services, New Delhi, India [8] Fortis Memorial Research Institute, Dept. of Nuclear Medicine, Gurugram, India [9] GE HealthCare, Molecular Imaging Application Specialist, Bengaluru, India [10] Sarvodaya Hospital, Dept. of Surgical Oncology, Faridabad, India [11] Sarvodaya Hospital, Dept. of Medical Oncology & Bone Marrow Transplant, Faridabad, India [12] Imam Reza International University, Cancer Research Center, RAZAVI Hospital, Mashhad, Iran (Islamic Republic of) [13] Bushehr University of Medical Sciences, The Persian Gulf Nuclear Medicine Research Center, Bushehr, Iran (Islamic Republic of) [14] Geneva University Hospital, Division of Nuclear Medicine & Molecular Imaging, Geneva, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate lesion-level dosimetry is essential for evaluating therapeutic response in radiopharmaceutical therapy; however, its reliability in SPECT/CT imaging is limited by partial volume effects, which can significantly underestimate activity concentration in small or heterogeneous lesions. These limitations become particularly important when comparing radionuclides with different emission characteristics, such as the widely used ¹⁷⁷Lu and the emerging ¹⁶¹Tb, which emits additional low-energy electrons that may enhance microscopic dose deposition. In this study, we performed a lesion-level dosimetric analysis of ¹⁶¹Tb-FAPI and ¹⁷⁷Lu-FAPI using a Monte Carlo simulation framework based on patient-specific SPECT/CT data. Two iterative partial volume correction methods, Richardson-Lucy and reblurred Van Cittert, were applied to assess their impact on absorbed dose estimation. Lesions were segmented on SPECT images, and voxel-wise dose maps were generated using GATE simulations, followed by lesion-level dose aggregation. Relative dose differences were calculated by comparing corrected and non-corrected images. Results show that partial volume correction significantly affects lesion dosimetry for ¹⁷⁷Lu-FAPI, with dose increases reaching approximately 30.6% in bone metastases and 23.2% in liver lesions, while changes in corresponding normal tissues remained minimal. In contrast, ¹⁶¹Tb-FAPI exhibited more stable behavior, with lesion-level variations generally limited to below 10% and moderate reductions observed in lung lesions (≈ −15%). Both correction methods produced consistent trends, with slightly lower magnitude changes for the reblurred Van Cittert approach. Overall, these findings indicate that lesion-level dose estimation for ¹⁷⁷Lu is highly sensitive to image correction, whereas ¹⁶¹Tb provides more robust dosimetric estimates.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 297Poster Number:MIC-15-297] A Quality Control Framework for Deep Learning-based Attenuation Map Synthesis in PET (#2579)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Lu (Autores: Z. Ji , Y. Li , C. Jiang , C. Sun , X. Wang , Y. Lu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] ShanghaiTech University, School of Information Science and Technology, Shanghai, China [2] Shanghai United Imaging Healthcare Co., LTD, Molecular Imaging Business Unit, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Deep learning-based attenuation correction (DL-AC) offers potential advantages over conventional CT-based attenuation correction (CT-AC) in PET imaging, including avoidance of additional radiation exposure and reduced susceptibility to PET-CT misalignment. However, in DL-AC application scenarios, when CT-derived attenuation maps (CT-μ) are unavailable as reference images, quality control (QC) of deep learning-derived attenuation maps (DL-μ) often relies on manual inspection. To address this limitation, we propose a patch-level 3D convolutional neural network (3D CNN) framework for automated anomaly detection and localization in DL-μ without requiring CT during inference. During training, CT-μ was used to assist patch-level annotation of DL-μ, and artifact-free CT-μ patches without observer-identified abnormalities were incorporated as normal samples to help the model learn normal attenuation patterns. During inference, only DL-μ was used, and sliding-window prediction was used to aggregate patch-level anomaly probabilities into a voxel-wise anomaly probability map. On the validation set (51 cases), the framework yielded patch-level performance with an AUC of 0.9984, an F1-score of 0.9802, a sensitivity of 97.06%, and a specificity of 98.86%. These results suggest that the proposed framework can provide spatial cues for DL-μ, potentially supporting efficient evaluation and reducing reliance on manual QC inspection.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 300Poster Number:MIC-15-300] Generating synthetic PET/CT scans with latent diffusion models (#2763)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. H. Leung (Autores: K. H. Leung , E. Mena , P. L. Choyke , S. Ray , Y. Du)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Russell H. Morgan Department of Radiology and Radiological Science, Baltimore, Maryland, United States of America [2] National Cancer Institute, Center for Cancer Research, Bethesda, Maryland, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence approaches require training on large amounts of data to achieve acceptable levels of performance as well as generalizability. However, there is a lack of available annotated datasets for nuclear medicine imaging modalities as they are a relatively low-volume clinical modality, especially when compared to other anatomical imaging modalities, such as CT and MRI. We aim to leverage a deep generative modeling approach based on latent diffusion models to generate synthetic PET/CT images to address this issue. 18 F-FDG PET/CT and 18 F-DCFPyL PET/CT scans of 668 patients with various types of cancer, including lung cancer, melanoma, lymphoma, and prostate cancer were used to train a latent diffusion model. The data were randomly partitioned into training and test sets using a 90%/10% split. A hierarchical, latent diffusion modeling approach was trained in multiple stages. A patch volume autoencoder was trained to learn a discrete latent representation of local image volume patches using a vector quantized-variational autoencoder. A diffusion model was then trained to generate image volumes sampled from random noise in the latent space. Image quality metrics, including peak signal to noise ratio (PSNR) and mean absolute error (MAE), were evaluated across the training and test sets. On the training set, the approach yielded PSNR values of 40.85 ± 5.50 dB and 36.77 ± 5.30 dB and MAE values of 0.015 ± 0.01 and 0.021 ± 0.011 between the generated and original PET and CT image volumes, respectively. On the test set, the approach yielded PSNR values of 40.00 ± 6.19 dB and 35.48 ± 5.75 dB and MAE values of 0.017 ± 0.012 and 0.030 ± 0.075 between the generated and original PET and CT scans, respectively. The approach achieved relatively high PSNR and low MAE values, respectively, indicating that the approach generated high fidelity PET and CT images. The present study demonstrated a proof of concept for generating realistic PET/CT volumetric scans.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 303Poster Number:MIC-15-303] Characterizing Noise in Clinical Nuclear Medicine Modalities via Quantum-Inspired Framework (#2977)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Hashemi (Autores: A. Hashemi , S. Abdar Esfahani , P. Silva , A. Sinagra , P. Heidari , H. Sabet)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Harvard Medical School/Massachusetts General Hospital, Department of Radiology, Boston, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Quantum-inspired denoising is employed for clinical PET/CT, PET/MR, and SPECT imaging by treating images analogous to disordered materials and analyzing the eigenfunctions of an associated Hamiltonian. Quantum localization is quantified by the participation ratio, enabling filtering of non‑localized, high‑participation modes that dominate the mid‑frequency range and are associated with diffusive noise. By suppressing these modes and reconstructing from the remaining localized modes, noise is reduced without training data or manual regularization. The framework is applied to 46 multi‑vendor, multi‑tracer patient datasets from Massachusetts General Brigham to characterize scanner‑dependent noise structure and its impact on image appearance. Across the cohort, quantum‑inspired filtering yields consistent decreases in blind image quality scores (PIQE and BRISQUE) together with increases in entropy and Laplacian variance, indicating lower perceived noise and enhanced structural detail in the denoised clinical images.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Nemati (Autores: N. Nemati , O. Rainio , S. Palonen , E. Lehtonen , T. Maaniitty , J. Teuho , J. Tuisku , M. Irfan , N. Miller , L. Nummenmaa , J. Knuuti , R. Klén)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Turku and Turku University Hospital, Turku PET Centre, Turku, Finland [2] Turku University Hospital, Department of Clinical Physiology, Nuclear Medicine and PET, Turku, Finland [3] Turku University of Applied Science, ICT and Industrial Engineering, Data Engineering and AI technologies, Turku, Finland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Patient motion remains a common challenge in dynamic cardiac positron emission tomography (PET), as it degrades image quality and complicates reliable evaluation of motion correction methods. Realistic motion simulation requires motion models that capture the variability observed in clinical data, but this remains difficult when simulations rely on only a limited set of motion patterns. In this work, we propose a data driven framework for motion model selection and simulation in dynamic cardiac PET. We characterize motion trajectories using physically interpretable features and analyze them using clustering and trajectory similarity based on dynamic time warping to identify a compact set of representative motion models. These models are integrated with patient-specific motion scaling for frame-wise simulation of motion-corrupted PET data. The proposed framework produces stable normalized error levels across 1308 patient-model evaluations while using only a small number of representative motion models. The results suggest that the selected models effectively capture dominant motion behaviors observed in the dataset and enable realistic PET motion simulation.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 309Poster Number:MIC-15-309] Initial Validation of a High-Precision External Head-Motion Tracking System for γβ + Brain PET Imaging (#3196)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. A. King (Autores: C. Lindsay , K. Kalluri , S. Pells , M. A. Kupinski , P. Kuo , S. Abbaszadeh , M. A. King , L. R. Furenlid)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School, Department of Radiology, Worcester, Massachusetts, United States of America [2] University of Arizona, Wyant College of Optical Sciences and the Department of Radiology and Imaging Sciences, Tucson, Arizona, United States of America [3] Kuo Radiology, LLC, Phoenix, Arizona, United States of America [4] University of California Santa Cruz, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Santa Cruz, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Patient head motion during positron emission tomography (PET) brain imaging degrades system spatial resolution and quantitative accuracy; even sub-millimeter displacements can blur fine structures in highresolution systems. We present the validation of an OptiTrack PrimeX 41 fourcamera near-infrared stereocamera system for use with a novel γβ + brain-imaging prototype targeting ≤0.200mm spatial accuracy and ≤250ms temporal synchronization with list-mode data acquisition. System calibration achieved a mean residual of 0.075mm, below the manufacturer's 0.1 mm specification. Tracking accuracy was characterized over 360,000 Euclidean-distance measurements using a Capintec brain phantom displaced by Zaber precision stages (repeatability ≤0.050mm) as ground truth, yielding RMSE of 0.018-0.038mm and maximum outliers ≤0.135mm across three orthogonal directions that were at least 5× better than the 0.200mm target. Three temporal synchronization strategies were evaluated; a network-based UDP broadcast produced a correctable 17.2±2.4ms transmission delay, yielding a combined synchronization uncertainty of 57ms versus the 250ms requirement. Performance was maintained in a clinically realistic configuration with a mock 40-cm imaging bore and supine patient positioning.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Zhang (Autores: D. Zhang , H. Liu , J. Qin , Y. Gu , W. Fang , L. Wang , J. Wu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Normal University, School of Physics and Astronomy, Beijing, China [2] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [3] Fuwai Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences & Peking Union Medical College/National Center for Cardiovascular Diseases, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Tracer kinetic modeling using the two-tissue (2T) compartment model remains challenging in dynamic SPECT imaging, particularly under realistic noise conditions. In this study, we propose a noise-robust Bayesian parameter estimation method that incorporates physiological prior information for the 2T model in dynamic SPECT imaging. To validate the proposed method, we conducted both simulation study and dynamic 99m Tc-4BOH clinical study. The proposed method was compared with the conventional nonlinear least-squares (NLS) method. In the simulation study, the proposed method yielded lower relative bias in the estimated kinetic parameters ( K 1 , k 2 , k 3 , and k 4 ) than the NLS method under both low and high noise conditions. In the clinical 99m Tc-4BOH study, K 1 estimated using the proposed method demonstrated significantly stronger agreement and lower relative bias with respect to head-to-head 13 N-NH 3 PET myocardial blood flow (MBF), which was used as the reference standard, than the NLS method. In conclusion, the proposed method substantially improved the accuracy and precision of parameter estimation for the 2T model compared with the NLS method.

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We propose a kinetic-consistent conditional flow matching framework for dynamic [11C raclopride PET SRTM parametric imaging. Conventional indirect SRTM fitting is vulnerable to frame-wise count noise, causing unstable voxel-wise R1 , k2 , and BPND maps. Using 105 scans from 35 subjects, count-reduced datasets were generated at 50%, 25%, and 10% of the original counts. The model refines reduced-count indirect SRTM estimates toward full-count SRTM pseudo-reference maps using kinetic consistency, count/noise conditioning, and physiological constraints, reducing BPND deviation, high-percentile errors, and kinetic-parameter disagreement compared with indirect SRTM and denoising and regularization-based baselines

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 318Poster Number:MIC-15-318] Treatment Monitoring System for Proton Therapy Based on Beam Range Measurement (#1067)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Jang (Autores: S. Jang , J. Cho , G. Lee , T. Eom , J. Lee , J.H. Jeong , S.H. Kim , S. Cho , K. Jo , C.H. Kim)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Hanyang University, Nuclear Engineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] National Cancer Center, Proton Therapy Center, Goyang, Republic of Korea [3] Samsung Medical Center, Department of Radiation Oncology, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In proton therapy, range uncertainties can result in insufficient dose delivery to the tumor or unintended dose delivery to organs at risk (OARs). To address this, several range verification methods have been investigated, and prompt gamma imaging is considered a promising method due to the strong correlation between the dose profile and prompt gamma distribution at the distal dose fall-off location. Based on prompt gamma imaging, a treatment monitoring system was developed to measure the in vivo beam range and detect range shifts during the treatment. The developed system consists of a 72-slit parallel collimator, 144 CsI(Tl) scintillation detectors, a dedicated field-programmable gate array (FPGA)-based data acquisition (DAQ) system, and a dedicated program with a graphical user interface (GUI). The DAQ system calculates pulse height and timing of each signal from 144 detectors. The dedicated program reconstructs 1D prompt gamma distribution using pulse data and determines the beam range of each spot using a dedicated range estimation algorithm [1]. The system's performance was evaluated using a clinical proton beam prescribed to deliver 0.5 Gy to a spherical clinical target volume (CTV) with 50 mm diameter in a homogeneous PMMA phantom. To evaluate range shift detection performance, range shifts were induced at both the global range shift (1-10 mm) and local range shift (5 and 10 mm) conditions. At the same time, the computation time for range deviation analysis was evaluated. The system detected global range shifts with an accuracy of 1 mm and identified the presence and location of local range shifts exceeding 5 mm. Furthermore, the time required for range deviation analysis per layer was found much shorter than energy layer switching time. These results demonstrate the system can verify the in vivo beam range during treatment in clinical practice.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 321Poster Number:MIC-15-321] Pixelated Cherenkov Crystals for Prompt-Gamma Imaging in Proton Range Verification (#1181)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Rebolo (Autores: L. Rebolo , S. Moreno Gomez , M. Kolstein , M. Backfish , M. Novotny , R. Sahebzada , S. St. James , B. Mehadji , E. Prebys , P. M. Correia , A.L. Silva , G. Ariño-Estrada)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidade de Aveiro, Física, Aveiro, Portugal [2] University of California Davis, Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America [3] University of California Davis, Physics, Davis, California, United States of America [4] University of Utah, Huntsman Cancer Institute, Salt Lake City, Utah, United States of America [5] Crocker Nuclear Laboratory, Davis, California, United States of America [6] Institut de Fisica d'Altes Energies - Barcelona Institute of Science and Technology (IFAE-BIST), Bellaterra, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Proton range verification (PRV) in proton therapy is an outstanding clinical need. Prompt-gammas (PG) emitted along the proton track constitute a strong signal to determine the Bragg Peak position. However, the high energy of PGs (1-7 MeV), the high particle flux and the presence of significant background radiation make prompt-gamma imaging (PGI) challenging. We report on the development of pure Cherenkov pixelated detectors for PRV. The detector consisted of an 8×8 pixelated PbF2 crystal array coupled to an 8×8 S14161-3050HS-08 SiPM array from Hamamatsu, read out by a row-column signal processing board. Two analytical event reconstruction algorithms were evaluated: rise-to-the-power with k=2 (RTP2) and k=3 (RTP3). The detector was exposed to both a sealed 228Th source and a 67.5 MeV proton beam at a current of 100 pA. Floodmaps were obtained using both RTP2 and RTP3 methods to resolve the 8×8 matrix of the crystal under laboratory source irradiation. Similar results were obtained under proton beam irradiation, showing the robustness of this detector concept. In this contribution we demonstrate for the first time the ability of a pixelated pure Cherenkov detector to provide spatial resolution information in clinically relevant proton beam conditions. The prompt emission of Cherenkov light and exclusive sensitivity to highly energetic PGs offer a very high count rate capability, effective background rejection, and capacity to multiplex signals, enabling to use less channels and low power readout electronics. Future work will focus on quantitative floodmap quality metrics, detector modeling to optimize the detector geometry, and acquisition of additional data in the proton beam line at higher proton energies and beam currents.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 324Poster Number:MIC-15-324] Coded-Mask PGI for Proton Range Verification With Pure Cherenkov Crystal Detectors (#1159)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. M. Gómez (Autores: S. M. Gómez , M. Kolstein , C. Gomà , S. Marcatili , A. Wrońska , M. Rafecas , G. Ariño-Estrada)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institut de Física d'Altes Energies - Barcelona Institute of Science and Technology (IFAE-BIST), Medical Detector Instrumentation and Imaging Physics group, Cerdanyola del Vallès, Spain [2] Institut d'Investigacions Biomèdiques August Pi i Sunyer (IDIBAPS), Translational genomics and targeted therapies in solid tumours, Barcelona, Spain [3] Laboratoire de Physique Subatomique et de Cosmologie (LPSC), Physics at the service of energy and health - Medical Applications, Grenoble, France [4] Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique (CNRS), Grenoble, France [5] Marian Smoluchowski Institute of Physics, Jagiellonian University, Department of Hadron Physics (ZFH), Kraków, Poland [6] Universität zu Lübeck, Biomedical Engineering - Medical Imaging, Lübeck, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany [7] University of California Davis, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate proton range verification (PRV) in proton therapy (PT) is an unmet clinical need and is essential to exploit the full potential of PT to maximize treatment effectiveness and minimize toxicity. We present a Monte Carlo (GATE 10) study of a Cherenkov-based prompt gamma imaging system combining an array of PbF2 crystal detectors with a MURA coded-aperture collimator for real-time PRV. The detector response was studied through detected Cherenkov photon distributions generated by prompt-gammas with energies ranging from 0.5 MeV to 7.0 MeV in steps of 0.5 MeV. A threshold of 15 detected Cherenkov photons was applied to reject low-energy background, which effectively suppressed 511 keV annihilation gammas and sub-MeV contributions while retaining the prompt gammas of interest. Image reconstruction was performed using the Maximum Likelihood Expectation Maximization algorithm, with the system matrix computed with 4.4 MeV point-like sources. The imaging performance was validated on isotropic gamma point sources in both 1D and 2D coded-mask configurations across a field of view of ∼130 mm. A direct comparison between discrimination based on energy deposition (E > 1 MeV) and discrimination based on the number of detected Cherenkov photons (nckv ≥ 15) showed comparable performance, with position residuals consistent with zero within statistical uncertainties in both cases. For the proton beam measurements, background rejection was performed exclusively via the Cherenkov photon count threshold. Under realistic proton beam conditions, the distal fall-off position was reconstructed with a systematic residual below 1.5 mm and a statistical precision of less than 2 mm for beam intensities above 10^8 protons, corresponding to approximately 10 ms of irradiation at a standard proton current of 2 nA (1.25 × 10^10 protons/s). This work presents the concept and shows the feasibility of using Cherenkov-based coded-aperture imaging for PRV by means of a simulation framework.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 327Poster Number:MIC-15-327] An FPGA-based data acquisition system for remote wireless radiation monitoring (#1302)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Miyaoka (Autores: P. S. Guntha , E. Ingalls , T. M. Whalen , M. Kim , W. C. Hunter , G. Jones , S. Hauck , R. Miyaoka)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Washington, Radiology, Seattle, Washington, United States of America [2] University of Washington, Electrical Engineering, Seattle, Washington, United States of America [3] Microsoft, Azure, Redmond, Washington, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Purpose: We are developing a Personalized Remote Radiation Tracking Portable Organ Dosimetry Device (PRRT PODD) for at-home monitoring of patients receiving radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT). We report on an FPGA-based data acquisition system capable of wireless communication in support of this goal. Methods: Our acquisition system supports16-radiation detectors and outputs an energy histogram for each using a time-over-threshold (ToT) energy measurement. The electronics consists of a custom analog board that converts each detector's analog signal into a digital ToT signal; an FPGA board for signal processing; and a microcontroller board that serves as the system controller. The microcontroller communicates with the FPGA via UART to retrieve energy histogram data, manages system configuration parameters, and provides Bluetooth Low Energy connectivity to a mobile Android app. The electronics fits within the PODD's base assembly and can operate on cell phone battery power. Each detector has a small thermistor for individual probe temperature monitoring and to characterize MPPC gain versus temperature. An Android app was developed to control data acquisition and wireless transfer of data to a remote workstation. The detector and electronics acqusition system was tested using Tc-99m, Na-22 and Lu-177 radioactive sources at clinically relevant counting rates. Results: Sixteen channel operation of our FPGA-based data acquisition system has been validated using a variety of radionuclides. The output properties of the probes have been characterized versus temperature to enable post acquisition normalization of signals. Conclusion and future work : A compact, wireless 16-channel gamma spectroscopy system for remote monitoring of Lu-177 RTP was designed and tested. Future work includes implementing real-time temperature compensation based on continuous temperature readings, ensuring stable operation without post-processing.
