sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 330Poster Number:MIC-15-330] Attenuation Images from Time‑of‑Flight PET for Metal Artifact Reduction: A Phantom Study (#1406)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A.-K. Lüvelsmeyer (Autores: F. L. Peltzer , A.-K. Lüvelsmeyer , C. M. Bäcker , J. Wulff , M. Teimoorisichani , W. Jentzen , B. Timmermann , C. Bäumer)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University Medicine of Essen, West German Proton Therapy Centre Essen, Essen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [2] University Medicine of Essen, West German Cancer Centre Essen, Essen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [3] TU Dortmund University, Physics, Dortmund, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [4] Siemens Medical Solutions USA Inc., Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America [5] University Medicine of Essen, Clinic for Nuclear Medicine, Essen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [6] University Medicine of Essen, Department of Particle Therapy, Essen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Metal implants can degrade CT image quality and introduce artifacts that affect dose calculation in particle therapy. This study investigates attenuation images (µ‑MLAA) reconstructed from time‑of‑flight PET data using maximum‑likelihood reconstruction of attenuation and activity for metal artifact reduction. The linearity of a calibration curve relating CT number to relative electron density was first evaluated using a PMMA phantom with metal and tissue‑equivalent inserts. Metal artifacts were then studied in a water phantom containing a Ti6Al4V total endoprosthesis (TEP) implant. µ‑MLAA attenuation images reconstructed from PET list mode data and CT images reconstructed using iterative metal artifact reduction (iMAR) were evaluated using gamma index analysis (10%, 1 mm) relative to an artifact‑free reference slice. The calibration curve remained linear in the presence of metal inserts ( R 2 > 0.999 ). For the TEP phantom, µ‑MLAA images achieved a higher gamma pass rate (96.3%) than iMAR CT (70.8%). Using the calibration curve, the relative electron density of the TEP shaft was estimated as n e, rel = 3.58±0.12 corresponding to a 3.5% deviation from reported reference values. These results indicate the potential of µ‑MLAA images for reducing metal artifacts and supporting implant characterization in radiotherapy imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 333Poster Number:MIC-15-333] Depth-Resolved Multi-Nuclide Decomposition of Carbon-Ion PET for Range Verification (#1499)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Q. Xie (Autores: X. Li , R. Liu , D. Mu , A. Qiu , W. Hu , J. Zhu , T. Hu , L. Wan , W. Li , N. Yuki , J. Liu , J. Zhu , Q. Xie)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Wuhan, China [2] Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan National Laboratory for Optoelectronics, Wuhan, China [3] University of Science and Technology of China, Department of Electronic Engineering and Information Science, Hefei, China [4] Chinese Academy of Sciences, Department of Radiation Oncology, Zhejiang Cancer Hospital, Hangzhou Institute of Medicine (HIM), Hangzhou, China [5] Huazhong University of Science and Technology, School of Software Engineering, Wuhan, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract PET-based range verification in ion-beam therapy requires decay correction for a depth-dependent mixture of positron emitters. We introduce a range-verification-oriented carbon-ion PET workflow that partitions beam-axis reconstructions into axial slices and fits post-beam-off time-activity curves with four fixed-half-life components ( 11 C, 15 O, 10 C, 13 N); the small 13 N term (~0.4%) was grouped with 11 C for comparison. The experiment contained 120 reconstructed 10-s frames, and corresponding GATE simulation modeled 221.48 MeV/u carbon ions with 2.0 x 10 7 primary particles and seven positron-emitting nuclides. Across 35 accepted PET slices (R 2 >= 0.9), fitted fractions were 82.6%, 12.1%, 4.9%, and 0.4%, showing clear 11 C dominance. After converting fitted amplitudes to observation-window counts, plateau PET fractions were 77.5%, 14.5%, and 8.0%, versus grouped simulation values of 63.2%, 27.1%, and 9.7% for 11 C+ 13 N, 15 O+ 14 O+ 17 F, and 10 C. Carbon-ion PET agreement is therefore nuclide dependent: 10 C showed the smallest residual bias after correction, whereas long-lived carbon/nitrogen activity remains high and oxygen-group activity remains low. This nuclide-aware comparison reveals isotope-group-specific discrepancies that total-activity range metrics cannot localize.

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The IRIS group at IFIC-Valencia, as part of the FARO (Feasibility of Adaptive Surface-Guided Radiation Oncology) project, funded under the VLC-BIOMED 2024 call (AP2024VLC-01), has developed a prototype to ensure the reproducibility of patient positioning, movement management in oncology applications and correlate the patient position across different scans. The system, based on Lighthouse v2 technology, uses base stations that emit infrared light and detectors that record these pulses. Experimental measurements at La Fe University and Polytechnic Hospital have been carried out using a torso phantom coupled to a motor that emulates different respiratory patterns. The results show that our non-invasive prototype is capable of calculating static position and reproducing respiratory movement with millimeter accuracy.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 339Poster Number:MIC-15-339] A Cherenkov-Based Prompt Gamma Imaging for Proton Range and Dose Prediction Using a Multilayer Perceptron (#1783)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 X. Zeng (Autores: X. Zeng , C. Huang , X. Jiang , H. Yang , M. Niu , J. Lei , E. Quan , Z. Gu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China [2] National Cancer Center/National Clinical Research Center for Cancer, Shenzhen, China [3] Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and Peking Union Medical College, Cancer Hospital & Shenzhen Hospital, Shenzhen, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate in vivo dose range verification is critical in proton therapy due to uncertainties in beam range. Prompt gamma imaging (PGI) is promising because PG emissions correlate with the Bragg peak. However, conventional detectors can suffer from signal pile-up under high-intensity proton beams. Cherenkov detectors are attractive for PGI due to their selective gamma sensitivity, ultrafast response, and high count-rate capability. In this work, a PGI system based on PbF₂, a pure Cherenkov-emitting material, was simulated, and a multilayer perceptron (MLP) model was employed to predict proton range and one-dimensional dose distributions. The detector comprises a 32 × 32 PbF₂ crystal array coupled to a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) array, with a knife-edge slit collimator providing one-dimensional PG projections. Proton beams from 70 to 120 MeV in 10 MeV intervals were simulated in a PMMA phantom using Geant4, and 1000 PG profiles per energy were generated via Poisson resampling. The MLP was trained on 70-120 MeV beams (80% training, 20% validation), while intermediate energies from 75 to 115 MeV (in 10 MeV intervals) were reserved for testing. Predicted dose distributions agree well with ground truth, achieving sub-millimeter proton range accuracy and mean relative errors (MRE) of 0.6-2.4%. These results demonstrate the feasibility of combining Cherenkov-based PGI with machine learning for accurate dose and range prediction, supporting future real-time, beam-by-beam verification in proton therapy.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M.-E. Tomazinaki (Autores: M.-E. Tomazinaki , A.-N. Rapsomanikis , E. Stiliaris)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Post-thyroidectomy whole-body imaging after Iodine-131 administration in differentiated thyroid cancer is performed to verify biodistribution, identify thyroid bed remnants, detect locoregional and distant metastases, and support patient-specific dosimetry. The clinical standard, planar scintigraphy with a high-energy parallel-hole collimator, suffers from photon collection efficiency below 1% and depth ambiguity that can mask small remnants. We present a GATE/Geant4 Monte Carlo comparison of a clinical planar gamma camera and a compact handheld silicon/cesium iodide Compton camera at the 364 keV photopeak of Iodine-131 This translates into shorter acquisition times in clinical practice. Preliminary results indicate a sensitivity advantage of 30% for the Compton camera over the gamma camera in planar mode. The handheld geometry enables point-of-care bedside imaging of high-activity post-therapy patients, with potential to transform post-radioiodine therapy monitoring and dosimetry in thyroid cancer.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 345Poster Number:MIC-15-345] Comparison of CNN-Based Reduced-Time-Point and Conventional Single-Time-Point Voxel Dosimetry for 177 Lu-DOTATATE SPECT/CT (#2030)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Varzakis (Autores: S. Varzakis , A. Denis-Bacelar , S. J. McQuaid , J. Dickson , M. Gaze , D. Priftakis , K. Thielemans)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University College London, Insitute of Nuclear Medicine, London, United Kingdom [2] National Physical Laboratory, Medical Physics, London, United Kingdom [3] Barts Health NHS Trust, Department of Nuclear Medicine, London, United Kingdom [4] University College London Hospitals, Department of Nuclear Medicine, London, United Kingdom [5] University College London Hospitals, Department of Oncology, London, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Patient-specific dosimetry in peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) using 177 Lu-DOTATATE commonly requires multiple quantitative SPECT/CT acquisitions to estimate time-integrated activity and absorbed dose distributions. Although multi-time-point imaging improves kinetic characterization, it increases clinical workload and patient burden. Single-time-point (STP) dosimetry approaches have therefore been proposed as practical alternatives, although conventional analytic STP methods may have limited accuracy in heterogeneous activity distributions. In this work, CNN-based voxel dosimetry frameworks for 177 Lu-DOTATATE SPECT/CT were compared against conventional Hänscheid-based STP dosimetry. Quantitative SPECT/CT datasets from 44 paediatric treatment cycles were retrospectively analysed. Reference voxel-level absorbed dose maps were generated using multi-time-point dosimetry and GATE Monte Carlo simulation. Conventional STP dosimetry was performed using the Hänscheid formalism and a GATE-derived dose voxel kernel (DVK). A 3D U-Net architecture was used to estimate voxel-level absorbed dose maps from co-registered activity and density distributions using either a single 96 h activity input or paired 4 h and 120 h activity inputs. CNN-based dosimetry demonstrated reduced organ-level absorbed dose deviations across the liver, spleen, kidneys, and tumour volumes relative to conventional STP dosimetry. Mean voxel-wise NMAE and NRMSE values decreased from 45.0 % and 54.3 % for conventional Hänscheid-STP dosimetry to 20.6 % and 27.4 % for CNN-STP dosimetry using a single 96 h activity input. The CNN model using paired 4 h and 120 h activity inputs further reduced these values to 18.8 % and 25.1 %, respectively. Improved preservation of heterogeneous tumour absorbed dose distributions was additionally observed in dose-volume histogram analysis.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 348Poster Number:MIC-15-348] Design and characterization of detector modules and readout electronics for a dual head PET system for proton therapy verification (#2108)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. Rato-Mendes (Autores: L. Freixas , J. Marín , J. Navarrete , J.C. Oller , O. Vela , P. Rato-Mendes)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CIEMAT, Technology Department, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positron emission tomography has been routinely used over the past 20 years for treatment delivery monitoring in charged particle radiotherapy. Based on previous work from our group on Monte Carlo simulations of real patient treatment plans, we report on the design and characterization of detector modules and readout electronics of a dedicated dual head PET system for treatment verification in proton therapy. The detector modules are made of LYSO:Ce matrices optically coupled to silicon photomultiplier matrices, with custom-designed compact readout electronics based on the 16-channel HRFlexToT ASIC, developed by our group in collaboration with the University of Barcelona. Each 64-channel detector module is read out by 4 ASICs, followed by an FPGA which records the time stamp of each event with respect to a global clock using a coarse and a fine counter, and digitizes the time-over-threshold output of each individual channel. Results from the characterization of the detector modules under irradiation of a 22Na source have shown that all channels are readout independently, with energy spectra for all channels yielding an average 16% energy resolution at the 511 keV photopeak. The time stamp of each event was calculated at FPGA level down to 87 ps binning, allowing time-of-flight PET image reconstruction. Moreover, individual readout of all channels allows the identification of intercrystal scatter events. We are currently developing a small prototype PET system based on these detector models and readout electronics to evaluate different treatment verification methods in proton therapy.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 351Poster Number:MIC-15-351] Characterization of Prompt Gamma-Ray Emission for Helium-Ion Beam Range Verification: A Monte Carlo Study (#2288)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 W. Duan (Autores: W. Duan , H. Zhang , J. Yan , Z. Zhao , S. Wang , Z. Wu , H. Liu , Y. Liu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Prompt gamma imaging is a promising technique for in vivo range verification in particle therapy. Compared with protons, Helium-ion (He 2+ ) beams may produce prompt gamma (PG) emissions different from proton beams, affecting energy-window (EW) selection and range-positioning performance. This study investigates the PG energy spectra, EW-dependent yields, and spatial distribution features of He 2+ irradiation in a homogeneous PMMA phantom. Monte Carlo simulations were performed using GATE for He 2+ pencil beams from 70 to 230 MeV/u. Secondary gamma rays generated within the phantom were recorded using a PhaseSpaceActor , including their production positions, kinetic energies, direction vectors, and particle information. The PG spectra were analyzed and compared with proton-induced spectra. Several energy windows were selected according to characteristic spectral regions, and their PG yields, longitudinal distributions, and range-positioning performance were evaluated using Falloff50% , Falloff80% , and Steepest Falloff metrics. The simulations showed He 2+ irradiation produced substantially higher PG yields than proton irradiation over the investigated energy range, while the main spectral peaks appeared at similar energies. For He 2+ , PG yield increased with incident energy in all selected windows. The broad 1.9-8 MeV window provided the highest yield and best statistical stability, whereas narrower characteristic windows showed stronger energy specificity but lower counting statistics. EW selection also affected the distal fall-off shape and the derived positioning value. Overall, the 1.9-8 MeV window combined with the Steepest Falloff metric provided the most robust PG range-positioning performance, supporting the development of helium-ion PGI range verification strategies.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 354Poster Number:MIC-15-354] GPU-Accelerated Voxel-Wise Mono/Bi-Exponential Fitting for Lu-177 SPECT Time-Integrated Activity Estimation (#2410)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Tan (Autores: H. Tan , J. Sun , G. Chen)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yunnan Vocational Institute of Energy Technology, Qujing, China [2] Hainan University, Department of Data Science and Big Data, Haikou, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Time-integrated activity (TIA) estimation is essential for patient-specific Lu-177 SPECT dosimetry, but voxel-wise time-activity curve fitting remains computationally demanding because nonlinear kinetic models must be solved independently across many voxels. This study developed a GPU-accelerated voxel-wise kinetic modeling framework for rapid Lu-177 SPECT TIA estimation. Four serial post-therapy SPECT/CT scans from anonymized Lu-177 DOTATATE datasets were analyzed. The framework used a hierarchical TAC model library, including one mono-exponential model and three bi-exponential variants, to characterize different uptake and clearance patterns. Model selection was performed using the Akaike information criterion, and voxels with insufficient fitting quality were processed using trapezoidal integration with tail extrapolation. GPU acceleration was implemented through batched voxel-wise optimization using CuPy-based array operations and compared with a CPU-based Levenberg-Marquardt implementation. Evaluation included fitting quality, model-selection distribution, agreement with dataset-provided reference TIA maps, organ/lesion-level relative error, and computation time. The GPU implementation preserved the CPU-derived model-selection distribution, with 60.7% mono-exponential, 31.2% bi-exponential, and 8.1% trapezoidal fallback voxels. The median regional voxel-wise fitting R² was 0.848. Relative differences from reference TIA maps were 4.2% for kidneys, 3.5% for spleen, 2.7% for liver, and 8.5% for tumor lesions. Computation time decreased from 552.1 s to 18.5 s per patient, corresponding to approximately 30-fold acceleration. These preliminary results support the technical feasibility of GPU-accelerated voxel-wise TAC fitting for practical Lu-177 SPECT dosimetry, although validation in larger multi-patient datasets remains necessary.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 357Poster Number:MIC-15-357] A Three-Stage Scintillator-Compton Camera for BNCT: From Point-Source Resolution to Phantom Reconstruction (#2560)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. López Martínez (Autores: S. López Martínez , C. Veiga , R. Speller , R. Moss)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University College London, Department of Medical Physics and Biomedical Engineering, London, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Boron Neutron Capture Therapy (BNCT) requires accurate in-vivo dose verification, yet current clinical methods rely on indirect blood-based boron concentration estimates that introduce substantial inter-patient variability. Imaging the 478 keV prompt gamma ray emitted during boron-10 neutron capture offers a direct route to real-time dose mapping. However, this requires a detector capable of efficient reconstruction at high gamma energies in the presence of significant background. Building on our previously reported scintillator-based Compton camera concept [1], we present the full computational characterisation of a three-stage system comprising scintillator cylinders arranged in a three-dimensional spherical array. The non-planar geometry offers multi-directional cone orientations, improving global spatial resolution compared to conventional planar designs. Geant4 Monte Carlo simulations were used to model a realistic BNCT irradiation scenario [2], incorporating a modified Snyder head phantom with clinically representative boron concentrations (25 ppm brain / 65 ppm tumour) [3]. Reconstruction performance is evaluated across scenarios of increasing complexity: an idealised point source, a distributed gamma-ray source, a treatment-like gamma source, and a full phantom simulation. This progressive approach illustrates how reconstruction quality is affected by increasing complexity and the high neutron-induced background inherent to BNCT environments, providing insight into the current limitations of the design and potential strategies to address them. These results establish a validated simulation framework for a scintillator-based Compton camera tailored to BNCT prompt gamma imaging, providing the foundation for forthcoming experimental characterization and clinical translation.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 360Poster Number:MIC-15-360] Impact of PET Energy Window Selection on Y-90 Radioembolization Dosimetry (#2682)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Strugari (Autores: M. Strugari , S. Romero García , F. Jansen , K.-H. Su , M. Spangler-Bickell , P. García-Polo , D. Pérez Enguix , L. Martí-Bonmatí , I. Torres Espallardo)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto de Investigación Sanitaria La Fe, Biomedical Imaging Research Group (GIBI230), Valencia, Spain [2] Hospital Universitario y Politécnico La Fe, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Valencia, Spain [3] GE HealthCare, Department of Engineering, Waukesha, Wisconsin, United States of America [4] GE HealthCare, Molecular Imaging and CT Engineering, Waukesha, Wisconsin, United States of America [5] GE HealthCare, PET/MR Engineering, Waukesha, Wisconsin, United States of America [6] GE HealthCare, Science and Technology Office, Madrid, Spain [7] Hospital Universitario y Politécnico La Fe, Department of Radiology, Valencia, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Selective internal radiation therapy using 90 Y microspheres provides targeted treatment of liver malignancies, with post-therapy PET enabling treatment verification and voxel-based dosimetry. Quantitative 90 Y PET imaging is challenged by a low signal-to-background ratio. The internal pair production branching ratio of 90 Y is low, yielding a weak 511 keV annihilation photon signal amid background contributions from bremsstrahlung following β - decay and intrinsic radiation from 176 Lu in PET systems constructed with LYSO scintillation crystals. These background events increase random coincidences and degrade spatial localization and dosimetric accuracy. This study evaluated the effect of PET energy window selection on 90 Y radioembolization dosimetry using standard (425‑650 keV) and narrow (480‑542 keV) energy windows. Six patients underwent post-therapy PET/MR imaging. Images were reconstructed using TOF‑OSEM, and absorbed dose distributions were calculated using local deposition modelling. Randoms fraction, apparent activity outside the perfused volume, dose-volume histograms, and dose-volume metrics were compared between protocols. The narrow-window protocol reduced the randoms fraction from 91 ± 3% to 60 ± 10% and apparent activity outside the perfused volume by 51 ± 16%, indicating reduced background contamination and improved confinement of the reconstructed activity distribution. Mean absorbed doses to the tumour and healthy liver were preserved, and healthy liver V 30 decreased by 13 ± 8%. Tumour D 70 changed by -15 ± 33%, and tumour dose redistribution effects varied substantially between patients without a consistent directional trend. These findings demonstrate that narrow-window PET acquisition improves activity localization in 90 Y radioembolization while preserving overall absorbed dose estimates and may influence patient-specific voxel-based dosimetry.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 363Poster Number:MIC-15-363] A Compton Camera Using GAGG Scintillators Coupled with SiPM Array Readout for Online Monitoring in Particle Therapy (#2860)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Wang, Y. Wang (Autores: Y. Wang , Y. Wang , J. Peng, J. Peng , J. Chen, J. Chen , Y. Yin, Y. Yin , J. Shao, J. Shao , C. Zhang, C. Zhang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lanzhou University, School of Nuclear Science and Technology, Lanzhou, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Particle therapy exploits the Bragg peak for precise dose deposition, yet the high-LET characteristic demands accurate real-time range verification and dose distribution monitoring. Compton cameras offer a promising collimator-free solution for the prompt gamma imaging induced during treatment. In this work, a Compton camera is constructed by using Gd 3 Al 2 Ga 3 O 12 :Ce (GAGG) scintillator coupled with silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) arrays. The scatter and absorber layers are both constructed from high-light-yield, high-energy-resolution GAGG with optimized geometry. An energy resolution of ~8% FWHM is obtained for 511 keV gamma rays, while the position resolution is 1.5 mm (scatter layer) and 2.0 mm (absorber layer) in both x and y directions. The scatter layer retains the capability for dual-ended readout, with an expected DOI resolution of ~2.5 mm. Image reconstruction is performed using GPU-accelerated LM-MLEM. Laboratory measurements with a 22 Na source demonstrate that an angular resolution of ~7° at 511 keV and ~6° at 1274 keV was achieved. Future work will focus on proton/carbon ion beam experiments and scaling the effective detector area to 100 mm × 100 mm.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 366Poster Number:MIC-15-366] In Silico Optimization of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 Therapy Regimens (#3011)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Ryhiner (Autores: M. Ryhiner , I. Fajnorova , I. C. Azrour , A. Fakharpour , J. Czernin , A. Rominger , C. Meyer , C. Mona , K. Shi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Bern, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Bern, Bern, Switzerland [2] University of California, Los Angeles, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Los Angeles, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study presents a data-driven framework for optimizing dosimetry regimens in radiopharmaceutical therapy using in vivo data from [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-617-treated murine models incorporating therapy resistance. Experimental data demonstrated improved long-term outcomes for cumulative (3 × 10 MBq) and de-escalation (20 MBq + 10 MBq) regimens compared with conventional single-dose (30 MBq) and escalation (10 MBq + 20 MBq) schedules. Building on these findings, additional treatment regimens were evaluated in silico to identify combinations of favorable therapeutic characteristics. Dose-rate kernels derived from dynamic SPECT/CT imaging were used to calibrate an integrated dose-response and tumor growth model. These kernels captured both the temporal evolution of dose rates following treatment and spatial intratumoral heterogeneity through region-specific dose quantiles. Therapy resistance across treatment cycles was incorporated using generalized dose-rate patterns derived from experimentally observed relationships between treatment response and previously administered activity ratios. The spatial distribution of dose-rate regions used for kernel generation was best described by an exponential decay model, yielding a lower Akaike Information Criterion (AIC: −139 ± 31) than alternative distributions. Simulations identified the 3-2-1 (15, 10, 5 MBq), 2-1-1 (15, 2 × 7.5 MBq), and 2-2-1 (2 × 12, 6 MBq) regimens as outperforming the experimentally tested schedules. These results demonstrate the potential of simulation-based optimization to support the design of biologically informed radiopharmaceutical therapy regimens and provide a framework for systematic in silico treatment planning.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 369Poster Number:MIC-15-369] Energy-Shifting: an efficient approach for Monte Carlo Particle Therapy Dose Calculation (#3092)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Bert (Autores: C.-H. Pham , D. Benoit , V. Bourbonne , U. Schick , D. Visvikis , J. Bert)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Brest, LaTIM, INSERM-UMR1101, Brest, France [2] Brest Hospital University, Radiotherapy Department, Brest, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract While recent deep learning techniques for accelerating Monte Carlo (MC) radiotherapy dose calculation have shown promising results, most state-of-the-art methods rely on a denoising paradigm. This approach aims to predict a high-sampling (HS) reference dose map from a fast low-sampling (LS) input. However, information loss and stochastic noise in LS inputs often limit the accurate recovery of fine structural details and dose gradients, and may lead to hallucinations. To address these limitations, we propose a novel learning framework, Energy-Shifting, which reconstructs a time-intensive polyenergetic HS dose distribution from a GPU-accelerated monoenergetic dose map. Our results demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms conventional denoising approaches in accuracy.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 372Poster Number:MIC-15-372] Human Single Time Point Dosimetry Using Weight-Based Extrapolated Mouse Effective Half-Life (#3228)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Yang (Autores: M. Almaslamani , J. Yang , I. Lim , K.I. Kim , S.K. Woo)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Division of Applied RI, Korea Institute of Radiological and Medical Sciences, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] University of Science & Technology, Radiological & Medico-Oncological Sciences, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [3] Korea Institute of Radiological and Medical Sciences, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Image-based dosimetry requires multiple-time-point (MTP) imaging to estimate the time-integrated activity (TIA), which can be challenging to implement in clinical practice. Moreover, Mouse-to-human extrapolation methods produces large errors. This study aimed to evaluate single-time-point (STP) dosimetry approach using extrapolated human effective half-life derived from preclinical activity scaling based on body weight and organ mass. Six patients underwent where administrated with 64 Cu-DOTA-rituximab and underwent MTP PET/CT imaging at 1, 24, and 48 h post-injection (p.i.), while four mice were imaged at 1, 24, 48, and 72 h p.i. Regions of interest were manually drawn for the kidney, liver, and spleen. Human MTP reference TIA was calculated using OLINDA with mono-exponential fitting. Mouse organ activity was converted to estimated human organ activity using body weight and organ mass scaling as: (%ID/organ) human =(%ID/g) mouse ×(kg WB ) mouse ×(g Organ /kg WB ) human . Human TIA was then estimated from the extrapolated activity curve. In the proposed approach, the extrapolated human time-activity curve was used to derive the extrapolated human effective half-life. This effective half-life was then combined with the measured human organ activity from STP scan and TIA was calculated as following: TIA=(A(T sc )/ln(2))×2 Tsc/Teff(extrapolated) × T eff(extrapolated). . The proposed STP approach reduced the estimation error for kidney from 88.7% with the conventional extrapolation approach to 29.0%, 40.6%, and 66.7% at 1, 24, and 48 h p.i., respectively. The corresponding errors decreased from 406% to 26.8%, 35.1%, and 65.3% for the liver, and from 480% to 42.2%, 57.7%, and 76.2% for the spleen, respectively. These results demonstrate that incorporating measured human STP activity with extrapolated human effective half-life improves TIA estimation and provide a practical dosimetry approach when full MTP imaging is not feasible.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 375Poster Number:MIC-15-375] Deep Learning-based CT-Free Deformable Registration for PET-CT Misalignment Correction (#1875)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Mehranian (Autores: A. Mehranian , S. Wollenweber , F. Kotasidis , Z. Chalampalakis , A. Lulinsky , H. Ratner , R. Johnsen , G. Kovalski)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] GE HealthCare, Oxford, United Kingdom [2] GE HealthCare, Waukesha, United States of America [3] GE HealthCare, Zurich, United Kingdom [4] GE HealthCare, Buc, France [5] GE HealthCare, Haifa, Israel
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Respiratory phase mismatches between PET and CT commonly cause artifacts in PET/CT, especially at lung-liver and lung-spleen interfaces. Since CT captures a single respiratory phase while PET reflects an average over breathing, this misalignment leads to attenuation correction errors and inaccurate lesion quantification, particularly near the liver dome. We propose a deep learning framework that uses PET-based pseudo-CT to guide deformable CT-to-PET alignment. A retrospective dataset of 10 18F-FDG exams with respiratory phase mismatch (banana) artifacts, scanned on a Total-Body BGO-based PET/CT scanner, was used for evaluation. A previously trained 3D residual neural network was used to generate pseudo-CT images from non-attenuation corrected (NAC) PET images. The pseudo-CT images, inherently aligned with the PET data, were then used as a reference for deformable registration of the CT images. The original and registered CT images were used for attenuation correction and reconstruction of the PET data using a BSREM algorithm. Regions of interested were placed in dome of the liver to quantitatively measure the SUV changes in those regions affected by the artifacts. Compared to baseline PET/CT without correction, the proposed method effectively reduced or eliminated respiratory-induced PET/CT misalignment artifacts were significantly reduced or eliminated. Quantitatively, the method achieved improvements in liver SUVmean towards the expected values. By leveraging the native alignment between PET and the generated pseudo-CT, the method avoids direct multimodal registration and instead enables accurate deformable alignment of CT to PET space. This approach improves attenuation correction and quantitative accuracy, with potential to enhance diagnostic confidence in routine clinical PET/CT imaging

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 378Poster Number:MIC-15-378] Investigation of Image Quality Gains Using Variable Time Windows in Long-Axial PET Systems (#1914)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Jiang (Autores: Y. Chen , Y. Hou , J. Jiang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Normal University, school of physics and astronomy, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The extension of the axial field-of-view (AFOV) represents a transformative advancement in PET, offering superior sensitivity and enabling ultra-low-dose 4D imaging. However, the increased AFOV necessitates wider acceptance angles and correspondingly larger coincidence time windows, leading to a substantially higher proportion of random coincidence events compared to conventional scanners. While traditional random correction relies on noisy, sparse delayed coincidence sinograms, the singles-rate method has been approved as a superior alternative for long-axial FOV (LAFOV) systems. A critical yet underexplored challenge in LAFOV PET is the significant variation in the required time window across different ring differences. Although object-specific customized windows have shown promise in short-axial systems, their application to total-body PET remains largely unoptimized. In this study, we propose a novel reconstruction strategy utilizing a variable time window tailored to specific ring differences to minimize random fractions. Using GATE simulations of a 1.5-m total-body PET system (uMI Panorama GS), we designed and evaluated a variable time window set based on practical coincidence time resolution (CTR). This approach was benchmarked against a standard fixed window (6.0 ns) and a 3-step window (4.7, 6.2, and 8.3 ns). Systematic analysis of simulated coincidence data reveals that the variable window design significantly reduces the random fraction. Comparative reconstructions of a uniform cylinder, NEMA, and torso phantoms demonstrate that this reduction directly translates to lowered image noise levels and enhanced signal-to-noise ratios within a consistent reconstruction framework. These findings establish that ring-difference-specific time windows provide a robust technical pathway for maximizing the quantitative performance of next-generation LAFOV PET systems.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 381Poster Number:MIC-15-381] Evaluation of TOF-DOI Crystal Topologies for the HD-MetaPET MRI Insert (#2140)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Meyer (Autores: T. Meyer , G. Terragni , D. Schug , Y. Kuhl , B. Weissler , E. Gegenmantel , O. Muelhens , H. Radermacher , M. Pizzichemi , E. Auffray , V. Schulz)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] RWTH Aachen University, Chair of Imaging and Computer Vision, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [2] CERN, Geneva, Switzerland [3] Hyperion Hybrid Imaging Systems GmbH, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [4] University of Milano-Bicocca, Milan, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The HD-MetaPET project is developing a high-resolution positron emission tomography insert for simultaneous magnetic resonance imaging. The insert will consist of 120 Hyperion Visor Max detector tiles with an area of 56.5 x 56.5 mm 2 , arranged in two semi-circles and coupled to LYSO:Ce crystal scintillators. A crucial optimisation parameter for the upcoming system performance is the crystal topology. This study evaluates Time-of-Flight and Depth-of-Interaction positioning performance across several crystal topologies: continuous slabs, pseudoslabs, and pixelated arrays with a light guide coupled to the face opposite the photosensitive detector. The study utilizes the Hyperion Visor Max and a custom development board, both featuring the TOFPET2 ASIC. Experimental measurements are performed using a 22 Na point source. The preliminary results with crystals of different materials show that pixelated arrays with light guides outperform continuous slabs. Specifically, pixelated designs achieved a Coincidence Time Resolution of ≈235 ps, compared to >400 ps for the slabs. The results indicate that the pixelated designs utilizing the light guide also demonstrated superior accuracy in the evaluation of the Depth-of-Interaction. The pixelated light-guide topology shows promising performance, circumventing the traditional compromise between spatial depth accuracy and timing resolution. Consequently, this configuration emerges as a good candidate for integration into the upcoming HD-MetaPET scanner. While these preliminary results are promising, the comprehensive evaluations utilizing final-scale crystals of the same material and the final scanner electronics will be presented at the conference.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 384Poster Number:MIC-15-384] Towards Clinically Compatible Dynamic PET: Enabling Kinetic Analysis with 20-Minute Acquisitions (#2711)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 I. Incicco (Autores: I. Incicco , D. Dall'Olio , I. Brusa , R. Mei , A. Farolfi , C. Nanni , B. A. Spencer , G. Wang , L. Nardo , S. Fanti , G. Castellani)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Bologna, Department of Medical and Surgical Sciences, Bologna, Italy [2] IRCCS Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria di Bologna, Nuclear Medicine, Bologna, Italy [3] University of California-Davis, Department of Radiology, Davis, California, United States of America [4] Alma Mater Studiorum University of Bologna, Nuclear Medicine, Bologna, Italy [5] IRCCS Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria di Bologna S.Orsola, 40138, Bologna, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dynamic PET imaging enables tracer kinetics characterization, offering complementary quantitative insights beyond static imaging. The advent of Long Axial Field-of-View (LAFOV) scanners, with high sensitivity, has renewed interest in kinetic modelling by enabling whole-body dynamic imaging in clinical settings. However, acquisitions can last up to 1 hour, limiting adoption due to reduced throughput. Clinically, reporting relies on late-phase images (1-hour post-injection), whereas kinetic modelling requires data from injection, creating a conflict between clinical requirements and feasibility. This work investigates whether dynamic protocols can be shortened to 20 minutes post-injection while preserving clinically relevant information by predicting late-phase time-activity curves (TACs) from early dynamic data. The cohort included 107 subjects imaged with 18 F-FDG, yielding 20,903 TACs extracted from multiple anatomical structures. Four approaches were compared: a three-exponential model, two-tissue compartment model (2TCM), a gated recurrent unit encoder-decoder, and a novel Neural Ordinary Differential Equation framework (NODE). At 60 minutes, all methods showed near-zero median residuals. Over 20-60 min, NODE outperformed competing approaches with the lowest root mean squared error (0.096) and χ 2 (0.43), and the highest concordance correlation coefficient (0.40), with reduced variability across TACs. Overall, prediction of late-phase PET information from 0-20 min data appears feasible. NODE provided the most accurate and stable results, although 2TCM remained competitive at 60 min, suggesting benefits from incorporating physiological priors. Future work will extend the analysis to voxel-wise reconstruction, with preliminary results showing promising outcomes, and will examine kinetic parameter consistency between observed early dynamics (0-20 min) and full predicted dynamic data (0-60 min).

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 387Poster Number:MIC-15-387] SADCA-ResDiff: A Structure-Aware Dual Cross-Attention Residual Diffusion Network for MR-Free Partial Volume Correction in Amyloid Brain PET (#1005)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Huang (Autores: R. Huang , Y. Liu , Z. Fang , Z. Hu , G.S.P. Mok)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Macau, Biomedical Imaging Laboratory (BIG), Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Faculty of Science and Technology, Macao, China [2] Chinese Academy of Sciences, Research Center for Medical AI, Shenzhen Institute of Advanced Technology, Shenzhen, China [3] University of Macau, Centre for Cognitive and Brain Sciences, Institute of Collaborative Innovation, Macao, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Partial volume effects (PVE) degrade quantitative accuracy and blur boundaries in PET. MR-guided partial volume correction (PVC) can mitigate PVE, but it requires anatomical information from MR, which may be unavailable. This work aims to develop a 2-stage deep learning-based PET to MR synthesis framework, SADCA-ResDiff, to provide structural priors for MR-guided PVC in 18F-AV45 amyloid brain PET. A total of 135 pairs of 18F-AV45 PET and MR were selected from ADNI [1]. A coarse MR is first generated from PET using a dual cross-attention UNet, while a residual diffusion network with an edge-aware mechanism is applied to refine the coarse MR. Joint mutual information, diffusion, reconstruction, and structure-aware symmetric consistency losses derived from a pretrained MR segmentation model were used to optimize the 2-stage network. Synthesized MR was segmented into gray matter (GM), white matter (WM), and cerebrospinal fluid masks using FSL [2] and applied to the Iterative-Yang (IY) PVC [3]. SADCA-ResDiff was compared with DeepPVC [4], using standard IY as reference. Structural similarity index (SSIM) and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) was measured on the whole brain while regional error was evaluated using relative mean absolute error (RMAE) for GM and WM. Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used for statistical comparison. SADCA-ResDiff achieved the highest SSIM and PSNR among all methods (0.97±0.02 and 32.62±3.43dB), significantly outperforming DeepPVC (0.93±0.02 and 27.95±3.67dB) and origin PET (0.90±0.02 and 26.73±3.89dB) (all p<0.05). It also yielded the lowest RMAE in GM and WM (0.12±0.05 and 0.08±0.05), compared with DeepPVC (0.14±0.04 and 0.15±0.03) and origin PET (0.16±0.04 and 0.15±0.03). SADCA-ResDiff provides effective anatomical guidance for PVC in amyloid PET, offering a practical solution for MRI-free PET quantification.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 390Poster Number:MIC-15-390] A comparison of deep-learning-based attenuation correction methods in brain perfusion SPECT (#1100)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Osorio Durán (Autores: R. Osorio Durán , G. A. Adame Ocampo , M. D.L. Martínez Gudiño , M. Rodríguez Villafuerte , A. Martínez Dávalos)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto Nacional de Psiquiatría, Departamento de Imágenes Cerebrales, CDMX, Mexico [2] Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Instituto de Física, CDMX, Mexico
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A locally developed database of human brain studies from 113 subjects has been used to develop and train convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for attenuation correction in SPECT. All subjects underwent brain perfusion SPECT imaging studies with 99m Tc-ECD, an X-ray CT scan, and MRI. Images were preprocessed for anonymization, removal of the table in CT, co-registration, and spatial and intensity normalization. Deep learning architectures encompassed U-Net, Residual U-Net, Attention U-Net and Residual Attention U-Net. Three methods were evaluated: (a) direct mapping of uncorrected SPECT to corrected SPECT, (b) multisequence MRI scans to synthetic CT (sCT) mapping, followed by iterative reconstruction with sCT attenuation correction, and (c) CNN reconstruction using sinograms to directly generate attenuation-corrected SPECT images. To evaluate the attenuation-corrected images, the mean square error (MSE), peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM) were calculated. Attenuation corrections were successfully applied using three different approaches, addressing various clinical scenarios found in clinical medical equipment that does not have CT for attenuation correction, such as dedicated SPECT or SPECT/MRI.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 393Poster Number:MIC-15-393] Assisting Total-Body Multiplexed PET Separation Using Synthetic Paired Data (#1368)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Prokopenko (Autores: D. Prokopenko , A. J. Reader)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] King's College London, London, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Multiplexed positron emission tomography (mPET) remains limited by the challenge of separating overlapping tracer signals, as tracers produce indistinguishable same-energy photon pairs. Existing deep learning-based separation methods are constrained by the limited real data availability, particularly in the context of total-body imaging. In this work, we propose a framework for training total-body dual-tracer mPET separation models using synthetic paired datasets generated from independent single-tracer acquisitions, and investigate the effect of synthetic data diversity on separation performance. Two score-based generative models were trained to generate synthetic [18F]FDG and [18F]PSMA PET images conditioned on attenuation maps. Complementary synthetic tracer images were combined with real PET acquisitions to construct paired dual-tracer datasets for training a Swin UNETR-based separation model. Quantitative evaluation on dual-tracer combinations demonstrated the feasibility of the proposed framework and suggested that increased diversity of synthetic samples may improve separation robustness. These results highlight the potential of generative augmentation as a scalable strategy for pretraining mPET separation models under limited paired-data availability.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 396Poster Number:MIC-15-396] A Multi-Client Split Federated Diffusion Framework for Resource-Efficient Cardiac-Gated MP-SPECT Denoising (#1592)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Sun (Autores: C. Li , J. Huang , Z. Fu , Y. Shi , Z. Sun , Z. Xu , Y. Zeng , H. Xiao , H. Wang , J. Sun)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Hainan University, Department of Data Science and Big Data, Haikou, China [2] Hainan Hospital of Chinese PLA General Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Sanya, China [3] The Second Affiliated Hospital of Hainan Medical University, Department of Radiation Oncology, Cancer Treatment Center, Haikou, China [4] The First Affiliated Hospital of Hainan Medical University, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Haikou, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Diffusion models have shown strong potential for cardiac-gated myocardial perfusion single-photon emission computed tomography (CG MP-SPECT) denoising. However, centralized or fully federated diffusion training requires each client to process a complete high-capacity model, which may be impractical for resource-limited nuclear medicine departments. This study presents a multi-client split federated learning diffusion framework (SFLDiff) for resource-efficient CG MP-SPECT denoising. SFLDiff vertically partitions the diffusion network into lightweight client-side encoders and a server-side reconstruction module, enabling local clients to perform shallow feature extraction while computationally intensive generative restoration is executed on the server. This architecture reduced client-side GPU memory consumption from over 4300 MiB to approximately 257 MiB with a training time of 2950.39 s while maintaining competitive denoising performance. Experiments on 8-/16- cardiac gated datasets showed that SFLDiff achieved image restoration accuracy comparable to centralized and federated diffusion baselines and superior to standard split learning, particularly under high-noise gated conditions. These results suggest that multi-client split federated diffusion provides a practical quality-efficiency trade-off for deploying advanced generative denoising models in resource-constrained CG MP-SPECT environments.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 399Poster Number:MIC-15-399] Weakly Supervised Cyclic Disentanglement for Delayed PET Image Synthesis (#1702)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Sun (Autores: Z. Sun , L. Fu , C. Li , Z. Xu , Q. Wang , Y. Zeng , H. Xiao , L. Tong , J. Sun)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Hainan University, Department of Data Science and Big Data, Haikou, China [2] Haikou Affiliated Hospital of Xiangya Medical College, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Haikou, China [3] The Second Affiliated Hospital of Hainan Medical University, Department of Radiation Oncology, Cancer Treatment Center, Haikou, China [4] The First Affiliated Hospital of Hainan Medical University, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Haikou, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dual-time-point positron emission tomography (PET) provides complementary temporal uptake information for lesion characterization, but delayed imaging increases examination time and clinical workload. This study proposes UCD-Net, a weakly supervised cyclic disentanglement framework for synthesizing delayed-pass PET from first-pass PET. UCD-Net decompose first-pass PET images into a delayed-equivalent component, a signal-dependent residual component, and a signal-independent residual component, followed by cyclic re-decomposition to improve latent-component separation. Reconstruction, zero-mean, identity-consistency, and noise-statistical constraints are used to preserve image content and suppress residual interference. A three-dimensional projection-excitation module captures global spatial statistics along depth, height, and width to enhance anatomical consistency. Real delayed PET images are incorporated as weak distribution-level guidance through a rank-based consistency loss, allowing the model to better recover delayed uptake patterns without direct image-to-image supervision. This retrospective study included 90 PET scans from 70 patients, including 86 ¹⁸F-FDG PET scans and 4 ⁶⁸Ga-PSMA PET scans, divided into training, validation, and test sets. The weakly supervised UCD-Net was compared with its unsupervised backbone and four baseline models, including EDCNN, CGAN, U-Net, and CVF-SID. Across three test scenarios, the weakly supervised UCD-Net achieved the best performance, with RMSE values of 0.0333, 0.0365, and 0.0236. Compared with unsupervised UCD-Net, weak delayed-image guidance reduced RMSE by 17.2%, 20.8%, and 30.0%. These results suggest that UCD-Net can synthesize delayed-equivalent PET images from first-pass PET and may reduce dependence on additional delayed imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 402Poster Number:MIC-15-402] Neural Radiance Field-Based Reconstruction of Object Changes in Stationary Computed Tomography with Linearly Distributed Sources (#1936)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Qian (Autores: H. Qian , Y. Xiao)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [2] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This research aims to detect and reconstruct object changes using computed tomography (CT). We focus on stationary CT with linearly distributed sources (SLCT), which enables rapid projection data acquisition without mechanical rotation. However, due to the lack of sufficient angular coverage, SLCT inherently suffers from a severely limited-angle imaging problem, where direct reconstruction leads to strong anisotropic artifacts. To address this issue, we introduce the pre-change object as prior knowledge and propose two Neural Radiance Field (NeRF)-based change modeling strategies. The first method, Full-Object Nerf (FO-NeRF), continues optimization from a pre-trained NeRF representing the pre-change object, refining it into the post-change object. The second method, Change-Filed NeRF (CF-NeRF), explicitly models a change field and directly learns the residual component between the pre- and post-change objects. We validate the proposed methods on 2D simulated objects composed of simple geometric shapes. Experimental results demonstrate that, with prior constraints, both methods can successfully reconstruct object changes while effectively mitigating limited-angle artifacts. These results indicate that, by leveraging object priors within a NeRF-based representation, the highly ill-posed limited-angle reconstruction problem can be transformed into a more stable and tractable optimization problem, enabling reliable change detection and reconstruction under severely incomplete projection data.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 405Poster Number:MIC-15-405] Methods for Reconstruction Aware Completion of Partial PET Sinograms (#2029)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Burbar (Autores: Z. Burbar , I. Hong)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Siemens Molecular Imaging, Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A partial-detector-ring Positron Emission Tomography (PET) system may be an option to reduce cost and/or enable integration within another modality for multimodality imaging. In some use cases, the PET system may not be able to rotate continuously to collect all lines of response needed to form an image, yet a rapidly available image is still required for image quality control or organ-motion detection when the detectors are stationary. In this setting, missing angular coverage yields incomplete projection measurements and degraded reconstructions. This work describes a learning-based method to generate results equivalent to full-ring acquisition from partial-ring data This work proposes a reconstruction-aware sinogram completion network that predicts a full-ring-equivalent sinogram while enforcing consistency after tomographic reconstruction. This method combines supervision in projection space with an additional image-space objective computed after reconstructing the predicted sinogram using standard PET reconstruction operators, encouraging outputs that both match full-ring sinograms and yield accurate reconstructed images. By incorporating reconstruction consistency, the reconstruction-aware approach is intended to enable partial-ring systems to produce full-ring-equivalent sinograms that can be reconstructed with existing pipelines without modification, supporting more practical imaging workflows when mechanical rotation is constrained.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 408Poster Number:MIC-15-408] Symmetry-Enhanced YOLOv11 for Bone Metastatic Lesion Detection in Whole-Body Bone Scintigraphy (#2214)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Weng (Autores: F. Weng , H. Gong , D. Li , N. Dang , Y. Lin , G. Chen , Y. Zan , Y. Liang , Q. Huang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Macao Polytechnic University, Faculty of Applied Sciences, Macao, China, Macao Special Administrative Region [2] National Cancer Center/National Clinical Research Center for Cancer/ Cancer Hospital & Shenzhen Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine, National Cancer Center/National Clinical Research Center for Cancer/ Cancer Hospital & Shenzhen Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and Peking Union Medical College, Shenzhen, China [3] Guangxi University of Foreign Languages, School of Digital Technology, Nanning, China [4] Vplus Technology Ltd., Research and Development Department, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Automated bone metastasis detection in whole-body bone scintigraphy (WBBS) is often hindered by subtle contrast, scale variation, and physiological interference. We propose an enhanced YOLOv11-based framework incorporating a symmetry-aware representation-utilizing ECC (Enhanced Correlation Coefficient)-registered mirrored images and difference maps-to model pathological asymmetry. To handle multi-scale lesions, we introduce a scale-sensitive architecture featuring a P2 detection branch and Efficient Multi-scale Attention (EMA). Furthermore, an extremity-specific refinement branch and an anatomical cross-view fusion strategy (integrating anterior/posterior projections) are employed to improve sensitivity in limbs and reduce single-view occlusion. Evaluated on 1,800 patient studies, our method achieved 0.959 recall, 0.820 precision and 0.785 mAP50, outperforming YOLOv8 and Faster R-CNN, particularly for small, low-contrast lesions. The exceptionally high recall demonstrates superior sensitivity to small and low-contrast lesions, highlighting the method's potential as a reliable screening tool to minimize missed diagnoses in clinical practice.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 411Poster Number:MIC-15-411] HyperAβ: Brain Region Hypergraph Neural Network with Dynamic Margin Loss for Amyloid PET/CT Classification (#2367)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Zhan (Autores: G. Zhan , X. Sun , Y. Yang , Q. Zhang , J. Yang , X. Liu , T. Ye , Z. Zeng , B. Jiang , L. Jiang , J. Zou , S. Xie)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China [2] Guangdong Provincial People's Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Guangzhou, China [3] Sun Yat-sen University, School of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China [4] Florida State University, Tallahassee, Florida, United States of America [5] Wenzhou University, Metaverse and Artificial Intelligence Institute, Wenzhou, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate Aβ PET/CT classification is critical for Alzheimer's diagnosis and anti-amyloid treatment eligibility, yet existing methods struggle to model higher-order inter-regionbrain relationships and handle class imbalance and per-class learning hardness. We propose HyperAβ, which constructs a 30 node brain-region hypergraph over SynthSeg-parcellated multimodal PET/CT features with 10 anatomically-defined hyperedges,and employs hypergraph convolution for higher-order multiregion interaction modeling. To address class imbalance and per-class learning hardness, we introduce GCA-D loss combining static per-class confidence calibration with EMA-based dynamic hardness tracking. Under 5-fold cross-validation, HyperAβ achieves ACC of 0.8784 and AUC of 0.9341, outperforming state of-the-art methods.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 414Poster Number:MIC-15-414] A Wavelet-Enhanced Trajectory-Refined Flow Matching Model for MR-to-CT Synthesis in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma (#2901)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Huang (Autores: Y. Huang , Z. Zhang , J. Da , T. Jiang , M. Yu , L. Qiang , T. Chen , Y. He , Y. Li)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shanghai University of Electric Power, College of Electronics and Information Engineering, Shanghai, China [2] Xiangya Hospital, Department of Radiation Oncology, Changsha, China [3] The First People's Hospital of Chenzhou, Chenzhou, China [4] Fudan University, College of Biomedical Engineering, Shanghai, China [5] ShanghaiTech University, School of Biomedical Engineering, Shanghai, China [6] Shanghai University, School of Life Sciences, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is common in southern China, Southeast Asia, and North Africa. Radiotherapy treatment planning (RTP) relies on magnetic resonance (MR) imaging and computed tomography (CT). MR provides superior soft-tissue contrast for target delineation, whereas CT provides electron density information for dose calculation. However, separate acquisition and subsequent registration of MR and CT not only increase time, cost, and radiation exposure, but also introduce registration and dosimetric errors. Diffusion model-based MR-to-CT synthesis offers an efficient, cost-effective, and radiation-free alternative for NPC radiotherapy. However, the nasopharyngeal region has highly complex anatomical structures. As a result, existing methods often fail to preserve anatomical details adequately and may suffer from mode averaging between adjacent slices, reducing slice-specificity and distributional separability. Accordingly, a wavelet-enhanced trajectory-refined flow matching model (WETR-FM) was proposed. A wavelet fusion convolution (WFConv) is introduced to strengthen the extraction of multi-frequency information in the feature space, particularly high-frequency structural details. A wavelet enhanced attention (WE-Attn) module is designed to enhance the network's ability to model critical multi-scale structural features through attention interactions among different frequency components. A trajectory refinement loss (TR loss) is incorporated to enlarge the differences among the denoising trajectories and terminal distributions of different slices. This helps alleviate distributional confusion between adjacent slices, while improving slice-specificity. Experimental results demonstrate that WETR-FM outperformed existing approaches (cycleGAN, sc-cycleGAN, pix2pix, DDPM, FM, SM) in terms of MSE and MAE by more than 35%, and improved by 4%-10% in PSNR. These findings demonstrated promising potential for application in NPC radiotherapy.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 417Poster Number:MIC-15-417] Quantitative Unpaired Low-Dose PET Image Translation with a Poisson-Aware Identity Loss (#2489)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Lee (Autores: S. Lee , R. Lee , E. Chung)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology, AI Graduate School, Gwangju, Republic of Korea [2] RMTEC, Gwangju, Republic of Korea [3] Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology, Department of Biomedical Science and Engineering; AI Graduate School, Gwangju, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Reducing positron emission tomography (PET) tracer dose lowers patient radiation exposure but degrades image quality and the quantitative accuracy of standardized uptake values (SUVs). Paired same-subject low/full-dose acquisitions are impractical to obtain at scale, motivating unpaired image translation. Applying Contrastive Unpaired Translation (CUT) to ultra-low-dose PET, we identify a quantitative failure mode in which the trained generator improves image appearance but introduces high-uptake SUV underestimation that can exceed the bias of the unprocessed low-dose input itself. We interpret this behavior as a mismatch between the fixed residual weighting of the intensity-space ℓ1 identity loss and PET's uptake-dependent Poisson-derived noise. To address this, we propose PA-CUT (Poisson-Aware CUT), which replaces the ℓ1 identity loss with one evaluated under the classical Anscombe transform, a Poisson-motivated variance-stabilizing reweighting of the identity term. A multi-dose training scheme yields a single model across multiple dose reduction factors (DRFs). On the UDPET 2024 challenge dataset, PA-CUT substantially reduces high-uptake SUV bias compared with CUT, with negligible changes in pixel-level and perceptual quality.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 420Poster Number:MIC-15-420] Deep Learning with Physics-Corrected Histo-Images for Robust Low-Dose Scatter Correction on uMI Panorama GS (#2657)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 X. Zhang (Autores: X. Zhang , Y. Zhu , L. He , Q. Ye , Y. Dong , H. Zeng , H. Xu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] United Imaging Healthcare, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Quantitative accuracy in PET relies heavily on effective scatter correction (SC), especially for long axial field-of-view (LAFOV) systems such as the uMI Panorama GS where low-count scenarios are increasingly prevalent. Conventional SC requires an emission map generated through iterative OSEM reconstruction, which is inherently sensitive to noise and degrades at low doses. Our prior work demonstrated that a deep learning (DL) approach using physics-corrected histo-images achieves high quantitative accuracy for SC under standard-dose conditions [2]. In this work, we extend this framework to low-dose scenarios on the uMI Panorama GS PET/CT system. We collected 220 static ¹⁸F-FDG cases and 21 dynamic cases. Low-dose conditions were simulated by randomly downsampling events at seven dose levels (0.1%-100%). A U-Net was trained to predict emission maps from physics-corrected histo-images, with full-dose reconstructions as targets. At standard dose, both the proposed and conventional methods achieved relative differences below 2% compared with the ground truth. At the 0.1% dose level, the conventional method showed organ VOI deviations approaching 10%, while the proposed method remained below 2% across all dose levels. In dynamic studies, the proposed method preserved time-activity curve accuracy at 0.5% dose and produced reliable Patlak Ki images at 1% dose. Combined with regularized reconstruction, the proposed method enables ultra-low-dose PET data to yield clinically usable images with high quantitative accuracy, demonstrating its potential for low-dose PET applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 423Poster Number:MIC-15-423] Quantum-Geometric Radiomics Classification of Pancreatic Lesions (#2704)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Yang (Autores: H. Yang , C. Min , H. Choi , S. Jeong)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yonsei University, Department of Radiation Convergence Engineering, Wonju, Republic of Korea [2] Wonju Severance Christian Hospital, Department of Radiation Oncology, Wonju, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study proposes Quantum Barren-Plateau Correction via Information-theoretic Regularization (QBPCIR), a hybrid quantum-classical architecture for CT radiomics-based pancreatic lesion classification. A parameter-shift-rule diagonal quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM) estimator quantifies per-class output curvature and adaptively amplifies minority-class gradient contributions to mitigate barren plateau-induced gradient suppression. Evaluated on 1206 training and 71 test portal-venous CT cases with 294 LASSO-selected PyRadiomics features, QBPCIR-VQC achieved AUC 0.916 and recall 0.859, outperforming a classical MLP (AUC 0.846) and a standard VQC (AUC 0.880), and approaching the recall of an expert radiologist reference (0.830). The BCE ablation confirmed that the inter-class Fisher trace asymmetry is a genuine quantum geometric effect, validating the information-theoretic rationale for the proposed correction

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 426Poster Number:MIC-15-426] Zero-Shot Vision-Language Refinement for PET-CT Multi-Organ Segmentation (#2885)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Duan (Autores: C. Duan , G. Krokos , A. J. Reader , D. M. Lilburn)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] King's College London, School of Biomedical Engineering and Imaging Sciences, London, United Kingdom [2] King's College London, PET Centre, London, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate organ segmentation in positron emission tomography (PET) is essential for quantitative analysis, treatment personalisation, and clinical decision-making. In current practice, organ masks are commonly derived from CT using tools such as TotalSegmentator (TS) and transferred to PET directly; however, PET-CT misalignment systematically degrades accuracy and biases downstream functional measurements. PET-native supervised approaches mitigate this misalignment but require costly expert annotation and lack generalisability to unseen organs or acquisition protocols. We propose a zero-shot vision-language refinement framework that adapts CT-derived anatomical priors to PET without any PET-specific training. TS masks are converted into multi-modal prompts for SAM3 - comprising organ bounding boxes, interior positive points, boundary negative points, and organ-specific radiological text descriptions - which are applied independently across axial, coronal, and sagittal views. A Prior-Anchored Refinement Gate (PARG) then constrains each SAM3 prediction by enforcing spatial overlap, area consistency, and eroded-core preservation with respect to the TS prior, suppressing anatomically implausible outputs. Evaluated on 12 held-out oncological PET-CT studies across liver, spleen, and bladder, our zero-shot refinement consistently outperforms TS, improving Dice from 0.744 to 0.835 for bladder, 0.936 to 0.941 for liver, and 0.870 to 0.879 for spleen. Our SAM3 features are further incorporated as auxiliary inputs to supervised training of nnUNet with very limited true labels. The resulting PET+TS+SAM3 configuration achieves Dice of 0.929 (bladder), 0.945 (liver), and 0.886 (spleen) with only eight annotated cases. These results demonstrate that our method effectively corrects PET-CT mismatch and offers a label-efficient, annotation-free pathway towards generalizable PET-CT multi-organ segmentation.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 429Poster Number:MIC-15-429] Beyond AUC: Decision-Level Discordance and XAI Interpretation of a CBAM-CNN and a Vision Transformer on PET Polar Maps (#2933)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Li (Autores: S.M. Hosseini , A. Li , A. Kazempour , S.E. Roshan , L. E. Juarez-Orozco , M. Vatandoust , J. Knuuti , A. Saraste , T. Maaniitty , R. Klén , J. Teuho)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Turku PET Centre, Turku University Hospital and University of Turku, Turku, Finland [2] Tabriz University, Tabriz, Iran (Islamic Republic of) [3] University MedicalCenter Utrecht,, Department of Cardiology, DivisionHeart & Lungs, Utrecht, Netherlands
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Convolutional neural networks and vision transformers are increasingly applied to medical image classification, yet their comparative decision-making behavior under equivalent aggregate performance remains poorly understood. We trained a convolutional neural network equipped with convolutional block attention modules and a vision transformer from scratch to predict major adverse cardiac events from nitrogen-13 ammonia positron emission tomography myocardial perfusion polar maps in a cohort of 1,079 patients. Across 100 independent training runs, both architectures achieved statistically indistinguishable area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (both 0.90; Wilcoxon signed-rank p = 0.897), yet discordance analysis revealed significantly different binary predictions on specific patients (McNemar p = 0.0013). Using architecture-appropriate explainability methods - gradient-weighted class activation mapping (the improved variant) for the convolutional network and attention rollout for the vision transformer - we propose a mechanistic hypothesis that the transformer's global self-attention integrates large-territory perfusion defects that the convolutional network's local spatial attention fails to aggregate. These findings demonstrate that equivalence in area under the curve does not imply decision equivalence, and motivate consideration of decision-level discordance when comparing architectures for clinical deployment.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 432Poster Number:MIC-15-432] Multitracer Conditional Diffusion Model for CT-Less Attenuation Correction in Preclinical PET Imaging (#3096)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Vachon (Autores: M. Vachon , A. St-Georges , C. Thibaudeau , O. Sarrhini , M. Gaudreault , R. Lecomte , J.-B. Michaud)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Sherbrooke, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Sherbrooke, Québec, Canada [2] University of Sherbrooke, Department of Medical Imaging and Radiation Sciences, Sherbrooke, Québec, Canada [3] Imaging Research & Technology, Sherbrooke, Québec, Canada [4] Sherbrooke Molecular Imaging Center, Sherbrooke, Québec, Canada [5] Institut Interdisciplinaire d'Innovation Technologique, Sherbrooke, Québec, Canada
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurately quantifying radiotracer uptake and metabolic activity in a subject using positron emission tomography (PET) requires correcting for photon attenuation. An attenuation map, typically produced using a second imaging modality, is required for attenuation correction but can increase radiation exposure, operational costs, and reconstruction complexity. To mitigate these drawbacks, methods for generating attenuation maps from the non-attenuation-corrected (NAC) PET image using deep neural networks were proposed. Preclinical PET images of small animals present additional challenges for artificial attenuation map generation because the attenuation is low and the subjects are not rigid bodies, making anatomical structures less consistent and more prone to artifacts. A conditional Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (cDDPM) was implemented to generate attenuation maps from NAC PET images. The model was preliminarily trained on approximately 60 paired NAC PET and CT images acquired on the LabPET8 scanner. The dataset consisted of mouse whole-body and body-without-head scans obtained with two radiotracers: 18 F-FDG, and 11 C-acetate. Preliminary slice-level evaluation showed that the generated pseudo-CT images were visually consistent with the reference CT images and preserved the main anatomical structures in the evaluated regions. The generated pseudo-CT images achieved a structural similarity index measure (SSIM) of 0.991, a mean squared error (MSE) of 4.47×10 -5 and a mean absolute error (MAE) of 8.51. These preliminary results suggest the feasibility of cDDPM-based pseudo-CT generation for preclinical PET attenuation correction, although full-volume validation and PET reconstruction studies using the generated attenuation maps are still required. Full results for more tracers and scanners will be presented at the conference.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 435Poster Number:MIC-15-435] Joint Self-Collimation Compton SPECT for Wide-Energy and High-SNR Imaging (#2)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. Li (Autores: P. Li , L. Lei , X. Zheng , Z. Lyu , R. Yao , T. Ma)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [2] University at Buffalo SUNY, Department of Radiology, Jacobs School of Medicine & Biomedical Sciences, Buffalo, New York, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Mechanical collimators enforce a strict resolution-sensitivity trade-off, necessitate hardware exchanges for wide-energy imaging, and suffer from poor high-energy performance due to septal penetration. We propose Joint Self-Collimation Compton (JSCC) SPECT as a wide-energy solution using a multi-layer stochastic mosaic detector. JSCC integrates geometric constraints with Compton kinematics to screen pathways and suppress artifacts. Cylindrical-coordinate-based fast modeling accelerates volumetric reconstruction. Simulations using Hot-rod, Contrast, and Hoffman phantoms demonstrate that JSCC achieves a significantly superior signal-to-noise ratio compared to parallel-hole SPECT. At 511 keV, JSCC resolves 16-mm and 10-mm rods in 2-minute and 20-minute scans, outperforming the baseline (22-mm and 16-mm). At 140 keV, it resolves 9-mm rods in 30 seconds without hardware modification. These results demonstrate the potential of JSCC as a wide-energy, high-SNR SPECT imaging paradigm for next-generation molecular imaging and theranostic applications.

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The growing integration of robotics in medical imaging applications [1], the maturation of high-resolution room temperature semiconductor detectors, and the push towards safe, cost-effective and easy-to-use imaging platforms [2], motivates the development of a robotic SPECT system designed to overcome the inherent limitations of traditional platforms. The high flexibility of the robot enables acquisition trajectories not attainable with standard gantry-based systems, practically implementing the concept of adaptive SPECT [3]. We propose a system based on a collaborative 7-degrees-of-freedom robot, a CZT detector panel, a custom-designed multi-pinhole tungsten collimator, a LiDAR sensor for environment awareness, and a 3D structured light camera for object localization and occupancy. Inverse kinematics and Bidirectional Rapidly exploring Random Trees are used for determining the robot configurations and collision-free movement. Energy calibration of the detector shows a FWHM of 4.94 keV at 122 keV, and an energy range up to 380 keV, suitable for imaging of most clinical and theranostics radiotracers. Integration of a LiDAR sensor and a 3D structured light camera shows high precision in object detection (AP 0.5 >0.90) and point cloud stitching via Eye-in-Hand calibration. Noisy Jaszczak phantom simulations show that robot-enabled spherical acquisition outperforms standard cylindrical scanning, yielding better metrics at the minimum NRMSE iteration: NRMSE improved by 18%, the peak-to-valley ratio for the 6.4 mm rods increased of 55.3%, and the average contrast-to-noise ratio and contrast recovery coefficient increased by 5.1% and 5.3%, respectively, with maximum gains over 13% for the smallest sphere.
