sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 441Poster Number:MIC-15-441] Estimating ejection fractions from standard of care F18-FDG PET/CT: a feasibility study (#1487)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Wilson (Autores: Z. Wilson , F. P. Jansen , K. M. Bradley , R. Johnsen , K.-H. Su , D. R. McGowan)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Oxford, Oncology Department, Oxford, United Kingdom [2] Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Department of Medical Physics and Clinical Engineering, Oxford, United Kingdom [3] GE HealthCare, Chicago, Illinois, United States of America [4] University Hospital of Wales, Wales Research and Diagnostic Positron Emission Tomography Imaging Centre, Cardiff, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract For patients undergoing cardiotoxic cancer therapies, baseline cardiac function is assessed using echocardiography to calculate left ventricle ejection fractions (LVEFs). At many sites, this requires additional patient visits and could delay treatment as use of these therapies increases. We investigate whether LVEF can be automatically derived from routine 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET/CT scans acquired on a high-sensitivity Omni Legend scanner. Our retrospective study of FDG PET lymphoma scans (n=437) was organised into three complementary cohorts addressing gating validity, preliminary clinical comparison, and real-world applicability. In 5 electrocardiogram(ECG)-gated PET/CT scans, algorithm-generated triggers showed strong agreement with ECG triggers, with standard deviation trigger shift < 0.03. Of patients with ground truth echocardiograms (n=5), algorithm-derived LVEFs showed good agreement with echocardiography (mean absolute error = 5.1%), within the clinically accepted range for echocardiographic reporting variability (10%). Across the full dataset, sufficient myocardial uptake for heart localization and edge detection was observed in 153/437 cases (35.0%), while 207/437 (47.4%) lacked sufficient uptake despite successful algorithm execution. This cohort data suggests the potential for automatic LVEF estimation for one third of patients. Future work will investigate pipeline improvements such as refining the basal plane localisation to enable a LVEF estimation for a greater proportion of patients. Overall, these preliminary results indicate the potential for FDG PET derived LVEF with good ECG gating agreement and acceptable early agreement against echocardiographic reference values. Ongoing analysis of ground truth EFs will further evaluate classification of abnormal LVEF (< 50%) and establish myocardial uptake thresholds to guide clinical applicability.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 444Poster Number:MIC-15-444] Experimental validation of inter-crystal scatter recovery using forward Compton kinematics and polarization correlations in PET imaging (#2032)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Makek (Autores: M. Makek , T. Bokulić , A.M. Kožuljević , S. Parashari , L. Pavelić)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Zagreb Faculty of Science, Department of Physics, Zagreb, Croatia [2] Institute for Medical Research and Occupational Health, Zagreb, Croatia [3] Instituto de Fisica Corpuscular, Valencia, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Compton scatter of gamma-rays within detector elements, denoted as inter-crystal scatter events, has been considered a resource for sensitivity improvement in PET imaging. The obstacle for their exploitation has been the resolution and contrast degradation due to inclusion of these events, related to the lack of knowledge of the first interaction position. We studied inter-crystal scatter events experimentally using a modular system based on single-end readout modules, also able to perform Compton polarimetry. Two modules comprising 16 x 16 GAGG:Ce scintillator matrices read out by silicon photomultipliers were mounted on a rotating gantry with 430 mm diameter. Two types of events were selected: (i) with a single pixel firing in one module and a two-pixel hit with forward Compton kinematics in the opposite module, and (ii) two-pixel Compton events in both modules with a pronounced polarization correlation. We imaged Ge-68 rod sources, and a NEMA NU-4 phantom with a Ga-68 solution. They results show that the statistics increases by 18 % using (i) and by an extra 8 % when adding (ii), compared to pure single-pixel events. At the same time, the inclusion of the selected inter inter-crystal scatter events has a marginal effect on image resolution (central field-of-view), shifting it from 2.5 +/- 0.1 mm (FWHM) for the single pixel events, to 2.7 +/- 0.2 mm (FWHM) for the combined sample, while the signal-to-noise and contrast-to-noise values are moderately increased. This validates the use of the inter-crystal scatter events for improved sensitivity and image quality in PET.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 447Poster Number:MIC-15-447] Development of a Dual-Modality Imaging Capsule for Laparoscopic Radio-Guided Surgery (#2174)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Patel (Autores: K. Patel , L. Confalonieri , S. Huh , M. Wilson , D. Caprotti , N. Ikoma , E. M. Zannoni)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The University of Texas at Austin, Walker Department of Mechanical Engineering, Austin, Texas, United States of America [2] The University of Texas at Austin, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Austin, Texas, United States of America [3] Rutherford Appleton Laboratory, Science and Technology Facilities Council, Didcot, United Kingdom [4] MD Anderson Cancer Center, Department of Surgical Oncology, Houston, Texas, United States of America [5] The University of Texas at Austin, Department of Diagnostic Medicine, Austin, Texas, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Minimally-invasive radio-guided surgery requires simultaneous functional nuclear guidance and anatomical visualization to enable precise intraoperative localization of radiolabeled targets [1]. We propose a dual-modality imaging drop-in capsule designed for deployment through a standard 15-mm laparoscopic trocar. It consists of a 2-mm thick semiconductor detector with a sub-millimeter pixel pitch [2,3], a custom lofthole collimator embedded within a 3D-printed tungsten capsule, and two miniaturized stereoscopic micro-cameras. Preliminary results show: real-time 3D depth maps validated against an ultrasonic distance sensor; a seamless 360° panoramic view stitched from sequential frames using cylindrical warping and multi-band Laplacian blending [4,5]; spectral localization of multiple isotopes 57 Co and 241 Am within a scattering biological medium; and a preliminary 2D co-registration overlaying the functional dataset onto the anatomical scene. We will present the system design and components, and discuss the steps towards a fully integrated prototype for laparoscopic radio-guided surgery.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 450Poster Number:MIC-15-450] Development of a High Sensitivity Cascade Gamma Photon Coincidence Imaging System (#2224)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Q. Wei (Autores: Q. Wei , Y. Zhao , K. Wang , Z. Yan , S. Xu , X. Zhou , J. Dang , H. Jia , H. Ye , Z. Hang , W. Huang , Z. Gu , H. Liu , J. Wu , Y. Liu , Z.-X. He)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Science and Technology Beijing, Beijing Engineering Research Center of Industrial Spectrum Imaging, School of Automation and Electrical Engineering, Beijing, China [2] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China [3] Tsinghua University, School of Biomedical Engineering, Beijing, China [4] Beijing Normal University, Center for Advanced Quantum Studies, School of Physics and Astronomy, Beijing, China [5] Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Beijing, China [6] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Lutetium-177 ( 177 Lu) is one of the most representative radionuclides in integrated nuclear medicine theranostics. To image 177 Lu, we have developed a full-ring, high-sensitivity cascade gamma photon coincidence imaging system. This work presents the system construction and preliminary performance evaluation. The detector ring consists of 40 continuous LaBr₃ crystal modules arranged in 10 radial × 4 axial configuration (each 50 × 50 × 6 mm³). The inner diameter of the ring is 110 mm, with axial module spacing of 60 mm. Each crystal is coupled to four MPPC arrays and read out via PETsys FEM256 electronics, with three FEB/D boards and one DAQ for data acquisition. Both the ASICs and MPPCs are cooled by a water-cooling system, maintaining water at 8 °C and ASIC temperature below 20 °C. The collimator assembly comprises 10 tungsten plates (26 × 128 × 8 mm³), each covering four axial detector modules. Plates are arranged alternately with pinholes and slits (1 mm), placed at a vertical distance of 36.5 mm from the ring center, creating an imaging field of Φ30 × 30 mm. The prototype hardware has been fully assembled and is capable of normal data acquisition. Simulation results indicate a coincidence sensitivity of 2.97 × 10⁻⁵ at the central field of view, spatial resolution of ~1.7 mm, and hot cylindrical object resolution up to 1.2 mm. Preliminary experimental tests have validated the feasibility of the system. Ongoing optimization includes crystal position calibration, energy resolution improvement, and collimator geometry alignment. The full system performance evaluation is expected to be completed before the upcoming conference.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 453Poster Number:MIC-15-453] Development of High-Time Resolution Ring-Type GFAG Pixel Detector System for pH Sensing via Time-Differential Perturbed Angular Correlation (#2325)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Uenomachi (Autores: M. Uenomachi , B. Feng , M. Fujiomoto , K. Nakamura , K. Shimazoe)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institute of Science Tokyo, Institute of Integrated Research, Tokyo, Japan [2] The University of Tokyo, School of Engineering, Tokyo, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positron emission tomography and single photon computed emission tomography are widely used nuclear medicine modalities. These modalities provide information on physiological and metabolic functions by visualizing radiotracer distributions. However, they cannot obtain local information, such as intermolecular interactions, pH, and other microenvironmental factors. We have proposed and demonstrated a novel nuclear medicine imaging and quantum sensing method utilizing the characteristics of cascade radionuclides. For imaging, the coincidence detection of cascade gamma rays enables localization of the source position using directional detectors. For sensing, changes in angular correlation between cascade gamma rays provide local information, such as pH [1]. In our previous studies, angular distribution information was used as an indicator of angular correlation changes because the time resolution of measurement system of approximately 50 ns was insufficient for time-differential perturbed angular correlation analysis. In this study, we developed the improved time resolution of the measurement system using GFAG pixel scintillator detectors, originally designed 64-channel slew rate limited time-over-threshold integrated application specific intesgrated circuits, [2] and 62.5 ps sampling data acquisition systems [3]. The time-dependent perturbation factor exhibited pH-dependent decay behavior consistent with a previous study [4], with slower decay at low pH and faster decay at higher pH. In addition, 111 In-labeled OctreoScan showed different after-effect behavior from aqueous 111 InCl 3 solutions, suggesting that time-differential analysis provides information beyond integrated angular distribution measurements. We will incorporate the time-differential perturbed angular correlation analysis into double-photon coincidence imaging and investigate its potential for nuclear medicine application.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 456Poster Number:MIC-15-456] Quantum entanglement of annihilation photons as a function of the annihilation mechanism (#2454)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Kumar (Autores: D. Kumar , S. Sharma , P. Moskal)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Jagiellonian University, Faculty of Physics, Astronomy and Applied Computer Science, Krakow, Poland [2] Jagiellonian University, Center of Theranostics, Krakow, Poland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In matter, a positron annihilates with an electron into two photons through several mechanisms, including direct annihilation and the formation of positronium, a metastable bound state that exists as either para-positronium or ortho-positronium. Each channel has a characteristic lifetime, allowing their contributions to be distinguished in time. The two photons are predicted to be entangled in their polarizations [1], and recent measurements indicate that the degree of entanglement depends on the annihilation channel [2]. In particular, the ortho-positronium decay is sensitive to the local concentration of molecular oxygen, and can serve as a probe of tissue hypoxia in PET imaging [3]. The Jagiellonian Positron Emission Tomograph is a scanner built from plastic scintillators, in which 511 keV photons interact predominantly through Compton scattering [4]. The Compton scattering plane of each photon is correlated with its polarization. We measure annihilations of positrons emitted by a sodium-22 source embedded in porous polymer. Sodium-22 emits a positron accompanied by a 1274 keV prompt photon, which provides a time reference for the positron lifetime. The polarization correlation distribution of the annihilation photon pairs is consistent with quantum entanglement, between the limits for maximally entangled and classically separable states [2]. Selecting events by positron lifetime reveals distinct polarization correlation distributions for different annihilation channels. A detailed comparison will be presented at the conference. These results motivate quantum-informed PET imaging, with tissue hypoxia as a clinical biomarker.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 459Poster Number:MIC-15-459] First In-Vivo Positronium Ratio Imaging (PRI) using F-18 FDG: A Preliminary Study with Phantom and a Mouse Model (#2615)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Fujimoto (Autores: M. Fujimoto , K. Nakamura , R. Sato , P. Caradonna , A. Ostuka , S. Ohta , M. Uenomachi , L. Stephenson , A. Montgomery , D. P. Watts , K. Shimazoe)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The University of Tokyo, Department of Bioengineering, Bunkyo, Japan [2] The University of Tokyo, Department of Nuclear Engineering and Management, Bunkyo, Japan [3] Institute of Science Tokyo, Laboratory for Zero-Carbon Energy, Meguro, Japan [4] University of York, School of Physics, Engineering and Technology, York, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This research presents the development and first in-vivo demonstration of Positronium Ratio Imaging, a novel functional imaging technique that uses the three-photon to two-photon decay ratio of positronium. While conventional Positron Emission Tomography primarily maps radiopharmaceutical distribution, Positronium Ratio Imaging provides insights into the tissue microenvironment by exploiting the sensitivity of ortho-positronium to local oxygen levels and morphology. We characterized the system's geometric stability using a four-rod phantom with varying dimensions and evaluated the results against Monte Carlo simulations using the Geant4 toolkit. The phantom study identified a size-dependent uncertainty baseline of approximately twenty percent, primarily arising from detector sensitivity and geometric factors. Furthermore, we achieved the first in-vivo ratio imaging using a tumor-bearing mouse model administered with fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose. Quantitative analysis revealed that the three-photon to two-photon ratio in brown adipose tissue was approximately two and a half times higher than in the heart and bladder. This significant contrast is consistent with theoretical trends derived from tissue-specific positronium lifetimes and far exceeds the established hardware-induced uncertainty. These findings validate the feasibility of using standard positron emitters for functional three-photon imaging without the need for specialized prompt-gamma emitters. Future work will focus on refining quantitative calculation methods, evaluating signal-to-noise ratios, and implementing hardware-specific calibrations to enhance absolute quantification. This technology lays a foundation for clinical applications such as the non-invasive visualization of tumor hypoxia and metabolic characterization of the tissue microenvironment, offering a breakthrough in functional molecular imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 462Poster Number:MIC-15-462] Ortho-Positronium Lifetime Measurements from Pile-up Single Events (#2939)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J.A. Avellaneda (Autores: J.A. Avellaneda , S. Gaitán , V.M. Nouvilas , E. Romero-Sanz , M. Oteo Vives , M.Á. Morcillo , J. Udias , L.M. Fraile , J.L. Herraiz)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Grupo de física nuclear & EMFTEL & IPARCOS, Madrid, Spain [2] CERN, ISOLDE, Geneva, Switzerland [3] CIEMAT, Unidad de aplicaciones médicas de la radiación ionizante, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positronium annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS) has recently attracted considerable interest as a potentially sensitive tool for tissue characterization. In standard PALS experimental setups, at least two detectors are needed to provide start and stop signals for positron emission and annihilation creation. However, due to the isotropic nature of prompt-gamma emission, in a very significant fraction of events, both prompt and annihilation photons are detected in the same detector, resulting in a pileup event. In this work, we propose using these pile-up events to simplify o-Ps lifetime estimation workflows, enabling estimation with a single detector. Using a 22Na source sample, we successfully measured the o-Ps lifetime using both standard coincidence PALS and the proposed approach with excellent agreement (1.88±0.04 and 1.90±0.07 ns). Measurements of o-Ps lifetime in an isopropanol-based liquid using 44Sc, as well as in ex-vivo biological samples from mice (liver and plasma) after a PET acquisition using 52Mn, were also obtained. These results demonstrate the feasibility of single-detector o-Ps measurement and open new lines of research, by facilitating the characterization of samples from PET studies.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 465Poster Number:MIC-15-465] Quantitative 4D PET Imaging of Photosynthate Transport and Rhizosphere Carbon Partitioning in Intact Plant-Soil Systems (#3049)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M.N. Ullah (Autores: M.N. Ullah , D. Hastings , D. Anders , W. Cheng , S. Abbaszadeh , C. S. Levin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Stanford University, Department of Radiology and Molecular Imaging Program at Stanford ( (MIPS)), stanford, California, United States of America [2] University of California Santa Cruz, Department of Environmental Studies, Santa Cruz, California, United States of America [3] University of California Santa Cruz, Electrical and Computer Engineering, Santa Cruz, California, United States of America [4] Stanford University, Departments Physics, Electrical Engineering, and Bioengineering, Stanford, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present quantitative 4D PET imaging of photosynthate carbon transport and rhizosphere exudation in intact Phaseolus vulgaris plant-soil systems using the R-PET (Rhizo-PET) scanner with the ¹¹C radiotracer (t₁/₂ = 20.3 min). Across N = 6 plants, time-activity curves (TACs) extracted from 225 cross-pattern ROIs per dataset-spanning 3 roots × 3 axial depths × ±3 mm radial extent-reveal a reproducible source-to-sink carbon allocation hierarchy: upper root zones receive ≈50% of total plant carbon, while root 2 (primary taproot) dominates at 20.8 ± 6.3%. Time-to-peak (TTP) increases from 31.5±4.4 min (upper) to 48.0±13.1 min (lower root 2), corresponding to a phloem transport velocity of ≈2.4 mm min⁻¹. Rhizosphere carbon exudation follows an exponential decay AUC(r) = A e⁻ᵏʳ with k = 0.10-0.20 mm⁻¹, placing the active deposition zone within 4-14 mm of the root surface-the first spatially resolved 3D+t measurement of this process in intact soil.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 468Poster Number:MIC-15-468] Investigating an Optical Approach for Microliter-Scale Droplet Geometry Correction in Radioactivity Quantification (#3086)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Shin (Autores: S. Shin , R. Carmichael , W. Deng , J.A.L. Doblado , D. Prout , R.M. van Dam , A. Chatziioannou)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California, Los Angeles, Department of Molecular and Medical Pharmacology, Crump Institute for Molecular Imaging, Los Angeles, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positron-labeled tracers are powerful tools for studying diseases and developing new therapeutics, yet conventional radiochemistry platforms are complex, costly, and low-throughput, making PET tracer development slow and resource-intensive. To address this bottleneck, we are constructing a high-throughput radiochemistry system that will enable multiple radiosyntheses to be performed in parallel. A key challenge is accurately quantifying radioactivity in each microliter-scale droplet throughout the radiosynthesis process. While plastic scintillators and an overhead CMOS camera offer a compact detection approach, the scintillation signal is confounded by variations in droplet volume and geometry. Geometry correction is therefore critical for reliable activity quantification. We investigated an optical approach to infer droplet geometry by leveraging its optical reflective and refractive properties. Droplets were illuminated with a ring light mounted around the camera lens, and we sought to infer their geometries from the resulting optical features. Experimental images were acquired from evaporating water droplets on a Teflon-coated silicon chip, and ray-tracing simulations were performed on droplet models reconstructed from side-profile images. Both revealed two distinct features from independent optical processes: a mirror reflection effect and a lensing magnification effect. These varied systematically with droplet volume, suggesting they encode geometry information and may provide complementary information for inference. These preliminary findings support the feasibility of this optical method for geometry estimation and radioactivity quantification correction. The approach adds minimal complexity to the existing system and is well-suited for integration into a compact radiochemistry robot. Future work will focus on refining droplet shape models, extending the method to off-axis droplets, and evaluating image-analysis approaches for robust geometry inference.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-16-01] How well do we know non-collinearity in PET? A simulation and a new analysis of past and recent experiments (#2250)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J.M. Udias (Autores: A. Espinosa , P. Galve , L. M. Fraile , J.L. Herraiz , J.M. Udias)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Grupo de Física Nuclear, EMFTEL & IPARCOS, Madrid, Spain [2] Spanish National Research Council (CSIC), Institute for Physical and Information Technologies "Leonardo Torres Quevedo", ITEFI, Madrid, Spain [3] CERN, ISOLDE, EP Department, Geneva, Genève, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positron-electron non-collinearity of the 511 keV annihilation-photon has been derived from several experiments. In the one hand, of the (anti-)correlation between Doppler broadening induced by the transverse momentum component of the annihilating pair, and photon non-collinearity. Direct non-colinearity measurements with pin-hole or slits provide also noncolinearity information. In the past, discrepancies in the non-collinearity derived from both kinds of experiments have arised, and the non-collinearity value generally accepted has been solely derived from Doppler broadening experiments. To better understand non-collinearity, we review the correlation between the kinematics of the initial electron-positron pair and the emitted non-collinear photon. We then use a detailed 3D simulation of the kinematics annihilation of the e-e+ pair, including the motion of the initial pair of leptons, which in turns introduces the energy broadening of the 511 keV peak, and the non-collinearity of the final photons, linked to the underlying electron kinetic-energy distribution. To this end, initial electron kinetic energies are sampled from a semi-Gaussian distribution, while initial electron directions are sampled isotropically. We fit the initial kinetic energy distribution of the electron-positron pairs to reproduce, after the detailed 3D simulation, the observables in each kind of experiments, either Doppler broadening or actual non-collinearity in slit experiments. We find that the same initial electron kinetic energy distribution explains both Doppler broadening and accurate slit experiments in water at room temperature. Finally, we compare our extraction for non-collinearity distribution, and found it similar to the one presented by Tuoissant et al in 2024, confirming that non-collinearity is being underestimated in most MC simulations of PET scanners.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-16-02] PAL-G4: A Geant4-based code with PAL parametrisation (#2072)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Ros (Autores: N. Castellanos , D. Niekaemper , W. Ramírez , L. Tellmann , J. Scheins , G. Llosá , C. Lerche , A. Ros)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto de Fisica Corpuscular (CSIC-UV), Valencia, Spain [2] Forschungszentrum Jülich, Institute of Neuroscience and Medicine 4, Jülich, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positron Annihilation Lifetime has previously been demonstrated to provide useful information in PET imaging. Due to the fact that the annihilation time depends on the tissue where the annihilation occurs, to disentangle the different times for heterogeneous tumors is extremely challenging. Geant4, the toolkit for the simulation of the passage of particles through matter developed at CERN, has been shown to be a good candidate for medical physics simulations. The main drawback is that Geant4 code does not include Positron Annihilation Lifetime information in the source code. The IRIS group at IFIC (Valencia) has developed PAL-G4, an unofficial version of Geant4 that introduces the possibility to add measured Positron Annihilation Lifetimes for different materials in order to be able to simulate realistic scenarios. In order to test the PAL-G4 code, the BrainPET-7T insert for magnetic resonance at the PET-physics group at the Forschungszentrum Jülich GmbH was simulated. Two cases were simulated, one in which the annihilation took place in a homogeneous medium, and another in a heterogeneous medium. The simulation results fit the expected behavior in terms of the detected annihilation times in both cases, thereby showing the suitability of using PAL-G4 for real case studies. Further measurements of annihilation times for various sources and tissues of interest in medical applications will be measured with the BrainPET-7T and used as input parameters for the PAL-G4 code. The simulations results will be compared with the measured data in all cases.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-16-03] Data-Driven System Response Modeling for SPECT via Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) of Directional Penetration Maps from Experimental Sparse Scanning Data (#2923)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Jin (Autores: Y. Jin , S. Mandot , L.-J. Meng)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Illinois at Urbana and Champaign, Department of Nuclear, Plasma, and Radiological Engineering, Urbana, Illinois, United States of America [2] University of Illinois at Urbana and Champaign, Beckman Institute for Advance Science and Technology, Urbana, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate system response modeling is essential for quantitative SPECT, but system response functions (SRFs) generated from nominal collimator geometry can deviate from the response of the actual system due to aperture imperfections, mechanical misalignment, and septal penetration. This mismatch is especially significant for a non-conventional aperture. We propose a data-driven SRF modeling method that reconstructs a directional penetration map from sparse point-source scans. In the proposed aperture-domain representation, each source-detector measurement is indexed by its aperture crossing position and ray direction, allowing measurements from different source locations and detector pixels to be pooled into a shared position-direction map. The map represents the effective material path length, which is estimated by maximum likelihood under a Poisson model with latent detector-depth sublayers, and the resulting problem is solved using an expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm. SRFs for arbitrary source locations can then be generated through the ray-tracing method by combining geometric factors with the learned path length and the photon-energy-dependent attenuation coefficient. Preliminary Geant4 validation using a 16-aperture micro-ring CZT-based SPECT model with controlled collimator tilting demonstrates that scan-based SRFs recover aperture-level response features missed by nominal-design SRFs and agree more closely with the ground-truth tilted-collimator response at non-scanned source positions. Experimental validation on the clinical AlphaSPECT system and image-domain evaluation will be presented at the conference.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-16-04] Wasserstein Pullback Metric for Intrinsic Difficulty of Scintillation Detector Inverse Problems (#2265)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Bae (Autores: S. Bae , J.S. Lee)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Seoul National University Graduate School, Interdisciplinary Program in Bioengineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] Seoul National University Graduate School, Integrated Major in Innovative Medical Science, Seoul, Republic of Korea [3] Seoul National University Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Scintillation detector inverse problems are limited by how sensitively photon distributions change with interaction or detector conditions. We propose a likelihood-free Wasserstein-geometric framework for quantifying this distributional sensitivity using a pretrained generative model for scintillation photon transport. By representing conditional photon distributions as pushforwards of a latent distribution, the Jacobian of the transport map induces a Wasserstein pullback metric on the condition space. We use the trace of this metric as a local sensitivity measure and its detector-level average as the expected distributional sensitivity (EDS). The proposed sensitivity captures DOI and crystal-dependent timing trends, correlates monotonically with interaction localization error across crystal dimensions (Spearman ρ=-0.88 for rough Teflon and -0.90 for polished ESR), and supports differentiable detector optimization. These results suggest that Wasserstein sensitivity can provide an estimator-independent measure of inverse-problem difficulty and a tool for detector characterization and optimization.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-16-05] Zero-Knowledge Calibration: PET Geometry Recovery from Unlocalized Point Sources (#2333)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Freye (Autores: T. Freye , J. Thull , Y. Kuhl , V. Schulz)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] RWTH Aachen University, Chair of Imaging & Computer Vision, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [2] Hyperion Hybrid Imaging Systems, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Mechanical detector misalignments in positron emission tomography (PET) scanners, caused by manufacturing tolerances as well as mechanical and thermal stress, lead to inaccurate line of response (LOR) positioning and consequently degrade image quality and quantitative accuracy. Existing calibration methods typically rely on dedicated measurements with known tracer distributions, requiring either calibration phantoms or precisely positioned point sources. These procedures are time-consuming, operationally demanding, and difficult to integrate into PET-MRI systems due to magnetic field constraints. This work proposes an unsupervised detector alignment calibration method that estimates detector misalignments from point-source measurements with unknown source positions. The proposed approach estimates source locations using an iterative likelihood-based optimization and derives detector alignment parameters from the resulting LOR geometry, eliminating the need for externally calibrated source positioning. The method is evaluated on a simulated PET scanner and achieves translational and rotational alignment accuracies of 0.95mm and 0.41°, respectively, while the source positions are recovered with an accuracy of 0.61mm using only 3×10 5 LORs. By avoiding specialized calibration hardware and requiring only limited acquisition data, the proposed method enables rapid, flexible, and easily deployable PET calibration. Its low operational complexity and short acquisition time make it particularly promising for routine clinical recalibration and for hybrid imaging systems such as PET-MRI.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-16-06] A Multi-Channel Positronium Decay Source Model in GATE (#2911)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 W. Krzemien (Autores: M. Bała , W. Krzemien , K. Dulski , W. Zdeb , A. Coussat)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Centre for Nuclear Research, Department of High Energy Physics, Otwock Swierk, Poland [2] National Centre for Nuclear Research, Department of Complex Systems, Otwock Swierk, Poland [3] Jagiellonian University, Faculty of Physics, Astronomy and Applied Computer Science, Krakow, Poland [4] INSA-Lyon, Université Claude Bernard Lyon 1, CNRS, Inserm, CREATIS UMR 5220,, Lyon, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positronium-based imaging [1-3] requires accurate Monte Carlo modelling of positronium decay in matter. Existing implementations in the Geant4 Application for Tomographic Emission simulation framework [4-5] are limited to at most two annihilation channels, which is insufficient to represent the multi-component lifetime structures observed in biological tissues and complex materials. We present a new modular positronium decay source model implemented in both GATE versions 9.4 and 10 [5], enabling the simultaneous definition of an arbitrary number of decay channels. Each channel is independently characterised by its mean lifetime, branching fraction, annihilation multiplicity into two or three photons, and optional prompt photon emission, as required for radionuclides such as scandium-44, gallium-68, and iodine-124. The model is validated through analytical and numerical benchmarks. Branching fractions are correctly reproduced within statistical uncertainties across all tested configurations. Practical applicability is demonstrated through simulations of a NEMA Image Quality phantom filled with tissue-mimicking positronium sources representing water, fat, muscle, and bone. The implementation is fully compatible with standard simulation workflows, providing the community with the first general-purpose, multi-channel positronium decay model integrated into a widely adopted medical physics simulation framework.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-17-01] Detection of deep seated anatomical changes in patients undergoing ion beam radiotherapy (#2562)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Martisikova (Autores: M. Martisikova , R. Kirchgässner , P. Ochoa , S. Harrabi , P. Schlegel , E. Bartelme , S. Yesilmen , L. Kelleter , J. Jakubek , M. Winter , J. Debus , O. Jaekel)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] German Cancer Research Center, Division of Medical Physics in Radiation Oncology, Heidelberg, Germany [2] University Hospital, Department of Radiation Oncology, Heidelberg, Germany [3] Nationatl Center for Tumor Disseases (NCT), HIRO-Heidelberg Institute for Radiation Oncology, Heidelberg, Germany [4] University of Heidelberg, Faculty of Physics, Heidelberg, Germany [5] University of Heidelberg, Faculty of Informatics, Heidelberg, Germany [6] University of Applied Sciences, Department of Science, Saarbruecken, Germany [7] Heidelberg Ion Beam Therapy Center (HIT), Departmen of Medical Physics, Heidelberg, Germany [8] ADVACAM s.r.o, Prague, Czech Republic
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Carbon-ion radiotherapy enables highly precise tumor treatment, particularly for locations near critical structures such as the brainstem or spinal cord. However, the focused dose distributions that make this modality effective also increase its sensitivity to variations in the beam path. Consequently, accurate monitoring and control of the dose distribution in the patient are essential. Despite this clinical need, radiation-free monitoring approaches are scarce. In order to investigate use of secondary ions for this purpose, we compare measured ion distributions across treatment fractions. For this approach, a contactless detection system for secondary-ion tracking was developed and clinically implemented at the Heidelberg Ion-Beam Therapy Facility (HIT), Germany. The system enables tracking of individual secondary-ions with high spatial and temporal resolution. The performance of the developed monitoring approach is currently being assessed within the clinical study "InViMo." To date, more than 100 patient measurements have been acquired. For the majority of patients, the measured data showed consistency across treatment fractions. However, pronounced inter-fractional variations were observed in several cases. These signals demonstrated clear spatial correlation with the anatomical ground truth derived from CT imaging, including challenging cases involving deep-seated tumors. In addition, the system enabled a worldwide first measurement of a patient treated with helium ions, a promising modality for several pediatric tumor indications. Considerable amount of secondary ion tracks was recorded. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method can detect clinically relevant anatomical changes in treated patients with high sensitivity and accurate spatial localization.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-17-02] Proton Range Verification in 3D Pencil Beam Scanning Lattice via a Dual-head Multi-slit 3D Prompt Gamma Imaging System (#2861)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Zhang (Autores: H. Zhang , B. Zhao , Z. Wang , J. Wang , P. Fan , Y. Yu , W. Duan , L. Gao , S. Wang , Z. Wu , T. Ma , H. Liu , Y. Liu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Ministry of Education, Key Laboratory of Particle & Radiation Imaging, Beijing, China [2] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [3] Chengdu NOVEL MEDICAL Equipment Co. Ltd., Beijing, China [4] Hebei Yizhou Cancer Hospital, Zhuozhou, China [5] China institute of Atomic Energy, Beijing, China [6] China Academy of Space Technology and Science, Beijing Institute of Spacecraft Environment Engineering, Beijing, China [7] Beijing Institute of Spacecraft Environment Engineering, Technology on Reliability and Environmental Engineering Laboratory, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Objective: Online range monitoring is critically important in proton therapy, as range uncertainties arising from patient positioning, anatomical variations, and range calculation algorithms remain a major limitation in precise dose delivery. Prompt gamma-ray imaging (PGI) offers a promising solution for real‑time range verification due to the ultra‑fast emission of prompt gamma rays. However, for the most advanced dose delivery technique-pencil beam scanning-proton beams are delivered in a three‑dimensional (3D) lattice, necessitating 3D online monitoring systems capable of spot‑by‑spot range and dose verification within a single acquisition. Approach: In this study, a dual‑head 3D PGI system based on multi‑slit collimated gamma‑ray cameras was evaluated for proton beams delivered to 3D lattices. Experiments were conducted in a clinical proton therapy treatment room using a proton beam of typical therapeutic energy incident on a polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) phantom. The precision and accuracy of both range verification and beam spot positioning were systematically assessed. Main results: At a typical low proton count level of 1 × 10⁸ protons per scanning spot, the system achieved accuracy and precision better than 1.5 mm for both range verification and beam spot positioning. At proton counts of 3 × 10⁸ or higher, both metrics improved to sub‑millimeter levels (<1 mm). Significance: These findings demonstrate that the dual‑head 3D PGI system is capable of high‑precision, spot‑by‑spot range and beam spot verification even at low proton counts, highlighting its potential for effective online in vivo monitoring in 3D pencil beam scanning proton therapy.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-17-03] Design and Experimental Validation of the REALPATH Prompt Gamma Camera for Range Verification in Hadrontherapy (#2605)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Piroddi (Autores: M. Piroddi , K. Urban , E. S. Bellotti , A. Forgione , F. Garzetti , D. Mazzucconi , C. Riboldi , L. Santini , G. Borghi , M. Carminati , G. Baroni , S. Agosteo , M. Pullia , C. E. Fiorini)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Politecnico di Milano, Department of Electronics, Information and Bioengineering (DEIB), Milano, Italy [2] Politecnico di Milano, Department of Energy (DENG), Milano, Italy [3] National Institute for Nuclear Physics (INFN), Milano, Italy [4] Centro Nazionale di Adroterapia Oncologica (CNAO), Pavia, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Hadrontherapy is a kind of radiation therapy that delivers highly localized radiation doses to treat tumors spearing healthy tissues. In this context, Prompt Gamma Imaging (PGI) is a promising technique towards real-time monitoring of the particle beam range, thereby enhancing both treatment precision and patient safety. The REALPATH project aims to develop a compact range verification system based on passive collimation and a pixelated gamma camera. The detector utilizes LYSO scintillator crystals coupled to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), organized into 64- channel base units that scale up to a 512-channel instrument with a 20 × 10 cm² footprint. The primary objective of this project is to overcome the physical and operational barriers that currently prevent PGI systems from being used during standard treatment workflows. For this reason, the detector and electronics are engineered to maximize detection efficiency, minime acquisition dead time, while reducing the footprint of the system. A novel "inverted" collimator design significantly reduces the overall instrument weight and allows the camera to be rigidly fixed beneath the patient couch. The experimental results obtained from measurement campaigns at CNAO facility in Pavia, Italy are also reported.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-17-04] First Tests of Hybrid n/gamma-ray Imaging for Proton Therapy Range Verification at a Clinical Proton Beam (#2027)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. T. Mueller (Autores: S. T. Mueller , S. Blorstad Thu , T. Jagt , I. Meric , A. Milde Bekkevoll , G. Pausch , H. Ratliff , K. Roemer , J. Turko , A. Wolf , T. Koegler)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] OncoRay - National Center for Radiation Research in Oncology, Dresden, Germany [2] Helmholtz- Zentrum Dresden- Rossendorf, Institute of Radiooncology - OncoRay, Dresden, Germany [3] University of Bergen, Bergen, Norway [4] Western Norway University of Applied Sciences, Bergen, Norway [5] Rapiscan Systems GmbH, Hofheim, Germany [6] Helmholtz- Zentrum Dresden- Rossendorf, Institute of Radiation Physics, Dresden, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Proton therapy provides highly conformal dose delivery and the integration of in-vivo range verification can further enhance treatment safety and efficacy by serving as a trigger for intervention and by decreasing safety margins [1]. The NOVO collaboration [2] investigates a novel hybrid detector concept that combines prompt gamma ray and fast neutron imaging in a compact organic-scintillator-based system to improve proton range verification. This dual-particle approach offers complementary particle information and thus improved localisation capabilities [3]. For the first time, the NOVO detector was operated at a clinical proton beam at the OncoRay proton therapy facility in Dresden, Germany [4]. The system's detection performance and imaging capability were investigated by irradiating different phantoms with numerous proton energies and beam currents and by varying the phantoms' position and compositions. The detector array demonstrated stable performance under clinically relevant mixed-field and high-rate conditions and achieved reliable neutron-photon discrimination. Furthermore, images could be reconstructed which provide the first experimental validation of the combined n/gamma approach in proton therapy and highlight its strong potential as a future real-time range verification technique.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-17-05] First Demonstration of Short-Interval Proton Range-Verification and FAZA PET on SIRMIO (#1636)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Toramatsu (Autores: C. Toramatsu , C. Steinbrecht , F. Evangelista , G. Lovatti , M. Chen , M. Nitta , J. Bortfeldt , N. Bassler , P. G. Thirolf , B. S. Sorensen , M. Busk , T. Yamaya , K. Parodi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology, Chiba, Japan [2] Ludwig Maximilians-University, Munich, Bavaria, Germany [3] Danish Centre for Particle Therapy, Aarhus, Denmark
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Biological washout, traditionally considered a source of error in range‑verification PET in particle therapy, is now emerging as a potential new biomarker for tumor diagnosis. At QST, proof‑of‑concept studies using animal irradiation at HIMAC demonstrated a correlation between hypoxia PET maps and washout rate maps derived from range‑verification PET. However, due to facility limitations, including radioisotope regulation constraints, hypoxia PET had to be performed on the day following irradiation. As a result, confounding factors such as tumor growth and delayed irradiation effects could not be fully excluded. In contrast, LMU has developed the Small Animal Proton Irradiator for Research in Molecular Image‑Guided Radiation Oncology (SIRMIO) that includes an in-beam PET scanner, and conducted experiments at DCPT, which offers close integration with a nuclear medicine division. Leveraging this environment, we designed an experimental protocol to perform both proton range‑verification PET (irradiation-PET) and hypoxia PET (FAZA-PET) on the same platform with a shortened interval using the SIRMIO system at DCPT. Considering that the activity level in range‑verification PET is much lower than that in FAZA-PET, ¹⁸F‑FAZA administration was performed after the irradiation-PET. The time interval between the two PET scans was reduced to < 4 hours, which is sufficient for FAZA uptake while minimizing biological changes in the tumor. The first proof‑of‑concept experiment was conducted using mouse models bearing SCCVII tumors. Mouse was positioned in a custom-made holder, and co-registration was ensured by on-board μCBCT. A low washout rate in hypoxic areas was observed, which may be explained by poor blood perfusion. Correlation to in-beam PET data will be analyzed and reported.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-17-06] Beyond short-lived positron emitters: feasibility of 18 F detection for range verification in carbon ion therapy (#1521)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Hamato (Autores: A. Hamato , C. Toramatsu , H. Wakizaka , H. Tashima , Y. Iwao , H.G. Kang , G. Akamatsu , K. Parodi , T. Yamaya)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology (QST), Advanced Nuclear Medicine Sciences, Chiba, Japan [2] Ludwig Maximilian University, Department of Medical Physics, Munich, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In carbon ion therapy, positron emission tomography (PET) is one of the most investigated methods for range verification that relies on short half-life β + emitters such as 11 C and 15 O. Consequently, in-beam PET or off-beam PET performed immediately after irradiation have been considered mandatory, and little attention has been paid to the existence of longer-lived β + emitters than ¹¹C. With a recent increase in PET system sensitivity, delayed acquisitions targeting longer-lived β + emitters have become increasingly feasible. In this study, therefore, we focused on the feasibility of off-beam detection of an irradiation-induced 18 F component for range verification in carbon ion therapy. Monte Carlo simulations were first performed to estimate the yield of 18 F and the other most important β + emitters induced in a polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) phantom irradiated by carbon ion beams. The yield of produced 18 F was one-eighth that of the 11 C, and the shifts of the dose peak and PET peak were 1.5 mm and 0.5 mm for in- and off-beam PET, respectively. To validate the simulation results, a PMMA phantom and a live tumor-bearing rat model were irradiated with a 12 C ion beam of 290 MeV/u at the carbon therapy facility of the Heavy Ion Medical Accelerator in Chiba (HIMAC) to evaluate 18 F production in both simplified and biologically relevant environments. One hour after irradiation, PET scans were carried out for 30 min for both the phantom and the rat. Time-activity curves (TACs) were extracted from the PET images, and they showed the presence and detectability of 18 F. A measured activity profile was obtained from the off-beam PET image of the phantom and compared with the measured dose. The dose peak and PET peak positions were matched, which is consistent with submillimeter (0.5 mm) shift of the peaks for off-beam PET predicted from the simulation. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of 18 F for range verification in carbon ion therapy using off-beam PET.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-18-01] Steerable Kernel Based Emission Tomography Reconstruction (#2137)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Wei (Autores: H. Wei , L. Livieratos , A. J. Reader)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Kings College London, School of Biomedical Engineering and Imaging Sciences, London, United Kingdom [2] Kings College London, Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, London, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Kernelized expectation maximization (KEM) has emerged as an effective and practical approach for improving image quality in emission tomographic reconstruction by incorporating high-quality prior information into the iterative reconstruction process. In conventional KEM, the kernel matrix is derived from a prior image and remains fixed throughout reconstruction. This may result in artifacts when the prior image and target emission data are not perfectly matched, especially in cross-modality or cross-scanner settings, such as MR-guided PET reconstruction and PET-guided SPECT reconstruction in theranostic imaging. In those settings, differences in scanner characteristics, acquisition time points, or tracer distributions may cause mismatch between the prior image and the target emission data. In this work, we propose a steerable kernel reconstruction framework that adapts the prior-derived kernel representation according to the measured data. The proposed method dynamically updates the kernel matrix during reconstruction to improve consistency with the measured data. We evaluate the proposed method on 2D brain phantom data for MR-guided PET reconstruction and on 2D thorax phantom data for PET-guided SPECT reconstruction in a theranostic setting. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed steerable kernel method mitigates mismatch-induced artifacts and achieves improved reconstruction fidelity compared with conventional fixed-kernel approaches. These findings suggest that adaptive kernel steering offers a promising direction for robust prior-guided emission tomography reconstruction under realistic mismatch conditions.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-18-02] Cross-Tracer PET Image Reconstruction Using an 18 F-FDG-Trained Deep Kernel Model (#2782)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Li (Autores: S. Li , X. Long , Y. Lv , G. Liu , J. Qi , S. R. Cherry , R. D. Badawi , L. Nardo , B. A. Spencer , G. Wang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California, Davis, California, United States of America [2] United Imaging Healthcare, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract PET image quality is affected by limited-count statistics and the ill-posed nature of tomographic image reconstruction. Deep learning methods have shown promise for improving PET image quality. However, most existing models have primarily been developed and validated using 18 F-FDG datasets. The generalizability of 18 F-FDG- trained models to less common radiotracers, particularly non- 18 F tracers with distinct biodistributions and physical properties, has not been well demonstrated. As the clinical and research use of diverse PET tracers continues to expand, there is a growing need for unified deep learning reconstruction methods capable of generalizing across tracers. We previously developed a pretrained deep kernel model using a large-scale 18 F-FDG total-body PET dataset and demonstrated its feasibility for tomographic image reconstruction in static PET imaging by using a single-frame MLEM image as the image prior. Unlike post-reconstruction denoising methods that learn tracer-specific activity distributions and directly output images, the deep kernel method learns to construct a kernel matrix that reflects spatial correlations, making it potentially transferable across tracers. In this work, we extend the deep kernel pretraining by incorporating additional 18 F-FDG data and then investigate whether the 18 F-FDG-trained model can be directly applied to other non- 18 F tracers without any tracer-specific training or fine-tuning. The proposed method was evaluated on fourteen 68 Ga-DOTATATE scans acquired with the uEXPLORER total-body scanner and compared against a state-of-the-art deep-learning denoising model that is also trained on 18 F-FDG total-body datasets. Results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces image noise and achieves improved lesion quantitative accuracy. This work demonstrates the feasibility of cross-tracer PET reconstruction using an 18 F-FDG-trained deep kernel model, supporting future evaluation in larger multi-tracer datasets.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-18-03] List-mode PET Image Reconstruction with Neural Radiance Fields (#1346)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Lu (Autores: H. Lu , C. E. Davey , L. A. Johnston)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Melbourne, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Parkville, Australia [2] University of Melbourne, Melbourne Brain Centre Imaging Unit, Parkville, Australia
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Numerous AI-based solutions to PET image reconstruction, an ill-posed inverse problem, have been implemented to enhance image quality or convergence speed, yet most suffer from reliance on high-quality paired dataset and lack of robustness. As an emerging methodology, implicit neural representations (INRs) demonstrate tremendous potential in continuous modelling of spatial distribution. However, the existing INR-based PET reconstruction methods generally suffer from loss of information due to compression in sinograms they utilise as input, and do not include corrections for noise caused by the physical factors like attenuation and normalisation. In this work, we present a self-supervised PET reconstruction method based on neural radiance fields (NeRFs), a special type of INR with list-mode coincidences as input, where sensitivity is incorporated as both the weight for sampling points along each LOR and combined corrections for attenuation and normalisation. LORs with no recorded coincidences function as data-driven regularisation and are augmented as part of the input. Results using simulated and experimental data show that our proposed method can achieve excellent image quality and improved contrast, and outperform conventional iterative algorithms and other AI approaches, particularly in recovering fine details in small hot regions.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-18-04] Dynamic image reconstruction for high-resolution SAVANT scanner using non-negative low-rank constraint (#3104)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Najmaoui (Autores: Y. Najmaoui , Y. Djebra , Y. Chemli , M. Gaudreault , K. Fontaine , M. Dhaynaut , J.-D. Gallezot , M.-A. Tétrault , R. Lecomte , M. Normandin , G. El Fakhri , C. Ma , T. Marin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yale University, Yale Biomedical Imaging Institute, New Haven, Connecticut, United States of America [2] Université de Sherbrooke, Institut interdisciplinaire d'innovation technologique, Sherbrooke, Québec, Canada [3] Université de Sherbrooke, Centre hospitalier universitaire de Sherbrooke, Sherbrooke, Québec, Canada
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dynamic Positron Emission Tomography (PET) imaging is an essential tool for research in neurodegenerative diseases through the modeling of tracer kinetics. However, achieving ultra-high spatial resolution in PET systems tends to reduce their overall geometric sensitivity. This leads to a possible compromise between dynamic frame duration, spatial resolution, and noise. This study presents the application of a non-negative low-rank-constrained reconstruction method tailored for the ultra-high-resolution SAVANT scanner. Traditional algorithms reconstruct PET images frame-by-frame without taking into account the natural spatiotemporal correlations within the data. This redundancy is leveraged by this method to reconstruct all the dynamic frames simultaneously. The method alternates between updating a matrix representing the spatial distribution for each temporal basis, and updating a matrix representing the translation from temporal bases to frame. In order to accommodate for the large memory and computational requirements associated with the SAVANT, we extended the nonnegative low-rank model to support list-mode data and optimized its implementation through Graphical Processing Unit (GPU) acceleration. In vivo evaluations using a dynamic [18F]DG scan demonstrate a visible improvement in image quality when using the proposed method compared to the conventional frame-by-frame MLEM algorithm. The low-rank constraint allows to preserve greater detail and shows sharper anatomical structures, which better showcases the high resolution of the SAVANT system.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-18-05] A Generalized Tuy-Type Completeness Analysis for X-Ray Scattering Tensor Tomography (#2612)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Liu (Autores: R. Liu , R. Deng , P. Song , L. Zhang , Z. Wang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [2] Radiation Imaging of Ministry of Education, Key Laboratory of Particle, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract X-ray scattering tensor tomography aims to recover orientation-dependent microstructural information beyond scalar attenuation or scalar dark-field CT. For quantitative reconstruction, however, an aquisition trajectory satisfying Tuy's condition should also provide enough independent angular sensitivity for the tensor model being reconstructed. We formulate this requirement as a generalized Tuy-type completeness condition for scattering tensor tomography, linking conventional geometric visibility with tensor sensitivity. This analysis shows that the former 15-component model is intrinsically incomplete: under each plane, only 12 independent tensor modes can be probed, so arbitrary 15-component fields require additional prior assumptions. In contrast, the reduced 6-component model satisfies the planar completeness requirement under sufficient angular coverage. Planar singular-value tests confirm both the 12-mode limit and the full rank of the reduced model, providing practical criteria for tensor-model selection and aquisition trajectory design and optimization.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-18-06] Hamiltonian Monte Carlo Ensemble Features for DATSCAN SPECT Analysis in Parkinson's Disease (#1511)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Leontiou (Autores: T. Leontiou , S. Jaafari , C. Likartsis , A. Frixou , Y. Parpottas , E. Stiliaris , C. N. Papanicolas)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Frederick University, Department of Mechanical Engineering, School of Engineering, Nicosia, Cyprus [2] Frederick Research Center, Nicosia, Cyprus [3] Limassol General Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Limassol, Cyprus [4] The Cyprus Institute, CaSToRC, Nicosia, Cyprus [5] National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, Department of Physics, Athens, Greece [6] The Cyprus Academy of Sciences, Letters and Arts, Nicosia, Cyprus [7] European University Cyprus, Department of Histology and Embryology, School of Dentistry, Nicosia, Cyprus
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) reconstruction is an ill-posed inverse problem, and standard clinical methods typically provide a single reconstructed image without an explicit characterization of uncertainty. In this work, we adopt a stochastic reconstruction approach based on Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), which generates an ensemble of radiotracer distributions consistent with the measured projection data and the assumed forward model. Rather than relying solely on the reconstructed mean image, this formulation enables both uncertainty-aware evaluation of conventional measures and the construction of new descriptors derived from ensemble variability. We investigate whether such ensemble-derived features can provide additional diagnostic information for DATSCAN SPECT analysis, complementing standard metrics such as striatal binding ratios (SBR). We show that normalized fluctuation measures extracted from the HMC ensemble exhibit distinct behavior between control and Parkinson's disease cases. These findings suggest that the stochastic reconstruction framework may provide additional diagnostic information and enhance the diagnostic capabilities of SPECT.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-18-07] Monte Carlo-based reconstruction in Ac-225 SPECT: impact on image quality, quantitative accuracy, and computational burden. (#1164)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Li (Autores: C. Li , P. Esquinas , J. Fowler , X. Hou , A. Rahmim , C. Uribe)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The University of British Columbia, Department of Physics & Astronomy, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada [2] BC Cancer Research Institute, Department of Basic & Translational Research, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada [3] BC Cancer, Department of Molecular Imaging & Therapy, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Purpose: Quantitative 225 Ac SPECT is challenging because of low counts, complex emissions, scatter, and septal penetration[1]. This study developed and evaluated a Monte Carlo (MC)-based reconstruction framework for 225 Ac SPECT, focusing on image quality, quantitative accuracy, and computational cost. Methods: SIMIND was used as an MC forward-projector for a vendor-specific SPECT system with a high-energy collimator, while an analytical back-projector was retained to improve efficiency[2]. Unlike conventional MLEM with TEW scatter correction, the MC model incorporated patient scatter, collimator penetration/scatter, detector backscatter, and system response. Performance was evaluated using both simulated and experimental phantom data. The simulated phantom contained 20, 40, and 72 mm spheres, and the experimental phantom contained a 60 mm sphere, both with a 10:1 sphere-to-background activity ratio. Reconstructions used a 218 keV photopeak with a 20% window and were assessed using the recovery coefficient(RC) and contrast recovery coefficient(CRC). Results: In simulations, MC reconstruction improved contrast recovery and reduced scatter and septal-penetration artifacts. At 25 iterations, mean CRCs for the 72, 40, and 20 mm spheres were 90.1%, 61.3%, and 21.9%, compared with 45.4%, 29.1%, and 9.4% for conventional reconstruction. MC reconstruction directly estimated activity in MBq and achieved RCs of 90.2% and 94.5% for the 72 and 40 mm spheres. Experimental results showed consistent improvement, with MC reconstruction more than doubling CRC at 25 iterations (75.4% vs. 29.2%) and achieving an RC of 88.5% for the 60 mm sphere. Reducing photon histories from 600 to 30 million per projection preserved accuracy for the 72 mm sphere while reducing runtime from 53 to 3.1 min per iteration. Conclusion: MC-based reconstruction substantially improves image quality and quantitative accuracy for 225 Ac SPECT and may support more reliable post-therapy imaging and dosimetry.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H.J. Lee (Autores: H.J. Lee , S. Bae , J.S. Lee)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Seoul National University Graduate School, Interdisciplinary Program in Bioengineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] Seoul National University Graduate School, Integrated Major in Innovative Medical Science, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Pre-treatment dosimetry for 177 Lu-DOTATATE therapy requires accurate reconstruction from low-dose sparse-view SPECT imaging, which remains challenging due to severe noise and limited projection information. We propose a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM)-based reconstruction framework with projection-domain optimization for sparse-view 177 Lu SPECT imaging. Experimental results on multi-timepoint 177 Lu-DOTATATE SPECT datasets demonstrated competitive reconstruction and dosimetry performance with substantially faster optimization under sparse-view conditions.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-19-01] Noise-Aware Brownian Bridge Diffusion Model for Denoising of Low-Dose PET Images (#2951)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 W. De Mits (Autores: W. De Mits , E. Taragola , B. Vervenne , M.E. Daube-Witherspoon , C. Vanhove , S. Matej , S. Vandenberghe , J.S. Karp , F.M. Muller)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Ghent University, Faculty of Engineering and Architecture, Ghent, Belgium [2] University of Pennsylvania, Department of Radiology, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study proposes a Noise-Aware Brownian Bridge Diffusion Model (NA-BBDM) for low-dose positron emission tomography (PET) denoising. The proposed NA-BBDM models a conditional diffusion path between paired low- and full-dose PET images and incorporates the estimated noise level from the input image into the network. The noise level is estimated from the variance of the residual between the low-dose image and a Gaussian-smoothed version. The diffusion path uses a parabolic variance schedule with zero variance at both endpoints (i.e., low- and full-dose images), parameterized by peak variance and number of diffusion steps. Both are treated as noise-dependent hyperparameters and optimized through grid search. Training data consisted of 25 18 F-FDG datasets acquired on the PennPET Explorer and subsampled to emulate dose levels from 1/5 to 1/300 of total counts. Performance was compared with a U-Net and evaluated on independent 18 F-FDG and unseen 11 C-carfentanil (CFN) datasets. The NA-BBDM produced images with reduced noise speckles (still present with the U-Net) and better-preserved high-uptake regions at ultra-low-dose levels. Quantitatively, the NA-BBDM also achieved lower SUV variability and mean squared error for 11 C-CFN, especially below 1/60th dose. Our results suggest that the NA-BBDM provides a robust framework for ultra-low-dose and cross-tracer PET denoising.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-19-02] N2N-DiffPET: Self-supervised Diffusion for Low-dose PET Image Denoising (#2281)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Q. Li (Autores: K. Fan , Y. Wu , Q. Li , H. Liu , N. Guo)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Department of Radiology, Boston, Massachusetts, United States of America [2] Zhejiang University, Department of Optical Engineering, Hangzhou, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Low-dose positron emission tomography (PET) imaging can reduce radiation exposure and shorten acquisition time, but reduced photon counts introduce strong count-dependent noise and degrade quantitative reliability. Supervised deep learning methods usually require paired low-dose and normal-dose PET images, which are difficult to acquire in clinical practice. We propose N2N-DiffPET, a self-supervised diffusion framework for low-dose PET denoising without normal-dose supervision. Inspired by recent self-supervised diffusion MRI denoising, N2N-DiffPET adapts iterative diffusion refinement to PET using paired noisy PET observations generated from independent low-dose measurements by event splitting or Poisson resampling. To better model PET noise, N2N-DiffPET constructs a fusion trajectory between the paired noisy PET images and perturbs it using pair-derived PET noise rather than synthetic Gaussian noise. Co-registered MRI is incorporated as an anatomical condition to improve structural preservation. During inference, bidirectional deterministic denoising is performed, and the two directional outputs are averaged to reduce directional bias. Normal-dose PET images are not used for training and are only used for evaluation. Experiments on BrainWeb-based PET/MR simulation data show that N2N-DiffPET suppresses noise while preserving anatomical structures and regional uptake, outperforming conventional denoising methods and self-supervised baselines in visual quality and quantitative metrics.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-19-03] Multi-Dose PET Image Denoising using Consistency Flow Matching (#1864)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J.H. Lee (Autores: J.H. Lee , S. Bae , J.S. Lee)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Seoul National University, Interdisciplinary Program in Bioengineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] Seoul National University, Integrated Major in Innovative Medical Science, Seoul, Republic of Korea [3] Seoul National University, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea [4] Brightonix Imaging Inc., Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Low-dose PET reduces patient radiation burden by decreasing injected radiotracer dose or scan duration, but the resulting reduction in photon counts introduces statistical noise that degrades diagnostic image quality. Most deep learning denoising methods are trained at a single fixed dose reduction factor and do not generalize to unseen dose levels. We propose Consistency Flow Matching (CFM), a multi-dose denoising framework that augments flow matching with a cross-dose consistency regularization. During training, pairs of low-dose images at two different dose reduction factors are jointly processed, and a consistency loss enforces agreement between their predicted normal-dose outputs, promoting a dose-invariant flow field. Dose conditioning is achieved through Spatial Feature-wise Linear Modulation with a log-sinusoidal dose embedding. Experiments on the UltraLow-Dose PET Challenge dataset show that CFM improves perceptual image quality and out-of-distribution generalization over standard flow matching, confirming the benefit of cross-dose consistency regularization.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-19-04] High-Temporal-Resolution Data-Driven Respiratory Motion Estimation in Cardiac PET Imaging (#1890)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Sun (Autores: H. Wei , C. Sun , Z. Feng , Y. Li , D. Zhang , Q. Ye , Y. Lu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] United Imaging Healthcare, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Cardiac PET is widely used for myocardial perfusion imaging and viability assessment, both of which require high image quality and quantitative accuracy. In free-breathing acquisitions, respiratory motion can induce cardiac displacement, particularly along the superior-inferior (SI, z-axis) direction, leading to image blurring, attenuation-emission mismatch, and quantitative bias. Reliable estimation of this translation is therefore essential for effective motion correction. In this work, we propose COD-S (Centroid of Distribution-Scaled), a data-driven method to estimate respiratory-induced SI cardiac translation in cardiac PET. COD-S integrates the high sensitivity and high temporal resolution of COD analysis with the physically scaled displacement provided by image registration. Specifically, the respiratory motion trajectory is decomposed into waveform and amplitude components, where the waveform is derived from COD and the amplitude are calibrated using registration-based estimates. This produces a high-temporal-resolution and physically interpretable cardiac translation trajectory without external respiratory hardware, providing a practical input for motion correction in cardiac PET.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-19-05] Spatial-variant fast non-linear energy calibration for a high resolution SSLE pixelated PET detector (#3118)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Jiménez Algarra (Autores: L. Jiménez Algarra , V. Sánchez Tembleque , L. Batres Mongil , D. Pérez Benito , J. J. Vaquero López)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Departamento de Bioingeniería, Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, Madrid, Spain, Departamento de Bioingeniería, Leganés, Spain [2] Instituto de Investigación Sanitaria Gregorio Marañón, Madrid, Spain, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract High-resolution PET detectors require position dependent energy calibration due to the spatial variability of their optical response. This work addresses that challenge for a novel hexagonal LYSO detector structured by subsurface laser engraving (SSLE) with a double honeycomb displaced crystal array, coupled to a custom 61-channel hexagonal SiPM. This design provides two depth-of-interaction (DOI) layers as well as a high-granularity for event's positioning. We first present a DOI separation method based on a dispersion metric computed from the per-channel light distribution, enabling crystal pixel specific calibration for each layer independently. After precise vertex identification, energy calibration is then performed per crystal pixel by fitting four reference points: the 202 and 307 keV intrinsic 176Lu peaks and the 511 and 1275 keV peaks from a 22Na source to a non-linear model accounting for SiPM saturation. These points are fitted to a non-linear response model that accounts for SiPM saturation and electronic nonlinearity. The proposed calibration produces stable photopeak positions across the detector and achieves an energy resolution of 15.2% at 511 keV, while preserving the DOI-resolved flood maps required for high-granularity event's positioning by PET imaging techniques.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-19-06] Random Coincidence Correction for Inter-Crystal Scatter Events in PET (#2588)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Shim (Autores: H. Shim , G.B. Ko)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Department of Nuclear and Quantum Engineering, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [2] Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Mechanical Engineering Research Institute, Daejeon, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Inter-crystal scatter (ICS) events in PET, in which a 511 keV photon deposits energy across multiple crystals, offer a route to higher effective sensitivity but are conventionally discarded by photopeak windowing. Prior work has focused on positioning the first-interaction crystal, yet positioning alone does not translate ICS recovery into a system-level sensitivity gain: accepting ICS events requires lowering the lower-level discriminator, which sharply increases the singles rate and raises three issues that have not been jointly addressed, how to group raw singles into candidate ICS events, how to reject uncorrelated groupings of independent-photon singles, and whether the resulting triple coincidences are compatible with the dual-coincidence random-correction framework. This study presents a unified pipeline that addresses all three. Candidate ICS events are formed from list-mode singles and screened for type-1 randoms (false ICS) by a joint timing-distance gate, suppressing the singles-level ICS-to-PE ratio from 15.5-18% to 7-7.5% with negligible activity dependence. Validated PE and ICS events are then paired into PE-PE and PE-ICS prompt coincidences, and the singles-prompt (SP) framework is extended to ICS events by symmetric deflation of the measured ICS rate, yielding a type-resolved SP estimator for type-2 random correction. Validated through GATE simulations of the Pharos PET scanner (Brightonix Imaging; Seoul, Korea), the type-resolved SP estimator achieves R̂/R true = 0.97-1.01 for PE-ICS coincidences across six activity conditions (200-667 μCi), outperforming the unified strategy and standard delayed-window and singles-rate methods. The complete pipeline delivers approximately 13% additional net true coincidences over a PE-only baseline, with essentially activity-invariant gain across the operating range examined.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-19-07] A Software-Based Coincidence Sorters for Simultaneous PET Emission and Lu-176 Intrinsic Transmission Data Extraction (#1792)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 X. Zhao (Autores: X. Zhao , Z. Wang , Z. Xie)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Peking University, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Conventional PET coincidence sorters focus on emission events, disregarding intrinsic Lu-176 background radiation in LYSO (Lutetium-Yttrium Oxyorthosilicate) crystals as unwanted noise. To enable simultaneous acquisition of emission and intrinsic transmission data, we developed a software-based multi-window coincidence processor capable of extracting mixed-energy coincidence events from list-mode singles data. The processor utilizes geometric constraints and a dynamic time-of-flight (TOF)-based limit to filter candidate pairs. To suppress severe 511 keV's backscatter contamination in the 202 keV transmission window, a dual-condition rejection strategy was integrated, reducing residual crosstalk to 15.9%. Quantitative validation against Monte Carlo simulation ground truth showed good agreement in count statistics, sinograms, and radial profiles. Tomographic reconstructions successfully recovered phantom structures, validating the fidelity of the simultaneously extracted emission and intrinsic transmission coincidences.
