sub_talks.title: [MIC-19-08] Characterisation of Positron Emission Particle Tracking (PEPT) Performance for In-vivo Blood Flow Estimation in Preclinical PET (#1869)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Vass (Autores: L. Vass , T. Gibson , R. De Torres , P. K. Marsden)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] King's College London, School of Biomedical Engineering and Imaging Sciences, London, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positron Emission Particle Tracking (PEPT) enables tracking of individual radiolabelled particles and is widely used in industrial applications (e.g. fluid dynamics), but remains underexplored for biomedical use. We recently demonstrated whole-body in vivo tracking of single nanoparticles in mice using a preclinical PET scanner, showing transit through the vasculature from the injection site. However, murine blood flow varies from a few to several hundred mm/s. Within this range, the conditions under which PEPT can reliably resolve motion remain poorly characterised. Trajectory estimation depends on a complex interplay between activity, particle velocity, acquisition settings (e.g. energy window, temporal sampling), and algorithm parameters, which have not been explored for murine blood flow estimation. We address this by establishing a controlled framework to evaluate PEPT performance on a 3-ring PET/CT system (Mediso nanoScan 123S). A modified FLSUN 3D printer generated programmable trajectories of Ga-68 radiolabelled beads (0.4-350 kBq) at speeds of 6-170 mms⁻¹. Ground-truth motion was validated via high-frame-rate video and frame-by-frame analysis. Trajectories were reconstructed using the Birmingham method; estimated speeds and positions were compared to ground truth to quantify accuracy and localisation error. Our results show that tracking a single particle at speeds up to 50 mms⁻¹ with RMSE <2.5 mm requires activity >1.2 kBq. At ≥0.7 kBq, speeds had 18-34% error with large RMSE. At ≤0.5 kBq, trajectories were not reliably resolved. Localisation error increased with decreasing activity and increasing speed, exceeding 10 mm RMSE in low-activity, high-speed regimes. These findings suggest activities >1.2 kBq are required for reliable intravascular speed estimation.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-20-01] Evaluation of Sparse-Geometry Designs for Long-Axial Field-of-View Preclinical SPECT (#1427)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. L. Avila (Autores: E. L. Avila , L. Confalonieri , X. Pan , C.-T. Chen , E. M. Zannoni)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The University of Texas at Austin, Walker Department of Mechanical Engineering, Austin, Texas, United States of America [2] The University of Texas at Austin, Department of Diagnostic Medicine, Austin, Texas, United States of America [3] The University of Chicago, Department of Radiology, Chicago, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study presents the design and preliminary performance evaluation of a long-axial field-of-view (LA-FOV) preclinical SPECT system for small-animal total-body imaging (TBI) [1]. The proposed full scanner consists of 240 CZT detectors distributed across 10 panels and coupled with a multi-pinhole collimator. The system offers a FOV of 74 mm in diameter, ideal for rat imaging, a high-sensitivity central region of 37 mm in diameter tailored for mice, and an axial coverage up to 20 cm. System performance was characterized through simulations to compute the system response function, 3D sensitivity map, and reconstructed image quality, assessed using a digital long-axial Derenzo phantom under both noiseless and Poisson-noise conditions. A 50% checkerboard sparse configuration was compared against the full configuration [2-3]. While the sparse configuration yielded a proportional 50% reduction in sensitivity, the volumetric uniformity was preserved. Both configurations achieve similar spatial resolution. In noiseless conditions, both can resolve hot rods as small as 1.62 mm with average peak-to-valley ratios (PVR) of 4.35 (full) and 5.32 (sparse). Under noisy conditions, both configurations can fully resolve the 1.93-mm hot rods with average PVR of 7.22 (full) and 7.58 (sparse). Notably, this performance is consistent along the 20 cm axial extent of the phantom. Future work will evaluate spiral sparse geometries at sparsity levels of 25%, 33%, 66%, and 75% to characterize the degradation of image quality, with quantitative analysis in terms of contrast-to-noise ratio and contrast recovery coefficient. This work supports a pathway toward cost-effective LA-FOV preclinical SPECT instrumentation suitable for TBI.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-20-02] Feasibility study of 68 Ga/ 18 F multiplexed PET imaging on a total-body PET scanner (#2284)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 W. He (Autores: W. He , C. S. Levin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Stanford University, Department of Radiology, Palo Alto, California, United States of America [2] Stanford University, Departments of Electrical Engineering, Bioengineering, and Physics, Palo Alto, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Multiplexed PET ( m PET) enables simultaneous multi-tracer imaging by detecting prompt gamma in positron plus prompt gamma emitters for triple-photon coincidence tagging, thereby distinguishing them from pure positron emitters. ⁶⁸Ga is a commonly used PET isotope and emits a prompt gamma at 1077 keV in ~1% of its positron decays. In this study, we assessed the feasibility of ⁶⁸Ga/¹⁸F m PET on the GE Omni 128 cm total-body PET/CT using Monte Carlo simulation. The scanner model was validated against NU2-2018 sensitivity and NECR measurements. A NU2-2018 image-quality phantom was simulated with a 1:1 ⁶⁸Ga/¹⁸F background (2.65 kBq/mL per isotope) and 4:1 hot-to-background ratio, with the two largest spheres assigned to ¹⁸F and the four smaller spheres to ⁶⁸Ga to represent a challenging case for triple-coincidence detection. Isotope unmixing employed an "alternating-update joint EM (AU-EM) algorithm" that we developed with a prompt-gamma detection efficiency map simulated from a ⁶⁸Ga point-source array. The simulation yielded 3.46 billion double and 57 million triple coincidences; triple events were dominated by randoms (55.6%), with ⁶⁸Ga true triples comprising 7.1%. Using true events only, AU-EM reconstructions successfully separated the ⁶⁸Ga and ¹⁸F distributions and achieved percent contrast comparable to OSEM reconstructions from ground-truth events, although percent background variability was degraded. These results demonstrate the feasibility of ⁶⁸Ga/¹⁸F m PET on a total-body PET scanner and motivate future work on random triple-coincidence estimation, variance reduction methods, and experimental validation.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-20-03] Positronium Lifetime Imaging on LAFOV PET: Impact of Estimation Methods and Count Statistics (#2317)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. U. Rauscher (Autores: L. U. Rauscher , W. Steinberger , E. Körner , P. M.-L. Linder , C. la Fougère , F. P. Schmidt)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University Hospital Tuebingen, Department of Preclinical Imaging and Radiopharmacy, Tuebingen, Germany [2] Siemens Medical Solutions, Inc., Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America [3] University Hospital Tuebingen, Department of Nuclear Medicine and Clinical Molecular Imaging, Tuebingen, Germany [4] University of Tuebingen, Cluster of Excellence iFIT (EXC 2180) "Image Guided and Functionally Instructed Tumor Therapies", Tuebingen, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positronium lifetime imaging (PLI) enables probing tissue microstructure via the lifetime of ortho-positronium (o-Ps). Robust voxel-wise lifetime estimation remains limited even for high-sensitivity long axial field-of-view (LAFOV) positron emission tomography (PET) systems due to a combination of low detection sensitivity for triple-coincidences and variability in o-Ps lifetime (o-PS-L) extraction methods. In this work, three established approaches for o-Ps-L estimation are presented: least-squares fitting (LS), Bayesian fitting (B), and exponential fitting of the late decay tail (LT). These methods were systematically evaluated using inorganic samples (Quartz, wet and dry Amberlite XAD-4) prepared with I-124. Data were acquired on a Siemens Healthineers Biograph Vision Quadra system in single event acquisition mode and analyzed using time difference distributions (TDDs). The o-PS-L for the Quartz sample was measured to be 1.572 | 1.573 | 1.574 ns (LS | B | LT), wet XAD-4 2.381 | 2.381 | 2.798 ns and dry XAD-4 2.719 | 2.719 | 2.915 ns. LS and B approaches showed consistent results across all samples, while the LT method exhibited systematic deviations under reduced o-Ps contribution. A subsampling analysis identified a minimum of 2500 events per TDD for stable o-PS-L estimation within 5% deviation from the full-statistics result. Based on this constraint, voxel-wise lifetime imaging was demonstrated in a metastatic thyroid cancer patient following injection of 37 MBq I-124 using a 15 min acquisition. To satisfy required statistics, a voxel size of 32 mm was selected, and lifetime estimates were restricted to regions with sufficient counts. These results identify count statistics as primary limiting factor for clinically viable PLI and define a practical threshold for stable voxel-wise lifetime imaging. Future work will focus on extending acquisition times to enable higher spatial resolution and improve robustness for clinical applications.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-20-04] Intercept Graphical Plot with Normalization for Total-Body PET Parametric Imaging with Reduced Input Function Data and Enhanced Inter-Subject Quantification (#2748)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Wang (Autores: Y. Wang , Q. Ye , S. Li , T. Li , B. A. Spencer , Y. Abdelhafez , X. Sun , A. Chandler , L. Hu , H. Li , L. Nardo , M. S. Chen , R. D. Badawi , S. R. Cherry , G. Wang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] United Imaging Healthcare, North America, Houston, Texas, United States of America [2] United Imaging Healthcare, Shanghai, China [3] University of California, Davis, Department of Radiology, Sacramento, California, United States of America [4] University of California, Davis, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America [5] University of California, Davis, Department of Internal Medicine, Sacramento, California, United States of America [6] King's College London, School of Biomedical Engineering and Imaging Sciences, London, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Patlak plot is a widely used kinetic modeling method for estimating the tracer net influx rate K i in dynamic PET imaging. However, the requirement for a full time course input function limits its routine clinical use. The Relative Patlak (RP) plot mitigates this constraint effectively by reducing the required acquisition time. Nevertheless, the quantified RP slope K i ' introduces a time-dependent and subject-specific scaling factor relative to K i , reducing the reliability for inter-subject analysis. In this study, we propose an Intercept Graphical (IG) plot with an associated normalization that requires the same imaging duration as the RP method. The quantified parameter K IG has a time-independent and approximately subject-independent scaling factor for estimating K i . We evaluated the proposed method using total-body dynamic PET images of 12 healthy and 10 cancer subjects. To evaluate inter-subject quantification performance, multi-organ and lesion K i ' and K IG were generated using the RP and IG methods, respectively, and then rescaled using population-mean scaling factors to recover K i . Using the Patlak K i as the reference standard, the organ or lesion K i estimated by the population-rescaled IG had an error that was 50-70% lower than that of the population-rescaled RP. Furthermore, group analysis indicates the K i yielded by the population-rescaled IG exhibits statistical behavior more similar to that of the Patlak K i and outperforms the population-rescaled RP K i . Overall, the proposed IG approach with normalization retains the low imaging time requirement and improves inter-subject quantitative robustness. It may enable more accurate K i quantification and improve the clinical feasibility of PET parametric imaging.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-20-05] Generative Consistency Model for Bayesian Kinetic Model Selection in Dynamic Total-Body PET (#2512)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Zhao (Autores: Y. Zhao , Q. Gu , G. I. Angelis , K. Amadita , A. J. Reader , Y. Fan , S. R. Meikle)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The University of Sydney, Camperdown, Australia [2] King's College London, London, United Kingdom [3] Commonwealth Scientific Industrial Research Organisation, Sydney, Australia
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The selection of compartmental models for dynamic PET analysis is compromised by three key scenarios-the unknown kinetics of novel tracers, mixed kinetics resulting from tissue heterogeneity and spillover, and the diverse multi-organ kinetics in total-body PET-where conventional model selection using nonlinear least squares and Akaike Information Criterion can fail. For this, we augmented our previous framework--kinetic parameter posterior estimation using generative consistency models--to perform Bayesian model selection. The objective is to simultaneously estimate both the model probability and the posterior distributions of the kinetic parameters across six commonly used kinetic models. The method involves training the consistency model on 6,000,000 simulated time-activity curves. Evaluation against a conventional method demonstrates significant improvements; across 6,000 simulated time-activity curves, the proposed method achieved an overall model selection accuracy of 86%, substantially outperforming the 34% accuracy of the conventional method. Furthermore, application to clinical total-body positron emission tomography data from a patient with metastatic cancer yielded physiologically plausible model selection maps that successfully differentiated complex underlying regional kinetics, such as healthy liver tissue versus tumour. Our results indicate that this proposed framework is useful in kinetic model selection in dynamic total-body PET and can have potential for evaluating new radiotracers in clinical practice.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-21-01] Experimental System Performance Characterization of Alpha-SPECT and Exploration of Angular Sampling Enhancement via Collimator Micro-Rotation (#3105)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Mandot (Autores: S. Mandot , Y. Jin , E. M. Zannoni , Y. Du , G. Sgouros , E. Frey , L.-J. Meng)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Department of Nuclear, Plasma and Radiological Engineering, Champaign, Illinois, United States of America [2] University of Texas at Austin, Walker Department of Mechanical Engineering, Austin, Texas, United States of America [3] Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Department of Radiology, Baltimore, Maryland, United States of America [4] University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology, Champaign, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Targeted Alpha Therapy (TAT) requires dedicated imaging infrastructure capable of tracking alpha-emitting therapeutics and their daughters in vivo across a wide energy range. We present the experimental imaging performance of AlphaSPECT - a whole-body CZT-based clinical SPECT scanner comprising 32 detector panels integrating 512 micro-pinhole cameras in a dual field-of-view (FOV) configuration. Each panel integrates 16 CZT detectors (20×20×6 mm³, 500-μm pixel pitch) bump-bonded to HEXITEC ASICs. A CT-derived precision rotating gantry enables seamless switching between a large-FOV mode (5-mm pinholes, 40×40×20 cm³) and a high-resolution mode (2-mm pinholes, 20 cm spherical FOV), with sub-10-μm rotational accuracy. Energy calibration across all panels achieved 4-7 keV FWHM at 122 keV following charge-sharing correction. System response matrices were generated via voxel-driven ray-tracing, with geometry parameters estimated via nonlinear optimization against experimental point-source projections. Phantom reconstructions demonstrate uniform response across all detector panels and qualitative compartmental contrast in a 3D Hoffmann brain phantom (8 mCi Tc-99m, 30-minute acquisition), with resolution-limited blurring and partial-volume effects motivating investigation into angular sampling and reconstruction improvements. Ongoing studies include spatial resolution evaluation using a NEMA-compliant hot-rod phantom, collimator micro-rotation to enhance angular sampling, and joint dual-FOV reconstruction - to be presented at the conference.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-21-02] First Validation of a BNCT-SPECT System Based on a Detector with Embedded AI in a Clinical-Like Facility (#2463)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Boron Neutron Capture Therapy (BNCT) requires precise, real-time monitoring of the distribution of boron neutron capture reactions to maximize its therapeutic selectivity. This work presents a major hardware evolution of the BeNEdiCTE detector, a SPECT-based system designed to track the 478 keV prompt gamma rays emitted during neutron capture. The detector is based on a co-doped LaBr3(Ce, Sr) monolithic crystal read out by Silicon Photomultipliers. The custom readout electronics have been entirely redesigned, utilizing boron-free substrates to eliminate background interference at 478 keV. Furthermore, the new module features embedded AI on a high-performance FPGA for real-time reconstruction of interaction coordinates (X, Y, and Depth-of-Interaction) of the gamma rays on the scintillator. To meet the high-flux demands of clinical BNCT, the dead time of the system has been reduced from 5.4 μs to 2.1 μs, and an hardware-based energy discrimination circuit has been designed to process only the small percentage of useful gamma rays across the whole spectrum. We report on the system's design and its upcoming validation at Nagoya University Accelerator-driven Neutron Source (Japan), marking the first SPECT measurement performed in a clinical-like facility. Preliminary Monte Carlo simulations using a Derenzo-like phantom demonstrate the system's high spatial resolution and its ability to distinguish lesion-sized volumes with boron concentrations as low as a few hundred ppm. These results set the stage for the upcoming SPECT validation, which aims to prove the system's readiness for the non-invasive, live monitoring of boron distribution during clinical patient treatment.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-21-03] Imaging of TAT in Clinical Phantoms with a CZT Compton Camera (#3012)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Das (Autores: B. Das , D. Goodman , M. Streicher , J. Lee , O. H. Matousek , R. Heller , V. Negut , Y. Seo , J. Caravaca)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California, San Francisco, Department of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging, San Francisco, California, United States of America [2] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Applied Nuclear Science Division, Berkeley, California, United States of America [3] H3D Inc., Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America [4] University of California, Berkeley, Department of Nuclear Engineering, Berkeley, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Targeted alpha therapy (TAT) has shown strong promise for cancer treatment because of its high linear energy transfer and localized cytotoxic effect. However, quantitative in-vivo imaging of TAT radiopharmaceuticals and its daughter remains challenging. The clinically administered activity is typically low, while the emitted gamma rays have low branching ratios, making conventional SPECT imaging sensitivity-limited and often requiring impractically long acquisition times. These limitations restrict accurate assessment of biodistribution, pharmacokinetics, and dosimetry, which are essential for optimizing TAT agents. This study investigates Compton imaging as a high-sensitivity alternative for visualizing TAT radiopharmaceuticals using a 5 cm × 5 cm single-layer 3D position-sensitive cadmium zinc telluride (CZT) camera. We performed a pilot imaging study with the alpha therapy radionuclide 225Ac in a clinical phantom filled with a low concentration of 6.2 kBq/mL surrounded by non-radioactive water. The phantom was scanned at 45 o rotational steps with 15-minute acquisitions each, and Compton images were reconstructed to evaluate source localization below clinically relevant low-activity conditions. This is the first time such a low-activity concentration has been imaged in a clinical phantom. The results demonstrate clear visualization of the radioactive inserts, supporting the feasibility of CZT-based Compton imaging for TAT monitoring. Based on these measurements, a multi-head configuration with at least eight detector modules could enable in-vivo imaging of 225 Ac daughters of target organs within less than 30 minutes, and is being planned as the next step. Additional experiments with 212 Pb further suggest that the proposed approach can operate across a broad photon-energy range. Overall, this work provides experimental validation that compact 3D CZT Compton cameras may overcome key sensitivity barriers in alpha-emitter imaging and support future image-guided TAT.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-21-04] Design of a PET&SPECT shared Detector with Low- and Medium-Energy Scintillator-as-Collimator for Lu-177 Imaging (#1720)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 X. Zeng (Autores: X. Zeng , H. Yang , W. Huang , M. Niu , Z. Gu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] shenzhen bay laboratory, Shenzhen, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Lu-177, a promising theranostic radionuclide emitting β particles for therapy and γ photons for imaging, enables integrated diagnosis and therapy. Lu-177 imaging is increasingly important in treatments where imaging guides therapy. Previous work has demonstrated the use of scintillator as collimators to achieve simultaneous and separate imaging of F-18 and Tc-99m. In this work, we present a novel three-layer shared detector with variable collimator thickness, enabling simultaneous PET, SPECT, and Lu‑177 imaging. The first two crystal layers are perforated, with the top layer functioning as a low-energy high-sensitivity (LEHS) collimator, the top and middle layers combined acting as a low-energy high-resolution (LEHR) collimator and medium-energy general-purpose (MEGP) collimator. This design allows flexible adaptation for Tc‑99m and Lu‑177 imaging without hardware changes.A 96 mm-diameter system was simulated to evaluate two collimation schemes. Simulation results indicate that for Tc‑99m, the system can achieve both LEHS and LEHR imaging, with hot-rod phantom spatial resolution reaching 3.5 mm. For Lu‑177 (208 keV), inserting high-density LYSO or BGO in the middle layer improved peak-to-valley ratio compared to GAGG, and BGO yielded 4 mm spatial resolution for hot-rod phantom imaging. This flexible collimator design enhances detector versatility and offers a promising solution for multi-radionuclide theranostic applications. Future work will focus on optimizing collimator thickness and evaluating the performance of a prototype system.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-21-05] Dosimetry Evaluation Studies in Non-Melanoma Skin Cancers Using a Novel Thin-Layer Scintillation Detector (#1851)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Tosetti (Autores: G. Tosetti , J.-M. Fontbonne , D. Lebhertz , I. Chaoufi , C. Moignier , R. Lafaye)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Université de Caen Normandie, ENSICAEN, CNRS/IN2P3, LPC Caen UMR6534, CAEN, France [2] Hassan II University, Laboratory of Mechanic and High Energy Physics, Department of Physics, Faculty of Sciences of Ain Chock, CASABLANCA, Morocco [3] Centre François Baclesse, Service de radiophysique, CAEN, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Conventional radiotherapy is a well-establish treatment for Non-Melanoma Skin Cancers (NMSCs). In this context, patient-specific quality assurance (PSQA) relies on accurate dose distribution measurements. However, current state-of-the-art technologies do not provide sufficient accuracy in assessing dose deposition within the superficial skin layers. To compensate for the buildup effect in radiotherapy, a bolus material is commonly applied over the tumor to mimic tissue equivalence. Nevertheless, anatomical changes during treatment, such as tumor shrinkage, may introduce air gaps between the bolus and the skin, potentially leading to underdosage. To address these limitations, a prototype detector, referred to as DQX, has been developed at Laboratoire de Physique Corpusculaire de Caen and experimentally evaluated at Centre François Baclesse . The device is based on a 100 μm thick plastic scintillator coupled to wavelength-shifting fibers and is designed to measure radiation dose in superficial tissue layers, targeting a relative measurement uncertainty below 1% for a 2 Gy photon beam at depths as shallow as 70 μm beneath the skin surface. This contribution presents a comparison of the DQX prototype and a range of commonly used dosimetric devices employed in PSQA for conventional radiotherapy. These include tools such as ionization chambers and radiochromic films, each of which exhibits inherent limitations when applied to superficial dose measurements. The evaluation focuses on the response under possible clinical conditions such as air gaps variations. By benchmarking the DQX detector against these established technologies, this study also aims to assess its potential to improve dose verification in the buildup region.

sub_talks.title: [WS-04-01] Radiotheranostics Beyond Boundaries: Hardware, AI, and the Future of Quantitative Imaging (#3328)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Seo (Autores: P. Correia , A. Gonzalez-Montoro , S. Abbaszadeh , J. Caravaca , J. Cates , Y. Seo)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Aveiro, Institute for Nanostructures, Nanomodelling and Nanofabrication (i3N), Aveiro, Portugal [2] CSIC-UPV, Institute for Instrumentation in Molecular Imaging (I3M), Valencia, Spain [3] University of California, Santa Cruz, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Santa Cruz, California, United States of America [4] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Nuclear Science Division, Berkeley, California, United States of America [5] University of California, San Francisco, Department of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging, San Francisco, California, United States of America [6] Siemens Healthineers, Molecular Imaging, Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America [7] University of California, Berkeley, Department of Nuclear Engineering, Berkeley, California, United States of America [8] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Molecular Biophysics & Integrated Bioimaging Division, Berkeley, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Cancer treatment has shifted from empirical, toxicity-based dosing toward precision oncology guided by the specific genetic and molecular profiles of individual tumors. Within this framework, physicians, medical physicists, engineers, and scientists share the responsibility of developing tools to deliver high-precision treatments, predict therapeutic responses, and track disease progression. Radiotheranostics contributes to this approach by leveraging advanced radiochemistry to design highly selective molecules that deliver diagnostic or therapeutic radionuclides to target cells. Although routine at major medical centers for metastatic disease, broader adoption requires advances in imaging performance and targeted radiopharmaceuticals. Conventional PET and SPECT systems remain constrained by physical limits in spatial resolution, sensitivity, and quantitative accuracy, all of which are critical for clinical translation. Addressing these gaps requires higher sensitivity and spatial resolution, refined reconstruction algorithms for improved image clarity, precise image-based dose calculations, and system standardization. These needs drive hardware development toward total-body and organ-specific PET and SPECT systems, as well as new gamma, x-ray, and hybrid imaging methods. For high linear-energy transfer approaches like targeted alpha therapy, ex vivo micro-scale imaging is increasingly important to measure dose heterogeneity at the suborgan/cellular level. Concurrently, artificial intelligence is improving image reconstruction and dose prediction. Finally, key translational challenges must be addressed: ensuring trial reproducibility, integrating new methodologies into clinical workflows, and demonstrating cost-effectiveness alongside tangible patient benefit. This workshop brings together experts across these areas to collaborate and advance next-generation radiotheranostic technologies.

sub_talks.title: [WS-04-02] A Long Axial-FOV PET System with Embedded Spectroscopic Gamma-Cameras for In Vivo Imaging of Radiopharmaceutical Therapy (#3322)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L.-J. Meng (Autores: Y. Jin , J. Du , S. R. Cherry , L.-J. Meng)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Illinois at Urbana and Champaign, Department of Nuclear, Plasma and Radiological Engineering, Urbana, Illinois, United States of America [2] University of California at Davis, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America [3] King's College London, School of Biomedical Engineering and Imaging Sciences, London, United Kingdom [4] University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology, Urbana, Illinois, United States of America [5] University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Department of Bioengineering, Urbana, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The development of radiotheranostics would greatly benefit from quantitative imaging techniques that can simultaneously map the distributions of diagnostic and therapeutic radionuclides across spatial, temporal, and functional domains. To address this need, we will present the design of a proposed preclinical PET/SPECT platform consisting of a long-axial-FOV PET scanner with embedded CZT pinhole camera modules. The system is designed to simultaneously image both PET tracers and typical SPECT isotopes, as well as therapeutic radionuclides, such as Lu-177, Ac-225, Ra-223, and At-211. The PET subsystem is based on dual-ended-readout BGO detectors with a diameter of 16 cm and an axial length of 16 cm. The BGO detectors in the central portion are purposefully positioned to leave small gaps to accommodate micro-gamma-camera elements (MGCE's) based on high-resolution CZT detectors with pinhole collimation for radionuclides. The MGCE's are designed to cover a wide dynamic range of 20 keV to 700 keV, so the combined PET and SPECT system will be capable of imaging virtually all commonly used SPECT isotopes and therapeutic radionuclides. In addition, data acquisition for the PET and SPECT subsystems is synchronized via a unified clock-and-trigger architecture. It enables coincidence detection of both PET and single-photon signals. Correlations among detected photons in the spectral and temporal domains are used to reject down-scattering noise in SPECT acquisition and to identify cascade emission of gamma rays from Lu-177 and Ac-225. In this presentation, we will discuss a comprehensive design study of an integrated PET/SPECT imaging system and its potential to characterize the complex pharmacokinetics of radionuclide therapies.

sub_talks.title: [WS-04-03] A High-Resolution Mobile Gamma-Camera for optimizing dosimetry in Molecular Radiotherapy : first clinical feasibility study for treatment of thyroid diseases with Radioactive Iodine (#3281)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Menard (Autores: T. Bossis , M.-A. Verdier , L. Vija , F. Courbon , D. Vallot , C. Nascimento , O. Caselles , T. Beaumont , F. Bouvet , L. Pinot , L. Menard)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Université Paris-Saclay, CNRS/INP3, IJCLab, Orsay, France [2] Université Paris Cité, IJCLab, Orsay, France [3] ASNR, LEDI, Fontenay-aux-roses, France [4] Nuclear Medicine Department, Oncopole Claudius Regaud, Toulouse, France [5] Nuclear Medicine Department, Oncopole Claudius Regaud and Toulouse University, Toulouse, France [6] Medical Physics Department, Oncopole Claudius Regaud, Toulouse, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Molecular radiotherapy requires personalized dosimetry for efficient treatment and reduced toxicity, but current clinical imaging systems and miniaturized gamma-cameras lack the required capabilities. We developed a mobile gamma-camera with a 10×10 cm 2 field of view tailored for quantitative assessment of 131 I biokinetics during therapy of thyroid diseases. The system combines interchangeable 3D-printed tungsten collimators, a monolithic scintillator read out by a SiPM array, and commercial electronics. It achieves an intrinsic spatial resolution of 1.15 mm FWHM and negligible deadtime up to 150 kcps. Images are reconstructed in real time using an experimental data-trained convolutional neural network. The collimators and shielding were adjusted with Monte-Carlo simulations in order to reduce septal penetration and scattering. Preclinical studies demonstrated high quantitative accuracy, with activity bias below 5%, even for small sources. These performances stem from the camera's compactness and mobile design, which enables shorter detector-to-target distances, optimized viewing angles, as well as from its high overall spatial resolution (4-6 mm at 365 keV). Its mobility also avoids transporting radioactive patients, reducing radiation exposure for staff and other patients. A first clinical feasibility study involving 20 patients with benign thyroid diseases was completed in March 2025, to assess patient acceptance and image quality during planning and post-treatment follow-up, compared with a standard gamma camera (Syngula). Results indicate unprecedented image quality around 400 keV with direct quantitative information, particularly for post-therapeutic imaging, enabling improved assessment of heterogeneous 131 I distribution, including for Graves' disease. This highlights the potential of the camera for personalizing administered activity and, more importantly, estimating the dose actually absorbed during treatment, directly linked to therapeutic success.

sub_talks.title: [WS-04-04] The Personalized Remote Radiation Tracking Portable Organ Dosimetry Device (#3335)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. S. Miyaoka (Autores: R. S. Miyaoka , W. C. Hunter , P. S. Guntha , G. Maliakal , E. Ingalls , T. M. Whalen , M. T. Kim , G. Jones , S. A. Hauck , A. M. Alessio)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Washington, Radiology / Nuclear Medicine, Seattle, Washington, United States of America [2] Michigan State University, CMSE, BME, and Radiology, Lansing, Michigan, United States of America [3] University of Washington, Department of Electrical Engineering, Seattle, Washington, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We are developing a Personalized Remote Radiation Tracking Portable Organ Dosimetry Device (PRRT PODD) for at-home monitoring of patients receiving radiopharmaceutical therapy. The goal of this work is to provide a user and facility friendly device to enable organ at risk (OAR) dosimetry for patients undergoing Lu-177 DOTATATE treatment. The PRRT PODD consists of a portable frame with wings that encircle the patient's torso from the base of their kidneys to the top of their liver. In addition, there is a registration pad that enables precise positioning of the patient in the PODD for daily measurements. The patient lies down in a PODD template during their therapy qualifying PET/CT scan. This registers the PODD to their anatomy. Using software tools, a sensitivity matrix between the patient's OAR and tumors is determined for a two-dimensional (2D) array of potential detector locations along the surface of the PODD. Using this matrix, 16-32 detector locations are selected based upon the patient's specific anatomy to enable activity estimation for the patient's OAR. After a quantitative SPECT/CT scan acquired 24-hours after treatment, a PODD measurement will be made in clinic to normalize with the SPECT/CT scan. The PODD will then be sent home with the patient for fourteen 5-minute daily measurements. The PODD utilizes a carbon fiber base plate, a vacuumable Styrofoam registration pad, 3D printed wings, compact pinhole SiPM-based radiation detectors, battery-operated acquisition electronics, and a cell phone app that supports wireless transmission from the PODD's detector to a remote computer workstation. Our updated simulation software supports placement of a virtual 2D array of detectors on the polygonal surface defined by the PODD. An overview of the PODD development along with results from simulations based on human imaging examples will be provided at the workshop.

sub_talks.title: [WS-04-05] Incorporating X-Ray and gamma-Ray Coincidence Detection for Improved Detection Efficiency and Image Quality in 177 Lu Imaging (#3306)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Q. Wei (Autores: K. Wang , T. Dai , Z. Hang , H. Liu , J. Wu , Y. Liu , Z. He , Q. Wei)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Science and Technology Beijing, Beijing Engineering Research Center of Industrial Spectrum Imaging, School of Automation and Electrical Engineering, Beijing, China [2] China-Japan Friendship Hospital, Department of Radiation Oncology, Beijing, China [3] Tsinghua University, Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital, Beijing, China [4] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [5] Beijing Normal University, Center for Advanced Quantum Studies, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In conventional 177 Lu imaging that relies solely on single photons or cascade gamma photons, the detection efficiency is fundamentally limited by the low photon emission probabilities. The decay of 177 Lu produces not only γ photons but also characteristic X-rays through the internal conversion process. In this work, we propose a multi-type time coincidence imaging strategy that exploits characteristic X-rays together with γ photons to improve the detection efficiency and image quality of 177 Lu imaging. The feasibility of X-X, X-γ, and γ-γ coincidence detection is analyzed based on the decay characteristics of 177 Lu, and a full-ring coincidence imaging system is subsequently employed for performance evaluation. Experimental results show that the integration of multiple coincidence-event types increases the system detection efficiency by 107.60\% and improves the contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) by 8.39\% compared with conventional γ-γ coincidence imaging, while preserving nearly unchanged spatial resolution.

sub_talks.title: [WS-04-06] Physics-Corrected List-Mode MLEM Reconstruction for Quantitative 177 Lu Cascade Gamma Coincidence Imaging (#3289)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Ye (Autores: H. Ye , H. Liu , Q. Wei , H. Jia , H. Hu , Z. Hang , T. Dai , Z. He , Y. Liu , J. Wu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Normal University, Center for Advanced Quantum Studies, School of Physics and Astronomy, Beijing, China [2] Beijing Normal University, Key Laboratory of Multiscale Spin Physics, Ministry of Education, Beijing, China [3] Beijing Normal University, Center for Health and Aging, Beijing, China [4] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [5] University of Science and Technology Beijing, School of Automation and Electrical Engineering, Beijing, China [6] Tsinghua University, School of Biomedical Engineering, Beijing, China [7] Tsinghua University Changgung Hospital, Changgung Hospital, Beijing, China [8] China-Japan Friendship Hospital, Department of Radiation Oncology, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Cascade gamma coincidence imaging is an alternative to conventional single photon imaging for therapeutic radionuclides such as 177 Lu by exploiting time-correlated cascade photon pairs. However, high spatial resolution and reliable quantitative accuracy remain challenging because of photon attenuation, scatter, partial volume effects. We developed a cascade-coincidence list-mode maximum-likelihood expectation-maximization (CCLM-MLEM) framework for a full-ring 177 Lu cascade gamma coincidence imaging system. Attenuation correction (AC) and scatter correction (SC) were incorporated into reconstruction, followed by absolute quantification and post-reconstruction partial volume correction (PVC). The system response matrix was modeled according to the cascade-photon detection geometry. The framework was evaluated using seven-point-source and hot-rod phantoms for spatial-resolution assessment, the modified image-quality phantom for quantitative evaluation, and the Mouse Whole-Body (MOBY) digital phantom for small-animal imaging. Direct backprojection (DBP) was used for comparison. CCLM-MLEM reduced the mean point-source FWHM from 2.20±0.10 mm with DBP to 1.51±0.27 mm and resolved 1.0-mm rods, compared with 1.5-mm rods using DBP. In the modified image-quality phantom, AC and SC improved activity and contrast recovery at comparable noise levels. In the MOBY phantom, the relative bias for a 4-mm tumor decreased from -57.19% without correction to 1.83% after AC, SC, and PVC. These results support high-resolution quantitative 177 Lu cascade gamma coincidence imaging and its potential for preclinical radiopharmaceutical imaging and dosimetry.

sub_talks.title: [WS-04-07] Learning Support Priors from 177 Lu with Projection-Domain Constraint for Quantitative 225 Ac SPECT Reconstruction (#3267)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Dong (Autores: Z. Dong , X. Meng , X. Jin , W. Liu , X. Ding , Y. Sun , L. Yuan , N. Li , Z. Yang , M. Lu , J. Li , Q. Ren , J. Yu , Z. Xie)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Peking University, National Biomedical Imaging Center, College of Future Technology, Beijing, China [2] Peking University Cancer Hospital & Institute, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Beijing, China [3] Peking University Cancer Hospital & Institute, Department of Gastrointestinal Oncology, Beijing, China [4] Beijing Sinotau International Pharmaceutical Technology Co., Ltd., Beijing, China [5] Peking University Health Science Center, Peking University, Institute of Medical Technology, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Background: 225 Ac targeted alpha therapy requires quantitative post-therapy SPECT for verification and dosimetry. Multiple emissions, scatter, and inter-window crosstalk complicate reconstruction. Methods: We developed a 177 Lu-informed deep support-driven kernel (DSDK). A support generator was pretrained on 63 clinical [ 177 Lu]Lu-DOTATATE SPECT scans using simulated projections at multiple count levels and a projection-consistency objective. For 225 Ac reconstruction, the learned support was used only to construct an image-domain kernel prior; activity remains governed by measured multi-energy projections and a Poisson model. Scatter and crosstalk are explicit projection-space physical models using MC-optimized DEW and self-consistent crosstalk correction for 218-keV, 440-keV, and joint-window reconstruction. Evaluation included MC calibration, single-sphere NEMA IQ scatter-window validation, dual-sphere IQ CNR-COV assessment at 15/30/60 s, and 10-patient [ 225 Ac]Ac-DOTATATE SPECT/CT evaluation. Baselines included OSEM, DDIP-TTA, and PET-guided methods; PET was not a DSDK input. Results: MC selected a narrow 5% lower scatter window beside ±10% photopeak windows, with projection MSEs of 0.16/0.10 at 218/440 keV. Single-sphere joint-window CNR/SBR rose from 3.032/8.390 without scatter correction to 3.104/9.081. Dual-sphere DSDK with crosstalk improved the CNR-COV trade-off, especially at 15/30 s; at a representative joint window, CNR/COV was 22.2/0.87 versus 17.1/1.19 for DDIP-TTA. Clinically, joint-window DSDK achieved TBR 2.43 ± 1.27 and the highest lesion CNR among non-PET-prior methods. DSDK also achieved the highest joint-window lesion SSIM, 0.88 ± 0.05, without a PET-derived prior. Conclusion: DSDK integrates support-level transfer, projection-consistent statistical reconstruction, and crosstalk physical modeling for quantitative multi-window 225 Ac SPECT and may support patient-specific dosimetry.

sub_talks.title: [WS-04-08] Rapid Extended-Distance 177 Lu Imaging with a Portable Telephoto-Lens Magic-Cube Gamma Camera for Intra-Procedural Theranostic Assessment (#3290)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Zhang (Autores: Y. Zhang , Z. Lyu , J. Xu , Y. Hu , Y. Zhang , W. Chi , Z. Zhao , W. Cheng , K. Chen , H. Cai , T. Ma)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua university, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [2] Greater Bay Area National Center of Technology Innovation, Guangzhou, China [3] Yale University, Department of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging, New Haven, Connecticut, United States of America [4] Sichuan University, Laboratory of Clinical Nuclear Medicine and Department of Nuclear Medicine, West China Hospital, Chengdu, China [5] Sichuan University, Sichuan Provincial Engineering Research Center of Radiopharmaceutical Clinical Translation, Chengdu, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Immediate visualization of therapeutic radionuclide distributions could provide useful spatial feedback during or shortly after interventional radionuclide therapy, but this use case requires a portable camera to acquire images quickly without close contact with the target region. We evaluated a Telephoto-Lens Magic-Cube portable gamma camera for rapid 177 Lu imaging using hybrid front-end long-hole geometric encoding and detector-side self-collimation encoding. A measured 177 Lu system matrix covered an 80 × 80 mm² field of view and source-to-camera distances of 8-22 cm. Across 54 point-source positions from 10-20 cm, mean absolute localization errors were 0.26, 0.32, and 2.58 mm along the x, y, and z axes, respectively. Representative dual-source reconstructions showed visually distinguishable hotspots separated by 5-7 mm at distances of 10-18 cm. At approximately 16 cm, all principal hotspots remained visible in 1 s reconstructions of three phantoms and an in vivo rat liver, with NCC values of 0.942-0.992 and transverse hotspot displacements of 0.27-1.12 mm relative to 300 s references. An excised rat liver containing 72.2 μCi of residual 177 Lu also showed a localized activity region. These results demonstrate the feasibility of rapid 177 Lu distribution imaging at extended working distances for procedure-room theranostic assessment.

sub_talks.title: [WS-04-09] Implementation of Radiation Detection Technologies, Quality Assurance, and Harmonized Control Standards for Theragnostic Programs in Emerging Healthcare Systems. (#3321)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 I. M. Rossi (Autores: I. M. Rossi , M. C. Plazas , P. N. Martinez)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidad Nacional de Colombia, Physics Department, Bogotá D.C., Colombia [2] IEEE, Colombian Section, New York, New York, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Theragnostic imaging is an emerging approach in precision oncology that combines molecular imaging with targeted radionuclide therapy. Its safe and effective implementation requires not only advanced radiopharmaceuticals, but also reliable radiation detection systems, standardized quality control (QC), and comprehensive quality assurance (QA) throughout the imaging and treatment workflow. This work focuses on the role of radiation detection technologies in theragnostics, including detector performance, calibration and verification of QC equipment, and radiopharmaceutical quality assessment. Particular attention is given to radionuclide and radiochemical purity, activity calibrator verification, measurement traceability, and harmonized QA protocols. The work also addresses challenges in conventional gamma spectrometry, particularly spectral overlap in composite and low-activity samples, highlighting maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE) approaches for improved activity quantification of theragnostic radionuclides using NaI(Tl) detectors. In addition, emerging detector materials such as graphene quantum dots are considered for their potential to enhance radiation detection technologies. The study discusses the challenges of implementing theragnostic programs in emerging healthcare systems, emphasizing the need for international standards, specialized training, appropriate infrastructure, and adaptable regulatory frameworks. These elements are essential to achieving accurate personalized dosimetry, reliable treatment planning, and safe, standardized theragnostic practices.

sub_talks.title: [WS-04-10] New Horizons in Ultra-High Resolution 3D CZT Detectors and its impact on preclinical SPECT/PET (#3309)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Cherlin (Autores: A. Cherlin , F. Beekman)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Kromek Ltd., Sedgefield, United Kingdom [2] TU Delft, dept. Radiation Science & Technology, Delft, Netherlands [3] Free Bee Int'l, Delft, Netherlands [4] The Molecular Imaging Foundation, Delft, Netherlands
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Clinical and preclinical demand for higher-precision molecular imaging across an extended energy range is pushing gamma-ray detectors beyond the limits of conventional SPECT. CZT detectors offer excellent energy resolution and good sensitivity for high-energy isotopes, but position resolution and spectral distortions, including charge sharing and depth dependence, remain limited by pixel size, detector thickness, and cost of scaling readout electronics. A novel approach is presented, using machine learning models trained on high-fidelity simulations to extract sub-pixel and depth-of-interaction (DOI) information from anode signals. Implemented in a prototype CZT gamma camera, the method achieves 10×10 sub-pixelisation of 2 mm pixels, DOI resolution of ~500-800 µm, and gamma-camera-level energy resolution with spatial precision approaching mid-range x-ray detectors, pointing toward a new class of high-resolution SPECT instrumentation. A key challenge is the increased demand on readout speed and bandwidth. Accurate positioning requires acquisition of positive and negative signals across pixel clusters, increasing data volume and processing requirements while limiting real-time operation and scalability. To address this, we explore neural network inference integrated directly into the detector front-end, enabling photon-by-photon signal processing. A dedicated ASIC will digitise and buffer electrode signals, which are then characterised by a neural-state machine that outputs high-level interaction data. A pulse-level simulation framework is being developed to train and validate front-end neural network models. We will present the first implementation of this framework on pixelated and drift-strip CZT detectors, with simulation results demonstrating improved multi-interaction event discrimination and reconstruction. This work provides a route to compact, high-resolution gamma detectors for next-generation theranostic imaging, from radionuclide therapy dosimetry to hybrid modalities. An example will be shown on what the impact of using high-end 3D CZT instead of traditional NaI Anger detectors could be on the architecture and performance of a new multi-isotope PET/PET PET/SPECT imaging module in Free Bee International's U-VET preclinical open PET/SPECT/CT/Optical/Ultrasound platform (World Molecular Imaging Society Innovation of the Year 2026 )

sub_talks.title: [WS-04-11] A multimodal C-arm enabling concurrent X-ray and nuclear imaging for cost-effective theragnostic interventions (#3316)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. R. Schaart (Autores: D. R. Schaart , M. M. Dietze , C. E. Kerckhaert , L. Schröder , M. Snoeyink , N. Wijnen , H. W. De Jong)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Delft University of Technology, Medical Physics & Technology, Delft, Netherlands [2] University Medical Center Utrecht, Radiology and Nuclear Medicine, Utrecht, Netherlands
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Theragnostic interventions commonly require both fluoroscopic and nuclear image guidance. In liver tumor radioembolization, for example, 90 Y microspheres are injected into the liver bloodstream under fluoroscopy. First, 99m Tc microspheres are administered, and a SPECT scan is made. Therapeutic 90 Y microsphere delivery is typically performed two weeks later, based on the results of the pre-treatment procedure. If a SPECT scan of the 99m Tc microsphere distribution can be made inside the intervention room, the pre-treatment and treatment procedures can be merged into a single session, enabling in-situ adaptation of the catheter position and near-real time, personalized dosimetric treatment planning. Moreover, the burden for the patient as well as the overall cost of treatment are reduced. To this end, a first prototype of an interventional X-ray and scintigraphy imaging (IXSI) system was built at UMC Utrecht. It consists of a C-arm equipped with an X-ray tube and a detector stack consisting of an adapted X-ray flat panel detector positioned in front of a gamma camera fitted with a cone-beam collimator. Here, we report on two recent developments. First, a clinical trial is ongoing in which the first patients with liver cancer are receiving single-session radioembolization using the IXSI prototype. Second, X-ray imaging is currently limited to 70 kVp and the X-ray tube is translated off-focus from the focal point of the cone-beam collimator by 5 cm, to avoid blinding of the gamma camera by X-rays penetrating through the flat-panel detector. To enable concurrent, intrinsically co-registered X-ray and nuclear imaging using X-ray spectra up to 120 kVp, a novel detector stack is under development, comprising a gamma camera based on a low-afterglow, pixelated NaI(Tl) scintillator read out by SiPMs. An update of these developments will be presented at the workshop.

sub_talks.title: [WS-04-12] Theranostic SPECT with High Energy Resolution CZT Detectors (#3334)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. G. Hotvedt (Autores: J. R. Kuchta , P. G. Hotvedt , Z. Ouyang , D. Paylan)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] MH3D Inc., Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America [2] University of Michigan, Nuclear Engineering and Radiological Sciences, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract An increasing number of isotopes have seen use in theranostic applications but have generally been limited by poor image quality or low quantification accuracy. These limitations are caused by factors like low emission intensities, clustered photopeaks, or lower system sensitivity. These factors drive the use of easier to image surrogate isotopes for biodistribution studies. Theranostic SPECT with CZT semiconductors reduces the need for traditional cut-and-count measurements and can produce quality reconstructions for isotopes that are otherwise difficult to image. The Alpha-SPECT TM Mini preclinical device utilizes CZT semiconductors as the detecting medium, providing the highest energy resolution with a full-body field-of-view for mice. This SPECT imager has a 2.5% single-pixel energy resolution at 140 keV, and it has been used in the imaging of popular isotopes such as 225 Ac, 213 Bi, 212 Pb, 211 At, 177 Lu, 111 In, and 99m Tc. The detectors' superior energy resolution allows for discrimination of the clustered photopeaks in the X-ray energy regions of 225 Ac and 212 Pb. Projection windows with sufficient separation from the tungsten characteristic X-ray at 60 keV allow for removal of excess scatter in reconstructed images, one of the major image degradation factors in low-emission isotope imaging. The system's high sensitivity enables the dynamic imaging of fast decaying isotopes over the whole body of a mouse, such as 213 Bi with its 45-minute half-life. The dynamic imaging function has been utilized for binning as small as 2 seconds for 99m Tc, 1 minute for 211 At, 15 minutes for 213 Bi, and 30 minutes for 225 Ac. This functionality unveils important information on theranostic isotope distribution shortly post-injection.

sub_talks.title: [WS-04-13] Fast Timing for High-Energy Gammas with GAGG and BGO for Improved Theranostic (#3313)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Pagano (Autores: F. Pagano , A. Gonzalez Montoro , F. Loignon-Houle , A. Olmos Risen , J. Cates , J. Caravaca , A. J. Gonzalez)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institute for Instrumentation in Molecular Imaging (I3M), CSIC-Universitat Politècnica de València, Valencia, Spain [2] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Nuclear Science Division, Berkley, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Time-of-flight (TOF) improves effective sensitivity and image signal-to-noise ratio in positron emission tomography (PET). Other medical applications that benefit from high time resolution include ion range verification in hadron therapy via prompt gamma imaging and dose verification in targeted alpha therapy via cascade gamma imaging. All these applications would benefit from intrinsically radiation-free scintillators, motivating the search for alternatives to LYSO. GAGG is a strong candidate due its high light yield, which enables good energy resolution, and to its fast decay time, which makes GAGG's time resolution very competitive. At high gamma energies - between 1-7 MeV, the range relevant to prompt gammas in hadron therapy and to characteristic gammas emitted in cascade by alpha-emitting isotopes - BGO also becomes particularly attractive, as its prompt Cherenkov photon yield increases significantly in this range. Here, we present a proof-of-concept measurement of the time resolution of BGO and GAGG at ~1 MeV. Pairs of 3×3×15 mm³ BGO and GAGG crystals, coupled to FBK-NUV-MT SiPMs, were read out using state-of-the-art high-frequency electronics. Each crystal pair detected in coincidence the gamma cascade from a 60 Co source (1173 keV and 1333 keV gamma rays emitted with a sub-picosecond half-life). In our preliminary studies, we achieved a coincidence time resolution (CTR) FWHM of 120 ps for GAGG and 188 ps for BGO, while for 511 keV the CTRs are 179 ps and 245 ps, respectively. Additionally, simulations are used to investigate Cherenkov photon detection yield and time resolution as a function of gamma-ray energy. These results highlight the potential of GAGG and BGO both for TOF-PET and other emerging applications involving high-gamma energies.

sub_talks.title: [WS-04-14] Event-Based Alpha- and Beta- Particle Imaging with iQID: From Quantitative Digital Autoradiography to Isotope Identification (#3326)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. W. Miller (Autores: B. W. Miller , J. W. Moore)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The University of Arizona, Radiation Oncology and Radiology & Imaging Sciences, Tucson, Arizona, United States of America [2] QScint Imaging Solutions, Tucson, Arizona, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The growth of radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) has created an increasing need to characterize RPT distributions at microscopic spatial scales, where heterogeneity can strongly influence absorbed dose and biological response. This is particularly important for alpha-particle therapies, where information of the activity distributions is needed at spatial scales comparable to alpha-particle ranges in tissue (40-100 µm). The ionizing-radiation Quantum Imaging Detector (iQID) is a high-resolution imaging system developed for quantitative digital autoradiography of alpha- and beta-particle emitters at these spatial scales. iQID combines scintillation-based detection with CMOS-camera imaging and real-time processing to localize individual particle interactions and record their spatial, temporal, and intensity information. Unlike phosphor imaging plate autoradiography, which integrates the cumulative signal from all radioactive decay events over an exposure, iQID detects and localizes individual scintillation events in real time. Event size, intensity, position, and time are retained as list-mode data, enabling high-resolution quantitative imaging of radioactive sources and radiolabeled tissue sections. Event characteristics can also distinguish alpha- and beta-particle interactions, allowing both emission types to be imaged simultaneously. The spatial and temporal information retained by iQID provides additional capabilities for characterizing radioactive sources. Changes in activity and decay behavior can be followed over time, and measured decay signatures can help distinguish radionuclides within mixed sources. This presentation will describe the iQID imaging approach and highlight applications in quantitative alpha/beta autoradiography, source characterization, isotope identification, radiopharmaceutical biodistribution, and micro-scale dosimetry.

sub_talks.title: [WS-04-15] How the next generation digital autoradiography can provide insight into theranostic bioequivalence (#3315)
sub_talks.speaker: S. Adler
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Frederick National Laboratory For Cancer Research, Clinical Research Directorate, Bethesda, Maryland, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Introduction: Theranostic cancer treatments rely on ligands which can be tagged with two different isotopes. One for imaging and one for treatment. The imaging ligand is used as a proxy for monitoring the ligand used to treat the target tissue. Key to using the imaging agent to measure the dosimetry of the treatment ligand is knowing the bio-equivalence of the ligand pair. Bio-equivalence is defined as equal biological interaction of two ligands within tissue. This can be achieved with the Quantitative Particle Identification Autoradiograph (QPID). Materials and Methods: The next generation of spectral autoradiograph has been developed which mates a Timepix3 sensor developed by the CERN Medipix collaboration with a CeBr3 scintillation crystal. This allows one to use the gamma emission energy in forming autoradiograph images of tissue samples harvested in bio-distribution studies. The QPID time resolution is on the order of 1.6 ns allowing for the detection of single decays, thus achieving alpha and beta identification through ionization topology and energy deposition in the Timepix3 sensor, and spectral gamma emissions from the imaged sample. Results: The QPID can segregate alpha and positron emissions, generating separate quantitative alpha and positron autoradiograph images from a sample which contains both an alpha and positron emitting ligand. This provides a mechanism to analyze co-injected theranostic imaging and treatment ligands. Using these separate images, one can measure the uptake and distribution in the same tissue sample. Furthermore, one can directly measure the pharmacokinetic properties of both ligands and measure their bio-equivalence. Conclusion: Measuring any bio-equivalent deviation of the two ligands can be used to adjust the imaging agent activity and pharmacokinetic properties to more accurately be used as a proxy to measure the treatment effects and dosimetry results of the treatment ligand.

sub_talks.title: [WS-04-16] Gamma-Positron Imaging and Event-Correlated Simulation for Emerging Theranostics (#3341)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. A. Kupinski (Autores: M. A. Kupinski , M. King , S. Abbaszadeh , L. R. Furenlid)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Arizona, College of Optical Sciences, Tucson, Arizona, United States of America [2] University of Arizona, Department of Medical Imaging, Tucson, Arizona, United States of America [3] University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School, Department of Radiology, Worchester, Massachusetts, United States of America [4] University of California, Santa Cruz, Baskin School of Engineering, Santa Cruz, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract PET and SPECT are often used even when radionuclides emit complementary radiations. Gamma-positron imaging exploits nuclides that emit a prompt gamma with a positron: annihilation photons define a PET line of response and prompt-gamma Compton interactions define a cone. Their intersection can estimate the radionuclide decay location more directly than PET alone. We are developing a brain-dedicated gamma-positron imager using crossed-strip CZT detectors, event-correlated radiation transport, and GPU-accelerated list-mode reconstruction. The system records PET coincidences, prompt-gamma Compton events, and triple events in which both signatures arise from one decay. We evaluated event-class-specific LM-MLEM, conventional joint-Poisson reconstruction, and an event-type-conditioned method designed to preserve the localization value of triple events. UAMonteCarlo preserves the lineage of prompt photons, positrons, annihilation photons, and secondaries from emission through detector interaction, allowing detector response, event classification, sensitivity, and reconstruction to be evaluated in one framework. In simulated 44Sc studies, all event classes localized point sources correctly. In a hot-rod phantom, rod-to-background contrast was 1.36 for PET-only, 1.14 for prompt-only, 4.93 for triple-only, 3.24 for conventional combined, and 3.86 for event-type-conditioned combined reconstruction, showing that triple events are uncommon but spatially informative. The project also applies complete radiation-transport histories to emerging theranostic imaging. For 149Tb, gamma-positron events from the positron branch could image the same radiopharmaceutical responsible for alpha therapy. We are also applying the framework to 203Pb surrogate imaging for 212Pb-targeted alpha therapy. Together, these studies show how preserving decay and particle histories can inform detector design, reconstruction, quantitative imaging, and dosimetry.

sub_talks.title: [WS-04-17] Multiplexed PET for Theranostic Imaging (#3342)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J.L. Herraiz (Autores: N. Encina-Baranda , A. Lopez-Montes , E.C. Pratt , T.-N. Nguyen , A. Rominger , L. Carter , J. Cabello , M. Conti , H. Sari , K. Shi , E. Körner , F. Schmidt , J.M. Udias , J. Grimm , J.L. Herraiz)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Complutense University of Madrid, Dep. of Structure of the Matter. Nuclear Physics Group., Madrid, Spain [2] Hospital Clinico San Carlos, Health Research Institute, Madrid, Spain [3] Bern University Hospital, Dep. of Nuclear Medicine, Inselpital, Bern, Switzerland [4] Stony Brook Cancer Center, Dep. of Radiology, Stony Brook, New York, United States of America [5] Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, Dep. of Radiology, New York, New York, United States of America [6] Siemens Medical Solutions USA, Inc., Tennessee, Tennessee, United States of America [7] Siemens Healthineers International AG, Zurich, Switzerland [8] University of Tübingen, Dep. of Nuclear Medicine and Clinical Molecular Imaging, Tübingen, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Multiplexed PET (mPET) enables simultaneous imaging of multiple radiotracers in a single acquisition by exploiting radionuclide-specific signatures beyond conventional 511-keV annihilation photons. Positron-prompt gamma emitters such as 124 I, 86 Y, or 44 Sc can generate triple coincidences that help distinguish them from pure positron emitters. This opens new opportunities for theranostic imaging, where complementary tracers could simultaneously characterize therapeutic targets and tumor biology, investigate intra- and inter-lesion heterogeneity, assess radiopharmaceutical biodistribution and dosimetry, or monitor early biological response to treatment. We present a modular mPET framework applicable to different radionuclides and scanners. It incorporates all the corrections and reconstructions required for quantitative PET while adapting to different scanner capabilities. When available, we exploit energy and time-of-flight information, while coincidence multiplicity alone provides radionuclide-specific information in more limited systems. The method also includes radionuclide-specific positron-range correction for each separated image. We quantitatively evaluated the approach with combinations such as 18 F+ 124 I, 18 F+ 52 Mn, 68 Ga+ 86 Y, and 89 Zr+ 86 Y across several preclinical and clinical PET scanners. Studies ranging from simultaneous tracer imaging in mice to multi-radionuclide phantom experiments demonstrated recovery of the individual radionuclide distributions across systems with different detector characteristics. These results demonstrate the translation of mPET across PET scanners and radionuclide combinations. mPET could extend PET from a predominantly single-tracer technique toward a multidimensional molecular imaging platform in which complementary aspects of patient selection, treatment delivery, and response are interrogated within the same imaging session.

sub_talks.title: [WS-01-01] Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks: A New Paradigm for Explainable Prediction
sub_talks.speaker: Ponente por confirmar
sub_talks.abstract:
M. J. Neuer (1,2), I. Garmaev (1) 1 RWTH-Aachen University 2 innoRIID-Ametek, Düsseldorf In 1957, the findings of Kolmogorov and Arnold showed that continuous multivariate functions can be represented by combinations of simpler, univariate functions. Based on this work, Liu et al. [1] presented in 2024 a novel architecture for formulating neural networks - the Kolmogorov-Arnold network (KAN). The paper will first introduce shortly the basic foundations of KAN, including how to design, train and apply them. Their structure differs from common multilayer perceptrons (MLP) because KANs train univariate functions on the edges of the network graph. In these functions, typically B-splines, instead of training weights like a MLP, KANs train the control coefficients of the splines. Nodes of the network consequently act as pure transfer points of the internal data. An advantage of this new network type is intrinsic explainability. After training, the splines on the edges represent human-interpretable mathematical functions. They can be visually studied to understand the decision logic within the network. The paper will also show the conversion of a KAN into an symbolic expressions. Secondly, several emerging KAN applications will be reviewed and compared to existing classical machine learning solutions. KANs have already been successfully applied to industrial problems, including cancer screening [2], mechanical predictions [3], time-series prediction [4], bioinformatics [5], soft-sensor solutions [6] and
hyperspectral image classification [7]. These recent works show the potential of the approach for application to radiation detection, nuclear security and safety, as well as nuclear medicine. The present paper will provide a brief outlook on how to use KAN for gamma spectroscopy. One canonical scenario - the differentiation of special nuclear material like weapon-grade plutonium (WGPu) and enriched uranium (HEU) from masking nuclides like iodine (I-131) or gallium (Ga-67, Ga-68) - is used to illustrate the
benefits of the new approach. [1] Liu, Z., et al. (2024). KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks. arXiv:2404.19756 [2] Wang, J., Zhang, L., & Liu, Y. (2025). Kan-AAE-driven synthetic SERS spectra generation method for cancer screening. Journal of Molecular Liquids, Volume 419, 126950 [3] Abueidda, Diab W.; Pantidis, Panos; Mobasher, Mostafa E. sub_talks.title: [WS-01-02] AI at the Front End: Machine Learning for Raw-Signal Processing in Semiconductor Detectors
sub_talks.speaker: Ponente por confirmar
sub_talks.abstract: A. Cherlin, N. Atkins, M. Exley, T. Winterbottom Kromek Ltd., County Durham, UK Over the past decade, ML (machine learning) methods in nuclear detection and medical imaging have advanced most rapidly at the back end of the processing pipeline, i.e. enhancement, correction and interpretation of already reconstructed images and spectra. In medical imaging, deep learning is now widely used to suppress noise, automate lesion segmentation, reduce patient dose and scan time, and flag abnormalities to support diagnostic decisions. However, ML application at the front end of low-level detector signal processing remains comparatively underexplored, even though the conversion of raw detector signals into event information significantly affects all subsequent steps. This review focuses on this stage, with particular attention to room-temperature semiconductor detectors, such as CdZnTe (CZT). Detector performance has traditionally been improved through theoretical and phenomenological modelling, extensive calibrations and, often, costly hardware modifications such as reducing pixel size to improve position resolution. The review outlines how ML is changing this landscape: models trained on raw detector signals can estimate energy, position and timing significantly more accurately than current signal processing methods, reducing the need for major hardware upgrades. The underlying ground truth of individual events cannot be measured directly, and characterising every detector in a real system in full detail is usually impractical. Such models therefore rely heavily on simulated training data, which can further be supplemented by experimental data. One of the central challenges is thus the gap between simulation and reality: real detectors exhibit material non-uniformities operating-condition drift, and other effects that simulations and calibrations usually do not fully capture. This review presents strategies reported to date for closing this gap: from generating more representative training data to adapting models to real measurements. These include the authors' recent results, which show that incorporating realistic calibration variations into simulated training data reduces the domain shift between simulated and real data and improves downstream spectral and image reconstruction. The review concludes with practical considerations for deployment, including real-time implementation and its impact on system performance.

sub_talks.title: [WS-01-03] Edge-AI with CMOS In-Memory Computing for Radiation Detector Acquisition Chains
sub_talks.speaker: Ponente por confirmar
sub_talks.abstract: M. Ronchi, M. Pandocchi, M. Amadori, M. Carminati, G. Borghi, C. E. Fiorini Politecnico di Milano, Dipartimento di Elettronica, Informazione e Bioingegneria, Milan, Italy Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare (INFN), Sezione di Milano, Milan, Italy We propose a review of digital and analog edge-AI in-memory computing (IMC) solutions for nuclear and medical imaging acquisition chains, with a focus on CMOS based approaches. We start by covering the motivation and historical context for IMC, driven by the von Neumann bottleneck, and its growing relevance to nuclear physics applications as high-density pixel detectors and high-luminosity, high-rate experiments push data-bandwidth demands higher. We then present the two main hardware directions pursued in the field: emerging non-volatile memory devices (memristors, phase-change memory, etc.) versus CMOS/SRAM-based IMC, comparing their trade-offs in maturity, reliability, and PDK availability. We survey how research groups across the nuclear field are approaching edge-AI implementation. We will then present a case study, that is our analog neural network ASIC (ANNA), an in-memory CMOS accelerator designed to be embedded in the analog front-end of Anger-camera PET/SPECT detectors. We briefly detail the initial ANNA V1 proof of concept and the ongoing ANNA V2 validation and monolithic crystal demonstrator. We discuss the advantages and disadvantages we observed with capacitive-based analog computing and the main difficulties encountered. We discuss figures of merit to compare in-memory computing devices, with a focus on energy efficiency (GOPs/W). We close by highlighting the main opportunities and unresolved questions for IMC adoption in nuclear instrumentation going forward. Although studies on the application of these devices to medical imaging and nuclear physics remain limited, we consider this a promising direction for the future of radiation and particle detectors.

sub_talks.title: [WS-01-05] AI in nuclear imaging and neuroscience: a look at the initial impact
sub_talks.speaker: Ponente por confirmar
sub_talks.abstract: L. Presotto University of Milano-Bicocca, Italy In the last decade, the number of medical devices approved for clinical use involving AI has increased exponentially. Most of them are for imaging based applications, due initially to the effectiveness of convolutional neural networks in extracting image features. Translating models into practice opens a large set of challenges, due to "distribution shifts". Such shift are often quite hard to predict and detect before the application is deployed to the end-user setting. In this review, I will focus mostly on imaging-based neuroscience, a field that developed robust automated analysis algorithms earlier than most others (SPM was released in 1996!). I will select a number of cases of interest to highlight which problems AI can effectively solve and where its inclusion in a full clinical or research pipeline is still suboptimal.

sub_talks.title: [WS-01-07] Delegate, Verify, Understand : Agentic AI in the Medical Imaging Research Workflow
sub_talks.speaker: Ponente por confirmar
sub_talks.abstract: G. Bélanger, M. Fromont, J.B. Michaud Electrical and Computer Engineering, Université de Sherbrooke Large language models have moved from conversational assistants to agents that can act within a research environment. Operating within a software harness that provides tools and feedback, they read code and data, run analyses, generate figures and revise their work based on what they observe. As these tools evolve rapidly, research groups need to consider how to adopt them in a controlled and transparent manner. Starting from a defined research question, this presentation examines where an agent may contribute at each step of the methodology and how its contribution can be verified. Agents can substantially accelerate tasks that are well established, precisely specified and easily verified, such as implementing known algorithms, standard statistical analyses, data visualization and publication figures, which occupy much of researchers' time. Tasks involving complex reasoning, such as literature synthesis, method selection or new numerical methods, remain possible but require closer supervision and independent validation. Two projects from our group illustrate both regimes. For a deterministic X-ray transport solver, an agent contributed to implementation, optimization and GPU porting, with validation against analytical and Monte Carlo references. For scatter estimation in time-of-flight computed tomography, an agent-assisted literature search led to a well-documented closed-form solution, complemented by active-set methods to enforce non-negativity, replacing our original purely iterative algorithm. Combined with a GPU implementation, this improved accuracy and reduced processing time, for example from about 11 minutes to 0.1 s per projection. Finally, we discuss the risks that accompany these tools. Results obtained with AI assistance should be understood and validated by researchers and reviewed by human peers; how to guarantee this in practice remains an open question.
