sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Dolenec (Autores: R. Dolenec , D. Gascon , A. Gola , J.M. B. Benlloch , D. G. Sanchez , R. Ballabriga , W. Weber , G. Elfakhri , R. Pestotnik)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Ljubljana, Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, Ljubljana, Slovenia [2] Jožef Stefan Institute, Experimental Particle Physics Department, Ljubljana, Slovenia [3] University of Barcelona, Dept. Física Quàntica i Astrofísica, Institut de Ciències Del Cosmos, Barcelona, Spain [4] Fondazione Bruno Kessler, Trento, Italy [5] The Institute of Instrumentation for Molecular Imaging, Valencia, Spain [6] Oncovision, Valencia, Spain [7] European Organisation for Nuclear Research - CERN, Geneva, Switzerland [8] Technical University of Munich (TUM-MED), Munich, Germany [9] University of California Davis, Dept. of Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract With coincidence timing resolution (CTR) below 100 ps positron emission tomography (PET) with limited angular coverage and even small flat panels could reach state-of-the-art image quality. The PetVision project is developing a novel modular PET detector concept based on high-resolution time-of-flight (TOF) capabilities that approach the physical limits of current scintillator technology. Achieving this performance requires dedicated development and optimized integration of key PET detector components. We are designing a low noise, high dynamic range frontend electronics, specifically a next generation ASIC with 20 ps intrinsic time resolution and on-chip time-to-digital conversion (TDC). Concurrently, we are advancing SiPM sensor technology to enhance photon detection efficiency and reduce jitter. We also explore 2.5D integration between the photodetector and electronics to minimise parasitic effects and timing dispersion. This contribution present the project's vision and progress in technology development, focusing on the ASIC design, production of dedicated SiPMs and preliminary tests of 2.5D integration approaches.

sub_talks.title: [WS-02-07] Recent progress in TSV, 2.5D and 3D integration of SiPMs at FBK (#3413)
sub_talks.speaker: A. Gola
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK), Trento, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract FBK is developing a set of integration technologies to overcome the limits of wire-bonded, front-side-contacted SiPMs in large-area, high-granularity detectors. We report on the latest progress of our through-silicon-via (TSV) platform. A first run of a glass-less TSV process has been carried out alongside the standard front-side production flow, and the transfer of the process to an external foundry has been assessed. TSVs allow 6x6 mm 2 SiPMs to be segmented into independently read sub-pixels down to 1 mm 2 on the same die, and a single-cell-access TSV layout, giving back-side access to individual microcells, has been taped out. In parallel, we are pursuing 2.5D and 3D integration with front-end electronics, including 3D stacking of SiPMs on readout ASICs developed with an industrial partner. These approaches enable four-side tileable modules with minimal dead area, and aim at finer segmentation and improved timing for TOF-PET, high-energy physics and space applications.

sub_talks.title: [WS-02-09] Status of project ASPIDES (#3415)
sub_talks.speaker: T. M. Floris
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universita di Pavia, Pavia, Italy [2] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Pavia, Italy [3] Fondazione Bruno Kessler, Trento, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract As part of the ASPIDES collaboration, a prototype of a fully digital SiPM in 110 nm CMOS technology, based on a fast parallel adder and featuring first-photon timing and time-over-threshold measurement capabilities, was submitted in December 2025. The development of a dedicated test board has been completed, and the measurement setup is currently being finalized. Pending the results of the initial experimental characterization, the design of a scalable demonstrator has been initiated. This new version is designed to interconnect multiple digital SiPMs, similar to those currently under evaluation, through a simplified serial input/output interface. This approach minimizes the physical interconnect overhead toward the control FPGA, thereby enabling a single FPGA to manage a considerably larger number of devices. The digital interface electronics must support two main functions: the configuration of internal structures and the retrieval of data from all integrated modules. The communication process is based upon a 32-bits instruction-based protocol, which enables individual module addressing, thereby supporting SiPM programming and command execution. This protocol includes functions such as pixel reset, acquisition window control, configuration register menagement and control of the output data format. The demonstrator is targeted for completion in spring 2027.

sub_talks.title: [WS-02-17] End-to-End SPAD Technology at Fraunhofer IMS (#3423)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Ruskowski (Autores: J. Ruskowski , P. vom Stein , M. Figge , S. Kolnsberg , A. Grabmaier)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Fraunhofer Institute for Microelectronic Circuits and Systems, Duisburg, Germany [2] University Duisburg-Essen, Duisburg, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The development of the Fraunhofer IMS SPAD technology was originally driven by the requirements of large-scale SPAD arrays for LiDAR. Today, a 200 mm backside-illuminated SPAD process with wafer-to-wafer bonding is available, providing a versatile platform for highly integrated photon detection systems. The approach allows SPAD detectors and CMOS circuitry to be designed and optimized separately and subsequently combined, with the electronics positioned directly underneath the detector to maximize the photosensitive area and reach perfect timing symmetry. Fraunhofer IMS covers the complete development chain, from SPAD and circuit design to semiconductor manufacturing and electro-optical waferlevel test, enabling sensor solutions tailored to specific detection challenges. The presentation will introduce this end-to-end approach, the rationale behind the technology, key lessons learned during its development, and its potential for highly integrated digital SiPMs, including applications in particle physics.

sub_talks.title: [NP-01-02] The Shape of Light
sub_talks.speaker: S. Cazzoli
sub_talks.affiliation: Instituto de Astrofísica de Andalucía, Spain
sub_talks.abstract:
The term Big Bang evokes a deafening sound. Yet in the Universe, it is not sound but light that serves, so far, as the most powerful messenger of information. Our eyes were the first instruments through which humanity began to understand the nature of our Universe.

Today, telescopes are our eyes to the cosmos, and they are coupled with a wide variety of instruments capable of collecting, manipulating, and transforming the light that we can ultimately study in order to unravel the secrets of the Universe. Thanks to them, we obtain information as distant and ancient as the Cosmic Microwave Background and as close and young as the whims of our own star, the Sun.

What stories do the different forms of light tell us? Whether through "simple" photon counts, spectra, or even the absence of light, its many forms reveal different information about our Universe.

Light is also a fundamental element in the arts. In the performing arts, it is crucial for creating emotions-often becoming a narrative language-in photography, it builds atmospheres, from the depth of black and white to the intensity of the most vivid colors; and in architecture, it defines spaces and highlights textures.

Light is an essential element both in the artistic experience and in our understanding of the Universe.
The Shape of Light is, more than a talk, a journey through light across astronomy, physics, and art.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-02-01] Ultra High-Rate Neutron Detection with ³He Tubes via CF₄ Prompt Scintillation Readout (#3034)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. M. Margato (Autores: L. M. Margato , A. Morozov , V. Solovov , B. Guérard , J. Marchal)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] LIP-Coimbra, Coimbra, Portugal [2] University of Coimbra, Dep. of Physics, Coimbra, Portugal [3] ILL-Institut Laue-Langevin, Grenoble, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents a novel neutron detector concept aiming to provide detection efficiency and background levels equivalent to conventional ³He-based detectors, whilst boosting the maximum counting rate by several orders of magnitude. The detector retains the form-factor of a standard ³He tube and uses the same working gas mixture of 3 He with admixture of CF 4 as the stopping gas. The key innovation is a fast optical readout of CF₄ prompt scintillation light using silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) sensors. The target performance is a detection efficiency equivalent to that of a standard ³He tube under identical gas filling conditions, gamma sensitivity below 10⁻⁶, and a maximum counting rate of 2 MHz/pixel, orders of magnitude improvement over existing detectors. The fast emission of CF₄ scintillation light is the enabling factor for achieving ultra-high counting rates. CF₄ exhibits a considerable photon yield, with one scintillation band in the UV and another in the visible region of the spectrum, with several thousands of photons emitted per neutron event. The efficient collection of light by the SiPMs constitutes a critical design parameter, addressed in this study through Monte Carlo optimization. The gas mixture composition is optimised to maximise the scintillation yield, and a gas purification system can be integrated into the detector to ensure long-term stability. The first experimental results of a detector prototype characterisation on a neutron beamline at the Institut Laue-Langevin (ILL) will be presented.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-02-02] Characterization of 3D ultra-thin silicon-based thermal neutron detectors (#3088)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Zamorano (Autores: F. Zamorano , I. Lopez , M. Pérez , J. Bravo , C. Fleta , C. Guardiola)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institute of Microelectronics of Barcelona, Barcelona, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Neutron contamination in advanced radiotherapy and other mixed radiation environments has become an increasing concern due to the limitations of conventional neutron detectors under intense gamma background conditions. In this work, ultra-thin 3D silicon neutron detectors specifically designed for operation in mixed radiation fields were experimentally characterized under thermal and high-energy irradiation conditions. The detectors, consisting of 20 µm-thick silicon sensors paired with ⁶LiF neutron conversion layers, were tested at the FANT thermal neutron facility and at the CERN High-Energy Reference Field (CERF). Measurements included reproducibility, angular dependence, bias voltage operation, and discrimination threshold effects using a low-voltage FPGA-based readout system. The results showed stable operation under mixed radiation fields, moderate angular dependence, and strong dependence of the response on detector bias and discrimination threshold. The ultra-thin detector architecture enabled high gamma rejection capability, enabling reliable neutron detection under intense photon background conditions. These results demonstrate the suitability of 3D ultra-thin silicon detectors for compact real-time neutron monitoring in radiation protection and medical applications.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-02-03] Scintillator Size Effects in Fiber-Based Neutron Detectors With Pulse-Shape Discrimination for BNCT (#2328)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H.-D. Liu (Autores: H.-D. Liu , C.-Y. Chang , Y.-H. You , Y.-C. Chang , Z.-F. You , T.-H. Lin , M.-W. Lin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Tsing Hua University,, Institute of Nuclear Engineering and Science, Hsinchu, Taiwan [2] Heron Neutron Medical Corporation, Nuclear Science Department, Zhubei, Taiwan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Scintillator-on-fiber (SOF) detectors utilizing Liglass scintillators show strong potential for neutron flux monitoring in intense radiation environments due to their high radiation hardness and fast response. Previous studies have typically employed fragmented scintillators in SOF detectors due to the difficulty of μm-scale machining. In this work, Li-glass scintillators with well-defined dimensions (1×1×0.5 to 0.25×0.25×0.5 mm 3 ) were precisely fabricated using laser cutting, enabling a systematic investigation of the effect of scintillator size on neutron response linearity in an acceleratordriven neutron beam. With pulse-shape discrimination (PSD), the results show that neutron signals measured with scintillator sizes larger than 0.5×0.5×0.5 mm 3 become blurred in the P SP -channel scatter plot due to gamma-ray contributions and pulse pile-up at an accelerator current of 250 μA. In contrast, the smallest scintillator (0.25×0.25×0.5 mm 3 ) maintains clear separation between neutron and gamma-ray signals. Analysis of the maximum shift error σ m of the neutron peak centroid further indicates that this smallest scintillator effectively suppresses pileup, achieving σ m = 0. In terms of linearity, scintillators with sizes below 0.75×0.75×0.5 mm 3 yield coefficients of determination R 2 > 0.99 when processed using a two-dimensional fiducial cut, satisfying the requirements for neutron flux monitoring in boron neutron capture therapy (BNCT). These results demonstrate the feasibility of optimizing Li-glass scintillator size and volume in SOF detectors to achieve reliable neutron flux monitoring in BNCT applications.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-02-04] Time-Resolved Imaging of Radioactive Gas with the 4π Gamma-Ray Imager C3G (#1185)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Kitayama (Autores: Y. Kitayama , H. Nakai , K. Enomoto , N. Yamada , K. Hitomi , M. Nogami , N. Kawachi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Fukushima Institute for Research, Education and Innovation, Plant Imaging research Unit, Fukushima, Japan [2] Tohoku University, Sendai, Japan [3] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology, Takasaki, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Coded Cube Camera for Gamma-ray (C3G) is a 4π gamma-ray imager designed to estimate gamma-ray source distributions from direction-dependent detector response patterns. In this study, we developed a 24-detector C3G consisting of 24 HR-GAGG scintillators and applied it to a plant radioisotope (RI) imaging experiment using 11 CO 2 gas. In the plant RI imaging experiment, approximately 300 MBq of 11 CO 2 gas was supplied to a plant placed in an experimental chamber to image the transport of 11 C-labeled photosynthates within the plant. During this experiment, the C3G was placed outside the chamber, and the dynamics of 11 CO 2 gas were continuously measured with an acquisition time of 1 s per measurement. As a result, the inflow of the gas into the chamber was clearly visualized. In addition, the reconstructed image intensity decreased exponentially over time. The half-life estimated from this intensity change was 20.70 min, which was in good agreement with the known half-life of 11 C, 20.34 min. These results demonstrate that the 24-detector C3G can visualize dynamic gaseous radioactive sources and estimate temporal changes in radioactivity from reconstructed image intensity. This capability is expected to be useful for applications such as radioactive gas leakage monitoring, environmental monitoring, and nuclear security.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-02-05] Method for determining lithium ore's grade based on photoneutrons' lifetime measurement (#1637)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Yu (Autores: M. Yu , Y. Yang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [2] Tsinghua University, Key Laboratory of Particle & Radiation Imaging, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Analysis of lithium ore grade is industrially significant for efficient lithium resource development and utilization, enabling improved production efficiency and reduced costs. Lithium has a large neutron absorption cross-section, and changes in lithium grade can affect the neutron lifetime, which is inversely proportional to the macroscopic absorption cross-section of ore. In this paper, a method for determining lithium grade through neutron lifetime measurements based on an e-LINAC driven photoneutron source is applied to the online analysis of lithium ore grade. Since lithium does not emit gamma rays upon neutron absorption, the neutron lifetime is measured from the time distribution of capture gamma rays induced by neutrons in the matrix elements of the medium. The feasibility of this approach has been demonstrated in experiments using various lithium nitrate solutions as simplified media. Meanwhile, the effect of neutron diffusion was investigated by simulations. The potential of neutron-induced prompt gamma analysis for reducing interference caused by variations in matrix composition is discussed. Further simulation studies and system design are in progress.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-02-06] Template-Matching Position Solving on FPGAs for a Thermal Neutron Detector (#1591)
sub_talks.speaker: M. Loyd
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Oak Ridge National Lab, Oak Ridge, Tennessee, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) based thermal neutron detectors have been developed at Oak Ridge National Laboratory for single crystal diffraction instruments. They have potential as good replacements for current 3He detectors on neutron reflectometers due to their high spatial resolution and fast scintillator decay time. The current software-implemented position fitting on these detectors is limited due to the processing required for the recursive least-squares algorithm. In this work, we present a fast method for determining neutron position that can be run on the Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) chip that is already installed on the detector. This method compares the collected event data with pre-determined shapes stored on FPGA memory in parallel, and determines the one with the least linear error. Using this method for neutron positioning takes less time than the hardware defined dead time. Count-rate and spatial resolution results collected at the High-Flux Isotope Reactor are presented, with output count rates > 500 kcps achieved, an order of magnitude greater than the software fitting method.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-02-07] Localization of uranium samples in large cemented nuclear waste using active photon interrogation and a Bayesian inversion (#1492)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Lebreton (Autores: M. Lebreton , B. Geslot , C. Carasco , B. Pérot , C. Michelet)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Commissariat à l'énergie atomique et aux énergies alternatives, CEA/DES/IRESNE, St Paul Lez Durance, France [2] Université de Bordeaux, CNRS-IN2P3/LP2IB, Bordeaux, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract CEA Cadarache currently manages over 6,000 historical 870 L nuclear waste packages. To ensure long-term safety, French regulatory authorities require a precise characterization of each unit, specifically regarding structural integrity, fissile material mass and total activity of alpha emitters. However, the high density and volume of 870 L concrete waste packages result in significant signal attenuation, making standard passive gamma spectrometry or passive and active neutron measurements inefficient to assess the mass of nuclear materials. To maximize the signal-to-noise ratio, a specific Active Photon Interrogation (API) approach is developed inside the CINPHONIE irradiation bunker of CHICADE facility, at CEA IRESNE, Cadarache, France. This method makes use of inorganic BGO scintillators to measure high-energy delayed gamma rays from short-lived photofission products induced with a high-energy bremsstrahlung photon source, i.e., a 18 MeV LINAC. A Bayesian framework is applied to infer both the mass and the position of nuclear materials from angular acquisitions. This article is focused on testing API framework in the case where the source of the signal is located in a homogeneous environment. Based on the promising results presented here, future developments will focus on the heterogenous case.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-02-08] Hybrid Temperature Compensation and Radiation Damage Recovery with Scintillation Detectors (#2243)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D.Y. Oh (Autores: D.Y. Oh , J. Hwang , G. Kim , C. Kim , J.-Y. Yeom)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea University, Department of Bioengineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] Korea University, Interdisciplinary Program in Precision Public Health, Seoul, Republic of Korea [3] Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [4] Korea University, School of Biomedical Engineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Gamma-ray spectroscopy is a fundamental technique for identifying radioisotopes in safety-critical applications. However, in scenarios such as nuclear accidents, high-temperature and high-radiation environments severely degrade photomultiplier tube performance. Conventional temperature compensation systems face physical voltage limits, and prior deep-learning algorithms fail because they require preserved spectral shapes. To overcome these limitations, this study presents a comprehensive strategy to enhance detector stability. First, an active high-voltage control system mitigates initial temperature-induced gain loss. Because this hardware compensation eventually reaches its physical safety limits, the system integrates a deep learning (DL) technique - bidirectional long short-term memory network - to interpret residual spectral distortions, successfully achieving accurate multi-isotope quantification up to 185 °C. Second, to address radiation-induced damage localized within the photomultiplier tube, a targeted active thermal annealing protocol was applied. Following a 1.55 kGy cumulative gamma irradiation, detector output dropped to 23.5% of its baseline. Subsequent thermal annealing of the photomultiplier tube body at 145 °C successfully restored the output to 89.4%. Ultimately, this integration of hardware, software, and active recovery lays a foundation for robust radionuclide identification under concurrent high-temperature and high-radiation constraints.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-02-09] Simulations of A Novel Time-of-Flight β/γ Transmission Tomography Scanner (#2255)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Carmichael (Autores: R. Carmichael , A. Chatziioannou)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California Los Angeles, Department of Molecular and Medical Pharmacology, Los Angeles, California, United States of America [2] University of California Los Angeles, Crump Institute for Molecular Imaging, Los Angeles, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Large cargo scanning presents a unique challenge for national security. Container size limitations pose challenges to tomographic imaging. This work proposes a new stationary, limited angle tomographic transmission scanner geometry with a unique β/γ source utilizing a pair of fixed flat panel detectors, known as Gamma Tomography (GT). A Gate 10 simulation evaluates the imaging capabilities of the scanner and explores time-of-flight (TOF) and energy discrimination as electronic collimation methods to reduce scattered radiation and improve image quality. A 600 μm thin plastic scintillator sheet encasing 100mCi of 60 Co as a near detector locally captures nearly all emitted β particles without significant γ interactions, while a far detector panel of 2 cm thick LYSO crystals captures the ~1.25 MeV energy 60 Co γ photons. Both panels were simulated as 50x80 cm with a thin, 2 cm thick, multi-material test object consisting of water, aluminum, titanium, steel, and uranium in the center of the field of view. The same simulation dataset was reconstructed with/without two separate electronic collimation schemes: valid coincidences with a 100 keV energy window around the 60 Co photopeaks, and valid coincidences with a 100 ps time resolution. Despite the short acquisition time (18sec), reconstructed images are low noise, with all objects visible above background and distinguishable. The images show attenuation coefficient under-estimation, due to object scatter. TOF and energy discrimination underestimate μ values by 25.8% and 34.3% respectively, but a large dynamic range and very high SNR in μ value is achieved for all reconstructions (SNR-water: 46, SNR-Uranium: 1369). Using time information in lieu of energy allows events scattered in the detector to be used to improve image quality and SNR, but further investigation will include achievable time resolution, panel construction, and source geometry optimization.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-02-10] Revealing Disorder Faster: Detector Upgrades for SANDALS-II (#2826)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. E. Mann (Autores: S. E. Mann , N. J. Rhodes , E. M. Schooneveld , G. Mauri , J. Day , O. L.G. Alderman , T.-L. Hughes , D. T. Bowron , G.J. Sykora)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] STFC, ISIS, Harwell Campus, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract SANDALS-II is an instrument being developed at the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source as a next generation diffractometer for the study of amorphous and liquid materials. This upgrade will deliver count rates up to 11 times higher than the existing SANDALS instrument and will significantly expand its scientific capabilities. This work focuses on developments of a large area scintillator detector that are essential for achieving enhanced performance. Scintillation detectors for SANDALS-II will cover a solid angle of 0.67Ω, 2.4 times greater detector coverage than the current instrument. These detectors are required to have high efficiency, particularly at higher neutron energies (short wavelengths), which is achieved using a unique design employing tiles made from alternating layers of glass and scintillator. Scintillator and glass options are explored to optimise detector and instrument performance. Different low Li and B content glasses were tested to determine the most suitable option for the instrument that provides good neutron transmission while maintaining affordability. The ratio of ZnS:Ag to 6 LiF in the scintillator will be altered from 4:1 to 2:1 to enhance neutron absorption and therefore detection efficiency. At 30eV (0.05Å) this offers a 60% improvement in detection efficiency. The applicability of low-afterglow scintillator, ZnO:Zn/ 6 LiF, for use in SANDALS-II is also explored. ZnO:Zn/ 6 LiF is shown to offer a 2x increase in count rate capability over ZnS:Ag/ 6 LiF, but a 6% lower neutron detection efficiency. As the reduction in efficiency using ZnO:Zn/ 6 LiF is modest, this alternative scintillator offers a viable solution for the high count rate regions of SANDALS-II. With optimised glass and scintillator selection, the performance required for the upgraded instrument can be delivered. This will enable faster measurements, smaller sample studies, and time resolved experiments, making SANDALS-II a world leading disordered material neutron diffractometer.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-02-11] Characterization and Radiation Damage Mitigation of Silicon Photomultipliers for Low Earth Orbit Applications (#1902)
sub_talks.speaker: S. Davarpanah
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Université de Genève, Département de physique nucléaire et corpusculaire, Genève, Genève, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) are attractive photosensors for space applications because of their compact size, low cost, low operating voltage, high photon detection efficiency (PDE), and single-photon sensitivity. Their use in space applications, however, is limited by radiation-induced increases in dark count rate (DCR). This work presents the characterization and radiation tolerance study of FBK NUV-HD-MT SiPMs for the focal plane of the Terzina Cherenkov telescope onboard the NUSES mission, which will operate in a Sun-synchronous low Earth orbit (LEO) at an altitude of approximately 550 km. Devices with micro-cell sizes ranging from 25 to 50 μm were evaluated through a comprehensive characterization campaign comprising static (current-voltage), dynamic (noise and pulse-shape), and optical (photon detection efficiency) measurements to identify the sensor configuration best suited for this application. The 30 μm bare sensors were selected as the optimal solution, achieving a PDE greater than 50% at 400 nm, optical cross-talk below 2%, and a DCR below 60 kHz/mm 2 at 10 V overvoltage. The radiation environment was modeled using SPENVIS, and dose deposition in the focal plane was evaluated with Geant4 simulations. In parallel, radiation effects were investigated experimentally through two irradiation campaigns: a 50 MeV proton beam test and electron exposure using a Sr-90 source. Proton-induced damage produced a significant increase in leakage current and DCR, while electron-induced degradation was substantially smaller. Temperature-dependent measurements were used to extrapolate in-orbit performance and to evaluate recovery through thermal annealing. The results indicate that performing periodic annealing cycles at temperatures above 50°C can reduce the radiation-induced current by up to 40% after approximately 84 hours, helping preserve detector performance over the three-year mission.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-02-12] Graphene Photodetectors for Vacuum-UV Through Visible Wavelengths (#3124)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Lindman (Autores: A. Lindman , M. Turqueti , L. Schlueter , G. R. Araujo)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, United States of America [2] University of Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Many experiments rely on measuring vacuum-ultraviolet light, which is emitted in situations as diverse as scintillation in cryogenic liquid noble gases (126.8 nm in argon) and laser spectroscopy of atomic hydrogen isotopes (121.6 nm). Graphene-monolayer photodetectors offer several attractive traits: they are naturally thin, sensitive to a broad range of wavelengths, relatively simple to fabricate (including with integrated readout circuitry with the same process), and can be made on flexible substrates. We present measurements with visible and UV light down to 115 nm, including at low intensity and with fast pulses, of graphene field-effect transistors (GFETs) of various sizes up to 2 mm square fabricated on silicon. These detectors show promise for experiments from neutrinoless double beta decay searches to absolute neutrino mass measurements, as well as dark-matter searches or other VUV-detection applications.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-02-13] FPGA-Based Real-Time SiPM Emulator with Sub-Nanosecond Temporal Quantization (#1987)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Carsi (Autores: A. Abba , S. Carsi , F. Caponio , E. Proserpio , V. Arosio)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Nuclear Instruments SRL, Lambrugo, Italy [2] Università dell'Insubria, Como, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents a real-time FPGA-based Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) detector emulator capable of reproducing physically accurate detector waveforms at 16-bit resolution and 2.5 GS/s analog output rate. The proposed architecture combines microscopic event simulation with a temporally quantized event-streaming model, enabling real-time waveform synthesis directly inside FPGA logic while drastically reducing bandwidth requirements compared to traditional waveform streaming approaches. The emulator separates event generation from signal shaping: software layers generate timestamped photon-hit sequences derived either from analytical distributions, Geant4 simulations, or SimSiPM microscopic detector models, while the FPGA reconstructs the analog waveform through parallel Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) filter banks implementing the SiPM transfer function; a look-ahead recursive transformation enables II = 1 operation across all banks at 156.25 MHz, consuming approximately 235 DSP48E2 slices. A multi-phase temporal quantization architecture provides 0.8 ns effective timing precision using a 156.25 MHz fabric clock and eight temporal sub-phases. Experimental validation demonstrates excellent agreement between hardware-generated waveforms and analytical as well as SimSiPM-generated references, including pile-up scenarios with overlapping scintillation events reproduced through linear superposition. The prototype operates with an end-to-end latency of approximately 83 ns.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-02-14] Self-Powered Wireless Communication via Ambient Gamma-Ray Harvesting at Fukushima Daiichi (#2629)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Fujiwara (Autores: T. Fujiwara , Y. Shoji , H. Kimura , S. Mae , H. Yoshimochi , K. Kawasaki , H. Kawamura , K. Miyako)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST), Tskuba, Japan [2] Chiyoda Technol Corporation, Tokyo, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Reliable long-term monitoring in nuclear decommissioning facilities is hampered by the absence of permanent power infrastructure and by the radiation fields that degrade conventional electronics. We present a scintillator-photovoltaic converter that captures ambient gamma radiation and transforms it into electrical energy sufficient for periodic wireless data transmission. The converter pairs a 750 cm³ CsI(Tl) crystal with a compact GaInP photovoltaic array mounted on a single end face, following a "large absorber, minimal semiconductor" strategy.) On-site evaluation inside a contaminated-material storage building at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant (~35 mSv/h) produced 273 nW per module. Two parallel modules, combined with ultra-low-power energy management and a sub-GHz radio, achieved seven autonomous transmission bursts totaling 32 packets over a 30 m link during a three-hour observation window-without any external power supply or dedicated radioactive source.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-02-15] Basic Development of a Wide-Field EUV Polarimeter for High-Energy Transient Sources (#3164)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Kuwabara (Autores: S. Kuwabara , S. Gunji , K. Chiba , A. Takahashi , M. Kitaura , E. Nakamura)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yamagata University, Graduate School of Science and Engineering, Yamagata, Japan [2] Yamagata University, Faculty of Science, Yamagata, Japan [3] Institute for Molecular Science, UVSOR Synchrotron Facility / Beamline Technical Staff, Aichi, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Polarization observations in extreme ultraviolet (EUV) band have not yet been achieved because it remains technically difficult to develop wide-field EUV detectors with sufficient sensitivity. However, EUV polarization measurements are expected to provide important insights into the emission mechanisms of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) and ultraviolet flashes associated with supernova explosions. In this study, we propose a novel EUV polarimeter based on Lobster-Eye Optics (LEO), which combines a wide field of view with polarization sensitivity. Optical simulations show that EUV reflectivity on metal surfaces strongly depends on polarization. For example, at 40 eV and an incident angle of 75° on a gold-coated mirror, the reflectivity is about 40% for p-polarization and 60% for s-polarization, respectively. This difference produces an asymmetric cross-shaped image on the focal plane detector depending on the polarization direction. To verify this principle, we developed a test chamber and conducted a synchrotron radiation experiment using a gold-coated mirror and a microchannel plate (MCP) detector. By rotating the mirror around the beam axis, we measured the modulation of the MCP count rate and evaluated the detector modulation factor. The experimental results are presented and discussed in this paper.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-01-01] Facile, scalable and high-yield synthesis of zero-dimensional copper halide Cs 3 Cu 2 Cl 5 scintillator with near-unity quantum yield for high-resolution X-ray imaging applications (#1659)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Shin (Autores: Y.S. Choi , J. Im , K. Heo , S.O. Cho , B.K. Cha , B. Shin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] KAIST, Materials Science and Engineering, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [2] KAIST, Nuclear and Quantum Engineering, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [3] Viewworks, Anyang, Republic of Korea [4] KERI, Ansan, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Metal halide perovskites, particularly copper halide variants, have emerged as promising scintillators owing to their large Stokes shift, high photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY), and efficient radioluminescence. Here, we demonstrate a dioxolane-mediated reaction synthesis as a simple, scalable, and high-yield strategy for producing Cs 3 Cu 2 Cl 5 powders with near-complete conversion. By employing low-polarity yet water-miscible dioxolane as the reaction medium together with an aqueous H 3 PO 2 additive, the solubility imbalance between the precursors inherent to low-polarity solvents is effectively addressed. This approach enables stoichiometry-controlled dissolution-precipitation under a low-polarity reaction environment and the formation of phase-pure Cs 3 Cu 2 Cl 5 powders with near-unity PLQY. The powders show bright green emission at ~530 nm and retain over 80% of their initial efficiency after 300 days of ambient storage without encapsulation, demonstrating remarkable intrinsic stability. Cs 3 Cu 2 Cl 5 -based composite films deliver an ultrahigh light yield of ~98,000 photons MeV -1 , greatly surpassing that of commercial scintillators such as Gd 2 O 2 S and CsI:Tl, and exhibiting excellent dose linearity and long-term irradiation stability. When integrated into commercial flat-panel detectors, the Cs 3 Cu 2 Cl 5 -based composite films successfully enabled high-quality 2D radiographic and 3D computed tomography imaging, directly verifying their compatibility with existing X-ray detection systems. This facile and efficient synthesis, together with the demonstrated device-level imaging performance, highlights Cs 3 Cu 2 Cl 5 as a scalable and practical candidate for next-generation X-ray scintillators.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-01-02] Hydrophobic Solvent-Based Polishing for Performance Enhancement of Water-Sensitive Perovskite Scintillator Crystals (#1236)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Song (Autores: S. Song , J. Seo , D. Lee , C. Park , B. Park , J.-Y. Yeom)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea University, Department of Bioengineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] Korea University, Interdisciplinary Program in Precision Public Health, Seoul, Republic of Korea [3] Korea Institute of Fusion Energy, Dajeon, Republic of Korea [4] Korea University, Global Health Technology Research Center, Seoul, Republic of Korea [5] Seoul National University, Research Institute for Future Technology and Policy, Seoul, Republic of Korea [6] Korea University, School of Bioengineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Halide perovskites are promising scintillator materials for radiation detection and medical imaging because of their excellent optical and scintillation properties. Since the surface quality of single-crystal scintillators strongly affects light extraction and detector performance, polishing is an essential step in scintillator fabrication. However, conventional wet polishing processes are not suitable for water-sensitive crystals such as Cs 3 Cu 2 I 5 (CCI). In this work, hydrophobic solvents were investigated as polishing media for water-sensitive CCI single crystals. Three hydrophobic solvents-squalane, silicone oil, and mineral oil- were used as dispersion media for 1 μm alumina abrasives, followed by toluene rinsing after polishing. Among them, squalane showed the best polishing performance, yielding the lowest surface roughness (R q =17.29 nm), the highest transmittance of 78.21%, and the narrowest rocking-curve FWHM of 0.025°. In addition, sequential polishing in squalane using P2000 sandpaper, P4000 sandpaper, and 1 μm alumina enhanced the light yield and improved the energy resolution from 6.53% to 5.83%. These results identify squalane as a promising polishing medium for water-sensitive halide perovskite scintillators.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-01-03] Organic Scintillator Light Yield Models for Sub-MeV Neutrons in EJ301D and d-stilbene (#1369)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. A. Irvine (Autores: C. A. Irvine , T. C. Borgwardt , R. A. Weldon Jr. , J. Mattingly)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Los Alamos National Laboratory, NEN-2, Los Alamos, New Mexico, United States of America [2] North Carolina State University, Nuclear Engineering, Raleigh, North Carolina, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Six commonly used models for neutron induced light yield in organic scintillators were fit and analyzed using measurements of a 2.54 cm diameter by 2.54 cm long right circular cylinder of EJ301D and a (5.08 cm)3 custom made cube of deuterated trans-stilbene-d12 (d-stilbene). Measured neutron energies spanned 300 keV to 2200 keV for the EJ301D scintillator and 200 keV to 2500 keV in d-stilbene. The model fits and experimental analysis methods were verified by examining the agreement between the predicted light output spectrum and the measured light output spectrum for several simulated quasi-monoenergetic neutron sources. Birks model inaccurately predicted highly quenched light yield for sub-MeV neutrons in both scintillators. The addition of a second order quenching term to the Birks model by Chou significantly improved the models accuracy, however its behavior is non-physical if extrapolated beyond the measured neutron energies. The model derived by Voltz accurately fit the measurement of both scintillators for all measured neutron energies. Further investigation into the ability to extrapolate based on these semi-empiric models would be valuable given the non-physical behavior of well-fitting models.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-01-04] Application of neutron sensitising layers to plastic scintillator (#2414)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. P. Taggart (Autores: J. R. Hitchens , C. Allwork , S. L. Chauhan , T. Crane , T. Heather , M. P. Taggart)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] AWE Nuclear Security Technologies, Reading, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Eljen plastic scintillator disks have been coated with layers of neutron sensitiser in a systematic study on the thickness of neutron detection layers. Here we discuss the impact of enhancing standard plastic scintillator (PVT) with coatings containing both lithium and boron isotopes. The application of these layers enhances the material to provide a mechanism for detecting neutron radiation. A systematic study was performed to assess the impact of sensitiser thickness on neutron detection efficiency and neutron-gamma pulse shape discrimination (PSD) performance. Samples were exposed to the mixed radiation fields of a 252 Cf source, and a sample of plutonium. The results demonstrate clear neutron-gamma discrimination in sensitised samples, with measured figures of merit in excess of 3 recorded for optimised lithium-rich coatings. This is comparable performance to established dual-mode detectors. These findings show that thin, externally applied neutron-sensitising layers provide an effective route to enhancing the performance of conventional plastic scintillators. This approach may offer a low-cost means of upgrading existing detector systems in nuclear security applications.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-01-05] Scintillation light quenching for energetic charged particles in GAGG:Ce (#1607)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Liang (Autores: F. Liang , N. Floyd , H. Jayatissa , P. Adsley , A. Alvarez , R. Bartsch , S. Fritz , T. Hankins , B. Harvey , K. Pham , E. Schnorrenberg , D. Shelden , S. Yennello)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Los Alamos National Laboratory, ISR Division, Los Alamos, New Mexico, United States of America [2] Texas A&M University, Cyclotron Institute, College Station, Texas, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Cerium-doped gadolinium gallium aluminium garnet (GAGG:Ce) is a novel scintillator with excellent scintillation properties. It is suitable for use in various basic science research and applications. Because the scintillation light is quenched for charged particle detection, it is necessary to use beams from accelerators to calibrate the energy response. Measurements of energetic charged particles incident on three GAGG:Ce crystals were performed using accelerated protons, 4 He, and 12 C at 0 o C and 20 o C in consideration for detecting charged particles in the earth's radiation belts for space weather modeling and for deploying in dosimetry devices in ion therapy, respectively. The Birks factor which quantitatively describes the extent of quenching was deduced from the experimental data. For all three GAGG:Ce scintillators, the Birks factor decreases with the atomic number Z of the incident ions. Furthermore, less light quenching, a smaller Birks factor, was observed for GAGG:Ce at 0 o C. The quenching for the Mg-codoped GAGG:Ce which has a shorter decay time constant, was found to be less temperature dependent compared to the other two GAGG:Ce crystals.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-01-06] Temperature Dependence of Pulse Shape Discrimination in SiPM-Based EJ-276D Detectors (#1585)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Di Fulvio (Autores: J. W. Fritchie , A. Di Fulvio , G. Gariazzo , G. Roche)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Nuclear, Plasma, and Radiological Engineering, Urbana, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The temperature dependence of pulse shape discrimination performance was investigated for three commercial silicon photomultiplier technologies coupled to an EJ-276D organic scintillator. Measurements were conducted at 22 °C, 30 °C, 40 °C, and 50 °C using PuBe sources. Pulse shape discrimination was quantified using the tail-to-total ratio and figure of merit. For all devices, the figure of merit increased at 30 °C. The Broadcom device exhibited the highest performance, increasing from 1.12 at 22 °C to a maximum of 1.17 at 30 °C before decreasing to 0.76 at 50 °C. The Onsemi and Hamamatsu devices showed smaller improvements, with figure of merit values increasing from 0.86 to 0.89 and 0.84 to 0.90, respectively, between 22 °C and 30 °C. At 50 °C, all devices exhibited reduced performance due to increased silicon photomultiplier thermal noise. Temperature-dependent changes in pulse shape were observed, with increasing temperature producing faster decay and modifying the balance of prompt and delayed scintillation light, improving neutron-gamma separation at intermediate temperatures. Despite degradation at higher temperature, all devices maintained effective discrimination up to 50 °C. These results demonstrate that silicon photomultiplier-based detectors are capable of robust neutron-gamma discrimination at elevated temperatures relevant to safeguards applications.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-01-07] Performance evaluation of GaGG(Ce) scintillators with different photosensors (#2850)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Caballero Rodríguez (Autores: M. Caballero Rodríguez , N. Bernier , V. M. Nouvilas , L. Fraile , O. Alonso-Sañudo , J. A. Briz , S. Gaitan , G. G. de Lorenzo , P. Gonzalez-Tarrio , A. Illana , J. Udias)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Facultad de Ciencias Físicas / Departamento de Estructura de la Materia, Física Térmica y Electrónica, Madrid, Spain [2] CERN, ISOLDE, EP Department, Geneva, Spain [3] CSIC, Instituto de Estructura de la Materia, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The HIE-ISOLDE Timing Array for Reaction Studies (HISTARS) project at CERN is developing a specialized detector system designed to measure the lifetimes of excited nuclear states. For efficient particle detection, thin square GaGG(Ce) are utilized alongside YSO due to their high density and fast scintillation properties. This work evaluates the performance of GAGG(Ce) crystals coupled with two distinct photosensors: a Hamamatsu R9779 photomultiplier tube (PMT) and an array of four silicon photomultipliers (SiPM) using a custom-designed circuit. These configurations were tested in combination with a LaBr 3 (Ce) detector to facilitate coincidence measurements. Data acquisition was performed using high-speed digitizer to extract timing and energy information. This article reports on the comparative performance of both readout methods, specifically characterizing pulse shape discrimination capabilities, energy resolution, and the coincidence time resolution for alpha-gamma events. Although the energy resolution is acceptable and it has a good pulse shape discrimination capability, the measured timing limitations show that the current configuration is not ideal for the HISTARS array. These results will guide the selection of better-suited materials for high-precision timing at HIE-ISOLDE.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-01-08] Combining cross-luminescent scintillators and μSiPMs for better timing in ToF-PET (#1249)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Herweg (Autores: K. Herweg , S. Bisi , C. Bruschini , E. Charbon , A. Gola , L. Parellada-Monreal , M. Penna , D. Schug , V. Schulz , S. Gundacker)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] RWTH Aachen University, University Hospital RWTH Aachen, Aachen, Germany [2] RWTH Aachen University, Institute of Imaging and Computer Vision, Aachen, Germany [3] Ecole polythechnique fédérale de Lausanne, Advanced Quantum Architecture Laboratory, Neuchatel, Switzerland [4] Fondazione Bruno Kessler, Trento, Italy [5] Austrian Academy of Sciences, Marietta Blau Institute for Particle Physics, Vienna, Austria
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Time-of-flight positron emission tomography (ToF-PET) has boosted PET image quality significantly in the last years. During its first inception it was built with cross-luminescent BaF 2 crystals, which have since been replaced by LYSO. Recently, cross-luminescence has regained popularity with new scintillators being developed. However, BaF 2 and the recently developed Cs 2 ZnCl 4 could not improve on the LYSO state-of-the-art coincidence time resolution (CTR) (56 ps for 2x2x3 mm³ and 95 ps for 3x3x19 mm³). As Cs 2 ZnCl 4 shows a significant Cherenkov production, we combined it with the DIGILOG approach to boost its timing performance. The DIGILOG approach segments the sensor into μSiPMs and has shown an improved timing performance for BGO due to its Cherenkov radiation and an improved SPTR. Here, we simulated a 3x3x3 mm³ and a 3x3x20 mm³ Cs 2 ZnCl 4 crystal coupled to seven different μSiPM arrays. The simulation included noise factors like dark counts, cross-talk, SPAD dead time and analog noise. It was designed with a PDE of 60 % and an SPTR of 25 ps. This resulted in an improved CTR of 34+/-4 ps for an array of 20x20 μSiPMs coupled to a 3x3x3 mm³ Cs 2 ZnCl 4 crystal compared to the non-segmented SiPM at 48+/-3 ps. Furthermore, for the 3x3x20 mm³ crystal, a CTR of 64+/-4 ps was reached with a 10x10 μSiPM array, while the non-segmented SiPM showed a CTR of 84+/-3 ps. The results of the segmented SiPMs improve on the LYSO state-of-the-art. Additionally, they demonstrate that the DIGILOG SiPM approach improves timing performance not just for BGO, but also for other scintillators with high Cherenkov yield, ultra-fast emission and low light yield. We also provide motivation to optimize sensors for Cs 2 ZnCl 4 , which could enable better timing performance than the LYSO state-of-the-art.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-01-09] Fast or Adapt: Proportional Gas in γ-ray Fields (#1278)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. O'Connor (Autores: J. Prchlik , E. Yokie , A. Petitjean , D. O'Connor)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Reuter-Stokes, LLC, Twinsburg, Ohio, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Background γ-ray fields complicate neutron measurements for Nondestructive Assay (NDA) of Nuclear Materials and the next generation of advanced reactor designs, including non-light water (non-LWR) and Small Modular Reactors (SMRs). Neutron sensitive proportional counter design for high γ-ray fields often focus on optimizing ion collection time and integrating low-Z materials. In these counters, the metal cathode produces most of the Compton scattered electrons, which deposit unwanted energy and signal in the gas. The long path length for Compton electrons in the counter gas means the counter gas pressures may be optimized to increase the ratio of ion-to-electron energy deposition. Here we present gas mixture and pressure optimization for ion-to-electron energy deposition using SRIM simulations. The simulation output is then tested experimentally for its effect on neutron sensitivity in γ-ray fields between 1 R/Hr and 100 R/Hr. The ion-to-electron energy deposition ratio shows promise as an additional design consideration for neutron sensitive proportional counters in γ-ray fields, even though the experimentally measured optimum pressure of 0.5 atm for He/N 2 95/5 is lower than the simulated optimum pressure. Future experiments with a current sensitive preamplifier (CAEN A1427) will improve neutron counting for 1 to 100 R/Hr γ-ray fields.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-01-10] Characterisation of edge-on fully-depleted monolithic CMOS silicon sensors (#1882)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Barbagiovanni (Autores: M. Barbagiovanni , A. Bjorklid , A. Bortone , R. Brunskog , M. Da Rocha Rolo , M. Danielsson , A. Elihar , U. Follo , S. Garbolino , J. Hartman , J. Herzen , D. John , F. L. Klaus , C. Mogler , L. Pancheri , J. Parnell , M. Persson , E. Posteraro , M. Sjolin , M. Y. Tamm , S. Wirtensohn)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Politecnico di Torino, Electronics and Telecommunications, Turin, Italy [2] INFN Sezione Torino, Turin, Italy [3] Prismatic Sensor, Stockholm, Sweden [4] Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm, Sweden [5] Università di Trento, Trento, Italy [6] KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden [7] TUM, Munich, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Monolithic silicon CMOS Sensors represent a considerable step forward in charged particle and photon sensing, and emerge as a promising embodiment for the design of novel deep-silicon photon-counting X-ray Computed Tomography scanners . This work presents the first characterization of the ARCADIA MD3 Fully-Depleted CMOS sensors, which technology is currently the baseline for the development of innovative sensors under the framework of the EIC Pathfinder Open 1MICRON project. We report on the characterisation results using an edge-on geometry and a focused synchrotron X-ray beam at the DESY test facility. The x-rays impinge on the edge of the sensor, increasing the active sensor depth seen by the photons, which consequently improves the quantum efficiency with respect to a face-on configuration. A 37 keV focused beam incident parallel to the sensor surface allowed scans along the two directions of the sensor edge, enabling the extraction of the active sensor thickness and mechanical tilt via pixel intensity profiles. Lateral scans across pixel boundaries revealed a periodicity of the spatial modulation of mean cluster size compatible with the pixel pitch of the matrix. Taking the cluster size as the main figure of merit, the performance of the sensor was evaluated at different thresholds and multiple bias voltages in order to assess the variation in the Coulomb cone and collection dynamic. The measurements are supported by Allpix Squared Monte Carlo framework, demonstrating good consistency between the simulated and the real domain.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-01-11] Gain suppression study on LGADs with different gain layer designs (#2025)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract High-energy physics experiments currently use Low Gain Avalanche Diodes (LGADs) as part of their time-of-flight layers to track particles, thanks to their unique temporal resolution and radiation hardness. With increasing deposited charge, the gain was observed to decrease. This gain suppression effect originates from the electrostatic field screening produced by the avalanche multiplication charge. This work investigates the resilience of the LGADs to the gain suppression by characterizing a set of detectors with different gain layer designs and thicknesses, using Transient Current Techniques.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-01-12] Pulse-Shape-Based Slow-Rising Pulse Rejection for Reliable Charge-Carrier Transport Characterization in a Semiconductor Radiation Detector (#2231)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Boo (Autores: J. Boo , B. Park , G. Kim)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Seoul National University, Department of Energy Systems Engineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] Seoul National University, Nuclear Research Institute for Future Technology and Policy (NIFTEP), Seoul, Republic of Korea [3] Seoul National University, Nuclear Engineering Department, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Mobility (μ), lifetime (τ), and mobility-lifetime product (μτ) are key metrics for semiconductor radiation detectors. Highly concentrated trapping centers or defects can distort the internal electric-field distribution, producing reduced-amplitude slow-rising charge-sensitive preamplifier pulses that degrade carrier-transit and charge-collection analyses. Although slow-rising-pulse rejection is commonly used to sharpen pulse-amplitude peaks and suppress low-amplitude tails, this work extends its use to charge-carrier transport characterization. A CdZnTeSe detector [1, 2] was characterized at room temperature under electron- and hole-transit-dominant conditions using ²⁴¹Am alpha irradiation. Pulse-shape analysis rejected slow-rising pulses for key metrics extraction. In electron-transit-dominant measurements, the fast-rising pulse events preserved the bias-dependent peak-centroid trend and yielded (μτ) e = 5.7 × 10⁻⁴ cm²/V, μ e = 576 cm²/V·s, and τ e = 1.0 μs, consistent with reported values [3,4]. For hole-transit-dominant measurements, all-pulse events obscured the pulse-amplitude peak and hindered Hecht fitting. After rejection, we obtained (μτ) h = 2.1 × 10⁻⁴ cm²/V, τ h = 0.7 μs, comparable to reported values [5], with μ h = 318 cm²/V·s. Using the rise-time peak as the representative transit time, both all-pulse and fast-rising-pulse events yielded similar μh values. However, when the median rise time of all-pulse events was used instead, drift velocity did not show a clear linear dependence on electric field, whereas fast-rising-pulse events retained linearity. This reflects the need for careful consideration of slow-rising components and the transit-time definition. These results show that slow-rising-pulse rejection enables reliable transport characterization beyond spectral improvement.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-01-13] Diagnosing Mechanisms for Charged Particle Attenuation Enhancement in Nanostructured Materials (#1508)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. P. Speck (Autores: N. P. Speck , G. J. Grey , D. A. Vecchio , K. A. Cotterill , A. I. Taub , M. D. Hammig)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Michigan, Nuclear Engineering and Radiological Sciences Department, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America [2] University of Michigan, Materials Science and Engineering Department, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a methodology for measuring the trajectories of high-energy electrons through materials utilizing a transmission electron microscope (TEM). This novel technique is implemented to diagnose and quantify the mechanism for enhanced radiation attenuation via nanostructures. Rather than an imaging technique, the TEM is applied to radiation shielding measurements as an adaptable electron source with functionality for various beam energies, amperage, alignments, and exposure times alongside an array of precise electron detectors. By utilizing energy filtering and direct electron detection capabilities, scattering profiles are measured with minimal background contributions. This TEM method is leveraged to describe particle transport in nanostructures. Palladium nanoparticles at various monodisperse sizes are synthesized via heat injection and deposited into an epoxy matrix. The palladium epoxy nanocomposites are sectioned with an ultramicrotome to thicknesses of 70 to 1000 nm containing nanoparticle sizes of 5 to 50 nm at 20% of the total weight fraction. Scattering profile measurements at various beam energies are conducted with a variety of sample thicknesses, nanoparticle sizes, and composite fractions. Scattering profile measurements also include bulk, homogeneous palladium samples in contrast to nanomaterials composed of identical atomic percentages. Simulation of the experimental scattering profiles demonstrate an understanding for the phenomena behind nanostructured attenuation enhancement, bolstering advanced nuclear technology via a foundational description for particle transport in nanostructures.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-01-14] Monolithic integration of cooling microchannels in all-silicon ladders for vertex detectors (#1940)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Fernández-Tejero (Autores: J. Fernández-Tejero , A. Dias , M. Duch , R. Mas , C. Orero , M. Vos , M. Ullán)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Centro Nacional de Microelectrónica (IMB-CNM, CSIC), Cerdanyola del Vallés, Spain [2] Instituto de Física Corpuscular (IFIC, CSIC), Paterna, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract New generation of vertex detectors must have excellent thermo-mechanical stability, and all-silicon ladders are considered as promising solutions for future detectors. However, power consumption asymmetries between the active area and periphery can induce large temperature gradients, and in some cases a combination of air and liquid cooling will be required to achieve homogeneous thermal profiles. Microchannel cooling offers a competitive alternative to traditional cooling systems. The short thermal path between the heat load and sink gives an increased thermal evacuation performance, combined with the reduced material needed for the integrated microchannels and the reduced Coefficient of Thermal Expansion mismatch between the cooling and sensor materials to obtain an optimized cooling for radiation detectors. The development of the technology needed for the integration of the sensor with the microchannels in a single piece is an ambitious challenge, as the conditions for the microchannel formation must be compatible with the sensor, requiring the optimization of the fabrication to ensure the compatibility with CMOS processes. As a demonstrator, all-silicon ladder prototypes with integrated cooling microchannels are presented. Power consumptions for the active area and periphery of the ladders are emulated using integrated aluminum heaters. The bulk in the active area is thinned from 600 to 50 microns, and the design of the microchannels cooling circuit, integrated in the periphery of the ladder, is optimized using finite-element simulation packages. Variations of prototype ladders with different sizes, microchannel dimensions, and integrated using different wafer bonding techniques are fabricated and evaluated in detail in this work.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-01-01] Exploring 4x4x3 cm 3 3D-CdZnTe Semiconductor Gamma-Ray Detectors (#1366)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. He (Autores: Z. He , Y. Zhu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Michigan, Nuclear Engineering and Radiological Sciences, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Three-dimensional position-sensitive single-crystal CdZnTe detectors (3D-CZT), with energy resolution of ~0.3% FWHM for single-pixel events and ~0.5% FWHM for all events at 662 keV, had been demonstrated previously on detectors with dimensions up to 2x2x1.5 cm 3 (total 6 cm 3 ). Larger volume single-crystal CdZnTe semiconductor gamma-ray detectors are needed to achieve higher intrinsic detection efficiency at higher gamma-ray energies. 4x4x3 cm 3 (total 48 cm 3 ) 3D-CZT detectors manufactured by Redlen Technologies have been explored for the first time. Energy spectra of Cs-137 were obtained on all three 4x4x3 cm 3 CZT detectors. An energy resolution of 1.05% FWHM at 662 keV was obtained for single-pixel events on one 4x4x3 cm 3 CZT detector #12R2. The feasibility of achieving close to 1.0% FWHM energy resolution on CdZnTe gamma-ray detectors with single-crystal detection volume of 48 cm 3 has been demonstrated.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-01-02] Visualizing the Hidden Physics of CdTe Detectors: Direct Spatiotemporal Imaging of Charge Clouds (#1397)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Cola (Autores: A. Cola , A. Valletta , I. Farella , V. Dědič , L. Dominici)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CNR, IMM, Lecce, Italy [2] CNR, IMM, Roma, Italy [3] CNR, IMM, Lecce, Italy [4] Charles University, Institute of Physics, Prague, Czech Republic [5] CNR, Nanotec, Lecce, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Carrier Dynamics by Pockels Imaging (CDPI) is a novel all-optical, quantitative, and non-invasive method for direct spatiotemporal visualization of charge carrier clouds in CdTe radiation detectors. CDPI achieves micrometer-scale spatial resolution and nanosecond temporal resolution, with sensitivity to electric field differences down to ~2 V/cm - enabling tracking of carrier densities just above the intrinsic level. We directly observe electron cloud formation and evolution, including Gaussian shape preservation, diffusion-driven broadening, and field-dependent reshaping. Under high optical excitation, we resolve space-charge perturbed regimes with cloud expansion due to Coulomb repulsion (width up to 400 µm) and pronounced asymmetric tails due to detrapping processes, possibly correlated with a defective layer near the cathode surface. Crucially, CDPI correlates internal cloud dynamics with external circuit currents, linking microscopic physics to macroscopic detector performance. Although demonstrated in one dimension, CDPI is intrinsically two-dimensional and readily extendable to investigate charge sharing in segmented electrodes or pixel arrays. The technique also supports studies of ultra-high photogenerated charge densities relevant to synchrotron and free-electron laser applications and enables direct visualization of carrier injection from the contacts. CDPI offers a powerful new diagnostic tool for understanding and improving CdTe and other compound semiconductor radiation detectors.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-01-03] Compton Imaging Capability of 1-cm-Thick Pixelated TlBr Detectors (#1525)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Hitomi (Autores: K. Hitomi , Y. Kitayama , M. Nogami , J. Lee , K. Watanabe)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tohoku University, Department of Quantum Science and Energy Engineering, Graduate School of Engineering, Sendai, Japan [2] Fukushima Institute for Research, Education and Innovation, Fukushima, Japan [3] Korea Institute of Nuclear Safety, Division of Radiation Protection for NORM & Cosmic Radiation, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [4] Kyushu University, Department of Applied Quantum Physics and Nuclear Engineering, Graduate School of Engineering, Fukuoka, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Thallium bromide (TlBr) is a promising compound semiconductor for the fabrication of gamma-ray detectors because of its high atomic numbers (Tl: 81, Br: 35), high density (7.56 g/cm 3 ), and wide bandgap energy (2.68 eV). The Compton imaging capability of 1-cm-thick pixelated TlBr detectors was characterized in this study. Pixelated TlBr detectors were fabricated from a crystal grown by the traveling molten zone method using zone-purified material. The crystal size for the detector was 12 mm x 12 mm x 10 mm. The electrodes were formed on the two 12 mm x 12 mm surfaces by vacuum deposition of Tl, followed by Ni and Au. The anode consisted of nine pixel electrodes (2 mm x 2 mm each) surrounded by guard electrodes. The cathode on the opposite side was a planar electrode. For single-pixel events, the TlBr detector exhibited energy resolutions of approximately 2% full width at half maximum or better at 662 keV for all nine pixels with depth correction and event selection based on electron drift time. Compton images of a 137 Cs gamma-ray source were obtained using non-adjacent two-pixel events via the list-mode maximum likelihood expectation maximization (LM-MLEM) algorithm. Clear images of the source were reconstructed at positions consistent with the actual source locations. These results demonstrate that the TlBr detector fabricated in this study possesses high energy resolution and Compton imaging capability.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-01-04] Effect of the Anode Irradiation by X-ray on the Polarization of a CdTe Imaging Sensor (#1944)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. Praus (Autores: P. Praus , E. Belas , M. Betusiak , R. Grill , S. Kacenga , Z. Melnikova , J. Jakubek)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Charles University, Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, Institute of Physics, Prague, Czech Republic [2] ADVACAM s.r.o., Prague, Czech Republic
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents a study of the influence of X-ray irradiation on the electric field profile in biased CdTe sensors with blocking contacts. The investigation focuses on the modification and potential stabilization of the internal electric field through controlled irradiation of the blocking anode under varying conditions. To emulate realistic detector operation, a silicon wafer was positioned in front of the anode to represent a readout chip, while the cathode was probed by laser-induced transient current technique to determine the electric field. A synchronized pulsed bias scheme enabled time-resolved monitoring of polarization dynamics. Transient current waveforms were recorded in a shielded setup with controlled X-ray exposure, and their temporal evolution was analyzed to assess changes in the electric field profile. The results show that, under dark conditions, the sensor exhibits pronounced space charge formation due to blocking anode. In contrast, appropriately tuned X-ray irradiation of the anode leads to a significant stabilization of the field within the sensor bulk. Under these conditions, the electric field remains nearly uniform over time. The observed behavior reflects the interplay between space-charge formation and X-ray-induced carrier generation, which can partially compensate accumulated charge, although the process remains sensitive to irradiation conditions and contact configuration. Furthermore, low-energy X-ray irradiation transmitted through a silicon layer produces effects comparable to optical excitation at the anode, indicating a similar mechanism of near-contact carrier generation. The presented results provide insight into the control of polarization effects and contribute to improving the operational stability of CdTe-based radiation detectors.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-01-05] Identification and control of interfacial limits enabling high-performance photon-counting perovskite radiation detectors (#2057)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Tumen-Ulzii (Autores: G. Tumen-Ulzii , S. D. Stranks)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Cambridge, Department of Chemical Engineering and Biotechnology, Cambridge, United Kingdom [2] University of Cambridge, Department of Physics, Cambridge, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Lead halide perovskite single crystals are promising for photon-counting radiation detection due to their high atomic number and favourable charge-transport properties. However, most perovskite detectors operate in hole-transport configurations, while currently existing readout electronics are optimised for electron collection. Bridging this mismatch requires a clear understanding of carrier-polarity-dependent transport and the underlying device physics governing perovskite detectors. We conducted polarity-resolved α-particle ( 241 Am, 5.48 MeV) measurements on FAPbBr 3 planar detectors (Au/FAPbBr 3 /Bi). Polarity-resolved α-particle measurements reveal strongly asymmetric degradation, with irreversible degradation localised beneath the Bi contact, whereas the Au interface develops a defect-rich recombination region that can be mitigated by ultrathin Ti or Cr interlayers, enabling stable bipolar transport operation. Detectors remain stable after ~100 h of continuous biasing at 5,000 V cm −1 and ~3 months of shelf-life storage. The combination of high-quality crystals and interfacial protection layers enables the detectors to achieve 1.3% energy resolution for 662 keV ( 137 Cs γ-ray source) and 6.1% for 5.48 MeV α-particles in an electron-transport configuration. This work establishes interfacial degradation as the dominant performance-limiting factor in perovskite radiation detectors and identifies interfacial engineering as the key pathway toward stable and high-resolution electron-transport spectroscopy.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-01-06] High-Z Sensor Characterisation and Readout Development for X-ray Detectors at PSI (#2720)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Mulvey (Autores: J. Mulvey , D. Greiffenberg , B. Schmitt , M. Anastasi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Paul Scherrer Institute, Center For Photon Science, Villigen, Aargau, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The newly upgraded Swiss Light Source (SLS) 2.0, a fourth-generation synchrotron, has begun operation. Photons with energies up to 80 keV will be available at increased flux compared to the third-generation source it replaces. In particular, the brilliance is expected to increase by two orders of magnitude. In this energy range, silicon is no longer an efficient detection material. High-Z semiconductors are therefore required, with GaAs:Cr, CdTe, and CdZnTe being promising candidates. Single sensors (2 × 2) cm 2 made up of 256 × 256 pixels with a 75 μm pitch have been bump-bonded to the JUNGFRAU readout ASIC. Developed at PSI, JUNGFRAU is a charge-integrating readout chip with three gain levels and dynamic gain switching. In this talk, we will discuss the ongoing characterisation of high-Z sensors using JUNGFRAU, with a focus on charge transport properties of CdZnTe produced by Redlen Technologies. Furthermore, recent efforts to improve the linear dynamic range of JUNGFRAU in electron collection mode will be discussed. We will also look towards the future with a discussion of full JUNGFRAU modules using GaAs from Dectris or recently acquired (4 × 4) cm 2 CdZnTe sensors from Redlen. Additionally, the new MATTERHORN photon-counting ASIC has been designed for both silicon and high-Z sensors, with assemblies using GaAs undergoing characterisation.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-01-07] Response of a Timepix4 CdTe spectral imaging detector for radiographic applications (#2859)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. A. Cerbone (Autores: L. A. Cerbone , J. Žemlička , B. Bergmann , P. Smolyanskiy , P. Manek , L. Cimmino , G. Mettivier , S. Pospíšil , P. Russo)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Scuola Superiore Meridionale, SPACE PhD program, Napoli, Italy [2] University of Naples Federico II, Dept. of Physics, Napoli, Italy [3] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Napoli, Napoli, Italy [4] Institute of Experimental and Applied Physics, Prague, Czech Republic
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We characterized a Timepix4 application-specific integrated circuit bonded to a 1-mm-thick cadmium telluride sensor for photon-counting X-ray imaging in the diagnostic energy range. A per-pixel energy calibration was performed using X-ray fluorescence and gamma-ray sources, followed by a cluster-wise linear correction to compensate for spectral distortions associated with multi-pixel charge sharing and front irradiation. Flat-field, photon-counting, and spectral imaging tests were performed using a tungsten-anode microfocus X-ray tube operated at 80 kV. The detector achieved an energy resolution of 3.3 keV at 59.5 keV for the Am-241 source. Spectral images were reconstructed using 1 keV energy bins after offline clustering and fluorescence recovery correction. The detector demonstrated high-quality radiographic imaging capability after flat-field correction, despite spatial inhomogeneities typical of fine-pitch CdTe hybrid pixel detectors. A limiting spatial resolution of 8 lp/mm at 10% modulation transfer function was measured for the detector biased at -450 V, at a counting rate approaching 10 7 cps per chip. The results demonstrate the potential of the Timepix4 CdTe assembly for spectral imaging applications.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-01-08] Exploring the X-ray imaging with single-crystalline integrated perovskite sensors (#1569)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 V. Bartosh (Autores: V. Bartosh , A. Sakhatska , K. Sakhatskyi , G. J. Matt , A. Kanak , S. Yakunin , M. Kovalenko)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] ETH Zurich, Laboratory of Inorganic Chemistry, D-CHAB, Zürich, Zürich, Switzerland [2] EMPA, Laboratory for Thin Films and Photovoltaics, Dübendorf, Zürich, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Metal halide perovskites emerge as promising materials for direct X-ray detection due to their high absorption efficiency, favorable charge-transport properties, and compatibility with scalable fabrication methods[1, 2]. While thin polycrystalline perovskite films integrated with pixelated electronics have already demonstrated high-resolution imaging[3], extending these approaches toward thicker highly crystalline absorbers remains essential for practical low-dose applications. Here, we investigate several perovskite multi-pixel detector architectures coupled to charge-integrating readout electronics for low-dose X-ray imaging. The developed devices exhibit stable operation, uniform photoresponse, and spatial resolution approaching pixel pitch limit. Highly crystalline film CsPbBr 3 detectors demonstrate spatial resolution up to 20 lp mm -1 , keeping high X-ray absorption and efficient charge collection together with scalable fabrication potential, while bulk single-crystalline integrated absorbers provide further improvements in charge collection and uniform low-dose response. Thick 3-4 mm single crystal sensors achieve modulation transfer function values of 35% at the Nyquist frequency under X-ray doses as low as 4 µGy air with a detective quantum efficiency of 48%. In addition, we demonstrate high-contrast radiographic imaging of packaged integrated circuit and computed tomography of small multi-material objects, highlighting the potential of perovskite detectors for next-generation high-resolution imaging systems.
