sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 91Poster Number:NSS-01-091] Radiation qualification of the interface Daughterboard for the ATLAS Tile Calorimeter Upgrade (#1565)
sub_talks.speaker: E. Valdes Santurio
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Stockholm University, Physics Department, Stockholm, Sweden [2] CERN, ATLAS Collaboration, Meyrin, Genève, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The upgrade of the ATLAS Tile Calorimeter readout system for the High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider requires radiation tolerant high throughput electronics capable of reliable long term operation under extreme radiation conditions. This work presents radiation qualification results of the Daughterboard, which interfaces on-detector electronics with off-detector trigger and data acquisition systems. Single point failures are minimized by means of two fully redundant halves, each integrating a CERN radiation tolerant GBTx ASIC for clock and configuration distribution, together with a Kintex Ultrascale FPGA for front-end control and data transmission via SFP+ modules. Radiation qualification targets require tolerance up to 32.71 Gy total ionizing dose, 4.38 × 10E12 n/cm2 non-ionizing energy loss, and 2.37 × 10E11 hadron/cm2 single event effects, including safety factors. Samples of Commercial off the shelf components were tested to evaluate batch variability. Results show all production components meet or exceed requirements. The MOSFETs exhibit degradation via a 15 mV threshold shift after 50 Gy, which does not affect the board functionality. Optical link single event upset error rates to about 9 errors/min over 3584 SFP+ modules, easily manageable by using forward error correction. While 0.65 functional errors/day are recoverable through targeted SFP+ module power cycle. Around 9.37 soft errors/min are expected over 1792 Kintex FPGAs, from which less than 0.20% (1.12 errors/hour) will require targeted FPGA reconfiguration. Radiation effects are mitigated using redundancy strategies and FPGA based soft error mitigation, reducing system impact to negligible levels. The results show that a hybrid architecture combining radiation tolerant ASICs with qualified commercial components enables a robust high bandwidth readout system for sustained operation withing the radiation conditions specified.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 93Poster Number:NSS-01-093] Design of the new Matterhorn detector for the 4 th generation synchrotrons (#1694)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Mezza (Autores: D. Mezza , M. Anastasi , A. Bergamaschi , M. Brueckner , R. Dinapoli , M. Carulla , S. Ebner , S. Emiliani , K. Ferjaoui , V. Gautam , D. Greiffenberg , E. Froejdh , S. Hasanaj , V. Hinger , M. Huerst , V. Kedych , T. King , S. Li , C. Lopez-Cuenca , L. Lunin , A. Mazzoleni , S. Moses , K. Moustakas , A. Mozzanica , J. Mulvey , M. Mueller , C. Ruder , B. Schmitt , S. Silletta , D. Thattil , X. Xie , J. Zhang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI), SLS Detector Group, Villigen, Aargau, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The new fourth-generation storage rings (diffraction-limited storage rings), such as those at MAX IV Laboratory, ESRF EBS, and Swiss Light Source 2.0, will provide significantly higher brilliance than third-generation sources, resulting in a much larger photon flux at the pixel level. This increased flux will exceed the count-rate capabilities of many single-photon counting detectors currently in use, making them unsuitable for future experiments at these facilities. Matterhorn is a 2-D hybrid pixel detector developed by the PSD detector group at the Paul Scherrer Institute for operation at SLS 2.0. Its main objective is to extend the count rate capability to a target of 20 Mcounts/pixel/s using multi-threshold circuitry implemented in each pixel. The Matterhorn ASIC features a 256 × 256 pixel matrix with 75 μm pitch and is implemented in UMC 110 nm technology. Each pixel includes a charge-sensitive amplifier and a shaper connected to four comparators with independently adjustable thresholds. Setting thresholds above the photon energy enables an extension of the effective count-rate capability. Each comparator is connected to an independently gateable 16-bit counter. The target frame rate for reading out one 16-bit counter per pixel is 10 kHz. To support this rate, the ASIC periphery includes four serial links operating in double data rate mode at up to 3.125 GHz, driven by a 1.5625 GHz clock generated by an on-chip PLL. A fully synthesized digital periphery provides flexible ASIC configuration. Since January 2026, the final ASIC, which is fully functional, has been under test to evaluate its performance. This contribution focuses primarily on the ASIC design and detector architecture, and reports the main performance parameters measured so far, while a detailed discussion of the full characterization results will be presented in a separate contribution.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 95Poster Number:NSS-01-095] A Low-Latency 28-nm CMOS ASIC for Superconducting Quantum Readout (#1815)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Zhang (Autores: Y. Zhang , C. Guo , X. Wang , W. Peng , F. Liang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Science and Technology of China, school of physical science, hefei, China [2] University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei National Laboratory,, hefei, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract As the scale of the superconducting quantum control system continues to expand, traditional field-programmable gate array architectures face bottlenecks such as high energy consumption, low scalability, and severe signal attenuation. This paper proposes a highly integrated, low-latency digital front-end architecture fabricated in a 28-nm CMOS process to meet dynamic feedback requirements and optimize power, performance,and area. The front-end includes an arbitrary waveform generator and a data acquisition module, independently managed by a microcontroller. At the transmitter, a digital-to-analog converter is used to output analog signals, with a measured spurious free dynamic range of 52 dB. At the receiver, a low-latency analog-to-digital converter captures analog signals, which the data acquisition module demodulates and ultimately uploads via a low-voltage differential signaling interface. The total hardware latency is restricted to approximately 100 ns. Under full-load testing conditions-including continuous waveform generation,concurrent demodulation of 16 qubits, and state feedback-the total digital power consumption is limited to 539 mW(33.7 mW/qubit). This design achieves extremely low latency and excellent energy efficiency, satisfying the real-time control demands of scalable fault-tolerant quantum computers.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 97Poster Number:NSS-01-097] Radiation Effects on COTS On-Board Computer and Boot/Data-Storage Media Configurations for Super-Low-Earth-Orbit Optical Satellites (#1893)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Sohn (Autores: J. Sohn , H. Lee , H. Yoon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute, Division of Space Exploration, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [2] University of Science and Technology, Department of Astronomy and Space Science, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [3] Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Department of Aerospace Engineering, Daejeon, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Super-low-Earth-orbit (SLEO) optical satellites require compact on-board computing and data-storage electronics, but commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) on-board computers (OBCs) and boot/data-storage media must retain boot, communication, and read/write functions under the mission radiation environment. This paper reports a configuration-level radiation screening of COTS OBC candidates for a 300 km-class, 2-year SLEO optical satellite. A SPENVIS/SHIELDOSE-2 dose assessment gave a total ionizing dose of 14.345 krad(Si) for the design case; therefore, a conservative 30 krad(Si) TID screening target was selected by applying a margin factor of approximately 2. The screening campaign included Arduino and Raspberry Pi family boards, and the detailed design interpretation focused on Raspberry Pi Compute Module 4 (CM4) with input/output board and nonvolatile boot/data-storage media, including Secure Digital (SD) cards, embedded MultiMediaCard (eMMC), solid-state drives (SSDs), and hard disk drives (HDDs). Devices were irradiated with cobalt-60 gamma rays, 10 MeV electrons, and 100 MeV protons, and were evaluated by boot status, communication, supply-current and voltage behavior, read/write operation, and recovery after irradiation. The results indicate that CM4-based configurations were more suitable than the other screened modules for the SLEO OBC candidate. Among storage options, eMMC showed the most favorable radiation and operational suitability, SSDs were identified as a practical secondary storage option after configuration-level verification, and HDDs were not recommended for spacecraft on-board use although some configurations survived to approximately 30 krad(Si), because rotating mechanical parts can affect spacecraft operation. These results support qualifying the exact OBC and boot/data-storage configuration, rather than only the processor board, for COTS-based SLEO on-board computing and storage electronics.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 99Poster Number:NSS-01-099] A Versatile High Linearity Front-End Preamplifier with Wide Dynamic Range for Multiple SiPM Sensors (#1920)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. García-Barrena (Autores: J. García-Barrena , V. Herrero , C. Mourani , R. Esteve , J. F. Toledo , F. J. Mora , F. Ballester , V. Álvarez , J. J. Gómez-Cadenas)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universitat Politècnica de València (UPV), Instituto de Instrumentación de Imagen Molecular (I3M), Valencia, Spain [2] Donosti International Physics Center (DIPC), San Sebastián, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The integration of Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) into high-resolution radiation detection systems has become increasingly relevant in the search for novel methodologies in precision energy measurement. This fact implies the need of front-end electronics capable of properly working with these sensors, whose parasitics change among different parts. In the signal processing chain, the initial stage must offer maximal linearity to preserve signal integrity throughout the subsequent architectures. A low-noise goal is also important in order to optimize energy resolution since first stage is critical in noise budget. Consequently, a specialized preamplifier design is presented in this paper in order to address these requirements. The primary design challenge involves achieving a very good linearity through high internal loop gain without compromising system stability. To ensure a controlled frequency response, the circuit employs a Miller compensation scheme whose dominant pole is inside the circuit. Constructing a robust stability topology, the architecture can handle diverse parasitic components in its input due to the use of different SiPM devices. In a first amplification stage, a key innovative structure has been developed as a translinear wideband inner gain stage. Furthermore, to ensure an extended dynamic range which allows working in both photon counting and high amplitude signal conditions without design reconfiguration, a digitally controlled attenuator system is integrated at the output of the first stage. The attenuator uses a R-2R ladder architecture implemented with MOSFET technology, allowing for direct gain adjustments and accurate calibration through external control logic.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 101Poster Number:NSS-01-101] SPAGHETTI : An original instrument for the continuous gamma-ray based monitoring of hydrothermal volcanoes (#2092)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Chanal (Autores: H. Chanal , C. Achard , J. Bonnard , V. Breton , E. Busato , C. Insa , J. Lao , G. Magaud , H. Croizet , M. Magne , V. Niess , D. Picard , V. Rabant , L. Terray)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Hydrothermal volcanic systems are associated with major hazards such as magmatic/phreatic eruptions and toxic gaz emissions. Monitoring fluid circulation within these systems is a key scientific challenge. The SPAGHETTI project (Spectral Panoptic Analyzers of Gamma rays in Hydrothermal Environments for Transport Time Inference) aims to develop an original instrument dedicated to the continuous and high-frequency monitoring of radon using gamma-ray spectroscopy. The instrument relies on NaI scintillation detectors coupled to a specific signal processing electronics. The whole system is designed to withstand high temperatures, extreme humidity, and acidic corrosion. This contribution focuses on the FPGA-based digital signal processing chain implemented on a low-cost ADC-SoC platform. Real-time triggering, digital filtering, and amplitude extraction are performed directly in programmable logic. First tests aiming to demonstrate the capability of the system to continuously acquire and process scintillation signals in conditions representative of volcanic hydrothermal environments will be presented.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 103Poster Number:NSS-01-103] Evaluating AMD's Versal Architecture for Tapped Delay Line Time-to-Digital Converters. (#2179)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Rossignol (Autores: J. Rossignol , S.I. Kwon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California, Davis, Biomedical engineering, Davis, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Performances of tapped delay line (TDL) time-to-digital converters (TDCs) in FPGAs are strongly linked to the FPGA fabrication process, with newer fabrication processes usually yielding smaller propagation delays, thus improving the resolution and precision of the fine measurement. This study evaluates TDLs designed inside the Versal architecture, AMD's newest architecture that uses a 7 nm fabrication process. Since the Versal architecture's new configurable logic blocks (CLB) allow for multiple propagation paths through them, three different implementations of a TDL were evaluated. Code density and single-shot precision measurements were performed on five pairs of channels for each implementation. The lowest quantization error, 4.47 ps, was obtained using a mix of the outputs of the carry propagation circuit and the look-up tables (LUTs) of the CLB, while the best single-shot precision, 7.51 ps, was obtained by using only the output of the LUTs. Because of the change in the CLB design, TDL TDCs perform significantly worse than in AMD's previous architecture.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 105Poster Number:NSS-01-105] Probing Sub-20 ps Intrinsic Timing Limits of MVT-SiPM Readout for TOF-PET (#2205)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Lao (Autores: H. Lao , Q. Xie , G. Su , Z. Wang , J. Chen , J. Wang , H. Xu , J. Yu , L. Li)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Science and Technology of China, Department of Electronic Engineering and Information Science, hefei, China [2] Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Biomedical Engineering Department, Wuhan, China [3] University of Science and Technology of China, School of Gifted Young, hefei, China [4] University of Science and Technology of China, School of Microelectronics, hefei, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Multi-Voltage Threshold (MVT) method is widely employed in particle detection. However, limited by discrete hardware architectures, existing FPGA-based digitization systems struggle to fully exploit the fundamental timing potential of photodetectors. To investigate these performance limits, we systematically evaluate the ultimate timing performance of a detection chain comprising a CMOS SiPM and an in-house-developed MVT ASIC. This ASIC features picosecond time quantization and a wide dynamic range. Experimental results show that, under excitation from a synchronized picosecond laser source, the MVT ASIC achieves an intrinsic electronic time resolution of 16.94 ps (FWHM) and a coincidence time resolution (CTR) of 16.58 ps (FWHM). Benchmarking against a high-performance digital oscilloscope demonstrates that the timing precision of the MVT ASIC closely approaches that of laboratory-grade instrumentation (11.74 ps). This work validates the potential of the MVT ASIC for time-of-flight (TOF) measurement systems and establishes a promising technical foundation for ultra-high-resolution TOF detection.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 107Poster Number:NSS-01-107] Graphene-Based Front-End Amplifier for Nuclear Instrumentation (#2349)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Turqueti (Autores: M. Turqueti , A. Lindman , O. Aggarwal , A. Poon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Engineering Division, Berkeley, California, United States of America [2] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Nuclear Science Division, Berkeley, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Front-end electronics for nuclear instrumentation require ultra-low noise, high bandwidth, radiation tolerance, and low power consumption to accurately process weak signals generated by radiation detectors. Conventional silicon-based amplifiers face increasing limitations in applications demanding extreme sensitivity, cryogenic operation, and compact integration. This work investigates the use of graphene-based electronic devices as a novel platform for next-generation front-end amplifiers for nuclear science applications. Owing to its exceptional carrier mobility, high thermal conductivity, mechanical flexibility, and potential for low-noise operation, graphene presents a promising alternative material for advanced detector readout electronics. We present the conceptual design and preliminary evaluation of a graphene-based front-end amplifier architecture intended for integration with nuclear radiation detectors including silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), cadmium zinc telluride (CZT) detectors, and other low-signal sensing systems. The proposed approach focuses on achieving improved signal amplification while minimizing electronic noise and power dissipation. Device-level considerations including transconductance behavior, impedance matching, frequency response, and low-temperature performance are analyzed to assess suitability for nuclear instrumentation environments. Theoretical analyses indicate that graphene-enabled amplifier structures can provide enhanced sensitivity and bandwidth compared to conventional semiconductor implementations, particularly in low-temperature and low-signal regimes relevant to modern nuclear physics experiments and radiation detection systems. The results demonstrate the potential of graphene-based front-end electronics as an enabling technology for next-generation nuclear instrumentation, with applications spanning particle physics, medical imaging, homeland security, and advanced scientific sensing platforms.

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A demonstrator chip integrating a matrix of 32 x 8 readout channels for hybrid pixel detectors has been designed and tested in the framework of the PiHEX project, funded by the Italian Ministry of University and Research. The front-end channels include a low-noise charge sensitive amplifier with detector leakage compensation, an asynchronous, differential comparator, and a 5-bit threshold tuning DAC. A Time-over-Threshold counter is integrated for signal digitization. The front-end channels have been developed in a 28 nm CMOS technology and feature an overall area of 25 um x 100 um with a current consumption close to 4.2 uA. Full details on the design and characterization of the prototype chip will be reported in the conference paper.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 111Poster Number:NSS-01-111] A 5.12-GS/s Time-Interleaved VCO-Based ADC With Digital Calibration for High-Speed Detector Waveform Digitization (#2436)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Chen (Autores: C. Chen , Y. Hu , S. Chen , X. Hu , J. Wang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a 5.12-GS/s time-interleaved voltage-controlled-oscillator-based analog-to-digital converter (VCO-based ADC) for high-speed detector waveform digitization in nuclear science and high-energy physics experiments. The proposed ADC employs an 8-channel time-interleaved architecture, where each sub-channel operates at 640 MS/s, resulting in an aggregate sampling rate of 5.12 GS/s. VCO-based quantization is adopted to exploit time-domain signal processing and inherent first-order noise shaping. Each sub-channel integrates a high-linearity bootstrapped sampling switch, a 15-stage ring-VCO quantizer, multi-phase sampling flip-flops, and an asynchronous coarse counter to realize hybrid coarse-fine quantization. To address the major performance limitations of VCO-based and time-interleaved ADCs, a digital calibration scheme is introduced to compensate for the VCO voltage-to-frequency nonlinearity and inter-channel timing skew. The ADC is implemented in a 55-nm CMOS process. Post-layout simulation results show that, at an aggregate sampling rate of 5.12 GS/s with a 2.4-GHz input signal, the ADC achieves an SNDR of 37.5 dB and an effective number of bits of 5.94 bits after calibration. The simulated power consumption is 75 mW from a 1.2-V supply, corresponding to a Walden figure-of-merit of 239 fJ/conversion-step. Full-chip performance measurement is currently underway, and the measured results will be reported at the conference. These results demonstrate the potential of the proposed digitally calibrated TI VCO-based ADC for compact, high-speed detector readout systems.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 113Poster Number:NSS-01-113] Development of an FPGA-based Hardware Data Injector for High-Energy Experiments (#2845)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. M. Boonen (Autores: M. M. Boonen , D. Cieri , O. Kortner , S. Kortner)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Most high-energy experiments at CERN are upgrading their trigger systems for the upcoming high-luminosity era of the LHC. At the same time, development started on the trigger systems of future collider experiments. To fully validate those new systems and developments, it is necessary to test both the algorithms and the underlying interfaces under consideration in a faithful manner. For the former, simulations are used, and for the latter small-scale hardware test stands are typically used. This project proposes the usage of an FPGA-based hardware data injector, which could replicate at the same time the expected fast trigger data rate and transmission protocols. By storing Monte-Carlo simulated data in a DDR4 memory and subsequently transmitting it continuously to a trigger board under test using Gigabit Transceivers, the emulator can mimic the expected low latency data flow.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 119Poster Number:NSS-01-119] Implementation of FPGA-Based Time-to-Digital Converters with Zero Measurement Dead Time (#1024)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 X. Qi (Autores: X. Qi , Y. Wang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Science and Technology of China, Department of Modern Physics, Hefei, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Field programmable gate array (FPGA)-based time-to-digital converter (TDC) has played a very important role in facilities of high-energy physics and scientific instrumentation. Some applications even require TDCs without measurement dead time. In this paper, normal tapped delay line (TDL) based TDC structure is modified towards the realization of zero dead time without losing any TDC original performance. The major challenge in this situation is that there will be more than one signal transition edge in the latched TDL status, therefore, a robust multi-signal transition edge detection circuit module and calibration module are crucial. On a Xilinx UltraScale FPGA, the latched TDL status is first decomposed into 32 divisions, which execute the transition edge picking up parallel before they are combined together to give out all the edges. Since there is only one calibration table in the system, all the edges have to be calibrated sequentially through a specially designed data queue. For performance evaluation, the TDC prototype is implemented on the FPGA with a system clock frequency of 700 MHz. The TDC resolutions for the rising and falling edges are measured as 2.44 ps and 2.31 ps respectively, meanwhile the root-mean-square (RMS) time-interval measurement precisions are measured in the range of 3.5 to 6.5 ps. Applying two trigger signals with 500 ps separation into the TDC repeatedly, all the edges are captured and correctly measured, which demonstrates the capability of zero measurement dead time of the design.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 121Poster Number:NSS-01-121] A Pre-Study of a General-Purpose Trigger Processing Unit for the CEPC TDAQ System (#1197)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Liu (Autores: D. Liu , J. Zhao , H. Wang , S. Dong , B. Chen , K. Zhu , W. Gong , C. Li , F. Li , X. Cao , Q. Zhao , Z. Liu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institute of High Energy Physics, Beijing, China [2] University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Circular Electron Positron Collider (CEPC) is a large-scale international high-energy physics facility with the Higgs boson as its primary scientific goal. Three operation modes are foreseen: Higgs, Z, and W+W-. The CEPC Trigger and Data Acquisition (TDAQ) system faces a fundamental challenge: extracting rare physics events from an extremely high background rate. For example, in the Higgs mode, simulation results indicate that the target physics event rate is approximately 0.5 kHz, while the bunch crossing rate reaches 1.34 MHz. To cope with this challenge, the required Level-1 (L1) trigger rate for the Higgs mode is about 20 kHz.This extremely low signal-to-background ratio demands a trigger system capable of making efficient and real-time trigger decisions to achieve high-purity event selection while maintaining high efficiency for rare physics signals.To facilitate research and verification of the trigger system design, this talk presents a general-purpose Advanced Telecommunications Computing Architecture (ATCA) processing unit for the CEPC TDAQ system. The unit features an AMD Virtex UltraScale+ field-programmable gate array (FPGA) as its computing core, providing high-density parallel processing. High-speed data transmission is achieved via the FPGA's Gigabit Transceiver (GT) and optical transceivers, offering standardized interfaces for electronic subsystems. The design incorporates 11 Quad Small Form-factor Pluggable (QSFP) modules providing 44 high-speed lanes up to 25 Gbps each, 16 GB of Double Data Rate (DDR) memory for hundreds of milliseconds of buffering, and an Intelligent Platform Management Controller (IPMC) + K26 system-on-module (SOM) for intelligent management. Developed as a flexible testbed, this unit enables the implementation and evaluation of various trigger algorithms and architectures. The test results of related trigger functionalities and performance will be presented in the talk at the conference.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 123Poster Number:NSS-01-123] Design of the Ultra-Low-Power Readout Electronics for the Large Area 3 He Tube Array Detector at China Spallation Neutron Source (#1266)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 W. Yin (Autores: W. Yin , Y. Lai , H. Liu , Q. Xiu , Y. Zhao)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The China Spallation Neutron Source (CSNS) is currently upgrading to CSNS-II, increasing the proton beam power to 500 kW and constructing several new neutron spectrometers. The CSNS-II upgrade poses significant challenges for detector and electronics systems, including higher counting rate, improved position resolution requirement, and vacuum operating environment. The large-area 3 He tube array detector has been adopted as the major neutron detector owing to the high detection efficiency, the excellent neutron/gamma discrimination, and the ability to construct the detector with large area coverage. In this paper, we present an ultra-low-power front-end readout electronics designed for ³He tube detectors in CSNS-II spectrometers. The circuit design, FPGA algorithms, and laboratory test results of the electronics will be discussed. Experimental results demonstrate that the new electronics system can achieve a single-tube counting rate of 100K/s while maintaining a position resolution about 6 mm. Test also confirmed the system's capability to operate under vacuum conditions. These results meet the requirements for neutron signal readout in CSNS-II spectrometers.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 125Poster Number:NSS-01-125] A modular, self-triggered firmware for the FPGA-based readout of electromagnetic calorimeters at the INSIGHT@ELSA experiment (#1294)
sub_talks.speaker: B. Otto
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Bonn University, Helmholtz-Institut für Strahlen- und Kernphysik, Bonn, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a modular, per-channel self-triggered firmware architecture for the FPGA-based readout of electromagnetic calorimeters at the INSIGHT experiment. The firmware integrates a compact deconvolution stage to compensate preamplifier trailing-edge ringing, a configurable, pipelined feature extraction chain (baseline estimation, peak-based trigger with interpolation, pileup detection), and a lightweight network module. The implementation uses a decomposition of the deconvolution kernel to reduce resource usage. Despite the computational demands, the implementation of the deconvolution is resource-efficient and leaves headroom for further extensions. A Python-based simulation framework guided the selection and tuning of algorithms and numerical parameters. Test-beam measurements with a detector module showed an effective ringing suppression without affecting the pulse amplitude and timing; cooling the detector to the nominal operating temperature in upcoming runs is expected to further reduce residual artifacts. The resulting firmware framework provides a base for both electromagnetic calorimeters, the Crystal Barrel and the PANDA forward endcap calorimeter, in the INSIGHT experiment and will reduce maintenance effort.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 127Poster Number:NSS-01-127] A Self-Triggered, Event-Driven Readout ASIC for the eXTP PFA X-ray Polarimeter (#1382)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Wang (Autores: N. Wang , K. Wang , Y. Zhang , K. Wei , Y. Shi , M. Li , T. Luo , Z. Chen , W. Lu , Y. Cui , W. Wei , W. Jiang , X. Liu , H. Li , H. Liu , H. Liao , H. Feng)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institute of High Energy Physics,Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China [2] School of Integrated Circuits, Peking University, Beijing 100871, Peoples R China, Beijing, China [3] School of Software and Microelectronics, Peking University, Beijing 100871, Peoples R China, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Polarimetry Focusing Array (PFA) onboard the planned enhanced X-ray Timing and Polarimetry (eXTP) observatory comprises three identical X-ray imaging telescopes, providing X-ray polarimetry in the 2-8 keV energy range with high spatial, spectral, and temporal resolution. To meet these requirements, each detector unit integrates a radiation sensor with a dedicated Application-Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC) for precise charge extraction and digitization of individual X-ray events. This paper presents a readout ASIC designed for this application. The proposed ASIC features a self-triggering mechanism that enables event-driven readout with dynamically configurable windows. To satisfy stringent performance requirements, a two-stage analog readout architecture is adopted. Although the target system employs a 352 × 304 pixel array, a prototype ASIC with a 70 × 60 pixel matrix and a pitch of 50 μm was fabricated in a 180-nm CMOS process to validate the design. Measurement results demonstrate an Equivalent Noise Charge (ENC) below 40 e⁻ rms. With a 12.5 MHz readout clock, the dead time for a typical event involving approximately 1000 pixels is maintained below 100 μs. These results verify the feasibility of the proposed ASIC architecture for the eXTP PFA instrument.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 129Poster Number:NSS-01-129] Pulse shape discrimination by digital pulse processing (#1608)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Liang (Autores: F. Liang , N. Floyd , H. Jayatissa , P. Adsley , A. Alvarez , R. Bartsch , S. Fritz , T. Hankins , B. Harvey , K. Pham , E. Schnorrenberg , D. Shelden , S. Yennello)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Los Alamos National Laboratory, ISR Division, Los Alamos, New Mexico, United States of America [2] Texas A&M University, Cyclotron Institute, College Station, Texas, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Cerium doped gadolinium aluminium gallium garnet (GAGG:Ce) is capable of detecting both photons and charged particles. Particle identification capabilities present GAGG:Ce as a useful detector in nuclear physics research, and in medical, industry, security and space applications. This work explores the feasibility of using trapezoidal filtering for pulse shape discrimination (PSD) to perform particle identification so that the pulse height analysis (PHA) mode in commercially available waveform digitizers can be used without developing custom PSD firmware. Waveforms recorded from proton and alpha scattering measurements were analyzed offline to optimize the trapezoidal filter parameters. Satisfactory pulse shape discrimination was achieved with a figure of merit of 0.68. Future work will incorporate the optimized parameters in the waveform digitizers for heavy-ion reaction experiments to improve particle identification in real time.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 131Poster Number:NSS-01-131] Intrinsic time jitter of alternate data acquisition systems for the HISTARS project (#1947)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 V. M. Nouvilas (Autores: V. M. Nouvilas , S. Gaitán , L.M. Fraile , M. Caballero , N. Bernier , A. Illana , J.A. Briz , J.M. Udías)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Grupo de Física Nuclear, Madrid, Spain [2] CERN, ISOLDE, Meyrin, Genève, Switzerland [3] CSIC, Instituto de Estructura de la Materia, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The HIE-ISOLDE Timing Array for Reaction Studies (HISTARS) is being developed for the measurement of lifetimes of excited nuclear states produced in reactions at HIE-ISOLDE (CERN). It is based on fast particle and gamma scintillator detectors that will require a fast data acquisition system capable of handling more than 60 channels with good time and energy resolution. Digitizing the fast scintillator signals will allow for a flexible signal processing, while preserving the pulse time structure, and potentially enabling high-precision timing. In this work we measure the intrinsic time resolution of several digitizer systems for data acquisition and processing of data stemming from fast scintillators, such as LaBr$_3$(Ce). A very promising high-performance candidate is the CAEN 2751 digitizer, providing 14-bit, 1 GS/s, 16 channels, and embedded FPGA processing for advanced waveform acquisition and digital pulse processing. The DRS4 Evaluation Board uses the DRS4 switched-capacitor array chip developed at Paul Scherrer Institute with 4 input channels, sampling rates of 0.7 to 5 GS/s with 1024 sampling cells at 14-bit resolution. The CAEN DT5742B is a 16-channel switched-capacitor digitizer based on the same DRS4 chip, providing 14-bit resolution and up to 5 GS/s sampling rate. The CAEN DT5751 is a desktop digitizer 4 channels, 10-bit resolution, and sampling rate of 1 GS/s per channel. An in-house custom microcontroller-based data acquisition system, capable of analog pulse integration and timestamp assignment based on a bespoke time to amplitude converter (TAC), is also included in the DAQ systems comparison. These results will guide the choice of the data acquisition system for the HISTARS project and determine its baseline contribution to the timing capabilities of the array.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 133Poster Number:NSS-01-133] Feasibility Study of Analog Pulse Processing ASIC for SDD Array in High Count Rate XRF (#2211)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Okubo (Autores: Y. Okubo , D. Matsunaga , C. Fiorini , G. Borghi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] HORIBA, Ltd., Advanced R&D Center, Kyoto, Japan [2] Politecnico di Milano, Dipartimento di Elettronica, Informazione e Bioingegneria, Milan, Italy [3] INFN, Sezione di Milano, Milan, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Silicon Drift Detectors (SDDs) are the most widely used sensors for energy dispersive X-ray detection in the energy range from a few hundred eV to some tens of keV. When connected to a state-of-the-art CMOS preamplifier, they provide high energy resolution at short peaking times, allowing for high count rates. In high-count-rate X-ray fluorescence (XRF) measurements, SDD arrays are also considered; however, using conventional Digital Pulse Processors (DPPs) requires a large number of ADCs and FPGAs, leading to an increase in overall system size. To keep the total system compact, this study proposes an approach using the analog pulse processing ASIC "SCARLET" and investigates its feasibility. Using an actual XRF setup, a single SDD signal was input into the ASIC as an initial evaluation of its fundamental throughput performance and energy spectrum at an input count rate of up to 1.8 Mcps. The results show that with a 400 ns shaping pulse width, the ASIC could potentially achieve faster throughput compared to a conventional DPP with an equivalent filter length. However, with a 200 ns pulse width, the throughput decreased, and incorrect energy measurements were observed, such as the appearance of an unexpected peak on the lower energy side. This indicates that there are remaining issues in the peak detection logic within the ASIC. This study provides fundamental insights into the effectiveness of the analog ASIC for high-count-rate XRF measurements and highlights areas for future improvement.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 135Poster Number:NSS-01-135] High-performance upgrade for Track Lab: processing Timepix4 hits efficiently at scale (#2433)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. Mánek (Autores: P. Mánek , B. Bergmann , P. Burian , T. Čelko , R. E. Mihai , P. Smolyanskiy)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Czech Technical University in Prague, Institute of Experimental and Applied Physics, Prague, Czech Republic [2] University of West Bohemia in Pilsen, Faculty of Electrical Engineering, Pilsen, Czech Republic [3] Charles University, Department of Computer Science Education, Prague, Czech Republic [4] Horia Hulubei National Institute for R&D in Physics and Nuclear Engineering, Department of Nuclear Physics, Bucharest-Magurele, Romania
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Timepix4 represents a significant advancement in the Timepix family of hybrid active pixel detectors, particularly attractive due to its fine time resolution (195 ps) and high supported hit rates (up to 5 GHz/mm2). To address performance challenges presented by these new features, an upgrade has been implemented for the Track Lab software package, which has become a standard tool for data collection and analysis of many Timepix-based systems. Above all, the presented upgrade adds support for a 40 Gb/s PCI-express readout interface, capable of reaching hit rates of 300-400 MHz. To facilitate efficient analysis of such data volumes, the presented work implements a number of optimizations, including memory-level bit packing, deduplication and GPU offload for hit clustering, a required step for most event-based analysis algorithms. This work will present details of these improvements, characterize Track Lab's response under heavy load and present results of a performance benchmark. The upgraded software is expected to find plentiful applications in high-intensity X-ray imaging, γ-imaging and the forthcoming high-luminosity campaign at the Large Hadron Collider.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 137Poster Number:NSS-01-137] A Scalable High-Throughput DAQ Architecture for Real-Time Proton Beam Monitoring Applications (#2452)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Deniz (Autores: B. Yerli , U. Demir , H. O. Caliskan , B. Deniz , F. Caliskan , M. Ayyildiz , K. Nurdan , B. Akgun)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] TÜBİTAK, Informatics and Information Security Research Center (BİLGEM), Kocaeli, Turkey [2] Bogazici University, Department of Physics, İstanbul, Turkey [3] Bogazici University, Center for Targeted Therapy Technologies, İstanbul, Turkey
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a scalable and high-throughput data acquisition (DAQ) architecture developed for real-time proton beam monitoring applications in advanced proton therapy systems. The proposed system is designed to support detector-based tracking of proton energy deposition, enabling continuous monitoring of beam delivery and allowing treatment parameters to be adjusted dynamically during operation. By providing precise localization of proton energy release within the target region, the system contributes to improved dose accuracy while minimizing radiation exposure to surrounding healthy tissue. The DAQ architecture integrates high-speed digitization, synchronized timing distribution, and efficient event aggregation within a modular rack-based platform optimized for detector readout applications. The system consists of eight digitizer boards supporting 64 analog input channels corresponding to 32 detector elements. Differential signal readout is employed to improve signal integrity and reduce noise susceptibility during acquisition. A dedicated Data Collection Board equipped with 40 Gbps QSFP+ communication links aggregates and transfers acquired event data to a host DAQ server with high bandwidth and low latency. System-wide synchronization is maintained through a centralized Clock Distribution Board, while an OpenVPX-compliant Power Supply Board ensures reliable operation of all modules. The proposed architecture provides a compact, scalable, and synchronized solution for real-time proton therapy monitoring and high-performance medical imaging applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 139Poster Number:NSS-01-139] A Modular High-Bandwidth DAQ System for the Medipix4 ASIC Based on FPGA Ethernet Readout (#2665)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N.V. Biesuz (Autores: N.V. Biesuz , R. Ballabriga , J. A. Alozy , R. Bolzonella , M. Campbell , M. Fiorini , X. Llopart)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare (INFN), Ferrara Division, Ferrara, Italy [2] CERN, EP Department, Geneva, Switzerland [3] Università di Ferrara, Ferrara, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Medipix4 ASIC is a hybrid pixel detector developed for high-rate spectroscopic X-ray imaging and photon-counting applications. Its synchronous frame-based architecture supports multiple acquisition modes and up to sixteen DDR output links, requiring scalable off-detector electronics. This work presents a modular FPGA-based Data Acquisition (DAQ) system developed for Medipix4 characterization and detector integration. The system is composed of a Xilinx Kintex UltraScale FPGA DAQ board and a dedicated CERN-developed Medipix4 chipboard directly interfaced through FMC connectivity. The firmware reuses the IPbus-based control path developed for the Timepix4 ASIC while implementing a dedicated Medipix4 synchronous acquisition pipeline. Sixteen independent DDR interfaces operate at selectable clock frequencies of 20, 40, 80, 160 and 320 MHz. Each detector link is connected to a deserializer implementing frame detection, header decoding and 64-bit payload reconstruction. The decoded headers allow the firmware to determine the active acquisition configuration, including counter depth, active links and payload size. The sixteen parallel data streams are packetized and transmitted through two independent 10~Gigabit Ethernet UDP links. The aggregate detector bandwidth of 10.24 Gb/s is compatible with the measured sustained transmission throughput of 2 X 8.85 Gb/s. The firmware uses reusable open-source HDL components where possible and is distributed within the Medipix collaboration as Open Hardware under the CERN Open Hardware Licence. Ongoing developments include migration toward lower-cost FPGA platforms and support for simultaneous acquisition from multiple Medipix4 ASICs.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 141Poster Number:NSS-01-141] Measurement of Energy-Dependent Neutron-Induced Single-Event-Upset Rates for Multiple FPGA Types (#2544)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Ueda (Autores: S. Ueda , H. Bae , E. Hamada , Y. Igarashi , Y. Nakazawa , S.-I. Meigo , H. Miyai , K. Oishi , K. Ueno , C. Yamada)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The University of Osaka, Toyonaka, Japan [2] Tohoku University, Sendai, Japan [3] High Energy Accelerator Research Organization, Tukuba, Japan [4] Japan Atomic Energy Agency, Naka, Japan [5] J-PARC Center, Naka, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We measured energy-dependent single-event-upset (SEU) rates for three field-programmable gate array (FPGA) types under neutron irradiation at the BL10 beamline of the Materials and Life Science Experimental Facility (MLF) at the Japan Proton Accelerator Research Complex (J-PARC). Two 28-nm complementary metal oxide semiconductor (CMOS) devices and one 65-nm CMOS device was irradiated with neutrons over a wide energy range from meV to MeV. Dedicated firmware detected SEUs with high timing precision, and the time-of-flight (TOF) method identified the neutron energies that caused the SEUs. We estimated the neutron fluence from a PHITS simulation of the beam spectrum and normalized the SEU counts to the fluence for each FPGA type. The SEU rates clearly depended on neutron energy. One 28-nm device had an SEU rate in the 10 -8 -10 -7 MeV region about one order of magnitude higher than that at 1 MeV, whereas the other devices showed no significant low-energy enhancement. Below 0.1 MeV, the SEU rate increased as neutron energy decreased, approximately following the 1/ v dependence, where v is the neutron velocity. The two 28-nm devices responded differently despite using the same process technology. In contrast, the 65-nm device had a low-to-high-energy change similar to that of one 28-nm device. These results suggest that device structure or neutron-sensitive materials, rather than process technology alone, contribute to neutron-induced SEUs.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 143Poster Number:NSS-01-143] Wireless Dosimetry System for Interventional Radiology (#2676)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Moniz (Autores: M. Moniz , P. M.M. Correia , A. L.M. Silva , J. F.C.A. Veloso , C. D.R. Azevedo)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Aveiro, i3N - Physics Department, Aveiro, Portugal
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents the design and characterisation of the front-end eletronics of a wireless active personal dosimeter for interventional radiology. The device is a low-cost, single-channel sensing unit that can be replicated across the thorax, neck, hands, and eyes, providing operators with continuous dose-rate feedback at these four anatomical regions. Each dosimeter consists of a tissue-equivalent plastic scintillator coupled to a silicon photomultiplier, read out by a charge-sensitive amplifier, a semi-Gaussian shaper with pole-zero cancellation, and a peak-and-hold circuit triggered by a comparator. Power management and wireless transmission are handled by a battery-operated microcontroller, keeping the assembly compact and unobtrusive to the operator. Dose-rate data are transmitted to a remote display with visual and sound alarms. The front-end has been characterised under dark-count conditions, with a dead time of 11.6 microseconds expected to extend to approximately 20 microseconds once analog-to-digital conversion is included in the readout loop. Energy and dose calibration of the coupled detector, together with the four-channel graphical interface, are the next development steps.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 145Poster Number:NSS-01-145] FPGA firmware for ³He resistive wire tube readout with CAEN R5560 ADC. (#2794)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Raspino (Autores: D. Raspino , A. Abba , E. Schooneveld , S. Carsi , J. Sykora)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] UKRI- STFC, ISIS, Chilton Didcot, United Kingdom [2] Nuclear Instrument, Comom, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents the development of a versatile FPGA firmware for the readout of ³He resistive wire tubes widely used in neutron scattering instruments. These detectors are deployed in large numbers across major neutron facilities, including ISIS, ILL, SNS, FRM2, ESS, MLF, and CNCS. In typical configurations, detector signals are first conditioned by front-end preamplifiers located near the tubes, then digitized by ADC systems positioned up to 40 m away. The FPGA-based processing extracts pulse amplitudes to determine the neutron interaction position along the detector. The implemented system is based on the R5560 ADC, operating at a sampling rate of 125 MHz. The firmware, developed using SCI-Compiler, is organized into two main blocks: signal processing and data transmission. The signal processing stage includes baseline correction and gain scaling to maximize ADC dynamic range, followed by configurable filtering. The latter consists of cascaded moving-average integrators and a differentiator, with user-defined parameters (number and length of filters) adjustable via control registers to accommodate different instrument requirements. To ensure compatibility with both legacy and next-generation data acquisition systems, the firmware supports multiple communication interfaces. At ISIS, the ADC serial interface is currently used for integration with the existing Data Acquisition Electronics (DAE), as demonstrated on the OSIRIS instrument. In parallel, a high-throughput UDP-based optical fibre link has been developed for future deployment, including WISH and μRWELL-based detector systems. Additionally, a TCP/IP Ethernet interface provides a flexible solution for diagnostics and lower-rate data acquisition. This architecture enables a scalable and adaptable readout solution for current and future neutron detector systems.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 147Poster Number:NSS-01-147] LDMX Silicon Tracker Data Acquisition System (#2807)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Reese (Autores: B. Reese , T. K. Nelson , M. Gignac , C. Bakalis)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, Menlo Park, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Light Dark Matter eXperiment (LDMX) is a proposed fixed-target experiment that will search for sub-GeV dark matter using a missing-momentum signature in high-rate electron interactions. Its Silicon Tagging Tracker (STT) and Silicon Recoil Tracker (SRT) measure incoming and outgoing charged particles around the target, providing trajectory and momentum information needed to identify events with invisible final-state particles and reject backgrounds. The Tracker data acquisition (DAQ) system is built around APV25-based silicon strip modules, front-end boards (FEBs), and a Bittware PCI Express back end integrated with the common LDMX timing, fast-control, and event-building infrastructure. Each FEB distributes APV25 clock, trigger, reset, I2C control, low-voltage power, and sensor bias. It also digitizes APV25 analog streams, formats three-sample channel records, and transmits Tracker event records to the back end. The architecture is constrained by the APV25 pipeline latency and must preserve bunch timing while scaling to the final multi-FEB Tracker. During the 2025 LDMX test at SLAC End Station A, a Tracker DAQ vertical slice operated one FEB with four silicon Hybrid modules and the Bittware back end. The system acquired coherent data with other LDMX subsystems, demonstrated stable noise performance, was timed in to beam, and observed beam-induced hits with the expected timing behavior.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 149Poster Number:NSS-01-149] Latest Upgrades and Operation of the Neutron Veto Data Acquisition System for the XENONnT Experiment (#2929)
sub_talks.speaker: S. Mastroianni
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] INFN, Sec. Naples, Naples, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Neutron Veto (NV) of the XENONnT experiment is a gadolinium-doped water Cherenkov detector surrounding the central xenon time projection chamber (TPC). It is instrumented with 120 photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) to reduce the nuclear recoil background induced by radiogenic neutrons originating from detector materials, which can mimic WIMP-like signatures. During the third science run (SR2), conducted between October 2023 and March 2025, XENONnT achieved a significantly reduced background configuration. In particular, the neutron background was suppressed by loading the water tank with 500 ppm of gadolinium sulfate, resulting in an approximately twofold reduction compared to earlier runs performed with pure water. Following maintenance activities initiated in summer 2025, the detector is currently being recommissioned in preparation for the next science run. This work presents the latest upgrades and the operational performance of the NV data acquisition (DAQ) and online processing systems. The NV DAQ is based on a fully triggerless architecture in which PMT waveforms are continuously digitized, enabling software-based coincidence searches within time windows of several hundred nanoseconds.To enhance long-term reliability and stability, the DAQ system has been upgraded with new-generation CAEN PCIe readout cards. Concurrently, the front-end server has been upgraded to ensure compatibility with latest operating systems, while improving fault tolerance, system monitoring, and integration with the experiment-wide online processing system. A further improvement is the deployment of a dedicated FPGA-based monitoring board for the NV data readout. This board processes digitizer monitoring signals such as buffer occupancy, busy and flow-control flags, timing and synchronization signals, and error conditions during both science data taking and calibration runs, enabling continuous checks of DAQ performance and stability.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 151Poster Number:NSS-01-151] Design and Integration of a Modular LiInP 2 Se 6 Neutron Detector Prototype for Single-Crystal Diffractometry Applications (#3158)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M.E.A. Benkechkache (Autores: M.E.A. Benkechkache , E. Hoegberg , A. Kargar , J. Christian , C. Sosa , H. Hong , M. Kanatzidis , K. Saheb , S. Imam , E. Lukosi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Tennessee, Nuclear Engineering Department, Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America [2] UT Institute for Advanced Materials & Manufacturing, Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America [3] Radiation Monitoring Devices, Inc., Watertown, Massachusetts, United States of America [4] Northwestern University, Department of Chemistry, Evanston, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Lithium Indium Phosphorus Selenide (LiInP 2 Se 6 ) has emerged as a promising semiconductor material for neutron detection due to its high neutron capture cross-section, suitable bandgap, and favorable charge transport properties. This work reports on the development of a modular LiInP 2 Se 6 detector prototype for single-crystal diffractometry (SCD) applications. The prototype consists of an 8 × 2 array of LiInP 2 Se 6 strip sensors with a 300 μm pitch configuration integrated onto a custom sensor baseboard. Initial sensor characterization includes electrical IV measurements and preliminary radiation-response evaluation. The sensors are coupled to a dual-ASICs daughterboard based on VATAGP7 ASICs for signal readout and processing, while detector control and data acquisition are managed through the LISeDAQ acquisition system. This work demonstrates the integration of LiInP 2 Se 6 sensors, front-end electronics, and acquisition hardware into a scalable detector module architecture toward future high-resolution SCD detector systems.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 153Poster Number:NSS-01-153] Improvement of Ambient dose equivalent rate Estimation for Airborne Radiation Monitoring Using Artificial Neural Networks with Vegetation and Topographic Information (#1454)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Miyahara (Autores: A. Miyahara , S. Miyuki , K. Suzuki , Y. Morishita , H. Funaki)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Japan Atomic Energy Agency, 1. Collaborative Laboratories for Advanced Decommissioning Science, Minamisoma, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In airborne radiation monitoring using unmanned aerial vehicles conducted in Japan following the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant accident, a flat-source model is used to estimate the ambient dose equivalent rate at ground level from count rates. However, its assumptions are not suitable for mountainous and forested areas. To improve reliability in these areas, an artificial neural network was constructed that incorporates topographic and vegetation information as input variables in addition to count rate information, and its impact on estimation performance was evaluated. The ambient dose equivalent rate map generated by the artificial neural network model reproduced spatial variation in more detail compared to the map created by the flat-source model. Vegetation information helped distinguish between forests and open land, contributing to improved estimation accuracy and precision. Topographic information reduced errors in mountainous areas where the relative position of the detector and the ground changes drastically. An artificial neural network incorporating this information can contribute to identifying hotspots and determining whether evacuation orders can be lifted for small areas.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 155Poster Number:NSS-01-155] Explainable Radionuclide Identification Using FWHM-Aware Adaptive Banding in Gamma-Ray Spectroscopy (#1543)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Jang (Autores: S. Jang , G. Song , U. Lee , J. Lee , D. Kim , J. Kim , G. Cho)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] KAIST (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology), Department of Nuclear and Quantum Engineering, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [2] Pusan National University, Nuclear Systems Major, School of Mechanical Engineering, Pusan, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Machine learning has shown strong potential for radionuclide identification using gamma-ray spectroscopy. However, its black-box nature limits the physical interpretation of model predictions. In this study, a spectroscopy-tailored explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) framework for a 1D-CNN-based radionuclide identification model was investigated using gamma-ray spectra measured with a NaI(Tl) detector. The model was trained to classify four radionuclides: 22 Na, 60 Co, 137 Cs, and 54 Mn. To identify the spectral regions contributing to the CNN predictions, Grad-CAM, LIME, and Kernel SHAP were applied. In particular, because perturbation-based XAI methods are strongly affected by the definition of input features, two spectral banding strategies were compared: conventional uniform banding and FWHM-aware adaptive banding. The results showed that compared with uniform banding, the proposed adaptive banding provided more localized and physically interpretable attribution results in several cases. These findings suggest that detector-resolution-aware banding can improve the reliability and interpretability of XAI for gamma-ray spectroscopy.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 157Poster Number:NSS-01-157] Source-Transferable Machine Learning-based Pulse Shape Discrimination in 3D-Printed Plastic Scintillators (#1703)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. K. Gourishetty (Autores: V. Anand , K. Shah , A. K. Gourishetty)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee, Roorkee, India
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work demonstrates source-transferable neutron-gamma pulse-shape discrimination in 3D-printed plastic scintillators using compact deep neural networks trained on experimental waveforms. Additively manufactured plastic scintillators are attractive for application-specific neutron detectors because printing can produce nonplanar and architected geometries. However, their pulse shapes can depend on resin chemistry, dopant loading, and curing conditions. Therefore, discrimination algorithms validated on conventional liquid or cast plastic scintillators cannot be assumed to transfer directly to printed scintillators. Pulses were collected from 252 Cf and AmBe sources using CAEN DT5751 and DT5730 digitizers, respectively, and analyzed using charge-comparison pulse-shape discrimination, unsupervised clustering, tree-based classifiers, one-dimensional convolutional neural networks, and fully connected deep neural networks. Charge-comparison methods were limited to 92-93% accuracy for the more overlapping 252 Cf dataset, whereas the optimized network used smoothed, peak-aligned, amplitude-normalized waveforms and achieved 99.55% test accuracy on 252 Cf. Without retraining, the same model achieved 99.91% inference accuracy on the independent AmBe dataset. Peak alignment was found to be essential as AmBe inference accuracy increased from 88.11% for unaligned raw waveforms to 99.91% for aligned waveforms. These results establish peak-aligned waveform learning as an effective route for robust neutron-gamma discrimination in 3D-printed plastic scintillators.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 159Poster Number:NSS-01-159] Spectro-Temporal Gamma-Ray Anomaly Detection with Context-Adaptive Background Modeling (#2215)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Parrilla (Autores: H. Parrilla , M. Bandstra , R. Cooper)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Gamma-ray anomaly detection and identification in complex environments requires background models that are accurate, robust to environmental variation, and interpretable enough to support adaptation given contextual information. We present Gaussian Process Prior NMF (GPP-NMF) spectro-temporal background modeling, combining the physically meaningful structure of Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) in the spectral dimension with a Gaussian process prior (GPP) in the temporal dimension, parameterized by a smoothing hyperparameter λ T . Evaluated on RADAI synthetic mobile search data, GPP-NMF outperforms standard spectral NMF in the low false alarm rate regime of operational interest, with a single fixed calibrated λ T . We validate a principled approach for λ T adaptation to contextual information by showing that the power spectrum of the logarithm of the total building solid angle seen by the detector - extractable from camera data in real time - closely matches the GPP prior power spectrum. Full contextual integration results, including on real-world data, will be presented.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 161Poster Number:NSS-01-161] Optical Readout of Geiger-Müller Survey Instruments on a Coordinated Multicopter Fleet for Distributed Count-Rate Mapping (#2225)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Junnarkar (Autores: S. Junnarkar , A. Junnarkar)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Field Viewers inc, Austin, Texas, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The primary objective is to describe and evaluate a multisensor architecture in which several small unmanned aircraft jointly support geographically registered ambient gamma survey without carrying a separate heavy scintillator and high-resolution pixel imager on every vehicle. The working hypothesis is that conventional handheld Geiger-Müller survey instruments, rigidly mounted with the numeric display visible to an onboard camera, can supply useful count-rate estimates when digits are recovered by image-space region selection, classification or template matching, and short-window temporal filtering that suppresses vibration-induced blur. The research design couples this optical readout path to a single mission manager that maintains a unified operator display, explicit multicopter formations to spread measurement locations along transects or grids, leader-follower roles with reassignment when radio links degrade, and a fixed policy in which facial-identity checks gate escalation to autonomous rerouting or alarm acknowledgement. Methods include hardware-in-the-loop bench comparison against an independent counting reference, latency measurement on embedded accelerators, and qualitative stress tests for glare, backlight change, and partial occlusion from neighboring rotors. Preliminary outcomes indicate stable decode at representative dose rates when temporal aggregation spans one to two seconds, inference on the order of tens of milliseconds per frame region, and graceful degradation when the display is shadowed. The conclusions are that display-mediated readout is a viable interface when spectroscopic identification is not required, and that formation metadata should be fused with decoded rates before mapping. Implications are outdoor line and grid flights with uncertainty accounting, handheld references, and optional spectrometer comparison before field deployment claims.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 163Poster Number:NSS-01-163] Generative Overlay Augmentation for Robust Structural Region Segmentation in Dual-Energy X-Ray Cargo Container Imagery (#2263)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y.-W. Kim (Autores: Y.-W. Kim , K. Kim , T. T.D. Pham)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Infiniq, AI Lab, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Non-intrusive inspection of cargo containers via dual-energy X-ray radiography increasingly faces threats concealed within the container's own structural void spaces, making segmentation of the structural region a necessary prerequisite for downstream anomaly detection. Two compounding factors hinder this task: inconsistent geometric distortion across operational scans, and path-integral structure-cargo overlay that prevents pixel-level human annotation in densely loaded regions. We formulate the task as binary segmentation and propose a regionwise generative overlay augmentation pipeline, in which Stable Diffusion is adapted via a three-stage scheme-LoRA, ControlNet, and inpainting-to synthesise structure-cargo overlay imagery. Polygon annotation is partitioned by visual confidence: structural polygons supply segmentation labels and ControlNet conditions, while cargo polygons serve as inpainting masks. The central hypothesis is that a model trained with the proposed structure-cargo overlay augmentation outperforms a baseline trained on real annotations alone, evaluated on two test partitions defined by the visual clarity of structure-cargo separation under overlay: Easy (clearly distinguishable) and Hard (separation challenging but feasible).

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 165Poster Number:NSS-01-165] Development of Realistic Gamma-ray Spectrum Database Using Geant4 and U-Net-based Sim-to-Real Translation (#2356)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Kim (Autores: G. Kim , J. Hwang , D.Y. Oh , C. Kim , J.-Y. Yeom)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea University, Department of Bioengineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] Korea University, Interdisciplinary Program in Precision Public Health, Seoul, Republic of Korea [3] Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [4] Korea University, School of Biomedical Engineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Reliable gamma-ray spectrum databases are needed for data-driven radioisotope identification, but direct measurements of accident-related or short-lived radionuclides are often limited by safety regulations and isotope availability. Geant4 can generate synthetic spectra, but simulated spectra may differ from measured detector-domain spectra because of detector response, energy resolution, gain variation, and channel-domain distortion. In this study, we evaluated a U-Net-based sim-to-real translation framework to transform Geant4-simulated spectra toward measured detector spectra. Measured detector energy-resolution broadening and channel-domain augmentation were applied before translation, and a spatial-transformer-integrated U-Net was used to compensate for gain- and offset-related channel shifts. In validation, the model achieved a mixed-isotope training mean absolute error of 0.045214 and leave-one-out mean absolute error values of 0.068125 for unseen ²²Na and 0.047816 for ¹³⁷Cs. A photopeak-based fidelity analysis showed that 44% of ²²Na samples and 24% of ¹³⁷Cs samples satisfied the defined peak-position and peak-height criterion and a peak-height difference threshold of 0.05. These results indicate that U-Net-based translation can partially reduce the sim-to-real discrepancy in gamma-ray spectroscopy, while consistent reconstruction of detailed photopeak structures remains limited.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 167Poster Number:NSS-01-167] Real-Time Nuclide Identification via Physics-Region Preprocessing (#2437)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Shin (Autores: D. Shin , I. Kwon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute, Department of Advanced I&C Research, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [2] Yonsei University, Department of Radiological Science, Wonju, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work addresses real-time identification of gamma-emitting nuclides released outside a damaged reactor using a network of low-cost Silicon photomultiplier (SiPM)-scintillator gamma detectors. Of all fission products, only a few reach the plant exterior in amounts sufficient to produce measurable photopeaks; using the NUREG-1465 source term for Pressurized Water Reactor (PWR) severe accidents, we reduce the monitored set to the dominant nuclides 85 Kr, 131 I, 132 Te, 137 Cs, 60 Co, and 140 Ba. For this set, we design a 2K+1 physics-region preprocessing front-end that places one region of interest on each target photopeak and Compton edge, producing compact features for small downstream classifiers, including the target on-chip deep-learning core. Because direct validation on a real off-site release is impractical, we evaluate the pipeline on a K=5 surrogate set of 133 Ba, 22 Na, 137 Cs, 54 Mn, and 60 Co spanning the same 80 keV-to-1.3 MeV band on a NaI(Tl)-SiPM detector. On this surrogate, the 2K+1 preprocessing achieves 83.9% accuracy at 25 photopeak counts per window and 97.8% at 100, compared with 75.4% and 94.3% for a raw pulse-vector baseline.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 169Poster Number:NSS-01-169] Development of a vehicle-mounted Directional radiation monitoring system using multiple NaI(Tl) detectors and an ANN algorithm (#2628)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H.K. Baek (Autores: H.K. Baek , J.W. Lee , S.M. Park , M.Y. Park , S.J. Jeong , S.H. Choi , J.S. Heo , Y.H. Chung , S.Y. Kim , J.K. Shin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Neosiskorea Co., Ltd., Daejeon, Republic of Korea [2] Yonsei University, Department of Radiation Convergence Engineering, Wonju, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Vehicle-based radiation monitoring systems are widely used for environmental radiation surveillance, nuclear emergency response, and radioactive contamination mapping. Conventional systems use large-area NaI(Tl) scintillation detectors with high sensitivity for low-count-rate radiation measurements. However, they have limitations such as poor energy resolution and the inability to provide directional information of radiation sources. To overcome these limitations, this study developed a vehicle-based radiation source direction detection system using nine NaI(Tl) detectors while maintaining high sensitivity and energy resolution. The system consists of nine Φ3" × 3" NaI(Tl) detectors. Four upper-layer detectors were arranged for rapid direction identification, one center detector was used for dose assessment, and four lower-layer detectors with lead collimators improved directional accuracy. Radiation source direction was estimated using detector count-rate ratios according to incident direction and distance. An ANN-based algorithm was applied for direction estimation. System performance was evaluated using a 137Cs (100 μCi). Energy resolution and sensitivity were evaluated at 23 cm, while angular resolution tests were conducted at 6 m with source angles varied from 0° to 90° at 10° intervals. The developed system showed approximately 6.8 times higher detection sensitivity than a conventional large-area NaI(Tl) detector system. The angular resolution was evaluated as 45° and 10° for the upper and lower detector layers, respectively, confirming the feasibility of radiation source direction detection in a vehicle-based system. Future work will focus on miniaturization through compact optical sensors, detector rearrangement, and signal-processing optimization.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 171Poster Number:NSS-01-171] Wavelet optimisation for improved photopeak extraction in low-count gamma-ray spectra (#2656)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Biggs (Autores: J. Biggs , C. Shenton-Taylor)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Surrey, School of Maths and Physics, Guildford, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Detector networks are a potential method of surveillance of radiological material moving through urban environments. Such a network would require ways of automatically assessing collected spectra for non-background isotopes, particularly in count-starved spectra collected in environments with complex backgrounds. In 2018, the London-based SIGMA trial gathered 1.5 billion one-second gamma spectra using both stationary and mobile scintillator detectors. This work presents a wavelet analysis method optimised for use with count-starved gamma spectra. A range of 137 Cs spectra were collected, both experimentally and simulated in Geant4, and combined with real-world SIGMA background data. A continuous wavelet transform was conducted on each spectrum, producing an associated scalogram with wavelet transform modulus maxima lines arising from spectral features. By using the 'straightness' of these lines, it was shown to be possible to identify the presence of 137 Cs with 95% accuracy, with a number of false positive identifications. Constraining certain metrics within the method reduced the number of false positives at the expense of overall detection accuracy. UK Ministry of Defence © Crown Owned Copyright 2026/AWE

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 173Poster Number:NSS-01-173] Real-Time Particle Hit Detection Using a 1D Convolutional Neural Network on a CAEN FPGA-Based Digitizer (#2722)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Tintori (Autores: C. Tintori , M. Brini , A. Potenza , F. Giordano , M. Zanetti , A. Triossi , M. Sapkas)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CAEN S.p.A., Viareggio, Italy [2] University of Padova, Physics and Astronomy, Padova, Italy [3] INFN Padova, Padova, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study proposes a 1D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture designed for real-time particle hit detection, moving beyond traditional rigid triggering thresholds. By processing continuous data streams, including high-noise environments, our model demonstrates superior sensitivity in low Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) regimes and pile-up events. We demonstrate that this approach successfully identifies particle signals and provides precise temporal metadata in real time, offering a robust alternative to conventional signal processing methods. Performance was evaluated on a scintillating detector.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 175Poster Number:NSS-01-175] Development of an ANN-based Gamma-ray Spectrum Correction Algorithm for PVT Detectors (#2762)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Ra (Autores: J. Ra , J. Kang , Y.S. Chung , Y.H. Chung)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yonsei University, Department of Radiation Convergence Engineering, Wonju, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Environmental radiation monitoring systems require detectors that can measure radiation in real time and rapidly identify radionuclides. This study developed an artificial intelligence-based spectrum Correction algorithm that converts gamma-ray spectra acquired from polyvinyl toluene (PVT) detectors with limited energy resolution into spectra comparable to those of NaI(Tl) detectors. The proposed model used an artificial neural network (ANN)-based multi-layer perceptron (MLP) regressor with two hidden layers, each containing 64 nodes. Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) and Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) were employed as the activation function and optimizer, respectively. The model was trained using PVT spectra as input and NaI(Tl) spectra as target output data to learn the spectral relationship between the two detector systems. Training datasets were generated using Geant4 Application for Tomographic Emission (GATE) for four radionuclides: Co-57, Ba-133, Cs-137, and Co-60. The simulation results demonstrated that the proposed model successfully generated NaI(Tl) photopeak features from PVT spectra. Representative results for Cs-137 yielded a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.9996 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.0038. Additionally, the energy resolutions at the 662 keV photopeak were found to be 5.94% for the actual NaI(Tl) spectrum and 5.96% for the predicted spectrum, indicating that the two spectra have highly consistent energy resolution characteristics. These results imply that the proposed model can generate spectra with characteristics comparable to those of NaI(Tl) detectors while maintaining the practical benefits of PVT detectors for radiation monitoring applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 177Poster Number:NSS-01-177] measurement-guided x-ray image restoration using fourier stochastic differential equations (#2948)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Oh (Autores: S. Oh , J. Lee , S. Yoo , J. Kim , H.K. Kim)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Pusan National University, school of mechanical engineering, Busan, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Industrial X-ray imaging for nondestructive inspection requires high spatial resolution and high sensitivity, but phosphor-based detectors face a trade-off because increased phosphor thickness improves X-ray absorption while degrading spatial resolution through optical spreading. This study investigates a measurement-guided Fourier stochastic differential equation for detector X-ray image restoration. The proposed method defines a degradation path in the Fourier domain using measured detector characteristics. The relative modulation transfer function (MTF) models deterministic resolution loss, and the measured noise power spectrum guides stochastic perturbation. A neural restoration network is trained to reconstruct high-resolution images from intermediate degraded states conditioned on low-resolution observations. Experiments on printed circuit board X-ray images compared the proposed method with Wiener filtering, a regression baseline, and a conditional diffusion model (CDM). The proposed method improved low-resolution images and achieved image domain restoration quality comparable to the regression baseline and better than Wiener filtering, while CDM showed slightly lower structural fidelity in representative regions. Frequency domain analysis using MTF, contrast transfer function (CTF), and NNPS showed that both CDM and the proposed method closely followed the high-resolution MTF and that the proposed method showed higher CTF recovery in the mid-to-high frequency range. These results indicate that X-ray image restoration methods should be assessed using both image domain metrics and frequency domain characteristics.
