sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 179Poster Number:NSS-01-179] A General-Purpose Radionuclide Identification Model for HPGe Gamma-Ray Spectrometry (#3209)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Zickefoose (Autores: J. Zickefoose , H. Persson , C. Cianci)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Mirion Technologies (Canberra) Inc, Physics, Meriden, Connecticut, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Radionuclide identification in high‑purity germanium (HPGe) gamma‑ray spectra can be a challenging and time‑consuming task, particularly when complex samples contain many radionuclides that produce overlapping spectral features. In addition to sample emissions, HPGe detectors measure contributions from naturally occurring and environmental radionuclides, referred to as background. The measured sample spectrum is therefore the sum of sample and background contributions, and in most applications it is desirable to identify only the radionuclides present in the sample itself. While background subtraction is commonly performed using a separate background measurement, accurate identification near critical detection limits remains difficult, especially for low‑count or cluttered spectra. We present a Siamese Neural Network (SNN)-based approach for radionuclide identification with background subtraction in HPGe gamma‑ray spectra that is generalizable to many detector models and geometries. By directly learning a similarity metric between foreground and background spectra, the method enhances sensitivity to weak spectral features while maintaining low false‑positive rates. The network is trained on a large dataset containing spectra from over 500 radionuclides, generated using Monte Carlo simulations spanning more than 50 detector and geometry combinations and augmented with measured background data. We present the data generation methodology, training procedure, and performance results on both simulated and measured spectra. The results demonstrate that the SNN approach achieves performance comparable to or exceeding that of traditional spectral analysis techniques. This work provides a foundation for robust, automated radionuclide identification across diverse measurement conditions.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 185Poster Number:NSS-01-185] High-Fidelity 3D MCNP Modeling for Waste Classification in PWRs (#1189)
sub_talks.speaker: C. Yoon
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Hydro & Nuclear CO., LTD, Central Research Institute, Daejeon, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate classification of radioactive waste is critical for determining disposal costs and ensuring safety during nuclear power plant decommissioning. However, generic models with simplified geometries and material compositions can lead to systematic misclassification. In this study, a high-fidelity 3D MCNP model of a pressurized water reactor (PWR) was developed to evaluate activation source terms and classify waste based on IAEA Safety Standards Series. The model includes the reactor pressure vessel (RPV), reactor vessel internals (RVI), and bioshield concrete, enabling realistic representation of complex structures. Activation analysis shows that Fe-55, Co-60, and Mn-54 are the dominant radionuclides in both the RPV and bioshield, qualitatively aligning with widely recognized reactor activation data and thereby validating the developed model. Based on specific activity, Fe-55 accounts for over 99% in both structures. However, applying radionuclide-specific activity limits results in a dramatic shift in the dominant contributor. In the bioshield concrete, the contribution of Fe-55 decreases from over 99% to approximately 16%, while C-14 becomes dominant at approximately 76%. This indicates that classification based solely on specific activity can lead to fundamental misclassification. The RPV is classified as low-level waste (LLW), whereas the bioshield meets the criteria for very low-level waste (VLLW). In contrast, generic models fail to accurately represent the reactor configuration, which can result in over-classifying the bioshield as LLW. The high-fidelity approach provides a quantitative basis for reclassification, directly contributing to the reduction of disposal volume. These results demonstrate that high-fidelity activation modeling is essential not only for improving classification reliability but also for avoiding systematic overestimation of waste classes and enabling more economically efficient decommissioning strategies.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 187Poster Number:NSS-01-187] Six-Degree-of-Freedom Pose Estimation for Safety Monitoring in a Nuclear Glovebox (#1287)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Mead (Autores: L. Mead , C. Kind , T. Scott)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University Of Bristol, Interface Analysis Centre, Bristol, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Nuclear glovebox monitoring must recognise not only which objects are present, but whether their position and orientation indicate an operationally relevant state, such as an inverted container, a handled tool, or an object moving close to a glove during potentially hazardous work. This paper evaluates a two-camera six-degree-of-freedom vision pipeline for advisory operator support in a tabletop analogue of a nuclear glovebox containing a can, pliers, and screwdriver. Offline colour-and-depth pseudo-labels are generated and filtered to train a lightweight object detector and keypoint regressor. During live operation, the system performs object detection, keypoint-based pose recovery, masked depth refinement, temporal smoothing, and safety-state logging. On the validation split, the detector achieved 99.3% mean average precision at an intersection-over-union threshold of 0.5, and the live keypoint-and-depth-refinement pipeline ran at 8.5 frames per second on constrained hardware. These results show that pose-aware monitoring can support prototype glovebox alarms and auditable event records without running a high- capacity pose model online, suggesting a practical route toward advisory systems that improve situational awareness and post- task review while preserving operator judgement. Before such systems could be used operationally, further work is required to establish independent ground truth, model articulated tools, validate longer-term reliability, and build the necessary safety case.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 189Poster Number:NSS-01-189] Photonuclear Processes in a Tungsten Matrix Collimator for Spatially Fractionated Radiation Therapy (#1326)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 I. E. Anokhin (Autores: I. E. Anokhin , D. Ramazanov)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institute for Nuclear Research, Kyiv, Ukraine
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Spatially fractionated radiation therapy using tungsten matrix collimators enables high peak-to-valley dose ratios and improved normal tissue sparing. At photon energies near 25 MeV, photonuclear interactions in tungsten induce activation and produce secondary neutrons, potentially affecting both dosimetric performance and radiation safety. In this work, these processes were investigated using FLUKA Monte Carlo simulations of a modular tungsten-matrix collimator irradiated by a 25-MeV photon beam. Secondary neutron fluence distributions, energy spectra, and absorbed-dose maps in a silicon detector plane were evaluated and normalized to a photon fluence of approximately 1 × 10⁹ cm⁻². The calculated absorbed-dose profile exhibits a pronounced mini-beam structure with a peak dose of 6.16 × 10⁻⁴ Gy, a valley dose of 2.53 × 10⁻⁵ Gy, and a peak-to-valley dose ratio of 24.4. Neutron production is highest at the entrance to the collimator and decreases significantly beyond approximately 5 cm along the beam path, indicating substantial attenuation within the 9 cm tungsten structure. Folding the neutron spectra with energy-dependent fluence-to-dose conversion coefficients yields an ambient dose equivalent of 102 µSv in the collimator region and 0.62 µSv in the phantom region for the same irradiation. The results demonstrate that photoneutron generation is strongly influenced by the collimator configuration and exhibits distinct spatial and spectral characteristics. Photoneutrons contribute to the dose outside the primary irradiation field, thereby increasing the valley dose and affecting the achievable peak-to-valley dose ratio. These findings underscore the importance of accounting for photonuclear effects during collimator optimization and shielding design for high-energy photon mini-beam therapy systems.

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Metallic foreign particles are critical safety hazards in lithium-ion battery manufacturing. To address the difficulty of detecting metallic microparticles in single-layer LiFePO 4 cells, this work proposes a nondestructive detection method based on low-energy X-ray transmission imaging. Cu, Fe, and Ni particles are analyzed through attenuation modeling and simulation to evaluate the effects of photon energy, particle material, and particle thickness on transmission contrast. Preliminary imaging experiments are performed using 40keV X-rays, and weak abnormal signals are extracted by normal-sample normalization, filtering enhancement, threshold segmentation, and local SNR analysis. The results show that metallic microparticles can produce detectable local attenuation anomalies in low-energy X-ray images.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 195Poster Number:NSS-01-195] Improved Scattering Modeling in CIVA-RT using a Next-Event Estimator (#1959)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Blas (Autores: S. Blas , A. Touron , H. Hutinet , O. Petit , J.M. Létang , C. Le Loirec)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Université Paris-Saclay, CEA, List, Palaiseau, France [2] CEA, DES, IRESNE, DER, Service de Physique des Reacteurs et du Cycle, Cadarache, France [3] Université Paris-Saclay, CEA, Service d'Etudes des Réacteurs et de Mathématiques Appliquées, Gif-sur-Yvette, France [4] INSA-Lyon, Université Claude Bernard Lyon 1, CNRS, Inserm, CREATIS UMR 5220 U1294, Villeurbanne, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In non-destructive testing (NDT), simulation is used to study radiation-matter interactions for various cases. CIVA software includes a radiographic testing (RT) module, which combines analytical and Monte Carlo (MC) approaches. The analytical component models primary photons, while the MC component handles scattered photons - a process that can become computationally intensive in complex configurations. Building on this, we introduce an estimator based on a split exponential track length method (seTLE) in the MC component of CIVA-RT, designed to reduce statistical variance and computational cost. This next-event estimator increases the probability of photon contributions to the detector by creating multiple pseudo-photons during the simulation. Its performance is evaluated using a convergence index and a Figure of Merit. Three configurations are studied: a simple configuration, a step wedge configuration with a distant detector, and an industrial weld case. Results show that the estimator provides significant efficiency gains. A detailed analysis of seTLE simulation shows that rare high-weight photons can cause sudden signal variations. These results demonstrate that the approach provides efficiency gains, making high fidelity simulations more tractable in industrial contexts.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 197Poster Number:NSS-01-197] Development of a spectral unmixing method for gamma-ray spectra analysis : application to airborne measurements (#2081)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Patryl (Autores: K. Castillo , L. Patryl , C.-P. Mano , H. Paradis , F. Carrel , J. Bobin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CEA, DAM-DIF, ARPAJON, France [2] CEA, LIST, SACLAY, France [3] CEA, IRFU, SACLAY, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The CEA develops and uses airborne detectors to carry out gamma mapping missions for various private and public entities, and various national and international authorities. The main objectives of these missions are : site monitoring (natural and anthropic contributions to environmental radioactivity), mapping contaminated areas, detecting and identifying radionuclides and radioactive sources. Methods for analyzing the spectra acquired during these missions are being studied, with a view to improve decision thresholds and detection limits for various radionuclides of interest. A spectral analysis method called "spectral unmixing" has been developed, using a full spectrum analysis instead of the reference method based on regions of interest. This algorithm takes into account the response of the detector under study to an individual radionuclide, and estimates the proportions of the different radionuclides using a likelihood estimator. This method was shown to be accurate for reconstructing radionuclide activities, with improved sensitivity compared to the reference method. The application of this algorithm to airborne detectors raises a number of challenging problems, such as taking into account the variability of spectral signatures linked to the environment and source shielding. An algorithm has been developed to address this problem. The algorithm was validated on simulated and experimental data, and improved the results of an airborne measurements campaign. This method can be implemented on the measurement system for real-time radionuclide identification.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 199Poster Number:NSS-01-199] Closed-Form Energy-Based Scatter Estimation for PET Image Reconstruction (#2160)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 W. A. Williams (Autores: W. A. Williams , G. Chinn , C. S. Levin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Stanford University, Molecular Imaging, Stanford, California, United States of America [2] Stanford University, Radiology, Stanford, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Scatter correction is a vital tool in enhancing SNR and contrast recovery in PET; however, existing techniques are computationally costly, need priors, and fail at lower counts. Our focus is to remedy these concerns using a novel closed-form solution. The technique differentiates itself by considering multi-Compton scatter (>2 scatter events) that twice convolve the single-scatter energy distribution revealing 9 states of joint probability density function. This then forms the Gram covariance matrix in our L2-regularized regression with Bhattacharrya weighting: an index of the probability density function overlap establishing appropriate penalties. Lastly, a quadratic cost function is implemented, and the solution is determined via gradient optimization method. Preliminary results from a Utah Phantom mimic's coincidence data simulated in our GenII PETCoil in GATE v.8.2 determined a 10-fold decrease in magnitude of the L2 lambda compared to our previous technique suggesting better conditioning. The global scatter fraction for the phantom, compared to the ideal estimate from GATE came remarkably close: ~0.08% with the median error per sinogram bin centered around 0.00% (99.7% CI [0.00%,0.00%]) within GATE's ideal scatter fraction within an average of 360-410 counts/sinogram bin after correction (using SF = 1-True Fraction) suggesting a near perfect scatter correction. To determine the potential benefit of a prior joint probability density function of the anatomical Utah Phantom, we reran the algorithm receiving a global scatter fraction error of 3.13% with a per sinogram bin error of -1.12% (99.7% CI [-1.17%,-1.06%]) indicating an overcorrection. Our results conclude the following: the KN derivation closed-form solution approaches the ideal and a probabilistic prior is not needed.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 201Poster Number:NSS-01-201] Hybrid Semantic-Keyword Analysis for the Classification of Nuclear Fuel Cycle Activities Using Open-Source Information (#2241)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y.W. Lee (Autores: Y.W. Lee , S.A. Choi , S.A. Kim , C.H. Min , Y.H. Chung , J.J. Ahn)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yonsei University, Division of Data Science, Wonju, Republic of Korea [2] Yonsei University, Department of Radiation Convergence Engineering, Wonju, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study proposes a hybrid semantic-keyword analysis framework for automatically identifying and classifying nuclear fuel cycle-related activities using open-source text data. In the safeguards system of the International Atomic Energy Agency, continuous monitoring and analysis of nuclear fuel cycle activities are required; however, existing approaches rely heavily on expert-driven manual review, limiting efficient processing of large volumes of unstructured text data. To address this issue, nuclear fuel cycle-related news articles collected from Google News were used to construct profiles for seven nuclear fuel cycle activities. Each activity was represented by combining semantic information derived from Sentence-BERT embeddings with keyword importance obtained using class-based TF-IDF. Subsequently, key sentences were extracted from IAEA news articles, and activity classification was performed by integrating semantic and keyword similarity for each activity category. Performance evaluation results showed that the proposed method achieved a Top-1 accuracy of 57.14%, a Top-3 accuracy of 85.71%, and a mean reciprocal rank of 0.738. In addition, the actual activity category was generally included within the top candidate groups, showing that the proposed framework reflects the semantic relationships and complex characteristics among nuclear fuel cycle activities. This study demonstrates the feasibility of automating open-source-based nuclear fuel cycle activity analysis and suggests the potential for future extension to an Additional Protocol-based automatic declaration target identification system. The results also highlight the applicability of data-driven analytical approaches for safeguards and regulatory support.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 203Poster Number:NSS-01-203] Selective Use of Directionally Informative Non-Photopeak Events for Low-Count Industrial Gamma Imaging (#2392)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Lei (Autores: L. Lei , D. Zhang , Y. Zhang , Z. Lyu , T. Ma)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract High-performance industrial gamma imaging under count-limited conditions is challenging, particularly for medium- and high-energy radionuclides where photopeak statistics are limited. However, some non-photopeak Compton-related events still retain directional information. We propose a directionally informed multi-energy-window reconstruction method that selectively incorporates such events. Monte Carlo spectral decomposition was used to define energy windows and estimate useful-event fractions. Window-specific projection data were paired with matched system matrices and jointly reconstructed using weighted MLEM. The method was evaluated with a self-collimating industrial gamma camera for ¹³⁷Cs imaging. In point-source experiments, 30 s multi-window reconstruction achieved localization accuracy comparable to 90 s photopeak-window-only MLEM. In structured-source and short-frame dynamic imaging, it reduced background artifacts and improved localization stability. These results show that selective use of directionally informative non-photopeak events can improve event utilization and reconstruction robustness under low-count industrial gamma imaging conditions.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 205Poster Number:NSS-01-205] An Optical Surrogate Framework for Three-Dimensional Fusion Source Reconstruction (#2548)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Zhang (Autores: Z. Zhang , Y. Yang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [2] Tsinghua University, Key Laboratory of Particle and Radiation Imaging, Ministry of Education, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Three-dimensional reconstruction of fusion neutron sources is critical for diagnosing burn-region morphology and implosion asymmetry in inertial confinement fusion, yet the recoverable morphology is severely limited by sparse and geometrically constrained diagnostic views. This work proposes an optical surrogate framework to study information-driven sparse-channel layout design for fusion neutron source reconstruction, offering controllable source morphology, low cost, and ease of iteration compared to direct neutron diagnostics. The core motivation is to treat limited-view reconstruction not only as an inverse-algorithm problem, but also as a constrained layout-design problem. A conceptual design employing Latin hypercube sampling generates candidate layouts within admissible geometries, followed by greedy selection. The optical surrogate tests the shared inverse-problem structure using movable point-like optical sources, directional fiber channels, rather than reproducing neutron transport physics. Preliminary fiber-response measurements reveal finite-acceptance soft-channel behavior with a transverse full width at half maximum of approximately 2.7 mm. Theoretical reconstruction using a discrete multi-point-source design yields a detector-domain residual of 0.038, a source-correlation coefficient of 0.998, and a maximum relative strength-ratio error of approximately 7.2%. These results establish a forward-model basis for subsequent layout optimization and future migration to neutron-response matrices.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 207Poster Number:NSS-01-207] Adaptive Tetrahedral Mesh Reconstruction for Industrial Computed Tomography (#2942)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Lee (Autores: J. Lee , Y. Hong , S. Yoo , S. Oh , H.K. Kim)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Pusan National University, Computational X-ray Imaging Laboratory, School of Mechanical Engineering, Busan, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Industrial X-ray computed tomography (CT) is widely used for non-destructive inspection and generation of geometric models. However, conventional voxel-based CT reconstruction on a fixed Cartesian grid causes partial-volume blurring and possible geometric errors when converted into surface or CAD models. This work presents an interface-adaptive tetrahedral mesh-based iterative reconstruction framework for industrial CT. The method estimates nodal attenuation coefficients directly on an unstructured mesh. X-ray projection and backprojection are performed by an NVIDIA OptiX-accelerated projector, which computes ray-mesh intersections, segment lengths, and barycentric weights, and backprojects residuals using the SIRT algorithm. To improve boundary representation, the reconstructed field is used to detect interface-related edges, locally refine the mesh, and displace vertices. For each candidate vertex, a local attenuation-gradient direction is estimated from neighboring nodes. The neighbors are divided across the estimated normal, and the vertex is shifted toward the attenuation mid-level between regions while enforcing element quality constraints. Simulated projection studies showed the proposed adaptive mesh reconstruction preserved overall structure while producing sharper material boundaries than voxel-based SIRT. Global structural similarity improved, particularly in regions containing material interfaces. These results indicate the framework reduces boundary blurring, supporting more accurate defect sizing and dimensional measurement in industrial testing.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 209Poster Number:NSS-01-209] Forward Simulation of High-Energy XPCI Using XRM-Derived Semiconductor Package Phantoms (#2980)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 U. Lee (Autores: U. Lee , S. Jang , D. Kim , S. Lee , Y. Kim , G. Song , J. Lee , G. Cho , J. Kim)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Department of Nuclear and Quantum Engineering, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [2] Pusan National University, Nuclear Systems Major, School of Mechanical Engineering, Busan, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study presents a forward simulation of high-energy X-ray phase-contrast imaging (XPCI) for semiconductor package inspection using an X-ray microscopy (XRM)-derived structural phantom. A projected phantom from an experimental laboratory XRM reconstruction stack was used as a geometry prior rather than quantitative material ground truth. The projected grayscale phantom was percentile-normalized and mapped to simplified Cu/Si refractive-index distributions. Under the proposed long-beamline high-energy synchrotron XPCI conditions, the simulated XPCI intensity and retrieved phase images reproduced characteristic package structures, including stacked layers and metal interconnect regions. The finite-source-induced blur was on the order of the detector pixel size, while the selected intra-bump feature showed higher local visibility in the retrieved phase image than in the simulated intensity image. This work extends idealized-phantom simulations to a laboratory-XRM-reconstructed semiconductor package structure under long-beamline high-energy synchrotron XPCI conditions.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 211Poster Number:NSS-01-211] Investigating Identifiability in Joint Transmission-Backscatter X-ray Image Registration with Energy-Dependent Source Geometry (#1740)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Choi (Autores: H. Joo , Y. Choi , J. Park , C.H. Lim , J. Lee , H.J. Yang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH), Department of Electrical Engineering, Pohang, Republic of Korea [2] Korea Research Institute of Ships and Ocean Engineering (KRISO), Daejeon, Republic of Korea [3] M1 International Inc., Daejeon, Republic of Korea [4] Seoul National University, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea [5] Seoul National University, Institute of New Media and Communications, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract X-ray scannings are widely adopted by customs to control containers. Transmission and backscatter X-ray imaging are often jointly employed to enhance material discrimination and detection robustness in cargo inspection systems. However, the two modalities typically operate at substantially different photon energy levels, leading to energy-dependent interaction volumes and effective source geometries that cannot be simultaneously aligned. As a result, image registration becomes a prerequisite for joint analysis and decision-making based on transmitted and backscattered measurements, yet it is fundamentally ill-posed because consistent spatial correspondence between the two imaging processes is not directly observable. In this work, we investigate this identifiability issue in joint transmission--backscatter X-ray image registration by explicitly modeling energy-dependent source geometry and imaging physics. We show that mismatched photon energies can induce structural ambiguity, such that multiple spatial alignments may remain similarly plausible under joint interpretation.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 213Poster Number:NSS-01-213] Development of a UAV-Mounted Radiation Survey System Integrating LaBr3(Ce) Detectors and LiDAR (#1003)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y.-Y. Ji (Autores: Y.-Y. Ji , W. Ji , K. Kim , M.J. Kim)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute, Environmental Safety Technology Research Division, Daejeon, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract To facilitate the highly efficient and accurate surveying of radioactively contaminated areas, this study presents the development of an advanced UAV-mounted integrated survey system capable of the simultaneous, real-time measurement of 3D geospatial information and environmental radiation data. The hardware architecture is robustly constructed, integrating two sets of two-inch LaBr3(Ce) detectors for high-resolution gamma spectrometry. This is combined with a LiDAR sensor for acquiring precise 3D terrain topography, a GPS, and a laser altimeter to ensure accurate spatial referencing. To guarantee operational stability during flight, the payload design incorporates specialized vibration-damping mounts and a lightweight 1.5-millimeter aluminum housing. Furthermore, a high-speed LTE router network was introduced to reliably handle the transmission of large-capacity data streams to the ground station. The practical efficacy of the system was rigorously validated through extensive flight tests conducted over radioactively contaminated regions in Fukushima. When aerial measurements were mathematically converted to dose rates at one meter above ground level, the results demonstrated highly satisfactory performance, showing a strong statistical correlation with baseline data obtained using conventional backpack-type ground survey equipment. Crucially, by mapping real-time energy spectra directly onto the acquired 3D geospatial models, the system successfully enabled the comprehensive, multi-dimensional identification of specific high-level contamination hotspots. Moving forward, by integrating AI to further refine advanced topographical correction algorithms, this autonomous system is expected to significantly enhance the rapid and precise generation of contamination maps, providing critical support for emergency response.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 215Poster Number:NSS-01-215] Development of a Handheld Uranium Enrichment Analyzer Based on LaBr3 Detector and Relative Detection Efficiency Self-Calibration Method (#1069)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Liu (Autores: G. Liu , H. Zhou , J. Li)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] China institute of atomic energy, Department of Radiochemistry, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract To meet the on-site inspection requirements for uranium materials, a handheld uranium enrichment analyzer based on a LaBr3 detector and the relative detection efficiency self-calibration method was developed. The adopted LaBr3:Ce crystal has a size of 38.1mm in diameter and 25.4mm in thickness, with an energy resolution of 2.9% at 662keV. The handheld uranium enrichment analyzer is equipped with a 4.5-inch touchscreen. It features overall dimensions of 145×75×58mm and a weight of 800g, supporting continuous operation for more than 8 hours. Test results from six NBS standard samples show that for uranium samples with a mass≥200g, a ²³⁵U enrichment≥0.711%, and a measurement time≥1800s, the relative deviation of the measured ²³⁵U enrichment is less than 8.0%. This device can be applied to the verification and measurement of ²³⁵U enrichment in uranium materials.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 217Poster Number:NSS-01-217] Neutron Response Evaluation of Miniature Spherical Li-glass scintillators for Optical-Fiber-Based Detectors (#1115)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Saito (Autores: Y. Saito , Y. Oshima , W. Kitsuki , K. Watanabe)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Kyushu University, Applied Quantum Physics and Nuclear Engineering, Fukuoka, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Boron Neutron Capture Therapy (BNCT) and high-flux pulsed neutron sources such as J-PARC require reliable real-time neutron monitoring with minimal perturbation of the irradiation field. We have been developing miniature optical-fiber-based neutron detectors using small Li-glass scintillators mounted at the fiber tip. Conventionally, the scintillator pieces were prepared by crushing bulk Li-glass, producing irregularly shaped fragments that introduce geometric uncertainties and complicate quantitative response evaluation by Monte Carlo simulation. To overcome this, an aerodynamic polishing technique was established to shape Li-glass fragments into well-defined spherical particles with diameters of 100 to 500 μm without significant degradation in light yield. The spherical geometry enabled quantitative prediction of the wall effect through PHITS Monte Carlo simulations with a quenching model based on Birks' law, and the simulated pulse-height spectra showed excellent agreement with experimental data obtained from spheres of various diameters (220-450 μm). This approach provides a robust framework for the precise design and manufacturing of miniature neutron detectors for high-intensity fields.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 219Poster Number:NSS-01-219] Time-Resolved Imaging of Radioactive Gas with the 4π Gamma-Ray Imager C3G (#1185)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Kitayama (Autores: Y. Kitayama , H. Nakai , K. Enomoto , N. Yamada , K. Hitomi , M. Nogami , N. Kawachi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Fukushima Institute for Research, Education and Innovation, Plant Imaging research Unit, Fukushima, Japan [2] Tohoku University, Sendai, Japan [3] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology, Takasaki, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Coded Cube Camera for Gamma-ray (C3G) is a 4π gamma-ray imager designed to estimate gamma-ray source distributions from direction-dependent detector response patterns. In this study, we developed a 24-detector C3G consisting of 24 HR-GAGG scintillators and applied it to a plant radioisotope (RI) imaging experiment using 11 CO 2 gas. In the plant RI imaging experiment, approximately 300 MBq of 11 CO 2 gas was supplied to a plant placed in an experimental chamber to image the transport of 11 C-labeled photosynthates within the plant. During this experiment, the C3G was placed outside the chamber, and the dynamics of 11 CO 2 gas were continuously measured with an acquisition time of 1 s per measurement. As a result, the inflow of the gas into the chamber was clearly visualized. In addition, the reconstructed image intensity decreased exponentially over time. The half-life estimated from this intensity change was 20.70 min, which was in good agreement with the known half-life of 11 C, 20.34 min. These results demonstrate that the 24-detector C3G can visualize dynamic gaseous radioactive sources and estimate temporal changes in radioactivity from reconstructed image intensity. This capability is expected to be useful for applications such as radioactive gas leakage monitoring, environmental monitoring, and nuclear security.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 221Poster Number:NSS-01-221] Performance Evaluation of a Fast Fission Neutron Coincidence Counting System (#1196)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Toh (Autores: Y. Toh , M. Maeda , M. Komeda)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Japan Atomic Energy Agency, Nuclear Science and Engineering Center, Ibaraki, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Characterization of nuclear fuel in fuel debris is essential for the decommissioning of the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station. The fast fission neutron coincidence counting (FFCC) method, which is less sensitive to neutron absorbers than conventional thermal-neutron-based techniques, was investigated using Monte Carlo simulations with PHITS. A cylindrical unit can containing fuel debris was modeled, and four detector configurations with 24-72 liquid scintillator detectors were compared. Fast neutron coincidence counting efficiency decreased as the number of detectors decreased, whereas the quantification limit did not vary monotonically; the 56-detector configuration provided the best performance. This indicates that an optimal number of detectors exists, as gains in coincidence events are offset by reduced efficiency in distant detectors and increased background counts. Evaluation of the effective dose showed that shielding with lead and boron-loaded polyethylene reduced the dose around the system below the access limit for personnel, without significantly affecting measurement performance. These findings provide useful guidelines for the design of practical FFCC systems.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. A. Wilson (Autores: L. A. Wilson , C. Horsfield , A. Leatherland , G. Davies , T. Harrington , S. Morley , S. Rice , S. Tanner , A. Stott , A. Simons , W. Tominey , V. Woolhead , D. Wright)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The ASP neutron facility at AWE - Nuclear Security Technologies (AWE-NST) Aldermaston, is undergoing upgrades to both the accelerator beamline and the supporting diagnostics. This is driven by evolving customer requirements, particularly its increasing use as a platform for fundamental nuclear data measurements. Neutron flux monitoring on ASP is provided by fission chambers and is supported by external activation foil calibrations and internal cross-calibration measurements. A recommissioned associated-particle technique provides improved accuracy for lower-fluence measurements, while ongoing work is improving neutron spectral characterisation using a range of techniques including activation, Single crystal chemical vapour deposited diamond detectors, proton recoil and Helium - 3 spectrometers. These activities reduce uncertainties in current measurements, and establish the diagnostic techniques required for a future facility (VENTURE) capable of delivering higher fluxes and a wider range of quasi-monoenergetic neutron energies. The calibration and diagnostics strategy for the VENTURE facility is outlined, with an emphasis on delivering the well characterised source required for nuclear data experiments. sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 225Poster Number:NSS-01-225] Development and test of a novel neutron and gamma imaging detector (#1280)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Yu (Autores: Y. Yu , Y. Liu , X. Liu , Z. Qiao , N. Jiang , Q. Wei , Y. Liu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Chengdu Novel Medical Equipment Ltd., Chengdu, China [2] Tsinghua University, Beijing, China [3] University of Science and Technology Beijing, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract As the demand for the detection of special nuclear materials increases, the use of imaging instruments that can sensitively image both gamma-ray and neutron signatures has become necessary. The radioactive waste streams can contain neutron-emitting radioactive materials, hence localisation of neutron sources plays an important part in nuclear decommissioning. Neutron detector design based on the MURA revealed promising results when tested in security applications. Due to the requirement of ensuring high detection efficiency for both neutrons and gamma rays, the plastic scintillator used is typically thick. As demonstrated in our previous study, the dual-layer design exhibits better imaging performance and produces fewer artifacts. In this paper, we propose a dual-layer DOI (depth of interaction) detector design and have successfully developed a prototype module. The first and second layer of the crystals are clearly resolved from the flood histograms, demonstrating its capability to provide two-layer depth encoding. The energy resolution of each layer is improved by 50% compared with that of a single-layer detector with the same thickness, and the neutron/gamma discrimination figure of merit (FOM) is also significantly enhanced. Validation and testing of the imaging performance are currently underway.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 227Poster Number:NSS-01-227] Multilayer Scintillator for Improved Gamma-ray Discrimination at Thermal Neutron Scattering Beamlines (#1365)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Moustafa (Autores: A. Moustafa , M. Loyd)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, Tennessee, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Scintillator-based thermal neutron detectors are utilized at scattering beamline facilities around the world. The Anger camera is one example that was designed and deployed at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. The camera uses enriched 6 Li-glass (GS20) that offers advantages over the widely used 3 He gas proportional counters, including sub-millimeter spatial resolution, higher count rate capability, and high neutron absorption efficiency. However, GS20 has higher γ-ray sensitivity due to its solid state, potentially reducing the neutron signal to background ratio. Gamma rejection using pulse height discrimination is feasible, but it suffers when there is greater overlapping between the neutron and gamma spectral features in intense background fields, like with certain beamline configurations. Additionally, pulse shape discrimination is unfeasible with GS20. Previous work demonstrated a new approach to discrimination by optimizing the scintillator shape and reducing its size. In this work, we demonstrate improved gamma discrimination by segmenting the GS20 scintillator layer of the Anger camera. The layer is divided into several thinner layers with the same overall thickness, and coupled together using non-scintillating quartz layers. The neutron absorption products fully deposit their energy in the GS20 layers due to their significantly shorter range compared to the Compton-scattered electrons from γ-rays that only partially deposit their energy. This allows for better separation between the respective features on the pulse height spectrum, and therefore improved discrimination, while maintaining the same high neutron absorption efficiency.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 229Poster Number:NSS-01-229] Feasibility of Organic Scintillator-Based Coincidence Counting for Photonuclear Nondestructive Assay of Nuclear Materials (#1414)

sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Research Institute of Police Science, Physics Section, Chiba, Japan [2] Institute of Science Tokyo, Laboratory for Zero-Carbon Energy, Tokyo, Japan [3] Kyoto University, Institute for Integrated Radiation and Nuclear Science, Osaka, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study demonstrates organic scintillator-based neutron coincidence counting as a promising approach for photonuclear nondestructive assay (NDA) of nuclear materials. Four organic scintillators-organic glass scintillator (OGS), EJ-276D, stilbene, and BC-501A-were systematically evaluated in terms of fast-neutron detection efficiency, pulse shape discrimination (PSD) capability, and timing response. In addition, three-detector coincidence counting systems based on OGS and stilbene detectors were constructed and tested using a 252 Cf source. Stilbene and BC-501A exhibited excellent PSD performance, EJ-276D showed high fast-neutron detection efficiency, and OGS provided superior timing response. The OGS-based system successfully measured neutron double- and triple-coincidence events with and without lead shielding, whereas the stilbene-based system showed a marked reduction in coincidence events under unshielded conditions. These results indicate that combining PSD, neutron coincidence counting, and gamma-ray shielding enhances the extraction of correlated neutron signals in photonuclear NDA. The proposed OGS-based approach is a promising for active interrogation systems in nuclear security and safeguards.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 231Poster Number:NSS-01-231] Localization of uranium samples in large cemented nuclear waste using active photon interrogation and a Bayesian inversion (#1492)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Lebreton (Autores: M. Lebreton , B. Geslot , C. Carasco , B. Pérot , C. Michelet)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Commissariat à l'énergie atomique et aux énergies alternatives, CEA/DES/IRESNE, St Paul Lez Durance, France [2] Université de Bordeaux, CNRS-IN2P3/LP2IB, Bordeaux, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract CEA Cadarache currently manages over 6,000 historical 870 L nuclear waste packages. To ensure long-term safety, French regulatory authorities require a precise characterization of each unit, specifically regarding structural integrity, fissile material mass and total activity of alpha emitters. However, the high density and volume of 870 L concrete waste packages result in significant signal attenuation, making standard passive gamma spectrometry or passive and active neutron measurements inefficient to assess the mass of nuclear materials. To maximize the signal-to-noise ratio, a specific Active Photon Interrogation (API) approach is developed inside the CINPHONIE irradiation bunker of CHICADE facility, at CEA IRESNE, Cadarache, France. This method makes use of inorganic BGO scintillators to measure high-energy delayed gamma rays from short-lived photofission products induced with a high-energy bremsstrahlung photon source, i.e., a 18 MeV LINAC. A Bayesian framework is applied to infer both the mass and the position of nuclear materials from angular acquisitions. This article is focused on testing API framework in the case where the source of the signal is located in a homogeneous environment. Based on the promising results presented here, future developments will focus on the heterogenous case.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 233Poster Number:NSS-01-233] Development and Performance Evaluation of a Four-Detector RMS in Compliance with IEC 60532 (#1540)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Yang (Autores: D. Yang , S.-H. Lee)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute (KAERI), Radiation Safety Management Division, Daejeon, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Radiation monitoring systems (RMS) are essential for continuous radiation surveillance and rapid alarm generation in nuclear facilities. This paper presents the development and performance evaluation of a miniaturized Local Processing and Display Unit (LPDU)-based RMS designed to reduce installation space and radioactive waste generation while maintaining reliable monitoring performance. The developed RMS adopts a 1:4 architecture that enables a single LPDU to process and display signals from four independent detectors. The system was implemented using a Texas Instruments TMS2800137-based edge device and a Canberra G64IC detector. Firmware was developed to support pulse counting, EEPROM operation, RS-232/RS-485 communication, and real-time data processing. A dedicated communication protocol with Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) verification was also implemented to enhance data integrity. In addition, a Centered Significant Test (CST)-based adaptive filtering algorithm was embedded in the edge device to improve noise suppression and detector signal monitoring under field conditions. Performance verification tests were conducted in accordance with IEC 60532:2010 using a calibrated Cs-137 gamma radiation source. The developed RMS satisfied the acceptance criteria for linearity, statistical fluctuations, response time, and alarm response time and stability. The maximum linearity deviation was 2.1%, the coefficient of variation was 0.0203%, and all response times were below 6 s. These results demonstrate that the proposed RMS provides reliable radiation monitoring performance in a compact multi-detector configuration.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 235Poster Number:NSS-01-235] Template-Matching Position Solving on FPGAs for a Thermal Neutron Detector (#1591)
sub_talks.speaker: M. Loyd
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Oak Ridge National Lab, Oak Ridge, Tennessee, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) based thermal neutron detectors have been developed at Oak Ridge National Laboratory for single crystal diffraction instruments. They have potential as good replacements for current 3He detectors on neutron reflectometers due to their high spatial resolution and fast scintillator decay time. The current software-implemented position fitting on these detectors is limited due to the processing required for the recursive least-squares algorithm. In this work, we present a fast method for determining neutron position that can be run on the Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) chip that is already installed on the detector. This method compares the collected event data with pre-determined shapes stored on FPGA memory in parallel, and determines the one with the least linear error. Using this method for neutron positioning takes less time than the hardware defined dead time. Count-rate and spatial resolution results collected at the High-Flux Isotope Reactor are presented, with output count rates > 500 kcps achieved, an order of magnitude greater than the software fitting method.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 237Poster Number:NSS-01-237] Method for determining lithium ore's grade based on photoneutrons' lifetime measurement (#1637)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Yu (Autores: M. Yu , Y. Yang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [2] Tsinghua University, Key Laboratory of Particle & Radiation Imaging, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Analysis of lithium ore grade is industrially significant for efficient lithium resource development and utilization, enabling improved production efficiency and reduced costs. Lithium has a large neutron absorption cross-section, and changes in lithium grade can affect the neutron lifetime, which is inversely proportional to the macroscopic absorption cross-section of ore. In this paper, a method for determining lithium grade through neutron lifetime measurements based on an e-LINAC driven photoneutron source is applied to the online analysis of lithium ore grade. Since lithium does not emit gamma rays upon neutron absorption, the neutron lifetime is measured from the time distribution of capture gamma rays induced by neutrons in the matrix elements of the medium. The feasibility of this approach has been demonstrated in experiments using various lithium nitrate solutions as simplified media. Meanwhile, the effect of neutron diffusion was investigated by simulations. The potential of neutron-induced prompt gamma analysis for reducing interference caused by variations in matrix composition is discussed. Further simulation studies and system design are in progress.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 239Poster Number:NSS-01-239] EJ309-Based Neutron-Photon Detection for Photoneutron Characterisation and High-Altitude Radiation Assessment (#1848)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Al Khouri (Autores: K. Al Khouri , M. Bony , V. Blideanu , B. Rapp)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Université Paris-Saclay, Laboratoire National Henri Becquerel at CEA, Paris, France [2] Université Paris-Saclay, IRFU at CEA, Paris, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents an EJ309 organic liquid scintillator system for neutron-photon detection in mixed radiation fields. The performances achieved are illustrated through two complementary use cases. The first concern photoneutron production in pulsed high-energy photon fields generated by a TrueBeam medical electron LINAC and it has been used to characterise neutron-photon pulse-shape discrimination, integrated-charge observables, pile-up and saturation signatures, and the response of the acquisition chain under short intense irradiation pulses. This configuration simulates closely enough the energies involved in high-altitude cosmic-ray neutron production allowing the use of the previously qualified detection system to be used for neutron monitoring at the Jungfraujoch research station (Switzerland, at 3600 m), where the neutron field is mainly produced by atmospheric secondary cascades, including proton- and alphainduced spallation reactions. The detection set-up and analysis framework will be used to measure time-resolved neutron-like and photon-like event populations, pulse-shape discrimination distributions, and spectral observables over long acquisition periods. The work demonstrates the use of EJ309 scintillators for fast-neutron detection in controlled photoneutron fields and supports their application to natural high-altitude cosmic-ray environments, atmospheric radiation monitoring, and photoneutron studies relevant to intense high-energy photon fields.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 241Poster Number:NSS-01-241] Multimodal extension of the Feynman model for thermal neutron multiplicity counters (#1916)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Chartier (Autores: G. Chartier , J. Dumazert , B. Laurent , L. Cavallini , M. Labalme)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Commissariat à l'Énergie Atomique, DAM, DIF, Arpajon, France [2] LPC Caen, Normandie Univ, ENSICAEN, UNICAEN, CNRS/IN2P3, Caen, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The point kinetics model can be extended to multiple regions or energy groups to account for system heterogeneities. This paper presents an extension of the Feynman-α technique in diverse measurement configurations relevant to nuclear safeguards. This extension is achieved by incorporating phase-type distributions into the heuristic derivation of the Feynman model. Phase-type distributions effectively capture the absorption times of finite-state Markov processes. The resulting expressions are specifically tailored to each experimental configuration. In a bare source configuration using an array of ³He-filled proportional counters, the neutron decay exhibits bimodal behavior. When a supplementary reflector is added to the setup, a third term emerges in the expression, as expected. However, the shape of this additional term depends on the type of reflector, due to assumptions in the system's transition matrix. When fitted to simulated datasets, these new models show the fundamental decay mode of the detector (approximately 70 µs) and are validated with a 95% confidence χ2 test.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 243Poster Number:NSS-01-243] Building a Two-Stage Compton Camera with LaBr 3 :Ce Detector Assemblies (#1962)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Mashinini (Autores: S. Hart , P. Jones , S. Mashinini , L. Pellegri , C. van Tubbergh)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] iThemba LABS, Separated Sector Cyclotron Laboratory, Cape Town, South Africa [2] iThemba LABS, Research and Development Technical Support, Cape Town, South Africa [3] University of the Witwatersrand, School of Physics, Johannesburg, South Africa [4] Stellenbosch University, Cape Town, South Africa
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A two-stage Compton camera prototype was developed for compact gamma-ray imaging applications in medicine [1]. Each camera layer consists of four monolithic 14 × 14 × 25.4 mm 3 LaBr 3 :Ce scintillation detector assemblies manufactured by CapeScint, each coupled to a single-channel silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) readout. This configuration does not provide intrinsic position sensitivity within individual crystals. Detector performance was experimentally characterised and modelled using the TOPAS Monte Carlo toolkit, with validation performed against standard gamma-ray calibration sources [2]. Data acquisition was performed using a XIA PIXIE-16 fully digital signal processing system operating in list-mode, enabling event-by-event energy and timing extraction with digital pulse processing [3]. The detectors achieved an energy resolution of approximately 3.4% at 662 keV and a coincidence timing resolution of 988(17) ps. Imaging performance was evaluated using a GBq 137 Cs source at multiple source-to-detector distances. Reconstructed experimental images were compared with validated simulations, with simulations yielding a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 3.36(1) mm and an angular resolution measure (ARM) of 1.47(13) o . Results demonstrate agreement between experiment and simulation, validating the modelling framework and supporting the feasibility of compact LaBr 3 :Ce-based Compton camera systems for medical gamma-ray imaging applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 245Poster Number:NSS-01-245] Dosimetry and Beam-Condition Characterization of Mixed-Field Irradiation Positions at CERN CHARM (#2131)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Fiore (Autores: S. Fiore , F. Ravotti , S. Danzeca)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CERN, Geneva, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Mixed-field irradiation facilities require accurate and traceable dosimetry to support the qualification of electronic components and systems for accelerator environments. This work presents an updated dosimetry and beam-condition characterization of the CERN High-energy AcceleRator Mixed-field facility (CHARM), focusing on the comparison of different irradiation positions and on the extension of the available test conditions to new high dose-rate and high fluence locations close to the target. The study combines active and passive dosimetry methods, including CERN RadMon radiation monitors, radiophotoluminescent glass dosimeters and alanine dosimeters, to evaluate Total Ionizing Dose and fluence-related quantities under representative operating conditions. Measurements acquired during commissioning are compared with data collected during user operation to assess the stability and reproducibility of the delivered radiation fields. In addition, the effect of upstream IRRAD samples on the residual beam reaching the CHARM target is investigated using the IRRAD beam position monitors and the multi-wire proportional chamber installed at the end of the T8 beam line. Variations in the upstream material configuration are shown to affect the transported beam properties, including divergence, with a measurable impact on the resulting mixed field. The combined dosimetry and beam instrumentation data are used to validate the new irradiation positions, compare independent dosimetry techniques and define operational reference conditions for CHARM tests. These results improve the traceability of dose and fluence delivery in mixed-field accelerator irradiation campaigns and support more robust interpretation of radiation effects tests performed at CHARM.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 247Poster Number:NSS-01-247] Hybrid Temperature Compensation and Radiation Damage Recovery with Scintillation Detectors (#2243)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D.Y. Oh (Autores: D.Y. Oh , J. Hwang , G. Kim , C. Kim , J.-Y. Yeom)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea University, Department of Bioengineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] Korea University, Interdisciplinary Program in Precision Public Health, Seoul, Republic of Korea [3] Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [4] Korea University, School of Biomedical Engineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Gamma-ray spectroscopy is a fundamental technique for identifying radioisotopes in safety-critical applications. However, in scenarios such as nuclear accidents, high-temperature and high-radiation environments severely degrade photomultiplier tube performance. Conventional temperature compensation systems face physical voltage limits, and prior deep-learning algorithms fail because they require preserved spectral shapes. To overcome these limitations, this study presents a comprehensive strategy to enhance detector stability. First, an active high-voltage control system mitigates initial temperature-induced gain loss. Because this hardware compensation eventually reaches its physical safety limits, the system integrates a deep learning (DL) technique - bidirectional long short-term memory network - to interpret residual spectral distortions, successfully achieving accurate multi-isotope quantification up to 185 °C. Second, to address radiation-induced damage localized within the photomultiplier tube, a targeted active thermal annealing protocol was applied. Following a 1.55 kGy cumulative gamma irradiation, detector output dropped to 23.5% of its baseline. Subsequent thermal annealing of the photomultiplier tube body at 145 °C successfully restored the output to 89.4%. Ultimately, this integration of hardware, software, and active recovery lays a foundation for robust radionuclide identification under concurrent high-temperature and high-radiation constraints.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 249Poster Number:NSS-01-249] Simulations of A Novel Time-of-Flight β/γ Transmission Tomography Scanner (#2255)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Carmichael (Autores: R. Carmichael , A. Chatziioannou)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California Los Angeles, Department of Molecular and Medical Pharmacology, Los Angeles, California, United States of America [2] University of California Los Angeles, Crump Institute for Molecular Imaging, Los Angeles, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Large cargo scanning presents a unique challenge for national security. Container size limitations pose challenges to tomographic imaging. This work proposes a new stationary, limited angle tomographic transmission scanner geometry with a unique β/γ source utilizing a pair of fixed flat panel detectors, known as Gamma Tomography (GT). A Gate 10 simulation evaluates the imaging capabilities of the scanner and explores time-of-flight (TOF) and energy discrimination as electronic collimation methods to reduce scattered radiation and improve image quality. A 600 μm thin plastic scintillator sheet encasing 100mCi of 60 Co as a near detector locally captures nearly all emitted β particles without significant γ interactions, while a far detector panel of 2 cm thick LYSO crystals captures the ~1.25 MeV energy 60 Co γ photons. Both panels were simulated as 50x80 cm with a thin, 2 cm thick, multi-material test object consisting of water, aluminum, titanium, steel, and uranium in the center of the field of view. The same simulation dataset was reconstructed with/without two separate electronic collimation schemes: valid coincidences with a 100 keV energy window around the 60 Co photopeaks, and valid coincidences with a 100 ps time resolution. Despite the short acquisition time (18sec), reconstructed images are low noise, with all objects visible above background and distinguishable. The images show attenuation coefficient under-estimation, due to object scatter. TOF and energy discrimination underestimate μ values by 25.8% and 34.3% respectively, but a large dynamic range and very high SNR in μ value is achieved for all reconstructions (SNR-water: 46, SNR-Uranium: 1369). Using time information in lieu of energy allows events scattered in the detector to be used to improve image quality and SNR, but further investigation will include achievable time resolution, panel construction, and source geometry optimization.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 251Poster Number:NSS-01-251] A Large-Area Spectroscopic Alpha Imaging Detector for Dual-Isotope Imaging of ²²⁵Ac and ²¹³Bi in Targeted Alpha Therapy (#2275)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J.-G. Kim (Autores: J.-G. Kim , B.S. Kim , I. Lim , K.C. Lee)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Institute of Radiological and Medical Sciences, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Alpha particle autoradiography is an emerging modality for mapping the biodistribution of alpha-emitting radionuclides in preclinical studies, supporting the development of radiopharmaceuticals for targeted alpha therapy (TAT). Considerable effort has been directed toward achieving high spatial resolution, with recent advances emphasizing single-event processing and energy-resolved detection to identify the nuclide of origin of individual alpha particles. Our previous work validated a spectrum decomposition method for dual-isotope imaging of ²²⁵Ac and ²¹³Bi using a spectroscopic alpha imaging detector, confirming its feasibility with therapeutic amounts of ²²⁵Ac. However, the active area of that system was constrained to 2.5 cm × 2.5 cm, limiting its applicability to small fields of view. To overcome this constraint and accommodate simultaneous imaging of multiple tissue sections or organs from larger animals, we developed a large-area spectroscopic alpha imaging detector with an active area of 5 cm × 5 cm, representing a fourfold increase over the prior system. The detector achieved an energy resolution of 4.3% FWHM at 5 MeV and a spatial resolution of approximately 600 μm, representing a substantial improvement over the prior system. Future work will include demonstration of dual-isotope spectral imaging of ²²⁵Ac and ²¹³Bi to support preclinical TAT evaluations.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 253Poster Number:NSS-01-253] Scintillator Size Effects in Fiber-Based Neutron Detectors With Pulse-Shape Discrimination for BNCT (#2328)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H.-D. Liu (Autores: H.-D. Liu , C.-Y. Chang , Y.-H. You , Y.-C. Chang , Z.-F. You , T.-H. Lin , M.-W. Lin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Tsing Hua University,, Institute of Nuclear Engineering and Science, Hsinchu, Taiwan [2] Heron Neutron Medical Corporation, Nuclear Science Department, Zhubei, Taiwan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Scintillator-on-fiber (SOF) detectors utilizing Liglass scintillators show strong potential for neutron flux monitoring in intense radiation environments due to their high radiation hardness and fast response. Previous studies have typically employed fragmented scintillators in SOF detectors due to the difficulty of μm-scale machining. In this work, Li-glass scintillators with well-defined dimensions (1×1×0.5 to 0.25×0.25×0.5 mm 3 ) were precisely fabricated using laser cutting, enabling a systematic investigation of the effect of scintillator size on neutron response linearity in an acceleratordriven neutron beam. With pulse-shape discrimination (PSD), the results show that neutron signals measured with scintillator sizes larger than 0.5×0.5×0.5 mm 3 become blurred in the P SP -channel scatter plot due to gamma-ray contributions and pulse pile-up at an accelerator current of 250 μA. In contrast, the smallest scintillator (0.25×0.25×0.5 mm 3 ) maintains clear separation between neutron and gamma-ray signals. Analysis of the maximum shift error σ m of the neutron peak centroid further indicates that this smallest scintillator effectively suppresses pileup, achieving σ m = 0. In terms of linearity, scintillators with sizes below 0.75×0.75×0.5 mm 3 yield coefficients of determination R 2 > 0.99 when processed using a two-dimensional fiducial cut, satisfying the requirements for neutron flux monitoring in boron neutron capture therapy (BNCT). These results demonstrate the feasibility of optimizing Li-glass scintillator size and volume in SOF detectors to achieve reliable neutron flux monitoring in BNCT applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 255Poster Number:NSS-01-255] Performance Evaluation of a DOI-Based Directional Radiation Monitoring System for Moving Radiation Source Tracking (#2334)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Kang (Autores: Y.S. Chung , J. Kang , J. Ra , Y.H. Chung)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yonsei University, Radiation Convergence Engineering, Wonju, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Radiation accident response requires real-time source-direction and radionuclide information. However, conventional systems are limited in simultaneously achieving radionuclide identification, direction estimation, 360° monitoring, real-time processing, and multiple-source detection. To address this, a directional radiation monitoring system (DRMS) using the depth-of-interaction (DOI) method was developed previously, and its feasibility for 360° monitoring and multiple-source detection was verified. This study evaluated the real-time direction detection performance of the developed DRMS under moving-source conditions. The DRMS consisted of a CsI(Tl) scintillator (1" diameter, 4" height), two photomultiplier tubes coupled to both ends, a cylindrical collimator with eight slots arranged in different directions, and an FPGA-based DAQ. The system calculated gamma-ray energy and DOI using the sum and ratio of the two PMT signals, respectively, and generated radiation distribution maps in real time based on the slot direction corresponding to the estimated DOI layer. Evaluation was conducted assuming an accident scenario in which a 5 TBq radiation source mounted on a vehicle moved at 40 km/h, 100 m from the system. To reproduce this in a laboratory, measurements used a 3.17 MBq 137 Cs source moved at 4.23 cm/min, 1 m from the system, under the same count-rate condition. Energy windows were applied to the data, and the nuclide was identified when counts within its window satisfied the criterion. A nuclide distribution map updated at fixed count intervals to reflect the real-time source position and an accumulated distribution map reflecting the total response were generated. The results confirmed that the system could visually reflect the position change and movement trajectory of a moving source. These results demonstrate the potential of the DOI-based DRMS for real-time source-direction monitoring in radiation accident response and mobile radiation detection.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 257Poster Number:NSS-01-257] Development of a Portable High-Gamma-Ray-resistant Alpha and Beta Dust Monitor (#2423)
sub_talks.speaker: M. Hirato
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Japan Atomic Energy Agency, Plutonium Radiation Control Section Radiation Protection Department, Muramatsu, Tokai-Mura, Naka-gun, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Measuring the radioactivity concentrations of airborne dust is crucial for selecting appropriate protective equipment for radiation workers and assessing internal exposure of them. In this study, we aim to develop a portable dust monitor that can measure alpha and beta rays simultaneously without being affected by ambient gamma rays. For the development, we utilize the clothing contamination monitor, which has been successfully put into practical use in previous research. We investigated whether it was possible to distinguish between alpha and beta rays based on their respective energy spectra by irradiation tests. The results showed that by setting appropriate regions of interest (ROIs), we were able to minimize the influence of gamma rays and successfully distinguish and measure alpha and beta rays.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 259Poster Number:NSS-01-259] Investigation of Structure-Dependent Neutron-Induced Displacement Damage in Silicon MOSFETs (#2564)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 O. Jinseok (Autores: O. Jinseok , H. Seop , K. Seo-Ryong , K. Inyong)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea University of Science and Technology (UST), Daejeon, Republic of Korea [2] Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute (KAERI), Daejeon, Republic of Korea [3] Yonsei University, Wonju, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work systematically characterizes how transistor geometry governs neutron displacement damage (DD)-induced degradation in silicon MOSFETs. A monolithic single-chip array integrating 1.8 V and 3.3 V NMOS/PMOS devices with seven channel widths and 1-, 5-, and 10-finger layouts was fabricated as the device under test, and a hierarchical 1 GHz multiplexing readout was developed to track 84 transistors in real time during irradiation at TRIUMF (10⁶-10¹⁰ n/cm², five incremental steps, annealing monitored up to 40 days). For 1.8 V NMOS devices, the post-irradiation output-voltage shift scaled with channel width, while the threshold-voltage shift after 40-day annealing varied strongly with finger configuration at the same total channel width. These results indicate a strong dependence of DD-induced degradation on finger topology, beyond what channel-width scaling alone can explain, with 10-finger layouts exhibiting anomalous nonlinearity attributable to parasitic coupling and non-uniform damage.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 261Poster Number:NSS-01-261] Solid-State Large-Area Contamination Detector Using Lightlink™ technology for Contamination and clearance equipment (#2688)
sub_talks.speaker: P. Talent
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Mirion Technologies, R&D, Lamanon, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a solid-state detection technology designed to improve large-area surface contamination measurements and enable integration into contamination and clearance equipment or robotics. The primary objective is to replace photomultiplier-based detectors with compact architecture using solid-state photosensors and embedded digital processing, while maintaining or improving detection performance. The proposed detector consists of a 579cm² sensitive surface divided into two independent channels, each coupled to integrated electronics performing biasing, signal processing, self-test, and communication. A daisy-chain configuration was implemented to evaluate system scalability, allowing up to fifty detectors to operate synchronously within a single network. Measurements demonstrate detection homogeneity better than plus or minus fifteen percent over the active area and typical hemispherical efficiencies up to forty-six percent for high-energy beta emitters. The acquisition architecture enables rapid readout compatible with moving platforms, with sampling rates reaching one hundred measurements per second for moderate network sizes. Compared with legacy systems, the proposed solution significantly reduces mass while improving robustness and insensitivity to magnetic fields and eliminates the need for complex external electronics. These results confirm that solid-state based large-area detectors can achieve high-performance contamination monitoring while enabling modular, scalable, and easily deployable systems. The approach opens new perspectives for robotic applications and large-area inspection in nuclear environments.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 263Poster Number:NSS-01-263] Performance Evaluation of the SNIPER-GN Portable Gamma-Neutron Detection System (#2692)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Davolio (Autores: P. Garosi , F. Davolio , C. Del Bene , G. Mangiagalli , M. Morichi , C. Uguccioni)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CAEN S.p.A., Viareggio, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents the experimental validation of SNIPER-GN, a portable gamma-neutron detection and identification system whose core innovation is a patented neutron identification algorithm (U.S. Patent No. 11835477). The algorithm enables robust and reliable neutron identification under challenging operational conditions, including shielding, moderation effects, and intense masking gamma radiation fields, representing a significant advancement over conventional detection approaches. The system integrates a high-efficiency gamma-neutron counter with a mid-high-resolution scintillation detector for rapid localization and characterization of radioactive threats, including Special Nuclear Material. The patented algorithm constitutes the enabling technology of the system and was the primary focus of the experimental verification campaign. Extensive performance testing was conducted in several international laboratories using calibrated sources under both static and dynamic measurement conditions. The system successfully identified neutron-emitting sources down to approximately 1 count per second with background levels below 0.1 counts per second, while gamma identification remained stable above 60 net counts per second over background. Tests employing polyethylene and lead shielding demonstrated identification success rates up to 100% depending on source geometry and activity, confirming robustness in realistic scenarios. Dynamic tests compliant with ANSI N42.53 confirmed reliable alarm performance for moving sources. Additional validation for field applications, such as rapid analysis of air-sampler filters and iodine cartridges for post-fallout monitoring, showed astonishing minimum detectable activities within measurement times shorter than five minutes. Overall, these results validate the patented technology and demonstrate the suitability of SNIPER-GN for homeland security, emergency response, and radiological field deployment scenarios.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 265Poster Number:NSS-01-265] Development of A Cold Neutron Imaging Detector based on Structured 10 B 2 O 3 -ZnS:Cu Screen (#2717)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Li (Autores: D. Li , P. Zhang , X. Yan , H. Li , B. Yuan)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] China Institute for Radiation Protection, Taiyuan, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Neutron imaging plays an irreplaceable role in the restoration of cultural relics and the study of lithium battery charging and discharging behaviors. The performance of neutron imaging detector directly determines the imaging quality. A cold neutron imaging detector based on a structured 10 B 2 O 3 -ZnS:Cu scintillation screen was developed and tested at China Mianyang Research Reactor (CMRR) Cold Neutron Radiography Facility. The structured screen was made of glass microchannel plate (MCP), B 2 O 3 , ZnS:Cu and UV-curable binders. The refractive index contrast between the MCP (1.5) and the UV curable adhesive(1.62) leads to total internal reflection, thereby forming a light confinement structure. The spatial resolution was measured to be about 33μm with a Siemens Star Chart, and the cold neutron absorption efficiency was measured to be 24.4%

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 267Poster Number:NSS-01-267] Revealing Disorder Faster: Detector Upgrades for SANDALS-II (#2826)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. E. Mann (Autores: S. E. Mann , N. J. Rhodes , E. M. Schooneveld , G. Mauri , J. Day , O. L.G. Alderman , T.-L. Hughes , D. T. Bowron , G.J. Sykora)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract SANDALS-II is an instrument being developed at the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source as a next generation diffractometer for the study of amorphous and liquid materials. This upgrade will deliver count rates up to 11 times higher than the existing SANDALS instrument and will significantly expand its scientific capabilities. This work focuses on developments of a large area scintillator detector that are essential for achieving enhanced performance. Scintillation detectors for SANDALS-II will cover a solid angle of 0.67Ω, 2.4 times greater detector coverage than the current instrument. These detectors are required to have high efficiency, particularly at higher neutron energies (short wavelengths), which is achieved using a unique design employing tiles made from alternating layers of glass and scintillator. Scintillator and glass options are explored to optimise detector and instrument performance. Different low Li and B content glasses were tested to determine the most suitable option for the instrument that provides good neutron transmission while maintaining affordability. The ratio of ZnS:Ag to 6 LiF in the scintillator will be altered from 4:1 to 2:1 to enhance neutron absorption and therefore detection efficiency. At 30eV (0.05Å) this offers a 60% improvement in detection efficiency. The applicability of low-afterglow scintillator, ZnO:Zn/ 6 LiF, for use in SANDALS-II is also explored. ZnO:Zn/ 6 LiF is shown to offer a 2x increase in count rate capability over ZnS:Ag/ 6 LiF, but a 6% lower neutron detection efficiency. As the reduction in efficiency using ZnO:Zn/ 6 LiF is modest, this alternative scintillator offers a viable solution for the high count rate regions of SANDALS-II. With optimised glass and scintillator selection, the performance required for the upgraded instrument can be delivered. This will enable faster measurements, smaller sample studies, and time resolved experiments, making SANDALS-II a world leading disordered material neutron diffractometer.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 269Poster Number:NSS-01-269] PGNAA-Based Composition Analysis Using LaBr₃(Ce) and NaI(Tl) Detectors (#2849)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Lee (Autores: K. Lee , H. Kim , H. Ha , K. Jung , J. Eo , J. Shin , J. Kim , J. Kim , K. Oh , J. Park , C. Baek)
