sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study evaluated the performance of a LaBr₃(Ce) scintillation detector for elemental identification and mass-fraction estimation in a thermal-neutron-based prompt gamma-ray neutron activation analysis (PGNAA) system, in comparison with a conventional NaI(Tl) detector. PGNAA spectra were acquired at the Four-Circle Diffractometer (FCD) beamline of the HANARO research reactor at the Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute. The measured samples included pure Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni samples; binary Fe-Mn, Fe-Co, and Fe-Ni mixtures; and ternary NCM622 and NCM811 samples simulating spent lithium-ion battery cathode materials. Elemental identification was performed using Gaussian-derivative-convolution-based peak detection, SNIP baseline correction, and Currie-criterion-based significance testing. Mass fractions were estimated using region-of-interest-based weighted non-negative least squares (WNNLS) with attenuation-integration correction. LaBr₃(Ce) produced higher Z-scores, smaller energy-matching errors, and more stable characteristic peak combinations in mixed samples than NaI(Tl). For NCM622 and NCM811, LaBr₃(Ce) achieved mean absolute errors of 4.3 and 1.9 percentage points, respectively, while also providing higher R² values for spectral-shape reproduction. These results indicate that LaBr₃(Ce) offers improved peak separation and compositional estimation capability for nondestructive analysis of complex industrial samples, including spent lithium-ion battery cathode materials.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 271Poster Number:NSS-01-271] Ultra High-Rate Neutron Detection with ³He Tubes via CF₄ Prompt Scintillation Readout (#3034)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. M. Margato (Autores: L. M. Margato , A. Morozov , V. Solovov , B. Guérard , J. Marchal)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] LIP-Coimbra, Coimbra, Portugal [2] University of Coimbra, Dep. of Physics, Coimbra, Portugal [3] ILL-Institut Laue-Langevin, Grenoble, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents a novel neutron detector concept aiming to provide detection efficiency and background levels equivalent to conventional ³He-based detectors, whilst boosting the maximum counting rate by several orders of magnitude. The detector retains the form-factor of a standard ³He tube and uses the same working gas mixture of 3 He with admixture of CF 4 as the stopping gas. The key innovation is a fast optical readout of CF₄ prompt scintillation light using silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) sensors. The target performance is a detection efficiency equivalent to that of a standard ³He tube under identical gas filling conditions, gamma sensitivity below 10⁻⁶, and a maximum counting rate of 2 MHz/pixel, orders of magnitude improvement over existing detectors. The fast emission of CF₄ scintillation light is the enabling factor for achieving ultra-high counting rates. CF₄ exhibits a considerable photon yield, with one scintillation band in the UV and another in the visible region of the spectrum, with several thousands of photons emitted per neutron event. The efficient collection of light by the SiPMs constitutes a critical design parameter, addressed in this study through Monte Carlo optimization. The gas mixture composition is optimised to maximise the scintillation yield, and a gas purification system can be integrated into the detector to ensure long-term stability. The first experimental results of a detector prototype characterisation on a neutron beamline at the Institut Laue-Langevin (ILL) will be presented.

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The response of Timepix detectors with different sensors (Si, SiC, GaAs, CdTe) to thermal, slow, and fast neutrons is studied. Measurements at tunable mono-energetic neutron fields are compared and analyzed with nuclear-reaction models and numerical calculations. Specific radiation-type and sensor-material interaction neutron detection channels are derived for each detector-sensor configuration. These results serve to better and more completely process radiation data acquired with these detectors. Combining multi-detector measurements expands and enhances the resolving power of field decomposition.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 275Poster Number:NSS-01-275] Characterization of 3D ultra-thin silicon-based thermal neutron detectors (#3088)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Zamorano (Autores: F. Zamorano , I. Lopez , M. Pérez , J. Bravo , C. Fleta , C. Guardiola)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institute of Microelectronics of Barcelona, Barcelona, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Neutron contamination in advanced radiotherapy and other mixed radiation environments has become an increasing concern due to the limitations of conventional neutron detectors under intense gamma background conditions. In this work, ultra-thin 3D silicon neutron detectors specifically designed for operation in mixed radiation fields were experimentally characterized under thermal and high-energy irradiation conditions. The detectors, consisting of 20 µm-thick silicon sensors paired with ⁶LiF neutron conversion layers, were tested at the FANT thermal neutron facility and at the CERN High-Energy Reference Field (CERF). Measurements included reproducibility, angular dependence, bias voltage operation, and discrimination threshold effects using a low-voltage FPGA-based readout system. The results showed stable operation under mixed radiation fields, moderate angular dependence, and strong dependence of the response on detector bias and discrimination threshold. The ultra-thin detector architecture enabled high gamma rejection capability, enabling reliable neutron detection under intense photon background conditions. These results demonstrate the suitability of 3D ultra-thin silicon detectors for compact real-time neutron monitoring in radiation protection and medical applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 277Poster Number:NSS-01-277] A Full Rank Pileup Deconvolution Scheme Suitable for Calorimeter Online Trigger Primitive Generation (#1091)
sub_talks.speaker: J. Wu
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, Batavia, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In this document, a pileup deconvolution scheme not relying on any mathematics guessing is presented. In high energy physics experiment, as the luminosity increases, pile-up issues on detectors such as calorimeters become non-negligible. Deconvolution approaches developed for data taken from DAQ systems are usually rank-deficient or underdetermined, having less equations than unknowns, even with the ADC values from multiple beam crossings are collected. These deconvolution approaches need mathematic pre-assumptions such as Sparse Representation. For online computation tasks such as for trigger primitive creation, signal availability is significantly different as in offline data analysis stage, and therefore, it is possible to use different (yet simpler) algorithms. In this situation, number of ADC values of the calorimeter outputs is the same as the number of beam crossings (or 4 times number of beam crossings, depending on the ADC sampling rate), and therefore, the number of equations can be arranged to be the same as number of unknowns. This way, a determined deconvolution scheme with a full-rank squared convolution (and deconvolution) matrix becomes possible. The robustness of deconvolution over long time windows is also studied in this paper.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 279Poster Number:NSS-01-279] In-orbit performance of the Tl 2 LiYCl 6 :Ce (TLYC) detector onboard the Neutron Radiation Detection Instrument-1A (NeRDI-1A) (#1372)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. G. Oñate Melecio (Autores: K. G. Oñate Melecio , A. L. Hutcheson , B. F. Phlips , J. M. Davis , T. T. Finne , W.N. Johnson , L. J. Mitchell , M. V. Johnson-Rambert , J. M. Wolf , R. S. Woolf , R. S. Perea)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Research Associate with the National Research Council, Resident at the United States Naval Research Lab, Washington D.C., United States of America [2] United States Naval Research Lab, Washington D.C., United States of America [3] Technology Service Corporation, Arlington, Virginia, United States of America [4] Former NRC Research Associate at the U.S. NRL, Washington D.C., United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Neutron Radiation Detection Instrument-1A (NeRDI-1A) is a technology demonstration payload on the International Space Station (ISS) as part of the Department of Defense Space Test Program (STP) mission STP-H9. The primary objective of NeRDI-1A is to space-qualify two detector technologies: a dual-mode gamma-neutron scintillator (Thallium-doped Cesium Lithium Yttrium Chloride, Tl 2 LiYCl 6 :Ce, or TLYC) and Domino microstructured semiconductor neutron detectors (MSNDs). The full NeRDI-1A suite includes a TLYC detector, three Domino MSNDs with varying moderation, and an EJ-270 plastic scintillator. This work focuses on the TLYC detector within NeRDI-1A. Here we present an analysis of the TLYC detector's response within distinct orbital regions--including the auroral regions and the South Atlantic Anomaly--during a period of minimal solar variability. We also present the evolution of the TLYC detector's performance over its operational lifetime.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 281Poster Number:NSS-01-281] Technical Design and Geometric Acceptance of the Assessing Lunar Ion-Generated Neutrons (ALIGN) Payload for Chang'E-8 (#1701)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Chaiwongkhot (Autores: K. Chaiwongkhot , K. Amratisha , K. Anuchit , S. Burom , S. Chindaratchakul , H. Donghui , P. Jamlongkul , P. Khonsri , J. Lakronwat , S. Manuthasna , T. Marsri , W. Mitthumsiri , P. Muangha , T. Panyalert , Y. Pittayang , K. Puprasit , D. Ruffolo , Z. Shenyi , J. Wannasorn , N. Treesakul , R. Plumanut , W. Hantrakul , P. Torteeka)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Mahidol University, Bangkok, Thailand [2] National Astronomical Research Institute of Thailand,, National Astronomical Research Institute of Thaila, Thailand [3] National Space Science Center, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China [4] Chulabhorn Royal Academy, Bangkok, Thailand
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Assessing Lunar Ion-Generated Neutrons (ALIGN) payload is an advanced spectrometer developed to characterize the lunar radiation environment during the Chang'E-8 mission. Designed to operate within a stringent mass allocation of 4.8 kg and optimized for low electrical consumption, the payload features a highly integrated coincidence telescope statically oriented at -30 degrees from the horizontal. This presentation details the instrumental architecture and multi-particle detection methodologies of the payload. The detector array comprises Double-Sided Silicon Strip Detectors (DSSDs), an EJ-254 boron-loaded plastic scintillator, and a primary CLYC calorimeter, all enveloped by an active BC-408 plastic scintillator veto. The system employs the Δ E-E technique-correlating initial energy loss in the DSSD transmission trackers with total energy deposited in the scintillators-to separate upward-moving albedo protons (20-140 MeV) from background electrons. Concurrently, intrinsic Pulse Shape Discrimination (PSD) within the CLYC crystal is utilized to accurately separate epithermal neutrons from gamma-ray interactions. To achieve definitive particle identification within these strict size, weight, and power constraints, a dedicated onboard FPGA executes priority-based signal processing. Geant4 simulations evaluated the instrument's overall geometric acceptance as a function of incident kinetic energy. By combining these advanced onboard logic techniques with a streamlined composite radiation shield, structural design is expected to successfully isolate lunar albedo signals from localized lander interference while fully satisfying the mission's strict engineering constraints.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 283Poster Number:NSS-01-283] Cluster Size Simulation to Predict LHCb Upgrade I VELO Performance (#1945)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. J. Williams (Autores: S. J. Williams , E. Buchanan , D. Friday , J. Velthuis)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Bristol, H.H. Wills Physics Laboratory, Bristol, United Kingdom [2] University of Edinburgh, School of Physics and Astronomy, Edinburgh, United Kingdom [3] University of Manchester, Department of Physics and Astronomy, Manchester, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The LHCb experiment recently underwent an extensive upgrade program to allow operation at higher luminosities. The VErtex LOcator (VELO) was redesigned to a hybrid pixel layout with 130nm CMOS technology. As a result of the upgrade, the VELO will be exposed to an extreme radiation environment - over an order of magnitude greater than before. At the end of its lifetime, the innermost regions are expected to be exposed to 8x10 15 MeV n eq cm -2 [1]. Previous analysis of bias voltage scans (presented at IEEE Yokohama, 2025) has shown the VELO is at risk of exceeding the maximum 1000V bias voltage limit to remain at operational performance. Here, we present a data-driven simulation of clusters in the VELO, to predict the performance at the end of its lifetime. Extensive validation of the simulation to testbeam data is performed, with angle and bias voltage scans showing very good agreement. Furthermore, charge sharing via diffusion in the simulation is authenticated with the charge collection vs intra-pixel hit position for size 2 clusters. Excellent agreement is seen. Comparison to Run III data is presented, showing good correspondence with the installed sensor. Extrapolations of the sensor performance at 8x10 15 MeV n eq cm -2 are performed. Preliminary results estimate the hit efficiency to be 89.41±0.14\% and the spatial resolution to be 19.98±0.37μm (a 19.8% increase from non-irradiated). These results highlight the need to make use of beneficial annealing for the rest of the sensor lifetime, to ensure performance remains as good as possible.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 285Poster Number:NSS-01-285] Design of Readout Electronics for a CdZnTe Detector Prototype for Polar-orbiting Solar Hard X-ray Imaging Telescope (#2200)

sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Purple Mountain Observatory, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Nanjing, China [2] University of Science and Technology of China, School of Astronomy and Space Science, Nanjing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract To support the X-ray Imaging Telescope (XIT) onboard China's Solar Polar Orbiting Observatory, which aims to perform the first-ever imaging of the Sun polar regions and study high-energy processes in solar eruptions, we have developed a prototype readout electronics system for a CdZnTe hard X-ray detector. The system consists of a 2 mm thick CdZnTe detector with an effective area of 15 × 15 mm² segmented into four strip electrodes with switchable area ratios, a front-end electronics board employing the IDE4281 charge-sensitive preamplifier ASIC, and a FPGA-based data acquisition unit with integrated calibration and high-voltage supply. The IDE4281 chip provides 12 channels with programmable shaping times, self-triggering, and peak-hold outputs. In the readout prototype, the equivalent noise charge after common-mode noise subtraction ranges from 149 to 189 e⁻ across all channels. Using a ²⁴¹Am radioactive source, the detector demonstrates a full-width at half-maximum energy resolution of 4.92 keV at 59.5 keV, fulfilling the scientific requirement of better than 5 keV at that energy. These results validate the prototype design and establish the basis for the forthcoming X-ray imaging telescope instrument.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Lesmes (Autores: C. Lesmes , B. Bergmann , M. Beneš , P. Broulím , P. Burian , M. Farkaš , T. Kulhánek , P. Mánek , S. Pospíšil , O. Růžička , P. Smolyanskiy , O. Urban , J. Zich)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Czech Technical University in Prague, Institute of Experimental and Applied Physics, Prague, Czech Republic [2] Czech Technical University in Prague, Faculty of Nuclear Sciences and Physical Engineering, Prague, Czech Republic [3] University of West Bohemia, Faculty of Electrical Engineering, Pilsen, Czech Republic
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Since its installation, the Timepix3 detector network has demonstrated utility within the ATLAS cavern by providing radiation field measurements and relative luminosity monitoring. This work evaluates the performance and internal stability of the network during the entire LHC Run 3. To ensure robust monitoring and assess systematic uncertainties, three distinct algorithms were evaluated and compared: cluster counting, thermal neutron counting, and heavy and straight track counting. Clean signal was achieved by identifying and masking noisy pixels and by modeling and subtracting background activation by a recursive growth and decay model. Internal consistency was verified through both short-term (intra-fill) and long-term (yearly) stability analyses across detectors situated at different distances from the interaction point. The presented results demonstrate that the distributed Timepix3 network provides a stable and robust relative luminosity measurement, complementing primary ATLAS luminometers during Run 3.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 289Poster Number:NSS-01-289] Radiation Studies for the LHCb Upgrade II Detector: Impact of the Upgraded Electromagnetic Calorimeter and Muon System Shielding (#2517)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. E.R. Medaer (Autores: S. E.R. Medaer , G. Corti)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CERN, LHCb Collaboration, Geneva, Genève, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The LHCb Upgrade II, planned for Run5, will operate at a substantially higher luminosity than previous runs, motivating dedicated FLUKA simulations of the resulting mixed-field radiation environment. This work addresses the impact of two major changes: the upgraded Electromagnetic Calorimeter, referred to as PicoCal, and the shielding of the Muon System. The increased fraction of high-density material in the PicoCal central modules modifies shower development and neutron production, while additional shielding is required to preserve Muon System performance. All comparisons are made with respect to the same Run4 reference configuration without additional Muon System shielding. Two Muon System shielding solutions are evaluated: i) replacement of the Hadronic Calorimeter by an iron-and-concrete shield with borated-polyethylene plates upstream and downstream, and ii) retention of the present Hadronic Calorimeter followed by a ductile cast iron, borated-polyethylene and steel wall. The simulations show increased local neutron production around the PicoCal central modules, while the existing polyethylene-and-boron shield upstream of the calorimeter limits the impact on upstream sub-detectors. For the Muon System, both shielding strategies reduce the charged-particle fluence relevant for detector performance, with different spatial and particle-composition trade-offs. These results support the optimization of the LHCb Upgrade II layout and illustrate the role of detector radiation studies for shielding design in mixed-field high-energy physics environments.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 291Poster Number:NSS-01-291] Timing properties of the FARCOS detection system (#2838)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Guazzoni (Autores: A. Castoldi , C. Guazzoni , A. Mason , M. Pozzi , R. Zambolo)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Politecnico di Milano and INFN, Dipartimento di Elettronica, Informazione e Bioingegneria, Milano, Italy [2] INFN, Sezione di Milano, Milano, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract FARCOS is a Femtoscope Array for Correlation and Spectroscopy designed to perform studies of two- and multi-particle and Intermediate Mass Fragments (IMFs) correlations in heavy-ion collisions at Fermi energies with stable and radioactive beams. The FARCOS system is a modular assembly of up to 20 telescopes to be used in combination with 4π detectors like the CHIMERA multidetector. Each telescope features two Silicon detection layers (32 + 32 channels Double Side Silicon Strip Detectors 300μm and 1500μm thick and a third calorimetric stage, made of four truncated pyramidal CsI(Tl) crystals arranged in a 2 x 2 matrix). Particular care has been posed in the design of the frontend electronics for the different stages. For the first time we performed a detailed qualification of the timing properties of the FARCOS frontend electronics and of the different detection stages. The achievable resolution was optimized thanks to an accurate analysis of the waveform shape. The remarkable time resolution measured at zero pf capacitive input load, with the FARCOS frontend electronics, below 100 ps rms at 1.1 MeV injected charge on the 100 MeV full-scale energy range, thanks to the excellent energy resolution below 15 keV FWHM paves the way to widen the range of experiments in which the FARCOS system will be applied. The measured time resolution improves to 25 ps rms at 5 MeV injected charge. The selectable gain factor allows the extension of the full-scale energy range up to a gain factor of 0.5mV/MeV over the full-scale range of 1.1V, with a small compromise on the time resolution, translating in a dynamic range of more than 15bits. The INL keeps below 0.5% over the full dynamic range. The timing performance of the Silicon layers of the FARCOS telescopes was then qualified with a near-infrared pulsed laser system and with alpha particles. This contribution presents the results of this qualification together with some highlights of the recent applications of the FARCOS telescopes.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 293Poster Number:NSS-01-293] Thermal and In Situ annealing tests for SiPM radiation damage mitigation (#2917)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Bez Baruah (Autores: S. Bez Baruah , M. S. Ruzzarin , F. Acerbi , A. Gola)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Fondazione Bruno Kessler, CRS, Trento, Italy [2] University of Trento, Physics, Trento, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) are solid-state photodetectors increasingly employed in astrophysics and space missions due to their high photon detection efficiency (PDE), compactness, insensitivity to magnetic fields, and operation at relatively low bias voltages. However, exposure to radiation, through both Ionizing Energy Loss (IEL) and Non-Ionizing Energy Loss (NIEL) effects, can degrade their key performance parameters. To mitigate radiation-induced damage, annealing strategies have been explored. This work presents the results of two annealing tests performed on FBK SiPMs, after x-ray irradiation and proton irradiation, highlighting their respective advantages and limitations: (1) thermal annealing, involves storing the devices in a climatic chamber without active heating, while periodically performing electrical measurements to track recovery over time. (2) In-situ current annealing progressively increases the SiPM bias current to induce self-heating via resistive effects. Electrical measurements have been done after each step, and a thermocamera have been used to monitor device temperature.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 295Poster Number:NSS-01-295] Axial Reactivity Profile Measurement of Polaris Using CR-39 Nuclear Track Detectors (#2958)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Alawabdeh (Autores: S. Alawabdeh , P. Young , N. Kaneshige , W. Hennig , D. Cech , J. Peterson , R. Grazioso , M. Hua)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Helion Energy, Nuclear Diagnostics, Everett, Washington, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents the measurement of the axial neutron emission profile of the Polaris field-reversed configuration (FRC) fusion machine using CR-39 solid-state nuclear track detectors (SSNTDs). Passive detectors were deployed at multiple axial positions along the Polaris compression section, accumulating neutron-induced proton recoil tracks over several pulses of moderate yield, sufficiently low to resolve tracks. Chemical etching in 6M NaOH at 85°C for 2.5 hours revealed latent damage tracks, which were analyzed using a custom Python-based image processing pipeline incorporating a trained Random Forest classifier achieving 94.1% ± 2.2% cross-validation accuracy in neutron track identification. The resulting axial track density profile is symmetric and centrally peaked, in agreement with MCNP-simulated neutron dose distributions for a thermonuclear DT fusion source confined within the FRC plasmoid. The absence of asymmetric structure - characteristic of beam-target dominated reactions - provides compelling experimental evidence of spatially confined thermonuclear fusion on Polaris. This represents the first deployment of CR-39 diagnostics for reactivity profiling on a pulsed FRC machine and establishes passive track detectors as an effective tool for fusion burn characterization.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 297Poster Number:NSS-01-297] On-detector Electronics for the ATLAS Liquid Argon Calorimeter Phase-II Upgrade at the High-Luminosity LHC (#2989)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E.J. Molina Gonzalez (Autores: E.J. Molina Gonzalez , N. Nikiforou)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The ATLAS Liquid Argon (LAr) calorimeter readout electronics are being upgraded for operation at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC), where up to 200 proton-proton interactions per bunch crossing will significantly increase detector occupancy, trigger rates, and radiation levels. While the calorimeter detectors themselves remain unchanged, the complete readout electronics chain is being replaced. The upgraded on-detector electronics readout system continuously amplifies, shapes, digitizes, and transmits calorimeter signals from approximately 182000 channels at the 40 MHz bunch-crossing rate. The new Front-End Boards (FEB2) integrate custom radiation-hard ASICs including the ALFE2 preamplifier/shaper, the COLUTA analog-to-digital converter, and lpGBT optical communication devices. Prototype boards and ASICs have been developed and extensively tested in laboratory and integration environments. This contribution presents the architecture, development status, and recent performance results of the Phase-II front-end electronics for the ATLAS LAr calorimeter.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 299Poster Number:NSS-01-299] Airborne Measurement of Terrestrial Gamma-Ray Flashes with the High Elevation Radiation Array (#2287)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. J. Manfredi (Autores: J. J. Manfredi , J. M. Chaffin , V. Clagett , M. Rynders , J. Weinberg , W. Erwin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Air Force Institute of Technology, Department of Engineering Physics, Wright-Patterson AFB, Ohio, United States of America [2] California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo, Physics Department, San Luis Obispo, California, United States of America [3] Air Force Research Laboratory, 711th Human Performance Wing, Wright-Patterson AFB, Ohio, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study investigates the unique high-energy radiation environment of thunderstorms, focusing on terrestrial gamma-ray flashes (TGFs). Led by the Air Force Institute of Technology, the United States Air Force School of Aerospace Medicine, and the Air Force Research Laboratory, this effort deploys custom-built High Elevation Radiation Array (HERA) instruments aboard ten WC-130J "Hurricane Hunter" aircraft. These planes fly into hurricanes and tropical storms for the purpose of measuring weather data, potentially bringing them into proximity of TGF radiation. Each HERA unit contains a sodium iodide scintillator, a plastic scintillator, and associated data acquisition hardware. HERA represents the largest airborne campaign to date for near-source TGF observations and aims to improve understanding of TGF mechanisms, occurrence rates, and associated radiation risks to aircrew and equipment. All HERA detectors have been installed on aircraft and will collect data during the full 2026 Atlantic hurricane season.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 301Poster Number:NSS-01-301] Systematic X-ray irradiations of a back illuminated, HPGe, microstrip sensor. (#1420)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Thacker (Autores: D. Thacker , M. Borri , M. Buckland , W. Helsby , A. Hill , K. Sutowski)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] UKRI - Science & Technology Facilities Council, Technology Department, Warrington, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Back illuminated, HPGe, microstrip sensors are operated in the cryogenic detector system called XH. XH enables the collection of energy dispersive X-ray absorption spectra to investigate near-instantaneous structural variations in experimental samples. XH detects the transmitted radiation of a bright, single flash of X-rays that is delayed with respect to a laser pulse, which also hits the sample and creates an excited state of matter. Each strip in the HPGe sensor detects the intensity of a spectral component (∆E ∼1.5 eV) of the transmitted, dispersed polychromatic beam, which has a typical bandwidth of ∼1 keV. The HPGe sensor can be exposed to beam intensities as high as 1 × 10 13 ph/mm 2 /s from polychromatic beams with a central energy in the range ∼5 keV to ∼25keV. The operation in this radiation harsh condition benefits from a systematic irradiation campaign to investigate ageing effects created by Total Ionising Dose (TID). The TID effects on the HPGe sensor are mitigated by design by adopting a back illumination approach in order to shield the strip contacts, and by the selection of a proprietary, commercial lithographic process. XH was irradiated at the X-ray Irradiation Facility at Daresbury Laboratory (UK). The 1024 strip sensor was repeatedly exposed to X-rays in finite time steps. Total leakage and strip currents were monitored regularly with X-rays on and off. The X-ray peak energy was limited to 20 keV, which was fully absorbed in the 1.5 mm thick HPGe sensor. This protected the strip contacts from radiation. Beam collimation within the active area of the HPGe sensor showed a steady performance, which was immune from TID. Evidence of deterioration in surface leakage current was measured when the beam was hitting the sensor edge and its supporting PCB.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 303Poster Number:NSS-01-303] Energy-resolved Laue Diffraction: a New Tool for Crystal Structure determination (#1715)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. P. Siddons (Autores: D. P. Siddons , A. K. Rumaiz , M.D. Drakopoulos , N. Vo , Z. Zhong , A. J. Kuczewski , J. Kuczewski , J. Li , W. Chen)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Brookhaven National Laboratory, NSLS-II, Upton, New York, United States of America [2] Brookhaven National Laboratory, Instrumentation, Upton, New York, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract White beam Laue diffraction is well-known as a means to orient single-crystal samples, but its use as a structure-determining tool is less exploited. One of the difficulties with the method is its incomplete measurement of the diffraction vector. Only its direction can be determined, but not its length, since conventional instrumentation does not provide the diffracted beam energy. In this paper we propose to use a high-resolution energy resolving detector to provide that information, together with NSLS-II's HEX beamline, which has a spectral range up to 200keV. We have developed a series of microstrip germanium detectors, and present here some measurements using one of them together with a horizontal aperture to emulate a 192 x 1 pixel detector with 250 micrometer pixels. By scanning this device in one dimension we could simulate a 2-dimensional detector with good energy resolution,. We have further designed and built a custom detector for this purpose, which has 192x2 pixels, each 250 x 250 micrometers, and so does not need the aperture, and which requires half the number of measurements. Data collected with these detectors will be presented.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 305Poster Number:NSS-01-305] Pile-Up Resilient X-Ray Spectroscopy via Direct Sampling and Waveform Fitting in SDDs (#1993)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Abba (Autores: A. Abba , V. Arosio , P. Barcella , F. Caponio , M. Carminati , E. Carlotti , S. Carsi , A. Cusimano , C. E. Fiorini , M. Lazzari , B. Pedretti , E. Proserpio , C. Tintori , Y. Venturini)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Nuclear Instruments SRL, Lambrugo, Italy [2] Politecnico di Milano, DEIB, Milano, Italy [3] CAEN SPA, Viareggio, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A fully digital readout architecture is described for high-throughput X-ray spectroscopy with silicon drift detectors (SDDs). The core challenge is the large-amplitude voltage ramp produced by transistor reset preamplifiers, which conventionally prevents direct digitization at spectroscopic resolution. In this work, sampling the preamplifier output with a 20-bit SAR ADC achieves a dynamic range exceeding 10⁶, eliminating any analog conditioning stage upstream of the digitizer. Throughput is sustained by combining four converters in a time-interleaved scheme, yielding an aggregate sampling rate of 160 Msps. A Zynq SoC provides the processing backbone, performing inter-channel timing alignment, gain equalization, and concurrent execution of the signal processing pipelines. Two energy estimation algorithms run in parallel on the digitised data: a ramp-corrected trapezoidal filter and a model-based least-squares fitter that uses linear regression over the full inter-event sample record, remaining accurate even when pulse separation shrinks to sub-microsecond intervals. Experimental characterisation with ARDESIA multi-pixel SDD arrays and KETEK single-pixel detectors yields an energy resolution of 120.7 eV FWHM at low rate, 150 eV at 1 Mcps, and 180 eV at 2 Mcps, with live time exceeding 90% throughout.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 307Poster Number:NSS-01-307] High-resolution Germanium Detector system for Fluorescence-Mode X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy (#2626)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. K. Rumaiz (Autores: A. K. Rumaiz , F. Capocasa , A. J. Kuczewski , G. Pinaroli , T. Krings , B. Ravel , D. P. Siddons)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Brookhaven National Laboratory, NSLS II, Upton, New York, United States of America [2] Brookhaven National Laboratory, Instrumentation Department, Upton, New York, United States of America [3] Forschungszentrum, Jülich, Germany [4] National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, Maryland, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Fluorescence-mode X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy (XAS) at high photon energies require detectors with both high stopping power and excellent energy resolution to measure weak element-specific fluorescence signals. Conventional silicon-based detectors suffer from poor absorption efficiency above ~20 keV, while most high-𝒁 semiconductor materials such as cadmium telluride (CdTe), cadmium zinc telluride (CZT), and gallium arsenide (GaAs) have largely been developed for imaging applications with comparatively limited spectroscopic performance. In contrast, Germanium combines excellent stopping power with superior intrinsic energy resolution owing to its low Fano factor and favorable charge transport properties, making it particularly attractive for spectroscopy in the 15-100 keV range. Here we report the development, fabrication, and characterization of Gepta-EX, a compact multi-channel high-purity germanium (HPGe) detector system designed for fluorescence-mode XAS. Gepta-EX incorporates a monolithic seven-channel HPGe pixel array integrated with low-noise CUBE charge-sensitive preamplifiers inside a thermally isolated compact cryostat operating near 90K. The detector achieves energy resolutions of 218 eV at 5.9 keV using an 55 Fe source and 373 eV at 59.5 keV using an 241 Am source, with uniform response across all channels. By avoiding the escape-peak interference commonly associated with silicon detectors while maintaining stable high-resolution performance at elevated X-ray energies, Gepta-EX provides a powerful platform for high-energy X-ray spectroscopy and fluorescence-mode XAS applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 309Poster Number:NSS-01-309] Visualization of beta-emitting nuclides in water using a CCD camera and CaF₂ scintillator (#1462)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Morishita (Autores: Y. Morishita , M. Kanno)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Japan Atomic Energy Agency, Collaborative Laboratories for Advanced Decommissioning Science (CLADS), Futaba County, Japan [2] PESCO Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract At nuclear facilities such as decommissioning sites and reprocessing plants, continuous monitoring of radioactive liquid waste is essential to prevent the spread of contamination. While gamma-emitting radionuclides can be detected relatively easily using gamma-ray detectors, radionuclides emitting only alpha or beta radiation are difficult to measure remotely because these particles are strongly absorbed in water. Conventional liquid scintillation counting requires sample collection and pretreatment, making real-time monitoring difficult. In this study, a real-time visualization method for beta-emitting nuclides in water was developed using a calcium fluoride (CaF₂) scintillator and an Electron Multiplying CCD (EM-CCD) camera. The scintillator was designed with a water-permeable structure to allow contaminated water to flow through it, enabling direct detection of beta radiation in water. Radiation source measurements were performed in a dark room using a 90Sr-90Y beta source. Scintillation light generated in the CaF₂ scintillator was captured by the EM-CCD camera. The results demonstrated that the position of the beta source could be successfully visualized with acquisition times as short as 1 s, and the detected intensity increased with measurement time. Measurements conducted while moving the source confirmed that changes in source position could also be visualized, indicating the capability to monitor moving contamination in water. In addition, water infiltration tests confirmed that water could successfully pass through the scintillator structure. These results demonstrate that the proposed system is promising for real-time monitoring and visualization of beta-emitting radionuclides in radioactive liquid waste and aquatic environments.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 311Poster Number:NSS-01-311] Diagnosing Mechanisms for Charged Particle Attenuation Enhancement in Nanostructured Materials (#1508)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. P. Speck (Autores: N. P. Speck , G. J. Grey , D. A. Vecchio , K. A. Cotterill , A. I. Taub , M. D. Hammig)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Michigan, Nuclear Engineering and Radiological Sciences Department, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America [2] University of Michigan, Materials Science and Engineering Department, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a methodology for measuring the trajectories of high-energy electrons through materials utilizing a transmission electron microscope (TEM). This novel technique is implemented to diagnose and quantify the mechanism for enhanced radiation attenuation via nanostructures. Rather than an imaging technique, the TEM is applied to radiation shielding measurements as an adaptable electron source with functionality for various beam energies, amperage, alignments, and exposure times alongside an array of precise electron detectors. By utilizing energy filtering and direct electron detection capabilities, scattering profiles are measured with minimal background contributions. This TEM method is leveraged to describe particle transport in nanostructures. Palladium nanoparticles at various monodisperse sizes are synthesized via heat injection and deposited into an epoxy matrix. The palladium epoxy nanocomposites are sectioned with an ultramicrotome to thicknesses of 70 to 1000 nm containing nanoparticle sizes of 5 to 50 nm at 20% of the total weight fraction. Scattering profile measurements at various beam energies are conducted with a variety of sample thicknesses, nanoparticle sizes, and composite fractions. Scattering profile measurements also include bulk, homogeneous palladium samples in contrast to nanomaterials composed of identical atomic percentages. Simulation of the experimental scattering profiles demonstrate an understanding for the phenomena behind nanostructured attenuation enhancement, bolstering advanced nuclear technology via a foundational description for particle transport in nanostructures.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 313Poster Number:NSS-01-313] Monolithic integration of cooling microchannels in all-silicon ladders for vertex detectors (#1940)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Fernández-Tejero (Autores: J. Fernández-Tejero , A. Dias , M. Duch , R. Mas , C. Orero , M. Vos , M. Ullán)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Centro Nacional de Microelectrónica (IMB-CNM, CSIC), Cerdanyola del Vallés, Spain [2] Instituto de Física Corpuscular (IFIC, CSIC), Paterna, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract New generation of vertex detectors must have excellent thermo-mechanical stability, and all-silicon ladders are considered as promising solutions for future detectors. However, power consumption asymmetries between the active area and periphery can induce large temperature gradients, and in some cases a combination of air and liquid cooling will be required to achieve homogeneous thermal profiles. Microchannel cooling offers a competitive alternative to traditional cooling systems. The short thermal path between the heat load and sink gives an increased thermal evacuation performance, combined with the reduced material needed for the integrated microchannels and the reduced Coefficient of Thermal Expansion mismatch between the cooling and sensor materials to obtain an optimized cooling for radiation detectors. The development of the technology needed for the integration of the sensor with the microchannels in a single piece is an ambitious challenge, as the conditions for the microchannel formation must be compatible with the sensor, requiring the optimization of the fabrication to ensure the compatibility with CMOS processes. As a demonstrator, all-silicon ladder prototypes with integrated cooling microchannels are presented. Power consumptions for the active area and periphery of the ladders are emulated using integrated aluminum heaters. The bulk in the active area is thinned from 600 to 50 microns, and the design of the microchannels cooling circuit, integrated in the periphery of the ladder, is optimized using finite-element simulation packages. Variations of prototype ladders with different sizes, microchannel dimensions, and integrated using different wafer bonding techniques are fabricated and evaluated in detail in this work.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 315Poster Number:NSS-01-315] A spin-selective detector for quantum sensing with neutrons (#1977)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Neulinger (Autores: T. Neulinger , S. Degenkolb , R. Gernhäuser , R. Georgii , C. Grüner , H. Haese , S. Kempf , T. Sandmann , J. Tremmel , M. Wegner)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Technische Universität München, Forschungs-Neutronenquelle Heinz Maier-Leibnitz, Garching, Bavaria, Germany [2] Universität Heidelberg, Physikalisches Institut, Heidelberg, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [3] Technische Universität München, E12 Dense and Strange Hadronic Matter, Garching, Germany [4] S-DH GmbH, Heidelberg, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [5] Institute of Micro- and Nanoelectronics Systems, Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Karlsruhe, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [6] Institute for Data Processing and Electronics, Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Karlsruhe, Baden-Württemberg, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present performance calculations for a proof-of-concept, spin-selective neutron detector in which the magnetic field of a microfabricated planar superconducting coil controls the quantum mechanical absorption resonance in a multilayer structure. For first tests with cold neutrons, depolarization calculations favor a parallel over a meander geometry, the latter of which should nevertheless offer enhanced detector sensitivity in the ultracold neutron regime. Simulations predict that spin contrasts can be efficiently demonstrated using polarized cold neutron reflectometry at existing facilities.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 317Poster Number:NSS-01-317] Higher-Order Gain-Drift Correction in Magnetic Microcalorimeters for Decay Energy Spectrometry (#2186)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Wood (Autores: R. Wood , I. Jovanovic , G.-B. Kim)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California, Berkeley, Nuclear Engineering, Berkeley, California, United States of America [2] Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Livermore, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Metallic magnetic calorimeters can provide excellent energy resolution for decay-energy spectrometry of alpha- and beta-emitting radionuclides, but temperature-dependent gain drift can broaden peaks during long acquisitions. This work compares two post-acquisition correction models for data acquired with a gold-erbium paramagnetic sensor in the MAGNETO-ν neutrino experiment. The pre-trigger baseline is used as an event-by-event proxy for detector temperature. The lower-order model includes linear baseline dependence, whereas the higher-order model adds baseline-energy cross terms and second-order baseline dependence to capture nonlinear drift. Model parameters are estimated with a likelihood-based fit to known plutonium and americium reference peaks, and each event is calibrated by solving the fitted response model for deposited energy. Performance is evaluated from isotope-resolved peak widths in the corrected alpha-decay region of the spectrum. Across the reference groups considered here, the higher-order model produces consistently narrower fitted peaks, with the clearest improvements in the higher-statistical-weight isotope groups. These results indicate that higher-order baseline terms can improve spectral resolution when baseline-correlated drift is present.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 319Poster Number:NSS-01-319] Pixelated Array for Low-Energy Electron Beam Mapping (#2374)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Turqueti (Autores: M. Turqueti , O. Aggarwal)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Engineering Division, Berkeley, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present a low-energy electron beam position detector based on a segmented capacitive sensing architecture designed for precision monitoring of electron beams in the 500 eV to 2000 eV energy range. The detector employs a 3 mm × 3 mm capacitive sensor structure optimized for non-invasive beam position measurements with micrometer scale spatial resolution. Low-energy electron beams present unique diagnostic challenges due to their sensitivity to electromagnetic perturbations, beam spreading, and reduced signal levels. Conventional beam diagnostics often suffer from limited sensitivity or introduce disturbances that alter the beam trajectory. The proposed detector addresses these limitations through a pixelated capacitive pickup array combined with low-noise front-end electronics and differential signal processing techniques. Variations in induced charge distribution along the sensing electrodes are used to reconstruct the transverse beam position with high precision while maintaining minimal interaction with the electron beam. The array enables accurate position tracking over extended beam paths and improves sensitivity to small beam displacements. Analytical modeling and preliminary experimental characterization demonstrate that the sensor can resolve beam motion at the micrometer level across the targeted energy range. The detector response was evaluated as a function of beam energy, beam current, and electrode geometry, showing stable operation and high linearity under low-energy conditions. Noise mitigation strategies, including shielding and optimized capacitance matching, were implemented to preserve signal integrity and reduce environmental interference. This detector architecture is well suited for applications requiring compact, high-resolution diagnostics of low-energy electron beams, including micro cathode ray magnetic probes, electron optics experiments, and vacuum electronic devices.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 321Poster Number:NSS-01-321] Self-Powered Wireless Communication via Ambient Gamma-Ray Harvesting at Fukushima Daiichi (#2629)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Fujiwara (Autores: T. Fujiwara , Y. Shoji , H. Kimura , S. Mae , H. Yoshimochi , K. Kawasaki , H. Kawamura , K. Miyako)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST), Tskuba, Japan [2] Chiyoda Technol Corporation, Tokyo, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Reliable long-term monitoring in nuclear decommissioning facilities is hampered by the absence of permanent power infrastructure and by the radiation fields that degrade conventional electronics. We present a scintillator-photovoltaic converter that captures ambient gamma radiation and transforms it into electrical energy sufficient for periodic wireless data transmission. The converter pairs a 750 cm³ CsI(Tl) crystal with a compact GaInP photovoltaic array mounted on a single end face, following a "large absorber, minimal semiconductor" strategy.) On-site evaluation inside a contaminated-material storage building at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant (~35 mSv/h) produced 273 nW per module. Two parallel modules, combined with ultra-low-power energy management and a sub-GHz radio, achieved seven autonomous transmission bursts totaling 32 packets over a 30 m link during a three-hour observation window-without any external power supply or dedicated radioactive source.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 323Poster Number:NSS-01-323] Optimizing Tritium Uptake and Detection Sensitivity in a Metal-Hydride Gas Detector (#2734)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T.-H. Lin (Autores: P. Kandlakunta , L. R. Cao , T.-H. Lin , R. Young , A. Hoffman)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The Ohio State University, Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Columbus, Ohio, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Metal-Hydride and Gas (MEGA) detector is a recently proposed approach for high-selectivity tritium (T 2 ) monitoring that combines hydrogen (H 2 ) storage metals with gas proportional counting. Previous work demonstrated the feasibility of T 2 absorption in palladium (Pd), formation of metal-tritide, and subsequent T 2 release into a proportional counter for measurement. In this work, we investigate pathways toward improving the overall detection efficiency of the MEGA detector through optimization of T 2 absorption, retention, desorption, and counting characteristics. A simplified efficiency framework is introduced to identify the dominant efficiency-limiting processes. The pressure-composition behavior of the Pd-H system is examined to evaluate approaches for enhancing isotope uptake at low T 2 partial pressures through reduced operating temperature and increased local pressure. Preliminary Monte Carlo simulations of tritium β-particle transport in Pd indicate strong self-absorption effects, with the simulated maximum penetration depth of 18.6-keV β-particles in Pd limited to a few hundred nanometers. These results support the need for optimized Pd geometry and efficient thermal desorption approaches to maximize gas-phase T 2 release and proportional counting efficiency. The present work establishes a quantitative framework for future optimization of MEGA detector sensitivity for environmental and nuclear safeguards applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 325Poster Number:NSS-01-325] Basic Development of a Wide-Field EUV Polarimeter for High-Energy Transient Sources (#3164)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Kuwabara (Autores: S. Kuwabara , S. Gunji , K. Chiba , A. Takahashi , M. Kitaura , E. Nakamura)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yamagata University, Graduate School of Science and Engineering, Yamagata, Japan [2] Yamagata University, Faculty of Science, Yamagata, Japan [3] Institute for Molecular Science, UVSOR Synchrotron Facility / Beamline Technical Staff, Aichi, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Polarization observations in extreme ultraviolet (EUV) band have not yet been achieved because it remains technically difficult to develop wide-field EUV detectors with sufficient sensitivity. However, EUV polarization measurements are expected to provide important insights into the emission mechanisms of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) and ultraviolet flashes associated with supernova explosions. In this study, we propose a novel EUV polarimeter based on Lobster-Eye Optics (LEO), which combines a wide field of view with polarization sensitivity. Optical simulations show that EUV reflectivity on metal surfaces strongly depends on polarization. For example, at 40 eV and an incident angle of 75° on a gold-coated mirror, the reflectivity is about 40% for p-polarization and 60% for s-polarization, respectively. This difference produces an asymmetric cross-shaped image on the focal plane detector depending on the polarization direction. To verify this principle, we developed a test chamber and conducted a synchrotron radiation experiment using a gold-coated mirror and a microchannel plate (MCP) detector. By rotating the mirror around the beam axis, we measured the modulation of the MCP count rate and evaluated the detector modulation factor. The experimental results are presented and discussed in this paper.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 327Poster Number:NSS-01-327] Cryogenic and Underground Performance of the Diffuse BGO Scintillator Array in the KAPAE Phase II Detector (#3216)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Jeong (Autores: D. Jeong , H.J. Kim , J. Cho , H. Park)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Kyungpook National University, Center for High Energy Physics, Daegu, Republic of Korea [2] Kyungpook National University, Department of Physics, Daegu, Republic of Korea [3] 2Central Research Institute, Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power Co., Ltd., DaeJeon, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The KNU Advanced Positronium Annihilation Experiment (KAPAE) Phase II searches for invisible positronium decays using a compact 4π BGO scintillation calorimeter. Stable operation, efficient photon collection, and low-background performance are essential for this rare-event measurement. We report the cryogenic and underground performance of a chemically diffused BGO scintillator array developed for KAPAE Phase II. The BGO crystal surfaces were chemically diffused to enhance photon collection and coupled to SiPM-based readout for low-temperature operation. At approximately −37 °C, reduced SiPM thermal noise and improved light collection yielded an energy resolution of 9% at 662 keV. The scintillation decay time was approximately 960 ns. This performance improves upon earlier BGO-based positronium calorimeters, including the ETH Zurich experiment, which reported an energy resolution of approximately 15% [1]. The detector was installed and operated at Yemilab underground. A continuous 120-day run demonstrated stable detector response, trigger operation, and long-term data-taking capability under cryogenic conditions. Calibration data were used to tune and validate a Geant4 detector simulation, which was applied to evaluate energy containment, gamma-ray leakage, and the expected sensitivity for invisible para-positronium decay searches. Based on measured performance and validated simulations, KAPAE Phase II achieves the expected sensitivity of 10−8 for invisible para-positronium branching-ratio measurements. This study demonstrates that chemically diffused BGO scintillator arrays can provide stable, high-resolution calorimetric performance under cryogenic underground conditions.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 329Poster Number:NSS-13-329] Organic Scintillator Light Yield Models for Sub-MeV Neutrons in EJ301D and d-stilbene (#1369)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. A. Irvine (Autores: C. A. Irvine , T. C. Borgwardt , R. A. Weldon Jr. , J. Mattingly)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Los Alamos National Laboratory, NEN-2, Los Alamos, New Mexico, United States of America [2] North Carolina State University, Nuclear Engineering, Raleigh, North Carolina, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Six commonly used models for neutron induced light yield in organic scintillators were fit and analyzed using measurements of a 2.54 cm diameter by 2.54 cm long right circular cylinder of EJ301D and a (5.08 cm)3 custom made cube of deuterated trans-stilbene-d12 (d-stilbene). Measured neutron energies spanned 300 keV to 2200 keV for the EJ301D scintillator and 200 keV to 2500 keV in d-stilbene. The model fits and experimental analysis methods were verified by examining the agreement between the predicted light output spectrum and the measured light output spectrum for several simulated quasi-monoenergetic neutron sources. Birks model inaccurately predicted highly quenched light yield for sub-MeV neutrons in both scintillators. The addition of a second order quenching term to the Birks model by Chou significantly improved the models accuracy, however its behavior is non-physical if extrapolated beyond the measured neutron energies. The model derived by Voltz accurately fit the measurement of both scintillators for all measured neutron energies. Further investigation into the ability to extrapolate based on these semi-empiric models would be valuable given the non-physical behavior of well-fitting models.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-02-01] Dead time and self-absorption corrections at high uranium grade for total count rate gamma probes (#1014)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Pérot (Autores: B. Pérot , T. Marchais , A. Miloudi , H. Toubon , T. Allen , R. Mieszkalski , Y. Bensedik , S. Hocquet , A. Gruel , C. Besnard-Vauterin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CEA, DES, IRESNE, Nuclear Measurement Laboratory, Saint-Paul-lez-Durance, France [2] Orano Mining, Châtillon, France [3] Orano Mining, CIME, Bessines-sur-Gartempe, France [4] Orano Canada Inc., Saskatoon, Canada
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In high-grade uranium mines such as the Orano Canada Inc. (OCI) operated McClean Lake Mine, gamma logging probes deal with a non-linear behavior due to both gamma self-absorption in uranium and electronics dead-time, which may lead to a significant underestimation of the resources. Up to now, quantitative uranium grade measurements were conducted through coring and subsequent laboratory analysis. However, the SABRE mining method involves larger diameter drilling, making systematic coring impractical due to the additional costs. Therefore, Orano Mining and CEA have developed and qualified a combined correction for electronics dead-time and gamma self- absorption. These phenomena are significant above a uranium grade of about 1% w/w U, leading to huge resource underestimations at high grade, for instance nearly a factor 3 at 50% w/w U, just for self-absorption. In this work, we detail the tests conducted at Orano La Hague irradiator to estimate the dead-time of different NaI(Tl) and Geiger Muller probes, the MCNP Monte Carlo calculations to assess uranium self- absorption on a large uranium grade range, a new method developed to jointly correct for these two phenomena, and its experimental qualification through the comparison of gamma logging with core sample analyses from high-grade boreholes.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-02-02] Identification and Reconstruction of Pair-Production Events in an Electron-Tracking Compton Camera via 3D Track Analysis (#1466)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Sato (Autores: T. Sato , A. Takada , H. Yoneda , S. Deguchi , S. Okumura , M. Abe , K. Matsunaga , T. Nakamori , H. Iiyama , S. Suzuki , T. Sawano , Y. Munakata , K. Okamoto , M. Mori , T. Oka , Y. Mizumura , K. Hamaguchi , J. Kushida , S. Kurosawa , K. Miuchi , T. Tanimori)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Kyoto University, Department of Physics II, Graduate School of Science, Kyoto, Japan [2] Yamagata University, Department of Science, Faculty of Science, Yamagata, Japan [3] Kanazawa University, Division of Mathematical and Physical Sciences, Graduate School of Natural Science and Technology, Kanazawa, Japan [4] Osaka Metropolitan University, Graduate School of Science, Osaka, Japan [5] Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg, Astronomy / AG Siegert, Würzburg, Bavaria, Germany [6] ISAS/JAXA, Institute of Space and Astronautical Science, Department of Interdisciplinary Space Science, Sagamihara, Japan [7] UMBC, Center for Space Sciences and Technology, Catonsville, Maryland, United States of America [8] Tokai University, Department of Physics, School of Science, Hiratsuka, Japan [9] Nagoya University, Department of Energy Engineering and Science, Graduate School of Engineering, Nagoya, Japan [10] Kobe University, Graduate School of Science, Kobe, Japan [11] Kitasato University, School of Frontier Engineering, Sagamihara, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The 1-30 MeV gamma ray observation holds key astrophysical signatures-nucleosynthesis, cosmic-ray interactions, and possible dark-matter signatures-yet remains the least explored window in high-energy astronomy. The electron-tracking Compton camera (ETCC) tracks the recoil electron to constrain the photon direction to a single point on the sky, enabling bijective imaging. We are developing the ETCC for SMILE-3, planned for 2028, extending the observation band to 5 MeV via a double-hit analysis. Beyond this, reconstructing pair-production events inside the time projection chamber (TPC) offers a further extension above ∼ 10 MeV and enables cross-calibration between Compton and pair-production channels in the same detector-an important advantage for MeV observations, where background control is critical. Additionally, identifying pair events removes a source of misreconstruction in the double-hit analysis, where atmospheric gamma rays above 10 MeV undergoing pair production are misidentified as Compton events and leak through the zenith-angle cut. We developed a geometry-based algorithm to identify pair-production events from the 3D point-cloud of TPC tracks. Voxelization and DBSCAN separate track clusters from noise; local PCA estimates direction vectors, and intersecting pairs define vertex candidates evaluated by a log-likelihood ratio (LLR) test. Accepted events are reconstructed from the vector sum of the two track directions. We validated the algorithm using inverse-Compton-scattered gamma rays at 3.3, 4.8, and 6.6 MeV from the UVSOR BL1U beamline. At 6.6 MeV, the 68% containment angle was 16.2◦ for beam-synchronous events and 12.0◦ for asynchronous events, consistent with the nuclear-recoil kinematic limit. Monte Carlo simulations with the SMILE-3 geometry are underway to quantify identification efficiency and leakage improvement.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-02-03] Design of a 2D neutron and gamma imager based on CPRE64 (#1589)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Zhao (Autores: C. Zhao , J. Han , J. Ren , K. Wang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Sichuan University, Institute of Nuclear Science and Technology, Chengdu, China [2] Harbin Engineering University, College of Physics and Optoelectronic Engineering, Harbin, China [3] Chinese Academy of Sciences, Institute of High Energy Physics, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dual gamma and neutron imaging is promising owing to their complementary characteristics, and has been widely applied in nuclear material monitoring, defect analysis of aerospace materials, and cultural heritage authentication. A gamma and neutron imager with an active area of about 20 cm × 20 cm is currently under development. The imager employs a home-developed Ce 3+ -doped lithium glass scintillator coupled to 4096 silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), each with a size of 3 mm × 3 mm. To achieve optimal imaging performance, each SiPM is individually read out using a newly custom-designed 64-channel application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC), designated CPRE64. A total of 64 CPRE64 chips are integrated into the system to read out the 4096 SiPM channels. This paper introduces the overall design of the two-dimensional (2D) neutron and gamma imager. A 2D neutron and gamma imager prototype, using a 25 mm × 25 mm × 5 mm scintillator coupled to an 8 × 8 SiPM array (3 mm × 3 mm pixel size), has been fabricated and characterized. The scintillator exhibits a light yield of approximately 4700 photon/MeV and an energy resolution of 14.5% for 662 keV gamma rays. Meanwhile, it provides a high light yield of roughly 7058 photon/neutron, which is approximately 1.18 times that of the reference GS20 glass. The baseline variation across CPRE64 channels was measured to be ± 10%, spanning from 1.3V to 1.7V, whereas the channel uniformity of the CPRE64 channels exceeded 90%. The prototype has been successfully used for gamma and neutron imaging, achieving an experimental neutron spatial resolution better than 1mm.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-02-04] Evaluation of a High-Efficiency Portable Compton-Imaging System for Radioactive Waste Characterization and Nuclear Decommissioning (#1393)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 V. Babiano-Suárez (Autores: V. Babiano-Suárez , J. Balibrea-Correa , J. Lerendegui-Marco , I. Ladarescu , P. Torres-Sánchez , A. Tarifeño-Saldivia , G. Cortés , J.L. Leganés-Nieto , C. Domingo-Pardo)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto de Física Corpuscular (CSIC - Universitat de Valencia), Experimental Nuclear Physics, Valencia, Spain [2] Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya, Escola Tècnica Superior d'Enginyeria Industrial de Barcelona (ETSEIB), Barcelona, Spain [3] ENRESA, Empresa Nacional de Residuos radiactivos, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Nuclear energy remains a pivotal low-carbon alternative for mitigating climate change, yet the management of radioactive waste presents significant technical and economic challenges. Optimizing waste characterization is essential to minimize disposal volumes and ensure safe decommissioning. This work evaluates a high-efficiency, portable Compton camera designed for the visualization and quantification of low- and intermediate-level waste (LILW). The system was validated through three extensive field campaigns at the El Cabril disposal facility and the Santa María de Garoña nuclear power plant in Spain. These evaluations encompassed diverse waste containers and isotopic inventories to assess characterization performance in real industrial environments. Our findings demonstrate the robustness of Compton imaging, particularly regarding detection efficiency and reduced acquisition times. The system's performance was enhanced by integrating computer-vision techniques with GPU-accelerated Maximum-Likelihood Expectation Maximization (MLEM) algorithms, enabling real-time radiological-visual fusion. Furthermore, we demonstrate the feasibility of 3D tomographic reconstructions derived from multi-pose measurements. A significant highlight is the first field deployment of GNVision, a novel dual-particle imager for simultaneous neutron and gamma-ray mapping, aimed at identifying actinide-bearing residues. These results underscore the potential of advanced imaging to streamline waste classification and enhance safety in decommissioning workflows.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-02-05] Development of a high-sensitivity portable gamma-ray imaging system for identifying radioactive material carriers (#1453)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Lee (Autores: G. Lee , J. Lee , T. Eom , J. Cho , S. Jang , C.H. Kim)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Hanyang University, Nuclear engineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Gamma-ray imaging is an emerging technology to identify individuals smuggling radioactive materials at international points of entry. However, imaging moving subjects requires high efficiency due to the limited data acquisition time as sources pass the imaging system. We developed a high-sensitivity gamma camera named the portable fast gamma imager (pFGI). The pFGI integrates an imaging module, an RGB-D camera, and other components into an enclosure. The imaging module combines Compton and coded aperture modalities using two position-sensitive detectors and a MURA coded aperture mask. Each detector comprises a monolithic NaI(Tl) scintillator (14.6×14.6×2.5 cm 3 ) coupled to a 3×3 square-type photomultiplier tube array. The detectors are placed 16 cm apart, with the mask 6 cm in front of the front detector. To achieve superior imaging performance across a broad energy range, a hybrid imaging method was employed, which acquires coded aperture and Compton images, respectively, and then fuses them via pixel-wise multiplication. Furthermore, an AI-based motion-compensated method was used to integrate data along the moving subject's trajectory. The YOLOv11 and BoT-SORT algorithms were applied to the RGB images acquired from the RGB-D camera to extract displacement vectors for each subject; then, the radiation image for each subject was translated and fused according to the trajectories. The pFGI achieved a 7° angular resolution and high sensitivity, imaging the location of a 137Cs source, producing an incremental dose rate of 0.1 µSv/h within 1 s. Additionally, in a dynamic multi-person scenario, the imager successfully and continuously imaged the moving source and identified the source carrier among multiple people. These results highlight the pFGI as a robust solution for national security.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-02-06] Development of a new gamma-ray spectrometer for measurements inside reservoirs (#1461)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Morishita (Autores: Y. Morishita , T. Yamada , K. Kajiyama)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Japan Atomic Energy Agency, Collaborative Laboratories for Advanced Decommissioning Science (CLADS), Futaba County, Japan [2] Japan Radiation Engineering Co. Ltd, Hitachi, Japan [3] NUCLEAR ENGINEERING Co. ,Ltd.,, Tokai-mura, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Radioactive materials released during the accident at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station were deposited not only on land surfaces but also in aquatic environments such as irrigation ponds. Monitoring radiation levels in these environments is important for environmental assessment and decontamination activities. In this study, a waterproof gamma-ray spectrometer based on a Ce-doped Gd₂Si₂O₇ (Ce:GPS) scintillator coupled with a photomultiplier tube was developed for underwater radiation measurements. The detector employed a 10 mm × 10 mm Ce:GPS scintillator and an FPGA-based data acquisition system for event-by-event signal processing and energy spectrum acquisition. To enable pond-bottom measurements, the detector was integrated into a pipe structure approximately 4 m in length. Field measurements were conducted in an irrigation pond in Fukushima Prefecture, where the detector was submerged and placed on the pond bottom. A clear 662 keV photopeak originating from cesium-137 was observed, and the measured energy resolution was 9.8% FWHM. Energy spectra were also measured at different heights above the pond bottom. The cesium-137 photopeak was clearly detected at the bottom and at 50 cm above the bottom, whereas scattered gamma-ray components became dominant at greater heights because of attenuation and scattering in water. The results demonstrate that the developed waterproof Ce:GPS spectrometer is effective for in-situ underwater gamma-ray measurements and radionuclide identification in aquatic environments contaminated by radioactive cesium.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-03-01] Dual Time-Over-Threshold Energy and PSD Readout of SiPMs Using FPGA-Based TDCs (#1724)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Nowack (Autores: A. Nowack , J. Leland , E. Brubaker , J. Steele , M. Sweany)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Sandia National Laboratories, Dept 08647 - Radiation and Nuclear Detection Systems, Livermore, California, United States of America [2] University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, Department of Nuclear, Plasma, and Radiological Engineering, Urbana, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Independent readout of highly pixelated organic scintillator detectors is needed for next-generation associated particle imaging, neutron radiography, and single-volume scatter cameras. Field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) are an attractive solution as they have hundreds to thousands of IO pins and can be programmed for a variety of applications while minimizing cost as compared to ASICs. We detail a dual time-over-threshold (ToT) method for measuring the deposited energy and pulse width of gamma and neutron interactions in scintillator using a Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) realized with an FPGA and minimal external components. We compare a simple DC threshold and an active feedback rising edge signal for PSD and energy estimation. Simulated ToT results using digitized data are presented, with hardware details for an upcoming data campaign. For each circuit, the performance of energy resolution and PSD capability is weighed against the complexity and power requirements of the external analog components. In this work we present each of these approaches for SiPM readout, detail current progress, and experimental results.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-03-02] Development of Readout Electronics for a SiPM-Based Compton Camera (#2016)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Brunamonti (Autores: A. Brunamonti , B. Morellato , F. Ghisio , G. Borghi , M. Carminati , G. Llosá , A. Iltis , C. Fiorini)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Politecnico di Milano, Dipartimento di Elettronica, Informazione and Bioingegneria, Milano, Italy [2] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Milano, Milano, Italy [3] Instituto de Fisica Corpuscolar (IFIC, CSIC-UV), Paterma, Spain [4] Damavan Imaging, Troyes, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work, conducted within the framework of the AIDER project, presents the design and preliminary characterization of an electronics readout architecture for SiPM-based Compton cameras (CCs) in nuclear applications. The system includes two front-end units, serving the absorber and the scatterer layers. Each module integrates four GAMMA ASICs to interface with up to 64 SiPMs per layer, performing individual charge integration while providing an aggregated sum-current output. To mitigate amplitude-walk effects over the broad energy spectra typical of Compton imaging, time stamps are extracted by a custom designed Constant Fraction Discriminator (CFD) circuit. A central FPGA with embedded Time-to-Digital Converters (TDCs) synchronizes energy and timing data across both layers. A pre-trained Artificial Neural Network (ANN) is embedded directly into the FPGA logic to provide real-time estimation of the interaction position, reducing data throughput. SiPM are biased by a custom module that dynamically compensates for temperature fluctuations. The electronics, coupled with a 25 mm x 25 mm x 5 mm LaBr3 scintillator and a 16 SiPMs tile, yielded an energy resolution of 3.6% FWHM at 662 keV. Preliminary characterization of the CFD circuit with current pulses injected into the ASICs yielded a 140 ps resolution at 511 keV maintaining a sub nanosecond resolution down to 45 keV. The amplitude walk on such dynamic range was limited to 2.15 ns.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-03-03] High Count-Rate Modular Readout System for SiPM-Based Gamma-Ray Detectors (#2622)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Forgione (Autores: A. Forgione , M. Piroddi , C. Riboldi , E. Ronconi , K. Urban , F. Garzetti , G. Borghi , M. Carminati , A. Geraci , C. E. Fiorini)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Politecnico di Milano, DEIB, Milano, Italy [2] National Institute for Nuclear Physics (INFN), Milan Section, Milano, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In this work, we present a scalable high-performance readout system for LYSO-coupled SiPMs. The project aims to enable real-time beam range monitoring in proton therapy through Prompt Gamma Imaging (PGI), detecting prompt gamma rays emitted during proton-tissue interactions [1]. This application requires operation over a wide energy range, from 3 MeV to 10 MeV, together with high count-rate capability up to 1 Mcps/channel. The resulting platform is suitable for a broad range of gamma-ray detection applications. A compact DAQ board has been developed integrating all the electronics required for gamma event acquisition, processing, and data transmission without the need for external units [2]. The system is able to detect gamma rays with energies above 10 MeV using 12-bit energy digitization and 300 ps (FWHM) timing resolution. The module is connected to LYSO-coupled SiPMs (Hamamatsu S14160-6015PS) featuring a 6 × 6 mm² photosensitive area and 15 μm pixel pitch. Tests with calibration sources show a 10.2% FWHM resolution at 511 keV and 6.2% at 1275 keV. A custom ASIC specifically developed for high-energy gamma-ray detection is used for the readout of SiPM currents. With a minimum integration and readout time of 350 ns, the ASIC supports output count rates above 1 Mcps/channel. While each module supports 32 SiPM channels, multiple identical modules can be connected in a daisy-chain configuration to support larger detector arrays. The PCB mechanical design allows multiple boards to be stacked without inactive regions between modules, with the only limitation being the available 10 Gbps transmission bandwidth.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-03-04] High-Rate FPGA-Based Fully Digital SiPM Readout for Photon-Number-Resolving Measurements in Quantum Optics and Quantum Communications (#2050)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Carsi (Autores: S. Carsi , A. Abba , A. Allevi , A. Pozzoli , M. Lamperti)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Nuclear Instruments SRL, Lambrugo, Italy [2] Università degli Studi dell'Insubria, Dipartimento di Scienza e Alta Tecnologia, Como, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Photon-number-resolving (PNR) detection based on Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) is emerging as a promising approach for high-rate quantum optics and quantum communication experiments, particularly for the possible implementation of hybrid schemes. We present a fully digital SiPM readout platform combining a 14-bit, 1 GS/s waveform digitizer with a real-time FPGA-based signal-processing chain optimized for fast charge extraction and photon-number reconstruction. The system is implemented on an open-FPGA architecture programmable through the Sci-Compiler framework, enabling custom firmware development without dedicated HDL design. The firmware performs real-time baseline restoration, digital pole-zero compensation, synchronous triggering, and charge integration entirely inside the FPGA pipeline at full sampling rate. The system supports synchronous operation with externally or internally triggered laser sources and enables deterministic acquisition windows with nanosecond-scale integration gates. Different Hamamatsu SiPM models were characterized using coherent and twin-beam optical states to evaluate the impact of detector gain, pixel pitch, pile-up, and photon detection efficiency on photon-number reconstruction. Measurements demonstrate reliable operation from mean photon numbers well below 1 up to more than 50 detected photons per pulse at repetition rates up to 1 MHz, with operation extendable toward 10-20 MHz depending on the analog front-end configuration. The digital processing chain significantly improves peak separation, dynamic range, and noise performance compared with conventional boxcar-based acquisition systems. The presented architecture demonstrates how modern FPGA-based real-time digital processing can transform SiPM detectors into scalable, high-speed PNR systems suitable for next-generation quantum optics instrumentation and quantum communication protocols.
