sub_talks.title: [NSS-03-05] Towards Multi-channel Direct Positron Emission Imaging using Cherenkov-Radiator-Integrated MCP-PMTs, FastIC+, and Time-to-Digital Converters in FPGA. (#2177)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Rossignol (Autores: J. Rossignol , R. Ota , J.M. Fernandez-Tenllado , J. Mauricio , J. A. Alozy , S. Gomez , R. Ballabriga , D. Gascon , S.I. Kwon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California, Davis, Biomedical engineering, Davis, California, United States of America [2] Hamamatsu Photonics K.K., Central Research Laboratory, Hamamatsu, Japan [3] University of Barcelona, ICCUB, Barcelona, Spain [4] CERN, Meyrin, Genève, Switzerland [5] Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya, Barcelona, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Direct positron emission imaging (dPEI) enables imaging of positron-emitting radionuclide distributions without tomographic reconstruction by directly localizing annihilation events using ultrafast time-of-flight measurements. This modality was first demonstrated experimentally in 2021 using two Cherenkov-radiator-integrated microchannel plate photomultiplier tubes (CR-IMPs) read out by an oscilloscope. However, to scale to a larger number of channels for clinical applications, the oscilloscope must be replaced with an embedded front-end and digitizer. In this study, a dPEI acquisition chain for multi-channel readout was designed using two CR-IMPs, a FastIC+ front-end, and a tapped delay line time-to-digital converter implemented inside an UltraScale+ FPGA. A single-shot RMS precision of 4.0 ps was achieved by the front-end and the TDC when measuring pulses from a function generator. This timing precision is sufficient to digitize CR-IMP signals while preserving the timing performance required to approach the best coincidence timing resolution (CTR) currently measured using an oscilloscope. After evaluating the combined FastIC+ and TDC system, a complete readout chain from two CR-IMPs through the FastIC+ to the TDC was successfully configured, and coincidence events from a Na-22 source were successfully acquired during preliminary operation. We are currently optimizing the front-end parameters to achieve the best CTR between the two CR-IMPs. This study highlights the capability of the FastIC+ to read out CR-IMP signals and the ability of the combined FastIC+ and FPGA-based TDC system to digitize events with sufficient precision for dPEI.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-03-06] TEMPOROC3 : A 64-channel SiPM read-out chip for time-of-flight measurement on monolithic crystal (#3068)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 V. Yeroshenko (Autores: S. Ahmad , J.-B. Cizel , C. Derrien , J. Fleury , A. Haddar , M. Morenas , F. Perrez , V. Yeroshenko)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Weeroc, Villebon-sur-Yvette, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract TEMPOROC3 is a 64-channel mixed-signal SiPM read-out application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) designed in TSMC130 technology. The ASIC aims at measuring the energy with a 10-bit analogue-to-digital converter (ADC), time-of-arrival (TOA) and time-over-threshold (TOT) with a 40-ps bin time-to-digital converter (TDC). The analogue front-end offers a dynamic range up to 500 pC. The dual discriminator allows for measuring either two TOA at different threshold levels or the time between a rising and falling edge, giving a TOT. The dual-gain charge measurement integrates the input signal over a tuneable range from 20 to 300 ns. The 64 channels are divided into 4 clusters, each outputting data at 320 Mbps. The clusters can be synchronised to stream all channel data whenever a channel from the matrix has triggered. The number of triggered channels (per cluster) required to launch the data serialisation is programmable, as well as the window duration for accepting new triggers. At 450 kEvents/s per cluster (with 1 TDC + 1 ADC per channel), the power consumption is about 8 mW per channel. The trigger scheme for the monolithic matrix readout was successfully validated by acquiring a gamma spectrum of an 11 Na source with a large LYSO(Ce) crystal coupled to a 61-channel SiPM. Event filtering using a charge discriminator was validated, allowing for data rate reduction in the ASIC. Temporal characteristics were evaluated using external trigger, charge injection, laser pulses with SiPM, and coincident gamma from an 11 Na source. Measurements in coincidence between 2 channels from 2 ASICs have shown TDC coincidence time resolution (CTR) as low as 60 ps FWHM. Coincident annihilation gamma measurement using LYSO(Ce) crystals with SiPM demonstrated spatial sensitivity to the source displacement, providing CTR as low as 139 ps FWHM. TEMPOROC3 has been shown to be a versatile read-out ASIC with numerous configuration parameters that can be applied in ToF-PET, Compton cameras, LIDAR.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-04-01] Very-High-Energy Electron FLASH Radiotherapy at the PEER Beamline - Dosimetry and Biological Benchmarking (#2494)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Cutajar (Autores: J. Cayley , D. Cutajar , E. Engels , C. Skee , A. Rosenfeld , Y.-R. E. Tan , M. Lerch)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Wollongong, Centre for Medical Radiation Physics, Wollongong, Australia [2] Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre and University of Melbourne Sir Peter MacCallum Department of Oncology, Melbourne, Australia [3] ANSTO, Australian Synchrotron, Melbourne, Australia
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Very-high-energy electrons delivered at ultra-high dose rates, are being investigated for their promise within radiotherapy to treat deep-seated tumours. VHEE FLASH radiotherapy research requires two major components; a real-time dosimeter that remains linear at the required dose-per-pulse, and an accelerator that is stable, biologically benchmarked, and suitable for in vivo studies. Investigations have been conducted at the Pulsed Energetic Electrons for Research (PEER) beamline of the ANSTO Australian Synchrotron to realise this reality. Utilising a 100 MeV electron linac, PEER provides irradiation fields comprised of 100 ps bunches with a 2 ns spacing, forming bunchtrains with average and instantaneous dose-rates as high as 10 8 Gy/s and 10 9 Gy/s, respectively. The MOSkin detector was tested for linearity with a dose-per-pulse as high as 23 Gy within 200 ns. During this work, EBT-XD radiochromic film was employed as a reference dosimeter, however, a dose-rate dependence of the film was discovered. This was confirmed with another experiment which allowed calculation of a correction factor, enabling use of the film as an independent measurement of dose. Three cell lines (A549, T98G, and MDCK) were irradiated utilising real-time dosimetry, and mouse cadavers were irradiated to assess the feasibility of small animal experiments. These results support PEER as being suitable for future in vivo VHEE FLASH research.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-04-02] New approach in 2D microdosimetry using Alpide pixelated detector (#3171)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Cutajar (Autores: L. Tran , Q. Lu , J. Vohradsky , A. Schilling , V. Panin , M. Petasecca , M. Lerch , S. Guatelli , O.H. Oddland , M. Richter , D. Röhrich , A. Rosenfeld , D. Cutajar)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Wollongong, Centre for Medical Radiation Physics, Wollongong, Australia [2] Tech Univ Kaiserslautern, Chair Sci Comp,, Kaiserslautern, Germany [3] University of Bergen, Bergen, Norway [4] Haukeland Hospital, Dept Oncol & Med Phys, Bergen, Norway
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work investigates the feasibility of using the ALPIDE pixelated detector for two-dimensional microdosimetry applications in proton therapy. The detector offers several advantages for microdosimetry, including low noise, fast readout capability, flexible spatial sampling, and very high spatial resolution. Detailed Geant4 simulations were developed to model an experimental setup using an 80 MeV proton beam passing through different aluminium thicknesses. A strong agreement was observed between the responses of the ALPIDE detector and the SOI microdosimeter, demonstrating the capability of ALPIDE to accurately characterise LET distributions in proton radiation fields. In addition, the proposed calibration approach showed that the cluster size measured by the ALPIDE detector can be reliably converted to LET in silicon. Thanks to its pixelated architecture, arbitrary groups of pixels can be selected and analysed, enabling high-resolution two-dimensional LET mapping of complex radiation fields. These results demonstrate the strong potential of the ALPIDE detector as a versatile and cost-effective tool for advanced microdosimetry and proton beam LET d characterisation.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-04-03] AlphaBeast : A CMOS-based detector for real-time neutron production monitoring (#1169)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L.V. Garcia Garcia (Autores: L.V. Garcia Garcia , N. Arbor , D. Betelgueriev , S. Higueret , T.-D. Le , J.-M. Horodynski)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Université de Strasbourg, CNRS, IPHC UMR 7178, Strasbourg, France [2] Ingénierie Radioprotection Sûreté Démantèlement (iRSD) - CNRS, Paris, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Neutrons produced around particle accelerators are a major concern for radiation protection in research, medical, and industrial facilities due to their contribution to occupational exposure, patient dose, and material activation. Accurate characterisation of neutron fields is therefore essential, but conventional techniques such as activation foils, Bonner sphere systems, and solid-state nuclear track detectors are limited by their lack of real-time capability. In this work, we present the AlphaBeast, a CMOS-based detector designed for real-time monitoring of thermal and fast neutrons. This sensor has been designed as an electronic alternative to solid-state track detectors, using polyethene and 10B converters for fast and thermal neutron detection with on-chip discrimination thresholds. The system was calibrated using the irradiation facilities available at the Institut Pluridisciplinaire Hubert Curien in Strasbourg, France. A GATE/Geant4 Monte Carlo model was developed to simulate the detector response and optimise its performance. The AlphaBeast sensor was then tested in various mixed radiation fields, including radiotherapy rooms and accelerator casemates. Experimental results show good agreement with simulations and demonstrate its potential for real-time neutron monitoring in particle accelerator facilities.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-04-04] Comparative Performance Evaluation of pnCCD Sensor Variants with 36 μm Pixel Size (#2493)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Š. Hadžić (Autores: Š. Hadžić , J. Treis , A. Bähr , R. H. Richter , J. Ninković , F. Schopper , M. Polovykh , M. Hensel , C. Koffmane , C. So , B. Kondasani , H. Ye , D. Mießner , I. Riazanova)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Semiconductor Laboratory of the Max Planck Society, Garching, Bavaria, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Fully depleted silicon pnCCD sensors are used for X-ray spectroscopy in applications ranging from X-ray astronomy to synchrotron radiation sources and free-electron lasers, due to their outstanding capabilities, such as high energy resolution, low electronic noise and excellent quantum efficiency. At HLL, a new series of pnCCD sensors with a 36 μm pixel size has been fabricated to investigate the performance of small-pixel pnCCD devices. Applications requiring high spatial resolution can benefit from smaller pixel sizes, utilizing position reconstruction based on charge sharing. This contribution focuses on the systematic comparison of different designs within this pnCCD production run. The investigated sensors include devices based on our standard JFET amplifier, as well as variants with modified readout anodes, different options for the biasing of the MOS structures between the p-registers, and an option for a sensor design with self-aligned channel guide implants. Since the devices share the same basic geometry and sensor thickness, their comparison allows design-dependent effects on the detector performance to be directly assessed, while also exploring possible simplifications of the fabrication process and the overall detector system. For this purpose, the sensor variants are tested under comparable operating conditions using a newly developed experimental setup at HLL. The sensors are read out in a column-parallel architecture using the VERITAS 2.1 ASIC. Their spectral performance is evaluated in terms of noise behavior, gain uniformity, charge transfer inefficiency, and energy resolution. The observed performance differences between the variants will be discussed as a basis for identifying optimization paths for future pnCCD sensor designs.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-04-05] fine-pitch HPGe strip detectors for high-rate gamma-ray spectroscopy and imaging (#3145)
sub_talks.speaker: J. M. Szornel
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Nuclear Science Division, Berkeley, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A prototype high-purity germanium (HPGe) double-sided strip detector has been developed to maintain high energy resolution and high throughput at count rates relevant to MHz-rate gamma-ray spectroscopy and imaging. Conventional HPGe detectors provide excellent energy resolution but suffer from throughput loss and resolution degradation at elevated count rates, limiting their use in applications such as beam diagnostics, nuclear decommissioning, medical imaging, and prompt spectroscopy of superheavy elements. This work presents the design, fabrication, and characterization of fine-pitch HPGe double-sided strip detectors developed for high-rate spectroscopy and imaging. A 0.5 mm strip pitch detector geometry was selected using analytical calculations and numerical simulations of efficiency, charge collection, throughput, timing, energy resolution, and position resolution. This prototype demonstrated an energy resolution of 1.8 keV FWHM at 662 keV under low-rate conditions, consistent with predicted performance, and has now undergone additional characterization at higher rates. Extensive characterization has also been performed on 1.16 mm-pitch HPGe strip detectors, providing a broader experimental basis for evaluating fabrication yield, leakage current, strip-to-strip uniformity, charge sharing, charge loss, and spectroscopic performance. Results from both the 1.16 mm-pitch and 0.5 mm-pitch detectors will be presented. Energy resolution and throughput are evaluated as functions of shaping time, strip geometry, and incident count rate. These results demonstrate progress toward fine-pitch HPGe detector systems capable of high-resolution spectroscopy, three-dimensional position sensitivity, and sustained performance in high-rate environments.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-04-06] Repairing Proton Radiation Damage on n-type, Cross-Strip Germanium Detectors (#1121)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. E. Haight (Autores: S. E. Haight , J. Roberts , S. Boggs , S. Pike , J. Gerber , E. Broadbent , J. Tomsick , J. Szornel , A. Shih , A. Valluvan , A. Zoglauer)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California San Diego, Department of Astronomy and Astrophysics, La Jolla, California, United States of America [2] University of California Berkeley, Space Sciences Laboratory, Berkeley, California, United States of America [3] NASA, Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, Maryland, United States of America [4] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We performed a high-energy proton irradiation on a cross-strip germanium detector with the goals of measuring the subsequent loss to detector spectral resolution and characterizing the effectiveness of high-temperature annealing in repairing radiation damage. This work aims to address the expected radiation damage to the Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI) during two-year primary mission in low-Earth orbit and evaluate methods for maintenance of spectral resolution. COSI's cross-strip germanium detectors are susceptible to damage induced by the space radiation environment. Negatively charged dislocations induced by high-energy protons trap charge carriers as they drift in the applied bias voltage. The result is a degraded hole-collection signal characterized by widened spectral lines and loss to detector spectral resolution. We irradiated a non-flight detector with a fluence of 1.1 - 10 7 p + /cm 2 - COSI's expected exposure over prime mission (95% confidence level). After irradiation, we executed a series of high-temperature anneals aimed at physically repairing the damaged germanium. We track spectral resolution by measuring the full width half maximum (FWHM) of the 662 keV spectral line emitted by the isotope Cesium-137. We repaired widened FWHMs through high-temperature annealing to within 12% of its preradiation value, repairing to 2.97 keV compared to the original 2.67 keV. We track spectral resolution across annealing processes and characterize a timescale for repair. We find the anneal time needed to repair damage from COSI's primary mission within 1% of the spectral broadening from residual damage. We project the repair time required at 90°C to be 54 +/- 10 hours.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-02-01] Next Generation Room Temperature Semiconductor Detectors, Sources, and Methods for Computed Tomography in Aviation Security (#2984)
sub_talks.speaker: W. C. Barber
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Rapiscan Systems, Detectors, Torrance, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Advanced X-ray imaging is a principal pillar supporting aviation security and provides materially segmented images of bags, luggage, and cargo. The images are processed to provide a high probability of detection for contraband and/or threats, at an acceptably low false alarm rate to allow sufficient throughput. As the list of contraband and threats increases, the challenge to maintain a high detection probability at a low false alarm rate is advancing the state of art in detectors, sources, scanning methods, reconstruction, recognition, and decision, with the goal of clearing items for air transport. Room temperature semiconductor detectors are currently being used in commercially available diffraction scanners. These are based on pixellated Cadmium Zinc Telluride spectroscopic detectors, which are being developed further for better performance and lower cost. Cadmium Telluride and Cadmium Zinc Telluride photon counting detectors are currently being developed for potential use in multi-energy transmission scanners to improve detection and lower false alarms compared to the dual-energy dual-layer scintillator based scanners that are in wide use. Sensor performance requirements and cost constrains for widespread use of room temperature semiconductor detectors in both transmission and diffraction scanners are presented, with a focus on next generation computed tomography methods in multi-modal system of systems approaches to achieve the imaging workflows required for aviation security. Detector array and source geometries to achieve combined transmission and diffraction imaging in the different concepts of operation for the various scanning applications in aviation security are discussed.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-02-02] A new compact prototype for 3D gamma coded-aperture spectro-imaging (#1218)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Rosso (Autores: G. Rosso , G. Amoyal , D. Fras , Q. Gendre , M. Michel , D. Tromson)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Université Paris-Saclay, CEA List F-91120, Palaiseau, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract During nuclear dismantling, remote measurements, as radiation gamma imaging, are particularly advantageous since they reduce the risk for users, providing a visual map of radioactivity even in inaccessible environments. However, 2D gamma imaging does not directly provide the distance between source and detector, neither the 3D localization of the source. The goal of this work is to overcome these limits by developing a new compact and light 3D coded-aperture spectro-imager for applications in nuclear dismantling. This study presents the developments of the prototype, consisting of a coded-aperture gamma spectro-imager and an RGB-D (color and depth) camera, in carrying out 3D gamma imaging in experimental laboratory conditions. The device weight 325 g, with dimensions of 18 × 10 × 2.8 cm, and can distinguish among the most common radionuclides in the nuclear industry with energies ranging from the 59.5 keV gamma ray line of 241Am, up to the 60Co 1332 keV emission. The 3D hotspot localization and reconstruction are achieved with a triangulation from different viewpoints, which is made possible using a SLAM (Simultaneous Localization And Mapping) algorithm. We tested the prototype using point-like radioactive sources both in single and multiple sources configurations. In both cases, using a minimum of three static poses of few minutes' duration, the sources localizations are correctly achieved with errors in the order of 2 cm for measurements taken at almost one meter. New tests on volumetric and extended sources are currently on-going.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-02-03] Characterization of a miniature prototype photon counting detector system and evaluation of its imaging performance for potential use in threat and explosive detection CT scanners; A new paradigm for security screening. (#1293)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Prekas (Autores: G. Prekas , B. Mercurio , C. Bosch , K. Rogers , E. Johnson)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] SureScan Corporation, Binghamton, New York, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Spectral photon counting technology (SPCCT) represents a critical leap for security screening, offering high-resolution imaging and accurate material identification to reduce false alarms and detect threats invisible to legacy systems. SureScan Corporation utilizes SPCCT and dual-energy CT (DECT) in airport explosive detection systems (EDS), focusing R&D on characterizing prototype components like the AMS-OSRAM AS5920M. This state-of-the-art, 4-side buttable system-in-package (BSIP) module features direct-conversion CdZnTe crystals with 341µm x 365µm pixels integrated with ultra-low noise ASICs. Each ASIC supports five configurable energy thresholds and operates with short dead times to sustain high photon flux without significant pile-up. Our performance evaluation includes per-bin count rates, spatial uniformity, and spectral fidelity under various beam conditions, alongside imaging metrics such as modulation transfer function (MTF) and detective quantum efficiency (DQE). Furthermore, we demonstrate the importance of spectrum unfolding to correct non-ideal detector responses. By utilizing energy response function models derived from synchrotron measurements at Brookhaven National Laboratory, we reconstructed true incident energy spectra, significantly improving the accuracy of material identification through proprietary empirical decomposition methodologies.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-02-04] Tileable Imager Architecture using HiSPECT Gamma Imaging Modules and Applications (#2049)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Montémont (Autores: G. Montémont , N. Billon-Pierron , M. Moulin , H. de las Heras Gala , S. Stanchina)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CEA-LETI, Grenoble, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract For low-flux radiation imaging applications such as gamma-ray imaging, nuclear medicine, and X-ray diffraction, spectral and spatial resolution are performance drivers.However, detector efficiency is essential as it determines the quantity of information collected. The primary challenge is to achieve high-resolution performance at a reasonable cost. Then, it becomes possible to increase detection volume and the amount of information that the system can gather within a limited time. Our HiSPECT CZT detector module addresses this challenge through several key principles: the anode is segmented into large pixels, which limits charge sharing, while high spatial resolution is achieved through sub-pixel positioning. The low electronics density reduces cost, power dissipation, and improves yield. Additionally, the absence of cathode readout simplifies integration, while the depth of interaction is retrieved through multiple anode readouts. In this work, we present how modules are combined to build larger systems, detailing the readout electronics and showcasing various imaging application cases, including coded aperture, collimator, positron, and Compton imaging modes.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-02-05] Activity Quantification Using Experimentally Imaged Source Distributions (#2702)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. G. Wahl (Autores: C. G. Wahl , R. Sobota , D. Goodman , J. Ghezzi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] H3D, Inc., Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Radioactive source activity quantification is critical in many applications. A limiting factor in estimating activity is often knowledge of the source distribution within a medium since the position of the activity can greatly impact the observed counts at the detector. Algorithms have been developed to use a Compton and coded aperture gamma-ray imaging detector to image the source distribution within the volume of interest using a set of stationary measurements or a free-moving measurement with a simultaneously localization and mapping (SLAM) system. The iterative 3D volumetric imaging algorithm will be described. The imaged source distribution can then be used to improve activity quantification over a uniform source assumption. This is demonstrated with measurements of various geometries.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-06-01] ARES: A Web-Based Platform for Registration, Access, and Analysis of Radiation Simulation Results (#3019)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. E.R. Medaer (Autores: S. E.R. Medaer , C. H. Ferreira Brito Filho , P. Glaser De Senna , A. Freitas Pacifico , J. Closier , G. Corti)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CERN, LHCb Collaboration, Geneva, Genève, Switzerland [2] Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro, COPPE/EE/IF, Rio De Janeiro, Brazil
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Radiation simulations are essential for the design, operation, upgrade, and radiation protection assessment of high-energy physics experiments and other complex accelerator or irradiation facilities. However, their outputs are often difficult to organise, document, retrieve, compare, and share consistently, particularly when many studies, configurations, and users are involved. We present the Analysis platform for Radiation Environment Simulations (ARES), a web-based system developed within the LHCb experiment to support the workflow from registration to analysis of radiation simulation results obtained with the FLUKA particle transport code. ARES provides a database-backed interface for registering radiation estimators together with metadata describing the simulation context, scoring configuration, estimator location, and other relevant information. This structured registration makes results traceable, searchable, reproducible, and easier to reuse. Users can browse and query available estimators through a dedicated search interface and open selected data in a standalone visualisation and analysis service. The platform has been deployed for LHCb radiation studies covering prompt radiation and induced activity use cases, supporting quantities such as fluence, dose, and activation-related estimators. By centralising validated results and providing common tools for access and analysis, ARES improves collaboration between stakeholders involved in simulation production, detector studies, operations, upgrades, and radiation protection. This work demonstrates that a dedicated data-management and analysis layer can make radiation simulations more accessible and more effectively exploitable within a large experimental environment. Future developments include support for additional Monte-Carlo based codes and broader applicability beyond current LHCb use cases.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-06-02] Monte Carlo simulation of a new Optical Neutron Detector geometry for generation-IV Sodium-cooled Fast Reactors (#1285)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 V. Gerenton (Autores: V. Gerenton , P. Filliatre , G. De Izarra)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CEA, DEN / DER / Instrumentation, Sensors and Dosimetry Laboratory, Saint-Paul-lez-Durance, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Generation-IV sodium-cooled fast reactors impose severe constraints on neutron flux measurement instruments, particularly due to sustained temperatures that can exceed 550 °C [1]. In this context, optical neutron detectors (ONDs) represent a promising alternative to conventional fission chambers. These devices convert the kinetic energy of fission fragments into optical photons via gas-plasma luminescence and transmit the signal via an optical fiber, allowing electronic components to be placed out of pile, away from radiation. However, the photon collection efficiency of current prototypes is only η ≈ 1.78 × 10 -7 , limiting detector sensitivity [2]. This work presents a dedicated Monte Carlo simulation code, written in C, that estimates the impact of a new OND geometry-combining a hemispherical fissile deposit and a parabolic mirror-on photon collection efficiency, while accounting for the thermal radiation generated at high temperatures. The code comprises three coupled Monte Carlo loops: heavy-ion transport in gas (using polynomial moderation laws from COSICAF), plasma-photon propagation by ray tracing, and thermal wall-radiation modeling at 600 °C. A parametric study identified the negligible impact of the focal length of the parabolic mirror around the geometrically calculated value and quantified the impact of the reflective surfaces, and gas density. The proposed geometry achieves η = 5.4 × 10 -6 , a factor of 30 improvement over to current prototypes. These results call for progressive experimental validation, from out-of-reactor thermal characterization to in-reactor testing.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-06-03] A Validated GEANT4 Model of a Dual-HPGe γ-γ Coincidence Spectrometer for Detection Sensitivity Evaluation (#1900)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. C. Stokes (Autores: T. C. Stokes , M. Goodwin , M. Jackson , A. Boston)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] AWE Nuclear Security Technologies, Aldermaston, United Kingdom [2] The Oliver Lodge Laboratory, The University of Liverpool, Liverpool, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Gamma-gamma (γ-γ) coincidence is an advanced radiometric detection technique that has been widely demonstrated to reduce detection limits for many radionuclides in a variety of sample types and applications. The superior selectivity of γ-γ coincidence spectrometry in comparison to traditional single detector analysis, reduces the sensitivity of detection limits to changes in the activity of impurity radionuclides. This is particularly true in the case of impurities that do not emit coincident gamma photons (e.g. 137 Cs). In this work, a GEANT4 model of a dual high-purity germanium γ-γ coincidence system has been developed and validated against experimental measurements. Additionally, a method to generate modelled time-stamped list mode (T-List) data is presented and demonstrated using long and short-lived radionuclides. By processing the modelled T-List data, the effect on the detection limit for an analyte of interest in the presence of an impurity radionuclide can be studied. These preliminary results demonstrate how the detection limit of 134 Cs shows no measurable dependence on the activity of 137 Cs over the simulated range of 0.2-100 kBq. Future work will seek to investigate the influencing factors on detection limits for coincidence spectrometry as well as demonstrate the use of γ-γ coincidence alongside radiochemical separations to accelerate analytical timelines.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-06-04] Monte Carlo Quantum Imaging with Annihilation Photons (#2481)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A.M. Kožuljević (Autores: A.M. Kožuljević , G. Jazvac , L. Lotina , M. Makek , S. Parashari , P. Žugec , L. Pavelić)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institute for Medical Research and Occupational Health, Divison of Radiation Protection, Zagreb, Croatia [2] University of Zagreb Faculty of Science, Department of Physics, Zagreb, Croatia [3] Instituto de Fisica Corposcular, Valencia, Spain [4] Nucleometrix d.o.o., Zagreb, Croatia
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Quantum imaging with annihilation photons has recently emerged as a promising imaging modality [1, 2]. Positron annihilation photons are correlated particles, carrying the same energy of 511 keV and opposite momenta. The technique relies on coincidence measurements of the annihilation photons' energies and positions, with an object placed in front of one of the detectors. As a result, a ghost image of the object forms in the other detector, and the real image is enhanced by background noise reduction, since the noise lacks the photons' correlations. In this work, we explore the limits of the modality for background noise reduction via Geant4 simulations. The coincidence measurements are simulated for an experimental setup encompassing two segmented scintillating detectors, comprised of 64 Gadolinium Aluminum Gallium Garnet (GAGG) crystals and assembled into an 8x8 square matrix with 3.2 mm pitch [3]. We have found that quantum imaging outperforms classical gamma transmission imaging by retaining the contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) of noiseless conditions regardless of the background noise intensity. We have also tested the penetrative aspect of annihilation gamma rays, exploring the possibility of detecting attenuation variations in optically dense, high-Z materials.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-06-05] Bringing Synchrotron X-ray Minibeam Radiotherapy into Clinical Relevance: Monte Carlo Validation of Clinically Relevant Treatment Fields at the Australian Synchrotron (#1459)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Cutajar (Autores: V. T. de Rover , K. Roughley , J.P. Bustillo , S. Au , M. Cameron , M. Tehei , E. Engels , M. Grams , S. Park , A. Rosenfeld , C. Phillips , M. Petasecca , D. Cutajar , S. Corde , S. Guatelli , M. Lerch)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Wollongong, Centre for Medical Radiation Physics, Wollongong, Australia [2] University of the Philippines Manila, Department of Physical Sciences and Mathematics, College of Arts and Sciences, Manila, Philippines [3] Australian Synchrotron, Imaging and Medical Beamline, Melbourne, Australia [4] Mayo Clinic, Department of Radiation Oncology, Rochester, Minnesota, United States of America [5] Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre, Parkville, Australia [6] Prince of Wales Hospital, Department of Radiation Oncology, Randwick, Australia
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract To progress synchrotron-based, spatially fractionated X-ray radiotherapy towards clinical trials, the efficacy of clinically relevant treatment fields must be assessed. In this paper, we present the development and validation of a Geant4 model for human-relevant broad beam (BB) and minibeam radiotherapy (MBRT) treatment fields (up to 7 x 7 cm 2 ) in an experimental hutch located 140m from the synchrotron source at the Imaging and Medical Beamline at the ANSTO Australian Synchrotron. Both broad beam and MBRT treatment fields were modelled for different beam energies and field sizes, with two minibeam fields of different peak spacing investigated. BB and MBRT (peak and valley) depth doses were investigated up to 7cm in a solid water phantom. There was excellent agreement in broad beam percentage depth dose curves (within 4%) as well as the minibeam peak depth dose curves (within 6%), with the model and experimental results agreeing within combined uncertainty for all depths and configurations investigated. There was good agreement in valley dose when comparing EBT-XD Gafchromic film to the model with most results within 10% and within uncertainty. However, there was disagreement between the valley dose measured by the microdiamond detector and the Geant4 model up to 15%. This model will be useful for further MBRT experiments performed at IMBL, with future work validating this model for 3D printed patient volumes.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-06-06] SimpleMC: A Simple and Flexible Monte Carlo Simulation Tool for Timepix Detectors (#2518)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C.-W. Huang (Autores: C.-W. Huang , J. Čeřovský , Š. Malec , V. Linhart , K. Sabirzyanova , K. Melovská , E. Soharová)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Czech Technical University in Prague, Faculty of Nuclear Sciences and Physical Engineering, Prague, Czech Republic [2] ADVACAM, Prague, Czech Republic
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Timepix type pixel detectors enable event-by-event radiation measurements [1], but classification of mixed fields remains challenging due to scarce labeled data and detector dependent effects. We present SimpleMC, an Allpix 2 [2, 3] based framework for generating realistic synthetic Timepix datasets by combining Monte Carlo transport simulation with detector response modeling and data driven refinement. Photon and electron benchmarks are improved using two complementary approaches: a tuned digitizer and a simplified Gaussian smearing model. These approaches enhance agreement with calibration and spectral measurements. For proton and alpha particles, generative models are used to bridge the sim-to-real gap, including Contrastive Unpaired Translation (CUT) and Conditional Diffusion Denoising Probabilistic Models (CDDPM). The models are trained to map simulated cluster representations to experimental-like responses. CDDPM outperorms CUT in capturing experimental variability and improving generalization to unseen geometries and irradiation conditions. The framework is evaluated across photons, electrons, and heavy charged particles, showing good agreement in both energy related observables and cluster morphology. Additional experimental datasets from complex radiation environments, including fusion relevant tokamak conditions, are collected for future validation. SimpleMC provides a flexible framework for realistic synthetic data generation, supporting detector characterization and the development of advanced simulation based analysis tools. It will be further developed into a user-friendly toolkit with documentation for the broader radiation detection community.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-06-07] Photodetector model for the ClearMind project: Toward ultra-high time resolution (#1979)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Zobundzija (Autores: Z. Zobundzija , V. Sharyy , D. Yvon , G. Daniel , T. Kaprelian , C. Morel , M. Dupont)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Université Paris-Saclay, CEA, IRFU/Département de Physique des Particules, Gif-sur-Yvette, France [2] Université Paris-Saclay, CEA, CNRS, INSERN, Laboratoire BIOMAPS, Orsay, France [3] Université Paris-Saclay, CEA, Service de Génie Logiciel pour la simulation, Gif-sur-Yvette, France [4] Aix-Marseille Université, CNRS/IN2P3, CPPM, Marseille, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The ClearMind collaboration is developing a next-generation Time-of-Flight PET detector aiming at sub-100 ps coincidence resolving time, high detection efficiency and precise spatial resolution. This presentation discusses the modeling of the ClearMind gamma detector, made of crystal with direct photocathode deposition and microchannel plate (MCP) electron multiplication. The simulation model uses Geant4 software to simulate gamma interactions within the crystal and the propagation of optical photons. Photoelectron generation, multiplication and signal processing are described through a parametrized simulation. This model is crutial for both understanding and optimizing the ClearMind prototype and for development of machine learning-based reconstruction algorithms. To validate the model, we compare simulation results with experimental measurments PbF 2 , PbWO 4 , BaF 2 and LYSO crystals assembled with the Incom HRPPD MCP-PMT in a conventional configuration. We also explore various factors contributing to the detector's time resolution, including photon collection efficiency, photocathode efficiency, single-photon time resolution and signal pile-up effects. Additionally, we investigated new estimators using deep learning models trained on simulation for time reconstruction and event-by-event associated uncertainty estimation enabling us to select the most precise events. The preliminary results show a time resolution below 100 ps.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-06-08] 3-D simulation of carrier transport and signal formation in silicon detectors for charged particle identification (#2910)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Castoldi (Autores: A. Castoldi , C. Guazzoni , F. Buda)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Politecnico di Milano, DEIB, Milano, Italy [2] INFN, Sezione di Milano, Milano, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Fast simulation of carrier generation, transport and signal formation is a powerful tool for the optimization of segmented detector arrays targeted to charged particle identification in nuclear physics experiments. A custom numerical tool for the self-consistent computation of the electron-hole dynamics has been used to study ion tracks in silicon and non-silicon detectors. The code includes the effect of thermal diffusion and Coulomb interaction among the mobile carriers in a microscopic fashion, essential for the correct simulation of high-density ionization tracks in which plasma-like effects (field screening, transient distortions, collection slowdown, and marked nonlinearities) become significant, like in the case of heavy ion interactions. We addressed the challenging case of intermediate mass fragments stopping in the typically few hundred microns of the first detection layer of a telescope configuration, where particle identification critically relies on pulse-shape analysis. Simulations were carried out for several ions - from Li6 to Na22 - impinging on a silicon detector with energies up to the punch-through condition. We studied the impact of the relevant properties of detector and preamplifier response and of the effectiveness of different pulse-shape algorithms to assess the minimum energy threshold and the achievable resolution in charged particle separation in mass (A) and atomic number (Z).

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-03-01] Flat-Panel Intensity Normalization for Fully Spectroscopic CT-Based Material Identification with 1 mm CdTe Timepix3 Detectors (#2597)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. K. Schütz (Autores: M. K. Schütz , G. Roque Romero , S. Useche Parra , M. P. Pichotka , M. Fiederle)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Freiburg, Freiburg Materials Research Centre (FMF), Freiburg im Breisgau, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [2] University of Freiburg, Medical Physics Division, Department of Radiology, Freiburg im Breisgau, Baden-Württemberg, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Fully spectroscopic photon-counting CT enables material identification by recording the energy-dependent transmission spectrum of an object. Timepix3 (TPX3) detectors extend conventional threshold-based photon counting CT by recording position, time-of-arrival and energy information for individual events, allowing for post-acquisition energy binning and extraction of spectral features such as K-edges. However, fully spectroscopic photon counting CT with TPX3 detectors remains limited by detector area, photon statistics, scan time and raw data volume. Previous work introduced a two-stage TPX3 acquisition scheme that combines frame-based and event-based readout. Here, we investigate whether the frame-based TPX3 intensity image can be replaced by a geometrically matched flat-panel intensity measurement. The CMOS/GdOS flat-panel detector provides full-field intensity projections, while a 12 x 1 TPX3 array with 1 mm CdTe sensors provides fully spectroscopic region-of-interest (ROI) information. The method combines the low-noise intensity information of the flat-panel detector with the material-specific spectroscopic information of TPX3. Projection geometry is matched by adapting cone-beam magnification, followed by empirical intensity mapping in the overlap region. The approach is benchmarked against the original TPX3-MPX-normalized acquisition reference. Initial results indicate that replacing the TPX3 intensity image with flat-panel projections preserves TPX3-derived material characteristics in the investigated ROI and enables material labels to be extrapolated to repeated structures in the full-field reconstruction.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-03-02] A Pixelated CCI TlBr Detector for Time-Resolved Multi-MeV Gamma Detection (#1612)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Rebolo (Autores: L. Rebolo , S. Moreno-Gómez , H. Kim , J. Christian , P. Correia , A. Silva , G. Ariño-Estrada)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California Davis, Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America [2] Institut de Física d'Altes Energies - Barcelona Institute of Science and Technology, Medical Detector Instrumentation and Imaging Physics, Barcelona, Spain [3] Radiation Monitoring Devices, Inc., Watertown, Massachusetts, United States of America [4] University of Aveiro, Aveiro, Portugal
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Cherenkov Charge Induction (CCI) detectors consist of transparent semiconductor detectors that combine the conventional charge induction readout with the detection of Cherenkov light generated by gammas depositing energy above the Cherenkov threshold. CCI detectors show strong potential for applications requiring time-resolved multi-MeV gamma detection, such as proton range verification in proton therapy. In this work we report on a pixelated CCI TlBr detector consisting of a 14×14×11 mm3 TlBr crystal with a 4×4 pixelated anode matrix of 2.3×2.3 mm2 pixels with 2.5 mm pitch. The lateral faces of the crystal were polished to maximize light extraction, and a 2×2 silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) array with 4×4 mm2 active area per channel was used for Cherenkov light detection. The detector was instrumented with a multi- channel acquisition system based on a CAEN R5560 open FPGA digitizer, enabling simultaneous acquisition of charge induction and Cherenkov light signals from all detector channels. The acquisition was triggered by the Cherenkov readout and a 22Na point source was used for detector characterization. First results demonstrate the feasibility of simultaneous Cherenkov light and charge induction acquisition using a multi-channel readout, with the optical signal successfully providing the acquisition trigger and a timing reference to estimate the electron drift time. Future work will focus on optimization of the triggering and synchronization scheme, waveform processing methods, and detector operating conditions to improve event selection and detector characterization.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-03-03] Self-Consistent Simulation of Charge Sharing in CZT Pixel Detectors (#2864)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Zappettini (Autores: S. Favilla , M. Bettelli , L. Abbene , M. C. Veale , A. Zappettini)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] IMEM-CNR, Parma, Italy [2] University of Palermo, aDipartimento di Fisica e Chimica (DiFC),, Palermo, Italy [3] STFC Rutherford Appleton Laboratory, Didcot, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Cadmium Zinc Telluride (CZT) detectors are widely used for X-ray and γ-ray detection due to their high atomic number, wide band gap, and excellent room-temperature performance. Their response is governed by charge transport processes, including carrier mobility, trapping, diffusion, and electric-field nonuniformities, which are critical in pixelated geometries where charge sharing and weighting-field effects dominate signal formation. In this work, a 3D CZT detector model is developed in COMSOL Multiphysics, solving semiconductor transport equations self-consistently without Gaussian charge-cloud approximations. Signal induction is computed using the Ramo-Shockley theorem applied to the full carrier distribution. Validation against synchrotron measurements shows excellent agreement in normalized charge collection profiles (r = 0.98), confirming accurate reproduction of charge transport and sharing effects.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-03-04] Waveform-Based Depth-of-Interaction Characterization in 5-mm Cross-Strip CdZnTe (#2149)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Teicheira (Autores: M. Teicheira , L. R. Furenlid , C. Huang , M. Kupinski , M. King , S. Abbaszadeh)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California, Santa Cruz, Electrical and Computer Engineering, Santa Cruz, California, United States of America [2] University of Arizona, Department of Radiology and Imaging Sciences, Tuscon, Arizona, United States of America [3] University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School, Radiology, Worcester, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Depth-of-interaction (DOI) estimation in CdZnTe detectors is conventionally based on the cathode-to-anode amplitude ratio (C/A), while timing-based methods have been explored as alternative indicators in pixelated geometries. However, DOI characterization in cross-strip CdZnTe detectors using digitized waveform signal parameters, including drift time, cathode amplitude, and anode rise time, and the degree to which these parameters provide independent depth information has not been systematically studied. In this work, we present a waveform-based DOI characterization of a 5 mm thick cross-strip CdZnTe detector (7 anode strips, 8 cathode strips, and 1 steering electrode). A collimated 137 Cs slit beam was scanned across 26 discrete depth positions 0.2 mm apart. Drift time and cathode amplitude exhibit a strong correlation (R 2 = 0.99), establishing that both contribute to the practical lower bound on the achievable single-event depth resolution. At each collimator slit position, the measured signal distributions reflect the distribution of interaction depths, due to finite beam width and intracrystal scatter. The C/A ratio computed from the two highest-amplitude cathode strips provides the best trade-off between DOI resolution and measurement consistency. Using a leave-one-step-out cross- validation framework, we obtain a DOI resolution of 1.35 mm RMSE with single-feature calibration and 1.12 mm RMSE using a 9-feature random forest regression model.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-03-05] Ultra‑High Resolution CZT Gamma Camera Using Machine-Learning Based 3D Interaction Localisation (#2496)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Cherlin (Autores: N. Atkins , M. Exley , I. Baistow , A. Cherlin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Kromek Ltd., Sedgefield, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract An ultra-high resolution CZT gamma camera platform is presented, integrating advanced detector readout, machine learning (ML) based signal processing and practical calibration procedures for sub‑pixel 3D interaction localisation. The system employs Kromek's D‑Matrix readout with 2 mm pixel pitch detectors and utilises an ML model trained on physics‑based simulations and calibrated with experimental flood‑field data. Recent developments focus on improving calibration flexibility, robustness to detector performance fluctuations and stability during prolonged operation through refined detector simulations, multi-model optimisation strategies and incorporation of measured data in the training process. Performance evaluation demonstrates improved spatial uniformity and significant suppression of inter‑pixel artefacts in uncorrected flood field images, with stable behaviour maintained over extended acquisition periods without recalibration. Previously reported intrinsic spatial resolution (~250 µm) and depth‑of‑interaction accuracy (~0.5-1 mm) are preserved, with improved consistency across the detector volume. Reduced reliance on flat‑field correction limits amplification of Poisson noise in reconstructed images, enhancing effective image quality. The ML predicted energy incorporates corrections that effectively eliminate energy DOI dependence and charge sharing losses, resulting in a strongly reduced low-energy tail of the spectrum. These results demonstrate a robust and scalable CZT gamma camera platform, addressing key practical limitations of earlier implementations. The integrated detector, calibration and ML based data processing framework enable reliable high‑resolution imaging under realistic operating conditions and supports straightforward scaling to larger field‑of‑view systems. A full‑scale camera is currently under construction, highlighting the potential for integration into advanced nuclear imaging applications.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-03-06] Optimized femtosecond laser ablation processing of hybrid semiconductor detectors for enhanced spectroscopic and imaging performance (#2556)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Melnikova (Autores: Z. Melnikova , E. Soharova , S. Syrovatka , V. Kudrna , J. Syrovatka , P. Kozmin , J. Jakubek)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] ADVACAM s.r.o., Prague 7, Czech Republic [2] Hofmeister, s.r.o., Pilsen, Czech Republic
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Hybrid semiconductor detectors based on the TimePIX-family read-out chips enable direct detection of ionizing radiation with high spatial and spectroscopic resolution. This work investigates the application of femtosecond laser ablation for precise structural modification of detector components while minimizing thermal damage and preserving detector functionality. The study focused on three-dimensional shaping of the read-out chip in a MiniPIX TimePIX3 detector with a 1 mm thick cadmium telluride sensor and on edge cutting of silicon sensors. An optimized laser ablation process enables significant thinning of the read-out chip while maintaining full detector operation. The modified configuration allows backside illumination of the detector, resulting in reduced X-ray attenuation and improved detection efficiency for low-energy photons in the energy range from 5 to 25 keV. Experimental measurements also demonstrate improved spectroscopic performance and enhanced spatial resolution. In addition, femtosecond laser ablation was applied to precise cutting of silicon sensor edges, enabling efficient integration of individual modules into large-area monolithic detection systems. The presented results demonstrate that femtosecond laser ablation is a promising tool for advanced modification of hybrid semiconductor detectors and can significantly expand their applicability in future radiation detection systems.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-03-07] Energy, Spatial and Timing Performance of CZT Drift Strip Detectors (#2701)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Abbene (Autores: L. Abbene , A. Buttacavoli , F. Principato , G. Gerardi , M. Bettelli , A. Zappettini , N. Auricchio , S. Del Sordo , E. Caroli)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Palermo, Dipartimento di Fisica e Chimica E. Segrè, Palermo, Italy [2] IMEM/CNR PARMA, Parma, Italy [3] INAF/OAS of Bologna, Bologna, Italy [4] INAF/IASF of Palermo, Palermo, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract High resolution detection modules for multi-isotope SPECT imaging are strongly required in nuclear medicine. In this framework, we proposed and developed new cadmium-zinc-telluride (CZT) drift strip detectors for room temperature gamma-ray spectroscopic imaging. As widely demonstrated, CdZnTe (CZT) is one of the key materials for the development of room temperature X-ray and gamma ray detectors and several research groups are still involved in advances in both device and the crystal growth technologies. The CZT detectors, equipped with orthogonal anode/cathode collecting strips, drift strips and dedicated digital pulse processing allow a detection area of 6 x 20 mm 2 , excellent room temperature energy resolution of 0.8% FWHM at 662 keV and sub-millimetre spatial resolution. The timing performance of the detectors will be also presented. These activities are within an Italian PRIN 2022 PNRR project (No. P2022SE49Y; CUP: B53D23024100001), funded by the Italian Ministry for University and Research (MUR).

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E.M. Zannoni (Autores: A. R. Whittemore , K. Patel , E.M. Zannoni)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract High-resolution Cd(Zn)Te radiation detectors are essential for quantitative imaging in medical diagnostics, high-energy physics, and industrial non-destructive testing [1]. This study examines the impact of charge sharing (CS) [2] in a 2-mm CdTe/Timepix detector with 55 μm pixels [3], and proposes a spectroscopic correction method. From Am-241 and Co-57 experimental data, we categorized interaction events by their multiplicity and a newly introduced shape descriptor called circularity. Analysis showed that non-circular events (C < 0.9) resulted in energy peaks shifting toward lower energies due to unrecorded below-threshold pixels. To address these high-multiplicity CS events, we developed a multi-stage spectroscopic correction method that corrects spectra based on circularity and multiplicity values. This approach improved the average FWHM for the Am-241 peak from 16.70% to 10.05% and for Co-57 from 9.64% to 6.73%. Additionally, AllPix-Squared simulations [4] were used to model charge cloud dynamics and quantify losses occurring during both propagation and digitization. This work enabled a more robust energy calibration and unbiased spectroscopic performance for small-pixel semiconductor detectors.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-05-01] Time-of-Flight Neutron Imaging With a Segmented Organic Imager Cell (#2120)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 W. Heriot (Autores: W. Heriot , D. Breitenmoser , P. Marleu , K. Vaigneur , S. Clarke , S. Pozzi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Michigan, Nuclear Engineering and Radiological Sciences, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America [2] Sandia National Laboratories, Livermore, California, United States of America [3] Oakridge National Laboratories, Oakridge, Tennessee, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Neutron imaging arrays are critical tools in nuclear non-proliferation, with applications in neutron source localization in wide-area source searches and cargo inspections. However, they commonly have large form factors due to needing large data acquisition systems, complicating deployment. A solution with simplified data acquisition is needed to make portable and field-deployable neutron imaging arrays. Organic scintillator-based neutron imaging arrays typically require pulse shape discrimination (PSD) to differentiate between neutron and gamma-ray events. This method requires full waveform data acquisition, which results in a high data throughput, and utilizes expensive analog-to-digital converters. In order to alleviate the need for full waveform acquisition, this work seeks to develop a system that instead leverages time-of-flight particle discrimination. To discriminate neutrons from gamma events using time-of-flight particle discrimination, a Segmented Organic Neutron Imager Cell, SONIC, has been constructed of 64 5x0.6x0.6 cm3 bars of EJ200. 14 of the 16 tested bars show typical pulse-integral spectra for Cs-137. This work details the introductory characterization of this imager array and evaluates its validity for future work in achieving a field-deployable, handheld neutron scatter imager.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-05-02] Development of an omnidirectional neutron imager with fractal geometry (#1531)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Matsubayashi (Autores: N. Matsubayashi , T. Torii , M. Sasaki , S. Kurosawa)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology, Tokyo, Japan [2] Fukushima University, Fukushima, Japan [3] Japan Atomic Energy Agency, Minamisoma, Japan [4] Nagoya University, Nagoya, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In areas where radiation sources are diffused three-dimensionally, it is important to develop a compact imaging sensor that can detect radiation distributions in the 4π direction. A radiation imager that detects the distribution of radiation sources with a fractal Sierpinski tetrahedron shape was developed before. The imager has 16 sensors arranged in a Sierpinski tetrahedron shape, with the space between the sensors filled with a shielding material. We have been developing a neutron imager to measure radiation distribution within the site of the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant (FDNPP) and in the environment contaminated by the FDNPP accident. The reactor buildings contain large amounts of radiation sources. Since the nuclear fuel and debris contained in the reactor pressure vessel (RPV) will be removed in the future, it is extremely important to identify neutron sources originating from nuclear fuel in high dose rate areas for criticality management and radiation protection of workers. Therefore, we developed a compact omnidirectional neutron imager to locate neutron sources in the reactor building. This sensor consists of thin triangular scintillators ( 6 LiF/ZnS:Ag) for neutron detection attached to a tetrahedral acrylic surface and arranged in a Sierpinski tetrahedron shape, with B 4 C mixed with resin for neutron shielding filled between the sensors. In this presentation, we report the results of performance evaluations of the imager using a neutron source and research reactor.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-05-03] Neutron Spectroscopy Using a Spatially Resolved He-3 Slab Detector (#2047)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. L. Lockhart (Autores: M. L. Lockhart , J. P. Hayward , A. Youmans , P. Kerr)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Tennessee, Department of Nuclear Engineering, Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America [2] Lawrence Livermore National Laboraatory, Livermore, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents a He-3 based slab detector for neutron spectroscopy that leverages spatially resolved detector response to infer incident neutron energy. In moderated detector systems, neutron energy information is typically degraded prior to detection, complicating spectrum unfolding. The proposed detector addresses this limitation through channel-by-channel list-mode acquisition, enabling analysis of spatial response variations correlated with neutron energy. Additional moderating and absorbing configurations are investigated to improve spectral sensitivity. A model of the detector is developed using Monte Carlo simulation and benchmarked against experimental measurements with monoenergetic neutron sources. This model will be used to generate energy-dependent response functions for use in spectral unfolding. Results indicate that combining spatial response information with multiple detector configurations will improve the conditioning of the neutron spectrum unfolding problem and enhance reconstruction accuracy. This approach provides a pathway toward information-optimized neutron spectrometry for nuclear security and safeguards applications.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-05-04] Residual Interpulse 14-MeV Neutron Emission in Active Interrogation with Neutron Generators (#2076)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 V. Fondement (Autores: V. Fondement , I. Jovanovic)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University Of Michigan, Nuclear Engineering & Radiological Sciences, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America [2] University of California, Berkeley, Nuclear Engineering, Berkeley, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We report residual 14 MeV neutron emission between pulses of a Thermo Fisher Scientific P 211 DT neutron generator operated at 100 Hz with a 0.1% duty cycle. Using a liquid organic scintillator with pulse-shape discrimination, we detect a significant population of neutron events with light output consistent with DT neutrons. The interpulse time structure follows a two-component exponential decay with time constants of 0.8 ms and 4.7 ms, inconsistent with 17 N β-delayed neutron emission. The interpulse yield represents 0.1% of the total emission (~10 -6 of instantaneous pulse intensity). These results demonstrate that the assumption of zero interpulse emission can be violated even when both the ion source and the high voltage are nominally pulsed, with direct implications for low-SNR delayed-signature measurements.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-05-05] Neutron Flux Monitor (NFM): A Micromegas-Based Beam Monitor for the European Spallation Source (#2999)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 I. Katsioulas (Autores: I. Katsioulas , A. Altingün , A. Gardikiotis , M. Kebbiri , C. Lampoudis , B. A. Moreno , T. Papaevangelou , E. Samouilidis , O. Sidiropoulou)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] European Spallation Source, Detector Group, Lund, Sweden [2] Université Paris-Saclay, IRFU, CEA, Gif-sur-Yvette, France [3] Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, Physics Department, Thessaloniki, Greece
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The European Spallation Source (ESS) requires advanced neutron-beam monitors capable of stable operation under high-rate conditions while maintaining low beam attenuation. To address these requirements, a Micromegas-based Neutron Flux Monitor (NFM) has been developed by the ESS Detector Group in collaboration with DEDIP (IRFU) and CEA Saclay. The detector employs a novel bulk Micromegas implementation directly on AlMg3 alloy substrates, minimizing the use of hydrogen-rich materials and therefore reducing neutron attenuation and moderation effects along the beamline. Initial detector characterization using X-ray sources demonstrated good gain uniformity, stable high-gain operation, and good energy resolution. Subsequent neutron measurements performed with different gas mixtures and front-end electronics confirmed stable operation under representative ESS-like conditions. Measurements performed at the EMMA beamline at ISIS investigated detector performance at high neutron rates and provided important input for the optimisation of the final NFM readout architecture for future ESS deployment.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-05-06] Development of a Handheld Fast Neutron Spectrometer Using Deuterated Scintillators and Spectrum Unfolding (#3014)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. A. Alcaide (Autores: A. A. Alcaide , T. C. Borgwardt , C. Brune , L. Fabris , M. Febbraro , J. J. Manfredi , T. Massey , J. Matta , D. Matthews , C. Parker , D. Rutstrom , N. Zaitseva)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Air Force Institute of Technology, Engineering Physics, Dayton, Ohio, United States of America [2] Los Alamos National Laboratory, Los Alamos, New Mexico, United States of America [3] Ohio University, Athens, Ohio, United States of America [4] Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, Tennessee, United States of America [5] Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Livermore, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Fast neutron spectroscopy has the potential to offer critical information for safeguards, nonproliferation, and field radiation detection applications where neutron energy distributions provide source characteristics inaccessible through conventional moderated neutron counters. Traditional portable neutron detection systems primarily rely on moderation and thermal neutron counting, which remove incident neutron energy information and limit spectroscopic capability. In this work, the nSpec system is developed as a handheld fast neutron spectrometer utilizing four novel deuterated polystyrene (dPS) scintillator detectors coupled to photomultiplier tubes in a compact, field-deployable architecture. By leveraging neutron--deuteron elastic scattering interactions, the system preserves energy-dependent neutron response while maintaining portability suitable for operational environments. Pulse shape discrimination is employed to separate neutron and gamma interactions, while detector response matrices (DRMs) derived from high-flux neutron characterization are used to reconstruct incident neutron spectra through maximum likelihood expectation maximization (MLEM) unfolding. Prototype evaluations using representative neutron sources, including AmBe and Cf-252, demonstrate successful spectral unfolding and source discrimination capability. Ongoing development focuses on onboard electronics integration, firmware implementation, shielding optimization, and validation against simulated and experimental DRMs. These results establish nSpec as a promising pathway toward practical handheld fast neutron spectroscopy for safeguards and field applications.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-05-07] Innovative neutron counting for high-rate double-differential cross-section in fragmentation events. (#2947)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 I. B. Rivas Ortiz (Autores: I. B. Rivas Ortiz , E. M. Data , V. Ferrero , E. Fiorina , S. Giordanengo , F. Mas Milian , A. Mereghetti , D. M. Montalvan Olivares , F. Pennazio , M. Pullia , S. Ranjbar , R. Sacchi , A. Vignati , P. Cerello)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Torino, Torino, Italy [2] Universita degli Studi di Torino, Torino, Italy [3] Universidade Estadual de Santa Cruz, Bahia, Brazil [4] Fondazione Centro Nazionale di Adronterapia Oncologica, Pavia, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Neutron production cross-sections are critical for dose assessment in particle therapy and space radiation protection, yet double-differential data remain scarce. We present a consistent framework for Time-Of-Flight (TOF)-based measurement built around the use of Low Gain Avalanche Detectors (LGADs) segmented into strips on the primary beam, enabling large statistical samples and precise time measurement, and a secondary neutron detector split into layers to accurately reconstruct neutron production as a function of kinetic energy and angular direction. A preliminary beam test was conducted to validate the methodology. The setup comprises an 8-strip beam monitor for primary particle tagging, a LaBr 3 (Ce) scintillator with Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) readout as secondary radiation detector, and a plastic veto for charged-particle rejection. Neutron kinetic energy is reconstructed via relativistic TOF analysis from approximately 16 MeV to several hundred MeV. A novel Beer-Lambert fitting approach enables efficiency-independent neutron flux estimation from the attenuation pattern along the detection depth, overcoming systematic uncertainties of conventional scaling methods. Monte Carlo (MC) simulations validate both TOF distributions and flux reconstruction at the few-percent level, with computed cross-sections in good agreement with MC truth values. Combined with a rotary-translation stage enabling systematic angular scanning for full double-differential cross-section mapping, the proposed approach provides a robust and scalable framework for neutron production measurements in fragmentation events, with direct application to out-of-field dose characterization in particle therapy and astronaut radiation exposure assessment.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-05-08] First 3D-PDC Experimental Measurements of Fast Neutrons and PSD Performance (#1598)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Steinhebel (Autores: A. Steinhebel , S. Charlebois , L. Fabris , P. Hausladen , G. Lessard , C. Pepin , J.-F. Pratte , T. Rossignol , N. Roy , F. Vachon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Bldg 3500, MS 6010, Oak Ridge, Tennessee, United States of America [2] Universite de Sherbrooke, Interdisciplinary Institute for Technological Innovation and Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Sherbrooke, Québec, Canada
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Novel Photon-to-Digital Converters (3D-PDCs) are arrays of Single Photon Avalanche Diodes (SPADs) vertically-integrated with low power CMOS digital readouts, offering high timing precision ($<200$ ps FWHM) and individual-pixel control. As single-photon counters, 3D-PDCs can be coupled to scintillators for radiation detection. This talk will discuss the first 3D-PDC measurements of fast neutrons. The 3D-PDCs are used to read out an organic plastic scintillator with Pulse Shape Discrimination (PSD) capabilities, making incident neutrons and gamma rays discernible by the pulse shape of the induced scintillator signal. First PSD results will be shown and compared to standard commercial silicon photomultipliers.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-07-01] Crucible-Free Growth of High Melting Temperature Scintillators by the OCCC Method (#2280)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Kamada (Autores: K. Kamada , T. Tomida , M. Yoshino , M. Kitahara , V. Kochurikhin , R. Murakami , Y. Shoji , K. Kakimoto , A. Yoshikawa)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tohoku Univ., Sendai, Japan [2] C＆A corp., Sendai, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract High-melting-point oxide scintillators are key materials for radiation imaging and harsh-environment radiation detection, but their scaling is limited by iridium crucibles, melt contamination, and composition fluctuation. We report crucible-free growth and scaling of Ce:LYSO and Y₂O₃ scintillators using the oxide crystal growth from cold crucible (OCCC) method. In OCCC growth, the oxide melt is directly heated by high-frequency induction and retained by a self-formed solidified raw-material layer in a water-cooled copper basket. Ce:LYSO was grown in air, and EPMA showed host-cation segregation coefficients close to unity for Lu, Y, and Si. The straight-body region exhibited light-output variation within ±20%, with a maximum light output of approximately 16,000 photons/MeV under ¹³⁷Cs 662-keV excitation. Most importantly, an ultrahigh-melting-point Y₂O₃ scintillator was successfully grown to a 3-inch diameter by OCCC, and polished Y₂O₃ samples exhibited transparent appearance and a clear scintillation response under ¹³⁷Cs excitation. The OCCC method is a promising platform for scaling high-melting-point oxide scintillators without precious-metal crucibles.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-07-02] Cs 3 Cu 2 I 5 Single Crystals Grown with Oleic- and Formic-Acid-Assisted Additives: Effects on Crystal Quality and Scintillation Properties (#2527)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Bansal (Autores: B. Bansal , V. Anand , G. A. Kumar)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee, Department of Physics, Roorkee, India
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Cs 3 Cu 2 I 5 single crystals were grown at room temperature via a solvent evaporation method using two organic acid additives: oleic acid (OA) and formic acid (FA), and their effects on crystal quality and scintillation performance were systematically investigated. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy confirmed the absence of Cu²⁺ features in both samples, demonstrating that organic acid additives effectively suppress Cu⁺ oxidation during growth. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction and rocking curve analysis revealed that formic-acid-assisted crystals exhibit superior crystalline quality, with a narrower rocking-curve FWHM of 0.009° compared to 0.016° for OA-assisted crystals. Scintillation measurements using a ¹³⁷Cs γ-ray source (662 keV) coupled to a SiPM photosensor showed an improved energy resolution of 5.4% for formic-acid-grown crystals versus 5.8% for OA-grown crystals. The enhanced performance of FA-assisted crystals is attributed to formic acid's ability to regulate iodide ion availability through slow reaction with I 3- species, reducing the crystallization rate and extending the metastable growth regime, thereby suppressing defect formation. In contrast, the long-chain nature of oleic acid promotes residual ligand incorporation and non-uniform solvent evaporation, slightly degrading optical transparency and crystallinity

sub_talks.title: [NSS-07-03] Novel Cs 3 Cu 2 I 5 :Tl Scintillator Films for X-ray Imaging (#2891)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Soundara Pandian (Autores: L. Soundara Pandian , J. Wang , G. Adhikari , E. van Loef , J. Glodo , V. Nagarkar)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Radiation Monitoring Devices, Inc., Imaging Sensors and Applications, Watertown, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Tl-doped cesium copper iodide (Cs 3 Cu 2 I 5 :Tl, CCI:Tl) has emerged as a promising scintillator for medical imaging, offering higher light yield than the long-established CsI:Tl while remaining non-hygroscopic and lead free. Its emission (445-500 nm) matches the quantum efficiency of CCD, CMOS, and flat panel readouts, making it an excellent choice as a converter for advanced X-ray detectors. Detectors based on CCI:Tl have potential for providing dose efficiency in medical applications including digital mammography, radiography, and cone-beam CT. The high brightness of CCI:Tl will enable their use in high framerate or otherwise light starved applications in both medical and industrial fields. We report on the development of polycrystalline CCI:Tl scintillating films grown by hot wall evaporation (HWE), a technique previously used to produce columnar, low stress CsI:Tl films and extended here to the ternary CCI system. CCI crystals were first grown and then used as the source for evaporation. Material quality was characterized by SEM and EDX. EDX confirms stoichiometric Cs:Cu:I ratio of 3:2:5. Scintillation properties were measured under gamma and X-ray excitation, including pulse-height spectra, emission, light yield relative to CsI:Tl, scintillation decay time, and afterglow. X-ray imaging performance was evaluated through quantification of contrast transfer function (CTF(f)) and measurements of modulation transfer function (MTF(f)) using a slit method. with films demonstrating resolution 5 lp/mm at 70 kVp for thickness in excess of 150µm. The results indicate structured growth and demonstrate that HWE grown CCI:Tl films offer a viable, potentially higher luminosity alternative to CsI:Tl for indirect medical‑imaging detection while also revealing the deposition parameters that govern film morphology and scintillation response. Results from both crystals and films and applications of CCI:Tl films will be presented.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-07-04] Growth and Pellet Fabrication of 2D Perovskite Scintillator Radiation Detectors (#2585)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. J. Dickinson (Autores: A. J. Dickinson , C. Crean , J. Ghosh , P. Petisiwaveth , P. Sellin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Surrey, School of Mathematics and Physics, Guildford, United Kingdom [2] University of Oxford, Department of Chemistry, Oxford, United Kingdom [3] University of Wollongong, School of Physics, Wollongong, Australia
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) metal halide perovskites have emerged as promising scintillator materials for radiation detection due to their high x-ray and gamma-ray absorption coefficients, high light yields, and fast scintillation decay times. Their structural flexibility enables precise tuning of optical and scintillation properties through variation of the organic spacer, halide composition, and dopant incorporation [1]. This work presents the synthesis, optical characterisation, and pellet fabrication of several 2D perovskite scintillators, including the Ruddlesden-Popper (RP) phase materials (BA)₂PbBr₄ and (PEA)₂PbBr₄, and the Dion-Jacobson (DJ) phase material (TMPDA)PbBr₄. Crystals were synthesised using a slow-cooling solution growth method and subsequently processed into pellets using a cold-pressing technique to increase thickness while improving uniformity and reproducibility. The effects of manganese and rubidium doping in (BA)₂PbBr₄ were also investigated, demonstrating enhanced light yield and tuneable emission behaviour. Under x-ray excitation, (PEA)₂PbBr₄ exhibited a light yield exceeding that of LYSO, while all investigated materials demonstrated promising gamma-ray scintillation responses with resolvable peaks. These results highlight the strong potential of 2D perovskite scintillators for next-generation radiation detection technologies.
