sub_talks.title: [RTSD-05-01] Performance Improvements on Perovskite Gamma-Ray Detectors Using Depth-Dependent Shaping Optimizations (#1338)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Robbins (Autores: M. Robbins , M. Unal , Q. V. Phan , K. S. Bayikadi , D. C. Young , M. Kanatzidis , Z. He)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Michigan, NERS, Ann arbor, Michigan, United States of America [2] Argonne National Labs, Materials Science Division, Lemont, Illinois, United States of America [3] Northwestern University, Department of Chemistry, Evanston, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract CsPbBr₃ is a perovskite room-temperature semiconductor crystal, with properties for high-resolution gamma-ray detection. This material has been fabricated in large volumes, with detectors up to 12 mm thick demonstrated to remain stable for up to 4 months under continuous bias, achieving energy resolutions of 1.1%-1.6% FWHM at 662 keV. This research employs depth-of-interaction analysis on a 12 mm-thick pixelated detector to investigate how optimizing digital pulse shaping parameters as a function of interaction depth and pixel electrode can improve energy resolution. Rather than applying a uniform set of shaping parameters across all events, each waveform is processed independently, allowing shaping to be tuned to the charge-transport characteristics specific to each depth bin and pixel pair. Two optimization methods are compared: a Linear 1D approach, in which rise time and flat-top time are constrained to be equal, and a Grid 2D approach, in which both parameters are varied independently across a wider search space. Our results show that both depth-dependent methods consistently outperform uniform shaping across all drift times. The 2D grid method achieves lower energy resolution than the 1D method but at a significantly higher computational cost (up to an order of magnitude slower). Using 1D optimization, per-pixel energy-resolution improvements of 4.1% to 15.4% were observed, with a best achieved resolution of 0.65% FWHM at 662 keV for near-pixel-side events, representing an improvement over previously reported thinner detectors while maintaining comparable stability.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-05-02] On Technological Aspects In The Development Of Perovskite Gamma Radiation Detectors (#1472)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Grundmanis (Autores: N. Grundmanis , V. Gostilo , A. Lupilov , A. Owens)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Baltic Scientific Instruments, Riga, Latvia [2] Czech Technical University, Institute of Experimental and Applied Physics, Prague, Czech Republic
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This paper outlines the technological steps and methods used to manufacture perovskite semiconductor radiation detectors and compares them with those used in the manufacture of other semiconductor materials, such as HPGe, Si, CZT, CdTe, and TlBr. We analyse the problems and limitations arising when implementing these technologies at this early stage of perovskite detector development. We examine and critique the technologies involved in crystal growth and processing; for example, mechanical (cutting, grinding, polishing...), chemical (etching, washing...), contact deposition and patterning (masking, photolithography) as well as the welding of contacts and micro assembly of detector crystals. Applying the processes described above to CsPbBr 3 crystals of dimensions of 5´5´3 mm 3 , we have manufactured a number of radiation detectors with different contact architectures - a planar contact structure, a planar structure with a guard ring and a ring-electrode type structure. The detectors provided FWHM energy resolutions of less than 1% at 662 and 1332 keV (0.79% and 0.86%, respectively) with a peak to Compton ratio of 11, The FWHM energy resolutions at 59.5 keV, 122 keV and 5.9 kV were 2.7 keV (4.5%), 3.9 keV (3.2 %) and ≤2.6 keV, respectively.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-05-03] Metal-Halide Perovskites for Fast Hard-Radiation Detection (#1576)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Sakhatska (Autores: A. Sakhatska , K. Sakhatskyi , G. J. Matt , A. Kanak , A. Szola , Y. Padnuik , Y. Kominko , A. Bhardwaj , S. Yakunin , M. Kovalenko)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] ETH Zurich, Laboratory of Inorganic Chemistry, Department of Chemistry and Applied Biosciences, Zürich, Zürich, Switzerland [2] EMPA, Laboratory for Thin Films and Photovoltaics, Zürich, Zürich, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Metal-halide perovskites are promising low-cost semiconductors for photon-counting X-ray imaging. However, their temporal response is often hindered by ion migration induced field screening, which can lead to an underestimation of charge carrier mobility. Here, charge transport is studied in CsPbBr 3 single-crystal detectors using time-of-flight technique and 241 Am (60 keV) gamma-counting spectroscopy under direct-current (DC) and alternating-current (AC) bias. In DC operation, polarization effects restrict the extracted hole mobility to ~36 cm 2 V -1 s -1 . Applying AC bias suppresses ionic accumulation and reveals substantially higher hole mobility, reaching up to ~560 cm 2 V -1 s -1 . Gamma counting under AC operation preserves energy resolution (~10-11%) while accelerating charge collection: the mean response time decreases from ~460 ns (DC) to ~110 ns (AC). These results show that alternating biasing mitigates ion migration induced field distortion and enables perovskite detectors to approach the response speeds required for fast photon counting.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-05-04] Growth of MAPbBr 3 Single Crystals for X-Ray, Gamma Ray Detection by Slow Solvent Evaporation at Room-Temperature (#1827)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Niraula (Autores: M. Niraula , R. Ohshima , S. Kamon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Nagoya Institute of Technology, Graduate School of Engineering, Nagoya, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Solution-grown lead halide perovskites are promising materials for next-generation radiation detectors. Inverse temperature crystallization (ITC) growth is widely used to obtain large crystals within a relatively short time. However, the rapid increase in supersaturation during heating promotes spontaneous nucleation, leading to compositional inhomogeneity and elevated defect density. To address this limitation, we investigated the growth of MAPbBr 3 single crystals using a slow solvent evaporation-induced crystallization method performed at a controlled, constant temperature near room temperature. X-ray diffraction confirmed the formation of high-quality single crystals with improved crystallinity compared to our standard ITC-grown crystals. Detectors fabricated in an Au/MAPbBr₃/Cr planar configuration exhibited reduced dark current and enhanced X-ray sensitivity relative to devices based on ITC-grown crystals. These results demonstrate that this growth strategy provides a viable pathway to improved crystal quality and device performance.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-05-05] Millimeter-Thick Perovskite Single-Crystal X-ray Detectors with Unity Charge Extraction in Photovoltaic Mode (#1868)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Sakhatskyi (Autores: B. Turedi , K. Sakhatskyi , V. Bartosh , G. J. Matt , A. Sakhatska , Q. Lung , S. Yakunin , M. Kovalenko)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] ETH Zurich, Department of Chemistry and Applied Biosciences, Zurich, Zürich, Switzerland [2] Empa - Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science and Technology, Laboratory for Thin Films and Photovoltaics, Dubendorf, Zürich, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Low-dose diagnostic X-ray imaging requires detector materials that combine high stopping power, low electronic noise, fine spatial resolution, and stable operation under clinically relevant X-ray energies. Cadmium telluride currently provides this performance in direct-conversion imagers, but its cost and crystal-growth constraints limit scalability. We report direct conversion detectors working in photovoltaic mode based on solution-grown mixed-cation methylammonium-formamidinium lead triiodide single crystals. The crystals were grown with controlled thicknesses up to 1 mm on charge-selective contacts and patterned indium tin oxide arrays. Optical and X-ray detection characterization shows millimeter-scale charge extraction without an externally applied field, with electron mobility-lifetime products up to 0.17 cm 2 V -1 and diffusion lengths of 3.5 mm. The devices achieve single-photon sensitivity and detective quantum efficiency above 90% at 60 keV, while the same growth route enables conformal integration into 40 µm-pitch linear arrays with spatial resolution up to 19-line pairs per millimeter. The detectors also maintain a stable response over up to two years of intermittent operation and storage. These results indicate that solution-grown perovskite single crystals can approach cadmium telluride-level low-dose imaging performance while retaining a scalable low-temperature materials platform for medical and industrial X-ray imaging.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-05-06] Multipixel 2D Perovskite Thin-Film Array for High-Resolution Proton Beam Profiling (#2090)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 I. Fratelli (Autores: I. Fratelli , L. Basiricò , G. Napolitano , A. Ciavatti , E. Verroi , I. Kymissis , B. Fraboni)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Bologna, Department of Physics and Astronomy, Bologna, Italy [2] INFN, Bologna, Bologna, Italy [3] Columbia University, Department of Electrical Engineering, New York City, New York, United States of America [4] Trento Institute for Fundamental Physics and Applications, Trento, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present a scalable and calibrated proton dosimetry platform based on flexible 2D perovskite (PEA₂PbBr₄) thin films, enabling high-resolution beam profiling in clinically relevant conditions. The devices consist of solution-processed thin films deposited on 75 µm Kapton substrates and operated as two-terminal coplanar detectors. Their response has been characterized under therapeutic proton beams (70-200 MeV), showing stable operation, good radiation tolerance up to 20 Gy, and a linear dependence of the collected charge on the total dose. The current response exhibits a reproducible sublinear dependence on dose rate, enabling the definition of calibration protocols. The scalability of the technology is demonstrated through multipixel linear arrays composed of up to 28 devices arranged side-by-side, showing good uniformity with pixel-to-pixel variations below 25% in sheet resistance and 15% in calibration parameters. After calibration, the system enables accurate reconstruction of transverse proton beam profiles in agreement with nominal beam shapes. A key feature of these detectors is their angular-independent response (<2% variation up to 90°), which enables operation in an edge-on configuration and a transition from pixel-pitch-limited to thickness-limited spatial resolution. This concept is extended to a stacked pixel-on-pixel multipixel architecture for high-resolution beam profiling (77 µm). Finally, the devices have been validated in an anthropomorphic phantom under clinical 200 MeV proton irradiation, demonstrating the capability to discriminate beam position shifts and reconstruct dose profiles consistently with radiochromic film and commercial dosimetry measurements. These results highlight the potential of flexible 2D perovskite detectors as a versatile platform for scalable, high-resolution, and real-time proton beam dosimetry.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-05-07] Phase-Pure Orthorhombic CsPbBr₃ Perovskite Materials for Low-Lag, Ultrahigh-Resolution Direct X-ray Detectors (#3093)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Motakef (Autores: A. Datta , B. Dunham , S. Motakef)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CapeSym, Inc., Research and Developement, Natick, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Room-temperature direct-conversion X-ray imagers require sensor materials that combine high stopping power, efficient charge transport, spatially confined charge collection, and stable temporal response. We report an all-inorganic perovskite detector platform in which phase purity of cesium lead bromide (CsPbBr₃, CPB) is used as the central materials control parameter. Low-impurity, spectroscopic-grade CPB crystals were produced by purification and optimized Bridgman growth, milled to nanopowder, and blade-coated into dense sensor films on active-pixel readout arrays at temperatures compatible with backplane electronics. X-ray diffraction of both precursor crystals and sensor films showed the stable orthorhombic Pnma phase with characteristic reflections, indicating preservation of phase through crystal-to-powder-to-film conversion. In contrast, unoptimized starting material contained a CsPb₂Br₅ tetragonal secondary phase, generated nonuniform slurries and aggregate-rich films, and produced degraded X-ray images due to interpixel charge sharing. The optimized CPB sensors demonstrated linear response to 30 keV X-rays, sensitivity of 55,400 μC Gy air ⁻¹ cm⁻² at 0.5 V/μm, a limit of detection of 417 pGy air s⁻¹, and a hole mobility-lifetime product of 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ cm²/V. Phase-pure CPB also produced low residual lag, reducing detector lag from 8.9% to 1.1%, while enabling 6.9 lp/mm at 20% modulation transfer function on a 100 μm-pitch amorphous-silicon array and 20 lp/mm on a fine-pitch CMOS readout. These results identify phase-pure orthorhombic CPB as a scalable room-temperature semiconductor for low-lag, high-sensitivity, high-resolution X-ray imagers.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-11-01] ML-based radiological clearance of activated metallic waste at CERN using synthetic data (#1357)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Gomes (Autores: A. Gomes , M. Helej , M. Magistris , F. Ogallar Ruiz , M.E. Stamati , C. Theis , H. Vincke)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CERN, HSE-RP, Geneva, Genève, Switzerland [2] University of Geneva, Physics Department, Geneva, Genève, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The maintenance and dismantling of high-energy accelerators at CERN generate activated waste with significant variability in irradiation history, cooling time, and material composition. If activity levels are negligible, waste can be cleared from regulatory control in Switzerland and reused as conventional material. We present a method for radiological classification which is conservative, without being as penalizing as more traditional approaches based on a worst-case scenario. More specifically, we classify accelerator components as conventional or radioactive based on a radiation measurement (e.g. with a bismuth germanate detector), and on the application of a predictive model. The models here presented were trained over ~60,000 synthetic waste items and their radiological properties. Each synthetic item represents a specific activation scenario, generated through probabilistic sampling of operational parameters. The associated radiological properties were computed with ActiWiz, a CERN-developed activation code based on FLUKA Monte Carlo simulations and evaluated neutron data libraries. Focusing on the classification of metallic accelerator components, we compare the performance of logistic regression based on a bismuth germanate detector response, with that of a neural network model incorporating both the detector response and the item mass. Results show that the neural network improves classification performance and robustness relative to logistic regression, reducing misclassification of borderline cases while maintaining compliance with Swiss regulatory criteria. The proposed framework establishes a robust and scalable clearance workflow, adaptable to the evolving requirements of large-scale research facilities.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-11-02] Inverse reconstruction of ¹³⁷Cs depth-dependent contamination in concrete from gamma spectrometry measurements (#1469)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Hayek (Autores: A. Hayek , J. Venara , G. Daniel , C. Lynde , P.-L. Antonsanti , M. Cuozzo , C. Mahé , Z. El Bitar)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CEA, Univ. Montpellier, Marcoule, DES, ISEC, DPME, SEIP, LNPA, F-30207 Bagnols-sur-Cèze Cedex, France [2] Université Paris-Saclay, CEA, Service de Génie Logiciel pour la Simulation, 91191 Gif-sur-Yvette, France [3] Université Paris-Saclay, CEA, Service de Physico-Chimie, 91191 Gif-sur-Yvette, France [4] Université de Strasbourg, CNRS, IPHC UMR 7178, 67000 Strasbourg, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Radiological characterization is a key step in nuclear decommissioning, particularly during final operations where contaminated concrete structures must be assessed prior to decontamination. Conventional approaches combine surface measurements with radiochemical analyses of samples at different depths, and use geostatistical methods to estimate 3D contamination distributions. Despite their efficacy, these methods remain intrusive, time-consuming, and costly. In this work, we investigate a complementary non-destructive methodology based on in situ gamma spectrometry conducted at the surface using a HPGe detector. The primary objective of this methodology is to reduce the need for destructive sampling and improving the understanding of contamination phenomena in concrete. This study focuses on the analysis of ¹³⁷Cs, a predominant gamma-emitting radionuclide frequently encountered in nuclear facilities. The proposed approach relies on inverse reconstruction of depth contamination profiles, where the volume of concrete is discretized into layers. The feasibility of the approach was confirmed through simulations. The detector response is modeled using Monte Carlo simulations with MCNP and is combined with the ML-EM algorithm to solve the inverse problem. However, investigations also revealed limitations, especially ambiguities and non-unique solutions in complex configurations. We propose to integrate prior knowledge on the contamination profile (Fickian diffusion) and demonstrate its benefits in addressing the aforementioned limitations. In controlled laboratory conditions, the experimental validation was executed with a calibrated ¹³⁷Cs point source shielded with a concrete barrier. With this configuration, the ability to estimate source position by using relevant energy ranges were demonstrated. These results highlight both the potential and inherent limitations of ML-EM, thus motivating hybrid approaches combining physics-based modeling and learning methods.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-11-03] Joint autoencoder-classifier network for particle-type identification in organic scintillator pulse pileup (#1374)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. R. McHugh (Autores: A. R. McHugh , K. Beyer , S. D. Clarke , S. A. Pozzi , M. I. Radaideh)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Michigan, Department of Nuclear Engineering and Radiological Sciences, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Charge-comparison pulse-shape discrimination in organic scintillators fails at high irradiation rates due to the effects of pulse pileup. While pileup rejection reduces particle misclassification, this severely degrades detector efficiency. We present a new machine-learning pipeline to extract particle-type information from piled-up trans-stilbene waveforms using a novel joint autoencoder-classifier design. Events are classified as single or pileup, then routed to separate multi-task convolutional autoencoders, which extract the important features of the input waveform and perform n/γ classification. Trained on 519,910 labeled Time-of-Flight waveforms and synthetically generated pileup data, the system achieves 97.66% accuracy for single/pileup detection, 99.42% n/γ classification accuracy on single pulses, and 90.15% classification accuracy of both constituents in pileup waveforms. This approach is shown to substantially outperform charge-comparison-based analytical pulse-shape discrimination by improving pileup detection and preserving neutron and gamma-ray counts.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-11-04] Joint Neutron Source Localization and Identification using Machine-Learning-based Spectral Imaging (#2042)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Breitenmoser (Autores: D. Breitenmoser , S. Clarke , S. Pozzi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Michigan, Department of Nuclear Engineering and Radiological Sciences, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Neutron source localization and identification are critical for nuclear safeguards and security, yet current scatter-based imaging pipelines typically decouple spatial reconstruction from spectral analysis, treating both as separate post-processing steps. This work introduces a unified machine-learning framework for joint spectral-directional neutron source inference using energy-resolved simple back-projection (SBP) images. The proposed framework combines unsupervised Gaussian mixture model localization with a lightweight k-nearest neighbors classifier. Despite its simplicity, the approach achieves strong performance on controlled laboratory data involving Cf-252 and PuBe sources in single- and mixed-source configurations, with a mean angular localization error <5º and a source classification accuracy >98%. These results demonstrate that low-complexity statistical learning applied to energy-resolved SBP data enables fully automated, end-to-end inference of both source direction and source identity without manual region selection or separate spectral analysis, offering a practical pathway toward more scalable and deployable neutron imaging systems for real-world safeguards and security operations.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-11-05] Machine-Learning-Based Real-Time Gamma-Ray Direction Estimation Using Fractal Radiation Imaging Element (#1755)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Sasaki (Autores: M. Sasaki , T. Torii , Y. Morishita , S. Kurosawa , N. Matsubayashi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Japan Atomic Energy Agency, Minamisoma, Japan [2] Fukushima University, Fukushima, Japan [3] Nagoya University, Nagya, Japan [4] Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology, Tokyo, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In this study, a real-time gamma-ray contribution direction imaging system using a Fractal Radiation Imaging Element (FRIE) detector and a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) was developed and evaluated. The system consists of an FRIE detector composed of sixteen GFAG scintillators, a 360-degree camera, and a PC for real-time analysis and visualization. Radiation contribution directions were estimated from count-rate data of the sixteen detectors using an MLP trained with Cs-137 point-source irradiation data including statistical fluctuations. Evaluation results showed that the average angular estimation error was approximately five degrees, and the estimation accuracy improved as the count rate increased. Experiments using measured data demonstrated that the estimated source direction gradually converged through temporal accumulation of measurement data, even under low count-rate conditions. Compared with the conventional similarity-based method, the proposed method reduced the direction estimation error while enabling real-time gamma-ray contribution direction estimation. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed system for real-time localization of gamma-ray sources in nuclear decommissioning environments.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-11-06] Evaluating isotope identification methods for use with count-starved gamma spectra (#2536)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Biggs (Autores: J. Biggs , C. Shenton-Taylor)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Surrey, School of Mathematics and Physics, Guildford, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Radiation detector networks provide a potential means of monitoring the movement of radiological material within urban environments. Such systems require automated methods capable of identifying non-background isotopes within collected spectra, particularly for count-starved measurements acquired in complex backgrounds. In 2018, the London-based SIGMA trial collected approximately 1.5 billion one-second gamma spectra using a combination of stationary and mobile scintillation detectors. This work presents a comparison between three viable isotope identification tools, to ascertain which is best placed to be used in environments with count-starved gamma spectra, such as those typically seen in large datasets like SIGMA. Representative spectra were created by combining laboratory collected spectra and Geant4 simulated spectra with real-world SIGMA background. Tranches of spectra were tested in each of the chosen methods: InterSpec, wavelets, and a convolutional neural network. Although all three methods showed promise when identifying a range of 137 Cs spectra, the CNN outperformed the others when presented with spectra with the smallest photopeaks, making it the preferred approach for isotope detection in urban landscapes. sub_talks.title: [NSS-12-01] PLATON: a plenoptic single-photon camera with sub-nanosecond time resolution for particle detection through monolithic scintillating volumes (#1339)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Sgalaberna (Autores: T. Dieminger , S. Alonso-Monsalve , K. Kaneyasu , M. Barbieri , V. Berardi , C. Bruschini , E. Charbon , D. Sgalaberna)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] ETH Zurich, Zurich, Zürich, Switzerland [2] EPFL, Lausanne, Vaud, Switzerland [3] Politecnico di Bari, Bari, Italy [4] Università degli Studi Roma Tre, Rome, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract High-resolution scintillator detectors achieve precise particle tracking through fine segmentation down to a few hundred micrometres, making complexity and costs prohibitive when scaling up to large volumes. We propose a change of paradigm: 3D imaging of particle interactions in an unsegmented monolithic volume of scintillator obtained by combining plenoptic imaging with a Single-Photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD) array sensor. We report the performance of the first SPAD-based plenoptic camera for particle detection, built around the SwissSPAD2 sensor. Results obtained from 90 Sr radioactive source, a point light source and a controlled two-photon-absorption setup as well as novel analytical and artificial-intelligence-driven 3D imaging techniques will be described. A simulation case study on neutrino detection demonstrates the unique potential of this approach and its scalability to medium (1 x 1 x 1 m 3 ) and large (10 x 10 x 10 m 3 ) scale scintillator volumes, with sub-millimeter 3D spatial resolution. A new custom SPAD array required to enhance the resolution currently under development is also presented. This work sets the path forward for a new system for high-precision particle tracking in dense volumes. Applications of the PLATON concept can also extend to medical imaging.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-12-02] A Capacitively Coupled GaAs SAM-APD with Cross-Delay Lines for Fully Digital 3D Hard X-ray Photon Imaging (#1810)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Lusardi (Autores: N. Lusardi , F. Arfelli , G. Biasiol , F. Driussi , M. Antonelli , M. Cautero , M. Colja , F. Garzetti , G. Cautero , R. H. Menk , A. Costa , G. Fiumicelli , E. Ronconi , G. Bonanno , G. Brajnik , S. Carrato , D. Curcio , S. Dal Zilio , D. Ercolani , A. Geraci , A. Pilotto , L. Sbuelz , R. Sergo , L. Stebel)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Politecnico di Milano, Dipartimento di Elettronica, Informazione e Bioingegneria, Milano, Italy [2] INFN, Trieste, Trieste, Italy [3] University of Trieste, Department of Physics, Trieste, Italy [4] CNR, ISTITUTO OFFICINA DEI MATERIALI, Trieste, Italy [5] Elettra Sincrotrone, Trieste, Italy [6] University of Trieste, DIA, Trieste, Italy [7] INFN, Milano, Milano, Italy [8] Università degli Studi di Udine, DPIA, Udine, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Time-resolved ultrafast phenomena with hard X-rays are central to applications such as pump-probe spectroscopy, driving advances in detector and multichannel acquisition technologies. This work proposes a fully digital 3D (x-y-time) imager for hard X-rays. Key challenges include improving time and spatial resolution-often limited by pixelated approaches-and overcoming the low quantum efficiency of silicon detectors at high photon energies. To address these issues, we adopt a Separate Absorption and Multiplication Avalanche Photodiode (SAM-APD) based on III-V semiconductors. GaAs alloys, with higher atomic number and carrier mobility than silicon, enable significantly improved absorption efficiency and faster response. On the readout side, the shift toward multichannel systems and stringent constraints on power and area per channel motivate a transition from voltage-mode pixel electronics to time-based acquisition, where spatial (x, y) and temporal information are encoded in the detection time. The proposed architecture couples a large-area GaAs SAM-APD (mm-scale diameter) with two Cross Delay Lines (CDLs) and a 4-channel Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)-based Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) with 15 ps precision. The main challenges are preserving spatial coherence between the interaction point on the detector and the corresponding charge readout location on the CDL, and ensuring capacitive coupling with high signal integrity. Preliminary tests were performed using a 10 × 5 mm² p-i-n diode and laser pulses achieving a spatial precision of <100 μm r.m.s. and a temporal jitter of 68.3 ps r.m.s. Additional measurements show intensity discrimination capability with resolvable signal changes of ~1.2-1.6×. The approach offers a compact and scalable alternative to pixelated detectors, eliminating the need for advanced lithography and per-pixel readout, while relying on only four acquisition channels.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Morozzi (Autores: F. Moscatelli , A. Morozzi , V. Sola , D. Passeri , P. Svihra , R. Novotny , V. Kracmar , J. Kroll , B. Regnery , R. White , M. Ferrero , M. Tornago , A.R. Altamura , M. Bruzzi , S. A. Onder , A. Dierlamm , T. Bergauer)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CNR-Istituto Officina dei Materiali (IOM), Perugia, Italy [2] INFN of Perugia, Perugia, Italy [3] University of Torino, Department of Physics, Torino, Italy [4] University of Perugia, Department of Engineering, Perugia, Italy [5] FNSPE CTU in Prague, Department of Physics, Prague, Czech Republic [6] FZU CAS, Department of Detector Development and Data Processing, Prague, Czech Republic [7] Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Karlsruhe, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [8] INFN Torino, Torino, Italy [9] University of Florence, Department of Physics and Astronomy, Firenze, Italy [10] MBI for Particle Physics, Wien, Austria
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The demand for radiation-hard 4D detectors capable of simultaneous high-precision timing and spatial resolution is driving the investigation of 4H-Silicon Carbide (4H-SiC) as a robust alternative to silicon. While 4H-SiC offers superior thermal stability and radiation tolerance, its wide bandgap and current epitaxial thickness limits necessitate the use of internal charge multiplication. This work presents an extensive performance evaluation of 4H-SiC LGADs and PN junction diodes fabricated by Onsemi on 6-inch wafers 50 μm epitaxial layer, n=5 ·10 13 cm -3 . The devices were subjected to 23 MeV proton irradiation, covering five fluences from 1.3 ·10 14 to 2 ·10 15 p/cm 2 . They have been characterized in terms of current-voltage I-V and capacitance-voltage C-V measurements. The study is complemented by ongoing Transient Current Technique (TCT) and Charge Collection Efficiency (CCE) measurements using a beta source. Furthermore, the impact of temperature (up to 200°C for I-V/C-V and 100°C for beta tests) is investigated to evaluate defect dynamics and the operational stability of 4H-SiC LGADs in extreme environments.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-12-04] Status of GRAiNITA, a next generation calorimeter (#1928)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Chanal (Autores: H. Chanal , D. Abbaneo , S. Barsuk , O. Bezshyyko , I. Boyarintseva , A. Boyarintsev , D. Breton , M. DeFranchis , A.M. Dubovik , L. Perez , D. Picard , M.-H. Schune , M. Selvaggi , N. Semkiv , I. Tupitsyna , M. Yeresko)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Université Clermont Auvergne, LPCA, CNRS/IN2P3, Clermont-Ferrand, France [2] Université Paris-Saclay, ,IJCLab, CNRS/IN2P3, Saclay, France [3] Institute for Scintillation Materials of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, Kharkiv, Ukraine [4] Kyiv National Taras Shevchenko University, Kyiv, Ukraine [5] CERN, European Organization for Nuclear Research, Geneva, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The GRAiNITA project aims to develop a novel design for a next-generation calorimeter. It is an innovative approach which uses a mixture of millimeter-sized inorganic scintillating crystals (approximately 1-2 mm) dispersed within a high-density, transparent liquid. Compared to other sampling calorimeter with sensitive material of plastic scintillator, liquid argon, or silicon detector the sampling fluctuation impact on the resolution is predicted by simulation to be much smaller (<2%/sqrt{E}) due to the high density of the scintillator grains compared to the liquid and the smallness of the grains. A test beam operated in June 2024 at CERN allowed to study the performance of a small-scale GRAiNITA prototype. The light light yield was confirmed to be approximately 10 kPE/GeV and we demonstrated the feasibility of achieving sub-2% stochastic and constant terms. Since, the project has advanced significantly. This article presents the latest developments, including the design of a full-scale demonstrator module, advanced Geant4 simulations which are used to evaluate its expected performance, and detailed characterization studies scintillation properties of ZnWO$_4$ using proton beams. These efforts pave the way for the comprehensive validation of a full-scale detector.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-12-05] Small Dose Monitor based on Silicon Carbide diodes for FLASH radiotherapy (#2594)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Fleta (Autores: C. Fleta , I. López , Á. Henao , S. Heinrich , C. Guardiola)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Center of Microelectronics (IMB-CNM, CSIC), Barcelona, Spain [2] University Paris-Saclay, Orsay, France, Institut Curie, Inserm U1021-CNRS UMR 3347, Orsay, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract FLASH radiotherapy (FLASH RT), delivered at ultra-high dose rates (>40 Gy/s), has shown potential to reduce toxicity in healthy tissues while preserving tumor control. However, accurate, real-time dosimetry at such conditions remains challenging due to limitations of conventional detectors, including saturation effects and insufficient temporal resolution. In this work, silicon carbide (SiC) diodes are investigated as a promising solution for ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) dosimetry due to their high radiation hardness, fast response, and low sensitivity to saturation [1]. A 4 × 4 array of SiC diodes (1 mm diameter, 2.2 mm pitch) and a single 2.2 mm diode were tested using pulsed 7 MeV electron beams under FLASH conditions. The detectors were evaluated in terms of linearity, time response, and spatial dose measurement capabilities using a clinical reference dosimeter and radiochromic films for comparison. The single diode demonstrated excellent linearity better than 3.5% up to 10 Gy per pulse, with no evidence of saturation or radiation damage. Time-resolved measurements confirmed the capability to resolve sub-microsecond pulse structures, consistent with accelerator signals. The SiC array prototype enabled spatially resolved dose measurements over areas up to 70 × 50 mm², producing 2D dose maps with millimeter-scale resolution under UHDR conditions. Good agreement with independent film measurements demonstrates its accuracy for beam profiling. These results highlight the feasibility of SiC-based detectors as scalable, position-sensitive dose monitors for FLASH RT [2]. Overall, this work demonstrates the potential of SiC technology for real-time, high-resolution dosimetry in FLASH radiotherapy, paving the way for future large-area detector systems and improved quality assurance in UHDR treatments.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-12-06] Thin-Film and Single-Crystal Perovskite Detectors for Real-Time FLASH Radiotherapy (#2664)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Bruzzi (Autores: M. Bruzzi , L. Baldesi , L. Basiricò , M.G. Bisogni , G. Casini , A. Cavalieri , C. Civinini , L. Forcieri , B. Fraboni , F. Di Martino , A. Vinattieri , E. Verroi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] INFN - Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Firenze, Firenze, Italy [2] Università di Firenze, Firenze, Italy [3] Università di Pisa, Pisa, Italy [4] INFN - Istituto di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Pisa, Pisa, Italy [5] INFN - Istituto di Fisica Nucleare, TIFPA - Sezione di Trento, Trento, Italy [6] Unit of Medical Physics, Pisa University Hospital, Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria Pisana, Pisa, Italy [7] Università di Bologna, Bologna, Italy [8] Centro Pisano ricerca e implementazione clinica Flash Radiotherapy (CPFR@CISUP), Pisa, Italy [9] Center for Instrument Sharing of the University of Pisa (CISUP), University of Pisa, Pisa, Italy [10] INFN- Istituto di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Bologna, Bologna, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) radiotherapy, commonly known as FLASH radio-therapy, is a revolutionary oncological approach that spares healthy tissue while preserving tumor control. Clinical translation of this method needs radiation detectors that provide real-time dosimetry under extreme dose rates, exceeding 40-100 Gy/s. Standard dosimeters, such as ionization chambers and traditional semiconductors, may face limitations like charge recombination and signal saturation in these environments. This study investigates full-inorganic metal-halide perovskites (CsPbBr 3 ) as viable detector material due to its high stopping power and moderately wide bandgap. We evaluated two distinct device architectures: thin-film (TF) and single-crystal (SC) detectors. The 1 μm-thick TF detectors were fabricated using radio-frequency magnetron sputtering (MS) on flexible Kapton substrates with interdigitated electrodes. SC detectors featured Schottky-Ohmic electrodes (Ti/Au and Au) deposited by DC-MS on pure commercial crystals. Characterization indicated a dominant CsPbBr3 phase, a forbidden gap of 2.32 eV, and a dark resistivity of approximately 10 7 Ωcm. Experimental validation was performed using a 9 MeV electron beam at Centro Pisano FLASH Radiotherapy (CPFR) and a 228 MeV proton beam at APSS (Azienda Provinciali Servizi Sanitari) Trento proton-therapy center. The tests with 9MeV electron beams covered a dose-per-pulse (DPP) range of 0.1 to 5.0 Gy delivered in 4us-long pulses, while proton testing reached dose-rates of 300 Gy/s with pulse durations of 10-25ms. Both detector types demonstrated good signal linearity and showed no evidence of saturation at the highest tested intensities. Ultimately, these results confirm that CsPbBr3 perovskite detectors are suitable for real-time monitoring in both electron and proton FLASH radiotherapy.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-12-07] Particle-by-Particle Characterization of Clinical Carbon Ion Beams with a Silicon Strip Detector and High-Rate DAQ Systems (#3038)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Mas Milian (Autores: F. Mas Milian , M. Fadavi Mazinani , P. Cerello , S. De Astis , M. D. Fernandez Moreira , V. Ferrero , E. Fiorina , D. Montalvan Olivares , F. Pennazio , M. Pullia , S. Ranjbar , I. B. Rivas Ortiz , R. Sacchi , A. Vignati , S. Giordanengo)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Section Torino, Torino, Italy [2] Università di Torino, Department of Physics, Torino, Italy [3] Centro Nazionale di Adroterapia Oncologica, Pavia, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract At CNAO, carbon-ion beams are delivered by the standard scheme which uses betatron-core extraction of a debunched beam, while RF Knock-Out (RFKO) extraction keeps the beam bunched and drives particles transversely toward extraction. To resolve the fine temporal structure of these modes beyond the 100 ms limit of standard ESA‑ABACUS readout, a High‑Rate DAQ system with 10 ns time bins was developed. The system used the LVDS outputs of 48 central channels from two ABACUS ASICs connected to a Xilinx Kintex-7 FPGA implementing custom VHDL firmware. Counts were aggregated in 10 ns windows, stored in DDR3 memory, and analyzed offline to reconstruct beam-rate waveforms and frequency components. Tests were performed at CNAO with clinical carbon-ion beams using Betatron and RFKO extraction at four energies (115, 209, 304, and 398 MeV/u) and three intensity levels (20%, 50%, 100%). A CAEN DT5203 picoTDC was also used as an independent acquisition system to record leading- and trailing-edge timing information from 32 ESA-ABACUS outputs in Streaming mode. The High-Rate DAQ resolved clear differences between the two extraction modes: RFKO showed a more compact and regular bunched time structure, while Betatron extraction showed the broader temporal distribution expected from a debunched coasting beam. Fast Fourier Transform analysis of the High-Rate DAQ waveforms allowed the main accelerator RF components to be estimated with deviations below 0.25% for all tested conditions. The DT5203 provided complementary hit‑by‑hit timing and enabled bunch‑spacing estimation with <1.5% deviations, but suffered rate saturation at high intensities. Overall, the High‑Rate DAQ proved suitable for fine beam‑structure measurements under clinical carbon‑ion conditions, supporting accelerator tuning, particularly for RFKO operation.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-12-08] Diamond Quantum Sensor for High Fluence Neutron Detection (#3048)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Cao (Autores: L. Shoen , Y. Tong , J. Lanza , J. Choy , R. Cao)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The Ohio State University, Nuclear Engineering, Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Columbus, Ohio, United States of America [2] University of Wisconsin at Madison, Electrical and Computer Engineering, Madison, Wisconsin, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work investigates diamond nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers as a new class of neutron dosimetry that uses neutron-induced defect formation as the sensing mechanism rather than treating radiation damage as a failure mode. There is no device fabrication, wire connection, or charge collection as the diamond works purely as a passive dosimeter. Fast neutrons generate carbon vacancies in nitrogen-enriched diamond, followed by high-temperature annealing to form stable NV centers exhibiting characteristic photoluminescence and optically detected magnetic resonance responses. Eight nitrogen-rich diamond samples were irradiated at The Ohio State University Research Reactor, with fluence ranging from 10 15 n/cm 2 to 10 17 n/cm 2 , and then annealed at 800 °C for a few hours. The results demonstrated a strong linear correlation between fluorescence intensity and neutron fluence, with up to 403× fluorescence increase observed after annealing compared to control samples. The results support the feasibility of applying diamond as compact, passive, and radiation-hardened sensors for high-fluence neutron detection in nuclear fission and fusion systems. The ongoing work is also exploring the real-time sensing using a diamond quantum sensor.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-03-01] Radiation-Hardened VCO in 28 nm FDSOI with Enhanced Frequency Stability Under Total Ionizing Dose (#1750)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M.A. Anwar (Autores: M.A. Anwar , D.S. Kim , S.R. Koo , I. Kwon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea University of Science and Technology (UST), Nuclear Science and Technology, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [2] Yonsei University Mirae Campus, Department of Radiological Science, Wonju, Republic of Korea [3] Korea University of Science and Technology (UST), Radiation Science, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [4] Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute (KAERI), Daejeon, Republic of Korea [5] Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute (KAERI), Gyeongju, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Ensuring reliable RF operation in radiation-prone is critical for wireless monitoring systems in nuclear and space applications. This work presents a radiation-hardened-by-design (RHBD) voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) implemented in a 28 nm Fully-Depleted Silicon-On-Insulator (FDSOI) process and experimentally evaluated under total ionizing dose (TID) conditions. The proposed RHBD VCO is compared with a conventional design up to 370 kGy(Si) using a Cobalt-60 gamma irradiation source at KAERI. Measurement results demonstrate that the RHBD VCO significantly improves frequency stability, achieving up to 57% reduction in frequency drift compared to the conventional counterpart. In addition, enhanced output power stability and reduced supply current variation are observed under irradiation. The results highlight the combined benefits of FDSOI technology and circuit-level hardening techniques, demonstrating a robust solution for radiation-tolerant RF circuit design.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-03-02] Preamplifier Readout Electronics for Summing SiPMs Enhanced Circuit (PRESSEC) for Advanced SiPM Camera (#1992)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Marín (Autores: D. Marín , A. López , D. Mateo , J. Altet , E. Barajas , X. Aragones , J. Serrano , J. Mauricio , R. Manera , E. Picatoste , S. Gómez)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universitat de Barcelona, Institut de Ciències del Cosmos, Barcelona, Spain [2] Universitat Politécnica de Barcelona, Electronics Department, Barcelona, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The next generation of imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescope (IACT) cameras is transitioning to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) due to their stability, robustness, and superior sensitivity compared to PMTs. Specifically, we are developing an ASIC for the advanced SiPM camera (AdvCam). This ASIC, designated as PRESSEC (Preamplifier Readout Electronics for Summing SiPMs Enhanced Circuit), is implemented in 65 nm CMOS technology. The PRESSEC utilizes a 32-input scheme for large-area sensor readout. Its primary function is to generate analog outputs by summing signals from four sensors into a single channel, effectively reducing the total output count to eight channels. The main functionality of this ASIC is housed in the energy path, which integrates a single-ended-to-differential converter and a pole-zero cancellation circuit. This structure is instrumental in reducing the pulse's Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) to 3 to 5 ns, thereby mitigating pileup effects in high activity environments. Simultaneously, these signals feed a trigger system for rapid event identification via a fast comparator. Additionally, a dedicated Night-Sky Background (NSB) monitoring circuit is included to measure ambient noise from sources like moonlight, employing a slow integrator with adjustable high-value pseudo-resistors to achieve integration time constants in the order of the milliseconds. Rigorous performance benchmarks, validated using Hamamatsu and FBK SiPMs, show a signal-to-noise ratio of at least 5, a dynamic range of 300 photons, and a linearity error below 3% for both energy and NSB paths, while presenting a power consumption of approximately 10 mW per input channel.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-03-03] Characterization of MAGIC: a SiPM Readout ASIC for Monolithic PET Detectors (#2162)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. D'Incà (Autores: L. Nassi , T. D'Incà , I. D'Adda , G. Borghi , C. E. Fiorini , M. Carminati)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] INFN - Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Milano, Milano, Italy [2] Politecnico di Milano, Dipartimento di Elettronica, Informazione e Bioingegneria, Milano, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The experimental characterization of MAGIC (Multichannel Analog Gamma- ray detection Integrated Circuit) is here presented. This ASIC is designed in CMOS 110 nm technology and it is intended to readout the current signals coming from SiPMs coupled with monolithic scintillators that are used in medical imaging applications. The circuit is divided into three main sections: an energy path that provides a differential voltage proportional to the energy of the gamma photon, a timing path that gives information about the time of arrival of the photon, and a validation path for event discrimination. For the experimental characterization two PCBs, a mainboard and a carrier, have been designed. In this testing phase all the functionalities have been validated and the key performance of the ASIC have been characterized, in particular the power dissipation (5 mW/channel), the linearity of the energy chain to demonstrate the direct proportionality between the measured charge and the one generated by photon interaction, and the time jitter which affects the propagation delay through the timing path. The results are within the specifications and confirmed by simulations: the linearity error is below 1% and the time jitter is below 20 ps. Such a low value enables its use also in TOF-PET applications.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-03-04] Photon Counting with FPGA Gigabit Transceivers: A Proof-of-Concept SiPM Readout for TOF-PET (#2884)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Turqueti (Autores: T. Prakash , J. W. Cates , W.-S. Choong , M. Turqueti)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Achieving 100ps FWHM coincidence time resolution (CTR) in time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET) is benefited by electronics that can resolve individual scintillation photons with high temporal precision. We report a proof-of-concept readout in which silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) single-photon pulses are discriminated by a high-speed comparator and digitized directly by GTY transceivers of a Xilinx Virtex UltraScale XCVU095 FPGA (VCU1287 board) at 16Gbps, encoding photon arrival times as bit positions with 62.5ps resolution. Signal integrity analysis showed that an initial LVDS comparator produced common-mode voltage and differential swing below GTY receiver specifications; switching to a CML comparator substantially reduced bit errors. Room-temperature SiPM dark count bitstreams were captured with a random FPGA clock trigger and post-processed to produce a finger plot showing 1-, 2-, and 3-photoelectron peaks, providing a preliminary validation of the bitstream-based photon-counting concept. These results support the feasibility of FPGA gigabit transceivers as scalable digitizers for single-photon pulse streams in next-generation TOF-PET detector modules.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-03-05] Design and Implementation of an FPGA-Based Nuclear-Like Signal Generator (#1615)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Yang (Autores: Y. Yang , X. Li , T. Tong , F. Meng , S. Liu , Z. Zhang , C. Wei , L. Wei)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Chinese Academy of Sciences, Institute of High Energy Physics, Beijing, China [2] Jinan Laboratory of Applied Nuclear Science, Jinan Laboratory of Applied Nuclear Science, Jinan, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Traditional radioactive source testing involves health risks, regulatory limitations, and operational inconvenience. To address these issues, this paper presents a nuclear-like signal generator capable of reproducing the waveform, amplitude, and timing characteristics of real nuclear radiation signals. The proposed system is implemented on a Xilinx K7 FPGA and supports parameter configuration through a touch screen, USB, Ethernet, or host computer software. In the waveform-generation module, photon emission timing is modeled according to scintillator light yield and decay time, while photoelectric conversion jitter and Gaussian pulse responses are introduced to synthesize realistic macroscopic waveforms. In the amplitude-generation module, a cumulative distribution function threshold table derived from measured energy spectra is used to reproduce statistical energy distributions. In the timing module, event occurrence is modeled as a Poisson process with exponentially distributed intervals. The system supports multiple radioactive sources and scintillator materials, including Na, Cs, LYSO, NaI, CsI, and BGO, with independent dual-channel output capability.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-03-06] High-performance preamplifier for spectroscopy systems based on High-Purity Germanium detectors (#1999)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Ojeda (Autores: F. Ojeda , B. Nelson)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] AMETEK ORTEC, Oak Ridge, Tennessee, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Preamplifiers play a primary role in the resolution, linearity, and sensitivity of ionizing radiation spectrometers, converting the small charges collected by photo detectors into usable voltage signals that are further amplified, digitized, and processed to obtain the intended spectra. Additionally, the accuracy and thermal stability of such charge-to-voltage conversion must be assured to keep a constant performance over time and across different detectors, wiring configurations, and radiation scenarios. This article presents electronic simulations and the first laboratory results showing recent improvements in a new preamplifier designed for High-Purity Germanium spectroscopy systems, in terms of dynamic response, noise, linearity, thermal stability, symmetry, tolerance to reactive loads, piling-up, saturation recovery, and power consumption. The impact of these improvements is also discussed.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-03-07] Preliminary Test Results on Latest Version of FESA Readout ASIC for TOF-PET Detectors (#2565)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Yang (Autores: Y. Yang , Y. Wang , X. Xu , X. Zhang , H. Huang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Science and Technology of China, Department of Modern Physics, Hefei, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The latest version of the low-power 64-channel Front-End readout chip for SiPM Array (FESA4.0) with the preliminary test results is presented in this paper. Using a row-column summing readout method, FESA compresses the 64 input signals into 16 output digital pulses, which then is digitized by the followed field programmable gate array (FPGA). In the pathway of each summing output, there are two threshold current comparators used for signal pickup, one with a low threshold for signal timing and the other with a high threshold for signal validation. Since the signal amplitude is converted into the pulse time-width via the linear discharge method, both the signals timing and amplitude can be measured by the time-to-digital converter (TDC) in the FPGA. The new version of FESA incorporates a time-over-threshold (TOT) measurement capability, which allows to identify the signals originating from different scintillators. The chip offers prominent advantages of simple architecture, low power consumption, and high performance. Through electronics tests, FESA4.0 has a measurement linearity of 99. 1% with a dynamic range of 140. The intrinsic time measurement precision is measured better than 30 ps. Combined with a TOF-PET detector with an 8×8 LYSO crystal coupled to an 8x8 SiPM, the energy resolution and time coincidence resolution are measured as 279 ps and 12.4% respectively. These test results show that FESA4.0 is very promising for the construction of highly integrated TOF-PET scanners.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-03-08] Single-Shot Precision Decomposition of a 64-Channel FPGA TDC for TOF-PET (#2381)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Sportelli (Autores: G. Sportelli , M. Morrocchi , N. Belcari)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Pisa, Department of Physics "E. Fermi", Pisa, Italy [2] INFN, Sezione di Pisa, Pisa, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We report a channel-level characterization of a calibrated 64-channel FPGA Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) for fast-timing TOF-PET, with explicit decomposition of the single-shot precision (SSP) into quantization and jitter contributions. The TDC is implemented on an Altera Cyclone 10 GX device and operates with a 256-tap, 64-bin tapped-delay-line (TDL) at ~400 MHz, calibrated offline via code-density histograms. Two implementation strategies are compared: the default arithmetic carry-chain inference, and a placement-aware variant in which the TDLs are constrained to regular structures. Across all 64 channels, controlled placement reduces the ultra-bin width from 160 ± 76 ps to 101 ± 12 ps, the equivalent LSB (LSBeq) from 83 ± 32 ps to 63 ± 4 ps, and the quantization noise σ Q from 24.5 ± 7.3 ps rms to 18.1 ± 0.8 ps rms. The placement-constrained implementation also substantially improves channel-to-channel uniformity. The constrained routing increases σ jitter which makes jitter the dominant SSP contribution once σ Q is reduced. A system-level projection onto previously characterized UTOFPET monolithic modules indicates that the TDC accounts for 59% of the measured CRT² in a 12 mm LYSO/256-channel module (CRT ≈ 150 ps FWHM), but only ~8% in 16-20 mm BGO/64-channel modules (CRT ≈ 400 ps FWHM). This identifies σ jitter as the dominant architectural ceiling and motivates wave-union/multi-TDC averaging or finer-node FPGAs for full LYSO exploitation.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-03-09] SEU Evaluation of an Atom Switch-based FPGA for Slow-Control Systems (#2501)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Ueno (Autores: K. Ueno , N. Taniguchi , T. Sakamoto , M. Miyamura)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The University of Osaka, Department of Physics, Osaka, Japan [2] KEK, Institute of Particle and Nuclear Studies, Tsukuba, Japan [3] NanoBridge Semiconductor, Inc., Tsukuba, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Atom Switch-based FPGAs (AS-FPGAs) are being developed as next-generation FPGAs with expected high radiation tolerance. Their application to various radiation environments is anticipated, and we are also investigating their potential use in detector electronics for future high-energy physics experiments. In this study, neutron irradiation tests were performed to evaluate the Single Event Upset (SEU) tolerance of digital resources implemented in a 65 nm AS-FPGA. A prototype slow-control board equipped with the AS-FPGA was developed and used for the irradiation test. Two independent block RAM (BRAM) blocks and D-type flip-flop (DFF) blocks were implemented in the FPGA for SEU evaluation, and data mismatches detected during irradiation were counted as SEU events. Neutron irradiation tests were carried out using the tandem accelerator at Kobe University. The neutron fluence reached 1.2 × 10 11 n/cm 2 . No SEUs were observed in the DFF blocks, while approximately 10 SEUs were detected in the BRAM blocks. The preliminary SEU cross section for the BRAMs was estimated to be on the order of 10 −9 cm 2 /Mbit. In parallel with the irradiation studies, stable acquisition of temperature and pressure data from a commercial environmental sensor connected to the prototype slow-control board was successfully demonstrated during neutron irradiation, indicating the applicability of the AS-FPGA to detector slow-control systems in radiation environments.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-03-10] MAPSSIC: Toward a Wireless Implantable Positron Probe for Molecular Neuroimaging of Awake and Freely Moving Rats (#2143)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Dupont (Autores: M. Dupont , S. El katera , F. Agnese , L. Ammour , J. Baudot , S. Bouvard , F. Gensolen , M. Kachel , J. Laurence , P. Pangaud , T. Weicherding , L. Zimmer , P. Lanièce , M.A. Verdier , C. Morel)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Aix-Marseille Univ, CNRS/IN2P3, CPPM, Marseille, France [2] Centre de Radiothérapie St. Louis, Toulon, France [3] Université Paris Cité, CNRS/IN2P3, IJCLab, Orsay, France [4] Université Paris Saclay, CNRS/IN2P3, IJCLab, Orsay, France [5] Université de Strasbourg,, CNRS, IPHC UMR 7178, Strasbourg, France [6] Nantes Université, CHU Nantes, Nantes, France [7] Universitée Lyon 1, CERMEP, CNRS, INSERM, HCL, Lyon, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Correlating molecular neuroimaging with behavior in preclinical models requires acquisitions in awake and freely moving animals, whereas most current positron emission tomography procedures are still performed under anesthesia. The MAPSSIC project addresses this limitation with an implantable intracerebral probe based on monolithic active pixel sensors (MAPS) for direct positron detection in targeted brain structures of awake, freely moving rats, thereby avoiding the pharmacological bias of anesthesia. Following sensor characterization and simulation studies previously reported, this contribution presents the transition to a fully wireless system. The acquisition chain combines four IMIC2 sensor chips, a STM32L4 microcontroller, 1 Gbit on-board flash memory, and a bidirectional 2.4 GHz radio link to a Raspberry Pi ground station. The complete software stack is implemented in Rust with the Embassy asynchronous framework, providing memory safety and concurrent peripheral management without dynamic allocation. Planned validation with 18 F, 11 C phantoms, and anesthetized implanted rats will mark the shift from sensor feasibility to system-level wireless validation.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-03-11] Realistic Detector Response Model for COMET Phase-I Cylindrical Drift Chamber (#2941)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Sun (Autores: S. Sun , M. Aoki , A. Jansen , M. Miyataki , Y. Nakatsugawa , Y. Uchida , K. Ueno , C. Wu , T. Xing , C. Yamada , Y. Yuan , Y. Zhang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The University of Osaka, Department of Physics, Toyonaka, Japan [2] Dresden University of Technology, Department of Physics, Dresden, Saxony, Germany [3] Wakayama Medical University, School of Medicine, Wakayama, Japan [4] Imperial College London, Department of Physics, London, United Kingdom [5] Institute of High Energy Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China [6] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Milan, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The COMET (COherent Muon to Electron Transition) Phase-I experiment at J-PARC searches for coherent muon-to-electron conversion in aluminum with a single-event sensitivity of 3 x 10^-15. A key detector challenge is the high instantaneous beam rate, which produces background hits in the Cylindrical Drift Chamber (CDC). In particular, low-energy protons can generate large ionization signals that drive the readout electronics into nonlinear regions, producing waveform saturation and pileups. These effects may reduce hit efficiency by masking later signal or background hits and therefore must be modeled realistically in performance studies. We developed a detector response model for the CDC that combines Geant4-based ionization with the Photon Absorption Ionization (PAI) model, Garfield++-based drift time calculation, and an electronics response emulation based on measured response functions. The model explicitly includes nonlinear saturation effects in the circuit and was validated using cosmic-ray test data. The measured-response model reproduces the main features of the data more accurately than a simple linear-response model. The remaining discrepancy corresponds to a limited uncertainty in the pileup-effect evaluation, providing a realistic basis for COMET Phase-I reconstruction and performance studies.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-03-12] Measurement and correction of high intensity effects on the pixel response of the DSSC DEPFET camera (#1557)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Ghisetti (Autores: A. Castoldi , M. Ghisetti , C. Guazzoni , S. Maffessanti , C. Danilevski , L. Le Guyader , D. Lomidze , Y. Ovcharenko , M. Porro)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Politecnico di Milano, DEIB, Milano, Italy [2] INFN, Sezione di Milano, Milano, Italy [3] DESY, Hamburg, Germany [4] European XFEL, Schenefeld, Germany [5] Università Ca' Foscari, Venezia, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work reports on the experimental characterization, modeling and correction of high intensity effects on the pixel response of the DEPFET Sensor with Signal Compression (DSSC) camera, an active pixel detector targeted at soft X-ray imaging experiments at the European XFEL. Experimental tests with up to 5 MeV/pixel deposited energy have been performed at the European XFEL, showing evidence of a shift of the pedestal value growing with X-ray intensity. Moreover, the signal compression provided by the DEPFET (DEpleted P-type Field Effect Transistor), integrated in each pixel, enhances the impact of this systematic effect on the measurement accuracy. The observed shift is assumed to be proportional to the signal dependent drop of the power supply lines along each ASIC column and can be modeled by two parameters. We devised a procedure to efficiently measure the two model parameters by means of a custom mask that shields a fraction of each ASIC column, irradiated with a flat field. The main results of the characterization of the signal dependent pedestal shift parameters and the application of the resulting correction to X-ray images of different patterned masks (dots, stripes, 2D shapes etc.) acquired at increasing intensities will be presented and discussed.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-03-13] Towards a 64-Channel Monolithic SDD X-Ray Spectrometer for High-Throughput Synchrotron Applications (#2776)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Pedretti (Autores: B. Pedretti , P. Barcella , A. Abba , G. Borghi , M. Carminati , C. Fiorini)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Politecnico di Milano, DEIB, Milano, Italy [2] INFN, Milano, Milano, Italy [3] Nuclear Instruments srl, Lambrugo, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The increasing brilliance of fourth-generation synchrotron sources drives a growing demand for energy-dispersive X-ray fluorescence (XRF) spectrometers capable of handling extreme photon fluxes. We present the design and characterization of the ARDESIA-64 instrument, a complete X-ray fluorescence (XRF) spectrometer for high-throughput synchrotron applications. The instrument integrates a highly scaled 64-channel monolithic Silicon Drift Detector (SDD) array, featuring a pixel pitch of 2.5 mm, within a compact, vacuum-compatible mechanical housing tailored for beamline integration. At the conference, we will present the instrument design and comprehensive spectroscopic characterization results. The collimated 450 μm-thick sensor variant demonstrates an excellent average energy resolution of 125.9 eV FWHM at 5.9 keV. Preliminary high-rate tests confirm exceptional throughput capabilities, sustaining Input Count Rates (ICR) exceeding 800 kcps per channel while preserving an energy resolution of ~150 eV. The readout is performed by a 64-channel Digital Pulse Processor (DPP) based on the CAEN DT5560SE digitizer with firmware specifically adapted for high-throughput X-ray spectroscopy in synchrotrons.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-03-14] Education kit for radiation measurements (#2477)
sub_talks.speaker: M. Nomachi
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The University of Osaka, RCNP, Ibaraki/Osaka, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We have been organizing schools on radiation measurements for students from ASEAN countries. Hands-on experience with radiation measurements is very important, and we prepare radiation measurement systems for practical exercises. To host as many students as possible, we considered organizing the schools in ASEAN countries. However, the shipping cost of the equipment was extremely high. As a result, we could not conduct hands-on exercises on radiation measurement. Driven by recent large-scale experiments, electronics for radiation measurements have become compact, highly integrated, and low-cost. This development now makes it possible to carry equipment to schools. Today, compact detector systems are available at affordable prices, making it much easier to conduct practical radiation measurement exercises in schools. However, modern compact electronics have introduced a new problem: they are too small to probe easily with an oscilloscope. In modern electronics, waveform processing is increasingly performed digitally. Nevertheless, we believe that analogue processing remains important and highly educational for students. This motivated us to develop electronics specifically for educational purposes. We have developed an "education kit" for radiation measurement education. By plugging in a SiPM and a small scintillator crystal module, the board functions as a complete radiation measurement system. An on-board FPGA interfaces with a PC through a USB connection. The board is the size of a Raspberry Pi board. Optionally, it can be plugged onto a Raspberry Pi. Although the board is compact, it provides sufficient space for probing signals. The design of the board will be released as open-source hardware. Students can modify the design and develop their own versions of the board. The "education kit" will serve as an entry point to radiation measurement electronics.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-04-01] Recoil electron tracking in 3D CZT drift strip detectors: a feasibility study (#2296)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Kossakowski (Autores: M. Kossakowski , A. Valverde Mahou , S. Hauberg , I. Kuvvetli)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Technical University of Denmark, Space Research and Technology, Lyngby, Denmark [2] Technical University of Denmark, Applied Mathematics and Computer Science, Lyngby, Denmark
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Bridging the MeV gap remains difficult due to the interplay of competing photon interaction processes, leaving a persistent sensitivity gap in gamma-ray astronomy. Compton telescopes based on 3D CZT Drift Strip Detectors (DSD) are promising candidates for bridging this gap, offering room-temperature operation, high stopping power, excellent energy and position resolution. A key open question is whether recoil electron tracking, which significantly improves angular resolution and detector sensitivity is achievable from raw detector signals. We investigate this using a machine learning approach trained on forward simulations of the 3D CZT DSD response. Principal Component Analysis of simulated electron tracks confirms that track structure is encodable in a low-dimensional representation, and neural network training to regress the recoil direction directly from detector waveforms is ongoing.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-04-02] CVAE-Based Synthetic Thermoluminescence Silica Glass Jewellery Bead Glow Curve Generation (#2606)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Tomaszewski (Autores: L. Tomaszewski , C. Shenton-Taylor)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Surrey, Department of Physics, Guildford, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Micro silica glass jewellery beads have emerged as a viable material for thermoluminescence dosimetry (TLD), offering a low-cost and widely accessible option for personal dose assessment. Their linear glow curve responses, governed by irradiation, thermal conditions, and sample characteristics, exhibit unique spectral elements and structure variability. While machine learning (ML) methods have been successfully applied to dose estimation and irradiation analysis, can ML be used to elevate silica glass beads beyond just decorative jewellery? In this work, a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) is implemented to model and generate thermoluminescent glow curves from silica glass beads conditioned on experimental parameters. The model is trained on a dataset of experimentally acquired responses, augmented with Poisson noise to increase the dataset size and robustness. Conditioning variables include temperature profiles, irradiation and sample characteristics, enabling the model to learn relationships between physical conditions and the glow curve. Results show that the CVAE model can generate realistic glow curves that reflect the underlying conditioning variables. Generated predications maintain peak structure and overall shape, while also reproducing the expected linear relationship between total counts and absorbed dose. Model performance remains consistent when evaluated on previously unseen testing data with a mean figure of merit of 7.5%, although accuracy declines at low dose levels due to diminished signal intensity. The proposed approach demonstrates the potential of generative ML techniques for supporting dosimetry simulation, calibration, and data augmentation workflows for future research. sub_talks.title: [N-LT-04-03] Characterizing Neutron Detection Efficiency in Timepix3: A Bayesian-Optimized FLUKA Approach (#3239)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Mukhopadhyay (Autores: A. Mercado , S. Mukhopadhyay , M. West , P. Connolly , S. Dewji)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Characterization of converter layer geometry is critical for determining the absolute detection efficiency of pixelated thermal neutron detectors. However, uncertainties in film deposition and source strength often lead to significant discrepancies between simulated models and actual experimental performance. This work addresses these challenges by implementing a Bayesian optimized FLUKA framework to determine the effective enriched Lithium-6 Fluoride converter thickness for an ADVACAM Timepix3 detector with a 1000 μm Silicon sensor. The FLUKA Monte Carlo model was benchmarked against experimental measurements using an Americium-Beryllium source with a nominal activity of 40 mCi and a documented tolerance of fifteen percent. The Bayesian optimizer successfully converged to an effective thickness of 5 μm after forty evaluations by minimizing the residuals between the nominal source activity and the simulation-implied activities. This methodology demonstrates a robust approach to resolving geometric uncertainties in hybrid semiconductor detectors where direct physical measurement of internal components is not feasible post-assembly. The resulting validated geometry provides a high-fidelity foundation for modeling future detection efficiency benchmarks across diverse neutron spectra. This work demonstrates a practical approach for integrating machine-learning optimization with Monte Carlo transport modeling to address geometric uncertainties in neutron detectors.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-04-04] Enhanced Spent Nuclear Fuel Characterization Using Sequential Detector Responses through Deep Learning (#2393)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Kwon (Autores: B. Kwon , W. Hong , J. Kim , G. Kim)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Seoul National University, Nuclear Engineering, seoul, Republic of Korea [2] Seoul National University, Energy Systems Engineering, seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate characterization of spent nuclear fuel (SNF) is essential for verifying operator-declared information in nuclear safeguards. Conventional nondestructive assay (NDA) approaches for such characterization based on gamma-ray spectroscopy typically rely on extracting specific photopeak information (ex. 662 keV peak of ¹³⁷Cs), which compresses high-dimensional detector responses into a limited number of variables and may lead to information loss. To address this limitation, we propose a deep learning-based SNF characterization approach that directly utilizes sequential detector-response data for advanced characterization performance. The training dataset was generated through integrated ORIGEN and MCNP simulations for 5000 realistic SNF conditions, covering variations in initial enrichment, burnup, and cooling time. The proposed C2C-GRU-v2 architecture was designed to process long sequential detector-response data by combining Coordinate-to-Context embedding and GRU-based recurrent sequence modeling, enabling both event-level contextual learning and sequence-level generalization. For comparison, a conventional spectrum-based regression method using ¹³⁷Cs peak counts was also implemented under identical conditions. The proposed approach demonstrated improved characterization performance compared with the conventional method, particularly for cooling time estimation, achieving Relative Root Mean Square Errors (RRMSE) of 0.157 for burnup and 0.0456 for cooling time prediction. These results demonstrate the feasibility of deep learning-based sequential detector-response analysis for advanced SNF characterization in nuclear safeguards applications.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-04-05] Robust Dual-Target Radioisotope Quantification Under Increasing Unseen Contaminant Complexity (#2217)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Kim (Autores: C. Kim , Y. Kim , G. Kim , D.Y. Oh)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [2] Korea University, Department of Bioengineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Gamma-ray spectroscopy is a fundamental technique for radioisotope identification and quantification across safety-critical applications, where deep learning models have recently emerged as a data-driven alternative to traditional library-dependent methods. However, most existing deep learning approaches operate under a closed-set assumption that all isotopes during deployment are present in the training set; field deployments frequently violate this assumption, and the introduction of unknown isotopes leads to silent degradation. Recent OOD-detection studies have been reported, but they treat OOD spectra as anomalies to be flagged rather than quantified, and systematic evaluation under increasing unseen contaminant complexity remains lacking. This study proposes a denoising autoencoder (DAE) framework that reconstructs the clean target spectrum (¹³⁷Cs, ¹³³Ba) from contaminated measurements while simultaneously estimating target fractions through a dual-head architecture. Using Ce:GPS scintillator pulse data under a leave-one-out unknown noise (LOO-UN) protocol, the DAE achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.024 at 20% out-of-distribution (OOD) contamination in the two-unseen configuration, outperforming NNLS-known (0.038) and MLP (0.031), with near-constant accuracy as the unseen contaminant count increased from one to two (0.025 → 0.024).

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-04-06] Automated Monte Carlo-Based Efficiency Transfer Integrated into HPGe Gamma Spectroscopy Workflows for High-Throughput Laboratories (#1579)
