sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Ametek, Ortec, Oak Ridge, Tennessee, United States of America [2] AMETEK GmbH, Meerbusch, Duesseldorf, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [3] AMETEK GmbH, InnoRIID, Duesseldorf, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract High-purity germanium (HPGe) detector systems are widely used for gamma spectroscopy; however, increasing throughput demands, expanding measurement configurations, and a declining base of expert users have made traditional efficiency calibration and transfer workflows increasingly impractical. Efficiency transfer between counting geometries has historically required manual configuration, custom made sources, and/or execution of Monte Carlo simulations by trained computational physicists, limiting scalability in routine laboratory environments. We present an approach that embeds Monte Carlo-based efficiency transfer directly within a commercial spectral analysis software stack, enabling automated operation without additional user intervention. At runtime, sample geometries-already specified by laboratory personnel using standard container templates such as Marinelli beakers-are used to drive a ray-tracing-based gamma transport simulation coupled to detector interaction and pulse-processing models. The approach operates over an energy range of 20 keV to 2.5 MeV and produces both full spectra and efficiency curves. Validation is performed through comparison of simulated spectra and efficiency curves against measured data and results from the Geant4 Monte Carlo toolkit. While not intended to match the full generality of Geant4, the proposed approach demonstrates comparable practical accuracy for routine laboratory configurations while significantly reducing user complexity. Additionally, seamless integration into existing workflows is demonstrated, enabling non-expert users to apply physics-based efficiency transfer without specialized training. This work provides a scalable solution for automated, high-throughput gamma spectroscopy, bridging the gap between rigorous Monte Carlo modeling and practical laboratory usability.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-04-07] Neutron and secondary photon dose mapping of deuterium-deuterium (D-D) and deuterium-tritium (D-T) neutron generators via PHITS simulations (#2970)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. G. Alipio (Autores: A. G. Alipio , C. L. Dulohan , B. Egwolf , A. Asuncion-Astronomo)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Santo Tomas, The Graduate School, Manila, Philippines [2] University of Santo Tomas, Department of Mathematics and Physics, Manila, Philippines [3] Department of Science and Technology, Philippine Nuclear Research Institute, Quezon City, Philippines
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Monte Carlo-based Particle Heavy Ion Transport Code System (PHITS) was used to model deuterium-deuterium (D-D) and deuterium-tritium (D-T) neutron generators for preliminary radiation safety assessment of the ongoing establishment of the Neutron Irradiation Facility (NIF) of the Philippine Nuclear Research Institute (PNRI). Neutron and secondary photon dose distributions were obtained for fully shielded, partially shielded, and unshielded configurations. In both D-D and D-T cases, the counting room dose rates were acceptable with respect to occupational dose limits for a 500-hour annual operating time. However, additional shielding should be explored for the D-T setup to further reduce dose rates in the work area. The dose maps presented the significance of the configuration of moderating and shielding materials in minimizing radiological doses during operation. The findings of this work will serve as a reference for the safe and reliable installation of the country's first neutron generator laboratory.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-04-08] Bayesian Filtering Image Reconstruction for SourceLocalization and Tracking in Compton Imaging (#2167)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Leland (Autores: J. Leland , C. Tarpau , M. Fang , Y. Altmann , A. Di Fulvio)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Nuclear, Plasma, and Radiological Engineering, Urbana, Illinois, United States of America [2] University of Edinburgh, Maxwell Institute for Mathematical Sciences, Bayes Center, Edinburgh, United Kingdom [3] Heriot-Watt University, School of Engineering and Physical Sciences, Edinburgh, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Stand-off detection of special nuclear materials (SNM) in safeguards and non-proliferation applications demands imaging systems capable of tracking sources across dynamic environments. In this work, we introduce a Bayesian-Filtering (BF) algorithm for simultaneous source localization and tracking where existing reconstruction methods, such as simple back-projection (SBP) and maximum likelihood expectation maximization (MLEM), are insufficient. We evaluate the BF algorithm using synthetic data generated with MCNPX-PoliMi for a simulated Compton imager consisting of a 4 x 7 array of LYSO scintillator crystals. Two independent sources are simulated, one sweeping in azimuth and one in elevation, each traveling from -90° to +90° at 1 m/s. The BF algorithm successfully tracked both sources across the full angular sweep, achieving mean angular errors of 6.4° and 6.03° for the azimuth and elevation cases, respectively. Additionally, preliminary results for multi-source tracking are successful with the algorithm tracking both sources up until their paths intersect which is a known challenge we are currently investigating.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-04-09] Count-Level Effects on Radiomics Robustness and Harmonization in Total-Body PET Imaging (#3090)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. S. Azimi (Autores: M. S. Azimi , M. Cheraghi , H. Zaidi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Geneva University Hospital, Division of Nuclear Medicine & Molecular Imaging, Geneva, Genève, Switzerland [2] Obuda University, University Research and Innovation Cente, Budapest, Hungary [3] Shahid Beheshti University, Department of Nuclear Medicin, Tehran, Iran (Islamic Republic of)
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Radiomics analysis in total-body PET imaging is highly sensitive to acquisition variability, particularly count reduction, which directly affects noise characteristics and feature reliability. In this study, we investigate the impact of count reduction and multi-parametric harmonization on the robustness of multi-organ radiomics. A retrospective dataset of 550 patients from two centers was analyzed. Multiple count levels were generated from list-mode data, including standard and reduced counts (reduction factors up to 100). Multi-organ segmentation was performed automatically, and 107 IBSI-compliant radiomics features were extracted from SUV-normalized images. Feature harmonization was applied using ComBat under different configurations, including scanner, voxel size, radiopharmaceutical, and scatter correction. Reproducibility was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients across count levels and anatomical regions. Results show that radiomics stability is strongly dependent on both count level and feature type. Approximately 31% of features achieved good reproducibility (ICC ≥ 0.75) in at least one organ. Shape and first-order features remained relatively stable under moderate count reduction (CRF ≤ 20), while higher-order texture features exhibited substantial degradation at extreme count levels (CRF ≥ 50). Harmonization improved feature consistency, particularly for scanner- and resolution-related variations, but had limited impact under severe noise conditions. Taken together, the results indicate that preserving quantitative reliability in low-count PET requires careful consideration of both feature selection and acquisition variability. Rather than relying solely on harmonization, robust radiomics analysis should incorporate count-aware strategies, especially when extending to multi-center or ultra-low-count imaging scenarios.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-04-10] Development of a Single-Layer Dual-Ended Readout Compton Camera Prototype for Enhanced Spatial Imaging (#1799)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Wen (Autores: H. Wen , C. Li , Y. Hou , K. Wang , J. Jiang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Normal University, Key Laboratory of Beam Technology of Ministry of Education, School of Physics and Astronomy, Bejing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Compton camera has emerged as a pivotal gamma-ray imaging technique, with critical applications in astrophysical observation, nuclear safety monitoring, and environmental radiation detection. In nuclear astrophysics, the detection and localization of gamma rays in the MeV range are indispensable for probing high-energy cosmic phenomena. Despite its importance, the advancement of MeV gamma-ray imaging instrumentation remains constrained by low interaction probabilities and high imaging complexity. This study presents a single-layer Compton camera prototype designed for enhanced spatial imaging, building upon the mission heritage of the BNU-120-a space-borne detector successfully deployed for monitoring gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). To transcend the original system's lack of spatial imaging capability, we propose a high-performance architecture that leverages the established BNU-120 framework while integrating a dual-ended readout to achieve a 4π detection solid angle. The prototype uses a 8×8 Ce:GAGG array coupled to Hamamatsu Multi-Pixel Photon Counters (MPPC, S14161-3050HS-08) at both ends. Each crystal measures 3×3×25 mm 3 and is optically isolated by 0.2-mm-thick BaSO₄ reflective layers. System characterization demonstrated an energy resolution of approximately 5% (FWHM) at 511 keV. Depth-of-interaction (DOI) information, extracted via the energy ratio method, yielded a DOI resolution of roughly 2 mm (FWHM) along the crystal axis. Computational validation using GATE simulations of a U-shaped 511 keV planar source showed that the source geometry was clearly distinguishable through a back-projection (BP) algorithm. Subsequent point-source experiments verified the detector's capability to localize discrete sources. Future work will focus on realistic physical imaging experiments and the exploration of more advanced reconstruction algorithms to fully evaluate the module's Compton imaging performance.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-04-11] Crystal Dual-Readout Calorimetry for Future e + e − Higgs Factories (#2842)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Campajola (Autores: M. Campajola , M. Alviggi , B. Argiento , E. Etiennette , A. Benaglia , M. Biasini , V. Bisignani , D. Boccanfuso , L. Borriello , C. Cecchi , F. Mirra , S. Moneta , P. Paolucci , S. Perna , B. Rossi , E. Rossi , J. Scamardella , G. Sekhniaidze)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] INFN, Sezione di Napoli, Napoli, Italy [2] Università degli Studi di Napoli Federico II, Napoli, Italy [3] Università degli Studi di Napoli Parthenope, Napoli, Italy [4] CERN, Ginevra, Switzerland [5] INFN, Sezione di Milano-Bicocca, Milano, Italy [6] Scuola Superiore Meridionale, Napoli, Italy [7] Università degli Studi di Napoli Perugia, Perugia, Italy [8] INFN, Sezione di Perugia, Perugia, Italy [9] Université de Strasbour, Strasbour, France [10] Università degli Studi di Milano-Bicocca, Milano, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Precision physics at future e+e− Higgs factories set stringent requirements on calorimetric performance, with 3%/√E for electromagnetic particles and ∼ 30%/√E for neutral hadrons identified as key benchmarks. A hybrid dual-readout approach, combining a homogeneous crystal electromagnetic section with a fiber-based hadronic section, offers a cost-effective path toward simultaneously achieving both targets. Reaching such performance requires enhancing the longitudinal and transverse granularity of the crystal section beyond what is available in conventional homogeneous calorimeters and equipping each crystal cell with two independent readout channels to simultaneously collect Cherenkov and scintillation light. These features enable advanced particle-flow dual-readout reconstruction algorithms to exploit the maximum available information from each event. This work will present extensive laboratory characterizations together with beam-test measurements carried out at CERN on single-crystal PWO, BGO, and BSO cells instrumented with optical filters and SiPMs. These studies demonstrate event-by-event separation of Cherenkov and scintillation light, with both scintillation and Cherenkov yields exceeding the thresholds required for optimal electromagnetic and hadronic energy resolution. The results have guided the technological choices for the ongoing construction of full-containment calorimeter prototypes

sub_talks.speaker: E. J. Mannel
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Brookhaven National Laboratory, Physics Dept, Upton, New York, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract ePIC is the general purpose detector for the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) that is being built at Brookhaven National Laboratory and will be ready for first physics when the Electron-Ion Collider turns on. ePIC is based on a new 1.7T superconducting solenoid magnet. The detector consists of precision tracking, particle identification and calorimeter (electromagnetic and hadronic) to measure the properties of electron-Ion collisions that will occur at the EIC. In this paper we will present the over all design of the ePIC detector, with a focus on the Barrel Hadronic Calorimeter (BHCal) which is the repurposed sPHENIX Outer Hadronic Calorimeter (HCal). We will also present the current status of the BHCal design, test stand and preliminary results of the new electronics readout system based on the CaloROC chip designed for ePIC

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-04-13] Off-detector Readout and Real-time Signal Processing for the ATLAS Liquid ArgonCalorimeter at the High-Luminosity LHC (#2635)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. Collado Soto (Autores: P. Collado Soto , N. Nikiforou)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CERN, Geneve, Switzerland [2] Universidad Autonoma de Madrid, Physics Department, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The ATLAS Liquid Argon (LAr) calorimeter readout electronics are being upgraded for operation at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC), where up to approximately 200 proton-proton interactions per bunch crossing will significantly increase detector occupancy, data throughput, and trigger rates. While the calorimeter detectors themselves remain unchanged, the full readout electronics chain is being replaced. The upgraded off-detector processing system continuously receives digitized calorimeter signals from approximately 182000 channels at the 40 MHz bunch-crossing rate through high-speed optical links. The processing architecture is implemented in Advanced Telecommunications Computing Architecture (ATCA) systems hosting large FPGAs performing real-time reconstruction of energy and timing while satisfying stringent trigger latency requirements. Prototype hardware and firmware have been developed and validated in integration setups combining front-end electronics, timing distribution, and data acquisition systems. In parallel, advanced reconstruction methods including machine-learning approaches optimized for FPGA implementation are being investigated to improve robustness against pileup and overlapping pulses.

sub_talks.title: [N-LT-04-14] The LS3 Enhancement of the LHCb Electromagnetic Calorimeter (#2898)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. Picatoste (Autores: E. Picatoste , S. Gómez)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universitat de Barcelona, Institute of Cosmos Sciences of the University of Barcelona, Barcelona, Spain [2] Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya, Barcelona, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract An upgrade of the LHCb electromagnetic calorimeter (ECAL) is planned for Long Shutdown 3 (LS3) to address significant aging effects in the central region caused by radiation damage and high particle flux. The innermost ECAL modules will be replaced with a new design based on Spaghetti Calorimeter (SpaCal) technology, optimized for radiation tolerance and improved performance under high occupancy conditions. A total of 176 SpaCal modules will be installed. These are based on scintillating plastic fibers embedded in dense absorbers. The innermost 32 modules will use 3D-printed tungsten absorbers to withstand the highest radiation levels, while the remaining 144 modules will employ lead absorbers produced through an innovative casting technique. Both configurations have been prototyped and extensively validated in test beam campaigns at DESY-II and CERN SPS. The measured energy resolution for electron beams is consistent with performance requirements and shows good agreement with detailed Monte Carlo simulations. The scintillating fibers will be read out using radiation-hard hollow light guides coupled to fast photon detectors. In total, 3072 new readout channels will be implemented with dedicated front-end electronics. In parallel with the installation of the new SpaCal modules, the current Shashlik calorimeter modules will be rearranged to better match the spatial distribution of particle occupancy. Simulation studies demonstrate a significant reduction in per-cell occupancy after the LS3 upgrade, improving detector performance in Run 4 conditions. Benchmark analyses of key physics channels confirm that this enhancement leads to a substantial gain in reconstruction efficiency and measurement precision. Overall, the LS3 ECAL upgrade represents a crucial step toward coping with higher luminosity conditions and anticipates key design features of the future PicoCal system foreseen for implementation during LS4.

sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CNR - Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche, DiaTHEMA Lab, ISM - Istituto di Struttura della Materia, Montelibretti, Italy [2] University of Rome Tor Vergata, C.H.O.S.E. (Centre for Hybrid and Organic Solar Energy), Department of Electronic Engineering, Roma, Italy [3] Università degli Studi Niccolò Cusano, Faculty of Engineering, Roma, Italy [4] CNR - Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche, IC - Istituto di Cristallografia, Montelibretti, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The performance under X-rays (with energies up to 40 keV) of self-powered detectors with a submicrometric metal-halide-perovskite (FAPbBr 3 ) active layer was systematically investigated as a function of the FAPbBr 3 film thickness, ranging from 180 to 840 nm. Results show that an intermediate thickness of 710 nm represents the best trade-off among sensitivity (up to 571.07 μC Gy -1 cm -2 ), limit of detection (down to 39.55 nGy s -1 ), linearity with the dose-rate, and stability over time (signal fluctuations <1% within 1 h of continuous irradiation).Very significantly, it is here shown that, in the case of submicrometric FAPbBr 3 film-based X-ray detectors, a better performance is not necessarily connected to a larger thickness; the benefits of a better X-ray absorption are indeed nullified by a drastic decrease of the photoconductive gain, due to increased interface charge accumulation and enhanced recombination.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-06-02] Optimization of FAPbBr 3 Single Crystals for Photon Counting Radiation Detection (#2520)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. Sellin (Autores: J. Jayarathne , A. Dickinson , J. Green , M. Zahid , C. Crean , S. Perera , P. Sellin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Surrey, School of Mathematics and Physics, Guildford, United Kingdom [2] University of Surrey, School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Guildford, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The organic hybrid perovskite FAPbBr 3 shows great potential as a radiation detector, particularly due to its synthesis using cost-effective room-temperature solution-based growth processes. In this paper we report on recent improvements in the quality of solution-grown FAPbBr 3 single crystals using a sulfonic zwitterionic ligand 3-(Decyldimethylammonio)­propane­sulfonate inner salt (DPSI). By optimizing the growth process we have produced X-ray and gamma ray detectors that show excellent charge transport properties, with a high hole mobility of 190 cm 2 /Vs and a high hole mobility-lifetime (µτ) product of 2.7 x 10 -3 cm 2 /V, combined with a low dark current of 2.9 nA cm -2 operating at a field strength of 1000 V/cm. These FAPbBr 3 detectors show well-resolved low energy gamma peaks from 241Am, with an energy resolution of 25.6% FWHM at 59.5 keV.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-06-03] Transient Currents in 4H-SiC Radiation Sensors with Graphene Electrodes (#2924)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. Belas (Autores: E. Belas , M. Betušiak , R. Grill , P. Praus , J. Kunc , R. Nag , K. C. Mandal)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Charles University, Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, Institute of Physics, Prague 2, Czech Republic [2] University of South Carolina, Department of Electrical Engineering, Columbia, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We investigate charge transport in both 4H-SiC semiinsulating bulk graphene/semiinSiC/Ni sensor and epitaxial graphene/epiSiC/subsSiC/Ni Schottky barrier diode structure. Using the laser-induced Transient Current Technique (L-TCT), combined with alpha spectroscopy and I-V characterization, we investigate charge transport across either the bulk or epilayer and adjacent substrate. Our results reveal rapid space charge formation at all structures, even under pulsed bias, attributed to electron depletion. It is shown that in contrast to metallic electrodes showing fast damped oscillations, the graphene electrodes lead to significantly slower non-oscillating exponential-like current waveforms. Observed phenomena were successfully described by theoretical model based on surface plasmons in both sensors. These findings highlight the importance of the transient current technique for the investigation of SiC sensors.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-06-04] Perovskite CsPbBr 3 Cherenkov charge induction gamma-ray detector with sub-ns timing resolution (#2971)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Pan (Autores: L. Pan , Q.V. Phan , M. Unal , S. Lee , D.Y. Chung , J. W. Cates , O. Aggarwal , M. Turqueti , G. Ariño-Estrada , M. G. Kanatzidis , J. Caravaca)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Nuclear Science Division, Berkeley, California, United States of America [2] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Engineering Division, Berkeley, California, United States of America [3] Argonne National Laboratory, Materials Science Division, Lemont, Illinois, United States of America [4] University of California Davis, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Perovskite CsPbBr 3 is promising as next-generation room temperature semiconductor gamma-ray detector. While remarkable energy resolution has been achieved (e.g., 1% at 662 keV) for CsPbBr 3 , its timing resolution is expected to be limited by the charge transport process as semiconductor (as a reference, timing resolution is several ns or worse for semiconductor CdZnTe or TlBr). Here, we report sub-nanosecond time resolution utilizing the prompt Cherenkov emission from the CsPbBr 3 as fast timing signal while maintaining its good energy resolution. We demonstrate successful simultaneous readout of semiconductor charge induction signal and SiPM Cherenkov light signal. By associating the Cherenkov light signal with the charge signal, good energy resolution of ~3% at 511 keV and sub-ns coincidence timing resolution of ~ 583 ps with 22 Na gamma-ray source were achieved simultaneously. We expect further improvement of time and energy resolution with a high-frequency SiPM read-out PCB and a dedicated charge-readout PCB with integrated high-performance pre-amplifiers. Built upon the high energy resolution and the ability to provide spatial information of gamma-ray interaction, the sub-ns fast timing capability would markedly broaden the applications of CsPbBr 3 gamma-ray detectors that are projected to have low cost compare to CdZnTe.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Napolitano (Autores: G. Napolitano , I. Fratelli , C. Martínez-Domingo , M. Makala , L. Fijahi , I. Kymissis , O. Jurchescu , B. Fraboni , M. Mas-Torrent , L. Basiricò)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Bologna, Department of Physics and Astronomy, Bologna, Italy [2] Columbia University, Department of Electrical Engineering, New York, New York, United States of America [3] Institute of Microelectronics of Barcelona, IMB-CNM-CSIC, Bellaterra, Spain [4] Wake Forest University, Deparment of Physics and Center for Functional Materials, Winston-Salem, North Carolina, United States of America [5] Institut de Ciència de Materials de Barcelona, ICMAB-CSIC, Bellaterra, Spain [6] INFN-BO, Bologna, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Organic field-effect transistors are promising candidates for ionizing radiation dosimetry due to their low-cost fabrication, large-area processability, and tissue-equivalent composition. However, their response is strongly affected by environmental species, such as oxygen and moisture, which can induce charge traps and compromise detector stability. Here, we investigate the role of Parylene-C encapsulation in TMTES:PS-based OFET X-ray detectors. The encapsulation layer preserves the pristine electrical performance while significantly improving shelf stability. Under X-ray irradiation, uncoated devices exhibit air-dependent transient dynamics, with recovery in air and integrative behavior in vacuum. In contrast, Parylene-C-coated devices show stable and cumulative response independently of the surrounding environment, indicating that encapsulation suppresses air-induced trap formation. Trap density of states analysis supports this interpretation, revealing additional shallow trap states only in uncoated devices irradiated in air. Encapsulated OFETs further display a dose-dependent threshold-voltage shift, with a maximum sensitivity of 0.109 ± 0.002 V Gy⁻¹ and long-lived retention of the absorbed dose information. These results demonstrate that Parylene-C encapsulation is not only an effective strategy to improve environmental stability, but also a key tool to control the radiation response of organic transistor-based dosimeters.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Boukhicha (Autores: M. Boukhicha , S. A. Reisbick , C. Luca , T. Thomas)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Brookhaven National Laboratory, Instrumentation, Upton, New York, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Efficient and scalable scintillators are critical for applications in medical imaging, nuclear security, and environmental monitoring. Here, we investigate lithium-6 and boron-10 doped CsPbBr 3 perovskite-polymer composites for dual-mode neutron and X-ray detection. A scalable ball-milling process was used to incorporate neutron-sensitive isotopes into CsPbBr 3 nanocrystals embedded in PMMA and PDMS matrices. The resulting composites combine the neutron capture capabilities of lithium-6 and boron-10 with the favorable optical properties of CsPbBr 3 , including high light yield, emission near 520 nm, and sub-nanosecond decay times. HR-TEM analysis confirmed a homogeneous distribution of ~10 nm nanocrystals throughout the polymer matrix. Synchrotron-based measurements further demonstrated strong radioluminescence and fast scintillation response under X-ray excitation. Preliminary studies also indicate promising neutron and alpha-particle scintillation performance, highlighting the potential of these flexible and scalable composites for next-generation radiation detection technologies.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-01-01] 3D Diffusion Posterior Sampling with Patient-Specific PET Priors for Ultra-Low-Count SPECT in alpha therapy (#2448)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Lopez Montes (Autores: A. Lopez Montes , A. Delker , K. Ramonaheng , D. Groschupf , R. Seifert , S. Resch , A. Rominger , G. Boening , M. Sathekge , A. Afshar-Oromieh , K. Shi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Bern, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Bern, Bern, Switzerland [2] University of Bern, Department of Digital Medicine, Bern, Bern, Switzerland [3] Ludwig Maximillian University, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Munich, Bavaria, Germany [4] University of Pretoria, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Pretoria, South Africa [5] Steve Biko Hospital, Nuclear Medicine Research Infrastructure (NuMeRI), Pretoria, South Africa
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Ultra-low-count SPECT imaging in alpha-particle radiopharmaceutical therapy (α-RPT) remains challenged by low administered activities and severe noise amplification associated with conventional reconstruction. We propose a fully three-dimensional diffusion posterior sampling (3D-DPS) framework for physics-informed SPECT reconstruction integrating learned generative priors with a Poisson-consistent likelihood formulation for emission tomography. A 3D unconditional diffusion model was trained on PSMA PET volumes to learn tracer uptake distributions. To further constrain the inverse problem, patient-specific prior adaptation was introduced through synthetic subject-specific uptake realizations designed to model physiologically plausible tracer variability during training. During reconstruction, the learned priors are coupled with a physics-based SPECT forward model through a Poisson log-likelihood formulation consistent with MLEM reconstruction. Validation was performed using realistic ultra-low-count 225 Ac-PSMA simulations, as well as two clinical 177 Lu-PSMA SPECT acquisitions retrospectively degraded to mimic 225 Ac imaging conditions using Poisson thinning (~10 5 detected photons) and angular downsampling (120 to 30 projections). Compared with MLEM and regularized MLEM, the proposed framework reduced reconstruction error (NMAE = 0.34 ± 0.04 versus 0.53 ± 0.02 and 0.41 ± 0.05, respectively) and improved structural similarity (SSIM = 0.90 ± 0.05 versus 0.77 ± 0.13 and 0.85 ± 0.08, respectively) while preserving anatomical detail and projection-domain consistency. Reconstructions from degraded clinical acquisitions demonstrated substantially improved noise suppression and lesion preservation compared with conventional reconstruction. These results demonstrate the potential of diffusion-based reconstruction for quantitative ultra-low-count SPECT imaging and α-RPT dosimetry.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-01-02] Joint Reconstruction of Activity and Attenuation with Motion Estimation in PET using Diffusion Models (#1403)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Phung-Ngoc (Autores: C. Phung-Ngoc , A. De Paepe , H.-P. Dang , O. Saut , D. Visvikis , A. Bousse)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Univ. Brest, LaTIM, Inserm UMR 1101, Brest, France [2] Inria Center, Univ. Bordeaux, MONC Project-Team, Talence, France [3] CentraleSupélec, IETR, CNRS UMR 6164, Cesson-Sévigné, France [4] Mathematics Institute of Bordeaux, UMR 5251, Univ. Bordeaux, CNRS, Bordeaux INP, Talence, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Respiratory motion and attenuation mismatch degrade positron emission tomography (PET) reconstruction. Furthermore, the additional scan required for attenuation correction (AC) may complexify the imaging workflow and increase radiation exposure. Joint reconstruction of activity and attenuation with motion estimation (JRAAM) methods address these issues by jointly estimating activity, attenuation, and motion solely from emission data. We propose JRAAM-DPS, a diffusion model (DM)-based framework that leverages a diffusion prior on activity-attenuation image pairs to recover motion-compensated and attenuation-corrected PET images directly from respiratory-gated PET data. We evaluated the proposed method on simulated data, and demonstrated improved image quality compared to maximum likelihood activity and attenuation (MLAA) and the non-motion-corrected JRAA-DPS

sub_talks.title: [MIC-01-03] Flow Models for PET Image Reconstruction (#1883)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Webber (Autores: G. Webber , A. Hammers , A. P. King , A. J. Reader)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] King's College London, School of Biomedical Engineering and Imaging Sciences, London, United Kingdom [2] Guy's and St Thomas' PET Centre, London, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Flow-based generative models can be used as pre-trained priors for inverse problems; however, their use in PET image reconstruction remains largely unexplored. We present a proof-of-principle study using flow priors for 2D PET reconstruction. A U-Net was trained by flow matching on simple brain phantoms and used as an unconditional image prior. We used the MPC-Flow (Model Predictive Control) framework to condition the pre-trained flow via direct control of the generative dynamics, and adapted it to the PET setting by incorporating a Poisson likelihood and an explicit intensity scaling to address the dynamic range mismatch between the generative model and PET data. This method was used to reconstruct images from simulated low-count PET sinogram data. On held-out phantoms, MPC-Flow achieved lower error than diffusion-based reconstruction and conventional iterative baselines, likely due to the explicit control objective, which balances likelihood maximization with a penalty on deviations from the learned flow trajectory. These results demonstrate that flow priors can be coupled with PET likelihoods in a principled framework. Evaluation on more realistic anatomical phantoms and clinical data, where the learned manifold may be less accurate, will be a necessary next step.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-01-04] Flow Matching for PET Image Reconstruction (#1731)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Hashimoto (Autores: F. Hashimoto , Z. Huang , K. Gong)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Generative models, especially diffusion models, have recently demonstrated strong potential for positron emission tomography (PET) image reconstruction. However, diffusion models often require many sampling steps and incur a high computational cost, which may limit their practical use in PET image reconstruction. Flow matching is an attractive alternative, enabling continuous generative modeling with a simpler sampling procedure and a stable, efficient training framework. In this study, we present flow matching-based PET image reconstruction methods. We first establish PET-FlowDPS as a baseline by incorporating Poisson likelihood guidance into the FlowDPS framework. We then propose a model-based PET image reconstruction method that uses a pretrained flow matching model as a prior. The proposed reconstruction method iteratively performs three steps: (1) flow-based destination estimation to obtain a clean image estimate, (2) penalized PET image reconstruction refinement to enforce data consistency, and (3) flow-based propagation to update the image to the next time step. The proposed reconstruction method was evaluated using 10 low-dose clinical brain [ 18 F]FDG datasets. Experimental results showed that the flow matching-based methods reduced image noise while preserving cortical structures compared with the maximum a posteriori expectation-maximization (MAPEM) algorithm. The proposed method further improved image quality compared with PET-FlowDPS in terms of PSNR. In addition, the computation time of the proposed method was less than 2 minutes. These results demonstrate that flow matching is a promising generative prior for PET image reconstruction.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-01-05] Data-Driven Kernel EM Reconstruction Using Attention-Based Learning for Dynamic PET (#3168)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Chang (Autores: H. Chang , W. Qi , J. Kolthammer , J. Qi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California, Davis, Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America [2] Canon Medical Research USA, Vernon Hills, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dynamic positron emission tomography (PET) reconstruction remains challenging due to low count statistics in individual frames and the ill-posed nature of the inverse problem. Kernelized expectation maximization (KEM) methods have been developed to incorporate prior information through a kernel matrix; however, their performance strongly depends on the design of the kernel and the prior information, as well as the associated hyperparameters. In this work, we propose a data-driven framework for kernel construction based on attention-guided learning from dynamic PET images. A neural network is used to learn spatial-temporal relationships from dynamic image frames, producing attention maps that encode pairwise similarities. These features are further analyzed via dimensionality reduction and clustering to identify regions of interest (ROIs) with similar spatial-temporal characteristics. The resulting ROI masks are used to define adaptive neighborhoods and compute kernel weights, producing a data-driven kernel that is subsequently integrated into the KEM reconstruction framework. Experiments on simulated data demonstrate that the proposed method not only improves image quality but also enables accurate estimation of time-activity curves (TACs) across different ROIs. In real PET data, the method achieves enhanced reconstruction quality, while exhibiting reduced sensitivity to the choice of clustering parameters compared with the baseline approach that performs clustering directly on the dynamic PET images without attention-guided learning. In particular, stable reconstruction performance is maintained across a wide range of cluster numbers, whereas baseline approaches show strong parameter dependence and introduce noticeable noise at larger cluster sizes. These results demonstrate that attention-based kernel learning provides a robust and effective strategy for improving dynamic PET reconstruction quality and quantitative accuracy.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-02-01] Development and Evaluation of Gym-PET for Functional Brain Imaging of Awake Running Mice (#2398)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 X. Yu (Autores: X. Yu , H. Liu , D. Liang , W. Zhu , W. Ma , Y. Zhang , J. Tao , H. Zhao , Q. Peng)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Shenzhen, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Awake functional brain imaging is crucial for behavioral neuroscience, but conventional preclinical PET scanners typically require anesthesia, which suppresses brain glucose metabolism and limits natural behavioral studies. To address these limitations, we developed Gym-PET, a 75 g head-mounted wearable PET system optimized for awake running mice. The wearable module features a compact detector ring (20.0 mm inner diameter) composed of 1 x 1 x 5 mm³ LYSO crystal arrays coupled to SiPMs, a short crystal design chosen to minimize parallax degradation under close-range conditions. To enable stable imaging during locomotion, the scanner is integrated with a customized treadmill platform using a lightweight suspension mechanism. Based on the NEMA NU-4 2008 standard, the system achieved 12.5% energy resolution, 0.8% peak sensitivity, and a high spatial resolution of 0.66 mm. Compared to conventional preclinical PET systems, Gym-PET demonstrated visibly improved delineation of small subcortical structures. To validate the system's in vivo capabilities, dynamic 18F-FDG PET imaging was performed. The results successfully captured exercise-induced metabolic activation in the brainstem and thalamus of awake running mice. Furthermore, a three-day sleep deprivation study revealed the system's sensitivity to global metabolic suppression without anesthesia interference. Ultimately, the Gym-PET platform significantly reduces anesthesia-related metabolic interference, establishing a highly effective tool for high-resolution molecular neuroimaging in awake behavioral models.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-02-02] Preliminary Validation of Flexible On-Demand Customized Ultra-Resolution System for Targeted Performance Enhancement in Preclinical PET (#3184)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Wang (Autores: K. Wang , R. Liao , Z. Yuan , Y. Chen , Y. Chen , H. Wen , C. Li , Y. Hou , S. Gong , Y. Tai , J. Jiang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Normal University, Beijing, China [2] Washington University in St. Louis, Mallinckrodt Institute of Radiology, St. Louis, Missouri, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study introduces Flexible On-demand Customized Ultra-resolution System for PET (FOCUS-PET), a novel technique designed to maximize spatial resolution and counting statistics within a predefined region of interest. The efficacy of FOCUS-PET was rigorously evaluated via Monte Carlo simulations and physical experiments using high-resolution add-on detector configurations. The simulated system employed an arc-shaped add-on detector comprised of a 4×2 module array, with each module housing 32×48 LYSO crystals (0.42×0.42×5.0 mm³). Sensitivity profiles were mapped using an axially stepped 22 Na point source, and a three-bed whole-body protocol was simulated utilizing a micro-Derenzo phantom. Simulation results demonstrated a 5.1% to 19.8% enhancement in absolute sensitivity. The system resolved 0.9-mm micro-rods, effectively surpassing native resolution limits, and improved the peak-to-valley ratio (PVR) and contrast recovery (CR) for 1.0-mm rods from 1.50 to 2.13 and 33.30% to 52.95%, respectively. Experimental validation was performed by integrating a flat-panel add-on detector-comprising two modules with 44×44 LYSO arrays (0.52×0.52×5.0 mm³)-into an ACTIVE 7 MAX preclinical scanner. Imaging of a physical Derenzo phantom was conducted to assess ultimate resolution and multi-bed stitching fidelity. Physical experiments corroborated the theoretical gains, with the flat-panel FOCUS-PET device consistently improving PVR (1.57 to 1.90) and CR (27.93% to 33.19%) for 1.25-mm hot rods compared to the baseline. In conclusion, FOCUS-PET significantly elevates system sensitivity and spatial resolution, providing a cost-effective pathway for ultra-high-resolution preclinical imaging and potential translation to clinical whole-body PET applications.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-02-03] Initial Performance Characterization of the SAVANT Ultra-High-Resolution Phoswich-Based DOI Brain PET Scanner (#2935)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Lecomte (Autores: R. Lecomte , Y. Najmaoui , M. Gaudreault , O. Sarrhini , J.-F. Beaudoin , T. Galarneau , É. Croteau , É. Lavallée , C. Thibaudeau , R. Espagnet , N. Viscogliosi , J. Bouchard , A. Samson , M. Toussaint , T. Marin , Y. Chemli , J.-B. Michaud , M.-A. Tétrault , R. Fontaine , G. El Fakhri)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Université de Sherbrooke, Sherbrooke Molecular Imaging Center and Department of Medical Imaging and Radiation Sciences, Sherbrooke, Québec, Canada [2] Yale University School of Medicine, Yale Biomedical Imaging Institute, New Haven, Connecticut, United States of America [3] CRCHUS, Sherbrooke Molecular Imaging Center, Sherbrooke, Québec, Canada [4] Université de Sherbrooke, Interdisciplinary Institute for Technological Innovation - 3IT, Sherbrooke, Québec, Canada [5] Imaging Research and Technology (IR&T) Inc., Magog, Québec, Canada [6] Nantes Université, Laboratoire CRCI2NA, INSERM, CNRS, Nantes, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract High spatial resolution is essential to resolve small structures in the brain and to enable imaging of neurological pathways at the onset of diseases. A key challenge with ultra-high-resolution (UHR) PET scanners is the significant degradation of resolution that occurs beyond the central area of the field-of-view (FOV). The UHR Brain PET scanner was designed with short (12 mm) LYSO crystals to mitigate the parallax error off the FOV center, but at the expense of reduced sensitivity. To address these limitations, the LabPET II technology platform was upgraded to implement depth-of-interaction (DOI) measurement using longer (15 mm) dual LGSO phoswich detectors in the SAVANT. Simulation results indicate an estimated 40% gain in sensitivity, while maintaining the resolution below 2 mm FWHM at the edge of the brain. For DOI determination, the crystal identification between slow (43-48 ns decay time) and fast (30-35 ns decay time) LGSO scintillators uses a model-based dual-threshold time-over-threshold (ToT) discrimination technique, currently achieving better than 70% accuracy. The 6.5/8.5 mm length ratio of the top slow and bottom fast LGSO scintillators resulted from trade-offs between off-center spatial resolution and balanced coincidence detection efficiency of the two crystal layers. We report the initial experimental characterization of the partially assembled scanner (182 mm axial extent), which demonstrate the improvement in sensitivity and resolution uniformity across the radial FOV achieved using this simple DOI discrimination scheme. Point source and phantom measurements taken at various radial positions demonstrate the gain in spatial resolution compared to non-DOI measurements, though not reaching the resolution predicted by simulation. Further refinement of the crystal identification process using AI-based classification is expected to yield the forecasted benefits from simulation. Preliminary results for imaging the human brain will be presented.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-02-04] A Physics-Guided Deep Learning Method for Fast System Matrix Modeling in Self-Collimating SPECT Using Sparse Point-Source Calibration (#2412)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Q. Ye (Autores: Q. Ye , D. Zhang , H. Xie , Z. Lyu , T. Ma)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Beijing, China [2] Fudan University, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Self-collimating SPECT (SC-SPECT) enables simultaneous high-resolution and high-sensitivity imaging using sparse-scintillator detector layers. Accurate system matrix (SM) estimation is essential but remains challenging in SC-SPECT, because dense point-source calibration is time-consuming and conventional modeling is limited by complex system physics, while geometry-dependent detector responses further complicate AI-based sparse-to-dense recovery. In this work, we propose a physics-guided sparse-to-dense SM modeling framework to recover the full SM from 10k point-source measurements. The framework uses a customized 3D encoder-decoder with anisotropic convolutions and modified down/up-sampling to preserve fine structures under limited sampling. Sparse response intensity, sampling positions, and detector angular information are encoded as four input channels, while LOR-directional profile and curvature-continuity losses enforce physically consistent recovery. The model is trained on simulated PPDFs, with ablation studies evaluating the input-channel, architecture, and loss designs. It is further validated using experimental SM-level metrics and MLEM reconstructions of hot-rod phantom and small-animal data. Results demonstrate improved PPDF recovery and reconstruction quality over interpolation-based SM estimation and a standard U-Net, while reducing the calibration time by over 97.5%.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-02-05] BuckyPET: Performance Evaluation and NEMA Adaptation for Compact PET Geometries (#3115)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Perez-Benito (Autores: D. Perez-Benito , L. Batres , L. Jimenez Algarra , M. Vidal , J. J. Vaquero)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, Departamento de Bioingenería, Madrid, Spain [2] Instituto de Investigación Sanitaria Gregorio Marañón, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dedicated brain PET systems are attracting renewed interest due to their potential to overcome key limitations of conventional whole-body PET, particularly limited sensitivity and spatial resolution for neurological imaging. In this work, we present BuckyPET, an innovative dedicated brain PET scanner inspired by fullerene-like geometry. The system is based on 234 regular hexagonal LYSO detector modules arranged to closely approximate a spherical configuration, arguably the most efficient geometry for brain PET imaging. Each detector is laser-engraved to create customizable optical barriers defining hexagonal scintillation pixels and is coupled to a hexagonal Hamamatsu MPPC with 61 individually read channels. Current clinical and preclinical NEMA standards rely on concepts such as sinograms, single-slice rebinning, axial axes, and transaxial planes, which are not directly applicable to spherical or highly enclosed geometries. We also discuss the need for a modified NEMA NU 2-2018-like protocol for non-cylindrical PET systems. We propose preserving the core performance metrics of the standard while reformulating the analysis in a geometry-independent framework. Preliminary results demonstrate the high-sensitivity capabilities of BuckyPET, alongside a high noise-to-count ratio and spatial resolution in the range of 1.5-2 mm. Ongoing work focuses on fine-tuning the electronics and acquisition system and assessing robustness under different operating conditions. Thus, the final figures of merit are expected to further improve, while ongoing advances in the reconstruction framework are anticipated to push the spatial resolution beyond the 1 mm frontier. First studies for the clinical validation are scheduled for summer 2026.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 2Poster Number:NSS-13-002] Gas Circulation and Pressure Protection System for the COMET Cylindrical Drift Chamber (#1762)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Nagai (Autores: R. Nagai , S. Kawano , S. Ueda , Y. Nakano , A. Sato , K. Ueno)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The University of Osaka, Department of Physics, Osaka, Japan [2] University of Toyama, Faculty of Science, Toyama, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The COMET Cylindrical Drift Chamber is a large, low-mass gaseous detector. Gas exchange through the detector volume affects gas quality, gain stability, and wire aging, which are important for stable detector operation. Increasing the gas-flow rate in a once-through operation would increase fresh-gas consumption and cost, and would also impose constraints on exhaust handling from the experimental area. For this reason, a gas circulation system is adopted. At the same time, safe operation of the chamber requires the differential pressure between the chamber volume and the surrounding atmosphere to be maintained within a narrow range, because the large-radius, low-mass inner wall adopted to suppress backgrounds imposes a strict mechanical limit on the allowable differential pressure. Pressure excursions caused by pump operation, environmental variations, or abnormal exhaust conditions must be suppressed. While the system consists of standard gas-system components, their configuration and operating parameters were quantitatively evaluated against the mechanical constraints and gas-flow requirements of the chamber. A simplified analysis based on a resistance-compliance model was introduced to interpret pressure propagation in the gas system. Preliminary gas-system commissioning tests, including pump-start and exhaust-transient measurements, were performed to characterize the pressure response and to evaluate the roles of buffer tanks and restricted flow paths. The results are being used to define the buffer-tank configuration, emergency-exhaust conductance, pump operating conditions, and a staged gas-commissioning procedure, enabling safe commissioning and stable long-term operation of the detector.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 4Poster Number:NSS-13-004] Performance of a 2D-THCOBRA Gaseous Detector with Ar/Xe Mixtures for X-Ray Imaging (#2168)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. L. Silva (Autores: F.D. Leite , S. Pessanha , J. Veloso , A. L. Silva)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidade Aveiro, Physics Department, Aveiro, Portugal [2] Universidade NOVA de Lisboa, Physics Department, Caparica, Portugal
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In this work, we present a systematic characterization of a 2D-THCOBRA detector operated in pure argon (Ar) and Ar/Xe mixtures (Ar/Xe 98/2, 95/5 and 90/10), exploiting the Penning effect to enhance detector performance. The detector is characterized in terms of gain, energy resolution, linearity, and intrinsic spatial resolution. The addition of Xe to Ar significantly reduces the required operating voltage, with equivalent gains achieved at voltages approximately 300 V lower than those required for pure Ar. The energy resolution improved from 24.4% (pure Ar) to 18.3% FWHM at 5.9 keV (Ar/Xe 95/5 mixture), and the intrinsic spatial resolution improves from 1.8 mm (pure Ar) to 1.5 mm FWHM Ar/Xe 95/5. These initial results demonstrate the strong potential of the 2D-THCOBRA operating in Ar/Xe mixtures for X-ray fluorescence imaging and spectral X-ray imaging applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 6Poster Number:NSS-13-006] The effect of hole geometry on the ion-backflow of a single gas electron multiplier foil (#2631)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Badran (Autores: H. Badran , E. Brücken , J. Heino , T. Hildén)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Helsinki Institute of Physics, Helsinki, Finland [2] University of Helsinki, Department of Physics, Helsinki, Finland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A systematic study of the ion-backflow (IBF) contribution of single GEM foils with respect to the hole sizes and geometries is presented. The effective gain and the IBF of single GEM foils in a standard gas enclosure with a 2D strip readout plane were measured, using Ar-CO2 (70-30) gas mixture. The X-ray exposure using 55 Fe source was performed separately for each foil segment to compare the performance differences of the different hole geometries. A clear dependency of the IBF to the size and shape of the GEM holes was found. The results were compared to simulations using the Garfield++ toolkit. We present that choosing the right foils for a TPC readout chamber can effectively limit the IBF.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 8Poster Number:NSS-13-008] Feasibility of a Compact Detector for LINAC Radioactivation Monitoring (#1053)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Kim (Autores: J. Kim , B. Park , J. Choi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Samsung changwon hospital, Research and Suport, Changwon, Republic of Korea [2] Samsung changwon hospital, Radition Oncology, Changwon, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A compact SiPM-GAGG(Ce) radiation detector without conventional front-end electronics was evaluated for LINAC radioactivation monitoring. The proposed detector employed a simplified signal-processing architecture without a preamplifier, shaping amplifier, or comparator. Spectroscopic performance was evaluated at SiPM operating voltages from 58 V to 61 V. The best energy resolution for the 662 keV photopeak of Cs-137 was 8.31% at 61 V, corresponding to an overvoltage of approximately 7 V from the measured breakdown voltage of 53.88 V. Mixed-source measurements using Ba-133, Cs-137, and Co-60 demonstrated distinguishable radionuclide peaks and channel-energy linearity greater than 0.99. The detector was subsequently applied to LINAC radioactivation measurements, where characteristic gamma-ray peaks of W-187 were successfully detected near the LINAC head after high-energy photon beam irradiation. The results demonstrate the feasibility of compact and simplified LINAC radioactivation monitoring using the proposed detector system.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 10Poster Number:NSS-13-010] Temperature Dependence of Energy Resolution in a SiPM-Based Scintillation Detector for PET Applications (#1177)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Rigotti Caiano (Autores: S. Rigotti Caiano , D. Alexandre Baptista Bonifacio , H. Massaharu Murata , M. Bottaro , M. Moralles)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of São Paulo (USP), Institute of Energy and Nuclear Research (IPEN), São Paulo, Brazil [2] University of São Paulo (USP), Institute of Energy and Environment (IEE), São Paulo, Brazil
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) are widely used in PET detectors due to their compact size and compatibility with magnetic fields. However, their performance is strongly dependent on temperature. In this work, the temperature dependence of energy resolution in a SiPM-based scintillation detector coupled to a LYSO crystal is experimentally investigated. Measurements were carried out over a temperature range from 10 to 50 degrees Celsius using a controlled climatic chamber. Preliminary results show a systematic degradation in energy resolution with increasing temperature. A simplified physical interpretation based on the temperature dependence of breakdown voltage, gain, photon detection efficiency (PDE), and noise contributions is proposed. Ongoing work focuses on developing a quantitative model and compensation strategies for detector stabilization.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 12Poster Number:NSS-13-012] Development of transparent ceramic Tl:NaI scintillators for gamma-ray detectors (#1187)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Yanagida (Autores: T. Yanagida , T. Kato , D. Nakauchi , N. Kawaguchi)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Tl-doped NaI (Tl:NaI) single crystal has been a one of the standard scintillators from mid 20 th century, and in this time, we will report a development of transparent ceramic Tl:NaI. Tl 0.05, 0.1, 0.3, and 0.5% doped NaI transparent ceramics were fabricated by the spark plasma sintering (SPS) method. Under X-ray irradiation, these ceramics showed a typical emission wavelength at 420 nm with a typical decay time (~200 ms) due to 3 P 1 → 1 S 0 electronic transitions of Tl + . When 662 keV gamma-rays from 137Cs were irradiated, all the samples exhibited a clear photoabsorption peak, and among all the samples, 0.1% doped one had the highest scintillation light yield, reaching to 36000 ph/MeV, which was equivalent to common commercial Tl:NaI single crystal.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 14Poster Number:NSS-13-014] Simulation of Electron Escape within Thin Organic Scintillators (#1248)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. Schneider (Autores: E. Schneider , C. Graham , E. Neely , D. Breitenmoser , S. Clarke , S. Pozzi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Organic scintillators are fast detectors that are sensitive to both neutrons and gamma rays. Measurements of neutron timing in an intense gamma-ray field can be studied with thin organics, as recoil electrons produced by Compton scatters have a path length significantly longer than those of recoil protons. Past work in characterization of such samples has been hindered by the lack of clear energy calibration with samples with thicknesses less than 2 mm, as the spectral features used for an energy calibration are significantly broadened from electron escapes. To address this issue, the gamma spectrum was observed for three gamma check sources, Cs-137, Na-22, and Co-60, within four organic glass scintillators, from 6 mm to 1 mm, and compared with Monte Carlo models MCNPX-PoliMi. A genetic algorithm was used to broaden the simulated spectra to match the measured spectra. Thinner samples displayed greater broadening of Compton edges, which suggests an increase in electron escape. Simulations show an increase in electron escape probability between the 6 mm sample and the 1 mm sample of 12% ± 1% to 26.1% ± 0.3%.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 16Poster Number:NSS-13-016] Alignments of the Dual-Layer Flat-Panel Detectors and their Modulation Transfer Functions (#1465)
sub_talks.speaker: D.S. Kim
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, Division of Semiconductor and Electronics Engineering, Sungnam, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In radiographic imaging, dual-layer flat-panel detectors (DFDs) can be used for two purposes: acquiring high-quality x-ray images and performing material decomposition. A convex combination of the x-ray images acquired from DFD can yield significantly improved detective quantum efficient. The DFD structure consists of stacked upper and lower flat-panel detectors, and can provide different modulation transfer function (MTF) characteristics depending on the orientation of the stacked detectors with respect to the incident x-ray. In this paper, we consider three different stacked structures for DFD and find the optimal DFD structure by experimentally observing the MTF curves using fabricated DFD prototypes. Because the inverted layers have a back-irradiation geometry, the MTF performance is better than that of the normal case. Therefore, we can select a DFD structure having an inverted lower layer to acquire high-DQE x-ray images.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 18Poster Number:NSS-13-018] Loading Surface-Modified LiAlO 2 Nanoparticles in Plastic Scintillators for Thermal Neutron Detection (#1484)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Koshimizu (Autores: H. Tsukahara , K. Watanabe , M. Koshimizu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shizuoka University, Graduate School of Integrated Science and Technology, Hamamatsu, Japan [2] Kyushu University, Department of Applied Quantum Physics and Nuclear Engineering, Fukuoka, Japan [3] Shizuoka University, Research Institute of Electronics, Hamamatsu, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We report the development of plastic scintillators for thermal neutron detection by incorporating surface‑modified LiAlO₂ nanoparticles. Conventionally, thermal neutrons have been detected using ³He gas counters, but the scarcity of ³He has driven the search for alternative technologies. Plastic scintillators are attractive due to their low cost and ease of fabrication; however, loading neutron‑reactive isotopes such as ⁶Li into plastics is challenging because conventional organometallic compounds suffer from poor solubility and strong quenching effects. To overcome these limitations, LiAlO₂ nanoparticles enriched with ⁶Li were synthesized via a sol-gel method and their surfaces were modified with trimethoxyphenylsilane to improve compatibility with a polystyrene matrix. Structural and spectroscopic analyses confirmed that the nanoparticles retained the γ‑LiAlO₂ phase and were successfully functionalized with phenyl groups, without significant changes in particle size. The surface modification greatly enhanced nanoparticle dispersion within the plastic scintillator, as evidenced by uniform elemental mapping. Scintillation measurements demonstrated that the emission originated from the organic fluor and that the modified nanoparticles did not introduce additional emission bands. The scintillation light yields of 2400-3000 photons per neutron were achieved, depending on nanoparticle loading, which is substantially higher than those of boron‑loaded commercial plastic scintillators and plastics containing unmodified LiAlO₂ nanoparticles. These results highlight surface modification as an effective strategy for improving the performance of nanoparticle‑loaded plastic scintillators for thermal neutron detection.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 20Poster Number:NSS-13-020] Development of Perovskite Quantum Dots with High Photoluminescence Quantum Yields and Their Loading in Plastic Scintillators (#1618)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Koshimizu (Autores: I. Ishihara , K. Asou , M. Koshimizu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shizuoka University, Faculty of Engineering, Hamamatsu, Japan [2] Shizuoka University, Research Institute of Electronics, Hamamatsu, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Fast plastic scintillators are attractive for radiation detection owing to their nanosecond decay times, low cost, and scalability; however, their practical application is limited by low scintillation light yield and poor detection efficiency for X‑ and γ‑rays. In this study, we report the development of plastic scintillators loaded with perovskite quantum dots (QDs) exhibiting high photoluminescence quantum yields (PL QYs). Cesium lead halide perovskite QDs with various halogen compositions were synthesized via a facile solution process under ambient conditions. Surface modification using oleyl amine was employed to passivate surface defects and enhance radiative recombination. Transmission electron microscopy revealed spherical QDs with diameters of approximately 10 nm and a narrow size distribution. The oleyl amine modification markedly improved PL QYs, achieving values exceeding 80% for CsPbBr₃ QDs. By tuning the halogen composition, the emission wavelength was controllably varied from ~420 to 540 nm. These high‑PL‑QY QDs were uniformly loaded into polystyrene‑based plastic scintillators. Scintillation spectra demonstrated dominant QD emission without defect‑related luminescence, indicating fast emission owing to the interband transition within the QDs. Although clear full‑energy peaks were not observed in pulse‑height spectra, enhanced scintillation responses were evident for samples containing surface‑modified QDs. These results demonstrate that surface‑engineered perovskite QDs are promising additives for improving the performance of fast plastic scintillators.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 22Poster Number:NSS-13-022] Effect of geometry on the properties of 3D-printed scintillators (#1708)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. K. Gourishetty (Autores: V. Anand , A. Sharma , U. Bajpai , B. Bansal , A. K. Gourishetty)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee, Roorkee, India
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work investigates how scintillator geometry influences light collection in 3D-printed plastic scintillators, motivated by the ability of additive manufacturing to fabricate detector shapes that are difficult to realize by conventional casting or machining. Four geometries, including a cylinder, truncated cone, cone, and paraboloid, were fabricated using a digital light processing based 3D printing method and evaluated experimentally. Complementary Geant4 optical-photon simulations were performed to study photon transport and collection trends for the same geometry family. Both experiment and simulation indicate that geometry modifies photon escape, internal reflection, and collection at the readout face. Taking the cylinder as the reference at 100%, the truncated cone, paraboloid-like geometry, and cone show increased relative light outputs of 151%, 156%, and 180%, respectively, suggesting that non-cylindrical 3D-printed scintillator shapes can improve photon collection at the readout face, most likely by reducing unfavorable optical paths and repeated reflections. The simulations reproduce the qualitative trend observed experimentally, although the absolute values do not agree number by number because the present model does not fully include fabrication-specific effects such as print-layer scattering, surface roughness, optical coupling variations, reflector response, and sensor nonuniformity. These results demonstrate that geometry is an important design parameter for additively manufactured scintillators and should be optimized together with material composition and photosensor coupling.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 24Poster Number:NSS-13-024] Development of a Gamma Camera for Real-Time Monitoring of High-Energy Gamma-Ray Environments (#1777)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Park (Autores: Y. Park , T. Lee , S. Jo , J. Yeom , H. Lee , K. Lee)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea University, Department of Bioengineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] Korea University, Interdisciplinary program in precision public health, Seoul, Republic of Korea [3] KEPCO KPS Global Institute of Technology, Naju-si, Republic of Korea [4] ARALE Laboratory, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In June 2025, Kori Unit 1, the first commercial nuclear power plant in the Republic of Korea, obtained final approval for decommissioning. This milestone highlights the growing need for radiation-imaging technologies that can support radiation surveillance during nuclear decommissioning and in other high-radiation environments. In this study, we developed a portable gamma camera for real-time monitoring of high-energy gamma-ray fields and evaluated its basic detector characteristics and imaging performance. The spatial response of the GAGG-SiPM detector array was investigated using flood-map measurements and line-profile analysis. The obtained flood maps showed that all scintillator pixels were distinctly resolved, with minimal signal overlap between adjacent pixels. The average full width at half maximum (FWHM) was measured to be approximately 0.58 mm, corresponding to about 41% of the 1.41 mm pixel pitch, indicating stable intrinsic spatial resolution across the detector array. The intrinsic energy resolution was assessed using a Co-60 point source. The measured energy resolutions were 7.42% and 6.68% FWHM at the 1.17 MeV and 1.33 MeV photopeaks, respectively. In addition, the detectable imaging distance was examined by acquiring Co-60 point-source images at source-to-detector distances from 10 cm to 300 cm. The source location was successfully identified throughout the tested range, and clear gamma-ray imaging was achieved even at a distance of 3 m. These results demonstrate that the proposed portable gamma camera provides stable detector response, high-energy gamma-ray imaging capability, and practical source-localization performance for radiation monitoring in nuclear decommissioning environments.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 26Poster Number:NSS-13-026] Study on the Influence of Grain Size for the GAGG powder-PMMA composite scintillator Detector (#1895)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Liu (Autores: Z. Zhang , Y. Feng , W. Zhou , X. Wang , X. Li , A. Wei , Y. Liu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Engineering Research Center of Radiographic Techniques and Equipment, Institute of High Energy Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China [2] School of Nuclear Science and Technology, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A SiPM-based detector using GAGG powder-PMMA composite scintillators was developed and evaluated. There were 8 scintillator samples with the identical GAGG mass fraction but different powder grain sizes. Each scintillator has an active area of 40 mm × 40 mm and a total thickness of 3.6 ± 0.1 mm. The detector system consisted of the scintillator module, front-end analog electronics for filtering, shaping, and amplification, and an 8-channel back-end digital acquisition system. Under identical measurement conditions, the count rate measured with a 50 µCi 22Na source increased from approximately 1.7 × 10 3 cps for Sample #1 to 1.6×10 4 cps for Sample #8. Waveform measurements also showed higher output amplitude for the larger-powder sample. The results indicate that the grain size of GAGG powder strongly affects photon transport and effective detector response in the composite scintillators.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 28Poster Number:NSS-13-028] Thermal Neutron Detection with Dy-doped LiF/CaF 2 Eutectic Composite (#2150)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Kawaguchi (Autores: N. Kawaguchi , H. Kimura , A. Nishikawa , T. Kato , D. Nakauchi , T. Yanagida)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Nara Institute of Science and Technology, Ikoma, Japan [2] National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology, Tsukuba, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We studied thermal neutron detection using a LiF/CaF 2 :Dy eutectic composite which can be used for thermoluminescence dosimetry. Emissions of the sample due to the self-trapped exciton of CaF 2 and 4f-4f transitions of Dy 3+ ions were confirmed in the X-ray excited spectrum and decay curve measurements. The thermoluminescence spectrum at 230 ℃ showed only the emission peaks due to Dy 3+ . This result indicates that Dy-doping in LiF/CaF 2 is efficient for thermoluminescence dosimetry applications. Thermal neutron detection was performed using the LiF/CaF 2 :Dy eutectic composite, and its light yield was 3000 photons/neutron. This measurement was achieved due to the fast emission of the self-trapped exciton. The LiF/CaF 2 :Dy eutectic composite can act as a dual functional material for radiation dosimetry and detection.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 30Poster Number:NSS-13-030] Development of Afterglow and NIR Decay Curve Measurement Systems using a Field Emission-type Pulsed X-ray Source (#2269)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Kimura (Autores: H. Kimura , H. Kato , K. Michishio , R. Suzuki , D. Nakauchi , T. Yanagida , K. Watanabe , T. Fujiwara)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology, Tsukuba, Japan [2] Nara Institute of Science and Technology, Ikoma, Japan [3] Kyushu University, Nishi, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Scintillation detectors are widely used in various fields. Since the performance of scintillators directly affects detector properties, the evaluation of scintillation properties is essential. Scintillators are required to exhibit specific properties, including a high light yield, a short decay time, and a low afterglow. So far, afterglow measurements have not yet been standardized, and each manufacturer employs its own measurement setup and evaluation criteria. In conventional systems, their temporal resolution is limited to several milliseconds, which is insufficient for accurate characterization of afterglow in the short-time region. Separately, although near infrared (NIR)-emitting scintillators have recently attracted considerable attention and their emission spectra have been investigated, their NIR decay curves have not been sufficiently evaluated. In this study, we developed the afterglow and NIR decay curve measurement systems by combining a field-emission pulse X-ray source with the two types of detection units: an afterglow detection unit and an NIR detection unit. The performance of the developed system was evaluated by measuring the afterglow of CWO, BGO, and CsI:Tl, as well as the NIR decay curve of the NIR-emitting Yb:Lu 2 O 3 transparent ceramics. The afterglow levels of CWO, BGO, and CsI:Tl were approximately 2.5, 0.5, and 450 ppm, respectively. The X-ray-induced NIR decay time constants of 0.1%-3.0% Yb:Lu 2 O 3 transparent ceramics were 0.66-1.05 ms. Since these values were comparable to previously reported afterglow levels and PL decay time constants, the present results are considered to be valid.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 32Poster Number:NSS-13-032] One Dimensional TPE-4Br Supramolecular Scintillator for High-Speed X-ray Imaging (#2373)
sub_talks.speaker: X. Liu
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Wuhan University of Technology, State key Laboratory of Advanced Glass Materials, Wuhan, China [2] Wuhan University of Technology, School of Materials Science and Engineering, Wuhan, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Next-generation radiation detection, such as TOF-PET and high-flux X-ray imaging, requires scintillators that combine high light yield with ultrafast response. However, organic scintillators are often limited by inefficient exciton utilization and non-radiative quenching of high-energy states. In this work, we report a 1D supramolecular organic architecture based on the luminophore TPE-4Br. By shifting the molecular packing from a discrete 0D form into an ordered 1D configuration, we achieve a structural "locking" effect that rigidifies the lattice and suppresses vibrational quenching. This configuration results in an increase in Young's modulus (6.44 GPa) and hardness (0.24 GPa) compared to 0D crystals. Under X-ray excitation, the 1D framework exhibits an enhanced light yield that is 1.5 times higher. Furthermore, real-time dynamic X-ray imaging at 67 fps is demonstrated, showing minimal afterglow and the ability to track moving objects with high signal fidelity. This combination of luminosity, timing, and mechanical robustness positions the TPE-4Br-based 1D framework as a candidate for high-speed nuclear instrumentation and medical CT systems

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents the development of a large-area flat-panel scintillation detector designed for prompt gamma monitoring in proton therapy. The detector comprises a 2x2 of ArrayJ-60035-64P silicon photomultiplier arrays, coupled with a 14x14 Lutetium-yttrium oxyorthosilicate crystal array. To address the challenge of high channel density, a diode-based row-column multiplexing circuit was implemented, reducing the total number of readout channels from 256 to 64. The system interfaces with the PETsys TOFPET2 ASIC via a custom adapter board utilizing LSHM-140 connectors. Preliminary laboratory tests using a 22Na point source demonstrate the feasibility of the multiplexing scheme and its potential for high-resolution gamma-ray imaging in clinical environments.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 36Poster Number:NSS-13-036] Development of a Hand-Foot Monitor for Visualizing Alpha Contamination (#2451)
sub_talks.speaker: N. Sagawa
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Japan Atomic Energy Agency, Plutonium Radiation Control Section Radiation Protection Department, Muramatsu, Tokai-Mura, Naka-Gun, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract When exiting controlled areas such as nuclear facilities, contamination control is of the utmost importance to prevent the removal of contaminants outside the area. Currently used hand and foot monitors and personnel contamination monitors are equipped with multiple detectors near the clothing and limbs, enabling the simultaneous measurement of radioactive contamination on the body surface. However, conventional detectors make it difficult to pinpoint contaminated areas in detail. Accurately visualizing contamination distribution is crucial for preventing internal exposure and conducting efficient decontamination operations. This study aimed to develop a personnel contamination monitor capable of visualizing contaminated areas. Contamination visualization is achieved by combining an electron-multiplying charge-coupled device (EMCCD) camera or a quantitative complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (qCMOS) camera with multiple scintillators, such as ZnS(Ag) scintillators and rare-earth complex high-luminescence scintillators. This device utilizes a CCD camera (ImagEMX2, Hamamatsu Photonics K.K.) or a CMOS camera (ORCA-Quest, Hamamatsu Photonics K.K.) in combination with a 3.25 mg/cm² ZnS(Ag) scintillator (EJ-440, Eljen Technology), a rare-earth complex high-luminescence scintillator (manufactured by Hokkaido University), and a large-area plastic scintillator containing dispersed europium complexes (manufactured by Hokkaido University). The system was irradiated with alpha rays, and the resulting images were analyzed using ImageJ. As a result, the luminous intensities of the various scintillators were confirmed, and we were able to select the optimal combination of scintillators and device configuration conditions for visualizing contaminated areas.
