sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 38Poster Number:NSS-13-038] Room-Temperature Synthesis of Na + -Doped Cs 3 Cu 2 I 5 Single Crystals: Structural, Optical and Scintillation Properties (#2545)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. A. Kumar (Autores: B. Bansal , G. A. Kumar)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee, Department of Physics, Roorkee, India
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Copper-based halide perovskite Cs 3 Cu 2 I 5 has emerged as a promising lead-free scintillator for ionizing radiation detection. In this work, Na⁺-doped and undoped Cs 3 Cu 2 I 5 single crystals were grown at room temperature via a formic-acid-assisted solvent evaporation method. Both crystals exhibit ordered diffraction planes and excellent crystallinity, confirmed by rocking-curve full width at half maximum (FWHM) values of 0.009° (undoped) and 0.008° (Na⁺-doped). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy confirms that Cu⁺ remains in its monovalent state in both samples. Optical analyses show that Na⁺ incorporation enhances the photoluminescence (PL) intensity by 11% and increases the self-trapped exciton (STE) decay time from 1090 ns to 1146 ns, attributed to shallow defect passivation and suppressed non-radiative recombination. The Na⁺-doped crystal demonstrates superior scintillation performance with a light output of 42,000 ph/MeV and an energy resolution of 4.9% at 662 keV, compared to 39,000 ph/MeV and 5.4% for the undoped crystal, corresponding to improvements of ~7.6% and ~9%, respectively. These results establish Na⁺ doping as an effective strategy for defect suppression and scintillation enhancement in lead-free halide perovskite single crystals.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 40Poster Number:NSS-13-040] Thermal Cycling of Optical Coupling Material to Investigate Performance Degradation in Detectors (#2575)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. H. Sharpe (Autores: Z. H. Sharpe , K. L. Loughney , C. Allwork , P. J. Sellin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] AWE NST, Reading, United Kingdom [2] University of Surrey, Physics, Guildford, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Thermal cycling is used to accelerate the ageing process through an exaggerated version of diurnal temperature variations a detector/material may experience during use/storage over the lifetime of a detector. For this investigation, samples of optical grease were thermally cycled between +5 and +75°C in an environmental chamber. Four sets of samples were created with different preparation methods, volumes and substrates used, consisting of: 0.02g between microscope slides, 2ml petri dish, and 1" & 2" diameter discs in petri slides. A total of 15 samples per set were created that were divided into three subsets: Cyclical (C), Duration (D) and Room (R) samples. The percentage transmission (%T) for all samples was measured using a spectrophotometer for a wavelength range of 300-700nm for comparison with the emission range of common scintillators, such as EJ200. Identical "blank" samples with air were used for baseline/zero corrections performed for the spectrophotometer, meaning all %T values are relative to air. C samples were recharacterised at the end of each year equivalent cycle, while D and R were only recharacterised after the final cycle as controls for the removal from the chamber and the passage of real time respectively. Samples were cycled to equivalent of a maximum 20 years, with an additional set of "no bubble" (NB) samples introduced at the start of the 11 th year equivalent cycle to determine the impact of air bubbles on %T. The 1" petri slide samples displayed the greatest average variation in %T across the range 400-500nm, with a drop of 20% %T value between pre and post-20 year characterisation (28% percentage difference), while 2" petri slide samples showed an average 10% decrease in %T value (15% percentage difference). Microscope slides and petri dish samples displayed a 2.6% average %T decrease (3% percentage difference) and 3.9% average %T increase (4.7% percentage difference) respectively. sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Scintillators play an important role in radiation detection and imaging. Thallium-doped cesium iodide (CsI:Tl) is one of the major scintillators that have been used for many applications for many decades. Coupling CsI:Tl crystals to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) makes them into compact and portable detectors, enabling them to be incorporated in many modular detector designs. This paper presents a performance study of improved CsI:Tl crystals coupled to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs). sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 46Poster Number:NSS-13-046] Optical Control of Valence State in LuAG:Ce,Ca (#2991)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Campbell (Autores: C. Campbell , S. Rand , J. Glodo , M. Muller , A. Kim , D. Wehe)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Michigan, NERS, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America [2] University of Michigan, EECS, Physics, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America [3] Radiation Monitoring Devices, Inc., Watertown, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Scintillator energy resolution is ultimately limited by light yield. One theoretical pathway for increasing this light yield in inorganic scintillators is optical re-excitation of activator ions. Lu 3 Al 5 O 12 (LuAG) with Ce 3+ activator ions is investigated as a candidate for verifying the mechanism. Ca co-doping is used to convert the Ce 3+ to Ce 4+ during manufacturing, so Ce 3+ is only present in the material after a radiation interaction occurs, allowing for multiplication of the radiation-induced signal. Optical spectroscopy is used to evaluate the impact of co-doping ratios on the concentration of Ce 4+ in several samples. The impact of stimulation wavelength on the intensity of previously observed optically-induced valence change indicates the valence change originates from charge-transfer absorption of the Ce 4+ . A dual-beam optical and x-ray excitation experiment with a chopperwheel and lock-in amplifier is used to compare the scintillation response of LuAG:Ce and LuAG:Ce,Ca samples to single- and dual-beam excitation. The difference between these responses is evaluated with a lock-in amplifier and using a program which superimposes the single-beam signals and minimizes the variance of this superposition with respect to the dual-beam signal. After optical characterization, the responses of LuAG samples with different Ce concentrations and co-doping ratios will be tested in this dual-beam experiment to identify optimal doping concentrations for re-excitation.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 48Poster Number:NSS-13-048] Study of elpasolite crystals for neutron/gamma spectroscopy : First measurements with CLYC:Ce (#3212)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 I. Zeghni (Autores: I. Zeghni , C. Delafosse)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CNRS, IJCLab, Orsay, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The spectroscopy of decay products is one of the three pillars of low-energy beam exploitation techniques produced by the ISOL method. Decay stations can be found in all facilities using the ISOL technique to produce radioactive beams, such as ALTO (France), ISOLDE (CERN), and IGISOL (Finland), as well as in future facilities like SPES (Italy) and DESIR (France), to name a few in Europe. In the context of β decay, it is important to note that the total energy released during this process, denoted as Q β , can exceed 10 MeV as we venture further from nuclear stability. At the same time, the energy required to remove a neutron (S n ) decreases, resulting in the emission of unbound neutron(s) alongside the expected γ-rays. Elpasolite crystals containing 35 Cl such as CLYC:Ce represent a promising way to detect and discriminate both neutrons and γ-rays coming from such decay while measuring their energies. The ANR project SENSE (Scintillating Elpasolite for Neutron Spectroscopy Enhancement) aims to study such crystals using detailed Geant4 simulations in association with experimental measurements. We started this project using a 3"x4" CLYC:Ce crystal in order to measure several physical quantities such as its resolution, efficiency and homogeneity. Those measurements were first performed for gamma only and are combined with simulations performed via Geant4 for comparaison. So far, the study of neutron interaction with the crystal is being studied and experiments using ALTO facilities are planned. Also, Geant4 does not implement well the cross-section of neutron interacting with chlorine and this part of the work is still in progress. Our presentation will share the results we have obtained for this CLYC crystal and the on-going work that is performed at IJCLab.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 50Poster Number:NSS-13-050] A feasibility study on CsPbBr3 perovskite crystals for time-of-flight PET (#1120)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C.-M. Kao (Autores: H. Kim , Y. Wang , S. Sundramoorthy , M. V. Nemallapudi , C.-T. Chen , C.-M. Kao)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Chicago, Department of Radiology, Chicago, Illinois, United States of America [2] University of Chicago, Department of Radiation and Cellular Oncology, Chicago, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We are evaluating the potential of CsPbBr₃ crystals as Cherenkov light generating materials for TOF PET applications. CsPbBr₃, a lead halide perovskite semiconductor, has recently emerged as a highly efficient and cost‑effective alternative to traditional radiation detection materials such as CZT and CdTe for X‑ray and gamma‑ray imaging. Its high carrier mobility and excellent energy resolution characteristics make it attractive for next generation radiation detector technologies. Furthermore, its high refractive index (∼2.4) enables efficient generation of Cherenkov light, positioning this material as a promising candidate for fast timing applications, including TOF PET. To assess its timing performance, we investigated the coincidence time resolution (CTR) of CsPbBr₃ samples. Two crystal sizes-5 × 5 × 10 mm³ and 3 × 3 × 3 mm³-were used to study how crystal length affects CTR. Each crystal was optically coupled to a Broadcom NUV‑MT SiPM (S4N44P014M or S4N66P014M) and irradiated with a ²²Na positron source in a coincidence timing measurement setup. A CTR of ~339 ps was achieved using a pair of 3 × 3 × 3 mm³ CsPbBr₃ detectors. This preliminary result is highly encouraging and demonstrates the strong potential of CsPbBr₃ crystals for fast‑timing radiation detection applications. In this work, we present our initial findings and discuss the associated challenges, along with potential strategies for further improving the CTR.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 52Poster Number:NSS-13-052] From Collision Cascades to Device Response: A Multiscale Study of Proton-Induced Defects in Silicon (#1178)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Shoorian (Autores: S. Shoorian , H. Jafari)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shahid Beheshti University, Nuclear Engineering, Tehran, Iran (Islamic Republic of)
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study presents a comprehensive multi-scale computational and experimental investigation into displacement damage effects induced by high-energy proton irradiation in silicon-based photodiodes. The developed methodology systematically integrates SRIM-based analysis of primary knock-on atom (PKA) energy spectra, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using LAMMPS to model atomic-level defect formation, and TCAD-based device-level electrical modeling in SILVACO. MD simulations revealed a nonlinear increase in stable Frenkel pair formation, ranging from minimal defects at low PKA energies (≤200 eV) to substantial defect clustering at higher energies (≥500 eV), with approximately 40 stable defects per 2 keV event. These atomistic results were used to inform TCAD models, which demonstrated that increasing mid-gap trap densities significantly amplify reverse-bias leakage currents via trap-assisted recombination mechanisms, consistent with the Shockley-Read-Hall (SRH) recombination theory. Experimental validation using BPX65 photodiodes irradiated with 3 MeV protons, corroborated simulation predictions. Leakage current increased dramatically with proton fluence, exhibiting linear trends at lower fluences. Forward current measurements showed only modest degradation, confirming trap-assisted recombination as the primary mechanism behind device deterioration. The combined results underscore the dominant role of trap-assisted recombination in leakage current enhancement and validate the SRH framework in describing carrier lifetime degradation due to mid-gap traps. Deviations at high fluence were attributed to interface effects and charge compensation mechanisms. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of integrating atomic-scale simulations with device-level modeling to predict and interpret radiation effects in semiconductor detectors, providing a foundation for future radiation-hardened electronics design.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 54Poster Number:NSS-13-054] DREAM : A miniaturized spectrometer for protons and electrons measurement in space (#1273)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Dufour (Autores: A. Dufour , R. Ecoffet , J. Mekki , A. Pierre-Louis , J. Sadowy)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CNES, Toulouse, France [2] STEEL Electronique, Martres-Tolosane, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This paper describes a compact charged particles spectrometer called DREAM (French abbreviation of « Détecteur Radiation Energétique Adaptable et Miniaturisé »). It is a cubesat compatible radiation monitor, designed to measure protons (13 MeV - 200 MeV) and electrons (350 keV - 3 MeV) in space, essentially in the Earth's magnetic field. Built around silicon diode detectors co designed with STEEL Electronique and N7 Consulting, DREAM weighs around 400 g, fits within a 0.6 U volume (55 × 100 × 100 mm), and consumes less than 3W at 5 V. The main goal of this instrument is to measure the dynamic behaviour of trapped charged particles flux in the magnetosphere, mainly disturbed by solar flares. It will then help to predict anormal fluxes that may damage satellites or humans in space. Experimental results show a good agreement between simulated and experimental spectra obtained at the UCL (62 MeV beam) and Partrec (184MeV beam) proton accelerators. Qualification activities (radiation latch up tests, vibration, thermal cycling in vacuum, …) have been performed in 2025 and a detailed summary will be available in the paper. This instrument is already identified in several missions (mainly for the spaceweather), like the ESA S2P (Space Safety Programme) mission.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 56Poster Number:NSS-13-056] Bulk Stoichiometry and van der Waals Interface Engineering of CdTe for Room-Temperature X/γ-Ray Detectors (#1617)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Q. Zhao (Autores: Q. Zhao , Z. Sun , T. Wang , V. Gnatyuk)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Northwestern Polytechnical University, School of Material Science and Engineering, Xi'an, China [2] Advafab Oy, Helsinki, Finland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Cadmium telluride (CdTe) is a leading room-temperature semiconductor for direct X- and γ-ray detection, but its performance is limited by bulk stoichiometric defects and interface-induced leakage current. Here, we report an integrated strategy combining vapor-pressure-controlled CdTe(Cl) crystal growth with noninvasive van der Waals (vdW) Au contacts to enhance bulk charge transport and interfacial charge control. Detector-grade CdTe(Cl) single crystals were grown by vertical gradient freeze using a Cd reservoir to stabilize Cd partial pressure and Cl doping to regulate compensation. This approach suppressed large Te inclusions below 5 μm, achieved ~60% infrared transmittance, and yielded high resistivity of 1.5 × 10 10 Ω·cm, electron mobility of 1055 ± 88 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹, and electron mobility-lifetime product of ~1.1 × 10⁻⁴ cm² V⁻¹. Planar Au/CdTe(Cl)/Au detectors showed clear ²⁴¹Am α-particle response. Mechanically transferred Au electrodes further formed vdW contacts that avoided atomic intermixing, preserved surface chemistry, reduced defect-related photoluminescence, and increased the Schottky barrier height from 0.78 to 0.83 eV. Consequently, vdW-contact CdTe detectors suppressed dark current and improved 59.5 keV γ ray energy resolution from 14.4% to 11.8%.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 58Poster Number:NSS-13-058] Alpha Particle Detection with sCMOS imager (#1770)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Sasano (Autores: M. Sasano , M. Hayashi , N. Teranishi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Mitsubishi Electric Corporation, Advanced R&D center, Amagasaki, Japan [2] Shizuoka University, Research Institute of Electronics, Hamamatsu, Japan [3] Hirosaki University, Institute of Radiation Emergency Medicine, Hirosaki, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We investigated the alpha-particle response of a back-illuminated CMOS imager for radionuclide measurements in nuclear decommissioning. A GSENSE2020-BSI sensor with an approximately 10 μm-thick sensitive layer was used. To prevent alpha particles from reaching the circuit layer, measurements were performed with an 11 μm-thick aluminum foil and aluminized polymer sheets. The alpha-particle energy was varied by changing the number of sheets, and the resulting event images and deposited energy were analyzed. The expected deposited energy was calculated using Geant4, and single events were extracted using OpenCV-based image processing. The image intensity was calibrated to deposited energy using a 241 Am gamma-ray source. Alpha-particle events appeared as spatially spread images. Under unsaturated conditions, the measured energy spectra agreed well with simulation, whereas ADC saturation caused underestimation at higher energies. Reliable energy information was obtained when the deposited energy was approximately 1.5 MeV or lower. The event area increased with deposited energy, following area is proportional to E dep 1/3 . These results demonstrate the potential of a back-illuminated CMOS imager for alpha-particle detection and nuclide identification.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 60Poster Number:NSS-13-060] Development of Silicon Drift Detector Technology from Single-Element Devices to a 19-Pixel Module for X-ray Spectroscopy Applications (#1826)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Bao (Autores: Z. Bao , Z. Li , Y. Liu , W. Li , Y. Wang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institute of High Energy Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing Synchrotron Radiation Facility and High Energy Photon Source, Beijing, China [2] University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China [3] Institute of High Energy Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, the State Key Laboratory of Particle Astrophysics, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Silicon drift detectors (SDDs) are promising sensors for high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy because of their low anode capacitance, good timing capability, and scalability to large-area and multi-pixel detector systems. This work presents recent progress on single-pixel and array SDD technologies developed for space astronomy and synchrotron radiation applications. Single-pixel SDDs with sensitive areas from 15 to 85 mm² were designed and fabricated through optimization of the drift field, anode structure, leakage-current suppression, and dedicated semiconductor process. Low-noise front-end electronics, semiconductor packaging, and digital pulse-processing readout electronics were developed to support detector characterization and module integration. A 30 mm² single-pixel detector achieved an energy resolution of 135 eV at 5.9 keV at −40 °C, demonstrating the effectiveness of the device and readout design. Based on these developments, a first 19-pixel SDD module with a hexagonal 1+6+12 layout was fabricated, packaged, and tested for the Spectroscopy Focusing Array of the enhanced X-ray Timing and Polarimetry mission. The module integrates the SDD sensor, ceramic substrate package, low-noise front-end electronics, and high-density flexible readout interface. Low-temperature X-ray measurements showed that most pixels satisfied the energy-resolution requirement, whereas the remaining pixels were mainly limited by increased dark current. The measured spectral response indicates the capability of the module to cover the required 0.5-10 keV energy range. These results validate the feasibility of the developed SDD technology for compact, low-noise, multi-pixel X-ray spectroscopy modules. The next stage will focus on the second-generation 19-pixel prototype and a 7-pixel SDD detector system for synchrotron radiation applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 62Poster Number:NSS-13-062] Oxygen-Ion-Assisted Amorphous PbO Layers for Direct-Conversion X-ray Detectors (#2091)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Nagicheva (Autores: G. Nagicheva , J. Rado , M. Vostokov , A. Stieh , A. Alexandrov , A. Reznik)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lakehead University, The Department of Physics, Thunder Bay, Ontario, Canada
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Lead oxide (PbO) is a promising high-atomic-number photoconductor for direct-conversion x-ray detectors because of its high x-ray stopping power and low intrinsic electron-hole pair creation energy. A key challenge is depositing detector-grade thick PbO layers directly onto flat-panel imaging electronics while keeping the substrate temperature compatible with thin-film transistor and CMOS readout arrays. In conventional physical vapor deposition, limited adatom mobility at substrate temperatures below approximately 200 °C can promote porous, platelet-like polycrystalline PbO with reduced charge collection, temporal lag, and structural instability. In this work, oxygen-ion-assisted thermal evaporation was investigated as a low-temperature route for producing amorphous PbO photoconductors. Low-energy oxygen-ion bombardment supplied additional energy to the growing film surface without increasing the substrate temperature. The deposition conditions were optimized with respect to x-ray-to-charge conversion, evaluated using the average electron-hole pair creation energy, W±​. Amorphous PbO layers with W±​ as low as approximately 7.5 eV/ehp and effective hole mobility on the order of 10 −1 cm²/V·s at 10 V/μm were achieved. These results indicate that oxygen-ion-assisted deposition can produce amorphous PbO layers with detector-relevant charge generation and transport properties for direct-conversion flat-panel X-ray detectors.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 64Poster Number:NSS-13-064] Custom Geometries for Broader Applications of the GAPS Si(Li) Detectors (#2180)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Yee (Autores: K. Yee , H. Fuke , T. Gupta , M. Kozai , W. Ostling , K. Pappas , K. Perez , Y. Shimizu , S. Vickers , M. Xiao)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States of America [2] Institute of Space and Astronautical Science, Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (ISAS/JAXA), Sagamihara, Japan [3] Columbia University, New York, New York, United States of America [4] Research Organization of Information and Systems, Tokyo, Japan [5] Kanagawa University, Yokohama, Japan [6] School of Physics and Astronomy, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The General Antiparticle Spectrometer (GAPS) is an Antarctic long-duration balloon experiment designed to measure low-energy (< 0.25 GeV/n) cosmic antinuclei as signatures of dark matter. The distinctive GAPS particle identification technique relies on a tracker composed of > 1000 lithium-drifted silicon (Si(Li)) detectors - over 10 m 2 of silicon sensors - that both captures an incoming antinucleus into an exotic atom and measures the de-excitation X-ray and nuclear annihilation products. The GAPS program established the techniques necessary to produce large-area Si(Li) detectors, operable 150 o C above the liquid nitrogen temperatures typically required to achieve fine X-ray resolution, for an order of magnitude lower cost than previous commercially-available detectors. The distinctive detector geometry, together with custom polyimide passivation coatings that protect against humidity and organic contamination, has enabled remarkably robust operation: stable performance has now been demonstrated after more than five years without requiring HV bias or low-temperature storage to prevent lithium redistribution. Detector segmentation, previously achieved through ultrasonic impact grinding, has now been demonstrated using a DISCO dicing saw, a less expensive alternative suitable for mass-production that opens new flexibility in detector and readout geometries. In this contribution, we review the features of such Si(Li) detector design and performance, and discuss the broader applications enabled by custom detector geometries.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 66Poster Number:NSS-13-066] Neutron Measurements of 252 Cf in High-Gamma-Ray Environments Using Silicon Carbide (SiC) Semiconductor Detector (#2326)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Nagai (Autores: K. Nagai , K. Aoyama , T. Suzuki , T. Nakamura , T. Matsumoto , A. Masuda , S. Manabe , J. Ishii , K. Shimazoe)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Tokyo, the Nuclear Enginnering and Management, the Graduate School of Engineering, Tokyo, Japan [2] Fuji Electric Co., Hino, Japan [3] Tohoku University, Sendai, Japan [4] National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology, Tsukuba, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Neutron measurement technology is essential for the decommissioning of the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant and for monitoring special nuclear materials. In the former case in particular, high-dose gamma radiation is present, and there are significant constraints on size and weight. As a neutron detector suited to these environments, we focused on a neutron detector using silicon carbide (SiC) semiconductors, which offer higher radiation resistance than silicon semiconductors. In this study, we verified whether it is possible to distinguish and detect neutrons emitted from a 252 Cf neutron source from gamma rays in a high-dose gamma-ray background environment. The results showed that it is possible to distinguish between neutrons and gamma rays in a gamma-ray environment of up to 132 Gy/h.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 68Poster Number:NSS-13-068] Development of amorphous germanium blocking contact multi-electrode coaxial HPGe detectors for highcount-rate applications (#2621)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Yu (Autores: S. Yu , Y. Tian , L. He , X. Li , L. Han , M. Yang , Y. Li , Y. Li)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [2] Key Laboratory of Particle & Radiation Imaging (Tsinghua University), Ministry of Education, Beijing, China [3] Greater Bay Area National Center of Technology Innovation, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract High-purity germanium (HPGe) detectors are widely used in high-resolution gamma-ray spectroscopy and high-count-rate radiation measurements because of their excellent energy resolution and detection efficiency. Multi-electrode HPGe detectors can improve count-rate capability and provide local response information, but the calibration and summation of segmented-electrode signals remain challenging due to charge sharing, inter-electrode coupling, crosstalk and transient induced signals. In this work, a coaxial four-electrode HPGe prototype based on amorphous germanium blocking contacts was developed and tested. The detector consists of a small boron-implanted central P⁺ electrode and three outer n-type segmented electrodes defined by amorphous germanium coating and aluminum metallization. The leakage current was below 10 pA at 200 V. Measurements with a 137 Cs source showed energy resolutions of 1.43-1.45 keV for the outer electrodes and 1.78 keV for the central electrode at 662 keV. Experimental and simulated four-channel waveforms were compared to evaluate induced responses in neighboring electrodes. Non-zero residual baselines observed in the experimental neighboring channels indicate coupling effects in the present frontend design. Simulated 137 Cs segment spectra and Ch1+Ch2 sum reconstruction further show that the central-electrode energy can serve as a reference for segment-energy calibration. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the amorphous-germanium-contact multi-electrode HPGe design and provide a basis for central-electrode-referenced correction and reliable segment-sum reconstruction in high-count-rate measurements.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 70Poster Number:NSS-13-070] A Novel Compton-Polarimeter in Telescope Configuration for X-Ray Energies up to 1 MeV (#2758)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Over-Winter (Autores: T. Over-Winter , A. Kononov , T. Krings , W. Middents , U. Spillmann , G. Weber , T. Stöhlker)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] GSI Helmholtzzentrum für Schwerionenforschung GmbH, Darmstadt, Germany [2] Friedrich-Schiller-Universität Jena, Institute of Optics and Quantum Electronics, Jena, Germany [3] Forschungszentrum Jülich, Nuclear Physics Institute, Jülich, Germany [4] Helmholtz-Institut Jena, Jena, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Compton polarimeters enable the detailed study of polarization sensitivity of fundamental radiative processes in the hard x-ray regime, i.e. for photon energies between 60 keV and 1 MeV. These detectors are based on double-sided segmented planar semiconductor crystals in which the recoil electron and the scattered photon of the Compton process are measured simultaneously. Within the SPARC collaboration (Stored Particles Atomic Physics Research Collaboration), a new Compton polarimeter in telescope configuration consisting of a Si(Li)- and a HPGe-detector has been developed, aiming for polarization experiments at particle accelerators and synchrotron facilities to analyze atomic or nuclear processes. A polarimeter consisting of only the first crystal, the Si(Li), was already operated in stand-alone mode in the energy range starting at 60 keV up to 250 keV. In a study of polarizazion-dependence of elastic scattering at the PETRAIII synchrotron facility of DESY, it proofed to be working well. Now the second crystal, the HPGe, was added to extend the accessible energy range up to the 1 MeV regime to widen the investigation of radiative processes. The main construction of the new detector system was performed at the detector laboratory of the Forschungszentrum Jülich, which is now relocating to the university of Cologne. We will report on the design of the novel Compton-polarimeter and first experimental applications.

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Mirion has been supplying sophisticated HPGe detectors and instrumentation which are used in cutting-edge materials analysis, fundamental nuclear physics research, and space studies to world's leading research institutes. The Clover [1] detector is one of Mirion unique product, recognized as an advanced gamma-ray detection system widely used in a variaty of different nuclear physics experiments. Clover detectors consist of four high-purity germanium (HPGe) crystals, arranged in a compact cloverleaf-like configuration within a single cryostat. This unique geometry enhances its efficiency, enabling precise gamma-ray detection and energy resolution. The detectors design minimizes dead space, improving sensitivity to weak signals and increasing the likelihood of coincident gamma-ray detection for advanced spectroscopic studies. The Clover detectors versatility is augmented by its segmented configuration, which allows for effective background suppression and Doppler shift correction, making it invaluable for nuclear physics experiments and high-energy gamma-rays. Recent advancements in signal processing and digital electronics have further enhanced the performance of Clover detectors which continue to be a cornerstone in gamma-ray spectroscopy due to its high efficiency, excellent energy resolution, and timing. This presentation will provide an overview of various technologies for Mirion Clover detectors, highlighting the benefits of recent advancements like electrical cooling, an expanded energy dynamic range, and more.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 74Poster Number:NSS-13-074] An automated testing and characterization system for SiPM device arrays (#1148)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Riboldi (Autores: S. Riboldi , A. Giaz , C. Boiano , S. Brambilla , F. Camera)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universita degli Studi di Milano, Dipartimento di Fisica, Milano, Italy [2] INFN, Milano, Milano, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Large-area photodetectors in the form of silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) array detectors are becoming increasingly widespread in basic physics, medical, industrial, and security applications. Various suitable devices are commercially available from companies such as Broadcom, Hamamatsu, and OnSemi. Alternatively, they can be constructed from individual SiPM devices. After repeated use and initial testing of self-constructed devices, it is useful to characterize the electrical properties of each SiPM photodetector to determine the operating conditions of the array. If the operational readout of the photodetector is based on a combination of theoretically available anode signals - for example, by short-circuiting all anode signals into a single readout channel - this verification procedure must be conducted using an independent test system. This paper discusses the possible general structure of a fully automated test system, its implementation details, and its practical application by the user. Through the implemented test procedures, the following can be determined: Short circuits and open circuits on the printed circuit board housing the array under test The individual I-V characteristic curves of the SiPM devices and the homogeneity of their operating parameters (e.g., breakdown voltage) The operability, electro-optical conversion gain, response time, and saturation level of the signal of the individual SiPM devices through the injection of optical photons from a light-emitting diode (LED) Depending on the tests performed, this test system can fully automatically determine the operational status of the SiPM device array within a time interval ranging from a few seconds to about ten minutes.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 76Poster Number:NSS-13-076] Construction and Testing of An In-Situ Magnetron Sputtering Plasma Monitoring Setup (#1340)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Bilki (Autores: B. Bilki , M. Tosun , S. Acikgoz)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Turkish Accelerator and Radiation Laboratory, Ankara, Turkey [2] Istinye University, Istanbul, Turkey [3] Ankara University, Ankara, Turkey
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Magnetron sputtering is a widely used technique for depositing both metallic and insulating thin films on diverse substrates. Its strength lies in the precise control it enables over film thickness and morphology, achievable through a detailed understanding of key physical processes such as gas ionization, plasma behavior, target sputtering, and film deposition. This level of control is particularly critical for high-energy physics detector technologies, where thin, uniform, and functional coatings such as those implemented in hybrid Resistive Plate Chambers are essential for optimizing detector performance, stability, and signal fidelity. A promising pathway toward improving this control is the investigation of plasma-emitted light, which encodes valuable information about the composition, density, and dynamics of both working gas species and sputtered material. However, existing studies have largely relied on external optical observations or diagnostic techniques that perturb the plasma, limiting their effectiveness. To address these challenges, we developed a high-precision, multi-parameter optical monitoring system capable of probing plasma emission directly within the sputtering chamber. The system samples light at key locations along the target-to-substrate trajectory with a timing resolution of up to 320 ps. Quartz optical fibers are integrated into the vacuum environment and coupled through a dedicated feedthrough to an external detection system. Signal acquisition is performed using Silicon Photomultipliers mounted on a custom-designed readout board. This approach provides detailed insight into the temporal and spatial evolution of magnetron plasmas, enabling improved understanding of thin-film growth mechanisms. These results will contribute to the optimization of coating processes for next-generation detector systems in high-energy physics, enhancing their performance, robustness, and scalability.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. E. Pooley (Autores: J.S. Lord , A. Abba , P.J. Baker , F. Caponio , P. Coode , S.P. Cottrell , D. Jack , K. Daniel , A. Lim , L. Malliolio , N. Daniel , D. E. Pooley , D. Templeman)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This paper reports on the recently deployed ISIS Digital Data Pipeline, which has facilitated an in-depth examination at the detector signals coming from the suite of Muon Spectrometers. Signal processing and event-mode analysis has been used to understand the afterpulsing characteristics of three types of photosensor; the HAMAMATSU R5505 1-inch PMT, the EMI-9954 2-inch PMT and S13360-1325PE HAMAMATSU SiPM. The R5505 was found to produce significant afterpulsing that can be identified via pulse shape discrimination due to their characteristically shorter fall time. This indicates impurity ionization, as the signals are not convolved with the scintillation response. The data pipeline has been tuned to suppress the afterpulses, producing data sets without this background contribution.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 80Poster Number:NSS-13-080] Dark Count Rate of LHCb Scintillating Fibre Tracker SiPMs as an In-Situ Radiation Monitor (#2507)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. E.R. Medaer (Autores: S. E.R. Medaer , F. Ronchetti , E. M. Niel , G. Corti , G. Haefeli)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CERN, LHCb Collaboration, Geneva, Genève, Switzerland [2] École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, Institute of Physics, Lausanne, Vaud, Switzerland [3] Leprince-Ringuet Laboratory, Institut Polytechnique de Paris, École Polytechnique, CNRS/IN2P3, Palaiseau, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In high-energy physics detectors, Silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) operated in mixed radiation fields show a dramatic increase in dark count rate (DCR), which affects detector performance. This work investigates whether the DCR of the SiPMs in the LHCb Scintillating Fibre Tracker can be used as an in-situ monitor of accumulated radiation exposure. The DCR at three delivered luminosities was recorded at the end of three consecutive yearly shutdowns and converted to area-normalized DCR. The results obtained were compared with radiation estimators obtained from particle-transport simulations using the latest detector geometry. The study focuses on total ionizing dose and 1 MeV neutron-equivalent fluence, which represent ionizing energy deposition and displacement-damage effects, respectively. The measured DCR was fitted as a linear function of each radiation estimator. Both estimators show a monotonic correlation with the measured DCR. The fitted slopes are approximately Gaussian after normalization, with relative dispersions of about 17 percent when all tracking stations are combined and about 13 percent when the stations are treated separately. This reduction indicates that part of the response spread is associated with station-dependent effects rather than with channel-to-channel variations only. The two radiation estimators cannot be uniquely separated with the present dataset. The results therefore support an empirical parameterization of DCR as a proxy for the considered radiation estimators, rather than a unique identification of the underlying damage mechanism. With appropriate station-wise calibration, this approach could provide a way to estimate the accumulated total ionizing dose or 1 MeV neutron equivalent fluence from post-shutdown DCR measurements.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 82Poster Number:NSS-13-082] Radiation-Hardened CMOS-SPAD Design for Stable Geiger-Mode Operation (#2314)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D.-H. Son (Autores: D.-H. Son , D. Eom , M.-J. Lee)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yonsei University, Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) are advanced semiconductor photodetectors that operate in Geiger mode, offering single-photon sensitivity and sub-nanosecond timing resolution for biomedical and space applications where robust radiation hardness is essential. In these environments, prolonged gamma-ray irradiation causes total ionizing dose effects, in which holes generated in silicon dioxide become trapped near the silicon/silicon dioxide interface, forming positive oxide-trapped charges and promoting interface trap formation. The progressive accumulation of these charges distorts the local electric field distribution near the guard ring periphery, causing field crowding that can promote premature edge breakdown and compromise stable Geiger-mode operation. This work employs technology computer-aided design (TCAD) simulations using the Sentaurus tool to compare a conventional virtual guard ring structure with a proposed physical guard ring realized by a deep p-well, available in complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) processes. Simulation results demonstrate that the virtual guard ring exhibits persistent edge field crowding exceeding the device junction field across all irradiation conditions, whereas the physical guard ring maintains its edge field below the junction level over a wide irradiation range. These results confirm that the deep p-well-based physical guard ring effectively reduces the risk of premature edge breakdown, offering a promising radiation-tolerant design strategy for CMOS SPADs.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 84Poster Number:NSS-13-084] ClearMind: fast photo-detection for TOF-PET (#2741)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 V. Sharyy (Autores: V. Sharyy , Z. Zobundzija , D. Yvon , E. Delagnes , D. Breton , J. Maalmi , M. Dupon , C. Morel , G. Daniel , T. Kaprelian , M. Minot , M. Popecki , A. Lyashenko)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CEA, IRFU, Gif sur Yvette, France [2] CEA, CNRS, INSERM, BIOMAPS, Orsay, France [3] CNRS, CPPM, Marseille, France [4] CNRS, IJCLab, Orsay, France [5] Incom Inc., Charltom, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The ClearMind project aims to improve Time-of-Flight Positron Emission Tomography by developing detection modules with a Coincidence Time Resolution of 100 ps FWHM or better. This performance is achieved through the simultaneous detection of Cherenkov and scintillation photons within the PWO crystal window of a Micro-Channel-Plate PhotoMultiplicator Tube read out by transmission lines. The first prototype, assembled by Photek (UK), demonstrated the feasibility of such technology but has a suboptimal time resolution of 370 ps (FWHM) when detecting 511 keV gamma photons. To address these challenges, we are improving the photocathode design, with the next prototype to be assembled by Incom (USA). As a first step, we evaluated the performance of standard Incom's High-Resolution Photon Detector (HRPPD) MCP-PMT with a capacitive readout. Tests were conducted using both a pulsed laser in single-photon mode and a 22 Na radioactive source. The HRPPD's capacitive readout system, which is compatible with the ClearMind's transmission line design, has achieved a single-photon Transit Time Spread as low as 50 ps (FWHM) for high-gain events and a spatial resolution of about 1 mm (FWHM). Photocathode deposition on PWO trials at Incom remains stable over time and confirms its feasibility. Through realistic simulations combined with machine learning-based reconstruction, we investigate the factors limiting the time resolution in ClearMind technology and demonstrate that a time resolution below 100 ps is achievable for large-size PWO modules under certain conditions.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 86Poster Number:NSS-13-086] Characterization of High-Speed Photomultiplier Tubes with LaBr 3 (Ce) scintillators (#2829)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Caballero Rodríguez (Autores: M. Caballero Rodríguez , L.M. Fraile , S. Gaitán , V. Martínez Nouvilas , V. Sánchez-Tembleque , J. Udias)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Fast-timing γ-ray spectroscopy based on LaBr 3 (Ce) scintillators coupled to photomultiplier tubes (PMT) is a well-established technique for measuring lifetimes of excited nuclear states in the picosecond-to-nanosecond range. In this work, we present a comparative characterization of different LaBr 3 (Ce) crystals of various sizes and geometries coupled to several Hamamatsu PMT models: R9779 (H10570), R13089 (H13719-Y006 and H13719-Y007), and R13408-Y006. The study focuses on timing performance, linearity, and energy resolution using digital signal processing. While the discontinued R9779 remains a benchmark for timing performance, the newer PMT models exhibit good linearity, comparable energy resolution for a given crystal, and competitive coincidence time resolution.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 88Poster Number:NSS-13-088] TID irradiations of a Shunt-LDO designed in a 110 nm CMOS process for EPIC-SVT (#1430)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Buckland (Autores: M. Borri , M. Buckland , J. J. Glover , L. Godfrey , A. Hill , A. Krieger , L. Ranatunge , I. Sedgwick , L. Teodorescu , C. S. Tse , R. Wastie)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] UKRI Science and Technology Facilities Council, Technology Department, Warrington, United Kingdom [2] University of Birmingham, Department of Physics, Birmingham, United Kingdom [3] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Engineering Division, Berkeley, United States of America [4] University of Oxford, Department of Physics, Oxford, United Kingdom [5] Brunel University of London, College of Engineering, Design and Physical Sciences, London, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Silicon Vertex Tracker (SVT) of the EPIC detector adopts a serial powering scheme to distribute electrical power to Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (MAPS) that are mounted on outer barrels, and electron and hadron end caps. Serial powering is an advantageous powering scheme because it reduces the mass required by electrical services. This is important in order to achieve the target material budget in staves and disks, which can be as low as 0.25% X/X 0 . The Shunt Low Drop Out (SLDO) voltage regulator is key to the serial powering scheme. Four SLDOs are connected to each MAPS to supply its 4 different power domains. This forms a coherent electrical unit that is repeated in a serial chain. A constant current is distributed through the SLDOs in this serial chain. The SLDO is a bespoke circuit design. It supplies up to ~1.0 A of output current with an output voltage in range 1.1 V to 1.4 V. The chip was designed in a 110 nm process. A series of SLDO chips were irradiated at the X-ray Irradiation Facility at Daresbury Laboratory (UK). X-rays were produced via Bremsstrahlung from electrons hitting a Tungsten target. The irradiation campaign studied the circuit response against the Total Ionising Dose (TID) requirements of the EPIC detector. The target TID for EPIC-SVT is estimated to be of the order of 200 krad(SiO 2 ), integrated over a period of 10 years of operations. This estimate is based on a worst case scenario where a beam of 100 GeV electrons collides with a beam of 275 GeV protons for a period of 6 months per year. TID irradiations characterised the performance of the SLDO chip for different settings of input voltage, output loads, and different temperatures. Irradiations were carried out at different dose rates, as high as ~100 krad(SiO 2 )/min. Annealing was monitored after irradiation.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 90Poster Number:NSS-13-090] Characterization of Single-Event Upsets in a 90 nm Commercial Off-the-shelf SRAM caused by Low-Energy Protons (#1482)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Ishihara (Autores: S. Ishihara , Y. Uchida , S. Toyama , W. Kada , S. Matsuyama)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tohoku University, Department of Quantum science and Energy Engineering, Graduate school of Engineering, Sendai, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In contradistinction to conventionally manufactured radiation-hardened devices, which demonstrate radiation tolerance and reliability, commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) devices may exhibit vulnerability to single-event effects (SEEs) resulting from direct ionization in environments dominated by protons, such as in low earth orbit (LEO). The issue of limited cross-section data availability for such protons with low energies has been addressed by a dedicated SEE, particularly single-event upset (SEU), evaluation field based on a 1MV tandem accelerator. In the present study, low-energy proton beams with an energy range of between 0.40 and 1.65 MeV have been irradiated to 90-nm COTS SRAM. The proton-induced SEU cross-sections were found to be several orders of magnitude lower than the predicted values through the Weibull plot derived from conventional data. Moreover, an approximate tenfold enhancement in SEU cross-section was observed at the energy of 0.447 MeV, coinciding with a roughly twofold increase in accumulated fluence. The findings present novel experimental insights into the energy- and ion-species- dependent mechanisms underpinning SEU occurrence in COTS.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 92Poster Number:NSS-13-092] Design and Implementation of an FPGA-Based Nuclear-Like Signal Generator (#1615)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Yang (Autores: Y. Yang , X. Li , T. Tong , F. Meng , S. Liu , Z. Zhang , C. Wei , L. Wei)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Chinese Academy of Sciences, Institute of High Energy Physics, Beijing, China [2] Jinan Laboratory of Applied Nuclear Science, Jinan Laboratory of Applied Nuclear Science, Jinan, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Traditional radioactive source testing involves health risks, regulatory limitations, and operational inconvenience. To address these issues, this paper presents a nuclear-like signal generator capable of reproducing the waveform, amplitude, and timing characteristics of real nuclear radiation signals. The proposed system is implemented on a Xilinx K7 FPGA and supports parameter configuration through a touch screen, USB, Ethernet, or host computer software. In the waveform-generation module, photon emission timing is modeled according to scintillator light yield and decay time, while photoelectric conversion jitter and Gaussian pulse responses are introduced to synthesize realistic macroscopic waveforms. In the amplitude-generation module, a cumulative distribution function threshold table derived from measured energy spectra is used to reproduce statistical energy distributions. In the timing module, event occurrence is modeled as a Poisson process with exponentially distributed intervals. The system supports multiple radioactive sources and scintillator materials, including Na, Cs, LYSO, NaI, CsI, and BGO, with independent dual-channel output capability.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 94Poster Number:NSS-13-094] Radiation-Hardened VCO in 28 nm FDSOI with Enhanced Frequency Stability Under Total Ionizing Dose (#1750)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M.A. Anwar (Autores: M.A. Anwar , D.S. Kim , S.R. Koo , I. Kwon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea University of Science and Technology (UST), Nuclear Science and Technology, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [2] Yonsei University Mirae Campus, Department of Radiological Science, Wonju, Republic of Korea [3] Korea University of Science and Technology (UST), Radiation Science, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [4] Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute (KAERI), Daejeon, Republic of Korea [5] Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute (KAERI), Gyeongju, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Ensuring reliable RF operation in radiation-prone is critical for wireless monitoring systems in nuclear and space applications. This work presents a radiation-hardened-by-design (RHBD) voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) implemented in a 28 nm Fully-Depleted Silicon-On-Insulator (FDSOI) process and experimentally evaluated under total ionizing dose (TID) conditions. The proposed RHBD VCO is compared with a conventional design up to 370 kGy(Si) using a Cobalt-60 gamma irradiation source at KAERI. Measurement results demonstrate that the RHBD VCO significantly improves frequency stability, achieving up to 57% reduction in frequency drift compared to the conventional counterpart. In addition, enhanced output power stability and reduced supply current variation are observed under irradiation. The results highlight the combined benefits of FDSOI technology and circuit-level hardening techniques, demonstrating a robust solution for radiation-tolerant RF circuit design.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 96Poster Number:NSS-13-096] A Radiation-Hardened R-2R Digital-to-Analog Converter with Branch-Local Diode-Replica Dummy Biasing (#1844)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Kim (Autores: D. Kim , G. Cho , I. Kwon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), Department of Nuclear and Quantum Engineering, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [2] Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute (KAERI), Advanced Instrumentation and Control Research Division, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [3] Yonsei University, Department of Radiological Science, Wonju, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract R-2R ladder converters in nuclear instrumentation are vulnerable to total ionizing dose (TID) because threshold-voltage shifts in NMOS switching transistors perturb on-resistance ratios that govern ladder accuracy. Preliminary irradiation measurements motivate a circuit-level solution: a modest on-resistance increase already drives worst DNL beyond 1 LSB. The proposed converter in 0.18 µm BCD employs a two-layer hardening strategy. The first layer uses a switch-compensated R-2R topology where all resistors share the same R+Ron unit, canceling Ron in the transfer function. The second layer preserves this cancellation through branch-local diode-replica biasing: a per-branch source-tracking loop and a scaled NMOS replica enforce uniform VGS,Ref on every dummy switch, with a constant-transconductance reference anchoring gm,rep to a poly-silicon ratio. Simulations across multiplicities 5-50 at 27 ℃ and 200 ℃ show the proposed converter achieves the 1 LSB target at multiplicity 15 vs. 40 for the conventional reference (2.7× area reduction). At multiplicity 20, worst DNL is 0.564 LSB at 200 ℃ vs. 2.471 LSB, with ~4.4× major-carry DNL improvement.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 98Poster Number:NSS-13-098] Preamplifier Readout Electronics for Summing SiPMs Enhanced Circuit (PRESSEC) for Advanced SiPM Camera (#1992)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Marín (Autores: D. Marín , A. López , D. Mateo , J. Altet , E. Barajas , X. Aragones , J. Serrano , J. Mauricio , R. Manera , E. Picatoste , S. Gómez)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universitat de Barcelona, Institut de Ciències del Cosmos, Barcelona, Spain [2] Universitat Politécnica de Barcelona, Electronics Department, Barcelona, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The next generation of imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescope (IACT) cameras is transitioning to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) due to their stability, robustness, and superior sensitivity compared to PMTs. Specifically, we are developing an ASIC for the advanced SiPM camera (AdvCam). This ASIC, designated as PRESSEC (Preamplifier Readout Electronics for Summing SiPMs Enhanced Circuit), is implemented in 65 nm CMOS technology. The PRESSEC utilizes a 32-input scheme for large-area sensor readout. Its primary function is to generate analog outputs by summing signals from four sensors into a single channel, effectively reducing the total output count to eight channels. The main functionality of this ASIC is housed in the energy path, which integrates a single-ended-to-differential converter and a pole-zero cancellation circuit. This structure is instrumental in reducing the pulse's Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) to 3 to 5 ns, thereby mitigating pileup effects in high activity environments. Simultaneously, these signals feed a trigger system for rapid event identification via a fast comparator. Additionally, a dedicated Night-Sky Background (NSB) monitoring circuit is included to measure ambient noise from sources like moonlight, employing a slow integrator with adjustable high-value pseudo-resistors to achieve integration time constants in the order of the milliseconds. Rigorous performance benchmarks, validated using Hamamatsu and FBK SiPMs, show a signal-to-noise ratio of at least 5, a dynamic range of 300 photons, and a linearity error below 3% for both energy and NSB paths, while presenting a power consumption of approximately 10 mW per input channel.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. Kalavakuru (Autores: P. Kalavakuru , K. Hansen , S. Maffessanti , C. Reckleben , I. Diehl , U. Ghosh)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] DESY - Deutsches Elektronensynchrotron, FE, Hamburg, Hamburg, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents a concept and feasibility study of a data readout circuit topology for a pixel matrix with in-pixel digitization, enabling continuous wave-mode X-ray detectors operating at MHz frame rates. The key components comprise dedicated high-speed column and row serializers based on custom-designed flip-flops with an optimized timing scheme. The readout topology is tailored to interface with silicon photonics electronic-photonic integrated circuits, enabling high-bandwidth and scalable data transmission. For a 64×64-pixel configuration, simulations confirm achievable frame rates of up to 4.5 MHz with the proposed architecture. At 1.125 MHz, the total readout circuitry consumes 100 µW per pixel at a supply voltage of 1 V. Design trade-offs in area, speed, mechanical integration and power consumption are analyzed, demonstrating the modularity of the architecture for high-frame-rate detector systems.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 102Poster Number:NSS-13-102] Characterization of MAGIC: a SiPM Readout ASIC for Monolithic PET Detectors (#2162)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. D'Incà (Autores: L. Nassi , T. D'Incà , I. D'Adda , G. Borghi , C. E. Fiorini , M. Carminati)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] INFN - Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Milano, Milano, Italy [2] Politecnico di Milano, Dipartimento di Elettronica, Informazione e Bioingegneria, Milano, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The experimental characterization of MAGIC (Multichannel Analog Gamma- ray detection Integrated Circuit) is here presented. This ASIC is designed in CMOS 110 nm technology and it is intended to readout the current signals coming from SiPMs coupled with monolithic scintillators that are used in medical imaging applications. The circuit is divided into three main sections: an energy path that provides a differential voltage proportional to the energy of the gamma photon, a timing path that gives information about the time of arrival of the photon, and a validation path for event discrimination. For the experimental characterization two PCBs, a mainboard and a carrier, have been designed. In this testing phase all the functionalities have been validated and the key performance of the ASIC have been characterized, in particular the power dissipation (5 mW/channel), the linearity of the energy chain to demonstrate the direct proportionality between the measured charge and the one generated by photon interaction, and the time jitter which affects the propagation delay through the timing path. The results are within the specifications and confirmed by simulations: the linearity error is below 1% and the time jitter is below 20 ps. Such a low value enables its use also in TOF-PET applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 104Poster Number:NSS-13-104] A Modular Warm Time-Division MultiplexedReadout Platform for SQUID Applications (#2181)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. A. Reese (Autores: B. A. Reese , G. Haller , S. W. Henderson , L. Sapozhnikov , Z. Ahmed)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, Menlo Park, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Many low-temperature detector experiments require a maintainable replacement for the warm Multi-Channel Electronics used for time-division multiplexed (TDM) readout of superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) amplifiers. This work presents a modular warm TDM readout platform whose architecture replaces the MCE backplane model with a common FPGA carrier, pluggable analog front ends, simple 12 V board power, and commodity network interfaces. The carrier hosts 16 two-channel fast DACs for 32 waveform outputs and an eight-channel 125 MSPS ADC. In a column-readout configuration, the fast DACs provide SQUID Series Array (SSA) feedback, Stage 1 SQUID (SQ1) bias, and SQ1 feedback for eight columns, while the column front end provides SSA bias, transition-edge sensor (TES) bias, and amplification of SSA return signals. In a row-select configuration, the same carrier drives 32 fully differential analog outputs that support two-level row and chip selection. Shared firmware provides timing distribution, configuration, data streaming, and communications, while role-specific firmware implements row-select sequencing or column ADC processing with SQUID flux-locked-loop feedback. Multiple carriers with attached front ends form scalable readout groups. One carrier in each group is configured as the coordinator and provides the SFP+ 10 Gb/s Ethernet interface to the back-end DAQ and configuration system. The platform has demonstrated 1 MHz row rates with 80 active rows.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 106Poster Number:NSS-13-106] A Scalable Test Vehicle ASIC in 28-nm CMOS for Cryogenic Device Characterization (#2278)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. Zarkos (Autores: P. Zarkos , A. Pena-Perez , M.G. Bautista , M. Garcia-Sciveres , C. Grace , T. Heim , S. Henderson , B. Lenardo , A. Papadopoulou , L. Rota , W. Henry)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, California, United States of America [2] Stanford Linear Accelerator National Laboratory, Menlo Park, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents the design and preliminary experimental validation of an ASIC developed as a test vehicle toward a comprehensive cryo-CMOS process development kit (PDK) for a commercially available 28\,nm bulk CMOS process. A CMOS device array utilizing a row-column addressing architecture for rapid characterization of nearly 2000 NMOS and PMOS devices with different geometries and threshold-voltage flavors, has been fabricated and experimentally validated. The complete transistor array can be evaluated using only 16 external wires, making the platform easily adaptable in a dilution fridge for deep-cryo testing. Separate gate-bias control of unselected devices is implemented to minimize leakage current, while a 4-wire sensing scheme improves measurement accuracy. The large-scale cryogenic characterization enabled by this approach represents an important step toward the development of accurate cryo-CMOS PDKs and reliable IC design methodologies for high-energy physics (HEP), quantum computing, and other cryogenic applications in deeply scaled CMOS technologies. The fabricated die comprises 13 subarrays covering 10 device flavors, including NMOS and PMOS transistors with high-, regular-, low-, and ultra-low-threshold voltage options, native as well as deep N-well NMOS devices. In addition, duplicated regular-Vt arrays are included to evaluate intra-chip process variations. An integrated scan chain selects one transistor at a time, with all remaining device gates independently biased to suppress leakage during measurement. Preliminary results confirm correct scan-chain operation and successful device selection, with measured I_d - V_{gs} characteristics showing expected current scaling across different device geometries. Comprehensive cryogenic characterization from 77K down to mK temperatures is planned as the next step toward completing the cryo-CMOS PDK.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 108Poster Number:NSS-13-108] Intermediate-Dose Close-In Phase-Noise Instability in a 55-nm CMOS PLL Irradiated to 100 Mrad(Si) (#2358)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. Zheng (Autores: P. Zheng , Y. Wu , C. Lv , W. Wang , X. Hu , J. Wang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Science and Technology of China, Department of Physics, Hefei, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents an in-situ total ionizing dose (TID) characterization of a 2.56 GHz charge-pump phase-locked loop (PLL) implemented in a commercial 55 nm CMOS process for high-energy physics front-end clocking applications. The chip was irradiated with X-rays up to 100 Mrad(Si), while phase noise, integrated jitter, supply current, and lock status were monitored throughout dose accumulation. Although the endpoint degradation is limited, with the RMS jitter integrated from 1 kHz to 10 MHz increasing from approximately 550 fs to 700 fs after 100 Mrad(Si), the in-situ measurements reveal a more critical intermediate-dose effect. Around 10 Mrad(Si), the PLL exhibits strong close-in phase-noise instability, mainly from 1 kHz to 100 kHz offset frequency. Standalone VCO measurements show no similar fluctuation, indicating that the observed behavior is unlikely to originate from the LC-VCO and is more consistent with radiation-enhanced low-frequency noise in the loop-control path. These results show that final-dose measurements alone may underestimate the worst-case phase-noise degradation of PLLs under TID exposure.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 110Poster Number:NSS-13-110] A Low-Noise Multi-Channel Readout ASIC for High-Purity Germanium Detectors (#2413)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. He (Autores: L. He , Y. Li , Y. Tian , Y. Li)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [2] Ministry of Education, Key Laboratory of Particle & Radiation Imaging (Tsinghua University), Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Multi-electrode High-Purity Germanium (HPGe) detectors are promising for high-count-rate gamma spectroscopy, but traditional JFET readouts suffer from excessive power (~200 mW per channel, >3.2 W for 16 channels), bulky volume, and severe outgassing. This paper presents a low-noise, high-integration readout ASIC implemented in TSMC 0.18μm CMOS, featuring 18 P+ and 18 N+ channels. Each channel consists of a continuous-feedback charge-sensitive amplifier (CSA), a CR-RC shaper employing ICON cells (1 GΩ equivalent resistance) for large time constants, and a class-AB buffer. A PMOS-input folded-cascode topology is utilized for optimal noise performance. Room-temperature measurements demonstrate a total power consumption of 594 mW (180 mA @ 3.3 V) for all 36 channels, presenting a significant advantage over JFET solutions. The ASIC achieves a gain of 11.3 mV/fC, an integral non-linearity (INL) < 1% over 40 keV to 1.5 MeV, and a rise time of ~65 ns. With a 10 μs shaping time, the equivalent noise charge (ENC) is approximately 58 e⁻ at zero input capacitance. Future work will focus on cryogenic evaluation with HPGe detectors and noise slope characterization.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 112Poster Number:NSS-13-112] A precision bandgap reference with improved noise performance for spectroscopy ASICs in 180 nm CMOS technology (#2577)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Zhu (Autores: Y. Zhu , F. Mele , G. Bertuccio)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Politecnico di Milano, Department of Electronics, Information and Bioengineering, Milano, Italy [2] Istituto Nazionale di Astrofisica (INAF), Istituto di Astrofisica e Planetologia Spaziali (IAPS), Roma, Italy [3] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare (INFN), Sezione di Milano, MIlano, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present the design of a low-noise and low-offset bandgap reference (BGR) circuit intended for front-end readout ASICs for semiconductor radiation detectors (SRDs). To suppress low-frequency noise and reduce process-induced dispersion of the reference voltage and proportional-to-absolute-temperature (PTAT) current, a voltage-domain BGR architecture employing local positive feedback is designed [1]. The circuit technique suppresses the dominant noise and offset contributions originating from the error amplifier. Compared to a conventional topology operating at the same power consumption of 50 μW, the proposed circuit achieves a tenfold reduction in low-frequency noise. The circuit is implemented in a 180 nm deep N-well CMOS process from amsOSRAM and operates from a 1.8 V supply voltage, occupying a total area of 0.024 mm 2 . Post-layout simulation results show a tenfold reduction in the 1/f noise, a voltage power spectral density of 200 nV/√Hz from 100 Hz up to 1 MHz and a DC accuracy of 0.06 %. In addition, the proposed BGR achieves a temperature coefficient of 30 ppm/ ◦ C over the temperature range from -40 ◦ C to 125 ◦ C.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 118Poster Number:NSS-13-118] A 640 MHz Phase Locked Loop for High Energy Physics Environment in 28nm CMOS Bulk (#3108)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. D'Ottavi (Autores: M. Chiariello , F. D'Ottavi , L. Palini , M. Malanchini , M. Privitera , C. Esposito , L. Gelmi , V. Vadalà , A. Stabile , M. De Matteis)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Milano-Bicocca, Milano, Italy [2] University of Pavia, Pavia, Italy [3] University of Catania, Catania, Italy [4] University of Milano, Milano, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents a Phase-Locked Loop (PLL) integrated in 28 nm Bulk CMOS HPC+ technology, developed within the INFN Ground-up iNITiative for Electronics developments (IGNITE) project. It is designed to generate low-jitter clock signals at 40 MHz for high-time-resolution charge measurement, and at 640 MHz for high-speed data serialization. In High Energy Physics, mixed-signal circuits must withstand severe radiation damage, both cumulative, in the form of Total Ionizing Dose (TID) up to 1 GRad, and event-driven, in the form of Single Event Effects (SEEs) induced by particles with Linear Energy Transfer (LET) values up to 60 MeV·cm²/mg. To address these effects, the PLL was implemented using radiation- hardened-by-design-oriented techniques. Experimental validation in time and frequency domains confirmed cycle-to-cycle jitter values of 11.437 ps RMS and 1.95 ps RMS for the 40 MHz and 640 MHz outputs, respectively. Power consumption is 8.4 mA from a 900 mV supply. The total active area is 0.0174 mm 2 .

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 120Poster Number:NSS-13-120] Machine-Protection System for the PIP-II Linear Accelerator: Architecture and Data Processing Schemes (#1193)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Wu (Autores: J. Wu , A. Waner , J. Eisch , M. Austin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, Batavia, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract PIP-II at Fermilab features a brand-new, 800 MeV leading-edge Linear Accelerator (Linac) that will enable the Fermilab complex to deliver more than a megawatt of beam power to the Long Base-line Neutrino Facility (LBNF), requiring a robust Machine Protection System (MPS) to prevent beam-induced damage to delicate cryomodules and vacuum components. Signals in various accelerator components, in both analog and digital format, are collected and processed to assest the operating conditions of the accelerator. In the situation a potential damage is foreseen, the beam permit signal will be drop. A critical element of this system is the fast Analog Machine Protection System, a high-bandwidth platform designed for real-time beam loss monitoring. The system utilizes a modular, FPGA-based architecture to digitize signals from beam-sensing devices, such as AC Current Transformers (ACCTs), non-invasive Ring Pickups (RPUs) and beam scrapers. To eliminate both high frequency as well as 60 Hz noise that might be picked up in the industrial environment, data processing schemes beyond regular digital filtering are planned and implemented.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 122Poster Number:NSS-13-122] Comparison of discrete non-gated charge-to-time converters for SPECT application (#1264)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. Lafoux (Autores: P. Lafoux , N. Chevillon , C. Fuchs , T. Robert , V. Bekaert , F. Boisson)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Université de Strasbourg, CNRS, Institut Pluridisciplinaire Hubert Curien UMR7178, Strasbourg, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In the context of tomographic imaging, a simple and modular readout combines non-gated charge-to-time converters (QTC), composed of few discrete analog components, and time-to-digital converters implemented in FPGA. The choice of discrete QTC's architecture depends on a compromise between number of components per channel, charge RMS resolution and dead time. Because temperature drift can lead to high measurement error and temperature compensation circuit costs lot of surface per channel, another key parameter to consider is the QTC's response stability to variation of temperature. This study compares three continuous-reset QTC topologies, named after their feedback circuit (RC, diode, and MOSFET). Each circuit is implemented with discrete components and tested in a dynamic range from 2 pC to 35 pC, for a Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) application. Unlike previous work, we compare them on conventional figures of merit and also evaluate their TOT-Q characteristics stability for temperature variation over 20 °C. Experimental results show that the RC QTC reduces dead time by a factor of 2 compared to linear designs, while the diode-QTC and MOSFET QTC achieve sub-0.1pC charge RMS resolution. However, the MOSFET QTC exhibits a 1.2 %/°C relative error due to temperature-dependent drain current. And diode-QTC requires a temperature compensation circuit to remain stable as RC-QTC (<0.2 %/°C).

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 124Poster Number:NSS-13-124] 150 Gbps data transfer Bay simulating Agata detector Readout (#1274)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Karkour (Autores: N. Karkour , X. LAfay)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Université Paris‒Saclay, CNRS/IN2P3, IJCLab 91405 Orsay, France, Electronic, Orsay, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Advanced Gamma Tracking Array (AGATA) spectrometer consists of 180 high-purity germanium detectors, each segmented into 38 segments. The trigger rate of each detector can go up to 50 kHz. The data transfer rate per detector ranges from 5 to 8 Gbps. Moreover, continuous monitoring data is sent over the network using another link, resulting in a total outgoing data rate of approximately 18 Gbps using User Datagram Protocol (UDP). The total transfer rate of 180 detectors can go up to 3.2 Tbps during a period of 1 to 3 weeks of continuous operation. The bay is designed in parallel with the Phase 2 front-end electronics development and production so that the complex readout system from these electronics to the computer farm is validated. The 10 Gbps UDP transfer is not totally secure; at such a data readout speed, the computer receiver uses most of its processing and memory capacities. The bay simulates the Phase 2 electronics data readout of more than 12 AGATA detectors using the Serial Transfer and Readout over Ethernet (STARE) modules. The bay is designed to validate the complex readout system from the Phase 2 electronics to the computer farm and to test the overall data acquisition system reliability. Data quality is mandatory for the scientific results, and any data loss could degrade the physics case and the system efficiency. This article will show how the bay simulates the multiple-source data readout to the computer farm at over 100 Gbps.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 126Poster Number:NSS-13-126] Performance Testing and Characterization of CPRE12-64CZT: A Low-Noise 64-Channel Readout ASIC for 3-D Position-Sensitive CdZnTe Detectors (#1303)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Wei (Autores: H. Liao , K. Wang , N. Wng , J. Cai , X. Li , X. Jiang , C. Wei , Z. Zhang , L. Shuai , Y. Yang , Y. Liu , L. Wei , X. Li)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institute of High Energy Physics,, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China [2] School of Nuclear Science and Technology, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China [3] Jinan Laboratory of Applied Nuclear Science, Jinan, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract CPRE64 is a 64ch readout ASIC specifically optimized for three-dimensional position-sensitive Cadmium-Zinc-Telluride (CZT) detectors, developed from the CPRE32 . The chip is capable of reading both cathode and anode signals, allowing it to match pixelated, virtual Frisch-grid CZT or silicon detectors. Each channel integrates a low-noise charge-sensitive amplifier (CSA), high-order shaper, peak detect-and-hold (PDH) circuit for energy measurement, and sample-and-hold circuit for timing measurement. Power consumption is below 5 mW per channel. The ASIC incorporates a layout designed for SEE hardening, resulting in a die area of 7.10 mm × 12.44 mm 2 . The chip layout features pins on three sides for permitting expansion to 128 channels . Experimental results show: when a CZT sensor connected and biased, the electronic resolution better than 150 e − (rms) for anode channel, better than 250 e − (rms) for cathode channel. The readout channel exhibits linearity with ≤1.5% integral nonlinearity, with a maximum dynamic range reaching 350 fC. Spectral measurements applying a simple depth correction demonstrated a single-pixel resolution of 0.78%(FWHM) at 662 keV.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 128Poster Number:NSS-13-128] Fast timing performance of a front-end ASIC designed for high purity germanium strip detectors (#1504)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Sleator (Autores: C. Sleator , E. A. Wulf , G. De Geronimo , A. Lowell , B. Mochizuki , J. M. Roberts , F. R. Rogers , J. A. Tomsick)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] U.S. Naval Research Laboratory, Space Science Division, Washington, United States of America [2] DG Circuits, Syosset, New York, United States of America [3] Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, New York, United States of America [4] University of California Berkeley, Space Science Division, Berkeley, California, United States of America [5] University of California San Diego, Department of Astronomy and Astrophysics, La Jolla, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We have developed an application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) to read out high-purity germanium (HPGe) strip detectors, which will be used as the front-end readout for the HPGe double-sided strip detectors flown aboard the Compton Spectrometer and Imager NASA Small Explorer mission. Here we present an overview of the ASIC, focusing on its fast timing capabilities. The ASIC has 32 channels, each of which contains two shaping circuits to allow for high-resolution measurements of both the charge collected, which is proportional to the energy deposited, and the time of collection. By taking the difference between the charge carrier arrival times on each side of the detector, we can determine the interaction depth in the detector. We evaluated the performance of the ASICs using engineering models of the COSI flight boards. To assess the timing performance in particular, we used a dual-channel function generator to pulse two ASICs, with one channel delayed from the other by various amounts. We also present preliminary measurements of the ASIC timing performance on a COSI-like detector using a fan beam collimator placed to illuminate discrete depths.
