sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 220Poster Number:NSS-13-220] Feasibility Study of Thermal-Neutron Localization Using a GAGG-Based Directional Probe (#1183)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Qiu (Autores: Y. Qiu , T. Dai , Q. Wei)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Science and Technology Beijing, School of Automation and Electrical Engineering, Beijing, China [2] China-Japan Friendship Hospital, Department of Radiation Oncology, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work evaluated the feasibility of thermal-neutron localization using a directional probe originally developed for gamma-ray source localization. The probe consisted of 30 GAGG scintillator bars surrounding a tungsten cylinder and was modeled by Monte Carlo simulation. Thermal neutrons were generated from a 252 Cf point source placed at the center of a spherical high-density polyethylene moderator. Localization was performed using a centroid vector method based on events recorded within the energy window around the characteristic 80 keV capture-related peak. Ten source directions at a source-to-detector distance of 0.5 m were evaluated under ideal noise-free conditions. Representative results showed the localization accuracy improved as the number of valid counts in the selected energy window increased. The mean angular bias decreased from 4.12° at 100 valid counts to 0.78° at 2700 valid counts, demonstrating sub-degree average localization accuracy at higher count levels. These results support the feasibility of thermal-neutron localization with a compact GAGG-based directional probe and suggest potential future use in simultaneous neutron and gamma-ray localization for nuclear security applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 222Poster Number:NSS-13-222] Empirical Test of Gamma Emission Tomography for Detecting Partial-defect within PWR-type Spent Nuclear Fuel (#1220)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H.J. Choi (Autores: H.J. Choi , H.-K. Baek , J.-K. Shin , S.-W. Kwak , C.H. Min)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yonsei University, Radiation Convergence Engineering, Wonju, Republic of Korea [2] NeosisKorea Co. Ltd., Daejeon, Republic of Korea [3] Korea Institute of Nuclear Nonproliferation and Control, Safeguards team, Daejeon, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Spent Nuclear Fuel (SNF) contains various radionuclides and emits significant levels of radiation; therefore, accurate and effective inspection methods for identifying partial defects within SNF are essential. In our previous study, we proposed and fabricated a scintillator-based Gamma Emission Tomography (GET) system named the Yonsei Single-photon Emission Computed Tomography (YSECT). The purpose of this study is to experimentally evaluate the its performance and applicability under conditions mimicking actual inspection conditions. The YSECT system consists of four detection modules, a data acquisition module, a Peltier-based cooling system, and a rotation module. For employing the YSECT instrument to partial-defect inspection, a waterproof test was conducted at a depth of 1.58 m for 120 minutes. In addition, the performance and applicability of the YSECT instrument were evaluated by acquiring projection and tomographic images. The waterproof test confirmed that water intrusion was not assessed into the instrument. While a comparison of projection images obtained in air and water revealed some degradation in image quality-specifically regarding noise levels and spatial resolution-and an exponential decrease in pixel intensities in the inner layers due to water attenuation and lead dummy pins, the source distribution remained clearly distinguishable across the entire SNF region. These results demonstrate that the YSECT instrument is highly effective for detecting partial defects in SNF. Future studies will focus on validating the system under actual SNF inspection conditions.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 224Poster Number:NSS-13-224] Enrichment-Dependent Neutron Interrogation Spectrum Optimization for Delayed Neutron Temporal Measurement (#1250)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. R. Wilson (Autores: C. R. Wilson , K. Ogren , S. Clarke , S. Pozzi , I. Jovanovic , O. Searfus)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California, Berkeley, Department of Nuclear Engineering, Berkeley, California, United States of America [2] Los Alamos National Laboratory, Los Alamos, New Mexico, United States of America [3] University of Michigan, Department of Nuclear Engineering and Radiological Sciences, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America [4] Sandia National Labratories, Livermore, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The time-emission profile of delayed neutrons (DNs) emitted by decaying fission fragments and induced by an external, time-modulated interrogating source can be used to identify the isotopic composition of uranium samples. In low- and high-enriched samples, a single isotope dominates the DN temporal profile, complicating measurements of isotopic composition. By suitably moderating the neutron spectrum of an interrogating neutron source, the large thermal fission cross-section of 235 U can be leveraged to amplify its signal, thereby improving the ability to measure lower enrichments. This work evaluates the use of neutron moderation in DN-based enrichment measurements using a Monte Carlo simulation. The 235 U-to- 238 U fission ratio serves as the optimization metric, since DN production is proportional to the number of fissions. Optimal moderating configurations that yield a near-unity 235 U to 238 U DN emission ratio for low-enriched and high-assay low-enriched uranium were determined. Based on this analysis, an experimental design has been developed for future validation. DN temporal analysis offers the prospect of nondestructive uranium assay across the entire 235 U enrichment range, from depleted (0.3% 235 U) to highly enriched (93.0% 235 U) uranium.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 226Poster Number:NSS-13-226] Improving contraband thermal neutron capture gamma detection in low and medium-Z cargo with pulsed D-T active neutron interrogation (#1300)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Joshi (Autores: K. Joshi , X. Wen , J. P. Hayward)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Tennessee, Department of Nuclear Engineering, Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Identification of shielded contraband like chemical weapons, explosives, and drugs being illegally transported in cargo containers can be achieved by detecting gamma rays produced using active pulsed D-T neutron interrogation. The time-dependent active gamma background produced by various low to medium-Z benign cargo-filling materials can interfere with contraband gammas and can make rapid and reliable detection of such contraband challenging. Using optimized timing gates depending on cargo-type for gamma spectra analysis can improve the signal-background ratio of contraband gammas. In this work we use a 6x6 array of 3"x8" NaI(Tl) detectors with coincidence-summing addback for full energy peak reconstruction and a pulsed D-T neutron generator to understand the gamma background produced by empty cargo, and paper and steel cargo filled to 0.6 g/cc density in our cargo inspection setup. We identify optimized timing windows for each cargo and validate the optimization with d a signal sensitivity calculations.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Green (Autores: B. Green , K. Mathur , A. Kennedy , D. Folley , S. Croft , D. Hambley , R. Mills , M. Joyce)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The detection of water in a mock advanced gas reactor slotted can has been carried out using non-radioactive surrogate materials. The method of detecting water is via prompt gamma activation analysis of hydrogen. This results in a prompt 2.223 MeV γ-ray. Due to the absence of hydrogenous materials in the fuel matrix, the 2.223 MeV γ-ray is indicative of the presence of water. GEANT4 simulations of the mock slotted can have demonstrated the variation in 2.223 MeV γ-ray intensity dependent on the location of water. High density polyethylene blocks equivalent to and above water mass detection limits set out in literature were exposed to 252 Cf sources. The γ spectra obtained were examined.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 230Poster Number:NSS-13-230] Development of a Portable Alpha-Beta Detection Device for Decommissioning Sites (#1464)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Morishita (Autores: Y. Morishita , N. Sagawa , M. Hirato , M. Sohma , J. Akedo , N. Yamaishi , J. H. Kaneko , M. Higuchi , Y. Kitagawa)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Japan Atomic Energy Agency, Collaborative Laboratories for Advanced Decommissioning Science (CLADS), Futaba County, Japan [2] Japan Atomic Energy Agency, Nuclear Fuel Cycle Engineering Laboratories,, Tokai-mura, Japan [3] National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST）, Tsukuba, Japan [4] Hokkaido University, Graduate School and School of Engineering,, Sapporo, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A compact handheld alpha-beta radiation detector was developed for field applications in nuclear decommissioning environments. At decommissioning sites such as the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, mixed contamination from alpha- and beta-emitting radionuclides requires rapid and reliable on-site radiation measurements. To address these challenges, the developed detector enables real-time alpha-beta discrimination while maintaining compact size, lightweight design, and battery-powered operation. The detector employs a Ce-doped Gd 2Si2O7 (GPS) scintillator coupled with a Multi-Pixel Photon Counter (MPPC). Signal processing and radiation discrimination were performed using an FPGA, and the measured count rates and energy spectra were displayed in real time on an LCD via a Raspberry Pi Pico microcontroller. The device weighs approximately 1.3 kg and can operate continuously for up to 8 hours on battery power. Pulse height spectra showed a speak for alpha particles, while beta particles exhibited continuous spectra. The detector achieved a detection efficiency of 90.7% under the measurement conditions. By applying a low-energy threshold (LLD) at channel 190, more than 80% of the alpha counts were retained, whereas the beta counts were reduced to 6.4%, demonstrating effective alpha-beta discrimination. Real-time measurement results, including count rates and spectra, were successfully displayed on the LCD screen. These results demonstrate that the developed handheld detector provides effective alpha-beta discrimination and is suitable for rapid, on-site radiation measurements in mixed contamination environments encountered during nuclear decommissioning activities.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Takeda (Autores: A. Takeda , R. Kawashima , A. Shiokawa , S. Kudo , K. Shimazoe , M. Uenomachi , K. Nagai , M. Yamada)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Miyazaki, Engineering, Miyazaki, Japan [2] The University of Tokyo, Engineering, Tokyo, Japan [3] Institute of Science Tokyo, Institute of Integrated Research, Tokyo, Japan [4] Tokyo Metropolitan College of Industrial Technology, Information and Telecommunication Engineering Program, Tokyo, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We report a proof-of-concept pulsed neutron de- tection experiment using SOFIST3, a silicon-on-insulator (SOI) pixel detector with per-pixel energy and timestamp recording. SOFIST3 was tested at the NOBORU beamline (BL-10) of J-PARC/MLF using a 10 B conversion layer. Two-dimensional spatial distributions of charge signal and timestamp were recorded, confirming simultaneous per-pixel energy and timing measurement under neutron irradiation. The pixel occupancy increased proportionally with beam intensity-from approximately 1.7 × 10 4 to 5.1 × 10 4 hits/cm 2 /s over a factor of ~3 in intensity-demonstrating count rate performance free from the system-wide dead time that limits conventional SOI pixel detectors. These results provide a foundation for developing dedicated high count rate neutron imaging detectors based on SOI pixel technology.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 234Poster Number:NSS-13-234] Experimental and Simulation Studies of FFCC Measurements Using a D-D Neutron Generator (#1563)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Maeda (Autores: M. Maeda , M. Komeda , Y. Toh)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Japan Atomic Energy Agency, Nuclear Science and Engineering Center, Tokai-mura, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Quantification of nuclear material in fuel debris at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station is expected to contribute to the streamlining of processing and management. The Fast Fission neutron Coincidence Counting (FFCC) method has been proposed as a non-destructive assay technique that utilizes fast neutrons, which are less affected by neutron absorbers contained in the debris. In FFCC measurements, an external neutron source is used to induce fission. Compared with conventional D-T systems, D-D neutron generators are more suitable for on-site deployment due to the absence of tritium and the lower neutron energy, which reduces shielding requirements. However, their lower neutron yield and smaller fission cross-sections pose challenges for measurement. In this study, the feasibility of FFCC measurements using a D-D neutron generator was experimentally demonstrated with EJ‑301 liquid scintillation detectors. Time-difference spectra were obtained from uranium samples with and without B 4 C neutron absorbers. Clear coincidence peaks were observed in both cases, indicating that fission neutrons can be successfully detected even in the presence of neutron absorbers, with less than a 10% reduction in counts. In addition, Monte Carlo simulations were performed using a designed measurement system to evaluate the feasibility of measurements within a practical measurement time. The results indicate that sufficient counting statistics can be obtained. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the FFCC method using a D-D neutron generator and its potential applicability to the non-destructive assay of fuel debris.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 236Poster Number:NSS-13-236] Compact and modular 6 LiF:ZnS(Ag) neutron detectors (#1609)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Liang (Autores: F. Liang , A. Esquibel , N. Floyd , H. Jayatissa)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Los Alamos National Laboratory, ISR Division, Los Alamos, New Mexico, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Neutron detection plays an important role in nuclear security, industrial applications, space exploration, and basic science research. Some compact neutron detectors made with 6 LiF:ZnS(Ag) and wavelength shifters have been deployed in portable instruments for nuclear security. In such detectors where photosensors are attached to one end of the wavelength shifter, high photon propagation efficiency for the wavelength shifter is required so that the signal-to-noise ratio of the photosensor is adequate for signal processing. Monte Carlo simulations using Geant4 were performed to study photon propagation efficiency for wavelength shifter panels and bars. Compact neutron detector modules were constructed according to the results of the Geant4 simulations. An initial test using a 252 Cf source shows the 10x10x45 mm 3 bar detects more neutrons than the 10x10x30 mm 3 bar and a majority of events have a small pulse height resulting from neutrons detected further away from the photodiodes. Although the count rate of the 45 mm bar for HDPE moderated neutrons was 67% lower than a 10 atm 3 He tube, its length is 3 times shorter than the 3 He tube.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 238Poster Number:NSS-13-238] Characterization of a Leak-Tight Radon Chamber for Exhalation Rate Measurements of NORM Products (#1748)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J.-G. Kang (Autores: J.-G. Kang , I.-H. Han , J. Lee , J. Kang , J.-S. Chae , G. Kim)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Institute of Nuclear Safety (KINS), Dept. of NORM Radiation Safety Assessment, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [2] Seoul National University, Dept. of Energy System Eng., Dept. of Nuclear Eng. and Institute of Eng. Research, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate quantification of radon (²²²Rn) exhalation rate from consumer products containing naturally occurring radioactive materials (NORM) is essential for source-term-based safety evaluation. This requires a sealed measurement chamber whose tightness and internal radon concentration homogeneity are characterized to ensure data integrity. We characterize a 0.343 m³ stainless-steel radon chamber housing two Durridge RAD7 alpha spectrometers for low-emanation NORM measurements. Chamber tightness, evaluated via the radon decay curve method over ~24 days, yielded a fitted leak rate constant statistically consistent with zero (1σ uncertainty 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ h⁻¹), more than an order of magnitude below the 5 % × λ Rn acceptance criterion. To support spatial homogeneity evaluation, a MATLAB advection-diffusion solver with a real Navier-Stokes velocity field (Chorin projection method) was developed as a transferable computational framework, deliberately trading full turbulence-model fidelity for accessibility. Preliminary simulations indicate that fan-driven advection (2.0 m/s) reduces the spatial coefficient of variation (CV) below the 5 % target within ~10¹ arbitrary time units, approximately three orders of magnitude faster than under natural diffusion alone (~10⁴ a.u.). Experimental cross-validation using a calibrated Pylon ²²⁶Ra source and two RAD7 units in a crossover configuration is in progress and will be presented at the conference. This integrated experimental and computational protocol qualifies the chamber for high-precision radon exhalation measurements of NORM products, enabling consistent and conservative safety regulation.

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Cultural heritage preservation requires non-invasive in-situ detection techniques to avoid irreversible damage to fragile relics. Compton scattering imaging (CSI), based on single-sided backscattering detection, offers a promising alternative to X-ray transmission imaging for nondestructive testing (NDT) at archaeological sites. This paper presents two push-broom CSI systems for on-site in-situ NDT of cultural heritage. A modified 2D CSI system was deployed at an auxiliary pit in Xi'an, effectively revealing shallow subsurface burial features and locating unexcavated relics. A 3D Compton scattering tomography system was further developed to address depth limitations, featuring a soil penetration depth of over 10 cm and a spatial resolution of 1cm with preliminary experiments verifying its technical feasibility for 3D structural characterization of buried artifacts.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 242Poster Number:NSS-13-242] In Situ 300-m Depth Underwater Environmental Radiation Monitoring System with Cesium Preconcentration (#1925)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M.S. Lee (Autores: M.S. Lee , J. Park , J. Seo , M. Jang , H. Cha , S.M. Kim)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Daegu Gyeongbuk Institute of Science and Technology (DGIST), Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Daegu, Republic of Korea [2] Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute, Environmental Radioactivity Assessment Team, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [3] Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology, Maritime ICT & Mobility Research Department, Busan, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The prompt detection of marine environmental radioactivity is essential in the wake of accidents such as the Fukushima event, yet conventional methods relying on bulk seawater sampling and offline analysis cannot provide timely information. We developed an in-situ underwater gamma-ray monitoring system, operable down to 300 m depth, that integrates real-time cesium preconcentration with a low-background gamma-ray spectrometer for deployment on unmanned surface vehicles, underwater gliders, and mooring platforms. The 18.54 kg system houses a seawater circulator, a pressure regulator, a dual-head gamma-ray detector, and a battery within a 58 cm × 21.4 cm watertight enclosure. Each detector head consists of a 2×2 tiled array of 48×48×20 mm³ monolithic GAGG:Ce crystals (96×96 mm² active area) coupled to a 16×16 SiPM array, with a KNiFC resin column placed between the opposing heads for selective ¹³⁷Cs adsorption. KNiFC-based preconcentration yielded over 92% ¹³⁷Cs recovery from spiked seawater. In a 30-bar pressure chamber, the system operated stably for 1 hour, and underwater background counts in the 662 keV region were reduced by a factor of 17 owing to water shielding. Under this low-background condition, two ¹³⁷Cs-preloaded adsorbent columns containing as low as 11.4 mBq and 73.2 mBq were observable within the 662 keV photopeak window, with net counts scaling consistently with the loaded activities. With a photopeak detection efficiency of 0.13, the system achieved a minimum detectable activity of 5.8 mBq/L for a 60 L sample within a 1-hour measurement, demonstrating sub-10 mBq/L sensitivity for in-situ ¹³⁷Cs detection in deep-sea environments.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 244Poster Number:NSS-13-244] Vehicle Based Detection System for Gamma-Neutron Background Measurements (#2083)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. G. Morris (Autores: L. G. Morris , T. Crane , M. B. Joseph , M. P. Taggart)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The variability of background radiation, primarily gamma rays and neutrons, can have a significant impact on the performance of detector systems. In nuclear security, background-limited minimal detectable activity constrains which sources can be detected with acceptable confidence. Furthermore, the radiation background can have direct impact on the false alarm rate; higher background levels can lead to increased false alarm rates, normally mitigated by increasing thresholds, which decreases the system sensitivity. The local environment is one of the main factors in background rate variation. Therefore, a vehicle-based system is a well-suited detector platform to investigate dynamically changing environments. This work summarises the design and creation of a custom vehicle-based system assembled at AWE-NST as a platform for experimental gamma and neutron background measurements. This platform can also be used to benchmark novel anomaly detection algorithms. This work details the results from the first measurement campaign taken in July 2025 with the system driven over 247 miles around the counties of Hampshire and Berkshire in the UK.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 246Poster Number:NSS-13-246] Performance Evaluation of a Portable MMXRF for Safeguards Environmental Sample Analysis under Transport-induced Alignment Changes (#2222)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S.-W. Kwak (Autores: S.-W. Kwak , W. Kim , J. Ryu , J. Kang , Y.H. Chung)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Institute of Nuclear Nonproliferation and Control, Safeguard Division, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [2] Yonsei University, Department of Radiation Convergence Engineering, Wonju, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Korea Institute of Nuclear Nonproliferation and Control (KINAC) has developed a portable Monochromatic Micro X-Ray Fluorescence (MMXRF) analyzer. This device is designed for the on-site measurement and evaluation of safeguards environmental samples to rapidly identify and respond to undeclared nuclear activities. Due to its portable nature for field inspections, the equipment is frequently subject to transportation. This movement can lead to misalignments between critical components which must remain precisely fixed for optimal performance. In this study, we conducted experiments to evaluate how transportation-induced alignment errors and environmental background noise affect the device's performance. The MMXRF system was transported from KINAC to two places. We measured the shift in the X-ray focal spot and background noise before and after each transit. Experimental results indicated a focal spot displacement of approximately 1.7 mm following transportation. While background noise levels remained relatively stable, significant performance degradation was observed during measurements of uranium-deposited swipe standard samples. These findings suggest that the shift in the X-ray focal spot is a primary driver of performance loss. In conclusion, this study confirms that the alignment stability of the X-ray generator is a critical factor in maintaining the reliability of portable safeguards equipment. We will discuss detailed methodologies and technical solutions to mitigate these alignment issues at the conference to ensure the high-fidelity performance of portable MMXRF systems in the field.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 248Poster Number:NSS-13-248] Measurement of 3-dimentional Distribution of 60 Co in a Graphite Block by Three Pinhole Gamma Cameras (#2268)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Kawarabayashi (Autores: J. Kawarabayashi , Y. Takabayashi , N. Hagura)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tokyo City University, Department of Nuclear Safty Engineering, Setagaya-ku, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Cobalt-60 isotopes are sometimes detected in graphite blocks used in research reactors with small cores. One possible cause of this cobalt-60 is the activation of impurities within the graphite blocks by neutrons. Another possible cause is the activation of rust adhering to the surface of the graphite blocks. When disposing of these graphite blocks, the distribution of radioactive materials measured by non-destructive methods would greatly contribute to improving the accuracy of radioactive material quantification. Therefore, we prototyped simple gamma camera combining a pinhole collimator and a phosphor plate. Using this camera, we imaged the block from three directions and attempted to measure the three-dimensional distribution of radioactive materials based on the acquired data. We prepared the detector response function in advance through Monte Carlo simulation. Images were captured by the gamma camera experimentally with a PLA resin block embedded with a cobalt-60 source and estimated the position of the source using ML-EM algorithm. From these results, when the source was placed at the corner of the block, the location of the source was estimated in the correct position. On the other hand, when the source was placed at the center, it was estimated to be at an adjacent position. Improving the accuracy of the response function is the next step of this study.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 250Poster Number:NSS-13-250] Verification of the Outer Space Treaty with trapped Protons in the VanAllen Radiation belt (#2270)
sub_talks.speaker: A. Danagoulian
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Nuclear Science and Engineering, CAMBRIDGE, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Outer Space Treaty (OST), opened for signature in 1967 and ratified by 117 countries including the U.S., Russia, and China, prohibits the placement of nuclear weapons in outer space. The OST, however, lacks any verification mechanism, and no peer-reviewed methodology for verification has been proposed in the open literature. Recent concerns over Russia's Kosmos2553, suspected of testing nuclear-armed anti-satellite (ASAT) components, and a U.S. executive order calling for the detection of nuclear weapons in space, have made the need for a credible verification capability urgent. A nuclear detonation in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) could destroy most LEO satellites, as the 1962 Starfish Prime test demonstrated. This study presents a concept and feasibility analysis for verifying a satellite's compliance with the OST by detecting neutrons induced by proton spallation on the thermonuclear device's high-Z (uranium) radiation case. The interrogating GeV-energy protons are naturally provided by the inner Van Allen belt, requiring no active source. The proposed inspector is a 9U-CubeSat-sized directional neutron detector consisting of two 30x30 pixel planes, with each pixel formed by an EJ-276 PSD plastic scintillator wrapped in CVD-diamond active vetoes. Geant4 simulations characterize anti-coincidence rejection of the harsh proton/electron environment, directional discrimination of spallation neutrons from atmospheric albedo neutrons via neutron-scatter-camera kinematic reconstruction, and dead-time effects due to the high charged-particle flux. Combined with IRENE AP9/AE9 belt models and Carpenter's spallation yield, the analysis shows that the 9U inspector can confirm the presence of a thermonuclear weapon from a stand-off of 4 km in approximately one week, with a false-positive rate <1.1%. A constellation of ten inspectors at 1 km reduces this to a single-flyby inspection.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 252Poster Number:NSS-13-252] Optimization of Detector Configuration for Enhanced Neutron Imaging Reconstruction Accuracy in Tokamak Fusion Reactor (#2283)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Choi (Autores: G. Choi , B. Kwon , I.-H. Han , K.-J. Chung)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Department of Energy System Engineering, Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study investigated the quantitative effects of neutron camera configuration with various parameter-the number of channels, colimator window diameter, and channel allocation for each port-on imaging performance in Deuterium-Tritium (DT) fusion reactor environments. Plasma neutron emission profiles were generated using the TRIASSIC code, which generating plasma shape, and detector signals were calculated in both 2-D and MCNP-based 3-D environments. Neutron image reconstruction was performed using the calculated detector signals, and reconstruction accuracy was evaluated using the Normalized Mean Square Error (NMSE). First, neutron image reconstruction was performed using the reference neutron camera configuration proposed for ITER and EURO-DEMO, resulting in an NMSE of 3.12%. To improve reconstruction accuracy, an expanded neutron camera configuration consisting of 10 and 16 channels for each vertical and radial neutron camera(VNC and RNC) port, respectively, was applied. The reconstructed results yielded NMSE values of 1.59% in the 2-D and 1.85% in the 3-D environment, both lower than the reference value. Reconstruction accuracy was strongly affected not only by the total number of detector channels but also by the channel distribution and Line-of-Sight (LoS) coverage. In particular, asymmetric detector distributions in the VNC ports generally produced lower NMSE values than symmetric configurations, while increasing the detector channel number in the RNC port improved reconstruction accuracy overall. These results indicate that appropriate neutron camera configuration can enhance neutron imaging performance in DT fusion reactor environments and may provide fundamental data for future neutron camera design and optimization for DEMO-class fusion reactors.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 256Poster Number:NSS-13-256] Characterization of Floating Gate Dosimeter Structures through a Standardized FPGA-Based Radiation-Test Platform (#2338)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. Leonida (Autores: E. Leonida , S. Fiore , A. Scialdone , S. Danzeca , F. Wrobel , J. Boch)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Montpellier, IES - Institute of Electronics and Systems, Montpellier, France [2] CERN, BE-CEM-EPR, Geneva, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Floating-gate dosimeters (FGDOS) are being investigated at CERN as candidates for the next generation of Total Ionizing Dose monitoring devices in the accelerator complex. This work presents the characterization of floating-gate dosimeter structures through a standardized CERN BE-CEM-EPR radiation-test platform using a common carrier board, dedicated sensor daughterboards with standardized pinout, and a Pynq FPGA readout implementing reusable gateware libraries and continuous-integration firmware validation. The platform allows the same device under test to transition from laboratory bring-up to irradiation facilities without setup modifications. The sensor is fabricated in a 0.6 μm CMOS process and exploits a digital control component - handling structure selection, bias control, charge injection, and frequency readout - combined with analog floating-gate NMOS structures, each paired with a matched dummy reference transistor for differential read-out. Two structures with different floating-gate area to NMOS readout transistor ratios were characterized: a reduced-area variant at one quarter of the baseline retaining the same NMOS (TC994), and a variant with larger sensor area and optimized NMOS for lower noise (TC994). Four recharge modes were compared: disabled, comparator-based, counter-based, and bit-based. Temperature dependence of the sensor frequency was observed and used to validate the acquisition chain; sensor-to- reference frequency ratios were evaluated as a first-order thermal compensation method. The platform is being extended to a new generation of structures integrating normal NMOS, high-voltage NMOS, and parasitic NMOS readout implementations (TC994), whose laboratory and irradiation results will be presented with emphasis on suitability for future RadMon and BatMon Total Ionizing Dose monitoring at CERN.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 258Poster Number:NSS-13-258] Physics-Informed Response Matrix Optimization for Neutron Flux Unfolding (#2476)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Ko (Autores: K. Ko , W. Kim , J. Kim , K. Shin , J. Kim , S. Kim , J. Kim , G. Kang , J. Hong)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Atomic Eneregy Research Institute, Radioisotope Research Division, Daejeon, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate characterization of neutron fields is crucial in applications involving neutron-emitting radioisotopes, as surrounding materials can alter these energy distributions. This necessitates a detailed reconstruction of neutron flux distributions beyond just dose-rate measurements. Reliable neutron flux reconstruction using compact organic scintillation detectors remains challenging under spectrally modified neutron fields owing to nonlinear light yield and detector resolution effects. In this study, we investigated the robustness of neutron flux unfolding using a stilbene scintillation detector with response matrices optimized using a physics-informed genetic algorithm (GA) framework. Although local differences in the unfolded flux distributions were observed under source-or neutron field-mismatched conditions, the overall spectral shapes remained stable. The approach aids neutron flux reconstruction for various safety and evaluation applications. It enhances assessments in mixed radiation fields and nuclear environments.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 260Poster Number:NSS-13-260] Comprehensive Modeling and Experimental Validation of a SiPM-Based Neutron-Gamma Pulse Shape Discrimination System (#2568)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 O. Halfon (Autores: O. Halfon , C. Riboldi , K. Urban , G. Borghi , M. Carminati , F. Camera , O. Maiatska , J. Stein , G. Pausch , C. Fiorini)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Politecnico di Milano, Dipartimento di Elettronica, Informazione e Bioingegneria, Milan, Italy [2] Università degli studi di Milano, Dipartimento di Fisica, Milan, Italy [3] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Milano, Milan, Italy [4] Rapiscan Systems GmbH, Wuppertal, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In recent years, increasing attention in nuclear and medical applications has focused on detectors capable of neutron-gamma discrimination, with Pulse Shape Discrimination (PSD) being one of the most widely used and versatile techniques. A compact real-time detector has been previously developed, providing an event-by-event digital PSD parameter and a flexible platform for both organic and inorganic scintillators, as demonstrated using the CLYC crystal and, more recently, the M-700 scintillator. The system is based on a scintillator coupled to NUV-HD SiPM arrays and compact front-end electronics enabling real-time acquisition and processing. The detector achieves moderate Figures of Merit (FOM) while ensuring reliable neutron-gamma separation. To investigate the factors limiting its performance, an analytical model of the full detection chain was developed, including scintillator-SiPM coupling, readout electronics, and the main noise contributions (electronic noise, statistical fluctuations, time jitter, amplitude walk, and finite bandwidth-induced shaping in the analog chain). This framework allows the decoupling and quantitative evaluation of the effects limiting discrimination accuracy. Preliminary results show good agreement with experimental data and identify the dominant limiting factors, providing guidance for targeted improvements and further performance enhancement.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 262Poster Number:NSS-13-262] Blade Checker - Radioisotope-free Positron Generator coupled with HPGe-based Doppler Broadening Spectroscopy for aircraft components maintenance operation (#2689)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Ralet (Autores: M. Ginsz , D. Ralet , J.-M. Rey)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] MIRION Technologies, Lingolsheim, France [2] POSITHOT, Villebon sur Yvette, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accessing an early stage of damage evolution is a key factor for the aircraft industry. Positron annihilation allows very accurate and nondestructive measurement of defect density, and its future evolution, as probed by Doppler Broadening Spectroscopy. Once the limited availability of positrons is addressed using a nonradioactive positron generator, application of positron annihilation can be foreseen for maintenance activity addressing the aircraft industry. The Blade Checker project is a proof of concept to demonstrate this capability. Although Blade Checker is focusing on the aircraft industry, this technique could be extended to other fields. It consists of a novel accelerator-based, radioisotope-free positron generator, custom HPGe detectors and an experimental setup allowing the defect density measurement on mechanical parts up to 3 dm 3 . The AM Gen is an accelerator-based positron generator, developed by POSITHOT, with a compact design and including the Xray shielding. Complemented by a beam stretching device, it provides a continuous positron flux of approximately 5.10 6 positrons per second. The generator has been commissioned by the French nuclear safety authority. The signals coming from the positron annihilation require the resolving power of a High Purity Germanium (HPGe) detector focusing on the 511 keV peak shape analysis. MIRION Technologies developed a custom, 7-element, electrically cooled HPGe detector placed inside a vacuum chamber as close as possible to the sample to be measured. Several small elements are preferred over one large crystal to avoid pile-up effects. A time-listed multi-channel data-acquisition is used to have in-beam time correlation and coincidence. A description of the systems, positron generator, HPGe system and readout, together with some results from material characterization and projected probing speed will be presented.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 264Poster Number:NSS-13-264] Optimization of the neutron source size for compensated neutron well logging (#2703)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y.X. Liu (Autores: Y.X. Liu , Y. Yang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Compensated neutron logging commonly employs isotopic neutron sources based on (α,n) reactions, such as Am-Be sources, which are typically approximated as point sources due to their small physical dimensions. However, alternative neutron sources based on (γ,n) reactions may require significantly larger target volumes to achieve sufficient neutron yield, making the point-source approximation no longer applicable. In this work, Monte Carlo simulations based on MCNP are performed to investigate the effect of neutron source length on compensated neutron logging response. A limestone-water formation model and a dual-detector configuration with near and far He-3 detectors are employed. The results show that the porosity sensitivity initially increases with source length, reaches a maximum at approximately 20 cm, and then gradually decreases. A figure-of-merit (FOM) combining sensitivity and statistical stability is further introduced, which increases monotonically with source length while gradually approaching saturation. The results provide a quantitative basis for neutron source optimization in compensated neutron logging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 266Poster Number:NSS-13-266] Three-Dimensional Radiation Source Reconstruction with a Compound-Eye Compton Camera Using a NeRF-Inspired Neural Field (#2721)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Xiao (Autores: W. Yu , M. Dong , Y. Xiao)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] tsinghua university, beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Compton cameras (CCs) have a large field of view and a wide energy detection range, and are useful in nuclear security monitoring, environmental radiation measurement, nuclear accident response, and radiation source localization. However, their depth accuracy is still limited in practical three-dimensional source localization. A single detector view provides weak spatial constraints, so traditional Compton reconstruction methods can produce depth errors, especially with few events, strong noise, or distant sources. Artifacts may also appear in the reconstructed images. To address this problem, we propose a three-dimensional radiation source reconstruction method for a compound-eye Compton camera based on a NeRF neural network structure. The aim is to improve localization accuracy by combining the compound-eye geometry with neural field learning. We simulated a compound-eye detector system with 25 scatterers arranged on a spherical surface and absorbers arranged in a plane. For each detector view, list-mode Compton event data were used to perform independent MLEM reconstruction, and a source distribution image was obtained. These reconstructed images and the corresponding detector pose information were then used as training data for the neural field network. Preliminary results show that, after training with multi-detector data, the reconstructed three-dimensional radiation intensity distribution becomes more concentrated. The peak intensity position is closer to the true source position, and the depth shift is reduced. These results show that multi-detector geometric constraints can provide useful information for three-dimensional radiation source reconstruction, and that combining a compound-eye Compton camera with neural field reconstruction is feasible.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 268Poster Number:NSS-13-268] Advancing Beam Diagnostics on ESS Neutron Beamlines: Simulation and Validation of Ionization Chamber Monitors (#2765)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. Samouilidis (Autores: A. Altingün , A. Gardikiotis , I. Katsioulas , M. Klein , C. Lampoudis , E. Samouilidis , C. J. Schmidt)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, Physics Department, Thessaloniki, Greece [2] European Spallation Source, Lund, Sweden [3] GSI Detector Laboratory, Darmstadt, Germany [4] CDT CASCADE Detector Technologies GmbH, Heidelberg, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The European Spallation Source (ESS), expected to start its scientific program in 2027, will be the world's most powerful neutron source. This facility requires advanced systems for accurate beam monitoring and diagnostics. To meet these requirements, dedicated detectors have been designed to operate at ESS, one of them being the Ionization chamber Beam Monitor (I-BM). This work presents detailed simulation studies, using Geant4, Garfield++ and LTspice, to investigate energy deposition, charge transport, induced current formation, and front-end electronics response. Experimental data from neutron beam test campaigns are also included to support the evaluation of the I-BM performance.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 270Poster Number:NSS-13-270] Indoor 3D Gamma Radiation Mapping Based on VSLAM and Its Application in NPPs (#2909)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Li (Autores: H. Li , H. Li , L. Liu , Q. Fan , M. Wang , F. Chen)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] China Institute for Radiation Protection, TaiYuan, China [2] University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Fast, spatially complete and digitally usable radiation information is essential for radiation protection in nuclear power plants (NPPs), particularly during maintenance, decommissioning and emergency response. Conventional surveys usually separate geometric measurement from dose-rate measurement, which makes data acquisition slow, labor-intensive and difficult to integrate with digital radiation-protection platforms. This paper presents an indoor three-dimensional (3D) gamma radiation mapping method based on visual simultaneous localization and mapping (VSLAM). The developed DoseMap system combines an RGB-D VSLAM module with a hot-pluggable Geiger--Muller gamma dose-rate detector. Environmental point clouds, measurement trajectories and gamma dose-rate data are fused through timestamp synchronization and an integral path midpoint method, enabling real-time 3D visualization, radiation-field interpolation and hotspot localization. Tests in laboratories and NPP environments show that more than 80\% of the reconstructed scene point cloud is within 0.2 m of the reference cloud, the trajectory localization error is approximately 4 cm, the single-source hotspot localization error is less than 0.2 m, and measurement efficiency is improved by a factor of 26.8 compared with traditional survey workflows. The method has also been linked with the smart radiation-protection support system(SMARP), demonstrating its potential for digital twins, ALARA planning and remote or robotic radiation surveys.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 272Poster Number:NSS-13-272] Photofission Prompt Neutron Measurements from Active Photon Interrogation of Depleted Uranium with a Superheated Droplet Detector (#2913)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Piekar (Autores: J. Piekar , J. Vinoy , V. Simic , A. Sari)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Université Paris - Saclay, CEA, LIST, F - 91120, Palaiseau, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Illicit transport of uranium-bearing materials remains a concern for nuclear security when passive radiation signatures are weak, shielded, or ambiguous. Active photon interrogation can induce photofission in uranium using a Bremsstrahlung field generated by 9 MeV electrons and provide neutron signatures from this reaction. Established photofission approaches commonly exploit delayed neutrons or delayed gamma rays measured after irradiation or in beam-off windows, which helps reject prompt radiation fields but imposes constraints on timing, sufficient decay statistics, and acquisition duration. Here, we propose a proof-of-concept measurement of prompt photofission neutrons using a depleted uranium bar and a commercial superheated droplet detector. Such passive neutron sensors rely on nuclear recoils that form bubbles when local energy deposition exceeds a thermodynamic threshold, while photon-induced low-LET interactions are strongly suppressed. Although superheated droplet detectors are established for neutron dosimetry and photon rejection, their use for measuring prompt neutrons from photofission during active photon interrogation has not, to our knowledge, been demonstrated experimentally. Measurements will be acquired with and without uranium under identical beam, geometry, shielding, and temperature conditions. The integrated response will be normalized to irradiation time under fixed beam settings, with beam-current or dose-monitor information used to check the stability of the photon output. A 20°C temperature-controlled bath stabilizes detector response. Polyethylene shielding is placed within the direct solid angle of the converter as seen by the detector, in order to reduce the linac-induced photoneutron component reaching the measurement region. The experiment will test whether uranium produces a reproducible excess above this background and will define requirements for prompt photofission neutron measurements at sub-10 MeV electron energy.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 274Poster Number:NSS-13-274] Characterization and Comparison of State-of-the-Art Handheld Gamma-Imaging Field Spectrometers (#3056)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. A. Alcaide (Autores: A. A. Alcaide , J. J. Manfredi , M. Ford , B. Parajuli)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Air Force Institute of Technology, Engineering Physics, Dayton, Ohio, United States of America [2] U.S. Air Force School of Aerospace Medicine, Dayton, Ohio, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Portable gamma-ray spectrometers with integrated imaging capability represent a significant advancement in field radiation detection by combining radionuclide identification with real-time source localization. These systems have the potential to reduce operator dose through stand-off detection while improving situational awareness in safeguards, emergency response, and radiological assessment missions. This work characterizes and compares two novel handheld gamma-imaging spectrometers: the PHDS GeGI, a mechanically cooled high-purity germanium (HPGe) system, and the H3D H420, a cadmium zinc telluride (CZT)-based detector employing room-temperature semiconductor technology. Baseline performance testing evaluated energy resolution, intrinsic photopeak efficiency, imaging capability, and operational factors including power consumption. Laboratory measurements confirmed that both detectors achieved manufacturer-stated energy resolution at 662 keV, with the GeGI demonstrating superior spectroscopic resolution while the H420 exhibited greater intrinsic photopeak efficiency across much of the tested energy range due to detector geometry and material characteristics. High-gamma-flux testing revealed that the H420 maintained functional spectroscopy and reliable gamma-imaging performance at significantly closer source distances, whereas the GeGI experienced degradation in spectral quality, imaging accuracy, and mission suitability under elevated exposure conditions. The results demonstrate complementary advantages between the two systems: the GeGI provides superior high-resolution isotope identification, while the H420 offers improved operational robustness, imaging stability, and field deployability. These findings support the development of expanded field-performance evaluation frameworks for next-generation gamma-imaging spectrometers and provide guidance for mission-specific detector selection.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 278Poster Number:NSS-13-278] Prototyping ALPIDE-based Modules for the R 3 B Target Recoil Tracker Detector (#1352)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Buckland (Autores: B. Amorim , P. Booker , M. Borri , M. Buckland , L. Godfrey , W. Helsby , A. Hill , O. Kiselev , M. Labiche , J. Lipp , P. Morrall , S. Paschalis , M. Petri , L. Rose , D. Seddon , K. Sutowski)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] GSI Helmholtzzentrum für Schwerionenforschung GmbH, Darmstadt, Germany [2] UKRI Science and Technology Facilities Council, Technology Department, Warrington, United Kingdom [3] University of Liverpool, Department of Physics, Liverpool, United Kingdom [4] University of York, Department of Physics, York, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract R3B is a fixed target experiment at the Facility for Antiproton and Ion Research (FAIR) (DE). The setup comprises different sub-detectors that perform kinematically complete measurements of reactions with high-energy radioactive beams. One such sub-detector is the Target Recoil Tracker (TRT), placed in vacuum around a target. The TRT aims to detect light charged particles with an efficiency of ≥ 65 % and provide precise tracking (≤ 10 μm), angular resolution (≲ 2 mrad), and reaction vertex reconstruction, over a large acceptance (≈10° to 90°). It consists of two concentric barrels with radii 5 cm and 6.5 cm, and a total active length of ∼ 27 cm. It utilizes silicon Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (MAPS) thinned down to 50 μm. The ALPIDE sensor, developed by ALICE/CERN, was chosen as its technology is mature and fulfills the R3B detector requirements. A module consists of 9 chips glued to an aluminum-based Flexible Printed Circuit (FPC) and wire-bonded, with a total material budget of ∼ 0.16% X/X 0 . The assembly has undergone extensive prototyping through low-, mid-, and high-readiness modules, during which assembly procedures, quality assurance, databases, manuals, and electrical tests were developed in preparation for launching pre-production. The last batch of high-readiness prototypes has been assembled with all final materials and tested. The prototypes show a functional response from all chips, demonstrating the ability to construct fully working production-level modules. Validation tests include a scan of the module with a 90 Sr source coupled to an external trigger, and vacuum tests down to 1×10 −4 mbar. This paper will present the latest developments from the last prototyping stage. UKRI-STFC Laboratories and the University of York aim to deliver 60 production-level modules to FAIR by October 2027.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 280Poster Number:NSS-13-280] Development of a Single-Layer Dual-Ended Readout Compton Camera Prototype for Enhanced Spatial Imaging (#1799)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Wen (Autores: H. Wen , C. Li , Y. Hou , K. Wang , J. Jiang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Normal University, Key Laboratory of Beam Technology of Ministry of Education, School of Physics and Astronomy, Bejing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Compton camera has emerged as a pivotal gamma-ray imaging technique, with critical applications in astrophysical observation, nuclear safety monitoring, and environmental radiation detection. In nuclear astrophysics, the detection and localization of gamma rays in the MeV range are indispensable for probing high-energy cosmic phenomena. Despite its importance, the advancement of MeV gamma-ray imaging instrumentation remains constrained by low interaction probabilities and high imaging complexity. This study presents a single-layer Compton camera prototype designed for enhanced spatial imaging, building upon the mission heritage of the BNU-120-a space-borne detector successfully deployed for monitoring gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). To transcend the original system's lack of spatial imaging capability, we propose a high-performance architecture that leverages the established BNU-120 framework while integrating a dual-ended readout to achieve a 4π detection solid angle. The prototype uses a 8×8 Ce:GAGG array coupled to Hamamatsu Multi-Pixel Photon Counters (MPPC, S14161-3050HS-08) at both ends. Each crystal measures 3×3×25 mm 3 and is optically isolated by 0.2-mm-thick BaSO₄ reflective layers. System characterization demonstrated an energy resolution of approximately 5% (FWHM) at 511 keV. Depth-of-interaction (DOI) information, extracted via the energy ratio method, yielded a DOI resolution of roughly 2 mm (FWHM) along the crystal axis. Computational validation using GATE simulations of a U-shaped 511 keV planar source showed that the source geometry was clearly distinguishable through a back-projection (BP) algorithm. Subsequent point-source experiments verified the detector's capability to localize discrete sources. Future work will focus on realistic physical imaging experiments and the exploration of more advanced reconstruction algorithms to fully evaluate the module's Compton imaging performance.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 282Poster Number:NSS-13-282] A GRID CubeSat Phoswich Payload for Space-Based Neutron Lifetime Measurement (#1825)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Q. Wang (Autores: Q. Wang , H. Qi , F. Sha , L. Li , X. Zhou , B. Sun , X. Zheng , M. Zeng)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [2] Beihang University, School of Physics, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A 1U-CubeSat payload for the Gamma-Ray Integrated Detectors (GRID) mission has been developed, expanding its scientific scope from transient gamma-ray burst (GRB) monitoring to include space-based neutron lifetime measurements in Low Earth Orbit (LEO). Constrained by a strict form factor (1U, 1.3 kg, 8 W), the payload retains two legacy GAGG scintillators for GRB detection while introducing two novel CLYC-plastic phoswich probes for thermal neutron measurement. To discriminate thermal neutrons within complex orbital backgrounds, the phoswich architecture enables robust pulse shape discrimination (PSD). To mitigate spacecraft-induced secondary neutrons, Gadolinium (Gd) shielding is applied to the sides and backs of both phoswich probes. Furthermore, a differential front-shielding design is employed to extract the thermal neutron flux. An in-orbit Charge Comparison Method (CCM) algorithm is implemented, which optimizes telemetry by processing the PSD signals in real-time, adding only two bytes per event. Ground calibrations demonstrate a neutron-gamma Figure of Merit (FoM) of 1.25, and preliminary cold neutron beam tests validate the differential shielding concept. The payload successfully balances multi-messenger astronomy and fundamental physics goals, verifying its readiness for flight.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 284Poster Number:NSS-13-284] Crosstalk and Charge collection in the ATLASPix3.1 (#2166)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Williams (Autores: S. Williams , A. Andreazza , R. Ballard , H. Bichard , R. Dong , J. Dopke , H. Fox , Y. Gao , E. Hutchinson , T. Jones , Y. Li , L. Meng , D. Muenstermann , I. Peric , F. Sabatini , F. Ustuner , J. J. Velthuis , F. Wilson , R. Zanzottera , S. Zeng)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Bristol, School of Physics, Bristol, United Kingdom [2] Università degli Studi di Milano and INFN Sezione di Milano, Milano, Italy [3] Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, ASIC and Detector Lab / IPE, Karlsruhe, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [4] Institute of High Energy Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China [5] STFC Rutherford Appleton Laboratory, Particle Physics, Didcot, United Kingdom [6] Lancaster University, Department of Physics, Lancaster, United Kingdom [7] University of Edinburgh, School of Physics and Astronomy, Edinburgh, United Kingdom [8] University of Liverpool, Department of Physics, Liverpool, United Kingdom [9] RheinMain University of Applied Sciences, Faculty of Engineering, Wiesbaden, Hesse, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The ATLASPix3.1 is a full reticle HV-CMOS sensor [1]. It is under study for future lepton colliders [2] and is part of the family of sensors leading to the MightyPix for LHCb and the MuPix for Mu3e. This makes detailed studies of the sensor performance important. We previously reported signal to noise, cluster size and position resolution [3]. Here a detailed study of cross talk and charge collection is presented. Between ATLASPix3.0 and ATLASPix3.1 masks were changed to improve the chip properties at the cost of introducing cross talk. Two types of cross talk were found. Type I yields small signal at fixed positions determined by the hit location. These typically have a signal less than 15% of the original signal. Around 99% of these clusters can be suppressed using a simple minimal signal cut. There is a second type of cross talk hits that yield high signals. An attempt was made to identify these cross talk hits using a gradient-boosted decision tree analysis with variables reflecting cluster shape & signal and signal spread over the pixels. We show that it is not possible to efficiently remove these hits based on cluster properties. This can result in a track candidates with similar χ 2 . This can be addressed in an updated design of the sensor and/or by further optimising settings. Using a grazing angle scan the charge collection was studied. In the depletion zone, the charge will be collected quickly. Charge generated in the non-depleted zone will yield a lower and later signal. The depth of the depletion zone was derived as a function of bias voltage. The results show that the depletion depth is proportional to the square root of the bias volrage as would be expected for a planar silicon detector. The experiments have shown that the sensor has very good performance, serving as a promising candidate for future lepton colliders.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 286Poster Number:NSS-13-286] Radiation-Tolerant Fast Analogue Pixel Test Structures in TPSCo 65 nm CMOS Technology for the ALICE ITS3 Upgrade (#2439)
sub_talks.speaker: U. Savino
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Torino, Department of Physics, Torino, Italy [2] INFN, Section of Torino, Torino, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The ALICE ITS3 upgrade represents a major advancement in silicon tracking, exploiting the commercial 65 nm CMOS imaging technology to develop ultra-thin monolithic active pixel sensors (MAPS) for high-energy physics applications. The target detector performance includes an extremely low material budget below 0.09% X0 per layer, with a spatial resolution below 5 μm, and radiation tolerance up to 4×10 12 1 MeV n eq cm −2 . Several pixel test structures have been designed and fabricated to investigate both sensor geometries and front-end architectures. In particular, analogue pixel test structures (APTS) featuring a fast operational amplifier (APTS-OA) as output buffer have been developed to study charge collection dynamics and the intrinsic timing performance of the sensor. Measurements performed in charged- particle beam tests demonstrated a best time resolution of 63 ps, combined with a charge collection efficiency above 99% and a spatial resolution better than 3 μm, while maintaining stable performance up to 1×10 14 1 MeV n eq cm −2 . Building on these results, a second engineering run (ER2) introduced three novel chip variants targeting enhanced detector performance and improved radiation robustness. In particular, the optimization of the low-dose n-implant located below the n-well collection electrode aims at reducing the sensor capacitance while enhancing the lateral electric field, thereby improving sensor depletion and restoring charge collection performance after radiation damage. This contribution presents the characterization of the new APTS-OA variants and discusses their impact on timing performance, charge collection efficiency, and radiation tolerance through measurements performed on both irradiated and non-irradiated devices. Laboratory characterization results will be presented providing insight into the effectiveness of the ER2 design optimizations for radiation-tolerant fast MAPS detectors.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 288Poster Number:NSS-13-288] Off-detector Readout and Real-time Signal Processing for the ATLAS Liquid ArgonCalorimeter at the High-Luminosity LHC (#2635)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. Collado Soto (Autores: P. Collado Soto , N. Nikiforou)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CERN, Geneve, Switzerland [2] Universidad Autonoma de Madrid, Physics Department, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The ATLAS Liquid Argon (LAr) calorimeter readout electronics are being upgraded for operation at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC), where up to approximately 200 proton-proton interactions per bunch crossing will significantly increase detector occupancy, data throughput, and trigger rates. While the calorimeter detectors themselves remain unchanged, the full readout electronics chain is being replaced. The upgraded off-detector processing system continuously receives digitized calorimeter signals from approximately 182000 channels at the 40 MHz bunch-crossing rate through high-speed optical links. The processing architecture is implemented in Advanced Telecommunications Computing Architecture (ATCA) systems hosting large FPGAs performing real-time reconstruction of energy and timing while satisfying stringent trigger latency requirements. Prototype hardware and firmware have been developed and validated in integration setups combining front-end electronics, timing distribution, and data acquisition systems. In parallel, advanced reconstruction methods including machine-learning approaches optimized for FPGA implementation are being investigated to improve robustness against pileup and overlapping pulses.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Campajola (Autores: M. Campajola , M. Alviggi , B. Argiento , E. Etiennette , A. Benaglia , M. Biasini , V. Bisignani , D. Boccanfuso , L. Borriello , C. Cecchi , F. Mirra , S. Moneta , P. Paolucci , S. Perna , B. Rossi , E. Rossi , J. Scamardella , G. Sekhniaidze)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] INFN, Sezione di Napoli, Napoli, Italy [2] Università degli Studi di Napoli Federico II, Napoli, Italy [3] Università degli Studi di Napoli Parthenope, Napoli, Italy [4] CERN, Ginevra, Switzerland [5] INFN, Sezione di Milano-Bicocca, Milano, Italy [6] Scuola Superiore Meridionale, Napoli, Italy [7] Università degli Studi di Napoli Perugia, Perugia, Italy [8] INFN, Sezione di Perugia, Perugia, Italy [9] Université de Strasbour, Strasbour, France [10] Università degli Studi di Milano-Bicocca, Milano, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Precision physics at future e+e− Higgs factories set stringent requirements on calorimetric performance, with 3%/√E for electromagnetic particles and ∼ 30%/√E for neutral hadrons identified as key benchmarks. A hybrid dual-readout approach, combining a homogeneous crystal electromagnetic section with a fiber-based hadronic section, offers a cost-effective path toward simultaneously achieving both targets. Reaching such performance requires enhancing the longitudinal and transverse granularity of the crystal section beyond what is available in conventional homogeneous calorimeters and equipping each crystal cell with two independent readout channels to simultaneously collect Cherenkov and scintillation light. These features enable advanced particle-flow dual-readout reconstruction algorithms to exploit the maximum available information from each event. This work will present extensive laboratory characterizations together with beam-test measurements carried out at CERN on single-crystal PWO, BGO, and BSO cells instrumented with optical filters and SiPMs. These studies demonstrate event-by-event separation of Cherenkov and scintillation light, with both scintillation and Cherenkov yields exceeding the thresholds required for optimal electromagnetic and hadronic energy resolution. The results have guided the technological choices for the ongoing construction of full-containment calorimeter prototypes

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 292Poster Number:NSS-13-292] The LS3 Enhancement of the LHCb Electromagnetic Calorimeter (#2898)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. Picatoste (Autores: E. Picatoste , S. Gómez)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universitat de Barcelona, Institute of Cosmos Sciences of the University of Barcelona, Barcelona, Spain [2] Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya, Barcelona, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract An upgrade of the LHCb electromagnetic calorimeter (ECAL) is planned for Long Shutdown 3 (LS3) to address significant aging effects in the central region caused by radiation damage and high particle flux. The innermost ECAL modules will be replaced with a new design based on Spaghetti Calorimeter (SpaCal) technology, optimized for radiation tolerance and improved performance under high occupancy conditions. A total of 176 SpaCal modules will be installed. These are based on scintillating plastic fibers embedded in dense absorbers. The innermost 32 modules will use 3D-printed tungsten absorbers to withstand the highest radiation levels, while the remaining 144 modules will employ lead absorbers produced through an innovative casting technique. Both configurations have been prototyped and extensively validated in test beam campaigns at DESY-II and CERN SPS. The measured energy resolution for electron beams is consistent with performance requirements and shows good agreement with detailed Monte Carlo simulations. The scintillating fibers will be read out using radiation-hard hollow light guides coupled to fast photon detectors. In total, 3072 new readout channels will be implemented with dedicated front-end electronics. In parallel with the installation of the new SpaCal modules, the current Shashlik calorimeter modules will be rearranged to better match the spatial distribution of particle occupancy. Simulation studies demonstrate a significant reduction in per-cell occupancy after the LS3 upgrade, improving detector performance in Run 4 conditions. Benchmark analyses of key physics channels confirm that this enhancement leads to a substantial gain in reconstruction efficiency and measurement precision. Overall, the LS3 ECAL upgrade represents a crucial step toward coping with higher luminosity conditions and anticipates key design features of the future PicoCal system foreseen for implementation during LS4.

sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Brookhaven National Laboratory, Physics Dept, Upton, New York, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract ePIC is the general purpose detector for the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) that is being built at Brookhaven National Laboratory and will be ready for first physics when the Electron-Ion Collider turns on. ePIC is based on a new 1.7T superconducting solenoid magnet. The detector consists of precision tracking, particle identification and calorimeter (electromagnetic and hadronic) to measure the properties of electron-Ion collisions that will occur at the EIC. In this paper we will present the over all design of the ePIC detector, with a focus on the Barrel Hadronic Calorimeter (BHCal) which is the repurposed sPHENIX Outer Hadronic Calorimeter (HCal). We will also present the current status of the BHCal design, test stand and preliminary results of the new electronics readout system based on the CaloROC chip designed for ePIC

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 298Poster Number:NSS-13-298] Operations and performance of a FD-MAPS Telescope based on the ARCADIA sensors (#3113)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. Giubilato (Autores: P. Giubilato , S. Mattiazzo , D. Pantano , C. Bonini , C. Pantouvakis , M. Rignanese , S. Ciarlantini , A. Zingaretti , M. Rolo , D. Falchieri , R. Santoro)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Padova, Physics and Astronomy, Padova, Italy [2] INFN, Padova, Padova, Italy [3] INFN, Torino, Torino, Italy [4] INFN, Bologna, Bologna, Italy [5] University of Insubria, Science and Advanced Technology, Como, Italy [6] University of Padova, Space Studies Center Giuseppe Colombo, Padova, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In the framework of the ARCADIA collaboration several INFN groups developed a Monolithic Active Pixel Sensor realized in 110 nm CMOS technology capable to operate with fully depleted substrate. Several prototypes embedding different substrate thickness have been produced and tested. In this contribution we detail the design and operation of the first multilayer particle tracking telescope realized with such technology, and successfully tested at the DESY II Test Beam Facility. The telescope uses 6 tracking planes, each realized with an ARCADIA sensor, and is paired to a 7th layer, the device under test, which was also an ARCADIA sensor, only with a different substrate thickness. The tracking apparatus includes a scintillator based triggering system, a complete synchronization electronics, and a parallel DAQ system for control and data readout. Together with a brief description of the sensor, the whole telescope system is depicted, detailing the relevant design choices and the expected performances. Maximum rates, resolution and other key metrics are derived from the telescope technical characteristics, and bench-marked against test-beam results. Measured performance are also compared with respect to the gold-standard MIMOSA telescope available at the same test-beam facility, which was used to characterize the same Device Under Test for reference. A discussion about the strength and weaknesses of the technology, as well as the foreseen improvements and potential applications will close the discussion. Also, potential area of application, both in physics research and in applied fields will be highlighted.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Ghisetti (Autores: A. Castoldi , M. Ghisetti , C. Guazzoni , S. Maffessanti , C. Danilevski , L. Le Guyader , D. Lomidze , Y. Ovcharenko , M. Porro)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Politecnico di Milano, DEIB, Milano, Italy [2] INFN, Sezione di Milano, Milano, Italy [3] DESY, Hamburg, Germany [4] European XFEL, Schenefeld, Germany [5] Università Ca' Foscari, Venezia, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work reports on the experimental characterization, modeling and correction of high intensity effects on the pixel response of the DEPFET Sensor with Signal Compression (DSSC) camera, an active pixel detector targeted at soft X-ray imaging experiments at the European XFEL. Experimental tests with up to 5 MeV/pixel deposited energy have been performed at the European XFEL, showing evidence of a shift of the pedestal value growing with X-ray intensity. Moreover, the signal compression provided by the DEPFET (DEpleted P-type Field Effect Transistor), integrated in each pixel, enhances the impact of this systematic effect on the measurement accuracy. The observed shift is assumed to be proportional to the signal dependent drop of the power supply lines along each ASIC column and can be modeled by two parameters. We devised a procedure to efficiently measure the two model parameters by means of a custom mask that shields a fraction of each ASIC column, irradiated with a flat field. The main results of the characterization of the signal dependent pedestal shift parameters and the application of the resulting correction to X-ray images of different patterned masks (dots, stripes, 2D shapes etc.) acquired at increasing intensities will be presented and discussed.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 302Poster Number:NSS-13-302] XSTREAM Pathfinder: A Modular R&D Framework for Next-Generation High-Throughput X-ray Detectors at the European XFEL (#1690)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Porro (Autores: M. Porro , M. Turcato)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] European XFEL, Schenefeld, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany [2] Ca' Foscari University of Venice, Department of Molecular Sciences and Nanosystems, Venezia, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present the XSTREAM Pathfinder, an exploratory R&D effort at the European XFEL aimed at defining detector technologies for a potential facility upgrade. The activity addresses a broad photon-energy range, from soft X-rays starting at about 250 eV to hard X-rays up to 50 keV, and is structured around three main building blocks: sensor and interconnection technologies, prototype readout ASICs, and a first-stage DAQ system at camera level. The goal is to investigate detector concepts combining pixel sizes of about 100 µm, MHz-rate capability, and flexibility with respect to possible future XFEL timing structures. Baseline sensor options include silicon diodes and MiniSDDs for soft X-rays, and (thick) silicon diodes for hard X-rays in the 9-12 keV range, with high-Z materials (e.g. CdTe, CZT) considered for extending the operation toward higher photon energies. More advanced options for soft X-rays, including DEPFETs and LGADs, are also under investigation. On the ASIC side, prototype developments will be implemented in scaled CMOS technologies (28 nm or 22 nm), aiming at maximizing the reuse of both analog and digital building blocks across different sensor implementations. While sensor-specific front-end adaptations are required, a common architecture is pursued for key elements such as analog filtering, predictive gain switching, in-pixel digitization, and high-speed data serialization. A central challenge is the development of a high-throughput readout enabling continuous operation at up to 1 MHz, opening the path toward CW or high-duty-cycle modes, while maintaining backward compatibility with burst-mode operation. The Pathfinder will progressively validate the readout chain from sensor to digital output, including early studies of DAQ-level real-time data reduction.

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Data Acquisition (DAQ) system of the DEPFET Sensor with Signal Compression (DSSC) megapixel (Mpx) camera at the European X-ray Free-Electron Laser (EuXFEL) is being revisited to support higher-performance detectors. The current digital front-end consists of two Field-Prgrammable Gate Array (FPGA)-based stages: the Input Output Board (IOB), responsible for initial data acquisition from Application Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs), and the Patch Panel Transceiver (PPT), which manages data reordering and remote control. In the present 1-Mpx configuration with 9-bit pixel resolution, each IOB serves 16 ASICs (0.29 Gbps), four IOBs form a quadrant (18.88 Gbps), and four PPTs handle the full camera (75.49 Gbps). Since the AISCs and IOBs operate inside a vacuum enclosure at about −20 °C, any upgrade must comply with strict constraints on size, power delivery, and thermal management. In this context, EuXFEL is exploring both near- and long-term upgrade paths driven by the evolution of DSSC toward a 4-Mpx detector with 10-bit pixel resolution and higher throughput. The current system stores about 8,000 frames per second out of the 27,000 pulses per second produced by EuXFEL; near-term targets are 10,000 fps and 27,000 fps, while the long-term goal is continuous operation up to 1 Mfps. These modes would increase the required data transfer rate by factors ranging from about 5.55 to 15 in the near-term, and up to 555 in the long-term scenario, highlighting the main limitation of the current IOB. The IOB must be redesigned with a more powerful FPGA to meet near-term targets while enabling advanced data processing for long-term scenarios (e.g., lossless compression). The current capacitor bank-a simple power approach for DEPFETs-is therefore reconsidered; its removal frees up to about 50% of the IOB area, allowing the integration of additional memory and paving the way toward significantly higher data rates.
