sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 306Poster Number:NSS-13-306] Towards a 64-Channel Monolithic SDD X-Ray Spectrometer for High-Throughput Synchrotron Applications (#2776)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Pedretti (Autores: B. Pedretti , P. Barcella , A. Abba , G. Borghi , M. Carminati , C. Fiorini)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Politecnico di Milano, DEIB, Milano, Italy [2] INFN, Milano, Milano, Italy [3] Nuclear Instruments srl, Lambrugo, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The increasing brilliance of fourth-generation synchrotron sources drives a growing demand for energy-dispersive X-ray fluorescence (XRF) spectrometers capable of handling extreme photon fluxes. We present the design and characterization of the ARDESIA-64 instrument, a complete X-ray fluorescence (XRF) spectrometer for high-throughput synchrotron applications. The instrument integrates a highly scaled 64-channel monolithic Silicon Drift Detector (SDD) array, featuring a pixel pitch of 2.5 mm, within a compact, vacuum-compatible mechanical housing tailored for beamline integration. At the conference, we will present the instrument design and comprehensive spectroscopic characterization results. The collimated 450 μm-thick sensor variant demonstrates an excellent average energy resolution of 125.9 eV FWHM at 5.9 keV. Preliminary high-rate tests confirm exceptional throughput capabilities, sustaining Input Count Rates (ICR) exceeding 800 kcps per channel while preserving an energy resolution of ~150 eV. The readout is performed by a 64-channel Digital Pulse Processor (DPP) based on the CAEN DT5560SE digitizer with firmware specifically adapted for high-throughput X-ray spectroscopy in synchrotrons.

sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Tennessee, Nuclear Engineering, Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America [2] University of Tennessee Space Institute, Center for Laser Applications, Tullahoma, Tennessee, United States of America [3] Argonne National Laboratory, Process Simulation and Safeguards, Lemont, Illinois, United States of America [4] Applied Diamond, Wilmington, Delaware, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Conducting isotopic level material control and accountancy of radioactive materials in fluids is challenging for multiple reasons: optical and electronic methods only provide elemental information, gamma-based methods face difficulties quantifying total concentrations, and destructive mass spectroscopy is costly and time consuming. Alpha-based techniques are typically not feasible due to the particles short (10-20 μm) range in dense matter and often require radiochemical separations in conjunction with electroplating. In this presentation we will present a novel sensor design that utilizes microfluidic structures which constrain the sample to a thin volume, limiting the energy loss of alpha particles, enabling spectroscopic measurements. If the alpha-particle energy is properly conserved it will allow for identification of the isotopes present, while the known sample volume will provide a means of calculating the isotope mass and subsequent concentration.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 310Poster Number:NSS-13-310] The Beta Rhizotron: a Radioisotope Imaging System for Plant Biology Research (#1603)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Weisenberger (Autores: S. J. Lee , E. Christy , K. Gnanvo , A. Weisenberger , S. Abbaszadeh , W. Cheng , G. Bonito , K. Domnanich , G. Severin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Thomas Jefferson National Accelerator Facility, Detector Development Group, Newport News, Virginia, United States of America [2] University of California Santa Cruz, Santa Cruz, California, United States of America [3] Michigan State University, East Lansing, Michigan, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The rhizosphere is the zone surrounding plant roots where there is mutual influence exerted between soil microbes and the roots. In this zone biological and chemical activity is driven by compounds exuded by or present in the root and consumed by specialized types of fungi and bacteria that inhabit or surround the roots. Understanding the dynamics occurring in the rhizosphere regarding plant-microbe, plant-plant and microbe-microbe interaction is the focus of much plant ecophysiology research. Plant biologists often use radioisotopes of carbon, iron, phosphorous and calcium to study this plant-microbe interaction but their radioisotope imaging methods are static and destructive. The Beta Rhizotron is a beta (b)particle imaging detector designed for dynamic, non-invasive, in-vivo/in-situ imaging of plant roots being studied using b-particle emitting radioisotope tracers. Potential tracers include 14 C, 32 P, 45 Ca and 64 Cu via detection of their emitted b-particles from roots grown in a special container called a rhizotron/rhizobox. The detector is a gas based charged particle detector known as a micro-pattern gaseous detector (MPGD). Large area MPGDs are used in particle physics research. The use of a MPGD coupled to a rhizobox for low energy b-particle detection requires an MPGD able to operate in a varying temperature and humidity environment of standard growth chambers to obtain dynamic images of the bio-distribution of b-particle emitting radioisotopes. A key optimization of MPGD construction we are reporting here is the choice of window material.To estimate the expected 2-D intensity histograms simulations were performed using GEANT4 for 64 Cu with the b+ endpoint energy of ~0.65 MeV.Simulated was an 8 µm Kapton window, a 6 µm aluminized Mylar MPGD cathode/window, a 3 mm thick MPGD drift gas volume and a 1 x 1 x 70 mm 3 water column with a uniform spatial distribution of the β-particle emitter to approximate a root. Results indicated adequate imaging results.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 312Poster Number:NSS-13-312] True Random Number Generation for Post-Quantum Applications (#1622)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. Cazalas (Autores: E. Cazalas , C. Blick)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Utah, Nuclear Engineering Program, Salt Lake City, Utah, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This project advances a self-contained, portable True Random Number Generator (TRNG) grounded in the quantum-physical randomness of radioactive decay, integrated with an AI-driven monitoring and adaptive control system, for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) in mission-critical environments where remote connectivity is unavailable or constitutes an unacceptable security risk. Conventional cryptographic methods are projected to be vulnerable to quantum computing attacks by 2030, and NIST has mandated migration to PQC standards (FIPS 203-205) by 2030-2035. A fundamental requirement of PQC is a hardware TRNG capable of producing certified entropy without software-based pseudo-randomness. Existing solutions, e.g., cloud-connected beacons, large optical facilities, are incompatible with the remote, radiation-exposed, and network-denied settings of nuclear power plants, satellites, submarines, and forward military installations. Silicon SoC (system on a chip)-based TRNGs further fail in these environments, as ionizing radiation effects (total ionizing dose, single event upsets, direct damage) can bias, degrade, or manipulate their entropy output. Radioactive decay is a quantum-physical process that is intrinsically random, radiation-environment-tolerant, and scalable to NRC-exempt activity levels, making it ideally suited to this application.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 316Poster Number:NSS-13-316] Optimization of working point for TES microcalorimetric gamma spectroscopy (#2121)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. I. Kowitt (Autores: N. I. Kowitt , A. Danagoulian)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Nuclear Science and Engineering, Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Cryogenic microcalorimeters are low-noise thermal detectors that have demonstrated gamma-ray resolution better than 100 eV at 100 keV, resolving lines unresolvable by conventional spectrometers. Achieving this resolution with an array of transition-edge sensors (TESs), however, requires that all TESs, each with a slightly different transition temperature, be simultaneously biased near their individual operating points. Because the TESs on a given readout line share a common bias, ensemble performance is determined by global parameters: the mixing-chamber temperature, the TES bias current, and the readout electronics configuration. A parametric study was performed to identify the operating point that maximizes the number of usefully contributing pixels and the combined energy resolution. Results of this study will be discussed, along with the methodology for combining and analyzing spectra across the array.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 318Poster Number:NSS-13-318] Radiation Damage to Quantum Dots (#2264)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. Cazalas (Autores: J. Snow , E. Cazalas)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] university of Utah, Nuclear Engineering Program, Salt Lake City, Utah, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract QD nanostructures have emerged as highly versatile materials for sensing ionizing radiation. However, comparatively little is known about how QDs respond to non-ionizing radiation such as fast and thermal neutrons, where neutron capture, rather than ionization, is the dominant interaction mechanism. This study examines the viability of graphene QDs as neutron dosimeters or neutron-gamma discriminators. Additionally, research into QDs can aid in nuclear non-proliferation and dosimetry. The goal of this research is to investigate the effects of neutron irradiation on the optical properties of graphene QDs for non-proliferation applications. The results of this work provide insight into the mechanisms through which neutrons alter QD electronic structure and optical response. This study will contribute to the broader effort to develop hybrid or stand‑alone QD‑based radiation sensors and markers capable of operating across diverse radiation environments and even being incorporated into fuel.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 320Poster Number:NSS-13-320] Simulation-based evaluation of a position-sensitive TES microcalorimeter for gamma-ray detection (#2462)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Hata (Autores: N. Hata , R. Moriyama , R. Arai , A. Kawamoto , N. Iyomoto , T. Ueno , N. Yamasaki , T. Hayashi , K. Mitsuda)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Kyushu University, the Department of Applied Quantum Physics and Nuclear Engineering, Fukuoka, Japan [2] Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, Insutitute of Space and Astronautical Science, Sagamihara, Japan [3] RIKEN, Nishina Center for Accelerator-Based Science, Wako, Japan [4] National Astronomical Observatory of Japan, Advanced Technology Center, Mitaka, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Transition-edge Edge Sensor (TES) microcalorimeters (TES) are attractive promising detectors for gamma-ray spectroscopy because of their excellent energy resolution[1]. However, TES detectors microcalorimeters generally have small sensitive effective areas, and large-scale arrays are required to achieve high detection efficiency. Since TESs operate at cryogenic temperatures, increasing the number of TESs increases Joule heating and readout complexity. To address this issue, a Position-Sensitive TES (PoST) structure microcalorimeters haves been proposed to realize a large effective detection area with a small number of TESs. The Our gamma-ray PoST consists of a long lead absorber with TESs attached to both ends, and the incident position of gamma rays is estimated from differences in pulse shapes. In this study, we evaluated the energy resolution and position resolution of the PoST detector by simulations considering thermal intrinsic noise and gamma-ray multiple scatteringinteractions. The simulations were performed using a finite element model coupling thermal conduction and TES electrical circuits. Sub-millimeter position resolution was achieved for 1333 keV1.33 MeV gamma rays.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 322Poster Number:NSS-13-322] Architecture and Qualification of the GlowRIA radiation monitor: An Optical fibre based dosimeter compatible with Cubesat missions (#2601)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Kerboub (Autores: N. Kerboub , N. Balcon , S. Fosset , M. Bergont , P. Cheiney , S. Girard , J. Mekki)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CNES, Toulouse, France [2] Exail, Lannion, France [3] Université Jean Monnet, Saint-Etienne, France [4] IUF, Paris, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Optical-fiber dosimetry, based on Radiation-Induced Attenuation (RIA) or Radiation-Induced Luminescence (RIL), has progressed from particle-accelerator research to space applications. The first space-borne implementation, the LUMINA experiment, flew on the International Space Station during the ALPHA mission. LUMINA used several kilometres of specially selected silica fiber to provide dose-rate-independent, temperature-independent, and particle-type-independent measurements, successfully monitoring the ISS radiation environment, including each passage through the South Atlantic Anomaly. To meet the more demanding radiation levels, mass, volume, and power constraints of CubeSat missions, we have miniaturized the LUMINA architecture into GlowRIA. In this new design, the fiber length was reduced to a few hundred metres and can be adjusted according to the expected mission dose. The optoelectronics, including the laser and photodiodes, were selected for lower power consumption and a more compact form factor. In addition, the read-out electronics were replaced by a radiation-tolerant microcontroller, eliminating the Raspberry-Pi board used on LUMINA and ensuring resilience to both cumulative dose effects and single-event effects. GlowRIA has been subjected to a comprehensive qualification campaign reproducing harsh orbital conditions such as vacuum, large temperature excursions, electromagnetic interference, and total ionizing dose. The tests confirm that the dosimeter retains its performance while meeting CubeSat power and mass budgets. We are also conducting Total Ionizing Dose calibration of the instrument using a Co-60 source, while Single Event Effects testing is planned at a later stage. The results of the environmental, radiation, and performance qualification campaigns will be presented in the full article.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 324Poster Number:NSS-13-324] Scintillation imaging with Coded Aperture masks (#2853)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 V. Cicero (Autores: V. Cicero , N. Tosi , A. Montanari , V. Pia , F. Mei , L. Martina , G. De Matteis)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Bologna, Bologna, Italy [2] Università del Salento, Mathematics and Physics, Lecce, Italy [3] Università di Bologna, Physics and Astronomy, Bologna, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Large volumes of liquid argon or xenon serve as highly effective media for detecting neutrino interactions and searching for dark matter. Conventional noble-liquid detectors typically use scintillation light for timing or calorimetric measurements only, while relying on charge drift in a time projection chamber for spatial reconstruction. Direct optical reconstruction of events by imaging scintillation light could provide an alternative to the slow charge collection, also eliminating the necessity for an electric drift field. The increased rate capability enables new applications, including detectors at high-intensity neutrino beams and medical imaging (whole-body PET). Thanks to finely segmented Silicon PhotoMultiplier arrays and appropriate optical systems, it is feasible to create cameras capable of ``photographing" the primary scintillation light. A significant challenge is presented by the fact that both argon and xenon emit scintillation light in the vacuum-ultraviolet spectrum. To overcome this, coded aperture masks are employed instead of conventional lenses, enabling the construction of thin cameras with wide and deep fields of view. A reconstruction algorithm based on Maximum Likelihood Expectation Maximization has been developed to generate a 3D map of energy deposition. The most recent results from simulations and reconstructions of particles tracks in a liquid argon detector equipped with these cameras will be discussed.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 326Poster Number:NSS-13-326] Application of a Compact Electrically Cooled HPGe Detector to Quality Control in Radiopharmaceutical Isotope Production (#2856)
sub_talks.speaker: G. Ilie
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Mirion Technologies, Radiometric Physics, Meriden, Connecticut, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Since their invention in the 1970s, high purity germanium (HPGe) detectors have been the gold standard for the detection and spectroscopy of gamma rays. Developments in the fabrication, packaging, and operation of HPGe detectors, as well as in readout electronics and signal processing, have led to their application in fields as diverse as fundamental nuclear and particle physics, nuclear security and safety, and nuclear medicine. Based on decades of experience in electrical cooling technology, in recent years Mirion Technologies has developed rugged germanium detectors that can be used in difficult conditions traditionally considered too challenging for HPGe detectors. An example of such a detector is our newest product: the MicroGe detector. Due to it is small form factor and rapid deployment capability, the MicroGe detector can be used in medical radioisotope production facilities where high resolution is critical to identify impurities in samples. The MicroGe detector is capable of going from storage to measurement in less than 30 minutes which is a revolutionary achievement for HPGes. This paper presents results of the evaluation of a novel ultra-compact electrically cooled germanium detector as a quality-control instrument for quantification of for radionuclide impurity of samples.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 194Poster Number:NSS-13-194] Graph-Based Modeling of Organ and Lesion Radiomics Interactions in Theranostic SPECT/CT Imaging (#3206)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. S. Azimi (Autores: M. S. Azimi , M. Cheraghi , M. A. Ghodsi-Rad , G. Divband , H. Zaidi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Geneva University Hospital, Division of Nuclear Medicine & Molecular Imaging, Geneva, Genève, Switzerland [2] Odense University Hospital, Deptartment of Nuclear Medicine, Odense, Denmark [3] Obuda University, University Research and Innovation Center, Budapest, Hungary [4] Shahid Beheshti University, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Tehran, Iran (Islamic Republic of) [5] Jam Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Tehran, Iran (Islamic Republic of)
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Current radiomics approaches primarily focus on individual organs or lesions, which limits the ability to describe interactions within the body holistically. To address this limitation, we introduce a graph-based framework for modeling radiomics relationships between organs and lesions in theranostic SPECT/CT imaging. A cohort of 57 patients treated with ¹⁷⁷Lu-based radiopharmaceuticals was analyzed using post-therapy SPECT/CT. Organs were segmented using a deep learning-based approach, and lesions were delineated semi-automatically on SPECT images. From each region, 107 standardized radiomic features were extracted. Interactions between organs and lesions were quantified using a combination of linear similarity measures (Pearson, Spearman, cosine) and a nonlinear dependency metric based on normalized mutual information. These relationships were then represented as patient-specific graphs to capture system-level radiomics organization. The results reveal a non-uniform interaction pattern, where only a subset of organs exhibits strong associations with lesion characteristics. The highest coupling was observed in physiologically active regions such as the kidneys, liver, and spleen, with normalized mutual information values reaching approximately 0.66. Across all regions, nonlinear dependencies consistently showed higher values than linear metrics, indicating that complex relationships dominate radiomics interactions. Network representations further demonstrated a densely connected structure without prominent hubs, suggesting a distributed interaction model. Stability analysis confirmed reproducible patterns across patients, with near-perfect rank consistency and high agreement among top-ranked regions. These findings demonstrate that radiomics interactions between organs and lesions are structured, nonlinear, and reproducible. The proposed framework enables system-level interpretation of imaging data and may support the development of more informative biomarkers.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 116Poster Number:NSS-01-116] Photon Counting with FPGA Gigabit Transceivers: A Proof-of-Concept SiPM Readout for TOF-PET (#2884)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Turqueti (Autores: T. Prakash , J. W. Cates , W.-S. Choong , M. Turqueti)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Achieving 100ps FWHM coincidence time resolution (CTR) in time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET) is benefited by electronics that can resolve individual scintillation photons with high temporal precision. We report a proof-of-concept readout in which silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) single-photon pulses are discriminated by a high-speed comparator and digitized directly by GTY transceivers of a Xilinx Virtex UltraScale XCVU095 FPGA (VCU1287 board) at 16Gbps, encoding photon arrival times as bit positions with 62.5ps resolution. Signal integrity analysis showed that an initial LVDS comparator produced common-mode voltage and differential swing below GTY receiver specifications; switching to a CML comparator substantially reduced bit errors. Room-temperature SiPM dark count bitstreams were captured with a random FPGA clock trigger and post-processed to produce a finger plot showing 1-, 2-, and 3-photoelectron peaks, providing a preliminary validation of the bitstream-based photon-counting concept. These results support the feasibility of FPGA gigabit transceivers as scalable digitizers for single-photon pulse streams in next-generation TOF-PET detector modules.

sub_talks.speaker: D. Meier
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Integrated Detector Electronics AS - IDEAS, Oslo, Norway
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract IDEAS has a long heritage in designing detector readout integrated circuits (ROICs) and electronic systems for scientific applications. You can use our VATA and IDE-type chips for reading out your high-channel-count detectors, e.g., strips or pixels on silicon, CZT, or scintillators with PMTs or SiPMs. For space applications, and with flight heritage, our radiation-hardened ASICs enable compact, low-power detectors. Building on this foundation, IDEAS is contributing to next-generation instruments and missions: Space radiation monitors deliver real-time dosimetry and particle spectra (NORM, and Galileo RMU). CZT-based systems (SRE4001, GDS-100) deliver high-resolution gamma spectroscopy and x-ray imaging in a modular form. Our new designs of ADC- and infrared controller ASICs (NIRCA) help minimizing infrared imaging systems and cameras. In my presentation I will focus on the ASICs and ROICs that we can supply and our new developments.

sub_talks.title: [TS-02-02] Toward Information-Efficient Photon Detection: CMOS SiPMs and Multi-Threshold Readout ASICs (#3352)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Lao (Autores: H. Lao , G. Su)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] RAYQUANT Technology Co., Ltd., Ezhou, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Detecting photons is only the beginning. How can we preserve and make better use of the information they carry? At Rayquant, we develop both CMOS silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) and multi-voltage-threshold (MVT) readout ASICs, linking photon detection with timing readout. This presentation highlights our latest SiPM devices, measured photon detection and timing performance, and timing results from our MVT ASIC and SiPM-MVT experiments. We will also share applications of our SiPMs in PET imaging and radiation detection. Beyond existing products, we will explore how detector-specific requirements can shape new SiPM and readout ASIC development, turning real detection challenges into working silicon.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Panesar (Autores: B. Panesar , J. Kalliopuska , S. Vahanen)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] ADVAFAB, Helsinki, Finland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Advanced radiation imaging requires sensor materials, electrode structures and interconnection processes tailored to the application and readout electronics. This presentation introduces Advafab's sensor fabrication and hybrid integration capabilities, with a focus on silicon and compound semiconductor sensors, including GaAs and Cd(Zn)Te, for scientific, medical and industrial imaging. We present the manufacturing route from sensor design and electrode processing to under-bump metallisation, wafer-level solder bumping, precision dicing and flip-chip bonding to readout ASICs. Particular attention is given to material-dependent processing requirements, compatibility between sensor contacts and interconnects, and electrical characterisation supporting detector quality. The presentation also outlines Advafab's development of compound semiconductor foundry capabilities and opportunities for customer-specific sensor fabrication and process development. Attendees will gain a practical overview of how Advafab supports detector development from initial prototypes towards repeatable production, connecting sensor manufacturing with the requirements of complete hybrid pixel detector assemblies.

sub_talks.title: [TS-02-04] Real-Time Pile-Up Recovery and High-Resolution Signal Processing for SDDs using PurSamurAI (#3305)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Takamaru (Autores: Y. Endou , M. Takamaru , K. Otomo)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] TechnoAP Co.,Ltd., Research and Development Department, Hitachinaka-City, Japan [2] TechnoAP Co.,Ltd., Sales Department, Hitachinaka-City, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In spectroscopy using Silicon Drift Detectors (SDDs), signal pile-up in high count rate environments remains a primary challenge, significantly degrading energy resolution and throughput. This presentation introduces "PurSamurAI" (Pile-up Recovery via Smart Algorithm for Multi-pulse Unmixing and Reconstruction AI), a novel algorithm designed to overcome this limitation. By implementing a pre-trained inference model specialized for waveform unmixing, PurSamurAI separates and recovers overlapping pulses in real time-events that are conventionally discarded. This approach minimizes spectral degradation even at extremely high input count rates, successfully achieving both high throughput and high energy resolution simultaneously. Furthermore, the architecture provides the flexibility for users to optimize the inference model tailored to their specific measurement applications. We will discuss the technical details of the PurSamurAI signal processing architecture and evaluate its real-time performance capabilities.

sub_talks.title: [TS-02-05] Sci-Compiler: Towards Cross-Platform FPGA Development and Automated CI/CD Workflows for Scientific Data Acquisition (#3405)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Abba (Autores: A. Abba , S. Carsi , D. Bianchi , F. Caponio , A. Cusimano , V. Arosio , M. Lazari , A. Giannini , S. Cuzzolin , Y. Venturini , G. Beccuzi , M. Bianchini , L. Colombini , C. Tintori , A. Mati)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Nuclear Instruments SRL, Lambrugo, Italy [2] CAEN S.P.A., Viareggio, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Sci-Compiler is a graphical FPGA development environment for custom digital signal processing and data acquisition in nuclear physics, radiation detection, and scientific instrumentation. This contribution presents a major evolution of the platform, including the highly anticipated introduction of Linux support and automated firmware compilation through CI/CD pipelines. The new alpha release for Linux represents a significant milestone, addressing a long-standing requirement from the scientific community and enabling Sci-Compiler to operate natively in Linux-based research environments. Together with newly introduced pipeline licenses, it opens the way to automated FPGA compilation, integration with Git-based workflows, reproducible firmware builds, and continuous validation of scientific instrumentation firmware. The signal processing library has been substantially expanded with advanced FFT/IFFT architectures, real-time frequency-domain filtering, programmable FIR and CIC filters, digital modulation, waveform averaging, statistical analysis, and configurable signal generators. Extensive support for time-multiplexed processing enables efficient implementation of multichannel algorithms for high-sampling-rate digitizers. Detector-oriented developments include improved trapezoidal processing for high-count-rate spectroscopy, pile-up rejection, rise-time discrimination, and flexible event packet generation. Extended simulation capabilities allow acquisition chains to be tested and waveforms, spectra, and event streams to be exported without physical hardware. A redesigned graphical editor further improves productivity through intelligent signal connections, searchable processing blocks, hierarchical design tools, and integrated documentation. These advances mark a transition towards an accessible, cross-platform and automated FPGA development ecosystem for modern scientific experiments.

sub_talks.title: [TS-02-06] Broadcom's Silicon Photomultiplier: Technology, Performance, Status and Roadmap (#3399)
sub_talks.speaker: S. Brunner
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Broadcom Inc, Regensburg, Bavaria, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This presentation provides an overview of Broadcom's silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) and photodetection technologies, including NIR- and NUV-SiPMs. Special focus is placed on initial results for the new HDR-NUV-MT SiPM, as well as the newly developed BroadR and NUV-DJ SiPM technologies. HDR-NUV-MT We present the recently released HDR-NUV-MT SiPM, a 3×3 mm² device designed for applications requiring high dynamic range. This is achieved using an 18 µm SPAD pitch, combined with a fast recharge time constant of about 17 ns. Additionally, this is the first SiPM in the NUV family featuring four subsegmented quadrants that can be read out individually. BroadR The newly developed BroadR technology utilizes a novel SPAD architecture enabling an unprecedented flat spectral response. A high photon detection efficiency (PDE) of 50% is maintained from 400 nm to 750 nm, bridging the spectral ranges traditionally covered by separate NUV- and NIR-SiPM technologies. Along with the high and flat PDE, the BroadR technology offers superior dynamic range. Indeed, the this PDE level is achieved with a SPAD pitch of 14 µm and a recharge time constant that can be designed to be well below 10ns. NUV-DJ The NUV-DJ technology significantly increases PDE at wavelengths above 420 nm compared to NUV-MT, while maintaining excellent NUV sensitivity from 250 nm to 420 nm. At 500 nm, PDE improves from 52% to 62% with the same 40 µm SPAD pitch. The correlated noise of NUV-DJ is also lower compared to NUV-MT at the same PDE. This high PDE and low noise enable best-in-class coincidence time resolution (CTR) for LYSO-based TOF-PET, expand applications to green-emitting scintillators like GAGG, and enable BGO-based Cherenkov TOF-PET. Initial characterization results for NUV-DJ will be presented. Broadcom's NUV SiPMs find application in TOF-PET, Cherenkov-PET, radiation spectroscopy, photon-counting X-ray detection & PCCT, flow cytometry, and time-gated fluorescence.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-01-01] SPECT Reconstruction via Diffusion Sampling from a PET Image Manifold for Theranostics (#1954)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Wei (Autores: H. Wei , L. Livieratos , G. Webber , A. J. Reader)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Kings College London, School of Biomedical Engineering and Imaging Sciences, London, United Kingdom [2] Kings College London, Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, London, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) remains the standard modality for uptake verification and patient-specific dosimetry in molecular radiotherapy (MRT), however it has limited spatial resolution and noise characteristics compared to pre-therapy positron emission tomography (PET). Existing approaches that incorporate PET priors into SPECT reconstruction are often constrained by hand-crafted feature representations and suffer from inter-modality mismatch and registration-induced artifacts. In this work, we employ a conditional generative framework to enhance SPECT reconstruction toward PET-level image quality. A denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) is trained to learn the distribution of high-quality PET images. During inference, the reverse diffusion process is conditioned on measured SPECT data and CT images, enabling anatomically consistent, high-fidelity image synthesis. The method is initially assessed using 2D Zubal phantom simulations. Performance is compared with conventional maximum likelihood expectation maximization (MLEM) and kernel based methods. Both quantitative metrics and qualitative analysis demonstrate that the diffusion-based approach achieves enhanced edge preservation and superior noise suppression. The reconstructed images show closer agreement with reference data compared to MLEM and kernel based reconstructions. By avoiding explicit PET-SPECT registration, the framework mitigates spatial misalignment and associated artifacts. These results indicate that conditional diffusion sampling provides a principled and flexible approach to improve resolution and noise limitations in SPECT, with potential to improve quantitative accuracy in MRT applications.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-01-02] Event-by-Event Energy-Dependent List-Mode Reconstruction for Quantitative 90 Y Bremsstrahlung SPECT (#2953)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Yan (Autores: C. Yan , H. Hu , J. Qin , H. Ye , C. Yang , F. Chen , R. Zhao , H. Li , Z. He , Y. Liu , H. Liu , J. Wu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Normal University, Center for Advanced Quantum Studies, School of Physics and Astronomy, Beijing, China [2] China Institute for Radiation Protection, Shanxi, China [3] Shanxi Provincial Key Laboratory for Translational Nuclear Medicine and Precision Protection, Shanxi, China [4] Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Beijing, China [5] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract 90 Y bremsstrahlung SPECT imaging remains challenging due to its broad continuous energy spectrum. In this study, we proposed and evaluated a novel event-by-event energy-dependent list-mode reconstruction algorithm for quantitative 90 Y bremsstrahlung SPECT. To enable real-time and reasonably accurate energy-dependent collimator-detector response modeling, we proposed and incorporated a True Half-Width method into the list-mode reconstruction framework. Monte Carlo simulations were performed using three energy windows: 90-160 keV, 105-285 keV, and 90-400 keV. Quantitative evaluation was performed using contrast recovery coefficient and background variability. Compared with projection-based reconstruction, list-mode reconstruction achieved the best quantitative performance using the 90-400 keV energy window, owing to accurate event-level energy-dependent system matrix modeling over the broad continuous energy spectrum. These results demonstrate that event-by-event energy-dependent list-mode reconstruction is essential for improving the quantitative accuracy of 90 Y bremsstrahlung SPECT.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-01-03] Introducing "T-Index"-A Metric for Quantifying Data Range and Sampling Sufficiency (#2039)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Taguchi (Autores: K. Taguchi , J. Xu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, Maryland, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Many image reconstruction methods for x-ray computed tomography (CT) use optimization approaches with cost functions that consist of a data fidelity term and a prior term. Extensive efforts have been devoted to construct better priors, some using machine learning, for high resolution, low dose, and spectral imaging. There seems to be a belief that a good prior can overcome any problems in data acquisition, downplaying the data fidelity term. It would be desirable if we could quantify the sufficiency of the problem setting (or adequacy of the data acquisition) toward a set of desired imaging properties. We propose "Truth index" or "T-index" to quantify data range and data sampling issues in this work. When fully developed, the T-index will show, independent of specific image reconstruction methods used, how much the solution can be trusted or has a risk of hallucination.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-01-04] Time-of-Flight X-ray Imaging with Scatter Rejection and Subtraction (#3042)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Lorenzon (Autores: A. Lorenzon , Z. Liu , X. Jiang , W. Zbijewski , J.W. Stayman)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Johns Hopkins University, Biomedical Engineering, Baltimore, Maryland, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract X-ray time of flight information can be used in computed tomography to characterize photon interactions and discriminate scattered from unscattered events. Specifically, photons undergoing Compton and Rayleigh scattering are subject to trajectory deviations that increase their path length relative to primary photons. Therefore, with adequate temporal resolution, scattered photons are detected with larger time delay with respect to primary photons, providing a physically grounded mechanism to reject scatter. Recent technological developments in ultra-fast X-ray sources (e.g: 50ps) and high-temporal-resolution photon-counting detectors may allow for this imaging modality. In this work, Monte Carlo (MC) simulations of a water cylinder were performed assuming Gaussian source pulse shape and detector timing jitter, with combined full-width-half-maximum as low as 50ps. A threshold-based scatter rejection method was applied, sweeping multiple thresholds to find the optimal balance between scatter rejection efficiency (η) and primary retention (ε). Filtered-backprojection reconstructions were performed and evaluated in terms of root mean square error and bias. Rejection performances were compared with an ideal, MC-based scatter subtraction technique, that leverages template fitting to estimate the average scatter contribution from time-delay histograms. A combined rejection-subtraction approach was also evaluated. For rejection only, the optimal reconstruction accuracy is obtained with a threshold T'=30 ps, corresponding to η=59% and ε=80%. Residual scatter leads to bias in the reconstructed attenuation, preventing the method from achieving the same reconstruction accuracy as the ideal subtraction. However, rejection yields lower noise levels compared to subtraction. Combining rejection and subtraction may provide a better compromise between bias and noise.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-01-05] Robustness to Scatter in Dual Energy Bone Suppression for Chest Radiography (#3063)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 W. Zbijewski (Autores: G. Shi , J. Schaefer , S. Vogt , A. Heshmat , L. Ritschl , S. Kappler , C. T. Lin , D. Oncel , S. Ocal , W. Zbijewski)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Johns Hopkins University, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Baltimore, Maryland, United States of America [2] Johns Hopkins University, Russel H. Morgan Dept. of Radiology and Radiological Science, Baltimore, Maryland, United States of America [3] Siemens Healthineers, Forchheim, Bavaria, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We quantify the impact of scatter on the performance of bone suppression in virtual non‑calcium chest radiographs (VNCa‑CXR) generated with (i) a multi‑layer flat‑panel detector (ML‑FPD, three 200-um thick CsI layers) and (ii) with a kV‑switching protocol (60/140 kVp). We show that in the setting of log-subtraction, the decomposition weight (DW) can be adjusted for scatter-to-primary ratio (SPR) such that the scatter-induced bias in VNCa is locally corrected (scatter-compensating weight, DW-scat). However, DW-scat is spatially varying. If a constant DW is used in log-subtraction, the magnitude of bone residual in VNCa radiographs will depend on the degree of spatial inhomogeneity in DW-scat. We investigate this effect is simulation studies in anthropomorphic chest phantoms (20 - 24 cm thickness) with and without an anti-scatter grid (ASG). Without a scatter‑compensating DW, scatter‑induced bone residual increased by >100% is most configurations except for ML-FPD with a grid. Applying DW-scat averaged over central lung region reduced the residual by up to 50% for ML-FPD without an ASG and by ~40% for kV-switching with an ASG. Overall, our results reveal that DE VNCa imaging is relatively robust to scatter in scenarios with a grid, where kV-switching appears to benefit from spatially-averaged scatter-compensating DW more than ML-FPD, likely due to differences in scatter content of the two energy channels. Without a grid, both configurations may require a spatially-dependent scatter compensation for optimal bone suppression.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-01-06] Unrolled relaxed algorithm for 3D SPECT reconstruction (#2388)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Constanza (Autores: C. Constanza , D. Sarrut , A. Etxebeste)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CREATIS, CNRS UMR 5220; INSERM U 1044, Université de Lyon; INSA-Lyon; Université Lyon 1, Villeurbanne, France [2] Centre de lutte contre le cancer Léon-Bérard, Lyon, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In this work, we propose an unrolled Block Sequential Regularized Expectation Maximization (BSREM) reconstruction framework in which the gradient of the regularization term is learned using a convolutional neural network. Building on our previous work, we adopt Jacobian-Free Unrolling (JFU) to enable memory-efficient training on 3D synthetic data. This training strategy backpropagates only through the final iteration of the unrolled optimization, significantly reducing memory consumption while improving training stability. We investigate the influence of relaxation strategies within the unrolled BSREM scheme and analyze their impact on convergence behavior, stability, and reconstruction quality. Experiments conducted on realistic simulated SPECT datasets and clinical 177 Lu-DOTATATE patient data show that JFU-based unrolling consistently outperforms classical unrolled training for an equivalent number of parameters and memory usage. Unlike classical unrolling, which requires strong relaxation to ensure stable training, JFU achieves optimal performance with weak or no relaxation. Excessive relaxation is shown to be suboptimal, leading to reduced quantitative accuracy. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate improvements in both global image quality and organ-level activity accuracy compared to OSEM and conventional BSREM with a Relative Difference Penalty prior. As observed in our previous study using Green's one-step-late algorithm, the proposed approach may introduce over-separation artifacts between regions of low and high activity. This behavior appears intrinsic to learning the regularization gradient rather than to the unrolling strategy itself. Overall, this work highlights the advantages of Jacobian-Free Unrolling for scalable and stable learning-based SPECT reconstruction and provides insights into the role of relaxation in unrolled optimization schemes.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-01-07] Three-Photon Bayesian Imaging of Ortho-Positronium (#2897)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 W. Krzemien (Autores: W. Krzemien , L. Raczyński , A. Coussat)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Centre for Nuclear Research, Department of High Energy Physics, Otwock Swierk, Poland [2] National Centre for Nuclear Research, Department of Complex Systems, Otwock Swierk, Poland [3] INSA-Lyon, niversité Claude Bernard Lyon 1, CNRS, Inserm, CREATIS UMR 5220, U1294, F-69373, Lyon, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positron emission tomography provides functional images from two-photon coincidences. In human tissue, approximately 40% of annihilations are preceded by positronium formation, of which the ortho-positronium component partially decays into three photons [1]. This three-photon channel carries additional information about the local micro-environment [1], including the three-to-two-photon yield ratio as a potential diagnostic marker [3,2], and its exploitation does not require a prompt photon, making it compatible with standard radionuclides such as FDG. We propose the Three-Photon Bayesian Imaging of Ortho-Positronium algorithm, a novel event-by-event reconstruction method formulated as a Bayesian maximum a posteriori inference problem, which unifies time-based trilateration [4], energy-based reconstruction [3], and a physics-informed prior derived from the quantum electrodynamics description of ortho-positronium decay [5-6] within a single probabilistic framework. Monte Carlo simulations modelled after the Siemens Biograph Quadra scanner [7] demonstrate an improvement of a factor of two over time-based trilateration and by an order of magnitude over energy-based reconstruction. The proposed approach is compatible with existing scanners capable of registering three-photon coincidences, broadening its applicability beyond positronium lifetime imaging to standard clinical radionuclides.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-01-08] Lutetium-176-Aided Joint Activity and Attenuation Reconstruction in TOF-PET Using Trust-Region Cubic Surrogate Optimization (#2772)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 X. Zhao (Autores: X. Zhao , Z. Zhao , Z. Wang , Z. Xie)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Peking University, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Joint Maximum Likelihood Activity and Attenuation (MLAA) provides a promising CT-less attenuation correction framework but suffers from global scaling ambiguity. Intrinsic Lu-176 background radiation provides patient-specific transmission information to reduce this issue, while introducing a highly nonlinear and ill-conditioned joint likelihood. We propose the Separable Cubic Surrogate with Trust Region (SCS-TR) algorithm, utilizing an analytical Lipschitz constant and a vectorized solver to ensure strictly monotonic convergence and avoid local optima. The reconstruction is initialized with Maximum Likelihood Transmission Reconstruction (MLTR) results. GATE simulations studies demonstrate that SCS-TR effectively recovers clear bone structures and smooth uniform regions without explicit regularization. The proposed method recovered clear bony structures and uniform soft-tissue regions without explicit regularization, and maintained structural fidelity under 20% count statistics.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-01-09] List-Mode Derived Synthetic Kernel-Based Image Reconstruction for Dynamic Total Body PET (#2844)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Dassanayake (Autores: M. Dassanayake , L. Vass , P. Marsden , J. A. Schnabel , A. J. Reader)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] King's College London, Department of Imaging Physics and Engineering at the School of Biomedical Engineering and Imaging Sciences, London, United Kingdom [2] Technical University Munich, School of Computation, Information and Technology, Munich, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Total-body positron emission tomography (TB-PET) provides significantly improved sensitivity, enabling ultra-short time framing for dynamic imaging. However, the resulting low count statistics lead to increased noise and unstable time activity curves (TACs), limiting quantitative accuracy. We investigate a kernel-based reconstruction approach within a list-mode (LM)-derived synthetic framework, where a vendor reconstruction is forward projected through an event-specific LM system matrix to generate synthetic data, implicitly includes attenuation, normalisation, scatter, and randoms effects while enabling flexible algorithm design. Spatial, temporal, and spatio-temporal kernels are evaluated for short-frame FDG data acquired on a Biograph Vision Quadra system, with features constructed from multiple dynamic intervals. Reconstructions are compared with a 10x higher count vendor reference images using spatial and temporal PRMSE. Spatially, the spatio-temporal kernel achieves the lowest error. In addition, we demonstrated that kernel methods benefit from larger neighbourhoods resulting in improved visual quality compared to synthetic PET. This was computationally feasible on consumer hardware by using region-of-interest specific reconstructions. These results demonstrate that LM-derived synthetic kernel reconstruction provides a flexible framework for incorporating spatial and temporal priors in TB-PET. While performance is currently limited by kernel parameter selection, the observed improvements in spatial and temporal behaviour indicate strong potential for optimisation through tuning the kernel strength and feature vector design.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-01-10] Unsupervised micro-CT reconstruction from limited-angle and truncated data in cone-beam geometry (#1238)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Izumitani (Autores: K. Izumitani , T. Shibuya , H. Kato , H. Haneishi , T. Okamoto)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Chiba University, Graduate School of Science and Engineering, Chiba, Japan [2] National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST), Research Institute for Measurement and Analytical Instrumentation, National Metrology Institute of Japan, Tsukuba, Japan [3] National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST), Non-Destructive Imaging Research Team, Integrated Research Center for Resilient Infrastructure, Tsukuba, Japan [4] Chiba university, Center for Frontier Medical Engineering, Chiba, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Micro X-ray computed tomography (micro-CT) enables non-destructive visualization of fine internal structures. Resolving finer details requires higher geometric magnification, typically achieved by reducing the source-to-rotation-center distance (SRD). However, short-SRD acquisition can suffer from a limited angular range due to physical interference with the X-ray source and from projection truncation when the object extends beyond the field-of-view (FOV), causing streak artifacts and structural distortions. Supervised learning-based reconstruction methods have been investigated to mitigate such artifacts but applying them to non-destructive high-magnification micro-CT is difficult because fully sampled, non-truncated reference data cannot be readily acquired without destructive sample preparation. Moreover, many existing methods are designed for 2D fan-beam geometry rather than 3D cone-beam geometry commonly used in micro-CT. We propose an unsupervised reconstruction method that simultaneously reduces limited-angle and projection-truncation artifacts by incorporating long-SRD measurements. Long-SRD acquisition provides full-view, non-truncated projections, albeit at lower spatial resolution, complementing the high-resolution but incomplete short-SRD acquisition. By jointly using these complementary measurements, the proposed method preserves fine structural details while recovering the global object structure without requiring ground-truth images. Numerical experiments demonstrated that the proposed method reduced streak artifacts and recovered structural information outside the short-SRD FOV. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first unsupervised 3D cone-beam reconstruction method to simultaneously address both artifacts in high-magnification micro-CT.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-02-01] Experimental Results from Novel Monolithic PET Detector and Application to Axillary Lymph Node Imaging (#1769)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Cotroneo (Autores: T. Cotroneo , D. Pare , L. Saleh , P. Vaska)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Stony Brook University, Biomedical Engineering, Stony Brook, New York, United States of America [2] Renaissance School of Medicine at Stony Brook University, Radiology, Stony Brook, New York, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Monolithic scintillators are a promising alternative to standard pixelated crystals in positron emission tomography, as they can be more cost-effective, reduce dead space, and capture an unobstructed light distribution, which can be used for depth of interaction estimation. We focus on the improvements seen by using an array of integrated corner reflectors (ICR) machined directly into the entrance face of the monolith, which we previously showed via simulation to improve light collection and narrow the light distribution. In this study, we built a physical prototype of the device using a CNC machining process. We compared this prototype with other monolithic block designs. We show that the ICR monolith with the CNN positioning algorithm has potential for high-resolution imaging with ~1 mm resolution at 12 mm thickness. Using GATE simulations, we constructed a full scanner with the performance of the monolithic blocks and tested the capabilities compared to existing systems. We show the improved spatial resolution and feasibility for a non-cylindrical design for axillary lymph node scanning.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-02-02] Spatial Characterization of PET Detectors Based on BGO Pseudo‑slabs (#1981)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Cucarella (Autores: N. Cucarella , L. Gil-Bosch , F. Paganao , F. Loignon-Houle , M. Gil , M. Freire , D. Sanchez , A. Gonzalez-Montoro , A.J. Gonzalez)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto de Instrumentación para Imagen Molecular (I3M), Centro Mixto CSIC-Universitat Politècnica de València,, DMIL, Valencia, Spain [2] Oncovision SA, Valencia, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Pixelated crystal arrays are the standard in commercial PET scanners. However, these detectors usually lack DOI information, essential to achieve a homogenous spatial resolution along the entire FOV. Yet, studies have been already performed with pixelated detectors with DOI capabilities but at the cost of using extra hardware material and/or crystal assembling. Inspired by semi‑monolithic crystal geometries, pseudo-slabs were proposed as an alternative. This geometry consists of an N × N pixel array optically isolated only in one direction, allowing light crosstalk in the orthogonal one. The N pixels sharing light in this direction form a pseudo-slab. The light sharing within a pseudo-slab is enough to enable DOI retrieval, while the physical separation between pixels confines the light more than in a pure slab geometry, yielding better time resolution. In this work we evaluated the DOI resolution of a BGO block formed by 8×8 pixels, each measuring around 3×3×15 mm 3 . Two different readout configurations were employed and compared. First, all the 64 channels corresponding to the TOFPET2 ASIC channels were digitized. Then, a multiplexing circuit was utilized, reducing the signals to 8+8 by summing rows and columns. The DOI was obtained using neural networks trained on experimental data. The results show a good DOI resolution for both readout configurations, achieving 3.8 ± 1.3 mm with the multiplexing circuit. These results show that pseudo-slabs are suitable for clinical PET scanners with DOI capabilities.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-02-03] SurfaceCam: A Close-Proximity Multi-Pinhole CZT Brain SPECT system with Enhanced Geometric Sensitivity and Spatial Resolution (#3121)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Mandot (Autores: S. Mandot , S. D. Metzler , L.-J. Meng)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Department of Nuclear, Plasma and Radiological Engineering, Champaign, Illinois, United States of America [2] University of Pennsylvania at Philadelphia, Department of Radiology, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States of America [3] University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Beckman Institute for Advance Science and Technology, Champaign, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract High-sensitivity, high-resolution brain-dedicated SPECT systems are critically important for advancing diagnosis and surgical planning in complex neurological disorders such as epilepsy, Parkinson's disease, and Alzheimer's disease. In this paper, we present SurfaceCam , a close-proximity multi-pinhole SPECT architecture with a radially adaptable rotating gantry, designed specifically for clinical brain imaging. The system comprises 15 detector-collimator panels distributed across three detector heads in a cylindrical arrangement, operating at a 1:8 minification geometry with a 28 cm bore. Each panel integrates 16 high-performance CZT sensors in a compact 2×8 configuration. The three detector heads translate radially to accommodate varying patient head sizes while maintaining close-proximity geometry, and the rotating gantry enables micro-rotation between acquisitions to facilitate angular super-sampling strategies. Pinholes are organized into groups of four with a twisted geometry, each subtending partial coverage of the 20 cm spherical FOV, while eliminating inter-pinhole projection multiplexing on the detector surface. Analytical comparison against a conventional 1:11 minification compound-eye reference design demonstrates approximately 1.4-fold higher geometric sensitivity and approximately 27% improvement in effective pinhole spatial resolution. The front-end electronics and data acquisition systems have been fully developed and validated, with Monte Carlo simulation studies and experimental phantom validation currently underway.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-02-04] In vivo Gold Nanoparticle Imaging in Mice for Tumor Detection Using SiPM-Based Photon-Counting CT (#1749)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Midorikawa (Autores: S. Midorikawa , M. Arimoto , F. Lucyana , Y. Furuta , S. Kobayashi , H. Kawashima , K. Okumura , A. Mizutani , N. Ohno , M. Oshima , J. Kataoka , R. Takahiro , R. MInagawa , K. Murakami , Y. Maeno , S. Terazawa)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Kanazawa University, Ishikawa, Japan [2] Waseda University, Tokyo, Japan [3] Ishikawa Prefectural University, Ishikawa, Japan [4] Proterial Ltd, Tokyo, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Photon-counting CT (PC-CT) is a powerful spectral imaging technique that identifies materials by counting individual X-ray photons. While direct-conversion systems are entering clinical practice, we are developing a cost-effective, large-area scintillator-based PC-CT system using YGAG:Ce coupled with silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs). PC-CT excels at identifying high-atomic-number elements like gold (Au) by utilizing its K-edge (80.7 keV). Gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) are promising for drug delivery, as their biodistribution can be controlled by particle size, enabling selective tumor accumulation via the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect. In this study, we evaluated the in vivo biodistribution of AuNPs in tumor-bearing mice using our SiPM-based PC-CT. Two sizes of AuNPs (1.9 nm and 15 nm) were intravenously administered, and their accumulation was quantitatively assessed using multi-energy CT concentration estimation. Results showed distinct size-dependent patterns: 1.9 nm AuNPs exhibited rapid renal clearance and bladder accumulation, while 15 nm AuNPs showed prolonged circulation and significant hepatic accumulation. Tumor accumulation was confirmed for both sizes, demonstrating the potential of our SiPM-based PC-CT for quantitative in vivo nanoparticle imaging.This presentation reports on the experimental setup, the analysis methods, and the results obtained.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-02-05] Quantitative Evaluation of Liver Disease through Multi-modality Approach Combining SiPM-based PC-CT and MRI-Approach to the Visualization of Inflammation through Water Fraction Estimation - (#1548)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Furuta (Autores: Y. Furuta , M. Arimoto , F. Lucyana , S. Midorikawa , S. Kobayashi , H. Kawashima , K. Okumura , N. Ohno , T. Tomoda , M. Oshima , K. Murakami , J. Kataoka , R. Minagawa , T. Ro , S. Terazawa , Y. Maeno)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Kanazawa University, Kanazawa, Japan [2] Ishikawa Prefectural University, Nonoichi, Japan [3] Waseda University, Shinzyuku, Japan [4] Proterial Ltd., Mishima, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract X-ray computed tomography (CT) is essential nondestructive internal imaging. Photon-counting computed tomography (PC-CT) acquires X-ray energy information to enable material identification and quantitative density evaluation. Combining PC-CT energy information with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data is expected to provide a novel diagnostic approach to visualize inflammation through tissue water fraction estimation. We developed a PC-CT system combining high-speed scintillators (YGAG:Ce) and silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), specifically utilizing multi-pixel photon counters, MPPCs, which are optical semiconductor devices. This study evaluated healthy and fatty liver rat models (fed a high-fat diet for two or four weeks). Liver fat fractions, estimated from energy-dependent linear attenuation coefficients, showed good agreement with MRI and pathological results. Furthermore, we performed a detailed pathological evaluation focusing on inflammation induced changes in tissue water content. By integrating high reliability MRI fat fraction data with PC-CT data, we improved the estimation accuracy of water content and quantitatively visualized tissue "water-richness" (edema). Increased water proportions in fatty liver groups suggested inflammation progression. These findings demonstrate that PC-CT is highly valuable for quantitative evaluation of liver disease within a multi-modality imaging approach.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-02-06] Position-, direction- and contrast-dependent measurement of MLEM-reconstructed PET resolution using a 3D-printed cube (#1967)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Schramm (Autores: S. Alvarado Orozco , M. Sevenois , G. Schramm)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] KU Leuven, Department of Imaging and Pathology, Leuven, Belgium [2] UZ Leuven, Division of Nuclear Medicine, Leuven, Belgium
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The reconstructed spatial resolution of a PET image is determined by both intrinsic scanner properties and the chosen reconstruction algorithm. Standard NEMA measurements use point sources reconstructed with FBP and therefore mainly characterize the scanner. They are thus suboptimal for predicting the resolution of images reconstructed with MLEM and point-spread-function modeling, as is common in clinical practice. We propose a 3D-printed resolution cube with an off-center inner compartment which, combined with a mid-acquisition phantom flip and a single reconstruction, produces sharp edges at finite (2:1) contrast along three orthogonal directions. Position-, direction- and contrast-dependent edge and line spread functions (ESFs, LSFs) are then extracted using smoothing-spline fits. As a proof of concept, the method is applied to the NeuroExplorer brain PET system at the isocenter and 10 cm off-center, with and without depth-of-interaction (DOI) modeling. The LSFs are non-Gaussian with pronounced negative side lobes. With DOI, the resolution is approximately 2.5 mm FWHM in all directions at both positions; without DOI it degrades radially to about 4 mm at 10 cm off-center. Notably, differences between finite and infinite contrast are small in most configurations. The method provides a position-, direction- and contrast-dependent characterization of PET resolution from clinically reconstructed images and complements NEMA point-source values for image quality comparison, harmonization and partial volume correction.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-02-07] A Clinically Viable, Scalable Implementation of Monte Carlo Scatter Correction for PET/CT (#2119)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Edelstein (Autores: D. Zeltser , E. Hait-Fraenkel , X. Zhang , M. Edelstein , G. Elkin-Basudo , Y. Mizrachi , Y. Grobshtein)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] GE HealthCare, Molecular Imaging, Haifa, Israel [2] GE HealthCare, Molecular Imaging, Waukesha, Wisconsin, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Monte Carlo scatter correction is well established as a highly accurate approach for scatter estimation in PET/CT imaging. It demonstrates superior robustness compared with model based scatter estimation methods, particularly under extreme variations in activity distribution and in the presence of patient motion, conditions under which model based approaches often produce artifacts. Despite these advantages, Monte Carlo scatter correction is computationally intensive, and does not inherently account for out-of-field scatter. In this work, we address both limitations and propose an implementation suitable for integration into routine clinical workflows. A multi-GPU implementation, as well as parallel processing with efficient data streaming significantly reduce the processing time. To handle out-of-field scatter, we separately handle regions where information about out-of-field distribution is known, and can be used for a highly precise estimation. In regions where out-of-field information is inaccessible, the effect on scatter is approximated by the measured data, while ensuring a smooth transition in which the high-accuracy region governs the final estimate. Our approach is scalable and robust across system designs ranging from a standard axial field-of-view to a long axial field-of-view, each presenting distinct considerations for scatter estimation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method using phantom and clinical data.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-02-08] Evaluation of Motion Correction Methods on the NeuroEXPLORER Using Multi-Tracer Human Data (#2130)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Zhang (Autores: J. Zhang , T. Zeng , Y. Hu , K. Fontaine , T. Volpi , T. Toyonaga , R. E. Carson)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate motion correction is critical for dynamic brain PET, particularly on the high-resolution NeuroEXPLORER (NX), where residual head motion can blur focal targets and bias time-activity curves (TACs). We evaluated multiple motion correction (MC) strategies using 17 multi-tracer human NX PET scans, including no motion correction (NMC), post-reconstruction registration (PRR), registration before attenuation correction (RBA), UMT-based frame-averaged correction (AVG), and UMT-based event-by-event correction (EBE). Performance was assessed using qualitative image comparison and ROI-based residual TAC variability (%SD res ) from 20-70 min. All MC methods reduced %SD res compared with NMC. Across all tracers, subjects, and ROIs, EBE achieved the lowest residual variability (1.40 ± 1.27%), followed by PRR (1.79 ± 1.49%), RBA (1.94 ± 1.64%), AVG (2.01 ± 1.63%), and NMC (4.68 ± 4.26%). Poisson noise-floor analysis further showed that residual motion effects were tracer- and count-statistics-dependent. Overall, UMT-based EBE provided the most effective reduction of residual motion effects in dynamic NX brain PET.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-02-09] SSS Optimised for Monte Carlo Scatter Estimation for PET (#3060)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Reeves (Autores: A. Reeves , S. ZamanPour , S. Noe , S. Arridge , K. Thielemans)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] KU Leuven, Department of Imaging and Pathology, Leuven, Belgium [2] University College London, Institute of Nuclear Medicine and the Hawkes Institute, London, United Kingdom [3] University College London, Department of Medical Physics and Biomedical Engineering, London, United Kingdom [4] University College London, Department of computer science, London, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Recent increases in computational power as well as new tools being more readily available have led to increased interest in Monte Carlo scatter estimation. However, Monte Carlo scatter simulation is still computationally expensive. This is exacerbated by the fact that model-based scatter estimation requires multiple iterations of scatter simulation and image reconstruction. We propose to combine the current clinical standard (analytic single scatter simulation and tail-fitting) with Monte Carlo scatter simulation.

sub_talks.title: [M-LT-02-10] Positron Range Confinement in Preclinical PET/MRI: A Multi-Isotope, Multi-Density Experimental Study (#1930)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Gonzalez-Montoro (Autores: F. Lopez-Berenguer , A. Gonzalez-Montoro , S. Berr , M. Williams , A. J. Gonzalez)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto de Instrumentación para Imagen Molecular (i3M), Centro Mixto CSIC-Universitat Politècnica de València, Valencia, Spain [2] University of Virginia, Department of Radiology and Medical Imaging, Charlottesville, Virginia, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The spatial resolution of PET imaging is fundamentally limited by the positron range, whose extent depends on both the emission energy of the radionuclide and the electron density of the surrounding medium. In integrated PET/MRI systems, the static magnetic field exerts a Lorentz force on the positrons, confining their trajectories in the transverse plane to the main magnetic field, potentially improving image resolution. Two complementary experiments were performed using a dedicated monolithic-crystal based PET insert operated at 0T and inside a 9.4T MRI: capillary line sources embedded in three tissue-equivalent phantoms of increasing density (EPF, PLA, and Rigid10k resin), and a microDerenzo phantom. Both tests were carried out with three positron emitters (¹⁸F, ⁸⁹Zr, and ⁶⁸Ga) eventually use in pre-clinical imaging. The results demonstrate that the magnetic field significantly enhances transverse spatial resolution for high-energy positron emitters in medium- and high-density materials, with FWTM reductions of ~60% for ⁶⁸Ga and ~18% for ⁸⁹Zr, while the axial direction remains largely unaffected. Rod resolvability improved at 9.4T from 1.5 mm to ~1.0 mm and from 1.2 mm to 0.9 mm for ⁶⁸Ga and ⁸⁹Zr, respectively. . These findings highlight the relevance of both positron energy and tissue-equivalent density in determining the magnitude of magnetic-field-induced resolution improvements in preclinical PET/MRI.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-03-01] LUCID: Model-Free High-Rate Photon Counting (#1041)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. Scoullar (Autores: P. Scoullar , C. Mc Lean)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Southern Innovation, Melbourne, Australia
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Conventional photon-counting systems rely on dead-time models [1], [2] that saturate at high flux, introduce systematic bias, and require per-channel calibration that scales poorly to large pixel arrays [3]. We present LUCID (Linear Unbiased Count-rate from Interval Detection), which estimates photon flux by measuring the silence between pulses rather than counting individual arrivals, eliminating dead-time modelling entirely. The method assumes only that photon arrivals follow a Poisson process - a condition satisfied by all common detector types at constant source output - and requires no detector-specific dead-time model. For a Poisson arrival process, the memoryless property of the exponential distribution ensures that gaps exceeding a configurable minimum duration θ_gap retain the full statistical information about the true rate λ, regardless of pile-up below that threshold. The unbiased estimator λ̂ = (N−1)/T_excess requires only two hardware-accumulated quantities - valid gap count N and cumulative excess gap duration T_excess - and a single division. No knowledge of pulse shape, dead-time, or detector material is required. The estimator variance Var(λ̂) ≈ λ²/(N_total·exp(−λθ_gap)) provides closed-form uncertainty quantification with graceful degradation at extreme rates rather than a hard saturation limit. LUCID has been validated from Monte Carlo simulation to commercial deployment, with no per-channel calibration. Simulation demonstrates sub-0.3% RMSE per pixel to 100 Mcps and continued accuracy to 300 Mcps. Eliminating count-rate non-linearity directly improves CT number accuracy, beam-hardening correction, and material decomposition fidelity in photon-counting CT. The architecture requires no high-speed ADC and is suited to FPGA, ASIC, or analogue comparator-integrator realisation [4]. We discuss current work extending the framework toward spectral recovery.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-03-02] Comparison of scintillator and semiconductor based photon counting detectors via a unique, modular, multi-level simulation framework (PC-SIM). (#2811)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 O. L.P. Pickford Scienti (Autores: O. L.P. Pickford Scienti , D. Darambara)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institute of Cancer Research and The Royal Marsden Hospital, Joint Department of Physics, London, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Spectral photon counting is widely seen as a revolution in medical imaging, however applications will be limited by the spectral performance of the x-ray sensor. Primarily these sensors are made of semiconductors such as CdTe, however in recent years there has been growing interest in whether scintillators could be used as an alternative. These materials lack the high energy resolution of the semiconductors, however they are not affected by the extensive low energy tailing seen in small pixelated semiconductor devices. As spectral photon counting is performed with coarse energy bins rather than fine spectral resolution, this raises the question of which factor is more important for spectral fidelity in energy binned tasks: a narrow intrinsic energy resolution (semiconductors) or the absence of charge sharing induced low energy tailing (scintillators)? This work sets out to compare the two sensor types to answer this question. To do this we use a new simulation tool called PC-SIM (Photon Counting Spectral Imaging Model), which is a modular framework, designed for flexible modelling of a range of spectral photon counting scanner designs. We combine this tool with Monte Carlo simulations performed in GATE to quantify the spectral fidelity of scintillator- and semiconductor-based detectors under a range of conditions, including various numbers of energy bins, pixel sizes, and differing beam spectra (polychromatic and monochromatic sources). This presentation will introduce PC-SIM, outlining its design philosophy, module options and how it was used to compare the scintillator and semiconductor systems as fairly as possible. Results will show under what conditions scintillators might provide comparable photon-counting performance compared with the current gold standard of semiconductor based detectors, but at a cheaper price-point. Limitations and assumptions of this work will be discussed, along with implications of the results.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-03-03] Single Energy Material Decomposition via X-ray Grating Interferometry (#1679)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Men (Autores: L. Men , P. Guo , J. Lu , L. Zhang , Z. Wang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We propose single-energy material decomposition (SEMD), a method that achieves quantitative basis material imaging from a single X-ray grating interferometry (XGI) acquisition without dual-energy scans. XGI inherently provides two independent spectra from a single acquisition, yielding the spectral separation required for material decomposition. SEMD is particularly valuable for dark-field CT, enabling material decomposition directly from the existing acquisition without requiring dual-energy hardware, greatly enhancing the clinical utility of these systems. Experimental results demonstrate that SEMD achieves decomposition accuracy comparable to conventional dual-energy material decomposition (DEMD), providing absorption, dark-field, and basis material images simultaneously from a single scan.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-03-04] Performance Evaluation of Low-Dose 3D Small-Animal Imaging Using YSO/SiPM-Based Photon-Counting CT (#2872)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Zheng (Autores: L. Pan , R. Zheng , D. Xi , Q. Hong , P. Xiao , Q. Xie)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Science and Technology of China, Department of Electronic Engineering and Information Science, Hefei, China [2] Hefei Comprehensive National Science Center, Institute of Artificial Intelligence, Hefei, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Photon-counting computed tomography (PC-CT) shows remarkable potential in low-dose spectral imaging by binning X-ray photons into discrete energy windows. This study presents a novel PC-CT system integrating scintillation detectors and multi-voltage threshold (MVT) digitizers, extends its application to 3D in vivo spectral imaging, and specifically evaluates the low-dose imaging performance. Validation results show that the system achieves a detection efficiency of 94.78%, a dark count rate of 0.08 cps/pixel, and a peak count rate of 0.85 Mcps/pixel. Dosimetric evaluations at 120 kVp reveal a central CTDI 100 of 0.15-0.375 mGy, yielding a dose-normalized figure of merit (FOM) nearly tenfold higher than that of conventional micro-CT. Furthermore, in vivo experiments validate the system's capability for high-fidelity 3D material decomposition, even under photon-starved conditions. These results substantiate the potential of the YSO/SiPM-based PC-CT system for precise in vivo material decomposition at low radiation doses.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-03-05] Photon-Counting Spectral Dark-Field Micro-CT for Enhanced Tooth Microcrack Detection (#3183)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Q. Ma (Autores: Q. Ma , J. Lu , S. Peng , Y. Bai , L. Men , L. Zhang , Z. Wang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [2] Tsinghua University, School of Clinical Medicine, Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Conventional absorption-based dental CT often fails to detect early tooth microcracks due to limited resolution and attenuation contrast. While X-ray dark-field imaging is highly sensitive to sub-pixel structures, traditional systems lack spectral capabilities. To address this, our study utilized a photon-counting grating-interferometry micro-CT system to perform energy-resolved CT imaging of an ex vivo human tooth. Using a 4.8 μm Talbot-Lau interferometer and dual-threshold detection (15 and 30 keV), absorption and dark-field signals were acquired across total-energy (TE), low-energy (LE), and high-energy (HE) channels. Results confirm the complementary nature of the two modalities: absorption imaging better differentiates enamel and dentin, whereas dark-field imaging reveals microcracks with significantly higher conspicuity. Regarding spectral performance, although increasing energy leads to higher overall image noise and decreased clarity (LE > TE > HE), microcrack contrast exhibits the exact opposite trend (HE > LE > TE), peaking in the HE channel with the maximum crack contrast. These findings highlight the advantages of photon-counting spectral dark-field micro-CT for highly sensitive dental crack detection.
