sub_talks.title: [MIC-03-06] ePixUHR-100k: A 100 kfps Full-Frame Imager for the LCLS X-Ray FEL Upgrade (#1812)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Pena-Perez (Autores: L. Rota , A. Pena-Perez , B. Markovic , A. Gupta , H. Hernandez-Herrera , G. Liu , P. King , H. Kim , M. Hammer , H. Shi , A. Miceli , A. Dragone)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] SLAC National Lab - Stanford University, TID-Instrumentation Division, Menlo Park, California, United States of America [2] Argonne National Laboratory, X-ray Science Division of the Advanced Photon Source, Lemont, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Next-generation X-ray sources, including 4th-generation synchrotrons and Free-Electron Lasers (FELs) such as LCLS-II, deliver photon rates that saturate conventional photon-counting detectors. ePixUHR-100k addresses this gap with a hybrid X-ray imager providing continuous 100 kfps readout with 104 dB dynamic range and single-photon sensitivity down to 2 keV, capturing single photon and > 1000-photon events with low cross-talk. Power-and area-efficient SAR A/D converters distributed across the pixel matrix enable massively parallel digitization, while a charge-integrating front-end with auto-gain switching sustains fluxes beyond 109 photons/s/pixel. Fabricated in a 130 nm CMOS process, the full-reticle 19.4 × 18.0 mm^2 ASIC is bump-bonded to a 144 × 192 pixel Si sensor and achieves 123 e- RMS noise. Validation of a prototype camera system with a 109Cd radioactive source and at the LCLS X-ray FEL confirms state-of-the-art continuous frame-rate and power-efficiency performance among reported X-ray detectors, including SPAD-based designs. Full ASIC architecture, A/D converter characterization, dynamic range evaluation, gain-switching performance, and comparison with state-of-the-art detectors will be presented at the conference. Scalability toward large-area X-ray cameras will also be discussed through tiled 2 × 2 and 2 × 3 ASIC configurations bump-bonded to large-format Si sensors, enabling systems from 0.5 to 16 Mpixels.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-03-07] Inverse Analysis of Pulse Pile-Up and Charge Sharing in Photon-Counting Detectors (#1582)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Sawada (Autores: R. Sawada , K. Taguchi , K. Amaya)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institute of Science Tokyo, Department of Systems and Control Engineering, Otaku, Japan [2] Johns Hopkins University, Department of Radiology and Radiological Science, Baltimore, Maryland, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Photon-counting detectors offer high spatial resolution and energy discrimination for advanced X-ray imaging. However, their performance is limited due to pulse pile-up and charge sharing, which distort the observed current waveforms. In this study, we propose a Bayesian inverse analysis framework to estimate photon events directly from observed current waveforms. The detector response is modeled by the drift-diffusion equation. Photon events are parameterized by their energy, arrival time, and interaction position. The event parameters are estimated using Bayesian inference. Prior probability distributions of the number of events and interaction depths are incorporated to obtain physically plausible solutions. Numerical simulation results demonstrated that the proposed method accurately estimated photon events under pulse pile-up and charge sharing conditions. Furthermore, the reconstructed energy spectra showed reduced distortion compared with the conventional method.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-03-08] Towards the first ToF-CT X-ray image: acquisition and scatter correction (#1314)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Belanger (Autores: G. Belanger , G. Lemaire , J. Rossignol , Y. Bérubé-Lauzière , A. Corbeil Therrien , M.-A. Tétrault , R. Fontaine)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universite de Sherbrooke, Electrical and computer engineering, Sherbooke, Québec, Canada [2] Universite de Sherbrooke, Institut Interdisciplinaire d'Innovation Technologique (3IT), Sherbrooke, Québec, Canada
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract All components of a first Time-of-flight CT scanner prototype are now assembled at Université de Sherbrooke where both timing and energy measurements enabled to create first line profiles. Previous simulation studies have shown that, by using these measurements, the contribution of scattered photons to an image can be estimated and removed without an using anti-scatter grid. The scanner prototype can now explore and confirm the measurement and scatter correction methods used in simulation studies. The experimental setup is composed of a scintillator coupled to an SiPM readout and a Weerock front end board. This board includes a Radioroc ASIC along with a picoTDC. An FPGA harvest data and send them to a PC for signal processing. From these data, primary and scatter counts in each pixel can be recovered through the use of an iterative deconvolution algorithm. The experiment successfully produced a small photon counting projection image of an ACR phantom and produced time-of-flight distribution measurements for each pixel with around 550~ps FWHM resolution for the full energy spectrum (30 to 120 keV). Scatter correction lead to a contrast resolution improvement of 195\% in the irradiated bone-water region of the phantom. Its accuracy was partially validated with an analytical calculation of the X-ray's penetration through a part of the phantom with a 5.2\% penetration calculated, and a 10.8\% and 5.7\% penetration before and after scatter correction respectively.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-04-01] Single-Source Cross-Tracer Brain PET Attenuation Correction via Anchored Flow Matching with Attenuation Maps from Simultaneous Reconstruction (#1516)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M.J. Cho (Autores: M.J. Cho , S.K. Kang , J.S. Lee)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Seoul National University, Interdisciplinary Program of Bioengineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] Seoul National University, Integrated Major in Innovative Medical Science, Seoul, Republic of Korea [3] Samsung Ventures, Seoul, Republic of Korea [4] Seoul National University, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea [5] Brightonix Imaging Inc., Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate attenuation correction (AC) is essential for quantitative PET imaging, but CT-free AC across diverse radiotracers remains challenging. MLAA-derived μ-maps are useful inputs for deep learning-based AC. However, tracer-dependent biodistribution introduces domain shifts that limit the generalizability of models trained only on ¹⁸F-FDG. We propose a single-source cross-tracer CT-free AC framework that combines tracer-robust U-Net regression with anchored flow matching. Local Gamma Field augmentation is used during U-Net training to mimic anatomy-preserving regional intensity and contrast variations in MLAA μ -maps, encouraging tracer-independent MLAA-to-CT mapping. The U-Net output is then used as an anchor for an unconditional flow-matching model trained on CT μ -maps, enabling generative refinement from a reliable deterministic estimate. The proposed method achieved the highest PSNR across all evaluated tracers and reduced MLAA noise, tracer-specific artifacts, and U-Net over-smoothing. AC PET analysis showed strong agreement with CT-based AC PET, with regional uptake correlations closest to the identity line. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework enables accurate and structurally faithful μ -map estimation across multiple tracers using only FDG training data.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-04-02] High-Energy Penetration Correction in Multi-Aperture SPECT Using Aperture-Plate Ray Decomposition (#1606)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Li (Autores: Y. Li , Q. Wang , L. He , H. Li)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] United Imaging Healthcare North America, MI, Houston, Texas, United States of America [2] United Imaging Healthcare, MI, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Multi-aperture single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) at 131I (364 keV) exhibits a detector-wide plate-penetration halo: a 1.8 cm tungsten plate transmits ~4 × 10−4 at μW = 4.4 cm−1. Prior corrections perform the aperture/plate split at the photon level via effective-radius point-spread function enlargement, or at the system-matrix level via per-ray full-physics tracing; both merge the two components at storage time, inflating memory by one to two orders of magnitude. We propose a storage-agnostic per-ray partition: a topological rule on the source-to-detector intersection list separates the response into a sparse, peaked aperture component A and a slowly varying plate halo B, upstream of any representation choice. The rule is mutually exclusive and jointly exhaustive, so Aij + Bij = Cij holds bit-exactly against the unsplit baseline for any per-ray contribution functional; the plate path length is a closed-form slab chord minus an analytic aperture chord at O(Nap) per ray. On a 34-module multi-aperture SPECT ring (small-aperture configuration), the identity holds bit-exactly across three projection modes (collimator-path, sensitivity, counts) for a centered single-photon source and across every pixel of 34 Jaszczak hot-rod 131I views, with per-pixel plate intensity ~10−4–10−3 of the aperture peak. OSEM correction with a lagged plate estimate will be presented at the conference.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-04-03] Improving Lutetium Background Radiation-based Attenuation Correction for CT-less PET Using Singles-derived Randoms (#2103)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Dai (Autores: B. Dai , S. C. Moore , M. E. Daube-Witherspoon , F. M. Muller , J. S. Karp)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Pennsylvania, Department of Radiology, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States of America [2] Ghent University, Faculty of Engineering and Architecture, Ghent, Belgium
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Lutetium background radiation in modern PET scanners enables activity- and tracer-independent transmission measurement for attenuation correction (AC) without CT scans. However, quantitative accuracy of attenuation maps (µ-maps) derived from lutetium transmission (Lu-Tx) is limited by low transmission statistics and noisy randoms estimation from delayed coincidences (DE). In this work, we investigate the use of singles-derived randoms (RS) to improve Lu-Tx-based AC for CT-less PET. Emission and Lu-Tx data were acquired simultaneously on the PennPET Explorer, a 142-cm long axial field-of-view (LAFOV) scanner. µ-maps were reconstructed using maximum-likelihood transmission reconstruction with randoms estimated from either delayed coincidences or singles data, then used for attenuation and scatter correction during PET image reconstruction. The methods were evaluated using physical phantoms, including uniform cylinders, a 190-cm pipe phantom, cylinders with non-uniform axial activity distributions, and an image quality (IQ) phantom. Data were subsampled to simulate low-count short clinical scans. RS produced substantially smoother sinograms while maintaining agreement with DE in total randoms counts. Incorporation of RS improved axial uniformity, reduced noise, and mitigated emission contamination-induced bias in µ-maps, particularly under low-count conditions and non-uniform activity distributions. In IQ phantom studies, AC PET images reconstructed using RS demonstrated contrast comparable to CT-AC PET, whereas DE led to reduced contrast and increased bias, especially for short scans. These results demonstrate that RS improves the quantitative accuracy of Lu-Tx-based AC and support the proposed method as a practical pathway towards CT-less PET for both long dynamic imaging and short clinical scans.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-04-04] Estimation of random events in PET imaging using the time differences of uncorrelated singles (#2578)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Toussaint (Autores: M. Toussaint , T. Carlier , S. Stute)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Nantes Université, Laboratoire CRCI2NA, INSERM, CNRS, Nantes, France [2] Nantes University Hospital, Nuclear Medicine Department, Nantes, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Correction of random coincidences is required in clinical PET imaging. Several methods have been proposed to estimate their distributions in a PET acquisition and they mostly use singles detection and/or a delayed coincidence window (DCW). We propose a new approach to achieve this task, which uses the differences in arrival times between consecutive single events that are greater than the coincidence window. This approach is thus less susceptible to bias induced by true coincidences and has more statistics than a DCW. As a proof of concept, a first implementation of this approach was compared to the classic methods using simulations from a small-sized PET scanner. The acquisition of four phantoms, each with different challenges in terms of randoms estimation, were simulated over a range of activities. Overall, the proposed method was less biased than the classical methods while also being more precise than DCW.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-04-05] Quantitative Activities Evaluation of Ac-225 and Daughter Nuclides Using the Alpha-SPECT Mini System (#3094)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Du (Autores: W. Zhao , X. Luo , L.-J. Meng , Y. Du)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, Maryland, United States of America [2] University of Illinois at Urbana and Champaign , Champaign Il, Champaign, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Alpha-SPECT Mini system integrates SPECT imaging with CT-based attenuation correction, providing a platform for quantifying in vivo distributions of alpha-emitting radiopharmaceuticals and daughter radionuclides. In this study, three Ac-225 filled syringes with different volumes, 0.5, 4.2, and 18.0 mL, respectively, were scanned with Alpha-SPECT Mini. The ground truth activities were[YD1] 26.12 µCi, 21.62 µCi, and 18.80 µCi from the smallest to the largest syringe, respectively. SPECT listmode acquisition was performed for 20 minutes for each syringe, together with an 80 kV CT scan for attenuation correction. SPECT images were reconstructed for the following photopeaks: 100 keV for Ac-225, 218 keV for Fr-221, 440 keV for Bi-213, and 117 keV for Tl-209. Activities of Ac-225 and these daughter radionuclides, were then estimated from SPECT images using CT defined ROIs and compared with ground truth. The results showed that quantification accuracy varied with the radionuclides and syringe sizes. Fr-221 and Bi-213 showed relatively lower errors (<5%), while Ac-225 and Tl-209 exhibited larger deviations. The higher errors likely due to the low abundance of low energy (100 keV for Ac-225 and 117 keV for Tl-209) photopeaks and interference from downscatter and collimator penetration from high energy photons. Tl-209 also exhibited larger deviations with a size-dependent trend, suggesting sensitivity to source geometry and scatter correction. Overall, the Alpha-SPECT Mini system showed potential for quantitative imaging of Ac-225 and daughter radionuclides. Future work includes further calibration and implementation of scatter correction.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-04-06] Physics-Driven Methods for Standardizing Radiomics Features in CT Data (#2771)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. W. Stayman (Autores: H. Din , Y. Yuan , G. H. Kim , M. F. McNitt-Gray , J. W. Stayman , G. J. Gang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Pennsylvania, Radiology, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States of America [2] Johns Hopkins University, Biomedical Engineering, Baltimore, Maryland, United States of America [3] University of California, Los Angeles, Radiology, Los Angeles, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Radiomics have demonstrated potential in numerous clinical applications. However, feature variability resulting from different scanner hardware and image processing degrades predictive ability and reduces model generalizability. We present a novel physics-driven framework for radiomics standardization. Assuming a linear, shift-invariant image formation model, we developed an analytical method to remove the dependency of radiomics features classes on known spatial resolution and noise properties. The method consists of two deconvolution operations: deconvolving the system blur from the reconstructed image, then deconvolving the noise probability density function from radiomics feature distributions. This approach is applicable to multiple feature classes. We further developed a workflow to implement this framework on a clinical CT scanner. The method was evaluated on an anthropomorphic lung phantom imaged at five dose levels and reconstructed using eight kernels. Results demonstrate that the standardization method effectively improves the consistency of radiomics features value with those at reference imaging conditions. As expected, standardizing from smoother kernels to sharp kernels is more challenging than the reverse. The proposed standardization method is a promising tool for improving the robustness and generalizability of radiomics models.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-04-07] Uncertainty estimation for 123 I-DaTSCAN (#2802)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. M. Ferreira (Autores: K. M. Ferreira , A. P. Robinson , K. M. Bradley , D. R. McGowan)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Department of Medical Physics and Clinical Engineering, Oxford, United Kingdom [2] National Physical Laboratory (NPL), Teddington, United Kingdom [3] University of Oxford, Department of Oncology, Oxford, United Kingdom [4] University Hospital of Wales, Wales Research and Diagnostic Positron Emission Tomography Imaging Centre (PETIC), Wales, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract 123 I-DaTSCAN is used to aid diagnosis of Parkinsonism. Visual analysis of 123 I-DaTSCAN is used in conjunction with patient clinical history and semi-quantification. Specific Binding Ratios (SBR) are commonly estimated for the right and left putamen and caudate using commercially available software. The estimation of uncertainties is not common for this clinical study; however, the benefits of estimating uncertainties have been recognised for other clinical applications. In this work, a method to evaluate the uncertainty associated with SBR is developed using phantom data and then applied to estimate uncertainties for imaging data from a cohort of patients. List mode data was acquired and bootstrapped to create equivalent sinograms. The sinograms were reconstructed and processed using BRASS software to obtain the distribution of SBR and respective standard deviations were estimated. The impact of estimating uncertainties in patient classification is also considered. For the patient data, the estimated standard uncertainties varied between 2.8 % and 19 %. The correlation of SBR uncertainty with patient classification within the cohort is presented. Initial analysis suggests the patient classification does not change when considering uncertainty, but does provide confidence in the results. This is the first time that uncertainties on SBR values are used to evaluate impact on patient classification. Future work will include analysing additional patient data to further investigate the impact of uncertainties in patient classification. Analysis to understand if the uncertainties can be reduced is also planned.

sub_talks.title: [MIC-04-08] Towards Absolute Resolution Characterization in OSEM Reconstructed Images without Ground Truth: Using FBP Reconstructed Images as the Bridge (#2809)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Hu (Autores: Y. Hu , L. Guo , T. Mulnix , T. Marin , R. E. Carson)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yale University, Department of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging, New Haven, Connecticut, United States of America [2] Yale University, Department of Biomedical Engineering, New Haven, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Absolute resolution characterization of OSEM-reconstructed images is challenging because the OSEM algorithm is nonlinear and its resolution strongly depends on the activity distribution and the number of iterations. In contrast, the linear FBP algorithm provides a more consistent resolution, albeit with higher noise. In this work, we propose using FBP-reconstructed images as a bridge to estimate the absolute resolution of OSEM images without requiring ground truth. Two FBP-bridge approaches are investigated: an image-domain Gaussian fitting method and a frequency-domain modulation transfer function (MTF) ratio method. Hoffman phantom experimental results show that the Gaussian fitting approach has better agreement with the reference FWHM obtained using the known phantom ground truth. Both methods are further applied to human brain PET scans. This method also allows pixel-wise visualization of spatially variant image resolution. Future work will investigate the effects of noise and FBP filter selection.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-14-01] ToRA : a 64-channel ASIC for the readout of gaseous detectors in a CMOS 65 nm technology (#1949)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Mazza (Autores: G. Mazza , M. Alexeev , O. Denisov , L. Marcellino , C. Alice , M. Mignone , R. J. Wheadon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] INFN - Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Torino, Torino, Italy [2] Università di Torino, Dipartimento di Fisica, Torino, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract ToRA is a 64 channel ASIC for the readout of gaseous detectors used in high energy physics experiments. Its driving application is the readout of the MicroMega detectors for the AMBER experiment upgrade. However, it is designed to be highly flexible in order to be used also for other types of gaseous detectors, e.g. straw detectors. Each ToRA channel provides programmable signal amplification and shaping. The ASIC provides the time measurement of the time of arrival, the time over threshold and the peak position of the shaper signal. Moreover, the peak value is hold and converted with a single ramp ADC. A fully digital interface, based on differential serial links and including a data and a control interface, has been implemented. The events are packed into 32-bit words and transmitted over two 200 Mb/s links.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-14-02] CHASER: A Charge Sensitive Amplifier and Sampling Circuit for CZT Detectors (#1963)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Bernardini (Autores: L. Bernardini , S. Formenti , A. Ciavarella-Ciavarella , G. Borghi , C. Fiorini , M. Carminati)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Politecnico di Milano, Dipartimento di Elettronica, Informazione e Bioingegneria, Milan, Italy [2] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Milano, Milan, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents an 8-channel ASIC designed in 180 nm CMOS technology for γ-ray spectroscopy as part of the EU-funded project i-RASE. i-RASE aims at developing a novel generation of radiation detectors capable of performing real-time processing by adopting artificial neural networks (ANN) to reconstruct energy, position, and timing of incoming photons. The ASIC is specifically tailored for room temperature detectors, featuring large detector capacitance (up to 50 pF), like CdZnTe. It includes dual-polarity charge sensitive amplifiers (CSA) with pulsed-reset and leakage current compensation (LCC), sample-and-hold circuitry controlled by a digital logic shared among the channels, and both single-ended and differential output architectures. Two readout modes are supported: a continuous mode, compatible with conventional analog and digital readout and shaping chains, and a high-speed sampling mode, in which a switched capacitor array (SCA) continuously samples the analog output of the CSA at frequencies up to 100 MHz. The samples are stored in 256 capacitors and subsequently buffered to an external differential ADC, triggered by the ASIC event thresholds, and controlled by the FPGA running the ANN. The preliminary results of the ASIC characterization (rise time of 100 ns, linearity of 0.5%), performed by injecting test signals, are presented and match simulations.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-14-03] Design and Experimental Characterization of a 65 nm CMOS Readout Channel for the Si(Li) Tracker Upgrade of the GAPS Experiment (#2371)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Ghislotti (Autores: L. Ghislotti , P. Lazzaroni , M. Manghisoni , L. Ratti , V. Re , E. Riceputi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] INFN, Sezione di Pavia, Pavia, Italy [2] Università degli Studi di Bergamo, Dipartimento di Ingegneria e Scienze Applicate, Dalmine, Italy [3] Università di Pavia, Dipartimento di Ingegneria Industriale e dell'Informazione, Pavia, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents the design and experimental characterization of a prototype channel developed in a 65 nm CMOS process for the readout of the large-area lithium-drifted silicon detectors of the General Antiparticle Spectrometer tracker. To simultaneously achieve high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy below 100 keV and a wide dynamic range up to 100 MeV, the charge-sensitive amplifier employs a dynamic-threshold MOS feedback capacitor exploiting dynamic signal compression. An enhanced Krummenacher network provides continuous feedback discharge, compensating detector leakage currents up to 200 nA. Experimental results demonstrate an energy resolution of 3.2 keV full width at half maximum (379 e⁻ rms equivalent noise charge) and an integral nonlinearity below 1.5%. A compensation technique to mitigate temperature-induced variations in the charge-sensitive amplifier response is also presented.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Macchiarulo (Autores: L. Macchiarulo , I. Mostafanezhad , E. Forsythe , G. Uehara , S. Mazza , J. Ott , K. Hoe , C. Chock)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Nalu Scientific, LLC, HONOLULU, Hawaii, United States of America [2] University of California, Santa Cruz, Santa Cruz Institute for Particle Physics (SCIPP), Santa Cruz, California, United States of America [3] University of Hawaii at Manoa, Electrical and Computer Engineering Department, Honolulu, Hawaii, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present the first measurements for the third revision of the High Pitch digitizer System-on-Chip (HPSoC), a 9 channel Readout Integrated Circuit (ROIC) prototype. The HPSoC concept is that of a high channel density and scalable waveform digitization ROIC with an embedded interface to advanced high-speed sensor arrays such as e.g. AC-LGADs. The chip was fabricated in 65nm technology and targets picosecond-level timing resolution via high speed waveform sampling (in excess of 10 Gsps), autonomous chip triggering and feature extraction. In this paper, we present the results of testing of the chip's timing generation and digitization.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-14-05] Cryogenic MOSFET Modeling Applied to CSA Design for Germanium Detector Readout (#2571)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Georgeous (Autores: J. Georgeous , C. Fiorini , F. Chiesa , A. Ciavarella-Ciavarella , M. Carminati , G. Borghi , M. Willers , S. Mertens)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Politecnico di Milano, Department of Information Technology, Milano, Italy [2] Technical University of Munich, Munich, Germany [3] Max Planck Institute for Nuclear Physics, Heidelberg, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The LEGEND (Large Enriched Germanium Exper iment for Neutrinoless double beta Decay) experiment aims to detect neutrinoless double beta decay (0νββ) in 76Ge using large scale cryogenic germanium detectors. A 0.35µm LUIGI ASIC was designed as a detector readout, ensuring low noise and high radiopurity conditions. Such front-end ASIC, when assembled to the Ge detector, must operate at cryogenic temperatures, typically 87 K using liquid argon (LAr). At cryogenic temperatures, semiconductor characteristics shift significantly, while standard transistor models, typically validated only to −55◦C (218.15 K), become inaccurate. therefore, this work presents a workflow for cryogenic MOSFET modeling based on BSIM4, using experimen tal data measured at 77 K. The model is extracted from mea surements at both room and cryogenic temperatures, validated with corresponding Cadence models at room temperature, and is then used to assess the impact of cryogenic effects on analog circuit performance. Further experimental characterization on a new set of transistors will be made is required to refine and improve the accuracy of the model.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-14-06] A Deep-Cryogenic CMOS Temperature Sensor Based on Threshold-Voltage Extractor (#1495)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Zhang (Autores: L. Zhang , S. Yang , X. Wang , F. Liang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Science and Technology of China, school of physical sciences, Hefei, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract On-chip thermometry is vital in cryogenic circuit systems implemented in the temperature of liquid nitrogen or even liquid helium, such as superconducting cubit controllers and astronomical detectors. As transistor density increases, the power consumption of the chip may induce localized overheating, leading to device failure. Typical CMOS temperature sensors can be mainly categorized as BJT-based, resistor-based, and MOSFET-based. Most of them are unable to work below 50 K, which is necessary for deployment in superconducting quantum control systems. Meanwhile, experiments have shown that the threshold voltage of a PMOS transistor exhibits a linear temperature dependence due to the Fermi potential, and this PTAT characteristic becomes even more sensitive as the temperature decreases into the deep-cryogenic region. In this paper, we present a deep cryogenic CMOS temperature sensor based on the threshold voltage of a PMOS transistor. We use a threshold voltage extractor circuit to monitor the targeted transistor and output its threshold voltage. Then the threshold voltage is transformed into current and fed into a integrator that operates on a capacitor charge-discharge cycle, producing a square-wave signal whose frequency is temperature-dependent. Subsequently, a counter is used to digitize the temperature by measuring this frequency. This article describes a deep cryogenic temperature sensor in 28-nm CMOS technology with an area of 0.05 mm 2 . With an output resolution of 0.1 K from 233 K to 398 K, it consumes 48.1 µW at 1.8 V at 233 K.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-14-07] A Fully Charge-Pump-Based Powering Scheme for SDDs in 180 nm SOI Technology (#1836)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Michel (Autores: T. Michel , P. Iskra , F. Wiest , W. Buttler , L. Maurer)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of the Bundeswehr Munich, Institute for Integrated Systems, Neubiberg, Bavaria, Germany [2] KETEK GmbH, Munich, Bavaria, Germany [3] KETEK GmbH, Munich, Bavaria, Germany [4] Ingenieurbüro Werner Buttler, Essen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [5] University of the Bundeswehr Munich, Institute for Integrated Systems, Neubiberg, Bavaria, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract X-ray fluorescence analysis is a fast, non-destructive technique for material characterization and recycling, where silicon drift detector-based systems provide high energy resolution. Portable applications require a high integration density, while conventional state of the art solutions depend on external highvoltage electronics occupying more than 250 mm 2 . To address this challenge, this work presents an application-specific integrated circuit fabricated in 180 nm silicon-on-insulator technology that generates all negative high voltages required for silicon drift detector operation in the range from -20 V to -130 V. Each voltage supply is implemented using a CMOS DC/DC converter based on a Pelliconi charge pump. The employed topology utilizes low-voltage transistors and a simple two-phase clock scheme driven by a ring oscillator at 10 MHz, enabling high efficiency while reducing chip area. The stability, noise, and spectral performance of a silicon drift detector operated with the proposed charge-pump-based supply is compared to those obtained with a conventional power supply. The results show that operation of a silicon drift detector module using an external ASIC-based charge pump is possible with high energy resolution for peaking times exceeding 1 μs, provided that the generated voltages are sufficiently smoothed using external capacitors. These results facilitate the development of more compact and cost-effective silicon drift detector power supply solutions.

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Analog Spectral Imager for X-rays (ASIX) is a technology demonstrator for a Hybrid Pixel Detector (HPD) aimed at delivering high-resolution measurements in both spatial and energy domains, thus enabling advanced X-ray spectral imaging. ASIX features 50~$\mu$m pixels arranged into a hexagonal array. An in-pixel ultra-low noise front-end (<30 ENC at Cd=100 fF), together with a self-triggering logic, and a highly segmented readout, enables precise identification of the charge clusters on a photon-by-photon basis. The readout architecture is based on regions. Each region comprises a 16 X 8 pixel matrix and dedicated readout electronics including a compact 10-bit SAR ADC, a data-out FIFO and the readout-controller sequencing logic. The full demonstrator chip will be composed of a 6 X 12 array of regions, corresponding to a 96 X 96 pixel matrix, together with a digital output logic responsible for collecting, formatting and serializing data. We developed a 2 X 2 mm^2 prototype readout chip in a commercial 65 nm CMOS process featuring a fully functional region. Given its 4-side abuttable layout and its almost exclusively digital interfaces, this can be regarded as the main building block for readout matrices in larger-scale ASICs such as the future full-scale demonstrator.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-15-01] Improving the Estimation Accuracy of the Inverse Estimation of the Radioactive Source Distribution at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station Using L2 Normalization (#1751)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Tateishi (Autores: D. Tateishi , M. Machida , S. Yamada , Y. Terasaka , Y. Sato , Y. Ichiba)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Japan Atomic Energy Agency, Fukushima Research and Engineering Institute, Collaborative Laboratories for Advanced Decommissioning Science, Radiation Sensing and Digitization Group, Naraha-machi, Futaba-gun, Fukushima, Japan [2] Japan Atomic Energy Agency, Fukushima Research and Engineering Institute, Naraha Center for Remote Control Technology Development, Facility Use Promotion and Technology Section, Naraha-machi, Futaba-gun, Fukushima, Japan [3] Japan Atomic Energy Agency, Center for Computational Science and e-Systems, Wakashiba, Kashiwa, Chiba, Japan [4] Tokyo Electric Power Company Holdings, Fukushima Daiichi Decontamination and Decommissioning Engineering Company, Ohkuma, Fukushima, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract To ensure the safe decommissioning of the reactor buildings at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station, it is essential to reduce the external exposure of workers. In order to achieve this objective, it is necessary to accurately estimate the distribution of contamination density - the primary source of external exposure - and to evaluate dose rates in each working space within R/Bs with high precision. 3D Air Dose Rate Evaluation System -Indoor (3D-AI) estimates distributions of contamination density and dose rate in the working space using dose-rate data and point clouds via LASSO regression. In this work, we introduce an L2-normalization method that balances each source's contribution to measurement points to improve sensitivity to remote contaminations. To test the ability of this method, we analyzed data measured near the startup transformer of the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station Unit 3 and compared them with maps estimated by the Compton camera. Results show that both conventional and new systems estimated contamination distributions and dose rates with high accuracy near the measurement points. In contrast, in areas distant from measurement points, the new method better matches the Compton images and improves surface dose-rate estimates, reducing the ~1/50 underestimation to within a few factors.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-15-02] Template-Based Decomposition of Gamma Spectra for NORM Quantification (#2804)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Davolio (Autores: M. Morichi , B. Angelucci , F. Davolio , C. Del Bene , E. Fanchini , P. Garosi , C. Uguccioni)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CAEN S.p.A., Viareggio, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This paper describes a template-based gamma spectral decomposition algorithm developed for quantitative analysis of Naturally Occurring Radioactive Material (NORM). The method uses a Monte Carlo-simulated template to decompose measured spectra into contributions from the 40K, and the 238U and 232Th decay chains, and to estimate the corresponding absorbed dose rates. The algorithm is integrated into the CAEN Gamon-Drone platform and supports both CeBr 3 and NaI(Tl) scintillation detectors. The proposed approach addresses two operational scenarios. In airborne surveys, dynamic integration and spectral reweighting are applied to continuously acquired spectra to reduce statistical fluctuations. This processing improves detection sensitivity and allows for high-resolution radiological mapping. In ground-based measurements, the same analytical framework provides rapid in situ characterization of soils, rocks, and construction materials through direct estimation of radionuclide concentrations. Validation tests showed strong consistency between reconstructed activities and reference values for multiple detector configurations and environmental conditions. The results demonstrate that Monte Carlo template decomposition can provide accurate and robust NORM quantification using compact scintillation-based gamma spectroscopy systems.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-15-03] Enhancing Low-Energy MVT Bi-exponential Convergence via Adaptive Initial Value Estimation (#2818)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Xu (Autores: B. Xu , H. Lan , Q. Xie)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Science and Technology of China, Department of Electronic Engineering and Information Science, Hefei, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Multi-Voltage Threshold (MVT) technology, serving as an advanced method for scintillation pulse digitization, achieves pulse waveform reconstruction and energy calculation in PET systems through a bi-exponential model. However, with the gradual application of crystal miniaturization and 1:1:1 readout technologies, the fitting of low-energy pulses faces severe convergence challenges. This leads to a large number of pulses being discarded, which severely restricts system sensitivity. To address this issue, this paper proposes an effective initial value estimation method. Experiments were conducted using four-threshold MVT sampling and bi-exponential fitting, utilizing the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of the fitted waveforms, the proportion of severe deviations, the absolute mean of the pulse area relative error, and the standard deviation as evaluation metrics. Results on low-energy band pulses (40-150 keV) indicate that after utilizing the proposed initial value estimation method, the waveform RMSE was effectively restricted, and the three relative area error metrics were improved by 61.5%, 105.8, and 341.0, respectively, thereby significantly reducing fitting convergence failures.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-15-04] Dual-Modality Muon Imaging via Trigger Optimization and Image Fusion (#2927)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Zhou (Autores: Z. Zhou , J. Zhang , Y. Zhang , Y. Wu , X. Zhao , L. Wang , W. Ding , N. Su , Z. Yin , Y. Huang , J. Cheng , Y. Liu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Normal University, School of Physics and Astronomy, Beijing, China [2] Beijing Normal University, Joint Laboratory of Jinping Ultra-low Radiation Background Measurement of Ministry of Ecology and Environment, Beijing, China [3] Jinping Deep Underground Frontier Science and Dark Matter Key Laboratory of Sichuan Province, Jinping, China [4] Beijing Normal University, Key Laboratory of Beam Technology of Ministry of Education, Beijing, China [5] Chengdu University of Technology, College of Nuclear Technology and Automation Engineering, Chengdu, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Muon scattering imaging (MSI) is sensitive to high-Z materials; however, the inherently low cosmic muon flux usually requires long acquisition times to achieve acceptable image quality. To address this limitation, we propose a statistically enhanced dual-modality muon imaging framework based on trigger redesign in a muon scattering tomography system consisting of 8 detector layers. By relaxing the conventional strict coincidence requirement and redesigning the event selection logic, previously discarded non-penetrating muon events can be effectively incorporated into muon absorption imaging (MAI), while penetrating events are retained for MSI reconstruction. This event reutilization significantly increases the effective statistics without additional hardware, thereby improving imaging efficiency and reducing the required measurement time. To further exploit the complementary information from MAI and MSI, multiple image fusion methods were investigated, including linear weighted fusion, Fourier decomposition filtering fusion, and Principal Component Analysis-based fusion. Experimental results show that the maximum a posteriori (MAP)-based fusion method achieves the best reconstruction performance. Imaging experiments were conducted using an eight-layer 50 cm × 50 cm plastic scintillator detector system. The target consisted of fifteen 5 cm × 5 cm × 5 cm lead blocks arranged in a U-shaped structure. A total of 4.3 × 10⁴ muon events were collected. Compared with conventional MSI reconstruction, the proposed framework produces clearer structural boundaries, higher contrast, and significantly suppressed background noise. Quantitative evaluation using the structural similarity index (SSIM) shows an improvement from 0.212 to 0.389, corresponding to an increase of approximately 83%. The proposed trigger optimization and image fusion strategy enable faster, higher-quality, and more practical muon scattering imaging for security and high-Z material identification.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-15-05] Effects of Inverse Compton Scattering Source Parameters on Output X-Ray Spectra for Medical Applications. (#3102)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Priestley (Autores: H. Priestley , G. Paterno , M. Jacquet , K. Dupraz , A. Wilson , J. Duffy , A. Bravin , S. Bugby , J. Spiga)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Loughborough University, Department of Physics, Loughborough, United Kingdom [2] University of Ferrara, Department of Physics and Earth Science, Ferrara, Italy [3] Universite Paris-Saclay, IJCLab, Paris, France [4] University of Warwick, Department of Physics, Warwick, United Kingdom [5] Università degli Studi di Milano-Bicocca and INFN, Dipartimento di Fisica, Milan, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work investigates Inverse Compton Scattering (ICS) sources and their potential for synchrotron-based medical applications, particularly Microbeam Radiation Therapy (MRT). As compact alternatives to large synchrotron facilities, ICS sources are rapidly approaching the flux and energy requirements necessary for MRT, but require detailed characterisation before clinical implementation can be considered. Geant4 Monte Carlo simulations inspired by the ThomX ICS source were performed to evaluate the influence of key source parameters on the emitted x-ray spectrum. Parameters studied included electron beam energy, energy spread, emittance, and laser wavelength. The simulations show that variations in these parameters produce measurable shifts in spectral peak energy, directly relevant to MRT beam optimisation, as well as asymmetric spectral broadening across the spectrum. These results are the first ICS simulations of these parameters at MRT relevant energies and aid the evaluation of ICS sources as compact alternatives to synchrotron radiation sources.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-15-06] Latent-Space Modeling for Multi-Organ Radiomics Phenotyping in ¹⁷⁷Lu-Based SPECT/CT Imaging (#3205)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. S. Azimi (Autores: M. S. Azimi , M. Cheraghi , M. A. Ghodsi-Rad , G. Divband , H. Zaidi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Geneva University Hospital, Division of Nuclear Medicine & Molecular Imaging, Geneva, Genève, Switzerland [2] Odense University Hospital, Deptartment of Nuclear Medicine, Odense, Denmark [3] Obuda University, Research and Innovation Center, Budapest, Hungary [4] Shahid Beheshti University, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Tehran, Iran (Islamic Republic of) [5] Jam Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Tehran, Iran (Islamic Republic of)
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Radiomics analysis in nuclear medicine is commonly performed on predefined features extracted from individual regions, which limits its ability to describe global imaging patterns across the whole body. In this work, we propose a latent-space digital twin framework to characterize multi-organ radiomics behavior in theranostic SPECT/CT imaging. Post-therapy SPECT/CT data from 57 patients treated with ¹⁷⁷Lu-based radiopharmaceuticals were analyzed. Multi-organ and lesion segmentations were obtained, and 107 standardized radiomics features were extracted for each region. These features were aggregated into patient-level representations and projected into a low-dimensional latent space using principal component analysis. Unsupervised clustering and distance-based analysis were then applied to identify underlying radiomics phenotypes and quantify inter-patient variability. The learned latent space revealed structured organization of radiomics patterns, with the first two principal components capturing more than half of the total variance (PC1: 34%, PC2: 19%). Distinct patient groups emerged with clear separation, characterized by lower intra-group distances (≈6) and substantially higher inter-group distances (≈12). Analysis of latent components indicated that structural regions predominantly contributed to the first component, while soft-tissue and vascular regions influenced the second component. In addition, the latent representation enabled identification of outlier patients, reflecting substantial heterogeneity in multi-organ radiomics profiles. These findings demonstrate that latent-space modeling provides a compact and interpretable representation of complex radiomics data. The proposed digital twin framework enables system-level phenotyping and may support improved patient stratification in theranostic SPECT/CT imaging.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-16-01] Asymmetry in time difference histograms for scintillators with different decay constants in coincidence (#2202)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Hamato (Autores: A. Hamato , N. Kratochwil , R. Ota , J. Glodo , T. Yamaya , S.R. Cherry , S.I. Kwon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology (QST), Advanced Nuclear Medicine Sciences, Chiba, Japan [2] University of California Davis, Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America [3] Radiation Monitoring Devices Inc., Watertown, Massachusetts, United States of America [4] Hamamatsu Photonics K.K, Central Research Laboratory, Hamamatsu, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Coincidence timing resolution is a critical performance parameter in time-of-flight PET and other timing sensitive applications. The timing performance of scintillation detectors is governed by intrinsic scintillator properties such as light yield, rise time, and decay constant. When detectors with different scintillation characteristics are in coincidence, these differences can distort the coincidence timing spectrum, leading to deviations from an ideal symmetric Gaussian distribution. Differences in scintillator decay constants can introduce measurable asymmetry in coincidence timing histograms. In this work, the influence of scintillator decay constant on coincidence timing histogram was investigated using several scintillators with different decay constants. The scintillators (Lu 2 O 3 :Yb, EPS-100 plastic scintillator, LaBr 3 :Ce, LYSO:Ce, GAGG, NaI:Tl, and BGO) with dimensions of 3×3×5 mm 3 mounted on identical silicon photomultipliers were placed in coincidence with a reference LYSO detector. Time difference histograms were acquired for each detector pair and quantitatively analyzed using the mean, median, and skewness of the measured distributions. The results showed nearly symmetric timing histograms for EPS-100, LaBr 3 , and LYSO scintillators, whereas other scintillators exhibited increasing asymmetry. The longest tail was observed for BGO on one side of the histogram. Time difference histograms were also analytically calculated based on the arrival time distribution of the 10 th detected photon. The analytical results reproduced the main trends observed experimentally. These findings demonstrate that scintillator decay constants significantly influence the shape and asymmetry of coincidence timing histograms for non-identical detector pairs with substantially different decay constants, providing insight relevant to the design and optimization of mixed scintillator timing systems.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-16-02] Ultrafast and Efficient 2D Perovskite Scintillators for Sub-50 ps TOF-PET and High-Resolution X-ray Imaging (#2541)
sub_talks.speaker: J. Liu
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Wuhan University of Technology, School of Materials Science and Engineering, Wuhan, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Ultrafast radiation detection has been persistently limited by the formidable challenge of achieving scintillators that combine sub-nanosecond response times with high scintillation efficiency. Here, we identify atomic-level exciton confinement, achieved through the synergistic regulation of A-site organic cations in 2D perovskites, as a critical factor for breaking this performance bottleneck. The resulting (1,4-CMA)PbBr 4 crystals exhibit a rare combination of a 0.62 ns radioluminescence decay time and a high light yield of 19,730 photons/MeV, surpassing leading commercial benchmarks such as BaF 2 and LYSO:Ce. Detectors based on this material achieved a record-breaking coincidence timing resolution (CTR) of 43.3 ps for reconstruction-free Time-of-Flight Positron Emission Tomography (TOF-PET) and a high spatial resolution of 32.3 lp mm -1 for X-ray imaging. These results establish rational lattice distortion engineering as a key principle for the development of high-performance, scalable perovskite scintillators for next-generation medical and industrial imaging.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-16-03] Thick Optical-guiding Scintillator with Enhanced Crystal Quality for High-Resolution and High-Sensitivity X-ray Imaging (#2557)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Nakata (Autores: Y. Nakata , K. Kamada , M. Yoshino , T. Kudo , R. Murakami , S. Ishizawa , Y. Yokota , A. Yoshikawa)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tohoku University, Department of Materials Science / Graduate School of Engineering, Sendai, Japan [2] Tohoku University, Institute for Materials Research, Sendai, Japan [3] Tohoku University, New Industry Creation Hatchery Center, Sendai, Japan [4] C&A Corporation, Sendai, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study presents the fabrication and evaluation of an Optical-guiding Crystal Scintillator (OCS), a structured scintillator that achieves both high spatial resolution and high detection sensitivity in X-ray imaging. Conventional scintillators face a trade-off between these two properties, and structured scintillators have been developed to overcome this trade-off. However, simultaneously achieving fine waveguiding channels with sufficient thickness at bulk scale remains a challenge. The OCS has been proposed to address this issue [1-2]. It has regularly arrayed single-crystal scintillator cores embedded in a low-refractive-index glass cladding. Each core confines scintillation light by total internal reflection. In this work, we grew Tl-doped Cs 3 Cu 2 I 5 (CCI:Tl, n = 1.92) single-crystal cores through directional solidification from a melt within the 5 µm-diameter channels of a borosilicate glass plate ( n = 1.47). Electron backscatter diffraction analysis of the cross-section sample confirmed that each core is a single crystal, and X-ray-excited radioluminescence showed an emission peak at 517 nm, consistent with previously reported values for CCI:Tl single crystals [3]. We evaluated spatial resolution by imaging test charts with a microfocus X-ray tube and calculating the contrast transfer function (CTF). A 500 µm-thick OCS achieved CTF = 35% at 10 lp/mm, compared with 10% for a commercial CsI:Tl columnar scintillator of the same thickness. The OCS maintained spatial resolution over a thickness range of 200 to 700 µm, whereas the commercial scintillator exhibited a sharp decline. Light yield was higher than that of the commercial CsI:Tl columnar scintillator. These results demonstrate that the OCS overcomes the conventional trade-off between spatial resolution and detection sensitivity, opening new possibilities for high-energy X-ray imaging, industrial nondestructive testing, and medical diagnostics.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-16-04] Development of 3D-Printable Plastic Scintillator Using Stereolithography for Radiation Detection Applications (#1653)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Puprasit (Autores: K. Puprasit , N. Mattayom , K. Chaiwongkhot , K. Amratisha , A. Phunpueok , N. Udee)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Chulabhorn Royal Academy/Princess Srisavangavadhana Faculty of Medicine/Medical Physics Program, Bangkok, Thailand [2] Chulabhorn Royal Academy/Personalized Radiotherapy and Imaging in Medicine (PRIME) Excellent Research Group, ฺBangkok, Thailand [3] Mahidol University/Faculty of Science/Department of Physics, ฺBangkok, Thailand [4] Rajamangala University of Technology Thanyaburi/Faculty of Science and Technology/Division of Physics, Pathum Thani, Thailand [5] Naresuan University/Faculty of Allied Health Sciences/Department of Radiological Technology, Phitsanulok, Thailand
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Plastic scintillators are widely used in radiation detection; however, conventional fabrication constrains detector geometry to simple shapes, limiting applicability in complex dosimetry configurations. We report the development of a geometrically flexible plastic scintillator fabricated via stereolithography (SLA) 3D printing, enabling arbitrary-geometry detector production. The formulation incorporated vinyltoluene (VT, 0-20 wt%) as an aromatic co-monomer, 2,5-diphenyloxazole (PPO, 1-2 wt%) as the primary fluorophore, 1,4-bis(2-methylstyryl)benzene (Bis-MSB, 0-0.01 wt%) as a wavelength shifter, and TPO as the photoinitiator in a commercial acrylate photopolymer host matrix. A post-print resin-dipping technique using the identical formulation improved optical transmittance from 11% to 72%. Main-effect analysis across nine formulations showed that VT at 10 wt% yields optimal optical clarity (~72% at 800 nm), while PPO at 2.0 wt% produces the highest emission intensity at 367-368 nm without concentration quenching. Self-absorption arising from PPO emission-absorption spectral overlap and a host-resin transmission cut-off at 410 nm was identified as the primary optical challenge, establishing Bis-MSB wavelength shifting as essential for light collection beyond the cut-off. Active scintillation was confirmed under Sr-90 via silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) readout, with pulse amplitude 20 times lower than EJ-200. Dosimetric characterization under Cs-137 and Co-60 with EJ-200 benchmarking will be presented.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-16-05] Energy Spectroscopy Using Tin-Loaded Organic Glass Scintillators of Varying Sizes (#2113)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. Neely (Autores: E. Neely , E. Schneider , C. Sosa , S. Clarke , S. Pozzi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Michigan, Department of Applied Physics, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America [2] University of Michigan, Department of Nuclear Engineering and Radiological Sciences, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America [3] Radiation Monitoring Devices, Boston, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Organic scintillators doped with heavy metals are promising for nonproliferation work as they combine the low-Z sensitivity to neutrons with the high-Z sensitivity to photoelectric absorption of gammas. Organic glass scintillators (OGS), in particular, are easy to shape and perform almost as well as trans-stilbene in light yield, energy resolution, and pulse shape discrimination. The Detection for Nuclear Nonproliferation Group (DNNG) at the University of Michigan has already completed work on 6-mm and 12-mm cubes of the tin-loaded OGS (or Sn-OGS), finding good agreement between experimental results and MCNP simulations of reasonable fidelity. The measured energy resolution of the photopeak from the 12-mm Sn-OGS is on the order of 10% and the intrinsic efficiency is visible on a log scale, both with uniform energy-dependent trends. DNNG and RMD have just entered into an agreement to further investigate this material in the form of a 1" x 1" cylinder. We anticipate that similar basic gamma spectroscopy will reveal increased photopeak efficiency and a diminished X-ray escape peak as multiple scatters are more likely in a larger volume; however, the effect of detector volume on energy resolution is unknown. In addition, we hope to present data from Compton coincidence experiments, and begin work with gamma/neutron sources for pulse shape discrimination. This work will also be compared to MCNP simulations.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-16-06] Position-Sensitive and Energy-Constrained Characterization of an Opaque Scintillation Detector (#1047)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Katz (Autores: S. Katz , G. Wendel , J. Moffatt , A. Wilhelm , M. Yeh , D. F. Cowen , I. Jovanovic)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California, Berkeley, Department of Nuclear Engineering, Berkeley, California, United States of America [2] Pennsylvania State University, Department of Physics, University Park, Pennsylvania, United States of America [3] United States Military Academy West Point, Department of Physics & Nuclear Engineering, West Point, New York, United States of America [4] Brookhaven National Laboratory, Chemistry Division, Upton, New York, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract LiquidO detectors stochastically confine scintillation and Cherenkov light around energy depositions by using media with a short optical scattering length. Wavelength-shifting fibers latticed throughout the volume capture the confined light, re-emit it, and transport it to photosensors, creating an optically segmented detector without physical optical barriers. Optical segmentation offers the prospect of effective particle identification and directional reconstruction by using the time of flight, energy deposition, and topology of events that deposit energy at multiple locations in the detector volume. A critical first step toward this capability is a position-sensitive calibration to evaluate detector homogeneity and single-scatter spatial and energy resolution. To achieve this, a four-liter LiquidO prototype detector was constructed and exposed to a collimated Cs-137 source in a tagged Compton scattering configuration. A sodium-iodide detector views the scattering region, providing spatially and energetically constrained event tagging. A Monte Carlo simulation of the experimental geometry models optical photon propagation, light collection, and photosensor noise. Initial measurements indicate a light collection of ~100 photoelectrons per MeV can be achieved in the detector center, and ongoing analysis compares measured and simulated detector responses to quantify the spatial and energy resolution.

sub_talks.title: [NSS-16-07] Large Scale Lu 2 O 3 :Yb Ceramics for High-Rate Calorimetry (#2903)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Soundara Pandian (Autores: L. Soundara Pandian , M. Muller , G. Adhikari , A. Kim , S. Kim , L. Zhang , H. Newman , P. Albert , J. Reiss , Y. Wang , J. Glodo)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Radiation Monitoring Devices, Inc., Watertown, Massachusetts, United States of America [2] California Institute of Technology, Physics, Mathematics and Astronomy Division, Pasadena, California, United States of America [3] Pennsylvania State University, Applied Research Laboratory, State College, Pennsylvania, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Future high‑luminosity collider experiments require scintillators that combine high density, ultrafast response, and strong radiation tolerance. Yb‑doped lutetium oxide (Lu₂O₃:Yb) is a promising candidate due to its 9.4 g/cm³ density, sub‑2 ns charge transfer luminescence, and light yield near 500 photons/MeV. Due to its very high melting point, Lu 2 O 3 is more effectively fabricated through ceramic processing, which enables scalable production of transparent, large volume components for calorimetry and fast timing systems. Our current effort advances two complementary ceramic routes for producing Lu 2 O 3 at detector relevant sizes. In collaboration with PSU/ARL, Field‑Assisted Sintering Technology (FAST) approach is being developed to achieve monolithic parts with target dimensions of 2 × 2 × 15 cm³. In parallel, RMD is fabricating 2.5 cm‑scale cubes and thin plates using a sinter‑plus‑HIP process. Optical and scintillation measurements show that thin plates, including 1‑inch squares and 14 × 14 × 3 mm³ samples, reach light yields near 500 ph/MeV, while larger cubes currently exhibit reduced output due to limited transparency. All samples emit near 350 nm under X‑ray excitation and maintain decay times of approximately 2 ns. In collaboration with Caltech we also produce Lu 2 O 3 plates for the RaDiCAL experiment as potential replacement for LYSO, leveraging the material's high density and ultrafast timing. The combination of fast response, radiation hardness, and scalable fabrication positions Lu 2 O 3 ceramics as a strong candidate for next‑generation HEP calorimeters and timing detectors. Our results from the latest FAST‑processed Lu 2 O 3 samples will also be presented at the conference.

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract XEMIS2 is a liquid xenon Compton camera developed at the Subatech laboratory in Nantes, France, designed to demonstrate 3 gamma nuclear imaging on small animals for the first time. This technique exploits the three gamma rays simultaneously emitted by Scandium-44, whose combined detection constrains the emitter position in 3D, enabling a reduction of the injected activity by a factor of 100 compared to conventional Positron Emission Tomography while maintaining equivalent image quality. The detector simultaneously measures two complementary signals: scintillation light, detected by 64 photomultiplier tubes surrounding the liquid xenon active volume, and ionisation electrons, drifted by a 2 kV/cm electric field toward a pixelised anode. Accurate image reconstruction relies critically on the precise calibration of the light acquisition system. The full light calibration chain developed for XEMIS2 is presented, covering the determination of detection thresholds, the photomultiplier tubes gain calibration procedure, and the inter-channel time delay correction validated on both simulation and experimental data.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-07-01] Physics-Informed 3D Gaussian Splatting for Multi-View Compton Camera Imaging (#1292)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Ma (Autores: R. Ma , L. Li)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract High-resolution 3D Compton imaging is essential for quantitative environmental monitoring. Traditional Maximum Likelihood Expectation Maximization (MLEM) suffers from voxel discretization penalties. Without ground-truth references, MLEM's required early stopping creates a dilemma between severe depth-elongation and late-stage noise deterioration. Meanwhile, modern deep learning models suppress noise but lack zero-shot generalization. To bridge this gap, we present a zero-shot, physics-informed 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework. Although likelihood computation utilizes differentiable voxelization, the fundamentally continuous nature of 3DGS introduces implicit spatial regularization, bypassing rigid voxel constraints. It rigorously decouples the morphological probability density from overall source activity via an analytical optimal scaling mechanism. In simulations, 3DGS eliminates background artifacts, yielding up to 5.7 dB Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) improvement over MLEM in 4-view phantom reconstructions. Validated experimentally on an H3D M400 detector within a 0.125 m³ workspace, 3DGS overcomes MLEM's depth-elongation and noise deterioration without arbitrary early stopping. It achieves an angular resolution of ~9° and excels in practical multi-isotope identification while strictly preserving relative activity linearity. This training-free paradigm offers a robust, quantitative tool for radiation monitoring.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-07-02] Benchmark of the H3DD_UMv5 Waveform Sampling ASIC for Pixelated Room-Temperature Semiconductor Detectors (#1336)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Zhu (Autores: Y. Zhu , G. D. Geronimo , Z. He)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Michigan, Nuclear Engineering and Radiological Sciences, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract H3DD_UM ASIC has been developed at the University of Michigan since 2017. This paper summarizes the performance of the most recent version H3DD_UMv5 ASIC. The electronic noise was measured to be 1.2 keV FWHM at 700-keV dynamic range with a 20×20×15 mm 3 CdZnTe detector attached but not biased. Such low noise enables an excellent energy resolution of 0.37% FWHM at 662 keV for single-pixel events. For all events, the measured energy resolution is 0.52 % FWHM. The low-energy threshold can be as low as 2.0 keV using the 200 keV dynamic range. The nonlinearity of the AISC is around 0.6% and it can be calibrated using the internal test pulse.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-07-03] Optimizing Array Configurations of Position-Sensitive Virtual Frisch-grid Detectors for Coded Aperture Telescopes (#3134)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Bolotnikov (Autores: A. Bolotnikov , P. Maj , E. Muller , U. Roy , R. James)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Brookhaven National Laboratory, Upton, New York, United States of America [2] Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, New York, United States of America [3] Savannah River National Laboratory, Aiken, New York, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We report recent progress in the development of CdZnTe (CZT) and CdZnTeSe (CZTS) position-sensitive virtual Frisch-grid (VFG) gamma-ray detectors and detector arrays. The high 3D position sensitivity enabled by the VFG design allows correction of response non-uniformities caused by crystal defects. A key challenge in current large-volume CZT/CZTS detectors is the lateral displacement of charge carriers, which may exceed 1-2 mm over a >1 cm drift distance, strongly affecting the imaging capabilities of gamma cameras. These displacements are closely tied to crystal defects, such as dislocations and sub-grain boundaries, which are always present even in the highest-quality crystals. To address this issue, we propose using detectors with smaller-than-typical cross-sectional areas (4×4 or 5×5 mm²), which match the size of the basic element in a coded-aperture imaging system. Improving position and energy resolution through the application of neural network algorithms is critical for the development of high-performance and reliable detector systems. We demonstrate that the neural network approach yields better results and requires significantly less calibration data because it handles the continuous distribution of events within the detector, whereas the conventional correction-matrix approach relies on discretized values resulting from detector segmentation. We present the results of testing these devices and discuss their advantages and shortcomings.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-07-04] Measurement of the energy response function of a photon counting prototype detector using the HEX-27 beamline at the Brookhaven National Laboratory; A method to derive an empirical model of the detector non-ideal behavior and to improve material discrimination by spectrum deconvolution. (#2142)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Prekas (Autores: G. Prekas , B. Mercurio , C. Bosch , K. Rogers , Z. Zhong , E. Johnson)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] SureScan Corporation, Binghamton, United States of America [2] BrookHaven National Laboratory, Upton, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Spectrum unfolding, or deconvolution, is a critical preprocessing step in X-ray image formation, particularly for spectral photon-counting detectors (PCDs). While an ideal detector records the full energy of an incident photon at a single pixel, realistic semiconductor detectors are governed by complex physical phenomena. Charge sharing, K-fluorescence escape, and pulse pile-up are the dominant factors that distort the recorded energy of the recorded signal. Thes first two effects are significantly exacerbated as pixel sizes decrease, leading to spectral degradation that compromises material discrimination and CNR, challenging the multi-energy imaging system. This study presents a comprehensive characterization of the energy response function (ERF) for a PCD module developed by AMS-OSRAM, utilizing a CdZnTe (CZT) crystal with a native pixel pitch of 341 µm × 365 µm coupled to three ultra-low noise ASICs. The work was conducted at the HEX-27 (High Energy X-ray Scattering) beamline at Brookhaven National Laboratory. The detector was exposed to monochromatic X-ray beams from 30 keV to 140 keV at a flux of 9 Mcps/mm². The complete spectral response was mapped at high resolution, by sweeping the detector's five energy thresholds. The measurements enabled the derivation of an empirical model describing the ERF of the AS5920M/CZT module, accurately capturing inherent spectral features and tailing effects. To verify this empirical model, the derived response was convoluted with ideal spectra generated via SpekCalc. The resulting reconstructed distorted spectra matched well the measured detector output. Finally, we propose a correction methodology applied to individual energy bins. By compensating for spectral distortions, enhanced contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) can be achieved, thereby significantly improving the accuracy of material separation.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-07-05] 3D Integration and Interconnects for the Readout of Hybrid Pixel Detectors (#2576)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Piernas Diaz (Autores: F. Piernas Diaz , J. A. Alozy , M. V. Barreto Pinto , T. Bodova , A. Fernandez Prieto , K. Kloukinas , M. I. Kovacs , X. Llopart Cudie , C. Scarcella , K. Wyllie)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto Galego de Física de Altas Enerxías (IGFAE), Santiago de Compostela, Spain [2] European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN), Experimental Physics Department, Geneva, Genève, Switzerland [3] University of Geneva, Geneva, Genève, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Future hybrid pixel detectors for particle tracking and imaging require dense, low-inductance interconnections that can distribute clean power, sustain multi-gigabit data transmission, and minimize non-sensitive area. Conventional wire-bonding constrains input and output access to the die periphery, and results in long internal power routing as well as dead area which prevents close tiling of chips. This contribution presents a three-dimensional integration approach for the readout of hybrid pixel detectors based on Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs) fabricated after complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor processing. Timepix4 readout chips are used as a test vehicle. Vias are etched from the back side of thinned chips, insulated from the substrate, metallized, and connected to a back-side redistribution layer that routes power and signals to an array of bonding pads on which solder balls can be deposited. The resulting interconnects replace wire bonds and allow the chip to be soldered directly to a carrier printed circuit board. Several processed Timepix4 batches have been evaluated. A custom-designed test system allows measurement of interconnect quality for signal transmission and power delivery. TSV-processed chips have also been co-integrated together with silicon-photonics into module demonstrators. The tests demonstrate successful operation of Timepix4 after TSV processing, including 5 Gbit/s data transmission and stable power delivery through the back-side interconnect stack. The presentation will discuss the processing flow, test system design choices, assembly and test results, and the suitability of solder ball-grid arrays and anisotropic conductive paste for permanent chip-to-board attachment.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-07-06] Carrier Dynamics and Polarization in GaAs:Cr Detectors Under High X-ray Flux (#2747)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Wang (Autores: T. Zhong , B. Wang , Y. Yang , H. Li , J. Kalliopuska , D. Nalyvaiko , V. Gnatyuk , X. Lai)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] ShanghaiTech University, School of Biomedical Engineering, Shanghai, China [2] Shanghai United Imaging Healthcare Advanced Technology Research Institute Co.,Ltd.,, Shanghai, China [3] Advafab OY, Helsinki, Finland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Gallium arsenide (GaAs) has broad application prospects as a material for photon counting detectors (PCDs). In this study, we investigate carrier dynamics and polarization in Cr-compensated GaAs (GaAs:Cr) via infrared transient current analysis and clinical X-ray temporal response experiments. The transient current results indicate that while massive carrier generation under high-intensity illumination can induce localized polarization, the deep energy levels introduced by Cr doping effectively preserve dynamic charge neutrality. By capturing and recombining excess carriers, this Cr-compensation successfully mitigates polarization effects, significantly improving detector signal stability up to an ultra-high clinical flux of 2.7 Gcps/mm^2.

sub_talks.title: [RTSD-07-07] Evaluation of Cr-Compensated GaAs Sensors with Different Thicknesses by Photon-Counting ReadoutElectronics (#2806)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Kalliopuska (Autores: J. Kalliopuska , D. Nalyvaiko , V. Gnatyuk , N. Masuda , S. Vähänen , E. Soharova , J. Jakubek , P. Spisek , B. Wang , H. Li , T. Zhong , X. Lai)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] ADVAFAB, Helsinki, Finland [2] ADVACAM, Prague, Czech Republic [3] School of Biomedical Engineering, ShanghaiTech University, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Advances in the fabrication of detector-grade GaAs semiconductors through chromium compensation have enabled the development of imaging sensors with high detection efficiency, energy resolution, high-flux tolerance, and enhanced radiation hardness, providing improved performance in the mid-energy X-ray range compared to conventional Si and Cd(Zn)Te sensors. Detection efficiency in semiconductor sensors strongly depends on sensor thickness, as the active detection volume scales directly with it. High absorption efficiency up to 80 keV is required in medical computed tomography (CT) and security imaging, which can be achieved using 2 mm thick GaAs sensors. GaAs sensors with thicknesses from 0.3 mm to 2 mm manufactured by Advafab were developed, characterized, and evaluated with different photon-counting readout electronics. High-resistivity GaAs wafers were processed using Cr compensation, followed by lithography, metallization, dicing, and flip-chip bonding to various readout ASICs. The sensors were evaluated under X-ray irradiation to investigate detection efficiency, count-rate uniformity, charge transport, stability, and imaging performance. The 2 mm thick sensors demonstrated excellent image uniformity and operation at extreme X-ray fluxes up to 1100 Mcnt/s/mm2 with stability better than 2% over 30 s. Sidewall etching of diced GaAs improved sensor performance by reducing leakage current and enhancing electric field uniformity. The results highlight GaAs:Cr as an effective material for photon-counting X-ray imaging in medical, synchrotron, and industrial applications.

sub_talks.speaker: M. Bombonati
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Hamamatsu Photonics Italia Srl, Arese, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Hamamatsu Photonics continues to develop a broad portfolio of photosensors and radiation detector technologies addressing the evolving requirements of nuclear science, high energy physics, medical imaging, and related applications. This presentation will provide an overview of recent developments across several detector platforms, including silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), advanced silicon electron multiplication devices, vacuum photodetectors, and emerging radiation detection technologies. Particular attention will be given to ongoing efforts aimed at improving photon detection efficiency, noise performance, timing characteristics, operation in demanding environments and detector integration. The presentation is intended as an overview of current development activities, providing attendees with insights into emerging detector solutions and their potential impact on future nuclear science and high energy physics experiments.
