sub_talks.title: [TS-03-02] Introduction to Representative Achievements of Jinan Laboratory of Applied Nuclear Sciences in the Field of Nuclear Technology Applications (#3425)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Liu (Autores: K. Liu , X. Yang , G. Wei , J. Cao , X. Xie)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Jinan Laboratory of Applied Nuclear Sciences, Department of Research management, Jinan, China [2] Institute of High Energy Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Nuclear Technology Application Center, Beijing, China [3] CAEA Center of Excellence on Nuclear Technology Applications for Nuclear Detection and Imaging, Jinan Base, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Jinan Laboratory of Applied Nuclear Sciences is a research platform established by the Institute of High Energy Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Our team focuses on nuclear technology applications in three key areas: non-destructive testing, radiation monitoring, and molecular imaging. We have developed and industrialized a broad portfolio of nuclear instruments. This presentation introduces our recent achievements and flagship products. Non-destructive testing - We invented the world's first curved-surface XRF spectrometer used for cultural heritage conservation, producing high-resolution 3D elemental maps of irregular bronze and jade relics. It has analyzed precious artifacts for the Palace Museum and other museums. Radiation monitoring - Our portfolio includes personal dosimeters, portable gamma cameras, radionuclide identifiers, neutron detectors, and nuclear electronics modules. Over 3,000 units are in service at universities, nuclear power plants, and hospitals. Our digital monitoring system supports wide-area imaging and semi-quantitative analysis to safeguard plant operations. Molecular imaging - Our panoramic small-animal PET-CT offers a 213 mm axial FOV, capturing whole-body dynamic rat imaging in a single bed position at sub-millimeter resolution for radiopharmaceutical R&D. XTOMO-CUBE, the world's smallest micro-CT, is compact, portable, and domestically built, delivering micron-resolution 3D reconstruction for archaeology, materials research, and teaching. Core components - We have also independently developed 150 kV X-ray source components with decetn in-lab performance, and we are carrying out equipment integration to further validate and optimize this technology. Visit us at Booth 53 for specifications, application cases, and live demos. We look forward to discussing collaboration with you.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 1Poster Number:MIC-05-001] Variable Angle Slant-Hole Collimator for Molecular Breast Imaging System (#1035)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Weisenberger (Autores: S. Lee , A. Weisenberger , B. Patt , J. Hugg)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Thomas Jefferson National Accelerator Facility, Nuclear Physics, Newport News, Virginia, United States of America [2] Smartbreast Corporation, Sherman Oaks, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A Variable Angle Slant-Hole (VASH) collimator has been developed for integration with the SmartBreast's Eve ClearScan e750 Molecular Breast Imaging (MBI) system, formerly known as the GE Discovery NM750b. This effort builds upon prior success implementing VASH technology in the Dilon 6800 camera platform, where slanted collimator geometries demonstrated improved resolution and lesion detectability in breast imaging applications. The SmartBreast MBI system incor-porates high-resolution cadmium zinc telluride (CZT) detectors, replacing earlier NaI(Tl)-based designs, and thus necessitates a redesigned collimator geometry to fully leverage the intrinsic resolution and detector compactness. The new VASH design incorporates a reduced hole pitch of 1.84 mm, fixed septal thickness of 0.4 mm, and a shortened collimator depth of 13 mm, in contrast to the original lead-based parallel-hole collimator (2.46 mm pitch, 0.4 mm septa, 21 mm depth). These parameters were selected to balance sensitivity and spatial resolution. Ana-lytical calculations indicate that the redesigned VASH achieves comparable or improved resolution and sensitivity performance at clinically relevant object-to-collimator distances up to 60 mm. The first prototype is under construction, with mechanical inte-gration, phantom imaging, and angular performance evaluation scheduled for upcoming testing. The VASH system offers imaging flexibility in clinical MBI and has potential implications for improving detection of lesions at variable depths in dense breast tissue.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 4Poster Number:MIC-05-004] Characterization of the CHLOE readout for dual-ended BGO crystals for PET with the FastIC+ (#1221)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. San Martín Valenzuela (Autores: C. San Martín Valenzuela , M. Maiorino , A. Pinto , N. Kratochwil , E. Medina , C. Puigdengoles , M. Chmeissani , G. Ariño-Estrada)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Institut de Física d'Altes Energies - Barcelona Institute of Science and Technology (IFAE - BIST), Bellaterra, Spain [2] University of California at Davis (UC DAVIS), Department of Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America [3] University of Aveirno, Aveiro, Portugal
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The performance of gamma detectors for time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET) has improved significantly over the last decade. With commercial systems surpassing the 200~ps coincidence time resolution (CTR) barrier, the avenues for improving TOF-PET detector performance become progressively more limited. We report on CHLOE (Cherenkov Light Module), a PET detector readout with high channel density composed of dual ended readout bismuth germanate (BGO) crystals coupled one-to-one to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) with the goal of providing a trade-off between 3D detector segmentation, energy resolution, and scalability in an intrinsic radiation-free crystal. The electronics were based on the FastIC+ chip and the complete readout chain, from the front-end to the back-end was customized for this concept. This work presents the first electronic and detector characterization of the CHLOE readout approach. The noise and dark counts contributions of the system are presented, including measurements of channel dependencies in the response. Energy spectra were obtained for $^{22}$Na and $^{133}$Ba sources. The work presented in this contribution represents the very first steps towards a full functional characterization of the CHLOE readout.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 7Poster Number:MIC-05-007] A 0.32 mm Pitch GAGG Array-Based SPECT Detector (#1596)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Xie (Autores: J. Xie , H. Wang , J. Qi , S. R. Cherry , J. Du)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California at Davis, Biomedical Engineering, Davis, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Multi-tracer preclinical single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) enables simultaneous tracking of multiple physiological processes inside organs, requiring detectors with high spatial and energy resolution over a broad energy range. In this study, we developed and evaluated a high-resolution detector comprising a 28 × 28 gadolinium aluminum gallium garnet (GAGG) array (0.32 mm pitch, 2 mm thickness) coupled to a linearly graded silicon photomultiplier (LG-SiPM) using radiation sources with different energies: 55, 122, 202, 307, 511 keV. Flood histograms demonstrated clear separation of crystal elements over a wide energy range from 55 keV to 511 keV. Furthermore, the detector achieved energy resolutions of 18% at 122 keV and 12% at 511 keV, along with excellent energy linearity across 55-511 keV (R² = 0.996). These results demonstrate that the developed detector is a promising candidate for high-resolution small-animal SPECT systems.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 10Poster Number:MIC-05-010] Sub-millimeter PET detectors using multiplexed readout with ASIC (#1718)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Liu (Autores: Z. Zhu , L. Zhang , H. Huang , H. Li , Y. Yang , Z. Liu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Institute of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shenzhen, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study presents a sub-millimeter resolution small-animal PET detector based on a dual-ended readout configuration with highly multiplexed signal processing, targeting applications in compact and MRI-compatible PET insert systems. The detector employs a LYSO crystal array coupled to silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) arrays on both ends. A row-column summation multiplexing scheme is adopted to compress multi-channel SiPM signals into a limited number of position-encoding outputs, while a dedicated multi-channel ASIC (MPT2321) is utilized for signal amplification, timing extraction, and digitization. The multiplexed signals are directly processed by the ASIC without requiring individual channel readout, significantly reducing the number of electronic channels and system complexity, which is particularly beneficial for integration in high-field MRI environments. Experimental results demonstrate that all crystal elements in the 26 × 26 LYSO array can be clearly resolved in the flood histogram. The detector achieves an average energy resolution of 15.3 ± 0.7%, a DOI resolution of 2.56 ± 0.46 mm, and a detector timing resolution (DTR) of 2.40 ± 0.20 ns. The proposed detector design demonstrates that highly multiplexed readout combined with ASIC-based signal processing can effectively reduce system complexity and cost while maintaining good spatial, energy, and DOI performance, making it suitable for high-resolution small-animal PET imaging and compact PET/MRI insert applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 13Poster Number:MIC-05-013] Performance Evaluation of a Position Sensitive SiPM for Decoding Ultra-Small Crystal Arrays (#1901)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Hua (Autores: J. Hua , X. Zhang , M. Niu , H. Yang , R. Dai , Z. Gu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We evaluate the spatial decoding capability and energy resolution of a position sensitive SiPM (PS-SiPM, model PSS 11-6060-S, Capital Photonics Technology, China) with an active area of 6.24 mm × 6.24 mm. The PS-SiPM is optically coupled to a checkerboard-pattern scintillator array, which is composed of alternating LYSO and BGO crystals with a 0.38 mm crystal size and a 0.46 mm pitch, arranged in a 28 × 28 array. To compensate for the lower scintillation light yield of BGO, a custom amplifier board with a nominal gain of 16 was incorporated into the readout chain. Delayed charge integration (DCI) technique was applied for distinguishing LYSO and BGO events based on pulse shape. The average rise and decay time constants were measured 31 ns and 313 ns for BGO, and 22 ns and 60 ns for LYSO, respectively. Using an Anger-logic positioning algorithm, the resulting flood image successfully resolved a 13 × 13 sub-region of the crystal array, with minimal edge decoding difficulty. It highlights the advantage of the PS-SiPM in identifying edge crystals. Energy resolution was evaluated within a central 9 × 10 crystal pixels to mitigate intrinsic geometric constraints. The 45 LYSO crystals in this region achieved an average energy resolution of 18.52% ± 2.39%, and the 45 interleaved BGO crystals achieved 25.54% ± 2.48%. These results confirm the feasibility of using a PS-SiPM for decoding sub-millimeter crystal array, and provide a performance reference for the implementation of PS-SiPMs in ultra-high-resolution nuclear imaging detectors.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 16Poster Number:MIC-05-016] Joint Deconvolution Framework for Photon-Train Reconstruction from Dual-Channel SiPM Readouts (#2012)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Yi (Autores: M. Yi , G.B. Ko , J.S. Lee)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Seoul National University, Interdisciplinary Program in Bioengineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] Seoul National University, Integrated Major in Innovative Medical Science, Seoul, Republic of Korea [3] Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Nuclear and Quantum Engineering, Seoul, Republic of Korea [4] Brightonix Imaging Inc., Seoul, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present a physics-constrained joint deconvolution framework for reconstructing photon arrival dynamics. In scintillator-based detectors, measured waveforms arise from the convolutional superposition of stochastic photon detection events, while finite analog signal shaping limits the observable temporal resolution. Mathematical deconvolution approaches implicitly assume continuous photon arrival recovery; however, such formulations are fundamentally ill-posed under band-limited measurements. In this work, we instead represent the latent photon arrival process on a discretized temporal grid as a sampled intensity. Dual-channel timing and energy waveforms are modeled as complementary observations of a shared latent process and jointly inverted using sparsity-constrained optimization. The proposed framework stabilized reconstruction in the presence of bipolar timing responses and temporal smearing, yielding physically consistent photon-train estimates. Joint modeling mitigates ambiguities inherent to single-channel reconstruction and improves robustness in timing extraction under degraded signal conditions. These results establish photon-train reconstruction as a physically grounded representation of detector response and a principled framework for interpreting temporally overlapping signals.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Mazzanti (Autores: D. Mazzanti , D. Guberman , J. Mauricio , J. A. Alozy , F. Nahuel , M. Campdell , R. Dolenec , G. El Fakhri , J. M. Fernández-Tenllado , A. Gola , S. sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universitat de Barcelona, Institut de Ciències del Cosmos, Barcelona, Spain [2] Universitat Politècnica de Barcelona, Barcelona, Spain [3] CERN, Microelectronics Section, Meyrin, Switzerland [4] Fondazione Bruno Kessler, Trento, Italy [5] Jožef Stefan Institute, Ljubljana, Slovenia [6] Yale University School of Medicine, New Haven, Connecticut, United States of America [7] University of California, Davis, Davis, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Over the past years, significant advances have been achieved in Time-of-Flight Positron Emission Tomography (ToF-PET) systems, reaching coincidence time resolution (CTR) values below 100 ps. However, this performance has been demonstrated in small-scale detectors using short scintillation crystals, which favor timing performance at the expense of detection efficiency, and high-power electronics. In contrast, realistic system designs require scintillator crystals with thicknesses of >=10 mm to ensure high detection efficiency. Pushing the CTR limits in large crystals remains challenging due to optical photon transport effects and depth-of-interaction (DOI) uncertainties. For this purpose, we investigate a dual-ended read out detector based on a 3x3x20 mm 3 LYSO:Ce,Ca crystal against a 2x2x3 mm 3 Fast-LGSO crystal used as a timing reference. The read out was performed with the FastIC+, a custom application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) multi-channel front-end with on-chip digitization. This ASIC is specifically design for fast-timing applications and optimized for the read out of high-gain photodetectors such as silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs). In this work, we apply an energy-based DOI correction method to improve the CTR performance of thick-crystal detectors. Using a dual-ended detector based on a 3x3x20 mm 3 LYSO:Ce,Ca crystal coupled to 4x4 mm 2 SiPMs and measured against a 2x2x3 mm 3 Fast-LGSO reference detector coupled to a 3x3 mm 2 SiPM, we achieve a CTR of (135 +/- 1) ps without DOI correction. After applying the correction, the CTR improves down to (110 +/- 1) ps. These results obtained for thick crystals opens a clear path toward sub-100 ps performance in realistic scanner configurations.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 22Poster Number:MIC-05-022] Deep Learning Depth-of-Interaction Estimation from Full-Waveform Single-Ended PET Readout: Spatial Resolution Limits (#2163)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Macchiarulo (Autores: M. Luck , L. Macchiarulo , C. Chock , I. Mostafanezhad , H. Sabet)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Nalu Scientific, LLC, honolulu, Hawaii, United States of America [2] Massachusetts General Hospital & Harvard Medical School, Radiology, Boston, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Depth-of-interaction (DOI) estimation is a bottleneck in next-generation PET, contributing to parallax error and degraded timing resolution. Existing solutions using double-sided readout, phoswich, monolithic, or layered crystals require substantial modifications to the readout or detector stack. As part of the development of the SymPET waveform-digitizing readout ASIC, we investigate whether photon arrival-time waveforms alone carry sufficient information to recover DOI without auxiliary sensing. Using DETECT2000 Monte Carlo simulations of 2×2 mm LYSO rods coupled one-to-one to SiPMs, we compare polished and unpolished surface treatments at 12 and 20 mm lengths and train a hybrid 1D CNN-Transformer regressor on 50 ps-binned photon arrival-time histograms. Unpolished surfaces yield lower per-Z MAE and residual std than polished. Bundled high-SNR events reach 0.18 mm worst-per-Z MAE, while single-event MAE is 2.53 mm. Showing the information is present in the waveform, closing this SNR gap is the open problem. (Preliminary results.)

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 25Poster Number:MIC-05-025] Optical-Guiding Crystal Scintillator for Single-Cell Resolution Imaging (#2253)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Nishikido (Autores: F. Nishikido , K. Kamada , Y. Nakata , T. Kudo , H. Wakizaka , A. Yoshikawa , T. Yamaya)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology (QST), Chiba, Japan [2] Tohoku University,, Sendai, Japan [3] C&A Corporation, Sendai, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study is aimed at the development of a dynamic micro imaging technique based on nuclear medicine methods. Single-cell resolution imaging is strongly required to study the properties and mechanisms of cells for improved efficiency of drug development. Conventional nuclear medicine imaging techniques are not suitable for this purpose due to their limited spatial resolution. Autoradiography works in terms of spatial resolution, but it cannot obtain dynamic images. Therefore, we are developing a micro radioisotope (RI) imaging system to realize dynamic cell observation. This system consists of a CCD camera and a scintillator plate. Instead of the eutectic scintillator that we introduced in the last IEEE MIC conference, which had non-uniformity and insensitive region issues for this purpose, in this study we use an optical-guiding crystal scintillator (OCS) which has a 10 μm fiber structure. We developed a prototype of the system using the OCS plate, an objective lens (x4) and an CCD camera (C9100-23B). The length, width and thickness of the OCS plate were approximately 2 mm × 5 mm and ~160 μm, respectively. The diameters of the cores in the OCS plate were ~10 μm. In evaluations, a slide chamber was filled with FDG solution, covered with an 8 μm thick polyimide film and then directly put on the OCS plate. The scintillation lights generated by irradiation of positrons from a FDG were detected with the CCD camera through an objective lens. As a result, optical and scintillation images were obtained with the developed system using the OCS. In addition, using half-life measurements, we confirmed the obtained scintillation images were exactly derived from the interactions between the positrons of the F-18 and the OCS. In the next step, we will evaluate performance of the prototype micro RI cell imaging system in measurements with actual cell samples.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 28Poster Number:MIC-05-028] Crystal Topology and Channel Compression Optimization for a high-resolution Neuro PET/MRI TOF-DOI PET Detector (#2364)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Meyer (Autores: T. Meyer , D. Schug , B. Weissler , E. Gegenmantel , O. Muelhens , G. Terragni , Y. Kuhl , H. Radermacher , C. Lerche , M. Pizzichemi , E. Auffray , V. Schulz)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] RWTH Aachen University, Chair of Imaging and Computer Vision, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [2] Hyperion Hybrid Imaging Systems GmbH, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [3] CERN, Geneva, Switzerland [4] Forschungszentrum Jülich, Institute of Neuroscience and Medicine 4, Jülich, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [5] University of Milano-Bicocca, Milan, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The S-PET project is developing a high-resolution positron emission tomography detector module intended for simultaneous brain positron emission tomography / magnetic resonance imaging. The detector needs to feature good position resolution including depth-of-interaction capabilities as well as good timing resolution. A core challenge is the limited space for electronics. The detector integrates 12×12 or even 16×12 SiPMs with one 64-channel TOFPET2 ASIC, necessitating efficient channel compression schemes without additional elements that leverage light-sharing for event positioning. Crucial optimization parameters for detector performance include the crystal topology and a matching compression scheme. This work evaluates Time-of-Flight and Depth-of-Interaction performance across multiple compression schemes and crystal topologies: continuous slabs, pseudoslabs, and pixelated arrays with a light guide coupled to the face opposite the photosensitive detector. This study utilizes modular development boards, that allow for quick swapping of the compression scheme without reattaching the crystal array, and the first full-scale sensor tile with one of these compression schemes, the Hyperion Visor HD. Preliminary results with a 48×48 mm 2 BrainPET 7T crystal array on the latter show planar resolutions with Mean Absolute Error below 1.5 mm. First tests without compression schemes on a development board with 16×16 mm 2 crystal arrays (2 mm and 4 mm pixel size) with light guide on top show good timing (Coincidence Time Resolution of 235 ps) and Depth-of-Interaction resolution (Mean Absolute Error <1.5 mm). While these preliminary results are promising, the comprehensive evaluations utilizing several crystal topologies combined with the different compression schemes will be presented at the conference.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 31Poster Number:MIC-05-031] An ultralow-afterglow γ-camera prototype for hybrid interventional X-ray and scintigraphy imaging (#2497)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Snoeyink (Autores: M. Snoeyink , L. Schröder , P. Menge , D. R. Schaart)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] TU Delft, TNW/RST, Delft, Netherlands [2] Luxium Solutions, Hiram, Ohio, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Radioembolization is widely used for treating cancer, e.g. in the liver. The procedure currently consists of two sessions, one for imaging and one for treatment, typically several weeks apart. Cost-effectiveness, accuracy of treatment, and patient experience could all be improved if both steps could be combined into a single interventional session. A multimodal detector that integrates an X-ray flat panel with a γ-camera would make this possible, by capturing anatomical information and dose distribution at the same time. During X-ray imaging, however, a portion of the radiation passes through the flat panel and blinds the γ-camera. In principle, γ-photons could be detected in between X-ray pulses, but the high afterglow of the currently used NaI(Tl) scintillator interferes with the γ-photon signals. To overcome this, we explore the use of a low-afterglow scintillator in a pixelated γ-camera design. Reducing afterglow facilitates γ-detection shortly after X-ray exposure. Pixelation further increases the γ-photon signal intensity relative to the afterglow background. The pixels are coupled one-to-one to silicon photomultipliers (SiPM). Here, we characterize a prototype module based on NaI(Tl,Sr,Y), which we previously showed to have a low afterglow of 500ppm at 100ms. The module is hermetically sealed to protect the hygroscopic scintillator and comprises 6 x 6 crystals of 3.75 x 3.75mm x 9mm, separated by 0.25mm thick Teflon reflectors. The central 4 x 4 pixels are coupled to a 4 x 4 SiPM array. The 20 inactive outer pixels ensure equal inter-crystal scatter conditions for all active pixels. Event positioning is based on a winner-takes-all algorithm. The performance of the prototype detector is evaluated by measuring Am-241, Ce-141 and Co-57 pulse-height spectra of all active pixels, with and without simultaneous exposure to a pulsed X-ray source.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 34Poster Number:MIC-05-034] CRYSP: towards an accessible TBPET (#2598)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Navarro-Cozcolluela (Autores: L. Navarro-Cozcolluela , S.R. Soleti , J.J. Gómez-Cadenas)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Donostia International Physics Center, Donostia, Spain [2] Universidad del Pais Vasco (UPV/EHU), Department of Physics, Bilbao, Spain [3] Ikerbasque (Basque Foundation for Science), Bilbao, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The dominant cost driver in total-body positron emission tomography (TBPET) systems is the scintillator material. Current commercial scanners rely on LYSO crystals, which are costly and depend on geographically concentrated rare-earth supply chains. CRYSP proposes an alternative TBPET design based on large monolithic pure cesium iodide (CsI) crystals operated at cryogenic temperatures (~100 K). At these temperatures, CsI achieves a light yield of ~10⁵ photons/MeV, yielding an energy resolution below 7% at 511 keV. The monolithic geometry provides inherent depth-of-interaction (DOI) capability, enabling millimeter-scale spatial resolution in all three dimensions and minimizing parallax error. These properties compensate for the lower sensitivity and absence of time-of-flight information, allowing image quality competitive with state-of-the-art TBPET scanners at substantially reduced cost. The slow decay time of cryogenic CsI (~800 ns) renders conventional readout electronics unsuitable; a front-end based on the CAEN CITIROC ASIC, providing pulse-height analysis well suited for slow scintillators, was adopted instead for the prototype. Event position reconstruction employs both analytic methods and a deep-learning algorithm trained on Geant4 simulations, achieving millimeter-scale resolution including DOI in Monte Carlo studies. As a first proof-of-concept, a small-scale PET scanner comprising 18 monolithic CsI(Tl) crystals operating at room temperature is under development, providing hands-on experience with the full acquisition and reconstruction chain before advancing to a cryogenic prototype.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 37Poster Number:MIC-05-037] Evaluation of a Low-Noise Ultra-Fast SiPM Time-of Flight Analog Readout Chip (LUSTAR) (#2690)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. W. Cates (Autores: J. W. Cates , J. Johnson , W.-S. Choong , C. Grace)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Applied Nuclear Physics, Berkeley, California, United States of America [2] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Engineering, Berkeley, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The precision to which the arrival time of 511 keV photons are able to be known directly affects the signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) for reconstructed images in time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET). Currently, significant research is ongoing to push the full-width-half-maximum (FWHM) coincidence time resolution (CTR) for TOF-PET systems well below 100 ps towards the few-10's-of-ps regime. In this work, we designed an application specific integrated circuit (ASIC) in a commercial 65nm CMOS process to translate ultra-fast timing performance currently demonstrated in state-of-the-art bench-top measurements into a fully integrated scalable topology for large scale time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF- PET) systems. We targeted a scalable, low-noise, ultra-fast silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) analog front-end that maintains excellent SNR for single photon response while achieving ≤35 ps FWHM electronic noise jitter for single photon detection with 4x4 mm 2 Broadcom AFBR-S4N44P014M Near-ultraviolet metal-trench SiPMs. This "analog" chip uses low-voltage differential signaling (LVDS) transmitters to drive discriminator data to an external time-to-digital converter (TDC). We present evaluation of achievable single photon time resolution and CTR with the first prototype test chip.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 40Poster Number:MIC-05-040] A Dual-Ended Readout PET Detector Module With 0.75 mm Pitch LYSO Arrays for High-Resolution Small-Animal Imaging (#2714)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 X. Huang (Autores: S. Yang , X. Huang , X. Han , H. Yuan , H. Liao , L. Wei , Z. Zhang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Chinese Academy of Sciences, Institute of High Energy Physics, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present a high-resolution PET detector module with fine-pitch crystals and dual-ended readout for small-animal imaging. The detector employs a 28 × 28 LYSO crystal array with a pixel size of 0.75 mm × 0.75 mm × 15 mm, separated by 0.08 mm BaSO 4 reflector layers and read out at both ends by SiPM arrays. Experimental results demonstrated clear crystal separation with a corrected depth-of-interaction (DOI) resolution of 1.59 mm (FWHM) and an energy resolution of 14.9% in the selected 1/4 detector region. These results indicate that dual-ended readout can effectively improve DOI resolution in fine-pitch crystal arrays while preserving crystal separation, demonstrating the feasibility of fine-pitch dual-ended PET detectors for high-resolution small-animal PET imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 43Poster Number:MIC-05-043] CNN-Based 2D Source Localization Using Collimator-Free Staggered Scintillator Arrays (#2914)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Casanelli (Autores: B. Casanelli , I. Neves , A. L. M. Silva , P. M. M. Correia)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Aveiro, Institute for Nanostructures, Nanomodelling and Nanofabrication (i3N), Department of Physics (DFis), Aveiro, Portugal
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Mechanical collimators in SPECT introduce a fundamental sensitivity-resolution trade-off that becomes critical in targeted radionuclide therapy (TRT) imaging, where administered activities are low. We explore a collimator-free detector concept based on an 18x18 pixelated GAGG scintillator array in which collimation is achieved through staggering, that is, height offsets between neighboring pixels that produce characteristic shadow patterns in the resulting flood map. Three configurations are evaluated: a flat array (stagger-0), a single-pixel checkerboard (stagger-1), and a 3x3-block checkerboard (stagger-3). For each geometry, OpenGATE 10 Monte Carlo simulations of a 140 keV point source were performed at 400 positions on a fixed-height plane. The resulting flood maps were used to train a 2D convolutional neural network that regresses the source coordinates. Evaluated on 40 test positions, the 3D root-mean-square error of the neural network decreases with increasing staggering degree, from 0.44 mm (stagger-0) to 0.40 mm (stagger-1) and 0.34 mm (stagger-3), a 23% reduction that supports staggering as a promising strategy for collimator-free source localization.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 46Poster Number:MIC-05-046] Development and Experimental Characterization of a Fine-Pitch CZT SPECT Detector Head with Simulation-Guided Matched-Pixel Collimator Selection (#3083)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Wang (Autores: Z. Song , R. Wang , P. Ke , X. Chen , Z. Hao , J. Gong , X. Lv , S. An)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shanghai United Imaging Healthcare Advanced Technology Research Institute Co., Ltd, Shanghai, China [2] United Imaging Healthcare Co., Ltd., Molecular Imaging, Shanghai, China [3] ShanghaiTech University, School of Biomedical Engineering, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A fine-pitch CZT detector-head prototype was assembled and experimentally characterized for SPECT imaging. The head consists of a 5 × 10 tiled array of CZT modules, each containing 16 × 16 anodes with 1.45 mm pixels and a 1.6 mm pitch. The prototype achieved a global energy resolution of 4.8% at 140 keV. The intrinsic integral and differential uniformities were 0.56% and 0.44%, respectively. To exploit the fine intrinsic spatial sampling of the CZT detector, a fast ray-tracing Monte Carlo framework was used to explore dual-layer 1H/4HMPD matched-pixel collimator candidates and to compare them with the 1HL30.5 reference design, defined as a one-hole-per-pixel collimator with a 30.5 mm hole length, under prototype-constrained geometric and mechanical conditions. A representative dual-layer candidate showed an alternative main-lobe sensitivity-resolution trade-off, but GATE point-source simulations revealed more pronounced non-Gaussian tails than the 1HMPD reference. Therefore, the 1HL30.5 configuration was retained as the near-term practical collimator design. GATE-simulated Derenzo phantom reconstruction of this configuration showed that 5 mm hot rods were visually distinguishable at 10M and 5M total projection counts. These results support the feasibility of the fine-pitch CZT detector-head prototype and justify retaining 1HL30.5 for subsequent experimental phantom validation.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 49Poster Number:MIC-05-049] Monte Carlo simulations of positrons in uniform magnetic fields with PENELOPE (#1298)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Alva-Sánchez (Autores: M. A. González-Ramírez , M. Rodríguez-Villafuerte , A. Martínez-Dávalos , H. Alva-Sánchez)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Instituto de Física, Mexico City, Mexico
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study investigates the influence of magnetic fields on F-18 and Ga-68 positrons and how they affect image quality metrics in tissue-equivalent phantoms relevant to PET/MR imaging. To this end, we performed Monte Carlo simulations using the PENELOPE code. Since the main PENELOPE routine penmain.f does not account for the influence of electromagnetic fields on radiation transport in matter, a modified version of the penfield.f module was used instead. Simulations were carried out in four representative media (lung, soft tissue, water, and cortical bone) and in NEMA-like image quality phantoms to assess the effect of uniform magnetic fields of 0, 3, and 9 T. We simulated positron point sources at the center of a 10 cm-radius spherical phantom of homogeneous materials and in a set of three image-quality phantoms to evaluate specific image-quality parameters: spill-over ratio, recovery coefficient, and lesion detectability, as in a previous experimental study. The results indicate that positron range significantly affects recovery coefficients and spill-over ratios, particularly for high-energy positron emitters in low-density tissues. In the recovery-coefficient phantom, when the cylinder separation distance is smaller than the positron range, a slight overestimation of the recovery coefficients is observed due to contributions from adjacent cylinders. The magnetic field reduces these effects in the direction perpendicular to the magnetic field lines, leading to improved spatial resolution and quantitative accuracy. These findings represent the maximum image quality that can be achieved under ideal conditions in a PET system in the presence of uniform magnetic fields and provide a physical basis for the development of positron-range correction methods in PET/MR imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 52Poster Number:MIC-05-052] Impact of a Breast PET Insert on Lesion Detectability in Whole-Body PET/MRI (#1405)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H.P. Vo (Autores: H.P. Vo , J. Roser , E. Olyaei , J. Hohnholz , L. Rauscher , F. P. Schmidt , M. Rafecas)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Luebeck, Institute of Medical Engineering, Luebeck, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany [2] Eberhard Karls University Tuebingen, Werner Siemens Imaging Center, Department of Preclinical Imaging and Radiopharmacy, Tuebingen, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [3] University Hospital Tuebingen, Department of Nuclear Medicine and Clinical Molecular Imaging, Tuebingen, Baden-Württemberg, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract To improve the detectability of small lesions and early metastases, we are developing a breast PET insert that operates in conjunction with a whole-body (WB) PET/MRI scanner. We implemented a joint reconstruction framework with attenuation correction that explicitly accounts for the different coincidence types from the insert and the WB-PET, aiming to improve spatial resolution inside the insert field of view (iFOV), as well as outside. Performance was evaluated using Monte Carlo simulations of an anthropomorphic phantom with lesions of 4, 8, and 12 mm diameter and contrast ratios of 4:1 and 8:1 relative to the breast background. Lesions were placed at clinically relevant locations, including within the breast, as well as in axillary and parasternal lymph nodes. Compared to WB-PET alone, the inclusion of all coincidence types improved lesion conspicuity, particularly for small (4-8 mm) and low-contrast lesions. Within the iFOV, breast lesions show increases in contrast recovery coefficent (CRC) of up to 16.4% (4 mm, 8:1) and 16.9% (8 mm, 4:1), with 4-mm lesions becoming resolvable. Similar trends were observed for axillary lymph nodes, with CRC increases of up to 11.9% (8 mm, 4:1). Future work will extend this study beyond the idealized 511 keV case to more realistic energy windows with finite energy resolution and higher scatter contribution, as well as incorporate spatially variant point spread function modeling and scatter correction into the reconstruction framework.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 55Poster Number:MIC-05-055] Proposal of an L-shaped Dual-detector Multi-pinhole Myocardial SPECT System Using a CNN (#1523)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Akatsuka (Autores: T. Akatsuka , K. Ogawa)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Hosei University, Applied Informatics, Graduate School of Science and Engineering, Koganei, Japan [2] Hosei University, Applied Informatics, Faculty of Science and Engineering, Koganei, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Dedicated cardiac semiconductor SPECT systems enable short acquisition times owing to their high sensitivity; however, artifacts may occur depending on patient body habitus, and quantitative reconstruction images cannot be obtained because attenuation correction using X-ray CT images (μ-maps) is not available. In this study, we propose a novel SPECT system in which two gamma cameras equipped with NaI scintillators are arranged in an L-shaped configuration, allowing data acquisition while keeping the detectors stationary, and achieving attenuation, scatter, statistical noise and collimator aperture correction using a convolutional neural network (CNN). To improve sensitivity, 44 multi-pinhole collimators were employed, and projection images were acquired in an overlapped manner and accurately separated using the CNN. A U-Net++ architecture was adopted to construct a unified framework for overlap separation of projection data, statistical noise reduction, aperture correction and attenuation/scatter correction without requiring μ-maps. Image reconstruction was performed using the ML-EM algorithm, and image quality was evaluated using the normalized mean squared error (NMSE) of the polar map. As a result, approximately uniform image reconstruction was achieved without using μ-maps, and the NMSE was 0.0402, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 58Poster Number:MIC-05-058] EduPETSIM: An Educational Web-Based Framework Integrating Simulation, Reconstruction, and Generative AI for Rapid Source Modeling (#1644)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Hoang (Autores: T. Hoang , M. Grossmann , A. Gonzalez-Montoro , P. M. Correia , A. L. Silva , J. F. Veloso , Y. Seo)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Science, VNU-HCM, Physics, Ho Chi Minh, Viet Nam [2] Vietnam National University, Ho Chi Minh, Viet Nam [3] Paul Scherrer Institut PSI, Villigen, Switzerland [4] Instituto de Instrumentación para Imagen Molecular (I3M), Centro Mixto CSIC-Universitat Politècnica de València, Detectors for Molecular Imaging Lab (DMIL), València, Spain [5] University of Aveiro, the I3N Physics Department, Aveiro, Portugal [6] University of California, San Francisco and Berkeley, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate physics-based simulations are essential for assessing and validating scanner geometries and reconstruction algorithms. EduPET is an NPSS-supported educational PET technology demonstrator. This work introduces the Educational PET SIMulation system (EduPETSIM), an integrated web-based framework designed for educational purposes to streamline the entire PET workflow. The platform unites an OpenGATE-based simulation engine, a custom coincidence sorter, and an image reconstruction module within a unified environment. A primary novel contribution of this framework is the integration of a Conditional Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Network (cWGAN) to facilitate rapid source modeling, which significantly reduces the computational overhead associated with traditional particle transport simulation. Current developments focus on fine-tuning the cWGAN model for a 22 Na source within the two-detector EduPET system, with the completed model available for the upcoming IEEE NPSS schools on medical imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 61Poster Number:MIC-05-061] Accelerating Monte Carlo Light Transport in Turbid Media with an Analytically Invertible Simplified Phase Function (#1704)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A.-N. Rapsomanikis (Autores: A.-N. Rapsomanikis , M.-E. Tomazinaki , E. Stiliaris)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, Department of Physics, Athens, Greece [2] University of West Attica, Athens, Greece [3] Institute of Accelerating Systems & Applications (IASA), Athens, Greece
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Modeling light scattering in biological media requires balancing the accuracy of Mie theory with the speed of simplified phase functions. We propose a new phase function that replaces the standard cos(θ) term with a quadratic θ 2 relationship, significantly improving large-angle fidelity compared to the Henyey-Greenstein (HG) model. A key advantage is the function's analytical invertibility, enabling direct Inverse Transform Sampling that accelerates Monte Carlo simulations by bypassing transcendental computations. Mathematical consistency is validated against the stochastic Rejection Method for various tissues. Transport simulations using the PhoSim package demonstrate enhanced spatial accuracy and closer alignment with the Mie ground truth, offering a high-speed framework for real-time IR tomography and Time-Resolved Optical Tomography.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 64Poster Number:MIC-05-064] Fast On-the-Fly System Matrix Computation for Broad-Energy Multi-Pinhole SPECT (#1808)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Gao (Autores: B. Gao , B. Wang , F. Zhou , L. He , Y. Dong)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] United Imaging Healthcare, Molecular Imaging Business Unit, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present a GPU-accelerated system matrix computation method for multi-pinhole SPECT based on spatial modeling of position-dependent point spread functions (PSFs). Sparse Monte Carlo-generated PSFs are fitted with an anisotropic Gaussian model, and the resulting parameters are expressed as geometry-dependent functions to enable estimation of voxel-dependent responses at unmeasured locations. Implemented in CUDA for forward and backprojection, the method supports on-the-fly iterative reconstruction without storage of a fully precomputed system matrix. This approach was evaluated using Derenzo phantoms and NEMA image quality phantoms filled with isotopes whose emitted photon energies range from 140 to 440 keV, demonstrating its potential for efficient multi-isotope and theranostic SPECT imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 67Poster Number:MIC-05-067] Monte Carlo Based Performance Evaluation of a Dual Panel PET&SPECT Trimodal Imager (#1888)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Yang (Autores: H. Yang , X. Zeng , Y. Zhao , Z. Wu , H. Li , M. Niu , Z. Gu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China [2] Harbin Institute of Technology, School of Astronautics, Harbin, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work presents a Monte Carlo based performance evaluation of a dual-panel PET&SPECT trimodal imaging system, in terms of spatial resolution, system sensitivity, and count rate performance following the NEMA NU 2-2018 standard. Spatial resolution measurements yield an average value of 1.01 mm for PET and 11.1 mm for SPECT. The SPECT sensitivity with a 700 mm length line source is 101.5 cps/MBq at the center of the field of view (axial offset z = 0 cm) and 103.0 cps/MBq at z = 10 cm. When using a 350 mm line source, SPECT sensitivity increases to 152.1 cps/MBq at z = 0 cm and 129.1 cps/MBq at z = 10 cm. The PET sensitivity measured with a 700 mm length line source achieves 43.4 cps/kBq at z = 0 cm and 43.5 cps/kBq at z = 10 cm. The PET peak noise equivalent count rate reaches 131.5 kcps at 193 MBq in standalone acquisition mode, and decreases under simultaneous PET&SPECT acquisition due to elevated dead time induced by SPECT detections. These results validate the overall system design, quantify the interference between PET and SPECT detections, and provide a foundation for further optimization toward clinical trimodal imaging applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 70Poster Number:MIC-05-070] Experimental Validation and Calibration of a GATE Simulation Model for a Dedicated Breast PET/MR Insert (#2013)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. Olyaei (Autores: E. Olyaei , J. Hohnholz , H. P. Vo , L. U. Rauscher , M. Rafecas , B. J.Pichler , F. P. Schmidt)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Tuebingen, Werner Siemens Imaging Center, Department of Preclinical Imaging and Radiopharmacy, Tuebingen, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [2] University Hospital of Tuebingen, Department of Nuclear Medicine and Clinical Molecular Imaging, Tuebingen, Baden-Württemberg, Germany [3] University of Luebeck, Institute of Medical Engineering, Luebeck, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Advanced detector designs employing multi-layer crystal configurations and multiplexed readouts introduce complex light transport and inter-crystal scatter effects. These result in position-dependent differences in energy response and crystal identification that are difficult to reproduce using idealized simulations. We present an experimentally calibrated GATE simulation framework for a dual-layer depth-of-interaction capable detector developed for a dedicated breast PET/MRI insert. The detector block consists of a 10×10 bottom LSO crystal array (1.5×1.5×9.81 mm³) and a 9×9 top array (1.5×1.5×5.19 mm³). Simulations were performed using GATE v9.4.1 for two geometries and compared against experimental measurements. A reference configuration of 18 detector modules in a 100 mm ring was used to derive crystal-specific correction factors, then applied to the same 18 modules in a 178 mm ring representing the breast insert geometry. Measurements were acquired using a centered Na-22 point source for three energy windows (250-760 keV, 511±50 keV, and 430-610 keV) with experimentally informed coincidence timing resolutions. The uncorrected simulations systematically overestimated experimental coincidence count rates, with the largest deviations at edge and corner crystals of the bottom layer. Prior to calibration, mean absolute deviations for the 178 mm geometry were 37.1%, 38.0%, and 43.0%; following calibration, deviations were reduced to 9.3%, 8.4%, and 8.8%. Experimental detector blocks additionally showed substantially larger crystal-to-crystal variations in energy resolution (top: 12.5±1.1%, bottom: 11.0±1.2%) compared with the fixed simulated values, indicating complex optical transport and detector-specific effects are not yet fully reproduced in the current model.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 73Poster Number:MIC-05-073] An Integrated Digital Twin Framework for Accurate Quantification of Preclinical Immuno-PET (#2128)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Dominguez-Borrero (Autores: C. Dominguez-Borrero , X. García-Otero , E. Ramos-Docampo , J. Rodríguez-Silva , N. Gómez-Lado , S. Groba de Antas , M. Gómez-Muñoz , J. Codesido , L. García-Varela , P. Aguiar)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Molecular Imaging Biomarkers Group, Center for Research in Molecular Medicine and Chronic Diseases (CIMUS), Universidad de Santiago de Compostela, Santiago de Compostela, Spain [2] Nuclear Medicine Department and Molecular Imaging Group, Health Research Institute of Santiago de Compostela (IDIS), Santiago de Compostela, Spain [3] Reina Sofia Alzheimer Center, CIEN Foundation, Madrid, Spain [4] Centro de Investigación Biomédica en Red en Enfermedades Neurodegenerativas (CIBERNED), Instituto de Salud Carlos III, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate quantification in preclinical PET remains a fundamental challenge due to the spatial resolution constraints inherent to small-animal imaging, where partial volume effects compromise biodistribution and dosimetry estimations in monoclonal antibody-based radiopharmaceuticals. Here, we present the first integrated digital-twin framework for immuno-PET quantification in preclinical imaging developed around a validated Monte Carlo model of the Bruker (BioSpec 3T) PET/MRI scanner implemented using the SimPET platform - which integrates the SimSET Monte Carlo engine and STIR reconstruction software - and validated following the NEMA NU 4-2008 standard. This validated model was then combined with physical and digital rodent phantoms to assess a highly accurate immuno-PET quantification pipeline. Scanner validation showed a good agreement between simulated and experimental data, with underestimation below 5%. On the other hand, quantification of a representative immuno-PET biodistribution using the Bio-Rat phantom revealed underestimations below 20% across most organs, consistent with partial volume effects at this spatial resolution. This framework establishes a reproducible strategy to characterize and correct quantification biases in preclinical PET, with direct impact on the translational development of radiopharmaceuticals.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 76Poster Number:MIC-05-076] Tensor-Based Multi-Stage Evolution for Generative Design of Arbitrary Permanent Magnet Geometries for PET-compatible Low-Field MRI (#2266)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M.S.H. Akram (Autores: M.S.H. Akram , F. Nishikido , T. Obata , T. Yamaya)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology (QST), Dept. of Advanced Nuclear Medicine Sciences, Chiba, Japan [2] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology (QST), Applied MRI Research, Chiba, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The development of portable, low-field MRI systems is currently limited by the computational complexity of optimizing high-density permanent magnet arrays. While traditional Halbach cylinders offer a baseline for transverse fields, achieving medical-grade homogeneity in non-standard, compact geometries remains prohibitive using conventional loop-based physics. This work introduces an ultra-vectorized "Gen-Tensor" engine that revolutionizes the magnet design process by replacing iterative loops with 4D broadcasting and tensor evolution. By parameterizing 300 discrete magnets into a multiple of 2,100-variable generative DNA block (encompassing 3D position, 3-axis rotation, and activation masks), the framework enables the autonomous synthesis of inherently shimmed, multi-layered topologies. A significant breakthrough of this study is the discovery of a non-standard Cassinian oval architecture that achieves a field magnitude nearly double that of traditional circular cylindrical benchmarks while maintaining high directional purity of the field. This 100% increase in field strength is achieved without an increase in the magnet budget, utilizing the algorithm's ability to exploit non-linear flux-path efficiencies and dynamic compaction. The optimization employs a dual-stage differential evolution protocol, transitioning from a high-entropy exploration phase to a low-mutation precision shimming phase. The resulting parallel flux streamlines, and high directional purity demonstrate a robust pathway for the realization of high-signal, portable MRI systems. This technology is specifically designed for side-by-side operation with existing PET systems in radiologically controlled environments, offering a computationally efficient solution for next-generation point-of-care molecular imaging without the need for intensive post-fabrication shimming.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 79Poster Number:MIC-05-079] Design of SSLE-PET with GATE Simulation Towards Sub-Second Dynamic Mouse Imaging (#2309)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H.G. Kang (Autores: H.G. Kang , H. Tashima , T. Sakai , T. Yamaya)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology (QST), Advanced Nuclear Medicine Science, Chiba, Japan [2] Hamamatsu Photonics, Hamamatsu, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Last year, we developed an ultrasensitive preclinical positron emission tomography (PET) scanner with 4-layer depth-of-interaction (DOI) detectors, thereby allowing sub-second dynamic imaging of a rat. However, the crystal pitch and DOI bins were 2.8 mm and 7.5 mm, which hampered mouse imaging. On the other hand, assembling smaller crystals remains technically challenging. In this study, we designed a novel preclinical PET scanner that uses a sub-surface laser engraving (SSLE) technique to fabricate the finely pixelized crystal elements, and we call it the SSLE-PET. The SSLE-PET consists of 12 DOI detectors, each of which has tapered LYSO crystals with a thickness of 20 mm. The LYSO crystals were pixelized by SSLE, providing fine crystal pitches (top=1.0 mm, bottom=1.6 mm) and 2.5 mm DOI bins. We used GATE simulation to investigate the effects of inner diameter (i.e. detector gap) and axial coverage on the performance of the SSLE-PET. To evaluate spatial resolution and sensitivity, a NEMA 22 Na source was used. For imaging performance evaluation, a resolution phantom was used. The GATE output was reconstructed by using a filtered back projection algorithm without any gap filling method. An energy window of 400-600 keV was used. The spatial resolution (1.27 mm) and resolvable rod diameter (1.0 mm) were not affected by the inner diameter. However, gap artifacts appeared for an inner diameter of 70 mm. Hence, an inner diameter of 65 mm would be the best choice to avoid any mechanical collision between detectors, while maintaining the image quality. With an axial coverage of 88 mm, sub-second PET imaging was demonstrated. As a next step, we plan to develop a prototype SSLE-PET scanner.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 82Poster Number:MIC-05-082] SPECT vs. Compton Camera for Prompt Gamma Monitoring in BNCT: a simulation study. (#2424)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Ferri (Autores: T. Ferri , F. Ghisio , M. Carminati , C. Fiorini , D. Mazzuzzoni , G. Mocerino , S. Agosteo , G. Borghi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Politecnico di Milano, Dipartimento di Elettronica, Informazione and Bioingegneria, Milano, Italy [2] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare (INFN), Sezione di Milano, Milano, Italy [3] Politecnico di Milano, Dipartimento di Energia, Milano, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Real-time monitoring in Boron Neutron Capture Therapy (BNCT) exploiting the 478 keV gamma rays emitted by the neutron capture reaction, remains a major challenge due to the intense background present in the irradiation room during treatment. To date, no clinically established system is available, and the choice between SPECT and Compton camera approaches remains an open and highly relevant question. Here, we present a Monte Carlo (MC) comparison study between a previously developed BNCT-SPECT detector and a LaBr3-based Compton camera for 478 keV prompt-gamma detection. The goal is to assess the capability of Compton cameras to exploit electronic collimation and directionality for background rejection, thereby improving the signal-to-background ratio (SBR) with respect to SPECT. The results confirm that, in the absence of shielding, SPECT detection is severely dominated by room-induced background. For a vial containing 1000 ppm of 10 B irradiated with a thermal neutron flux of 3 × 10 6 n cm −2 s −1 , the SPECT configuration yielded an SBR of only 0.009, while the Compton camera achieved an SBR of 3.2. These findings suggest that a Compton camera-based system may represent a promising strategy to address one of the main limitations of BNCT-SPECT systems towards clinical applicability. However, the choice between the two approaches remains challenging, since properly shielded SPECT configurations can still provide high SBR values, while clinically relevant neutron fluences may increase the single-interaction rate in Compton cameras, making true-coincidence identification more demanding and possibly requiring dedicated shielding as well.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 85Poster Number:MIC-05-085] A Novel Inter-Crystal Scatter Positioning Method Using Variable-Bin Stochastic Conditional Probability Based on Energy and Depth-of-Interaction Ordering (#2695)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Shim (Autores: H. Shim , G.B. Ko)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Department of Nuclear and Quantum Engineering, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [2] Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Mechanical Engineering Research Institute,, Daejeon, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Inter-crystal scatter (ICS) in PET detectors causes multiple interactions within a detector block, and misidentification of the first interaction crystal can lead to incorrect LOR assignment and image degradation. Rejecting all ICS events avoids this error but reduces system sensitivity. This study proposes a stochastic conditional-probability-based ICS positioning method using ordering information from deposited energy and DOI. The method estimates first-interaction events by applying conditional probabilities defined over binned observables, where the conditioning variable is either the energy or DOI difference between two crystals involved in an ICS event. These probabilities were obtained statistically from GATE simulations of an 8×8 LYSO crystal array with 3.2 mm pitch. Point sources were placed at 5, 10, 20, and 25 cm, and two-crystal ICS events were selected for validation. The effects of bin count, binning strategy, and detector resolution were evaluated using 2, 4, and 8 bins with equiquantile and equal-width binning. Accuracy exceeded 85% using only 3% of the validation data, corresponding to approximately 20,000 ICS counts per detector block. DOI-based conditioning achieved slightly higher accuracy than energy-based method, suggesting that DOI ordering provides useful geometric information for first-crystal identification. However, the performance difference was small, indicating that either DOI or energy ordering can be used depending on detector readout capability. Accuracy was insensitive to bin count, binning strategy, and detector resolution. These results demonstrate that reliable ICS positioning can be achieved using predetermined conditional probabilities matched to detector characteristics, supporting practical recovery of ICS events without requiring high detector resolution or excessive readout complexity.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 88Poster Number:MIC-05-088] Validation of Compton camera simulations using GATE version 10 through experimental data (#2793)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. J. Hurani (Autores: Z. J. Hurani , L. Barrientos , K. Brzezinski , G. Llosá , D. Sarrut , A. Etxebeste)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CREATIS, CNRS UMR 5220, INSERM U1044, Université de Lyon, INSA-Lyon, Université Lyon 1, Lyon, France [2] Instituto de Física Corpuscular (IFIC), CSIC, Universitat de València, Valencia, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Compton cameras are electronically collimated imaging devices that reconstruct the origin of gamma rays using Compton kinematics, making them particularly suited for targeted radionuclide therapy (TRT), where conventional gamma cameras struggle with high-energy and low-activity emitters. The European project AIDER is developing a high-performance scintillator-based Compton camera to improve imaging and enable dosimetry in TRT, including targeted alpha therapy. Accurate Monte Carlo modeling is essential in this context for detector design and image reconstruction optimization. We present the validation of Compton camera simulations using GATE version 10, a major evolution of the Geant4-based Monte Carlo toolkit for medical physics with a Python based user interface. To this end, data acquired with MACACO1, a two-layer Compton camera prototype based on monolithic LaBr₃ scintillation crystals, developed at IFIC-Valencia, was employed. A Monte Carlo model of this system was previously validated using a dedicated Compton camera module in an older version of GATE based on legacy static macro-based files. In this work, the model was developed using GATE 10. The detector response was modeled by a digitizer chain that includes the measured energy and spatial resolution of the prototype. Time coincidences were obtained offline using a time coincidence window of 50 ns. Simulated and experimental coincidence energy spectra showed good agreement despite small discrepancies at low energies. The angular resolution measure at 1275~keV was in good agreement between both simulated and experimental data with a relative difference of 0.7%. The validated framework for Compton camera simulations with the new GATE 10 modular version, provides a flexible platform for detector design and image reconstruction optimization.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 91Poster Number:MIC-05-091] Convertible Whole‑Body Extension of a Brain‑Dedicated Whole Gamma Imaging System:A Simulation Study (#3053)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Akamatsu (Autores: R. Abe , G. Akamatsu , H. Tashima , T. Yamaya)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology, Imaging physics groupe, Chiba, Japan [2] Chiba University, Medical Engineering Course, Department of Fundamental Engineering, Graduate School of Science and Engineering, Chiba, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Whole gamma imaging (WGI) is a hybrid nuclear medicine technique under development at QST that integrates PET and Compton imaging by placing a scatterer detector ring inside a PET detector ring. This configuration is expected to enable simultaneous PET and SPECT tracer imaging and to allow high‑sensitivity PET acquisition using radionuclides such as 89 Zr, which emit both positrons and prompt gamma rays. In this study, we investigated the feasibility of extending a previously optimized brain‑dedicated WGI design to a whole‑body configuration by scaling the scatterer‑detector ring diameter. Our proposed system expands the scatterer detector ring diameter in the whole-body mode, and fills the missing data due to the detector gaps by a mechanical rotation. Monte Carlo simulations using Geant4 were performed to evaluate the detection performance of the proposed system for 89 Zr imaging in the whole-body mode, with particular emphasis on the effects of inter‑detector gaps introduced by geometric scaling and the necessity of mechanical rotation in the scatterer‑detector system. Point‑source simulations were conducted to assess Compton sensitivity and angular resolution measure (ARM), and sparse detector configurations were reproduced by masking half of the scatterer detectors. The results showed that Compton sensitivity was approximately doubled when all scatterer modules were installed, indicating that sensitivity is primarily determined by the number of available detectors rather than the presence of gaps. In contrast, ARM exhibited minimal variation across configurations, suggesting that mechanical rotation has little influence on angular‑resolution performance. These findings provide essential design guidelines for whole‑body WGI systems and will be further validated through imaging simulations to quantify the impact of detector gaps and rotation on reconstructed image quality.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 94Poster Number:MIC-05-094] Translating CLS Detector Technology from Brain to Whole-Body PET Imaging: A Simulation Study (#3161)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Furuta (Autores: M. Furuta , H. Tashima , G. Akamatsu , T. Yamaya)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology (QST), Department of Advanced Nuclear Medicine Sciences, Chiba, Japan [2] Chiba University, Faculty of Engineering, Chiba, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We have achieved 1 mm rod separation performance in a brain-dedicated PET system, CLS-7, which employs our original crosshair light-sharing (CLS) detector with both time-of-flight (TOF) and depth-of-interaction (DOI) capabilities. From that work, our next question to explore is how CLS technology can improve whole-body PET imaging. PET is widely used in cancer diagnosis, and improving spatial resolution with low image noise is important for detecting small lesions at earlier stages. In this study using Monte Carlo simulation, we investigated the imaging performance of a whole-body PET system using CLS detectors. A whole-body CLS-PET system was modeled using the Geant4 with a ring diameter of 750 mm and an axial field-of-view of 228 mm. The detector was modeled as a 14 × 14 LGSO crystal array with 1.45 × 1.45 × 15 mm³ crystals divided into three depth segments for DOI modeling. The system had 92 detector blocks per ring and seven rings. Spatial resolution and image quality were evaluated by simulating point-source and image quality phantom measurements based on the NEMA NU 2 standard and compared to cases with and without DOI and TOF information. As a result, we found the use of DOI information improved spatial resolution by 40% compared with the no-DOI information condition, while TOF information substantially reduced image noise in the image-quality evaluation. These results suggest that whole-body PET using CLS detectors can suppress peripheral spatial-resolution degradation and improve contrast recovery for small lesions .

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 97Poster Number:MIC-05-097] Photon-Counting CT in the Context of Ultra-Low-Dose PET/CT (#2394)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Mostafapour (Autores: S. Mostafapour , J. F. Hop , J. Braaksma , M. J. Greuter , J. van Sluis , A. A. Lammertsma , C. Tsoumpas)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University Medical Center Groningen, University of Groningen, Nuclear medicine and molecular imaging department, Groningen, Netherlands [2] University Medical Center Groningen, University of Groningen, Department of Radiology, Groningen, Netherlands
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Reducing radiation dose in positron emission tomography / computed tomography (PET/CT) is possible, but ultra-low-dose (ULD)-CT increases image noise which may affect quantitative reliability and accuracy due to attenuation correction. Photon-counting CT (PCCT) offers improved noise characteristics compared with conventional energy-integrating detector CT (EID-CT), particularly at low dose levels. This study compares PCCT and EID-CT under low-dose (LD) and ULD-CT conditions using a cadaver, an anthropomorphic phantom (PBU-60), and a tissue characterization phantom (Gammex 467). Quantitative evaluation is performed using CT values in HU and corresponding linear attenuation coefficients ( μ ). Results show that ULD increases noise in both systems, with stronger degradation and reconstruction dependency in EID-CT. Compared with EID-CT, PCCT shows less changes in mean HU values between LD and ULD acquisitions, particularly in dense materials, although noise remains present. After HU-to- μ conversion, variability is substantially reduced for both systems, though not uniformly across all conditions. These findings indicate that attenuation coefficients are less sensitive to dose reduction than CT values and suggest that PCCT may provide more robust quantitative performance than EID-CT under ULD conditions. However, given non-matched acquisition and reconstruction settings results should be interpreted with caution, and require validation in further standardized and PET-based studies.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 100Poster Number:MIC-05-100] DMGR-Net: Dual-Modal Gated Residual Network for Lightweight PET/MRI Brain Parcellation (#2634)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Wang (Autores: M. Wang , G. Zhan , Y. Tong , J. Yang , X. Liu , Y. Li , S. Feng , J. Zou , S. Xie)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Sun Yat-sen University, School of Medicine, Shenzhen, China [2] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China [3] Sun Yat-sen University, Zhongshan School of Medicine, Guangzhou, China [4] Sun Yat-Sen University, School of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China [5] Florida State University, Tallahassee, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Automated parcellation of the brain into correct regions using dual-modal PET and MRI is essential for quantitative neuroimaging. Existing high-performing fusion networks often rely on large model sizes, which limits their deployment in resource-constrained settings. This paper presents the DualModal Gated Residual Network (DMGR-Net), a lightweight architecture that integrates Bidirectional Cross-Modal Feature Gating (Bi-CMFG) and Residual Soft Deep Supervision (RSDS). Bi-CMFG performs spatial attention across modality-specific encoder branches to preserve fine structural details, while RSDS applies a boundary-weighted loss at multiple decoder scales to sharpen parcellation boundaries by explicitly penalizing errors along anatomical interfaces. Built upon a depthwise-separable 3D U-Net with only 0.121M parameters, DMGR-Net contains 0.206M parameters and 5.30 GFLOPs, yet achieves the lowest HD95 and ASSD among compared methods, surpassing substantially larger models on surface-distance metrics. Ablation studies confirm the complementary roles of each module, and qualitative comparisons illustrate progressively refined boundaries across configurations, demonstrating that a lightweight design can deliver precise surface delineation.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 103Poster Number:MIC-05-103] New Hyperion Detector Platform Electronics: Highly Integrated Mainboard, Tile Cable, and Sensor Tile (#2834)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Weissler (Autores: B. Weissler , D. Schug , E. Gegenmantel , O. Muelhens , T. Meyer , H. Radermacher , J. Thull , M. Breuer , C. Lerche , V. Schulz)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] RWTH Aachen University, Institute of Imaging & Computer Vision / Institute for Experimental Molecular Imaging, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [2] Hyperion Hybrid Imaging Systems GmbH, Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [3] Forschungszentrum Juelich, Institute of Neuroscience and Medicine 4, Juelich, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Combined PET/MRI is a powerful tool for studying neurological diseases, but resolving cortical structures requires a spatial resolution of about one millimeter. Dedicated brain inserts can achieve this by bringing high-resolution detectors close to the head, provided that the detector electronics meet stringent constraints on integration, thinness, width, length, and MRI compatibility. The S-PET project develops such a scalable PET detector platform for neuro PET/MRI. The detector module concept is built around a single mounting and cooling structure that spans the full module length and carries sensor tiles, mainboard, and power supply. The Visor HD sensor tile (49 × 49 mm²) combines a 12 × 12 Broadcom 4 mm NUV-MT SiPMs with a PETsys TOFPET2 ASIC. A dedicated compression scheme maps the 144 SiPM outputs to its maximum 64 ASIC channels: 36 SiPMs are read out directly, while the remaining channels each combine four spatially separated SiPMs that can be disambiguated through their direct neighbors. The SuperVisor mainboard (134 × 49 mm²) hosts six sensor-tile connectors, an AMD/Xilinx Kintex-7 FPGA, individual voltage and current regulation per tile, and fiber-optic transceivers on a second PCB layer to keep the board short. A separate, exchangeable power-supply board feeds the module. Thin flex-PCB tile cables, produced in precise lengths up to 454 mm, connect the sensor tiles to the mainboard on the opposite side of the cooling structure. A first measurement with a BrainPET 7T crystal array (three DOI layers of LSO at 2 mm pitch), scanned across a fan-beam-collimated ²²Na source, yields a mean absolute error below 1.4 mm in both planar directions, confirming that the Visor HD compression scheme works as intended. SuperVisor PCBs are in production and expected in time for the conference.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 106Poster Number:MIC-05-106] Development of a Shielded Digital PET Detector System for a Brain PET/MRI Insert (#3066)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Krauze (Autores: B. Krauze , Y. Shepelytskyi , V. Batarchuk , B. Baldassi , M. Albert , A. Reznik , O. Bubon)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lakehead University, Physics, Thunder Bay, Ontario, Canada [2] Radialis Inc., Thunder Bay, Ontario, Canada [3] Thunder Bay Regional Health Research Institute, Thunder Bay, Ontario, Canada
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Simultaneous positron emission tomography/magnetic resonance imaging (PET/MRI) can combine PET functional information with MRI soft-tissue contrast in a single imaging session, offering potential benefits for neurological applications such as neurodegenerative disease assessment and brain tumor localization. However, fully integrated PET/MRI systems remain limited, motivating the development of compact PET inserts that can operate inside or around existing MRI scanners. In this work, radiofrequency shielding was developed and evaluated as an enabling step toward an MRI-compatible Radialis brain PET insert using digital detector electronics. Shielding was implemented for the digital front-end modules, data-acquisition electronics, high-speed data-transmission cable, and auxiliary power cable of a Radialis PET detector array. Each detector module consisted of a 24 × 24 cerium-doped lutetium yttrium orthosilicate scintillator array coupled through a borosilicate light guide to an 8 × 8 silicon photomultiplier array. The shielded detector configuration was evaluated during simultaneous acquisition on a 3.0 T MRI system using a ²²Na point source in a water phantom positioned within the MRI brain-coil geometry. The redesigned shielding enabled stable PET data acquisition, coincidence processing, and point-source image reconstruction during MRI operation. PET energy resolution was maintained at approximately 22.5-22.6% during simultaneous acquisition, although reconstructed image signal-to-noise ratio decreased from 76.64 outside the MRI environment to 37.83 during PET/MRI acquisition, likely reflecting residual MRI-related effects, head-coil attenuation, and source-positioning differences. These results demonstrate that targeted shielding of Radialis digital PET electronics enables reliable simultaneous PET/MRI operation and supports further development of a high-sensitivity brain PET/MRI insert.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 109Poster Number:MIC-05-109] Design and Performance Evaluation of a Full-Ring SPECT System Based on the Continuous LaBr3(Ce) (#1199)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Wang (Autores: K. Wang , T. Dai , Q. Wei)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Science and Technology Beijing, Beijing Engineering Research Center of Industrial Spectrum Imaging and School of Automation and Electrical Engineering, Beijing, China [2] China-Japan Friendship Hospital, Department of Radiation Oncology, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Small-animal single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) serves as a cornerstone of functional nuclear imaging, with extensive applications in preclinical research, drug discovery, and life sciences. Building upon our previously developed full-ring cascade gamma coincidence imaging system with continuous LaBr3 crystals, this work redesigns a multi-pinhole collimator to enable full-ring SPECT imaging for 99m Tc. To optimize computational efficiency, the system transfer matrix is implemented using a sparse storage strategy. Furthermore, GPU acceleration is employed for key processes, including system matrix calculation, forward and backward projections, and image updates, significantly enhancing the performance of the iterative reconstruction algorithm. Experimental results demonstrate that the storage requirement for the system transfer matrix is reduced from 10.06 GB to 77.7 MB. Concurrently, the computational efficiency is significantly enhanced, achieving a single iteration time of 0.94 ms in binning mode. Moreover, the full-ring SPECT system achieves a 1.0×10 -3 detection efficiency and successfully resolves 1.2 mm diameter hot rods. In conclusion, the proposed full-ring SPECT system achieves a high-performance balance between detection sensitivity and spatial resolution.
