sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 112Poster Number:MIC-05-112] Image quality assessment of a positron emission mammography prototype (#1431)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 V. Pérez-Martínez (Autores: V. Pérez-Martínez , K. F. Goyes-Acosta , H. Alva-Sánchez , T. Murrieta-Rodríguez , A. Martínez-Dávalos , F. G. Moncada-Gutiérrez , M. Rodríguez-Villafuerte)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Instituto de Física, CDMX, Mexico
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract At the Biomedical Imaging Laboratory of the Institute of Physics, UNAM, a dual-panel positron emission mammography (PEM) prototype is under development. This work evaluated its spatial resolution through the line spread function, and image quality via recovery coefficients. A custom variable-geometry phantom was developed using 3D-printed supports for four 18 F line sources with a 0.69 mm internal diameter. Data acquisitions were performed at 11 in-plane positions and at different cross-planes heights to map the 17.4 cm × 17.4 cm × 6.0 cm effective field-of-view. Experimental setup included a panel separation distance of 6.0 cm, 8 ns coincidence window and a 360 - 757 keV energy window. The interaction position of each event is estimated using a raise-to-a-power center-of-gravity algorithm. Images are reconstructed using a list-mode ordered subsets expectation-maximization algorithm (3 iterations, 4 subsets) using a 1 mm isotropic voxel. Image quality was evaluated with a NEMA-like phantom containing 4 spherical lesions (diameters of 4, 6, 8 and 10 mm) filled with 18 F, placed at different field-of-view positions and phantom orientation. The effect of restricting oblique lines of response was also studied. In addition, the sensitivity was analyzed using a point-like 22 Na source in different field-of-view positions. The best spatial resolution was 2.1 ± 0.2 mm at the center of the PEM field-of-view and decreasing to 4.5 ± 0.3 mm at the PEM edges. FWHM values closest to the real sphere diameters were obtained at the detector center. Limiting oblique lines-of-response to reduce depth-of-interaction effects resulted in lower spatial resolution. Overall, the prototype showed good performance, with adequate image quality regardless of spherical-lesion position or orientation.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 115Poster Number:MIC-05-115] Experimental Results from Novel Monolithic PET Detector and Application to Axillary Lymph Node Imaging (#1769)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Cotroneo (Autores: T. Cotroneo , D. Pare , L. Saleh , P. Vaska)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Stony Brook University, Biomedical Engineering, Stony Brook, New York, United States of America [2] Renaissance School of Medicine at Stony Brook University, Radiology, Stony Brook, New York, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Monolithic scintillators are a promising alternative to standard pixelated crystals in positron emission tomography, as they can be more cost-effective, reduce dead space, and capture an unobstructed light distribution, which can be used for depth of interaction estimation. We focus on the improvements seen by using an array of integrated corner reflectors (ICR) machined directly into the entrance face of the monolith, which we previously showed via simulation to improve light collection and narrow the light distribution. In this study, we built a physical prototype of the device using a CNC machining process. We compared this prototype with other monolithic block designs. We show that the ICR monolith with the CNN positioning algorithm has potential for high-resolution imaging with ~1 mm resolution at 12 mm thickness. Using GATE simulations, we constructed a full scanner with the performance of the monolithic blocks and tested the capabilities compared to existing systems. We show the improved spatial resolution and feasibility for a non-cylindrical design for axillary lymph node scanning.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 118Poster Number:MIC-05-118] Spatial Characterization of PET Detectors Based on BGO Pseudo‑slabs (#1981)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Cucarella (Autores: N. Cucarella , L. Gil-Bosch , F. Paganao , F. Loignon-Houle , M. Gil , M. Freire , D. Sanchez , A. Gonzalez-Montoro , A.J. Gonzalez)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto de Instrumentación para Imagen Molecular (I3M), Centro Mixto CSIC-Universitat Politècnica de València,, DMIL, Valencia, Spain [2] Oncovision SA, Valencia, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Pixelated crystal arrays are the standard in commercial PET scanners. However, these detectors usually lack DOI information, essential to achieve a homogenous spatial resolution along the entire FOV. Yet, studies have been already performed with pixelated detectors with DOI capabilities but at the cost of using extra hardware material and/or crystal assembling. Inspired by semi‑monolithic crystal geometries, pseudo-slabs were proposed as an alternative. This geometry consists of an N × N pixel array optically isolated only in one direction, allowing light crosstalk in the orthogonal one. The N pixels sharing light in this direction form a pseudo-slab. The light sharing within a pseudo-slab is enough to enable DOI retrieval, while the physical separation between pixels confines the light more than in a pure slab geometry, yielding better time resolution. In this work we evaluated the DOI resolution of a BGO block formed by 8×8 pixels, each measuring around 3×3×15 mm 3 . Two different readout configurations were employed and compared. First, all the 64 channels corresponding to the TOFPET2 ASIC channels were digitized. Then, a multiplexing circuit was utilized, reducing the signals to 8+8 by summing rows and columns. The DOI was obtained using neural networks trained on experimental data. The results show a good DOI resolution for both readout configurations, achieving 3.8 ± 1.3 mm with the multiplexing circuit. These results show that pseudo-slabs are suitable for clinical PET scanners with DOI capabilities.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 121Poster Number:MIC-05-121] Positron Range Confinement in Preclinical PET/MRI: A Multi-Isotope, Multi-Density Experimental Study (#1930)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Gonzalez-Montoro (Autores: F. Lopez-Berenguer , A. Gonzalez-Montoro , S. Berr , M. Williams , A. J. Gonzalez)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto de Instrumentación para Imagen Molecular (i3M), Centro Mixto CSIC-Universitat Politècnica de València, Valencia, Spain [2] University of Virginia, Department of Radiology and Medical Imaging, Charlottesville, Virginia, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The spatial resolution of PET imaging is fundamentally limited by the positron range, whose extent depends on both the emission energy of the radionuclide and the electron density of the surrounding medium. In integrated PET/MRI systems, the static magnetic field exerts a Lorentz force on the positrons, confining their trajectories in the transverse plane to the main magnetic field, potentially improving image resolution. Two complementary experiments were performed using a dedicated monolithic-crystal based PET insert operated at 0T and inside a 9.4T MRI: capillary line sources embedded in three tissue-equivalent phantoms of increasing density (EPF, PLA, and Rigid10k resin), and a microDerenzo phantom. Both tests were carried out with three positron emitters (¹⁸F, ⁸⁹Zr, and ⁶⁸Ga) eventually use in pre-clinical imaging. The results demonstrate that the magnetic field significantly enhances transverse spatial resolution for high-energy positron emitters in medium- and high-density materials, with FWTM reductions of ~60% for ⁶⁸Ga and ~18% for ⁸⁹Zr, while the axial direction remains largely unaffected. Rod resolvability improved at 9.4T from 1.5 mm to ~1.0 mm and from 1.2 mm to 0.9 mm for ⁶⁸Ga and ⁸⁹Zr, respectively. . These findings highlight the relevance of both positron energy and tissue-equivalent density in determining the magnitude of magnetic-field-induced resolution improvements in preclinical PET/MRI.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 124Poster Number:MIC-05-124] Resolution-Sensitivity Optimization with Expanded Position Maps in the CLS-7: A TOF-DOI Brain PET System (#2329)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Narita (Autores: K. Narita , G. Akamatsu , Y. Iwao , E. Yoshida , H. Tashima , M. Takahashi , T. Yamaya)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology (QST), Institute for Quantum Medical Sciences, Chiba, Japan [2] Chiba University, Graduate School of Science and Engineering, Chiba, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The aim of this study was to optimize detector parameters of crosshair light-sharing (CLS) detectors to achieve a better resolution-sensitivity balance in the CLS-7, a brain-dedicated PET prototype we developed in 2025. In particular, we focused on position lookup tables (LUTs), which are generated from flood histograms calculated using Anger logic. In the 2025 model, restricted position LUTs fitted to crystal clusters were used to reduce inter-crystal scattering (ICS), thereby improving spatial and time-of-flight (TOF) resolution at the cost of decreased system sensitivity. In this study, we employed expanded position LUTs and compared the performance of restricted and expanded LUTs in the CLS-7. The detectors consisted of 15-mm-long fast-LGSO scintillators arranged with a crystal pitch of 1.6 mm. Sensitivity, noise-equivalent count rate (NECR), and TOF resolution at the peak NECR were evaluated for both settings. In addition, image quality was evaluated using a rod phantom, an IQ phantom, and a Hoffman phantom. Compared with the restricted LUTs, the expanded LUTs significantly improved sensitivity and the peak NECR by factors of 1.7 and 1.9, respectively. The loss in TOF resolution was only 12%, and no significant difference was observed in the rod phantom results. In both the IQ phantom and the Hoffman phantom, images obtained using the expanded LUTs had lower noise levels than those obtained using the restricted LUTs. These results demonstrate that expanded position LUTs can improve overall image quality despite some degradation in TOF resolution in the CLS-7 system.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 127Poster Number:MIC-05-127] Performance evaluation of N-PET, a high-resolution TOF-DOI PET dedicated to brain imaging (#2442)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Niu (Autores: M. Niu , X. Zeng , H. Yang , X. Jiang , W. Huang , X. Zhao , C. Huang , Z. Wu , H. Li , X. Zhang , Y. Zhao , J. Hua , J. Wu , Q. Wei , J. Dai , Y. Liang , Z. Gu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China [2] University of Science and Technology Beijing, School of Automation and Electrical Engineering, Beijing, China [3] Beijing Normal University, School of Physics and Astronomy, Beijing, China [4] Shenzhen Institute of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shenzhen-Hong Kong Institute of Brain Science, Shenzhen, China [5] National Cancer Center, Cancer Hospital & Shenzhen Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Shenzhen, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study presents a performance evaluation of N-PET, a high-resolution TOF-DOI PET system designed for human brain imaging. The system has a compact ring geometry comprising 18 detector modules, with a ring diameter of 302 mm, a transaxial FOV of 210 mm, and an axial FOV of 52 mm. Each module employs dual-layer, multi-resolution LYSO detectors that enable both high spatial resolution and DOI measurement. System performance was first evaluated through count-rate measurements and phantom studies. Using a monkey-sized phantom, the scanner achieved a peak NECR of 44.0 kcps at 66.8 MBq, with a scatter fraction of 36.0%. After component-based normalization, the images of an image quality phantom showed a uniform background and high contrast hot spheres. Hot rod phantom imaging further demonstrated the high resolution of the system. With the phantom placed at the center of the FOV, rods of 1.2 mm diameter were resolved. When the phantom was placed at a 5-cm radial offset, reconstructed images using four DOI bins yields improved rod separation compared to that with one or two DOI bins, highlighting the benefit of DOI information in reducing resolution degradation near the edge of the FOV. In the Hoffman brain phantom images, gray matter structures are clearly delineated, and the PET images correlated well with anatomical structures derived from the CT image. The imaging performance of N-PET was further evaluated in animal studies. In small animal scans, a rat 18 F - FDG imaging visualized the rat heart, while 18 F-NaF imaging clearly depicted rib structures. In a rhesus macaque brain study, PET and fused PET/CT images revealed major brain anatomy, with elevated FDG uptake in the cerebral cortex and subcortical nuclei. These results demonstrate that N-PET can provide high-resolution PET images in phantoms, small animal, and non-human-primate studies, supporting its feasibility for human brain imaging studies.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 130Poster Number:MIC-05-130] DOI-Dependent Energy Window for Reducing Lu Background in In-Beam SIRMIO PET (#2637)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Nitta (Autores: M. Nitta , G. Lovatti , F. Evangelisat , J. Bortfeldt , Z. Huang , N. Bassler , P. Poulsen , H.G. Kang , C. Gianoli , T. Yamaya , P. Thirolf , K. Parodi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Ludwig Maximillian University Munich, Medical Physics, Garching, Bavaria, Germany [2] Aarhus University Hospital, Danish Centre for Particle Therapy, Aarhus, Denmark [3] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology, Chiba, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We have developed a high resolution small-animal in-beam PET scanner as part of the SIRMIO project for accurate image-guided proton irradiation at clinical facilities. The scanner consists of 56 three-layer depth-of-interaction (DOI) LYSO detectors with 1.0 mm-pitch scintillator pixels arranged in a compact spherical geometry with a with an entrance radius of 72 mm. Using different irradiation platform, we successfully demonstrated small-animal in-beam PET imaging. Since the number of positron emitters generated during irradiation is limited by the prescribed dose, intrinsic Lu background can contribute to background noise. In this study, we investigated the optimal energy window settings for different activity levels using Monte Carlo simulations based on coincidence count statistics in the SIRMIO PET scanner. The three-layer DOI detector structure enables independent energy window settings for each DOI layer. Since 511 keV gamma rays are more likely to interact near the shallow side of the detector, wider energy windows were selectively applied to shallow DOI layers, while narrower windows were used for deeper DOI layers to suppress Lu-176 background contributions. Geant4 simulations were performed for source activities ranging from 0.05 to 50 kBq. Net significance was evaluated for combinations of lower energy thresholds of 250 - 450 keV with a fixed upper threshold of 600 keV. For low-activity cases such as 0.05 kBq, the optimal lower energy thresholds were 400, 450, and 450 keV for the first, second, and third DOI layers, respectively. In contrast, wider energy windows became more advantageous at higher activity levels. These results indicate that layer-dependent energy window optimization is an effective method for improving low-count in-beam PET imaging performance.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 133Poster Number:MIC-05-133] NEMA NU-2 performance tests of a prototype PET scanner using novel detectors capable of measuring the gamma interaction point in 3D (#2832)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Blomgren (Autores: A. Blomgren , B. Brunt , M. Palm , C. Vallgren , K. Ziempekis , M. Viscione , A. Rominger , K. Shi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Bern, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Bern, Bern, Switzerland [2] Terapet SA, Geneva, Genève, Switzerland [3] Inselspital - University hospital of Bern, Bern, Bern, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Background: Depth-of-interaction (DOI) is one of the remaining challenges for high resolution PET. The resolution degradation stems from incorrect LOR endpoint estimation when photons impinge on the detector at oblique angles. This problem increases with distance from the symmetry axis and poses a challenge for LAFOV PET, where more LORs are acquired at oblique angles. Terapet SA manufactures radiation detectors capable of localising gamma ray interactions in 3D within the detector volume, potentially mitigating this effect. The aim of this project was to characterise the performance of a prototype PET scanner using Terapet's proprietary detectors, particularly the potential of DOI artefacts reduction. Method: The NEMA NU-2 performance tests were conducted at the Department of Nuclear Medicine at Inselspital, Bern. Additionally, so far, two patient scans have been performed. Results: The prototype achieved a FWHM of 2.56, 2.60 and 2.96 mm, averaged over all axes, at 10, 100 and 200 mm radial offset, respectively. The loss of resolution with increasing radial offset was lower in the prototype than in other clinical scanners, particularly along the radial axis. The prototype had a low detection sensitivity of 0.99 cps/kBq. This is explained by the restrictive selection requirements on single- and coincidence events, optimised for high-quality data rather than high sensitivity. The image-quality phantom and two patient images have been acquired. Results will be presented at the conference. The expectation is improved contrast recovery due to the improved spatial resolution, particularly for the smallest sphere. Conclusion: The prototype demonstrated improved spatial resolution with the proprietary detectors. In particular, the spatial resolution is maintained with increasing radial offset. Future work will be aimed at improving the image reconstruction algorithms and correction methods. Construction of a LAFOV scanner using the same proprietary detectors is ongoing.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 136Poster Number:MIC-05-136] SurfaceCam: A Close-Proximity Multi-Pinhole CZT Brain SPECT system with Enhanced Geometric Sensitivity and Spatial Resolution (#3121)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Mandot (Autores: S. Mandot , S. D. Metzler , L.-J. Meng)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Department of Nuclear, Plasma and Radiological Engineering, Champaign, Illinois, United States of America [2] University of Pennsylvania at Philadelphia, Department of Radiology, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States of America [3] University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Beckman Institute for Advance Science and Technology, Champaign, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract High-sensitivity, high-resolution brain-dedicated SPECT systems are critically important for advancing diagnosis and surgical planning in complex neurological disorders such as epilepsy, Parkinson's disease, and Alzheimer's disease. In this paper, we present SurfaceCam , a close-proximity multi-pinhole SPECT architecture with a radially adaptable rotating gantry, designed specifically for clinical brain imaging. The system comprises 15 detector-collimator panels distributed across three detector heads in a cylindrical arrangement, operating at a 1:8 minification geometry with a 28 cm bore. Each panel integrates 16 high-performance CZT sensors in a compact 2×8 configuration. The three detector heads translate radially to accommodate varying patient head sizes while maintaining close-proximity geometry, and the rotating gantry enables micro-rotation between acquisitions to facilitate angular super-sampling strategies. Pinholes are organized into groups of four with a twisted geometry, each subtending partial coverage of the 20 cm spherical FOV, while eliminating inter-pinhole projection multiplexing on the detector surface. Analytical comparison against a conventional 1:11 minification compound-eye reference design demonstrates approximately 1.4-fold higher geometric sensitivity and approximately 27% improvement in effective pinhole spatial resolution. The front-end electronics and data acquisition systems have been fully developed and validated, with Monte Carlo simulation studies and experimental phantom validation currently underway.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 139Poster Number:MIC-05-139] Local Activity and Uncertainty Quantification for Pre-clinical Compton Imaging of 213 Bi (#3138)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 O. H. Matousek (Autores: O. H. Matousek , J. Lee , B. Das , J. Caravaca , K. Vetter)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California, Berkeley, Nuclear Engineering, Berkeley, California, United States of America [2] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Nuclear Science Division, Berkeley, California, United States of America [3] University of California, San Francisco, Department of Radiology, San Francisco, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract α-emitting radiopharmaceutical therapies (αRPT) show great potential to treat solid and diffuse tumors. However, following α-decay, the recoil energy and chemistry of daughter isotopes separate them from the targeting vector, exposing healthy tissue to an elevated radioactive dose. These effects must be studied in small animal experiments before new αRPTs make it to clinical trials. However, since extremely low activities are used, current single-photon emission computed tomography is insufficient due to its low sensitivity, especially for the 440 keV gamma ray emitted by 213 Bi (a daughter of one of the most promising radionuclides for αRPT, 225 Ac). In previous work, we used a high-purity Ge Compton camera as a high-sensitivity solution for pre-clinical imaging of αRPT. We demonstrated quantitative Compton imaging of 213 Bi using total-variation maximum- a posteriori expectation-maximization and a post-reconstruction global activity calibration. In this work, we improve upon this by implementing non-region-of-interest (nROI) reconstruction and a Gaussian Process Prior (GPP). We image a mouse phantom at relevant activity concentrations and measurement times to demonstrate that nROI reconstruction mitigates artifacts by redistributing events outside of the field-of-view across the image. We also show that, by using a GPP that correlates the activity in proximate voxels, we improve activity concentration quantification in all the volumes of the mouse phantom with respect to ML-EM. We modify both methods from previous iterations for local activity and uncertainty quantification, which is not straightforward in conventional ML-EM, and compare uncertainties obtained with the Laplace Approximation and preconditioned Crank-Nicholson Markov-Chain Monte Carlo to explain discrepancies from the ground truth. Finally, we experimentally measure a spatial resolution of ~3mm FWHM with a mini-Derenzo phantom.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 142Poster Number:MIC-05-142] A Compact X-ray Dark-Field Imaging Setup and Corresponding Image Optimization (#1107)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 X. Yan (Autores: X. Yan , C. Hoeschen)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Otto-von-Guericke- Universität Magdeburg, Institute of Medical Technology, Chair of Medical Systems Technology, Magdeburg, Saxony-Anhalt, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Grating-based X-ray interferometry dark-field (DF) imaging provides exceptional sensitivity for detecting microstructures below the spatial resolution of standard detectors. Traditionally, this technique requires either large-scale synchrotron facilities or the integration of a source grating into a conventional X-ray tube setup. This study investigates a compact, simplified Talbot interferometer configuration utilizing a microfocus X-ray tube paired with a pixelated, energy-resolved photon-counting detector. In this setup, the microfocus source ensures the necessary spatial coherence, while the detector's energy-resolving capability enables the selection of specific energy bins-directly correlated to wavelength-to optimize reconstruction at the pixel level. Validation was conducted by imaging a metallic screw (0.5 mm pitch) using the phase-stepping method. Results demonstrate that while the sharp thread lines were heavily blurred in attenuation and phase-contrast modalities, they were clearly resolved in the dark-field images. Two optimization methods were evaluated for the full-energy dataset. Method 1, based on fitting effect correction through pixel filtering and interpolation, increased the Contrast-to-Noise Ratio (CNR). Method 2, based on the probability distribution approach, further improved the dark-field image quality compared to Method 1. This method resulted in a brighter signal along the threadline and significantly fewer rejected pixels, ensuring a more complete and better-defined representation of the object. These results demonstrate that high-resolution dark-field imaging is achievable through a compact laboratory setup combined with targeted data-processing optimizations.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 145Poster Number:MIC-05-145] Digital phantoms that can reproduce diseases aiming for virtual radiation imaging experiments (#1256)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 R. Nishigami (Autores: R. Nishigami , T. Asahara , N. Kimoto , M. Mitani , D. Kobayashi , T. Kasue , N. Akagi , T. Iguchi , T. Hiraki , H. Hayashi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Kanazawa University, Graduate School of Medical Sciences, Kanazawa, Japan [2] Okayama University, Department of Radiological Technology, Faculty of Health Sciences, Okayama, Japan [3] Junshin Gakuen University, Department of Radiological Science, Faculty of Health Sciences, Fukuoka, Japan [4] Okayama University Hospital, Division of Radiological Technology, Medical Support Department, Okayama, Japan [5] Okayama University, Department of Radiology, Faculty of Medicine, Dentistry and Pharmaceutical Sciences, Okayama, Japan [6] Kanazawa University, College of Transdisciplinary Sciences for Innovation, Kanazawa, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Virtual X-ray imaging experiments are a crucial research technique in the development of X-ray technology. In recent years, advanced imaging detectors, such as photon-counting detectors, have been developed and are increasingly being used in clinical applications. It further increases the importance of virtual X-ray imaging experiments. To improve the reproducibility of patients in virtual experiments, the development of digital phantoms having diseases is desired. The purpose of this study is to develop a procedure for creating digital phantoms that can reproduce diseases. Virtual monoenergetic images (VMIs) at 40 keV and 130 keV were generated using a clinical photon-counting CT (PC-CT) system, and effective atomic number (Z eff ) and effective physical density (ρ eff ) were calculated using a newly developed algorithm. Z eff was calculated by using the correlation between the ratio of measured linear attenuation coefficient (μ) values and atomic number (Z). ρ eff was calculated from the fitting coefficient obtained by fitting the reaction cross-section (σ) of each Z material to the measured μ values. Then, 10 patient data examined using PC-CT were analyzed, and digital phantoms were created. We investigated the reproducibility of Z eff and ρ eff values of the disease tissues. Our procedure could reproduce the disease tissues by continuous Z eff and ρ eff distribution. In conclusion, we developed a methodology for constructing digital phantoms of patients having diseases from VMIs acquired with PC-CT.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 148Poster Number:MIC-05-148] A novel computational scatter estimation method in CBCT with half ASG (#1343)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Zhu (Autores: J. Zhu , Y. Tan , Z. Huang , H. Wu , Y. Ge)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shenzhen, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract CBCT image quality is strongly degraded by scattered radiation. Conventional anti-scatter grids (ASGs) are commonly used to mitigate this effect; however, they can only remove a portion of the scattered photons. In this study, we propose a novel computational scatter estimation method based on a half anti-scatter grid (h-ASG), which covers only half of the flat-panel detector. The full scatter distribution is estimated by combining two reconstructed CBCT images: one containing the full scatter component and the other containing a reduced scatter component. Experimental results using CatPhan and anthropomorphic head phantoms demonstrate that the proposed method effectively suppresses scatter-induced artifacts and significantly improves CBCT image quality.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 151Poster Number:MIC-05-151] Quantitative Evaluation of Liver Disease through Multi-modality Approach Combining SiPM-based PC-CT and MRI-Approach to the Visualization of Inflammation through Water Fraction Estimation - (#1548)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Furuta (Autores: Y. Furuta , M. Arimoto , F. Lucyana , S. Midorikawa , S. Kobayashi , H. Kawashima , K. Okumura , N. Ohno , T. Tomoda , M. Oshima , K. Murakami , J. Kataoka , R. Minagawa , T. Ro , S. Terazawa , Y. Maeno)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Kanazawa University, Kanazawa, Japan [2] Ishikawa Prefectural University, Nonoichi, Japan [3] Waseda University, Shinzyuku, Japan [4] Proterial Ltd., Mishima, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract X-ray computed tomography (CT) is essential nondestructive internal imaging. Photon-counting computed tomography (PC-CT) acquires X-ray energy information to enable material identification and quantitative density evaluation. Combining PC-CT energy information with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data is expected to provide a novel diagnostic approach to visualize inflammation through tissue water fraction estimation. We developed a PC-CT system combining high-speed scintillators (YGAG:Ce) and silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), specifically utilizing multi-pixel photon counters, MPPCs, which are optical semiconductor devices. This study evaluated healthy and fatty liver rat models (fed a high-fat diet for two or four weeks). Liver fat fractions, estimated from energy-dependent linear attenuation coefficients, showed good agreement with MRI and pathological results. Furthermore, we performed a detailed pathological evaluation focusing on inflammation induced changes in tissue water content. By integrating high reliability MRI fat fraction data with PC-CT data, we improved the estimation accuracy of water content and quantitatively visualized tissue "water-richness" (edema). Increased water proportions in fatty liver groups suggested inflammation progression. These findings demonstrate that PC-CT is highly valuable for quantitative evaluation of liver disease within a multi-modality imaging approach.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 154Poster Number:MIC-05-154] Introducing "T-Index"-A Metric for Quantifying Data Range and Sampling Sufficiency (#2039)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Taguchi (Autores: K. Taguchi , J. Xu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, Maryland, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Many image reconstruction methods for x-ray computed tomography (CT) use optimization approaches with cost functions that consist of a data fidelity term and a prior term. Extensive efforts have been devoted to construct better priors, some using machine learning, for high resolution, low dose, and spectral imaging. There seems to be a belief that a good prior can overcome any problems in data acquisition, downplaying the data fidelity term. It would be desirable if we could quantify the sufficiency of the problem setting (or adequacy of the data acquisition) toward a set of desired imaging properties. We propose "Truth index" or "T-index" to quantify data range and data sampling issues in this work. When fully developed, the T-index will show, independent of specific image reconstruction methods used, how much the solution can be trusted or has a risk of hallucination.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 157Poster Number:MIC-05-157] In vivo Gold Nanoparticle Imaging in Mice for Tumor Detection Using SiPM-Based Photon-Counting CT (#1749)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Midorikawa (Autores: S. Midorikawa , M. Arimoto , F. Lucyana , Y. Furuta , S. Kobayashi , H. Kawashima , K. Okumura , A. Mizutani , N. Ohno , M. Oshima , J. Kataoka , R. Takahiro , R. MInagawa , K. Murakami , Y. Maeno , S. Terazawa)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Kanazawa University, Ishikawa, Japan [2] Waseda University, Tokyo, Japan [3] Ishikawa Prefectural University, Ishikawa, Japan [4] Proterial Ltd, Tokyo, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Photon-counting CT (PC-CT) is a powerful spectral imaging technique that identifies materials by counting individual X-ray photons. While direct-conversion systems are entering clinical practice, we are developing a cost-effective, large-area scintillator-based PC-CT system using YGAG:Ce coupled with silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs). PC-CT excels at identifying high-atomic-number elements like gold (Au) by utilizing its K-edge (80.7 keV). Gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) are promising for drug delivery, as their biodistribution can be controlled by particle size, enabling selective tumor accumulation via the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect. In this study, we evaluated the in vivo biodistribution of AuNPs in tumor-bearing mice using our SiPM-based PC-CT. Two sizes of AuNPs (1.9 nm and 15 nm) were intravenously administered, and their accumulation was quantitatively assessed using multi-energy CT concentration estimation. Results showed distinct size-dependent patterns: 1.9 nm AuNPs exhibited rapid renal clearance and bladder accumulation, while 15 nm AuNPs showed prolonged circulation and significant hepatic accumulation. Tumor accumulation was confirmed for both sizes, demonstrating the potential of our SiPM-based PC-CT for quantitative in vivo nanoparticle imaging.This presentation reports on the experimental setup, the analysis methods, and the results obtained.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 160Poster Number:MIC-05-160] End-to-End Simultaneous Combined Scatter Correction and Metal Projection Segmentation for CBCT Metal Artifact Reduction Network (#2385)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Zhou (Autores: J. Zhou , H. Qiao , K. Chen , Z. Wang , S. Xie , H. Tang , Z. Wu , Y. Chen)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications, School of Communications and Information Engineering, Nanjing, China [2] Qilu University of Technology, School of Computer Science and Technology, Jinan, China [3] Southeast University, School of Computer Science and Engineering, Nanjing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is a vital imaging modality rooted in nuclear science. It uses ionizing radiation and information processing to provide patients' internal anatomical details. When patients with metal implants undergo CT scans, projection data is contaminated. Consequently, reconstructions produce severe metal artifacts, compromising diagnostic accuracy. Thus, developing high-performance metal artifact reduction (MAR) methods for CBCT is essential for accurate clinical diagnosis. Some existing MAR methods ignore physical phenomena, like X-ray scattering, during imaging. Others use scatter correction as a preprocessing step; however, this non-end-to-end approach increases complexity. Here, we propose an end-to-end MAR method incorporating scatter correction and metal segmentation within the projection domain into a single network, followed by morphological post-processing and artifact suppression. Qualitative and quantitative analyses on simulated and real datasets demonstrate the superiority of this end-to-end method.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 163Poster Number:MIC-05-163] X-ray Scattering in Dual-Layer Flat-Panel Detectors (#2510)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D.S. Kim (Autores: E. Lee , D.S. Kim)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Seoul National University, College of Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea [2] Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, Semiconductor and Electronics Engineering, Yonin, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In radiography imaging, dual-layer flat-panel detectors (DFDs) can be used for two purposes: acquiring high-quality x-ray images and performing material decomposition. When using cone beam projection in DFD, the x-ray beam is scattered inside the object, increasing and distorting the intensity. In this paper, we experimentally observe x-ray scattering in acquiring images from DFD. The image acquired from the lower detector layer shows more scatter to prime ratios (SPRs) than the upper layer case due to the scattering inside the upper and intermediate layers. We perform parameter modeling for experimental SPR curves and simulations regarding the measurement of bone mineral density (BMD) estimates, including scattering intensity. We can observe that using the 2nd-order polynomial BMD function or fully connected neural network can successfully estimate BMD functions without scatter correction.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 166Poster Number:MIC-05-166] Development and Experimental Validation of a Low-Cost Benchtop Micro-CT System (#2591)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. M.M. Correia (Autores: P. M.M. Correia , J. M. Reis , A. L.M. Silva)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidade de Aveiro - i3N, Department of Physics, Aveiro, Portugal
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The growing demand for accessible, high-resolution imaging in pre-clinical and materials research has driven interest in low-cost micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) platforms. In this work, a bench-top micro-CT system was designed, assembled, and experimentally characterized, built around a microfocus X-ray tube, a CMOS flat-panel detector, low-cost open-source electronics based on an STM32 microcontroller, and the open-source TIGRE toolbox for volumetric reconstruction. A step-and-shoot acquisition strategy --- in which the sample rotates incrementally, and the detector captures frames only during active X-ray exposure via a hot duration trigger mode --- was employed for synchronized image acquisition. Three reconstruction approaches were implemented and comparatively evaluated: filtered back projection (FBP), Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) algorithm as the primary volumetric reconstruction method, and iterative techniques for noise suppression. System performance was assessed through established phantom protocols evaluating image uniformity, noise, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and a QRM micro-CT Bar-pattern phantom for spatial resolution characterization. While a persistent precession artefact attributed to rotation stage mechanical instability was identified as the primary performance limitation, the system demonstrated tomographic imaging capability and sub-millimeter spatial resolution, establishing a promising foundation for the development of accessible and cost-effective micro-CT platforms for laboratory research.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 169Poster Number:MIC-05-169] Development of a Robot-Arm-Based Automated Transmission and Backscatter X-ray Image Acquisition System for AI Training Data Generation (#2733)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Lee (Autores: J. Lee , C. Lim , J. Park , Y. Choi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Research Institute of Ship & Ocean Engineering, Dejeon, Republic of Korea [2] XsCan Inc, Dejeon, Republic of Korea
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A large-scale X-ray image dataset acquired under diverse specimen and imaging conditions is essential for developing robust AI-based container-structure inspection models. However, single-view transmission imaging often fails to resolve structural ambiguities in complex container environments, where X-ray attenuation and scattering characteristics vary significantly with specimen geometry, material composition, and overlap conditions. In this study, a robot-arm-based automated transmission and backscatter X-ray image acquisition system was developed to enhance the diversity, reproducibility, and traceability of AI training data. The system employs a 225 kV, 13 mA X-ray source to sequentially acquire vertical and horizontal transmission images and horizontal backscatter images. The transmission unit consists of 1,408 detection channels based on eleven 1×128-pixel line-detector modules, whereas the backscatter unit incorporates four 600×500 mm plastic scintillation detectors. By precisely controlling specimen orientation using a robot arm, the system stores acquired images together with preprocessing results, quality-assessment data, and imaging-condition metadata for subsequent AI model training, validation, and evaluation.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 172Poster Number:MIC-05-172] Robustness to Scatter in Dual Energy Bone Suppression for Chest Radiography (#3063)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 W. Zbijewski (Autores: G. Shi , J. Schaefer , S. Vogt , A. Heshmat , L. Ritschl , S. Kappler , C. T. Lin , D. Oncel , S. Ocal , W. Zbijewski)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Johns Hopkins University, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Baltimore, Maryland, United States of America [2] Johns Hopkins University, Russel H. Morgan Dept. of Radiology and Radiological Science, Baltimore, Maryland, United States of America [3] Siemens Healthineers, Forchheim, Bavaria, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We quantify the impact of scatter on the performance of bone suppression in virtual non‑calcium chest radiographs (VNCa‑CXR) generated with (i) a multi‑layer flat‑panel detector (ML‑FPD, three 200-um thick CsI layers) and (ii) with a kV‑switching protocol (60/140 kVp). We show that in the setting of log-subtraction, the decomposition weight (DW) can be adjusted for scatter-to-primary ratio (SPR) such that the scatter-induced bias in VNCa is locally corrected (scatter-compensating weight, DW-scat). However, DW-scat is spatially varying. If a constant DW is used in log-subtraction, the magnitude of bone residual in VNCa radiographs will depend on the degree of spatial inhomogeneity in DW-scat. We investigate this effect is simulation studies in anthropomorphic chest phantoms (20 - 24 cm thickness) with and without an anti-scatter grid (ASG). Without a scatter‑compensating DW, scatter‑induced bone residual increased by >100% is most configurations except for ML-FPD with a grid. Applying DW-scat averaged over central lung region reduced the residual by up to 50% for ML-FPD without an ASG and by ~40% for kV-switching with an ASG. Overall, our results reveal that DE VNCa imaging is relatively robust to scatter in scenarios with a grid, where kV-switching appears to benefit from spatially-averaged scatter-compensating DW more than ML-FPD, likely due to differences in scatter content of the two energy channels. Without a grid, both configurations may require a spatially-dependent scatter compensation for optimal bone suppression.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 175Poster Number:MIC-05-175] Time-of-Flight X-ray Imaging with Scatter Rejection and Subtraction (#3042)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Lorenzon (Autores: A. Lorenzon , Z. Liu , X. Jiang , W. Zbijewski , J.W. Stayman)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Johns Hopkins University, Biomedical Engineering, Baltimore, Maryland, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract X-ray time of flight information can be used in computed tomography to characterize photon interactions and discriminate scattered from unscattered events. Specifically, photons undergoing Compton and Rayleigh scattering are subject to trajectory deviations that increase their path length relative to primary photons. Therefore, with adequate temporal resolution, scattered photons are detected with larger time delay with respect to primary photons, providing a physically grounded mechanism to reject scatter. Recent technological developments in ultra-fast X-ray sources (e.g: 50ps) and high-temporal-resolution photon-counting detectors may allow for this imaging modality. In this work, Monte Carlo (MC) simulations of a water cylinder were performed assuming Gaussian source pulse shape and detector timing jitter, with combined full-width-half-maximum as low as 50ps. A threshold-based scatter rejection method was applied, sweeping multiple thresholds to find the optimal balance between scatter rejection efficiency (η) and primary retention (ε). Filtered-backprojection reconstructions were performed and evaluated in terms of root mean square error and bias. Rejection performances were compared with an ideal, MC-based scatter subtraction technique, that leverages template fitting to estimate the average scatter contribution from time-delay histograms. A combined rejection-subtraction approach was also evaluated. For rejection only, the optimal reconstruction accuracy is obtained with a threshold T'=30 ps, corresponding to η=59% and ε=80%. Residual scatter leads to bias in the reconstructed attenuation, preventing the method from achieving the same reconstruction accuracy as the ideal subtraction. However, rejection yields lower noise levels compared to subtraction. Combining rejection and subtraction may provide a better compromise between bias and noise.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 178Poster Number:MIC-05-178] Iodine Sensitivity in Photon Counting CT Using Conventional and Diffusion-Based Material Decomposition Algorithms (#3123)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. J. Gang (Autores: S. Liao , G. J. Gang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Pennsylvania, Radiology, Philadelphia, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Spectral CT enables material-specific imaging but suffers from noise amplification in low-concentration iodine decomposition. This work investigates advanced material decomposition algorithms for improving iodine detectability in a simulated four-channel photon-counting CT system. Diffusion Posterior Sampling (DPS) with hybrid priors was compared with conventional image-domain and projection-domain decomposition methods. Results demonstrate improved noise suppression and low-concentration vessel detectability while highlighting the noise-bias tradeoff in diffusion-based material decomposition.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 181Poster Number:MIC-05-181] TCMnet: An Automatic Tube Current Modulation Policy Based on Neural Network (#3217)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Zhang (Autores: H. Zhang , Z. Zeng , Y. Xing)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, the Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) is essential for mitigating radiation risks to patients, and its effectiveness is significantly enhanced by automatic tube current modulation (TCM) that optimizes photon allocation across different projection angles to maintain image quality at reduced doses. However, most traditional methods offer fixed modulation strategies based on typical human phantoms, thereby ignoring individual anatomical variations and failing to achieve personalized dose allocation. This paper proposes a personalized TCM method driven by an end-to-end neural network (TCMnet). Specifically, we construct a differentiable optimization chain that integrates the modulation strategy, forward projection, and image reconstruction into a unified framework, allowing the system to learn optimal, patient-specific current profiles by directly minimizing reconstruction errors under specific dose constraints. Experimental results demonstrate that, under identical photon count (radiation dose) constraints, the proposed method yields significantly higher reconstruction quality compared to conventional approaches. By analyzing the performance of these optimized profiles across varying dose levels, this study reveals an important physical phenomenon: under extreme low-photon-count conditions where photon resources are severely limited, the optimal modulation strategy shifts from seeking a globally balanced noise distribution to concentrating photons on fewer key projection angles in high-attenuation regions. This finding not only validates the optimization capabilities of the end-to-end framework under complex constraints but also provides new insights and design concepts for TCM mechanisms for ultra-low-dose CT.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 184Poster Number:MIC-05-184] A Fully Quantitative Reconstruction Framework Tailored for Depth-of-Interaction PET Systems (#1140)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Chen (Autores: Y. Chen , Z. Yuan , Y. Chen , C. Li , K. Wang , Y. Hou , J. Jiang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Normal University, School of Physics and Astronomy, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Depth-of-interaction (DOI) encoding in positron emission tomography (PET) systems effectively mitigates parallax errors and improves spatial resolution, however, it introduces substantial complexities for accurate and efficient image reconstruction. Specifically, the dramatic increase in valid lines-of-response (LORs) and the inherent limitations of conventional correction methods-such as component-based normalization (CBN) and single scatter simulation (SSS)-often compromise quantitative accuracy in DOI enabled systems. To address these challenges, we propose a fully GPU-accelerated reconstruction framework specifically designed for DOI-PET with complete correction techniques. The proposed framework extends standard CBN and SSS methods through sub-layer-based geometric modeling, enabling layer-specific normalization and scatter correction. A maximum-likelihood-based strategy is introduced to estimate DOI-dependent scatter scaling factors, incorporating inter-layer attenuation effects and axial response variations. The framework was evaluated using Monte Carlo simulations of the NeuroEXPLORER scanner. Our results demonstrate that the reconstructed uniform cylinder phantom exhibits high spatial homogeneity. Furthermore, the spatial resolution quantified via the Derenzo phantom and the quantitative accuracy achieved in a digital brain phantom are consistent with previously established benchmarks. These findings suggest that the proposed framework provides a robust and computationally efficient solution for high-resolution, quantitative reconstruction in DOI-PET systems.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 187Poster Number:MIC-05-187] Unsupervised micro-CT reconstruction from limited-angle and truncated data in cone-beam geometry (#1238)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Izumitani (Autores: K. Izumitani , T. Shibuya , H. Kato , H. Haneishi , T. Okamoto)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Chiba University, Graduate School of Science and Engineering, Chiba, Japan [2] National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST), Research Institute for Measurement and Analytical Instrumentation, National Metrology Institute of Japan, Tsukuba, Japan [3] National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST), Non-Destructive Imaging Research Team, Integrated Research Center for Resilient Infrastructure, Tsukuba, Japan [4] Chiba university, Center for Frontier Medical Engineering, Chiba, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Micro X-ray computed tomography (micro-CT) enables non-destructive visualization of fine internal structures. Resolving finer details requires higher geometric magnification, typically achieved by reducing the source-to-rotation-center distance (SRD). However, short-SRD acquisition can suffer from a limited angular range due to physical interference with the X-ray source and from projection truncation when the object extends beyond the field-of-view (FOV), causing streak artifacts and structural distortions. Supervised learning-based reconstruction methods have been investigated to mitigate such artifacts but applying them to non-destructive high-magnification micro-CT is difficult because fully sampled, non-truncated reference data cannot be readily acquired without destructive sample preparation. Moreover, many existing methods are designed for 2D fan-beam geometry rather than 3D cone-beam geometry commonly used in micro-CT. We propose an unsupervised reconstruction method that simultaneously reduces limited-angle and projection-truncation artifacts by incorporating long-SRD measurements. Long-SRD acquisition provides full-view, non-truncated projections, albeit at lower spatial resolution, complementing the high-resolution but incomplete short-SRD acquisition. By jointly using these complementary measurements, the proposed method preserves fine structural details while recovering the global object structure without requiring ground-truth images. Numerical experiments demonstrated that the proposed method reduced streak artifacts and recovered structural information outside the short-SRD FOV. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first unsupervised 3D cone-beam reconstruction method to simultaneously address both artifacts in high-magnification micro-CT.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 190Poster Number:MIC-05-190] A Self-Supervised Framework for Simultaneous Reconstruction of Activity and Attenuation in TOF-PET (#1404)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Jia (Autores: T. Gong , H. Liu , W. Huang , H. Jia , Y. Liu , Z. He)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, School of Biomedical Engineering, Beijing, China [2] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [3] Tsinghua University Changgung Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Time-of-flight PET (TOF-PET) enables CT-free attenuation correction (AC) through simultaneous activity and attenuation (SAA) reconstruction from emission alone. In this study, we propose a self-supervised SAA framework based on implicit neural representation. The proposed framework employs parallel hash encoders and multilayer perceptrons to learn the mapping from spatial coordinate to image space, thereby jointly reconstructing activity and attenuation maps. To further accelerate reconstruction and reduce GPU memory consumption, an ordered-subset training strategy is introduced, in which projection angles used for supervision are progressively increased during optimization. The proposed method was evaluated using analytical simulations based on a BrainWeb brain phantom with 18 F-FDG uptake. Compared with non-attenuation-corrected MLEM, maximum likelihood reconstruction of attenuation correction factors (MLACF) and maximum-likelihood activity and attenuation (MLAA), OSIR demonstrated improved visual consistency and quantitative accuracy. For activity reconstruction, OSIR achieved the highest PSNR of 24.62 dB and the lowest NRMSE of 5.87%, with SSIM comparable to MLAA. For attenuation reconstruction, OSIR outperformed MLAA across all evaluation metrics. In addition, OSIR reduced the reconstruction time from 60 min to approximately 40 min. These results demonstrate that OSIR provides an efficient and robust solution for CT-free attenuation-corrected TOF-PET reconstruction, enabling accurate joint estimation of activity and attenuation maps without requiring CT images or large-scale training datasets.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 193Poster Number:MIC-05-193] Extended Field-of-View Reconstruction for Full-Ring Multi-Pinhole SPECT (#1639)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Q. Liu (Autores: Q. Liu , Y. Lv , F. N. Gür)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Global Institute of Future Technology, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Full-ring multi-pinhole SPECT offers high sensitivity and compact detector coverage, but eFOV reconstruction remains challenging due to projection truncation, incomplete angular sampling, and reduced peripheral sensitivity, especially for large-body or off-center activity distributions. We propose a staged deep-learning-assisted OSEM framework for eFOV recovery. The framework combines a physics-based forward model, two-stage sinogram completion, and image-domain refinement. Truncated projections are first reconstructed by OSEM as the baseline. Two residual U-Nets then sequentially restore missing detector-width information and angular views in the sinogram domain. Finally, an image-domain network suppresses residual artifacts and improves structural continuity in the eFOV region. Simulation studies used FDG activity distributions with randomized body scaling, translation, sparse sampling, and peripheral lesion insertion. Evaluation metrics included recovery coefficient, MAE, RMSE, SSIM, and lesion-level recovery. Compared with truncated-data OSEM, the proposed method improved peripheral lesion recovery and reduced reconstruction errors. In representative cases, recovery coefficient increased from 25.9% to 96.6% at 550 mm and from 10.1% to 82.5% at 650 mm. Preliminary 3D validation also showed lower errors and higher structural similarity in axial and sagittal views. These results suggest that combining physics-based modeling with dual-domain deep learning is feasible for eFOV reconstruction in full-ring multi-pinhole SPECT. Future work will validate the framework using physical phantom and clinical data.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 196Poster Number:MIC-05-196] CT Image Reconstruction Using Deep Image Prior with VoxelMorph (#1782)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Hori (Autores: K. Hori , F. Hashimoto , T. Hashimoto)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Juntendo University, Department of Radiological Technology, Bunkyo-ku, Japan [2] University of Florida, J. Crayton Pruitt Family Department of Biomedical Engineering, Gainesville, Florida, United States of America [3] Kyorin University, Department of Radiological Technology, Mitaka-shi, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Motion during scanning results in motion artifacts that distort anatomical structures in computed tomography (CT) images. In radiation therapy, planning CT scan duration are high-speed, whereas linear accelerator gantry mounted CT takes more than 15 seconds, making them more susceptible to motion artifacts. Recently, CT image reconstruction methods using supervised learning have been shown to suppress motion artifacts. However, obtaining sufficient training data is difficult because actual organ motion cannot be directly visualized. In this study, we propose an unsupervised CT image reconstruction method incorporating deep image prior and VoxelMorph (DIP-VM). The proposed method iteratively alternates between DIP-based image reconstruction and VM-based estimation of the motion vector field, in which planning CT images are leveraged as reference images. The main advantage of the proposed DIP-VM is its ability to correct patient motion using only patient-specific data, without requiring large training datasets. The proposed DIP-VM was evaluated on an XCAT phantom with cardiac and respiratory motion. Experimental results demonstrate that, using only patient-specific projection data, the proposed DIP-VM method reduces motion artifacts more effectively than the comparison methods. This study provides an effective solution for suppressing motion artifacts using only patient-specific projection data, without requiring large training datasets.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 199Poster Number:MIC-05-199] A Boosting Diffusion Model for Ultra-Sparse-View CT reconstruction (#1840)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Kimura (Autores: Y. Kimura , S. Ozaki , H. Obara , M. Aoki)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Hirosaki University, Graduate School of Science and Technology, Aomori, Japan [2] Hirosaki University School of Medicine and Hospital, Department of Radiology, Division of Medical Technology, Aomori, Japan [3] Hirosaki University, Department of Radiation Oncology, Aomori, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Recent advances in diffusion models for natural image processing [1] have led to the development of several diffusion prior-based methods for medical image reconstruction [2,3,4,5,6]. For these diffusion model-based methods, balancing fidelity to the observed data (e.g., projection data) and the diffusion prior is essential. In diffusion models, low noise levels correspond to fine-grained details and therefore better preserve consistency with the observed data, whereas high noise levels correspond to coarse-grained information and rely more heavily on the diffusion prior. In our previous study, we proposed an ensemble method using multiple diffusion priors [7]. This method successfully optimized the balance between observed-data fidelity and diffusion priors in moderately sparse-view settings. However, we found that the advantage of the ensemble method decreases in extremely sparse cases with fewer than 25 views. Under such extremely sparse conditions, a diffusion prior with a large time step alone performed better than the ensemble method. In this study, we propose a boosting diffusion model for sparse-view CT reconstruction, particularly targeting cases with severe information loss in the observed data. In the proposed method, image reconstruction is first performed using a large time step, resulting in a coarse-grained reconstruction. Subsequently, reconstruction is refined using smaller time steps, leading to fine-grained image reconstruction. We compared the proposed method with existing methods, including iterative reconstruction (IR), DPS, and SDPS, in terms of SSIM and PSNR. The results demonstrated that the proposed method outperforms the existing methods in extremely sparse-view cases with fewer than 25 views.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 202Poster Number:MIC-05-202] SPECT Reconstruction via Diffusion Sampling from a PET Image Manifold for Theranostics (#1954)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Wei (Autores: H. Wei , L. Livieratos , G. Webber , A. J. Reader)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Kings College London, School of Biomedical Engineering and Imaging Sciences, London, United Kingdom [2] Kings College London, Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, London, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) remains the standard modality for uptake verification and patient-specific dosimetry in molecular radiotherapy (MRT), however it has limited spatial resolution and noise characteristics compared to pre-therapy positron emission tomography (PET). Existing approaches that incorporate PET priors into SPECT reconstruction are often constrained by hand-crafted feature representations and suffer from inter-modality mismatch and registration-induced artifacts. In this work, we employ a conditional generative framework to enhance SPECT reconstruction toward PET-level image quality. A denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) is trained to learn the distribution of high-quality PET images. During inference, the reverse diffusion process is conditioned on measured SPECT data and CT images, enabling anatomically consistent, high-fidelity image synthesis. The method is initially assessed using 2D Zubal phantom simulations. Performance is compared with conventional maximum likelihood expectation maximization (MLEM) and kernel based methods. Both quantitative metrics and qualitative analysis demonstrate that the diffusion-based approach achieves enhanced edge preservation and superior noise suppression. The reconstructed images show closer agreement with reference data compared to MLEM and kernel based reconstructions. By avoiding explicit PET-SPECT registration, the framework mitigates spatial misalignment and associated artifacts. These results indicate that conditional diffusion sampling provides a principled and flexible approach to improve resolution and noise limitations in SPECT, with potential to improve quantitative accuracy in MRT applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 205Poster Number:MIC-05-205] Plug-and-Play PET Image Reconstruction Using Diffusion Models (#2071)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Minagawa (Autores: T. Minagawa , F. Hashimoto , K. Hori , T. Hashimoto)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Toho University Ohashi Medical Center, Radiology, Tokyo, Japan [2] University of Florida, J. Crayton Pruitt Family Department of Biomedical Engineering, Florida, United States of America [3] Juntendo University, Radiological Technology, Tokyo, Japan [4] Kyorin University, Medical Radiological Technology, Tokyo, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Diffusion models (DMs) have recently demonstrated remarkable performance in positron emission tomography (PET) image reconstruction. However, in diffusion posterior sampling, data fidelity and diffusion prior are coupled within each sampling step, which can make the balance between them sensitive to parameter selection. In this study, we propose a plug-and-play diffusion-based PET image reconstruction method (PnP-DM) that enables explicit incorporation of a DM as a prior within a penalized reconstruction. The proposed method is formulated based on Bayes' theorem and employs a half-quadratic splitting algorithm to decouple the likelihood and prior terms into penalized reconstruction and diffusion sampling. The proposed method alternates between the likelihood and prior steps, where the likelihood step penalizes deviation from the diffusion result, while the prior step is guided by the reconstructed image from the likelihood step, thereby maintaining data consistency throughout the optimization process. We evaluated the proposed method using simulated [ 18 F]FDG BrainWeb phantom datasets. The proposed method suppressed noise while preserving structural details and achieved higher contrast-to-noise ratio and contrast recovery coefficient than maximum likelihood-expectation maximization (EM) and maximum a posteriori-EM. These results suggest that the proposed PnP method provides diffusion-based reconstruction that enables more stable optimization and flexible balancing between data fidelity and diffusion prior.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 208Poster Number:MIC-05-208] List-Mode Reconstruction for Gamma-Positron Imaging (#2124)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. A. Kupinski (Autores: M. A. Kupinski , M. A. King , S. Abbaszadeh , L. R. Furenlid)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Arizona, College of Optical Sciences, Tucson, Arizona, United States of America [2] University of Arizona, Department of Medical Imaging, Tucson, Arizona, United States of America [3] University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School, Department of Radiology, Worcester, Massachusetts, United States of America [4] University of California, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Santa Cruz, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We present a GPU-accelerated list-mode reconstruction framework for gamma-positron brain imaging that models PET coincidences, prompt-gamma Compton events, and triple events, in which one decay produces both detected event classes. The goal is to reconstruct the radionuclide decay distribution, rather than only the positron annihilation location, by combining the sensitivity of 511-keV coincidences with the geometric constraint from a coincident prompt gamma. The framework uses UAMonteCarlo emission and detector simulations to generate sorted list-mode events and voxelized sensitivity maps for an edge-on crossed-strip CZT geometry. The test configuration contains 690 detectors on a 30-cm-diameter ring surrounding a 24-cm water sphere and models 44Sc, including emission and transport of a 1474 keV-max positron and a 1157 keV prompt gamma. Event likelihoods are evaluated for PET-only events, two-interaction prompt-gamma events, and triple events. PET likelihoods include annihilation-photon attenuation and positron range effects; prompt-gamma likelihoods include Compton kinematics, energy deposition, detector interaction type, and attenuation; triple-event likelihoods combine PET line-of-response and prompt Compton-cone constraints. The reconstruction code computes event probabilities on the GPU and applies a list-mode maximum-likelihood expectation-maximization update. Initial consistency studies with simulated 44Sc point-source data show that PET-only and prompt-only reconstructions recover point-source locations after three iterations using 2000 events per mode, while sensitivity maps and likelihood images show the tradeoff between high-sensitivity PET/prompt events and lower-sensitivity, higher-weight triple events. These results establish machinery for combined gamma-positron reconstructions and motivate tests with triple events, mixed event-type reconstructions, and further phantom studies.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 211Poster Number:MIC-05-211] Pilot Clinical Evaluation of CT-Less PET Attenuation Correction Using Back-Scatter Coincidences on the NeuroEXPLORER System (#2352)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Liu (Autores: Z. Liu , T. Li , L. He , S. Tang , Y. Dong)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shanghai United Imaging Healthcare Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China [2] Wuhan United Imaging Life Science Instrument Co., Ltd., Wuhan, China [3] United Imaging Healthcare North America, Inc., Houston, Texas, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Attenuation correction (AC) is essential for quantitative PET imaging and is conventionally performed using CT-derived attenuation maps. In this work, we present an initial clinical evaluation of a CT-less AC approach based on detector backward inter-crystal scattered (BKS) coincidences on the NeuroEXPLORER (NX) PET/CT system. Two patient datasets were acquired with a full-energy-window protocol that preserved standard emission coincidences, BKS events, and (^{176})Lu background events within the same list-mode dataset. For each patient, three reconstruction pipelines were compared: CT-AC+OSEM, Lu-AC+OSEM, and BKS-AC+OSEM. Results showed that, in the higher-activity case, Lu-background data were more strongly affected by random events, leading to a noisier attenuation map, whereas the BKS-derived attenuation map showed improved quality, particularly in the skull region, and yielded PET images in closer agreement with the CT-AC reference. In the lower-activity case, BKS- and Lu-derived attenuation maps were generally comparable. A short-acquisition study further showed that BKS-derived attenuation maps remained reasonably consistent for acquisition times of 5 min or longer. These results indicate that BKS-based AC is a promising direction for CT-less PET attenuation correction and warrants further evaluation in larger studies.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 214Poster Number:MIC-05-214] Unrolled relaxed algorithm for 3D SPECT reconstruction (#2388)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Constanza (Autores: C. Constanza , D. Sarrut , A. Etxebeste)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CREATIS, CNRS UMR 5220; INSERM U 1044, Université de Lyon; INSA-Lyon; Université Lyon 1, Villeurbanne, France [2] Centre de lutte contre le cancer Léon-Bérard, Lyon, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In this work, we propose an unrolled Block Sequential Regularized Expectation Maximization (BSREM) reconstruction framework in which the gradient of the regularization term is learned using a convolutional neural network. Building on our previous work, we adopt Jacobian-Free Unrolling (JFU) to enable memory-efficient training on 3D synthetic data. This training strategy backpropagates only through the final iteration of the unrolled optimization, significantly reducing memory consumption while improving training stability. We investigate the influence of relaxation strategies within the unrolled BSREM scheme and analyze their impact on convergence behavior, stability, and reconstruction quality. Experiments conducted on realistic simulated SPECT datasets and clinical 177 Lu-DOTATATE patient data show that JFU-based unrolling consistently outperforms classical unrolled training for an equivalent number of parameters and memory usage. Unlike classical unrolling, which requires strong relaxation to ensure stable training, JFU achieves optimal performance with weak or no relaxation. Excessive relaxation is shown to be suboptimal, leading to reduced quantitative accuracy. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate improvements in both global image quality and organ-level activity accuracy compared to OSEM and conventional BSREM with a Relative Difference Penalty prior. As observed in our previous study using Green's one-step-late algorithm, the proposed approach may introduce over-separation artifacts between regions of low and high activity. This behavior appears intrinsic to learning the regularization gradient rather than to the unrolling strategy itself. Overall, this work highlights the advantages of Jacobian-Free Unrolling for scalable and stable learning-based SPECT reconstruction and provides insights into the role of relaxation in unrolled optimization schemes.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 217Poster Number:MIC-05-217] Multiple Emission Tomography: GPU-Accelerated LM-OSEM Reconstruction for Compton Events (#2640)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. N. Colombo (Autores: M. N. Colombo , M. Pizzichemi , G. Terragni , F. Pennazio , M. Paganoni , L. Presotto)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Milano-Bicocca, Milan, Italy [2] CERN, Meyrin, Genève, Switzerland [3] INFN Torino, Turin, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Multiple Emission Tomography (MET) detector, a single-layer ring of LYSO:Ce scintillators, offers a versatile imaging platform combining Positron Emission Tomography (PET) with collimator-free Compton-mode Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT). However, Compton reconstruction for single-layer cylindrical geometries remains a major challenge due to high data dimensionality and a dense system matrix. In this work, we present a GPU-accelerated reconstruction framework based on List-Mode Ordered Subset Expectation Maximization (LM-OSEM). Building on the open-source CoReSi library, our framework introduces several contributions. i) High-Performance Architecture: we implement a vectorized PyTorch pipeline with fused broadcasting and event batching. This approach achieves O(batch size · voxels) peak GPU memory occupancy, enabling the processing of massive datasets. ii) Advanced Physics Modeling: we introduce a system matrix that incorporates a per-event Angular Resolution Measure (ARM). This model integrates Doppler broadening, energy resolution, and detector spatial resolution, allowing for optimal event weighting and noise suppression. iii) Geometry-Specific Sensitivity: we propose a novel sensitivity model tuned for the MET cylindrical geometry, accounting for solid-angle coverage and LYSO self-absorption.The framework is validated through Monte Carlo simulations of the MET prototype. We evaluate spatial resolution and noise on reconstructed images from 511 keV to 1 MeV. Spatial resolutions between 5 mm and 10 mm are achievable, confirming MET's potential for imaging high-energy exotic nuclei inaccessible to conventional gamma cameras. This work provides a scalable, fast, and physically accurate foundation for next-generation multi-modal molecular imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 220Poster Number:MIC-05-220] List-Mode Derived Synthetic Kernel-Based Image Reconstruction for Dynamic Total Body PET (#2844)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Dassanayake (Autores: M. Dassanayake , L. Vass , P. Marsden , J. A. Schnabel , A. J. Reader)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] King's College London, Department of Imaging Physics and Engineering at the School of Biomedical Engineering and Imaging Sciences, London, United Kingdom [2] Technical University Munich, School of Computation, Information and Technology, Munich, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Total-body positron emission tomography (TB-PET) provides significantly improved sensitivity, enabling ultra-short time framing for dynamic imaging. However, the resulting low count statistics lead to increased noise and unstable time activity curves (TACs), limiting quantitative accuracy. We investigate a kernel-based reconstruction approach within a list-mode (LM)-derived synthetic framework, where a vendor reconstruction is forward projected through an event-specific LM system matrix to generate synthetic data, implicitly includes attenuation, normalisation, scatter, and randoms effects while enabling flexible algorithm design. Spatial, temporal, and spatio-temporal kernels are evaluated for short-frame FDG data acquired on a Biograph Vision Quadra system, with features constructed from multiple dynamic intervals. Reconstructions are compared with a 10x higher count vendor reference images using spatial and temporal PRMSE. Spatially, the spatio-temporal kernel achieves the lowest error. In addition, we demonstrated that kernel methods benefit from larger neighbourhoods resulting in improved visual quality compared to synthetic PET. This was computationally feasible on consumer hardware by using region-of-interest specific reconstructions. These results demonstrate that LM-derived synthetic kernel reconstruction provides a flexible framework for incorporating spatial and temporal priors in TB-PET. While performance is currently limited by kernel parameter selection, the observed improvements in spatial and temporal behaviour indicate strong potential for optimisation through tuning the kernel strength and feature vector design.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 223Poster Number:MIC-05-223] Three-Photon Bayesian Imaging of Ortho-Positronium (#2897)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 W. Krzemien (Autores: W. Krzemien , L. Raczyński , A. Coussat)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Centre for Nuclear Research, Department of High Energy Physics, Otwock Swierk, Poland [2] National Centre for Nuclear Research, Department of Complex Systems, Otwock Swierk, Poland [3] INSA-Lyon, niversité Claude Bernard Lyon 1, CNRS, Inserm, CREATIS UMR 5220, U1294, F-69373, Lyon, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positron emission tomography provides functional images from two-photon coincidences. In human tissue, approximately 40% of annihilations are preceded by positronium formation, of which the ortho-positronium component partially decays into three photons [1]. This three-photon channel carries additional information about the local micro-environment [1], including the three-to-two-photon yield ratio as a potential diagnostic marker [3,2], and its exploitation does not require a prompt photon, making it compatible with standard radionuclides such as FDG. We propose the Three-Photon Bayesian Imaging of Ortho-Positronium algorithm, a novel event-by-event reconstruction method formulated as a Bayesian maximum a posteriori inference problem, which unifies time-based trilateration [4], energy-based reconstruction [3], and a physics-informed prior derived from the quantum electrodynamics description of ortho-positronium decay [5-6] within a single probabilistic framework. Monte Carlo simulations modelled after the Siemens Biograph Quadra scanner [7] demonstrate an improvement of a factor of two over time-based trilateration and by an order of magnitude over energy-based reconstruction. The proposed approach is compatible with existing scanners capable of registering three-photon coincidences, broadening its applicability beyond positronium lifetime imaging to standard clinical radionuclides.
