sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 226Poster Number:MIC-05-226] Event-by-Event Energy-Dependent List-Mode Reconstruction for Quantitative 90 Y Bremsstrahlung SPECT (#2953)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. Yan (Autores: C. Yan , H. Hu , J. Qin , H. Ye , C. Yang , F. Chen , R. Zhao , H. Li , Z. He , Y. Liu , H. Liu , J. Wu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Normal University, Center for Advanced Quantum Studies, School of Physics and Astronomy, Beijing, China [2] China Institute for Radiation Protection, Shanxi, China [3] Shanxi Provincial Key Laboratory for Translational Nuclear Medicine and Precision Protection, Shanxi, China [4] Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Beijing, China [5] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract 90 Y bremsstrahlung SPECT imaging remains challenging due to its broad continuous energy spectrum. In this study, we proposed and evaluated a novel event-by-event energy-dependent list-mode reconstruction algorithm for quantitative 90 Y bremsstrahlung SPECT. To enable real-time and reasonably accurate energy-dependent collimator-detector response modeling, we proposed and incorporated a True Half-Width method into the list-mode reconstruction framework. Monte Carlo simulations were performed using three energy windows: 90-160 keV, 105-285 keV, and 90-400 keV. Quantitative evaluation was performed using contrast recovery coefficient and background variability. Compared with projection-based reconstruction, list-mode reconstruction achieved the best quantitative performance using the 90-400 keV energy window, owing to accurate event-level energy-dependent system matrix modeling over the broad continuous energy spectrum. These results demonstrate that event-by-event energy-dependent list-mode reconstruction is essential for improving the quantitative accuracy of 90 Y bremsstrahlung SPECT.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 229Poster Number:MIC-05-229] Evaluation of Cash C as a Cost Function for xSPECT Conjugate Gradient (#2962)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Massanes (Autores: F. Massanes , A. H. Vija)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Siemens Medical Solutions, MI SPECT Research, Hoffman Estates, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract xSPECT CG (Conjugate Gradient) SPECT reconstruction uses the Mighell Chi-Square (χ 2 ) statistic as its optimization cost function [3]. While effective under standard count conditions, the Mighell statistic is known to be suboptimal when Poisson statistics are poorly approximated at low counts. The Cash C statistic offers an alternative formulation derived from a modified chi-square for Poisson data, better suited to low-count regimes[2]. This work evaluates Cash C as a direct replacement for Mighell χ 2 in xSPECT CG, assessing resolution-noise trade-offs across count levels using a standard phantom. Resolution was quantified using a metric based on the approach described in [1], further developed here to handle arbitrary source-to-background contrasts. Cash C consistently achieved better noise properties at equivalent resolution compared to Mighell χ 2 , with both algorithms converging to similar minimum resolution values 16.4 mm FWHM) at high update steps for the 8 mL sphere, confirming no loss of performance at high-count conditions. These characteristics are particularly relevant for clinical applications with limited count statistics, including cardiac SPECT [4] and emerging theranostic radiopharmaceuticals.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 232Poster Number:MIC-05-232] Investigation of Ray Driven Collimator Detector Response Model for Multi-Photopeak SPECT Reconstruction (#3098)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. Merlin (Autores: T. Merlin , B. Laurent , D. Visvikis)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CHRU de Brest, Brest, France [2] LaTIM INSERM UMR 1101, Bâtiment 1, premier étage CHRU Morvan, Brest, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In SPECT imaging, accurate modeling of the collimator-detector response (CDR) function is essential for improving image resolution and quantitative accuracy. The CDR profile depends on several physical factors whose modeling can be complex and computationally demanding, particularly for multi-photopeak datasets, since the CDR, photon attenuation, and Compton scattering are energy dependent. In this work, we investigate the modeling of the CDR function using profiles generated through Monte Carlo simulations and its incorporation into the reconstruction process using a multi-line projector approach. Monte-Carlo simulations were processed in order to generate CDRs of a SPECT intevo system with MELP collimator using 177Lu point sources located at different distances of the imaging system. These data were combined to generate CDR reponses for both 208kev and 113kev photopeaks. A multi-lines projector was implemented to integrate these profiles and processes the corrections specific to each photopeak. Simulations of NEMA IQP phantom was conducted to assess the proposed implementation, as well as phantom data acquired with the same system and variable source to collimator distance for each projections. The proposed model improves the CRC-versus-noise trade-off as well as the overall image quality. Although increasing the number of projection lines enhances the signal-to-noise ratio, the evaluated metrics show limited improvement beyond a certain number of lines. These results suggest that for the studied acquisition and reconstruction setup, a reduced number of lines per detector channel may be sufficient to accurately model the CDR while limiting the computational cost of the reconstruction process. Ongoing work includes the evaluation of the proposed implementation with different collimator geometries exhibiting various septal penetration and scattering characteristics. Future investigations will focus on simulations involving high-energy photon-emitting radionuclides.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 235Poster Number:MIC-05-235] Deep Kernel Gaussian Process Prior for Robust, Anatomically Guided Radiation Image Reconstruction (#3129)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Lee (Autores: J. Lee , J. Caravaca)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Applied Nuclear Physics (ANP), Berkeley, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Newly emerging radiation imaging modalities-such as Compton camera imaging of alpha-emitting radiopharmaceuticals, positronium lifetime imaging, and dynamic PET imaging-frequently operate under count-starved, low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions, where the conventional maximum likelihood expectation maximization (ML-EM) algorithm is prone to severe overfitting. While recent neural network-based reconstruction methods have achieved impressive results, they require large amounts of task-specific training data, often neglect physics constraints, and largely lack principled uncertainty quantification frameworks. In this work, we propose a Bayesian image reconstruction algorithm incorporating a Gaussian process (GP) prior with a neural network-based kernel, combining the robustness and principled uncertainty quantification of the GP framework with the representational flexibility of neural networks. The proposed method is highly robust against measurement noise, naturally incorporates physics constraints through the forward model, supports anatomically guided reconstruction through co-registered structural imaging data, and provides a full posterior covariance characterization via variational inference. We demonstrate significant improvement in reconstruction quality over the conventional ML-EM algorithm alongside meaningful uncertainty estimates.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 238Poster Number:MIC-05-238] ChameleonIQ: Bridging NEMA NU-2 and NU-4 Standards through Automated Image Analysis (#1243)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. Y. Ulin-Briseño (Autores: E. Y. Ulin-Briseño , S. Jiménez-Serrano , A. J. Gonzalez)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CSIC-Universitat Politècnica de València, The Institute for Instrumentation in Molecular Imaging (I3M), Valencia, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Quantitative positron emission tomography (PET) requires standardized and reproducible image quality assessment to ensure comparability across scanners, protocols, and institutions. However, current workflows for NEMA-based evaluation often rely on manual region-of-interest (ROI) definition and fragmented analysis tools, limiting reproducibility and scalability. In this work, we present ChameleonIQ, an open-source, configuration-driven framework for automated PET image quality assessment. The platform supports both NEMA NU-2 2018 and NEMA NU-4 2008 protocols within a unified pipeline, providing automated ROI definition, deterministic metric computation, and structured reporting. Validation was performed using standardized IEC Body and NU-4 IQ phantoms. For the NEMA NU-2 protocol, contrast recovery ranged from 29.5% (10 mm sphere) to 55.1% (37 mm sphere), with background variability maintained between 6.1% and 7.0%. For the NEMA NU-4 phantom, recovery coefficients exceeded 0.8 for rods larger than 3 mm. The framework demonstrated high quantitative fidelity, achieving an average error in hot rod recovery of only 3.9% compared to reference manual evaluations. By providing a semi-automated pipeline that maintains this high precision while removing operator bias, ChameleonIQ facilitates efficient protocol optimization and multi-center benchmarking.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 241Poster Number:MIC-05-241] Position-, direction- and contrast-dependent measurement of MLEM-reconstructed PET resolution using a 3D-printed cube (#1967)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Schramm (Autores: S. Alvarado Orozco , M. Sevenois , G. Schramm)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] KU Leuven, Department of Imaging and Pathology, Leuven, Belgium [2] UZ Leuven, Division of Nuclear Medicine, Leuven, Belgium
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The reconstructed spatial resolution of a PET image is determined by both intrinsic scanner properties and the chosen reconstruction algorithm. Standard NEMA measurements use point sources reconstructed with FBP and therefore mainly characterize the scanner. They are thus suboptimal for predicting the resolution of images reconstructed with MLEM and point-spread-function modeling, as is common in clinical practice. We propose a 3D-printed resolution cube with an off-center inner compartment which, combined with a mid-acquisition phantom flip and a single reconstruction, produces sharp edges at finite (2:1) contrast along three orthogonal directions. Position-, direction- and contrast-dependent edge and line spread functions (ESFs, LSFs) are then extracted using smoothing-spline fits. As a proof of concept, the method is applied to the NeuroExplorer brain PET system at the isocenter and 10 cm off-center, with and without depth-of-interaction (DOI) modeling. The LSFs are non-Gaussian with pronounced negative side lobes. With DOI, the resolution is approximately 2.5 mm FWHM in all directions at both positions; without DOI it degrades radially to about 4 mm at 10 cm off-center. Notably, differences between finite and infinite contrast are small in most configurations. The method provides a position-, direction- and contrast-dependent characterization of PET resolution from clinically reconstructed images and complements NEMA point-source values for image quality comparison, harmonization and partial volume correction.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 244Poster Number:MIC-05-244] Evaluation of Motion Correction Methods on the NeuroEXPLORER Using Multi-Tracer Human Data (#2130)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Zhang (Autores: J. Zhang , T. Zeng , Y. Hu , K. Fontaine , T. Volpi , T. Toyonaga , R. E. Carson)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate motion correction is critical for dynamic brain PET, particularly on the high-resolution NeuroEXPLORER (NX), where residual head motion can blur focal targets and bias time-activity curves (TACs). We evaluated multiple motion correction (MC) strategies using 17 multi-tracer human NX PET scans, including no motion correction (NMC), post-reconstruction registration (PRR), registration before attenuation correction (RBA), UMT-based frame-averaged correction (AVG), and UMT-based event-by-event correction (EBE). Performance was assessed using qualitative image comparison and ROI-based residual TAC variability (%SD res ) from 20-70 min. All MC methods reduced %SD res compared with NMC. Across all tracers, subjects, and ROIs, EBE achieved the lowest residual variability (1.40 ± 1.27%), followed by PRR (1.79 ± 1.49%), RBA (1.94 ± 1.64%), AVG (2.01 ± 1.63%), and NMC (4.68 ± 4.26%). Poisson noise-floor analysis further showed that residual motion effects were tracer- and count-statistics-dependent. Overall, UMT-based EBE provided the most effective reduction of residual motion effects in dynamic NX brain PET.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 247Poster Number:MIC-05-247] A Clinically Viable, Scalable Implementation of Monte Carlo Scatter Correction for PET/CT (#2119)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Edelstein (Autores: D. Zeltser , E. Hait-Fraenkel , X. Zhang , M. Edelstein , G. Elkin-Basudo , Y. Mizrachi , Y. Grobshtein)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] GE HealthCare, Molecular Imaging, Haifa, Israel [2] GE HealthCare, Molecular Imaging, Waukesha, Wisconsin, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Monte Carlo scatter correction is well established as a highly accurate approach for scatter estimation in PET/CT imaging. It demonstrates superior robustness compared with model based scatter estimation methods, particularly under extreme variations in activity distribution and in the presence of patient motion, conditions under which model based approaches often produce artifacts. Despite these advantages, Monte Carlo scatter correction is computationally intensive, and does not inherently account for out-of-field scatter. In this work, we address both limitations and propose an implementation suitable for integration into routine clinical workflows. A multi-GPU implementation, as well as parallel processing with efficient data streaming significantly reduce the processing time. To handle out-of-field scatter, we separately handle regions where information about out-of-field distribution is known, and can be used for a highly precise estimation. In regions where out-of-field information is inaccessible, the effect on scatter is approximated by the measured data, while ensuring a smooth transition in which the high-accuracy region governs the final estimate. Our approach is scalable and robust across system designs ranging from a standard axial field-of-view to a long axial field-of-view, each presenting distinct considerations for scatter estimation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method using phantom and clinical data.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 250Poster Number:MIC-05-250] Down-Scatter Correction for PET-induced contamination in simultaneous PET&SPECT imaging (#2341)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Li (Autores: H. Li , H. Yang , X. Zeng , M. Niu , J. Wu , Z. Gu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China [2] Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen), International Research Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Shenzhen, China [3] Beijing Normal University, School of Physics and Astronomy, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In simultaneous PET&SPECT imaging, PET-induced down-scatter contaminates SPECT data, degrading image quality and quantitative accuracy. This study presents a correction method that estimates PET down-scatter based on PET source modeling and corrects contaminated SPECT data to suppress PET interference. A PET&SPECT simultaneous imaging system is modeled using GATE Monte Carlo simulation. The system adopts a dual-head detector rotating around the field of view. An image quality phantom consisting of background region, cold region, and multiple PET and SPECT hot regions is simulated to evaluate cross-modality interference. PET and SPECT activities are modeled using 511 keV annihilation photons and 140 keV gamma photons. A uniform PET activity distribution is simulated to establish a voxel-wise PET down-scatter contribution model. The actual PET activity distribution is obtained from reconstructed PET images, and the corresponding down-scatter components are estimated from the model and subtracted from the SPECT projections. Experimental results demonstrate that PET-induced down-scatter significantly degrades SPECT projections and reconstructed image quality. The auxiliary energy window (AEW) method partially mitigates this degradation, while the proposed method achieves more effective suppression, yielding images closer to a pure SPECT reference. Quantitative evaluation shows that the proposed method outperforms AEW in terms of spillover ratio and contrast, confirming its effectiveness in simultaneous PET&SPECT imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 253Poster Number:MIC-05-253] A Quantitative Reconstruction Framework for Variable-Pitch Multi-Layer DOI Brain PET (#2420)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Chen (Autores: Y. Chen , Y. Chen , X. Zeng , M. Niu , Z. Gu , J. Jiang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Beijing Normal University, School of Physics and Astronomy, Beijing, China [2] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A dedicated brain positron emission tomography (PET) system utilizing multi-resolution depth-of-interaction (DOI) detectors is under development at Shenzhen Bay Laboratory. These detectors employ variable-pitch, multi-layer scintillators to optimize intrinsic spatial resolution and coincidence timing resolution while minimize parallax errors. However, the multi-resolution architecture introduces structural and detection heterogeneities that complicate quantitative image reconstruction. This study proposes an extended quantitative correction framework to address these challenges. We adapted standard component-based normalization (CBN) and single scatter simulation (SSS) via sub-layer-based geometric modeling to achieve layer-specific normalization and scatter correction. Specifically, a 3D fan-sum method was implemented to calculate crystal efficiencies by treating lines of response (LORs) within shared DOI layers as independent subsystems. Furthermore, a likelihood-based optimization framework was formulated to derive layer-specific scatter multipliers, compensating for detection biases caused by inter-layer shielding and axial sensitivity fluctuations. The framework was validated using GATE simulations. Ablation studies on uniform cylinder data confirmed the necessity of the integrated correction suite for spatial uniformity. Quantitative evaluation of a custom IQ phantom yielded contrast recovery coefficients (CRC) of 84.53%-65.13% and background variability (BV) of 1.69%-3.07% for spheres ranging from 37.0 to 13.0 mm. Reconstructed Derenzo phantom images resolved 1.0 mm rods at both central and off-center positions, validating its high spatial resolution. Finally, digital brain phantom studies indicate that the system's imaging performance is visually comparable to the NeuroEXPLORER benchmark.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 256Poster Number:MIC-05-256] Intra-frame motion correction for dynamic PET using mutual information-based registration (#2653)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Noë (Autores: S. Noë , M. Spangler-Bickell , A. Rezaei , J. Nuyts , G. Schramm)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] KU Leuven, Department of Imaging and Pathology, Nuclear Medicine & Molecular imaging, Leuven, Belgium [2] GE HealthCare, Waukesha, Wisconsin, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Patient motion remains a challenge for dynamic positron emission tomography (PET) imaging of the brain, due to long acquisition times. Data-driven registration-based motion estimation for static PET using sum of squared differences or normalized cross correlation as alignment metric (while popular for their simplicity and generalization potential) are not suitable for dynamic PET, as they cannot handle the changing tracer distribution throughout the scan. Alternative methods for dynamic PET motion estimation rely on the availability of a good kinetic model or suitable training data for deep learning, reducing their generalization potential. We therefore propose a registration method based on mutual information that makes it suitable for dynamic PET, and included the motion estimates in a listmode reconstruction using event-by-event motion correction. We tested this approach for 3 tracers on 2 patient scans each.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 259Poster Number:MIC-05-259] Head Motion Correction Improves Machine Learning Classification of Alzheimer's Disease from PET (#2752)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. V. Lieffrig (Autores: E. V. Lieffrig , T. Toyonaga , J. Zhang , J. Onofrey)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yale University, Department of Biomedical Engineering, New Haven, Connecticut, United States of America [2] Yale University, Department of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging, New Haven, Connecticut, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Head motion during PET data acquisition is a common source of artifact that degrades image quality and biases tracer uptake quantification. We hypothesize that motion correction improves the performance of a machine learning (ML) classifier for Alzheimer's disease versus cognitively normal subjects using brain PET images alone. A ResNet10 feature extractor combined with a Support Vector Machine classifier was applied to two cohorts encompassing a total of 301 11 C-UCB-J and 18 F-FDG PET. On motion-corrected images, the classifier achieved AUROC of 0.96 ( 11 C-UCB-J) and 0.94 ( 18 F-FDG), with accuracy increases of 5% and 10%, respectively, when motion correction was applied. Our results highlight the critical need for efficient motion correction solutions to enable effective ML analysis of PET AD imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 262Poster Number:MIC-05-262] CT-less Data Corrections For Dedicated Cardiac PET Scanners (#2950)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F.M. Muller (Autores: F.M. Muller , S. Majumder , E.J. Li , M.E. Daube-Witherspoon , P. Bravo , M.J. Parma , J.S. Karp , S. Surti)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Pennsylvania, Department of Radiology, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States of America [2] Ghent University, Faculty of Engineering and Architecture, Ghent, Belgium [3] University of Pennsylvania, Department of Bioengineering, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This work develops and evaluates CT-less data correction methods for quantitative cardiac PET by combining deep learning-based attenuation correction (DLAC) with energy-based scatter (EBS) estimation. Robustness was assessed in three human FDG studies spanning a wide BMI range (24-50 kg/m²). DLAC showed stable performance across BMI groups, with mean myocardial SUV biases below 5% relative to CT-based AC (with single scatter simulation). For a low BMI case, the DLAC+EBS method resulted in low myocardial SUV bias (mean: 1.7%, P 5 -P 95 : [-2.1%, 10.8%]) relative to standard CT-based reconstruction. To assess generalization, the DLAC model (originally trained on supine non-cardiac human data) was extended to cardiac 82 Rb studies in pigs using transfer learning. These pig studies served as a surrogate for evaluating whether the network could be adapted to other imaging conditions (cross-tracer, cross-species, and other patient positionings, e.g., seated cardiac imaging) with limited re-training. With limited additional pig data (n=8), relative biases in mean myocardial SUV decreased to within 2%. Overall, these findings support CT-less data correction for cardiac PET systems.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 265Poster Number:MIC-05-265] AmyPET: A Comprehensive Automated Framework for Static and Dynamic NeuroPET Quantification (#3013)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. J. Markiewicz (Autores: P. J. Markiewicz , A. Bollack , K. Erlandsson , A.M. Wink , M. Yaqub , L. E. Collij , N. Dijk , R. Wolz , R. Manber , D. Vállez García , B. Holman , T. Szyszko , A. Hammers , J.D. Gispert López , F. Barkhof)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] London South Bank University, School of Computer Science and Digital Technology, London, United Kingdom [2] Royal Free Hospital, London, Nuclear Medicine, London, United Kingdom [3] GE HealthCare, Chalfont St Giles, United Kingdom [4] University College London, Medical Physics and Biomedical Engineering, Hawkes Institute, London, United Kingdom [5] University College London, Institute of Nuclear Medicine, London, United Kingdom [6] Vrije Universiteit, Amsterdam UMC, Department of Radiology & Nuclear Medicine, Amsterdam, Netherlands [7] IXICO, London, United Republic of Tanzania [8] Barcelonaβeta Brain Research Center (BBRC), Pasqual Maragall Foundation, Barcelona, Spain [9] Hospital del Mar Medical Research Institute (IMIM), Barcelona, Spain [10] King's College London, School of Biomedical Engineering and Imaging Sciences, London, United Kingdom [11] King's College London, King's College London & Guy's and St Thomas' PET Centre, London, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Existing software solutions for PET quantification in neurological disorders remain fragmented and lack comprehensive end-to-end pipelines suitable for multi-site studies involving heterogeneous tracers, and scanners, including Total-Body PET systems. We present AmyPET, an open-source toolkit for automated end-to-end preprocessing and quantification of static and dynamic PET data directly from raw DICOM images. The framework supports processing in both native and MNI image spaces and integrates multiple brain atlases, motion correction, partial volume correction, and harmonised analysis within a single modular environment. AmyPET comprises four integrated processing engines for static and dynamic PET analysis: (1) an alignment engine for moderate motion correction based on a novel displacement metric, (2) spatial normalisation and tissue segmentation, (3) regional sampling and image extraction, and (4) a post-processing engine enabling kinetic modelling, Centiloid quantification, and additional quantitative analyses, including dual-time-window acquisitions. Automated quality-control outputs are generated for all processing stages. The framework has been calibrated against the GAAIN reference datasets for amyloid PET and is extensible to tau and TSPO tracers. Validation was performed using multiple amyloid PET cohorts, including test-retest studies, an amnestic mild cognitive impairment cohort, and the AMYPAD Prognostic and Natural History Study comprising more than 1500 scans. AmyPET demonstrated high repeatability (within-subject coefficient of variation, wCV=3.5%; ICC>0.98) and strong agreement with established clinical and research pipelines (R 2 >0.96), supporting its use as a robust and scalable framework for quantitative neuroPET imaging.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Reeves (Autores: A. Reeves , S. ZamanPour , S. Noe , S. Arridge , K. Thielemans)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] KU Leuven, Department of Imaging and Pathology, Leuven, Belgium [2] University College London, Institute of Nuclear Medicine and the Hawkes Institute, London, United Kingdom [3] University College London, Department of Medical Physics and Biomedical Engineering, London, United Kingdom [4] University College London, Department of computer science, London, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Recent increases in computational power as well as new tools being more readily available have led to increased interest in Monte Carlo scatter estimation. However, Monte Carlo scatter simulation is still computationally expensive. This is exacerbated by the fact that model-based scatter estimation requires multiple iterations of scatter simulation and image reconstruction. We propose to combine the current clinical standard (analytic single scatter simulation and tail-fitting) with Monte Carlo scatter simulation.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 271Poster Number:MIC-05-271] Quantitative Activities Evaluation of Ac-225 and Daughter Nuclides Using the Alpha-SPECT Mini System (#3094)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Du (Autores: W. Zhao , X. Luo , L.-J. Meng , Y. Du)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, Maryland, United States of America [2] University of Illinois at Urbana and Champaign , Champaign Il, Champaign, Illinois, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Alpha-SPECT Mini system integrates SPECT imaging with CT-based attenuation correction, providing a platform for quantifying in vivo distributions of alpha-emitting radiopharmaceuticals and daughter radionuclides. In this study, three Ac-225 filled syringes with different volumes, 0.5, 4.2, and 18.0 mL, respectively, were scanned with Alpha-SPECT Mini. The ground truth activities were[YD1] 26.12 µCi, 21.62 µCi, and 18.80 µCi from the smallest to the largest syringe, respectively. SPECT listmode acquisition was performed for 20 minutes for each syringe, together with an 80 kV CT scan for attenuation correction. SPECT images were reconstructed for the following photopeaks: 100 keV for Ac-225, 218 keV for Fr-221, 440 keV for Bi-213, and 117 keV for Tl-209. Activities of Ac-225 and these daughter radionuclides, were then estimated from SPECT images using CT defined ROIs and compared with ground truth. The results showed that quantification accuracy varied with the radionuclides and syringe sizes. Fr-221 and Bi-213 showed relatively lower errors (<5%), while Ac-225 and Tl-209 exhibited larger deviations. The higher errors likely due to the low abundance of low energy (100 keV for Ac-225 and 117 keV for Tl-209) photopeaks and interference from downscatter and collimator penetration from high energy photons. Tl-209 also exhibited larger deviations with a size-dependent trend, suggesting sensitivity to source geometry and scatter correction. Overall, the Alpha-SPECT Mini system showed potential for quantitative imaging of Ac-225 and daughter radionuclides. Future work includes further calibration and implementation of scatter correction.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 274Poster Number:MIC-05-274] Exploring a Novel Timing Calibration Approach for a Brain-Dedicated Time-of-Flight PET Scanner (#1341)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. D. Ho (Autores: J. D. Ho , M. N. Ullah , G. Chinn , G. H.-S. Park , E. Ram , W. Park , C. S. Levin)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Stanford University, Physics, Stanford, California, United States of America [2] Stanford University, Radiology, Stanford, California, United States of America [3] Stanford University, Molecular imaging, Stanford, California, United States of America [4] Stanford University, Electrical Engineering, Stanford, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract PETcoil Gen II is a novel MRI-compatible time-of-flight (TOF) PET system for simultaneous PET-MRI brain imaging. Current calibration uses an annulus phantom to correct time skew on a per line-of-response (LOR) basis, leading to a large number of correction factors (order $n^2$). We propose a convex-optimization calibration method to calculate and store per-channel (order $n$) time skew offsets using rod phantoms. We evaluate the method using simulated annulus and rod phantoms with known applied skew offsets and point-source validation. The proposed per-channel approach achieves a mean absolute timing error of 19.9 ps (annulus-based) and 18.8 ps (rod-based) compared to 142 ps for the per-LOR method. When applied to point-source correction, the proposed approaches improve coincidence time resolution (CTR) performance by +18.7\% and 13.4\% using annulus and rod phantoms respectively, whereas the per-LOR approach resulted in a -70.0\% degradation relative to uncorrected data. Results demonstrate improved calibration accuracy and robustness in using rod-based phantoms. Future work will validate these methods experimentally and assess the quality of reconstructed images.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 277Poster Number:MIC-05-277] Preliminary Study on Thick-Slab Image Generation of Digital Breast Tomosynthesis (#1451)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Hyun (Autores: S. Hyun , D. Kim , S. Lee , D. Lim , S. Cho)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] KAIST, Nuclear and quantum engineering, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [2] Mayo clinic, Radiology, Rochester, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) improves lesion detection compared with 2D digital mammography (DM), but its large number of reconstructed slices leads to increased reading time and workload for radiologists. As a potential solution, thick-slab image generation can be used to combine adjacent reconstructed slices into fewer representative slab images. However, conventional slab generation methods typically rely on simple slice-combination strategies, such as maximum intensity projection (MIP) or average intensity projection (AIP) of adjacent slices, which may reduce image sharpness and obscure diagnostically relevant details. To overcome these limitations, we propose a new thick-slab image generation method. For each slab, the proposed method adaptively blends a representative slice with the corresponding MIP image. The representative slice is selected from the DBT slices within the slab based on linear structure information obtained using the oriented bins method. The blending map is generated by applying a 1D high-pass filter to the MIP image along the X-ray source travel direction. Using a numerical phantom, the proposed method was compared with conventional MIP- and AIP-based slab generation methods and showed improved image sharpness and structural preservation. These preliminary results suggest that the proposed thick-slab image generation method has the potential to reduce DBT review time by decreasing the number of images to be reviewed without substantial loss of diagnostically relevant information.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 280Poster Number:MIC-05-280] Torch-Enabled STIR: Validation on CPU and GPU (#1661)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Efthimiou (Autores: N. Efthimiou , Z. Li , V. Cosmi , K. Thielemans , C. Tsoumpas)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] UMCG, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Groningen, Netherlands [2] UCL, Institute of Nuclear Medicine, London, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract STIR is a widely used open-source framework for PET and SPECT image reconstruction; here we explored PyTorch as an alternative array backend for STIR. We replaced the STIR arrays with a tensor-based variant while preserving the existing reconstruction framework and backwards compatibility. Correctness was assessed using existing and newly developed unit tests. Performance was evaluated with dense arithmetic benchmarks, stir_timings, and stir_math. For image-based operations, the tensor backend accelerated in-memory processing, with the largest gains observed for larger volumes. In projection-data workflows, initial performance was limited by layout-conversion and storage overhead, but targeted optimization substantially reduced these costs. In projection-data stir_math tests, the Torch-backed implementation was faster than the native STIR Array backend in end-to-end execution, with gains of roughly 7% to 23% depending on the operation. Initial GPU benchmarking further showed that the tensor backend can exploit consumer GPU hardware for dense arithmetic, achieving an approximate 3.7x speedup over CPU in the tested workload. However, projector-style kernels based on sparse, irregular scalar access did not yet benefit consistently from direct backend substitution, indicating that these critical paths require further redesign.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 283Poster Number:MIC-05-283] Post-Reconstruction Spill-In Correction Methods in Lung PET Under Heterogeneous Conditions (#1891)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 C. J. Brooks (Autores: C. J. Brooks , D. Pérez-Benito , M. Felipe-Maestre , C. Mayet , C. Joly , J. Lemaitre , T. Nanink , R. Le Grand , J.J. Vaquero)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, Departamento de Bioingeniería, Leganés, Spain [2] Immune Diseases, Microbiology and Innovative Therapies, Université Paris-Saclay, INSERM, CEA U1184 IMVA-HB/IDMIT, Fontenay-aux-Roses, France [3] Instituto de Investigación Sanitaria Gregorio Marañón, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate quantification of pulmonary PET activity is often limited by spill-in contamination from adjacent tissues. Although reconstruction-based partial volume correction techniques effectively reduce resolution-related blurring, residual spill-in can remain significant in pulmonary analysis due to respiratory motion and proximity to high-uptake extrapulmonary structures. Post-reconstruction correction methods often assume homogeneous activity within clearly defined anatomical compartments, assumptions not satisfied in inflammatory whole-lung volumes. As a result, manual refinement of the lung boundary is often necessary but is also time-intensive. Here, we compare three automatic post-reconstruction spill-in correction strategies in 18F-FDG PET scans of tuberculosis-infected macaques, using manually refined lung masks as a reference. Two methods directly adjust PET values within the lung: the first estimates spill-in from local background activity, while the second applies a more conservative correction using extrapulmonary hotspots. The third method automates conventional morphological mask refinement by adjusting the lung boundary. The value-based spill-in correction methods achieved higher agreement with manual refinement (mean log ratio 0.032 and 0.116) but showed greater sensitivity to boundary perturbation, whereas morphological correction showed lower boundary sensitivity but systematically underestimated uptake (mean log ratio -0.408). These findings suggest that localized spill-in correction methods may provide a practical alternative to manual mask refinement in 18F-FDG PET pulmonary imaging by reducing extrapulmonary contamination while preserving anatomical boundaries.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 286Poster Number:MIC-05-286] Data-Driven Motion Artifact Correction for Wearable PET (#2279)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Q. Peng (Autores: K. Hu , R. Meng , H. Liu , W. Qu , Y. Lin , X. Yu , D. Liang , Y. Lin , X. Zhang , J. Tao , D. Shi , W. Li , H. Zhao , Y. Zhang , G. Luo , Q. Peng)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China [2] Harbin Institute of Technology, College of Artificial Intelligence, Harbin, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Wearable brain PET enables neuroimaging during free movement, but head motion causes severe degradation. Compact scanners are particularly sensitive because their small detector rings ( ∼ 100 mm) amplify angular displacements at the event level. We compare five data-driven motion correction approaches on a wearable scanner using programmed Derenzo phantom motion, with all-data 3-DOF control groups isolating event retention from algorithmic accuracy. The hybrid phase-correlation with mutual-information 6-DOF method achieves the best resolution-noise trade-off-FWHM 4.68 mm vs. 5.42 mm for all-data 3-DOF and 15.15 mm for uncorrected-with SNR of 4,586. Results confirm that 6-DOF event-level correction is essential for compact-geometry wearable PET.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 289Poster Number:MIC-05-289] Radiographic Scatter Correction via Pixelwise Alpha Blending of Dark and Bright Channel Priors (#2340)

sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yonsei University, Department of Radiation Convergence Engineering, Wonju, Republic of Korea [2] Yale School of Medicine, Department of Therapeutic Radiology, New Haven, Connecticut, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Radiographic image quality is degraded by X-ray scatter, which reduces contrast and obscures fine anatomical structures, especially in thick body regions. This study proposes a calibration-free software scatter correction method for radiographic imaging based on pixelwise alpha blending of dark channel prior and bright channel prior. The observed radiograph was modeled as attenuated primary radiation plus additive scatter. Scatter intensity was estimated using self-guided filtering, and transmission maps were generated from dark and bright channel priors. Because dark channel prior can fail in bright anatomical regions such as bone, an attenuation-based alpha weight was used to adaptively combine the two transmission maps. The restored radiograph was obtained using the estimated scatter intensity and refined transmission map. The method was evaluated using in vivo animal radiographs acquired with a mobile radiographic imaging system at 100 kVp and 40 mA. Rabbit, beagle dog, and mixed-breed dog images were used to assess performance across different body sizes and scatter conditions. Image quality was compared among the observed image, dark-channel-prior-only correction, and the proposed alpha-blended correction. The proposed method improved anatomical visibility and reduced overcompensation artifacts in bright bone regions. The contrast-to-noise ratio increased from 0.85 in the observed image and 1.78 with dark-channel-prior-only correction to 2.18 with the proposed method. These results demonstrate that pixelwise blending of dark and bright channel priors can improve radiographic contrast and fine-structure visibility without additional hardware or calibration.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 292Poster Number:MIC-05-292] Adapting Timepix4 single-particle trackinginstrumentation for medical X-ray imaging (#2440)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. Mánek (Autores: P. Mánek , B. Bergmann , P. Burian , L. A. Cerbone , R. E. Mihai , S. Pospíšil , M. P. Pichotka , P. Russo , N. R. Schäfer , J. Žemlička)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Timepix4 hybrid pixel detectors, originally optimized for single-particle tracking applications, are increasingly attractive for medical X-ray imaging owing to their large area (∼7 cm2), 4-side buttability and appreciable data-driven throughput (3.6 × 106 hits/mm2). Adapting them to imaging workflows, however, demands a substantial shift in data handling. A notable challenge is presented by coping with intensity-dependent data rates, and efficiently aggregating hits and clusters into fixed-size structures under heavy loads. This contribution describes a collection of stackable software tools that adapt an established event-driven tracking framework for Timepix-based systems to X-ray imaging, organized over a modular processing pipeline. The presented platform includes energy-band splitting of hit and cluster streams and corrections for commonly seen effects: internal fluorescence of CdTe sensors, per-pixel high-energy correction, cluster-volume energy loss, non-uniform flat field response and beam hardening. The composition order of these operations is treated as a user-driven parameter, permitting construction of dedicated processing workflows depending on the imaging task at hand. Fluorescence recovery, high-energy correction, and cluster volume correction are already operational and have been tested experimentally; the remaining features are under active development. The full platform is expected to be applied to representative medical imaging tasks over the summer of 2026, with quantitative results to be presented at the conference.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 295Poster Number:MIC-05-295] A phase shifting method to provode three dimensional position information of an incident gamma ray (#2533)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Zhao (Autores: S. Zhao , H. Takahashi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The university of Tokyo, Graduate school of Engineering, Bunkyo City, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Phase-shifting sub-pixel sampling can improve the spatial granularity of compact gamma-ray detector modules without using analog charge sharing or Anger-logic interpolation.In this work, the phase-shifting concept is extended toward depthof-interaction (DOI) estimation by combining controlled detectordisplacement with double-sided MPPC readout. A monolithic scintillator is coupled to two readout sides, denoted as A and B, and the DOI-sensitive observable is defined by the signal ratio A/ ( A + B ). The detector is translated laterally by 1 mm steps relative to a narrow slit so that the effective irradiation position changes within the scintillator thickness. Coincidence signals are then analyzed using A-B correlation plots. The measured slopes vary systematically from the B-side region to the A-side region, indicating that interaction depth information is preserved in the double-sided signals. These results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating phase-shifting sampling with DOI estimation for compact SPECT or Compton camera detector modules.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 298Poster Number:MIC-05-298] Simultaneous Dose Reduction and Resolution Recovery in Preclinical SPECT via Deep Learning (#2608)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 E. Taragola (Autores: E. Taragola , S. Neyt , W. Van de Velde , S. Vandenberghe , C. Vanhove , F. Muller)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Ghent University, Department of Electronics and Information Systems, Faculty of Engineering and Architecture, Ghent, Belgium [2] University of Pennsylvania, Department of Radiology, Perelman School of Medicine, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Micro-single photon emission computed tomography (µSPECT) is constrained by an inherent sensitivity-resolution trade-off imposed by the collimator. High-sensitivity collimators mitigate statistical noise but blur spatial details, whereas high-resolution collimators limit count sensitivity, thereby amplifying noise. To bridge this trade-off and overcome both low sensitivity and poor resolution, we propose and compare three frameworks for joint µSPECT denoising and super-resolution: a single Joint U-Net, a sequential Cascade U-Net, and a Dual-Encoder U-Net utilizing task-specific encoders and a shared decoder. Models were trained on paired mouse datasets to map noisy low-resolution acquisitions (10-50% of standard counts) to high-resolution targets, acquired with two different collimators. The Dual-Encoder architecture most effectively balanced the competing objectives of noise suppression and edge preservation by extracting distinct representations before merging. Compared to the input, the model achieved a 32% reduction in overall RMSE and an 8% improvement in SSIM. Furthermore, it demonstrated superior resolution recovery relative to the Joint and Cascade approaches, reducing edge map and spectral errors by 27% and 21% compared to the input, respectively. Visually, it was the only model capable of resolving rod peaks in a Derenzo phantom. This approach enables significant reductions in acquisition time or dose while maximizing precision for preclinical quantification.

sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Nantes Université, École Centrale de Nantes, CNRS, LS2N, Nantes, France [2] CHU Nantes, Serive de médecine nucléaire, CRCI2NA, INSERM UMR 1307, Nantes, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract PET reconstruction aims to transform raw sinograms data into images using analytical, iterative or deep learning approaches. In addition to the ill-posedness of the problem, inherent Poisson noise in sinograms makes the problem more difficult, especially in low-dose contexts. Using deep learning for image denoising and reconstruction has shown promising performances. However, supervised training requires large sets of paired data with corrupted images and their associated ground truth, which is hard or even impossible to acquire in the medical field, especially in emission tomography. In this work, we adapted Noise2Noise, a self-supervised framework, to PET imaging in order to learn how to denoise images from noisy measurements only.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Taheri (Autores: N. Taheri , M. Toussaint , A. Merasli , S. Stute)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] CRCI2NA, INSERM UMR 1307, Nantes University, Nantes, France [2] Nuclear Medicine Department, Nantes University Hospital, Nantes, France [3] Hematology Biology, Nantes University Hospital, Nantes, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Modern PET reconstruction methods increasingly rely on advanced optimization strategies and deep learning-based priors. However, integrating such approaches into established reconstruction toolkits remains challenging due to limited interoperability with high-level programming environments. In this work, we present a framework that enables Python integration within the CASToR reconstruction platform, allowing direct interaction between C++ reconstruction routines and Python-based modules. As a proof of concept, we implemented an end-to-end PET reconstruction approach incorporating the Deep Image Prior (DIP) and a forward projection model. This example illustrates how the proposed integration facilitates the use of modern Python libraries for deep learning within a physics-based reconstruction framework. This work opens the door to rapid prototyping and deployment of advanced reconstruction algorithms within CASToR using the Python ecosystem.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 307Poster Number:MIC-05-307] DOI Calibration and Resolution Estimation in PET Detector Panels Using Uncollimated Irradiations (#3133)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. E. Enriquez-Mier-y-Teran (Autores: F. E. Enriquez-Mier-y-Teran , A. Z. Kyme , S. R. Meikle)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The University of Sydney, Faculty of Medicine and Health, Sydney, Australia [2] The University of Sydney, Brain and Mind Centre, Sydney, Australia [3] The University of Sydney, School of Biomedical Engineering, Sydney, Australia
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract High-resolution PET systems require accurate DOI calibration to reduce parallax errors. Conventional DOI calibration methods rely on lateral detector access and collimated irradiations, resulting in complex and time-consuming experimental setups. In this work, we investigated the use of an analytical DOI model and a multilayer perceptron (MLP) network for DOI calibration and DOI resolution estimation using only detector front-face irradiations. The methods were evaluated on a dual-ended-readout 4 × 4 detector panel. Crystal-wise DOI calibration estimates obtained using the analytical model and the MLP showed good agreement with ground-truth measurements, with median calibration RMSE values below 0.6 mm and 0.7 mm, respectively. However, the MLP yielded superior DOI resolution prediction, with consistent mean DOI resolution estimates of approximately 2.0 mm.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 310Poster Number:MIC-05-310] Virtual Imaging Trial to Evaluate the Impact of Acquisition Protocols on Harmonized Radiomic features in multi-site PDAC CT (#2788)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 D. Pal (Autores: D. Pal , I. Montero , J. Luo , A. Thomas , E. Abadi , K. I. Shoghi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Washington University School of Medicine, Department of Radiology, Saint Louis, Missouri, United States of America [2] Washington University in St. Louis, Imaging Science Program, Saint Louis, Missouri, United States of America [3] Washington University School of Medicine, Department of Surgery, Saint Louis, Missouri, United States of America [4] Duke University School of Medicine, Department of Radiology, Durham, North Carolina, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Radiomics is used to extract high-dimensional features from medical images such as computed tomography. However, radiomic features are susceptible to acquisition protocols in a multi-center setting. This results in domain shift in data distribution even when the patient anatomy is the same. This can increase intraclass variability and lead to algorithms learning protocol-specific artifacts rather than clinically relevant imaging information. In this work, we developed a virtual imaging trial (VIT) of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) patients scanned across multiple scanners and protocols to quantify protocol-induced radiomic variability post harmonization. A virtual patient cohort of 50 patients was generated using the XCAT. PDAC tumors extracted from clinical cases were implanted in individual virtual patients. DukeSim was used to simulate Siemens clinical scanners. For each scanner, two clinically representative acquisition protocols were designed by varying tube current, pitch, and reconstruction kernel. Radiomic features were extracted from tumor regions and harmonized using scanners and protocols as batch effect. Scanner and protocol dependency of each feature was assessed using Wilcoxon and Kruskal-Wallis tests, respectively. Feature robustness was quantified using intraclass correlation coefficient. Protocol-related batch effects were prominent in the non-harmonized data, with 85.98% of radiomic features dependent on protocols. Protocol-based CovBat achieved the best overall performance, reducing protocol-dependent features to 19.63% and increasing reproducible features by 3.8% post harmonization. Therefore, the proposed VIT-based framework can be used to evaluate harmonization methods and assess radiomic feature robustness before developing clinical decision-support models.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 313Poster Number:MIC-05-313] Allometric Scaling of PSMA Uptake as a Novel Biomarker for Predicting Biochemical Response in Prostate Cancer (#2104)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Yousefirizi (Autores: F. Yousefirizi , T.J. McColl , R. Samimi , E. Hosseinzadeh , G. Divband , B. Nickkholgh , Z. Adinehpour , S. Dastgerdi , C. Uribe , A. Rahmim)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of British Columbia, Department of Radiology, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada [2] BC Cancer Research Institute, Department of Basic and Translational Research, Vancouver, Canada [3] BC Cancer, Vancouver, Canada [4] Shahid Beheshti University, Tehran, Iran (Islamic Republic of) [5] Jam Hospital, Tehran, Iran (Islamic Republic of) [6] PET/CT Centre, Tehran, Iran (Islamic Republic of) [7] The Ottawa Hospital and University of Ottawa, Ottawa, Ontario, Canada [8] University of Isfahan, Isfahan, Iran (Islamic Republic of)
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET/CT enables standardized quantitative tumor burden assessment, yet routine SPARC-aligned metrics, molecular tumor volume (MTV), total lesion activity (TLA), and total lesion fraction (TLF), show limited predictive value for early biochemical response. Allometric scaling laws (TLA ∝ MTV^β) govern metabolic activity superlinearly (β > 1) across multiple cancers, but their application to PSMA PET outcome prediction remains unexplored. We hypothesized that each patient's deviation from the cohort-level scaling line, the Distance from the Scaling Law (DSL), encodes biologically distinct information beyond raw burden metrics and predicts PSA50 biochemical response (PCWG3: ≥50% PSA decline). In 103 prostate cancer patients with PSMA PET/CT and paired PSA measurements from a real-world clinical cohort, we fitted the allometric law (TLA = α × MTV^β) and computed per-patient DSL residuals. The cohort exhibited a superlinear scaling law: TLA = 0.574 × MTV^1.157 (R² = 0.782, p < 0.0001) consistent with literature values (β ≈ 1.22-1.28). DSL ranked 4th among 12 candidate features in univariate discrimination (AUC = 0.668), outperforming standard SPARC burden metrics including TLF (0.589), TLA (0.588), and MTV (0.523). Non-responders showed lower DSL than responders (mean −0.243 vs +0.018; rank-biserial r = 0.336), indicating hypoactive PSMA uptake relative to tumor volume as a failure signature. Nine cost-sensitive classification strategies under 5-fold stratified cross-validation reached balanced accuracy of 0.57-0.64, constrained by extreme class imbalance (93.2% responders). These findings establish DSL as a physics-grounded, automatically computable biomarker that outperforms conventional burden metrics and is deployable within SPARC workflows.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 316Poster Number:MIC-05-316] A Cucker-Smale Flocking Model for Edge-Aware Medical Image Analysis (#3017)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Hashemi (Autores: A. Hashemi , H. Sabet)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Harvard Medical School/Massachusetts General Hospital, Radiology Department, Boston, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract We propose a flocking‑based framework for image structure analysis inspired by the Cucker-Smale model, interpreting pixels as interacting agents whose alignment patterns reveal self-organized regions. Here, we model each pixel as coupling with its neighbors through distance‑weighted interactions, and identify structural boundaries via a normalized measure of local misalignment. This yields an edge‑aware representation that suppresses intra‑region variation while emphasizing transitions between self-organized flocks. We evaluate the method on diverse medical imaging data, including brain MRI, retinal fundus images, and microaneurysm patches. Across modalities, the approach robustly captures both large‑scale anatomical boundaries and fine pathological details, adapting to different contrast regimes without requiring reference images. Quantitatively, strong‑edge masks achieve edge/non‑edge contrast ratios of ~66 in MRI, ~11 in fundus images, and ~4.4 in microaneurysm patches, with edge fractions ranging from 0.06 to 0.15-demonstrating high structural selectivity and reduced sensitivity to noise.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 319Poster Number:MIC-05-319] ComBat-Driven Latent Representation Learning for Robust Multicenter Radiomics in Theranostic SPECT/CT Imaging (#3106)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. S. Azimi (Autores: M. S. Azimi , M. Cheraghi , M.A. Ghodsi Rad , G. Divband , M. Alhashim , M. Alabedi , N. Ibrahim , E. Alwuhaib , Z. Mansouri , Y. Salimi , H. Arabi , J.M. Beauregard , A. Rahmim , H. Zaidi)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Obuda University, Doctoral School of Applied Informatics and Applied Mathematics, Budapest, Hungary [2] Obuda University, University Research and Innovation Center, Budapest, Hungary [3] Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences, PET-CT Unit, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Tehran, Iran (Islamic Republic of) [4] Shohada-e Tajrish Medical Center, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Tehran, Iran (Islamic Republic of) [5] Jam Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Tehran, Iran (Islamic Republic of) [6] Imam Abdulrahman Bin Faisal University, Department of Radiology, College of Medicine, Dammam, Saudi Arabia [7] King Fahad Specialist Hospital Dammam, Medical Imaging Services Center, Dammam, Saudi Arabia [8] Geneva University Hospital, Division of Nuclear Medicine & Molecular Imaging, Geneva, Switzerland [9] Université Laval, Cancer Research Centre and Department of Radiology and Nuclear Medicine, Quebec, Canada [10] University of British Columbia, Departments of Radiology and Physics, Vancouver, Canada
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Multicenter SPECT/CT radiomics is highly sensitive to variations in imaging protocols, reconstruction settings, and scanner configurations, limiting reproducibility and masking biological patterns. To address this challenge, we propose a harmonized latent radiomics framework for robust patient-level modeling in theranostic imaging. A retrospective multicenter dataset of ¹⁷⁷Lu-DOTATATE SPECT/CT scans from three institutions was analyzed. A total of 93 IBSI-compliant lesion-based radiomic features were extracted and harmonized using ComBat to reduce inter-center variability. Principal component analysis was then applied to generate a compact latent representation, followed by unsupervised clustering for lesion phenotype discovery. Patient-level representations were constructed by aggregating lesion embeddings. In addition, a perturbation strategy was implemented to assess latent-space stability and responsiveness. ComBat substantially reduced center-related variability, with η² values decreasing from 0.75 to near-zero levels (0.000-0.006). The latent representation demonstrated improved biological interpretability, with stronger association to intensity-related characteristics (0.351 to 0.956) and reduced dependence on texture-related confounding (0.967 to 0.528). Clustering results showed that lesion grouping was primarily driven by intrinsic phenotypic patterns rather than acquisition center. Perturbation analysis further revealed low phenotype transition rates (<10%) with gradual centroid shifts, indicating stable yet responsive latent behavior. The proposed framework combines harmonization and latent representation learning to improve robustness in multicenter radiomics and provides a promising foundation for digital twin modeling in theranostic imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 322Poster Number:MIC-05-322] Evaluation of Dose Rate Dependent Alanine/ESR Response under Carbon Ion FLASH Irradiation (#1286)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S.M. Lee (Autores: S.M. Lee , K.-T. Han , M. Tashiro , S. Inagaki , C.H. Min)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Yonsei university, Department of Radiation Convergence Engineering, Wonju-si, Germany [2] Korean Association for Radiation Application, Radiation Technology and Research Center, Jeongeup, Germany [3] Gunma University, Gunma University Heavy Ion Medical Center, Gunma, Germany [4] Gunma University, Department of Medical Physics for Heavy Ion Therapy, Graduate School of Medicine, Gunma, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate dosimetry for ultra-high dose rate (FLASH) carbon ion irradiation is challenging because ionization chambers can exhibit dose rate dependent recombination and charge-collection inefficiency. Alanine/ESR dosimetry is a passive technique for high dose verification, but its response under FLASH conditions remains unclear. This study evaluated dose rate dependent alanine/ESR response by comparing calibration curves under conventional and FLASH irradiation. Alanine pellets were irradiated with a 290 MeV/u carbon ion beam at 10-100 Gy. Measurements were performed at SOBP centers under conventional irradiation at 0.09 Gy/s and FLASH irradiation at 174-265 Gy/s. An Advanced Markus chamber provided the reference absorbed dose to water. Monte Carlo simulations examined possible geometry-related dose perturbations and beam-quality effects. Under conventional irradiation, the ESR response was highly linear, and reconstructed doses agreed with the reference dose within 2%. However, applying this calibration to FLASH-irradiated alanine produced dose dependent deviations, with errors up to 28.6% in the low dose region and approximately 3-4% at higher doses. Simulations showed that chamber related scatter and positional dose differences at the alanine locations were below 1%, indicating that the discrepancy was not mainly caused by the irradiation geometry. A FLASH-specific calibration restored agreement within 1.31%, with an approximately 7.4% lower slope than the conventional calibration. These results indicate that alanine/ESR response is modified under FLASH irradiation, likely due to combined FLASH delivery and high-LET beam-quality effects. Therefore, conventional carbon ion calibration shows limited direct transferability to FLASH conditions, requiring FLASH-specific calibration for accurate dose verification.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Q. Xie (Autores: W. Hu , S. Ou , D. Mu , J. Zhu , A. Qiu , M. Chen , Y. Lai , X. Rao , L. Wan , Q. Ma , Q. Liu , P. Qi , Z. Yang , Q. Xie)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate dose delivery in proton therapy requires reliable control of the proton range to ensure that the beam deposits its energy at the planned treatment position. However, the proton range is highly sensitive to tissue heterogeneities, anatomical changes, and patient positioning errors, making in vivo range verification an important component of proton therapy quality assurance. Positron emission tomography (PET) provides a non-invasive approach for range assessment by detecting proton-induced positron-emitting nuclei generated in the irradiated material. In this work, we demonstrate preclinical proton range verification using a dedicated in-room All-Digital PET system installed in a clinical proton treatment room. The system was evaluated using polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) phantoms irradiated with a 130 MeV proton pencil beam. Controlled range perturbations were introduced using intact, 1 mm air-gap, and 4 mm air-gap phantom configurations. PET data were acquired for 300 s following irradiation, and one-dimensional activity profiles were extracted. At 130 MeV, the PET-derived activity profiles exhibited distinct distal fall-off shifts that correlated with the introduced air gaps. These results demonstrate the capability of the system to resolve millimeter-scale range perturbations under the tested phantom conditions and provide experimental support for future preclinical animal studies and clinical in-room proton therapy verification.

sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Santiago de Compostela (USC), Instituto Galego de Física de Altas Enerxías (IGFAE), Santiago de Compostela, Spain [2] TripleAlpha Innovation, Santiago de Compostela, Spain [3] OncoRay - National Center for Radiation Research in Oncology, Medical Faculty and University Hospital Carl Gustav Carus, TUD Dresden University of Technology, Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden - Rossendorf, Dresden, Saxony, Germany [4] Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden - Rossendorf, Institute of Radiooncology - OncoRay, Dresden, Saxony, Germany [5] Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden - Rossendorf, Institute of Nuclear Physics, Dresden, Saxony, Germany [6] Instituto de Física Corpuscular (IFIC), CSIC-UV, Paterna, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Proton therapy is recommended as the "new standard-of-care option for patients with head and neck oropharyngeal cancer". Still, the absence of a monitoring tool equivalent to electronic portal imaging hinders its upmost potential, and forces the application of safety margins and field-patching, thereby increasing the dose to normal tissue. Prompt gamma-rays produced along the proton track can cover this shortfall, since their production cross section is strongly correlated with the proton dose depth profile. We present the first experimental proof of principle of proton range verification with a single-channel prompt gamma-ray detector located behind the treated area, in coaxial geometry. Simple heterogeneous targets were irradiated with 1e8 protons at clinically realistic energies at beam currents of 1.6 nA. The mean statistical precision was 1 mm (sigma). The absolute experimental error with respect to the ground truth predicted by a Monte Carlo simulation was 2 mm on average. These findings encourage further investigations with anthropomorphic phantoms and realistic treatment plans, and could open up the door for proton range verification with a single scintillation detector, that may have better prospects of integration into rotating gantries and compact treatment rooms than collimated multi-channel systems.

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Positron emission tomography (PET) has been widely investigated for range verification in carbon-ion radiotherapy (CIRT). All-Digital PET, based on multi-voltage threshold (MVT) direct digital signal acquisition with high count-rate capability, represents a promising new approach for in-beam monitoring. However, its application in CIRT remains largely unexplored, and experimental validation under realistic irradiation conditions is still lacking. In this study, we report the preliminary experimental validation of an in-beam All-Digital PET system for range verification in CIRT. A discrete 7x7 raster-scanned carbon-ion field (261.03 MeV/u) with a spot spacing of 5 mm and a delivery of 2000 MU per spot was delivered to a polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) phantom (6x6x15 cm³). To simulate localized anatomical heterogeneity, a cylindrical air cavity with a diameter of 1 cm was embedded at a depth of 5 cm from the beam entrance, introducing an approximate local range shift of 10 mm. Two-dimensional distal range maps successfully revealed the irradiation field and clearly identified the cavity boundary. Within the region of interest, the measured localized range shift was 9.14 mm, with a residual error of only 0.86 mm compared with the ground truth. These results demonstrate the feasibility of All-Digital PET for accurate in-beam range verification under clinically relevant raster-scanned carbon-ion delivery conditions and support its potential for future CIRT applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 334Poster Number:MIC-05-334] Effect of Radionuclide Distribution on DNA Damage Yields: A Comparative Study between 134 Ce/ 134 La and other radionuclides (#1512)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Lee (Autores: S. Lee , J. Shin , Y. Huh , K. N. Bobba , R. R. Flavell , G. Cho , Y. Seo)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Department of Nuclear and Quantum Engineering, Daejeon, Republic of Korea [2] University of California, San Francisco, Department of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging, San Francisco, California, United States of America [3] National Institutes of Health, Division of Cancer Epidemiology and Genetics, National Cancer Institute, Rockville, Maryland, United States of America [4] Seoul National University Hospital, Department of Radiation Oncology, Seoul, Republic of Korea [5] Seoul National University Medical Research Center, Institute of Radiation Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea [6] University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Department of Nuclear Engineering, Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America [7] University of California, San Francisco, Department of Pharmaceutical Chemistry, San Francisco, California, United States of America [8] University of California, Berkeley, Department of Nuclear Engineering, San Francisco, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Targeted radionuclide therapy employs therapeutic radiation-producing radionuclides bound to targeting agents to selectively damage cancer cells. Recent interest has expanded beyond conventional beta emitters to include alpha emitters and Auger electron emitters. We investigated the therapeutic potential of the 134 Ce/ 134 La pair by comparing its DNA damage induction with commonly used radionuclides. A simplified human fibroblast cell model was implemented using Monte Carlo track-structure simulations to evaluate single-strand and double-strand DNA break yields. Particular attention was paid to the various spatial distributions of the radiation source. In this simulation, radionuclides were distributed at the cell surface, cytoplasm, and nucleus surface; both physical and chemical stages of radiation interaction were modeled, including indirect damage mediated by hydroxyl radicals. The results show that double-strand break yields increase as radionuclide localization approaches the nucleus, while single-strand break yields remain relatively stable. Indirect effects dominate DNA damage formation across all radionuclides and spatial distributions. The 134 Ce/ 134 La pair demonstrates DNA damage yields comparable to established beta and Auger electron emitters under all tested conditions. Although these findings do not directly translate to therapeutic efficacy, they indicate that this radionuclide pair has competitive radiobiological effectiveness and warrants further investigation for potential application in targeted radionuclide therapy.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 337Poster Number:MIC-05-337] Range Monitoring and Tissue Identification in Particle Therapy with the TIARA Detector (#1641)

Grenoble Alpes, CNRS, Grenoble INP, LPSC-IN2P3, Grenoble, France [2] Aix-Marseille Univ, CNRS/IN2P3, CPPM, Marseille, France [3] Università Roma Tor Vergata, Roma, Italy [4] Centro Nazionale di Adroterapia Oncologica (CNAO), Pavia, Italy [5] Centre Antoine Lacassagne, Nice, France
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Particle therapy with protons and carbon ions offers conformal dose delivery, but its clinical benefit strongly depends on accurate verification of the beam range inside the patient. The TIARA (Time-of-Flight Imaging ARray) detector has been developed to address this challenge through the exclusive measurement of Prompt-Gamma (PG) Time-of-Flight (TOF). The system combines a fast plastic beam monitor with arrays of Cherenkov gamma detectors based on PbF 2 crystals coupled to SiPMs, enabling sub-nanosecond timing performance and real-time treatment verification. An 8-channel prototype has been tested with proton and carbon-ion beams delivered by cyclotrons, synchro-cyclotrons and synchrotrons. Measurements with 63 MeV protons at the MEDICYC cyclotron demonstrated a range accuracy of 3.3 ± 0.1 mm (2σ) for irradiation spots of about 2×10 7 protons, corresponding to roughly 3200 detected PG events. Experiments with carbon ions at the CNAO synchrotron achieved a range accuracy of 4.74 ± 0.36 mm (2σ) at clinical intensity by grouping four spots of 2.4×10 6 ions each, with approximately 5600 detected PGs. These results confirm the high sensitivity of the TOF approach for proton and carbon-ion therapy. Beyond range monitoring, TIARA implements the Prompt Gamma Time Imaging (PGTI) method to identify anatomical changes occurring between treatment planning and dose delivery. An iterative reconstruction algorithm was developed to merge the TOF information from multiple detector modules and reconstruct both the PG emission profile and the proton beam average velocity evolution inside the patient. The method was validated using a RANDO head phantom irradiated at the Proteus One accelerator under two anatomical configurations simulating an empty and filled sinus cavity. The reconstructed PG distributions enabled localisation of the induced anatomical change, demonstrating the potential of TIARA for adaptive particle therapy and in vivo tissue identification.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 340Poster Number:MIC-05-340] Secondary Electron Bremsstrahlung Imaging with a Knife-Edge Slit Camera for Range Verification in Carbon-Ion Therapy (#1876)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Tsuda (Autores: M. Tsuda , M. Yamaguchi , Y. Nagao , H.G. Kang , T. Yabe , E. Yoshida , T. Yamaya , M. Sakama , H. Mizuno , N. Kawachi , H. Watabe)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology (QST), Takasaki Institute for Advanced Quantum Science, Gunma, Japan [2] Postdoctoral Research Fellow of the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science (JSPS), Tokyo, Japan [3] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology (QST), Institute for Quantum Medical Science, Chiba, Japan [4] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology (QST), QST hospital, Chiba, Japan [5] Fukushima Institute for Research, Education and Innovation (F-REI), Radiation Science, Medicine and Drug Development, & Industrial Applications for Radiation, Fukushima, Japan [6] Tohoku University, Research Center for Accelerator and Radioisotope Science (RARiS), Miyagi, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate in-vivo range verification is essential for realizing the full dosimetric advantage of carbon-ion therapy [1]. Secondary electron bremsstrahlung (SEB), a low-energy photon emission produced along the beam trajectory inside the patient, has attracted attention as a prompt signal for non-invasive range monitoring [2]. While our prior work demonstrated the principle using a pinhole collimator, the limited collection efficiency of a pinhole aperture imposes a fundamental constraint on range estimation precision [3]. A knife-edge slit geometry offers a one-dimensional focusing advantage that substantially raises the collected photon flux compared to the pinhole-based approach. In this study, a knife-edge slit camera equipped with a Ce:GAGG scintillator array was constructed and evaluated through irradiation experiments with a 290 MeV/u carbon-ion beam at the Heavy Ion Medical Accelerator in Chiba (HIMAC). The camera employed a tungsten knife-edge slit collimator with a slit width of 1 mm and a thickness of 48 mm, positioned 490 mm from the beam axis with a collimator-to-detector distance of 49 mm. The Ce:GAGG scintillator array consisted of 1.5 × 1.5 × 1 mm³ crystals arranged in a 16 × 16 matrix with a pitch of 1.6 mm. One-dimensional SEB profiles were measured over a range of beam range conditions by varying the range-shifter thickness, and representative results are presented. The acquired distributions exhibited a systematic dependence on beam range, with a 5 mm increment reliably distinguished by visual inspection. Quantitative range estimation yielded an uncertainty of 2.89 mm for 10⁸ ions; further details will be presented at the conference.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 343Poster Number:MIC-05-343] A Deep Learning-Based 3D Dose Reconstruction Using a Dual-Panel PET in Proton Therapy (#1929)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 X. Jiang (Autores: X. Jiang , C. Huang , H. Yang , X. Zeng , Y. Zhao , J. Lei , E. Quan , M. Niu , Z. Gu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen, China [2] Harbin Institute of Technology, School of Electronics and Information Engineering, Harbin, China [3] Southern University of Science and Technology, Department of Electronic and Electrical Engineering, Shenzhen, China [4] Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and Peking Union Medical College, National Cancer Center/National Clinical Research Center for Cancer/Cancer Hospital & Shenzhen Hospital, Shenzhen, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Proton therapy requires accurate in vivo dose verification because proton range uncertainties may compromise treatment precision. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a deep learning-based method for three-dimensional (3D) dose reconstruction using positron emission tomography (PET) in proton therapy. A dual-panel PET system with time-of-flight and depth-of-interaction (TOF-DOI) capability was modeled using GATE Monte Carlo simulations. PET activity images and corresponding ground-truth dose maps were generated for single pencil beams with energies across 60-120 MeV. A U-Net-based neural network was developed to reconstruct the 3D dose distributions from reconstructed PET activity images. Quantitative evaluation was performed using 3D gamma passing rates (GPRs) and distal range metrics ( R 50 and R 90 ). The proposed method accurately reconstructed 3D dose distributions while reduced the impact of limited-angle artifacts inherent to the dual-panel PET geometry. GPRs exceeded 99% under the 3%/3 mm criterion and 98% under the 2%/2 mm criterion for all validation datasets. Submillimeter accuracy was achieved for distal range verification, with maximum deviations of 0.15 mm for R 50 and 0.11 mm for R 90 . The results demonstrate the feasibility of using a dual-panel PET system with a deep learning method for accurate 3D dose reconstruction and proton range verification, supporting its potential in proton therapy quality assurance.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 346Poster Number:MIC-05-346] Validation of Dose-to-PET Conversion for OpenPET Range Verification in Carbon-Ion Therapy (#2077)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Tashima (Autores: H. Tashima , T. Du , C. Toramatsu , T. Masuda , G. Vallari , M. Pinto , A. Hamato , Y. Iwao , H.G. Kang , M. Tajiri , H. Mizuno , T. Inaniwa , M. Koto , H. Ikawa , M. Shinoto , K. Parodi , T. Yamaya)
