sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In-beam PET is a promising technique for range verification in particle therapy because positron emitters are produced along the beam path through nuclear fragmentation reactions. Over the past years, QST has developed a human-scale OpenPET system that enables three-dimensional PET imaging during and/or immediately after carbon-ion therapy. In parallel, LMU has developed an analytical approach based on a pencil beam algorithm for irradiation-plan-based PET image prediction. In the present study, we combine these two developments toward the clinical implementation of OpenPET for range verification in carbon ion therapy. The approach involves comparing measured OpenPET images with predicted PET images. Phantom experiments were performed at HIMAC. OpenPET data were acquired during and after irradiation. To simplify PET image prediction, the present analysis was limited to the post-irradiation period, and list-mode data acquired from 0 to 600 s after the end of irradiation were extracted and reconstructed as the measured OpenPET image. A predicted PET image corresponding to the same 0-600 s post-irradiation period was generated from the irradiation plan and PET measurement conditions by modeling positron-emitter production and physical decay. The predicted PET images showed an activity distribution corresponding to the planned irradiation fields, and the comparison indicated reasonable agreement between the predicted and measured images. These results demonstrate the feasibility of combining OpenPET with the irradiation-plan-based PET prediction, and they support the potential of the clinical use of OpenPET for range verification in carbon-ion therapy.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 349Poster Number:MIC-05-349] EasyPET.3D imaging of positron-emitter distributions in proton-irradiated PMMA phantoms (#2152)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Silva (Autores: A. C. Magalhães , P. Correia , M. Grossman , D. Meer , J. Veloso , A. Silva)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] I3N -University of Aveiro, Physics Dpt., Aveiro, Portugal [2] Paul Scherrer Institut, PSI, Villigen, Switzerland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate quality assurance (QA) is essential in proton therapy, where the steep dose gradient of the Bragg peak requires precise knowledge of beam position to spare healthy tissue while ensuring full tumor coverage. This work presents the experimental evaluation of easyPET.3D, a compact and cost-effective preclinical PET scanner, as a potential tool for pretreatment QA in proton therapy using phantoms.Homogeneous PMMA phantoms were irradiated at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) Gantry 1 facility with proton energies ranging from 138 to 195 MeV, delivering up to 6.4 × 10 11 protons per irradiation. The resulting 3D β+ activity distributions were reconstructed and analyzed to characterize both longitudinal range and transverse beam profiles. A temporal convergence study determined the minimum acquisition time required for stable range estimation. In addition, a controlled displacement experiment, with longitudinal offsets of 1, 2, 3, and 5 mm, was performed to assess the system's ability to detect range variations.Transverse analysis revealed energy-dependent beam broadening, with mean FWHM values decreasing from 12.3 mm at 138 MeV to 9.6 mm at 195 MeV, and a characteristic widening near the distal end consistent with proton stopping at the Bragg peak. Range estimation converged within 10-12 cumulative frames (~30-35 min). Sensitivity tests showed that the system could detect longitudinal phantom displacements as small as 1 mm, with a linear response and a systematic overestimation of 13%, attributed to manual positioning uncertainties.These results demonstrate that easyPET.3D is a promising and accessible solution for pretreatment QA in proton therapy workflows.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 352Poster Number:MIC-05-352] Dosimetry-Oriented Structure-Weighted CT-Guided Registration for Multi-Time-Point SPECT/CT in Radionuclide Therapy (#2369)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Du (Autores: Y. Du , Z. Wu , S. Wang , Y. Chen , C. Qi , H. Liu , Y. Liu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Department of Engineering Physics, Beijing, China [2] The Affiliated Hospital of Southwest Medical University, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Luzhou, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Multi-time-point SPECT/CT is used for patient-specific dosimetry after Lu-177-PSMA therapy. However, inter-scan motion, anatomical deformation, and time-dependent uptake variations can compromise volume-of-interest (VOI) activity extraction and time-integrated activity (TIA) estimation, thereby requiring accurate inter-time-point SPECT registration. This study proposes a structure-weighted CT-guided registration method for longitudinal SPECT/CT. Organ-specific dosimetric priorities and an uptake-derived activity-concentration term were integrated into a spatial weight map, which was incorporated into the CT registration similarity metric to emphasize structures with greater dosimetric relevance. The resulting CT-derived transformation was applied to SPECT images using physical-coordinate inverse mapping. Compared with Elastix and an unweighted baseline, the proposed method improved SPECT VOI Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) from 0.82 with Elastix and 0.87 with the unweighted baseline to 0.90. It also reduced fitting-residual-based TIA normalized root-mean-square error (nRMSE) across all evaluated structures, with additional reductions relative to the unweighted baseline of 15.8% in kidneys, 23.2% in prostate, and 49.2% in tumors. These results indicate that incorporating dosimetric structure weighting into CT-guided registration can improve dosimetry-relevant spatial consistency and temporal fitting stability in multi-time-point SPECT/CT workflows for radionuclide therapy.

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Boron Neutron Capture Therapy (BNCT) is a binary radiation treatment relying on the selective uptake of B-10 in tumors, requiring a high thermal neutron flux with minimal fast neutron and gamma ray contamination. The reaction between the thermal neutron and the B-10 releases an alpha and lithium nucleus, two high-LET particles that deposit their energy inside the cell causing lethal damage. This work characterizes a BNCT-optimized irradiation field at a TRIGA Mark II reactor and compares the effects on various cell samples to standard radiation fields. The irradiation setup was localized within the graphite thermal column of the TRIGA reactor (Mainz). Gamma contamination was mitigated using lead shielding, while additional graphite bars further thermalized the neutrons. Dosimetric profiling was conducted using radiochromic films paired with specific radiation converters. Additionally, PADC plates were employed to quantify the alpha particle tracks emitted by the BNCT reaction, as well as proton tracks generated by the elastic scattering of fast neutrons. For biological validation, FaDu tumor cells and isolated lymphocytes were exposed to nominal doses (1-6 Gy) to evaluate clonogenic survival and DNA double-strand breaks (DSB) via the γH2AX foci assay. Experimental data were cross-referenced with Monte Carlo (GATE/Geant4) cellular microdosimetric models. Dose contributions from primary beam components were assessed across different shielding configurations to optimize the thermal neutron field, and microdosimetric models were applied to estimate biological sample doses. Results demonstrated linear dose-response relationships for lymphocyte DNA damage, while tumor cell survival was reduced compared to photon reference data, due to relative biological effectiveness of thermal neutrons. Ultimately, this integrated experimental and computational methodology validates the reactor facility for advanced BNCT research.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 358Poster Number:MIC-05-358] MACACO III+ Compton camera imaging of 225 Ac in mice (#2614)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 K. Brzeziński (Autores: K. Brzeziński , L. Barrientos , J. Rodríguez , U. Cossío , J. Llop , G. Llosá)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto de Física Corpuscular (IFIC), CSIC-UV, Valencia, Spain [2] CIC biomaGUNE, Basque Research and Technology Alliance (BRTA), San Sebastián, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Compton cameras are a potential tool for assessing translational targeted alpha therapy (TAT) treatments using 225 Ac in murine models. For this application, gamma cameras perform sub-optimally due to the extremely low activities used. The IRIS group at IFIC-Valencia is developing Compton cameras based on lanthanum bromide (LaBr 3 ) crystals, capable of visualizing 225 Ac distributions through the detection of the 440 keV gammas emitted during the decay of its short-lived daughter nuclide 213 Bi. Following successful imaging tests with 131 I in live mice at CIC biomaGUNE in San Sebastián, Spain, this work presents measurements performed using the current Compton camera prototype, MACACO III+, and a mouse phantom filled with 225 Ac. The system was shown to be capable of visualizing 225 Ac distributions in the phantom with two combinations of organ compartments filled with activity. Images obtained using the Compton camera are of comparable quality to those obtained using commercial pre-clinical SPECT systems at 440 keV. Monte Carlo simulations of a mouse phantom filled with 225 Ac have also demonstrated the improved image quality that can be achieved with an augmented Compton camera, MACACO IV, featuring a larger first plane detector and currently under development. Measurements using MACACO III+ for imaging live mice grafted with AR42J tumor cells and injected with [ 225 Ac]Ac-DOTATATE are planned for the near future.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 361Poster Number:MIC-05-361] Boron Imaging with a Compton Camera: Toward Real-Time Dosimetry in BNCT Treatments (#2726)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. Torres-Sánchez (Autores: P. Torres-Sánchez , S. Valladares-Sánchez , V. Babiano-Suárez , J. Balibrea-Correa , B. Gameiro , I. Ladarescu , J. Lerendegui-Marco , S. Bortolussi , S. Fatemi , I. Postuma , C. Domingo-Pardo)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Instituto de Física Corpuscular (CSIC-UV), Grupo de Espectroscopía Gamma, Valencia, Spain [2] Università di Pavia, Dipartimento di Fisica, Pavia, Italy [3] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Pavia, Pavia, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Boron Neutron Capture Therapy is a binary cancer treatment modality in which a tumour-selective boron-carrying drug is administered to the patient prior to irradiation with a neutron beam. The highly localised nuclear reaction between thermal neutrons and ¹⁰B deposits a lethal radiation dose selectively within tumor cells. After recent advances driven by accelerator-based neutron sources and improved boron compounds, a critical gap remains: there is currently no method to image boron distribution in vivo during treatment, preventing real-time dose verification. We present the development of a Compton camera system designed to detect the 478 keV prompt gamma rays emitted following ¹⁰B neutron capture, thereby enabling direct spatial mapping of boron dose deposition. The detector is based on LaCl₃ and CeBr₃ scintillators arranged in a pyramidal geometry, inherited from nuclear physics instrumentation developed at CERN-n_TOF, which provides intrinsically low neutron sensitivity and high gamma-ray detection efficiency. Experimental validation was carried out at Institut Laue-Langevin (ILL, Grenoble). A boron sample in water at 65 ppm, within the clinically relevant concentration range, was successfully imaged, yielding a signal-to-background ratio of 12. This constitutes, to our knowledge, the first experimental demonstration of Compton imaging of boron at clinical concentration levels. At treatment-level neutron fluxes, however, the original detector suffered from count rate saturation. To address this, we redesigned the detector incorporating pixelated crystal arrays. The pixelated prototype was subsequently validated at the LENA reactor (U. Pavia) achieving a reduction in per-crystal count rate by a factor of approximately 250. These results represent a substantive step toward a clinically deployable real-time boron imaging system, with implications both for treatment monitoring of patients and preclinical pharmacokinetic studies with animal models.

sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Washington University in St. Louis, Imaging Science Doctoral Program, St. Louis, Missouri, United States of America [2] Washington University in St. Louis, Radiation Oncology, St. Louis, Missouri, United States of America [3] Washington University in St. Louis, Radiology, St. Louis, Missouri, United States of America [4] Washington University in St. Louis, Electrical and Systems Engineering, St. Louis, Missouri, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Proton therapy enables conformal tumor irradiation while reducing dose to surrounding healthy tissues. But anatomy, motion, and delivery uncertainty can cause differences between planned and delivered dose. PET can detect proton-induced positron-emitting radionuclides such as 15 O, 13 N, & 11 C, providing a method for post-irradiation in-vivo dosimetry verification. We evaluated a mobile PoC-PET system for imaging validation & MLEM-based radionuclide decomposition. PoC-PET used 8 TOF detector modules. Imaging performance was evaluated with a Derenzo-style tumor phantom 3.3-11.4mm lesions at a 20:1 tumor:background ratio and with a FDG-injected mouse. To evaluate radionuclide decomposition, three vials with known 15 O, 13 N, & 11 C activities were imaged for 60 minutes. Counts were binned in 30s windows and reconstructed into PET image series. ROIs generated decay curves modeled as mixtures of exponential decay components using an MLEM-based fitting approach. PoC-PET resolved all tumor clusters by the VPR < 0.735 criterion. Mouse imaging clearly showed regional FDG uptake with spatial agreement to MicroPET. In the multi-isotope experiment, the MLEM fit matched the large-ROI decay curve with a ~1% nRMSE. The fitted isotope allocation captured expected isotope behavior: 15 O dominating early, 13 N showing intermediate decay, and 11 C persisting throughout the scan. The injected mixture was 29% 11 C, 16% 13 N, and 55% 15 O, the MLEM estimated 27.7%, 15.7% and 56.6% respectively. These results demonstrate the feasibility of using a mobile PoC-PET system and radionuclide decomposition for post-irradiation radionuclide characterization.

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Multi-time-point SPECT/CT imaging enables improved characterization of radiotracer kinetics for quantitative dosimetry, particularly in emerging radiopharmaceutical therapies. However, activity quantification is affected by partial volume effects (PVE), which introduce time-dependent bias in both lesion and organ dose estimation. This issue is especially relevant for novel radionuclides such as ¹⁶¹Tb, where complex emission characteristics may lead to varying sensitivity to image correction across time. In this study, we analyze the temporal behavior of lesion and organ dosimetry for ¹⁶¹Tb-FAPI-2286 and evaluate the influence of partial volume correction at multiple imaging time points (2 h, 24 h, and 96 h post-injection). Patient-specific SPECT/CT data were used, with lesions and organs segmented using semi-automatic and deep learning-based approaches. Two iterative correction methods, Richardson-Lucy and reblurred Van Cittert (RVC), were applied prior to dosimetric analysis. Absorbed dose values were estimated using Monte Carlo simulations, and relative differences were computed between corrected and non-corrected images. Results indicate minimal impact of correction at early imaging, with relative differences generally below ±3%. In contrast, substantial and heterogeneous variations were observed at later time points, with lesion-level dose changes ranging from approximately −30% to +38%. Bone lesions exhibited the largest positive deviations, whereas lung lesions showed consistent reductions at delayed imaging. Both correction methods demonstrated similar temporal patterns, with slightly lower variability for the RVC approach. These findings highlight the time-dependent nature of PVE in ¹⁶¹Tb-based dosimetry and emphasize the importance of incorporating correction methods in delayed imaging. Temporal-aware quantitative strategies are therefore essential for improving the reliability of lesion-level dose estimation in emerging theranostic applications.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 370Poster Number:MIC-05-370] COXIRIS: A Novel Real-Time Platform for Integrated Cancer Detection, Medical Imagen and Targeted Treatment; Deep EDXRF Detection (#3141)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 B. Casanelli (Autores: R. G. Figueroa Saavedra , B. Casanelli , J. Sagardia , M. A. Valente , N. S. Villar , M. Cerna , A. L. Silva)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidad de la Frontera, Center for Physics and Engineering in Health Please and Department of Physical Sciences, TEMUCO, Chile [2] Aveiro University, Department of Physics, AVEIRO, Portugal
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The development of integrated strategies for simultaneous cancer detection and treatment is driving advanced theranostic platforms. In this context, the COXIRIS system (Confocal Orthovoltage X-Ray Induced Radiation Integral System) introduces a large-scale X-ray fluorescence (XRF) imaging architecture designed to combine real-time functional imaging with precision-guided therapy.This work evaluates the feasibility of COXIRIS for imaging and guiding treatment of tumors labeled with high-Z biomarkers or nanoparticles (e.g., Au, Gd). The system uses XRF detection with a collimated X-ray source directed toward a focal inspection region, while a synchronized high-sensitivity detection system performs three-dimensional scanning and tumor localization. The partially confocal detection geometry improves spatial selectivity at macroscopic scale and enables guidance of therapeutic modalities including radiotherapy, ablation, drug delivery, and surgical assistance.Experimental results demonstrated tumor localization at depths up to 15 cm in tissue-equivalent media using low radiation dose levels. Gadolinium-based targets were detected in less than 2 seconds at this depth. Although acquisition times are currently comparable to some nuclear medicine procedures, scalability through larger detector areas and optimized geometry indicates potential for sub-second detection.COXIRIS represents a novel large-scale XRF imaging and theranostic guidance platform that addresses limitations of existing micro-scale XRF techniques. Its compatibility with conventional radiotherapy systems, including linear accelerators and orthovoltage units, supports its translational potential for real-time and personalized cancer treatment.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 373Poster Number:MIC-05-373] Attenuation Correction Using 176Lu Background in Limited-Angle Flat-Panel Total-Body PET (#1490)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 T. D'Hulster (Autores: T. D'Hulster , J. Maebe , S. Vandenberghe)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Ghent University, MEDISIP, Ghent, Belgium
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A novel flat-panel total-body walk-through PET system under development at Ghent University aims to improve patient throughput and cost-eﬀectiveness compared to conventional total-body scanners. Its high sensitivity enables low-dose imaging protocols, where CT may be omitted to minimize radiation exposure. In this setting, an alternative CT-less attenuation correction method is required. The high sensitivity and large number of LYSO detector elements in the walk-through geometry also result in a substantial and potentially exploitable intrinsic background signal from 176 Lu. This GATE simulation study investigates the feasibility of leveraging this intrinsic 176 Lu background activity in the LYSO detectors for transmission-based attenuation estimation. The limited angular coverage inherent to the flat-panel design introduces additional challenges for implementation of this method. To address this, a maximum likelihood transmission reconstruction (MLTR) algorithm was implemented. MLTR is particularly interesting for low-dose applications because it is independent of emission data and computationally eﬃcient, making it suitable for clinical integration. The eﬀect of limited-angle artifacts on attenuation map convergence was evaluated, along with their impact on attenuation correction in PET image reconstruction, using a full angular coverage flat-panel geometry with side panels as reference. Simulations with a NEMA image quality phantom and the XCAT phantom demonstrated that limited angular coverage has minimal impact on attenuation correction in emission image reconstruction. These transmission-based attenuation maps may further serve as initial estimates for more advanced approaches, such as maximum likelihood reconstruction of attenuation and activity (MLAA) or physics-informed deep learning methods.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 376Poster Number:MIC-05-376] System Characterization of a DOI-Enabled High-Resolution Total-Body TOF PET Scanner (#1642)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Q. Peng (Autores: D. Liang , Y. Lin , H. Liu , X. Yu , H. Zou , Y. Xu , H. Zhao , J. Tao , W. Zhu , Y. Lin , W. Ma , W. Li , Y. Zhang , D. Shi , J. Zeng , Q. Ren , Z. Xie , W. Liu , Q. Peng)

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A DOI-enabled total-body TOF PET system with a 200-cm axial field of view was developed using 2-mm-pitch LYSO crystal arrays and light-sharing-window-based DOI encoding. The system consists of seven detector rings with a transaxial diameter of 70 cm. Phantom experiments, including SZBL logo, Derenzo, and dynamic line-source phantoms, were performed to evaluate imaging performance. The reconstructed logo phantom demonstrated clear visualization of 2-mm structures, while rods down to 2.0 mm could be distinguished in the Derenzo phantom, indicating high spatial resolution consistent with the detector crystal pitch. Dynamic imaging results demonstrated continuous tracer propagation across consecutive 5-s frames, indicating high sensitivity and short-frame dynamic imaging capability. In addition, TOF resolution measurements based on the NEMA NU 2-2018 method achieved approximately 330 ps for both single-ring and dual-ring configurations. These results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating DOI capability, high spatial resolution, dynamic imaging capability, and stable TOF performance within a long axial field-of-view total-body PET system.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 379Poster Number:MIC-05-379] Implementation and Evaluation of TOF and Scatter correction for the IMAS TB-PET (#1989)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A.J. Gonzalez (Autores: Á. Anreus-Valero , M. Freire , D. Sanchez , S. Jimenez-Serrano , N. Cucarella , A. Gonzalez-Montoro , A. Rios , I. Torres-Espallardo , L.F. Vidal , M. Gil , A.J. Gonzalez)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] the Instituto de Instrumentación para Imagen Molecular (I3M), Centro Mixto CSIC-Universitat Politècnica de València, Valencia, Spain [2] Oncovision S.A., Valencia, Spain [3] Full Body Insight, Valencia, Spain [4] Hospital La Fe, Clínical Area of Medical Imaging, Valencia, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Total-Body Positron Emission Tomography systems offer substantially increased sensitivity due to their extended axial FOV, enabling reduced dose, shorter acquisitions, or improved image quality. Incorporating TOF information further enhances image reconstruction by improving Signal-to-Noise Ratio. We have recently developed and installed a novel TB-PET scanner (IMAS) at Hospital La Fe in Valencia (Spain). The system is based on semi-monolithic LYSO crystals and provides TOF and Depth of Interaction (DOI) capabilities. In this work, we present the implementation and evaluation of TOF and scatter correction for the IMAS system, and we also present ongoing developments related to random, dead time, and quantification corrections are presented. For the TOF information, an iterative skew correction was used. Scatter correction was applied using a TOF-based scaling method. For the random, dead-time and quantification correction study, the acquisition mode was modified allowing the acquisition of coincidences and singles at the same time. A system CTR of 690 ps was measured at the NECR peak. The combined use of TOF and DOI information and the inclusion of scatter correction demonstrated a reduction in positional errors for off-center lesions and an improvement of the SNR, contributing to improving the image quality of the IMAS system.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 382Poster Number:MIC-05-382] Addressing Scatter Phantom Length Limitations: A Single-Scan Multi-Position Method for NEMA NU 2 Testing of Long Axial FOV PET Systems (#2290)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Xu (Autores: H. Xu , Y. Wu , Y. Liu , L. He , Y. Dong)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] United-imaging Healthcare Co., Ltd., MI-RECON, Shanghai, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The NEMA NU 2 scatter phantom (70 cm, ~20 kg) was designed for conventional PET scanners with axial fields-of-view (AFOV) under 30 cm. For long axial field-of-view (LAFOV) systems exceeding 70 cm, this phantom provides only a localized assessment that fails to capture out-of-FOV scatter and randoms from the full body. Scaling the phantom to 1.2-1.75 m would increase its weight to 34-50 kg, rendering routine use impractical. We propose a single-scan multi-position protocol that exploits the idle intervals between static acquisitions in a standard decay experiment to reposition the phantom axially within each time slot. A center-plus-off-center demonstration was performed on a uMI Panorama GS (1.5 m AFOV). The 70-cm phantom was measured at both the AFOV center and 10 cm beyond the AFOV edge, with the off-center position sampled twice per slot to enable interpolation to a common activity level. The two off-center acquisitions showed close agreement across all count rate metrics and scatter fraction (SF), confirming reproducibility. The SF at the off-center position was elevated due to out-of-FOV scatter contributions, consistent with total-body imaging conditions. This approach enables evaluation of LAFOV systems at multiple axial positions without additional phantom preparation, offering a practical basis for NEMA NU 2 evalution metrics related to the scatter phantom experiment.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 385Poster Number:MIC-05-385] Characterizing Smoking Effects Across Lung Cancer Subtypes by Integrating Systemic Metabolic Networks and Tumor Habitat Imaging from Total-Body 18 F-FDG PET/CT (#2779)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Wang (Autores: H. Wang , Y. Wu , Y. Duan , L. Li , L. Sun , X. Tao , N. Zhang , X. Zhao , J. Liu , Z. Guan , H. Zheng , D. Liang , R. Chen , Z. Cheng , M. Wang , G. S.P. Mok , Z. Hu)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Shenzhen Institute of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shenzhen, China [2] Key Laboratory of Biomedical Imaging Science and System, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shenzhen, China [3] Henan Provincial People's Hospital, Henan, China [4] The First Affiliated Hospital of Shandong First Medical University, Jinan, China [5] Ren Ji Hospital, School of Medicine, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China [6] University of Macau, Faculty of Science and Technology, Macau, China, Macao Special Administrative Region [7] University of Macau, Faculty of Health Science, Macau, China, Macao Special Administrative Region
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Lung cancer (LC) is increasingly recognized as a systemic disease, with metabolic alterations that may vary across histological subtypes. Smoking is a major LC risk factor, but its effects on systemic metabolism and tumor phenotypes across LC subtypes remain insufficiently characterized. We integrated systemic metabolic networks and tumor habitat imaging from static and dynamic total-body 18 F-FDG PET/CT to characterize smoking effects across LC subtypes. This multicenter study included 125 LC patients and 200 healthy controls from three centers. Thirty-seven regions spanning the central nervous system and peripheral organs were analyzed. Regional SUL mean values and time-activity curves were harmonized using ComBat and adjusted for demographic covariates. Population-level metabolic networks were constructed from bootstrapped Pearson correlations of regional uptake, while individual-level networks were derived from residual time - activity curve correlations after third-order polynomial fitting to calculate organ-specific abnormality strength. Tumor habitats were defined using PET/CT intensity and entropy features, and their associations with smoking and organ abnormalities were assessed by multivariable regression and mediation analyses. Both network analyses showed that smoking disrupted systemic metabolic coordination in a subtype-dependent manner, with the liver emerging as a central hub. Tumor habitat imaging revealed a smoking-associated shift toward hypometabolic tumor microenvironments. Mediation analysis suggested that habitat composition modulated the association between smoking and hepatic metabolism, linking local tumor heterogeneity to systemic metabolic responses. These findings demonstrate that integrated metabolic network and tumor habitat imaging from total-body 18 F-FDG PET/CT provides quantitative insight into smoking-related systemic metabolic reprogramming in LC and may support imaging-based characterization across histological subtypes.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 388Poster Number:MIC-05-388] Improving Generalization of PET Image-Enhancing Deep Learned Models Through Domain Randomization (#1058)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 P. Aguiar (Autores: J. Poveda-Martínez , J.P. Gómez-González , F. J. López-González , C. Dominguez-Borrero , M. A. Belzunce , G. Webber , A. J. Reader , P. Aguiar , J. Silva-Rodríguez)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidad de Santiago de Compostela, Molecular Imaging Biomarkers and Theragnosis Lab, Center for Research in Molecular Medicine and Chronic Diseases (CIMUS), Santiago de Compostela, Spain [2] Qubiotech Health Intelligence, Research & Development, La Coruña, Spain [3] Reina Sofia Alzheimer Centre, CIEN Foundation, Madrid, Spain [4] King's College London, School of Biomedical Engineering and Imaging Sciences, London, United Kingdom [5] Instituto de Ciencias Físicas, Universidad Nacional de San Martínez, Buenos Aires, Argentina [6] Centro Universitario de Imágenes Médicas, Universidad Nacional de San Martínez, Buenos Aires, Argentina
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Deep learning models for PET image enhancement often struggle to generalize across unseen scanner configurations due to limited training data diversity. We introduce a Domain Randomization (DR) framework that utilizes Monte Carlo simulations via the SimPET platform to randomize scanner geometries and reconstruction protocols within clinically operational ranges. To mimic biological variability, this approach is supplemented by a tailored activity augmentation pipeline, resulting in a training dataset of 232 activity maps. To validate this methodology, we trained a 2.5D Attention U-Net to map simulations to high-quality activity maps. Performance was assessed across incremental data regimes ranging from 20 to 236 training instances. On unseen scanner domains, the DR strategy consistently outperformed the no-DR baseline in SSIM and relative contrast. Conversely, on the in-distribution source domain, the DR model achieved perceptual equivalence to the baseline, despite a minor trade-off in absolute pixel precision. Real-world validation with a Hoffman Phantom acquisition on a Philips Vereos scanner suggested a remaining sim-to-real gap on real data distributions. By demonstrating improved generalization without compromising structural fidelity on synthetic domains, this work presents a promising pathway for future research and democratizes access to high-quality, annotated training data through scalable and cost-effective deep learning tools.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 391Poster Number:MIC-05-391] Unsupervised Deep Learning for Prompt Gamma Emission Reconstruction in Time and Space (#1173)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 J. Werner (Autores: L. Hellwege , J. Werner , J. Kasprzak , V. Ferrero , F. Pennazio , T. M. Buzug , M. Rafecas , M. Stille)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Luebeck, Institute of Medical Engineering, Luebeck, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany [2] Fraunhofer Research Instution for Individualized Medical Technology and Engineering IMTE, Luebeck, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany [3] Universitá degli Studi di Torino, Department of Physics, Torino, Italy [4] Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Torino, Torino, Italy
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Spatiotemporal Emission Reconstruction from Prompt Gamma Timing data (SER-PGT) has the potential to verify the stopping power through passive measurements during proton therapy. The underlying inverse problem is ill-posed and offers some unusual challenges compared to conventional emission or transmission reconstruction scenarios.In this work, we introduce an unsupervised deep learning framework for reconstructing prompt gamma emission distributions from simulated data, without requiring ground-truth images during training. Our method combines a physics-informed Poisson likelihood loss in the data domain with a UNet++ architecture with ResNeXt101 encoder. It operates on pseudo-inverse reconstructions from a system matrix modeling 110 detectors, 160 depth bins, and 100 time bins. Evaluation on 200 test samples yields comparable performance to MLEM in terms of Mean Absolute Error and Peak-Signal-to-Noise-Ratio in both image and data domains, demonstrating that accurate reconstruction is achievable through self-supervised learning. The approach showcases fast execution speed and a flexible framework. This makes it a promising candidate to move SER-PGT closer towards stopping power estimation in clinical scenarios.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 394Poster Number:MIC-05-394] Supervised Contrastive Pretraining Enables Few-Shot Alzheimer's Disease Classification on Multi-Site ECD SPECT (#1384)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y.-C. Ni (Autores: H.-C. Yang , F.-P. Tseng , Y.-C. Ni , Y.-W. Wu , G.-U. Hung , C.-Y. Lin , Y.-C. Liu , Y.-M. Fan , S.-Y. Wang)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Atomic Research Institute, Department of Radiation Protection, Taoyuan, Taiwan [2] Far Eastern Memorial Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine, New Taipei City, Taiwan [3] National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, School of Medicine,, Taipei, Taiwan [4] Chang Bing Show Chwan Memorial Hospital, Changhua, Taiwan [5] Cardinal Tien Hospital, Department of Neurology, New Taipei City, Taiwan [6] Cardinal Tien Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine, New Taipei City, Taiwan [7] Fu Jen Catholic University, School of Medicine, New Taipei City, Taiwan [8] Yuan Ze University, Electrical and Communication Engineering College, Taoyuan, Taiwan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This study investigates the cross-site generalization of deep learning for Tc-99m ethyl cysteinate dimer (ECD) brain perfusion single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), where site-specific imaging variability often limits cross-site generalization of deep learning models. To address this, a multi-site supervised contrastive learning (SupCon) pretraining framework was developed using a 3D ResNet-18 encoder, which was trained on 2,242 images collected from five sites across eight diagnostic categories. The pretrained representation achieved a latent-space silhouette score of 0.815, while t-SNE visualization showed that samples from different sites were well mixed within diagnostic clusters, indicating that the learned features were more disease-discriminative than site-specific. To simulate deployment at a new hospital, a sixth site that had been entirely excluded from pretraining was reserved for downstream evaluation. In this hospital-held-out setting, where only 46 balanced samples were available for adaptation, few-shot fine-tuning achieved 80.4% accuracy for Alzheimer's disease-versus-Normal classification, with a macro F1-score of 0.801 and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.819. This performance substantially exceeded that of a randomly initialized baseline, which achieved 60.9% accuracy, a macro F1-score of 0.568, and an AUC of 0.639. These results suggest that multi-site SupCon pretraining may provide a practical route toward scalable cross-site deployment of brain SPECT classifiers with minimal site-specific annotation, potentially enabling rapid clinical adoption at new hospitals.

It describes a novel method for encoding volumetric data into a discrete set of tokens, which are then used to condition the text generated by a pre-trained foundational language model. Design considerations and model architecture are outlined, and the feasibility of the technique is demonstrated for generating descriptive captions of image volumes with information related to imaging modality, administered radiopharmaceutical and anatomical scan range.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 400Poster Number:MIC-05-400] Preliminary Region-Aware MRI-to-sCT Synthesis for Radiotherapy-Oriented Imaging in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma (#1752)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Z. Sun (Autores: Q. Wang , J. Xu , C. Li , Z. Sun , H. Xiao , W. Huang , Y. Zeng , J. Sun)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Hainan University, Department of Data Science and Big Data, Haikou, China [2] The Second Affiliated Hospital of Hainan Medical University, Department of Radiation Oncology, Cancer Treatment Center, Haikou, China [3] The First Affiliated Hospital of Hainan Medical University, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Haikou, China [4] Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital, School of Clinical Medicine, Tsinghua University, Department of Nuclear Medicine, Haikou, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Synthetic computed tomography (sCT) generation from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is an important component of MRI-only radiotherapy planning because MRI provides excellent soft-tissue contrast but lacks quantitative Hounsfield unit (HU) information for electron-density assignment. However, MRI-to-sCT synthesis remains challenging due to the indirect MRI representation of bone, the ambiguity between intra-body air and external background, and the heterogeneous HU distributions across anatomical regions. This study proposes a region-aware 3D supervised MRI-to-sCT synthesis framework using paired CT-referenced MRI and CT volumes. The network combines 3D convolutional feature extraction with a Project-and-Excite (PE) attention module to enhance volumetric anatomical representation. To improve HU fidelity in clinically relevant regions, MRI masks were used for input background suppression, CT body masks were used to define valid supervision and evaluation regions, and HU-derived masks were used to impose region-weighted constraints on body, background, intra-body air, and bone regions. The method was evaluated on 24 paired MRI/CT cases, including 16 training, 5 validation, and 3 independent testing cases. In ablation analysis, the full body-background-air-bone loss achieved the highest PSNR of 19.65 dB, while SSIM decreased to 0.53, suggesting improved control of large HU deviations rather than simple maximization of structural similarity. These preliminary results support the feasibility of region-aware HU optimization for MRI-to-sCT synthesis, while larger-scale validation, region-wise HU analysis, and dosimetric assessment remain necessary before clinical application.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Hu (Autores: Y. Hu , C. Boccalini , G. Hajianfar , V. Garibotto , H. Zaidi , A. Sanaat)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Geneva university hospital, Division of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging, Geneva, Genève, Switzerland [2] University of Geneva, Geneva University Neurocenter and Faculty of Medicine, Geneva, Genève, Switzerland [3] University of Groningen, Department of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging, Groningen, Denmark
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Tau positron emission tomography (PET) is strongly linked to cognitive impairment and disease progression in Alzheimer's disease, but direct tau imaging is not always available in routine clinical or research workflows. This study evaluated a multimodal deep learning framework that uses amyloid PET and fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET to estimate binary 18 F-flortaucipir (FTP) positive/negative status. A total of 340 participants from Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) and the Geneva University Hospital cohort with available amyloid, FDG, and FTP PET were included. Images were registered to Montreal Neurological Institute space and used as two-channel volumetric input to a SwinUnetR-based classifier. The multimodal model setting was evaluated using stratified five-fold cross-validation on the combined cohort. The model achieved an accuracy of 0.853, sensitivity of 0.823, specificity of 0.871, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.904. These findings suggest that combined amyloid and FDG PET contains complementary information relevant to tau status and may provide practical decision-support evidence when direct tau PET is unavailable or when the indication for tau imaging remains uncertain.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 406Poster Number:MIC-05-406] Compton Camera Image Reconstruction Using Compton Physics-Prior Fusion and Set Transformers for Actinium-225 Targeted Alpha Therapy (#2148)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Balasmeh (Autores: Y. Balasmeh , I. Fleck , R. Obermaisser)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Siegen, Department of Physics, Siegen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany [2] University of Siegen, Embedded Systems, Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Siegen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract In this work, a physics-aware neural network architecture is proposed for Compton camera image reconstruction. The model incorporates physics-based features from coincidence events and uses backprojection as a prior. It is applied both to mono energetic sources as well as to targeted alpha therapy using Actinium-225 where the presence of multiple gamma-ray lines makes image reconstruction more challenging for existing medical imaging devices, such as single-photon emission computed tomography. The input data are preprocessed and categorized into scattering-only, absorption-only, and coincidence events. These data are used to generate feature maps through neural network layers and a transformer-based model, followed by an image reconstruction decoder. Training and testing data were generated using the Geant4 simulation toolkit. The model was first evaluated using controlled single-source simulations with different source sizes, energies, positions, and event statistics. It was then tested under more realistic conditions using a mouse phantom with Actinium-225 activity distributed in tumor and background regions. CPPF-Net achieved a mean peak-localization error of 1.0 ± 0.7 mm and a structural similarity index of 0.99 ± 0.01. These results indicate that CPPF-Net can provide accurate Compton camera image reconstruction for Actinium-225 targeted alpha therapy. Experimental validation with measured data is foreseen for the near future.

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Prostate cancer is one of the most commonly diagnosed cancers in men worldwide. Accurate detection using 18 F-prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) enables reliable identification of the disease and supports clinical staging. In this study, we propose a deep learning framework for the slice-level classification of 18 F-PSMA PET/CT images using convolutional neural networks trained on axial, coronal, and sagittal views. The models achieved high discrimination performance, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.98 and a specificity of 0.98, while showing orientation-dependent differences in sensitivity and classification balance. However, lower performance in the hold-out dataset indicates limited generalization capability, highlighting the importance of imaging plane selection in prostate tumor classification. The classification model serves as a preliminary step for downstream segmentation by enabling slice-level localization of the region of interest.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 415Poster Number:MIC-05-415] Equilibrium Matching for PET Image Denoising: Signal vs. Velocity Parameterization Under Identical Conditions (#2453)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Afshari (Autores: S. Afshari , C.-Y. Chou)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Taiwan University, Department of Biomechatronics Engineering, Taipei, Taiwan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Low-count Positron Emission Tomography (PET) suffers from severe Poisson photon-counting noise, yet existing deep learning denoisers either rely on supervised regression networks that tend to oversmooth anatomical detail or on diffusion-based generative models designed for Gaussian corruption that require iterative, noise-level-dependent sampling at inference time. Equilibrium Matching (EqM) was recently proposed as a generative modeling framework that learns a time-invariant equilibrium gradient field toward the data manifold, but has not yet been explored for medical image restoration. We present a novel adaptation of EqM to PET denoising, reformulating its interpolation scheme for Poisson-corrupted acquisitions and introducing noise-level conditioning via Adaptive Group Normalization, and conduct a controlled comparison of its two parameterizations under identical training conditions: the signal form, which predicts the clean image directly with hyperparameter-free inference, and the velocity form, which predicts the noise residual via iterative Euler updates. Signal EqM achieves up to +5.26 dB PSNR gain at severe noise (N_peak = 50) with no step-size tuning. Velocity EqM consistently outperforms signal EqM on both PSNR and FID at all seven noise levels, with the PSNR gap growing from 0.13 dB at N_peak = 50 to 1.23 dB at N_peak = 5000, mirroring the x- vs. velocity-prediction trade-off in flow-based generative models.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 418Poster Number:MIC-05-418] CT-VDETR: Semi-supervised 3D Trauma Detection in Computed Tomography (CT) scans using Dense Vertex Relative Position Encoding (#2592)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 S. Chaudhary (Autores: S. Chaudhary , S. Bhat , A. Maier)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg, Pattern Recognition Lab, Erlangen, Bavaria, Germany
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Accurate detection and localization of traumatic injuries in abdominal CT remain challenging because voxel-level annotations are limited and expensive to obtain. We present a label-efficient framework for 3D abdominal trauma detection that combines self-supervised pretraining with semi-supervised transformer-based detection. First, we use Masked Image Modeling (MIM) on 1098 CT volumes to pretrain a 3D U-Net encoder for anatomical representation learning. Next, we adapt V-DETR to dense volumetric CT through a feature adapter that converts the encoder feature grid into a compact token sequence for transformer decoding. The pretrained encoder is then integrated with V-DETR and 3D Vertex Relative Position Encoding (3D V-RPE) to improve the localization of irregularly shaped injuries. Finally, semi-supervised teacher-student consistency regularization leverages 2,000 additional unlabeled volumes during detector training. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of a 3D DETR-style detector to the RSNA abdominal trauma detection task. On this benchmark, the proposed method achieves 31.33% test mAP@0.50 using only 78 labeled training volumes, corresponding to a 1.53× improvement over supervised-only training. These results show that combining medical-domain pretraining with semi-supervised learning is an effective strategy for label-scarce 3D medical detection.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 421Poster Number:MIC-05-421] An AI Model for Breast Density Estimation using Spectroscopic X-Ray Data (#2672)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. A. Eaton (Autores: M. A. Eaton , E. Lewis , M. Wilson , S. Pani)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Surrey, Department of Physics, Guildford, United Kingdom [2] Royal Surrey County Hospital, Department of Medical Physics, Guildford, United Kingdom [3] STFC Rutherford Appleton Laboratory, Detector Development, Didcot, United Kingdom
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract High breast density is a known risk factor for breast cancer. Current gold standard methods of density measurement are highly variable, and as such, reporting of density is not standard practice worldwide. The use of artificial intelligence has shown promise, but a lack of a definitive ground truth leads to less reliable predictions. This work combines artificial intelligence with spectroscopic X-ray imaging, which preserves compositional tissue information, as a novel density estimation method. A proof-of-concept study was performed by simulating the breast imaging process for breast tissue-equivalent phantoms to build a training set for a custom machine learning tool. This gave good results, having a mean squared error in the model's output of 0.013 +/- 0.002 %. Based on these results, further work focused on increasing the realism of the simulation and training data by modelling the charge transport in the detector as well as including anthropomorphic breast phantoms. This work will provide the foundations towards building a reliable and accurate way to measure breast density, allowing early cancer detection by tailoring patient pathways, and improving health outcomes.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 424Poster Number:MIC-05-424] Positron Range Correction with Texture Preservation in 82 Rb PET (#2819)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Encina-Baranda (Autores: N. Encina-Baranda , Y. Zheng , J. Cabello , R.J. Paneque-Yunta , A. Lopez-Montes , M. Conti , J.L. Herraiz)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Complutense University of Madrid, Grupo de Física Nuclear, EMFTEL & IPARCOS (), Madrid, Spain [2] Bern University Hospital, Department of Nuclear Medicine,, Bern, Switzerland [3] Siemens Medical Solutions USA, Inc., Knoxville, Tennessee, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The positron range (PR) is a fundamental resolution-limiting factor in positron emission tomography (PET), particularly for high-energy radionuclides such as ⁸²Rb. In cardiac PET, the long PR of ⁸²Rb causes spatial blurring, activity spill-out, and reduced myocardial contrast, especially across heterogeneous tissue interfaces. Deep learning-based PR correction (PRC) provides a practical post-reconstruction strategy, but supervised regression networks often produce over-smoothed outputs by attenuating high-frequency stochastic fluctuations. We propose a model-consistent framework that decouples structural PR correction from texture preservation by combining PRC, matched smoothing estimation, and deterministic texture reinjection. In simulated ⁸²Rb PET studies, the proposed framework improved the recovery coefficient by 13.8% relative to the uncorrected ⁸²Rb input, while restoring noise levels closer to the reference (9.74 ± 1.85% vs. 10.62 ± 0.82%), supporting structure-texture decoupling as a promising strategy for PET imaging.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 430Poster Number:MIC-05-430] Genetic algorithm-based PET sinogram denoising using a Poisson noise fitness criterion (#2975)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 F. Guedan (Autores: F. Guedan , J.E. Ortuño , G. Kontaxakis)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Universidad Politécnica de Madrid, ETSI Telecomunicación, Madrid, Spain [2] Universidad Politécnica de Madrid, Biomedical Image Technologies Group, ETSI Telecomunicación, Madrid, Spain [3] Instituto de Salud Carlos III, CIBER de Bioingeniería, Biomateriales y Nanomedicina, Madrid, Spain [4] Universidad Politécnica de Madrid, Information Processing and Telecommunications Center, ETSI Telecomunicación, Madrid, Spain
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a genetic-algorithm-inspired methodology for denoising positron emission tomography (PET) sinograms from a single noisy acquisition. The method assumes that a noise-free sinogram (NFS) is embedded within the noisy sinogram (NS) and formulates denoising as the search for chromosome-encoded parameters capable of recovering it. Each chromosome generates a candidate NFS by fitting continuous exponential curves to the measured sinogram data, with the exponential order and other generation parameters encoded in a reduced-size chromosome. For each candidate, the residual noise is computed as the difference between the NS and the generated NFS. The selection criterion is based exclusively on the statistic al properties of this residual noise, without requiring a ground-truth image or supervised training data. Since PET measurements are governed by photon-counting statistics, the residual noise is expected to exhibit Poisson-like behavior. Accordingly, the fitness function evaluates the mean-to-variance ratio over homogeneous count regions obtained by percentile-based stratification of the residual noise map. A ratio close to 1.0 indicates consistency with Poisson statistics. Experiments on simulated brain phantoms show a strong correlation between this noise-statistical criterion and the inverse of PSNR and SSIM after filtered back-projection reconstruction. These results indicate that chromosomes whose residual noise better satisfies Poisson statistics tend to produce higher-quality reconstructed images. The proposed method therefore provides a reference-free and interpretable framework for PET sinogram denoising, reducing dependence on annotated datasets and offering a mathematically evaluable alternative to supervised deep-learning approaches.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 433Poster Number:MIC-05-433] Comparative Analysis of Cross-Validation Strategies for Classification of Major Adverse Cardiac Events Using Stress-phase PET Polar Maps (#3097)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 M. Vatandoust (Autores: M. Vatandoust , J. Teuho , R. Klén , S.M. Hosseini , L. J. Orozco , J. Knuuti , E. Lehtonen , R. J. Knol , F. V.D. Zant)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Turku, Turku PET Centre, Turku, Finland [2] UMC Utrecht, Utrecht, Netherlands [3] Cardiac Imaging Division, Department of Nuclear Medicine, NWZ, Alkmaar, Netherlands
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The choice of cross-validation (CV) strategy can significantly affect reported performance in deep learning studies, but systematic comparisons of CV methods for medical image classification remain limited. This study systematically benchmarks seven common cross-validation strategies across nine mainstream deep learning models and a logistic regression baseline to classify major adverse cardiac events (MACE) utilising stress-phase PET MPI polar map data. For each model and CV combination, evaluated on identical data splits, we report average precision (AP) and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) as primary metrics, with confidence intervals estimated by bootstrapping. Quantitative analysis shows that Stratified Shuffle consistently yields the highest and most stable AP and AUC scores, exemplified by SqueezeNet achieving an AP of 0.52, AUC of 0.85, and delivering reduced variability across models compared to the bootstrap approach. These results highlight the critical impact of CV strategy on reliable and reproducible model evaluation for imbalanced and limited-size biomedical datasets.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 436Poster Number:MIC-05-436] High-Sensitivity Compton Imaging via a Virtual Multi-Stage Edge-On CZT Architecture (#1139)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Shoop (Autores: G. Shoop , G. Romancheck , M. Kupinski , L. Furenlid , M. King , S. Abbaszadeh)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California, Santa Cruz, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Santa Cruz, California, United States of America [2] University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Department of Nuclear Plasma and Radiological Engineering, Champaign, Illinois, United States of America [3] The University of Arizona, James C. Wyant College of Optical Sciences, Tucson, Arizona, United States of America [4] The University of Arizona, Department of Medical Imaging, Tucson, Arizona, United States of America [5] University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School, Department of Radiology, Worcester, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Optimizing detection efficiency and angular resolution in Compton cameras (CC) remains a challenge for its use in nuclear medical imaging of targeted alpha therapy (TAT) and prompt-gamma (γ) Positron Emission Tomography (PET) isotopes. A trade-off between detection efficiency and angular resolution must be considered when designing scattering layer material, thickness, and distance to the absorbing layer. We propose a novel approach by repurposing a cross-strip edgeon Cadmium Zinc Telluride (CZT) PET detector system as a high-sensitivity, single-layer CC. By leveraging 40 mm of CZT thickness and binning coincidences based on scattering distance, the system functions as a virtual multi-stage CC within a single volume. GATE simulations of γ's from 137Cs (662 keV) and 133Ba (356 keV) yield event sensitivities up to 4,508±7 and 1,239±4 cps/MBq and angular resolutions of 10.8° and 16.3° respectively. This work demonstrates the advantages of high energy resolution edge-on CZT, operating as a dual-mode PET/CC, providing a high-sensitivity where angular resolution can be further enhanced without sacrificing sensitivity. Future work aims to improve the existing design with advanced reconstruction algorithms, depth-of-interaction (DOI) correction, and detector optimization.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 439Poster Number:MIC-05-439] 3D reconstruction of radioluminescence microscopy data via MAP with optimized total variation regularization (#1231)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Seo (Autores: G. T. Gullberg , Q. Lyu , G. Pratx , Y. Seo , Y. Sung)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of California San Francisco, Radiology and Biomedical Imaging, San Francisco, California, United States of America [2] University of California San Francisco, Radiation Oncology, San Francisco, California, United States of America [3] Stanford University, Radiation Oncology, Stanford, California, United States of America [4] University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, Biomedical and Mechanical Engineering, Milwaukee, Wisconsin, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract A new microscopic nuclear imaging instrument using radioluminescence microscopy (RLM) has been developed to image living cells at high resolution with radiotracers tagged with positron emitters. These are used in biological samples to mimic clinical applications in order to evaluate their effectiveness to target receptors, antigens, and proteins that are overexpressed during growth of cancerous cells. The methodology has demonstrated impressive results for planar applications using optical reconstruction of β-ionization tracks (ORBIT); however, 3D imaging presents a challenging problem of reconstructing the 3D distribution of the source requiring backtracking of the ionization track of the positron in the scintillator in order to determine its position and 3D orientation at the detector surface. Four microlens arrays are used to record projections, limiting the angle of projection measurements to 360° sampling in the azimuthal angle φ and 40° sampling in the polar angle θ. The angle information acts as a collimator but the limited angle acquisition presents a challenging reconstruction problem which increases in difficulty for sources further from the scintillator. We consider reconstruction of the image x as a hierarchical maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation problem under a Poisson data model with a total variation (TV) prior. In our algorithm we treat the prior weight β as a variable and jointly estimate x and β by minimizing the sum of the negative Poisson log-likelihood and a TV penalty. An alternating optimization scheme is used in which x is updated by MAP-TV reconstruction and β is updated from the current image total variation using a deviance-based adaptive update method. Good results are demonstrated using Geant4 simulations of point sources as far as 98 μs from the face of the detector. The novelty is the microscopy application to image individual cells three-dimensionally with radiopharmaceuticals.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 442Poster Number:MIC-05-442] Physics-Informed Jointly Constrained Spectral Signal Decomposition for High-Resolution X-Ray Fluorescence Computed Tomography (#1630)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 L. Li (Autores: H. Sun , L. Li)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] TsingHua University, Beijing, China [2] Key Laboratory of Particle Radiation Imaging, Beijing, China
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract X-ray fluorescence computed tomography provides element-specific imaging, but weak fluorescence peaks are often obscured by a broad Compton-scatter continuum in photon-counting spectra. The objective of this study was to improve fluorescence projection extraction before reconstruction by replacing local empirical background fitting with a physics-informed hierarchical full-spectrum unmixing method. Each measured spectrum was modeled under Poisson counting statistics as the sum of a Klein--Nishina-constrained scatter template and a calibrated fluorescence-line template. The estimator was built hierarchically, progressing from pixel-wise spectral fitting to detector-plane joint unmixing and cross-angle projection-stack refinement. The method was evaluated on a simulated polymethyl methacrylate phantom with known fluorescence projections and on an experimental spectral data set. Under the default simulated Poisson-noise setting, the proposed method reduced projection root-mean-square error from 7.98 to 3.54 and background standard deviation from 3.92 to 1.39 relative to polynomial background extraction. On experimental data, it achieved the lowest contrast-to-noise-ratio-based detection limit, 0.305 mg/ml, compared with 0.370 mg/ml for polynomial extraction. These results indicate that structured full-spectrum unmixing can improve weak fluorescence extraction and downstream detectability while remaining compatible with existing reconstruction pipelines.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 445Poster Number:MIC-05-445] Evaluation of Dual Tracer [¹⁸F]FDG:[¹¹C]choline PET: A Simulation Study (#2094)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Elkayee Dehno (Autores: A. Elkayee Dehno , Z. Li , J. van Sluis , W. Noordzij , A. A. Lammertsma , A. H. Brouwers , C. Tsoumpas)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Groningen, University Medical Center Groningen, Department of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging, Groningen, Netherlands
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract [¹⁸F]FDG and [¹¹C]choline ([¹¹C]CH) are used in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) lesions for more accurate characterization across various differentiation stages. In this study, we investigate a simultaneous dual tracer protocol, in which [¹¹C]CH is administered immediately following [ 18 F]FDG scanning, and assess whether dual tracer images can provide diagnostic information comparable with single tracer [ 18 F]FDG and [¹¹C]CH. We simulated single and dual tracer datasets to evaluate the impact of residual [ 18 F]FDG activity on [¹¹C]CH quantification. Realistic activity distributions were used, and lesions of varying sizes (1-4 cm) were inserted in the liver and spleen with different tumor-to-background ratio (TBR) uptake patterns. Analytic simulations were performed using STIR library for a long axial field-of-view PET scanner. Results indicated that all lesions remained detectable in dual tracer images, and TBR preserved differentiation dependent patterns. Averaged relative differences and standard deviation for SUV mean , SUV max and SUV peak between the dual tracer and [¹¹C]CH images were -21.1±10.5%, -22.5±10.6% and -18.0±8.2%, respectively. To improve quantification, voxel-wise [¹⁸F]FDG subtraction was applied as a separation step, reducing the mean absolute relative difference to 1.2±1.1% for SUV mean , 4.4±4.1% for SUV max and 1.2±1.08% for SUV peak . These results demonstrate the clinical feasibility of a dual tracer [¹⁸F]FDG:[¹¹C]CH imaging protocol and motivate further optimization of separation methods for simultaneous dual tracre clinical implementation.

sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. L.M. Silva (Autores: A. L.M. Silva , T. Gomes , C. Cuccui , A. Gonzalez-Montoro , M. Grossmann , S. Ritt , H. T.K. Trang , Y. Seo , J. Veloso , P. Correia)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] University of Aveiro, I3N - Physics Dpt., Aveiro, Portugal [2] Universitat Politécnica de Valência, Instituto de Instrumentacion para Imagen Molecular (I3M), Centro Mixto CSIC, Valencia, Spain [3] University of Science - Ho Chi Minh City, Department of Nuclear Physics, Ho Chi Minh City, Viet Nam [4] Vietnam National University - Ho Chi Minh City, Ho Chi Minh City, Viet Nam [5] Paul Scherrer Institut PSI, Villigen, Switzerland [6] University of California, San Francisco and Berkeley, California, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The Nuclear Plasma Science Society (NPSS) Educational Committee (EduCom) oversees educational initiatives and manages the NPSS Schools as its main vehicle for sustainable education. One such initiative is the EduPET project, which aims to develop an educational system to be used in EduCom's instrumentation schools. The EduPET system was designed to demonstrate the fundamental principles of Time-of-Flight Positron Emission Tomography (ToF-PET) using modern detector instrumentation. The current prototype consists of two opposing detector modules, each comprising a 2×2×30 mm 3 LYSO:Ce crystal coupled to a Hamamatsu S13360-2050 silicon photomultiplier (SiPM), with signal digitization performed by a DRS4-based WaveDREAM board. Initial measurements included energy spectroscopy, coincidence timing, and ToF-based source localization using a 22 Na point source positioned at multiple locations along the detector axis. Coincidence time resolution (CTR) values ranging from 463 to 591 ps FWHM were obtained across the different positions. The timing resolution achieved was sufficient to resolve source displacements and demonstrate the probabilistic nature of ToF-based position estimation, confirming the suitability of EduPET system as an effective educational platform for illustrating key ToF-PET concepts and advanced instrumentation techniques. Future developments will focus on expanding the detector geometry toward a complete tomographic system.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 451Poster Number:MIC-05-451] Telephoto-Lens Magic-Cube: A Hybrid-Encoded Portable Gamma Camera for Extended-Distance Intraoperative Radiotracer Imaging (#2251)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 Y. Zhang (Autores: Y. Zhang , Y. Hu , Z. Lyu , Z. Zhao , Y. Zhang , W. Chi , R. Yao , H. Cai , T. Ma)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Tsinghua University, Beijing, China [2] Greater Bay Area National Center of Technology Innovation, Guangzhou, China [3] Yale University, Department of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging, New Haven, Connecticut, United States of America [4] Sichuan University, West China Hospital, Chengdu, China [5] Sichuan University, Sichuan Provincial Engineering Research Center of Radiopharmaceutical Clinical Translation, Chengdu, China [6] University at Buffalo SUNY, Department of Radiology, Jacobs School of Medicine & Biomedical Sciences, Buffalo, New York, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Intraoperative radiotracer imaging requires gamma cameras to maintain adequate imaging performance at relatively large source-to-camera distances, because surgical targets are often separated from the detector by tissue, instruments, surgical access constraints, or sterile operating space. In this work, we propose a Telephoto-Lens Magic-Cube gamma camera based on a hybrid encoding mechanism. The proposed system integrates front-end long-hole geometric encoding with detector-side self-collimation encoding, allowing distant radioactive sources to generate distinguishable detector responses. The proposed system was evaluated using numerical simulations and radioactive-source prototype experiments. In simulations, the Telephoto-Lens Magic-Cube maintained better spatial resolution at large source-to-camera distances than the Magic-Cube system without the Telephoto-Lens and two conventional parallel-hole collimator systems. It also successfully detected low-activity hot spots under background activity at large distances, whereas the reference systems failed to provide reliable detection. Prototype experiments demonstrated a mean sensitivity of 118 cps/MBq over 50-200 mm, dual-source resolution of 3 mm at 100 mm and 5 mm at 150 mm, and accurate lateral localization of 10 μCi point sources. In an anthropomorphic prostate lymph-node phantom, the system visualized five low-activity deep lymph-node-like sources under background activity and organ-uptake interference. These results suggest that the hybrid-encoded Telephoto-Lens Magic-Cube gamma camera is promising for intraoperative localization of deep low-activity lesions or lymph nodes.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 454Poster Number:MIC-05-454] Whole gamma imaging prototype V: a proof-of-concept system with thin HRGAGG toward simultaneous PET/SPECT imaging (#2353)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 G. Akamatsu (Autores: G. Akamatsu , Y. Iwao , H. Tashima , R. Abe , E. Yoshida , H.G. Kang , F. Nishikido , F. Obata , H. Wakizaka , S. Ito , K.J. Kim , K. Kamada , A. Yoshikawa , M. Ishibashi , Y. Imai , M. Takahashi , T. Yamaya)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology (QST), Chiba, Japan [2] Mirai Imaging Inc., Fukushima, Japan [3] Tohoku University, Miyagi, Japan [4] Nippon Medical School, Tokyo, Japan [5] Dokkyo Medical University, Tochigi, Japan
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Whole gamma imaging (WGI) is a novel imaging concept combining both PET and Compton camera using a dual-ring detector arrangement. We previously developed a series of WGI prototypes for proof-of-concept. In WGI Prototype IV (WGI-IV), reported in 2025, we targeted imaging of 909 keV γ-rays from 89 Zr, achieving a 3.0-mm rod resolution by Compton imaging. In this study, we aimed at further improving Compton imaging performance by using thin scatterer detectors, considering a potential extension to typical SPECT tracer imaging, and we developed WGI Prototype V (WGI-V). Compton imaging performance is determined mainly by the spatial resolution and energy resolution of scatterer detectors. Therefore, we used fine and thin 0.9×0.9×2.0 mm 3 HRGAGG scintillators to obtain high spatial resolution and high energy resolution. The outer absorber ring (304 mm diameter), which was composed of 216 fast-LGSO crystal blocks, was the same as that in WGI-IV. The inner scatterer ring (109.4 mm diameter) was remodeled with 10 HRGAGG crystal blocks (22×22 array). We evaluated energy resolution for scatterer detectors using 133 Ba, 241 Am, 99m Tc and 176 Lu (background). Then, we evaluated small rod resolution using a 89 Zr-filled rod phantom (rod diameters: 1.0-4.8 mm). Energy resolutions for scatterer detectors were 37.6% at 31 keV, 27.3% at 59.5 keV, 21.5% at 81 keV, 15.0% at 141 keV, and 7.5% at 307 keV. These were superior to those for the previous scatterer detector (HRGAGG, 1.45×1.45×15 mm 3 , 14×14 array). In the 89 Zr-filled rod phantom measurement, the 2.2-mm rods were resolved by WGI-V, whereas they could not be resolved by WGI-IV. High-resolution Compton imaging (2.2-mm rod resolution) was achieved by WGI-V with 0.9×0.9×2.0 mm 3 HRGAGG scatterer detectors. An application of the WGI-V to SPECT tracers will be presented at the conference.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 457Poster Number:MIC-05-457] Methodology to determine the absolute values of 3γ/2γ annihilation rate ratio with J-PET (#2566)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 N. Chug (Autores: N. Chug , P. Moskal)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Jagiellonian University, Faculty of Physics, Astronomy and Applied Computer Science, Krakow, Poland [2] Jagiellonian University, Center of Theranostics, Krakow, Poland
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract The measurement of the three-photon to two-photon annihilation rate ratio (R 3γ/2γ ) in positronium decays emerges as a promising diagnostic indicator for accessing tissue hypoxia [1, 2, 3]. The triplet state of positronium (ortho-positronium) is highly sensitive to local molecular oxygen concentrations [4, 5]; thus, the R 3γ/2γ ratio could reflect on the oxygenated level of tissues [6, 7]. This study presents methodology for determining the absolute values of this annihilation ratio using the Jagiellonian Positron Emission Tomograph (J-PET), the first PET scanner based on plastic scintillators [8]. We performed measurements with sodium-22 source enclosed in metal to characterize the detector response and geometrical acceptance for the R 3γ/2γ ratio. Since the positronium formation is suppressed in metals the resulting annihilation ratio serves as a detector-dependent reference value. After calibrating with sodium-22 in metal, we have performed the studies with porous polymer material where the positronium formation is enhanced. The two-photon and three-photon annihilation events selection are described, and their respective lifetime distributions are presented. The results presented validate the event selection methodology and establish the detector calibration baseline for future quantitative R 3γ/2γ studies in biological sample with J-PET.

sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Compton cameras (CCs) can be designed as compact and portable systems that can be employed in combination with other imaging modalities. These imaging systems provide 3D images with just one device. However, the resolution in the axis perpendicular to the first detector is degraded with respect to the parallel plane, especially at positions far from the detectors. Placing two CCs orthogonally can improve the uniformity of the 3D spatial resolution and also increase the usable size of the field of view (FOV). Following an initial study based on simulations carried out by the IRIS group, the current work aims at an experimental verification of operating two CCs positioned orthogonal to each other in the dual-CC MACACOX2 system. In this work, simulations are performed using a geometry that replicates the laboratory setup. Coincidence data are simulated with sources located at the center of the geometry, such that the scatterers of both CCs are positioned 30 mm from the center of the FOV. The image reconstruction algorithm has been developed and optimized by the group specifically for this imaging modality and is being applied in this work. Images of a 22 Na point source array obtained using the simulated two head CC system and reconstructed at 511 keV are obtained. Point sources separated by 8 mm can be clearly resolved at two, three, and four cm from the detector surface. Such successful findings provide foundation for the ongoing laboratory experiments with the MACACOX2 system.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 463Poster Number:MIC-05-463] MEDICAL THERMAL TOMOGRAPHY: EXPERIMENTAL DEMONSTRATION WITH HARDWARE PHANTOMS (#2959)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 A. Frixou (Autores: A. Frixou , E. Stiliaris , C. N. Papanicolas)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] The Cyprus Institute, Nicosia, Cyprus [2] National and Kapodistrian University of Athens,, Department of Physics, Athens, Greece [3] The Cyprus Academy of Sciences, Letters and Arts, Cypru, Nicosia, Cyprus
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Medical thermal imaging has long been explored as a non-invasive diagnostic modality for detecting localized sub-surface abnormalities associated with pathological processes. However, despite decades of investigation, conventional thermography has not achieved widespread clinical acceptance due to inconsistent and unreliable results. In this work, we experimentally validated a framework for medical thermal tomography combining high-precision thermal measurements in a controlled and monitored environment with physics-informed tomographic reconstruction. Following software-phantom studies, the methodology was validated using a dedicated automated experimental setup together with a suite of calibrations and temporal and spatial corrections, reducing the uncertainty in panoramic thermal projections to approximately 25 ◦ C. Reconstruction was performed using physics-informed forward thermal diffusion models within the AMIAS/RISE framework. Using this methodology, localized hot-spots with temperature differences as low as ∆T = 1.5 ◦ C were successfully detected and reconstructed at depths up to 3.3 cm in hardware phantoms. The reconstructed positions and temperatures were in good agreement with independent thermocouple and μCT measurements. These results provide strong evidence that thermal tomography is feasible when combined with precision thermal measurements and physics-informed reconstruction methods.

sub_talks.title: [Poster panel: 469Poster Number:MIC-05-469] A Computational Assessment of Quantum SimulationVersus Classical Simulation for Quantum-InspiredMedical Imaging (#3117)
sub_talks.speaker: 🎤 H. Sabet (Autores: A. Hashemi , H. Sabet)
sub_talks.affiliation: [1] Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Radiology, Boston, Massachusetts, United States of America
sub_talks.abstract: Abstract Quantum-inspired formulations have emerged as a promising approach for medical image denoising and segmentation by recasting image processing tasks as eigenvalue problems. While computationally demanding on classical hardware, these methods align naturally with quantum computing paradigms, particularly the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE). In this work, we assess whether quantum simulation on classical hardware is justified in the absence of real quantum devices by comparing classical computing (CPU-based diagonalization), quantum simulation on CPU, and GPU-accelerated quantum simulation using Qiskit. Experiments on synthetic data and a clinical PET/CT case show consistent reconstruction and segmentation quality across implementations. Quantitatively, classical methods are faster for small problems (e.g., 0.0063 s vs 0.0229 s), while GPU-based quantum simulation reduces this gap (~0.003 s) and becomes slightly faster at larger scales (660.78 s vs 669.1 s). These results indicate that quantum simulation is not advantageous for small cases, but can become competitive or beneficial for larger problems within a quantum-inspired framework.
